## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

# Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library, Entire, Uniform, Convenient, Economical, of All the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers Who Flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III

A chronological reprint of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed through the first twelve centuries of the Church, corrected with the utmost care by comparison with the most accurate editions and with certain manuscripts; continually illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the most extensive editions produced in the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following either individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters properly set within the text itself and with headings at the upper margin of every page distinguishing and indicating its subject matter; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal which nevertheless possess some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers wrote on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily ascertain which Fathers, and in what places in their works, commented upon each text of each book of Scripture.

A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the course of the whole work, the modest price, and especially this single, methodical, and chronological collection of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, now for the first time brought together in our library from works pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In which are issued the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, editor of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology has been committed to print in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The 1,200 volumes of the Latin edition are sold for 1,000 francs; the 1,300 volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for 800 francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are supplied in it only in Latin translation.

## The Ordinary Gloss Follows

[Col. 0009]

# The Prophecy of Jeremiah (G)*

## Jerome’s Prologue to Jeremiah

(See volume IX of his works, col. 847.)

## Preface

[Col. 0009A]

This interpretation belongs to Jerome. If anything in it causes difficulty, it should be examined according to the Hebrew manuscripts. There is another version, that of the Seventy Interpreters, used in the Churches. Although it contains certain things differently from what is found in the Hebrew manuscripts, nevertheless both versions—that according to the Seventy and that according to the Hebrew—have been confirmed by apostolic authority. The Seventy are understood to have expressed or arranged certain matters differently, not through error or in criticism of the earlier version, but according to a definite plan. We mention this beforehand so that no one may wish to correct one version from the other; for the truth of each must be preserved within its own kind.

## Argument

[Col. 0009B]

Jeremiah of Anathoth, which is a village three miles distant from Jerusalem, was stoned to death by the people at Thamnas in Egypt. He lies buried in that place where King Pharaoh had formerly lived. And because, at his request, the serpents were driven away from that place, making the Egyptians safe from the attacks of asps, the Egyptians venerate him there with great religious devotion.

# Chapter One

### Verse 1—“The words of Jeremiah.”

*(Jerome.)* The Septuagint has, “The word of God,” because the words of Jeremiah are the word of the Lord.

### Verse 2—“In the days,” etc.

*(The same.)* The mercy of God is marvelous. Although captivity is already near and the Babylonian army is surrounding Jerusalem, he nevertheless calls the people to repentance, preferring to save those who are converted rather than destroy those who persist in wrongdoing.

### Verse 5—“Before I formed you.”

Not because he existed before conception, as the heretics suppose, but because the Lord foreknew that he would come into being; for to him things that are to be done are already done, and he calls things that do not exist as though they existed.

[Col. 0010A]

### Verse 6—“Ah, ah, ah, Lord God!”

He rejects an office that he cannot bear because of his age. He displays the same modesty with which Moses says that he is weak and slow of speech. Yet Moses is rebuked as though he were of mature and robust age, whereas this child is granted pardon, since he is adorned with modesty and shame.

### Verse 9—“And he stretched out,” etc.

*(The same.)* It should be noted that here the hand of God is sent, etc., up to the point at which he receives confidence for preaching.

*(The same.)* Four sorrowful things are followed by two joyful ones, etc., up to the command that he should offer the cup to all nations.

### Verse 11—“The rod of vigilance.”

*(The same.)* The rod of vigilance, etc., up to the statement that it is said to have blossomed at the Lord’s resurrection.

### Verse 13—“And it happened.”

Sinners are rebuked gradually. Those who were unwilling to be corrected or amended by the striking rod are cast into a burning pot, concerning which Ezekiel speaks more fully.

“Burning pot.” From this passage the Lord says to Job, etc., up to “but this is a violent and perverse interpretation.”

### Verse 14—“The inhabitants of the land.”

Concerning these, in the Apocalypse, etc., up to Peter’s words: “To the elect exiles of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia.”

### Verse 17—“Therefore gird yourself,” etc.

*(The same.)* Job too is commanded, etc., up to “but the entire city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.”

### Verse 18—“And into a pillar.”

Concerning this the Apostle says: “The pillar and foundation of truth” (1 Timothy). Peter, James, and John, who were thought to be pillars of the Church, gave the right hands of fellowship to Paul and Barnabas.

“Against the kings of Judah.”

*(The same.)* If at any time the kings of Judah, etc., up to “let him hope in the Lord, that he may conquer.”

# Chapter Two

### Verse 2—“Your youth.”

*(Jerome.)* This is read more fully in Ezekiel, where the Lord joins Jerusalem to himself in marriage and, under the figure of a wife, unites her to his embraces. Or, to show a more ardent affection, he calls her a girl and a betrothed. For what we do not yet possess, we desire more ardently.

### Verse 3—“All who devour her.”

*(Jerome.)* Just as those who devour the firstfruits, etc., up to “the firstfruits are owed to the priests, not to enemies.”

### Verse 4—“Israel.”

*(The same.)* Both names, Jacob and Israel, are used—not according to the two and the ten tribes, but with reference to the whole people, since Jacob himself was afterward called Israel.

### Verse 5—“What did your fathers find?”

God speaks of an offense committed by the fathers—not because the sins of the fathers are charged to their children, but because the children, who resemble their fathers, are punished both for their own crime and for that of their parents. For the sake of the holy fathers, God has mercy on their children.

### Verse 6—“Nor did man dwell there.”

*(The same.)* He who is always hastening toward greater things, etc., up to “but struggle and an uncertain outcome of future things.”

### Verse 7—“And I brought you in.”

As if he said: In return for the labor of an exceedingly difficult journey, etc., up to “and we make his inheritance abominable.”

### Verse 10—“Kittim.”

*(The same.)* Kittim, that is, either Italy or the western regions—for Cyprus, an island near Judea, has a city of this name—from which came Zeno, the leader of the Stoics.

“And consider.”

*(The same.)* We can say this against those who pursue vices with greater zeal than virtues. To them it is said: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh; just as you presented your members to serve impurity and iniquity unto iniquity” (Romans 6), etc.

### Verse 11—“My people.”

Like those who give God a human form: taking the occasion of the passage, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1), they obstinately maintain that the immense and simple substance of divinity is composed according to our features and human form.

### Verse 12—“Be astonished, O heavens.”

*(The same.)* The Septuagint has, “The heaven was astonished,” etc., up to the observation that both *coeli* and *coelum* are called by the same name, as are Thebes and Athens.

### Verse 13—“They have forsaken me.”

I gave the command, saying: “I am the Lord your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” And, according to what is written in the same place, “Let there be no strange gods before me”; instead, he followed demons.

“A fountain of living water.”

*(The same.)* A fountain is perpetual and has life-giving waters. Cisterns and pools are filled from streams and turbid waters by rainwater.

### Verse 15—“Is Israel a servant?”

*(The same.)* From this passage those of Judah who were lifted up in pride, etc., up to “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant to his brothers” (Genesis 9).

“Lions.”

According to the allegorical sense, we understand lions, etc., up to “All of them commit adultery; their hearts are like an oven” (Hosea 7).

### Verse 16—“Even to the crown of his head.”

According to the passage: “From the sole of the foot even to the crown,” etc., up to “those who pollute the purity of the Church by their own disgrace.”

[Col. 0012A]

### Verse 19—“Your wickedness shall reprove you.”

*(The same.)* Note that wickedness and transgression, etc., up to “because she has forsaken the Lord her God.”

### Verse 20—“From of old you broke.”

*(The same.)* This can be said of him, etc., up to “and make their feet straddle for every passerby.”

### Verse 21—“A choice vine.”

In Hebrew, *soreth*, which is a type of excellent vine. From its cutting Israel was planted, and it is astonishing that a true seed and a choice vine should have been turned into bitterness and become foreign.

“How then have you been turned?”

Let no one be secure if he is a planting, etc., up to “if he remains in what was planted.”

### Verse 22—“Borith.”

*(The same.)* This is the Hebrew word itself. The Septuagint, however, has “fullers’ herb,” which grows in Palestine in moist and green places and has the same power for washing away dirt as natron.

### Verse 23—“See your ways.”

That is, look toward the Valley of the Sons of Hinnom, which is watered by the springs of Siloam. There you will see the shrine of Baal, whom you worshiped after abandoning God.

### Verse 25—“Keep your foot back.”

When they were about to celebrate Passover, etc., up to “which ought to be trodden down and crushed by the evangelical foot.”

### Verse 27—“They turned.”

They cast my words backward. For whenever a teacher commands, etc., up to “but then they indicate the swelling of their spirit by the gesture of their body.”

### Verse 28—“According to their number.”

Either the same gods or different ones were worshiped by individual cities, so that they did not appear to agree even in impiety; rather, superstition, fighting against itself, followed a different error.

[Col. 0012C]

### Verse 29—“What do you want?”

Human perversity is inclined to excuse itself, and what it deservedly suffers seems to it unjustly imposed.

### Verse 30—“Your children.”

So that through the blows inflicted on your children you might learn that you required a more severe medicine for healing, and so that you might not perhaps say, “You were unwilling to rebuke those who were sinning.”

### Verse 31—“To see the word of the Lord.”

Moses saw the voice of the Lord. The apostle John also says that he saw and touched the Word of God.

### Verse 32—“Will a bride forget?”

*(The same.)* He who withdraws from the Lord loses his ornament and the understanding of doctrine, which is signified by the breast. Hence John reclined upon the Lord’s breast at the supper (John 13), and among other things the breast-piece of the victims is reserved for the priests.

### Verse 34—“In all.”

In these places; or, according to another reading, “under every oak.” For the Hebrew word signifies both “oak” and “these things.” In pleasant places they sacrificed in the shade and among the foliage.

### Verse 35—“And you said.”

These words must be used against them, etc., up to “not to mourn, but to put forward excuses.”

“Behold, I am entering into judgment.”

*(The same.)* Let the new heresy hear from the old one that the greatest wrath of God consists in refusing humbly to confess sin and instead shamelessly boasting of righteousness.

### Verse 36—“And from Egypt.”

So that the assault of the Egyptians, etc., up to “therefore they are rebuked because, after abandoning God, they place their hope in human beings.”

### Verse 37—“Upon your head.”

*(The same.)* In the manner of mourners: Tamar, after being violated by Amnon, scattered ashes upon her head, placed her hands upon it, and thus returned to her house.

# Chapter Three

### Verse 1—“It is commonly said: ‘If a man dismisses.’”

Behold, concerning a woman who has committed fornication and been abandoned, etc., up to “how much more does he still not disdain to call her.”

“If a man dismisses.”

*(Jerome.)* We can say this against those who abandon the Lord’s faith and become entangled in the errors of heretics. After many acts of fornication and the deception of their own souls, they pretend to return to the former truth—not to put away the poisons in their hearts, but to insinuate them into others.

“But you have committed fornication.”

Or: “You have had many shepherds to your offense,” so that you might offend God; and those who ought to have been teachers, restraining others from every error, became authors of impiety.

“Nevertheless, return.”

“If you return to me,” says the Lord. He rebukes the shamelessness of the harlot, who dares to return to her husband after adultery.

### Verse 2—“Lift up your eyes.”

According to the allegorical sense, those who promise to abandon heretical errors are commanded to lift their eyes straight ahead. Unless they see what is straight, they cannot condemn their former perversity.

“Like a thief.”

Just as thieves customarily do toward evening, etc., up to “and lies in ambush along the roads for those descending from Jerusalem to Jericho.”

### Verse 3—“The forehead of a woman.”

*(The same.)* We can say this about heretics who boast in their errors. Since she previously said, “I have not sinned,” he rebukes her as a shameless woman who is not ashamed to stoop to anyone.

### Verse 4—“You are the guide of my virginity.”

“Will you be angry forever?” etc., up to “so much more wretched is the harlot who refuses to accept healing.”

### Verse 6—“Have you seen what she has done?”

*(The same.)* He makes a comparison, etc., up to “and this is what he says: ‘Have you seen what she has done?’”

“Israel the adversary.”

*(The same.)* He speaks under the figure of two sisters who were born from one stock, that of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He calls the first an adversary because she set up golden calves in Dan and Bethel.

### Verse 7—“And she saw.”

The sufferings of some are remedies for others, etc., up to “and appointed for the jealousy and emulation of the Lord.”

### Verse 11—“She has justified her soul.”

“Your sister Sodom has been justified in comparison with you.” And elsewhere: “This man went down to his house justified rather than the other” (Luke 18).

### Verse 12—“And I will not turn away my face.”

Hence: “Turn your face away” (Psalm 50), etc., up to “of whom it is truly said: ‘They devour my people like the food of bread.’”

### Verse 13—“Nevertheless, know this.”

As if he said: When I have had mercy on you, do not think yourself righteous; but always remember your iniquity and lower the necks of your pride, so that you who offended through arrogance may be able to appease God through humility.

### Verse 14—“Return.”

*(Jerome.)* The Jews think that this has been fulfilled, etc., up to “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah” (Romans 9).

### Verse 16—“And when you have multiplied.”

*(The same.)* Some refer this to the end of time, etc., up to “but they will pursue spiritual food.”

### Verse 17—“They will call.”

Those who once said, “You who sit upon the cherubim, manifest yourself” (Psalm 79), etc. Between the two cherubim upon the Lord’s mercy seat the divine majesty appeared and spoke to Moses and the priests; but now it is otherwise, in the age of faith.

### Verse 18—“In those days.”

This is fulfilled specifically at Christ’s coming, when the twelve tribes together believe the Gospel, leave the land of the north, and abandon the dominion of the devil.

[Col. 0014B]

### Verse 19—“As sons.”

*(Jerome.)* Among the number of sons who believed from the nations: “As many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God” (John 1).

### Verse 20—“A woman who loves another.”

*(The same.)* Once joined, seeing him, etc., up to “she despised the Lord the Savior, to her own destruction.”

### Verse 21—“A voice was heard on the roads.”

The Lord willingly receives the penitent. He runs to meet the son exhausted by want and squalor, clothes him in his former garments, and restores grace to the one who returns—provided that he comes back to his father with weeping and lamentation.

### Verse 22—“Your apostasies.”

Some read “your conversions.” Although we turn to him by our own will, unless he draws us and strengthens our desire by his protection, we cannot be saved. We understand this both of the Jewish people returning to him and of heretics who have abandoned the Lord.

### Verse 25—“We shall lie down.”

The voice of Israel, which did not hear its God, and of the penitent heretic. For knowing and confessing our sins is part of salvation. Hence: “First declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified” (the same passage).

# Chapter Four

### Verse 1—“If you return.”

*(Jerome.)* The Septuagint has: “If Israel returns, says the Lord, let him return to me.” Another reading has, “You will return”; that is, if you desire salvation and say that you have sinned, return fully—that is, believe the one whom you denied.

“If you remove.”

It is clear that when we are shaken and say, “But my feet were almost moved; my steps were almost poured out” (Psalm 72), we suffer this not from weakness of nature, but because we set our stumbling-blocks and idols against God.

[Col. 0014D]

### Verse 2—“And you will swear, ‘As the Lord lives,’” etc.

*(The same.)* This is said as a reproach to dead gods, by whom every idolater swears.

“Break up new ground.”

*(The same.)* By rooting out thorns and briars, etc., up to “a mind filled with the troubles of the world cannot receive the seed of God and bear fruit.”

“Circumcise yourselves.”

*(The same.)* Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem are commanded to abandon the letter that kills and follow the Spirit that gives life.

“Lest perhaps.”

*(The same.)* He warns and foretells, lest he be compelled to do what we approve in the case of the Ninevites, to whom a sentence was announced so that they might avert the impending wrath by repentance.

[Col. 0015A]

### Verse 7—“A lion has gone up.”

*(Jerome.)* If anyone is a supporter or author of perverse doctrines, this can be said of him: “A lion has gone up from his lair,” etc.

“And the destroyer.”

Of him it is said: “He shall rule over all his enemies” (Psalm 9). He boasts, saying: “I have gone around the earth and traversed it” (Job 2). For who is there whom the devil’s poisons do not touch, except the one who says: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14)?

“From his place.”

From the abyss, in which he is to be bound, into which he begs not to be sent.

### Verse 8—“Because of this.”

Without repentance we cannot escape the most savage beast, and unless we turn to God not only in mind but also in body. For while the Church is being devastated, the wrath of God is revealed.

[Col. 0015B]

### Verse 9—“The princes.”

*(Jerome.)* Those who ought to have taught the law and defended their subjects from the lion.

“The priests.”

Those who are thought to be wise: “God made foolish the wisdom of this world,” because through it they did not know God.

“The prophets shall be dismayed,” etc.

Aquila has, “They shall be insane.” For who would not go mad or lose heart when he saw princes, kings, and priests once his own, beneath the lion?

### Verse 10—“And I said: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God.”

Since he previously said, “At that time they will call Jerusalem the throne of the Lord,” etc., and now says, “The heart of the king shall perish,” etc., the prophet is troubled and thinks that God has lied to him. He does not understand that the former event lies far in the future, whereas this one is to occur soon.

### Verse 11—“A scorching wind.”

*(Jerome.)* Namely, when the sword has reached even to the soul, etc., up to “it will come not at all against the people, but against me, so that my wheat may be scattered.”

### Verse 12—“A spirit full.”

Some interpret this passage to mean that, after the threshing floor has been cleansed, the remnant will be saved. Hence it is written: “A spirit of fullness will come to me”; and hence the Evangelist says: “From his fullness we have all received” (John 1).

“And now I.”

This is an aposiopesis, as Virgil says (*Aeneid*):

> “Whom I—but it is better to calm the stirred waves.”

The prophet, about to speak of prosperity, restrains himself and joins sorrow to sorrow.

### Verse 13—“Behold, he comes like,” etc.

He sees future events as though they were present. He describes the army of the Babylonians, whose chariot wheels’ noise is compared with a most savage storm and whose horses’ speed is compared with eagles.

The army of the devil—that is, the chariots and horsemen of Pharaoh—is understood by the ecclesiastical man who says: “Woe to us, for we have been laid waste.” He believes that saying: “When you groan after turning, you will be saved.” “Woe to us,” because the prophet, as though pointing with his finger, has shown it, and the people groan. He says not that these things will happen, but that they have already happened: “Woe to us.”

### Verse 14—“Wash your heart from wickedness.”

The prophet—or rather, in the prophet, the Lord—responds: “Wash.” Hence: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isaiah 1), namely with the water of baptism, the saving water of repentance.

### Verse 15—“For a voice announcing.”

He speaks according to the geographical position of Judea. The tribe of Dan, near Mount Lebanon and the city now called Paneas, faces north, from which Nebuchadnezzar will come.

“From the mountain.”

After the tribe of Dan comes the land of Ephraim, through which one travels toward Jerusalem.

Allegorically:

*(Jerome.)* The judgment of the Lord comes upon the land that has offended the Lord, together with the full abundance of punishment.

[Col. 0016A]

### Verse 16—“Watchmen.”

That is, adversaries who besiege it so diligently and surround the city with fortifications that you would think them guardians of vineyards and fields rather than enemies. The Lord wishes all the surrounding nations to know his sentence; and, once Jerusalem has been scourged, he wishes all to receive instruction.

### Verse 18—“Your ways.”

*(Jerome.)* Whatever evil befalls us, etc., up to “how much less those who once belonged to the city of God?”

### Verse 19—“My belly.”

*(The same.)* The Lord speaks this when he sees sedition and discord in the Church, and when he sees the partridge crying out in its assemblies and God’s rest turned into wars. Hence it follows:

### Verse 21—“How long shall I see?”

The voice of the prophet—and through the prophet, of God—mourning over the ruin of his people, whose entrails are torn asunder like those of a man. The Savior wept at the death of Lazarus and over Jerusalem. He does not conceal his grief in silence, and the blare of the trumpet and the tumult of battles disturb his affection, while evils are piled upon evils and the entire land of the two tribes is laid waste.

### Verse 22—“For my people are foolish.”

*(Jerome.)* Because the princes of my people did not understand, etc., up to “whom he always desired to see.”

“They are wise,” etc.

*(The same.)* “Wise in wickedness,” etc., up to “it is called not wisdom but cunning and craft.”

### Verse 23—“I looked upon the earth.”

The prophet sees in the spirit what is about to happen, so that the people, hearing it, may be terrified and repent, and may not endure what they fear.

Whatever is said historically about Judea and Jerusalem, let us refer to the Church of God. When she has offended God and has been devastated by vices and persecution, where once there was a company and joy of virtues, there may instead be a multitude of sins and mourning.

### Verse 27—“For thus says the Lord.”

*(Jerome.)* The Lord’s mercy is mingled with wrath: the earth is abandoned but not consumed, so that those who understand his mercy may remain.

[Col. 0016D]

### Verse 28—“I have purposed and have not repented,” etc.

He had purposed to remove the sentence already announced, so that the wrath of the one who raged would not reach its end. The Lord threatened through Jonah, but the magnitude of tears and groans overcame the impending sword.

### Verse 29—“At the voice of the horseman.”

He describes the raging army, from fear of which the people abandoned the city and climbed the heights. Yet they could not escape the wrath of God.

All this can be referred to the Church when she has offended God and has been handed over to adversaries during persecution, or to vices and sins.

### Verse 30—“But you, when you have been devastated.”

*(Jerome.)* The same must be said against those who have lost conjugal affection and the chastity of true faith.

“When you clothe yourself.”

You prepare these things also for your lovers, and a narrow bed cannot contain both. Nor does God accept the ornaments by which you previously pleased your lovers.

[Col. 0017A]

### Verse 31—“For I heard a voice like,” etc.

*(Jerome.)* Two examples are presented, that of a woman in labor and that of a mourner, so that whatever a woman suffers, whether in childbirth or in the death of her children, Jerusalem might suffer among the peoples.

# Chapter Five

### Verse 1—“Go around the ways.”

*(Jerome.)* Great is the love of justice: not merely, according to Abraham’s question and God’s answer, that God would spare a city already on the point of perishing for the sake of ten righteous men, but that, if he should find one who practices justice and seeks faith, he would spare it.

### Verse 3—“Lord, are not your eyes?”

*(The same.)* The works of the Jews—in which they rejoiced according to the ceremonies of the law—are condemned by the faith of Christians, through which we have been saved by grace.

“You struck them.”

*(Gregory.)* Every divine stroke, etc., up to “and there is one scourge that begins in time and is completed in eternal punishments.”

“And they did not grieve.”

Punishments are inflicted so that vices may be corrected, but Jerusalem is not amended, not even through torments.

### Verse 4—“Perhaps they are poor.”

*(Jerome.)* As in the passage: “I will send my son; perhaps they will reverence him” (Matthew 21). God uses the speech of one who doubts, so that from the ambiguity of the statement and the suspension of the words the freedom of the human will may be shown.

### Verse 5—“Behold, I will go to the great,” etc.

According to the tropological sense, those who are considered great in the Church, because they loose the yoke and break the bonds, are handed over to shameful passions so that they may do what is improper.

“Bonds.”

*(Jerome.)* The commandments of God, not those of the Pharisees, concerning whom it is said: “Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke from us” (Psalm 1).

### Verse 6—“The watchful leopard.”

This signifies the assault of Alexander, who, with the various nations subjected to him, like a variegated leopard, took up arms against the Medes and Persians. But since he weaves a history not only of the future but also of the past and of events already almost future, he says nothing about the Roman empire.

[Col. 0017D]

### Verse 7—“I filled them.”

*(Jerome.)* Let the person who serves luxury after receiving riches hear this.

### Verse 8—“Lustful horses.”

*(The same.)* As horses, when they do not see a female animal, etc., up to “He was likened to foolish beasts and became like them” (Psalm 48).

### Verse 10—“And destroy.”

*(The same.)* Let the Church hear how quickly the walls, etc., up to “because of the judge’s mercy, not because of the merit of sinners.”

### Verse 12—“They denied the Lord,” etc.

*(The same.)* Let the negligent Church hear this, since, rejecting God’s providence, she must endure both sword and famine unless she believes the things that are said are going to come.

### Verse 14—“Behold, I am making,” etc.

*(The same.)* So that unbelievers may be consumed by your word, etc., up to “if we build upon the foundation of Christ.”

### Verse 15—“You will not understand the language,” etc.

In Hebrew: “You will not understand what he says.” For it is a comfort amid evils if you have enemies whom you can address and who understand your prayers.

### Verse 17—“And it will eat the crops,” etc.

He describes the devastation of the land, the slaughter of many, the driving away of livestock, and the overthrow of cities and walls: everything is seized by the hostile sword.

### Verse 18—“Nevertheless,” etc.

*(Jerome.)* The remnant will be saved—either those who were led away to Babylon, or those left behind to cultivate the land of Judea, or those who, after the heat of persecution, preserved faith in God either by flight or by confession.

[Col. 0018B]

### Verse 19—“And if you say,” etc.

*(The same.)* Tropologically, this can be understood of heretics, etc., up to “live—indeed, serve—those whose gods you worship.”

### Verse 21—“Hear this, foolish people.”

He speaks specifically to Judah and to the house of Jacob. Israel had already been in exile among the Assyrians for a long time.

“You who have no heart.”

He indicates that, without a command, we ought naturally to understand what is right.

“You who have eyes,” etc.

Something similar is said: “They have eyes and will not see,” etc.; “Let those who make them and all who trust in them become like them” (Psalm 113).

### Verse 25—“Your iniquities,” etc.

*(Jerome.)* If at some time the sea should cross its boundaries, etc., up to “among whom the workers in the vineyard are promised one eternal reward.”

[Col. 0018C]

### Verse 27—“Like a cage.”

While they hunt one another to the death and fill their houses through the losses and expenses of others, in accordance with that saying of the philosophers: “Every rich man is either unjust or the heir of an unjust man.”

Would that these things were done only by those who are outside, and not by us; and would that those who come to us looked not at their hands but at their faces.

### Verse 28—“They have grown fat,” etc.

Something similar is said: “He grew fat, became thick, and became sleek; he forsook God who made him” (Deuteronomy 32). And: “The beloved grew fat and kicked” (the same passage).

“And they have grown fat,” etc.

Trusting in material goods, as if he said: “Soul, you have many good things laid up for many years; rest, eat, and drink” (Luke 12).

# Chapter Six

[Col. 0018D]

### Verse 1—“Strengthen yourselves,” etc.

*(Jerome.)* Since Nebuchadnezzar is now already about to come from the north, etc., up to “among these there is another village called in the Syriac and Hebrew language Bet-haccerem, situated on a mountain.”

### Verse 2—“The beautiful one.”

The beauty of Jerusalem is described. Jerusalem is itself Zion, although one name denotes the entire city and another the citadel of the city. For Zion is interpreted as “citadel,” that is, “watchtower,” and she is compared to a beautiful woman.

### Verse 3—“Shepherds.”

*(Jerome.)* The word is very elegantly placed here, etc., up to “some of whom reveal themselves in order to pollute the harlot, and others for the destruction of the city.”

[Col. 0019A]

### Verse 4—“Woe to us,” etc.

*(Jerome.)* When those men say, “Rise and let us go up,” these answer: “Woe to us,” etc. The sense is: If we suffer this by day, what shall we suffer by night?

### Verse 5—“Rise.”

Those who said, “Rise, let us go up,” etc., urge one another to battle with these words: “Rise, let us go up by night,” so that the adversaries may know that victory does not depend upon the time but upon valor.

### Verse 7—“Like a cool spring.”

Without the warmth of faith. The Church is fervent in spirit, but the wicked are cold. Hence: “The love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24). And also: “I shall be like those who descend into the pit” (Psalm 28).

It is enough to have said once that *lacus* here does not mean a pond, according to the Greek, but a cistern, which in Syriac and Hebrew is called *gab*.

### Verse 8—“Be instructed.”

*(Jerome.)* From this we learn that God scourges, etc., up to “through every sorrow and scourging you shall be instructed, Jerusalem.”

### Verse 9—“Even to the remnant.”

*(The same.)* As when Jerusalem has been devastated, etc., up to “as into a basket or winepress.”

### Verse 10—“Uncircumcised ears,” etc.

It should be noted that circumcision is spoken of in the Scriptures in three ways: of the foreskin, of the heart, and of the ears. Hence: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matthew 11).

### Verse 11—“Therefore I am full of fury.”

*(Jerome.)* As if he said: I foresee the wrath of God coming, and I am filled with his fury and anger, and can no longer endure it; nor do I dare to entreat God on behalf of sinners.

[Col. 0019C]

### Verse 12—“I will stretch out.”

*(Jerome.)* The Septuagint has, “I will lift up.” Both expressions describe the posture of one who strikes. Hence: “And still his hand is stretched out,” or “raised up” (Isaiah 5).

### Verse 14—“And they healed the wound.”

*(The same.)* As if he said: Although they were committing such great evils, etc., up to “preparing them all the more for punishment and for the wrath of God.”

### Verse 15—“They were ashamed.”

*(The same.)* This should be read more explicitly, etc., up to “rather, they increased their sin through contempt.”

They did not know. They were unwilling; but through excessive contempt and the vice of violent evil they could not even understand. It is a grave impiety not only to fail to avoid sins, but not even to wish to understand them, and to recognize no distinction between good and evil deeds.

**VERSE 16.**—Stand upon the roads. Let us read the Gospel parable in which the good merchant sold everything in order to buy one precious pearl: namely, that through the patriarchs and prophets we may come to him who says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). Hence, “Stand upon the roads,” and so forth.

**VERSE 17.**—The sound of the trumpet. (JEROME.) “The sound of the trumpet”: the commandments of the Gospel or the teaching of the apostles. Hence: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion; lift up your voice like a trumpet, you who announce Jerusalem.”

**VERSE 20.**—Why is incense for me? (ID.) As though he said: “In vain do you bring it to me for the preparation of perfumes,” and so forth, up to the point where Scripture says, “The redemption of a man’s soul is his own riches” (Prov. 13).

**VERSE 21.**—Fathers and sons. (ID.) The sons of the fathers follow their blasphemies, daily accepting that imprecation: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27).

**VERSE 22.**—Behold, a people, and so forth. This is properly said of the Babylonians, who are about to come against Jerusalem. The whole array of arms and the onset of the combatants are described, so that, shaken by terror, they may do penance and appease the most merciful God.

**VERSE 23.**—His voice is like, and so forth. Allegorically. (JEROME.) We can misuse this testimony, and so forth, up to the point where, like the waves of a very violent sea, they overwhelm those who resist.

**VERSE 25.**—Do not go out. (ID.) The Gospel also teaches, and so forth, up to the point where they should protect themselves most firmly with fortifications.

**VERSE 27.**—And you shall test. (ID.) As though he said: “So that, when you have tested and learned the way,” and so forth, up to those who, like deaf asps, stop up their ears so that they will not hear the voice of the enchanters.

All these. (GREGORY, *Moral Interpretations*, book 18, chapter 14.) The princes are those who depart from the Lord and are disobedient, and so forth, up to the one who disagrees with the unity of the Church and does not love his neighbor.

# CHAPTER 7

**VERSE 2.**—Stand in the gate of the house of the Lord, and so forth. (JEROME.) Through it the multitude of the people enters to entreat the Lord, and so forth, up to the point where, because of the opportunity and the solemnity of the place, they are compelled to hear the word of the Lord.

**VERSE 4.**—The temple of the Lord. (ID.) This can apply to those virgins, and so forth, up to the place in which there are true faith, holy conduct, and a chorus of all the virtues.

**VERSE 8.**—Behold, you trust in yourselves. (ID.) These sins show that they place their trust in the temple in vain, and so forth, up to the point where they burst into such madness that they boast of having been set free because they have withdrawn from the worship of God.

**VERSE 11.**—A den of thieves, and so forth. (ID.) I think that what is said in the Gospel was taken from this passage, and so forth, up to the point where my eyes have observed what you think is hidden.

**VERSE 12.**—Go to my place in Shiloh, and so forth. (ID.) Namely, where my tabernacle was first located, and so forth, up to: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18).

**VERSE 13.**—Rising early to address you, and so forth. (ID.) Not because any time is too early for him, and so forth, up to the point where they are called children of light and not of night or darkness; nor are they sleeping, namely, those who preserve the commandments of God.

**VERSE 14.**—As I did to Shiloh. I rejected Shiloh, and I will reject the temple; I rejected the ten tribes, and I will reject the two tribes also. Whatever he threatens that people, let us fear for ourselves as well, lest we do similar things.

**VERSE 16.**—Therefore you, do not, and so forth. (JEROME.) Lest the prophet appear to ask without obtaining what he requests, the Lord commands, and so forth, up to the point where this impenitence, this blasphemy, or this word against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness forever.

**VERSE 17.**—Do you not see? Let us not think God cruel: although he does not permit himself to be entreated, he gives the reason why he does not listen: “Do you not see?”

**VERSE 20.**—It is kindled. (JEROME.) As though he said: “What I long refused to do, I am compelled to do by the multitude of your sins, against human beings and against animals.” When God is angry, human beings also, and the things belonging to human beings, experience a similar severity.

**VERSE 22.**—For I did not speak. (ID.) He clearly shows that he first gave the Decalogue, and so forth, up to the point where evangelical grace was therefore necessary, by which he would preserve them not through their merit but through God’s mercy.

**VERSE 27.**—And you shall speak to them. (ID.) Do not hesitate to harden your necks, and so forth, up to: “At least now speak to them with my words.”

**VERSE 28.**—This is the nation. This happened in the time of the prophets and preceded it in shadow. It was completely fulfilled in Christ, whose discipline they refused to hear; hence the elegant conclusion: “Faith has perished and has been taken away.” That faith properly belongs to Christians.

**VERSE 29.**—Cut off your hair. Among the ancients it was customary for mourners to cut their hair; now, conversely, letting the hair grow is a sign of mourning.

**VERSE 31.**—The high places of Tophet. (JEROME.) *Tophet* in Hebrew means “breadth” in Latin; it is a place, and so forth, up to the point where, even if a dog, donkey, or any unclean animal had first met the lord, he ought not to have offered it.

**VERSE 32.**—Behold, days are coming. (ID.) When he departed from fidelity to his lord, the siege began. But when the king of Egypt came and liberated Jerusalem, Nebuchadnezzar drove him away. Afterwards Nebuzaradan besieged and captured it, led Zedekiah to Antioch, and there deprived him of his sight.

**VERSE 34.**—And I will make to cease. When the place of idolatry has been turned into tombs, so that where they had offended God, there their unburied corpses might lie.

# CHAPTER 8

**VERSE 1.**—At that time, and so forth. (JEROME.) All that prophetic speech describes, and so forth, up to the gold and silver that, according to ancient custom, were placed in tombs.

**VERSE 4.**—And you shall say. After so many evils he calls those who remain to repentance. Or, before what he has threatened comes, he urges them to conversion and points out a place for repentance. “He has turned away,” or “he has turned.” As though he said: One who turns back can resist and avert the wrath of God through prayers.

**VERSE 5.**—Why, then, and so forth. (JEROME.) The more I called them to repentance, the more they withdrew—not so much from a desire to sin as from a desire to overcome me.

**VERSE 6.**—No one does what is good, and so forth. (ID.) Every kind of human being is inclined toward evil (Gen. 8). In the time of the Savior, all turned aside; together they became worthless; there is no one who does good (Ps. 13). Hence he himself says: “Save me, Lord, for the holy one has failed” (ibid. 11). Where, then, are those who say that it lies within our power to be free from every sin?

**VERSE 7.**—The kite in the sky. (ID.) As though he said: Even birds know their seasons, so that they understand when, hastening toward warmer places, they should avoid the harshness of winter, and at the beginning of spring return to their customary regions.

**VERSE 10.**—Therefore I will give. (ID.) They received their reward, and those who rejected the word of the Lord have themselves been rejected.

**VERSE 11.**—And they healed the wound. (ID.) As though he said: Good physicians wished to heal the wounds of others with words, and so forth, up to the disgrace of those who deceive by saying, “Peace, peace,” and so forth.

**VERSE 12.**—Therefore they shall fall. (ID.) So that those whose dignity was conspicuous might also be mixed with the people’s ruin, since from the least to the greatest all are devoted to greed (Jer. 6).

**VERSE 13.**—There is no grape, and so forth. As though he said: When the seasons pass, summer gives way to autumn, and the leaves of the trees fall in winter, you will see everything from afar but will obtain no food from it.

**VERSE 14.**—Why do we sit? The voice of the people is introduced, responding, confessing their vices, and encouraging one another. “Assemble and let us enter the fortified city.” Or one city, Jerusalem; the others had already been captured.

**VERSE 16.**—From Dan the sound is heard. Where the river Jordan rises: Nebuchadnezzar is described as coming from Dan through Phoenicia with his army.

**VERSE 17.**—I will send serpents among you. (ID.) So that they may strike you incurably, and so forth, up to the point where those who despise the utterances of the Lord are handed over to hostile powers.

**VERSE 18.**—My sorrow. (ID.) These words should be read as spoken by the Lord, mourning the overthrow of Jerusalem and unable to endure its misery.

**VERSE 19.**—And behold, a voice. He describes the weeping and howling of the city when the enemies have entered. The enemies coming from a distant land cry out against the city, or the citizens cry out against the enemies.

**VERSE 20.**—The harvest has passed. The words of the people enclosed in Jerusalem by a long siege, because the seasons have changed and the cycle of the year has revolved. But our hope has been frustrated.

**VERSE 21.**—Over the wound. The Lord’s response, for he appears to be afflicted in Jerusalem’s affliction.

# CHAPTER 9

**VERSE 1.**—Who will give? (JEROME.) The king of Jerusalem, with the city besieged by enemies, and so forth, up to the point where this can be understood either as spoken by the Lord or by the prophet.

**VERSE 2.**—Who will give me, and so forth. As though he said: It is better to dwell in solitude than to live among such human crimes. Hence in the Gospel: “How long shall I endure you?” (Matt. 17). And elsewhere: “He who understands will sit, for it is an exceedingly evil time” (Lam. 3; Mic. 2).

**VERSE 3.**—For they pass from evil, and so forth. (JEROME.) Sinners pass from evil to evil, and so forth, up to the tongue of those who arm themselves for blasphemy.

**VERSE 4.**—Each one, and so forth. (GREGORY.) When the crafty enemy sees that he is being expelled from the hearts of the good, he seeks those who are greatly loved by them and speaks flattering words through them—those who are loved more than the others—so that, while the force of affection pierces the heart, the sword of persuasion may easily break into the innermost depths of uprightness.

From his neighbor. (JEROME.) For “a man’s enemies are his household” (Mic. 6). The affection of brothers is also rare. “The father will hand over the son, and the son the father. And two will be divided against three, and three against two” (Luke 12).

**VERSE 5.**—They labored to act wickedly. (GREGORY.) As though it were said plainly: Those who could have been friends of the truth without effort labor in order to sin; and, because they refuse to live simply, they impose labors upon themselves so that they may die.

**VERSE 7.**—And I will test them. (JEROME.) In the furnace of tribulation. “The furnace tests the vessels of the potter” (Sir. 27), so that whatever adulterated material is in us may be melted away. “The silver of the Lord, tested by fire, approved by the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 11).

**VERSE 9.**—Shall I not for these things? (ID.) He often repeats this verse, so that, after enumerating their evils, he may show that he acts justly in doing what he does.

**VERSE 10.**—Upon the mountains. (ID.) Tropologically. Weeping is taken up over the mountains, and so forth, up to those who are able to ascend on high, down to the simple who have departed from God.

**VERSE 11.**—And I will make Jerusalem. (ID.) When ecclesiastical teachers fail, and so forth, up to the one who says, “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (Lev. 26).

**VERSE 14.**—Of their heart. One must trust not in our own heart but in the Lord. The human heart is crooked; from it proceed crooked thoughts.

**VERSE 15.**—Therefore thus says the Lord. This may be prophesied of the near future, when they were captured by the Chaldeans, and properly of the time when they were scattered among all the nations and dispersed throughout the whole world.

**VERSE 16.**—The sword. (JEROME.) Either the material or the spiritual sword, by which they are divided so that they do not agree in evil, but perish in the fact that they are evil.

**VERSE 17.**—And summon. Summon the mourners because of the future captivity, and so forth, up to the point where, with measured voice, they may pour the people into tears.

**VERSE 18.**—Our eyes. Therefore—or else God himself joins himself to the compassionate feeling, so that he is said himself to endure and feel what the people endure.

**VERSE 19.**—How we have been devastated. Let the crowds say this during the persecution of believers. They have been devastated and confounded because they abandoned the law of the Lord and deserted their tabernacles.

**VERSE 20.**—Hear, therefore. Above he said, “Summon mourners,” and so forth. Now, as though they were present, he addresses them—to the reproach of priests, teachers, and all men—so that, while they cease from teaching, women may hear the word of the Lord.

**VERSE 21.**—For it has ascended. For the strength and speed of the enemies will be so great that they will not wait at the door but will climb through windows and over roofs.

**VERSE 22.**—Speak: Thus says, and so forth. (JEROME.) The Hebrew word written with three letters, and so forth, up to the point where there is no one to bury those who fall.

**VERSE 24.**—I who exercise mercy. (ID.) Although some things may appear unjust, nevertheless everything, and so forth, up to: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10).

**VERSE 25.**—Behold, days are coming. (ID.) Many nations, especially those bordering Judaea and Palestine, and so forth, up to the point where circumcision is of no benefit unless one observes the law.

# CHAPTER 10

**VERSE 1.**—Hear the word, and so forth. (JEROME.) He speaks specifically against them, and so forth, up to the point where they should regulate earthly things according to the causes of heavenly things.

**VERSE 3.**—Wood. (ID.) What we have said concerning idols, and so forth, up to the point where it is also characteristic of those who do not know God.

**VERSE 4.**—With silver and gold. (ID.) So that it may seize and deceive the simple by the brilliance of the material. This error has reached us, so that we suppose religion to consist in riches.

**VERSE 5.**—Therefore do not fear them. Many of the nations are accustomed to worship demons lest they harm them, and to entreat others so that they may prosper. Hence Virgil, *Aeneid* 3:

> A black sheep for winter, a white one for the favorable west winds.

**VERSE 6.**—There is none like you. There is none like you, Lord, among the gods—namely, those fabricated by heretics.

**VERSE 7.**—For yours it is. (JEROME.) Although heretics, according to the wisdom of the world, and so forth, up to: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the understanding of the prudent” (1 Cor. 1).

**VERSE 8.**—Wrapped up. (ID.) Otherwise it does not deceive; falsehood is wrapped up, whereas truth, and so forth, up to the point where they display to themselves the color of heaven and promise heavenly things.

**VERSES 11–12.**—The heavens and the earth. Those who are fellow workers with Christ, who are called gods and lords, have partly made these things through ecclesiastical teaching.

The one who makes. (ORIGEN, *Homilies on Jeremiah*.) The Lord who makes the earth by strength, and so forth. The prophet assumes, in a certain manner, three virtues of God, and so forth, up to the point where, if they are heavenly things, they carry their treasurer into a region near them.

**VERSE 13.**—Clouds. (JEROME.) They know, namely, over whom they should suspend rains and upon whom they should bestow them. Moses spoke like a cloud when he said, “Let the earth await my words as rain” (Exod. 9). And Isaiah: “Hear, O heaven, and listen with your ears, O earth, because the Lord has spoken” (Isa. 1).

From the extremities. “Whoever wishes to be first among you must be last of all.” Otherwise no one becomes a cloud.

Lightning into rains. (ORIGEN.) It is said that lightning is generated from the collision of clouds or rains, and so forth, up to the point where Jeremiah and Baruch, speaking together, also send forth shining lightning.

And he brings the wind out of his treasuries. (ID.) The winds that blow across the lands are not in God’s treasuries, and so forth, up to the point where it follows that one is wise, another faithful, and so on.

**VERSE 14.**—Foolish. (JEROME.) Foolish in comparison with God, and so forth, up to the point where God assumed all opposites in order to dissolve opposites.

It is false. (ORIGEN.) What he fashions according to its order. For what he cast is false, just as every human being is foolish apart from knowledge, and what he makes is also foolish.

There is no spirit. (JEROME.) It should be noted that in this chapter wind and spirit are called by one name among the Hebrews: *ruaḥ*.

**VERSE 15.**—They are vain. For either they are rustic, like wood; or they ring with beautiful speech, like silver; or, fabricated from their own understanding, they speak falsehoods, like gold.

At the time of visitation. Heresy is useful for a time, so that those who are approved may become manifest (1 Cor. 11). But when God’s visitation comes and his eye has looked upon everything, all things will fall silent.

**VERSE 17.**—Gather. (JEROME.) Jerusalem is commanded to gather into the most heavily fortified city whatever possessions it has outside and to prepare provisions far in advance for the siege. For God is not threatening what will happen far in the future, as before, but what will happen immediately.

**VERSE 19.**—Woe is me, and so forth. (ID.) Jerusalem complains that it has been grievously afflicted and struck with an incurable wound.

**VERSE 20.**—The tabernacle. (ID.) Jerusalem laments that its overthrow has been made so easy, and so forth, up to the point where a large part of them was killed and destroyed.

**VERSE 21.**—The flock. (ID.) The Septuagint has “cattle.” This cannot stand according to the historical sense: during such a long siege the cattle would not have survived.

**VERSE 22.**—A sound of report. (ID.) All these things that the preceding and present discourse describe, and so forth, up to those who acted foolishly and did not seek the Lord.

Of dragons—or ostriches. Symmachus has “sirens,” so that, in place of human beings, there may be dragons and all kinds of poisonous creatures; or ostriches, which are familiar with solitude and are born and raised in deserts. Or sirens, namely certain monsters and phantoms of demons.

**VERSE 23.**—I know, and so forth. Let those be ashamed who say that each person is governed by his own free choice. For “a man’s way is not his own,” and so forth. Hence David: “The steps of a man shall be directed by the Lord” (Ps. 36).

**VERSE 24.**—With judgment, and not in wrath. (JEROME.) As though he said: “What we suffer is just,” and so forth, up to the point where the nations that did not know you deserve not judgment but indignation.

# CHAPTER 11

**VERSE 1.**—The word. (ORIGEN, *Homily on Ezekiel*.) Namely, the Word who was in the beginning with God, and so forth, up to the point where he said to the disciples, “I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28).

The word that came to be. (JEROME.) The title does not state at what time, and so forth, up to the point where the discourse is directed to the men of Judah and Jerusalem.

**VERSE 2.**—Hear, and so forth: the men of Judah, and so forth. Allegorically, namely Christians; for Christ arose from Judah. Concerning him it is truly said: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hands shall be upon the backs of your enemies” (Gen. 49), and so forth.

Jerusalem. The Church, which is the city of the great King and the vision of peace. For peace is multiplied and seen in it.

**VERSE 3.**—Cursed. (ORIGEN.) The Jews are cursed because they did not hear God’s covenant when he led them out of the land of Egypt. But we who believe in Christ obey his covenant, which was handed down through Moses; and this is said to us so that we may not be cursed.

**VERSE 4.**—I brought them out. (JEROME, ORIGEN.) God also brought us out of Egypt and from the iron furnace, and so forth, up to the point where obedience to the commandments in the law is here a likeness of God.

And you shall be. God is not the God of everyone, but only of those to whom he gives himself. Hence: “I am the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel” (Ezek. 14). And elsewhere he says: “I will be their God” (Exod. 3); and, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Explaining this, the Savior says: “God is not the God of the dead but of the living” (Luke 20). The sinner is dead.

**VERSE 5.**—With milk and honey. (JEROME.) “Milk and honey” signifies an abundance of all things, and so forth, up to the point where it means either, “May it be so, Lord”—that is, may what you have given remain forever.

**VERSE 7.**—Because, solemnly testifying, and so forth. The words “so that they might do these things” are not found in the Septuagint. What follows, “And they did not do them,” belongs to them; it has been placed at the end of the preceding chapter. “Hear the words of this covenant,” and so forth.

**VERSE 9.**—A conspiracy was found. (ORIGEN.) A bond was found among the men of Judah, and so forth. If we sin, and so forth, up to the point where you will become a son of God in Christ Jesus.

**VERSE 11.**—They will cry out. In their necessities, and I will not hear, because they did not wish to hear me. Saul also suffered this, and so forth, up to the point where what is now said pertains to Judah and Jerusalem, upon whom captivity is impending.

**VERSE 13.**—According to the number. (ID.) In the Books of Kings and Chronicles we find that Judah and Jeremiah had far worse things, and so forth, up to the point where they had so many altars for their own confusion, upon which they sacrificed to idols.

**VERSE 14.**—Therefore you. (ID.) The prophet is commanded not to pray for those against whom, and so forth, up to the point where we learn from this that it is useless to pray for one who does not deserve to receive.

**VERSE 15.**—What is this, and so forth. (ID.) Let us say this to the leaders of the churches and to the wealthy, when they seize what belongs to others and do not remove the wickedness of their hearts, yet think that they deserve God’s mercy.

Are holy meats? But now the names of those who offer publicly are recited, and the redemption of sins is turned into praise; nor is the widow of the Gospel remembered, although she put more than everyone else into the treasury.

**VERSE 16.**—At the sound of speech. (JEROME.) As though he said: “Exalted through pride, you did not understand your creator and master with humility, but, speaking arrogantly against the Lord, you will be consumed by his fire and reduced to nothing.”

**VERSE 17.**—And the Lord. As though he said: “Your lord called you and planted you as a luxuriant, beautiful, fruitful olive tree; but because of the sound of your arrogant speech, his flame has descended upon you.”

**VERSE 18.**—But you. (JEROME.) The Jews and our Judaizers refer this to the person of Jeremiah, and so forth, up to the point where they might perhaps say that the people had thought but had not acted.

(ORIGEN.) “But you, Lord,” and so forth. Or: “Make me know, Lord, and I shall understand” (Ps. 142). According to the Psalmist, the Lord teaches human beings knowledge (ibid. 93). Hence: “Do not be called teachers upon the earth, for one is your teacher, who is in heaven” (Matt. 23)—namely, the one who instructs human beings, and so forth, up to the point where, when the wood of Jesus Christ comes and the Savior’s word descends into it, it is sweetened.

**VERSE 20.**—For to you. (JEROME.) Because I am crucified not through my own merit but through their crime. “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14).

**VERSE 22.**—Therefore thus says the Lord. This appears contrary to the preceding sentence, in which, and so forth, up to the point where what is fulfilled in Jeremiah at present is prophesied concerning the Lord in the future.

# CHAPTER 12

**VERSE 1.**—Indeed, you are just, and so forth. (JEROME.) This is an argument against all who act wickedly, as in that Psalm of the Psalmist: “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright” (Ps. 72), and so forth. But especially against heretics.

**VERSE 3.**—And you, Lord. (ID.) As though he said: There is no scandal if the impious or heretics flourish for a time, and so forth, up to the point where they have been slaughtered by the ecclesiastical sword.

**VERSE 5.**—If with footmen. As though he said: If the captivity of neighboring nations has wearied you—namely, of the Moabites, Philistines, Ammonites, and Edomites, who, because of the difficulty of the terrain, are suited less for battle than for banditry—what will you do when you come into captivity in Chaldaea? For the Chaldeans and Persians delight in horses.

**VERSE 6.**—For even your brothers, and so forth. (JEROME.) This can be understood of Christ, against whom his brothers cried, “Crucify him! We have no king but Caesar” (John 19).

**VERSE 7.**—I have abandoned my house. Hence: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Luke 13); and: “Rise, let us go from here” (John 14).

**VERSE 8.**—My inheritance, and so forth. (ORIGEN.) It is not surprising if the inheritance was then compared to a savage beast, since even today there are lions in the forest anathematizing Christ, blaspheming, and lying in wait for the faithful.

**VERSE 9.**—Is a many-colored bird? The Septuagint has: “Has a hyena’s cave become my inheritance for me?” (JEROME.) The hyena is a nocturnal beast that devours the corpses of the dead, digs bodies out of tombs, and feeds on every kind of filth; Israel is compared to its uncleanness.

**VERSE 10.**—Many shepherds, and so forth. (JEROME.) Let those who wish to be leaders hear this, and so forth, up to the point where they have scattered the people of God.

**VERSE 11.**—With desolation. (ORIGEN.) Because the Jews filled up the measure of their fathers and added the Savior himself to the killing of the prophets, and so forth, up to: “Let us sow not in the flesh but in the spirit, so that we may not reap corruption from the flesh but eternal life from the spirit” (1 Cor. 17).

**VERSE 12.**—There is no peace, and so forth. (JEROME.) Flesh cannot receive God’s peace within itself. For “the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God,” and those who are in the flesh cannot please God (Rom. 8).

**VERSE 13.**—They have sown. This is also said to ecclesiastical leaders, and so forth, up to: “From the one to whom more has been entrusted, more will be required” (Wis. 6).

From the fruits. The Septuagint has: “From your boasting.” (JEROME.) Namely, from expensive clothing, decorated houses, many possessions, and worldly wisdom. “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1); and “in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6); and “in his weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in him” (2 Cor. 12).

**VERSE 14.**—Neighbors. (JEROME.) Literally, the Edomites, Philistines, Moab, and Ammon. Allegorically, heretics who are called Christians and are more closely related to the holy land than they are inhabitants of it.

# CHAPTER 13

**VERSE 1.**—Thus says the Lord. (JEROME.) The holy man is called the loincloth of God, having been taken from the mud of the earth, and so forth, up to the point where he is, in a certain way, swallowed up by the innumerable multitude of nations and regarded as nothing.

**VERSE 5.**—And I hid it, and so forth. (ORIGEN.) The Jews proved unworthy of God and were cast away by him, and so forth, up to the point where, if one is not joined to the Lord, one is one spirit in Christ.

**VERSE 7.**—And you, loincloth. (JEROME.) In captivity. It signifies that the prophet, and so forth, up to the point where, for this reason, he wastes away in eternal destruction.

**VERSE 12.**—Every little bottle. (ID.) This is the drunkenness by which we forget God’s commandments and, through vices and sins, and so forth, up to: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7).

**VERSE 14.**—And I will scatter. (ID.) With rational anger, so that I may bring them back from error through pains and torments, and so forth, up to the point where the whole people of Jerusalem must be drunk with the cup of Babylon and overwhelmed by captivity.

**VERSE 16.**—Give to the Lord, and so forth. (ID.) He calls them to repentance before they are led into Babylon, and so forth, up to Sophonias: “A day of darkness and storm” (Zeph. 1).

**VERSE 17.**—But if you will not hear this. (ID.) Let us say this to the Jews and to our Judaizers, who cling to the letter, and so forth, up to the point where the prophet’s soul will weep because of their pride.

He has been captured. By the devil or by Nebuchadnezzar, or else he has been crushed. Israel was once the Lord’s flock. But because they judged themselves unworthy of salvation, the discourse turned to the Gentiles. Let the wild olive, grafted contrary to nature into the good olive, beware lest it too be crushed.

**VERSE 18.**—Say to the king and to the mistress. (JEROME.) The Hebrew word *Gebirah*, Aquila and Symmachus translated as “mistress” and “lady,” and so forth, up to the point where some angels supposedly suffered for the redemption of demons, and after the judgment the gates of hell would be closed and no one would be punished there—a view Origen seems to hold, but it is frivolous.

**VERSE 21.**—For you yourself taught them, and so forth. (ID.) When Hezekiah showed the treasury to the messenger of the king of Babylon. “For you yourself,” and so forth. Let the negligent Church hear this: it teaches its adversaries how they can seize it in spiritual captivity and tear apart its flock with bestial cruelty.

**VERSE 22.**—Because of the multitude, and so forth. (ID.) From this we learn that as long as sins are smaller, and so forth, up to: “These will rise to eternal life, and those to everlasting disgrace and confusion” (Dan. 12).

**VERSE 23.**—If he can change, and so forth. (ID.) Those who try to assert different natures use this testimony, and so forth, up to: “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength” (Jer. 9), and similar passages, in which the power of Christ works in all things.

**VERSE 26.**—I have stripped you. (ID.) Let us ask Christ that he reveal neither our shameful parts in the present nor in the future, but erase our iniquities and not permit our crimes to appear.

**VERSE 27.**—Upon the hills. Allegorically. He fornicates upon the hills and in the fields and is never cleansed—he who, with neck held high through pride, is not humbled beneath the powerful hand of God but trusts in his crimes.

# CHAPTER 14

**VERSE 1.**—And its gates, and so forth. (JEROME.) The meaning is, namely, the senses through which discipline is conceived in the mind, and so forth, up to the point where, even to the present day, the lack of rain produces scarcity not only of crops but also of drinking water.

**VERSE 4.**—Farmers. One of whom says: “You are God’s cultivation” (1 Cor. 3). And elsewhere: “We are God’s fellow workers.”

**VERSE 5.**—For even the hind, and so forth. (GREGORY.) “For even the hind”—or “hinds”—gave birth in the field. This statement is directed against teachers who carelessly abandon the children they have begotten, and so forth, up to: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6).

**VERSE 6.**—They drew in the wind. (ID.) The perverse, like dragons, draw in the wind when they are puffed up by malicious pride.

Their eyes failed. (JEROME.) Unable to see the clear light, and so forth, up to those who learn but do not teach.

**VERSE 8.**—The expectation of Israel. (ID.) Let us also say, in a time of drought and scarcity of water: “We have sinned against you and done evil before you” (Ps. 50). We await your coming, you who save Israel—not through its own merit but through your grace.

Like a tenant farmer. (GREGORY.) For one who is not heard as Lord is not the owner of the field but a tenant farmer, and so forth, up to the passing traveler who neglects the things that meet him on the roads.

And like a traveler. (JEROME.) The Jews explain this passage as follows: “Why do you withdraw yourself?” and so forth, up to the point where, with Israel abandoned, he proceeds toward the Gentiles—from place to place, from people to people, from the temple to the Church.

**VERSE 10.**—To move their feet, and so forth. (ID.) It should be noted in the holy Scriptures that the feet of sinners are always moving, and so forth, up to those who built the tower of Babylon and moved their feet from the East.

**VERSE 11.**—Do not pray. (ID.) It is foolish to pray for one who has sinned unto death, and so forth, up to the point where one who has once been assigned to the sword, famine, and pestilence is rescued by no prayers. Hence: “Do not pray,” and so forth.

**VERSE 13.**—The prophets say to them, and so forth. Let teachers who promise prosperity to sinners and to those who persist in vices hear this. There are many such people today who do not care where an offering comes from but consult their own greed. It is said that one such man acted as follows: he persuaded people to confess their secret sins before God at the altar, while he himself sat opposite; he listened and gave them this assurance: “Only give generous alms, and it is enough.”

**VERSE 15.**—Thus says the Lord. (JEROME.) Let the false prophet beware, lest those who deceive and flatter the people of God perish together with those they have deceived, lie unburied, and have no one to cover their disgrace with the dust of repentance.

**VERSE 17.**—Let my eyes pour forth. (ID.) This passage can be understood in two ways: either God himself, and so forth, up to the point where there is a crushed virgin, a stricken daughter, and a destroyed people.

**VERSE 18.**—If I go out, and so forth. (ID.) Let our prophets and priests hear this: neither outside nor inside, and so forth, up to the point where those who prophesied prosperity and ought to have opened the commandments of the law have gone into a land they did not know—that is, they have been taken captive.

**VERSE 19.**—Has he rejected, and so forth. (JEROME.) So that where the worship of God and tranquility had been, there might be sedition and the hostile roar. Whenever our Zion and our Judah, having become abominable, are rejected, let us not be surprised, but let us say what follows.

**VERSE 20.**—We acknowledge, Lord, and so forth. (ID.) As though he said: Both we and our fathers, through the same madness, neglected God’s commandments, and so forth, up to the point where they had not yet reached the culmination of wickedness; this was completed in the death of Christ.

**VERSE 21.**—The throne of glory. The temple, or any holy person, in whom, as it is written, “You struck his throne down to the earth.” It is struck down and destroyed when God is offended by the multitude of sins in him. But because he is ruined by guilt, he is sustained by the Lord’s mercy, which is changed into the severity of the sentence if the Lord makes void his covenant by which he promised us salvation.

**VERSE 22.**—Are there among carved images, and so forth? (JEROME.) After many varied discourses he returns to the title of the prophecy, and so forth, up to the point where you alone are able to instruct your people, and those who await you await the distributions of your graces.

# CHAPTER 15

**VERSE 1.**—And the Lord said. (GREGORY, *Moral Interpretations*, book 9, chapter 12.) With so many fathers passed over, only Moses and Samuel are brought forward, and so forth, up to the point where the other is expelled from the leadership and says: “Far be this sin from me, that I should cease to pray for you” (1 Sam. 12).

**VERSE 3.**—And I will visit them. (JEROME.) The four plagues to which the people of Judah were handed over are also shown by the prophet Ezekiel: the sword, and so forth, up to the point where, with the Creator neglected, the whole of creation would not rise up against sinners.

**VERSE 4.**—And I will give them over to agitation, and so forth. (ID.) This was partly fulfilled under the Babylonians, and so forth, up to the point where, if free people and descendants commit similar acts, they pass on to later generations. This Manasseh was utterly wicked: he cut Isaiah apart with a wooden saw, and Amon led his son through fire in honor of idols and Tophet.

**VERSE 5.**—For who will pity you? No one can plead with an offended God on behalf of the offenses of sinners, because a creature cannot be as merciful as the Creator, nor can one who is foreign to outsiders be as merciful as the Lord is to his own.

**VERSE 6.**—You have turned backward, and so forth. (JEROME.) Although, according to the Apostle, he ought to forget what lies behind and stretch toward what lies ahead, he desired the Egyptian meats.

**VERSE 8.**—They have been multiplied for me. (JEROME.) God wishes to save sinners by different medicines, so that those who despised him when he coaxed them may fear him when he threatens.

**VERSE 9.**—Seven. (ID.) The Hebrew word *Saba* can mean “seven,” “an oath,” or “many.” Hence, and so forth, up to the point where she is confounded forever, losing her people by the spiritual sword.

### Chapter 15

**Verse 10.—“Woe is me, my mother...”** (The same.) This can be understood synecdochically of Jeremiah, who was not throughout the whole world, etc., up to the point where we also find Jeremiah frequently asking for the people in this book.

**Verse 11.—“If your remnant...”** The Lord’s answer to what Jeremiah had said above: “Woe is me, my mother...” As if he said: “Do not consider only present things, but future ones. For your remnant will be for good,” etc. In the present also, when your enemies wished to overwhelm you, I came to your aid and protected you. “If your remnant will be for good.” These things can also be said of Christ according to his humanity: “If your remnant...” They can be understood of Jeremiah, who was compelled to prophesy at the worst of times, when captivity was imminent, and to endure harsh treatment from an unbelieving people.

**Verse 12.—“Will iron be joined with iron?”** (Jerome.) As if he said: “Do not grieve that your people are hostile,” etc., up to the point where it reached such wickedness that it was enclosed by a harder metal, that is, bronze.

**Verse 13.—“And treasures...”** (Origen.) One treasure is Jeremiah, another Isaiah, or Moses and the others. God took these treasures away from the Jews and gave them to us; hence: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21). “To them were entrusted first the oracles of God” (1 Cor. 1), and afterward they were given to us. They do indeed have the Law and the Prophets, but they do not understand them.

**“In all your sins.”** (Jerome.) That is, because of your sins, which have reached all your borders, etc., up to the point where, after rising again, Christ appeared no longer to his slayers but only to believers.

**Verse 14.—“It will burn.”** It cannot be extinguished, because you supplied the material for the blaze, so that my fire may consume what is in you—wood, hay, and straw. The cause of the burning therefore lies not in the Lord but in those who provide fuel for the conflagration.

**Verse 15.—“Do not receive me in your patience.”** The voice of Christ. As if he said: “You have always been patient with this sinful people, but since it has also raised its insolence against me, do not now continue to be patient.” But if you consider the times of the Lord’s Passion and of Jerusalem’s ruin, you will see that he was altogether patient. From the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar until the destruction of the Temple, forty-two years are reckoned, because a period for repentance had to be granted on account of those who would believe through the apostles.

**Verse 17.—“I did not sit...”** (Jerome.) The Hebrews think that this is spoken in the person of Jerusalem, because she alone sat, filled with bitterness, etc., up to the point where by her deed she will show that all her bitterness was like flowing waters.

**“Because of the face of your hand.”** (Origen.) The face of God’s hand is the striking of just judgment itself, which humbles the proud, etc., up to the point where, if we do not cease from sinning, it adds [them] further to eternal punishments.

**“I sat alone.”** (Gregory, *Moralia*, Book IV, chapter 35.) As if he said: “While I consider what I now suffer through the experience of judgment from the tumult of temporal desires, I tremblingly seek a withdrawal of the mind, because I still fear more keenly those eternal punishments which you threaten.”

**Verse 19.—“If you separate...”** (The same, *Moralia*, Book XVIII, chapter 23.) The present world is indeed cheap in God’s sight, while what is precious to him is ..., up to the point where he tears the human soul away from love of the present age by saying whatever he can.

**“Like my mouth.”** (Jerome.) Let us consider how great a reward a teacher’s speech possesses if he wishes to free someone from error and recall him from the number of sinners.

## Chapter 16

**Verses 1–2.—“And the word came to pass...”** (Jerome.) Since captivity was imminent, do not add to your own grief the misery of a wife and children. The Apostle therefore rightly commands: “Because the time is short and the consummation is near, let those who have wives be as though they had none” (1 Cor. 7).

**Verse 4.—“By deaths of sicknesses.”** (The same.) Observe that wasting away through prolonged illness is the wrath of God; thus Joram, son of Jehoshaphat, was consumed by illness. And the Apostle says: “For this reason many among you are weak and sick” (1 Cor. 11), etc.

**Verse 5.—“Do not enter a house.”** (Jerome.) Hence: “Do not even eat with such a person” (1 Cor. 5). Nor should you say “Hail” to him. The apostles too were forbidden this, etc., up to the point where one thing is to die by the common law of nature, and another to have fallen under God’s sentence. Jeremiah was sent by the Lord as a young man to preach; hence he says: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord, I do not know how to speak.” He was also a virgin and chaste, and without children, so that he might preach more freely.

**Verse 6.—“Nor will they mourn.”** (The same.) This was a custom among the ancients and remains so to the present day, etc., up to the point where they daily lay out in the Church the funerals of the deceived.

**Verse 9.—“Behold, I will take away...”** Thus God also takes away all joy and gladness from the sinful Church. Concerning this it is said: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4).

**Verse 12.—“But you also...”** (The same.) Lest they perhaps say: “The sentence is unjust: the father ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge.”

**Verse 14.—“Behold, days are coming...”** (The same.) Miracles are foretold which, according to the literal sense, were partly fulfilled under Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest, etc., up to the point where he brought them back to their own land, that is, the Church which he gave to their fathers, namely, the apostles and apostolic men.

**Verse 16.—“Behold, I will send fishermen.”** The Jews think that by “fishermen” the Chaldeans are signified, and by “hunters” the Romans, who hunted the wretched people from mountains and hills and from caves in the rocks.
