**“From caves in the rocks,” etc.** (Jerome.) The apostles and apostolic men: for “the Rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10); but he also gave [this] to Peter, etc., up to the point where they received double punishments for their iniquities.

**Verse 18.—“Double iniquities,” etc.** (The same.) Because “the servant who knew his master’s will and did not do it will be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12). It is fitting that those from the nations should receive single sins, but that we should receive double ones. Hence: “For those who sin voluntarily, no sacrifice for sins remains” (Heb. 6).

**Verse 19.—“To you the nations will come,” etc.** (The same.) After Israel has been cast out and carried away by fishermen and hunters, the multitude of the nations is consequently called, and confesses its former error.

**“From the ends.”** The first of the earth are the world’s wise men, nobles, rich men, and powerful men. But God chose the ends—that is, the foolish things of the world—in order to confound all that is strong. “The nations will come,” that is, those who are last upon the earth: foolish, ignoble, and despised.

**Verse 20.—“Gods.”** (Jerome.) People make gods for themselves not only from bodily images, etc., up to the point where they worship the work of their hands, thinking that what they have fashioned is real.

## Chapter 17

**Verse 1.—“The sin of Judah is written...”** (Jerome.) As if he said: “The sins of the nations have been erased,” concerning which it is said to Moses, “Leave me,” etc., up to the point where: “Cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils” (Isa. 2).

(Origen.) Perhaps “the sin of Judah” means our sin, since we believe in Christ from the tribe of Judah, etc., up to the point where, if you wish to understand it of Judas the betrayer, “The sin of Judah is written” conflicts with what follows concerning “their” sin, etc.

**Verse 3.—“The high places.”** (Jerome.) Which are called *Ramoth* in Hebrew. Heretics are signified, who set their mouth against heaven, etc., up to the point where the slavery of demons, who are enemies and avengers, is signified.

**Verse 5.—“Cursed is the man.”** (The same.) Cursed, therefore, are Paul of Samosata and Photinus, who, although holy, etc., up to the point where the two might become one, and we might worship not the creature but the Creator.

**Verse 7.—“Blessed is the man,” etc.** (Jerome.) As if he said: “Cursed are the Jews and heretics who have no hope in the Lord,” etc., up to the point where he once died for us and does not die again; and he says: “I am life” (John 14).

**Verse 8.—“That toward the moisture...”** (The same.) As if he said: “He passes from Jewish dryness to the grace of baptism.”

**Verse 11.—“In the midst of his days.”** (The same.) His days are those of this age. Christ rescued us from this evil age, and we leave it during the day. Its last one will be foolish, when all things have been subjected to Christ. “The last enemy to be destroyed is death.”

**Verse 14.—“Heal me, Lord.”** (The same.) Many physicians have healed, etc., up to the point where he desires to be cured and healed, whose praise and medicine are true.

**Verse 15.—“Behold, they themselves say to me: Where is the word...”**

**Verse 16.—“I was not troubled, following you as shepherd.”** (The same.) The more you follow Christ, etc., up to the point where the day of judgment is evil for those who suffer torments.

**Verse 19.—“Go and stand...”** As if he said: “Because they refuse to hear your words,” etc., up to the point where they should hear whether they wish to or not, as though they had not heard before.

**Verse 21.—“Guard your souls.”** Lest we tear apart the commandment of the Sabbath, restored through Jeremiah, we set it down all together, so that we may understand everything at once.

**“So that you do not bring burdens through the gates of this city on the Sabbath day.”** (The same.) If our Judaizers, etc., up to the point where he also called his father God.

**Verse 27.—“But if you will not listen to me, to sanctify the Sabbath day, and not to carry a burden or bring it through the gates of Jerusalem...”** As if he said: “These are the rewards of those who sanctify the Sabbath and are burdened by no weight. But if ...”

## Chapter 18

**Verse 1.—“The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying.”** (Jerome.) Through all the senses he proceeds toward judgment, etc., up to the point where he might hear the Lord’s commandments there.

**Verse 4.—“And it was spoiled,” etc.** It was spoiled by divine providence, so that the ignorant craftsman might, through his own error, fashion the parable.

**Verse 7.—“Suddenly I will speak.”** (The same.) He signifies free choice, etc., up to the point where the grace of the giver may excel in all things.

**Verse 11.—“Behold, I...”** (Jerome.) He fulfills the parable which he taught both by what he showed and by his speech.

**Verse 12.—“According to their thoughts.”** (The same.) Where there is no grace of God, etc., up to the point where all the nations around him are included.

**Verse 14.—“From the rock?”** As if he said: “As from the summits of Lebanon,” etc., up to the point where: “My people has forgotten me.”

**Verse 16.—“So that the land might become...”** (Jerome.) This seems to have been fulfilled more fully after the Lord’s coming, when no Jew is permitted to enter the land or the holy city. But when they come to lament, they marvel and mourn over the prophecies of the prophets, which have been fulfilled.

**Verse 17.—“Like the wind.”** (The same.) This sentence remains to the present day, etc., up to the point where then all Israel will be saved.

**Verse 18.—“Come.”** (The same.) This was then the Jews’ opposition to Jeremiah or to Christ, etc., up to the point where they persecute the prophecy with every confidence of words and meanings.

**Verse 19.—“Attend, Lord, to me, and hear the voice of my adversaries.”** (The same.) In the type of the Savior, etc., up to the point where: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27).

**Verse 23.—“Do not forgive their iniquity,” etc.** This is not contrary to the preceding sentence, etc., up to the point where sin would not remain unpunished for them as an example.

## Chapter 19

**Verse 1.—“Thus says the Lord: Go and take a potter’s flask.”** (Jerome.) Holy Scripture wishes to teach the people not only through their ears but also through their eyes. For what is perceived by sight is retained in the mind more firmly than what is perceived by hearing.

**“A potter’s flask” for “a potter’s flask,” etc., up to “and *Hierihoh* for *Chiricho*.”

**Verse 4.—“Because...”** (The same.) Every heretic abandons God, etc., up to the point where they burn to idols the children whom they have begotten in heresy.

**Verse 5.—“Which I did not command.”** I did not command or conceive it, etc., up to the point where these things must be understood of God, like the others.

**Verse 6.—“Topheth and the valley of the sons of Hinnom,” etc.** (The same.) What the valley of the son of Hinnom is, etc., up to the point where [it may be understood] historically, when Babylon ravaged it.

**Verse 7.—“And I will give the corpses...”** Although these things happened to the people in the Babylonian captivity, etc., up to the point where they made tombs of their own bellies for their children.

**Verse 11.—“So I will break this people.”** Under Aelius Hadrian the city lost both its name and its status, to break the pride of its inhabitants. The names “holy cross” and “resurrection,” however, do not signify the city but the place.

(The same.) The Jews’ golden and jewel-adorned Jerusalem, etc., up to the point where everything is reserved for the true Judge.

**“And they will bury in Topheth,”** etc., up to the point where what threatens this place may happen as it did at Topheth.

**Verse 13.—“And the houses of Jerusalem and the houses of the kings...”** Every house of the kings of Judah will be like the place of Topheth. This is not found in the Hebrew, but is inserted by the Septuagint.

## Chapter 20

**Verse 1.—“And Pashhur heard.”** (Jerome.) He was the high priest of the Temple, etc., up to the point where he considers the one who commands.

**Verse 3.—“And when it had dawned.”** The prophet’s patience and prudence must be noted. Sent to prison, he is silent and conquers the injury through silence; yet he does not conceal what he knows is going to happen, so that at least the priest of God might cease from sinning and implore God’s mercy.

**“Not Pashhur.”** According to the preceding interpretation, etc., up to the point where you look this way and that and fear the approaching adversaries.

**Verse 7.—“You deceived me, Lord.”** (The same.) The prophet says that he was deceived by the Lord, etc., up to the point where he endures persecutions and afflictions.

**“I have become a laughingstock.”** (The same.) The prophet had thought that what the Lord threatened would happen immediately; and the people thought that, since it had not happened immediately, it would not happen at all.

**Verse 12.—“But you, Lord of hosts,” etc.** (The same.) God alone is ..., up to the point where he is therefore dead in his sins.

**“Let me see.”** Although the righteous man knows that he has God as his defender, nevertheless, in the patience of human frailty, he now desires to see what he knows is going to happen.

**“For to you...”** You who say: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Heb. 10), etc. Blessed is the conscience whose cause is revealed to the Lord. Hence the Apostle says: “Everything that is made manifest is light” (Eph. 5).

**Verse 13.—“For he has delivered.”** (The same.) The poor in spirit, having obtained vengeance from the Lord, praises him and rejoices that he has been snatched from the hand of the wicked. This, however, does not happen by merit but by the grace of him who delivered the poor man, who does not love the riches of the fallen proud but the humility of the delivered poor.

**Verse 14.—“Cursed...”** Jeremiah was born in the fifth month, that is, August, etc., up to the point where they suppose that it foretells the future destruction of the Temple.

**Verse 15.—“Cursed is the man,” etc.** Those who think that souls existed in the heavenly regions, etc., up to the point where: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. 5), etc.

## Chapter 21

**Verse 1.—“The word which...”** “When he sent.” (Jerome.) It must be noted that in the prophets, etc., up to the point where they are mentioned in what follows.

**“Pashhur, son of...”** Above, Pashhur or Phascor, who struck Jeremiah, had Immer as his father; but this Pashhur is the son of Malchiah, for they are not the same person.

**Verse 4.—“Behold, I...”** As if he said: “You resist and prepare weapons of war in vain; you will use them only in the middle of the city, and only so much that you may appear to be armed. For the enemies will have no one whom they must defeat, but only people whom they must capture.”

**Verse 7.—“I will give Zedekiah.”** First he prophesied concerning the whole city, etc., up to the point where he should hope for no mercy after violating the covenant by perjury.

**“Into the hand.”** Into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and into the hand of his enemies.

**Verse 8.—“And to the people...”** To the king’s messengers who had come, etc., up to the point where he says: “Cursed be the day on which I was born.”

**“Behold, I set before you...”** Some explain this passage tropologically as follows: It is better to surrender oneself to secular disciplines, especially philosophical ones, than to remain in that Church in which there is a famine of the word of God, and in which the whole people dies by the sword of heretics, by lack of teaching, and by heretical pestilence.

**Verse 12.—“Judge in the morning.”** (Jerome.) In this passage God’s mercy is demonstrated, etc., up to the point where it would happen to them through their own fault, not through the harshness of the one threatening.

**Verse 13.—“Behold, I am against you, inhabitress...”** He speaks against Jerusalem, which is under siege; or, just as Tyre is surrounded by the sea, so she is enclosed by the Babylonian army and cannot escape; or she thinks herself unconquerable and strong like an extremely hard rock, because of the solidity and size of her walls.

**Verse 14.—“In the forest.”** (The same.) Jerusalem and the surrounding region—which had no fruit-bearing trees of good works and was therefore worthy of burning—he aptly calls a level valley, as though accessible to enemies, not a lofty mountain that is difficult to climb.

## Chapter 22

**Verse 1.—“Thus says...”** (Jerome.) Here the word of the Lord came, etc., up to the point where he should flee from God’s sentence.

**Verse 3.—“Do justice.”** Whatever was said to the royal house, let them understand, etc., up to the point where they walk with measured steps in the Church.

**Verse 6.—“If I do not make...”** (The same.) He threatens the royal house, etc., up to the point concerning those who minister to the Lord.

**Verse 10.—“Do not weep for the dead,” etc.** (The same.) It seems to me that this is said specifically concerning Zedekiah, etc., up to the point where everything is to be understood of Zedekiah.

**Verse 11.—“Concerning Shallum,” etc.** (The same.) Josiah, the righteous king, had three sons, etc., up to the point where the kingdom of Judah ended in them.

**Verse 13.—“Woe to him who builds...”** (The same.) Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, whom Pharaoh appointed in his place, etc., up to the point where he relates that he died and was not buried; we will speak of him later.

**Verse 18.—“They will not mourn for him,” etc.** (The same.) What we have set down from the Hebrew, etc., up to the point where brigands finally killed him.

**Verse 24.—“As I live, says...”** (The same.) Above he had spoken to the royal house, etc., up to the point where it may be understood of the Lord of majesty.

**“For if he should be...”** (The same.) Grunius miserably, etc., up to the point where, if he wishes to read it, let him read it as a philosopher, not as a churchman.

**Verse 28.—“Is this man...?”** (The same.) Since this is said of Jeconiah, etc., up to the point where he is cast out of the Lord’s hand and delivered to the king of Babylon.

**“This man.”** (The same.) Jeconiah is interpreted as “the Lord’s preparation.” In the present passage its first syllable, *ie*, that is, the Lord’s name, is removed, and he is called Coniah, so that he may be understood to have been prepared for destruction and ruin.

**Verse 30.—“Write...”** (The same.) Christ was born from his seed, etc., up to the point where even the semblance of the kingdom was completely destroyed.

**“Childless,” etc.** Aquila’s first edition has “childless”; the second, “not increasing.” Symmachus has “empty”; the Septuagint and Theodotion, “abominable and rejected.”

## Chapter 23

**Verse 1.—“Woe to the shepherds,” etc.** (Jerome.) Since all hope of the Jewish kingdom has failed, he turns to the leaders of the Church; and with the synagogue abandoned and condemned along with its shepherds, the word is addressed to the apostles, concerning whom it is said: “I will raise up shepherds over them” (Ezek. 34), etc.

**Verse 5.—“Behold, days are coming, says...”** (The same.) After the shepherds of the synagogue—namely, the scribes and Pharisees—have been rejected and the apostles substituted in their place, Christ, the shepherd of shepherds, is introduced.

**Verse 7.—“Therefore...”** (The same.) This entire chapter is absent from the Septuagint. Its meaning here is: God’s people are not delivered from Egypt through Moses but from the whole world through Christ. This will be completely fulfilled when they come from east and west and north and south and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and when the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved (Rom. 11).

**Verse 9.—“Like a man drenched with wine.”** He has no understanding and no wisdom, etc., up to the point where Jeremiah is interpreted as “exalted of the Lord.”

**“Before the face of the Lord,” etc.** (The same.) Having looked upon the face of almighty God—that is, of the Father—and the face of the Son, who is the radiance of his glory and the exact representation of his being, the prophet trembles in soul and body and understands that he is nothing. Hence: “I became like a beast before you.”

**Verse 10.—“The land mourned.”** Whatever you understand literally concerning the land of Judea, you can refer to the congregation of believers. For adultery, lies, and perjury are followed by barrenness of virtues and graces.

**Verse 11.—“For the prophet...”** When evils are found in the Church of God, and especially among its leaders, we know that this has been fulfilled: “For both prophet and priest are polluted.”

**“I will bring evils upon them.”** Not that the evils are ..., etc., up to the point where it is called the correction and torment of the sinner.

**Verse 14.—“And among the prophets...”** Just as the prophets of Samaria prophesy in Baal whatever they say, so heretics, whether in the Church or outside it, speak through demons in order to overthrow the people of Israel, who formerly saw God.

**Verse 15.—“From the prophets.”** (The same.) For we use this testimony, etc., up to the point where they attempt to defame and sow blasphemies everywhere.

**Verse 18.—“For who...?”** Do not believe the false prophets who say these things. How can they know the Lord’s counsels? Who has seen them and announced them?

**Verse 19.—“Behold, a whirlwind.”** As if he said: By contrast it is clear that the prophets do not know what they are saying. In place of the peace and security they promise, the Babylonian storm is coming.

**Verse 25.—“I have heard what they said.”** (Jerome.) There are many kinds of prophecy, etc., up to the point where the hearts of ungoverned tyrants might, through their own conscience, feel the majesty of the Lord.

**Verse 27.—“Their dreams which...”** There are dreamers in the Church even today who turn their errors into the Lord’s prophecies, frequently saying, “I dreamed.” Against them it is said: “How long will this be?” etc.

**Verse 28.—“What has straw [in common]...?”** The doctrine of heretics is aptly compared with straw, which has no marrow and provides no nourishment.

**Verse 29.—“Are not my words...?”** What the prophets lied about among the former people, etc., up to the point where the Lord therefore threatens that he will come against teachers of this kind.

**“Like fire.”** It is written concerning churchmen that hammer and axe were not heard in the house of the Lord.

**Verse 30.—“Who steal...”** For falsehood always imitates truth; otherwise it cannot deceive.

**Verse 39.—“And I will abandon...”** We know that this happened at the time of the Babylonian captivity, etc., up to the point where it specifically signifies the mystery of the Trinity.

## Chapter 24

**Verse 1.—“He showed.”** (Jerome.) It must be noted that this vision occurred in the time of Zedekiah, after Jeconiah had been led away into deportation, not into captivity, because he had surrendered voluntarily.

**“Two baskets.”** Two baskets or hampers of bad and good figs, etc., up to the point where they are referred to the good figs and the excellent basket.

**“Placed before the Temple.”** Not outside, etc., up to the point where the bad figs are very bad.

**Verse 2.—“And one basket...”** (The same.) We who seek simple histories, etc., up to the point where he was led to Babylon and died there.

**Verse 4.—“And it came to pass.”** (The same.) The allegorical interpreter raves at this point, etc., up to the point where they are to die in this land and in the valley of tears.

**Verse 6.—“And I will set my eyes.”** In the captivity he set his eyes upon them, etc., up to the point where a large part returned to Jerusalem.

## Chapter 25

**Verse 1.—“The word.”** (Jerome.) These events precede the vision already mentioned, etc., up to the point where the lyric song does not observe this.

**“In the fourth year.”** In the fourth year of King Jehoiakim, etc., up to the point where Jehoiakim was killed in the eleventh year of his reign.

**Verse 3.—“From the thirteenth year.”** From the thirteenth year of Josiah’s reign, etc., up to the point where he is recalled only by constant admonition from the Lord.

**Verse 4.—“And the Lord sent to you all his servants.”** He admonished his people not through one prophet but through all of them; and, as though stationed on watch and guard duty, he rose early to warn them, but they did not listen. Thus, the more frequent the warning, the greater their contempt.

**“Nor did you incline.”** (The same.) Such was their hardness, etc., up to the point where he does not inflict punishment for the crime.

**Verse 6.—“After other gods,” etc.** As if he said: “While I was warning you about these things and those preceding, I told you not to serve foreign gods, not to provoke me to anger, and not to force me, against my will, to punish you.”

**Verse 9.—“And I will take...”** “Nebuchadnezzar, my servant.” Not as the prophets and other saints who serve God, but because, in the overthrow of Jerusalem, he serves the Lord’s will.

**“And I will bring them,” etc.** These are the rewards of those who despise and refuse to hear God. Whatever evil is therefore brought upon us is deserved by our sins; and just as nations were brought against Jerusalem, so today they serve against the negligent Church.

**Verse 10.—“And I will destroy...”** This is confirmed in the assembly of the wicked, so that their teachers do not teach the word of God but hiss like a serpent. Among them the voice of joy and gladness has perished, so that they do not hear the Apostle: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4).

**Verse 11.—“And they will serve.”** Just as Jerusalem, etc., up to the point where he describes it in prophetic speech.

**Verse 12.—“When they are completed.”** Observe that Jeremiah prophesies not only against Babylon but against all the nations that were in Babylon’s army and fought against God’s people.

**Verse 15.—“Take the cup of the wine of wrath,” etc.** (The same.) The offering of the cup is an indication of the Lord’s wrath, etc., up to the point where the cup is offered, but as punishment.

**Verse 18.—“Jerusalem and the cities of Judah,” etc.** As if he said: “I thought I would offer the cup only to the nations, and therefore had gladly offered myself for this ministry; but among the other nations, indeed before the others, I offered it to Jerusalem and the cities of Judah,” etc.

**Verse 19.—“To Pharaoh, king of Egypt,” etc.** After Jerusalem, Pharaoh, king of Egypt, drank, along with his servants, his princes, and all his people, as well as those who were not Egyptians but lived in his territories.

**Verse 20.—“The Philistines and Ashkelon,” etc.** By a general name he signifies the land of the Philistines, etc., up to the point where Isaiah writes that the Philistines were captured and devastated by the Babylonians.

**Verse 22.—“Tyre and all the kings,” etc.** Tyre and Sidon are on the coast of Phoenicia, etc., up to the point where the Hebrew language is largely related to it.

**Verse 25.—“To the kings of Elam and all...”** Because Elam and the kings of the Medes follow, they think that Zimri is a region of Persia; unless perhaps, because Arabia preceded it, they are understood as kings of the desert.

**“And the king of Sheshach,” etc.** As if he said: “All who are around,” etc., up to the point where he is to be destroyed before the Antichrist, according to Daniel.

**Verse 31.—“The judgment belongs to the Lord.”** Since the merits of the nations differ, “the one who does not believe has already been judged,” in the very fact that he does not believe; but those who do not believe will be afflicted with different punishments.

**Verse 32.—“Behold, it will go forth,” etc.** Let those be ashamed who, doing violence to Holy Scripture, interpret the Lord’s threats in a favorable sense.

**Verse 34.—“Howl, shepherds.”** (Jerome.) The howling of the leaders of the flock, etc., up to the point where the good things of peace will fall silent and be taken away in the Lord’s wrath.

## Chapter 26

**Verse 1.—“At the beginning of the reign,” etc.** (The same.) This prophecy is earlier than the preceding one, although it occurred under the same king. The former took place in the fourth year, while this one occurred at the beginning of that same king’s reign. Therefore the historical order should not be woven into the prophecy, since earlier events are sometimes stated later and later events earlier.

**Verse 2.—“In the court of the house.”** So that you may also speak to people from the surrounding cities. He aptly stands in the court and in the vestibule of the Temple, so that those who gather to pray may be compelled to hear his words.

**Verse 3.—“Perhaps they will listen,” etc.** (The same.) As if he said: “Perhaps they will listen,” etc., up to the point where: “Perhaps they will fear my Son.”

**Verse 4.—“If you will not listen.”** It lies within our will, etc., up to the point where it is not once and from the beginning, but continually and attentively.

**Verse 6.—“I will make this house like Shiloh.”** As, after the Temple had been built upon the threshing floor, etc., up to the point where he was made a curse for us.

**Verse 10.—“The gates of the house.”** It is called “New” because those who sat there and presided over judgment resisted the accusations of the priests and false prophets.

**Verse 11.—“And they spoke.”** While the city’s leaders sat at the gate of the Temple, etc., up to the point where they were thinking about future goods.

**Verse 12.—“And he said.”** While Jeremiah’s accusers were bringing the charge and accusation, etc., up to the point where: “For in truth the Lord sent me to you.”

**Verse 13.—“Now therefore, good...”** As if he said: “If you are angry,” etc., up to the point where nothing is taken away from the truth.

**Verse 16.—“And they said.”** The city’s leaders and the people understood, etc., up to the point where we can free them by changing the sentence.

**Verse 20.—“There was also...”** It is asked, since Uriah [said] the same, etc., up to the point where Christ too escaped from the hands of his persecutors.

**Verse 22.—“And the king sent.”** It is asked how King Jehoiakim, etc., up to the point where this prophecy is said to have been made when he had begun to reign.

**Verse 24.—“Nevertheless, the hand of Ahikam...”** Although Jeremiah was freed by the Lord’s help, the credit is nevertheless assigned to the one through whom he freed his prophet.

## Chapter 27

**Verse 1.—“At the beginning of the reign,” etc.** (Jerome.) Many think this is the beginning of what follows; but it must be joined to the preceding passage, so that whatever is reported as said or done may be understood to have occurred at the beginning of Jehoiakim’s reign.

**Verse 2.—“Thus says the Lord.”** The preceding vision occurred at the beginning of Jehoiakim’s reign; but this one occurred under Zedekiah, who reigned last in Jerusalem, under whom the city was captured and destroyed.

**Verse 5.—“The earth and human beings.”** The order is reversed. In Genesis, living creatures are made first and the human being afterward; here he names the human being first and afterward the things subjected to him.

**“In strength.”** Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

**“And I gave,” etc.** This signifies that all things have been granted to the human race through grace.

**Verse 6.—“Into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar.”** (The same.) What great misery Israel suffers, since by comparison Nebuchadnezzar is called God’s servant!

**“Moreover...”** Every kind of animal. Along with the human being, all things subject to him are delivered; or savage nations are signified, so that they may serve the one who did not know how to serve.

**Verse 7.—“Until he comes,” etc.** Lest Nebuchadnezzar’s kingdom be thought eternal, he signifies that Nebuchadnezzar himself will be captured by the Medes and Persians.

**Verse 12.—“And to Zedekiah.”** After all the nations, he turns to Zedekiah and threatens him with the same things. The Jews do not deserve a privilege, since they have sinned either similarly, or more seriously, or more greatly than the nations; and those who disdain to listen are consumed by pestilence and famine.

**“Do not listen.”** In this passage the allegorical interpreter, etc., up to the point where they will not regain their former position.

**Verse 14.—“You will not serve.”** It is better to serve voluntarily, have God as a friend, and cultivate foreign soil than to serve as captives under compulsion.

**“The words of the prophet.”** It must be noted that in the Holy Scriptures false prophets are called prophets.

**Verse 16.—“And to the priests.”** After the nations and kings, he speaks to the priests and to the people, who had already announced destruction through the prophets, saying: “And I will cast you out,” etc. He speaks of the same things as above.

**Verse 17.—“So that you may live.”** Note God’s mercy, etc., up to the point where it is shown that God can be restrained by the prayers of the saints.

**Verse 18.—“Let them meet the Lord.”** (The same.) Let them come forward and demonstrate by deeds that what they predict has been fulfilled; then the prophecy will be proved true.

**Verse 19.—“Concerning the pillars.”** (The same.) He lists the vessels that were carried to Babylon after Zedekiah had been captured, the city burned, and the Temple overthrown.

## Chapter 28

**Verse 1.—“And it came to pass.”** (Jerome.) This was before Ezekiel prophesied in Babylon to those who had been led away with Jeconiah.

**“In the house of the Lord.”** There he speaks boldly because he promises prosperity to the people; and lies are gladly heard, especially lies that promise what is desired.

**Verse 3.—“All the vessels,” etc.** Jeremiah had said that the remaining vessels too were to be carried away; this man asserts that those already carried away will be brought back.

**Verse 6.—“Amen, so be it,” etc.** He wishes to happen what the other man falsely asserted, etc., up to the point where he confirms the truth by the example of others.

**Verse 7.—“Nevertheless.”** He could have said, “You are lying,” etc., up to the point where those who hear may await the outcome.

**Verse 10.—“And he took.”** (Jerome.) Jeremiah’s prudence must be considered, etc., up to the point where their knowledge belongs to God alone.

**Verse 13.—“Hananiah.”** He is called a supposed prophet. For many things in the Holy Scriptures are stated according to the opinion of the time in which events are reported, not according to the truth of the matter.

**Verse 14.—“And you will make...”** After Jeremiah had gone away and silently swallowed the insults, the word of the Lord came to him—not so that he might address Hananiah, boasting in his lie, in his own words and say, “Thus says the Lord,” although Hananiah himself had said it; but falsehood always imitates truth.

**“Chains.”** He shows that, while retaining the lesser punishment, etc., up to the point where they were confined in the bodies of brute animals.

**Verse 15.—“And he said.”** (The same.) It must be noted that Jeremiah, having suffered the insult and not yet having received the word of the Lord addressed to him, remains silent; afterward, having been sent by the Lord, he boldly rebukes him and announces imminent death to the liar.

**Verse 16.—“This year.”** (The same.) If, whenever we die, we are freed from the prisons of our bodies—as in the passage which heretics wrongly interpret, “Bring my soul out of prison”—how can death be imposed as a punishment?

**Verse 17.—“In the seventh month.”** Perhaps he died in the seventh month, which usually signifies rest; for this reason they falsely say that he died so that he might be freed from the body’s evils, according to the saying: “Death is rest for a man.” We, however, know that the bodies of believers are temples of God if the Holy Spirit dwells in them.

## Chapter 29

**Verse 1.—“And these things...”** (Jerome.) He intends to persuade them not to yield to the false prophets who promised them a return to Jerusalem after a short time. But they should know that they will remain in Babylon for a long time.

**“The words of the book.”** (The same.) This little book of Jeremiah, etc., up to the point where he persuaded the people concerning what had been commanded him by the Lord.

**“To the remnant of the elders.”** First the letter is addressed to the remnant of the elders, then to the priests, third to the prophets, and fourth to all God’s people; it is sent according to the order of age.

## Chapter XXIX

### Verse 6

“Take wives,” etc. Jeremiah is commanded—for the captivity of Jerusalem is near—not to take a wife or beget children. But if, because of the urgency of the time, the use of wives is withdrawn from those who have them, how much more is it commanded that those who do not have them should not take them.

### Verse 8

“Let them not deceive you.” (The same author.) The false prophets, [Col. 0044A] etc., up to the one who was likewise of Zedekiah’s reign.

### Verse 10

“When they begin.” Do not believe the false prophets who promise you a return close at hand: the seventy years will first be completed for you before you return.

“Seventy years.” For so long we remain amid the confusion of the world, etc., up to “and then there is the end of our labor and endurance.”

### Verse 14

“And I will bring you back.” So that you may know more certainly that you should not hope for this return as something near, but should build houses, plant orchards, beget children, and await the promised time.

### Verse 17

“Like figs.” Theodotion has *suarinas*, that is, “second”; Symmachus has “last,” which in Hebrew is *suarim* (the Hebrew term is left unidentified in the source).

[Col. 0044B]

### Verse 19

“From the night.” (The same author.) I did not cease warning them that they should imitate you, who enjoy secure leisure in the exile, until God’s promises should be fulfilled.

### Verse 21

“To Ahab.” The Hebrews say that these were elders, etc., up to the point that, after performing penance, they might possess their former place after the true Sabbath.

### Verse 24

“To Shemaiah.” Shemaiah of Nehelam, etc., up to “but discernment of spirits is a spiritual gift.”

### Verse 27

“Why did you not rebuke?” By a lie he anticipates the truth and imposes upon others what he himself deserved, because the children of darkness are wiser than the children of light, and they inflict upon others what they fear for themselves.

### Verse 31

“Thus says.” Shemaiah, truly a Nehelamite, etc., up to the words that follow against them: “Behold, I will visit.”

## Chapter XXX

[Col. 0044C]

### Verse 1

“This word.” (Jerome.) Jeremiah was promising a return, etc., up to “But when Israel and Judah return to their land.”

### Verse 7

“Alas, because it is great.” (The same author.) First, grievous things are announced, etc., up to the point that they will hold not weapons in their hands, but their loins like women in labor.

### Verse 9

“And David.” That is, Christ. For just as the first Adam and the second are written according to bodily reality, so also David. For Christ is from David according to the flesh.

### Verse 10

“My servant.” (The same author.) He calls him familiarly, just as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are called servants of God. Moses also and the other prophets, and Paul at the beginning of his Epistles, glory in this title.

[Col. 0044D]

### Verse 12

“Wound.” (The same author.) A friend strikes in one way, an enemy in another; a father in one way, an adversary in another. The former strikes in order to correct; the latter strikes in order to kill.

### Verse 16

“Therefore.” (The same author.) We recognize that these things happened under Zerubbabel, etc., up to the point that they are fulfilled more fully and perfectly in Christ.

### Verse 18

“Behold, I will restore.” (The same author.) Since the type went before, etc., up to the point that they are fulfilled more fully and perfectly in Christ and in the apostles.

### Verse 19

“Of those who play, and I will multiply them,” etc. Not according to the passage, “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. XXXII), but as David played before the ark of the Lord (1 Chron. XIII).

## Chapter XXXI

[Col. 0045A]

### Verse 1

“In that time.” (Jerome.) When the work has been completed, the craftsman is recognized; when health has been obtained, the physician’s skill. Thus, when Jerusalem has been overthrown and the former people cast away, it is understood that the rejection of the Jews is the salvation of the Gentiles.

### Verse 3

“The Lord appeared from afar.” Because Israel had offended the Lord, etc., up to the point that he was saved not by merit.

### Verse 5

“They shall plant,” etc. (The same author.) Those who, after Israel’s captivity, were possessed by foreigners, to whom it is said: “Plant plantations and harvest vineyards” (Deut. XXVIII).

### Verse 7

“The remnant of Israel.” Those who are saved according to election.

### Verse 8

“Behold, I will bring,” etc. Through the apostles and apostolic men, who are watchmen crying out on Mount Samaria, to whom it is commanded: “Sound the trumpet; sing” (1 Kings XVIII), etc.

“The lame.” (The same author.) Such are addressed through Elijah: “How long will you limp on both feet?” But afterward they ran in Christ; and the one who walked in darkness saw a great light.

“They shall come with weeping and with,” etc. (The same author.) The Jews think that this has been fulfilled, etc., up to the point that they can prove that these things were fulfilled.

### Verse 9

“And Ephraim.” Ephraim, who is a type of the Gentile people, etc., up to the point that he first obtained the kingdom in Samaria, etc.

### Verse 11

“From the hand of the stronger,” etc. (The same author.) From the opposing power, which is stronger by nature. We, however, are stronger through faith, provided that we are delivered from him who binds the strong man [Col. 0045C] and plunders his house.

### Verse 14

“The soul of the priests.” Those who possess knowledge of God, from whose mouth they inquire of the law, who believe in him who is priest forever.

“With fatness, and my people shall be filled with my good things, says the Lord,” etc. Hence the Lord was seized in the valley of Gethsemane, that is, “of fatness.”

### Verse 15

“A voice in.” (The same author.) Certain Jews explain this passage in this way, etc., up to the point that they can show that the Hebrews expressed in their own language what they read in Hebrew.

“Rachel weeping.” Rachel, the mother of Joseph, etc., up to the point that she is said to weep for the children killed beside her.

### Verse 16

“And they shall return.” (The same author.) We understand this better of the little ones, etc., up to the point that the infants will rise as a perfect man.

[Col. 0045D]

### Verse 18

“I was instructed.” As though he said: Correction advances salvation, and what for the present appears to be sorrow afterward produces the fruit of peace.

### Verse 19

“Since I endured.” (The same author.) He says that he sinned through the ignorance of youth, so that he may more easily obtain pardon; hence: “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances.” And in what follows, God called him a little one and one abounding in delights, because of the greatness of his riches and the fertility of the land, clearly alluding to Psalm XXIV.

### Verse 20

“If Ephraim is an honored son,” etc. When Ephraim repented and said, “You instructed me, Lord, and I was instructed,” etc., the Lord answered and supports the one fully converted with this oracle: “If Ephraim is an honored son,” etc.

[Col. 0046A]

“Therefore, disturbed.” As though he said: He received my words with eager desire and preserved them, yet I will have mercy on him, because even human righteousness needs God’s mercy.

### Verse 21

“Set up for yourself,” etc. He calls her to satisfaction, so that she may consider the things in which she sinned and, performing penance, return to her former grace, according to the passage: “Remember from where you have fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev. II).

“Direct your heart.” (The same author.) She directs her heart along the right way, etc., up to the point that she does not consent to turn aside through the luxuries of the world.

“Return, virgin Israel; return to these cities of yours.” (The same author.) Although some understand these things according to the historical sense, etc., up to the point that she ceases to wander through the luxuries of the world.

### Verse 23

“They shall still say.” (The same author.) This refers to Christian times, when the Lord turned away the captivity of his people.

“May he bless you.” These things appear in part under Zerubbabel, etc., up to the point that they are understood according to the Jews and our Judaizers in a carnal manner.

### Verse 25

“For I have intoxicated.” A change of persons, etc., up to the point that the people returning from captivity answer: “Therefore I awoke,” etc.

### Verse 26

“Therefore, as though.” So that I might imitate the one saying, etc., up to the point that he awaits the day of resurrection.

### Verse 27

“Behold, days are coming, says the Lord.” All promises of this kind, etc., up to the point that God may be all in all.

### Verse 30

“The teeth shall be set on edge.” (The same author.) The teeth of those who eat cannot perceive sweetness, etc., up to the point that it is not because of the harshness of the food, but because of the defect of the teeth.

### Verse 31

“Behold, days are coming.” Paul uses this testimony, etc., up to the point that circumcision and the Sabbath would be fulfilled spiritually.

### Verse 34

“And he shall not teach.” So that they may not seek Jewish teachers and human commandments, but may be taught by the Holy Spirit, provided that they are the temple of God and the Spirit of God dwells in them—he who breathes where he wills and has diverse gifts. Nevertheless, knowledge of the one God is possession of every virtue.

“For all shall know.” (Jerome.) Because all will be, etc., up to the point that he was not hidden in the nature in which, even when he appeared, he remained concealed within himself.

### Verse 35

“He who gives the sun.” (The same author.) According to Genesis, the sun was placed in heaven for the light of day, and the moon and stars for the light of night. The Psalm also reads: “Day pours forth the word to day, and night gives knowledge to night,” because days and nights succeed one another in turn.

### Verse 36

“If they fail,” etc. If the heavens will perish and thus grow old like a garment, how can the seed of Israel be perpetual? Yet the heavens will perish.

### Verse 37

“If they can be measured.” As though he said: How can the things of creation, etc., up to the point that it will never cease.

### Verse 38

“Behold, days are coming.” He who speaks of a thousand-year reign, etc., up to the point where Ananehel is written with the letter *mem*.

### Verse 39

“Up to the Corner Gate.” (The same author.) For there is no true righteousness, etc., up to the point that this building will remain forever.

## Chapter XXXII

[Col. 0047A]

### Verse 1

“The word that,” etc. (Jerome.) Not only the words but also the deeds of the prophets are examples of virtues for us. Jeremiah could have announced prosperity and enjoyed the king’s friendship, but he preferred to obey God, who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.

### Verse 2

“In the court of the prison.” (The same author.) The king’s clemency is to be noted: he ordered the prophet to be confined not in the prison but in the vestibule, in free custody, so that he could not escape—as though all Jerusalem, enclosed by fortifications, had not been a common prison.

### Verse 3

“For he had shut him up.” With the captivity already near, the city already consumed by plague and famine, Zedekiah nevertheless persisted in his decision.

“Why do you prophesy?” The terror before a rebuke in words is more grievous than enduring the torment of punishments and seeing the one whom you fear.

### Verse 5

“I will visit him.” He moderated the sentence so that it could refer either to good or to evil, for visitation signifies both consolation and punishment.

### Verse 7

“Behold, Hanamel, the son.” Hilkiah and Shallum, etc., up to the point that he shows the beginning of this volume.

“Buy for yourself a field.” This field, which was priestly and whose purchase and possession are offered to Jeremiah, is in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin. The first of these names signifies “obedience,” the second “son of the right hand”; and fittingly he seeks to purchase the place in which the obedience and strength of the Lord were active.

### Verse 8

“In the land of Benjamin.” (The same author.) That is, among the suburban lands, etc., up to the point that those who attempt to claim things by means of false witnesses should listen.

### Verse 13

“And I commanded Baruch.” (The same author.) Baruch, whose name means “blessed,” etc., up to the point that he may present an open scroll to those wishing to read it.

### Verse 14

“In an earthen vessel,” etc. So that, being placed outside, they might not suffer robbery, etc., up to the point that they are nevertheless moved by the word of God.

### Verse 15

“Houses and fields shall still be possessed.” This is what Jeremiah said above: that he had understood the word of God and therefore had bought the field.

### Verse 18

“You show mercy.” Great is the mercy of the Creator, etc., up to the point that punishment long delayed may be repaid.

“Most mighty, great,” etc. (The same author.) These names indicate the Creator’s power, but “Father” is properly the name of God; hence: “Father, I have manifested your name to men” (John XXVII).

### Verse 19

“Great in counsel,” etc. Therefore let no one intrude into God’s secrets or presume to judge his judgments.

“To repay each person.” It signifies that sometimes, etc., up to the point that at last he was overwhelmed by the waves of the Red Sea.

### Verse 20

“You who established signs.” He passes from the general to the particular and briefly reviews what he specifically did for Israel.

“And wonders,” etc. By which it was afflicted up to this day, etc., up to the point that he notes how Israel separates itself from all others.

### Verse 21

“And you brought out your people.” He beautifully said “your people,” for at the time when they were brought out they were serving at the Lord’s command.

### Verse 23

“And they entered.” (The same author.) There is nothing intermediate between possession and disobedience: abundance produces security, security produces negligence, and negligence produces contempt.

“And they did not obey.” That is: They promised in vain, saying, “Whatever the Lord commands, we will do.” For the reward is found not in the response but in the deed.

### Verse 24

“Behold, siegeworks have been raised.” It was the tenth year of Zedekiah, and the city was under siege, as was said above, while Jeremiah was in the court of the prison. Hence what follows: “Behold, siegeworks.”

“That it may be captured.” As though he said: They have no one whom they need to conquer, but people whom they need only capture, since they have already been consumed by famine and plague.

“And whatever you have spoken.” From created things he proclaims the Creator, etc., up to the point that he prefaces all this in order to introduce, as though in reproach of the divine judgment: “And you say to me, Lord God, ‘Buy the field.’”

### Verse 25

“And you say.” He does not reproach but asks, etc., up to the point that he should buy a field he will not possess.

### Verse 27

“Behold, I am the Lord.” Not merely of all nations or of the people of Israel, etc., up to the point that some things were made for their own sake and others for human use.

### Verse 28

“Behold, I will give this city.” Because I care for ruling all things, ordering everything, and repaying each according to his ways.

“This city.” First it was surrounded by the army of the Chaldeans, while Nebuchadnezzar was absent; it was then captured, and Zedekiah was handed over to the king at Riblah.

### Verse 29

“And the Chaldeans shall come.” Aquila has “they shall enter,” which is better. For they were not absent, so that those besieging the city needed to come; but the Hebrew verb means both “they shall come” and “they shall enter.”

“And the houses on whose roofs.” Just as the world is written as destined to perish, according to the passage, “Heaven and earth will pass away,” because it lies in the evil one, so the house itself and the places in which crimes were committed will also be subject to God’s anger.

### Verse 30

“Continually doing evil.” Without end, etc., up to the point that they are in your sight.

### Verse 33

“And they turned their backs to me.” Hence elsewhere: “They turn their retreating shoulder against me” (Zech. VII). For one who prays pours himself out prostrate on the ground with bowed neck; but one who turns his back indicates by the gesture of his body that he disregards the one threatening him.

“When I was teaching them.” Once the darkness of error and the worship of idols had been driven away, I wished to enlighten them and teach them what is right.

### Verse 34

“And they set up their idols,” etc. It was not only then that Judah placed an idol in the temple of God; even today an idol is placed in the Church or in the heart of believers when a new doctrine is established and secretly worshiped.

[Col. 0049A]

### Verse 35

“And they built,” etc. Properly, the tribes of Judah and Benjamin worshiped images of demons in the shrine of Baal and Molech; the ten tribes worshiped golden calves in Dan and Bethel. This was so detestable that the Lord testifies that he had never even conceived of it.

“In the valley of the sons of Hinnom.” (Jerome.) This valley lies beneath the springs of Siloam, and by its pleasantness invited the people to luxury, which is followed by the worship of idols.

### Verse 37

“Behold, I will gather.” Many think that this occurred in the time of Zerubbabel, etc., up to the point that the election of the remnant is saved.

“And I will bring them back to this place, and they shall dwell.” Just as those who hope for help, etc., up to the point that despair and humility may merit God’s help.

### Verse 38

“They shall be my people, and I will be,” etc. [Col. 0049B] He joins joyful things to sorrowful ones and promises a return to the captives; but first he shows the cause of the offense and of the just fury. The greater the guilt, the greater the clemency toward sinners.

### Verse 39

“And I will give them.” (Cassiodorus.) He clearly reveals the beginning for us, etc., up to the point that by this they may merit either rewards or punishments.

### Verse 40

“And I will put my fear in their heart.” (The same author.) Thus he grants free choice, so that the fear bestowed by grace may be understood as the gift of the giver.

### Verse 41

“With all my heart and with all my soul.” If these are the words of the Savior, etc., up to the point that this is like the passage: “I hate your festivals” (Amos V), etc.

“For thus says the Lord,” etc. These things are understood according to the literal sense, etc., up to the point that spiritually they have been fulfilled more fully in Christ and in the apostles.

## Chapter XXXIII

### Verse 1

“And it came to pass.” He foretells that, just as vengeance comes upon sinners, etc., up to the point that they are scattered by the Romans throughout the whole world.

### Verse 3

“Cry to me, and I will answer him.” He shows that through the prayers of the prophets and saints who were among the people, the Lord was appeased and revealed to them the return to their land, which until then had remained hidden.

Now it says: “Cry to me, and I will answer you.” Because the Lord did not wish to avert the impending captivity, so that they might first pay the penalty for their sin; afterward he did not deny the return, which he now promises.

### Verse 10

“It shall still be heard in this place,” etc. So that the Jews might not despair because of the threats and future captivities, he promises the blessings of restoration, so that the place which had been deserted because of the crimes of its inhabitants might be inhabited because of their correction and amendment.

### Verse 12

“Of those who lie down among the flocks.” The flocks of the Church, gathered from the Gentiles, that is, etc., up to the point that there are many who belong to the faith of Christ and to the number of his sheep.

### Verse 14

“To the house of Israel.” Concerning them Isaiah says: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains,” etc.

### Verse 17

“Thus says the Lord.” Above he had spoken of the creation of the sun, moon, and stars, etc., up to the point that Christ’s kingdom and priesthood will remain forever.

## Chapter XXXIV

### Verse 1

“The word that came,” etc. (Rabanus.) Although he was a most wicked king, etc., up to the end of the chapter.

## Chapter XXXV

### Verse 1

“The word that came to pass.” (Rabanus.) While in the preceding chapter the prophet speaks of Zedekiah, etc., up to the end of the chapter.

## Chapter XXXVI

### Verse 3

“If perhaps the house of Judah, when it hears,” etc. Immense clemency, etc., up to the point that through God’s mercy they may obtain forgiveness.

### Verse 4

“Therefore he called.” The prophet’s ready obedience corresponds, etc., up to the point: Who, being released and free, neglect to spend the word of God for the benefit of their neighbors?

### Verse 9

“They proclaimed a fast in the sight of the Lord,” etc. So that those who had sinned through luxury, etc., up to the point that they might confess the things in which they had sinned most greatly.

### Verse 16

“Therefore, when they had heard,” etc. Even hearers need, etc., up to the point that they were able to hear the words of God with the bodily ear but not with the heart.

### Verse 18

“He spoke from his own mouth,” etc. It signifies that the apostles and prophets suffered neither the necessity of laboring to formulate their message nor any poverty of speech; rather, they brought everything forth readily and easily.

### Verse 23

“And he cast it into the fire.” The wickedness of an hardened heart is astonishing, etc., up to the point that they might not believe and repent.

[Col. 0050C]

### Verse 26

“But he hid,” etc. Against him human presumption struggles in vain. For the Lord guards all who love him and will destroy all sinners.

### Verse 30

“Therefore,” etc. A deserved vengeance, etc., up to the point that he would be burned by the heat of the sun and the frost of the night.

## Chapter XXXVII

### Verse 1

“And King Zedekiah reigned,” etc. That Zedekiah came after Jehoiakim, etc., up to the point that all were wicked and idolaters and therefore perished.

### Verse 3

“Pray for.” He certainly did not ask him to pray for himself, because he refused to obey the divine commandments: “Whoever turns his ear away so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be accursed.”

### Verse 4

“Therefore the army.” How the Chaldeans withdrew, etc., up to the point that Jeremiah prophesied things both contrary to expectation and true.

## Chapter XXXVIII

### Verse 5

“And King Zedekiah said,” etc. Zedekiah’s father, without pure affection, etc., up to the point that afterward, after scourging him, he handed him over to the Jews to be crucified.

### Verse 7

“Now Abdemelech heard.” Like those princes who sent the prophet, etc., up to the point that we hold ourselves all the more strictly guilty.

### Verse 17

“If you go out and surrender,” etc. The prophet, foreseeing that the city would be delivered into the hands of the Chaldeans, advised the king to surrender himself into the hands of the king of Babylon, so that he might thereby calm his furious spirit [Col. 0051A] and receive a lighter sentence; but his hardened mind could not be corrected.

### Verse 22

“Behold.” It signifies that a fleeting thought, etc., up to the point that it will burn the soul with unquenchable fire.

## Chapter XXXIX

### Verse 17

“And I will deliver you.” “Those who hope in the Lord will not be confounded” (Wis. XIX). “All who do wicked things will be confounded” (Ps. XXIV). Behold, the princes who sought Jeremiah’s life are taken captive. The eunuch who had freed him obtained perfect freedom. So also, when holy preachers are freed, their persecutors will be punished with eternal vengeance.

## Chapter XL

### Verse 1

“The word that came to pass,” etc. It is asked how this word of the Lord, etc., up to the point that he was freed according to the word of the Lord.

### Verse 2

“Then, taking him.” After the devastation of the city, the slaughter and captivity of the people, and the king’s treachery have been described, what happened to Jeremiah and to the remnant of the people follows. The prophet had warned them by the word of the Lord to remain in their land and serve the king of Babylon; but they preferred to go to Egypt, where Nebuchadnezzar later slaughtered them and devastated Egypt itself.

### Verse 3

“And it has happened to you.” From this passage also it is clear that God, etc., up to the point that they proclaimed God’s judgment to be just.

## Chapter XLI

### Verse 8

“Ten men were found among them,” etc. “We have a treasure.” For a treasure in a field, etc., up to the point that by the heel, which is the end of the body, the completion of an action is signified.

### Verse 16

“Then Johanan son of Kareah took, along with all the commanders of the warriors who were with him,” etc. Isaiah had foretold long beforehand this flight of the remnant and their journey into Egypt against the word of the Lord, which Jeremiah later unfolded here in a lengthy narrative—one hundred and fifty years earlier, namely the interval between Isaiah and Jeremiah—saying: “Woe to the rebellious sons, says the Lord, who make a plan, but not from me” (Isa. XXX), etc.

## Chapters XLII–XLIII

*The sacred text without exposition.*

## Chapter XLIV

### Verse 15

“But they answered Jeremiah,” etc. A foolish response. They confess that he speaks in the name of the Lord, yet they do not comply; instead, they follow the counsel of their perversity.

Mystically: All heretics are in Egypt, that is, established in the darkness of error. They offer sacrifices not to the true God but to demons, when they write fabrications and perverse doctrines in order to deceive people and overturn the faith. Therefore evils will come upon them, and they will become desolation and astonishment.

### Verse 26

“As the Lord lives,” etc. The prophet, speaking by the word of the Lord, contradicts them so that his name may not be invoked by the mouths of the Jews in the land of Egypt, since those who had gone there against God’s command were not to have the Lord’s protection there.

Mystically, however, the name of the Lord is not invoked by the mouths of heretics in the land of Egypt, because neither their speech nor their prayer, while they remain in error, is acceptable to God. “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. XV). Therefore those who persist in error will perish beneath the sword of strict judgment. But those who abandon error, return penitently from Egypt to the land of Judah, and thereafter hold the Catholic faith will be saved.

## Chapter XLV

### Verse 1

“The word that Jeremiah spoke,” etc. Baruch, still inexperienced in enduring the sufferings he was destined to undergo, was terrified by the calamity of the captivity that threatened in the time of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah. Hence he complains that sorrow has been added to his sorrow. The Lord’s answer was that he was seeking peace for himself uselessly, while the whole people was laboring beneath the burden of tribulations.

This signifies those who, under the pressure of the tribulations or persecutions by which the present Church is weighed down, falter through faintheartedness while seeking the consolation promised for the future. Hence: “You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John XVI).

## Chapter XLVI

### Verse 1

“The word that came to pass,” etc. (Rabanus.) Up to this point the prophet has treated intermittently, according to the suitability of the narrative, Judah and Israel, the Chaldeans and the Egyptians, etc., up to the year of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, when Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, fought Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish and was defeated.

### Verse 9

“Mount the horses.” (The same author.) Heretics and schismatics, arising from different provinces, vainly prepare wars against the city of God, etc., up to the point that they are handed over to him who has set his throne toward the north, so that he may cast them into the lake of fire and sulfur.

### Verse 11

“Go up to Gilead.” (Jerome.) It is a mountain to which Jacob came on the seventh day while fleeing from Haran. It lies behind Phoenicia and is joined to the hills of Arabia and Lebanon; it stretches through the wilderness as far as the region beyond the Jordan where Sihon, king of the Amorites, dwelt. It fell by lot to the sons of Reuben and Gad and to half the tribe of Manasseh.

“Take resin.” (Rabanus.) The Greeks call it *rhētinēn* (ῥητίνην); for *rheō* (ῥέω) is said of that which flows, etc., up to the point that they will not receive healing from them, but confusion.

### Verse 12

“The nations have heard.” (The same author.) Because the consolation of idols has failed, etc., up to the point that they do not receive victory of the truth but, taken captive by error, fall together into the pit of destruction.

### Verse 14

“Announce it in Egypt.” As though he said: You who have heard my prophecy, announce to Pharaoh that the time and tumult of war are near.

### Verse 18

“For as Tabor.” This is understood by comparison with fertile places, as though they had been submerged in the sea; thus you may understand the great downfall of the Egyptians.

(Jerome.) Tabor is the boundary of Zebulun, a mountain in the middle of the plain of Galilee, rising with remarkable rounded elevation. It is ten miles from Diocaesarea toward the eastern region. Carmel, which also formed the boundary between the tribes of Issachar and Naphtali, is where Nabal the Carmelite lived; now there is a village called Carmela, ten miles from the town of Hebron, extending toward the east, where there is a Roman garrison.

(Rabanus.) Mystically, because Tabor, etc., up to the point that they are submerged in the sea of this age and in eternal damnation.

### Verse 20

“A heifer.” Because the Egyptian people, raised in luxury, untamed and wanton, refused the yoke of discipline.

### Verse 21

“Mercenaries.” (Rabanus.) He calls the princes of the Egyptians not shepherds but mercenaries, etc., up to the words: “But the mercenary, and the one who is not the shepherd, when he sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep and flees” (John X).

### Verse 26

“And after this,” etc. (The same author.) Although he seems to indicate that the kingdom of the Egyptians was not irreparably destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, etc., up to the words: “The Lord will strike Egypt with a plague and heal it” (Isa. XIX), etc.

### Verse 27

“And you, do not fear,” etc. This promise does not fit the Jews well, since they have been scattered throughout the whole world, etc., up to the words: “A partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters; and then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI).

## Chapter XLVII

### Verse 1

“The word that came to pass,” etc. Jeremiah, like Isaiah and Ezekiel, foretells the coming plagues of neighboring nations, because they harassed the people of God and rejoiced in their adversity. Thus, to the Philistines, as previously to the Egyptians, he announces the captivity that is to come.

### Verse 4

“And it shall be scattered.” He shows that Tyre and Sidon belong to the Philistines, although Tyre fell by lot to Naphtali and Sidon was the boundary of the Canaanites in the territory of Asher. Yet Israel did not possess it, because it was unable to drive out the enemies.

“The remnant of the island of Cappadocia.” The Cappadocians lived there after the former inhabitants had been killed. This is the boundary of the Canaanites near Egypt; it fell by lot to Judah, but Judah did not obtain it because the Anakim—that is, the giants among the Philistines—resisted with great strength. It is still to this day a notable city of Palestine, although it was prophesied concerning it: “Gaza shall become an everlasting mound.” Yet scarcely any traces remain where it formerly stood, for it was built in another place.

### Verse 5

“Gaza has become bald,” etc. (Rabanus.) He signifies the coming plague of heretics, schismatics, and all enemies of the Church, etc., up to the point that through lust he burns the minds of the carnal, but at the last he will cast them down.

### Verse 7

“How shall it be quiet,” etc. As though he said: The sword cannot rest unless the Lord commands it, since it exercises his vengeance; or as though he had spoken to the sword of the Lord from the person of those afflicted, and the sword now responds in its own person.

## Chapter XLVIII

[Col. 0054A]

### Verse 1

“Concerning Moab, thus says the Lord,” etc. (Rabanus.) Just as there is carnal and spiritual circumcision, so there is carnal and spiritual Moab. Moab is interpreted, etc., up to the point that Moab is a province of the Arabs, and Nebo a famous city in which there was the idol Chemosh, also called Baal-peor.

### Verse 6

“Save your lives.” Those who wish to save their soul should flee the perverse teaching of philosophers and heretics, where destruction is certain; through the humility of confession they should do penance for their error, remain in the wilderness of strict abstinence, and abide in the simplicity and truth of Catholic doctrine.

### Verse 9

“Give a flower,” etc. He who seemed to flourish through human invention and secular learning will be reduced to desert and solitude. But because every hypocrisy displeases God, as the following judgment shows:

### Verse 10

“Cursed is he who does,” etc. For it is necessary not only to consider what we do but also with what discernment we do it.

“Cursed.” (Rabanus.) Sloth is born through torpor, fraud through private affection, etc., up to the point that they often fail when sloth intervenes and waste away when love grows cold.

“And cursed.” This curse can apply to all who follow the world’s flow and neglect to chastise their bodies and subject them to service, according to the passage: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh” (Gal. V), etc. For without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins. “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (II Cor. XV). Cursed, therefore, is the one who keeps the sword—that is, the word of God—from the blood by which the matter of sins is animated. Whatever carnal and earthly thing has grown up in our members must be poured out and cut away by the sword of God’s word.

(Gregory.) To keep the sword from blood is to restrain the word of preaching from putting carnal life to death. Concerning this it is said: “My sword shall devour flesh” (Isa. I). Hence Paul says: “I testify today that I am clean from the blood of all. For I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts X).

### Verse 11

“Fertile.” Moab is shown to have passed from abundance into hatred and arrogance and to have despised the afflicted people of God, because it suffered no affliction or captivity.

### Verse 12

“I will send him,” etc. (Rabanus.) Whoever trusts in human philosophy while despising the faith of the Church and its simple teaching, etc., up to the point that they will go with the devil and his angels into eternal fire, while the righteous will go into eternal life.

### Verse 17

“Console yourselves.” He speaks ironically, or calls them to repentance, so that through suitable satisfaction they may escape misery.

Mystically: The wise men of this world and the heretics, whom Moab signifies, if they do not correct their folly by converting to the Catholic faith, will suffer ruin and devastation in all their cities—that is, their various sects. Whatever lies far or near from the truth will be overthrown when the Gospel shines forth.

### Verse 25

“His horn has been cut off.” (Jerome.) Just as he prophesied against Babylon and the Philistines, etc., up to the point that whatever pertains to earthly knowledge and is thought strong is overthrown, so that nothing is approved that had been considered most powerful.

### Verse 29

“We have heard.” Because in the preceding sentence he was calling those who had gone astray to repentance and urging them to convert to Christ so that they might remain perpetually in his faith, he now recognizes that many are incorrigible and obstinate. Speaking from the perspective of those who were saved from Moab and learned its arrogance through their own experience, he says: “We have heard of the pride of Moab,” etc. He accuses Moab of pride because it exalts itself beyond what its strength can accomplish or require.

### Verse 31

“Therefore I will lament over Moab.” He displays the power of its former prosperity and the wound of its sudden overthrow.

“I will cry out over all Moab.” Moab is interpreted as “their strength” and signifies the very strong doctrines of heretics, constructed dialectically, in which the strength of error appeared to reside.

### Verse 32

“I will weep for you, vineyard of Sibmah.” The storm of this age. He seems to signify that some from Moab wish to be converted to the Lord. Sibmah is interpreted as “some conversion.” “The vineyard of Sibmah,” etc. It raises itself to a height, because pride attempts to erect a tower to heaven.

### Verse 34

“From Zoar to Horonaim.” Zoar is a city overlooking the Dead Sea, where the boundary of the Moabites lies. He therefore indicates that the howling will resound as far as the extreme boundaries of the province.

Concerning this Isaiah says: “Its bars reach as far as Zoar, the heifer that is throwing itself down” (Isa. XV), that is, one of mature age. For just as the thirtieth year is strongest among human beings, so among cattle and beasts the third year is the most vigorous.

“And the waters of Nimrim.” Isaiah says: “The waters of Nimrim shall be desolate” (Isa. XV), etc. What is said more briefly here is explained fully in Isaiah. Nimrim is a town above the Dead Sea.

### Verse 35

“And I will take away from Moab.” As the sect of human wisdom perishes, the pomp and clamor of words cease, so that neither philosophers nor heretics who have gone out from the Church find anything in their doctrine useful for human life.

### Verse 37

“For every head is bald.” (Rabanus.) Among the ancients, shaving the beard and head was a sign of mourning, etc., up to the point where Isaiah says: “On all their heads there is baldness; every beard is shaved” (Isa. XV).

### Verse 38

“For I have broken Moab.” All the teaching of philosophers and heretics, because it is fragile and useless, is crushed and dispersed by the truth.

### Verse 41

“And the heart of the mighty men of Moab.” He aptly compares Moab’s heart to the heart of a woman in labor, because great sorrow follows great luxury.

VERSE 45.—“They stood in the shadow of Heshbon.” Because he hoped to find aid in its fortification, but in vain: for the fire of vengeance, with the just Judge repaying it, crushed the summit of the tumult of the sons of Moab.

VERSE 46.—“Woe to you, Moab.” For neither the fortification of the cities nor the power of the idols was able to defend you. Thus there will be perpetual woe for those who trust in human wisdom and serve various errors.

VERSE 47.—“And I will restore the captivity of Moab.” He seems to signify the time of grace, in which whoever calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved (Joel II).

## CHAPTER XLIX

VERSE 1.—“To the sons.” After Moab, the words turn to the sons of Ammon, and they are reproved because they dared to invade the land of Israel. Accordingly, a fitting vengeance is foretold for them, and Israel is predicted to possess its former possessors.

VERSE 2.—“The daughters of Rabbah.” The metropolis of the Moabites, now called Ariopolis, a name compounded from Hebrew and Greek, because it is called Ἄρεως, that is, “the city of Mars.”

[Col. 0056B] VERSE 6.—“And after these things.” Because after the conversion of heretics to the true faith, the captivity of sin will be dissolved, and those who had departed from the communion of the Church will be received back into it. “And the captives.” By the sons of Ammon we can understand heretics, who were begotten from Lot in a cave, in drunkenness and incest, according to the saying, “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (John II).

VERSE 7.—“Against Edom.” (RAB.) Tropologically, Edom is earthly and carnal pleasure, which rises up against the spirit, so that we do not do the things that belong to the spirit, and the soul, etc., up to: “For when the flesh has been subjected to the spirit, Edom will pass over into Judah, and the flesh will serve reason.”

VERSE 9.—“If thieves.” Heretics, who steal enough for themselves and daily snatch some people from the Church, entering the vineyard of the Lord which he transferred from Egypt, desire to plunder everything, so that scarcely a grape-cluster may remain in it. But the Lord, on the contrary, brings into the open all their secrets and brings forward the ecclesiastical men and teachers as the patriarchs of Esau, who first devised the heresies. His first victory is to disclose what had been concealed.

(HIER.) The saying was made against the Jews, who envy Christians, etc., up to: “so that, by putting our members to death”—namely, fornication, impurity, and the like—we may attain eternal victory in Christ.

VERSE 14.—“I have heard.” This sentence, and much of this chapter, is contained in nearly the same words in Obadiah.

[Col. 0056D] VERSE 15.—“For behold.” (RAB.) As if he said: “O Edom, who are the least among all the surrounding nations,” etc., up to: “therefore I would bring you down and restore you to the land of the other nations.”

“I have made you small among the nations.” O heretic, although you may seem great to yourself and despise the smallness of the Church, you are nevertheless small and contemptible.

VERSE 16.—“When you have exalted yourself,” etc. (RAB.) Because heretics promise themselves the height and likeness of eagles, which gather around the Lord’s corpse, etc., up to: “But what was said against heretics and the flesh can also be understood as having been said against the Jews.”

VERSE 19.—“Behold, like a lion.” (ID.) Just as the Lord chastised the pride of the Jews, whom he brought across the Jordan, etc., up to: “but as a most savage lion he will thrust them into Tartarus to be tormented forever.”

VERSE 21.—“At the sound of the ruin,” etc. When the devastator comes, the crash of their ruin will resound far and wide, striking terror into the neighboring provinces.

VERSE 23.—“She has been put to shame.” (RAB.) After the Philistines, Moabites, Ammonites, and Idumeans, the prophet turns to Damascus, that is, Arabia, etc., up to: “for when the Jewish people was captured, Damascus, which Arethas ruled, was likewise captured.”

VERSE 24.—“Dissolved.” Damascus is interpreted as “a cup of blood,” or “drinking blood,” or “the blood of sackcloth”; all of these suit the pagans, etc., up to: “For just as a heap of stones is piled from scattered stones, so from all the nations a heap of believers is gathered amid the ruin of the falling Jews, while the Gentiles rise.”

VERSE 28.—“Against Cedar.” These are the Hagarenes, but by an assumed name they are called Saracens, and they dwell throughout the wilderness. Of them the poet says: “Wandering far and wide, the Agi.” [The final word is uncertain in the supplied text.]

(RAB.) Mystically: Cedar, which is interpreted as “darkness,” and Hazor, etc., up to: “who pretend to be sons of the East, although they are sons of darkness.”

VERSE 29.—“The tents.” All these specifically signify the nation of the Saracens, who remain in tents and, wherever night compels them, have their dwelling places, with many herds, flocks, and herds of camels. But they have no doors or bars, for they do not live in cities but in the wilderness. All these were destroyed by the Babylonians.

VERSE 35.—“Behold, I will break,” etc. (RAB.) Elam is a region of Persia, from which the Elamites come. For the prophet foretells, etc., up to: “The Elamites are also interpreted as ‘despisers’ or ‘testers,’ and they signify the persecutors of the Church.”

## CHAPTER L

VERSE 1.—“The word.” After completing the prophecy against Egypt, the Philistines, Moab, the sons of Ammon, Damascus, and Cedar, the word is directed against Babylon and the Chaldeans, so that those whom he previously reproved covertly may now be openly exposed in their crimes, and the devastation and desolation that follow may be plainly declared. Isaiah and Ezekiel likewise prophesied similar things against the Babylonians and Chaldeans.

VERSE 2.—“They have been put to shame.” Isaiah says something similar: “Behold, I will raise up the Medes against them, who will not seek silver, nor desire gold” (Isaiah XIII).

VERSE 4.—“The sons of Israel will come.” (RAB.) This promise signifies the return of God’s people from captivity, etc., up to: “so that they may be joined to him by an everlasting covenant.”

VERSE 6.—“A lost flock.” By this saying the kings of the Israelites are indicated, for they caused the people to err and turn to idolatry. The first of these was Jeroboam, son of Nebat, who caused golden calves to be worshiped; after him came the other transgressors of the Law.

VERSE 8.—“Withdraw,” etc. According to the historical sense, he warns the Israelites who were destined to be taken captive to Babylon not to regard themselves as going to have a permanent possession there, but to retain hope of returning. When the captivity was loosened, they were to flee from there, because it was going to happen that the Medes and Persians would lay it waste.

(ORIG.) Just as our body exists in some place on earth, so the soul, according to its condition, is figuratively said to be in some place on earth. Our body, etc., up to: “Thus in Egypt one lives in Taphnis, another in Memphis, another in Syene, another in Bubastis.”

VERSE 12.—“Your mother has been utterly put to shame,” etc. Isaiah says something similar: “And that glorious Babylon, renowned among kingdoms, in the pride of the Chaldeans, will be overthrown as the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah” (Isaiah XIII). “Behold, she will be the last,” etc. At the end of the world, or at each person’s death, all the glory and pride of the Chaldeans and the shame of the world will depart from us. Thus everything will be overthrown, as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and there will no longer be any state of pleasure or of the world.

VERSE 15.—“As she has done, do to her.” That is, just as she devastated the surrounding nations through Nebuchadnezzar, so repay her in kind.
