VERSE 16.—“From the face of the sword of the dove.” The dove is called foolish because it feeds the young of others; so too did Nebuchadnezzar, both oppressing and nurturing others. He also calls Nebuchadnezzar a dove, not because of simplicity but because of the foolishness of pride.

VERSE 17.—“Lions have driven them out,” etc. Tiglath-pileser, who transferred a large part of the Jews to the Assyrians, and Sennacherib, who led the ten tribes away into the mountains of the Medes, are called lions.

VERSE 18.—“Behold, I will visit.” (RAB.) The Lord visits the king of Babylon—that is, of confusion—as he visited the king of Assyria, which is interpreted, etc., up to: “but the new people will rejoice forever in the new city.”

VERSE 21.—“Against the land of the rulers.” The preachers of Christ are commanded to strive to overthrow the kingdom of the devil, together with his evil works and most wicked counsels, so that they may kill all the sinners of the earth and destroy from the city of the Lord all who practice iniquity.

[Col. 0058D] VERSE 23.—“How the hammer has been broken,” etc. (ORIG.) The devil is the hammer of the whole earth. But there is one who does not care about the hammer of the whole earth, namely, a man standing upon adamantine walls, etc., up to: “For he is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can he be; and Babylon was found and seized because it resisted the Lord.”

VERSES 25–27.—“The Lord has opened his treasury,” etc. (ID.) Another edition reads: “Open its storehouses,” etc., as the Apostle says (Romans VI): “He endured with great patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to show the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy,” etc. Some, therefore, are vessels of mercy and others vessels of wrath, etc., up to: “Who maintains that the stars are not the causes of the things that happen on earth, especially of the things that happen to Christians, carries out the command of the Lord.”

VERSE 28.—“The voice of those who flee.” (ORIG.) Would that this were our voice, O catechumens: of those fleeing from Babylon, and fleeing, etc., up to: “Kill all the sinners of the earth who are in you, and all the Babylonians, so that, once cleansed, you may cross over into Jerusalem, the city of God.”

VERSE 31.—“Behold, I am against you.” (RAB.) Mystically, he foretells the Antichrist, who will exalt himself above everything that is called God, etc., up to: “because they did not fear to bring accusation and captivity upon God’s people.”

VERSE 37.—“And they will be like women.” (ID.) Unwarlike like women, he destroyed them through the Medes and Persians, etc., up to: “because their synagogue is a land of carved images, and they glory in portents, that is, false fabrications.”

VERSE 44.—“Behold, like a lion.” (ID.) It seems to signify that Nebuchadnezzar, after he had subdued the kingdom of the Jews, etc., up to: “and to show that this happened not through Cyrus’s power but by the Lord’s judgment, it is added: ‘For who is like me?’”

## CHAPTER LI

VERSE 5.—“For it was not,” etc. Because the Lord sent them for vengeance upon his people, whom he did not chastise by correction but crushed by savage violence. Hence: “Woe to Assyria, the rod of my fury” (Isaiah X).

VERSE 6.—“Flee from the midst,” etc. After the plagues of Babylon, he turns his exhortation historically to the Jews and mystically to the faithful, so that they may flee from the midst of Babylon, that is, from worldly confusion.

(ORIG.) Not gradually or little by little, but leave quickly, whoever has a confused soul, etc., up to: “Similarly, when the sins are lesser, God uses ministers; but when they are more serious, he himself hastens to retribution.”

VERSE 7.—“A golden cup,” etc. Babylon’s golden cup is not always, nor is it always in the Lord’s hand. For when it comes for vengeance and is placed in the Lord’s hand, it will become the earth that was made in Job. Nor is it held continually in the Lord’s hand, but only when the Lord restores to it what it deserves.

(ORIG.) “A golden cup.” Nebuchadnezzar, wishing to deceive people through Babylon’s cup, did not mix it in an earthen vessel, etc., up to: “Often I have seen a golden cup in beautiful verbal ornament, and, examining the poisons of its doctrines, I recognized Babylon’s cup.”

“Inebriating,” etc. (ID.) See that all people are drunk. We are drunk with anger and sadness; we are drunk, etc., up to: “By him we are all drunk as long as we are on earth.”

“Of the wine.” (ID.) Just as in those who drink bodily wine beyond measure we observe the movement of the drunken body, etc., up to: “The nations drank; therefore they were shaken.”

VERSE 8.—“Suddenly she fell.” This signifies the sudden future consummation of the world, which will happen not in stages but all at once, just as Jericho quickly or suddenly perished when it collapsed. But if you turn to Christ’s coming and see his great work—how he overthrew all the doctrines of the nations in order to free believers from the yoke of error—you will see that Babylon suddenly fell and was crushed in his Passion. Let each person see whether Babylon has fallen in his own breast. For in whose heart has it not fallen, Christ has not yet come to him. Babylon falls; Jerusalem, the holy city of God, is built.

“Wail.” (HIER.) Because no soul is incurable before God, he gives counsel to those who are able, etc., up to: “but because it did not wish to be healed, the good physicians fulfill their duty and say:”

VERSE 9.—“We have healed.” (ORIG.) See whether God may at some time command angels to prepare medicines for your sick soul, etc., up to: “God brings forth his judgment in order to humble what has been exalted.”

[Col. 0060B] VERSE 16.—“He who raises the clouds,” that is, preachers and prophets, who defend us from the heat of the coming judgment by the rain of their eloquence when they announce future things. “Lightning.” The preachers of the prophets are lightning when they strike enemies; they are rains when they wash the devoted from sins and pour in the rain of salvation. Thus spiritual fruits may sprout and grow into a mature harvest. “And he brings forth the winds from his treasuries.” The winds are the apostles, whose preaching traverses the world like a swift wind. Of them it is said elsewhere: “He made his arrows into burning ones” (Psalm VII). To these winds wings are attributed because of the rapidity of their journeys; hence: “He flew upon the wings of the winds” (ibid. XI).

VERSE 17.—“Every man has become foolish.” After Babylon’s overthrow he rightly reproves the makers of idols, because through the foolishness of the human mind vain and laughable works were made. For there is neither spirit nor voice nor any efficacy in them; therefore they cannot free either themselves or their worshipers on the day of visitation.

“He has been put to shame.” (RAB.) Having demonstrated Babylon’s overthrow, the prophet returns to the author of so great a judgment, because there is no authority except from God, who rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whomever he wishes.

VERSE 25.—“Behold, I am against you,” etc. The pestilential mountain is Nebuchadnezzar and the kingdom of the Chaldeans; or it is the devil, who elsewhere is called a dark mountain because of the darkness of error. “And I will make you.” To this mountain belong the Jews, heretics, blasphemers, and all the impious who persist in wickedness and do not convert so as to become living stones in God’s building.

[Col. 0060D] VERSE 30.—“They have ceased,” etc. When Cyrus and Darius came, the strength of Babylon and its princes ceased.

VERSE 33.—“The daughter of Babylon,” etc. The people of Babylon existed when, through the power of the kingdom and the abundance of riches, it threshed and crushed the nations. But the time of its harvest came when it was compelled to receive what it had done. Concerning it, in the person of the Jewish people, it is subsequently said: “Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, has eaten me and devoured me.”

“And I will make the sea a desert,” etc. (RAB.) Mystically, the sea signifies the turbulence of this age, which the Lord makes desolate. For he will cause its luxury to cease, and the wicked who served the confusion of errors and vices will be scattered.

[Col. 0061A] VERSE 41.—“How has Sheshach been captured?” (RAB.) Sheshach is interpreted as “the linen of a sack” or “the hand of a sack”; just as Babylon means “confusion,” etc., up to: “so that they may leave their fellowship, lest they perish with them.”

VERSE 45.—“Go out from the midst of her.” (ID.) Whoever wishes to save his soul, etc., up to: “but diligent in meditation upon his Law and in the practice of virtues.”

VERSE 52.—“Therefore,” etc. (ID.) He enumerates the plagues of Babylon that will come upon its nobles, leaders, magistrates, and entire people, etc., up to: “Come out of her, my people, lest you share in her sins and receive none of her plagues” (Revelation XVIII), etc.

VERSE 64.—“Thus Babylon will be submerged.” For historically Babylon was submerged in the Euphrates, although it was reduced to a wilderness. But he foretells the eternal destruction of spiritual Babylon, which will be plunged into the depth of hell with its prince, the devil. Hence John says: “A mighty angel lifted up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying: ‘With such violence Babylon will be thrown down’” (Revelation XVIII).

## CHAPTER LII

VERSE 1.—“A son of twenty.” The historical account that relates the capture of Zedekiah and the devastation of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans is contained in full in the Book of Kings.

VERSE 4.—“And it came to pass.” The number nine, being less than ten, signifies the imperfection of the Law, etc., up to: “Surrounded by the darkness of sins, they flee; and when they see the wolf coming, they abandon the sheep.”

[Col. 0061C] VERSE 7.—“By the way of the gate.” He covertly reproves the inactivity of the teachers, who, stationed between the walls of the two Testaments, seek not to wage war but to escape, and prefer to abound in pleasures—which the garden signifies—rather than resist their enemies with the shield of faith.

VERSE 8.—“He pursued,” etc. (RAB.) In the Book of Kings it is read as follows: “Zedekiah fled by the way,” etc. When evil spirits surround the people, the ruler does not flee, etc., up to: “Having therefore seized the king, they brought him to the king of Babylon at Riblah,” etc.

VERSE 11.—“And the king led him away,” etc. Because the soul, bound in the confusion of sins and fettered by vices, is led by evil spirits into the house of imprisonment until the day of death, and is confined in anguish of mind so that it may await the sentence of death.

VERSE 12.—“But in the fifth month,” etc. The order of time accords with the logic of vengeance. In the fifth month the city is devastated because it despised the Pentateuch; on the tenth day of the month because it acted contrary to the Decalogue of the Law, flattering itself about its security because of its dwelling in holy places. Hence above: “Do not trust,” etc.

(GREG.) While Scripture narrates Zedekiah’s captivity, it announces the order of inward captivity, etc., up to: “For sometimes even the light of the whole power of reason is closed off, because it is weighed down by corrupt practice and the multitude of its iniquity.”

“Nebuzaradan came,” etc. (RAB.) By the just judgment of God, Nebuzaradan, commander of the king of Babylon’s army, came against Jerusalem and burned, etc., up to: “He burns every house with fire—that is, each person’s conscience with the flame of illicit love.”

“Of the poor,” etc. (ID.) Those who could have been useful in word and example, etc., up to: “but the thorns and thistles of vices.”

VERSE 20.—“The pillars also,” etc. Through the various vessels, the various offices in the Church are signified. Evil spirits remove these from the service of God and convert them to their own use.

VERSE 21.—“Of the pillars,” etc. (RAB.) The description of the workmanship of the pillars, with their capitals, latticework, and pomegranates, shows, etc., up to: “Let him read our work on the Book of Kings, where what the holy Fathers have thought about these matters is explained.”

VERSE 24.—“And the captain took,” etc. The devil deceives and captures even the strong in the Church. Hence: “His food is choice” (Habakkuk I), etc.

VERSE 25.—“From the city he took,” etc. Namely, those who do not have the oil of grace and mercy in their breasts, like the foolish virgins, who are appointed over fighting men in vain because they have not first considered how to avoid arrogance.

VERSE 26.—“Seven men,” etc. That is, sanctified by the sevenfold Spirit. But because they lost grace, they were handed over to seven more wicked spirits. They do not attend to the commands of the heavenly king but obey the will of the infernal king. “And the scribe,” etc. The Book of Kings calls him Sophar, which is interpreted as “dispersing” or “dividing.” He signifies those who, in the Church, disperse by wicked examples the inexperienced whom they ought to have nourished for Christ’s service, and separate them through error from the assembly of the faithful.

“And sixty men,” etc. Namely, foolish co-workers, who are rightly called by the name of the common people because they neglected to discern and fulfill the usefulness of divine counsel.

VERSE 27.—“And the king of Babylon struck them,” etc. The king of Babylon aims at this: that those whom he tears away from the Church he may bring to the slaughter of eternal death.

[Col. 0062D] VERSE 28.—“This is the people,” etc. (RAB.) Nebuchadnezzar devastated Judea for the third time. First, under Jehoiakim, etc., up to: “and thrusts them back into the prison of hell, where the condemned groan forever.”

VERSE 31.—“And it came to pass.” (ID.) He signifies God’s wondrous power, which works equally through the good and the wicked, etc., up to: “He mercifully regarded the corrected man, and, freeing him from punishment, restored him to peace and honor.”

[Col. 0063]

## LAMENTATIONS. (G)*

The edition of the theologians of Douai appends to the Book of Lamentations an exposition by Paschasius Ratpert, who flourished around the year of the Lord 880. Walafrid, who was certainly forty years older than Ratpert, did not know this work; therefore we have judged that it should now be omitted, intending to give it in its proper place among the works of Paschasius Ratpert.

(EDITOR.)

## THE PROPHECY OF BARUCH. (G)*

### PREFACE

This book, which is designated by the name of Baruch, is not found in the Hebrew canon, but only in the Vulgate edition. [Note: The Vulgate edition mentioned in the prologue to Baruch is explained in the prologue to Ezekiel. The rest is clear.] The Epistle of Jeremiah is likewise absent from the Hebrew canon. Nevertheless, these writings are included here for the information of readers, because they indicate many things concerning Christ and the last times.

## THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW. (G)*

### PROLOGUE

[Col. 0063A]

After Matthew had first preached the Gospel in Judea, wishing to pass over to the Gentiles, he was the first to write the Gospel in Hebrew, leaving it as a memorial for the brothers from whom he was departing. For just as it was necessary to preach the Gospel for the confirmation of faith, so it was also necessary for it to be written against heretics. Although many have written Gospels, only four have the testimony of authority, because through the four parts of the world they announce the faith of the Trinity. They are like the four wheels of the Lord’s chariot, which carries him through the preaching of the Gospel; and the human race, slain by a fourfold death, was to be brought to life by their preaching. Hence the Gospels of the others fell away and were not received, because they did not wish the predetermined number to be discontinued on account of the power of the mystery.

The evangelists are also represented by four figures, which are not deceptive but conscious of a delightful mystery. Matthew is understood as a man, because he dwells principally upon Christ’s humanity. Mark is represented by a lion, because he deals with the resurrection. Luke is represented by a calf, because he treats of the priesthood. John is represented by an eagle, because he writes of the mysteries of the Divinity. Christ, whom they describe, was a man born from a virgin; a calf in his sacrifice; a lion in his resurrection; and an eagle in his ascension. Or: in the man, his humanity is expressed; in the calf, his priesthood; in the lion, his kingship; and in the eagle, the mystery of his Divinity.

The Gospel according to Matthew begins here.

## CHAPTER I

VERSE 1.—“The book of the generation.” (HIER.) The Hebrews give their books titles from their beginnings, as the book of Genesis, etc., up to: “But this is customary in many books, especially among the prophets, as in ‘The vision of Isaiah,’ where the sense is, ‘This is the vision.’”

“Son of David.” The order is inverted so that, once Abraham had been mentioned first, the sequence of the genealogy would not be interrupted. He is specially called the Son of these two, because one was first among the patriarchs and the other among the kings to whom the promise concerning Christ was made, in order to show the Jews that Christ would come from the Law and that in him they would see the prophecies fulfilled.

“Son of David, son of Abraham.” Of all the fathers, he chose these two, whose Son Christ is called, so that it might be evident to the Jews to whom he writes—who knew from the Law that Christ would come—that this was the one who had long been promised, in whom all the prophecies would be seen to be fulfilled. For in the Old Testament the promise is read as having been made to these two alone: “In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis XXII).

Abraham and David are two pillars standing in the Law, as in a vestibule before the door that is Christ. A cord of twelve cubits, that is, the faith of the apostles, surrounds them. The genealogy embraces these fathers, from whose midst Christ, the door, is opened to believers.

VERSE 2.—“Abraham begot Isaac, and Isaac begot Jacob.” It is fitting that the genealogy should begin from the one to whom the promise was first made, in whom lies the blessing of all.

Matthew begins the genealogy from the beginning of the promise. This theme is also pursued to the end of the book, so that the one who was born from this genealogy may be understood as God and man.

From the beginning he starts with the one to whom the promise of faith was first made, so that in this father to whom the promise was first given people may learn who and what sort of persons those ought to be who wish to be blessed in his seed. Matthew begins or reckons the genealogy by descending, because he shows Christ’s humanity, through which God descended to human beings. Luke, reporting it by ascending, discloses the form of the mystery. Beginning from baptism, he ascends to God, showing that the baptized ascend in order to become sons of God.

“He begot.” Matthew says “begot,” since he counts only sons by nature. Luke says “who was,” since he inserts some sons according to the Law or by adoption. Matthew says “begot,” not “generated,” perhaps so that the one revealed at the end might be recognized, concerning whom it is said: “Today I have begotten you” (Psalm II).

“Judah and his brothers.” He names Judah alone specifically so that you might recognize the one who had been promised from his stock.

He mentions Judah’s brothers while passing over the brothers of Isaac and Jacob, because the latter were rejected as though alien from the people of God, whereas the former, like heirs written in the book of life and like the twelve patriarchs, signify the number of the apostles. They are not named individually, lest the genealogy be extended beyond the number of the mystery.

In the seed of the fathers mentioned above, Christ entered Egypt. Anticipating this, the enemy oppressed the people and killed not the females but the males, in order to extinguish him.

Christ came from Judah, and all the nations received him; when he came, the foreigner Herod was already ruling.

[Col. 0066B] VERSE 3.—“Judah, however.” Judah begot Perez and Zerah before he entered Egypt; afterward both of them crossed over into Egypt with their father.

“Perez begot Hezron.” In Egypt Perez begot Hezron, Hezron begot Aram, Aram begot Amminadab, and Amminadab begot Nahshon. Then Moses led them out of Egypt. Nahshon was a leader under Moses in the tribe of Judah through the wilderness, and there he begot Salmon. This Salmon was a prince in the tribe of Judah, who entered the Promised Land with Joshua. In the Promised Land this Salmon begot Boaz by Rahab.

Christ is Perez, that is, “division,” because he will separate the sheep from the goats. He is Hezron, that is, “arrow” or “court,” because he penetrates the hearts of his hearers. He also possesses the breadth of charity, by which he loved even his enemies.

VERSE 4.—“Aram, however.” Aram is interpreted as “chosen” or “exalted.” He is the Chosen One concerning whom the prophet says: “Behold my servant whom I have chosen” (Hosea XI). And elsewhere: “The Lord is exalted above all nations” (Psalm CXII). He is Amminadab, that is, “willing,” who says: “I will sacrifice willingly to you” (ibid. XXXIII). He is also Nahshon, that is, “augury,” because he knows past, present, and future things. Or Nahshon means “serpentine,” because Christ, in the manner of a serpent, avoided all snares.

VERSE 5.—“Salmon begot Boaz.” Christ is Salmon, that is, “perceptive,” because he perceives all things. He took Rahab, that is, the Church from the Gentiles. Rahab means “hunger,” or “blessedness,” or “impetus,” because the Church of the Gentiles hungers and thirsts for righteousness and, enlarged throughout the world, converts philosophers and kings by the force of its teaching. Rahab displayed scarlet in the window; that is, through confession she declares in her mouth the Passion of Christ. Rahab the prostitute, who received Joshua’s messengers and whom Salmon, prince of the tribe of Judah, joined to himself in marriage, signifies the Church from the Gentiles, which is joined to the Prince from Judah, that is, to Christ. She alone is saved with her household, while Jericho—that is, the present age—surrounded by the seven walls of vices, is besieged for seven days by the trumpets of preaching, until at the last trumpet all the walls fall and the last death is destroyed.

“But Boaz.” Boaz is Christ, concerning whom it is said: “Behold, the Lord God will come in strength” (Isaiah XL). Observe that none of the holy women is included in Christ’s genealogy, but rather women whom Scripture censures. He had to be born from sinners, since he had come for sinners, so that they might learn that the sins of their fathers do not harm them. Hence the lamb to be sacrificed at Passover was commanded to be taken from goats and sheep—that is, to be generated from the just and from sinners.

“From Ruth.” From Ruth the Moabite woman, to show that Isaiah’s prophecy was fulfilled: “Send forth the lamb, O Lord, the ruler of the earth” (Isaiah XVI). Through her the seed of Abraham is led down to Christ. The Church from the Gentiles, signified by Ruth, before it came to Boaz—that is, to Christ—belonged to the father, the devil.

Ruth signifies the Church that comes from Moab, that is, from the Gentiles, from the father the devil and from the rock of the wilderness because of idolatry, from which God raised up children for Abraham. Having forgotten its former nation, it came to Boaz, who is called “strong,” that is, to Christ, who raises up the seed of his brother, namely Moses, who died childless, because the Law brought nothing to perfection (Hebrews VII). Ruth means “seeing” or “hastening,” because the Church sees God with a pure heart, hastens toward the prize of heavenly vision, and resolves to persevere in faith and love.

“But Jesse.” David’s father is more often called Isai, but he had two names. Here he is called Jesse so that one might know that he had come concerning whom Isaiah says: “A shoot will come forth from the root of Jesse” (Isaiah XI), etc. He is the flower whose fragrance Isaac perceives when he says: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field” (Genesis XXVII), because the Spirit filled him most abundantly.

[Col. 0067C] “A king.” Not because he alone was a king in this genealogy, but because he was the first king from Judah and the beginning of the kings, on account of whom the others are also preserved upon the royal throne. Through him the sequence of the genealogy runs down to Christ, who possesses the kingdom of David.

VERSE 6.—“David the king.” Mystically, David is Christ, who overcame Goliath, that is, the devil. He is “strong of hand” or “desirable in appearance.” Concerning him it is said: “The Lord is strong and mighty” (Psalm XXIII), etc. And again: “Beautiful beyond the sons of men” (ibid. XLIV).

“Of Uriah.” Uriah means “my light is God,” namely, the devil, who said: “I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah XIV). Christ loved the Church, which had been joined to him in marriage, from the balcony of the Father’s majesty, and, having made her beautiful, joined her to himself in marriage. Uriah, who is a figure of the devil, is interpreted as “God is my light”; for the devil still transforms himself into an angel of light and makes himself the light of God.

VERSE 7.—“Solomon, however.” Christ is Solomon, that is, “peaceful,” because he is our peace, who made both one. He is Rehoboam, that is, “the impetus of the people,” because he swiftly converts peoples to the faith.

“Rehoboam.” Concerning him it is said: “I will give him the tribe of Judah, so that David’s lamp may remain all the days in Israel” (3 Kings XI). This cannot be understood literally, because Israel did not exist for all days, nor was there any ruler from David in Israel after Christ. But Christ is the eternal lamp in the heavenly Israel, and therefore he is preserved forever. Christ is said to sit upon David’s throne because David’s temporal kingdom prefigured Christ’s eternal kingdom.

“Abijah.” “The Father is the Lord,” that is, Christ, who says: “I will be a Father to him,” because, as Lord, he did everything whatever he wished (Psalm CXIII). He is also Asa, that is, “lifting up,” because he took away the sins of the world.

VERSE 8.—“Jehoshaphat,” etc. “Judging” or “the judgment of God,” namely Christ, who judges the world in righteousness.

“Joram begot.” Christ is Joram, that is, “exalted,” who says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III).

VERSE 9.—“Uzziah, however.” Under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, Isaiah prophesied concerning Christ. Because of the sins of the rulers, the mouths of the prophets were closed.

“Hezekiah.” “The Lord is strong.” He is the one who says to the apostles: “Do not be afraid.” When Hezekiah was childless, it was said to him: “Set your house in order, for you will die and will not live” (Isaiah XXXVIII). Therefore he wept, not for the sake of a longer life—since he knew that Solomon had pleased God precisely because he had not asked for additional years—but because he feared that God’s promise might not be fulfilled, since he knew that he belonged to David’s lineage, through whom Christ had to come. He was childless, and therefore he also said: “I shall not see the Lord God”; and again: “I shall no longer look upon man,” etc. On the other hand, he believed because the one who had promised was faithful. But God changed the sentence he had pronounced in order to test his faith and granted him time to beget children.

VERSE 10.—“Manasseh.” “Forgetful.” He is the one who said to the repentant sinner, as it were: “I will remember none of all his iniquities” (Ezekiel XVIII).

“Amon,” that is, “faithful” or “nourishing,” signifying Christ, concerning whom it is said: “The Lord is faithful in all his ways,” who calls together his children as a hen gathers her chicks (Psalm CXLIV).

VERSE 11.—“Josiah,” that is, “the salvation of the Lord,” or “incense.” He is the one who says: “Let my prayer be directed like incense” (Psalm CXL), etc.

Josiah, the just king—not his sons whom he begot, nor in the transmigration, since he never migrated—but according to God’s predestination for migration, places Jeconiah and his brothers together, so that, since their iniquity is shared, their misery too may be alike. Jeconiah means “preparation of the Lord,” because the Lord prepared both father and son for transmigration.

[Col. 0068D] (ISID.) The truth of the history holds that there were two Jeconiahs: one was the father at the end of the preceding group of fourteen, and the other at the beginning of the following one. But mystically, according to Augustine, there is one and the same person at the end of the preceding group and at the beginning of the following one. But why was Jehoiakim, the father of Jeconiah, omitted? Perhaps, in order to make Jeconiah a type of Christ, he counted Jeconiah twice and omitted Jehoiakim so that the number would not be increased.

All those who are counted from David up to the transmigration of Babylon were kings.

Jeconiah. The first Jeconiah is called “resurrection of the Lord,” the following Jeconiah “preparation of the Lord.” Both meanings [Col. 0069A] suit Christ, who is “the resurrection and the life” (John XI).

**VERSE 12.**—Shealtiel. “My petition is God,” which suits Christ, who says: “Holy Father, keep those whom you have given me, so that they may be one, just as we are” (John XVII).

**VERSE 13.**—“But Zerubbabel begot Abiud.” “Master of Babylon,” that is, of confusion. This suits the one who recalled the world from the error of idolatry to the way of truth. There were zealous men among the Jews called Heriles because of the closeness of their kinship to Christ; they were Nazarenes, who, retaining the order of Christ’s genealogy partly by memory, partly from the Books of Chronicles, and partly from their grandfathers and great-grandfathers, wrote it out in due order. Abiud, that is, “my father.” This suits Christ, of whom it is said: “He called upon me: You are my father” [Col. 0069B] (Psalm LXXXVIII), and so forth. Eliakim. “The Lord who raises up.” He is the one who says: “Everyone who sees the Son and believes in him will have eternal life, and I will raise him up” (John VI), and so forth.

**VERSE 14.**—Azor. “Helped.” He is the one who says: “Behold, God has helped me; the Lord is the protector of my soul” (Psalm LIII). Zadok. “Just,” that is, Christ, of whom it is said: “The Lord is just and has loved justice” (ibid. X). Achim, that is, “my brother.” Who else is meant but the one who wished to become human, so that he might have brothers, of whom he would say: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers” (ibid. XXI)? Eliud, that is, “my God,” suits Christ, who says: “My God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew XXVII).

**VERSE 15.**—Eleazar, that is, “my God is a helper.” [Col. 0069C] He is the one who, speaking in the person of a human being, said: “My God, I will hope in him” (Psalm XC). Matthan. “Giving” or “given.” He is the one who gave good things to human beings, and of whom it is said: “God so loved the world that he gave his Son” (John III).

Through these fathers Christ came into the world, and he bore in himself the office of all of them. It is fitting, therefore, that we ascend to him by the same line of holiness by which he deigned to descend to us.

**VERSE 16.**—Joseph. “Adding.” Christ added the Gentiles to the Jews. Joseph is also called Christ’s father: he adoptively received him, born of his own wife; he is also called his putative father. Matthew says that Joseph was the son of Jacob, and Jacob the son of Matthan. Luke says that Joseph was the son of Heli, and Heli the son of Matthat. But Matthan and [Col. 0069D] Matthat each begot a son by the same wife, named Hesta. Matthan, descended through Solomon, married her first; after leaving one son, Jacob, he died. Afterwards Matthat, descended through Nathan from David, married the same woman and begot Heli. Thus Jacob and Heli were uterine brothers. Jacob, taking the wife of his brother Heli, who had died childless, in order to raise up his brother’s seed, begot Joseph as his natural son, but according to the law as Heli’s son. The claim that a son is called by the name of the man for whom the seed is raised up is not true, since Boaz called the son whom he begot from Ruth not Elimelech, for whom the seed was raised up, but Obed. [Col. 0070A]

“Husband of Mary.” What relevance does a genealogy traced from David to Joseph have to Christ, since Christ was not from Joseph’s seed? But it is not the custom of Scripture to weave the order of women into genealogies. Therefore Christ is introduced through Joseph, not through Mary, since Joseph and Mary were from the same tribe. Hence he was also obliged to take her as a relative, lest one tribe become intermixed with another. For this reason they likewise professed together, as though from one stock, that they were returning to Bethlehem, each to his own city.

Mary’s example makes clear to married believers that, with equal consent preserved, continence can remain and the marriage still be called a marriage—not through bodily intercourse, but through the preservation of the affection of the mind. Thus Joseph is called Mary’s husband, because a true marriage exists where the effect of love is preserved, and in Mary the fruit of marriage is found.

[Col. 0070B] **VERSE 17.**—“Thus all.” Having completed the order of the genealogy, the evangelist finally concludes by recapitulating it under a mystical number.

**VERSE 18.**—“Now the generation of Christ.” He writes simply “of Christ,” without adding “Jesus,” so that you may understand him of whom the prophet says: “God, your God, has anointed you.” He reserves the name Jesus—which properly belongs to him in substance—for the angel, so that the one who will later be said to have been conceived by the Holy Spirit may have his proper name declared more sublimely from the office of salvation. “Thus it was.” As it was said: the origin of Mary was from Joseph, and through him she would also be shown to be from David; yet Christ was not from Joseph’s seed. Thus, as God and human being, through the genealogy he is shown to be human, while through his being born of a virgin by the Holy Spirit he is shown to be God. Thus, I say, it was as previously prescribed and shortly to be stated, just as it was later manifested by signs and wonders, [Col. 0070C] so that the entire book might demonstrate that God and human being were born. This must be believed in order that it may be understood. For human understanding fails here, where there is not nature but power: whoever does not believe does not understand that a virgin gave birth, that the Word became flesh.

“When she was betrothed.” (ORIGEN.) She was betrothed in order to signify the Church, which is both virgin and bride; and so that through Joseph, and so forth, up to the point where betrothal took place several days before habitual cohabitation, and meanwhile she was a wife under the protection of her husband.

“Before they came together.” Not that they came together afterward, just as if we said, “Before he repented, he was overtaken by death.” It does not mean that they came together afterward; rather, it indicates the approaching time of the wedding, when the wedding ceremonies are celebrated.

[Col. 0070D] “She was found to have a child in her womb.” Joseph found that she had a child in her womb, but he did not know that it was from the Holy Spirit. Later, when he deliberated in doubt about dismissing her, the apostle adds this so that no suspicion might meanwhile insinuate itself into the reader’s mind. How this happened, in what order, or in what city Christ was conceived is explained by Luke, though it is omitted here.

**VERSE 19.**—“Just.” Through the faith by which he believed that Christ would be born of a virgin, and he wished to humble himself before so great a grace.

That he was just is a testimony to Mary’s chastity: whoever protects an innocent person is called just. He was also pious, since he did not wish to expose her; through his awareness of her chastity he was just, and through fear he was pious. He knew that she was blameless, but he did not know from where or what this was. Therefore he chose a middle course of escape, so that he would neither betray an innocent woman nor, by consenting to an unknown matter, make himself guilty before God. True virtue exists when neither piety is without justice nor justice without piety; separated from one another, they collapse.

“And did not wish her.” He did not wish to take into marriage the woman to whom he was betrothed, lest he appear to be concealing what he did not understand. Or he did not wish to expose her to the punishment in which he knew there was no disgrace, because he knew that he had received her as a virgin and had kept her untouched.

**VERSE 20.**—“But while he was considering these things.” Here we are taught that uncertain matters should be deliberated over for a long time, lest one sin through the rashness of levity. “Behold, an angel of the Lord.” Because he considers the matter piously, he deserves consolation, and his plan is changed by a better plan. “Son of David.” Recognize what was promised to the house of David, from which you and Mary come, and see that it has been fulfilled in her. “Do not fear.” Even though the matter is as great as you believe, do not fear on account of guilt, but embrace it with the perspective of love. “Your wife.” She was his wife not by intercourse but by affection, not by bodily union but by the joining of souls.

Note that she is called a wife from the first pledge of betrothal. Therefore it is a matter of dispensation if someone is permitted to marry another woman after the sacrament of betrothal, even if he can never discharge the marriage debt.

Joseph is rightly called the husband and Mary the wife, since the affection of love is preserved in him—which constitutes a true marriage—and in her the fruit of marriage exists without intercourse.

“What has been born in her.” To be born from her means to be brought forth into the light. [Col. 0071C] To be born in her, however, means to be conceived; or, according to the angel’s presence, which he has from God, what is future is called “born” as though it were past. “It is from the Holy Spirit.” The Holy Spirit is called God, and the gift of God, and love; and love alone caused him to become incarnate.

**VERSE 21.**—“She will give birth.” Lest Joseph seem unnecessary to him, he adds: “She will give birth.” And thus you will be necessary for the administration of the matter. “And you shall call his name Jesus.” He says the same thing to Joseph that he had foretold to Mary, so that through the spoken word he might show to men and women alike that the promised Savior had already come. “For he himself.” The name is interpreted.

**VERSE 22.**—“Now all this,” and so forth. That she was betrothed to a close relative; that she was found to have a child in her womb; that a virgin gave birth; that he was called Jesus; that he saves. This is what the evangelist says once all these things had already been fulfilled. [Col. 0071D]

“So that it might be fulfilled.” The prophecy of Isaiah is a sign of God’s foreknowledge, because what he says is certainly foreknown by God; and therefore it ought to be feared by human beings. No sign, however, causes the thing that it signifies; it merely signifies what it displays. Thus prophecy does not impose necessity upon the things it foretells, but is a sign of God’s foreknowledge.

(HIER.) There is no necessity imposed upon events by the utterance of the prophets, but only the manifestation of truth. Prophecy did not create the necessity of the things it declares; it is a sign of God’s foreknowledge.

One kind of prophecy proceeds from God’s predestination, and must occur in every respect, without our free choice, as in the matter under discussion here. Another proceeds from God’s foreknowledge, to which our free choice is joined. A third, called a threat, is made as a sign of divine retribution, so that they may flee from before the chosen bow, and the unwary may justly perish—not from foreknowledge, since it is known in a very different way from the manner in which it is threatened as future.

**VERSE 23.**—“Behold, the virgin.” The prophet Isaiah marvels and, as though rousing everyone from sleep, says: “Behold, the virgin will have a child in her womb” (Isaiah VII). To the Holy Spirit the present was already known, although in time it did not yet exist. “Behold, the virgin,” and so forth. The Jews say that this word does not signify virginity but merely a young woman of a certain age. But how, then, is it a sign? He follows Isaiah’s meaning, not his words. In place of “she will conceive,” he writes: “She will have a child in her womb”; and in place of “you will call,” “they will call,” or “he will be called.” [Col. 0072B]

“Emmanuel.” This is proper to Christ, as is “Jesus,” because he continually remains with those whom he saves, always helping them.

For three reasons he establishes from the Old Testament the things he sets forth in the Gospel: as testimony, so that he may have testimony from the Law and the Prophets; as confirmation of faith, because we believe more easily when we see fulfilled what was foretold; and for the joining of the New and Old Testaments.

**VERSE 24.**—“But Joseph, rising,” and so forth. (BEDE.) Morally: whoever is moved by God should cast off delay and rise from sleep; he should do what is commanded. “He did as he was commanded.” Perfect obedience. He did not merely do what the angel commanded, but did it as he commanded. Obedient in the performance of service and in the effect of love, he is rightly said to have done as he was commanded. [Col. 0072C] “The angel of the Lord.” There is no room for lying where the ministry of angels is being celebrated. “And he took his wife,” and so forth: to avoid dishonoring the virgin, to conceal the Savior’s coming, and to provide the necessary service for the child who was to be born.

**VERSE 25.**—“Until she gave birth.” It does not mean that there was intercourse afterward, as is more clearly established by many indications, since he recognized in many ways that the one who had been born was God.

It does not mean that he knew her afterward. Rather, “until” is used in place of “and,” or with reference to eternity, as in: “Until I make your enemies your footstool” (Psalm CIX). It is said that Joseph could not see Mary face to face, because the Holy Spirit had completely filled her from the moment of conception. Therefore he did not know face to face the woman to whom he was betrothed until the womb had been emptied. [Col. 0072D] This matter is not being discussed here. “Firstborn,” and so forth. Everything that opens the womb is called firstborn, whether another child follows or not. Or he is firstborn among all the elect through grace. Properly, however, the only-begotten is said of God the Father or of Mary.

# CHAPTER II

**VERSE 1.**—“When, therefore, he had been born,” and so forth. Although Matthew passes over the birth itself, in reporting the coming of the Magi he briefly mentions it, saying: “When, therefore.” (RAB.) Four things strengthened by the prophets are set forth here: the birth, the name, the place, and the time, and so forth, up to the point where Luke is silent about the coming of the Magi, while Matthew explains it.

[Col. 0073A] “Bethlehem of Judea.” To distinguish it from the one in Galilee, in the tribe of Zebulun. There are two Bethlehems. The first was called Ephrathah; Bethlehem means “house of bread,” because there the Living Bread who descended from heaven was to be born and placed in a manger, so that he might make irrational animals companions of the angels. It also signifies the Church, which is the house in which the Living Bread is eaten.

“In the days.” (HIER.) He does not say this merely with reference to time, but so that it may be seen to have been fulfilled, and so forth, up to the point where the Jews indicate the place but do not recognize the time of the coming.

(AUG.) Jesus was manifested neither to the learned nor to the just; for he prevails, and so forth, up to the point where no great person might become proud and no weak person despair.

[Col. 0073B] “Magi came.” Not after a year, since then he would not have been found in the manger but in Egypt, but on the thirteenth day. They came from the land of the Persians, where the river Saba also is, from which the region is named; Arabia lies nearby, and the Magi were kings there. Although they are said to have offered three gifts, this does not prove that there were no more than three. Rather, they prefigured the Gentiles, descended from Noah’s three sons, who would come to the faith. Or they were as many rulers as brought many people in their retinue. The Magi therefore inquire especially at Jerusalem because they had heard through Balaam that the one who was to be born would come from Israel. The new star indicated the new human being. The star is Christ, whom we ought to follow; unless he rises in hearts, the King of the Jews is not sought in the East.

[Col. 0073C] **VERSE 2.**—“Where is he who has been born king,” and so forth. This is the Jews’ disgrace: they learn Christ’s birth from the Gentiles, and, if they do not believe, they are without excuse. “For we saw his star.” This star, the messenger of the Lord’s birth, had never appeared before. The child created it at that time and appointed it for the Magi; once its service was completed, it immediately ceased to exist. A mute star proclaims the still-unable-to-speak Christ; afterwards the apostles announced him when he spoke, to the Jews as rational beings. The rational substance, that is, an angel, announced Christ’s birth. But the Magi, the first fruits of the Gentiles who did not yet use reason, were led by an irrational thing, that is, a star. Angels spoke to the shepherds, a star to the Magi, yet to both the language of heaven spoke, because the language of the prophets had already ceased. It is uncertain whether the star arose in the East or whether the Magi, who were themselves there, saw it born in the West. [Col. 0073D] It could have been born in the East and led them to Jerusalem. But when they seek human assistance, as though according to the Law, they are abandoned by divine assistance. Through the star they understood that he had been born in Judea, and therefore they came to Jerusalem. After learning the place, they then began their journey, recognizing the star that went before them.

Allegorically. The star is the illumination of faith that leads to Christ. When they turn aside to the Jews, they lose it, because when they seek counsel from the wicked, they lose true illumination.

(LEO.) Three men follow the guidance of heavenly light, accompanying with attentive contemplation [Col. 0074A] the sign of the preceding radiance, toward recognition of the truth, and so forth, up to the point where the mystery of so great a vision would not remain hidden from them, and what was shown to their eyes as extraordinary would not be obscure to their minds.

**VERSE 3.**—“When Herod heard,” and so forth. He is called “king” so that, by comparison with the one who is being sought, this man may be understood to be an outsider, since the proper king had already failed.

“When Herod heard.” He wanted another king of the Jews to be sought rather than himself, for although he was a foreigner, he wished to appear the legitimate king. Therefore he burned the books in which the genealogy was recorded.

“He was troubled,” and so forth. Either because he feared the end of his reign, or because he feared the anger of the Romans if this were allowed, since they had decreed that no one should be called king or lord without their counsel. When the King of heaven was born, the king of earth was troubled, for earthly exaltation is indeed confounded when heavenly exaltation is proclaimed.

“With him.” Because of popular favor, since the people often unjustly favor those whom they endure even when they are cruel. Hence Solomon says: “An unjust king has all wicked ministers” (Proverbs XXIX).

**VERSE 4.**—“And gathering all the chief priests,” and so forth. Note the diligence of the inquirer: if he should find the answer, he would do what he later showed that he wished to do; if not, he could be excused before the Romans. He was also investigating whether their king would make the Jews sorrowful or joyful. “Where Christ was to be born.” He asks the Jews for the place and the Magi for the time, so that he might be certain of both.

**VERSE 5.**—“In Bethlehem of Judea.” They identify the place of the birth, which they had learned from the testimony of Scripture [Col. 0074C], so that their knowledge itself might become a testimony condemning them, while serving us as an aid to faith.

From this it is clear that they refused to believe not through ignorance but through hardness of heart.

**VERSE 6.**—“And you, Bethlehem.” He presents it in the way they stated it, because, even if not in the exact words, they in some manner convey the truth of the meaning.

**VERSE 7.**—“Secretly calling the Magi.” He had removed the priests and scribes, for he feared that the Jews, if they sensed that he wanted to kill the child, might conceal what had been promised through God’s oracle. He therefore also promised that he would worship him, so that no one might perceive his deceit, and so that they would report the child to him without suspicion, out of favor toward him.

**VERSE 8.**—“Worship him.” Herod professes devotion but [Col. 0074D] sharpens the sword, painting the wickedness of his heart in the color of humility. In face and words he pretended to worship the one whom in his envious mind he was planning to kill. Hypocrites represent his character: they falsely seek God and never deserve to find him.

**VERSE 9.**—“And behold, the star that they had seen.” After entering Judea, they are deprived of the star’s guidance, so that they are compelled to inquire from the Law. Or they are deprived of divine assistance because they seek human assistance. It was not fitting for the sign given to unbelievers to appear to those who were familiar with the Law and the Prophets, since, “if they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if someone should rise from the dead,” and so forth. The star did not follow heavenly paths, but remained very near the house; otherwise they would not have been able to distinguish the house.

[Col. 0075A] Morally. The star is a good exhortation leading to Christ. Or rather, it is faith, which is the illumination of the mind. Through it, the one who enters sees Christ, who is the morning star; and, having seen him, rejoices with joy and does not cease to worship.

**VERSE 10.**—“They rejoiced with exceedingly great joy,” and so forth. One rejoices with joy when one rejoices because of God, who is true joy. He adds “great,” than which nothing is greater. And “they rejoiced exceedingly,” because, even from something great, one person can rejoice more and another less.

**VERSE 11.**—“And entering the house,” and so forth. The three Magi come by one route to worship God, because in the one Christ, who is the way, they were to worship the inseparable Trinity. “The child with Mary his mother,” and so forth. He is often called a child so that they may recognize him of whom it was said: “A child is born for us.” [Col. 0075B]

Why was Joseph not also found with Mary by the Magi? So that no opportunity for an evil suspicion might be given to the Gentiles, who, as soon as the Savior was born, sent their first fruits to worship him.

“They worshiped him.” Thus they confessed him to be God, while understanding that he had become human; and they indicated that he would die through the myrrh.

“And opening,” and so forth. Through their mystical gifts they publicly professed their faith. Closed gifts signify faith in the heart; opened gifts signify—and so forth, up to the point where through these three things royal power, divine majesty, and human mortality are intimated in the same Christ.

**VERSE 12.**—“And having received an answer.” Just as Moses [Col. 0075C] cried out silently, so these men, with devout affection, asked what the divine will commanded. This answer was not given through an angel but by God himself, because no one else established the way of return except the one who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” The child did not speak to them, lest his divinity be revealed before the proper time and his true humanity be preserved. Therefore he is immediately sent into Egypt: faith had to be nourished for its reward, and the life of his teaching had to be prepared for its journey. “By another way,” and so forth. Here a pattern is given to believers: they should come devotedly to God and attend to what he commands, namely, that they should not return to the devil, but come to their homeland by the paths of virtue; and that those who have fallen through contempt should rise again through obedience.

(LEO.) They worship the Word in the flesh, wisdom in infancy, power in weakness, and [Col. 0075D] the Lord of majesty in the truth of human nature, and so forth, up to the point where what was proper to the substances was not different in the person.

**VERSE 13.**—“Take the child,” and so forth. (HILARY.) When he signified that she was betrothed to a just man, he called her his wife; but after the birth, she is shown to be Jesus’ mother alone. Thus, just as Mary’s marital union in virginity was assigned to the just Joseph, so her venerable virginity as Jesus’ mother might be displayed.

**VERSES 14–15.**—“He arose.” Joseph is a figure of preachers, who carried Christ with his mother—that is, the faith of Christ and the Church—to the Gentiles, leaving Herod, that is, the unbelief of the Jews. “By night.” [Col. 0076A] He descended secretly through his flight to enlighten Egypt, leaving the Jews in the night.

He took him into Egypt by night because he left them in the night of ignorance, those unbelievers from whom he himself had departed. When he returns, there is no mention of night, because at the end of the world the Jews, receiving the faith like Christ returning from Egypt, will be enlightened.

“Into Egypt, and he was there,” and so forth. He shows that God came to people of every race, because Christ, not received by the Jews, passes through preaching to the Gentiles. He fled into Egypt as he had been born, in order to restore corrupted nature. He fled in such a way as to call back those who flee. His flight was a matter of mystery, not fear, so that he might give his own an example of flight. He did not flee death, since he had come to die; nor did he fear ambushes, since he had come to expose the devil’s deceptions. [Col. 0076B] Isaiah foretold this flight: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud,” that is, flesh without sin, “and he will enter Egypt” (Isaiah XIX). He remained hidden in Egypt for seven years.

“From Egypt I called.” In Hosea, according to the Hebrew truth, this is found; or in the Book of Numbers, as some assert, because everything was done by God’s arrangement.

**VERSE 16.**—“Then Herod, seeing,” and so forth. It is plausible that, when the Magi had reported nothing to Herod, he believed they had been deceived by the false star and therefore had not returned to him. Hence he remained at peace for so long regarding the search for the child. Afterwards, when what had happened and been said in the temple became widely known, he realized that he had been deceived by the Magi. Hurrying toward Christ’s death, he killed the children.

[Col. 0076C] It is plausible that Herod raged against the children for a year and four days after Christ’s birth. Perhaps he delayed for this reason because he had gone to Rome, either because he had been accused there or to consult the Romans about what was being said concerning Christ. Perhaps he therefore refrained from searching for the child for so long so that he might apprehend him more carefully and prevent him from escaping in any way.

“He killed all the children.” As soon as Christ appeared to the world, persecution against him began; this prefigured the persecution of the saints. While the infant is sought, infants are killed; in them the pattern of martyrdom is born, at the moment when the infancy of the Church is consecrated.

The death of the little ones represents the passion of all the martyrs, who, being little, humble, and innocent, were killed. They suffered not only in Judea but everywhere [Col. 0076D] at the hands of the wicked, whom Herod signifies. They were two years old because they were perfected in teaching and in works. When they were killed, Christ escaped, because bodies can be destroyed, but divinity cannot be touched.

“And in all its territories.” He was not content with the devastation of Bethlehem but devastated the neighboring regions as well. He showed no mercy regarding age, from the son of one night old to the son of two years old, but killed them all.

“From two years old.” He began with two years so that, just as Herod had anticipated the boundaries of the city, he might also anticipate the other year. He also began with two years because he feared that the child, whom the stars served, might conform his appearance to someone slightly older or younger than his actual age.

[Col. 0077A] **VERSE 17.**—“Then it was fulfilled.” It is called “fulfilled” because, before it happened, it was only half-complete for readers: what sounded in the letter secretly promised something yet to come.

(CHRYSOSTOM.) He says that the star appeared for a year, just as signs appeared in the sky at the destruction wrought by the Romans, when the voice of angels was heard: “Let us depart from these dwellings.”

**VERSE 18.**—“A voice in Rama.” That is, a voice spread far and wide in a high place.

Allegorically. Or it is the voice of the Church, mourning the death of its members, rising as far as the throne of the heavenly Judge. “A voice in Rama.” Because of the Levite’s wife, who was killed on account of fornication, all Israel [Col. 0077B], after dividing her into twelve parts according to the number of the tribes, destroyed the tribe of Benjamin except for three hundred men. The lamentation and wailing of those who survived were heard as far as Rama, a place near Gibeah, twelve miles from Bethlehem. “She was heard.” He intensifies the expression, so that Rachel, already dead, may hyperbolically be said to weep for her children in the affection of one who mourns. Thus, through this passage, a history concerning the Chaldeans is woven, indicating that a devastation similar to the earlier disaster would befall the Jewish people. But more truly, with the Spirit revealing it through the evangelist, the prophecy is understood of the killing of the children. He therefore says that what had been spoken was fulfilled then, because, although the prophetic speech looks toward the captivity that was imminent, the future truth of the slaughter of the infants is proclaimed in it as in a shadow.

“Rachel.” Because she was buried near Bethlehem [Col. 0077C] and received the name of mother from the earthly lodging of her body. Or because many from Benjamin and Joseph were killed. Benjamin was born from Rachel, but Bethlehem does not belong to his allotment, only to the tribe of Judah. Yet because the tribes of Judah and Benjamin adjoin one another at the borders of Bethlehem, many from the tribe of Benjamin were also killed.

Note that the sacramental figure is better suggested through Rachel than if she were said to have wept through Bethlehem, because through her the form of the Church is commended in every respect. The Church weeps not so much for those transferred by death as for those slain by punishment. “Rachel,” that is, the Church, weeps for her slain tender lambs. She does not wish to be consoled in the present, because they are no more, but transfers all hope and consolation to eternal life.

The Church weeps and does not wish to be consoled here [Col. 0077D] because her children are not of this world. Or she weeps because, while she gives birth, she possesses justice, as it is said: “You will weep,” and so forth; but consolation is added: “Your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John XVI).

**VERSE 19.**—“But when Herod was dead, behold,” and so forth. When Jewish unbelief has been lulled to sleep, and Elijah and Enoch are preaching, Judea will receive the word of God.

When the king dies, his accomplices immediately perish. Thus, when persecution of the Church has ceased, she is invited to heavenly things.

**VERSE 20.**—“Into the land.” He does not specify which part, so that, while Joseph is uncertain, the angel may return and, through his frequent address, make Joseph more certain. Since he did not distinguish which region, Joseph understood him to mean Judea, the more distinguished part of the kingdom. “Those who were dead.” [Col. 0078A] Some report that Herod arranged for the nobles of the Jews to be killed at his funeral, so that he might thereby force the Jews to mourn his death.

**VERSE 21.**—“He arose.” Allegorically. Joseph represents the apostles, through whose ministry Christ is carried about. The apostles first came into the land of Israel because they first preached to the Jews. But because of Herod—that is, because hereditary unbelief remained—they became afraid and withdrew, having been warned to preach grace to the Gentiles and to transfer Christ to them.

When the land of Israel was named, Joseph thought that such a child ought to dwell nowhere except in Jerusalem, where there was a temple and the celebration of the prophets. Yet the angel intended Galilee [Col. 0078B], which the Jews also inhabited, thereby showing that it had been predestined in this way, because he would be called a Nazarene.

**VERSE 22.**—“He was afraid to go there.” If he feared Judea because of Archelaus, the heir of his father’s cruelty, why did he not also fear Galilee, where another Herod, his brother, reigned? Because Archelaus obtained the monarchy of the whole kingdom after his father, but, becoming arrogant, was deposed by Tiberius Caesar and exiled to Lugdunum. Then the kingdom was divided into four tetrarchies, one of which—Galilee—was obtained by his brother Herod.

It is asked why Joseph did not fear going into Galilee as he did into Judea, since Archelaus also reigned there. But he could more easily hide in Nazareth, which was remote, than in Jerusalem, where the capital of the kingdom was and where Archelaus was constantly present.

“He withdrew into the districts.” [Col. 0078C] The fact that Christ is not transferred to the place where Archelaus reigned signifies that Christ will be hidden from those among whom the Antichrist will reign.

**VERSE 23.**—“Nazareth.” Nazareth is interpreted as “new shoot” or “flower of the field.” From the root of this shoot, the Holy of Holies is read to have arisen, signifying the substance of his eternity. Therefore, just as he chose the time in which he would be born and the place, so he also chose the city in which he would grow up. Its name indicates that the very holiness, nurtured in holiness, is rightly called the Holy of Holies. Hence his disciples were first called Nazarenes, but afterwards were called Christians after Christ.

Nazareth of Galilee, to which he is transferred, signifies a part of the same people that was to receive the faith. Hence it is interpreted as “flower,” because the more ardently the Church migrates from earthly things to heavenly things, the more abundantly it [Col. 0078D] flourishes and puts forth the flower and shoot of virtues.

“Through the prophets.” He says “prophets” in the plural because we do not have a fixed example from Scripture. He shows that he has taken the meaning, not the words. Or the same words occur in Isaiah according to the Hebrew truth: “A Nazarene will rise from his root” (Isaiah XI).

# CHAPTER III

**VERSE 1.**—“Now in those days.” He passes over many things and moves on to John’s preaching. “In those days” includes not only the years of childhood but all the years up to John’s preaching, that is, when he was almost thirty years old. Luke expresses the times more precisely: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar.” “Preaching.” He who had previously been silent manifested himself by baptizing [Col. 0079A] and preparing the way for the Lord. “In the desert of Judea.” Because the Jews had been abandoned by God and needed repentance in order to return.

**VERSE 2.**—“Repentance.” The herald announces what Truth itself would announce afterward. Repentance precedes; the promise of the kingdom follows. Whoever truly repents first laments past errors in himself and then raises his mind toward the heavenly kingdom. If forgiveness is freely given in baptism, why is repentance preached? There are three forms of repentance. The first is to renounce and condemn errors and all evils committed before baptism; this is necessary for those who are coming to Christ. The second is the restoration through repentance of those who have fallen after baptism. The third is that by which the saints are daily cleansed from such sins as are inseparable from human life.

[Col. 0079B] To repent is to lament past deeds and not commit deeds that must be lamented. The kingdom of heaven is said to be near for those who repent. It is not an earthly kingdom, as in the Old Law, but one brought about through obedience to Christ. John was the first to preach this kingdom of heaven: “Repent.” The first virtue is, through repentance, to put the old human being to death and hate vices. Whoever does not do this not only fails to attain the virtues but also does not escape punishment. The virtue of repentance is conceived through fear, which is the beginning of wisdom. Repentance comes from punishing, by which each person punishes what he has unlawfully committed.

“To practice repentance” means to produce fruits worthy of repentance. “The kingdom of heaven,” that is, Christ, through whom the saints reign in heavenly places; or the Gospel, by which he invites people to the kingdom.

[Col. 0079C] “For it has drawn near,” and so forth. Unless it had drawn near, no one could return, because the weak and the blind lacked the way, which is Christ. John prepares that way and sets it before the repentant.

**VERSE 3.**—“The voice of one crying out.” John is the voice; Christ is the Word, who cries out in John. No word is heard without a voice, nor is a voice effective without the understanding of the word. The voice prepares the way for the Word, so that he may be received. Hence: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” (Psalm CXXXI).

“In the desert.” This is a pattern for the penitent: the place of their way of life is not the crowd of human beings but the desert. Their clothing is not soft and flowing but rough; their food is sparse and unusual.

Typically, the desert signifies the life of the saints, set apart from the enticements of the world.

[Col. 0079D] “The way of the Lord.” The way of the Lord is directed toward the heart when his word is heard attentively.

**VERSE 4.**—“John himself.” The one who preaches repentance displays the garment of repentance. In him the lowliness of clothing and food is praised, while their use by the rich is condemned.

John himself teaches penitents in his own person and presents a pattern of life by dwelling in the desert, living on locusts, and wearing camel’s hair.

A servant of God ought not to have clothing for adornment or pleasure, but only for covering nakedness. Hence John was clothed in hair.

**VERSE 5.**—“Then people went out to him,” and so forth. Unless someone goes out from evil, he is not cleansed. Hence it appropriately follows: “They were baptized by him in the Jordan,” which is interpreted as “descent,” because they descended from the pride of the old human being to the humility of confession and amendment. Already then an example was given to those being baptized: to confess sins and promise better things. [Col. 0080A]

### VERSE 6

**In the Jordan.** Because the figure of baptism preceded in it, and its name requires a descent from pride, which is appropriate to the baptized.

**Confessing.** Confession of sins is the testimony of a conscience that fears God. For whoever fears God’s judgment is not ashamed to confess sins. Perfect fear removes all shame. Confession of sin involves shame, and the very blush of shame is a severe punishment. Therefore we are commanded to confess our sins, so that we may suffer shame as punishment. For this itself is part of divine judgment.

### VERSE 7

**Many of the Pharisees, etc.** These are among [Col. 0080B] the heretics of the Jews. The Pharisees prefer the righteousness of observances and traditions. Hence they are called Pharisees—that is, “separated from the people”—because of their private righteousness. The Sadducees, that is, “the righteous,” claim for themselves what they are not. They deny the resurrection, saying that the soul perishes with the body; they accept the five books of Moses but reject the prophets. John rebukes them when they come to baptism, because they especially needed correction and repentance.

**Brood of vipers, etc.** That is, poisonous children of poisonous parents, because they envy the good and persecute them, and injure their neighbors just as their fathers did.

The viper kills its father; so the Jews killed the prophets who were their fathers.

### VERSE 8

**Therefore produce worthy fruits.** *(Bede.)* [Col. 0080C] As though he were saying: Why do you not first lay aside your poisons, so that you may come to baptism, etc., up to “grace is what perceives, and, perceiving, seeks holiness.”

### VERSE 9

**For I say.** He turns them away from the flesh, so that they may consider the works of God’s predestination. The first rudiments of faith are to believe that God can do whatever he wills: he who created all things from nothing can form children of Abraham from stones or dust.

**From stones.** Demonstratively, he refers to those stones which Joshua caused to be transferred from the Jordan, toward which, as though extending his finger, he says this.

Joshua caused twelve stones to be carried from the middle of the Jordan onto the land, and others to be restored from the land into the same riverbed. Through these, the blinding of the Jews and the transformation of the Gentiles to the light were prefigured.

[Col. 0080D] Or he calls the Gentiles “stones,” and the meaning is: Do not boast of descent from the flesh, because only those are children of God who have been enlightened by grace and raised inwardly. He significantly says “to raise,” because Christ took Sarah—that is, the Church—and by grace raises children of Abraham, who had died without children, so that so great a patriarch, having died without children, would not be deprived of the promises. As a foreshadowing of this event, God once produced a son from Sarah.

### VERSE 10

**For already the axe.** So that they would not seem exempt if they separated themselves from such sacred rites, he threatens them.

**The axe.** Christ, who consists of a handle and iron: humanity, by which he is held, and divinity, by which he cuts. It has been placed there because, although he waits patiently, he nevertheless sees what he is going to do.

[Col. 0081A] **At the root.** That is, at the end of the Jewish people, so that he may remove from the land of the living those who do not believe in Christ.

Or the axe is the sentence of judgment, or the preaching of the Gospel.

**At the root.** Note that it is not placed at the branches but at the root. When the children of evil people are removed, what else are they than the branches of an unfruitful tree being cut off? When the entire offspring is removed together with its parent, the tree is cut off by the roots, so that nothing remains from which a new shoot might arise.

The roots are thoughts, by which those who have been planted are either lifted upward toward heaven or sent down to the depths of hell. The tree is the human race. Its branches are of several kinds: some are dry—that is, pagans, fit for burning; others are green but without fruit, such as hypocrites, who display the appearance of holiness but are empty within; others are fruitful but poisonous, namely heretics, who produce [Col. 0081B] fruit by preaching, but deadly fruit; others, namely Catholics, bear good fruit.

Thus every tree—such as the Gentiles and hypocrites, who bear no fruit, and the heretics, who bear evil fruit—is included.

### VERSE 11

**I indeed.** So that he would not seem to threaten on his own authority, he begins to reveal how great his dignity is—whose presence threatens, or whose benefit he commends:

**I indeed baptize you with water.** I wash only bodies, because I cannot absolve sins. Thus, just as I precede him by birth and preaching, so I precede him in baptism, directing penitents—whom I distinguish from the impenitent by this sign—to Christ’s baptism.

**He who is coming after me.** Although I urge you to produce worthy fruits of repentance and to cast away pride, I still cannot free you from sins.

**He is stronger than I.** Because I baptize unto [Col. 0081C] repentance, but he unto remission. I possess the Spirit; he gives the Spirit. I proclaim the kingdom of heaven; he gives it.

**Whose sandal-strap I am not worthy, etc.** Some write: “Whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to loosen.” John could have said both, either in sequence or at different times, so that one evangelist took up one wording and another the other. All, nevertheless, narrated the truth. In this he intends to show Christ’s excellence and his own humility.

Or, according to the allegory: the sandal is the mystery of the incarnation; the strap is the bond of the mystery. John therefore is not able to loosen the strap, because he is not sufficient to investigate the mystery of the incarnation.

[Col. 0081D] Or: “I am not worthy to loosen his sandal-strap,” that is, I do not claim for myself the bridegroom’s name, nor do I wish to be believed or called the bridegroom, but rather the bridegroom’s friend. For it was customary that, if someone did not wish to take as wife the woman who was properly his, the man who approached her as bridegroom by right of kinship would loosen his sandal. John, therefore, who was not the bridegroom, says: “I am not worthy,” etc. As though he were saying: I cannot uncover the Redeemer’s footprints, because I do not claim for myself the name of bridegroom.

Or he simply humbles himself; or he is not worthy to carry the sacraments of the Gospel by preaching, since this was not assigned to him but entrusted to the apostles. I am not worthy to explain the nature of divinity in relation to humanity. Or: I am not worthy to bear the preaching of the [Col. 0082A] Gospel or to claim the bridegroom’s name.

John, as a mere human being, could not give the Spirit by whom guilt is remitted. Christ, however, gives him because he is God, and he baptizes in the Word, concerning which it is said: “And you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John 15); and elsewhere: “Cleansing them by the washing of water in the word of sanctified life” (Ephesians 5).

**In the Holy Spirit.** Or, in the Spirit of sanctification, and in fire—that is, in the testing of tribulation. Or he washes in the Spirit in the present; afterward, if any stain steals in, he will burn it away completely in purgatorial fire. This is to be understood of lighter sins.

Hence, in Leviticus, fire sent from heaven always burned upon the altar: that is, the fire of divine love, which rebaptizes and burns away [Col. 0082B] the vices of the flesh of all those who are offered in Christ—that is, upon the altar.

### VERSE 12

**Whose winnowing-fan.** The winnowing-fan in his hand is the examination of judgment by which those who are light and empty of good works are separated.

**In his hand.** Because the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.

**He will thoroughly cleanse.** That is, he cleanses daily from various temptations. Or, “He will thoroughly cleanse” when the perverse person is expelled from the Church for manifest sins, or condemned after death.

**But the chaff.** Chaff comes from the same origin as the wheat—that is, from the seed—whereas weeds come from another source. Chaff, therefore, signifies those who are instructed in the sacraments of the faith but are not solid; weeds signify those who are separated from the elect both in conduct and profession.

Of these it is said: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged,” and therefore no mention is made here of them.

[Col. 0082C] **Unquenchable.** Because it will not be extinguished, nor will it extinguish those tormented; rather, it will punish them eternally. It is said this way to distinguish it from the fire of which it is said: “You tested us by fire” (Psalm 65), etc.

### VERSE 13

**Then Jesus came.** When John was preaching and baptizing, namely when Jesus was thirty years old, showing that no one should become a priest or preacher before reaching a suitable age. Thus Joseph, at the age of thirty, assumed the kingdom of Egypt; David began his reign at that age; Ezekiel attained the prophetic office.

Jesus came for these reasons: to approve John’s baptism; because, as a human being, he was to fulfill all righteousness and the humility of the law; and, by sanctifying the waters, to show through the dove in the washing the coming of the Holy Spirit.

He came not from any need [Col. 0082D] for cleansing, but so that no one, however holy, would judge the grace of baptism superfluous.

**From Galilee to the Jordan.** Galilee means “migration”; Jordan means “descent.” Whoever wishes to be baptized must therefore migrate away from vices and, descending, humble himself.

### VERSE 15

**Let it be so now.** Let me now be baptized by you, so that afterward you may be baptized in the Spirit by me. For it is fitting to give an example of fulfilling all righteousness, so that all may learn that no one is perfect without the water of baptism.

**Then he allowed him.** Having understood that righteousness was to be fulfilled in this order, he allowed him, because true humility does not abandon obedience as its companion.

The Spirit taught him in an instant what he had previously not known [Col. 0083A] Therefore, what he had earlier feared, he humbly and dutifully fulfilled.

### VERSE 16

**When he had been baptized.** Christ sanctified the waters of baptism, because the one whose work it is to create also has the work of sanctifying.

Just as a human being consists of two things, body and soul, so he is reborn through two things: water, which cleanses filth and buries us with Christ; and the fire of the Spirit, by which, once purified, we are snatched up to heaven.

Thus, after baptism, the Church seeks the summit of the virtues through certain stages of growth, just as Christ, having been baptized, rose from the water. So those who advance in virtue rise after baptism; those who were previously carnal and children of Adam become spiritual and children of God.
