**The heavens were opened, etc.** This too was for the fulfillment of righteousness. [Col. 0083B] The heavenly things did not first become open to him then, nor was the Holy Spirit then first given to him; rather, he showed us that, through the baptism received, the way to heaven is open and the Holy Spirit is given.

The fact that the heavens were opened, that the Holy Spirit came, and that the Father’s voice sounded—these things are mystically present for us.

The way into heaven is open to those reborn through Christ, a way that had been closed through Adam.

**Like a dove.** He took, for that hour, a true body formed in the likeness of a dove, because otherwise the Spirit could not have been seen by human beings—not because it was truly a dove, but because the Spirit appeared in bodily form without itself being a body.

The same understanding applies to this manifestation as to the others in which God appeared: once their function had been completed, they dissolved.

The Spirit appropriately appeared in a dove [Col. 0083C], which descended simply and gently, indicating both the simplicity of its own nature and the gentleness of him upon whom it descended, the herald and giver of mercy.

Similarly, all who are reborn through baptism ought to be filled with the seven virtues signified by the dove.

The dove is free from the bitterness of gall, by which we are warned against anger. It harms no one with its beak or claws, signifying innocence. It does not attack even the smallest birds, among which other birds nourish themselves and their young, and thus we are warned against robbery. It feeds on pure grain, signifying abstinence. It shelters others as though they were its own young—behold charity. It gives a groan instead of a song—behold compunction. It sits upon the waters so that, seeing the hawk’s shadow in the water, it may avoid it—behold vigilance.

The Spirit appeared over the Lord in the form of a dove because he came to gather us through gentleness. [Col. 0083D] Over the disciples he appeared in fire, because he came to kindle them against themselves for the consuming of the rust of sin.

Adam lost heaven by sinning. Christ, glorified by the Holy Spirit through the dove, appeared; and he extinguished the flashing flame that had barred the way, through the water of baptism, because water is opposed to fire.

**I am well pleased.** That is: I have established my good pleasure, so that you, in whom nothing but good pleases me, may please me; and through you others may please me—not in themselves but in you, that is, united to you by faith and splendor.

## CHAPTER IV

### VERSE 1

**Then Jesus.** After baptism, because there is no delay before temptation: so that he might immediately teach the baptized [Col. 0084A] to depart from the world and devote themselves to God in quiet. Thus the children of Israel, after crossing the sea, went up through the desert and ate manna until they came to the land of promise.

**Then Jesus was led, etc.** *(Rabanus.)* This is the order of right conduct: after receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit, we are to gird ourselves more tightly against the devil. By this path the Samaritan descended, because, clothed in flesh, he endured the same temptations.

**By the Holy Spirit.** The Spirit sends those whom he fills, strong for battle. Whoever goes into battle without this Spirit quickly falls.

**To be tempted by the devil.** He is tempted by the devil only because he has gone out into the desert—that is, because he has begun to pursue what is good.

### VERSE 2

**And when he had fasted.** *(Bede.)* He fasts in order to be tempted; he is tempted because he fasts; and he gives us an example of fasting [Col. 0084B], etc., up to “and so, as long as we are here, let us always mourn our sins,” because the present life is indicated by this number.

*(Leo.)* While the concerns of this life are stretched out through its various activities, it is necessary to cleanse ourselves of worldly dust, etc., up to “so that in whose resurrection we have been raised together, in his passion we may be found to have died together.”

**Afterward he was hungry.** This is truly a mark of humanity, and through it an opportunity for temptation arises. His power is hidden; his weakness is visible.

### VERSE 3

**And the tempter approaching.** Because hunger is a sign of weakness, temptation is not absent from us in abstinence. Through outward weakness he tempts Christ, in whom he found no law of sin.

**If you are the Son [Col. 0084C] of God.** One thing belongs to the tempter’s investigation, another to his temptation: he appears to confess God while attempting to mock him in this way. He tempts in order to investigate what he fears; he investigates in such a way that, by tempting, he may deceive.

**If you are the Son of God.** He knew that the Son of God had come into the world, whether through prophets, through angels announcing him, or through John pointing him out. But because he saw in him humble things, what he had suspected concerning his divinity became doubtful to him through pride. Hence he craftily inquires.

Nor was it unworthy that Christ should be tempted, since he had come to be killed, so that by overcoming temptations he might give us power to overcome temptations, just as by his death he took away our mortality.

*(Rabanus.)* Christ did not permit himself to be tempted until after baptism, signifying that those who go to him will suffer greater [Col. 0084D] things, etc., up to “but Christ was tempted only by suggestion, because the pleasure of sin did not wound his mind.”

### VERSE 4

**It is written.** He does not use power but the authority of Scripture, teaching us to fight by doctrine rather than by miracles.

**Man does not live by bread alone.** As though he were saying: Your suggestion is a temptation, because you are speaking about food for the body and not food for the mind. The lower part of a human being is sustained by bread; the other part is refreshed by the word of God. But because you are speaking about the lower part, it is clear that you are the tempter.

**But by every word, etc.** Every word is charity, in which all things that proceed from the mouth of God are fulfilled. For whatever is spoken through the ministry of anyone belongs not to that person but to God. But if anything contrary is inserted, that is not from God.

[Col. 0085A] From one word—that is, from the wisdom of God—proceeds whatever the saints, who are his mouth, speak.

### VERSE 5

**Then he took him.** The first and last temptation occurred in the desert; the middle one likewise occurred historically; the last occurred after he had returned to Jerusalem. [The transmitted wording is internally difficult.] Matthew does not follow the historical order but the order of Adam’s temptation; Luke follows the order in which the events happened.

Because the devil was defeated and left uncertain by Christ’s answer, he went from the first temptation to the second.

The fact that Christ allowed himself to be taken was not weakness but patience; in the devil it was not virtue but pride.

Note that all these things were completed through bodily senses. Nor is it surprising that he allowed himself to be carried about, if [Col. 0085B] “taken” is understood in this way, since he allowed himself to be crucified.

**Above the pinnacle.** *(Rabanus.)* In Palestine the roofs were flat above, and there was the seat of teachers there, etc., up to “he shows that we should obey anyone commanding good and exalted things, but resist one who wishes to cast us down.”

**If you are the Son.** *(Bede.)* In all the temptations he acts so that he may understand, etc., up to “it is likely that the devil appeared in human form.”

**Throw yourself down.** This command suits the one who strives to cast everyone down. In it he is shown to be weak, since he can harm no one unless that person first throws himself down.

He was suggesting that Christ test by some sign how much he could accomplish with God. But no one should tempt God when human reason provides a course of action.

[Col. 0085C] Hence, although he could do everything, he nevertheless said to his own: “If they persecute you in this city, flee into another.” He himself likewise fled, departed, and remained hidden.

Now he could have descended from the temple by another way than by throwing himself down in ostentation. When human reason fails, a person should commend himself to God, not by tempting him but by devoutly confessing.

**For he has commanded his angels concerning you.** *(Bede.)* What is rightly said of the body, the devil wrongly interprets of the head, etc., up to “but he speaks of the angels’ assistance as though to a weak person and remains silent about his own being trampled underfoot.”

### VERSE 8

**Again he took him.** This temptation preceded in chronological order, but it is narrated out of order according to what happened with Adam. [Col. 0085D]

**He showed him, etc.** This does not mean that he enlarged the vision of the one who sees all things, but that he presented the vanity of worldly pomp, which he loved, as though it were beautiful, etc., up to “not that he looked upon it with the eye of desire as we do, but this showing took place in the mind, just as physicians see diseases without injury.”

### VERSE 9

**All these things I will give you.** He says this out of arrogance, not because the whole world belongs to him.

From the beginning the devil has labored to usurp what belonged to God. Therefore, so that he might be worshiped in these things, he invented idols.

In these three things gluttony, avarice, and pride are noted.

*(Rabanus.)* Luke places avarice in the middle [Col. 0086A] and pride last, etc., up to “all kinds of temptations are contained in these three.”

### VERSE 10

**It is written.** David struck down Goliath with three stones from the torrent, and Christ struck down the devil with three testimonies from the Law.

**The Lord your God.** This may be said [Col. 0086B] to the devil—not because he would fulfill it out of devotion, but so that, in opposition to what he himself was attempting, Scripture might show that God, not he, is to be worshiped.

Or it is not said to the devil but to Christ according to his humanity, and to every human being, to indicate that this command applies to them. Likewise, the command “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” refers to the Son, the Father, and the Holy Spirit, who is one God.

God is worshiped, and service is rendered especially to him for his own sake.

Here it is shown that Christ as man is to be worshiped as God and Lord, as a matter of duty.

**You shall serve.** In Greek, *λατρεύσεις* (*latreuseis*), for *latreia* means service. Service rendered commonly to God, a human being, or anyone else is called *douleia* in Greek. But that service which is owed to God alone is called *latria*. Hence *idolatry*, which gives to idols what is owed to God alone.

Note that the devil is defeated in the very things in which he overcame Adam: he tempted him through gluttony when he urged him to taste the forbidden tree; through vainglory when he said, “You will be like gods” (Genesis 3); and through avarice when he said, “Knowing good and evil.”

### VERSE 11

**They came.** Not as though they were approaching for the first time, but, watching the Lord’s contest from a distance, they waited lest they appear to have needed their assistance or to have conquered through it. But when the devil departed, defeated, they came prepared to serve him.

Just as [Col. 0086C] our warfare is equipped in this contest, so a glorious reward in the service of the angels is taught.

### VERSE 12

**When he had heard.** *(Rabanus.)* Here Matthew, like Mark and Luke, omits the Lord’s first coming into Galilee, after which, etc., up to “Jesus made the beginning of his signs.” And again: “John had not yet been cast into prison.”

**John, etc.** This happened for the sake of the Gospel. Jesus, preaching the same message more perfectly, withdraws and flees for a time, so that he might be an example to his own.

**Into Galilee.** There are two Galilees: one is called the Galilee of the Jews; the other of the Gentiles, because of the Gentiles who inhabited it. Solomon gave this region to the king of Tyre, who placed Gentiles there.

[Col. 0086D] ### VERSE 13

**Nazareth.** *(Rabanus.)* From this Christ is called the Nazarene. It is a village in Galilee near Mount Tabor, etc., up to “because, standing firmly in the midst of the Gentiles for the spreading of the word of God, he shows believers a refuge and, for those in danger, a harbor of faith.”

### VERSE 15

**Land of Zebulun.** *(The same.)* The evangelist omits what was placed first, namely: “At the first time he lightly afflicted the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali” (Isaiah 9), as well as what comes in the middle, etc., up to “but, as a figure of those who were to be called from the Gentiles, he mentions here the region that belongs to the Gentiles.”

### VERSE 16

**The people.** *(Augustine.)* This people, which was first led into captivity and was in the darkness of vices, was the first to see the light of Christ’s preaching. Then [Col. 0087A] the Gospel was spread among all. Hence it follows: “Those dwelling in the region.”

**The shadow of death.** Death is in hell. The shadows of this death are sins, which are never without death. Whoever, therefore, wishes to flee death must avoid its shadow.

### VERSE 17

**From that time.** After he had been baptized. Baptism makes people suitable for preaching.

“From that time,” that is, after John had been handed over. When the Law comes to an end, the Gospel follows, as the sun follows the dawn.

He is a humble teacher, who does not obstruct the disciple’s teaching but waits until he has completed his course. In this he teaches that no one should despise a message because of the inferior status of the person speaking. Hence the Apostle says: “If something is revealed to another, let the first be silent.”

**Repent.** He preaches the same message as the herald, [Col. 0087B] so that it may be shown that the one speaking is no other than the one who cried out in the voice.

Christ is the Word that cries out in the Jordan as its instrument and in all those who, from the beginning, have spoken anything divinely. Yet John alone is called the voice, because through him the present Word is revealed, which others announced from afar.

There is nothing between voice and word: as soon as the voice sounds, the word is immediately perceived. Thus, when John was imprisoned, he ceased; Christ shone forth through his powers.

John is therefore a figure of the prophets and the Law, who truly are the voice crying out the wisdom of God. John is their end; when they cease, the Word that had sounded in them is revealed by itself.

*(Rabanus.)* This preaching of Christ began in Capernaum with miracles flashing forth, etc., up to “he began to preach after the Baptist had been imprisoned.”

[Col. 0087C] ### VERSE 18

**Who is called Peter.** Either this name was given to him when Andrew first brought him, when it was said, “You shall be called Cephas” (John 1), which is interpreted as Peter, although here it appears to promise something future.

Or it was said to him when he confessed, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16).

*(Bede.)* Peter means “knowing”; Andrew, “manly”—which is appropriate to teachers, because these alone, etc., up to “but because the first man went out disobedient, the second entered obedient.”

*(Rabanus.)* Matthew says that Jesus called the disciples after settling in Capernaum. John says, etc., up to “before Jesus came to Cana of Galilee, Andrew brought Peter, but [Col. 0087D] they were not yet disciples.”

**Casting a net.** Because he often sees them longing for earthly profits, he calls them to heavenly desires. Through them he rescues others from the depths of iniquity by the nets of the Gospel. Hence he adds: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (John 1).

### VERSE 19

**Fishers.** One who is going to fish goes through fishing places.

**Mystically.** When he became incarnate and took flesh, he saw divinely spiritual fishers in the sea of the world and showed others what they were, those whom he had foreseen from eternity.

### VERSE 20

**Immediately.** Perfect obedience is to leave behind one’s imperfect things.

**Leaving their nets.** Even if they later take them up again [Col. 0088A], they do so without greed or possessive attachment. In them an example is given to those who wish to follow.

The intention is changed, not the fishing; the nets are changed into doctrine, greed into love of souls. The sea becomes the world, the ship the Church, and the fish good and evil human beings.

### VERSE 21

**He saw two other men.** Here the number four, representing the evangelists, is prefigured: they draw souls out of the world from its four quarters.

They are called two by two because charity exists only between two. Their calling is understood either according to the election of grace, as it is said, “Those whom he called” (Romans 8), etc.; or according to the saying, “Many are called” (Matthew 10).

*(Augustine.)* It is asked how Matthew and Mark say that Jesus called two at a time—first Peter and Andrew, etc., up to “therefore he sent uneducated fishermen to preach, so that faith might be attributed to the power [Col. 0088B] of God, not to human eloquence.”

**Of Zebedee and John.** Zebedee means “fugitive,” that is, the devil. James means “supplanter,” who is assisted by John—that is, by the grace of God.

**And he called them.** “They,” however, etc. He called others as well, but it is enough to name these.

### VERSE 23

**And Jesus went around all Galilee.** After calling his assistants, he devoted himself to preaching, teaching that a teacher ought to be diligent.

**Teaching in their synagogues.** Teaching about morals to those engaged in the active life.

**Preaching.** Teaching about future things to those perfected in the contemplative life.

He taught natural righteousness, namely chastity, humility, and similar things that human beings possess naturally.

**Preaching the Gospel of the kingdom.** The Gospel includes [Col. 0088C] the mystery of righteousness, the good beginning, the promise of blessedness, the remission of sins, adoption, resurrection, the heavenly inheritance, and fellowship with the angels.

**In the synagogues.** A teacher should not run about idly and in vain, but should preach where there are many.

**The Gospel.** Because righteousness is burdensome to one living in the flesh, the labor of righteousness is not undertaken unless the reward of the work is expected. Therefore Christ proclaims blessedness, so that he may stir people to endure good works.

**And healing.** It was not a great thing to cure sickness and weakness, since those healed would later die. But this was done so that they might thereby be lifted toward the kingdom.

Morally, he instructs preachers also to provide earthly assistance to those under their care and thus draw them toward the kingdom.

### VERSE 24

**And his reputation spread.** *(Bede.)* [Col. 0088D] Works of salvation do not shine sufficiently before hearers without the fame of a good fragrance, nor does fame profit without works: without these, etc., up to “he cures bodies so that they may listen more readily to invisible things.” Otherwise, it would have been of little value to care for those who were soon to die.

### VERSE 25

**Great crowds followed him.** *(Augustine.)* The crowds were fourfold, namely: some, etc., up to “others, wishing out of envy to accuse him and catch him in something.”

## CHAPTER V

### VERSE 1

**When Jesus saw this.** *(Augustine.)* Luke agrees with this account, saying: “It happened in those days that he went out to the mountain to pray” (Luke 6), etc. But Luke says, etc., up to “for not all people can do all things.” It is considered more likely [Col. 0089A] that this was one and the same event, although the two accounts may also be understood as having occurred together.

**He went up.** He teaches his followers to ascend and not remain in the crowd. He was going to teach a higher righteousness than that of the scribes and Pharisees.

He himself, the mountain, ascended the mountain in order to teach the heights of virtue, and, preaching from the Church above which he sits, he showed that the Church must be raised higher by the Lord’s command. Through this same teaching he would more fully instruct it until the end of the world.

He leads the apostles away more prominently, so that they may first receive from the mountain the mountains of peace for the people.

**He sat down.** His sitting signifies his humanity, through which he is recognized. Hence: “The world did not know him” before the incarnation.

**They approached.** So that those who were hastening to fulfill his teaching inwardly might hear more closely.

### VERSE 2

[Col. 0089B] **And opening his mouth.** The opening of the mouth signifies the depth of the mystery. He opened it like an abyss, like a treasure, like a river of paradise.

On this mountain he writes the New Testament in the hearts of his children, beginning with blessedness, just as on Mount Sinai he gave the Old Testament on stones to servants, beginning with terror.

*(Augustine.)* The sermon that our Lord spoke on the mountain, as it appears in the Gospel, etc., up to “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them I will compare to a wise man” (Matthew 7).

### VERSE 3

**Blessed.** *(Gregory of Nyssa.)* Blessedness, in my opinion, is the comprehension of all those things which, etc., up to “for misery consists in harsh and grievous events and calamities that do not befall us according to our own will. [Col. 0089C]”

**Blessed are the poor.** The number and order of the sayings must be carefully noted. Blessedness begins with humility.

*(Jerome.)* **Blessed are the poor in spirit.** It is not necessity but faith and devotion to poverty that make people blessed, etc., up to “just as the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, so poverty is the beginning of blessedness.”

*(Chrysostom.)* The poor in spirit are humble and contrite in heart. Here he calls the spirit the soul and the will. Since many are humble not voluntarily but under compulsion, he calls the voluntary humble blessed first.

### VERSE 4

**Blessed are the meek.** The meek are those who rule over evil habits. Possession of one’s character is perfect virtue.

[Col. 0089D] *(Theophylact.)* The meek are not those who never become angry at all, etc., up to “thus a person’s teaching is recognized through patience.”

**They shall possess the earth.** *(Augustine.)* I believe this is the land of which it is said in the Psalm: “You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living” (Psalm 141).

### VERSE 5

**Blessed are those who mourn.** They mourn for their own sins or the sins of others. This mourning comes from the lower irrigation, whereas mourning from the higher irrigation arises from desire for the heavenly homeland.

The former washes away present stains; the latter kindles more intensely those who love eternal things. Whoever has laid aside sins, corrected his conduct through gentleness, and also wept can now hunger and thirst for righteousness—something he previously could not do.

This virtue is not fulfilled without the spirit of fortitude [Col. 0090A], because through it we shall eventually come, by hungering, to satisfaction.

**Blessed are those who mourn.** After what has been said, it remains to cleanse the filth of ruins through mourning. Mourning for sins or for heavenly desire deserves consolation; no other mourning does.

These people are enlightened by the spirit of knowledge, so that they may know the evils in which they are entangled.

*(Hilary.)* For those who mourn not bereavements, insults, or losses, but weep over former sins and are burdened by the consciousness of crimes by which we are defiled, this diligent consolation is prepared in heaven.

### VERSE 6

**Blessed are those who hunger.** They are lovers of the good word, for whom it is not enough to be righteous; they always thirst for the work of righteousness.

[Col. 0090B] Righteousness is to give each person what is his: to oneself, to one’s neighbors, and to God. This righteousness will not be fully accomplished until God is all in all. Therefore, here we can hunger but not be satisfied.

The light of righteousness is mercy; the virtue of mercy is righteousness. This mercy requires the spirit of counsel, without which no one shows mercy prudently.

The beginning is to have mercy on oneself; the end is to die for another. For the order of showing mercy is that each person should begin with himself. Christ reveals the end: out of mercy he died for sinners.

### VERSE 7

**Blessed are the merciful.** Mercy arises from what precedes. If true humility has come first, and the mind has become gentle, and one has mourned one’s own and others’ falls, and has hungered for righteousness, then true mercy is born.

Then a person makes the miseries of others [Col. 0090C] his own and helps them according to his ability. If the means of helping are lacking, compassion will not be absent:

“Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6). That is, show mercy for the same purpose as God does, so that goodness may overflow in everyone.

Mercy without justice is called indulgence and lukewarmness; justice without mercy is called severity and harshness.

### VERSE 9

**Blessed are the peacemakers.** *(Rabanus.)* Peacemakers are those who compose all the movements of the soul and subject them to reason, because nothing opposes those who are like the Father, etc., up to “but when God is all in all, then the blessedness of adoption will be given.”

### VERSE 10

**Blessed are those who suffer persecution.** In the seven preceding beatitudes the manifestation and testing of perfection are presented. Those who possess what has been described are able to suffer persecution; and rightly does [Col. 0090D] the one who has received these things hold them who is prepared to die for them.

### VERSE 11

**Blessed are you when they curse you.** Up to this point he has stated the sayings generally, as though addressing absent people, although they also applied to those present. Now he turns his words to them, although this too applies to others, foretelling how much they would suffer for his name.

He wished to make them aware of the dignity of their rank, saying: “You are the salt of the earth; you are the light of the world,” so that from the sorrowful things they might receive humility, and from the joyful things consolation.

**When they curse you.** The older translation has: “When people hate you, and say every evil thing, and expel you.” The meaning in our version is nevertheless the same, since curses arise from hatred of the heart.

Whoever desires the glory of heaven does not fear reproach on earth. The more someone rejoices in human praise, the more he is saddened by reproach. The one whom praise exalts is depressed by criticism. Whoever seeks to be praised only by God does not fear [Col. 0091A] being put to shame before human beings.

**Lying.** He adds this so that no one may glory in accusations that are truly deserved.

He also adds: **Because of me**, since false things are sometimes said, arising from human recklessness; yet those who do not follow Christ do not suffer these things because of him.

### VERSE 12

**For your reward is abundant in heaven.** It is not in things that turn and pass away, since the eternal reward should not be in mutable things but in spiritual firmaments, where everlasting righteousness dwells.

Already those who rejoice in spiritual goods experience this reward. But it will be perfected when this mortal nature puts on [Col. 0091B] immortality.

“For thus they persecuted, etc.” He moderates the severity of suffering by an example. Persecution occurs in three ways: through hatred in the heart, through words, and through deeds.

### VERSE 13

**You are the salt of the earth.** Here the office of the apostles is shown: namely, that they are the salt of the earth and the light of the world.

This applies especially to the apostles, who ought to be adorned with the virtues mentioned above—poverty and the others—so that they may be the finest salt, seasoning others by their teaching and by the example of their lives.

Salt means preservation from corruption. Hence the prophet says: “I have appointed you as a light to the nations, so that you may be my salvation to the ends of the earth.”

But if the salt, etc. That is, if you, through whom others are to be seasoned, yield to adversity or prosperity: by whom will error be removed from you, when God has chosen to raise you above [Col. 0091C] others? It is useful for nothing, because, as another Evangelist says, it is useful neither for the earth, which it prevents from sprouting by being cast upon it, nor for the manure heap, which it does not allow to become fertile. Thus the person who turns back produces no fruit himself and is unable to cultivate others; he is cast out of the Church, and these words are spoken mockingly of him: “This man began to build and was not able to finish.” If the salt has lost its savor (Luke IV), that is, if through fear or desire the teacher has abandoned the flavor of wisdom, by whom will his foolishness be corrected? This applies specifically to the apostles; what follows applies to all teachers: “It is useful for nothing any longer,” etc. At the end he concludes concerning everyone as follows: “Unless your righteousness abounds,” etc.

And is trampled by men. The holy and true minister of Christ, although mocked by the wicked, cannot be trampled down, because, fixed in mind in heaven, he remains there.

**VERSE 14.**—You are the light of the world. Salt is mentioned before light because life comes before teaching: life leads to knowledge of the truth. Whoever fears God is not lacking in knowledge.

Light of the world. There is another reason why they must not fail: they have been enlightened by Christ in word and example; wherever they are brought into the world, they must minister the light of faith and knowledge. And just as, because they are salt, they must drive away corruption, so also, because they are light, they must dispel darkness.

A city cannot, etc. Since the apostles are foundations, they are appropriately called a city. Upon a mountain. The place indicates the mountain of righteousness, which is lofty, and upon which you are displayed [Col. 0092A], so that you may not hide yourselves. For there is no possibility of evading or doing anything secretly. Therefore govern those under you mercifully within by counsel, and defend them outside by fighting against adversaries on behalf of righteousness. This belongs to the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

**VERSE 15.**—Nor do they light a lamp. By domestic examples he teaches that they must not conceal the light of the word entrusted to them. They do not light it—that is, the doctrine of preaching was not given for them to conceal it and subject it to the servitude of the body while they fear certain things. Rather, they should subject their bodies to the service of God, so that through their voice and the other functions of the body the superior light may appear to everyone. Hence it is said: “I chastise my body,” etc. (1 Cor. IX).

Alternatively, Christ lights the lamp when he fills the vessel of human nature with the flame of his divinity [Col. 0092B]; he neither hides it from believers nor confines it under a bushel—that is, within the measure of the Law—or within the boundaries of a single nation. Rather, upon the lampstand—that is, the Church—he affixed the faith of his incarnation, where all who are in the house, that is, in the Church or in the world, can behold it. Hence he adds: “Let your light shine,” etc. The lampstand. Just as Christ is the lamp, the cross is the lampstand, upon which he was to be lifted up. The Church is the lampstand, carrying the word of life in the present age.

**VERSE 16.**—Let your light shine, etc. Do all these things in such a way that you do not make the praise of men the goal of your good work. That they may see, etc. I require works so that they may be seen and thus the teaching may be confirmed; but this is not to be done for your own glory.

**VERSE 17.**—Do not think. After exhorting them to endure all things for the truth, not to conceal it, and to glorify God, he begins to teach what they are to teach. It is as though he said: What is this that you forbid to be hidden and for which you command us to endure everything? Is it something contrary to the Law? “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it,” either by doing what it says or by supplying what was lacking and incomplete.

**VERSE 18.**—The iota. (Bede.) Here it is shown that the things regarded as least in the Law are full of spiritual mysteries, and everything, etc., up to the point that the iota signifies ten, that is, the Decalogue, whose culmination is the perfection of the Gospel.

Let everything be done. Let them be fulfilled spiritually, or let what was imperfect be perfected, and let the things signified be completed through fulfillment.

[Col. 0092D] **VERSE 19.**—Whoever therefore abolishes, etc. The least things are the cross of Christ and his passion; whoever is ashamed of them is least, while whoever confesses them is great. Alternatively, he is referring to the Pharisees, who abandoned God’s commandments for their own traditions, which are worthless, since they pass over even the least thing contained in the Law. Morally speaking, a person abolishes the Law when he does not fulfill it but holds to it as though it had been given only to the weak. Or he abolishes it when he does not understand it spiritually. To abolish is not to do what one rightly understands, or not to understand what one does not corrupt, or to diminish the integrity of Christ’s additions.

He will be called least, etc. In the kingdom of heaven, the least will be called the person who is unworthy to be in it—although in that kingdom no one is least, but all are great.

[Col. 0093A] But whoever does them. Whoever does not abolish them and thus teaches them is not least, though he is not yet great; rather, he does what he teaches. For only those who do the Law are righteous before God (Rom. II).

**VERSE 20.**—But I say to you. When he says, “I say,” he impresses upon them the great force and profound meaning that must be considered; he shows how he adds to the Law. Yet he does not nullify the things he had previously commanded. It is more to love enemies than merely not to hate them; more to refrain from desiring than merely not to commit adultery; more not to become angry than not to kill.

Unless, etc. That is, unless you fulfill not only the least commandments of the Law but also those that I add. For when the additions are carried out toward perfection, the things previously stated for beginning are also fulfilled more fully: whoever does not look at a woman in order to desire her does not commit fornication, and whoever does not become angry does not kill.

Your righteousness. He calls the righteousness of the Pharisees all those things that were actually commanded for the worship of God, or the mystical things instituted according to the letter alone as figures.

**VERSE 21.**—You have heard, etc. He explains what the righteousness of the Pharisees is; whoever fulfills it is not immediately great, but ascends a certain step.

**VERSE 22.**—But I, etc. He begins to explain the perfection that he came to fulfill, and how their righteousness ought to abound more greatly.

Everyone who is angry. Because they did not know murder to be anything other than killing, he reveals that every movement of the soul toward harming another is counted as murder. Christ’s command is not contrary to the Law, but contains the Law in itself in a broader form [Col. 0093C]. Whoever does not become angry does not kill. But the converse does not follow: that permission to become angry is the cause of murder. Remove anger, and murder does not occur.

**VERSE 23.**—Therefore if you offer your gift. He explains the greater righteousness by showing that, if it is not lawful to be angry with a brother, much less is it lawful to retain in one’s mind something that seeks to turn into hatred. If we have anything evil in mind against our neighbor, we cannot offer anything pleasing to God.

Therefore if you offer. According to the letter, this is absurd. There is therefore an altar in the inner temple, that is, faith; any gift—psalm, hymn, prayer, or something of that kind—will not please God unless it is founded upon faith. And there, etc., that is, when you are about to offer such a gift in your heart, which is the inner temple, if it comes to mind that your brother has something against you, whom you have injured. For if he has injured you, it is not he but you who have something against him; nor should you then ask him for forgiveness, but give it, just as you wish forgiveness to be given to you.

**VERSE 24.**—Leave it there, etc. He does not say “bring it back,” because what is rightly offered may not be changed. Rather, leave it until you can offer it in a more conciliatory spirit. For he does not reject the gift but seeks love of neighbor, without which no one reaches the love of God. Hence: Let the person who wishes his gift to please God first fulfill love toward his neighbor.

Go. Not with your feet, but in your mind; humbly prostrate yourself before him in the presence of the one to whom you are about to offer it. Or ask forgiveness if he is present.

You will offer. This comes from the spirit of piety, by which a person becomes gentle, understands the divine word piously, obeys through understanding, and raises his heart toward fulfillment.

**VERSE 25.**—Be in agreement. Just as he has already commanded reconciliation with a brother and afterward commands love of enemies, so here, while we are running along the way of this world, he exhorts us to peace and concord, as it is said: “If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Rom. XII). In place of “be in agreement,” the Greek has “kindly” or “well-disposed.”

Quickly, so that you do not postpone it until tomorrow: while you are on the way, while it is still possible to work.

If you have injured your brother, be reconciled to him. If he has become your adversary, be well-disposed toward him, so that he may become your friend.

With him on the way. The divine word is with us on the way of Christ. The adversary is with us on the way of this world. [Col. 0094B] The divine word is the way for us along which we run. Hence: “I have run in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. CXVIII).

Lest perhaps he hand you over. He has tempered the statement so as not to eliminate the possibility of repentance. For it might be thought that, if the adversary died and it was no longer possible to be well-disposed toward him on the way, the person would necessarily be handed over to the judge. But he both left room for repentance and handed the unrepentant person over to the judge, saying: “The judge will hand you over to the officer.” He will hand you over, that is, he will be the cause of your being handed over into the hands of Christ, to whom the Father has given all judgment. The officer is Christ’s angel, who will gather the weeds.

**VERSE 26.**—The last quadrans. That is, minor sins, because nothing will remain unpunished. Or by the last quadrans earthly sins are signified, because the first part of the world is heaven, the second air, the third water, and the fourth and final part earth. Therefore, until you pay the last quadrans—that is, until you expiate the sins that you have contracted from the earth.

**VERSE 27.**—You have heard. (Rabanus.) Again he says: “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it” (Mark XI). He adds how greatly it ought to abound, etc., up to the point where the soul, having abandoned the higher Law, is corrupted by being prostituted through a shameful desire to lower things.

Whoever looks at a woman. (Bede.) A great addition. “Look” is used for every movement that is, etc., up to the point that a person is not accused or defended according to what he was able to do but was not permitted to do; rather, he is accused or defended according to what he desired and deliberately proposed in his conscience.

In order to desire her. So that it may pass into the affection of the heart and dispose him to act, where the will is not lacking but only the opportunity. This is called passion, which is death in the house. *Propasion* is a sudden affection of the soul, whether of anger or love. Passion is a form or deliberation of the soul arising from consent. Hence someone is called angry or loving.

(Isidore.) If contemplation turns into weariness or arrogance, abandon it and pass over to the active life; for it is better to be saved through the active life than to perish through the contemplative.

**VERSE 29.**—Pluck it out. Literally, no bodily member is commanded to be plucked out. Rather, the inner sight, which is called the right eye, and the outer sight, which is called the left, must be recalled or removed through the devoted labor of discipline if they cause harm; they must even be put far away, so that they are not retained in memory. The eye is plucked out when an evil habit is broken. It is cast away when it is utterly destroyed and is not permitted to enter.

**VERSE 30.**—Your right hand. Prosperous activity, or some energetic helper amid the affairs of life: if such a person is a stumbling block in the Law of God, it is better to be saved after cutting him off than to be damned with him.

Cut it off, etc. If anyone preaches this concerning bodily members, he should not be heard in a spirit of piety. Rather, what must be cut away is the wickedness of conduct and the perversity of actions: whatever in the eye of the mind turns us from the way of righteousness and moral integrity, and whatever externally assails our practice of the virtues, must be driven far away.

Into Gehenna. The name Gehenna is not found in the ancient books; it is first used by the Lord. The origin of the name is as follows. The idol Baal stood near Jerusalem at the foot of Mount Moriah, where Siloam was. This valley was watered, wooded, and full of delights, and a place within it was consecrated to idols. The people of Israel became so insane that, abandoning the Temple, they sacrificed there and burned their children to demons. This place was called *Gehennon*, that is, the valley of Hinnom. God threatened to fill that place with corpses, so that it would be called *polyandrium*, that is, a tomb of the dead. Thus future punishments are designated by the name of this place.

**VERSE 31.**—Let him give her. (Augustine.) Moses wrote in Deuteronomy that, if a wife does not please her husband because of some disgrace, he should divorce her. Christ explains this, etc., up to the point that one should love an enemy not insofar as he is an enemy and evil, but insofar as he is a human being, so that he may be saved together with oneself.

(Chrysostom.) Moses permitted a bill of divorce to be given so that blood would not be shed because of hatred. He permitted evil things to be done, etc., up to the point that we cannot completely restrain the evil desires of human beings.

**VERSE 32.**—Except on account of fornication. For in this the faithfulness of chastity and marriage is broken. The man does not make her commit adultery; she herself is the cause of her guilt. If he divorces her on account of fornication, he must remain free from fornication and may not take another wife while she lives.

On account of fornication. This may refer to the woman who has committed fornication, or to the man, lest he fornicate—for example, if his wife compels him to idolatry, avarice, or other unlawful desires. For fornication does not mean only sexual immorality [Col. 0095D], but generally whatever causes a person to stray from the Law of God.

And whoever, etc. (Chrysostom.) Do not say that her husband divorced her; for even after she has been divorced, she remains the wife of the man who divorced her.

**VERSE 33.**—But you shall repay. If it happens that you swear an oath, swear by the Creator, not by a creature. For whatever someone swears by, he venerates; he loves it and fears it. Therefore the Law commands that one swear only by God.

But I, etc. He teaches that nothing among created things is so insignificant that a person ought to swear falsely by it; thus he forbids oaths from the highest to the lowest—from heaven to a hair. Whoever swears by God is convicted of perjury, for heaven is his throne and everything that exists belongs to him.

[Col. 0096A] By heaven. Either they supposed heaven to be something more than it is, or, when swearing by it, they did not think themselves bound by their oath. Therefore he moderates the statement so that heaven is understood to be God’s creature, not something more, and so that, because it is his throne, perjury may be feared. The same applies to the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet. Whoever therefore swears by a creature owes his oath to the one who created and governs it; it is not rightly thought to be rendered to anyone else.

Let us not swear by creatures in order to venerate them beyond what is proper through our use of them, nor to regard them as worthless, as though, when we swear by them, we thought we were not swearing at all.

Nor by the earth. Others understand this as referring to the health of Pharaoh, who by God’s judgment was placed among the lowest. “There is no authority except from God” (Rom. XIII); in this also you swear by God.

[Col. 0096B] Nor, etc. Whatever is not your work but God’s; thus, by swearing by the smallest things, you can incur perjury.

Whoever swears by his head owes his oath to the one whose image and power remain in it.

**VERSE 36.**—Because you cannot, etc. Since the things stated above are lofty and difficult, no one keeps them without the spirit of fortitude. He compels us toward perfection by removing the occasion for swearing.

**VERSE 37.**—Let your “Yes” be yes and your “No” be no. He says each twice so that what you say with your mouth you may prove by your works. What you deny in words, do not confirm or establish by deeds.

He did not absolutely forbid swearing, but forbade it because of the occasion for perjury. He taught what is more perfect, showing that to be farther from evil is the superior way. The Apostle swears in order to persuade people of the faith [Col. 0096C], and the Church also permits her members to swear for the sake of a pact of peace and faith. But Christ taught what is more perfect, excused what belongs to weakness, and cut away what is superstitious.

The truth of the Gospel does not admit an oath, but another person’s weakness compels it when he does not believe the truth.

It is from evil. Not that it is itself evil, since, although it is not good, it is necessary; rather, it is from evil—not your evil, but that of the person who compels you to swear, that is, from his weakness, which is evil.

**VERSE 38.**—You have heard. (Augustine.) The Law established the measure of retaliation: “An eye for an eye.” If this can be said, etc., up to the point that it is done for love of righteousness: the just is given for the unjust, which is good for evil, as even a judge does.

[Col. 0096D] When it says, “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth,” it does not wish to remove one or the other, but to preserve both while threatening retaliation. It also imposes retaliation within bounds, so that vengeance does not exceed the injury. This is the beginning of peace and, as it were, the beginning of justice.

**VERSE 39.**—Do not resist. The righteousness of the Law instructs beginners at the beginning of righteousness: do not return more than has been inflicted. The righteousness of the Gospel, which leads people to the kingdom, is not to resist evil. “Do not resist,” as he himself says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. XI). And David: “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil” (Ps. VII). Jeremiah: “I gave my cheek to the one who struck me” (Lam. III). Behold, the Lord of both the Law and the Gospel is the same.

[Col. 0097A] Offer it to him. Do not merely refrain from striking back; if he wishes to strike the other cheek, endure it patiently. This concerns an injury to the body. As for necessities, if he takes one of them, allow him to take the other as well. What, then, should be said about superfluous things?

The other. (Chrysostom.) First, it is an unworthy thing for a faithful person to stand in judgment before the presence of an unbelieving judge. For even if he is an unbeliever, etc., up to the point that, once you have entered into judgment, you no longer desire the truth of the case to appear, but only to emerge victorious by whatever means.

**VERSE 40.**—And to the one who, etc. This is advice given before you contend. The weak may indeed reclaim what belongs to them, but they should not quarrel. Luke states it in the opposite order: “Whoever takes away your cloak, do not withhold your tunic also.” This should be done not only with these things but with all temporal possessions.

Your tunic. Alternatively, the tunic is the soul. If someone does not wish to lose it, let him surrender the cloak—that is, the body—to martyrdom. Spiritually, the teacher takes away the tunic when he causes inner vices such as envy, pride, and the like to be confessed. The other adds, “and the cloak,” when he does not blush to confess outward sins such as theft and fornication.

**VERSE 41.**—A thousand paces. This is the distance of a Sabbath journey, by which spiritual perfection is signified, because it is not lawful to perform servile work on the Sabbath. Two more. A person goes two more when, although the body alone has been reduced to servitude, he is prepared to bring spirit and soul—that is, reason and will—into servitude as well.

**VERSE 42.**—Give to him. Give what can honestly and justly be given. If the means are lacking, give goodwill through a word or service.

[Col. 0097C] Give to him. Give in such a way that you harm neither yourself nor another; justice must be weighed. In this way you will give to everyone who asks, even if you do not give what he asks, but something better, when you correct him who asks unjustly.

And to the one who wishes. He embraces two kinds of giving. We either give generously, or lend to one who will repay. Sometimes the person who gives does not wish to lend, as though there were no reward in it when the debtor repays what he has received. Yet the one who commands even this truly gives a return. Therefore he says: “Do not turn away,” that is, do not alienate your will. “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. IX). In the same way, the spiritual teacher ought to lend the word of God to his hearers as an investment, so that he may receive from them the repayment of good works and hope for a reward from God.

**VERSE 43.**—You have heard. He who came to fulfill the Law brings it at the end to complete love, which is the fulfillment of the Law.

You shall hate. This may perhaps be understood according to what was said above: “An eye for an eye,” etc., or as referring to withdrawing the duties of human kindness.

**VERSE 44.**—Love. The Church is attacked in three ways: by hatred, by words, and by bodily torture. The Church, by contrast, loves, does good, and prays. This is the new commandment; through it he makes children of God out of children of wrath. Hence it follows: “So that you may be sons.” Adoption as sons is acquired solely through love.

Do good. By supplying food for the mind or body. This is done even by the person who says that such a person should not receive food. Everything has the same goal: that they may become brothers. [Col. 0098A] Each part of malice is countered by a corresponding good, so that all its aspects may be overcome by goodness. The imprecations of the prophets may appear contrary to this, but they are not spoken as wishes of those who desire evil; rather, they are spoken by the spirit that foresees what will happen.

Pray. (Augustine.) He does not say this concerning brothers in whom there are sometimes sins more serious than the persecution of enemies, etc., up to the point that, although they confess that they have sinned and deeply regret having done evil, they nevertheless retain dispositions of mind by which they do not humble themselves to ask forgiveness.

It may also be asked why John, in his Epistle, seems to exhort us only to the love of God and neighbor, when the Lord says that we must also pray for enemies. But brothers are understood to include not only those who already believe but also those who will believe, for whom we ought to pray so that they may be joined to us by the bond of brotherhood.

**VERSE 45.**—Sons. Not degenerate ones. It is as though he said: Having received the power, act through works so that you may become sons by being reborn through love.

Of the Father. He is already called Father. See to it that you are sons reborn from God, who is love.

Who makes the sun. This visible sun. For, they say in the book of Solomon, “The sun of righteousness did not shine upon us” (Wis. V). Concerning the rain of teaching the prophet says: “He rained upon one city and did not rain upon another” (Amos IV), etc. It is as though he said: The sun, which he made, belongs to him; indeed, all things properly belong to him, since he created them from nothing. What, then, shall we do with the things we have received as gifts from him?

**VERSE 46.**—Publicans. Collectors for the Romans, whom the Jews call by this name because they administered public affairs. They are also said to have taken their name from the Roman king Publius [Col. 0098C], who first organized them.

**VERSE 47.**—And if you greet. If you pray only for those who are joined to you by some relationship, what greater benefit do you have than unbelievers? It is necessary to love brothers and greet them humbly, but that is little.

**VERSE 48.**—Perfect. In love of God and neighbor. The fullness of perfection is to love even enemies and pray for them, just as Christ did.

# CHAPTER VI

**VERSE 1.**—Take heed, etc. Up to this point he has commanded mercy; now he commands purity of heart, by which God is seen. For if works of mercy are done not with a simple intention but for the praise of men, they are not approved by God. The praise of men must not be sought, but should follow, so that it may invite others by example. Thus far he has spoken of the righteousness of the Gospel, which is superior to the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees. Now he teaches by what purity of heart this same righteousness must be fulfilled; this is observed in almsgiving and prayer. For here he does not command either prayer or almsgiving as such, but teaches with what disposition they should be performed. The subject is the cleansing of the heart.

Before your Father. His glory is what sons ought to seek, referring all good things to the purpose of pleasing him.

**VERSE 2.**—Therefore when, etc. He proceeds from the whole to the parts, explaining which good things must not be done for the praise of men.

To sound a trumpet. Perhaps they did this in order to summon people, so that everyone would go as though to a spectacle.

[Col. 0099A] Before you. The person who sounds a trumpet before himself is one who wishes to be praised before others, so that he may appear greater than they.

They have received. From God, who examines the heart, they receive the punishment of their deceit. Of such people it is said: “Depart from me, you workers of deceit; you had my name, but you did not do my works.”

**VERSE 3.**—Let not know. The left hand signifies vices; the right hand, virtues. Therefore what virtue does, let not pride, vainglory, or any vice know; rather, let the light of right action drive away the darkness of sin.

**VERSE 4.**—In secret. Almsgiving is done in secret when it is mixed with no darkness: the light is within, and the darkness outside.

He sees in secret. For God to see is for him to approve. He approves only those things that are hidden; the things that are external do not please him, nor does he approve them.

[Col. 0099B] **VERSE 5.**—And when you pray. This sentence is joined to what was said above. Earlier he had said: “Take heed that you do not practice your righteousness before men”; here he adds: “And when you pray.” He does not forbid prayer, but forbids being like the hypocrites in prayer.

In the corners. As though they were hiding their prayers, yet doing so in the marketplaces so that they might be seen, and thereby receive greater glory.

Allegorically. The person who prays in a corner is one who pretends to pray in secret while seeking fame in the marketplace. The corners of the marketplaces are places where a road passes through the crossing of another road and forms a crossroads. It is not wrong to be seen, but it is wrong to desire to be seen.

They have received. In such people not only is the true reward emptied out by a corrupt intention, but the vice of pretense and mockery against God is increased.

**VERSE 6.**—But you. Understood simply, this teaches that the vain glory of the world must be avoided. Yet it seems more likely that he commands us to pray to God while shutting the thought within the breast and compressing the lips.

The room is the secrecy of the heart. The door is the carnal sense, through which external things intrude improperly and crowds of imaginings interrupt those who pray. It is therefore not enough to enter the room if the door lies open to intrusive thoughts. The carnal sense must be resisted, so that spiritual prayer may be directed to God from the innermost heart.

With the door shut. With the senses closed, lest crowds of external imaginings come upon us.

Alternatively, he calls the love or fear of this world the door. Just as every good thing arises from fear and love of God, so every evil arises from love and fear of the world. With these doors shut—that is, removed—pray.

[Col. 0099D] (Chrysostom.) What then, you ask? Is it not necessary to pray in church? Indeed it is very necessary, but with this intention: that you look upon the one who has the power to grant what you ask. For wherever God is, he looks to see with what intention you do something.

The Father. You have him within through faith. Hence: “With myself prayer is offered to the God of my life” (Ps. XLI).

**VERSE 7.**—But when you pray. Just as it belongs to hypocrites to display themselves and please men, so verbosity belongs to the Gentiles, from whom this practice began. They devote more attention to exercising the tongue than to cleansing the mind, transferring this kind of frivolous performance even to the attempt to bend God through prayer, thinking that just as an advocate can persuade a judge, so they can persuade God.

[Col. 0100A] (Chrysostom.) If one should pray with few words, why did Luke set forth the parable that one must always pray, etc., up to the point that both Christ and Paul commanded that prayers be brief but frequent, with only short intervals between them?

(Cassian.) The Fathers consider brief but very frequent prayers more useful, etc., up to the point that we should avoid them in concise brevity.

For they think. They think that God is soothed by persuasive words, or that, if he is absent, he can be summoned, and that what he does not know can be taught to him through verbal circumlocutions.

**VERSE 8.**—Therefore do not become like them. We must not deal with God through words but through actions, the intention of the heart, and a simple affection. When we say these things, we do not teach him; rather, at the time of prayer we remind ourselves.

[Col. 0100B] For your Father knows. Why then do we speak to the one who knows? Not to make our will known to him, but to awaken the service of devout dedication.

**VERSE 9.**—Our Father. (Bede.) Among the other salutary and divine instructions by which he provides for believers, he set forth a form of prayer, etc., up to the point that true worshipers are those who, as sons through grace, worship the Father in spirit and truth.

No prayer is more spiritual than the one that proceeded from the mouth of the Son, who is the Truth.

Our Father. We serve him not out of fear but out of love for the inheritance. When “Father” is said, let us think of adoption, so that we may return a devoted affection to the Father. When “our” is said, we are reminded of brotherhood, since adoption is common to all. No one should say “my Father,” which properly belongs to the Son, whose Father is so by nature [Col. 0100C]. Hence elsewhere: “I am going to my Father” (John VII), specifically by nature, “and your Father,” joined to you by grace. He is called “our Father” because he is common to all; no one should say “my Father,” which belongs only to Christ, who is Son by nature. To others is granted the common grace of adoption.

(Rabanus.) The noble and rich person is warned not to be proud, etc., up to the point: What will he deny his sons, when he has already given them what it means to have him as Father?

(Augustine.) Nowhere is the people of Israel found to have been commanded to say “Our Father,” or to pray, etc., up to the point that they did not depart from his commandments. As in the saying: “I have begotten and raised up sons” (Isa. I), etc.

In heaven. In spiritual realities, so that we may learn to hasten toward the spirituality in which he dwells and seek heavenly things from him.

Hallowed be your name. The distinction among these seven petitions must be considered. Since our life is conducted temporally while eternal life is hoped for, the first petitions are, etc., up to the point that liberation makes free people—that is, sons—so that, in the spirit of adoption, we may say, “Abba, Father.”

“Amen” signifies that in all these petitions the Lord undoubtedly grants what is asked, if we do not neglect to keep the agreement contained in the final condition. Hence he adds: “If you forgive,” etc.

Hallowed, etc. Here we pray for the spirit of wisdom, so that we may not first in any respect depart from the sanctification of the name, but that the Father’s name may be displayed in the conduct and life of his sons.

[Col. 0101A] The Father’s name is in us, who are called sons, and we ask that it be sanctified. This does not mean that he himself should become holier, but that the increase of his sanctification may work in us; for the sanctification of his sons is attributed to his name. Thus one says that it is sanctified just as it is glorified and magnified in us: “Hallowed,” that is, let it be regarded by human beings as holy, just as it is, and let God become known to them in such a way that they do not suppose anything to be holier.

**VERSE 10.**—Your kingdom come. Here the spirit of understanding is requested, by which the heart is cleansed so that God may be seen. The hardness and power of the devil are excluded, and this will happen more perfectly in the future, when he has emptied every principality and power and the kingdom has been handed over to God the Father. It appropriately follows that, after adoption as sons, we should seek the kingdom that is owed to sons.

[Col. 0101B] The kingdom of God always exists; but let it come—that is, let it be manifested to human beings, who do not see it, like the blind do not see light. No one will be able to remain ignorant of it when the Son comes to judge. In it the saints will also reign, as it is said: “Receive the kingdom prepared for you” (Matt. XXV), etc.

The future kingdom is disclosed to those entering it by the spirit of understanding, and purity of heart is attributed to them; through that purity God, reigning there, will be seen as he is. There the spirit of wisdom will be fulfilled, the seventh sanctification of his name. In the perfection of the six petitions, the coming of the kingdom is requested, so that we may all run toward the perfect man. Then, when we rest in him, may he himself be sanctified in us while we are sanctified in him. We rightly ask that his rest be sanctified in us, so that, sanctified eternally in him, we may rest in him. In this sanctification the peace of blessedness is established and complete wisdom is bestowed.

Your will be done. Here the spirit of counsel is requested, by which God’s will is sought so that it may be fulfilled by us.

God’s will is ordered on earth as in heaven by the spirit of counsel. We also need the spirit of counsel, so that God’s will may be directed in us and we may be able to be merciful in action. God’s will is always done, but we pray that the freedom of our will may be joined by grace to his will, which is our sanctification and eternal life. God’s will is the keeping of his commandments.

As in heaven. As it is done among the angels, so among human beings. Or, as it is done among the righteous, so among converted sinners. Or, as in Christ, so in the Church. Or, as with the mind I serve the Law of God, so also in the flesh.

According to the spirit, we are heaven; according to the flesh, we are earth. Therefore we pray that, just as in heaven—that is, in the spirit—so also on earth the will may be done, so that flesh and spirit may constitute the spiritual person of whom it is said: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God.” Nor do we merely pray that we may wish for good things; rather, let the will be done in us so that we may live for you and not for ourselves. These three things are possessed more perfectly in the future, but for now we pray for them partially, so that afterward they may be possessed more perfectly. The four petitions that follow are the supports of the present life.

**VERSE 11.**—Bread. The hunger for righteousness, so that it may reach satiety, is supported by the spirit of fortitude. Therefore we pray: “Give us our daily bread,” without which we would die of hunger.

Bread is the body of Christ, or the word of God, or God himself, whom we need daily, or the one who is above all substances. This is the living bread that descended from heaven (John VI), whose nature is exalted above all substances.

Our. Because Christ has become ours, and God the Father has given us all things together with Christ. Therefore we pray that what is ours through the gift may be given daily through its effect.

Supersubstantial. Or daily. For “those who eat me will still hunger” (Eccl. XLIV). Here it is daily; in the homeland it is eternal. This bread must continually refresh us inwardly through faith and love, because no one can live without it. Alternatively, spiritual commandments are called bread, since they must always be practiced or preserved.

**VERSE 12.**—And forgive, etc. After food he asks forgiveness of sins, so that the person who is nourished by God may live in God and reach eternal life.

When we say, “Forgive us our debts,” we ask for the spirit of knowledge, by which we understand offenses that cannot be understood without the spirit of knowledge. Knowledge pertains to the use of temporal things; it is the virtue by which evils are avoided and good things sought, so that we may lament our own contagions and those of others and desire good things.

As. Behold the caution by which we are bound: he inclines us to mercy toward one another, promises forgiveness to those who sin against us, and promises forgiveness to us and, through us, to others.

We must not refuse forgiveness for guilt. Hence: “When you pray, forgive if you have anything against anyone”; otherwise your Father will not forgive your sins.

One may lawfully demand repayment of money from another, but one may never justly refuse forgiveness to a person who asks it for sins.

**VERSE 13.**—And do not lead us. Rather, enlighten us by the spirit of knowledge, so that we may know by what evils we are entangled; and we ask that our tears may be useful when we say: “Forgive us our debts.”

And do not lead us, etc. This does not mean that he himself leads us into temptation, but that he abandons us and permits us to go. We do not pray not to be tempted, but not to be overcome even briefly. Temptation is necessary for the crown.

And do not lead us, etc. Do not abandon us in temptation so that we are overcome; even if you permit us to be tempted, without temptation no one has been tested.

But deliver us from evil. This one petition contains as much as all those preceding it.

So that by the Spirit of the fear of God all harmful things may be driven away, inwardly and outwardly, and we may live blessedly in poverty.

**But deliver us.** Do not permit us to be led into that which has not yet occurred, and deliver us from that into which we have been led. When this has been accomplished, nothing is to be feared and nothing remains to be requested.

**From evil, from every evil, visible and invisible.** This deliverance is necessary daily, since no one lives without evil of soul and body; but it will be completed at the end, when we shall be immortal and incapable of suffering. From the lowest things to the highest we ascend gradually in this way. We are delivered from evil through the Spirit of fear [Col. 0103A]; once delivered from it, we desire to be poor in spirit and in material things, while saying, “Do not lead us into temptation.” We ask for the Spirit of piety, so that the inner person may become gentle and meek and not be shaken by temptation.

**VERSE 14.**—“For if you forgive.” He established the form according to which we wish to be judged. Hence confidence before God in obtaining what is asked corresponds to those who forgive; but those who demand repayment are gnawed by the punishment of vengeance or condemnation.

**VERSE 15.**—“But if you do not forgive.” No excuse is left, because each person will be judged in the future according to this sentence. From this it is clear that each person is condemned in his own unbelief.

**VERSE 16.**—“When you fast.” After teaching how one should pray, he teaches about fasting, which likewise pertains to purity of heart [Col. 0103B], so that the heart may not cease to be single toward God while it is drawn toward outward things. “Do not become.” He does not prohibit the virtue, but the pretended appearance of virtue.

It is good, through fasting, to be sorrowful for sins unto repentance and to humble our soul; hence: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psalm 50). But he prohibits the sorrow that is displayed for praise. Hence he does not simply say, “Do not fast,” but adds, “like the hypocrites, sorrowful.”

**“They disfigure themselves.”** That is, they cover themselves beyond the limits of human condition. Just as ostentation is shown through the brightness of clothing, so it is shown through excessive squalor and emaciation. To disfigure is almost to scatter and destroy, and to reduce the beauty of the face almost to nothing. “Their faces.” With mournful filth [Col. 0103C], in which there is also ostentation; and by this appearance of religion they deceive people all the more.

Note that sheep ought not to cast off their own skins, but to be clothed with them, even if wolves sometimes conceal themselves in those skins.

**VERSE 17.**—“Anoint your head.” Refresh your mind with spiritual joy during the days of abstinence, so that the fragrance of love may spread through works of mercy. Wash your conscience with tears, so that it may be clean before God. For the work of mercy without a clean conscience is not sufficient, nor is a clean conscience sufficient without that work. It was customary among the Palestinians to anoint the head at festivals. Therefore, “anoint your head,” that is, present yourself as festive and cheerful; refresh your mind with spiritual oil; and do not seek outward praise for your fasting. But since you have thus turned away from the world, rejoice before God; and in this way you will cleanse your face—that is, your heart—from its filth. Once these have been removed [Col. 0103D], you will be able to see God.

“Anoint your head.” Behold, not everything in the New Testament is still to be understood according to the letter. For it would be ridiculous for people to be smeared with oil while fasting. Rather, the mind must be anointed with the spirit of his love, and we must mortify ourselves by sharing in his sufferings—not with the oil of flattery; otherwise fasts are vain.

Christ became an ointment for us; poured out through the passion of his death, he filled his Church with his fragrance. Therefore we ought not to fast for the sake of anyone else; rather, filled with his Spirit, let us mortify the flesh through abstinence and share in his passion. Let us therefore be anointed with him, so that works of mercy may abound and charity may be poured out inwardly, because without him the cup of our fasting is not made drunk with the affection of piety.

He fasts for God who mortifies himself for love of him and gives to another what he takes away from himself. [Col. 0104A]

**VERSE 18.**—“And your Father.” The Father is within through faith, and he rewards deeds done in secret. Therefore fasting must take place where he himself sees. It is necessary that the person fasting should fast in such a way as to please the one whom he carries in his breast.

**VERSE 19.**—“Do not store up treasures.” He commands earthly possessions to be distributed for the sake of purity of heart.

**VERSE 20.**—“But store up treasures.” As though he were saying: When you fast or perform some good work, store it where corruption cannot approach.

**“In heaven.”** That is, place all your hope in heavenly things, advancing by faith and embracing charity. “In heaven,” that is, in the spiritual firmament [Col. 0104B], which does not pass away: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.” If, then, the heart is in heaven, it is clean, because heavenly things are clean. But if it rolls about in earthly things, how is it clean? That is, if it does something in order to obtain earthly things, how is it clean? For even if a thing is clean in its own category, a nobler thing becomes defiled when it is mixed with an inferior one, as gold with silver, or silver with lead.

**VERSE 21.**—“For where your treasure is.” If it is on earth, the heart is below; if it is in heaven, the heart is fixed in Christ.

**VERSE 22.**—“The lamp.” He continues concerning purity of heart. Just as the eye directs the limbs toward action, so intention and the light of faith direct all virtues. A lamp is a light in a vessel; so charity is in faith. When faith ceases [Col. 0104C], charity alone will be light.

With regard to the outward person, he teaches the function of the inner person: through the intention of the mind and the light of faith all virtues are illuminated, so that they make the body luminous.

Again, this passage itself pertains to purity of heart, or it may be understood in relation to the grace of the preceding works that appear openly.

**“If the eye is,” etc.** If with a pure intention you do the good that you are able to do, your works are works of light, even if they do not appear so to people. If the intention is perverse, whatever is done is evil, even if it appears right.

The eye is one and single—namely, charity—which now shines in faith as in a vessel.

[Col. 0104D]

**VERSE 23.**—“But if the eye.” If the intention does not arise from faith, the whole inner person is dark. For whatever is not from faith is sin.

**“It will be dark.”** Since the intention gives form to the work that follows. Therefore, if the good things you do are darkness because they are done with an evil intention, what of those things that are evil in themselves and are done with an evil intention?

**“If therefore the light.”** The intention by which we do whatever we do, and which is known to us, is called light. The outcome of the matter, however, is uncertain: when I give or do something for someone, I do not know whether it will turn out for that person’s good or harm. Therefore he calls it darkness. He says, then: If the intention by which you act—which is known to you—is sullied by the desire for temporal things, how much more the deed itself, whose outcome is uncertain? For even if what you do turns out well for another, what you do without a good intention will benefit you nothing, because what is imputed to you is how you acted, not how it turned out for the other person.

[Col. 0105A]

**VERSE 24.**—“No one can,” etc. As though he were saying: You cannot do good in the sight of people and, on that account, please God. You cannot store up treasures simultaneously in heaven and on earth, nor serve both vices and virtues. Whatever you do is done either from love of God or in slavery to the devil.

Since the kingdom of God and that of the devil are opposed to one another, no one can serve in both at the same time. Hence those who are baptized renounce the devil and his works.

**“Either he will hate the one.”** There is no middle position. Whatever you do is done either from love of God or in slavery to the devil.

**(AUGUSTINE.)** The devil must always be hated; God, however, etc., up to: “but they despise him, overcome by their own desire and by the devil’s persuasion.”

**“Or he will cling to the one.”** (The same author.) He does not in fact love him [Col. 0105B]—for no one loves the devil—but, entangled in his own desire, etc., up to: “even though he does not love the one whose maidservant he loves.”

**“He will despise the other.”** He will not in fact hate him, for no conscience can hate God. Augustine later reconsidered this, saying: “I do not see that this ought to have been said.” For many are described in the words: “The pride of those who hate you” (Psalm 3), etc.

**“And Mammon.”** Mammon, in the Syriac language, means riches; to serve them is to deny God. He does not say that one may not possess them—for that is permitted if one administers them well—but that one must not serve them, which is characteristic of the greedy. This name is said to belong to a demon who presides over riches—not because riches are in his power, but because he uses them to deceive by entangling people in the snares of wealth.

[Col. 0105C]

**VERSE 25.**—“Therefore I say to you,” etc. Because you cannot serve God and Mammon. “Do not be anxious,” which is to serve riches. Throughout the whole discourse he has commanded contempt for the world and confidence in future things, ordering us both to endure evils without taking revenge, to love enemies, and to flee human glory. Now he wishes to strengthen this through faith in the hope of eternal things, because many are made sluggish by love of present things and despair of future ones.

Bread is prepared in the sweat of the face, but labor must be undertaken while anxiety must be removed—the anxiety that disturbs the mind when it fears either that possessions will perish or that what has been worked for will not be obtained.

**“For your souls.”** That is, for the animal life to which these things are necessary. Commit all your hope to God, because you can acquire or retain nothing except what he has decreed. [Col. 0105D]
