Here “soul” is used for life, which is sustained by food, as in: “He who loves his soul will lose it” (John 12).

Animal life is nourished by food and here stands for life: it lives together with beasts. Whoever loses it for Christ’s sake will find it spiritual, unto eternal life.

**“Is not the soul?”** etc. Life is not for the sake of food, nor the body for the sake of clothing, but the reverse. Therefore the mind should not be anxious in order to obtain what was created for its sake.

As though he were saying: He who gave the greater things—that is, life and the body—will also give the lesser things—that is, food and clothing. [Col. 0106A] Let no one doubt these promises of truth. Let a person be what he ought to be, and all things for whose sake they were made will immediately be added to him.

**VERSE 26.**—“Consider.” This concerns food. The saints are rightly compared with birds because they seek heaven; some are so removed from the world that they already do nothing on earth but dwell in heaven through contemplation alone. Of them it is said: “Who are these who fly like clouds?” (Isaiah 60), etc.

These examples do not prohibit diligence in laboring for one’s needs, but anxiety, so that your entire confidence may be in God, since even birds live without anxiety.

**“And your Father.”** He magnifies and confirms the confidence of the children, because if the Father’s goodness extends even to those things, how much more to the children of adoption?

[Col. 0106B]

**VERSE 27.**—“But which of you,” etc. Leave the care of governing the body to the one who brought it to this measure.

**VERSE 28.**—“And concerning clothing.” This does not mean that it is unsuitable to work and provide for oneself, but that all anxiety must be cast aside and hope placed in God. “Consider the lilies of the field.” He confirms his exhortation concerning clothing with a fitting example.

**VERSE 29.**—“For not even Solomon,” etc. What royal purple, what woven design, can be compared with flowers? The color itself is called the covering of flowers, just as we say, “Blush covered him.”

**VERSE 30.**—“If therefore the grass of the field.” If God adorns so beautifully things that exist only for temporal use and will quickly wither and be burned in the fire—

[Col. 0106C] “Tomorrow” is used in Scripture for the future, as Jacob says: “Tomorrow my righteousness will answer for me” (Genesis 30).

**“It is thrown into the oven.”** Some books read: “into the fire,” or “into a heap that has the appearance of an oven.” How much more will he clothe you. Therefore all confidence must be placed in him. If we are not confident even concerning these things, how do we hope for invisible things? Faith is very small if it is not certain even concerning the least things. Therefore he also instills confidence concerning eternal things and condemns unbelief.

**“You of little faith.”** Whoever doubts any promise has little faith; and the more he doubts, the less he finds those things for which he was anxious.

[Col. 0106D]

**VERSE 31.**—“Therefore do not be anxious,” etc. He repeats and reinforces more fully what he taught at the beginning of the discourse: that we should live without anxiety.

**“Do not,” etc.** Here those seem to be reproved who, scorning ordinary food or clothing, seek more luxurious or more austere nourishment or garments than those with whom they live.

**“To be anxious.”** Anxiety chokes the word of God so that it bears no fruit, and makes a person like a pagan—that is, an unbeliever.

**VERSE 32.**—“For all these things.” What more, then, does he have than a pagan, whose unbelief troubles his mind and exhausts him with the cares of this life?

**“The nations.”** The nations have no concern for future things, but it belongs to the children to seek the kingdom.

**“For he knows.”** These things have been provided by God, who knows that they are necessary for us along his way.

**“Your Father.”** In this way he makes his children secure concerning the goodness [Col. 0107A] and providence of the Father, that is, free from anxiety.

**VERSE 33.**—“Seek therefore.” Here he clearly shows that these things are not to be sought as our goods, even though they are necessary. The kingdom of God, however, must be sought, and our end must be placed in it, so that we may do everything for its sake. For example: Let us eat so that we may evangelize, not evangelize so that we may eat. When he says “first,” he signifies what comes afterward, not in time but in worth. The former is to be sought; the latter is necessary for its sake. Therefore, seek first the kingdom of God—that is, place it before all other things.

**“And all these things.”** All things belong to the children; therefore all these things will be added even to those who do not seek them. If they are taken away, it is for testing [Col. 0107B]; if they are given, it is for thanksgiving, because all things work together for good.

**VERSE 34.**—“Anxious.” That is, with the fear, sorrow, and distress of cares that disturb the mind.

**“For tomorrow.”** (AUGUSTINE.) For the future; concerning present things he permits labor, hence the Apostle says: “Night and day we worked, so that we would not burden anyone” (1 Thessalonians 2). But concerning future things, which divine providence arranges, this is not fitting, etc., up to: “because the one who commanded this, and whom the angels served, had a purse for this very example to be given; from it he provided what was necessary for use, and Judas was its keeper.”

**“The day.”** Not the day that the Lord made, but the day that Job and Jeremiah cursed—that is, the day the devil discovered.

**“It is sufficient.”** And because care for the present overwhelms minds, the evil of the day must not be allowed to germinate.

# CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0107C]

**VERSE 1.**—“Do not judge.” This concerns doubtful matters, because judgment is made concerning manifest things, not concerning those whose purpose is uncertain; no one judges such matters without danger.

Judgment is rash when those to whom judgment has not been entrusted judge, whether the matter concerns manifest or hidden things. Judgment is entrusted either to the teachers of the Church or to the rulers of the earth. If these judge manifest things—that is, things established by conviction or confession—they do not judge rashly. If they judge uncertain things, they judge rashly. These are the judgments he prohibits.

**VERSE 2.**—“For with what judgment,” etc. As though he were saying: With the intention with which you do good, you will be delivered; and with the intention with which you do evil, you will be punished. He is speaking of those matters in which we either offend by judging rashly or are excused by acting rightly. Therefore he adds: “With what measure.” [Col. 0107D]

And justly: those whose will had no end of sinning, although their sinning had an end, will have no end of punishment; and those whose judgment was without mercy will be judged without mercy.

**“With what measure.”** In the measure by which one thing has been measured, such as wheat, another thing may be measured, such as barley; and there may be different quantities, for example, one bushel of one thing and a hundred of another. God does this, and not unjustly, so that it may remain with them eternally.

The disgrace itself, or the evil that you have suffered, is also the reason why you incur the punishment that is due.

[Col. 0108A] Justly, those who wish to enjoy sin eternally also find eternal punishment; their will had no end of sinning, nor will their torment have an end.

**VERSE 3.**—“But why do you see,” etc. Here is a moderation of judgment: one who is preoccupied with greater faults must not judge another concerning lesser ones. Many, preoccupied with greater faults, prefer to criticize and condemn lesser faults in a brother rather than correct them. Thus, if they are full of hatred, envy, or malice, they condemn in another what anger makes him do—anger being like a speck, while hatred is like a beam. An angry person may sometimes wish another to be corrected; one who hates cannot wish this. Therefore it is said to be impossible for one who carries a beam to remove a speck from his brother. First, then, the beam of hatred, envy, deceit, and every kind of malice must be cast out, so that we may rebuke our brother mercifully, with regard to God and not ourselves. [Col. 0108B] Whether the correction benefits him or not, we shall nevertheless be secure because our own eye is single.

Someone free from this vice is scarcely found, because each person favors himself and easily reproves what belongs to another. By tolerating another’s faults more harshly than his own, he assumes authority to rebuke without the example of correcting himself.

At least in the very matter in which they judge rashly, they have a beam in their eye.

**VERSE 4.**—“Or how can you say to your brother?” That is, you cannot correct a lesser fault—such as anger—in your brother until you have driven the greater fault—hatred or envy—from your own heart.

**VERSE 5.**—“Hypocrite, cast out.” Such people, out of hatred and spite, undertake to accuse everything and wish to appear advisers without the example of their own correction. A teacher is not qualified to heal another who has not yet healed himself. [Col. 0108C]

**VERSE 6.**—“Do not give what is holy,” etc. Once the eye has been purified, the stewards of the Church may chastise others, but they must not give what is holy to dogs. For just as it is dangerous to hide it, so it is wasteful to give it to dogs. Mysteries must not be opened to such people, but the Holy of Holies must be covered with a veil. Things that are clearer and, as it were, more ordinary may be spoken.

“Do not.” The holy thing and the pearl signify the same thing—that is, the Gospel and the Church’s sacraments. It is holy because by nature it is inviolable and must not be corrupted by anyone. It is a pearl because it lies hidden and is drawn, as it were, from open shells; it is a precious gem that cannot be corrupted.

Dogs are truly those who bark and tear apart what is whole [Col. 0108D]; pigs are those who despise and trample it. Alternatively, dogs are those who have returned to their vomit; pigs are those who have not yet been converted but wallow in the mud of vices.

**“And turn.”** Lest they tear apart something else that they hear—not the pearls that they trample, but you in their indignation. For it is not easy to find anything pleasing to such people.

**VERSE 7.**—“Ask.” By these steps, the way, the truth, and the life are granted to those who contend lawfully. Christ is the way on which one walks, the truth by which one finds, and the door at which one knocks, so that we may enter to him through him.

**(AUGUSTINE.)** I thought it necessary to explain laboriously how these three differ from one another, but it is much better, etc., up to: “For he did not say to those asking, seeking, and knocking.”

[Col. 0109A]

**VERSE 8.**—“For everyone,” etc. To provide constancy in persevering, diligence in seeking, and confidence in obtaining, he adds this. “Everyone,” etc. Above he taught what we should ask for—namely, the kingdom. Here he teaches confidence, so that we may ask without hesitation. He does not deny himself to those who ask, since he freely offered himself to those who did not ask. Those who seek will find him who gave them the means of finding even when they did not seek; and he will open to those who knock, who cries: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock” (Revelation 3).

**VERSE 9.**—“Or who is there,” etc. He explains what should be asked for and, from human benevolence toward children, commends the Father’s diligence toward us. To those asking for Christ, right faith does not give a stone of stumbling or hardness of heart. [Col. 0109B] Likewise, if you ask your Father for charity, without which all other things are nothing, it is like a table without bread, whose opposite is hardness of heart.

**VERSE 10.**—“If he asks for a fish.” By the fish is meant faith, nourished beneath the flowing waters of the Holy Spirit.

He calls faith in invisible things a fish, either because of the water of baptism, or because it is caught from invisible places, or because it is not broken by the waves of this world. In Luke’s Gospel the comparison of the egg and the scorpion follows. In the egg hope is also understood, because the embryo is not yet fully formed in it but is hoped for through incubation. In the scorpion, whose sting must be feared from behind, the opposite of hope is understood—namely, looking backward, when hope ought to extend toward what lies ahead.

[Col. 0109C]

**VERSE 11.**—“If therefore you,” etc. Since fathers give good things to their children, much more will our Father, who is incomparably good, give good things to those who ask him as children.

**“You know how to give good things.”** According to the understanding of those who regard these things as good, although they are also good by their nature and belong to this life—things that the evil person does not give from his own possession. “The earth is the Lord’s” (Psalm 23), etc.

Alternatively, the apostles are called evil in relation to themselves, in comparison with God, who alone is good, from whom all good things come.

**“He will give good things.”** That is, the Holy Spirit; or good things—namely, eternal things—which are given only to children.

**“To those who ask him.”** He is the distributor of all spiritual goods, so that works of charity may be fulfilled.

**VERSE 12.**—“Therefore everything,” etc. To love one who loves is natural; but to be compelled by benefits to love one who does not love is the perfection of Christ. When he commanded us first [Col. 0109D] to do to others what we want done to us, he immediately confirms the same meaning by saying: “Therefore, whatever things,” etc. That is, the good things you wish to receive from others, do the same to them, so that love of neighbor may be fulfilled; without love it cannot rightly be perfected.

Therefore he adds: “This is the law and the prophets,” etc. For neither is God loved without one’s neighbor, nor is one’s neighbor loved without God. One’s neighbor must not be judged out of hatred or envy. Therefore, with the charity by which you would wish to be admonished, act toward others.

**“That people should do to you.”** Because he adds “people,” he speaks only of love of neighbor. Hence he does not add “the whole law,” but leaves aside the love of God. If he had said, “Whatever you wish done to you, do to others,” he would have embraced both, in which [Col. 0110A] the whole law is contained, written for the salvation of humanity in the prophets and the law.

**VERSE 13.**—“Enter.” Although it is difficult to do to others what you wish done to yourself, nevertheless it must be done so that we may enter.

**“Through the narrow.”** The narrow way is sought, but it is not found by everyone. Nor do all who find it enter through it, because, captured by the world, they turn back.

**“And the broad.”** Even if they do not seek it, everyone finds this way, because everyone is born in it. Pleasure, like an importunate prostitute, invites everyone with its delights; therefore many enter through it.

**VERSE 14.**—“How narrow.” It is very narrow to leave everything else aside, to love only one thing, to seek only one thing, to knock daily at one door, not to pursue prosperity, and not to fear adversity.

**“And few.”** If few find it [Col. 0110B], fewer still strive to enter through it. No one enters without labor and purity of spirit.

**VERSE 15.**—“Beware.” After saying that the narrow way is found by few, lest his own people become entangled in the errors of false prophets, he added: “Beware.” What he had said above about the broad gate, he now speaks more openly of as false prophets.

“Beware.” Although this may be understood of all who show one thing in dress and speech and another in their deeds, it applies especially to heretics. Covered by a certain garment of piety, they are ravenous wolves in their poisoned minds and harmful intentions, either persecuting outwardly when opportunity is given or corrupting inwardly.

**“To you in sheep’s clothing.”** In the sight of people they resemble ministers of righteousness when they fast, pray, and give alms; but their fruits are not theirs [Col. 0110C], because this is reckoned to them as vice.

**“By their fruits.”** (JEROME.) Not by their clothing but by their works; this applies to manifest things, etc., up to: “but sheep ought not to cast off their skins, even if wolves sometimes conceal themselves in them.”

**VERSE 16.**—“Can it be?” Allegorically: Thorns and thistles are heretics, from whom no wise person can obtain holiness or truth; rather, they tear and wound those who approach. Alternatively, thorns and thistles are the cares of the world and the prickings of vices.

Grapes and figs are the sweetness of the new way of life for which Christ hungered in us, and the fervor of love that makes the human heart rejoice. Therefore grapes and figs do not come from thorns and thistles, because a mind still oppressed by the habits of the old person can pretend, but cannot produce [Col. 0110D] the fruits of the new person.

If the words or deeds of evil people sometimes benefit the good, the evil do not accomplish this; it comes about through God’s providence. It is not their fruit, but the fruit of the vine that sometimes flourishes above thorns. The cluster is to be gathered, but the thorn avoided.

The vine is Christ. His own are the branches that bear grapes—that is, the works of the Spirit that intoxicate the mind.

**VERSE 17.**—“So every tree.” That is, according to the impossibility stated above: a fruit of sweetness cannot burst forth from a bad root. Good fruits must be expected from a good tree.

A good or bad tree does not mean nature, which was created good by God in all people, but a good or bad will. The fruits are works [Col. 0111A], which can be neither good when the will is evil nor evil when the will is good.

The fruits of a good tree are joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, and so forth; only a good will produces these fruits. Conversely, an evil intention nourishes evil fruits.

**VERSE 18.**—“It cannot.” He does not say: “A bad tree cannot become good, or a good tree bad,” because Paul became an apostle from being a persecutor; and while the soul’s nature remains intact, the disposition of the will is either corrupted or changed for the better.

The will of each person is a good or bad tree. Just as a tree is rooted in the earth, so the will is rooted in the soul.

The fruits of a bad tree are the works of the flesh, namely, unclean fornication and wantonness.

[Col. 0111B]

**VERSE 19.**—“Every tree.” By this sentence he condemns hypocrites and false prophets, and confirms by this example what he taught above concerning purity of heart: no one obtains good fruit from a bad intention, nor reaps anything but good from a good intention.

**VERSE 20.**—“Therefore by their fruits.” As though he were saying: Beware of false prophets, and recognize them by their fruits.

[Col. 0111C]

**VERSE 21.**—“Not everyone who says.” Just as those who possess the appearance of a good life but hold an evil doctrine must be avoided, so here, conversely, those who possess sound faith and teaching but live shamefully must also be avoided. Both are necessary: works must be confirmed by speech, and speech by works.

**“Who says, ‘Lord, Lord.’”** The road to the kingdom of God is obedience, not the utterance of a name. This is not truly and properly to say it when the utterance disagrees with the will. Concerning this the Apostle says: “No one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12).

**VERSE 22.**—“Many will say.” Above all, one must beware of those who, because of Christ’s name, even possess miraculous powers. Although the Lord performed these miracles for the sake of unbelievers, he nevertheless warned us not to be deceived by such people, thinking that invisible wisdom is present where there is a visible miracle. Hence he adds: “Many will say.”

How pure and single the eye must be, therefore, so that the way of wisdom may be found amid so many deceptions.

**VERSE 23.**—“I never knew you.” Light does not know darkness—that is, it does not look upon it, because if it did, darkness would not exist.

**“You who work iniquity.”** He does not say “you who worked,” lest he remove the possibility of repentance, but “you who work” in the judgment. Even if you no longer possess the power to sin, you still possess the inclination. [Col. 0111D]

**VERSE 24.**—“Therefore everyone.” As though he were saying: All the things stated above must be held firmly, because whoever holds them will be made like Christ, while whoever does not hold them will be made like the devil.

**“Who hears these words of mine.”** He says “which were spoken on the mountain” to show that the sermon delivered on the mountain is complete in all the commandments by which Christian life is formed.

**“Will be made like.”** Just as Christ constructs one Church from various persons, teaches it, governs it, and prepares it for eternal life, so this person builds for himself an everlasting dwelling from various virtues, and at its future dedication he will rejoice with Christ.

**“A man.”** [Col. 0112A] The one who says: “As a wise architect I laid the foundation in Christ.”

**“Who built.”** He builds in Christ who does what he hears from him.

**“Upon the rock.”** From this Peter received his name because of the firmness of faith; that is, he built the Church upon himself.

**VERSE 25.**—“And the rain descended.” The devil attacks in three ways: through the desire of the flesh, through the outward delights of the world, or by himself, when he loosens the whole force of the winds of temptation.

**“The rain.”** Desire, by which each person is tempted, and which softens the firmness of faith. If this does not prevail, greater floods arise.

**VERSE 26.**—“Who hears my words,” etc., outwardly. Therefore he has no excuse, but his ruin is great, because he despised warnings of salvation.

**“A foolish man.”** Of him it is said: “An enemy has done this,” whose works are all unstable and exposed to ruin.

**“Upon the sand.”** [Col. 0112B] Whatever things are founded upon the desire for vices will not stand.

**VERSE 27.**—“And it fell, and its ruin was great.” Every conscience that does not remain fixed in hope in God cannot endure in temptations. It is shaken all the more violently as it is separated from higher things and attached more deeply to worldly things. Truly, all evil people, and all who are good only in appearance, become worse when any temptation breaks upon them.

**VERSE 28.**—“The crowds.” Or some people among the crowd, because they were unbelievers; or, rather, everyone was astonished at the excellence of his wisdom.

# CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0112C]

**VERSE 1.**—“When he had come down.” After the Lord’s descent from the mountain, etc., up to: “he shows after how great an interval of time.”

**“When he had come down.”** According to Luke, he delivered the sermon in a level place, perhaps the sermon he had already given above.

**“They followed.”** Some because of love, others because of his teaching, others because of wonder and healing.

**VERSE 2.**—“He worshiped him, saying, ‘Lord.’” Before asking, he displayed reverence for his divinity.

**“If you are willing, you can cleanse me.”** I do not doubt his willingness as though I were suspicious of his compassion; rather, conscious of my own filth, I do not presume.

**VERSE 3.**—“Stretching out.” After the sermon he performs miracles by which the sermon is confirmed among its hearers.

**“He touched.”** Not because he could not heal without touching, but to indicate that he was not subject to the law, but Lord of the law [Col. 0112D], who does not fear contagion.

**“He touched.”** Because of his humanity, to teach us not to despise anyone because of bodily pollution.

Grace appears above the law—which excludes the leper—for grace heals him, as he says: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it,” etc.

**“I am willing.”** He healed him in the manner in which he had been entreated, and then he commanded: “Be cleansed.” Behold the power.

**VERSE 4.**—“See that you tell no one,” etc. He commanded him to keep silent, yet the man could not keep silent. This does not mean that he wished something and was unable to accomplish it. Rather, he gave an example that his own people should wish to remain hidden in the great things they do, but that, in order to benefit others, they should be revealed against their will.

**“Tell no one”** (Mark 1). Yet Mark says that the man proclaimed this after he had gone out, as though he had become an evangelist.

**“Go.”** [Col. 0113A] He sends him to the priests out of humility, so that he might show honor to the priests, whom the law commands those who have been cleansed to offer gifts; and so that, when they saw him, they might believe, or, if they did not believe, might be without excuse; and so that he would not appear to violate the law.

**“Show yourself to the priest.”** So that the priest might understand that he had been healed not by the order of the law but by the grace of God above the law.

**“Offer,” etc.** Because I do not abolish the law, since the true sacrifice has not yet begun.

**“For a testimony.”** That is, so that they may believe in the Lord if the leprosy of impiety departs.

**“For a testimony.”** For spiritual healing, a spiritual offering must be presented: the person himself.

**VERSE 7.**—“I will come and heal him.” And the centurion answered, etc., up to: “lest he be thought physically unable to go.”

[Col. 0113B]

**VERSE 8.**—“I am not worthy.” Because of his awareness of a pagan way of life, he fears that Christ’s presence will burden him rather than help him. For even if he possessed faith, he had not yet been instructed in the sacraments. Yet he knew that grace could give what our weakness does not presume.

**VERSE 9.**—“For I also,” etc. “If I, a man,” etc., up to: “as Cornelius is called a just man who feared God” (Acts 10).

**VERSE 11.**—“They will come from east and west and recline.” Or the east signifies those who, once enlightened, immediately pass onward; the west signifies those who endure sufferings until death. These two regions of the world designate the nations that were to be called.

**VERSE 12.**—“But the children of the kingdom will be cast out.” Because in this world they enjoy God’s benefits, according to the saying: “He makes his sun rise upon the just and the unjust.” Now they seem to be in the presence of the Lord [Col. 0113C], but then they will not be.

**“Into the outer darkness.”** Because they will be expelled outside by the Lord, etc., up to: “he repents that he persisted in sin.”

**“Weeping.”** By this the greatness of the torments is shown. Weeping signifies the torment of the soul; the gnashing of teeth signifies that of the body.

**VERSE 14.**—“And when he had come,” etc. Matthew does not state when this happened, etc., up to: “to bring matters to his memory for narration.”

**“And she was feverish.”** The Greek term for “fever” is omitted in the supplied text; in Latin it is called *fervor* (“heat”). If this illness sometimes causes trembling, that belongs to human nature.

**VERSE 15.**—“And he touched,” etc. Luke says that they asked him, etc., up to: “Who understands his transgressions? Cleanse me from my hidden faults” (Psalm 18).

**“And she arose,” etc.** [Col. 0113D] It is natural for those suffering from fever to become weak when recovery begins, etc., up to: “she ministers in the spirit.”

**VERSE 16.**—“When evening had come,” etc. The setting of the sun signifies the death of Christ, through which he healed more demoniacs than, while living in the flesh, he had healed sick people before.

**VERSE 18.**—“When Jesus saw.” It is clear that this was another day, etc., up to: “let us cross the bitter waves of the world.”

**VERSE 19.**—“And one who approached.” What Matthew says happened when he commanded them to cross the strait, while Luke says it happened as they were walking along the road, is not contradictory, because they were walking along the road in order to come to the strait.

**“Teacher.”** [Col. 0114A] As though he were one among many. He was also learned in letters, but not a spiritual hearer.

**“Teacher.”** He did not say “Lord,” but “teacher,” regarding him as one among many teachers.

**VERSE 20.**—“Foxes have dens.” As though he were saying: Why do you seek me for the profits of the world, etc., up to: “there is no place for Christ’s divinity.”

**“But the Son of man has nowhere,” etc.** Although people call him the Son of God, he himself calls himself the Son of man, because of humility.

**VERSE 21.**—“But another.” Note that this man was called by Jesus.

**“Lord.”** The one who intruded upon him calls him “teacher,” like an exalted Pharisee; the other, who was received, humbly calls him “Lord,” like the tax collector.

**VERSE 22.**—“His own dead.” Those who departed through guilt, since they themselves live with guilt.

**“To bury the dead.”** This means to support sinners in their sin.

[Col. 0114B]

**VERSE 23.**—“And when he had boarded.” He who did great things on earth crosses over to the sea, so that he may do them there also, and may appear as Lord of earth and sea.

### VERSE 24

“Behold, a storm arose.” The storm did not arise of itself, but at his command, so that the disciples might fear more and ask him, and that, when they asked, he might display his power. “He was sleeping.” The Lord sleeps in us—that is, faith in the Lord sleeps—when we act carelessly; and therefore there is a storm. But if faith rises again, it commands the winds and the waves.

### VERSE 25

“They awakened him.” First, Jesus must be aroused by prayers amid tribulations, so that, rising after his rebuke, he may command the winds and the sea, and there may be a great calm.

### VERSE 26

“O you of little faith,” and so forth. If you know that he is powerful on land, why do you not believe also at sea? The one who believes little is rebuked; the one who believes nothing is despised. “He commanded,” and so forth. Whatever is commanded perceives the one who commands. Note that every creature perceives its Creator. Things that are insensible to us are sensible to them.

### VERSE 27

“What sort of man is this?” and so forth. (ORIGEN.) “What sort of man is this, greater than Moses?” and so forth, up to “they obey, though they have no hearing.”

### VERSE 28

“Into the region of the Gerasenes.” Gerasa is a city of Arabia, and so forth, up to “visited by Christ through preachers.” “Two possessed men.” Mark and Luke mention one, and so forth, up to “they displayed the foulness of their bodies.” “Fierce.” Mark says that no one could any longer [materially uncertain: something concerning] the demoniac, and so forth, up to “they attacked anyone attempting to pass.”

### VERSE 29

“Jesus, Son of God.” (HILARY.) They should be regarded as having suspected rather than known this. (AMBROSE.) “Jesus, Son of God.” They knew as much about him as he wished them to know, and so forth, up to “they saw this in him but did not believe.” “Before the time.” For they knew that this was destined for them at God’s judgment, and so forth, up to “for there were two thousand, as Mark says.” “To torment us.” Christ’s presence is a torment to them; or they are tormented when they are driven out of the bodies whose torment they enjoyed, just as God’s presence is the refreshment of the angels.

### VERSE 31

“Send us.” Note that they have far less power to harm human beings by their own authority, since they cannot even harm animals. Unless someone has lived like a pig, the devil does not gain power over him, except perhaps for the purpose of testing him.

### VERSE 32

“And behold, with great…” Man is more worthy than beasts, since two thousand swine perished for the salvation of two human beings. Once the people of the nations had been delivered, the unbelievers practiced evil rites in hidden places, submerged in blind and profound curiosity.

### VERSE 33

“But the herdsmen fled.” For even certain leaders of the ungodly, although they flee the faith of Christ, do not cease to announce his power with wonder.

### VERSE 34

“They went out to meet him.” (BEDE.) Those who come out signify certain people bound by habit: they indeed marvel at and venerate Christ’s law, but are unwilling to suffer it; hence they ask him to depart. “And they found the man,” as Luke says, “clothed and sitting in his right mind at the feet of Jesus” (Luke 8). “They begged him.” They beg not out of pride but from humility, judging themselves unworthy, as Peter did, and the widow did with Elijah. They feared that the presence of his holiness would destroy them because of their sins, just as it had destroyed the swine.

## CHAPTER IX

### VERSE 1

“Into the city.” Do not suppose that this was Nazareth, and so forth, up to “Capernaum, as it were the capital.”

### VERSE 2

“They brought him.” These are teachers who lift up and bring people to Christ by admonishing and interceding. “Faith.” This shows how much one’s own faith avails before God, with whom another’s faith was so effective that it healed the man both within and without. “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you.” Luke says, “Man,” and so forth, up to “after removing the cause of the illness, he then heals the body.”

### VERSE 5

“Which is easier?” Note that illnesses sometimes occur because of sins, and so forth, up to “therefore: ‘With a double destruction the Lord will crush them.’” (BEDE.) “Which is easier?” Since you do not believe this spiritual reality, let the matter be proved by a visible sign, which is no less a display of power, so that you may recognize in the Son of Man the hidden power of majesty that can forgive sins as God.

### VERSE 6

“Then he said to the paralytic.” Behold: by the remission of the punishment, understand the remission of the guilt. “Rise.” To rise is to draw the soul away from carnal desires. “Take up your bed” means to raise the flesh from earthly desires to the will of the spirit. “Go to your house” means to return to paradise, or to return to the inner guardianship of oneself, so as not to sin again. “Take up your bed and go to your house.” Thus what had been a testimony of infirmity becomes proof of health.

### VERSE 7

“And he rose.” Great is the power where salvation immediately accompanies the command. Therefore, deservedly, those who were present, abandoning their blasphemies in astonishment, turned to praise such great majesty.

### VERSE 9

“He saw a man.” Here it seems more probable that he records something omitted earlier, since he chose the Twelve before the Sermon. “In the tax office.” Greek *telos*, Latin *vectigal*, “tax” or “tribute.” “Matthew” in Hebrew, *donatus* in Latin, “given,” because he received so great a gift of grace. “Levi” means “added” or “taken up,” because divine election took him up and added him to the number of the apostles. “Matthew.” The other Evangelists, out of modesty, and so forth, up to “the discourse mentioned above took place.” “Rising.” (BEDE.) Luke says more fully: “leaving everything, he followed him,” both in body and in mind. He was drawn not by fickleness but by the truth of his works and by divine power working inwardly. In perfect obedience and perfect renunciation, he abandoned his profits, eager to follow Christ.

### VERSE 10

“In the house.” He does not say whose house it was, but Luke makes it clear, and so forth, up to “the conversion of penitents is shown.” “Behold, many tax collectors.” A good omen: already many are being converted by his example. Already he is drawing many after him, destined to become an apostle and teacher of the nations. (JEROME.) “Tax collectors and sinners.” Tertullian says that these were gentiles, and so forth, up to “he commanded: ‘Do not go into the way of the nations.’” “Sinners came and reclined at table.” They were penitents, hoping for forgiveness through Matthew’s example; hence Mark says here that “many followed him” (Mark 2).

### VERSE 11

“Why does he eat with tax collectors?” The whole question, and so forth, up to “everything he did serves salvation.”

### VERSE 12

“But Jesus, hearing this, said.” He further strengthens the penitents whom he has received in faith, and calls the proud to the grace of humility and compassion. “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.” Christ is the physician, and so forth, up to “they cannot hunger, since they receive the word of God.”

### VERSE 13

“Go and learn.” To those puffed up with false righteousness he gives the counsel of correction, and so forth, up to “the sheep, the drachma, and the two sons.” “For I have not come to call the righteous.” What of Nathanael, Peter, Andrew, and so forth, up to “they now no longer seem righteous to themselves.”

### VERSE 14

“But your disciples do not fast.” John, Mark, and Luke, and so forth, up to “understand grace and power.”

### VERSE 15

“Can the wedding guests?” He means: You will act like mourners, and so forth, up to “but from all earthly things.” “To mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them.” By this word he expresses that fast, and so forth, up to “afterward they will fast, but they will not mourn.” “And then they will fast.” This mourning over the bridegroom’s absence was not lacking among the fathers before the Incarnation, nor after the Passion, except during the time when he lived with the disciples in the flesh. “They will fast.” From love of the world, not only from food. For since spiritual fasting is part of the new life, it is not yet suitable for those who are still devoted in other ways to the old life.

### VERSE 16

“But no one.” He means: Those who are carnal, not yet strengthened by faith in the Passion and Resurrection, and so forth, up to “it does not suit the oldness itself.” “For it takes away.” That is, the perfection of the new life, which is one, is divided, and the faith possessed by the old order is taken away from it, although the perfection of the new life was owed to it.

### VERSE 17

“Nor do they put.” He compares the same disciples to old wineskins, and so forth, up to “within we are renewed in the newness of understanding.”

### VERSE 18

“Behold, one of the rulers came.” Mark and Luke say that he was a ruler of the synagogue, and so forth, up to “he began to hope for and seek a remedy.”

### VERSE 20

“A woman who…” The gentile people seized, with firm hope, the salvation prepared for the Jews. “Twelve years.” She had suffered from the flow for twelve years, just as that daughter had grown for twelve years, because from the time when the synagogue began to serve God, the gentile people began to be polluted by idolatry and sin. She approached, believed, and spoke; for through these three—faith and deed—every salvation is obtained.

### VERSE 21

“If I touch.” The fringe, not the garment. Since she did not see the Lord in the flesh, she received through the apostles the word of the Incarnation. Blessed is the one who touches even the outermost part of the word with faith.

### VERSE 22

“Take courage, daughter.” She certainly believed when she asked, but he impresses upon her the strength and perseverance of faith.

### VERSE 23

“When he saw.” The flute players are those singing a mournful song. They are teachers who soothe their subjects with their own grief, and the crowd of Jews who kick against Christ’s teaching. “And the crowd.” Since the synagogue, and so forth, up to “appeared in its reception.”

### VERSE 24

“It is not…” She is dead to you. But to God, who can raise her, she sleeps, both in soul and in body.

### VERSE 25

“And when the crowd had been put out.” That is, when the mockers had been rejected, he entered the minds of the elect. “And he took her by the hand.” Unless the hands of the Jews are first, and so forth, up to “the hidden things can be erased by repentance.”

### VERSE 27

“As he passed on.” That is, from the ruler’s house to your house. The ruler’s house is the synagogue; his own house is the heavenly Jerusalem. “Two blind men,” and so forth. The two blind men signify two peoples without understanding, and so forth, up to “the same event, but another similar one.”

### VERSE 32

“A man.” He signifies the gentile people, or the whole human race, which, led to Christ through preaching and freed from idolatry, confessed Christ. Greek *kōphos* is more commonly used, but both “mute” and “deaf” are nevertheless said without strict distinction.

### VERSE 34

“But the Pharisees.” The unbelief of the Jews is signified in the Pharisees.

## CHAPTER X

### VERSE 1

“And having summoned.” From the healing of Peter’s mother-in-law, and so forth, up to “the healing of the centurion’s servant.” “Twelve.” These are the laborers who were to be sent and who would summon the four quarters of the world to the faith of the Trinity. So that their preaching might carry the weight of authority, power was given them to heal every illness.

### VERSE 2

“Peter and Andrew.” He joins together pairs and yokes of apostles, and so forth, up to “Christ, in whom he believed.”

### VERSE 3

“Thomas.” “Abyss”: because through certain faith he penetrated the depth of divine power in the Resurrection. Or Thomas means “twin,” which in Greek is *didymos*, because of his hesitant heart in believing.

### VERSE 4

“And Judas Iscariot.” A great example of instruction for us: although he knew everything, Christ did not hesitate to choose a betrayer as a disciple and appoint him an apostle. Christ has a witness aware of his purity, since he does not hesitate to choose his own betrayer.

### VERSE 5

“Into the way.” After the Resurrection he says, “Teach all nations.” But here he says this beforehand, because first it was necessary to preach to the Jews, so that they would have no excuse for not receiving him on the ground that he had sent the apostles to the nations.

### VERSE 7

“The kingdom of heaven is near.” Through faith the kingdom is near. For just as the sinner is earth, so the righteous person is heaven, in whom God presides; hence it is said: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17), and so forth. Behold what they must preach: “The kingdom of heaven is near.”

### VERSE 8

“Heal the sick.” The Church strengthens the sick in the condition of good works; it raises the dead in sins, or those without faith; it cleanses lepers sprinkled with errors; and through exorcisms it drives out demons. “You received freely.” So that Judas, who kept the money box, might not wish to collect money from the power mentioned above, the Lord suppresses his wickedness by saying: “You received freely,” and so forth. He also condemns here the faithlessness of the Simoniac heresy. Spiritual gifts lose their value when sold for a price.

### VERSE 9

“Neither gold nor silver.” Those who possessed such things would seem to preach not for the sake of salvation but for profit. “Nor money in your belts.” There are two kinds of necessities: one by which necessities are purchased, and the other consisting of the necessities themselves. By “money in your belts” he means the means by which things are purchased; by “a bag,” what is purchased and stored there. Concerning this he says during the Passion: “When I sent you without purse and bag, did you lack anything?” They answered, “Nothing.”

### VERSE 10

“Nor sandals.” Plato too says that the two extremities of the body should not be covered, and that the head and feet should not be accustomed to softness. When these have firmness, the other parts are stronger. “Nor a staff.” Matthew and Luke say “nor a staff,” while Mark mentions only a staff; by this term, and so forth, up to “it is shown that he must proceed on the journey of preaching.” “The laborer is worthy.” How, then, are necessities to be obtained? Receive only as much as suffices for necessity, so that, free from anxiety, you may devote yourselves more fully to eternal things.

### VERSE 11

“Ask who is worthy.” A host should be chosen on the testimony of his neighbors, lest his infamy harm the preaching. “If he is worthy.” Thus he may know that he receives grace more than he gives it. “Remain there.” (AMBROSE.) He gives a general command of steadfastness, so that they may observe the rights of hospitality; therefore the house should be chosen so that no occasion arises for changing one’s lodging or violating the bond of hospitality.

### VERSE 14

“Shake the dust from your feet.” By shaking off the dust, the loss of the journey is understood. “Shake off the dust,” as a testimony to the earthly labor which they had undertaken for them in vain, and so forth, up to “they are said to have been washed by the Savior himself.”

### VERSE 16

“Behold, I am sending.” Their punishment will be reserved for the future, and so forth, up to “he must not inflict evils but endure them.” “As serpents.” The serpent’s cunning is, and so forth, up to “he has put off the old man.”

### VERSE 18

“For a testimony.” So that the perverse may perish from it, and so forth, up to “a testimony to their innocence.”

### VERSE 19

“For it will be given you in that hour what you should say.” Offer your will for Christ; Christ himself will speak for himself.

### VERSE 21

“But brother will hand over brother.” The evils inflicted by strangers cause less pain; those we suffer from people whose minds we trusted cause greater pain, because together with bodily loss, we are tormented by the loss of charity.

### VERSE 22

“But whoever…” He teaches the virtue of endurance and patience, and so forth, up to “we begin to possess precisely what we are.”

### VERSE 23

“But when…” This pertains to the time when it was said, “Do not go into the way of the nations.” They should not fear persecutions but avoid them, so that the occasion of tribulation may become the seedbed of the Gospel.

### VERSE 24

“A disciple is not…” Do not be indignant at enduring what I endure, since I am the Lord, doing what I will, and the teacher, teaching what I know to be useful.

### VERSE 25

“If they have called the master of the house…” He displays their slanders so that, by his example, they may bear injuries. Hence he said: “Sufficient for the day is its own evil.” “Beelzebub.” *Beel* itself is *Bel*; *zebub* means “fly,” and so forth, up to “man of flies,” or “one who has flies.”

### VERSE 26

“Therefore do not fear them.” Do not fear their savagery or blasphemies, because the day will come when God will judge the hidden things of human beings. Then their wickedness will be uncovered, and your intention, now known only to God, will be known to everyone.

### VERSE 27

“What I tell you…” This is what I want you to be steadfast in, and so forth, up to “preach after trampling down the dwelling of the flesh.”

### VERSE 29

“Are not two sparrows…” He speaks according to the custom of Palestine, and so forth, up to “proclaim it throughout the whole world.” “Are not two sparrows?” Luke says: “Are not five sparrows sold for a *dipondius*?” (Luke 12.) There is not much difference: two are sold for an *as* and five for a *dipondius*. For a *dipondius* consists of two *asses*. What is one in number is an *as* in weight, and what is two is a *dipondius*. “And one of them…” How, then, does the Apostle say: “Does God care for oxen?” (Luke 9.) Care is one thing; knowledge is another.

### VERSE 30

“Numbered.” This means the knowledge of God, and so forth, up to “that even small and idle words escape him.”

### VERSE 32

“Whoever confesses.” A person confesses Jesus with the faith that works through love; he denies him who does not obey God’s commands.

### VERSE 33

“But whoever…” He is denied by the Son before the Father to whom the Son and the Father are not revealed in the power of divinity. He is confessed by the Son before the Father who, through the Son, has access to the Father.

### VERSE 34

“Peace.” A good war has been sent so that a bad peace might be broken.

### VERSE 35

“For I have come.” Here Luke says: “There will be five in one house divided, three against two and two against three will be divided.” How, then, and so forth, up to “circumcision and the other carnal observances.” “To separate.” That is, to extinguish private affections of the flesh, by which people love one another so much that they serve God less. Or, they must be turned away altogether—not because father and mother are not to be honored, but after God; this is the order of charity.

### VERSE 37

“Whoever loves father…” They are to be loved after God; but if both cannot be preserved, hatred toward one’s own is devotion toward God.

### VERSE 38

“And whoever does not take up…” The cross is carried in two ways, and so forth, up to “the love of Christ may be shown.” “And follows me.” Someone may mortify the flesh for empty glory, or suffer with his neighbor carnally in order to favor his sin. Such a person seems to carry the cross, but he does not follow the Lord.

### VERSE 39

“Whoever finds…” By the word “soul,” the present life is signified.

### VERSE 40

“Whoever receives…” When he sends them to preach, and so forth, up to “that they ought to receive their support.”

### VERSE 42

“And whoever…” The one who denounced the danger of those who would not receive them through the testimony of shaken-off dust commends the merit of those who do receive them beyond what was expected. Note that God looks more to the devout affection than to the quantity of what is offered. “To one of the least.” The least are those who possess absolutely nothing in this world, and they will be judges with Christ.

## CHAPTER XI

### VERSE 2

“Now John…” While Christ was preaching, and so forth, up to “it is not apparent who preserves the order of what happened.”

### VERSE 3

“Are you…” He does not say, “the one who came,” as though he were saying: Since I am about to descend to the lower regions, should I announce you to those in the underworld, I who announced you to those above? Is it fitting for the Son of God to die, or are you going to send another for these mysteries?

### VERSE 6

“Whoever does not…” Whoever has not doubted the power of divinity should not be thought to have said this against John, whom he immediately praises so highly.

### VERSE 7

“About John.” Christ’s precursor wished to assure the disciples concerning Christ because he sensed that they were doubting. Concerning the precursor, Christ taught the doubting crowds not to doubt, since they considered him soft and lightweight.

### VERSE 8

“Behold, those who wear soft clothing…” Those who place cushions under the elbow, who flatter the lives of sinners rather than prick them.

A strict life and preaching ought to avoid the palaces of the soft, which those dressed in softness frequent while flattering them.

(CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA.) Blessed John, rejecting even the hairs of sheep, which exude luxury, chose camel hair, and so forth, up to “he withdrew from every empty pursuit, every vain appearance of goodness, and every sordid and ungenerous adornment.”

### VERSE 9

“More than a prophet.” (BEDE.) Because he is an angel not by nature but by office.

### VERSE 11

“Greater than John.” In this he is not placed above the patriarchs and all human beings, but is shown to be equal to the other saints. “But whoever…” That is, every saint who is already with God is greater than one who is still in the world. Or: I, whom the opinion of many makes lesser, am greater than he in the Church of the saints. Or: the last angel of heaven is better than any human being. “In the kingdom.” The kingdom of heaven is understood in two ways: either as the heavenly kingdom above, in which we are not yet present, or as the present Church, in which we still live and already reign in a certain sense.

### VERSE 12

“From the days of John.” The Lord had commanded the apostles to go to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel, so that they might be brought back to the kingdom. But this preaching was turned toward the advancement of tax collectors and sinners who believed. The people do not believe John; Christ’s works are not credited to their author, because the cross is a stumbling block. Prophecy has now ceased; the law has now been fulfilled. Christ is preached to some and received by others: his own reject him, enemies accept him. Therefore the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, because the glory of Israel owed to the fathers, announced by the prophets, and offered by Christ is seized and taken possession of by the faith of the nations.

Or: “from the days of John,” who preached the presence through which the sinner comes back to life—and not before, because the law imposed punishment and did not give life through repentance. The heavenly homeland suffers violence when the sinner enters it through repentance as though into a foreign place. Great is the violence by which one is born on earth, seizes heaven, and possesses by virtue what one cannot possess by nature.

### VERSE 13

“For all…” Not because there were no prophets after John, such as Agabus, but because whatever they prophesied, they prophesied about the Lord. “For all…” Because whatever they said concerned the one who was to come, whereas John showed him already coming.

### VERSE 14

“And if you are willing to receive it.” This is so that you may be less excusable, since you did not receive him. He is Elijah in power, not in person: equal in severity of life and firmness of mind, preceding Christ’s first coming as Elijah will precede the second.

### VERSE 16

“But to what…” Having praised John, he turns to rebuke those who were not moved even by John’s preaching, or who despise Christ’s own preaching. John is such a one and so great, as I have said, and so worthy that he ought to be believed. But to whom are you to be compared, since you refused to believe him?

“It is like children.” The children are teachers humble in spirit. Their synagogue—or Jerusalem itself—is where the laws of God’s commandments were stored. They are fellow citizens who used to reproach them because they did not rise to God’s praises with devoted hearts, their bodily agility signifying this by dancing. Nor were they turned to repentance by the laments of the prophets over destructions already carried out or still to come.

### VERSE 17

“We sang to you.” As in David: “Rejoice in God our helper; shout for joy to the God of Jacob” (Psalm 80), and similar passages. “We mourned.” As in: “Turn to me with all your heart, with fasting and weeping and mourning” (Joel 2), and similar passages.

### VERSE 18

“For John came.” Then, as now, you reject both ways of salvation. “We mourned” for John; “we sang” for Christ. This is the whole matter: this generation neither weeps with John when he weeps nor rejoices with Christ when he rejoices. It is no wonder that they despise the twofold way of salvation, since they reject both fasting and fullness when these are offered. If fasting is pleasing, why is John displeasing? If fullness, why is the Son of Man displeasing?

### VERSE 19

“And wisdom was justified…” He shows that the children of wisdom understand that righteousness consists neither in abstaining nor in eating, but in equanimity when enduring poverty and in moderation so as not to be corrupted by abundance. “The kingdom of God is not food and drink.” In these things it is not their use but their desire that is censured. Some books read: “Wisdom was justified by her works,” because wisdom does not seek the testimony of words but of works.

### VERSE 20

“Then…” Having until now rebuked the Jews collectively, he now names the cities that, although they frequently heard the teaching and saw so many signs, refused to believe. He does not wish evil upon them but foretells what will come.

### VERSE 21

“Woe to you…” Above, where it is written that Jesus went around the cities and all the villages, healing every illness, it should be understood that among the others the Lord also performed mighty works in Chorazin and Bethsaida. “Chorazin” is interpreted as “my mystery”; “Bethsaida” as “house of fruits” or “house of hunters.”

“If the miracles had been done in Tyre…” We now see this fulfilled, because Chorazin and Bethsaida refused to believe while the Lord was present. Tyre and Sidon later believed when the apostles preached, so devotedly that, when Paul departed from Tyre, they all accompanied him with their wives and children as far as the ships. Why, then, did he preach to those who would not believe and avoid those who would believe? He himself knows whose ways are mercy and truth. Nevertheless, he had proposed not to exceed the boundaries of Judea, lest he give the Pharisees and priests a legitimate occasion for persecution. At that time there were also people in Chorazin who were destined to be called, yet they were not to be punished more severely for their contempt.

“Tyre” means “narrowness.” “Sidon” means “hunting.”

### VERSE 23

“And you, Capernaum.” Woe will come not only upon Chorazin and Bethsaida but also upon you, Capernaum. “Will you be exalted to heaven?” Are you not the city made famous by the reputation of my hospitality and by the signs performed in you, yet you resisted my preaching with the greatest pride?

“Capernaum” is interpreted as “most beautiful village.” In it faithless Jerusalem is condemned, to which it is said: “Your sister Sodom was justified in comparison with you”—that is, in comparison with you, since she was not corrected by the example of Lot, whereas you were always shown to be ungrateful toward the words and miracles of the Son of God.

### VERSE 25

“Jesus answered.” He answers a silent objection, as though the question were being asked: Why did the Jewish people, worshipers of God, obstinately reject the Son of God coming in the flesh, while the gentiles received him with such eagerness?

“Lord of heaven and earth.” You who make the heavens and leave those whom you wish in earthly things—or understand it literally. “To little ones.” He does not oppose the wise and prudent to the foolish and dull, but to little ones, proving that he condemns arrogance, not intelligence.

### VERSE 26

“Yes, Father.” He speaks with the affection of one who flatters, so that the benefit begun in the apostles may be completed. Here we receive an example of humility, lest we rashly presume to investigate the heavenly counsels concerning the calling of some and the rejection of others. For when he had mentioned both, he did not immediately give a reason, but said that it was pleasing to God, showing that what pleases the just one cannot be unjust. Therefore, in all that is arranged externally, the rational cause is open, but the justice of the will is hidden.

“Because this was pleasing before you.” Let no one ask again why he chooses the humble and rejects the wise.

### VERSE 27

“All things have been handed over to me…” Understand mystically the Father as the one who hands over and the Son as the one who receives. Otherwise, if you understand it according to our weakness, once the receiver begins to possess, the giver will begin not to possess. Recognize that the Son is co-omnipotent in all things: the things handed over are his by the right of one substance according to his nature, not gifts received by grace.

The things handed over are not heaven and earth and the other things he made, but those who through the Son have access to the Father—those who formerly rebelled and later began to acknowledge the Lord.

“And no one knows the Son…” He reveals himself. “And no one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son has wished to reveal him.” The latter expression refers back to both clauses. For the Father declares himself through his Word, and the Word declares himself because he is the light of our mind.

“Except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes…” This is mutual knowledge, which exists through equality of nature. The small amount of knowledge that exists in us comes through the condescension of the one who reveals.

### VERSE 29

“Take my yoke…” The yoke of Christ is the Gospel, which joins Jews and gentiles in one faith. “Take it upon you.” That is, hold it in honor, not beneath you as something to despise. “You who labor,” through the difficulty of the law, “and are burdened,” namely with sins, “I will refresh you,” if you take up the yoke—that is, my commandments.

What is sweeter than his yoke? What is lighter than his burden? To become approved, to abstain from evil, to will what is good, to love everyone, to pursue eternal things, not to be captivated by present things, and not to wish to do to another what you do not want to suffer yourself.

“Learn from me.” He teaches by word and example, so that you may be humble in mind and gentle in conduct. Humble, so that you despise no one; gentle, so that you harm no one. “In heart,” so that what is outwardly done in the work may also be in the heart, lest a serpent lie hidden in the appearance of a dove.

### VERSE 30

“For my yoke…” How is the Gospel lighter than the law, when in the law works are condemned, while here even desire is condemned? In the law many things are commanded which the Apostle says cannot be fulfilled; here the will is sought, and the will lies within our power. It alone can suffice and receive a reward.

Again, how is Christ’s yoke sweet when it is said above: “Narrow is the way that leads to life”? It is narrow because one begins only through a narrow entrance; but as time advances, it is widened by the ineffable sweetness of love.

“My burden.” Because “this momentary lightness of our tribulation is producing an eternal weight of glory for us in the heavens” (1 Corinthians 4).

## CHAPTER XII

### VERSE 1

“At that time.” Having recounted the preaching and miracles performed during one year before John’s question, he moves on to those that occurred in another year—namely, after John’s death, when Christ was already contradicted in every way.

“Hungry.” As another Evangelist says, they did not even have an opportunity to eat because of the crowds, on account of their excessive persistence. The other Evangelists add that they rubbed the grain in their hands (Luke 6). Hence Peter is also told: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10).

### VERSE 2

“It is not lawful.” This is according to the commandment of the law. But since another Scripture says, “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice” (Hosea 6), it was better to rescue a human being from the danger of hunger than to offer sacrifice to God, because the pleasing offering is the salvation of human beings. They do not accuse them of wasting the crops, because the law permits them to eat from them.

### VERSE 3

“But he said…” From this deed we learn nothing other than that the Sabbath must be understood not literally but spiritually. “Have you not read?” If David and Abimelech are not blamed—although both transgressed the commandment of the law through a reasonable necessity—and the cause here is likewise hunger, why do you not approve the same conduct in the apostles?

### VERSE 4

“The loaves of the Presence.” This signified that priestly food would pass into the use of the peoples. Or because we must all imitate the priests. Or because we are all priests.

### VERSE 5

“Because on the Sabbaths the priests…” Here he shows that the Sabbath is violated without necessity by the very people who bring accusations. One example concerns royal power, in David; another concerns priestly power, in those who violate the Sabbath through the service of the temple. How much less, then, does the charge of plucking ears of grain on the Sabbath apply to him who is the true king, priest, and Lord of the Sabbath?

### VERSE 6

“But I say to you.” He means: If the figurative temple could defend the priests serving it, why can the spiritual temple not defend the disciples who believe in it?

### VERSE 7

“But if…” To show you that everything contained the form of what was to come, he added: “If you knew”—that is, that God had determined to free the people through grace and not through external observances—you would not condemn mine if they omit the old observances.

### VERSE 8

“For the Son of Man is Lord…” If David, when fed, and the priests who violated the Sabbath through the ministry of the temple are without guilt, how much more the Son of Man, who is the true king, priest, and Lord of the Sabbath?

### VERSE 10

“And behold, a man.” This man is said to have been a mason, because the hand to which the care of the spiritual building had been entrusted was withered until the time of Christ.

“Behold, the man’s hand…” This signifies the human race, dried up in the fruitfulness of good works because of the hand stretched out toward the fruit. The innocent hand stretched out on the cross healed it. The hand was rightly withered in the synagogue, because where there is the greater gift of knowledge, there the transgressor is subject to greater guilt.

“They questioned him.” Since he had excused the disciples from violating the Sabbath by a plausible example, they wanted to accuse him himself—so that if he did not heal, they might accuse him of cruelty or weakness; but if he did heal, they might accuse him of transgression.

“On the Sabbaths.” Jesus especially teaches and works on the Sabbaths, not only because of the particular Sabbath but also because of the larger gathering of the people, seeking the salvation of all.

### VERSE 11

“Who among you…” He answers the question with an appropriate example, showing that those who accuse him of violating the Sabbath themselves violate it through a work of greed, and accuse him of violating it through a work of charity. He rebukes those who interpret the law badly, saying that one must cease from good works on the Sabbath. One must cease only from evil works; hence it is said: “You shall do no servile work on it” (Leviticus 23)—that is, no sin. Likewise, in eternal rest they will cease only from evil, not from good.

### VERSE 13

“Stretch out…” Nothing contributes more to healing than generosity in almsgiving; hence it is said: “Let your hand not be extended to receive, but gathered together to give” (Ecclesiasticus 4). For in vain does one stretch out his hands to God to ask forgiveness for sins if he does not extend them, as far as he can, to the poor.

“As the other.” Before Christ’s coming, a person had a diseased right hand because he was sluggish in almsgiving, while his left hand was healthy because he was intent upon his own advantage. But when Christ came, the right hand was healed like the left, because what he had greedily collected he now distributes in charity.

### VERSE 15

“He withdrew from there.” Note the example: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matthew 10). “They followed him.” The learned pursue him after seeing his miracles; the unlearned, led by his reputation, follow him in love, and therefore deserve to be healed.

### VERSE 16

“And he commanded.” This was not from fear that he might be betrayed and killed, but from mercy toward the Jews, lest they be slaughtered by envy because of his innocence and gentleness. Here he mystically instructs us not to seek praise publicly when we accomplish something great.

### VERSE 18

“My soul.” By “soul” every affection is signified.

### VERSE 20

“A bruised reed.” He will not immediately condemn the Jews, who yield to every wind and have been scattered by disagreeing among themselves, but will support them. “A bruised reed.” Whoever does not extend a hand to a sinner, nor carry his brother’s burden, breaks the bruised reed. Whoever despises the small spark of faith in little ones extinguishes the smoldering wick. Christ did not do this; rather, he came to seek what had been lost. He preserved patience until the judgment being carried out in him reached victory, and, having cast out the ruler of the world, he returned to the kingdom, sitting at the right hand of the Father until he placed his enemies beneath his feet.

“A smoldering wick.” The gentiles are those whom the smoke of error—most bitter and harmful in smell—enveloped, with the fire of the natural law almost extinguished. He did not extinguish them, but raised them from a small spark to the great ardor of the fire of God.

“Until…” His preaching shines upon the world, overcome by no ambush, until he establishes judgment on earth and the saying is fulfilled: “Your will be done, as in heaven so on earth.”

### Verse 22

“And he healed.” Three signs occurred simultaneously, and these also occur daily in the conversion of human beings: once the demon has been expelled, they see the light of faith and praise God.

### Verse 24

“In Beelzebub.” Beel—that is, Baal—“of flies,” because of the filth of sacrificial blood: he is the god of Ekron, by which name they call the prince of demons.

### Verse 25

“Every kingdom.” He refutes them by a necessary argument. For either Christ casts out demons by the power of God, or by the power of the prince of demons. If by the power of God, they accuse him without cause. If by the power of the prince of demons, his kingdom is divided and will not stand; therefore they should withdraw from his kingdom. He implies that they have chosen it for themselves, since they do not believe in him.

### Verse 26

“And every city.” The same reasoning applies to a city and a house as to a kingdom. Jerusalem, always glorious, after it was inflamed against Christ and the apostles, fell through division and destruction.

### Verse 27

“And if I cast out demons by Beelzebub.” If the expulsion of demons in your sons is attributed to God and not to demons, why does the same work in me not have the same cause?

“Their sons,” and so forth. The contemptible things of the world, in which the holy simplicity of my power is apparent. Or rather, this may be understood as follows: “sons,” that is, the apostles, who were well aware that they had learned no evil art from him. Therefore they themselves are witnesses of my judgment, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

### Verse 28

“But if I.” That part—“If I cast out demons by Beelzebub”—has been led to several absurd consequences; now the other part of the argument is being considered.

“But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God.” Here Luke says, “by the finger” (Luke 11). The Holy Spirit is called a finger because of the distribution of gifts.

“The kingdom of God”—he either means himself, as elsewhere: “One stands among you whom you do not know” (Luke 11; John 1); or the kingdom that John and Jesus themselves preached: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matthew 21).

There is also a third kingdom, that of Holy Scripture, which is taken away from the Jews and given to a nation producing its fruits. Or “the kingdom” means all the regions of the world, distributed to the apostles and their successors for conversion.

### Verse 29

“Or how can he.” The Lord therefore shows by an obvious parable that he does not cooperate with demons in a deceitful operation, as they accused him of doing, but frees human beings from the demon by divine power. Thus they commit a grave crime when they proclaim that what they have recognized as God’s work belongs to the devil. For they cannot be in agreement, since their works are different. Hence he adds: “Whoever is not with me,” and so forth.

“His house.” Or “the house,” that is, all the regions of the world, which he distributed to the apostles and their successors for conversion.

### Verse 30

“Whoever is not with me,” and so forth. That is: whoever performs works unlike mine is opposed to me. He draws people toward vices; I draw them toward virtues.

### Verse 31

“Every sin and blasphemy.” What is contracted through human frailty can be forgiven, if the congregation is not abandoned. But if, through diabolical obstinacy, one never returns from dispersion to the congregation, the sin is judged incapable of being loosed.

(JEROME.) “Every sin.” Not all sins are forgiven to everyone, but to those, and so forth, up to his assertion that all will obtain forgiveness after the universal judgment, even though many ages will have passed.

“But the Spirit.” Whoever clearly understands the works of God, and, since he cannot deny their power, nevertheless, when provoked, slanders them out of envy and says that they are Beelzebub—this person will not be forgiven. This does not mean that forgiveness would be denied him if he repented; rather, because this blasphemer, in accordance with the demands of his evil merits, will never attain either forgiveness or repentance. Thus the evangelist John says of certain people blinded on account of the merit of their blasphemy: “For this reason they could not believe” (John 10). Isaiah said the same again: “He has blinded their eyes” (Isaiah 6).

Those who believe and say that the Holy Spirit does not exist, or is lesser than the Father, because they do this not through diabolical envy but through human ignorance, are not held by an unforgivable crime. But those who, in the likeness of the devil, attack the majesty of God against their own conscience have no forgiveness forever, as Mark plainly declares. After setting down this testimony of the Lord, he added: “Because they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit’” (Matthew 3).

### Verse 32

“And whoever.” (AMBROSE.) Even one who, scandalized by the weakness of my flesh, should suppose me to be merely a human being or a glutton, will be forgiven.

“But whoever.” Whoever does not recognize the grace of the Holy Spirit, by which repentance is inspired and one returns to the congregation, and remains with an impenitent heart—since this is no longer human but diabolical—will not be forgiven.

“Neither in this age.” For some sins are loosed in this age, while others—namely, lesser ones—are loosed even in the age to come. Such sins indeed weigh upon a person after death, but they are also forgiven if, through good works in this life, he has merited that they be forgiven there.

“Nor in the age to come.” Because there are certain slight sins which, if they have not yet been forgiven in this life, weigh upon a person after death; but they are also forgiven if the persons are worthy.

### Verse 33

“Either make the tree.” There is no middle position: the works of a good author are only good, and those of an evil author only evil. He constrains them by his argument on every side and presses them with either horn. If the devil is evil, he does not perform good works; if the works are good, they do not belong to the devil.

“Either make the tree,” and so forth. Mystically, the good tree is Christ; its fruit is the preaching of the Gospel; its healings are redemption. The evil tree is the devil and his own—that is, the scribes and Pharisees—and the other evil fruits are envy, slander, blasphemy, heresy, and things of this kind.

### Verse 34

“Brood of vipers,” and so forth. He shows that they are an evil tree and that they bear the fruits of blasphemy.

“From the abundance.” A human being is often deceived when he weighs the heart from the mouth and from conduct. But God judges works and words from the heart, which he knows. Therefore the mouth of the one who knows from what intention a word proceeds speaks from the abundance of the heart.

### Verse 35

“The good person.” The treasure of the heart is the intention from which God judges works, so that at times lesser works may have a greater reward, and greater works a lesser one. In this passage he either shows from what sort of treasure the Jews bring forth blasphemy, or this is connected with what precedes: just as a good person cannot bring forth evil things, nor an evil person good things, so neither can Christ perform evil works, nor the devil good works.

### Verse 36

“Idle word.” If a person will give an account on the day of judgment even for an idle word, how much more will you, who say that the works of the Holy Spirit are Beelzebub?

(GREGORY.) An idle word is one that lacks either the usefulness of righteousness or the rationale of a just necessity, and so forth, up to the point where he says that here a person will be held guilty not of an idle word but of a criminal one.

### Verse 37

“From your words.” Death and life are in the power of the tongue.

### Verse 38

“Then they answered.” Since the scribes and Pharisees were entirely unable to refute his words, they seek to test him in his works, asking to see signs, as though the signs they had seen had not been signs.

### Verse 39

“Except the sign of Jonah.” He shows that the Jews are criminal like the Ninevites and, unless they repent, are near destruction. But just as punishment is announced to the Ninevites and a remedy is shown to them, so the Jews ought not to despair of forgiveness if, at least after Christ rose from the dead, they heed the warning and repent, because the death of Christ is the reconciliation of the world.

### Verse 40

“For just as Jonah was.” Jonah—that is, “suffering”—signifies the one who bore our sufferings. Or “dove”: the fish that swallowed him in the sea signifies the death he suffered in the world. Just as Jonah was cast out onto dry land, so Christ rose into glory.

“For three days.” This follows the custom of the ancients, who counted the day together with the preceding night. Count the part of the day during which he was buried, together with the preceding night, as a night and a day—that is, as a whole day by synecdoche. Count the night and the day of the Sabbath in full. Count the Lord’s night together with the dawn of that same day as a part standing for the whole, and thus you have three days and three nights. The first days are counted because of humanity’s future fall from light into night; these are counted because of humanity’s restoration from darkness to light.

Mystically, the three days are the three periods: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. The three nights are the three dead whom the Lord raised.

### Verse 41

“The men of Nineveh.” The meaning is this: Jonah preached for only a few days and without signs to an unbelieving nation, and he succeeded; I preach for a long time, to the people of God, and with many signs, yet in vain. Those who are unfaithful despite possessing the Law are all the more unworthy of forgiveness, since those who did not know the Law possess the greater faith.

“Nineveh,” meaning “beautiful,” signifies the Gentile world, which Christ loved when it was foul, in order to make it beautiful. In the Ninevites and the queen of the South, the faith of the Church is signified. It is reconciled to God no less through repentance for its former folly than through the diligence with which it learns wisdom. For the Church has two parts: the one that does not know sin, and the one that ceases to sin. Repentance abolishes sin; wisdom guards against it.

### Verse 43

“But when,” and so forth. It is as though he said: You are not like the Ninevites or the queen of the South, because when I preached repentance you did not repent, and when I taught wisdom you did not learn. Rather, you are like a man from whom the devil has been expelled but then enters again.

There is a distinction between my works, which cleanse what has been polluted by the world, and Satan’s works, which more grievously corrupt what has been cleansed.

“He walks through places.” He examines the hearts of the faithful, cleansed of the softness of fickle thought, to see whether he can plant any footsteps there. Since he cannot, he returns to wet places.

### Verse 44
