“I will return to my house.” He sleeps beneath the shade, in the hidden recess of a reed, and in damp places. The dark shade is the conscience; the reed, bright on the outside but hollow within, is the hypocrite; the damp place is a wanton and soft mind.

### Verse 45

“Seven other spirits.” Seven vices opposed to the seven spiritual virtues.

“More wicked.” Because such a person not only possesses vices but also pretends to possess virtues. They are more wicked in proportion to their greater cunning.

“Seven,” because there were that many graces destined to be associated with Christ.

The seven vices are seven demons opposed to the seven spirits, contrary to the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, and so forth.

“So it will be,” and so forth. What he said about one individual is fulfilled in this entire nation. The unclean spirit went out from the Jews when they received the Law. He went to the Gentiles, who later believed in the Lord; finding no place among them, he said: “I will return to the Jews,” who were empty of the protection of God and the angels, cleansed by rebukes and corrections, and adorned with superfluous observances. Seven are added because those who blaspheme Jesus are possessed by a far greater number of demons than were those possessed in Egypt. The number of vices corresponds to the seven spirits of virtue.

### Verse 46

“Behold, his mother.” (RABANUS.) Mystically, the mother and brothers are the Jewish people, who cannot enter while Jesus is teaching within, because they do not understand his words spiritually, and so forth, up to the statement that the Lord’s brothers are his cousins: the sons of his maternal aunt Mary, who is called the mother of James the younger, Joseph, Judas, and Simon.

### Verse 47

“But he said to him.” They ask this deceitfully, to discover whether he prefers the flesh to spiritual work. Therefore he pretends not to know his mother and relatives by natural acquaintance, but says that they are close to him through the union of the spirit.

### Verse 48

“Who is my mother?” He does not reject the services of his mother, but places the Father’s work first. He does not despise his brothers, but prefers spiritual work to kinship, so that we too may prefer the spirit to the flesh. Hence: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10).

“Behold, my mother,” and so forth. These are my mother: those who beget me in the hearts of believers. These are my brothers: those who do the works of my Father. A brother and sister come through believing; a mother through preaching.

## Chapter XIII

### Verse 1

“On that day.” By this he indicates that the event took place in sequence, unless perhaps “day” is used for “time,” as is customary in Scripture. Mark preserves the same order. Luke moves on to another matter, but does not contradict this account.

(RABANUS.) Not only the Lord’s deeds and words, but also his journeys, and so forth, up to the statement that the Jews did not enter these things but remained outside, fixed in the letter.

### Verse 2

“The crowd was standing.” These are the people who had recently come to listen. They are separated from the waves of the sea and, not yet instructed in the heavenly mysteries they desire, ascend with Christ.

### Verse 3

“He spoke many things.” Because the crowd does not possess one opinion but various desires, he speaks to them in many parables, so that according to their different inclinations they may receive diverse teachings.

“The one who sows.” He is Christ himself, who sowed among human beings, through himself or through his own servants, the word of truth that he had seen with the Father. He who spoke the mysteries to the disciples went out to sow God’s word among the crowds.

### Verse 4

“Beside the way.” The way is the mind, worn smooth and dried out by the continual traffic of evil thoughts. The seed perishes there in two ways: it is trampled by the passage of thoughts, as Luke says, and it is snatched away by birds. Demons are called birds either because they are of a heavenly and spiritual nature, or because they fly through the air.

“And they came.” According to Luke, it was trampled by human beings, because it was taken away by the wicked persuasion of the impious.

“And they ate.” Because they stole it away from the minds of human beings.

### Verse 5

“On rocky ground.” Rocky ground seeks to produce shoots quickly, but the root is not established because the soil is not deep—that is, because there is little desire for salvation. From this exposition of the Lord we learn that things do not always carry the same meaning. Here, the rock signifies hardness; the soil, the gentleness of the mind; and the sun, the heat of persecution. Elsewhere the sun has a good meaning: “The righteous will shine like the sun” (Matthew 13); the rock signifies the strength of faith in the foundation; and the soil signifies earthly thoughts.

“The depth of the soil.” The depth of the soil is the uprightness of a spirit trained in heavenly disciplines and tested in temptations.

### Verse 8

“Sixtyfold.” Since the adornment of the world was completed in the number six, good works are signified by it.

### Verse 9

“Whoever has ears to hear.” Whenever this admonition is inserted in the Gospel or in the Apocalypse of John, it indicates that what is being said is mystical.

### Verse 10

“And the disciples came,” and so forth. How did the disciples come when the Lord was sitting in the boat? Perhaps it should be understood that they had boarded the boat with him earlier and, standing there, asked him.

### Verse 11

“To you it has been given.” Note that not only the Lord’s words but also his deeds are parables—that is, signs of mystical realities—which many who are outside do not understand.

### Verse 12

“For whoever has.” That is: if the apostles, who possess faith, have anything less in the virtues, it is granted to them; but from the Jews, who do not believe in the Son of God, whatever good they possess by nature is taken away. For those who do not possess the head of wisdom can understand nothing wisely.

“It will be taken away from him.” He will not rejoice in the sweetness of true wisdom.

### Verse 13

“Therefore in parables.” It is said that they were blinded for this reason and that the Lord’s teaching was hidden from them in parables, so that afterward they might be converted more beneficially. Since they did not understand what had been spoken obscurely, they therefore did not believe in him, and so crucified him. Then, after the resurrection, terrified by the miracles and pierced by awareness of their greater guilt, they were moved to repentance. Having received pardon, they burned with a greater love.

But John presents this passage in the following way: “For this reason they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: ‘He has blinded their eyes, so that they may not see’” (John 11). There he plainly says that the blindness was not brought about so that, warned by it and grieved that they did not understand, they might eventually be converted. They could not have done this unless they believed. Rather, they were blinded so that they would not believe, which they had deserved through their other sins.

“Seeing, they do not see.” A miser has many possessions and none, because they are useless to him.

### Verse 14

“Hearing, you will hear.” These words were prophesied about the crowds, because they stand on the shore and are not worthy to hear the Lord’s teaching.

### Verse 15

“Their eyes.” That is: they themselves were the cause of God’s closing their eyes.

“Lest at any time.” That is: because they refused to open their eyes and ears, they did not merit being converted at any time. Yet this too was done for them mercifully.

### Verse 16

“Blessed.” Truly blessed, because they were even granted to see and hear in the present what none of their predecessors, however deserving, had merited, although many had greatly desired it.

### Verse 17

“And righteous men.” Luke calls them “righteous kings,” because they rule their impulses well.

### Verse 18

“You, then, hear.” He explains the first parable so that they may attend to the same meaning in the others. He explains it not according to each individual word but according to the substance of the meaning.

(AUGUSTINE, *On Genesis*.) Therefore, what the evangelist narrated—and it also happened—namely, that the Lord spoke such things, and so forth, up to the distinction that the narrator wrote about past events, whereas the one who foretold spoke only of future events.

### Verse 20

“On rocky ground.” Those who receive the word well are sown on rock and among thorns, but either adversity through frightening them or prosperity through flattering them hinders them from reaching perfection. Riches are joined by the anxiety of guarding them, which afflicts, and by pleasure, which causes them to dissipate.

### Verse 22

“The deceitfulness of riches.” (CHRYSOSTOM.) Those whom we heard are choked by thorns, not indeed through any fault of the thorns themselves but through the fault of the person who possesses them, and so forth, up to the statement that riches contain two opposing vices: one inflames anxiety and obscures the mind with cares; the other makes people softer through pleasures.

### Verse 23

“Another, indeed, a hundredfold.” (RABANUS.) There are three distinctions in good soil, just as there were in bad soil. Thirty refers to marriage; sixty to, and so forth, up to the explanation that the thirtyfold refers to married people, because this is the age of those engaged in battle, and they face the greater struggle lest they be overcome by lust.

### Verse 24

“Another parable.” It is as though a wealthy householder, having invited guests, refreshes them with various foods, so that each may receive different nourishment according to the condition of his stomach. Hence he says “another parable,” not “a different one,” so that it may be understood that more will follow.

This parable is proposed after the crowds have been dismissed and is explained at home to the disciples who ask about it. Here he teaches good will, caution, patience, discernment, endurance, and justice.

### Verse 25

“Men.” These are those appointed over others for protection and guardianship, the leaders in the Church; or, when the apostles receive the sleep of death.

### Verse 28

“Do you want us to go?” When a spiritual person hears that this is from the devil, who is powerless against God’s will, a desire may arise in him to remove such people from the world if he has the ability. But he consults God’s justice: whether he ought to do this, and whether God wishes this duty to belong to human beings.

The Truth replies that a human being does not know what one who is now in error will become in this life, or what benefit his error may bring to the good. Therefore such people should not be removed, lest those who may perhaps become good be killed, or lest this harm the good whom they benefit, and so forth.

He says that this should be done at the appropriate time, when it is no longer possible for the person’s life to be changed or for him to benefit others; and then he says that it is done not by human beings but by angels.

### Verse 29

“And he said: No,” and so forth. Here we see patience. When he heard of the injury, he did not flare up in anger or immediately wish to avenge himself. In the same way, let us patiently endure those who injure us.

“Lest perhaps.” Here an opportunity for repentance is granted, and we are warned not to cut off too quickly, because one who errs today may perhaps defend the truth tomorrow. If he were uprooted now, the wheat he was destined to become would be uprooted. Or it is necessary that the wicked be mixed with the good, so that the good may be exercised by them; or so that, in comparison with them, they may strive toward what is better. Once those people were removed, the height of charity would wither, and that would be uprooting.

The wicked must be patiently tolerated there where some are found whom they may help, while the good are helped by them.

(AUGUSTINE.) The multitude is not to be excommunicated, nor is the leader of the people.

### Verse 30

“Allow them.” This appears contrary to the apostolic command: “Remove the evil one from among you” (1 Corinthians 5). But just as there is little difference between darnel and wheat so long as they are still grass, so the Lord warns us not to judge what is ambiguous. The Lord will condemn it on the day of judgment, not suspiciously but openly.

In enduring, let us meditate on justice; in judging, let us not neglect justice.

“And at the proper time.” The one who endured patiently, in accordance with justice, gave a fitting recompense. For the virtues are distinct but not opposed.

“And bind them.” In this life there is no binding; otherwise so many people would not turn back from error.

### Verse 31

“The kingdom is like,” and so forth. The kingdom of heaven is the preaching of the Gospel, concerning which he says elsewhere: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruit” (Matthew 21). Or it is knowledge of the Scriptures.

“To a mustard seed.” It is compared to a mustard seed because of the fervor of faith, since it is said to drive out poisons—that is, all false doctrines. The humility of the Lord’s incarnation may also be understood in the mustard seed. Joseph received the body of the crucified Savior and buried it in a garden; thus, having received it, a person “put it in his garden.”

“It spread its branches in which the birds of heaven will rest,” because he scattered preachers throughout the world, so that in their words and consolations the faithful might breathe again after the weariness of this life.

### Verse 32

“But when it has grown.” This may be understood throughout the whole world or in the soul of each individual, since no one becomes perfect suddenly. It grew and became a tree because it rose and ascended into heaven.

Or “when it has grown” means when the minds of human beings have come to know how great its power is. Other plants appear, which grow and wither quickly—lacking vitality and already decayed. But this does not remain a plant; it becomes a tree, with leaves together with fruit, and spiritual people rest in its various meanings.

“It becomes a tree from plants.” That is, from the teachings of philosophers, which quickly grow and wither, promising nothing living.

### Verse 33

“In three measures of flour.” This signifies that spirit, soul, and body, brought together into one, do not disagree among themselves. Or the three powers of the soul are brought into unity: in reason we possess prudence, in anger hatred of vices, and in desire longing for virtues.

Or the woman, the Church, mixes the faith of human beings into three measures of flour: faith in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. When it has been fermented into one, it does not lead us to knowledge of a threefold God but to knowledge of one divinity, because the nature of each is not different.

“Until it was fermented.” Charity, hidden within the mind, must grow for as long as necessary until it transforms the whole mind into its perfection, so that it loves or remembers nothing except God. This begins here and is perfected in the other life.

### Verse 34

“In parables to the crowds.” Because everything said there about the army of Israel, and all the signs, are hidden mysteries.

### Verse 44

“With a treasure hidden in a field.” The treasure may be understood as the word of God, hidden in the flesh of Christ. Or it may be Scripture, in which knowledge of the Savior has been stored. Or it may be the two Testaments in the Church, for whose understanding all other things are renounced so that they may be studied in leisure.

He compares the kingdom of heaven to earthly things so that the mind may rise from what is known to what is unknown and love it.

“He hid it, and because of his joy over it.” So that it may be preserved from evil spirits and from human praise. Let the work be public, while the intention remains hidden.

### Verse 45

“To a merchant.” We must all trade for the blessedness from which we were stripped by the guilt of the first human being, by understanding rightly and acting well.

“Good pearls.” The good pearls are the Law and the Prophets. The one precious pearl is knowledge of the Savior, for which a person, like Paul, renounced all the mysteries and observances of the Law.

### Verse 46

“When he had found it.” That is, Christ, who presides over all human beings; or the spiritual commandment of love. Or it is the understood word that was with God, having penetrated the shell of the flesh. Or it is the sweetness of heavenly life, for the sake of which all things become worthless.

### Verse 47

“A net cast.” Jeremiah’s prophecy is fulfilled: “Behold, I am sending many fishermen to you” (Jeremiah 16). After Peter and Andrew, James and John heard, “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of human beings,” they wove a net for themselves from the Old and New Testaments and cast it into the sea of the world. It is still being drawn and stretched through the waves to this day, catching whatever falls into it, good and bad alike. It draws them to the shore—that is, to the end of the world—so that then the division may take place. Hence it follows: “So it will be at the consummation of the age,” and so forth.

The net is compared with the Church or with evangelical preaching, which draws people from the waves of the world toward heaven.

### Verse 48

“And beside the shore.” The shore is the end of the world, at which the good will be sent to heaven and the wicked to darkness. In the present life they were mixed together.

### Verse 52

“Therefore every scribe instructed,” and so forth. Because you understand the mysteries that I reveal to you, I will make you preachers, and you will be like me, bringing forth new and old things from the treasure of my knowledge, so that you may do the same.

The apostles are Christ’s scribes and notaries, inscribing his words on the tablets of the heart. They possess the wealth of the householder, bringing forth new and old things from the treasure of their teachings, because whatever is preached in the Gospel is confirmed by the words of the Law and the Prophets.

### Verse 54

“So that they were amazed.” Great blindness: they recognize Christ by his words and deeds, yet despise him because they know his family.

### Verse 55

“The carpenter’s son.” He did not wish to be called the carpenter’s son without reason—not the son of the carpenter they suppose, but of the Maker of all things. But the Jews, ignorant of this mystery, despise the works of divine power when they contemplate his human ancestry. They do not consider his present works but remember the weakness of his infancy.

### Verse 57

“A prophet.” Christ is called a prophet. Hence Moses says: “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your own people” (Deuteronomy 18).

“In his homeland.” That is, among the Jewish people. But he performs greater works among the Gentiles.

### Verse 58

“And he did not perform.” He performed some miracles, but not many, lest he condemn the unbelieving. Or, because he was despised, he performed a few, so that they might not be entirely without excuse; but he performs greater works among the Gentiles.

## Chapter XIV

### Verse 1

“At that time Herod heard.” Luke has it this way: “Herod the tetrarch heard” (Luke 9), and so forth.

When he says, “This is John” (John 4), he either spoke after hesitation, confirmed by the opinion of certain people, or he was still doubtful. These words can be understood in either way.

### Verse 2

“And he said.” Note the envy of the Jews. This foreigner says that John, who performed no sign, has risen again. Yet they insist that Jesus, approved by so many miracles, has not risen.

“And therefore.” For they perceived that the holy ones who would rise from the dead would possess a power greater than those weighed down by fragile flesh.

### Verse 3

“For Herod.” Since he had spoken of the opinion that John had risen without saying anything about his death, he returns to the matter and explains how and why John died.

This Herod and Philip were brothers, sons of the Herod under whom the Lord fled into Egypt.

“His wife Herodias.” Herodias was the daughter of King Aretas. Her father himself took her from Philip and, to Philip’s grief, gave her to Herod, Philip’s enemy.

### Verse 4

“It is not lawful.” Herod perhaps observed the Jewish Law, and therefore John prohibited him from adultery.

### Verse 5

“He feared the people.” He feared the people, but love prevailed, and for its sake he put God second. Fear of God corrects; fear of human beings delays, but does not remove the will. Thus it makes those whom it has sometimes restrained from crime even more eager for crime.

### Verse 7

“With an oath.” Perhaps he swore this in order to create an opportunity by which he might appear to do unwillingly what he was doing willingly. For he would not have carried out against someone he loved what he carried out against the prophet; indeed, he would have done it earlier if he could have excused himself.

(BEDA.) If it should happen that we have sworn something rashly, and so forth, up to the statement that he did not regret having contracted any guilt through such perjury.

(ISIDORE.) An oath by which evil is rashly promised must not be kept, as, for example, if, and so forth, up to the statement that it is more tolerable not to fulfill an oath than to remain in sexual sin.

### Verse 9

“He was saddened.” So it appeared to those reclining at table. Such was Herod’s sadness—namely, like Pharaoh’s repentance.

### Verse 10

“And he beheaded him.” John was diminished by the loss of his head, while Christ was exalted on the cross: the fame of the former decreased, while that of the latter increased. Hence: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3).

In the severed head of John, it is shown that the Jews lost Christ, who is the head of all the prophets.

Morally, John’s death signifies the end of the Law. Once it has ended, one rightly passes over to Christ, who is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

### Verse 13

“When Jesus heard this.” After the Law and the prophet among the Jews have lost both their head and their voice, Jesus passes into the desert of the Church, which previously had no husband.

“He withdrew.” He did not withdraw out of fear, but spared his enemies, lest they add murder to murder, and gave an example of avoiding rashness. Or he withdrew in order to test the faith of believers. Hence: “When the crowds heard,” and so forth.

“On foot.” By their own exertion, to show the ardor of their minds. They leave the cities—that is, their former ways of life. They have the will to reach him but not the strength. Therefore Jesus goes out to meet them and, moved by compassion, heals them, so that complete faith may immediately receive its reward. Behold how greatly he delights in the devotion of believers.

### Verse 15

“When evening came,” and so forth. Jesus withdraws from Judea and goes into the desert. The crowds follow him; he meets them and heals them. This occurs not in the morning or at midday but in the evening, when the sun of righteousness has set and the end of the world is approaching.

“His disciples.” They are carnal and ignorant of the future miracle of nourishment. They had been told: “Do not go on the way of the Gentiles” (Matthew 10).

Mystically, the Jews are displeased that the Gentiles are received and murmur. Isaiah uses their voice: “Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket” (Isaiah 40); and again: “All the nations are as though they were not, yet they are before him.” But the Lord determined to refresh them through the apostles; hence it follows: “But Jesus,” and so forth.

“Send the crowds away.” They have long followed idols and therefore are not to be nourished by us with the bread of the word of God.

### Verse 16

“Give them something.” He urges them to give, so that when they testify that they do not possess anything, the greatness of the sign may become more evident. He also indicates that through them the hungry hearts are to be nourished.

### Verse 17

“Five loaves and two fish.” Through the five loaves and two fish, the whole Old Testament is signified.

By the five loaves, the five books of Moses are signified. They are appropriately barley loaves, since barley is food for animals, and rough, coarse food must be given to the uneducated. “The natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 1). Yet within them lies the marrow of the sweetest meaning.

By the two fish, the Prophets and the Psalms are signified. Hence, after the resurrection, he says: “The things written concerning me in the Law and in the many Prophets” (Luke 24).

### Verse 19

“Having taken the five,” and so forth. He took five loaves; he did not create new ones, because when he came in the flesh he preached nothing other than what had been foretold, and he fulfilled it in his work.

“He blessed.” By opening their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures, he multiplied them through the gift of inner sweetness.

“He broke.” He brought forth the mysteries of the Law into the midst.

### Verse 20

“The fragments.” The more hidden things, which the uneducated cannot grasp, must not be neglected. They must be diligently investigated by the twelve apostles, signified by the twelve baskets, and by their successors. Servile tasks are carried out with baskets. “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Corinthians 1).

### Verse 21

“Besides women and children.” The weaker sex and younger age are considered unworthy of being numbered. This signifies those who are weak in faith and not yet fit for battle.

### Verse 22

“And immediately he compelled,” and so forth. (RABANUS.) Those who, as John says, were going to come and make him king (John 6), because they had seen the miracle of the loaves, and so forth, up to the exhortation that we pray that such things may not soften us.

### Verse 23

“He went up.” He fed the crowd as God; he went up to pray as a human being. This was not because he did not possess everything in his power, but so that he might fulfill the form of a human being. After this act of piety there follows the remarkable miracle of his power.

“When evening came.” It is rightly said that this storm occurred in the evening, because while the Church is in tribulation she is said to be as though in the night, and the sun of righteousness appears to have hidden itself.

### Verse 24

“But the boat.” The boat is in the middle of the sea, while Jesus alone is on the land, because sometimes the Church is not only afflicted but also defiled, so that she appears entirely abandoned by God. Yet God does not abandon her. Hence Mark says: “He saw them struggling at the oars” (Mark 6). Even if he is not present, and even if he delays, he nevertheless sees and strengthens them.

### Verse 25

“But in the fourth watch.” They are in danger throughout the entire night, because when a person examines himself, he finds nothing except the darkness of anxieties and the heat of enemies.

“He came to them.” Mark says: “He intended to pass them by,” although he came to free them. This happens so that, after being troubled for a while and then quickly delivered, they may be more greatly astonished and give thanks. The same thing often occurs in the sufferings of the saints.

### Verse 26

“And when they saw him,” and so forth. It often happens that when some calming of a long tribulation suddenly arises, people do not immediately believe that the deliverance is real. Therefore, while their former fear remains intense, prayer is directed toward deliverance.

### Verse 27

“I am he; do not be afraid.” He does not add “who I am,” because they could recognize him from his familiar voice. Or because he is the one who said: “He who is has sent me to you” (Exodus 3).

### Verse 28

“Lord, if it is you.” If you are that deliverer, command me to come to you by overcoming these pressures in imitation of you.

### Verse 29

“And getting out.” Despairing of human help, he tramples down the pressures in his mind so that he may be conformed to Jesus.

“He was walking,” and so forth. Behold, a human being walks upon the waters. Therefore do not doubt that Christ possessed a true body, because he walked upon the waters.

He made him walk upon the sea in order to show divine power. He causes him to sink so that he may not forget his weakness, think himself equal to God, or become proud.

### VERSE 30.—

And when he had begun, etc. He is left for a little while to the temptation, so that faith may be increased; for just as he believed that by Jesus’ command he could be supported upon the waves, so, while he is sinking, he believes that he can be saved by his power.

### VERSE 32.—

The wind ceased. Whenever God is present in anyone through grace, all conflicts immediately fall silent.

### VERSE 33.—

And they worshiped, etc. Having seen the sign, they confess him to be the Son of God. Why, then, does Arius maintain that he is a creature?

### VERSE 34.—

Into the land of Genesar. Allegorically: *Genesar* is interpreted as “garden of princes.” Through the type of the apostles and the boat, therefore, we are to understand that the Church, delivered by the Lord from persecutions, is brought to the shore—that is, to rest—where the inheritance of paradise and the delight of the first robe will be restored.

### VERSE 36.—

The fringe of his garment, etc. That is, the least commandment; or the flesh through which we come to the Word of God. Whoever touches him by believing is healed from every disease of impiety.

## CHAPTER XV

### VERSE 1.—

Then they approached. The people of Genesar, less learned, believe; but those who seem wise come to do battle.

(CHRYSOSTOM.) “Then,” he says—that is, when he had performed countless signs, when, etc.—up to the point where he showed their great wickedness.

### VERSE 2.—

For they do not wash. Those who are inwardly defiled by envy accuse nothing inwardly. They preserve their baptisms in vain, since they neglect to wash away the uncleanness of their hearts and bodies.

### VERSE 3.—

Why do you also? If you disregard God’s commandments because of human traditions, why do you accuse the disciples, who set aside human ordinances in order to keep God’s decrees?

### VERSE 4.—

Honor your father. (HIER.) In Scripture, honor consists not so much in greetings and the performance of duties as, etc.—up to the point that children should honor their parents even by providing them with the necessities of life.

### VERSE 5.—

But you say, etc. Your tradition, however, is contrary. You compel children to say this to their parents: “Whatever I was going to offer to God, I am using for your food”; and it benefits you, father, to fear eating what has been consecrated. Or: “What I offer to God benefits you yourself.” Whoever says this—namely, he will be worthy of eternal life. Or “says,” that is, it will be beneficial to say it. “It will be beneficial,” as if he were saying: “No; rather, you would be sacrilegious if you accepted it, because I have vowed it to God.” Or: “It will benefit you, if I give it to God.”

### VERSE 7.—

He prophesied well, etc. In the Spirit he foretold the Jews’ hypocrisy: that they would oppose the Gospel deceitfully.

### VERSE 8.—

He honors me with his lips. “Teacher, we know that you are truthful” (Mark 12). Or, while commending outward cleanliness, he indicates that the inward cleanliness—which is the true one—is not in them.

### VERSE 11.—

Not what enters. Nothing outside a person defiles him inwardly; nor is sacrificial food (*idolothyton*) defiled by the fact that it is God’s creation. With one statement he abolishes every superstitious observance, since religion is thought to consist in distinguishing foods.

### VERSE 12.—

Then the disciples approached. The Pharisees display great religious concern regarding foods, and when they heard this saying they were scandalized—that is, they were indignant.

“They were scandalized.” In Greek, *σκάνδαλον* (*skandalon*); in our language we may say “an offense,” “a ruin,” or “a stumbling of the foot.” Hence: “Whoever scandalizes anyone,” that is, gives an occasion for ruin.

### VERSE 14.—

Leave them, etc. Allow them to follow their own judgment, since they are beyond correction. Hence Paul says: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second correction” (Titus 3).

### VERSE 15.—

Explain it. What was said plainly, the apostles think was said as a parable. The hearer is defective who wishes either obscure things to be understood plainly or plainly stated things obscurely.

### VERSE 19.—

From the heart, etc. These things are not implanted by the devil; they arise from one’s own will. The devil is an instigator, not the author, since he knows a person’s inner thoughts only through habits and actions.

### VERSE 20.—

With unwashed hands. The prophets’ spiritual sayings concerning the purification of heart and body, such as: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isaiah 1). The Pharisees understood this carnally as referring only to the body, which is vain.

### VERSE 21.—

And departing, etc. He leaves the slanderers and goes into the region of Tyre and Sidon in order to free the daughter and, through the faith of a gentile woman, to expose the unbelief of the scribes. His leaving the slanderers signifies that after the resurrection he would leave behind the unbelief of the Jews and go to the gentiles through preaching.

### VERSE 22.—

She cried out, etc. She cries out through faith; hence she knows to call him “Son of David,” confessing Christ’s incarnation. She asks on behalf of her daughter—that is, on behalf of her people, who do not yet believe—that they may be freed from the devil’s deception. Or, the daughter is the soul or conscience of any member of the Church enslaved to the devil, for whom the mother Church prays; alternatively, the person himself prays for his defiled conscience.

### VERSE 23.—

He did not answer her. Not out of pride, but so as not to contradict his own decree: “Do not go into the way of the gentiles” (Matthew 10). Thus he avoids the Jews’ accusation, while the salvation of the gentiles is reserved for the time of his passion and resurrection.

### VERSE 24.—

I was not sent. As if he were saying: “First I must complete among the Jews the mystery of my coming, and then bring in the other sheep.” He postpones the granting of this request because of that sign.

### VERSE 26.—

The children’s bread. The word of salvation, which is owed first to the Jews, is not good to give to dogs—that is, to gentiles, who continually bark with canine fury.

### VERSE 27.—

Yes, Lord. Under the woman’s persona, the Church’s remarkable faith, patience, and humility are proclaimed. Faith, because she believes that her daughter can be healed. Patience, because, though repeatedly despised, she persists in prayer. Humility, because she compares herself not to dogs but to puppies.

“For even the puppies.” The table is sacred Scripture. The children’s crumbs are the inner mysteries by which the humble are nourished beneath the table, because the gentiles are humble puppies, submissive to Scripture in humility. The little ones eat neither loaves nor crusts—that is, not the surface of the letter but its marrow.

### VERSE 28.—

Great is your faith. Thus earlier concerning the centurion: “I have not found such faith in Israel” (Matthew 8). He likewise foreshadowed the faith of the gentiles, as this Canaanite woman does. Great is the faith of the gentiles, who obey upon hearing and obtain salvation from God for themselves and their own. The fact that he heals the centurion’s servant and the Canaanite woman’s daughter without going to them signifies that the gentiles, to whom he did not come in bodily presence, would be saved through his word.

And she was healed. Here an example is given of catechizing and baptizing infants, who can neither understand nor do anything for themselves, but are freed from the devil through the faith and confession of their parents.

### VERSE 29.—

And when he had crossed over. After foreshadowing the salvation of the gentiles in the daughter of the Canaanite woman, he returns to Judea, because, when the fullness of the gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.

Into the mountain. The Lord sits upon the mountain; the Word sits on high, because he could not be understood in his own majesty.

### VERSE 30.—

The blind. The blind are those who do not understand, even if they obey those who command them. The deaf are those who do not obey, even if they understand.

### VERSE 32.—

But Jesus. He summons the disciples in order to teach teachers to share their counsels with their inferiors, or so that from his speech they may understand the greatness of the sign.

I have compassion on the crowd. The crowd endures the Lord for three days, because faithful penitents turn to the Lord in deed, word, and thought. They would faint on the road of the present life if they were sent away in the state of their conscience without the nourishment of instruction. In the earlier sign, relatives and neighbours—the five senses—are mentioned; the Lord does not recall them, but the disciples do, when evening had come and the sun was already declining. Here the Lord says that he has compassion, and explains why: “because they have now continued with me for three days.” In the whole world there is a third period, the time in which grace is given: the first before the Law, the second under the Law, the third under grace, and the fourth is in the future, where there will be day without night. As one journeys toward that time, one is refreshed along the way.

### VERSE 33.—

Bread in the desert. The preachers call themselves loaves and the desert—that is, unproductive. As if they were saying: “Where are we to obtain such eloquence that we can satisfy listeners so eager?”

### VERSE 36.—

And taking them. He shows that he rejoices with us over the salvation of human beings and teaches us to give thanks even for temporal things.

Seven loaves. He feeds them with the sevenfold Spirit, joined with apostolic authority, as though with the flavor of the few fish that refresh us through the example of their life or death. The seven loaves are the Scripture of the New Testament, in which the grace of the Holy Spirit is both revealed and given. They are not barley loaves, as above, because here—unlike in the Law—the vital nourishment of the soul is not concealed beneath figures as under extremely tenacious chaff. Here there are not two fish, as in the Law, where two were anointed, king and priest, but a few: the saints of the New Testament, who have been rescued from the waves of the world, endure its turbulent sea, and refresh us by their example, so that we do not faint on the way.

(BEDA.) There, above the grass, so that the desires of the flesh might be restrained; here, upon the earth, where the world itself also is, etc.—up to the point that both meals were celebrated on a mountain, because the Scripture of both Testaments commands the height of heavenly precepts and rewards; both proclaim the height of Christ.

And what remained. The higher mysteries, which the common crowd cannot contain, the apostles lift up and fill seven baskets—that is, the hearts of the perfect, enlightened for understanding by the sevenfold grace of the Spirit.

Seven baskets. Baskets are customarily woven from rushes and palm leaves. They signify the saints, who place the root of their hearts in the very fountain of life so that they do not wither, like a rush in water, and who retain in their hearts the palm of eternal recompense.

### VERSE 39.—

And having dismissed the crowd. Here he teaches that preachers, after ministering the word to the crowd, ought themselves to be refreshed within the chamber of their hearts by the fruits of virtue.

Into the region. Magedan, otherwise called Dalmanutha, is a region around Gerasa. Its name is interpreted as “fruits” or “messengers,” and it signifies the garden of which it is said: “A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed,” where the fruits of virtues grow. There the name of the Lord is proclaimed.

## CHAPTER XVI

### VERSE 1.—

And they approached, etc., asking for a sign from heaven, etc.—that he who had fed many with little might rain down manna by which he could refresh everyone. Hence, after the distribution of the bread, John says: “What sign do you perform, so that we may see and believe you? What do you work? Our fathers ate manna in the desert” (John 6). They asked this by way of testing him, so that he would send fire from on high after the manner of Elijah, or, in the likeness of Samuel, make thunder roar in summertime—as though they could not also slander those signs and say that they resulted from hidden and various disturbances of the air.

### VERSE 2.—

When evening came. He reproaches them for distinguishing the days according to the order of the elements while ignoring the signs of the times, although the whole Law and the prophets signify the indications of his coming through the marvel of the works he would perform.

### VERSE 3.—

For it glows red. After the resurrection the apostles suffer. Through them you can know that I will judge in the future, because, since I do not spare my own good people from suffering, I will not spare others in the future.

### VERSE 4.—

Signs. The signs relating to the time of grace, foretold by the prophets, cannot make you believe in my coming.

But the sign. He spoke of the signs of the times concerning his coming or passion, to which the red sky in the evening is analogous; and likewise concerning the tribulation preceding his future coming, to which the red sky accompanied by sadness is analogous.

It will not be given to him. Yet it is given to the faithful from heaven, when, in the sight of the apostles, he ascended into heaven and sent the Holy Spirit.

### VERSE 5.—

They forgot to take bread. How can they lack bread, when they had just filled the baskets, boarded the boat, and, as they sailed, heard him warn them to beware of the Pharisees’ leaven? Nevertheless, Scripture says that they forgot to take loaves with them because they were captivated by the sweetness of the one true and inward bread—which was with them—and judged that they should care little about bodily concerns and necessities, since even natural refreshment had slipped from their minds.

### VERSE 6.—

Of the leaven. Leaven is perverse doctrine, which, even in a small quantity, corrupts the whole mass and draws it into its own flavor.

### VERSE 8.—

Why are you thinking? Why are you thinking that I spoke of earthly bread, about which you ought not to doubt, when from so few loaves I made such abundant remains?

### VERSE 11.—

Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees. Beware of their superstitious doctrine, which, in the manner of leaven, pretends to possess the substance of true bread. By this he indicates what the five or seven loaves signify. For if he calls leaven heretical doctrines, the loaves are true doctrine.

### VERSE 13.—

Into the region of Caesarea Philippi. This is the place where the Jordan rises at the foot of Lebanon, from two springs, Jor and Dan.

Human beings. They are human beings who speak of the Son of Man; those who understand his divinity are gods.

The Son of Man? The Lord professes concerning himself the humility of humanity; the disciples understand his divinity.

### VERSE 14.—

Some say John the Baptist. They could have erred concerning Elijah or the others, just as Herod erred concerning John when he said: “John, whom I beheaded, has risen from the dead; and therefore powers are working in him” (Mark 6). He wishes their errors to be explained so that, once these have been rejected, the disciples may proclaim the truth—not from popular opinion but from the Lord’s revelation.

### VERSE 17.—

Simon Peter answered. One answers, and the answer is given to one on behalf of all, so that unity may be preserved in everyone.

Of the living God. This distinguishes him from false gods, whom the gentiles fashioned for themselves either from dead human beings or from perceptible matter.

Barjona. He is rightly called “son of the dove,” because he followed the Lord with devout simplicity, or because he was full of spiritual grace. He is called the son of the Holy Spirit, who appeared in the form of a dove, by the one whom he had called the Son of the living God. The Father reveals this to the son of the dove, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one operation. He reveals, I say, the mystery of faith, because flesh and blood could not reveal it—that is, human beings puffed up with carnal wisdom, who are not sons of the dove and therefore are alien to the wisdom of the Spirit. Of such people he said above: “Some say John the Baptist, others …,” and so forth.

### VERSE 18.—

You are. He does not say, “You will be called,” but “You are Peter,” because of the firmness of faith and the constancy of confession.

Peter. From me, the rock; yet in such a way that I retain for myself the dignity of the foundation. You will arrange pure stones upon me and cast away the leprous.

Just as the apostles received from the Lord names such as “light” and the others—“You are the salt of the earth”—so he gave Simon the name Peter from himself.

And the gates. The gates of hell are sins, threats, flatteries, and heresies. Through these the weak rush into death, since they are thought to have built the house of their profession—that is, their confession of faith—not truly upon the rock but upon sand: not following Christ with a simple and true intention, but putting forward a religious appearance for some earthly reason. Whoever receives the faith of Christ in the innermost love of the heart easily conquers whatever assaults him from outside.

### VERSE 19.—

And whatever you bind. That is, whoever you adjudge to eternal punishments while persisting in sins; or whoever you release as humble and truly penitent—so shall it be in heaven also.

And whatever you bind on earth. (HIER.) The other apostles also possess the same judicial authority, to whom, after the resurrection, he said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20), etc.—up to the point where lepers are commanded in Leviticus to show themselves to the priests. The priests do not make them lepers; they discern who are clean and who unclean. So also here.

### VERSE 20.—

That he should tell no one, etc. Above, he commands them to preach his coming; here he commands them not to say that he is Jesus. For it is one thing to preach “Christ,” which is a common title of dignity, and another to preach “Jesus,” which is the personal name of the Savior. As if he were saying: “It is not useful for my majesty to be publicly preached to the peoples, who are going to see me suffer many things. This will be permitted only when the resurrection has displayed the power of my divinity.”

Jesus Christ. The Savior, so that they would not be scandalized by the one whom shortly afterward they would see spat upon and crucified.

### VERSE 21.—

From that time onward, etc. Here is the reason why preaching was prohibited. As if he were saying: “Preach me only after I have suffered these things, because before then it is not beneficial.”

### VERSE 22.—

Far be it. Peter does not want his confession destroyed, nor does he think that the Son of God can be killed.

### VERSE 23.—

Go. Above, all those glorious things were promised for the future, not given in the present: “I will build my Church, and I will give you the keys,” etc. If he had given these immediately, error would never afterward have found a place in him.

Because you do not. You do not wish me to redeem the world through my death, which is the Father’s will; rather, you understand these things carnally.

### VERSE 24.—

If anyone wishes. After foretelling his passion and resurrection to the apostles, he urges both them and the crowds to follow him.

Let him deny himself. Let him reject what belongs to the old condition, so that he may receive what lies beyond himself. Once vices have been removed, let virtue follow; let him take up his cross and follow me. He had denied what belonged to the old condition who said: “I live, yet no longer I.” But he had begun to possess what lay beyond himself: “Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2).

Let him take up his cross. The cross is taken up either when the body is afflicted through abstinence or when the soul is afflicted through compassion for one’s neighbor. Paul bore the cross of abstinence when he said: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” (2 Corinthians 11). He also bore the cross of compassion when he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?”

### VERSE 26.—

For what does it profit? The Church has a time of persecution and a time of peace. He designates these times in his commands. In the time of persecution, one must lay down one’s life; in the time of peace, earthly desires must be broken.

Or what, etc. Neither profit, nor fear, nor anything else should withdraw anyone from salvation, because “what exchange will a person give,” etc.: “I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm 115). Or, a person can give nothing earthly in exchange for a lost soul.

### VERSE 27.—

For the Son. Let it not seem harsh that he must suffer this, because “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8).

### VERSE 28.—

There are some. Because the apostles were inexperienced, some consolation is promised to them even in the present life, so that they may believe more certainly concerning the future.

In the kingdom. In the kingdom of eternal blessedness; or by displaying his power in the present Church.

## CHAPTER XVII

### VERSE 1.—

And after days, etc. Mark says the same, but Luke says eight. Thus these two place the intervening days, while Luke adds them, etc.—up to the point that in the future they will be separated in every respect, when he hides them in the shelter of his face from the disturbance of human beings.

Peter. The names of these men are fitting. Each person ought to be a Peter—that is, firm in faith. Hence James, that is, one who overthrows vices. Hence John, that is, one who attributes everything to divine grace in opposition to the pride of life, which commonly arises from virtues.

### VERSE 2.—

He was transfigured. He displayed the form that he possessed by nature without abandoning the flesh that he had assumed by his will. That body which he possessed by nature he gave to his disciples at the supper: it was neither mortal nor corruptible.

His face shone. This was an example of the future blessedness and glory that the righteous will see, after the impious have first been removed.

His garments, etc. They became white in a way they had not been before, because what we will be has not yet appeared; but when it appears, we will be like him. Mark says that they were such as no fuller on earth can make. That is, God cannot make garments so bright in this life, because no one is without sin. No one on earth can cleanse himself in the way God does in heaven, cleansing his garment from every stain. The fuller is either the teacher of souls or the purifier of his own body.

### VERSE 3.—

And behold. What they said and of what they spoke, Luke makes clear: “They appeared in glory and were speaking of his departure, which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem” (Luke 9)—that is, of his passion and resurrection. They signify the prophetic oracles, etc.—up to the point that, if Peter, seeing the glorified humanity, is affected by such joy that he never wishes to be separated from its contemplation, what must we think of those who have deserved to see the divinity?

### VERSE 5.—

While he was still speaking. Let the one who sought a tabernacle learn that, in the resurrection, they are to be protected not by the shelter of buildings but by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Behold, a bright cloud, etc. As with the Lord’s baptism, so also with his glorification the mystery of the Holy Trinity is displayed. The glory that we confess by believing at his baptism, we will praise by seeing at the resurrection. There the Holy Spirit appeared in a dove; here, in a bright cloud. For whoever now preserves the faith with a simple heart will then contemplate openly what he has believed, and will be protected by the grace with which he is illuminated.

And behold, a voice, etc. Because he had asked imprudently, he did not deserve an answer from the Lord; but the Father’s voice bears witness to the Son and teaches Peter, and through him the others, the truth.

This is the Son. Moses and Elijah are servants, and together with us they ought to prepare a tabernacle for the Lord in their hearts.

Listen to him. The Father now commands what Moses, bearing witness to the incarnation, foretold: “The Lord will raise up a prophet” (Deuteronomy 18), etc. As if he were saying: “This is the one whom Moses promised.”

### VERSE 6.—

And when the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces. With a deeper understanding, they perceived the one divinity of both. They were afraid either because they recognized that they had been mistaken, or because the cloud overshadowed them, or because they heard the Father’s voice.

### VERSE 7.—

Rise, etc. When fear has been driven away, instruction is given; while fear remains, it would not be heard.

### VERSE 8.—

But when they lifted up their eyes, etc. Once the cloud had been removed, they saw Jesus and realized that Moses and Elijah had vanished. For after the shadow of the Law and the prophets, which had covered the apostles with its veil, had departed, the true light is found in the Gospel.

Jesus alone. If Moses and Elijah had remained with Jesus, the Father’s voice would have seemed uncertain as to whom it had preferred to honor.

### VERSE 9.—

Tell no one, etc. Otherwise the glory of the future kingdom, shown beforehand, would seem unbelievable, and the subsequent cross would cause scandal among the inexperienced.

### VERSE 10.—

That Elijah must come, etc. It is a tradition of the Pharisees, in accordance with the prophet Malachi, that Elijah will come before the Savior’s coming, turn the hearts of the fathers toward the children and of the children toward the fathers, and restore everything to its ancient condition. The apostles therefore think that the final transformation of glory is the one they have seen, and they say: “If you have now come in glory, how is it that your precursor has not appeared?”—especially since they had also seen Elijah depart.

### VERSE 13.—

Then they understood, etc. They understood from the indication of his passion, which he had often foretold, and of his precursor, whose work they saw completed.

### VERSE 14.—

And when he had come. The circumstances correspond to the events, etc.—up to the point where he strengthens the weak, teaches, and chastises.

Because he is a lunatic. Mark calls him deaf and mute, etc.—up to the point where the creature insults the Creator.

### VERSE 15.—

And I brought him, etc. He covertly accuses the disciples, since the inability to heal often arises not from the fault of those healing but from the fault of those who are to be healed.

### VERSE 16.—

Answering. He is not overcome by weariness and does not burst out in anger, for he is gentle in speech; rather, he speaks as a physician to a sick person acting against his instructions.

### VERSE 17.—

And he rebuked him. He was angry not with the person but with the vice, and through one person he rebuked the Jews for their unbelief. Hence he adds: “Bring him here to me.”

And the demon went out from him. Mark says, etc.—up to the point where he was more tormented than before, when the demon possessed him in a quiet state.

### VERSE 19.—

Because of your unbelief. Here we see that when we are not heard, the problem is not the inability of the one who grants the request but the fault of the one who prays. Conversely, if your faith were as ardent as it was distressed, it would grow hotter and hotter.

Like a grain of mustard seed. He compares perfect faith to a grain of mustard seed, humble in appearance but burning in the heart: insignificant to those who see it and apparently powerless, yet when crushed by afflictions it displays what it contains within.

### VERSE 20.—

But this kind. He shows how the devil’s insolence is overcome, so that we may know that the more serious evils must be conquered through fasting and prayers, and that God’s anger toward us can be appeased by this remedy.

Except through prayer. This instability of carnal pleasures is not changed, etc.—up to the point where it is said: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5).

### VERSE 21.—

The Son of Man. He always mingles sad things with joyful ones, so that when they arrive they may be borne with less distress, as things already foreseen.

### VERSE 22.—

And they were greatly saddened. This did not arise from unbelief but from affection, because they could not bear to hear anything humiliating about him.

### VERSE 23.—

And when they had come to Capernaum. Through the emperor Augustus, Judea was made tributary, etc.—up to the question whether he would pay the tribute or resist Caesar.

### VERSE 24.—

What do you think? Before Peter could suggest anything, the Lord asks the question so that the disciples would not be scandalized by the demand for tribute when they saw that he knew what had happened in his absence.

The kings of the earth. Our Lord, according to the flesh, was also the son of a king, born from David, and he was the Word of the Almighty. Therefore, as the son of kings, he did not owe tribute; but, because of the humility of the flesh, it was fitting for him to fulfill all righteousness.

### VERSE 25.—

Then the children are free, etc. The children of every kingdom are free within that kingdom; how much more, then, are the children of that kingdom under which all earthly kingdoms exist, free within any earthly kingdom?

## CHAPTER XVIII

### VERSE 1.—

Who, do you think, etc. Because of the equality of the price at which Peter had been compared with the Lord in the payment of the tribute, they supposed that Peter had been placed above all the apostles.

In the kingdom of heaven. Alternatively, the kingdom of God is the teaching of the Gospel, which we must obey simply and without any hesitation, just as a child does not contradict his teachers.

### VERSE 2.—

And calling him. According to Mark, Jesus embraces the child, signifying that the humble are worthy of his embrace and love.

A little child, etc. He used a child of that age in order to demonstrate the likeness. Or he placed himself in their midst, since he came not to be served but to serve. Or “a little child” means that he placed the Holy Spirit in their hearts, so that they might avoid pride through humility.

### VERSE 4.—

Whoever therefore humbles himself, etc. The Lord invites his disciples and everyone else to possess through virtue what the child has by nature: innocence and humility.

Like this little child. He will be innocent like this little child, who does not persist in anger; Jesus does not remember an offense; he does not desire a woman merely because he has seen her.

### VERSE 6.—

But whoever causes scandal. Although this is said generally against everyone, etc.—up to the point where it is necessary for us to take prudent measures, etc.

It is better. It is much better to undergo a brief punishment for one’s fault than to be preserved for eternal torments. For God will not judge the same matter twice.

### VERSE 7.—

Woe to the man. He is not judged according to the benefit that results from the matter, but according to the outcome he intends.

### VERSE 8.—

But if your hand. Above he taught that we must not scandalize believers, etc.—up to the point where, under the pretext of compassion, you expose yourself to scandals.

It is better for you, etc. It is better to lead a solitary life than to lose eternal life for the sake of the necessities of the present life.

### VERSE 10.—

See that you do not despise. Thus I command you to abandon all friendships with severity, etc.—up to the point where you should care as much as you can for the salvation of the weak.

For their angels. Why must they not be despised? Because angels are sent daily for them.

(HIER.) Great is the dignity of souls, since each person has, from the beginning of his birth, an angel assigned to guard him.

They always see, etc. They enjoy the manifest vision of God, etc.—up to the point where those who are everywhere run within him who is everywhere.

### VERSE 12.—

If someone has a hundred, etc. The Lord had a hundred sheep, etc.—up to the point where they lack unity for perfection.

Will he not leave, etc.? (GREGORY.) Because he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, etc.—up to the point where the unjust person condemns only what he has done wrongly.

### VERSE 13.—

He will rejoice, etc. The Lord rejoices more over our restoration—because he makes us rejoice more—than over the angels’ immutability. The greater power and humility of God are recognized in our restoration than in our creation.

### VERSE 15.—

But if he sins against you, etc. If he sins against God, the matter is not subject to our judgment. In this order we must avoid scandals: we must not injure anyone, correct the sinner out of zeal for justice, and open the compassion of our heart to the penitent.

Reprove him, etc. He does not command us to forgive the sinner indiscriminately, but the penitent. The person who sees a brother sinning and remains silent sins just as the person who does not forgive the penitent. For when he said, “If he repents, forgive him,” he had first said, “If he sins, reprove him.” Forgiveness should be neither difficult nor indulgence careless.

### VERSE 17.—

Tell it to the Church. So that the Church may hold him in abhorrence, etc.—up to the point where divine judgment confirms the human sentence.

As a gentile. The person who acts under the name of believer is more detestable, etc.—up to the point where he acts through thefts and perjuries.

### VERSE 18.—

Amen, I say, etc. So greatly is your judgment confirmed by the divine judgment, whether in receiving the penitent or rejecting the stubborn.

### VERSE 20.—

If two. Typically: when spirit, soul, and body agree, so that there is no conflict among them—with the flesh desiring against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh—whatever they ask will be done. For if the body desires what the spirit desires, the request concerns only good things.

There I am in their midst. Every saying urges concord and peace, which he commends so strongly that he says God is in their midst, because peace and charity establish their dwelling among the peaceful; and he confirms that, by the merit of unity, everything asked for ought to be obtained.

### VERSE 23.—

Therefore it is like. So that you may know that one must forgive fellow servants, I will show this by a comparison: if that king and lord forgave his servant, how much more should a person forgive his fellow servants?

### VERSE 25.—

And his wife. He handed over not only the people but also their rulers and subjects, together with their entire families and possessions, to foreign nations according to the magnitude of their offenses, so that what they had refused to pay by choice they might pay through punishment. He ordered that they pay penalties for their greed and deeds, as though for a wife and children.

### VERSE 27.—

But moved with compassion. The merciful Lord not only released the Jewish captivity but also promised, at Christ’s coming, to grant forgiveness for all sins if they persisted in what they had begun.

He forgave him. That is, he released him from the burden of carnal observances and forgave the debt—that is, his former transgressions.

### VERSE 28.—

He found one. He wearied the gentile people, as though they were his debtors, saying that the grace of Christ was not given to them for salvation. He demanded carnal observances from them not only by persuasion but also by torments.

### VERSE 32.—

Wicked servant. “I often forgave you your debts when you asked in your distress; but once freed, you had no compassion. Rather, you persecute the prophets and apostles, and, ungrateful and presumptuous in your claim to justice, you despise the gentiles, judging them unworthy of your fellowship in Christ.”

## CHAPTER XIX

### VERSE 3.—

And they approached. They intended to trap him by their question. If he said that a wife should be dismissed for any reason and another taken, the preacher of chastity would act against himself. If he said that she should not be dismissed, he would act against the teaching of Moses and of God. Therefore he moderates his answer concerning the natural law, setting the first judgment of God against the later concession, which was granted not by God’s will but because of the necessity created by sinners.

### VERSE 4.—

And female. He does not say “females,” so that there may be one marriage rather than several, which was being sought through the dismissal of the first wives.

### VERSE 5.—

He will cling to his wife. If the wife is morally bad, luxurious, or anything of that kind, she must be endured whether one wishes it or not. For although we were free, we voluntarily subjected ourselves to servitude. If a free woman is joined to a slave, or a free man to a female slave, it is not regarded as a marriage once the matter has been discovered; the same applies to relatives.

And the two will be one flesh. The reward of marriage is that two become one flesh. Chastity joined to the spirit becomes one spirit. By God’s salutary counsel it was arranged that a man should embrace in a woman a portion of his own body, lest he consider foreign to himself what he knew to have been fashioned from himself.

### VERSE 6.—

Let no human being separate. A human being separates when, out of desire for a second wife, he dismisses the first. God separates—he who also joins—when, by mutual agreement for the worship of God, because the time is short, “those who have wives” live “as though they had none.”

### VERSE 7.—

Why then did Moses, etc.? (CHRYSOSTOM.) The teaching displeases sinners, etc.—up to the point where the interpretation of the truth is silenced.

### VERSE 9.—

And marries another, he commits adultery. And he who [marries] the dismissed woman. For it could happen that someone would slander an innocent woman and, because of a second marriage, bring a charge against his first wife. Thus he commands the first wife to be dismissed so that, while she is alive, he may not have a second. And lest the wife do the same to her husband, the same precaution is prescribed, so that she may not have a second husband.

And because an adulterous woman does not fear disgrace, Scripture says of the man who marries such a woman that he is guilty of adultery: “He who keeps an adulteress is a fool and impious” (Proverbs 18).

### VERSE 10.—

It is not expedient. They saw the heavy burden of wives—women who are angry, drunk, and of this sort—who nevertheless must be endured, because, although we were free, we subjected ourselves to servitude.

### VERSE 12.—

For there are. There are three kinds of eunuchs. Two are bodily: those who are born so, and those who have been castrated through captivity or through the pleasures of their mistresses. The third is spiritual: those who, although they could be husbands, practice continence for Christ.

Those who have made themselves so. Among these are also counted those who pretend to chastity under the appearance of religion.

Whoever is able. This is the voice of one exhorting, not commanding, as though each person should consider his own strength and whether he is able to fulfill the precepts of virginity and chastity.

### VERSE 14

“Let the little children come.” If they are going to be holy, why do you forbid them to come to the Father? If they are evil, why do you pronounce judgment before the offense? “Of such.” For what they are now, it is indeed my concern that you honor them; what they will be afterward is their own concern, that you may pity them. He does not say “of these,” but “of such,” to show that it is not age but character that reigns; and he promises a reward to those who possess similar innocence and simplicity.

### VERSE 15

“And when he had laid his hands upon them.” He lays his hands upon the little children whenever he grants the humble the help of grace.

### VERSE 16

“And behold, one came.” (Bede) He had heard that those who were like a little child were worthy of the kingdom, and he wanted to learn more certainly—not through parables but openly—by what merits one might attain life. (Jerome) This young man was both rich and proud. According to another Evangelist, he questioned him not with the desire of a learner but as one who was testing him.

### VERSE 17 [Col. 0149A]

“Why do you ask me about what is good?” Because he had called him a good teacher, but had not confessed him to be God or the Son of God, he says that no holy man is good in comparison with God. Christ, however, did not reject the testimony to his goodness; rather, he excludes the error of calling him a teacher apart from God. He does not deny that he is a good teacher, but says that no teacher apart from God is good.

“Keep the commandments.” He had asked, “What shall I do?” Christ does not answer, “Learn,” because God had taught him, as a rational creature, what to do. He shows that the one who asks about what is good is not good, but the one who does what is good. [Col. 0149B]

### VERSE 20

“The young man says to him.” (Bede) This man should not be thought—as some say—to have tested the Lord or to have lied about his life; rather, he confessed simply how he had lived. Otherwise, as another Evangelist says, Jesus would not be said to have loved him after looking into the secrets of his heart. He loves those who keep the commandments of the law, but he adds what is lacking for those who wish to be perfect; hence it follows:

“If you wish to be perfect.” “All these things.” (Jerome) He is lying. For if he loved his neighbor as himself, he would have fulfilled this in practice and would not have been saddened when he was ordered to give his possessions to the poor.

### VERSE 23

“A rich man enters with difficulty.” It is not the rich who remain rich, but those who cease to be rich, who will enter. In every respect it is safer neither to possess nor to love riches. [Col. 0149C]

### VERSE 24

“How difficult it is for a rich man.” (Isidore) No rich man will enter—that is, no one who trusts in riches—as Jesus explains according to Mark.

### VERSE 25

“They were astonished.” They counted among the rich all who loved riches, even if they did not possess them. Otherwise, since the crowd of the poor was larger, they would not have said, “Who can be saved?”

### VERSE 26

“God.” He is the one who turns a person from love of earthly things toward love of eternal things—not so that the greedy and proud may enter.

### VERSE 28 [Col. 0149D]

“In the regeneration.” There are two regenerations: the first from water and the Holy Spirit, the second in the resurrection. Thus there are two adoptions and two resurrections.

“Son of Man.” That is, when he who was judged in the form of a servant exercises judicial authority, you also will be judges with me.

“Upon twelve thrones.” By the twelve thrones is understood the whole company of those who judge; by the twelve tribes, the whole company of those who are judged. Those who left everything and followed the Lord will be judges. Those who possessed lawful things and used them rightly will be judged, and to them it will be said: “Come, blessed of my Father; for I was hungry, and you gave me food.” For there are two orders of the good.

### VERSE 29

“A hundredfold.” That is, whoever has abandoned carnal things for the Lord will receive spiritual things, which in comparison and according to their worth will be as though a hundred were compared with a small number.

Mark says: “A hundred times as much now in this time, with persecutions, brothers and sisters, and in the age to come eternal life” (Mark 10). That is, in this life, which is full of persecutions, they taste the joy of the kingdom and enjoy the sincere love of all the elect. But because many grow lukewarm or turn back, he adds: “But many who are first will be last” (Luke 15), and so forth. [Col. 0150A]

## CHAPTER XX

### VERSE 1

“The kingdom is like.” He shows by the parable that the first will be last and the last first.

This householder is our Creator, who has a vineyard: the universal Church. From Abel to the last elect who will be born at the end, it has produced as many holy people as it has sent forth branches. This father went out to cultivate the vineyard in the morning, at the third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours, hiring laborers from the beginning of this world to its end. To instruct the people of the faithful, he does not cease to send preachers. [Col. 0150B]

“The kingdom is like.” It is like not merely a man, but the whole undertaking carried out by a man, and similarly in comparable matters.

“Early in the morning.” Clearly, he began with the first righteous person to invite preachers, for an eternal reward, to plant the Church.

### VERSE 2

“By agreement.” That is, with the promise confirmed that they would be restored to the image of God if, by building up the Church, they persisted in the commandments of the Decalogue.

“For a denarius.” (Jerome) The denarius bears the image of the king, and so forth, up to “repent even at the last.”

“From the last onward,” and so forth. Those who were called to the kingdom at the Lord’s coming arrive without any delay and become equal to those who began from the beginning of the world. All receive the same heaven, but “star differs from star in glory.” He began with the last when he brought the thief into paradise before Peter. Those who come late are sometimes rewarded first because they depart from the body before those who were called in childhood. [Col. 0150C]

### VERSE 15

“Or is it not lawful for me?” A foolish question against the goodness of God. One should ask not whether he gave what he ought not to have given, but whether he failed to give what he ought to have given.

“Or is your eye,” and so forth. The Jews truly had an evil intention when they prohibited the apostles from speaking to the Gentiles so that they might be saved.

### VERSE 16 [Col. 0150D]

“So the last will be first.” (Augustine) That is, the Jews will be turned from the head to the tail, and the Gentiles from the tail to the head. Hence Moses says in the book of Deuteronomy: “The foreigner who dwells with you will rise above you; he will be the head, and you will be the tail.” Yet not all the first, nor all the last, belong to the number of the elect.

### VERSE 18

“Behold, we are going up,” and so forth. (Jerome) He had often said this to them, and so forth, up to “let them have no doubt that he would rise again.”

### VERSE 19

“To mock him,” and so forth. The Lord did not wish to prosper in the world but to suffer grievous things, in order to show us who fell through pleasure with what bitterness we must return.

### VERSE 20 [Col. 0151A]

“Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to him.” Having heard of the resurrection, she thought that he would immediately reign—forgetful of the second coming—and in feminine eagerness desired present things, forgetful of future ones.

### VERSE 21

“Say that,” and so forth. The desire is good, but the request is inconsiderate. Therefore it is not the will or intention that is blamed, but ignorance; and if simplicity does not deserve to obtain what it asks, it does not deserve to be put to shame.

### VERSE 22

“You do not know.” You who ask for or seek the seat of glory, which you have not yet deserved, are delighted by the height of honor even though you have not yet undergone the path of labor.

“Can you?” He knew that they could imitate his passion, but he says this so that, when he asks and they answer, we may all hear that no one can reign with Christ unless he has imitated his passion.

### VERSE 23 [Col. 0151B]

“The cup.” James, beheaded by Herod, and John, cast into a vessel of boiling oil and banished to Patmos, did not lack the courage for martyrdom.

“It is not mine to give.” This means that the kingdom of heaven belongs not to the one who gives but to the one who receives. For there is no partiality with God; whoever is worthy receives what is prepared not for a person but for a life. If, then, you are such that you may obtain what the Father has prepared for victors, you will receive it.

Or, “It is not mine to give” means that it is not mine to give to the proud, as you still are, but to others for whom it has been prepared. Therefore, do not remain what you are, but become other than you are: humble yourselves, you who already wish to be exalted, and it has been prepared for you.

### VERSE 24

“When the ten heard this.” Just as the two had carnally requested to be above all the others, so the others were carnally grieved that anyone should be placed before them.

### VERSE 30 [Col. 0151C]

“And behold, two blind men.” Mark mentions one of them because he had been the most famous in that city. Having been cast down from great prosperity, he was notorious for his misery: blind, of course, and a beggar. Mark therefore also mentions his name and that of his father—Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus—which is not easily found elsewhere, except in the case of Jairus, who was also prominent in that place. The fame of the man who was healed gave great renown to the miracle.

As he was entering Jericho, he healed one, as Luke says, because, approaching death, he preached the light of the Gospel to the Jews. As he was leaving, he healed two, because after the resurrection he preached both to Jews and to Gentiles. Mark mentions one of them because he writes for the Gentiles.

## CHAPTER XXI

### VERSE 1 [Col. 0151D]

“And when they had drawn near.” Here Matthew omits what happened before Jesus entered Jerusalem, which the others treat at greater length.

“And when they had drawn near.” The Lord drew near spiritually to Jerusalem when, having become incarnate, he visited the Church, in which there is the vision of peace, and reconciled it to himself through confession.

For Bethphage is interpreted as “house of the jaw.” Bethphage was a village of priests on the Mount of Olives, on the slope of which was the city of Bethany. Bethphage means “house of the jaw”; Bethany, “house of obedience.” As the Lord proceeded through these places, he exalted Jerusalem by his presence, because before his passion he filled many, through teaching, with the gifts of devout confession and obedience.

Those cities were situated on the Mount of Olives—that is, in Christ the Lord, from whom anointing and light come to all. Hence: “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden.”

“To the Mount of Olives: then Jesus,” and so forth. Looking toward the height of mercy, ἔλεος (*eleos*) is interpreted as “mercy.” The nature of oil serves light, is a solace in labors and sorrows, and surpasses other liquids. [Col. 0152A]
