“He sent.” Because he does not wish to hide the lamp he has received under a bushel.

“Two disciples.” Two were sent because they would preach the knowledge of truth, purity of works, and the mystery of twofold love. Some say that these two were Peter and Philip, who first brought the Gentiles to Christ: Philip brought Samaria, which they interpret as “she-ass,” and Peter brought Cornelius, understood as the colt of Samaria.

### VERSE 2 [Col. 0152B]

“And the colt.” The colt is the people of the Gentiles, upon whom none of the teachers had imposed the bridle of correction: free and wanton, yet itself entangled in the bonds of sins. “For all have sinned and lack the grace of God” (Romans 3).

Others speak only of the colt; Matthew, who writes for the Hebrews, also speaks of the she-ass, teaching that the Hebrews should not despair of salvation if they repent. Mark says that the colt was found before the door at a crossroads. The door is Christ, outside whom the people of the Gentiles stood bound—not on one road of faith, but amid various errors.

### VERSE 5

“Tell the daughter of Zion.” The daughter of Zion is Jerusalem, situated on Mount Zion.

Mystically, she is the Church belonging to the Jerusalem above, which is the mother of us all; at that time a considerable part of her was among the people of Israel.

“King.” Do not say, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19).

“To you.” If you believe; against you if you do not believe.

“Mounted on a she-ass,” and so forth. He did not literally sit upon both animals, but in the hearts of both peoples. The Lord was able to mount upon both, descending from one and ascending upon the other. [Col. 0152C]

### VERSE 7

“And they brought them.” Thus the apostles, by the power of Christ, also released the world from the power of the devil and placed their garments upon it. But the rest of the crowd—that is, the Jews—spread garments, meaning the commandments of the law, because these were to be trampled by Christians, on the road—that is, in Christ.

“Upon them.” The garments of the apostles are the divine commandments and spiritual grace, by which the ugliness of our flesh is covered. Formerly these peoples were naked, but now, adorned through the apostles, they have Christ as their rider.

The lesser crowd does not place garments upon the she-ass, but on the road, and not where it might cause offense. For the holy martyrs, stripping off the flesh, prepare the way for the simpler by the example of their blood.

### VERSE 8 [Col. 0152D]

“Branches from the trees,” and so forth. They cut branches or foliage because they excerpted words and judgments from the books of the Fathers, or examples.

### VERSE 9

“Hosanna.” (Jerome) *Osi* means “save” or “make safe.” *Anna* is the interjection of one who pleads, as though saying, “Save, I beg you.” *Hosanna* is wholly Hebrew and signifies that Christ’s coming is the salvation of the world. Hence it follows: “Blessed.”

“Hosanna,” that is, “Save.”

“In the highest.” Christ’s coming is the salvation not only of human beings but of the whole world, joining earthly things to heavenly things, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Philippians 2).

“In the highest.” It is also the salvation of the angels, whose number he completes.

### VERSE 10 [Col. 0153A]

“When he had entered.” He had often entered the city of Jerusalem, but never with such praises. He is called king only now, when he ascends in order to suffer—a title he had always avoided. This happened in order to stir up their envy against him more intensely, because the time of his passion was already approaching.

### VERSE 12

“And he was driving out.” (Augustine) He had driven them out on an earlier occasion also, as John alone relates; but the others speak of this final expulsion.

“The tables of the money-changers.” Since people came to the temple from every region, the priests sold animals to those who did not possess all that was required, including doves for the poor to offer, so that afterward they might receive the offerings once they had been sold. But because some had nothing with which to buy, they set up money-changers who would lend to them. Since the law forbids usury, the money-changers accepted various commodities in its place—fruit, grapes, and things of that kind. He drove these men out.

Mystically, he likewise drives such people out of the Church every day. He regards as guilty of one crime both those who sell and those who buy ecclesiastical offices. “And the seats of those who sell.” These are the seats of teachers; that is, he destroys the priesthood of those who accept payment for the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is given. Hence the heresy of Simon is condemned. [Col. 0153B]

Literally, however, it is absurd to say that sellers of doves sat in chairs.

### VERSE 13

“Of thieves.” A thief is one who pursues profit. Such a person persecutes bodily those who do not give, spiritually kills those who do give, and, while contemplating injury against his neighbor, sits like a thief in a cave.

### VERSE 14 [Col. 0153C]

“And the blind and the lame came to him.” Mystically, he heals simple sinners who approach him through repentance: first illuminating those who are blind in understanding and directing those who are lame in action into a life of righteousness.

### VERSE 15

“The wonderful things that he did,” and so forth. Nothing more astonishing could he have done than to drive out so many people with one lowly scourge and overturn the tables. Something fiery and star-like radiates from his eyes; the majesty of his divinity shines in his face.

### VERSE 16

“He said to them.” He does not leave himself open to accusation. He does not say, “They are doing well,” or, “They are doing badly,” nor does he spare their age; rather, he moderates his response, and, while remaining silent, confirms the children’s words through the testimony of Scripture.

“From the mouths of infants and nursing children.” They are witnesses to the miracles. They are called Christ’s infants not because of age but because of simplicity. They are called nursing children because they are delighted, as with milk, by the sweetness of the miracles. The miracles are called milk, while perfect doctrine is bread.

### VERSE 17 [Col. 0153D]

“He went out.” Because he was poor and flattered no one, he found no host in so great a city, but was received by Lazarus.

### VERSE 19

“The fig tree.” Just as he spoke many things in parables, so he also acted them out. For why would he seek fruit on a fig tree whose season everyone knew had not yet come, and condemn it to eternal barrenness, unless he meant by this action to terrify the people whom he taught by his word, so that no one who has leaves—that is, words of righteousness—without the fruit of works might deserve to be cut down?

“Leaves.” These are the traditions of the Pharisees, without the fruit of truth. Hence another Evangelist says that the time of Israel’s salvation had not yet come, because the people of the Gentiles had not yet entered; or because the time of faith had passed, when, having been rejected, he turned to the Gentiles.

“Never may fruit come from you.” The Creator does no injustice to what he possesses if he uses his creature according to his own will and for the benefit of others. [Col. 0154A]

### VERSE 20

“And when they saw this.” Since the Lord was going to suffer and bear the scandal of the cross, he ought to strengthen the minds of his disciples in advance through the sign. Hence they wondered that the fig tree had withered. By the same power he could have withered his enemies, unless he had awaited their salvation through patience.

### VERSE 21

“Faith.” He has perfect faith who works through love; such a person can move mountains. Others obtain forgiveness for sin if they themselves forgive others.

### VERSE 22

“You will receive.” Even if it is delayed until the appropriate time, and even if it is not granted to those for whom it is asked, it is nevertheless granted to those who ask worthily.

[Col. 0154B]

### VERSE 24

“I also will ask you,” and so forth. He could have refuted them openly, but he asks them so that they may be condemned either by their own silence or by their own answer, and may recognize for themselves by what authority he acts, in accordance with the saying: “God will crush their teeth in their own mouths.”

### VERSE 27

“Neither do I tell you.” Truth is concealed for two reasons: either because the hearers are incapable of receiving it—hence, “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now”—or because they are contemptuous—hence, “Do not give what is holy to dogs.”

### VERSE 28 [Col. 0154C]

“A certain man had two sons, and he approached,” and so forth. After receiving a guarded answer from the priests, he immediately introduces a parable which both accuses them of impiety and teaches that the kingdom of God is to be transferred to the Gentiles.

### VERSE 31

“They say to him.” In some manuscripts, “the last” is found instead of “the first.” They understood the truth, but through evasion refused to say what they thought, as with the question concerning John’s baptism.

### VERSE 32

“John came in the way of righteousness.” The Jews despised John and neither understood the way of righteousness nor repented of their evil works.

“But you.” (Gregory) Because they openly refused to answer wisdom, they are caught through parables.

### VERSE 33 [Col. 0154D]

“A vineyard.” The vineyard is mentioned by Isaiah (chapter 5): “The vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth,” and so forth.

“He dug a winepress in it.” In the digging, fear is signified, because they observed those legal commandments not out of love but out of fear.

### VERSE 34

“When the time of the fruits had drawn near,” and so forth. He rightly says “the time of the fruits,” not “the fruits,” because there was no fruit in that disobedient people.

### VERSE 37

“Finally,” and so forth. Observe the patience of the householder, who waits for repentance.

“They will reverence my son.” As though he were saying: “I will do what belongs to me; let them see to what belongs to them.”

### VERSE 38 [Col. 0155A]

“This is the heir.” It is clear that the chief priests killed Jesus not through ignorance but through envy, since they knew that he was the one of whom it is said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm 2). Hence, when they were taking counsel among themselves, they said: “If we let him go on this way” (John 11), and so forth.

“We shall possess his inheritance.” Christ’s inheritance, which he possessed when he rose again, is the Church. The Jews tried to seize it by extinguishing faith in him and attempting to persuade the Gentiles to embrace the righteousness that comes from the law.

### VERSE 39

“They cast him outside the vineyard.” Mark changes the order, saying: “They killed him and cast him outside the vineyard” (Luke 20), as though he were a worthless corpse. This signifies their obstinacy: after killing and resurrecting the Lord, they excluded him from their own boundaries and sent him to the Gentiles.

### VERSE 42

“The builders.” They appeared to be building a house for God out of the people placed under their authority.

“And whoever falls upon it,” and so forth. Whoever believes yet sins falls upon the stone, but is not crushed; rather, he is bound, because through patience he is preserved for salvation. But upon whomever the stone falls—that is, upon one who denies—it falls completely, so that he is utterly crushed and not even a fragment remains.

Or, the stone falls upon one who now despises and insults him. Such a person has not yet completely perished, but is shaken so that he no longer walks uprightly. The stone falls upon him when, coming in judgment, it overwhelms him, as he says: “Go into the eternal fire.” [Col. 0155B]

## CHAPTER XXII

### VERSE 2

“The kingdom of heaven is like.” Again he reproves them through parables. He does not remain silent because they have been provoked, but tells them through another parable that a worse wrath of God is going to come upon them.

“The wedding feast.” The bridal chamber of the wedding feast is the virgin’s womb. Matthew alone relates the invitation to the wedding feast. Luke gives another similar account, in part, concerning a dinner—that is, the eternal banquet—from which no one who has entered is sent away, just as from the present Church. [Col. 0155C]

### VERSE 4

“Bulls.” First the prophets, and afterward the apostles, suffered at the hands of unbelievers. Those who are now examples to you show what you ought to believe.

“Come,” that is, believe, in agreement with the rest.

The bulls are the fathers of the Old Testament, to whom permission was granted to strike enemies as though with horns.

“Fattened animals,” from *alere*, “to nourish,” signify the preachers of the New Testament, fattened inwardly by charity and seeking the heights on the wing of contemplation.

“Slaughtered,” either because they had been such, or because, through the death of the flesh, they were already placed in rest.

### VERSE 5

“Another went to his farm.” To go to a farm is to devote oneself excessively to earthly labor. To conduct business is to long for earthly profits.

### VERSE 7 [Col. 0155D]

“But the king.” Above, he was a man when he invited and performed works of mercy; now he is a king in vengeance alone.

“And having sent,” and so forth. Having sent armies—that is, angels through whom he will exercise judgment—he destroys the persecutors. He will also burn the city—that is, the flesh in which they dwelt with their souls—in Gehenna.

### VERSE 8

“The wedding feast is indeed ready.” The whole mystery of the Incarnation has been accomplished: birth and passion.

“To the roads,” and so forth. Actions are the roads; the exits are the failures of actions. For those whom no prosperity accompanies in earthly activities are often converted easily.

### VERSE 11

“To see those reclining.” That is, he causes the merits of those who are to be judged to be displayed, and he makes a distinction among them.

“Not clothed in a wedding garment.” After refuting the Pharisees, he adds that not all who are in the Church are worthy of the kingdom, lest his own people grow sluggish. [Col. 0156A]

### VERSE 12

“Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” He is called “friend” because he was invited to the wedding. “How?” accuses him of shamelessness.

### VERSE 13

“After binding his hands and feet.” Those who here refused to be bound—that is, restrained—from evil are bound by punishment.

The hands are those not extended toward almsgiving. The feet are those slow to do good. There each individual member will be subjected to punishments because here each served its particular vice.

“Outer darkness,” and so forth. Here they possess the inner darkness of the heart.

### VERSE 14 [Col. 0156B]

“For many are called, but few are chosen.” After dismissing the one in whom the whole body of the wicked is represented, he adds a general judgment:

“For many are called.” As though he were saying: Although I have spoken of one, it must be understood of many.

### VERSE 16

“Speaking with the Herodians.” They approached as though they were strangers, so that they might deceive him more easily, because they feared the crowds. What they themselves did not dare to do, they attempted through the hands of the governor.

“With the Herodians.” That is, with Herod’s soldiers. Under Caesar Augustus, when the census was taken, Judea became tributary. Herod, the foreigner and proselyte son of Antipater, was placed over these taxes and appointed king of the Jews by Augustus.

There was therefore a dispute among the people. Some said that taxes ought to be paid for the sake of security and peace, since the Romans fought on behalf of everyone. The Pharisees, on the contrary, insisted that the people of God, who paid tithes and observed the other things prescribed by the law, ought not to be subject to human laws. The Pharisees therefore sent people to see whether they could deceive him. [Col. 0156C]

“You do not care,” and so forth. They provoke him so that he will fear God more than Caesar and therefore say that taxes ought not to be paid, enabling the Herodians to seize him as an instigator of rebellion.

### VERSE 18

“Hypocrites.” Because they are one thing and pretend to be another.

### VERSE 21

“Therefore give back.” Just as Caesar demands the imprint of his image, so God desires the soul marked with the light of his countenance.

### VERSE 23 [Col. 0156D]

“The Sadducees,” and so forth. There were two heresies among the Jews: that of the Pharisees, who preferred the righteousness of traditions and observances, and that of the Sadducees, who likewise claimed for themselves what they were not—that is, righteousness.

For “Sadducees” is interpreted as “righteous.” They do not believe in the resurrection of bodies and think that souls perish with the body. They invent an absurd story to deride those who affirm the resurrection. It is possible, however, that something of this kind once occurred among their people.

### VERSE 29

“You are mistaken.” The reason is that you do not know the Scriptures. Hence it follows that you do not know the power of God.

### VERSE 30

“In the resurrection.” Bodies will indeed rise—bodies that could marry and be given in marriage, which is said of those who possess sexual organs—but they will not marry for another reason.

### VERSE 31 [Col. 0157A]

“Have you not read?” In Moses, whom you accept. Otherwise he could have offered clearer testimonies from the prophets concerning the resurrection, but the Sadducees do not accept the prophets.

### VERSE 32

“The God of Abraham,” and so forth. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had already died when he said this. Therefore, by this statement he proves that souls continue after death; for he would not be called the God of those who do not exist.

In this way the resurrection of bodies is also introduced, since bodies acted either well or badly together with their souls:

“The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” By this he proves the eternity of souls, and immediately adds: “He is not the God of the dead,” and so forth. Once he has proved that souls continue after death, the resurrection of bodies—which acted either well or badly together with the souls—is consequently introduced.

### VERSE 34 [Col. 0157B]

“Silence.” Observe that the poisons of envy can be overcome, but that it is difficult for envy to become quiet.

“They came together.” In order to overcome by numbers the one whom they could not overcome by reason. Those who are opposed in doctrine come together in testing him. They had already been refuted in the matter of the denarius; they had already seen the Sadducees fall silent, yet malice and jealousy continued to nourish their shamelessness.

### VERSE 35

“Testing him.” Mark says that, because he answered wisely, the Lord said to him: “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” It could happen that the man who came to test him was converted by the Lord’s answer.

Or the testing was not evil, as though he wished to deceive, but arose from the desire to investigate more fully what was unknown.

### VERSE 37 [Col. 0157C]

“You shall love the Lord your God.” With his first answer, the Lord strikes the false conscience of the questioner.

“Your God is one.” “You shall not take the name of your God in vain.” “Observe the Sabbath day.” These three pertain to the love of God: you are to consider his unity, his truth, and his will.

“With all your heart.” The integrity of faith is expressed.

“With all your soul.” Perfect obedience is required.

“With all your mind.” Perseverance is demonstrated.

### VERSE 42

“Concerning Christ.” Whether you say that he has come or believe that he is still to come, you assert that he is merely human.

### VERSE 44

“He said.” To say this is to beget a son equal to himself.

“To the Lord.” Not according to the way in which he was born from him, but according to the way in which he always existed from the Father.

### VERSE 45

“How?” These things are contradictory according to your understanding.

### VERSE 46

“And no one was able,” and so forth. Observe that the poisons of envy can be overcome, but that it is difficult for envy to become quiet.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### VERSE 1 [Col. 0157D]

“Then he spoke.” After refuting those who were deceitful, he instructs those who are capable of receiving instruction. Nevertheless, he urges them to submit to the scribes and Pharisees on account of their priesthood and the dignity of their name, considering not their works but their teaching.

### VERSE 4

“Heavy burdens.” They mix the commandments of the law with their own traditions, urging people to live according to them and not to come to the easy and delightful grace of Christ. Hence the earlier saying: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened.”

### VERSE 5

“But all their works.” He had said that such teachers should be heard but not imitated. Now he shows the reason why they cannot believe Christ: they do everything in order to be seen by human beings. For one who desires earthly glory cannot believe Christ, who preaches heavenly things. [Col. 0158A]

### VERSE 8

“But you.” For two reasons he commands them to distance themselves from such people: lest we be led astray by their pretense, and lest we be inflamed by rivalry.

### VERSE 9

“There is one.” He is the one who illuminates a human being. Another human being does not do this; he merely exercises a ministry, and by teaching does not grant understanding.

“Your Father.” God is called Father and Teacher by nature; a human being is called father through kindness. He is called father so that honor may be shown to age, not so that he may be regarded as the author of life. He is called teacher through association with the true Teacher, as his messenger; and he is honored out of reverence for the one by whom he is sent.

### VERSE 13

“You shut.” Either by their evil example or by removing the mysteries of Scripture. For through the example and teaching of those who are teachers, some people do not receive Christ. [Col. 0158B]

### VERSE 15

“You go about.” Throughout the whole world you disparage the Gospel; and if anyone adheres to you, he is a son of double punishment, because he neither receives remission of sins nor avoids falling into the society of those who persecuted Christ. Whoever is called the son of someone is one who performs that person’s works.

“Proselyte.” Proselytes are people from the Gentiles who were received into the synagogue. Their scarcity is signified by the singular, because scarcely anyone became one after Christ.

### VERSE 16

“Whoever.” The Pharisees, who did everything for profit, said that gifts offered to the temple or altar were even holier than the temple or altar itself, so that people would be more eager to offer gifts than to pour out prayers in the temple or perform acts of righteousness. In this they attended not to the fear of God but to their own greed. Therefore the Lord accuses them of folly and fraud. [Col. 0158C]

### VERSE 22

“In heaven.” Through the creature: where you do not think there is perjury, one swears by heaven—that is, by creation subject to the divinity and by the divinity presiding over creation.

### VERSE 23

“Woe to you.” Here also he accuses them of greed, because they omit nothing that serves their own advantage.

“You tithe.” God had commanded tithes of all things to be offered for the nourishment of the priests. Observe that almsgiving does not purchase some degree of impunity for those who remain in iniquity.

“These things you ought to have done.” Lest he appear to reject almsgiving and the fruits of the earth, he added this. [Col. 0158D]

### VERSE 24

“Blind guides.” Under the pretext of religion, you display diligence in the smallest matters that bring profit; but you swallow and neglect the great commandments concerning judgment, faith, and mercy.

“Straining out.” Mystically, in the name of the gnat, the seditious murderer Barabbas is signified, because this creature disturbs by buzzing and delights in blood. In the name of the camel, because of its humility in undertaking burdens, the Lord is understood.

Thus the Jews strain out the gnat—that is, they observe small matters—because they released Barabbas, who had not observed the Sabbath; and they swallow the camel, that is, they despise greater things, because they killed Christ, who spiritually revealed the Sabbath through judgment, mercy, and faith—things that they despised. [Col. 0159A]

### VERSE 25

“Woe to you.” Through various comparisons he accuses the Pharisees of pretense and falsehood: they display one thing to people but do another at home.

“You cleanse.” In vain you pretend to outward holiness, as though someone cleansed a cup on the outside while leaving filth within, even though its use is internal.

Luke has it this way: “Fool, he who made what is outside also made what is inside” (Luke 11). That is, he who made both aspects of the human being also wished both to be cleansed. Therefore no one should think that fornication and similar bodily vices alone are serious, while greed, pride, anger, and the other spiritual vices are light.

### VERSE 26

“Of the cup.” This is said by way of comparison, not because their superstition is literally in the cup and the dish. [Col. 0159B]

### VERSE 29

“You build.” You construct memorials for those who were killed, seeking the favor of the crowd so that you may appear righteous; yet you also condemn the crimes of your fathers.

### VERSE 31

“Therefore.” Because you condemn the crimes of your fathers merely as a display of holiness, while by persecuting Christ and the apostles you do the same things, your actions prove that you are their children not only by flesh but also by an evil imitation. It is clear that they sin knowingly.

That is, you speak against yourselves when you condemn your fathers, for you act in the same way.

### VERSE 32

“And you.” Having proved that they are the children of murderers, he sets forth what he intended: “And you, fill up what they lacked.” They killed the prophets; you kill the Lord of the prophets. He does not command them to do this, but shows what they are going to do. [Col. 0159C]

### VERSE 33

“How will you escape?” (Jerome) Will you escape by building the tombs of the saints, or rather by cleansing your hearts from malice? Will the saints whose tombs you adorn deliver you? Certainly not. The saints are not friends to the enemies of God. Those who despise holiness honor the saints in vain.

### VERSE 34

“Wise men.” Those who know what word they should bring.

“Scribes.” Those learned in the law.

### VERSE 35 [Col. 0159D]

“So that there may come upon you.” He does not mean only those who are present, but the entire generation of wicked people, both preceding and future, because they are all one city and one body of the devil.

“Abel the righteous.” Abel’s righteousness was approved through the acceptance of his offerings.

“Up to the blood.” Why does he go only as far as this, when many were killed after Abel before Christ’s birth, and, after Christ was born, children were immediately slain by this generation?

But because Abel was a shepherd of sheep and was killed in a field, while Zechariah the priest was killed in the court of the temple, he wished under their names to indicate martyrs of both ranks: lay people and those devoted to the office of the altar.

Zechariah, who was killed by King Joash between the temple and the altar, as the history of the Kings relates, was the son of Jehoiada. In the Gospel used by the Nazarenes, however, he is read as the son of Jehoiada instead of the son of Barachiah. But so that the righteousness of Jehoiada the priest might be proclaimed, he himself is called Barachiah, that is, “blessed of the Lord.”

This Zechariah was one of the Twelve Prophets, just as the father of John was one of the prophets.

### VERSE 36 [Col. 0160A]

“Upon this generation.” This generation is reckoned from the first murderer to the final son of perdition. It is as though he were saying: They will be alike in punishment just as they are alike in guilt.

### VERSE 37

“Jerusalem.” As though he were saying: You are guilty of blood, and deservedly so, because many times I sent messengers to gather you, and you were unwilling.

“How often.” It is as though he were saying: “I was willing, but you were unwilling”; and whenever I gathered those whom I gathered by my effective will, I did so despite your unwillingness, because you were always ungrateful.

“A hen.” This animal has great affection for its young, so that it becomes weak when they are weak, and, protecting them with its wings, fights against the kite. Thus the Wisdom of God, made weak through the flesh, protects and defends us from the devil.

### VERSE 38 [Col. 0160B]

“It will be left.” The city, deprived of God’s help, will be left to its own power. It was rightly abandoned when it was abandoned by God.

**VERSE 39.—“Blessed is he who comes.”** The crowd said this to the Lord as he was coming to Jerusalem. But when, after these events, the Lord says this, it must be understood mystically as referring to the advent of his charity, when they will confess the Son whom they crucified.

## CHAPTER XXIV

**VERSE 2.—“Not one stone here will be left upon another.”** Mystically: When the Lord departed from the temple, all the structures and arrangement of the Law were destroyed, so that nothing could be fulfilled by the Jews. Divine providence, however, arranged that as the grace of the Gospel increased, that temple with its ceremonies would be removed, lest, while they remained standing, any weak person in the faith should find an occasion for Judaism. He who had threatened this in words demonstrated it by a sign, when he departed from them after making the threat.

**VERSE 3.—“And as he was sitting.”** Mark says, “opposite the temple.” He sits opposite the temple when he discusses its ruin and the destruction of the nation, so that the position of his body also corresponds to his words. Mystically: He sits on the Mount of Olives—that is, in the Church—remaining at rest and detesting the arrogance of the proud. **“Tell us.”** Because he had said that everything would be destroyed, they ask about the time and signs of the destruction. They ask three things: at what time Jerusalem would be destroyed; when Christ would come; and when the consummation of the age would occur.

**VERSE 4.—“See.”** When these things happen, we should not think that the day of the Lord is at hand; its sign is clearly set out in what follows. He forewarns them, so that they may not be disturbed or fall away through deception, as in the case of Simon Magus, or through tribulation and persecution, as under Nero. Note that the things which would come before the destruction of Jerusalem are similar, and almost identical, to those which will occur at the consummation of the age; thus he speaks of one as though he were speaking of the other.

**VERSE 5.—“Many.”** As the destruction of Jerusalem approached, there were many leaders who claimed to be Christs and said that the time of liberty was near. There were also many in the Church in the times of the apostles who, among other false claims, said that the day of the Lord was at hand.

**VERSE 6.—“You will hear.”** These things abounded in Judea after the Lord’s Passion. The apostles are warned not to be terrified by them and abandon Jerusalem and Judea, because the end would not come immediately, but after forty-two years.

**VERSE 8.—“But all these things.”** All these things are beginnings, not the consummation, like heralds of Antichrist or of the city’s destruction. Some concern the overthrow of the Jews, and some the day of judgment, because the apostles asked about both.

**VERSE 9.—“Then they will hand you over.”** He adds the reason why these things would befall the Jews: after killing Christ, they persecuted the heralds of his name and faith.

**VERSE 11.—“And many false prophets.”** Some refer this to the overthrow of the Jews. But at that time there was no faithful person among them to whom an exhortation could be addressed; it is better understood of heretics, whose first was Simon Magus. The last, greater than all, is Antichrist. It must be carefully observed which of the signs refers to the destruction of the city and which to the day of the Lord. For the Lord answered concerning the things that would follow from that time, whether concerning the destruction of Jerusalem or his own coming.

**VERSE 14.—“And it will be preached.”** Because the Lord knew that the disciples’ hearts would be saddened by the destruction and ruin of their nation, he lifts them with this consolation, so that they might know that far more companions of eternal joy would be gathered from the whole world. Hold fast to this sign as well: the day of the Lord, or the desolation of Jerusalem, will not come before the apostles have been dispersed throughout the whole world, except for the two Jameses, who were first killed in Judea. They were dispersed, I say, so that if they grieved over the destruction of their nation, they might have the consolation of knowing that more companions had been gathered from every nation.

**VERSE 15.—“The abomination,” etc.** If this refers to the destruction of the city, “the abomination” means an idol. For Pilate placed an image of Caesar in the desolated temple. Or this may refer to the equestrian statue of Hadrian, which stood for a long time in the very place of the holy things.

**VERSE 16.—“Then those who are in Judea.”** These things literally took place when, as the extermination of the Jews approached, all the Christians, warned by an oracle, fled into the kingdom of Agrippa, who was subject to the Romans.

**VERSE 22.—“And unless.”** What hope, then, would there be for the elect except the grace of God, which grants the godly patience so that it may more quickly curtail the power of the wicked? For the more severe this tribulation would be, the more it would be moderated by its brevity. Or by the word “days,” the evils themselves are signified. **“Those days would have been shortened.”** Not in measure, but in number, so that the delay of time would not shake the faith of believers. For these evils will last only three and a half years. **“Here is Christ.”** Each heresy has its own particular regions of the world, hence the saying, “Here he is,” or, “There he is.” Or it deceives human curiosity in secret or obscure gatherings, hence the sayings, “Here he is in the inner rooms,” and, “Here he is in the wilderness.” There will be many who will not believe that Christ is the common salvation of all, but only of some; hence the saying, “Here” or “there.”

**VERSE 24.—“If it were possible.”** That is, if it could somehow happen that God’s predestination were changed; and therefore this cannot be understood of the true elect. **“The elect.”** This does not mean that divine election is frustrated, but those who, by human judgment, appear to be elect.

**VERSE 26.—“Behold, he is in the wilderness.”** Many also believe that he will not come into public view, but in the wilderness. Many believe that Christ gave more secret teachings of the faith to some, not to everyone; hence the phrase, “in the inner rooms.” Do not believe that Christ is in the wilderness or in the inner rooms; rather, his faith shines clearly and openly from East to West among the Catholics. Therefore one must not believe schismatics. By the names East and West he designates the whole world.

**VERSE 31.—“From the highest places of heaven.”** Lest anyone think that the elect will be gathered from the four quarters of the earth, and not from all its extremities, including the inland regions, it is added: “From the summit of the earth to the summit of heaven”—that is, directly from the farthest ends of the earth to its ultimate boundaries, where, for those looking from a distance, the circle of heaven appears to rest upon the earth.

**VERSE 32.—“From the tree.”** Mystically: From the people of Israel, in whom blindness occurred in part, and who became like a condemned fig tree. But when, from the dry wood, a branch of faith and charity has blossomed in it, and leaves—that is, words of preaching—have appeared, summer is near: the eternal serenity that is awaited, and the desired renewal of those being reborn. For when Israel’s unbelief has finally been removed and all Israel has been saved, we must not doubt that the day of judgment is near.

**VERSE 35.—“Heaven and earth.”** They will be renewed, their former appearance having been laid aside, while their substance remains; hence it is said: “The earth will stand forever.”

**VERSE 36.—“Concerning the day.”** Lest, after hearing the signs, they should also seek a definite limit for that day, he says: Do not be anxious about the last day—after how many years or days it will come. It has not been determined for anyone whether the judgment will occur by day or by night; “day” is said because of its manifestation, and “night” because of its hiddenness. **“No one knows,”** etc. In some manuscripts there is added, “nor the Son.” He certainly knows everything with the Father, but does not make human beings know, as the Apostle says: “In him are hidden the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians II). He does not make it known because it would be useless to know it. But let us always be uncertain about the Judge’s coming, so that we may live each day as though we were to be judged on the next. Neither did the elect angels make anyone know. Or God granted knowledge of this day to none of the holy angels, nor to his adopted Son—that is, to none of the holy human beings.

**VERSE 37.—“But just as.”** He confirms by many examples that the day of his coming will be sudden: he compared it to lightning swiftly flying across everything, and to the days of Noah, or, according to another Evangelist, of Lot.

**VERSE 38.—“Eating and drinking, marrying,” etc.** It is not food and marriage that are condemned, but the immoderate use of what is lawful. After wars, famines, earthquakes, and so forth, a brief peace will follow, so that it may be proved whether the faithful, once the evils have passed, expect the Judge to come. Hence it is said: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (1 Thessalonians V).

**VERSE 40.—“Then,”** etc. Luke says, “on that night”—that is, in that tribulation by which they are tested, in which some remain and others fall. **“There will be two.”** There are two classes among those mentioned in the Church, as among laborers in a field: those who sincerely proclaim Christ and those who adulterate the word of God.

**VERSE 41.—“Two women grinding.”** There are two classes among those who follow the changing affairs of the world, which are designated by the feminine gender because women are governed by men through the counsel of their elders. **“Two in bed.”** These are those who choose leisure and rest, signified by the name “bed,” and who are occupied neither with secular nor ecclesiastical affairs. **“One will be taken.”** This is the person who strives to practice continence for God’s sake, so that, living without anxiety, he may think about the things of God. But whoever chooses the monastic life for human praise or through some corruption of the vices will be abandoned by God.

There are no other kinds of people in the Church than these three. Hence Ezekiel saw three men delivered: Noah, Daniel, and Job—that is, rulers such as Noah, continent persons such as Daniel, and married persons such as Job. Corresponding to these three kinds of people, he sets out three parables. In the first he speaks of those laboring in the field, which is where he says, “Therefore keep watch.” In the second he speaks of those who are in bed, which is where he says, “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins.” In the third he speaks of those grinding at the mill, which is where he says, “For it is like a man going abroad,” etc.

**VERSE 42.—“Therefore keep watch.”** *(Jerome.)* He did not say, “because we do not know,” but “because you do not know,” showing that he himself is not ignorant of the day of judgment.

**VERSE 43.—“If he had known,”** etc. While the master of the house is unaware, the thief breaks into the house, because, while the spirit sleeps, neglecting its own watchfulness, unexpected death bursts into the dwelling of the flesh and drags it to punishment. He would resist the thief if he were watchful, because, anticipating the Judge’s secret coming, he would meet him through repentance.

**VERSE 45.—“Who, do you think, is the faithful servant?”** By three comparisons—of lightning, of the thief, and of the submersion of the Pentapolis—he introduced the terror of judgment generally to everyone, so that they might keep watch and be ready. Now he speaks specifically to prelates, who ought to be humble and prudent, not seeking what is good for temporal gain, but feeding the sheep by word, example, and deed.

**“Who, do you think,”** as if he were saying: You must be admonished. For how rare is the person who serves the Lord for the Lord’s sake, feeding Christ’s sheep not for profit but out of love for Christ. **“Prudent.”** One who provides for himself in the future. **“Whom he appointed.”** How rare is the one who has been called by God, like Aaron, rather than thrusting himself forward, and who feeds the sheep rather than himself.

**VERSE 46.—“Blessed is that servant.”** He will be glorified with eternal blessedness who, when the Lord comes for judgment, is found faithfully distributing the food of the word and keeping watch over the care of the flock. A faithful or prudent person is rarely found; but whoever is found to be such is blessed.

**VERSE 47.—“Over.”** That is, over all the joys of the heavenly kingdom. He will make the others—that is, the good hearers—recline, and, passing among them, will serve them.

**VERSE 49.—“To strike his fellow servants.”** To injure them, or to corrupt the consciences of the weak by evil speech or example. Hence Luke says “servants or maidservants” (Luke XII): the weaker their age or sex, the easier their downfall.

**VERSE 51.—“With the hypocrites,”** etc. That is, with those who were in the field and those who were grinding, and yet were abandoned. They are called hypocrites both in the field and at the mill: they appeared to do good, but the outcome revealed a different intention. **“Weeping.”** By an analogy with bodily members, the magnitude of the torments is shown.

## CHAPTER XXV

**VERSE 1.—“Ten virgins.”** Virgins are all those who abstain from the luxuries of the world. **“And brides.”** Together they are the bride who is now betrothed, a virgin untouched by the corruption of the world. She will marry when the mortal is joined to the immortal.

**VERSE 2.—“Five.”** Continence in relation to carnal temptations is divided into five parts: namely, that they restrain themselves from pleasures in the five senses.

**VERSE 5.—“But while the bridegroom was delayed.”** There is a considerable interval between Christ’s first and second coming. **“They all became drowsy and slept.”** Because they would later be awakened.

**VERSE 6.—“But at midnight a cry was made.”** That is, when no one knew or expected it. Hence: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians III).

**VERSE 8.—“Give us some of your oil,”** etc. Those whose deeds are supported by the praise of others fail when that praise is withdrawn, and out of habit they always seek what usually gives the mind joy. Thus people who do not see the heart seek to have the testimony of human beings before God, who is the examiner of the heart.

**“They are going out.”** That is, at the Judge’s coming they are darkened within and receive no reward from God, because they have received praise.

**VERSE 9.—“Perhaps not.”** Each person will give an account for himself, and no one is helped before God by another’s testimony, since his secrets are open to him. Each person scarcely suffices for himself, so that his own conscience may bear witness on his behalf. Perhaps each person will receive a reward for his own deeds; on the day of judgment the virtues of some cannot lift up the vices of others. **“Go to the sellers.”** The sellers are flatterers, because they give praise and receive some payment.

**VERSE 10.—“But while they were going.”** While they inclined themselves toward the things outside and sought their customary joys, since they did not know the things within, the one who judges came. **“The door was shut.”** After judgment there is great severity in the one whose mercy beforehand was ineffable.

**VERSE 11.—“But finally.”** Through true repentance, through barren tears, those left outside knock. It is not said that they bought oil, because, with no joy remaining from the praises of others, they return in distress to implore God.

**VERSE 13.—“Keep watch.”** Namely, so that we may prepare for ourselves the testimony of a good conscience, lest we remain outside with the foolish virgins. **“You do not know the day or the hour.”** Not only the day of judgment, but also the day of each person’s death, or the hour in which the one who is found ready will be found ready. And because he desires to find us prepared, he adds another parable concerning the same matter.

**VERSE 14.—“A man going abroad called his servants,”** etc. The earth is the place of the flesh; therefore Christ took our flesh to a foreign place when he ascended into heaven.

**VERSE 15.—“And immediately he went away.”** He did not change his location, but allowed them the free power to work.

**VERSE 16.—“He worked with them.”** By guarding himself from visible things and exhorting others as far as he could, so that they might pass from visible things to invisible ones. Or, by preaching to both sexes and instructing them in good conduct, he doubled the talents he had received.

**VERSE 19.—“But after a long time.”** He began to examine the actions of each person, as conscience accused or excused each one.

**VERSE 20.—“Behold, another five.”** As many as he converted from error, so many did he offer to the Lord, with his conscience bearing witness that, through the grace given to him, he not only benefited himself but also gained as many others as he could.

**VERSE 21.—“Over a few things.”** The good things of the present life are few, even though they seem many, because they are not without the admixture of some trouble. The eternal goods, however, are many, since they are without any trouble from corruption. **“Enter into the joy of your Lord.”** Admitted into the choirs of the angels, rejoice inwardly in the gift, so that there may no longer be anything outward over which you must grieve because of corruption.

**VERSE 22.—“The one who had received two talents.”** This man doubled in the Gospel whatever he had learned in the Law according to his abilities. Or he understood his conscience and the works of the present life as representations of future blessedness.

**VERSE 24.—“You are a hard man.”** Because the way that leads to life is arduous, and because the higher the step, the more serious the fall.

**VERSE 25.—“And being afraid, I went away,”** etc. Being afraid to undertake the higher stage of life, lest, while seeking another’s salvation, I should endanger my own. **“I hid your talent.”** I did not preach what I understood because you had given it.

**VERSE 26.—“You knew that,”** etc. Why did this thought not instill fear in you, so that you would know that I would seek my own things more carefully? What he said as an excuse is turned into a charge.

**VERSE 27.—“With the bankers.”** Or with the other teachers, such as apostles and bishops. Or with all believers who can double the money.

**VERSE 28.—“Give it to him,”** etc. We often see this happen in the Church: many, while faithfully administering the external things they have received, are brought by the accompanying grace to a mystical understanding as well.

**VERSE 29.—“For to everyone,”** etc. Many who are naturally wise and perceptive, if they are sluggish, lose the good of nature; and the reward promised to them seems to pass to others who, although they possess less by nature, acquire it through diligence. Or, whoever has faith and a good will, even if he has less in works, will receive from the good Judge. But whoever does not have faith also loses the virtues he naturally possesses, without which they are not virtues. Or, whoever has love for the word is given the capacity to understand; but whoever does not have it, even if he is skilled through natural study, falls short. Or, whoever does not have charity loses every good he possesses.

Note that whatever is given to each person in worldly or spiritual matters is reckoned as a talent, concerning which he will have to give an account.

**VERSE 31.—“But when.”** As he was about to be handed over to the cross, he first proclaimed the glory of the triumphant one, so that the scandals that would follow might be balanced by this promise. After the parables concerning the end of the world, the Lord now explains the manner of the future judgment.

**VERSE 32.—“The sheep from,”** etc. There will be two orders at the judgment: the elect and the rejected. But among the elect, some will judge, to whom it is said: “You also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” Others will be judged, to whom it is said: “I was hungry, and you gave me food.” Likewise, among the rejected, some are outside the Church and will not be judged; others will be judged, to whom it is said: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” etc.

**VERSE 33.—“The goats.”** The goat is a wanton and foul-smelling animal, which was offered for sins in the Law, and signifies sinners. He does not say “she-goats,” which can bear offspring.

**VERSE 34.—“Blessed of my Father.”** Promoted by the favor of my Father to obtain the glory in which you will reign without corruption, to which you were predestined from the foundation of the world.

**VERSE 37.—“Then they will answer.”** They will not distrust the Lord’s words, but will either be astonished by the greatness of the King’s majesty, or because everything good they have done seems little to them. Hence it is said: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory” (Romans VIII), etc.

**VERSE 40.—“Of these brothers.”** My brothers and mother are those who do the will of my Father.

**VERSE 42.—“You did not give,”** etc. What does one deserve who has seized what belongs to another, if the person who did not give from his own is eternally condemned?

**VERSE 44.—“Lord, when,”** etc. They strive to excuse themselves, as though they could deceive God, who sees through human beings. But those who were unwilling to turn from evil and give alms have no excuse. Hence he adds: **“As long as you did not do it for one,”** etc.

**VERSE 46.—“Into eternal punishment.”** Origen therefore promises in vain that evil human beings, and even the demons themselves, will be liberated after many years. **“Into eternal punishment.”** *(Augustine.)* In this matter Origen was certainly more merciful: he believed that even the devil and his angels, after punishments more severe and longer in proportion to their merits, would be rescued from those torments and joined to the holy angels. But the Church rightly rejected him for this and several other reasons, especially for his belief in alternating blessedness and misery without end, and in interminable comings and goings from one state to the other at fixed intervals of the ages.

## CHAPTER XXVI

**VERSE 1.—“And it came to pass, when he had finished.”** He had completed his teaching concerning the consummation of the age and the separation at the judgment; or, from the beginning of the Gospel up to the Passion, he had completed everything by doing and preaching. After the discourse in which he foretold that he would come in glory, he showed that he would suffer, so that he might remind them that the mystery of the cross was joined to the glory of eternity.

**VERSE 6.—“But when.”** After the council had been held, the order of the narrative moves there, when one of the Twelve departed, so that Judas’s deed might be joined to the priests’ council. It returns, however, to the day that was six days before Passover, saying: “But when,” etc. **“Of Simon.”** His former name remains, so that the power of the healer may be displayed. By that house understand the portion of the people that believed in the Lord and was healed. **“Simon,”** that is, “obedient.”

**VERSE 7.—“A woman came.”** *(Jerome.)* Observe carefully what is said about the two women concerning the head. The sinful woman anointed his feet, whereas the woman who is said not to have been sinful anointed his head. **“A woman having.”** Mary Magdalene, the sister of Lazarus, now just and familiar with him, who once came as a sinner and washed his feet with tears, now anointed his head and feet—his feet, as John says. **“Precious ointment.”** Mark says “spikenard,” that is, made from spikes and leaves, which is more precious. John says “pistic nard,” that is, faithful or genuine, not adulterated with other herbs: *pistis* (πίστις) in Greek, *fides* in Latin.

Mystically: This devotion of Mary signifies the faith of the Church. When it proclaims Christ’s divinity, it anoints his head; when it proclaims his humanity, it anoints his feet. Matthew, Mark, and John speak of this ointment in the house of Simon the leper in Bethany. Luke, however, relates another similar event that occurred earlier in the house of another Simon, a Pharisee who was not a leper, and not in Bethany, involving the same woman, who then came as a sinner.

**VERSE 8.—“The disciples were indignant.”** John says that Judas spoke these words, and that he did so out of greed. The others may have agreed with his words, or may even have said the same thing, but out of concern for the poor.

**VERSE 11.—“But you will not always have me,”** etc. He means in bodily presence; otherwise he says elsewhere: “Behold, I am with you always, until the consummation of the age.”

**VERSE 12.—“For by pouring.”** This is the service of burial, which you think is waste. Nor is it surprising if she gives me the fragrance of faith, for which I will soon pour out my blood.

**VERSE 15.—“What will you give me,”** etc. Like a slave being handed over as a cheap possession, he places in the buyers’ power how much they wish to give.

**VERSE 17.—“Where do you want us,”** etc. They did not have a fixed house, by which the construction of unnecessary buildings is condemned.

**VERSE 18.—“To a certain man.”** He means the same person whom Mark and Luke call the master of the house. When he says “to a certain man,” as though speaking in his own person rather than the Lord’s, he indicated him briefly for the sake of concision. **“To a certain man.”** Not to just anyone, but to a particular person, whom he would rightly have named when speaking in his own person. But now, after setting down the Lord’s words, “Go into the city,” he himself inserts “to a certain man”—not because the Lord said this, but so that he might imply, without giving the proper name, that there was a certain man to whom they were sent.

**VERSE 19.—“And the disciples did as.”** In another Gospel it is written: “They found a large upper room furnished.” The upper room is the spiritual Law, which, emerging from the narrowness of the letter, receives the Savior in a lofty place. For one who follows the letter celebrates Passover below; but one who follows the bearer of water—that is, the herald of grace—into the house of the Church transcends the letter through the Spirit and prepares refreshment for Christ in the height of the mind.

**VERSE 21.—“One of you.”** He who had foretold the Passion now foretells the betrayer, so that, seeing that his deed was not hidden, he might repent. He places the crime among the number, so that the guilty man might repent, but does not identify him specifically, lest he become more shameless.

**VERSE 22.—“They began, one by one.”** They believe the teacher more than themselves; and, fearing their own weakness, they ask about a sin of which they have no awareness.

**VERSE 23.—“The one who dips.”** While the others were saddened and withdrew their hands from the food, he, with the same shamelessness with which he betrayed him, put his hand into the dish with the teacher, so that audacity might pretend to possess a good conscience. Behold the humility and patience with which he admits the betrayer to the table.

**“In the dish.”** Mark says, “in the bowl.” A *paropsis* is a square vessel for food, named from equal sides; a bowl is an earthen vessel suited to holding liquid. It could have happened that the table contained an earthen, square vessel. Punishment is foretold, so that the announced torments might correct the one whom shame had not overcome.

**VERSE 24.—“It would have been good for him.”** It would be much better not to exist at all than to exist wickedly; he says this in the ordinary and simple sense. For it cannot be well with one who does not exist. Or does he say that it was good for the devil not to have been born unto sin? Or was it good for him not to have been born for Christ through a calling, so that he would not become an apostate through betrayal? Or we may simply say: It would be better not to exist than to exist wickedly.

**“Rabbi.”** Others say, “Lord,” while this man says, “Rabbi”—as though betraying the teacher were a lesser sin than betraying the Lord, or as a form of flattery.

**VERSE 25.—“You have said it.”** Here too it is not openly said whether he was the one; it can be understood as though he were saying, “I did not say it.”

**VERSE 26.—“As they were dining,”** etc. When the solemn joys of the old Passover, celebrated in memory of God’s liberation of his people from Egypt, had ended, he passed to the new Passover, which he wished the Church to celebrate in his memory. In place of the flesh and blood of the lamb, he would substitute the sacrament of his body and blood, and show that he himself was the one concerning whom the Lord swore and would not repent: “You are a priest” (Psalm CIX), etc.

**“He took.”** *(Jerome.)* After the typical Passover had been fulfilled and he had eaten the lamb’s flesh with the apostles, he took bread. **“And he blessed and broke it.”** He subjected the humanity he had assumed to death in such a way as to show that the power of immortality was present in it and that he would therefore rise quickly. He broke it to show that the breaking of his body would not take place without his own will. He blessed it first because, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he filled the nature he had assumed with the grace of divine power. He gave his body after the meal because the typical Passover first had to be completed, and only then could the sacrament of the old Passover be replaced.

But we, out of reverence for so great a sacrament, are first nourished by the sacraments of the Lord’s Passion before bodily food.

**VERSE 27.—“He gave thanks.”** He showed what each person ought to do under the scourge of his own fault, since he himself endured with equanimity the fault of another. Bread strengthens the body, while wine produces blood.

**VERSE 29.—“I will not drink.”** I will not delight in the ceremonies of this people, in which the sacred rites of the paschal lamb are primary. After the Passion I will not take flesh until I take the new flesh that is now mortal.

**“The new [wine] in my Father’s kingdom.”** By calling one “new” and the other “old,” he shows the body: namely, the body derived from the old Adam, which will be changed through immortality. **“With you.”** Through this, immortality is promised to his own as well, although not at the same time. **“From this fruit.”** The same bodies will rise. The day of my resurrection will come when, raised up in the kingdom of God—that is, in the glory of immortality—I will be filled with new joy with you over the salvation of that same people, regenerated by spiritual grace.

**VERSE 30.—“And having sung a hymn.”** This is what the psalm says: “The poor will eat and be satisfied” (Psalm XXI), etc. Or, according to John, he sang a hymn giving thanks to the Father, in which he prayed for himself, for the disciples, and for those who would believe. **“They went out to the mountain,”** etc. Through the reception of the sacraments and his intercession, he teaches us to ascend to higher gifts, by which we may be anointed in heart: there is refreshment from labor and consolation in sorrow.

**VERSE 31.—“You will all be scandalized.”** He foretells what they will suffer, so that afterward they may not despair, but be freed through repentance.

**VERSE 32.—“After.”** Just as he foretold the place of the Passion, so he foretells the place of the resurrection, so that, just as they are saddened by the Passion, they may rejoice when glorified by the resurrection or by the vision. **“I will go before you,”** etc. He would console their weakness by promising his return.

**VERSE 33.—“Even if all.”** This was neither a lie nor recklessness, but faith and ardent love, to such an extent that he did not consider his own weakness or the truth of God’s words.

**VERSE 36.—“And pray.”** Near to death, he rightly prays in the valley of abundance, because through humility and the richness of charity he underwent death for us.

**VERSE 37.—“He began to be sorrowful.”** Not out of fear of the Passion, for he had come for this purpose, but because of the apostles’ scandal and the destruction of the wicked. *(Jerome.)* “He began to be sorrowful,” to prove the reality of the humanity he had assumed. He was truly sorrowful, but his suffering did not dominate his soul; it was a fore-suffering, hence he says, “He began to be sorrowful.” He was sorrowful not from fear of suffering, for he had come for that purpose, but on account of wretched Judas, the apostles’ scandal, the rejection of the Jews, and the overthrow of Jerusalem.

**VERSE 38.—“Sorrowful.”** It is the soul that fears and becomes sorrowful. Peter, being inferior, does not fear, saying, “I will lay down my life for you,” because, as a human being, he does not understand the power of death. Christ fears because, as God established in a body, he displays the weakness of the flesh; since he assumed a body, he had to undergo everything proper to the body.

**“Even unto death.”** *(Hilary.)* Not because of death, but until he freed the apostles through his Passion. It is not death but the time of death that is feared, because after the power of the resurrection the faith of believers had to be strengthened.

**VERSE 39.—“If it is possible.”** He says this not out of fear but out of mercy, lest the Jews, who have no excuse based on ignorance, should kill him. Hence he says, “this”—that is, the cup of the Jewish people—not simply the cup: If it is possible for the Gentiles to believe without the destruction of the Jews, I reject the Passion. But if they must be blinded so that the Gentiles may enter, let not my will but yours be done.

**“Not as I will.”** *(Augustine.)* He transforms his own people into himself, those who will nothing other than what the Father wills, as in the saying, “I was hungry and you gave me food,” and, “Why do you persecute me?” He teaches them to correct and direct their private will according to the divine will.

*(Ambrose.)* He demonstrated the human being whom he truly showed by equating him in feeling, saying: “But not as I will, but as you will.” He assumed my will; he assumed my sorrow. I confidently call it sorrow when I proclaim the cross.

**VERSE 41.—“But the flesh.”** He certainly does not say this about himself, but about those who had said that they would never deny him.

**VERSE 42.—“Again, a second time.”** He prays a second time: if Nineveh cannot otherwise be saved unless the gourd—that is, the Jewish people, which was formerly his shelter—has withered in order to kill me.

**VERSE 44.—“He prayed a third time.”** He prayed three times so that we too might pray for forgiveness of past sins, protection from sins for which we repent, and caution against future dangers, and so that we might direct every prayer to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Likewise, just as temptation by desire is threefold, so is temptation by fear. There is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and worldly ambition. There is also fear of death, fear for one’s welfare, and fear of pain. Against all these he teaches us that we must be fortified by prayer. Thus, because of the threefold temptation of the Passion, the Lord may be understood to have prayed three times.

**VERSE 47.—“With swords and clubs.”** The deed corresponds to the changed mind. For now he comes with clubs, whereas, as long as he was at peace, he behaved more calmly.

**VERSE 48.—“He gave them a sign.”** He thought that the signs he had seen were performed not by divine power but by magic; and he feared that the one whom he had heard was transformed on the mountain might now escape from their hands in the same way. Therefore he gave them a sign. **“The one whom I kiss.”** He still retained something of a disciple’s shame, since he did not hand him over openly to his persecutors but through the sign of a kiss.

**VERSE 49.—“And he kissed him.”** The Lord accepted the kiss, not to teach us to pretend, but lest he appear to flee betrayal. Hence: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceful” (Psalm CXIX).

**VERSE 52.—“They will perish by the sword.”** By that fiery sword which turns before paradise—that is, by divine vengeance—and by the sword of the Spirit, that is, the word of God.

**VERSE 53.—“Or do you think that,”** etc. As if he were saying: I do not need the help of twelve apostles, since I can have twelve legions of angels—seventy-two thousand in whom the languages of all nations are expressed. He indicates that there is no need to fear if all nations rise up against Jesus, since he himself has far stronger armies of angels.

Alternatively: This number signifies the entire human race that would wage war against the Jews under the Roman Empire. These are the angels of God who, after the resurrection, in the forty-second year, destroyed those murderers with Titus and Vespasian and burned their city.

**VERSE 55.—“You have come out with swords.”** It is foolish to seek with swords and clubs one who willingly hands himself over, and to investigate by night, as though he were hiding, one who taught daily in the temple. But you gather in darkness because your power is in darkness.

**VERSE 57.—“To Caiaphas.”** The name suits the action. Caiaphas means “investigator” or “shrewd,” for the fulfillment of the wickedness of his deceit; or “vomiting from the mouth,” because he was shameless in uttering lies and demanding murder.

**VERSE 58.—“From a distance.”** Rightly from a distance, since he was soon to deny him at close range. This signifies that the Church would imitate Christ’s Passion in a very different way: the Church suffers for itself, but Christ suffers for the Church.

**VERSE 64.—“You have said it.”** Mark says, “I am,” which is the same thing. His response before Pilate and Caiaphas is similar, so that they may be condemned by their own judgment. **“The Son of Man.”** Me exalted in the form in which you judge me, and possessing the name that is above every name.

VERS. 65.—He tore his garments. The fury that made him rise from his seat also made him tear his clothing. In a great mystery: although the Lord’s garment could not be torn even by the soldiers. For it signifies that their priesthood, because of their crimes, had to be completely dissolved; but the solidity of the Church—which is called God’s garment—will remain unbroken until the end of the age. It is the custom of the Jews, when they hear something blasphemous, to tear their garments.

Paul and Barnabas did this in Lycaonia when they were called Jupiter and Apollo.

VERS. 67.—Then they spat. Just as he was then spat upon by the saliva of unbelievers, so now he is dishonored by the reproaches of false believers and struck with blows—that is, with their blasphemies.

VERS. 68.—Prophesy. They utter this insult to one who wished to be regarded by the people as a prophet. For, according to Mark, they covered his face—not so that he would not see their crimes, but so that they themselves might conceal from themselves the grace of knowing him. It was like the veil over Moses’ face, which remains to this day.

VERS. 69.—One maidservant. Why does a maidservant first expose him, when men could more readily have recognized him, unless to show that this sex sinned in the killing of the Lord, and was redeemed through his Passion? Therefore a woman was the first to receive the mystery of the Resurrection and kept the commandments, so as to erase the ancient error of transgression. Just as the ancient enemy first deceived the first parent through a woman, so through a woman he compels the ruler of the Church to deny the Master whom he had confessed to be Christ, the Son of God.

VERS. 72.—I do not know the man. How harmful are the conversations of the wicked, which compel Peter to deny Christ, or to deny that he knows the man whom, among the disciples of God, he had confessed to be the Son of God.

VERS. 73.—Those who were standing there. John and Luke mention one person, a relative of Malchus. But perhaps the plural is used for the singular. Or perhaps one had seen him and was the principal speaker, while the others, following him, made the same accusation.

VERS. 74.—And immediately the cock crowed. The cockcrow follows the third denial. The mysteries of events are signified through the sequence of times. At midnight he denies; at cockcrow he repents; after the Resurrection, in the light, he professes three times that he loves the one whom he had denied three times. For what he had forgotten in the darkness of oblivion, he corrected by remembering the light already hoped for; and by the presence of that true light he completely raised up whatever he had altered.

VERS. 75.—He remembered. In another Gospel it is said, “The Lord looked at Peter” (Luke 22), and by his gaze summoned him to tears, as though bringing to his mind how often he had denied him and what he had foretold. He could not remain in darkness when the Light of the world had looked upon him. And he went out. Separated from the counsel of the ungodly, he washes away his guilt outside, which he had not done within. For this reason he was permitted to hesitate, so that in the chief of the Church a remedy of repentance might be established, and no one might dare to trust in his own strength.

## CHAPTER XXVII

VERS. 1.—But in the morning. Matthew and Mark connected the narrative of what happened with the Lord until morning, but afterward returned to narrate Peter’s denial; once that was concluded, they returned again to the morning, so that they might continue the rest of the narrative from there.

VERS. 4.—I have sinned by betraying, etc. As though it lay within his power to change the persecutors’ sentence. Although he changed his intention, he nevertheless did not change the outcome of his original intention. What is that to us? What does this have to do with us? You see to it; you know what you have done. Or: What do you judge to concern us? What does the price received concern us? You had approved it; do with it what you wish. Those who sin unto death possess such ignorance and blindness that they are neither troubled by their crimes nor tormented by the pain of repentance.

VERS. 5.—And having thrown down. Just as his repentance was fruitless, so this offering in the temple was accursed. And departing. (HIER.) It did Judas no good to have practiced repentance, by which he could not correct his crime. But when a brother sins against a brother in such a way that he is able to amend what he has done, it can be forgiven him. But if the deeds remain, repentance is taken up in vain by words. This is what is said of him: “Let his prayer become sin” (Psalm 108), so that he not only could not amend the wickedness of his betrayal, but added the crime of his own murder, making himself still more wicked.

VERS. 6.—It is not lawful for us to put them. Truly they are people who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel. For if they do not put the money into the *corban*, that is, into the treasury, that is, among the offerings to God, because it is the price of blood, why then is the blood itself shed? And what reward is it for them if with it a field is bought for the burial of the poor?

VERS. 9.—Through Jeremiah. (HIER.) This is not read in Jeremiah but in Zechariah, though in different words. Recently I read an apocryphal work of Jeremiah, in which I found these words written. Nevertheless, it seems to me more likely that this was taken from Zechariah according to the custom of the apostles, who, omitting the order of the words, bring forth only the meaning from the Old Testament.

From the children of Israel, etc. From those from whom it was least appropriate, since they ought to have magnified him.

VERS. 11.—You are the king of the Jews. According to Luke, they had brought two charges against him: namely, that he forbade tribute to be given to Caesar and that he said he was a king. Therefore Pilate asks about the kingdom, because he does not know. As for the tribute, because he had heard that Jesus had answered, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s” (Zech. 2), he disregards the accusers’ obvious lie. Hence Mark says: “Their testimonies were not consistent” (Mark 14). By the fact that Pilate asks him about no other charge than whether he is the king of the Jews, the Jews are convicted of impiety, since they could not even find a false accusation to bring against the Savior.

VERS. 16.—Who was called Barabbas. In the Gospel according to the Hebrews, *Barabbas* is interpreted as “son of the father” or “their master.” He is the Antichrist, whom those people prefer to Christ, of whom it is said: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8). Pilate, whose name is interpreted as “the mouth of the hammerer,” signifies the devil, who is the hammer of the whole earth, through whom the Lord permits his vessels to be tested; and finally he crushes them, when he will break them in the final condemnation.

VERS. 17.—Whom do you want? Wishing to satisfy the people, he gives them a choice, although he does not doubt that Christ ought to be chosen, knowing that he had been handed over through envy. Who is called Christ. The same as what Mark says: “the king of the Jews,” whose king Christ was called.

VERS. 19.—From the judgment seat. The tribunal is the seat of judges, just as the throne is the seat of kings and the chair the seat of teachers. His wife. The wife of a Gentile understands in a vision what the Jews, while awake, refused to understand. Have nothing to do with him. Now at last the devil, understanding that he would lose his spoils through Christ, just as he first brought death through a woman, now wishes through a woman to free Christ from the hands of the Jews, lest through his death he lose the dominion of death.

VERS. 21.—Barabbas, etc. They chose the son of the devil in place of the Son of God, so that they might destroy the Savior together with his salvation and release the betrayer. Their request still clings to them today, though they have lost their nation, place, and freedom, because they wished to destroy the giver of freedom.

VERS. 22.—What then shall I do with Jesus? He sought many opportunities to release him with the goodwill of the people. First, by comparing a robber with the just man. Then: “What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” And when they said, “Let him be crucified,” he did not immediately agree, but, following the suggestion of his wife, said: “For what evil has he done?” By saying this, Pilate acquitted Christ.

VERS. 24.—He washed his hands. He signifies the Gentile people, alienated from the impiety of the Jews who cried out, “Crucify, crucify him.”

VERS. 25.—His blood. The curse persists to this day, and Christ’s blood is not removed from them.

VERS. 26.—Then he released Barabbas to them. Barabbas, a seditious robber and author of murders, was released to the Jewish people. (ISID.) The devil, who long ago was expelled from the homeland of light because of pride and had been sent into the prison of darkness. Therefore the Jews cannot have peace, because they preferred to choose the leader of seditions. Or Barabbas bore the figure of the Antichrist.

But Jesus, having been scourged. Pilate should therefore be believed to have scourged Jesus and handed him over to the soldiers for mockery, so that, satisfied with his punishments and insults, the Jews would no longer thirst for his death. Jesus, however. He was serving the Roman laws, which command that those who are to be crucified should first be scourged.

VERS. 28.—A scarlet cloak. (HIER.) In the scarlet cloak he sustains the bloodstained works of the Gentiles. In the crown of thorns he dissolves the ancient curse. With the reed he kills poisonous animals. Or he holds the reed in his hand so that he might write the sacrilege of the Jews. He is not mocked in his own garments, but in those which he bore because of our sins. When he was crucified, he immediately recovered his own adornment, because the elements are disturbed and creation bears witness to the Creator.

VERS. 32.—The Cyrenian. Behold, not a Hebrew but a foreigner is subjected to the reproach of Christ, so that it may be shown that the fullness of the mysteries passes from circumcision to the uncircumcision.

VERS. 33.—Golgotha. It is Syriac and is interpreted as “of the Skull,” not because of the baldness of Adam, whom they falsely claim to have been buried there, but because of the beheading of the condemned. Adam is read to have been buried near Hebron in the Book of Joshua.

VERS. 34.—Mixed with gall. Another Evangelist says “mingled with myrrh,” that is, extremely bitter. Both mixtures—of gall and myrrh—could have been present. And when he had tasted it, he would not drink. Mark omits this: he did not wish to drink. This is what Mark says: “He did not accept it,” namely, in order to drink it.

VERS. 35.—They divided. John explains this more distinctly: the garments were divided into four parts, so that the Church might be signified in the four parts of the world. The tunic, assigned by lot, signifies the unity of all the parts through the bond of charity, which comes by lot—that is, by the grace of God—not by human judgment.

VERS. 37.—The charge. The reason for which the Jews handed him over to Pilate. By means of the cross the king did not lose his kingdom but confirmed it, whether the Jews wished it or not.

VERS. 38.—One on the right. One on the right, by whom the mortification of the flesh for heavenly glory is signified; one on the left, by whom the mortification of the flesh for some worldly cause is again signified.

VERS. 39.—They blasphemed him. It had been foretold in the Book of Wisdom (chapter 2): “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death. For there will be regard for his words.
