If he is truly the Son of God, he will receive him and deliver him from the hand of his enemies.” Therefore, because he was crucified and was not delivered, they believed that he was not the Son of God. For this reason they insulted him hanging on the wood and shook their heads:

VERS. 40.—If you are the Son of God. If, yielding to those who insulted him, he had descended from the cross, he would not have demonstrated the power of patience.

VERS. 42.—And we will believe him. A fraudulent promise: he does something greater by rising from the tomb, and you do not believe; therefore, if he descended from the cross, you would not believe. But the demons put this into their minds. For they immediately perceived the power of the cross and that their own strength had been broken, and they acted so that he might descend from the cross. But the Lord, knowing this, remained in order to destroy the devil.

VERS. 44.—The robbers also did the same. At first both blasphemed; then, seeing the signs, one believed. So both peoples first blasphemed God, but one, terrified by the signs, repented and now reproves the Jews.

VERS. 45.—Now from the sixth hour. Observe that the Lord is crucified as the sun is about to withdraw from the center of the world, because he dies for sins; and Adam, after he had sinned in the afternoon, heard the voice of the Lord. It is reasonable, therefore, that at the time when he closed the gate against the transgressing Adam, he should open the gate of paradise for the repentant robber. The reason Mark says that the Lord was crucified at the third hour is that he might show that the Jews, who excuse themselves, crucified him more with their tongues than the soldiers did with their hands: for at the third hour they shouted that he should be crucified. When he was crucified, however, it was approximately the sixth hour—that is, not yet fully the sixth hour.

VERS. 46.—And about the ninth hour. When the day had declined toward evening and the sun had been cooled from its heat, he completed his Passion, showing that he died because of our sins, through which we had fallen from the divine light and love into this night. The Lord rose in the morning, teaching that he would bring those raised again in soul into the light of eternal blessedness. Eli, Eli, lamma. He who assumes the nature of those whose misery he laments. In this he shows how much those who sin ought themselves to weep. Do not be surprised at the lowliness of the words and the complaints of one forsaken, when, knowing the form of a servant, you see the scandal of the cross.

VERS. 47.—But some of them. Not all, perhaps Romans who were ignorant of the proper meaning of the Hebrew language. Or certain Jews, considering Christ inferior to Elijah, so that he might implore his help.

VERS. 49.—Wait, let us see. Because they misunderstood the Lord’s voice, they were foolishly awaiting the coming of Elijah.

VERS. 51.—And behold, the veil of the temple. So that the ark of the covenant and all the mysteries of the Law that had been covered might appear and pass to the Gentiles. Josephus says that the angelic powers who had formerly guarded the temple then cried out together, “Let us depart from these dwellings.” The veil that was called the outer veil: for now we see in part; but when that which is perfect has come, then the inner veil will be torn. The earth was shaken. All the elements demonstrate their crucified Lord. The earth is moved, unable to bear its Lord hanging there. The rocks. That is, the hearts of the Gentiles, or the prophecies of the prophets, who are called rocks because of Christ, the Rock, so that whatever had been closed within them by the hard covering of the Law might be split open and lie exposed to the Gentiles.

VERS. 52.—And the tombs. Yet, when the tombs were opened, they did not rise before the Lord had risen, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. The bodies of the saints. They should be believed to have ascended with the Lord in bodily form when he ascended.

VERS. 53.—Into the holy city. Jerusalem, which is called holy because of the temple and the Holy of Holies, as no other city is.

VERS. 54.—Now the centurion. These men confess God in the scandal of the cross. Arius preaches a creature in the Church, whom the blind Jews do not believe even after so many miracles. In the centurion the faith of the Church is signified: when the veil of the heavenly mysteries has been opened through the Lord’s death, the Church confirms Jesus as the Son of God while the Synagogue remains silent.

VERS. 55.—Many women. Matthew and Luke say that Mary Magdalene stood at a distance. John, however, says that she was near the cross, because she was at such a distance that she could still be called “near”: she was present within his sight and was farther off in comparison with the nearer crowd. We may also say that those who were with the Lord’s mother, after he had entrusted her to the disciple, began to leave, so that they might withdraw from the density of the crowd and observe the other things that happened from farther away. Ministering to him. It was a Hebrew custom for women to minister from their possessions to their teachers; the Lord accepted this so as to give an example to the apostles.

VERS. 56.—James’s. James son of Alphaeus is called “the younger,” to distinguish him from James, who was called and chosen by the Lord among the first apostles.

VERS. 57.—A rich man. For no one could approach the governor unless he was rich—not because the Evangelist commends riches. He was also called a decurion because he belonged to the order of the curia and performed the office of administration. Through this he was able to have the means; through being a disciple he was worthy of this ministry. He was a disciple of Jesus. This man came to Pilate. Although secretly, previously avoiding the hostility of the Jews, in this final service he cared nothing for them.

VERS. 59.—In a clean linen cloth. Mystically: he wraps Jesus in a clean linen cloth who receives him with a pure mind. Hence the Church also has the custom of celebrating the altar sacrifice not with silk or dyed cloth but with pure linen.

VERS. 60.—In his own new tomb. For if he had been placed in a tomb in which someone else had been laid, someone else might perhaps have been imagined to have risen. In a rock, so that, if it had been built of many stones, he would not be said to have been secretly removed after the foundations of the mound had been undermined.

VERS. 61.—Now they were there. While Jesus’ other acquaintances returned to their own homes, only the women who loved him more closely watched over the funeral service, awaiting what Jesus had promised; and therefore they were the first to see the Resurrection.

VERS. 63.—After three days. This is a part taken for the whole: the sixth day on which he was crucified, together with its night, counts as one day. The Sabbath in full. The third day is counted from its first part, that is, the whole night together with its daylight; and thus there are three days.

VERS. 66.—They secured the tomb. Their diligence benefited our faith. For the more carefully it was guarded, the more clearly the power of the Resurrection was demonstrated.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

VERS. 1.—In the evening, etc. (HIER.) The fact that the times of these women differed, etc., up to the point that they could not approach, while in the morning they did approach. Mary Magdalene and the other Mary. Two women of the same name and devotion signify two peoples embracing the Passion and Resurrection of Christ with equal devotion.

VERS. 2.—An earthquake. Just as an earthquake occurs in the Passion and in the Resurrection, so it signifies that the hearts of earthly people must be moved to repentance through faith in the Passion and Resurrection. He rolled away the stone. He who was born when the womb of the Virgin was closed could leave the tomb when it was closed. The rolling away of the stone signifies the opening of Christ’s mysteries, which had been covered by the veil of the letter. When that veil was removed, the Resurrection, the abolition of death, and eternal life began to be proclaimed throughout the whole world.

VERS. 3.—Like lightning. In the whiteness of the garment he signified gentleness toward the righteous; in the terror of lightning, he signifies what will be terrifying to the reprobate.

VERS. 5.—Do not be afraid. You see your fellow citizens. Let those who do not belong to their fellowship be afraid.

VERS. 7.—And going quickly. We have not been granted to keep this joy hidden in the secrecy of our hearts, but to reveal it similarly to those who love him.

VERS. 8.—With fear and joy. There are two emotions in them: fear and joy. One arose from the greatness of the miracle, the other from desire for the one who had risen; and each of them hastened the women’s steps.

VERS. 9.—And behold, Jesus, etc. Thus Christ comes to assist all who are beginning the way of virtue. And they took hold of him. It was said above that he had come out of the tomb while it was closed, so that you might understand that his body was immortal; here his feet are held, so that you might recognize the reality of his flesh. And because they trembled at so great a vision, fear was first driven away: “Do not be afraid,” so that with tranquil minds they could hear what was said. These women hold his feet as they worship the risen one; but the woman who did not yet know that the Son of God had risen rightly hears: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20).

VERS. 10.—Tell it. Just as the woman who brought death narrated the serpent’s words, so now she narrates the words of the one who gives life: from the woman through whom death came then, life now comes. My brothers. Earlier he had also called them servants; now he calls them brothers, so that he might teach that after the Resurrection he had resumed the same humanity and that they should hope for the same.

VERS. 12.—A large sum of money. (HIER.) Those who abuse the Church’s property for other purposes by which they may satisfy their own will are like the scribes, Pharisees, and priests who purchase a lie and the Savior’s blood.

VERS. 13.—His disciples came by night and stole him while we were sleeping. (AUG.) If they slept, how did they see? If they did not see, how could they have been witnesses? Greed, which had taken captive the disciple who accompanied the Lord, also deceived the soldiers guarding the tomb; and thus it led the Jews astray, as follows: “And this report has been spread abroad.”

VERS. 16.—They went away. From Jerusalem to Galilee. Onto the mountain: because the body received from common earth had been raised above all earthly things. And he admonishes us that, if we wish to see him, we should be lifted from low things to heavenly ones. Christ, the firstfruits of those who sleep, went before; the others follow in their own order and, seeing him, worship him—that is, praise him without end.

VERS. 17.—But some doubted, as Luke says: they thought that they were seeing a spirit, which he had yielded up when dying.

VERS. 18.—And Jesus came. Therefore the merciful teacher both strengthens them in faith and calls the doubting to faith, indicating to what great glory he had attained. All authority has been given to me. He does not say this of the coeternal divinity of the Father, but of the humanity he assumed, in which he was lower than the angels, in which he was also crowned with glory and honor and placed above all.

VERS. 19.—Go. That which until then had, for certain reasons, been doubtful to people has now come into the light. Teach. The order is appropriate. First the hearer must be taught; then he must be imbued with the mysteries of faith; afterward he must be instructed to keep the commandments. For unless the soul first receives faith, baptism ought not to be given; nor can it be cleansed if afterward it does not persist in good works.

VERS. 20.—And behold, I am with you. What reward of a devout way of life, and what pledge of future blessedness, is even now present for the faithful, he adds: “Behold, I am with you,” etc. This he promises through succession to the universal Church through the apostles. Note that until the end of the age those who are worthy of the divine indwelling will not cease to exist.

(AUG.) “At dawn on the first day of the week,” etc., up to the angel’s saying to them: “So he will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1).

# THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK (G)*

## PROLOGUE OF BLESSED JEROME

*(See his works.)*

## CHAPTER ONE

VERS. 1.—The beginning of the Gospel. (ISID.) *Gospel* means “good announcement,” which properly concerns the kingdom of God and the remission of sins. Hence: “Repent and believe in the Gospel,” and “the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.”

(HIER.) The four Gospels are one, and the one is four. Thus Mark’s book is called the Gospel, and likewise the books of the others, because all are one and the one is all.

Of Jesus Christ. (HIER.) *Jesus* is *Jesus* in Hebrew, *Soter* in Greek, and *Salvator* in Latin: “Savior”; *Christ* is *Messias* in Hebrew and *unctus* in Latin, “anointed,” that is, king and priest. He is said to be from the lineage of David the king and from the Levitical line.

The Son of God. (BEDA.) Matthew says, “the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1). Mark says, “the Son of God,” so that he proceeds gradually from lesser things to greater, etc., up to the point that John begins from the eternity of the Word of God and brings it to completion in the Lord’s Resurrection.

VERS. 2.—As it is written. Mark puts the testimonies of the prophets first, by which he asserts that these things are ancient, not new, but foreknown and foretold by the prophets. In this way he invites the Jews, who had received the Law and the Prophets, to the Gospel, and urges the Gentiles, who held the Gospel, to venerate the Law and the Prophets, so that no one, like the heretics, might accept one without the other.

Behold, I send. (BEDA.) John is called an angel not by a sharing of nature, as Origen falsely claims, but by the dignity of his office, just as the priests, of whom it is said: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2).

(ID.) Note that this testimony, “Behold, I send my angel,” etc., belongs to Malachi, yet he says that both belong to Isaiah, because, etc., up to the point that all the prophets spoke by one Spirit, as though with one mouth.

VERS. 3.—Of one crying out. (ISID.) To the Jews, deaf because of their sins and situated far away, deserving the cry of indignation. In the wilderness. In the wilderness there is a voice and a cry, because the house of Judah, deserted, empty, swept, and without the Spirit of God, has been deprived of prophet, king, and priest. Therefore Jesus and John seek what has been lost in the wilderness. Where the devil conquered, there he is conquered; where man fell, there he rises again.

Prepare. (ISID.) Do penance and preach. Hence *Parasceve* comes before the Sabbath, etc., up to the point that we may possess the desirable land in peace.

The way of the Lord. (HIER.) The way of the Lord by which he enters human beings is repentance, through which God descends to us and we ascend to him. Hence angels are remembered ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.

Make his paths straight. (ISID.) He commands that, walking along the royal road, we should love our neighbors as ourselves, and ourselves, etc., up to the point that the mouth should not be separated from the deed, nor the deed from the mouth.

The paths follow the way, because moral commandments are explained after repentance according to Mark or Matthew. The way is prepared through faith, baptism, and repentance.

Straight paths are made through austere signs: clothing, belt, food, drink, and a very humble voice.

VERS. 4.—John. (ISID.) The grace of God. He begins from the grace of God, whence it follows: “baptizing,” etc. Through baptism sins are forgiven; hence: “What you have received freely, give freely” (Matthew 10). And the Apostle says: “You have been saved by grace” (Ephesians 2).

Baptizing. (HIER.) He gave the baptism of repentance and preached baptism for the remission of sins, but did not give it. Just as through preaching, etc., up to the point that now, through the friend of the bridegroom, the bride is brought in, like Rebecca, veiled in a white garment by the servant.

VERS. 5.—In the Jordan. (ID.) *Jordan* means “alien descent,” where sins are absolved. For the ark, etc., up to the body of Christ: it does not benefit the unclean, but changes them for the worse.

Confessing, etc. (ID.) “Confession and beauty are in his sight” (Psalm 115), that is, in the sight of the bridegroom. Hence the bride leaps down from the camel when the Church humbles herself before Christ, who is represented by Isaac, at whose birth God caused Sarah to laugh. As it is said to Mary, who is a ruler with God: “Blessed are you among women” (Luke 1).

(BEDA.) Those who confess their sins are baptized. For those who receive baptism ought to promise the newness of a better life, etc., up to the point that, thus cleansed and promising the Christian religion, they are changed into members of the Church.

VERS. 6.—And John was, etc. (HIER.) The prophet’s clothing, food, and drink signify the entire austere life of preachers, and the Gentiles, etc., up to the point that all things come from the grace of the Gospel, in which there is no distinction between Jew and Greek.

(BEDA.) Clothed in camel’s hair. Because he did not indulge sins but rebuked them harshly, saying: “Brood of vipers,” etc. A leather belt, etc., up to the point that in honey there is sweetness, in the locust an agile flight, but one that quickly falls.

VERS. 7.—Mightier than I. (HIER.) Who is mightier than the grace by which sins are washed away? He who, etc., up to the point that it reaches one hundred forty-four thousand.

To loosen the strap. (BEDA.) It was the custom among the ancients that if someone did not wish to take as his wife the woman who was appropriate for him, he, etc., up to the point: “I am not able to uncover the Redeemer’s feet, because I do not claim the name of the bridegroom for myself.”

(HIER.) The strap of the sandals, that is, the mystery of God’s Incarnation. For the heel, etc., up to the point that the bride is in the patriarchs, the friend in the prophets, the close companion in Mary and Joseph, the beloved in John the Baptist, and the dove in Christ and the apostles.

VERS. 8.—I baptized you with water. (BEDA.) John does not yet openly say that he is God or the Son of God, because his hearers were still inexperienced; but gradually, through glorified humanity, he leads them to faith in divinity, saying: “He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.” Later, when he saw that they had become more capable, he openly preached that he was the Son of God, saying: “He bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John 3).

(ISID.) “I baptize you with water, but he,” etc. God’s river is always full, always equal, concerning which it is said: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Psalm 45). There is a great difference, etc., up to the point that Christ’s anointing passes from the bitterness of the Passion to the glory of the Resurrection. Hence the Apostle says: “Have this mind among yourselves, which was also in Christ Jesus,” etc., up to: “Therefore God also exalted him” (Philippians 2).

VERS. 9.—And he was baptized in the Jordan. For three reasons: to fulfill righteousness and humility; to confirm John’s baptism; and, by sanctifying the waters of the Jordan through the descent of the dove, to show that the Holy Spirit is present in baptism.

(HIER.) Mark is like a deer longing for springs of water: he leaps, plucks the tops of meadows, carries palms on his head, and, like a honey-bearing bee, briefly tastes the flowers of the field—whose fragrance is compared with that of the true Isaac. Hence, Jesus coming from Nazareth of Galilee to baptism, etc., up to: “To the one who conquers I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God” (Revelation 2).

VERS. 10.—He saw the heavens opened, etc. (BEDA.) The mystery of the Trinity is demonstrated in baptism: the Son is baptized, the Spirit is in the dove, and the Father speaks in the voice. The heavens are opened, etc., up to the point that the Spirit will remain among us and will be in us according to the measure of faith. But of Christ it is said: “Full of grace and truth” (John 1).

Remaining in him. The Spirit remains in him not from the time when he was baptized, but from the time when he was conceived. But the fact that it descended at baptism signifies that spiritual grace is given to us in baptism; after we have been regenerated from water and the Spirit for the remission of sins, a greater grace of the Spirit is customarily given to us from heaven through the laying on of the bishop’s hands.

VERS. 11.—You are my beloved Son. (BEDA.) It is not that one who did not know is being taught, but that what we ought to believe is shown to us: namely, that he is, etc., up to the point that the Spirit rightly descended in the form of a dove, which is a simple animal without gall, because he seeks the simple and does not dwell in impure minds.

VERS. 12.—The Spirit. (ID.) So that there might be no doubt which spirit was meant, Luke deliberately says beforehand: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan”; then he adds: “and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness,” so that no one might suppose that an unclean spirit had been able to do anything against him.

VERS. 13.—For forty days. (ID.) This signifies the entire period during which the devil tempts his members. For the four-part world, by observing the ten commandments and fighting against the devil, serves the Lord. Four times ten makes forty. Everywhere and always the adversary is present, who does not cease to impede our journey.

And he was with the wild beasts. If we too, in the wilderness of holy conduct, endure the beastly behavior of human beings with an undefiled mind, we merit the mystery of the angels, by whom, once freed from the body, we will be transferred to heaven.

VERS. 14.—Now after. (ISID.) We have received grace in place of grace; carnal things are put to death, spiritual things are brought to life. When the shadow ceases, truth is present. John is in prison, the Law is in Judea, Jesus is in Galilee, and salvation is among the Gentiles.

Preaching, etc. (HIER.) “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for they shall possess [it]” (Matthew 5), etc. Earthly rule is succeeded by poverty, and poverty by the everlasting kingdom of Christians. Hence: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18); for every earthly honor is foam, smoke, and sleep.

VERS. 15.—Repent. (HIER.) The sweetness of the fruit compensates for the bitterness of the root; the hope of the harbor delights amid the dangers of the sea; the hope of health alleviates the pain of medicine. Let the one who desires the kernel break the nut; let the one who wishes to cling to eternal good practice repentance. Those who have deserved to reach the palm of forgiveness can proclaim the praises of Christ. Hence preachers are chosen after repentance.

VERS. 16.—He saw Simon. (HIER.) Simon means “obedient”; Andrew, “manly”; James, “supplanter”; John, “grace.” Through these names, etc., up to the point that through prudence we obey, through justice we act manfully, through temperance we trample serpents, and through fortitude we merit the grace of God.

(ID.) Whom does secular eloquence not intoxicate? It is difficult for powerful, noble, and rich people—and much more difficult for eloquent people—to believe in God. Their minds are blinded by riches, resources, and luxury; surrounded by vices, they cannot see virtues. They judge the simplicity of Holy Scripture not by the majesty of its meanings but by the usefulness of its words.

(ID.) Four fishermen are called—Simon, Andrew, James, and John—and, leaving everything, they follow. By this four-horse chariot we are carried to the heavens, etc., up to the point that we are covered with Solomon’s skins, by which the bride boasts that she is beautiful.

(BEDA.) It is asked how he first called Peter and Andrew and, shortly afterward, James and John, as he narrates, etc., up to the point that they followed the one calling and commanding them, not having drawn the boats onto land as though concerned about returning, but as those who followed the one calling and commanding.

And they enter. (HIER.) Mark, arranging the sayings of the Gospel within himself without following the historical order, preserves the order of the mysteries. Hence he narrates the first miracle on the Sabbath, saying: “And they enter,” etc.

Capernaum. (ID.) Capernaum means “village of consolation”; the Sabbath means rest. A man with an unclean spirit signifies the human race, in which there is uncleanness, etc., up to the point that Pharaoh, having dismissed Israel, pursues him; when the devil is despised, he rises up into scandals.

(BEDA.) By healing and teaching especially on the Sabbath, he shows that he is not under the Law but above it. He teaches us the true Sabbath, namely, that while devoting ourselves to the salvation of souls, we should abstain from every servile work—that is, from everything unlawful.

VERS. 22.—For he was, etc. (BEDA.) The scribes spoke what had been written in Moses and the prophets; Jesus, as God and Lord, freely added to or changed the Law of Moses itself where it was lacking. Hence in Matthew: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients,” etc.; “But I say to you.”

VERS. 24.—What have we to do with you, etc. (ID.) This is not a confession of the will but an extorted confession of necessity, just as a runaway slave fears seeing his master and begs to be spared the blows. For when the demons saw the Lord on earth, they immediately believed that they were to be judged.

VERS. 25.—Be silent. (ID.) In fitting order, the serpentine tongue that first spread its poison is first closed, so that it may spread no further; then, etc., up to the point that the same order of restoration may be found in the Lord as of destruction in the first-formed man.

VERS. 26.—Convulsing him. (ID.) Or “shaking him violently,” as some manuscripts have. Luke says that it did him no harm. But what Mark says, “convulsing him,” is the same as what Luke says: “having thrown him into the midst.” What he adds, “and did him no harm,” should be understood to mean that this tossing did not weaken him, just as demons depart after some limbs have been cut off or torn away.

“(Same author.) By the man freed from the demon we understand the mind cleansed from unclean thought. By the woman subsequently healed of fever, we understand the flesh restrained from the heat of lust through the precepts of continence.

**VERSE 27.**—What does this mean? By the things they see, they are stirred to inquire into the things they have heard. For this reason the Lord himself also performs signs and gave his disciples power to perform them, so that through this the Gospel might be believed more firmly: those who promise heavenly things to earthly people perform heavenly and divine works on earth.

**VERSE 30.**—And immediately they tell him, etc. Luke says that they pleaded with him on her behalf. For now the Savior, when entreated, heals; now he heals of his own accord, so that he might show that, against the passions of vices also, he is always present to the prayers of the faithful, and that to those who piously ask he either grants what they do not understand to be understood, or mercifully forgives what they have failed to understand. Hence: “Who understands his offenses? Cleanse me from my hidden faults” (Psalm 18).

**VERSE 31.**—He took her by the hand. Peter’s mother-in-law, feverish, is taken by the hand and raised up. Fever is intemperance; from it we, the sons of the Synagogue, are healed through the hand of discipline and the raising up of desire, and we minister to the will of the one who heals us as he declines from us toward evening.

He ministered to them. “(Bede.) Allegorically: that is, let the members which had served impurity serve righteousness.”

**VERSE 32.**—But when evening came. “(Same author.) The setting of the sun is the death of Christ. They brought to him all who were ill. For he healed more people through the apostles after his death than he preached to the Jews while living in the flesh.”

**VERSE 33.**—At the door. “(Jerome.) Morally, the door of the kingdom is repentance with faith, which works salvation amid various illnesses. For the vices by which the city of the world languishes are various.”

**VERSE 34.**—Because they knew him. “(Bede.) Luke states it more plainly: ‘Demons also came out of many,’ etc., because they knew him to be Christ. Thus the demons know that Christ is the Son of God, etc., up to the passage: Hence Paul says, ‘None of the rulers of this age understood it; for if they had understood it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory’ (1 Corinthians 2).”

**VERSE 35.**—And early in the morning. “(Same author.) Just as the setting of the sun signifies death, so dawn signifies the resurrection of Christ, whose manifest light went forth into the desert of the Gentiles; and he prayed among the faithful because he stirred their hearts to prayer.”

**VERSE 38.**—For this is why I came. “(Victor of Antioch.) The Evangelist appropriately adds this. For here the authority of his divinity is not merely foreshadowed; the humility of his voluntary self-emptying is also expressed. Luke, wishing to convey the economy of the Word, writes, ‘For this is why I was sent.’ Thus he designates the Father’s good pleasure concerning the incarnation of the Word by the name of apostleship.”

**VERSE 39.**—And he was preaching in their synagogues. “(Bede.) This preaching also includes that sermon delivered on the mountain which Matthew records; for, etc., up to: ‘And behold, a leper came and worshiped him, saying, “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean”’ (Matthew 8).”

**VERSE 40.**—And kneeling, etc. “(Bede.) Humble and ashamed. Everyone ought to blush at the stains of his life, but shame should not suppress confession: let him show the wound and ask for a remedy.”

“(Jerome.) The leper, kneeling and imploring the Lord’s will, is cleansed—he who does not desire the death of a sinner, but, etc., up to: ‘Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you’ (Luke 11).”

“(Bede.) The leper signifies the human race, which, according to Luke, is said to have been full of leprosy. For all, etc., up to: and truly to offer their bodies to the true priest as a living, holy sacrifice, pleasing to God (Romans 12).”

If you will, you can. “(Same author.) In his will he attributes the power, and he does not doubt as an unbeliever concerning the Lord’s will; rather, conscious of his own pollution, he does not presume.”

“(Same author.) He who, excluded by the law of the Lord, asks to be healed by his power judges that grace is above the law. For just as there is authority of power in the Lord, so there is constancy of faith in him.”

**VERSE 41.**—He stretched out his hand. “(Same author.) The law prohibits touching a leper; but because he is Lord of the law, he does not submit to the law but makes the law. He does not touch him because he was unable to heal without touching him, but in this way he demonstrates that he was not subject to the law.”

I will; be clean. “(Same author.) This is marvelous: by the very manner in which he is entreated, he heals. ‘I will; be clean’; and when he had said this, immediately the leprosy departed from him. There is nothing between the deed and the command. ‘He spoke, and they came to be’ (Psalm 32). You see that the will is power. Therefore, etc., up to: ‘He says “I will” for Photinus, commands for Arius, and touches for the Manichaean.’”

**VERSE 44.**—See that you say nothing, etc. “(Same author.) Not because he desired something he could not accomplish—for ‘he has done whatever he has willed’ (Psalm 113)—but he teaches that our benefits should be restrained not only from monetary reward but also from gratitude.”

Show yourself, etc. “(Same author.) So that he may understand that he was healed not according to the order of the law, but by grace, which is above the law. He commands him to offer the sacrifice in order to show that he does not abolish the law but fulfills it: while walking according to the law, he heals above the law those whom the remedies of the law did not heal. Nor should the sacrifice signifying this have ceased, since what was signified had not yet been confirmed by the constitution of the apostles and the faith of believers.”

**VERSE 45.**—But after he went out. “(Same author.) The salvation of one compels many to come to the Lord. He cannot keep silent about the benefit, even when commanded by the one who gave it. The Lord commanded that it be concealed. For he wishes us to desire that what we do in goodness remain hidden, which is humility; and that we be unwillingly revealed so that we may benefit others, which is great sublimity, since even if we ourselves wished it, works cannot be concealed.”

So that Jesus could no longer, etc. “(Jerome.) Jesus was not manifested to all who serve broad avenues and plane trees with praise and their own pleasures, but to these, etc., up to: those whom nothing can separate from the love of God.”

## CHAPTER II

**VERSE 2.**—So that there was no room, etc. “(Bede.) When the Lord was preaching, they could not fit inside the house, nor even at the door. For while Christ was preaching in Judea, the Gentiles had not yet wished to enter to hear him; nevertheless, though standing outside, he directed the words of his teaching to them through his preachers.”

**VERSE 3.**—A paralytic. “(Jerome.) Paralysis is a type of torpor, by which a sluggish person lies in the softness of the flesh while desiring salvation; but because of the crowds, etc., up to: so that by another route he might return with the Magi to his own region.”

He was carried by four. “(Bede.) For the mind is raised in confidence toward the Lord by four virtues. Concerning these it is said in the Book of Wisdom: ‘She teaches sobriety and wisdom, knowledge and virtue’ (Wisdom 8), which others call prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice.”

**VERSE 4.**—They uncovered the roof where he was. The roof of the house in which Christ teaches is the sublimity of Scripture, by which a young person corrects his way: “by keeping your words” (Psalm 118).

“(Bede.) According to another Evangelist, the house of Jesus is said to be roofed with tiles, because the spiritual meaning is covered by the lowliness of the letter. He is lowered before Jesus with the pallet because, even while established in this flesh, he ought to recognize Jesus.”

**VERSE 5.**—When he saw, etc. “(Same author.) Personal faith is of great value before God, since the faith of another was so powerful that a man, healed inwardly and outwardly, suddenly rose up, and his offenses were forgiven through the merits of others.”

Son. What marvelous humility: he calls a man despised by all, with all his limbs paralyzed, “son.” Or certainly he does so because his sins are forgiven.

**VERSE 6.**—Your sins are forgiven you. He shows that the man had been struck by illness on account of his sins, and therefore could not be healed unless these were first forgiven. As with the paralytic at the pool: “Behold, you have been healed; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5). “(Bede.) People are afflicted with bodily troubles for five reasons: either to increase their merits, as with Job and the martyrs; or because of humility, etc., up to Lazarus, whose illness was not for death but for the glory of God; or as the beginning of eternal damnation, as with Herod.”

**VERSE 7.**—Who can forgive? “(Same author.) They speak truly: God alone can do this, and he alone forgives through those to whom he has granted the power of forgiving sins; therefore he is truly God. They testify to the truth, but they go astray by denying Christ’s person. Thus they err: although they believe that he is God and forgives sins, they do not believe that he is Christ. But the Arians are even more foolish: they do not dare deny that Christ exists and forgives sins, yet they do not fear denying that he is God.”

**VERSE 9.**—Which is easier? “(Same author.) As though he were saying: By the same power by which I perceive the hidden things of the heart, I forgive sins. As though he were saying: From yourselves, understand what follows for the paralytic.”

**VERSE 10.**—The Son of Man. “(Same author.) God alone forgives sins, and the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins; therefore he is both God and the Son of Man. Thus Christ the man forgives sins through his divinity, and through his humanity can die for sinners.”

**VERSE 11.**—Go to your house. “(Same author.) He who had been ill carries the pallet home; when the soul has been healed by the forgiveness of sins, it returns with the body to the prolonged guardianship of itself, lest it again admit anything by which it might be struck.”

**VERSE 13.**—And he went out, etc. “(Same author.) After healing the paralytic in Capernaum, he goes out toward the sea because he instructs not only the citizens but also the inhabitants of the sea; and by the firmness of faith, etc., up to: he draws those separated from the waves of desires into solitude, into the quiet conduct of life that rests in hope of heavenly things.”

**VERSE 14.**—Levi. “(Jerome.) Levi means ‘added,’ because, leaving the customs office of worldly business, he follows the single word that says: ‘Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple’ (Luke 14).”

“(Bede.) Out of modesty and in honor of the Evangelist, Mark and Luke do not use the familiar name. He himself, in accordance with what is written—‘The righteous man is first of all his own accuser’ (Proverbs 18)—calls himself Matthew and publican, to show that no convert ought to despair of salvation, since an apostle and Evangelist was suddenly made from a publican.”

He followed him. “(Same author.) Luke gives the fuller account: ‘And leaving everything, he followed him’ (Luke 5). He follows so that, as a poor man, he may follow Christ not so much by the movement of his body as by the affection of his mind; he leaves everything, etc., up to: therefore, deservedly, he who by obedience despised human business was made a steward of divine talents.”

**VERSE 15.**—And it came to pass. “(Same author.) Luke says: ‘Levi made a great banquet for him in his house’ (Luke 5). For whoever receives Christ within is delighted by the abundance of pleasures, and the Lord gladly enters and reclines in his affection. This is the spiritual banquet of the good poor, which the rich person needs and the poor person enjoys.”

Publicans. Those who collect public taxes, or those who pursue the profits of the world; they are converted by the example of the publican and now presume upon salvation, not slandering like the Pharisees while remaining in their vices, but repenting.

“(Bede.) He goes to the banquet of sinners so that he may have an opportunity to teach and impart spiritual food. In going to sinners, the Lord’s humility is displayed; in the conversion of the penitent, the power of his teaching is revealed.”

“(Same author.) Through the calling of Matthew, the faith of the Gentiles is signified: they leave the profits of the world and feast with the Lord at the banquets of charity and good works. Through the haughtiness of the Pharisees, the envy of the Jews concerning the salvation of the Gentiles is signified, to whom it is said: ‘Tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of God’ (Matthew 21).”

**VERSE 17.**—There is no need. “(Same author.) If he calls himself a physician, he is one who, by a wondrous manner of healing, was wounded ‘because of our iniquities, and by whose bruising we were healed’ (Isaiah 53).”

**VERSE 18.**—And the disciples were, etc. Other Evangelists say that the Pharisees and John’s disciples asked this. Here he seems to say that those who were moved by concern for the same matter asked it. From this it is gathered that the question was raised by several groups: by the Pharisees, John’s disciples, the guests, or any others.

“(Same author.) John’s disciples and the Pharisees fast because those who glory in the works of the law, or—what is worse—follow traditions, etc., up to: he ate with sinners, so that, seeing grace, you might recognize power.”

**VERSE 19.**—Surely they cannot? Matthew has it this way: “Can the wedding guests mourn while the bridegroom is with them?” etc. (Matthew 9). Christ is the bridegroom, the Church is the bride; from this spiritual marriage the apostles were created. They cannot mourn and fast while they see the bridegroom with the bride. When the wedding has passed and the time of the passion and resurrection has arrived, then they will fast.

“(Bede.) As long as the bridegroom is with us, we are in joy and cannot fast or mourn; but when he withdraws and flies away because of sin, then fasting must be proclaimed and mourning multiplied.”

**VERSE 21.**—No one sews a patch, etc. “(Same author.) He calls the disciples garments that are old—that is, still carnal, not yet renewed by the firmness of faith, etc., up to: wine, the fervor of faith, hope, and charity, by which our inner sense is reformed in the sight of God through the newness of our understanding.”

**VERSE 22.**—But new wine. They were new when, after the Ascension, they were renewed by hoping and praying out of their desire for his consolation. Then they received the Holy Spirit, by which, like new wineskins filled with new must, they were filled.

**VERSE 23.**—On the Sabbath. “(Bede.) Note first that the apostles establish the letter of the Sabbath against the Ebionites, who, although they receive the other disciples, reject Paul as a transgressor of the law.”

And plucking the heads of grain. They are hungry as human beings, having no opportunity to eat because of the crowd. But they provide an example of a stricter life: they seek not prepared dishes but simple food.

“(Bede.) The disciples pass through the grainfields when prelates look around upon their subjects with pious concern and diligently consider how they may draw each person to the faith, etc., up to: the Lord approves this, while foolish defenders of the Sabbath condemn it; they love only the surface of the letter, know nothing of the refreshment of the mind, and do not understand the rest of souls.”

**VERSE 25.**—Have you never read, etc.? Above all others he brings forward David, who might seem to have opposed the sanctity of the law. He does this with the purpose of restraining, through the honor and reverence they paid to David, the shameless slander which they maliciously directed against the apostles. As though he were saying: Do you not remember that David was bound by the servitude of the law? Yet I, although I am called the Son of Man, am Lord of the Sabbath.

**VERSE 26.**—In the time of Abiathar, etc. Let it not trouble you that others say “Ahimelech”; both were present there at that time: Ahimelech the father and Abiathar the son. After his father was killed by Saul, Abiathar became David’s companion in exile; when David reigned, he became high priest, more renowned than his father. For this reason he was worthy for the Lord to mention him as high priest, even while his father was still alive.

The bread of the Presence. “(Bede.) As though he were saying: If David and Ahimelech are not blamed by us but excused because of hunger, why do you disapprove in this case what you approve in others? Although it is, etc., up to: and all the sons of the Church are priests, joined in a holy priesthood, offering themselves as spiritual sacrifices to God.”

And he gave it to them. He followed the saying, “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6): he judged it better to free people from the danger of hunger than to offer sacrifice. The sacrifice pleasing to God is the salvation of human beings.

**VERSE 27.**—The human being was made for the Sabbath. “(Bede.) The Sabbath was commanded to be observed in such a way that, if necessity arose, a person would not be guilty, etc., up to: if someone breaks a fast because he is ill, he is not held guilty.”

**VERSE 28.**—Therefore the Lord. As though he were saying: If King David and the priests—according to another Evangelist—because of the ministry of the temple violated the Sabbath without guilt, how much more the Son of Man, the true King and Priest! Therefore, as Lord of the Sabbath, he is not held guilty on the Sabbath for the offense of plucking the heads of grain.

## CHAPTER III

**VERSE 1.**—A withered hand. “(Bede.) The hand which was extended toward the forbidden fruit withered from good work; through the hands of Christ extended on the cross, it was restored to the nourishment of good works.”

“(Jerome.) This man signifies the avaricious, who, unwilling to give, wish to receive—to plunder and not to distribute. They are told to extend their hands: that is, let the one who stole steal no longer, but rather labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to one in need (Ephesians 4).”

**VERSE 2.**—And they watched him. “(Bede.) Because he had plausibly excused the disciples, they watch him, so that if he heals on the Sabbath they may accuse him of transgression, and if he does not heal, of cruelty or weakness.”

It is lawful to do good on the Sabbath. “(Same author.) He rebukes them because by a perverse interpretation they violate the precepts of the law, judging that one must refrain from doing good on the Sabbath, although the law says, etc., up to: he set forth the example of the sheep and concluded that it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.”

A life. “(Same author.) The whole human being is signified by a part. Or because he did this for the sake of the soul, or because the healing of this hand signifies the salvation of the soul.”

To destroy. “(Same author.) Not that the supremely merciful one could destroy anyone, but that failing to save someone is to destroy him. Thus it is said that he hardened Pharaoh’s heart—not that he made it hard, but that he did not soften a heart already hardened.”

**VERSE 5.**—Stretch out your hand. “(Bede.) No remedy is better for the soul’s unproductive weakness than the distribution of alms; hence: ‘Whoever has two tunics should give to one who has none; and whoever has food should do likewise’ (Luke 3). And in Ecclesiasticus: ‘My son, do not let your hand be stretched out to receive and closed when it is time to give’ (Ecclesiasticus 4). For in vain does one stretch out one’s hands to the Lord in prayer who does not extend them to a widow asking.”

And his hand was restored. In their great zeal for wickedness, they count it as a crime that his hand was healed at a word. Nor can he who spoke and it came to be be convicted of having labored on the Sabbath, while they themselves carry food on the Sabbaths, offer cups, and provide the other necessities of life.

**VERSE 6.**—But after they went out. Those who cannot act alone seek companions in iniquity.

With the Herodians. Herod’s servants, because of the hostility that Herod himself exercised against the man, pursued Jesus with plots and hatred—the Jesus whom John preached.

**VERSE 7.**—He withdrew. He fled as a man because his hour had not yet come, and there was no place for his passion outside Jerusalem.

“(Bede.) He withdraws from the synagogue to the sea, etc. He leaves Judea and comes to the Gentiles with his disciples—that is, he approaches the hearts of the Gentiles while the apostles preach; and thus he received many who came to him and gave them the salvation they desired.”

And a great crowd. “(Same author.) The teachers of the people and the king’s servants pursue him out of hatred; the uneducated populace follows him out of love, and many deserve to be healed.”

**VERSE 9.**—A boat. The Church gathered from the Gentiles, crossing the waves of the world in mind. The more broadly it expands the bosom of its heart to receive grace, the more securely it treads upon the waves of the world.

Lest they should crush him. They crush who disturb the peace of the Church. They touch who receive faith with a true heart and love; those who touched him are said to have been healed. He flees from those pressing upon him and goes up into the boat.

**VERSE 11.**—And unclean spirits, etc. “(Bede.) Both those afflicted with diseases and the unclean spirits are mentioned. But the sick have a pious intention toward salvation; the demoniacs—or rather, the demons within them—not only are compelled by fear to fall down, but also to confess his majesty. Terrified by his presence, they could not conceal the one whom they already knew to be the Son of God. They are sounder than the Arians, who even today deny that he is the Son of God.”

**VERSE 12.**—That they should not reveal him. “(Same author.) Not only are the demons, who confess unwillingly, or those healed by him, who confess willingly, commanded to be silent; the apostles too, who would preach throughout the whole world after the passion, are commanded to remain silent before the passion, lest the preaching of his divine majesty delay the passion and thus the salvation of the world.”

**VERSE 13.**—And he went up. “(Same author.) After forbidding the unclean spirits to preach him, he chose holy men who would preach him and drive out the wicked spirits.”

This mountain signifies the height of righteousness, by which they were to be instructed and which they were to preach. Through the place he admonishes them to be raised toward heavenly things; likewise, he gave the law on a mountain.

“(Jerome.) It is the custom of divine Scripture to speak allegorically; but let us apply lofty things to our understanding in such a way that we preserve the truth of the history, etc., up to: those who are called to the mountain are exalted both in merit and in word, so that the place corresponds to their lofty merits.”

**VERSE 14.**—That they might be twelve. God loved the likeness of Jacob when the Most High divided the nations and separated the sons of Adam. He established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel, so that they might be upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. To them power was given—the power which the Son received from the Father according to the flesh—so that they might perform the works that he himself performed, and greater works than these.

“(Bede.) He also gave them power to raise the dead, as Matthew says, so that the power displayed might produce faith, etc., up to: because tongues are for a sign not to believers but to unbelievers (1 Corinthians 14).”

**VERSE 16.**—And he appointed. “(Same author.) Not only at first, but also when Andrew brought him and he said: ‘You shall be called Cephas,’ which is interpreted as Peter (John 1). But here the Evangelist makes you attentive by saying that, etc., up to: or hearing the sorrow of death, namely when he is told: ‘Another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go’ (1 Corinthians 4).”

**VERSE 17.**—And James. He who has the desires of the flesh supplanted.

And John, who received by grace what others received through labor.

And he gave them the name Boanerges, which means “sons of thunder.” Their sublime merit deserved to hear on the mountain the thunder of the Father thundering through the cloud concerning the Son: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 17), so that through the cloud of the flesh they too might scatter Christ’s fire and lightning as rain upon the earth. “For the Lord has made lightning into rain,” so that mercy may extinguish what judgment consumes by fire. Hence: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Psalm 100).

James. He supplanted the care of the flesh when the Lord called him and despised that same flesh when Herod slew him.

John. “(Bede.) In him there is grace, or the grace of the Lord. Because of the special grace of love which he earned through virginal glory, he reclined upon the breast of his Redeemer at supper.”

Sons. “(Same author.) One of them, thundering forth a theological voice—one which no one had previously known how to utter—proclaimed: ‘In the beginning was the Word,’ etc. (John 1). He left it pregnant with such weight that, if he had wished to thunder a little more, even the world itself could not have contained it.”

**VERSE 18.**—And Andrew. “(Jerome.) He who manfully does violence to his own destruction, so that he always has within himself the sentence of death and always holds his soul in his hands.”

And Philip. “(Same author.) He is the mouth of the lamp; he illuminates with his mouth what he received, and he was given the work of an illuminated mouth. Scripture often recalls this kind of expression, when names are assigned because of mysteries; here the Evangelist inserts it with intense reference to the person of God.”

And Bartholomew. “(Same author.) He is the son of the one who suspends the waters, namely the one who said: ‘I will command my clouds not to rain’ (Isaiah 5). The name ‘son of God’ is acquired through peace and love: ‘Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God’ (Matthew 5). And: ‘Love your enemies, so that you may be sons of God’ (Luke 6).”

And Matthew. He is “given”; not only forgiveness of sins but also a place among the apostles is granted to him, so that the lion and the ox may eat together, and the wolf with the lamb (Isaiah 11).

Note that the other Evangelists place Matthew first and do not call him a publican. He places himself after Thomas and calls himself a publican.

And Thomas. “(Same author.) He is the abyss. For many know deep things but do not bring them forth. Hence: ‘I know a man in Christ,’ etc., up to: ‘which it is not lawful for a man to utter’ (2 Corinthians 12).”

“(Bede.) Thomas is the abyss because he penetrated the depth of virtue in the resurrection. Or ‘twin,’ in Greek *didymus*, that is, doubtful, because of his doubtful heart, since he scarcely believed the resurrection.”

And James of Alphaeus. That is, “learned” or “a thousandth,” from whose side a thousand will fall, and ten thousand at your right hand (Psalm 90).

“(Bede.) James of Alphaeus, who is also called the brother of the Lord, because Mary was the sister of Alphaeus, etc., up to: immediately after the resurrection he was appointed bishop of Jerusalem, as the learned man or son of the learned.”

Thaddaeus. Guardian of the heart. Luke names him in the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles “Judas of James,” because he was the brother of James, the brother of the Lord. Hence he is called the son of Mary, the mother of James and Joseph and Judas and Simon.

“(Jerome.) And Thaddaeus, who is *corculus*, that is, guardian of the heart, who keeps his heart with all vigilance. For God is seen through purity of heart, as through clear glass.”

And Simon. “(Bede.) Simon the Cananaean, from Cana, a village of Galilee; he is also Simon the Zealot, that is, the zealous one. Cana means ‘zeal’; Cananaean means ‘Zealot.’”

And Simon the Cananaean. He is also Simon the Zealot, Simon who brings or possesses sorrow. For blessed are those who mourn, because they will be comforted (Matthew 5). He who seeks the future consolation fulfills a threefold mourning. He laments his own sins with David and Mary. With Paul he weeps with those who weep. And he weeps greatly with John, who said: “And I wept greatly, because no one was found worthy to open the book and break its seals” (Revelation 5). He is called a Zealot because zeal for the house of God consumed him, as it did Phinehas: “And the plague ceased” (Numbers 25).

**VERSE 19.**—And Judas Iscariot. He does not erase his sin through repentance, nor is it erased through remembrance. Hence: “May the sin of his mother not be erased; may it stand continually before the Lord” (Psalm 108).

Judas means “confessing” or “glorious”; Iscariot means “the memory of death.” There are many confessors in the Church who are proud and glorious, the first being Simon Magus, and others among the heretics; their deadly memory is celebrated in the Church so that it may be erased.

“(Jerome.) Judas Iscariot is named either from the village in which he was born or from the tribe of Issachar. Issachar means ‘payment,’ namely the price of destruction; Iscariot, etc., up to: the example of one humbles others for fear, as the fall of the angel of light does, and as it is written: ‘Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom’ (Jeremiah 9), but ‘let the one who glories glory in the Lord’ (1 Corinthians 1).”

And they come, etc. “(Bede.) Those who have undertaken the care of others ought diligently to guard the gift of conscience, so that they may govern themselves first, and then others.”

**VERSE 20.** “(Jerome.) The house in which they gather is the primitive Church. The crowds that prevent them from eating bread are sins and vices, because whoever eats the Lord’s body unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the Lord’s body (1 Corinthians 11). Hence the Lord is aroused to anger when he says: ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life’ (John 6).”

**VERSE 21.**—And when his people heard, etc. The crowd frequents him; his own people despise him as though he were mad. In this the salvation of the Gentiles is signified and the envy of the Jews rejected, concerning whom it is said: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 6).

**VERSE 22.**—And the scribes. “(Bede.) If some, because of slowness of mind, do not understand the word of God, hope of salvation nevertheless remains, in case they should perhaps understand. But for those who do not wish to understand and pervert what they do understand, there is no hope. Hence ‘scribes,’ that is, wise men, etc.”

From Jerusalem. This signifies that he would be persecuted by his fellow citizens unto death. Above we read that a crowd followed him from Galilee and Jerusalem, from across the Jordan and from the region around Tyre and Sidon, which are cities of the Gentiles; but the scribes from Jerusalem blasphemed. For the crowd of the Jewish people brought him in with palms and praises; the Gentiles desired him; the scribes and elders of the people plotted his death.

He has Beelzebul. A “lord of flies,” or “one who has flies”; by this name they called the prince of demons because of the filth of sacrificial blood.

**VERSE 23.**—How can Satan cast out Satan, etc.? “(Bede.) Let them choose whichever they wish. If Satan cannot cast out Satan, they say nothing against the Lord. But if he can, let them withdraw from his kingdom, which cannot stand divided.”

**VERSE 27.**—And then he will plunder his house. “(Same author.) He plundered the house because he distributed among the apostles and their successors, as though among divided provinces, all the regions of the world possessed by the devil, so that they might convert the peoples to the faith.”

**VERSE 29.**—But whoever blasphemes. “(Jerome.) He does not deserve to perform repentance so as to be received who, understanding Christ, said that he was the prince of demons, etc., up to: ‘Whoever does and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven’ (Matthew 5).”

“(Bede.) Matthew says: ‘Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit or the word,’ etc. There he shows that certain things will be revealed in the future. This is to be understood of lesser matters, such as an idle word or excessive laughter; for these things also this life has obtained pardon.”

Forever. This is directed against Origen, who promises forgiveness to all sinners after judgment, once countless ages have passed.

He will be guilty of an eternal sin. “(Bede.) Not because he says that the Spirit does not exist, or that he exists but is not God, or that he is God but lesser than the Father and the Son—for this arises not from diabolical envy but from human ignorance, etc.”

**VERSE 31.**—Brothers. “(Jerome.) They are not the children of Mary ever-Virgin, as Helvidius falsely claims, nor children of Joseph by another wife, as others chatter, but relatives.”

“(Bede.) The mother and brothers, the Jewish people from whom Christ came according to the flesh, stand outside in the literal sense. The crowd in the house signifies the Gentiles in the spiritual mystery. The Jews wish to see Christ outside because, not seeking spiritual understanding, they compel or seek to make him go out to teach them carnal things.”

**VERSE 33.**—Who is my mother? “(Same author.) He does not refuse obedience to his mother, who says, ‘Honor your father and your mother’ (Exodus 20); rather, he shows that he owes more to the mysteries of the Father than to maternal affections. He demonstrated the same thing by his saying: ‘Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me’ (Matthew 10). Nor does he contemptuously reject his brothers; he places spiritual work above kinship, teaching that the bond of hearts is better than that of bodies.”

**VERSE 34.**—Behold my mother, etc. “(Jerome.) So that we may know that we are both his brothers and his mother if we do the will of his Father, so that we may be coheirs, since he distinguishes not by sex but by deeds. One is sister and brother through believing, and mother through preaching, when through preaching the love of Christ—as Christ himself—is generated in the heart of the hearer.”

## CHAPTER IV

**VERSE 1.**—And again he began to teach. “(Bede.) Coming out of the house where he is said to have had the demon, he teaches by the sea, to show that because of the guilt of unbelief he would leave Judea and go to the Gentiles. Therefore it is appropriately stated beforehand that, while he was preaching in the house, his mother and brothers stood outside.”

“(Jerome.) He began to teach by the sea so that the place might indicate hearers who were bitter and unstable. And therefore, etc., up to: he who makes bitter things sweet, turns sadness into joy, and sickness into salvation.”

Going up into a boat, etc. “(Bede.) The Church, which is in the sea among unbelievers, which God illumines by the grace of his visitation and consecrates as a dwelling beloved by him.”

And the whole crowd was by the sea. “(Jerome.) These are those who have recently come to hear the word and, moved by the piety of their hearts, have followed him away from the bitterness of the wicked as from the sea. But they are not yet with the Lord in the boat, because they have not yet been imbued with the heavenly mysteries or sacraments that they desire.”

**VERSE 2.**—In many parables. A parable is a comparison made under a certain likeness between things differing in nature. He speaks according to his customary wisdom, so that those unable to comprehend heavenly things might grasp them through an earthly likeness. In Greek, *parabolē* means “comparison,” when we indicate what we wish to be understood through various comparisons—for example, when we compare iron with someone who is hard, or with the winds and birds when we speak of speed. The same pattern appears in the thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruit—that is, in the law, the prophecy, and the Gospel—which consists in the mystery of the kingdom displayed upon the mountain through the mouths of three witnesses: Moses, Elijah, and Jesus.

**VERSE 4.**—Some fell beside the road, etc. Luke says: “It was trampled, and the birds of the sky ate it” (Luke 8). The road is the mind worn down by the passage of carnal thoughts; therefore the seed perishes and bears no fruit, and is snatched away by birds—that is, by demons, who are called birds of the sky either because they are of a heavenly and spiritual nature or because they dwell in the air.

**VERSE 15.**—But these, etc. He sets forth the differences among those who hear the word. There are some, such as the Gentiles, who do not even hear.

**VERSE 19.**—The remaining desires, etc. This is what is commanded. For it is commanded: “Desire wisdom; keep the commandments” (Proverbs 7), etc. And elsewhere: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he will greatly delight in his commandments” (Psalm 3). These are good desires; whoever desires what remains goes astray.

**VERSE 21.**—A lamp, etc. “(Jerome.) The lamp is the word of God. The bushel or the bed is the hearing of the disobedient. The lampstand is the apostles, whom the word of God illumined. What is hidden and concealed becomes public when it is handled by the Lord.”

“(Bede.) The bushel is our life, measured by divine foreknowledge. The bed is the flesh, in which, etc., up to: because he places the desires of the flesh above it.”

Is it not so that it may be placed on a lampstand? “(Same author.) So that the preaching of truth may rule and the service of the body may be subordinate; through that service, however, the teaching appears more exalted, just as a lamp is elevated by means of a lampstand.”

## Verse 22

[Col. 0195B]

**“For there is nothing…”** As though he were saying: “Do not be ashamed of the Gospel, because nothing is now hidden that will not be made public at the judgment, when God will bring to light the things hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts” (Matt. 10); there, God’s praise will await you, but eternal punishment will await them.

## Verse 24

**“In what measure…”** (Jerome.) Indeed, according to the measure of faith, understanding of the mysteries is distributed to each person, and the gift of knowledge will be added to us; virtues also will be added.

## Verse 25

**“For whoever has…”** That is, whoever has faith will have virtue, and whoever possesses the work of the word will possess understanding of the mystery. Conversely, whoever does not have faith fails in virtue; whoever does not have the work of the word lacks its understanding; and whoever does not understand loses even what he has heard, as though he had not heard it.

[Col. 0195C]

## Verse 26

**“So is the kingdom of God.”** (Jerome.) Divine Scripture displays heavenly mysteries through earthly likenesses, as is evident throughout the whole body of the Gospels. The kingdom of God is the Church, which … up to: “For the harvest is present,” that is, the consummation of the age, in which the righteous will rejoice who sowed in tears.

## Verse 29

**“He sends the sickle.”** (Victor of Antioch.) The harvest is indeed the time of the consummation; the sickle is the word of God, more penetrating than any two-edged sword. Moreover, the sickle in this passage does not signify … up to: “For all bear grain, although not all bear an equal amount.”

## Verse 31

**“Like a grain.”** (Jerome.) Again he compares this seed to a mustard grain, which is very small in fear but great in charity, which is greater than [Col. 0195D] all vegetables, because God is charity, and all flesh is grass, and let the one who is weak eat vegetables. It produces branches of mercy and compassion. Beneath its shade the poor of Christ, who are the creatures of heaven, delight to dwell.

**“When it has been sown.”** By Christ or by a human being in the earth, or in the field—that is, in his own heart. This human being is our understanding and spirit; nourishing the grain of preaching with the moisture of faith, he makes it sprout in the field of his breast. **“It is smaller,”** etc. As though he were preaching contemptible things: at first he is not believed, because he preaches a God who became human, died, and was crucified; compared with the eloquence and wisdom of the philosophers, this is found to be inferior.

[Col. 0196A]

## Verse 32

**“It grew up,”** etc. It surpasses the nature of plants in height, breadth, and age. It is high because it raises people to heavenly things; broad because it has occupied the whole world; enduring because it cannot come to an end.

**“Than the vegetables.”** (Bede.) Than philosophical disciplines, which become more openly developed and therefore more worthless; for, like vegetables, they quickly wither.

## Verse 34

**“Without a parable.”** (The same.) Not because he made no discourse plain to the crowds, but because no discourse of his is found in which something of a parable is not present.

**“But privately to the disciples.”** (Jerome.) They were worthy to hear the mysteries in the innermost chamber of wisdom: having removed the tumult of their thoughts, they remained in the solitude of the virtues. For wisdom must be learned in a time of leisure.

[Col. 0196B]

## Verse 36

**“In the boat.”** (Bede.) Allegorically: the sea is the turmoil of the world. The little boat is the cross by which we rise above the waves of the world and reach the shore of our heavenly homeland. The other boats … up to: “For perhaps those boats had recently been made and had merely been brought into the harbor, or had been brought back into the harbor after the dangers of the sea.”

## Verse 38

**“In the stern.”** (Jerome.) The stern holds the living within dead skins, keeps back the waves, and is strengthened with wood, etc., up to: “Great tranquility”—the peace of the Church after its afflictions, or the contemplative life after the active life.

**“Sleeping.”** (Bede.) Christ falls asleep while the disciples are sailing because, while the faithful meditate upon the rest of the future kingdom and, by the favorable breath or rowing of the Holy Spirit, cast the waves of the world behind them through their own exertion, suddenly Christ’s Passion comes upon them. When he has ascended, etc., up to: “But let us flee to the helmsman; let us diligently awaken him who does not serve the winds but commands them, who will calm everything and grant the harbor of salvation.”

## Verse 39

**“Be silent; be quiet.”** Note that every creature perceives the command of its Creator—not that all things are animate, as the heretics falsely claim, but that through the majesty of the Creator those things are perceptible to him which are imperceptible to us.

[Col. 0196D]

## Verse 40

**“Why are you afraid?”** (Bede.) As though he were saying: “Why are you afraid while I am present?” This resembles what he reproached them with after the Resurrection: their unbelief and hardness of heart, because those who saw him rise did not believe (Mark 16). Likewise: “O foolish men and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that Christ should suffer and thus enter into his glory?” (Luke 24).

**“And they were afraid.”** Matthew says: “But the men marveled, saying, ‘What sort of man is this?’” (Matt. 8). Therefore it was not the disciples but the others who were in the boat who marveled, doubting about the one whom the sea and the wind obeyed. Or the disciples themselves are rightly called “men,” because they did not yet know the Savior’s power.

# Chapter V

## Verse 1

**“And they came,”** etc. (Bede.) Gerasa, a notable city of Arabia beyond the Jordan, adjoining Mount Gilead in the tribe of Manasseh and not far from the lake of Tiberias, [Col. 0197A] into which the pigs were driven headlong, signifies … up to: “And the one who was far away was brought near in the blood of Christ.”

## Verse 2

**“A man in the spirit.”** (Isidore.) This most desperate man is the people of the Gentiles, whom the Apostle enumerates: haughty, proud, unclean, bloodthirsty, idolatrous, dishonorable, etc., up to: “For when a fool is chastised, the wise man becomes wiser or more prudent.”

## Verse 3

**“And not even with chains,”** etc. (Bede.) Heavy chains and fetters signify the two laws of the Gentiles by which sins were restrained in their public life. When the chains were broken—as Luke writes—he was suddenly driven by the Lord into the desert, because, even after transgressing those laws, they were carried away by desire toward crimes that exceeded ordinary custom.

[Col. 0197B]

## Verse 7

**“That you torment me.”** (The same.) It is a great torment for him to cease from harming the human being, and he lets go all the more painfully the longer he possesses him.

## Verse 9

**“What is your name?”** (Bede.) He does not ask as though he were ignorant, but so that, once the public plague which the man had endured had been confessed, the power of the healer might appear more glorious. Even the priests of our own time who cast out demons by exorcism commonly say that sufferers cannot otherwise be cured unless, insofar as they are able to understand, they openly confess everything that they experienced from demons—through sight, hearing, or any other sense of body or mind—whether awake or asleep.

**“My name is Legion.”** (The same.) This signifies the Gentile people enslaved to innumerable forms of idolatrous worship; against whom there is … up to: “But the reprobate are confused by the separation of sects, more numerous than languages.”

[Col. 0197C]

## Verse 12

**“Send us.”** (The same.) Luke says: “And they begged him not to command them to go into the abyss” (Luke 8). Therefore they knew that at some future time, through his coming, they would be sent into the abyss; not that the future things … up to: “For unless someone has lived in the manner of a pig, the devil does not gain power over him, except perhaps for testing and not for destruction.”

## Verse 13

**“The herd was driven headlong.”** (Bede.) Because, once the Church has been glorified and the people of the Gentiles freed from the domination of demons, they perform sacrilegious rites in hidden places, etc., up to: “For two thousand pigs are drowned for the salvation of one man.”

## Verse 14

**“But those who…”** Because certain leaders of the impious, although they flee the Christian law, nevertheless proclaim its power throughout the nations in astonishment and wonder.

[Col. 0197D]

## Verse 15

**“And they see him.”** (Bede.) Luke says: “Sitting at his feet.” This signifies those who have been corrected from their sins and, with fixed attention of mind, look upon the footsteps of the Savior in order to follow them.

**“Clothed.”** With the devotion to virtues which he had lost through his deranged mind. Hence, when the prodigal son returns to his father, he is immediately clothed with the first robe and a ring: because whoever truly repents in heart can, by the grace of Christ, recover the former works of righteousness from which he had fallen, together with the ring of inviolate faith.

**“And they were afraid.”** For many, delighted by their former way of life, say that they wish to honor the Christian law but do not wish to suffer it, because they cannot fulfill it; nevertheless, they marvel at the faithful people healed from their former conduct.

[Col. 0198A]

## Verse 17

**“And they began to beg him.”** (Rabanus.) Like Peter: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man,” etc. (Luke 5). Let them not touch the ark of God, like Uzzah.

## Verse 19

**“Go to your house.”** (Bede.) Thus, after the resurrection from sins, let each person return to a good conscience and serve the Gospel for the salvation of others, so that afterward he may rest with Christ. Let him not, while hastily wishing already to be with Christ, neglect the mystery of preaching adapted to the redemption of his brethren.

[Col. 0198B]

(Jerome.) The healed man is sent to his house—that is, to the spiritual observance of the law—and he preaches, etc., up to: “For moral precepts must be observed according to the letter.”

(Bede.) Matthew says that two men were healed, while Mark and Luke speak of one, because one of them had the more distinguished name and was more famous; therefore his healing was more famous. Allegorically: the two signify the Gentiles descended from the two sons of Noah. For although Noah fathered three sons, one was taken into God’s possession, while two were devoted to idols.

## Verse 22

**“And one of the rulers,”** etc. (Jerome.) After this Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, comes, because when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel … up to: “Abraham, Moses, and Samuel intercede for the dead people, and Jesus follows their prayers.”

(Bede.) Jairus means “illuminating” or “illumined,” because he illumined the people with the words of life; and, in order to do this, he was illumined by the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0198C]

## Verse 23

**“Because my daughter…”** (Bede.) Luke says: “For he had an only daughter, about twelve years old, and she was dying” (Luke 8). The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue is the Synagogue, possessing only legal instruction, etc., up to: “Overwhelmed suddenly by the weakness of error, she abandoned the spiritual ways in despair.”

## Verse 24

**“And they pressed upon him.”** While he goes to heal the girl, he is pressed by the crowd; because, while offering the Jews counsels of salvation by which he might raise their sick conscience, he was burdened by the harmful custom of carnal peoples.

## Verse 25

**“And a woman,”** etc. As the Lord proceeds toward the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, a sick woman seizes healing after twelve years, [Col. 0198D] and afterward the daughter is healed and raised: because the salvation of the human race was so arranged that first some from Israel, then the fullness of the Gentiles, and thus all Israel would be saved.

(Bede.) It should be noted that the girl was twelve years old, while the woman had suffered a flow of blood for twelve years, etc., up to: “While Christ was beginning to heal Judea, she, already prepared for salvation and promised to others, anticipated it with certain hope.”

## Verse 26

**“Having suffered many things,”** etc. These are the false theologians, philosophers, and teachers of secular laws who promised that they would give useful precepts for living. Demons also, etc., up to: “They began both to hope for and to seek a remedy for their illness.”

[Col. 0199A]

## Verse 27

**“She came in the crowd.”** (The same.) “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John 12). And elsewhere: “You shall walk after the Lord your God” (Hos. 11). Or because she does not see God present in the flesh, but afterward comes to the grace of recognition through faith, etc., up to: “Through the sacraments of the Gospel, as though through her own garments, she cleanses the sources of her shameful blood.”

## Verse 31

**“Touched.”** (Bede.) The faithful woman alone touches the Lord, whom the crowd accompanying him presses from every side. For the one who is burdened by the various heresies of those who gather together in disorder, or by perverse conduct, is touched only by the faithful heart of the Church. Hence: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20). For to touch him truly is to believe that he is equal to the Father.

[Col. 0199B]

(Jerome.) The dead woman is raised by the seventh power, but on the way the woman suffering from hemorrhage touches the fringe from behind; when, together with salvation, she receives substance, etc., up to: “The cymbal signifies confession; the pomegranate signifies the will to martyrdom and the brightness of the virtues.”

## Verse 33

**“But the woman.”** (Bede.) Behold the purpose of the questioning: namely, that the woman should confess the truth of her long illness, her sudden faith, and her healing; thus she herself would be strengthened in faith and provide an example to others.

## Verse 35
