**“While he was still speaking,”** etc. (Bede.) As soon as the woman is healed, the girl is reported dead: because, once the Church of the Gentiles has been healed from the stain of vices and because of the merit of faith, etc., up to: “But what is impossible for human beings is possible for God.”

[Col. 0199C]

## Verse 36

**“To the ruler of the synagogue.”** The ruler of the synagogue is the assembly of teachers of the law, concerning whom it is said: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat” (Matt. 23). If they are willing to believe, the Synagogue subject to them will also be saved.

## Verse 37

**“And he allowed no one,”** etc. (Bede.) Mysteries are not to be revealed to blasphemers and mockers, but to the faithful who honor them. Hence elsewhere: “Wisdom is justified by all her children” (Matt. 11).

## Verse 38

**“Weeping and wailing.”** (The same.) “Let all who hope in the Lord rejoice, and they will exult forever, and you will dwell in them” (Ps. 5). The Synagogue lost this joy through the merit of its unbelief; and therefore it lies dead among those who weep and howl. But Jesus does not permit it to perish utterly.

[Col. 0199D]

## Verse 39

**“She is not dead.”** To me, in whose disposition her soul lives after being received, while her flesh rests in expectation of resurrection. Hence it is customary among Christians that the dead, whom we do not doubt will rise again, be called “sleeping.” Thus: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who are asleep” (1 Thess. 4).

(Bede.) Although the soul that has sinned dies, nevertheless the soul which the Lord foresees for eternal life may rightly be said by us to have been dead, but to have fallen asleep for him.

## Verse 40

**“Having put them all out.”** (The same.) The crowd is put out so that the girl may be raised: because, unless the multitude of worldly cares is expelled from the heart, the soul lying dead within is not raised. For while it scatters itself through all its thoughts, it cannot gather itself at all for consideration of itself.

[Col. 0200A]

## Verse 41

**“Talitha cumi.”** In the Syriac expression which the Evangelist gives, this means no more than: “Girl, arise.” But perhaps, to express the force of the Lord’s command, he added: “I say to you, arise,” and took care to convey the speaker’s meaning rather than his words. Thus the apostles and Evangelists often, when they take up a testimony, give the sense rather than the words.

(Jerome.) To the girl he says, “Talitha cumi,” that is, “Girl, arise.” To the ruler of the synagogue, etc., up to: “Hence it is said: ‘Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness’” (James 2).

[Col. 0200B]

(Bede.) That Christ raised three dead persons signifies three kinds of souls. He raises the girl, etc., up to: “He heard of a fourth dead person when a disciple announced it; but because there were no living people available to bury him, he said: ‘Let the dead bury their own dead’” (Matt. 8).

# Chapter VI

## Verse 2

**“From where did this man get these things?”** What remarkable blindness! They can recognize Christ in his deeds and words, but despise him solely because they know his family.

## Verse 3

**“The carpenter.”** (Bede.) He who works with fire and spirit; hence: “He himself will baptize you with fire and the Spirit” (John 1). He is the carpenter who fashioned the dawn and the sun.

[Col. 0200C]

## Verse 4

**“A prophet is not without honor.”** It is almost natural for citizens to envy their fellow citizens, because they remember not his works but the childhood which they saw.

(Isidore.) Lowly status often accompanies one’s origin. Thus: “Who is the son of Jesse?” (1 Kings 12). But: “The Lord regards the lowly, and knows the lofty from afar” (Ps. 137).

## Verse 5

**“And he could do no mighty work,”** etc. Either so that, by performing many wonders, he would not condemn his unbelieving fellow citizens even more severely; or because he was despised in his homeland, he performed few wonders and signs there, so that they might not be entirely without excuse. Every day he performs greater signs among the Gentiles, not so much in the healing of bodies as of souls.

## Verse 6

**“And he marveled.”** (Bede.) Not as though this were unexpected, but he presented it as something marvelous, because they believed neither the prophets nor the one whom they themselves saw present.

[Col. 0200D]

## Verse 7

**“And he called.”** (Jerome.) The twelve apostles are sent, and authority is given to them to teach the commandments, so that word and deed might accompany one another; and when invisible promises are joined with virtues, then, when they anoint the sick with oil, they strengthen the weakness of faith by the power of virtue.

**“And he gave them,”** etc. The gracious Lord and teacher does not begrudge his disciples and servants his power. He acts by his own power; if they accomplish anything, they do so in their own weakness, and they confess the Lord’s power, saying: “In the name of Jesus, rise and walk” (Acts 3).

## Verse 8

**“That they should take nothing,”** etc. Let their confidence in the Lord be so great that they know with certainty that nothing will be lacking, lest, while providing for temporal things, they provide less for eternal things.

[Col. 0201A]

(Bede.) Matthew and Luke record that the Lord told the disciples not even to carry a staff; Mark says that they should take nothing except a staff. They accept the staff literally. Mark understands by the staff the authority to receive necessities from those subject to them.

## Verse 9

**“Shod with sandals.”** (The same.) So that the foot would be neither covered nor bare upon the ground—that is, so that the Gospel would neither be hidden nor rely upon earthly advantages.

**“And not to put on two tunics.”** (The same.) This means that they should walk simply, not duplicitously.

## Verse 11

**“Shake the dust from your feet.”** (The same.) The dust is shaken from their feet as testimony to their labor: that they entered the city and that the preaching reached even them. Or because those who despised the Gospel accepted nothing from them for their necessary sustenance.

[Col. 0201B]

## Verse 13

**“And they anointed with oil.”** (The same.) James says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil” (James 5), etc. Hence it is clear that the apostles handed down this custom: that the possessed and other sick persons should be anointed with oil consecrated by the bishop.

## Verse 14

**“And the king heard.”** (The same.) Luke says: “Herod the tetrarch heard of all that was happening,” etc. (Luke 9). Therefore it must be understood either that, believing the words of others, he confirmed what he said, or that he was still hesitating, etc., up to: “They preferred to believe that he had not risen but had secretly been carried away.”

## Verse 17

**“Of Philip his brother.”** (Bede.) An ancient history says that Philip was the son of Herod the Great and the brother of the Herod under whom the Lord suffered; that he married Herodias, the daughter of Aretas; and that afterward, when enmity arose, Aretas took his daughter away and joined her in marriage to Herod, Philip’s enemy, to Philip’s grief. Hegesippus—or Josephus—nevertheless tells the story quite differently.

[Col. 0201C]

## Verse 18

**“It is not lawful for you to have,”** etc. (The same.) He who came in the spirit and power of Elijah rebuked Herod and Herodias, just as … up to: “For a human being is born for labor, and the saints pass through death into rest.”

## Verse 23

**“And he swore.”** (Bede.) His oath does not excuse him from perjury. Perhaps he swore for the very purpose of finding an opportunity to kill him. And if she had asked for the death of her father or mother, Herod certainly would not have granted it.

[Col. 0201D]

## Verse 26

**“And he was distressed,”** etc. (The same.) In accordance with Scripture’s customary manner of speaking, he was distressed—not in reality, but in the opinion of many. So also Joseph himself, etc., up to: “So that under the pretext of piety he might become impious.”

## Verse 27

**“His head on a platter.”** (The same.) The head of the law, which is Christ, is cut off from the body, etc., up to: “But Christ, who is the light of the world, when the days begin to grow longer.”

## Verse 29

**“And they took it away.”** (The same.) Josephus says that John, after being bound, was brought to the fortress of Machaerus and beheaded there. Ecclesiastical history says that this occurred in Sebaste, a city of Palestine formerly called Samaria.

[Col. 0202A]

In the time of Julian, etc., up to: “After cleansing the temple of Serapis from its impurities, he placed those same bones there and consecrated a basilica in honor of Saint John.”

## Verse 30

**“And gathering together.”** (Jerome.) Rivers return to the place from which they flow. They always give thanks to God for the things they have received.

**“Everything.”** The apostles did not report to the Lord only what they themselves had done and taught, but also what John had suffered while they were teaching. Or this may refer to the disciples of John or of the apostles, as Matthew writes.

## Verse 31

**“Come away privately.”** (Bede.) This does not signify merely a withdrawal for rest, but mystically signifies that, after Judea—which … up to: “He comes apart and leads those whom he chooses, so that, living among those who live badly, they may not attend to evil things,” like Lot in Sodom, Job in the land of Uz, and Obadiah in the house of Ahab.

**“Rest.”** Like birds in the branches of the mustard plant. Here there is little rest for the saints and long labor; but afterward it is said to them that they should rest from their labors.

**“For there were many,”** etc. (Jerome.) In Noah’s ark the animals that were inside were sent outside, and those that were outside burst inside. So in the Church Judas, etc., up to: “Then the wind and storm will cease, with Jesus sitting and reigning in the boat, which is the universal Church.”

[Col. 0202B]

## Verse 32

**“They went away into a deserted place.”** (Bede.) By requesting solitude, he tests whether the crowds will follow him, and he rewards those who have been tested with a worthy recompense. The crowds, neither on animals nor in vehicles but by the labor of their own feet, undertake the journey into the desert and display their desire for salvation. Again, by receiving the weary, teaching the ignorant, healing the sick, and refreshing the hungry, he reveals how much he delights in the devotion of believers.

[Col. 0202C]

## Verse 33

**“And on foot.”** Note that they did not reach another shore of the sea without crossing the Jordan by boat. Rather, after crossing some strait or lake, they went to nearby places of the same region, which the local inhabitants could also reach on foot.

## Verse 34

**“And he had compassion.”** (Bede.) Matthew explains more fully how he had compassion, in these words: “And he had compassion on them and healed their sick.” This is truly to have compassion on the poor and those without a shepherd: to open the way of truth, heal the sick, and, by refreshing the hungry, encourage them to praise the generosity from above. The following events show that he did these things.

[Col. 0202D]

## Verse 35

**“And when the hour was already late.”** As the day declined, the Savior refreshes the crowds, because either, as the end of the age approaches, or when the sun of righteousness set for us, we were freed from the long hunger of spiritual starvation.

(Bede.) Many companies of the faithful follow Christ, who seeks the deserts of the Gentiles, leaving behind the walls of their former way of life and disregarding the protection of various doctrines. When God was first known in Judea, then his glory was exalted above the heavens and over all the earth.

## Verse 37

**“Give them something.”** He urges the apostles to distribute bread, so that when they testify that they do not possess any, the greatness of the sign may become known. He also intimates that every day hungry hearts must be fed through them, when we are roused to love heavenly things by their examples or words. It should be noted that, when John was about to write of this miracle of the loaves, he first mentioned that Passover was near. Matthew and Mark say that this occurred immediately after John was killed; from this it is inferred that John was beheaded as Passover approached, and that the Lord was crucified at the following Passover.

[Col. 0203A]

## Verse 38

**“Five.”** (Bede.) The five loaves signify the five books of Mosaic law, in which are found knowledge of divine eternity, the creation of the world, the course of the present age, and the true worship of God, etc., up to: “Finally, by a great gift he grants the elect to eat and drink at his table in his kingdom.”

[Col. 0203B]

## Verse 39

**“According to companies.”** (The same.) The various arrangements of those reclining signify the distinct orders of the churches, which together make one Catholic Church.

## Verse 40

**“By hundreds and fifties.”** The fifty signifies the rest of the Jubilee. Fifty taken twice makes one hundred; therefore it signifies the perfection of both kinds of rest, namely, of body and mind. Whoever rests from evil deeds has bodily rest; whoever rests even from perverse thoughts has rest of mind.

It is rightly on green grass that those who are fed with God’s nourishment recline: those who, through devotion to abstinence and by trampling underfoot the allurements of the flesh, devote themselves to hearing and fulfilling the words of God.

[Col. 0203C]

Some are therefore in groups of fifty and others in groups of one hundred, because one first rests from evil works, so that afterward there may also be rest in the mind.

## Verse 41

**“And having taken them.”** He does not create new kinds of food because he became incarnate, nor does he preach anything other than what had been written; rather, he demonstrates that the law and the prophets are pregnant with mysteries.

**“He broke.”** He distributed them to his disciples to place before the crowds, because he disclosed the sacraments to the holy teachers who would preach them throughout the whole world.

## Verse 43

**“And they took up,”** etc. (Bede.) More advanced people diligently investigate the deeper mysteries, which the inexperienced cannot grasp. The twelve apostles are signified by the baskets; and by the apostles, the teachers who follow are represented—despised outwardly, but inwardly filled with the remnants of saving food to nourish the hearts of the humble. Servile works are performed in baskets; yet that bread of fragments filled them which chose the weak things of the world in order to break or confound them.

[Col. 0203D]

## Verse 44

**“Five thousand.”** (The same.) Because of the five bodily senses. Those who followed the Lord signify people who, while still situated in a worldly way of life, know how to use well the external possessions they have. They are rightly fed with five loaves, because such people must still be instructed in legal precepts. Those who entirely renounce the world are four thousand and are refreshed with seven loaves—that is, they are exalted by evangelical perfection and instructed inwardly by spiritual grace.

[Col. 0204A]

## Verse 45

**“And immediately he compelled.”** He gives us an example, so that in all the good things we do we may avoid the reward of human favor, lest the practice of virtue bend us toward the desire for temporal things. The Lord himself teaches us this: when those who admired his virtues wanted to make him king, he fled to the mountain to pray. He went out readily to meet those who would crucify him, so that we might be prepared to endure adversity, cautious about flatteries when they smile upon us, and, lest they deceive us by softening us when they abound, might implore the Lord with frequent prayers.

**“To Bethsaida.”** (Bede.) Bethsaida is a city in Galilee, near the lake of Gennesaret, belonging to Andrew, Peter, and Philip. But Mark says, etc., up to: “Both are cities in Galilee beside the lake of Gennesaret, which is also called Tiberias after the city of Tiberias.”

[Col. 0204B]

## Verse 46

**“He went up onto the mountain.”** (The same.) He prays well who seeks God by praying, progressing from earthly things to higher things and ascending the summit of the loftier court. He who, concerning riches, etc., up to: “He can do everything he wishes, because he is both our advocate and our judge: the one is an office of mercy, the other a mark of power.”

## Verse 47

**“And he himself was alone,”** etc. At times he appears to have entirely abandoned the Church in its dangers; hence: “Why, O Lord, do you stand far away?” (Ps. 10), etc. But although he delays help, he does not withdraw assistance.

## Verse 48

**“And about the fourth watch.”** (Bede.) Military stations and watches are divided by periods of hours. It is therefore clear that they … up to: “For Lucifer is said to illuminate three hours of the night, that is, the whole morning watch.”

**“And he intended to pass them by.”** (The same.) So that, being troubled for a while, but immediately delivered, they might marvel more greatly at their deliverance and at their rescuer, etc., up to: “When you walk through fire, you will not be burned, and the flame will not consume you.”

[Col. 0204C]

## Verse 49

**“They thought.”** (Bede.) Even now the heretics think that he was a phantom and that he did not assume true flesh from the Virgin. For Theodore, etc., up to: “And how, without feet immersed in the water, possessing bodily weight and material burden, he walked upon a fluid and unstable substance.”

## Verse 50

**“Do not be afraid.”** The first assistance is to drive away fear; the second is to restrain the storm by the power of his presence. Nor is it surprising that, when the Lord ascends into the boat, the wind ceases: for in whatever heart he is present through the grace of his love, all the battles of vices, the hostile world, and evil spirits immediately grow quiet.

[Col. 0204D]

## Verse 52

**“For they did not understand.”** (Bede.) Through the miracle of the loaves he showed that he was the Creator of all things. By walking upon the waves, he showed that his whole body was free from every burden of sin. By calming the winds and waves, he showed that he ruled the elements. But the disciples were still carnal: they were indeed astonished at the greatness of his virtues, but they did not recognize the truth of his divine majesty.

## Verse 54

**“They recognized him.”** By report, not by his face or by the greatness of the signs; he was also known to many by his appearance.

[Col. 0205A]

## Verse 56

**“The fringe of his garment.”** (Bede.) The least commandment—whoever transgresses it will be called least in the kingdom of heaven—or the assumption of flesh through which we come to the Word of God.

# Chapter VII

## Verse 1

**“And they gather together.”** (The same.) This makes clear how true is the Lord’s confession to the Father: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11). The unlearned come and bring the sick, so that they may at least touch his fringe, and therefore they suffer the salvation they desire. But the Pharisees and scribes, who ought to have been teachers of the people, come together not to hear the word and not as to a physician, but for battles of disputation.

[Col. 0205B]

## Verse 2

**“With common hands.”** (Jerome.) “Unclean,” or “common” hands signify the communion of the Gentiles. The purity of the Pharisees is sterile, while the communion of the apostles does not entirely extend its branches to the sea. **“Unwashed.”** They criticize unwashed hands of the body, although nothing unclean is found in their works. They themselves, washed outwardly with water, are inwardly polluted by the envy of their conscience.

[Col. 0205C]

## Verse 3

**“The Pharisees.”** (Bede.) The superstitious tradition of human beings required frequent washing before eating and for similar purposes. But the necessary teaching of truth commands those who desire to eat the bread of life that came down from heaven to cleanse their deeds frequently through almsgiving and other fruits of righteousness.

## Verse 4

**“Baptisms.”** They uselessly preserve the ritual washings of vessels while neglecting the filth of their hearts and bodies. For this was not said about material hands, but about the cleansing of minds, the correction of deeds, and the sanctification and salvation of souls.

## Verse 5

**“Why do your disciples,”** etc. What remarkable stupidity! They rebuke the Son of God because he does not observe human precepts. But hands—that is, works—not of the body but of the soul, must be washed, so that the Word of God may come to dwell in them.

## Verse 6

**“He prophesied well.”** (Jerome.) He restrains the barking of the Pharisees with the fork of reason, that is, with the rebuke of Moses and Isaiah, so that we too may be able to overcome heretics with the words of Scripture.

[Col. 0205D]

## Verse 9

**“You nicely nullify.”** He refutes their false accusation by true reasoning, as though he were saying: “Because of human tradition you despise and neglect God’s commandments. Why then do you rebuke my disciples, who disregard the commands of the elders in order to keep God’s commandments?”

## Verse 11

**“But you say.”** (Bede.) In consideration of the weakness arising either from the age or the poverty of parents, the Lord commanded, etc., up to: “The offering to the Lord, who is the true Father, is to be preferred.”

**“Whatever benefit you might have received from me.”** (Isidore.) What is consumed for your own uses is sacrilege. Or it may be understood interrogatively: “Will it benefit you?” He means: “It ought not.” Fearing this, fathers were afflicted by hunger.

## Verse 15

**“Nothing outside,”** etc. (Bede.) Nor is an offering to idols unclean insofar as it is food, since it is a creature of God; rather, the invocation of demons makes it unclean. Hence: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons” (1 Cor. 10).

The Jews boast that they are God’s portion and call “common foods” those which all people use, such as oysters, hares, and animals of that kind, which neither divide the hoof nor chew the cud, and which, among fish, do not have scales.

[Col. 0206A]

## Verse 18

**“And are you also without understanding?”** They are rebuked because they consider things that are obvious in themselves to be mystical. From this we learn that the hearer is defective who wants to understand obscure things plainly, or plainly stated things obscurely.

[Col. 0206B]

## Verse 19

**“And into the latrine.”** (Bede.) From this certain heretics slander the Lord, as though, ignorant of natural philosophy, he thought all foods … up to: “Through hidden passages—which the Greeks call *poroi*—it flows down to the lower parts and goes into the latrine.”

(Augustine.) Some things enter in such a way that they both change and are changed. Thus food itself, losing its form, is transformed into our body, and we, refreshed, are changed into strength.

## Verse 21

**“From the heart of human beings.”** (Bede.) The principal seat of the soul is not, according to Plato, in the brain, but, according to Christ, in the heart. They are also rebuked, etc., up to: “If he frequently sees us looking at a beautiful woman, he understands that we love her.”

## Verse 24

**“And rising from there.”** Leaving behind the scribes and Pharisees who were making accusations, he withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon in order to heal the Tyrians and Sidonians.

**“No one.”** (Bede.) Although he could not remain hidden, what he wished did not happen. But this provides an example, etc., up to: “So that he might free the daughter of the Syrophoenician woman from the demon and, through the faith of the Gentile woman, rebuke the unbelief of the scribes and Pharisees.”

[Col. 0206C]

## Verse 25

**“For a woman.”** Mark says that the Lord was in a house when the woman came to him. Matthew says that she cried out after him (Matt. 15), thereby indicating that she uttered her prayers while following him. The woman therefore came to him in the house; but because Matthew says, “He did not answer her a word,” he makes it understood that both of them were silent and entered in silence. Thus the remaining details are woven together, and they disagree in nothing.

[Col. 0206D]

(Jerome.) The woman is our mother, the Roman Church. Born as a demonic Western barbarism, through her faith she made a sheep out of a dog. She seeks crumbs of understanding and does not desire the unbroken bread of the letter.

(Bede.) The Gentile woman, coming to the Lord with faith, signifies the Church gathered from the Gentiles, which, on behalf of her daughter, etc., up to: “Who abandon the former dwelling places of their unbelief and transfer themselves, in devout dedication, into the house of God, that is, into the Church.”

### Verse 27

“Let the children first be satisfied.” As if he were saying: “It will happen that you Gentiles also will attain salvation; but first it is necessary that the Jews, who by their ancient election are called the children of God, be refreshed with the heavenly bread, and that only then the nourishment of life be supplied to the Gentiles.”

“Of the children.” (Bede.) A remarkable reversal: Israel was once the child, while we are the dogs. According to the diversity of faith, the order of the names is changed. Of them it is said: “Many dogs have surrounded me” (Psalm 21). Of us: “I have other sheep, which are not of this fold” (John 10).

### Verse 28

“From the crumbs.” “I am not worthy to receive whole foods; I am content with the leftovers of the little dogs, so that in this way I may come to the complete bread.”

(Bede.) “From the crumbs,” etc. The table means Scripture, whence: “You have prepared a table before me,” etc. (Psalm 22). “The crumbs of the children,” etc., up to the point that through the merit of humility they may raise themselves to hope for the heavenly rewards promised by the Lord.

### Verse 29

“Because of this saying.” (Bede.) Here an example is given of instructing and baptizing infants, because through the faith and confession of their parents in baptism, little children are freed from the demon, although they are not yet able by themselves either to understand or to do anything good or evil.

### Verse 31

“Tyre.” (Jerome.) Tyre, signifying distress, represents Judaea, to which the Lord says: “The bed is too narrow, and the short covering cannot cover both,” so that it may transfer itself to other nations (Isaiah 18).

“Sidon.” (Jerome.) Sidon means “hunting”; it is the wild, untamed creature—our region or nation.

“Decapolis.” (Bede.) The region of the ten cities beyond the Jordan toward the east. When it is said, “He came to the Sea of Galilee, between the borders of Decapolis,” this does not mean that he entered Decapolis itself. For it is not said that he crossed the sea by boat, but that he came as far as the sea and reached a place that looked toward the borders of Decapolis, situated far beyond the sea.

(Jerome.) The Savior is led by the apostles to save the nations, and he teaches what he answered the young man who questioned him: “You know the commandments; do this and you will live” (Luke 18).

### Verse 32

“A deaf man and one who could not speak.” (Bede.) That is, one who opens neither his ears to hear the words of God nor his mouth to speak. Such people must be brought to the Lord for healing by those who have learned through long practice both to hear and to speak the word of God, so that the right hand of grace may save those whom human weakness cannot.

(Jerome.) The human race, like one man consumed by various diseases in the first-created man, is blinded while seeing, becomes deaf while hearing, has his nose cleared while smelling, grows mute while speaking, becomes maimed while raising its hands, is bent over while being raised up, becomes dropsical while desiring, is lame while advancing, is covered with leprosy while being cleansed, is filled with a demon while seeking divinity, and dies by death while boldly making excuses.

“And they begged him.” The prophets and patriarchs longed for the Lord’s incarnation.

### Verse 33

“And taking him aside,” etc. The one who deserves to be healed is led away from turbulent thoughts, disordered actions, and confused speech. The fingers placed in his ears signify the words of the Holy Spirit, concerning whom it is said: “This is the finger of God” (Exodus 8); and: “The heavens are the work of your fingers” (Psalm 8).

“He touched his tongue,” etc. The spittle from the Lord’s flesh signifies divine wisdom, which dissolves the ignorance of the human race, so that it may say: “I believe in God the Father almighty,” etc.

“Taking him aside.” (Bede.) The first path of salvation is to be led out from the crowd. The Lord leads the sick man out from the crowd when he removes the mind from sins, etc., up to the point that, spitting upon the tongue of the mute so that he may be able to speak, he touches it when by the contact of his mercy he shapes lips that have long been brutish for bringing forth the words of wisdom.

### Verse 34

“And looking up,” etc. (Jerome.) “He groaned.” He taught us to groan and to raise the treasure of our heart toward heaven; through compunction of heart it is cleansed from the frivolous joy of the flesh, as it is said: “I roared because of the groaning of my heart; Lord, all my desire is before you,” etc.

“And he said to him: ‘Ephphatha,’ which means ‘Be opened.’” “With the heart one believes unto righteousness” (Romans 10), etc.

“And immediately his ears were opened,” etc. The ears are opened to hymns, songs, and psalms. The tongue is released so that it may pour forth a good word, which neither threats nor words can restrain or prevent. Hence Paul says: “I am bound, but the word of God is not bound in me” (2 Timothy 2).

### Verse 36

“And he commanded them to tell no one.” He taught that one must not glory in miracles, but in the cross and in humiliation. “The more he commanded them,” etc. A city set on a mountain, visible from every side, cannot be hidden (Matthew 15); humility always precedes glory.

“Be opened.” This properly refers to the ears. The ears had to be opened for hearing, while the tongue had to be released so that it could speak. Hence what follows: “Immediately his ears were opened,” etc.

### Verse 35

“And he spoke correctly.” (Bede.) He alone speaks correctly—whether confessing the Lord or preaching to others—whose hearing divine grace restores so that he may listen to and obey the heavenly commandments. The Lord, by the touch of wisdom, which he himself is, instructs his tongue to speak. Such a person can say: “Lord, open my lips” (Psalm 5), etc.

### Verse 36

“The more he commanded them,” etc. He who knows all things before they happen knew that they would preach all the more. By commanding the sluggish, he wished to show how much more diligently and frequently—or more fervently—they ought to preach, since those who were forbidden to speak could not keep silent.

## Chapter VIII

### Verse 2

“I have compassion on the crowd.” Because he is truly human, he shows mercy and compassion with the feeling of human weakness. That he fed four thousand people with seven loaves and a few small fish is an act of divine power, directed against the error of Eutyches.

“They have been with me for three days.” Why they remained for three days Matthew says as follows (Matthew 15): “And going up onto the mountain, he sat there, and they came to him,” etc. The crowd remains with the Lord for three days because of the healing of its sick, when all the elect, enlightened for the Lord by faith in the Holy Trinity, earnestly implore him for their own sins and those of their people—that is, for the illnesses of the sinful soul.

The great crowd remains with the Lord for three days when the multitude of the faithful, turning away from its sins through repentance, turns to the Lord in deed, speech, and thought.

(Bede.) This miracle signifies that we cannot pass safely through the way of the present age unless Christ refreshes us with the nourishment of his word. This, figuratively, etc., up to the point that he refreshes with the bread of heaven the soul drawn away from lowly pleasures and kindles it toward a desire for heavenly sweetness by giving it the pledge of spiritual food.

### Verse 3

“If I send them away.” Because converted sinners fail along the road of the present life if they are sent away in their conscience without the nourishment of instruction.

“From far away.” Morally speaking: whoever, having experienced nothing of carnal corruption, hastens to serve God does not come from far away. Whoever has been stained by no impurity or crime, but has experienced only marriage, likewise does not come from far away. Others come after many crimes, and therefore come from far away.

### Verse 5

“Seven.” (Bede.) This is the mystery of the New Testament, in which the grace of the sevenfold Spirit is believed and given more fully. Nor are the loaves barley loaves, as were the five by which five thousand people were fed, lest, as in the Law, the nourishment of the living soul should be concealed beneath bodily sacraments. For the marrow of barley is covered by a very tenacious husk.

(Jerome.) The seven loaves are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. The four thousand signify the year of the New Testament with its four seasons. The seven baskets signify the seven early churches. The fragments of the loaves are the mystical understanding of the first week. The blessed little fish are the books of the New Testament: just as the risen one asks for a portion of roasted fish, and presents a fish placed upon the coals to the disciples in the catch of fish.

### Verse 6

“Upon the ground.” (Bede.) At the feeding with the five loaves, the crowd reclined upon the grass; but those who were to be refreshed with the seven loaves were commanded to recline upon the ground, because through the law of the flesh, etc., up to the point that here, with every carnal desire removed, the guests of the New Testament are held by the firmness of enduring hope, like the solidity of the mountain itself, with no grass interposed.

### Verse 7

“Little fish.” (Bede.) The saints of that age, through whom the same Scripture was composed—or whose faith, life, and sufferings Scripture itself contains. Rescued from the waves of the world and consecrated by divine blessing, they offered us refreshment through the example of their life and death, so that we might not fail in the course of this world.

### Verse 8

“They ate.” (Bede.) There are many who, although they cannot leave all they possess or accomplish the higher things of this world, are nevertheless filled when they hunger and thirst for righteousness, since by hearing the commandments of God they attain eternal life.

“What remained.” (Bede.) The higher commandments, exhortations, and counsels, which the general multitude of the faithful cannot attain, such as: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have” (Matthew 19), etc.

“Seven baskets.” The seven baskets are filled with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. Baskets are made from rushes and palm leaves. The rush grows upon the waters; the palm crowns the victor. Likewise, the saints, lest they dry up from the moisture of eternity, place themselves at the very fountain of life and await the palm of eternal reward.

### Verse 10

“And immediately.” In Matthew we have this instead: “He got into the boat and came to the region of Magadan.” But there is no doubt that the same place is meant by both names. For many manuscripts also have “Magadan” in Mark.

### Verse 11

“Seeking,” etc. As though the things they had seen had not been signs. But what they were seeking is determined by the phrase “from heaven”: either fire from above in the manner of Elijah, or thunder roaring in summer, or lightning or rain in the likeness of Samuel—as though those who slandered what they had seen with their eyes, touched with their hands, and experienced through its benefit could not also slander these things.

Or they sought signs from heaven such as manna, so that the one who had fed many thousands with a few loaves might now, like Moses, refresh the whole people everywhere with manna sent from heaven. Hence John says that after the distribution of the loaves the crowds asked: “What work will you do? Our fathers ate manna in the desert” (John 6), etc.

### Verse 12

“If a sign will be given.” (Augustine.) Concerning the harmony of the Evangelists: he says that in Mark it is written, “No sign will be given to it.”

(Bede.) “To this generation”—that is, to those who tempt God and contradict his words—no sign from heaven will be given. Those who tempt him, etc., up to the point that, through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he poured out the grace of the Holy Spirit from heaven upon many believers.

### Verse 13

“He went up into the boat.” (Bede.) After the seven baskets had just been filled, they immediately got into the boat and came to the region of Magadan. While they were sailing there, they were told to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. But Scripture says that they forgot to take bread, thereby showing that, being attentive to the Lord’s presence, they had little concern for the flesh.

### Verse 17

“What are you thinking about?” (Bede.) Taking the opportunity, he teaches what the five loaves, the seven loaves, the few little fish, and the five or four thousand people signify. If the leaven of the Pharisees and the traditions of Herod signify perverse and heretical doctrines, why should the foods by which the people of God were nourished not signify true and complete doctrine?

### Verse 23

“And spitting,” etc. (Bede.) Spittle proceeds from within, from the Lord’s head; the hands, however, are bodily members placed on the outside. Therefore, spitting into the blind man’s eyes, he lays his hands upon him so that he may see, because he removed the blindness of the human race both through the invisible gifts of divine mercy and through the outward signs of the humanity he assumed.

He could have healed him completely and all at once with a single word, but he heals him gradually, in order to show the magnitude of human blindness, which scarcely and as if by degrees returns to the light, and to indicate his grace, by which he assists each successive increase toward perfection.

### Verse 24

“I see people,” etc. (Jerome.) He considers everyone superior to himself, judging himself not a man but a dead dog and a single flea. At first, however, etc., up to the point that by the second laying on of his hands the Lord restored to this man the light by which he could see everything clearly—namely, what must be believed, how one must live, and what rewards must be hoped for.

### Verse 25

“Then again,” etc. (Jerome.) So that he might see everything clearly—that is, understand invisible things through visible works, and contemplate with the clear eye of a purified heart the condition of his soul, which the rust of sin had obscured. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5).

### Verse 26

“And he sent him away.” (Jerome.) So that he might see in himself what he had not previously seen. A despairing person does not think that he can accomplish at all, through hope, what he can do after being enlightened.

Mystically: the Lord admonishes all who are illumined by the knowledge of truth to return to their heart, carefully consider how much has been given to them, and respond to God’s benefits with actions worthy of them.

“Tell no one.” (Bede.) His command to keep the healing silent is an example for his followers, so that if they perform marvelous works they may not seek human favor, but be content to please the divine sight.

### Verse 27

“Who do people say that I am?” He beautifully asks first for the opinion of the people, so that their confession may not appear to have been weakened by popular opinion rather than strengthened by recognition of the truth, and so that they may not seem, like Herod, to have hesitated over what they had heard. Hence, according to Matthew, he says to Peter: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you” (Matthew 16)—that is, human teaching.

“People.” Those who give differing opinions about the Lord according to human custom are appropriately called people. But those who recognize the truth of his power with devout minds deserve to be called not people but gods. Hence he says to them: “But you,” etc. As if he were saying: “They are people, thinking human thoughts; but you are gods—who do you say that I am?”

### Verse 29

“You are the Christ.” (Bede.) He embraces everything who expresses both the nature and the name, in whom is the fullness of virtues. Paul says, etc., up to the point that nevertheless no one may be ignorant of the faith concerning his generation.

### Verse 30

“And he charged them.” (Bede.) He did not wish himself to be preached before his passion and resurrection, because, once the sacrament of his blood had been completed, he more suitably said to the apostles: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 18). It would not have been beneficial for him to be publicly preached when they were going to see him scourged and crucified and suffering many things.

### Verse 31

“For it is necessary,” etc. (Jerome.) Just as a skilled helmsman anticipates a storm during calm weather and wants his sailors to be ready, so he prepares his own. As elsewhere: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matthew 16), etc.

### Verse 32

“And taking him aside.” (Bede.) He spoke with the affection of one who loves: “Far be it from you, Lord.” Or, as it is better expressed in Greek: “Be propitious,” etc., up to the point that he took him aside in affection, or led him away privately so that he would not appear to rebuke the Master in the presence of the others.

### Verse 33

“Get behind me.” (Bede.) Many think that it was not Peter but the adversarial spirit who was rebuked, since the Apostle spoke this at its prompting. But Peter’s error, arising from affectionate devotion, will never seem to me an incitement of the devil. “Get behind me” is said to the devil: “Get behind me, Satan.” To Peter: “Get behind me,” etc.—that is, “Follow my judgment.”

“The things that are God’s,” etc. My will and the Father’s is that I die for the salvation of human beings. You do not want the grain of wheat to fall into the ground so that it may bear much fruit.

### Verse 34

“If anyone wishes,” etc. (Bede.) After revealing the mystery of his passion and resurrection, he exhorts everyone to imitate the example of his passion and promises salvation to all souls. But to the more perfect he disclosed how much he would suffer and that he would rise from the dead, providing a model for preaching, so that each person might be instructed according to his capacity and higher matters might not be entrusted to the weak.

“Let him deny himself.” He cannot grasp what lies beyond him if he does not know how to slay what he is. Unless a person fails with respect to himself, he does not draw near to God, who is above him.

“Let him take up his cross.” Either by disciplining the body through abstinence or the soul through compassion. Paul speaks of the body: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” (2 Corinthians 9), etc. He speaks likewise of compassion of soul: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Corinthians 11.)

### Verse 38

“For whoever,” etc. (Bede.) The Church signifies two periods: one of persecution, when the soul must be laid down; the other of peace, when earthly desires must be broken.

“For whoever is ashamed of me,” etc. Many overcome greed and despise passing things, but, hindered by shame, do not express aloud the uprightness of the faith they possess. He adds: “For whoever is ashamed of me,” etc.

### Verse 39

“Amen, I say.” (Bede.) Since he was speaking about the life to come, it was necessary that he make this promise concerning the life of penitence, so that the disciples, still inexperienced, might be strengthened by this consolation. Thus it is said of the Jewish people: “He gave them the lands of the nations, and they possessed the labors of the peoples, so that they might keep his justifications and seek his law” (Psalm 104).

“The kingdom of God,” etc. That is, the Church raised up against the glory of this world; or the future blessedness in heaven, which they saw on the mountain. This was done by a gracious providence, so that eternal joy, although tasted for a brief moment, might inspire them more strongly to endure adversity.

## Chapter IX

### Verse 1

“And after six days,” etc. (Jerome.) After the threat of the cross, the glory of the resurrection is shown; hence what follows:

“And after six days,” etc. This was so that those who had seen with their own eyes the glory of the future resurrection would not fear the reproaches of the cross.

(Bede.) “And after six days.” Luke says: “It happened about eight days after these words,” etc., up to the point that we may not be punished by the angry Judge in the eighth age, the time of retribution.

“On a high mountain.” On the mountain, in order to pray, etc., up to the point that then they will deserve to rejoice in his eternal vision.

“He was transfigured.” He did not lose the true substance of his flesh, but showed the glory of his future resurrection—or of our resurrection. After judgment he will appear in this form to all the elect. At the judgment he will appear in the form of a servant to both good and evil, so that the impious, who despised him; the Jews, who denied him; the soldiers, who crucified him; and Pilate and Herod, who judged him, will be unable to recognize the Judge.

### Verse 2

“And his garments.” The Lord’s garments signify the saints. Hence: “All you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3). These garments appeared despised while the Lord remained in the world, but when he went up the mountain they shone with new brightness. For now we are indeed children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3). Hence it is added:

### Verse 3

“And there appeared,” etc. Moses, the holy man who had died, and Elijah, who had been taken alive into heaven, were seen in majesty with the Lord—as Luke says—and signify the future glory in him of all the saints, who at the time of judgment will either be found alive in the flesh or will be dead.

“Elijah with him.” (Bede.) The Lawgiver and the eminent prophet appear; they speak with the Lord living in the flesh, showing that he is the one whom the Law and the prophets promised. They are not in lowly places but on the mountain with him, because those who pass beyond earthly desires in mind perceive the majesty of Holy Scripture, which has been fulfilled in the Lord.

### Verse 4

“Rabbi.” Although he was astonished, etc., up to the point that they had one tabernacle—that is, the Church of God.

“It is good.” It is therefore much better to take part in the choirs of the saints and enjoy the vision of the Godhead, if the transfigured humanity of Christ and the companionship of the two, displayed for a moment, are so delightful.

### Verse 6

“A cloud overshadowing them.” Since he had sought a material tabernacle, he received the shade of a cloud, so that he might learn that in the resurrection the saints would be protected not by the covering of houses but by the Holy Spirit.

“This is he.” As if he were saying: “This truly is the one whom this Moses promised to you,” etc., up to the point that it itself will be illumined by grace and protected forever.

### Verse 7

“And immediately.” (Bede.) When the voice was spoken over the Son of Man, he was found alone. For when he reveals himself to the elect, God will be all in all; indeed, Christ himself, together with his own, will be one in every respect: the head will shine together with the body. Hence: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3).

### Verse 8

“He commanded them.” He does not wish the glory of the future kingdom and triumph that he had shown on the mountain to be preached publicly, lest, because of its greatness, it seem incredible, and lest the cross that followed such glory should cause scandal in inexperienced minds.

### Verse 9

“They kept the word.” (Jerome.) That is, when death has been swallowed up in victory, former things will no longer be remembered, when the Lord has removed the filth of the daughter of Zion and taken every tear from the eyes of the saints.

### Verse 10

“What then?” The scribes teach, according to Malachi, that Elijah will come before the Savior’s advent, turn the hearts of the fathers to their children, and restore everything to its ancient state. The disciples therefore think that the glory of this coming is what they had seen on the mountain, and they say: “If you have already come in glory, why does your forerunner not appear?”—especially since they see that Elijah has departed.

### Verse 11

“He will restore,” etc. That is, he will turn the heart of the fathers to the children and the heart of the children to the fathers. For he will restore to death what death is owed and what he took away through long living. Hence he adds: “How is it written?” As if he were saying: “Just as the prophets wrote in many ways about Christ’s passion, so Elijah too will suffer many things.”

“He will restore everything.” First, he will restore the hearts of the people of that time to believe in Christ and resist Antichrist. Then he will lay down his life for Christ.

### Verse 13

“A great crowd.” (Jerome.) There is no rest under the sun. Envy is always killing the little ones; lightning strikes the great mountains. Some come to the Church learning with faith, others envying with pride.

“They were questioning.” (Bede.) The Evangelist does not say what they were questioning, but it may be understood that the question concerned why the disciples could not free the demoniac who was among them. This may be inferred from what follows.

### Verse 15

“And he asked.” (Bede.) Note that places correspond to events. On the mountain he prays, is transformed, and opens to the disciples the secrets of his majesty; below, he is received by the crowd and assailed by the weeping of the miserable. Above, he discloses the mysteries of the kingdom to the disciples; below, he reproaches the crowds for the sins of unbelief. Above, he reveals the Father’s voice to those able to hear; below, he drives out evil spirits. Now, according to the quality of their merits, he does not cease either to make some ascend or to descend to others.

“And he asked.” (Jerome.) He knows and asks so that confession may produce salvation and the murmuring of our heart may first be dissolved through words, as it is written: “Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified.”

### Verse 17

“And I said to your disciples.” He subtly shifts the blame onto the disciples, since healing is often hindered not by the fault of those who heal but by that of those who are to be healed.

### Verse 18

“O generation.” He is not angry with the person but with the vice. He does not say this out of weariness with human feeling, but like a physician addressing a sick person who acts against his instructions. Through one man he reproves the Jews for their unbelief.

### Verse 19

“Immediately the spirit,” etc. When we wish to turn to the Lord after sin, we are attacked more fiercely by the devil, so that he may either shake off our virtue or avenge his expulsion.

### Verse 20

“From childhood.” (Jerome.) This signifies the Gentile people, into whom the worship of idols grew from birth, so that they foolishly sacrificed their children to demons. Hence what follows:

### Verse 21

“And often,” etc. Some worshiped fire, others water.

“Help.” (Jerome.) Our faith is weak, like a faltering tongue, unless it rests upon God’s help. Faith with tears obtains the desired petitions, as it is written: “Let it be done for you according to your faith” (Matthew 9).

### Verse 25

“Tearing him,” etc. (Jerome.) The devil tears apart those who approach salvation, for they are his beloved food. He desires to drag them into his belly through terrors and losses, as with Job: “He was made,” etc. (Isidore, Rabanus), etc.

For those who have been healed it is said: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3). Hence the weakness of Christians is not death but the likeness of death.

### Verse 28

“This kind,” etc. (Jerome.) Foolishness belongs to the luxury of the flesh and is healed by fasting. Anger and laziness are driven away by prayer. The medicine appropriate to each wound must be applied to it. What heals the eye does not heal the heel; the passions of the body are healed by fasting, and the diseases of the mind by prayer.

### Verse 30

“They will kill him,” etc. He mingles sorrow with favorable things, so that when they come they may not be borne by minds unprepared. If it saddens them that he will be killed, it should gladden them that he will rise on the third day.

### Verse 31

“They did not understand.” This was not so much because of slowness of intellect as because of love. Since they had recognized the true God, they could not believe that he would die. And because he had been accustomed to speak to them in figures, they thought, horrified by his death, that he was speaking figuratively in this matter also.

### Verse 32

“Capernaum.” (Jerome.) “Village of consolation”: it agrees with the preceding statement, “Killed, he will rise on the third day” (John 12). The grain of wheat dies so that it may be gathered in greater abundance; if it does not die, it remains alone.

“What were you discussing on the road?” On the road they were discussing primacy; the place corresponds to the subject. For primacy enters through force, is abandoned in the same way, and slips away while it is being held. It is uncertain in which dwelling—that is, on which day—it will end. Hence he says: “Whoever wishes to be first,” etc.

### Verse 33

“They disputed among themselves.” (Bede.) This dispute appears to have arisen because they had seen Peter, James, and John led apart onto the mountain and believed that some secret had been entrusted to them there. They had also heard that the keys of the kingdom of heaven had been promised to Peter, as Matthew says, and that the Church would be built upon the rock of faith from which he himself had received his name. They therefore thought either that those three were preferred to the others or that Peter was preferred to them all.

### Verse 34

“And sitting down,” etc. They were discussing primacy as they went, while he teaches humility as he sits. Leaders labor; the humble rest. He wishes to heal the desire for glory through humility, and first admonishes them with a simple command, then with the example of a child’s innocence.

### Verse 35

“Embracing him.” He signifies that the humble are worthy of his embrace and may rightly glory and say: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song of Songs 2).

### Verse 36

“Whoever receives one.” Either, in a simple sense, he shows that Christ’s poor are to be received by those who wish to be greater, for Christ’s honor. Or he urges them to become little in malice, so that they may be simple like children.

“And whoever,” etc. Because he taught that he was received in children, as the head in the members, lest he be thought to be only what he appeared to be, he added: “And whoever receives me,” etc.

### Verse 37

“He answered him.” Since he had said: “Whoever receives one of these children receives me,” John understands that those who do not walk sincerely do not receive them in his name. Hence he says: “Teacher, we saw someone,” as if he were saying: “This person ought not to be received in your name.”

“And we forbade him.” He thought that one who does not perform the office should be excluded from its benefit, but he is taught that no one should be kept away from the good that he possesses in part; rather, he should be encouraged toward what he lacks. Hence: “Do not forbid him.”

### Verse 38

“Do not forbid him.” (Bede.) Hence the Apostle says: “Whether in pretense or in truth Christ is proclaimed,” etc., up to the point that we ought to detest and forbid them.

### Verse 41

“And whoever causes scandal,” etc. Although this is a general statement, it can nevertheless be directed, according to the sequence of the discourse, against the apostles, who were disputing about primacy and could destroy by their example those whom they were calling to the faith.

(Bede.) Note that in our good work we must sometimes guard against giving scandal to our neighbor, and sometimes regard it as nothing. Insofar as we can do so without sin, we ought to avoid scandalizing our neighbors. But if scandal arises on account of truth, it is better to allow it to arise than to abandon the truth.

“A millstone turned by a donkey.” (Jerome.) According to the custom of the province, etc., up to the point that even if the punishment of hell tormented him, it would nevertheless be more tolerable.

### Verse 42

“And if he causes scandal.” Because he had taught above that we must not scandalize those who believe in him, he now teaches how carefully we must avoid those who cause scandal.

Σκάνδαλον (*skándalon*) in Greek means “an offense,” “a ruin,” or “a striking of the foot.” Others translate it as “a scruple.” Therefore the person who gives his brother an occasion of falling by word or deed causes scandal.

“Your hand.” A friend, whose help and counsel we need every day. But if this person wishes to harm us in a matter concerning the soul, he must be excluded from our fellowship, lest, if we wish to share in this life with one who is lost, we perish together with him.

“Than the two hands.” (Jerome.) The two hands signify primacy, humility and pride. Cut off pride; retain humble authority.

### Verse 43

“Where the worm is.” (Bede.) The stench of worms comes from the corruption of flesh and blood. For this reason fresh meat is preserved with salt, so that when its bloody moisture has been dried out, worms cannot exist. Flesh and blood therefore produce worms, because carnal pleasure, when not resisted by the seasoning of self-restraint, generates eternal punishment for the lustful. We must therefore chastise the body with the salt of continence and the mind with the seasoning of wisdom, cleansing them from the stain of error and vices.

### Verse 48

“For everyone will be salted with fire.” Since he mentioned fire and the worm for a third time, he shows how we can avoid both. “Everyone with fire”: this is wonderfully said. What is salted with salt keeps away the corruption of worms. But what is salted with fire—that is, placed in fire—also consumes the flesh when salt has been sprinkled upon it.

These things were done according to the Law in the sacrifices burned upon the altar, where it was commanded that salt be offered with every victim and sacrifice: “Every victim shall be salted with salt.”

For he is truly the Lord’s victim who offers body and soul, etc., up to the point that he must renounce those who are beloved and close to us.

“Every victim shall be salted with salt.” (Jerome.) The victim is the human race, which here is salted with the salt of wisdom or reason, while the corruption of blood, the preservation from decay, and the mother of worms are consumed here and will afterward be examined through purgatorial fire.

### Verse 49

“But if the salt,” etc. That is, if someone who has once been refreshed with the seasonings of truth returns to apostasy, by what other teacher can he be corrected, when he rejects the wisdom he has tasted, whether frightened by adversity or enticed by prosperity? Hence: “Who will heal the enchanter bitten by the serpent?” (Ecclesiasticus 12.)

In this passage Judas and his companions are believed to be signified: corrupted by the love of money, he did not hesitate both to lose the apostleship and to betray the Lord.

But because there are many whom greater knowledge lifts up and separates from the fellowship of others, and the more they know, the more they lose their good sense regarding the virtue of concord, he adds: “Have salt in yourselves and peace.”

(Bede.) To have salt without peace is not a gift of virtue but an indication of condemnation. For the better someone understands, the worse he sins.

## Chapter X

### Verse 1

“And rising from there.” Up to this point he has recounted what he did and taught in Galilee; from here he narrates what he did, taught, and suffered in Judaea. First, what he did beyond the Jordan toward the east; then what he did on this side of the Jordan, when he came to Jericho, Bethany, and Jerusalem.

Although the entire province of the Jews is generally called Judaea in distinction from other nations, more particularly the southern region is called Judaea in distinction from Galilee, Decapolis, and the other regions within the same province.

### Verse 2

“The Pharisees were questioning him.” There is a great difference between the crowds and the Pharisees. The crowds come together to be taught and for the sick to be healed, as Matthew clearly says; the Pharisees come in order to deceive him by testing him. Devotion to piety brings the former; the goad of envy brings the latter.

“Is it lawful for a man?” (Bede.) He tested him with a horned syllogism, etc., up to the point that it was granted on account of the necessity of sinners.

### Verse 5

“Because of the hardness of your heart.” (Bede.) Is God then opposed to himself? etc., up to the point that the marital bond may persist through hatred and murder.

### Verse 8

“And the two will become one flesh,” etc. The reward of marriage is that two become one flesh. Chastity joined to the spirit becomes one spirit.

### Verse 9

“What God has joined, let no one separate.” This refers to the desire for a second wife. God, who joins them, separates them when, by mutual consent and for the service of God—because the time is short—they have wives as though they had none.

### Verse 10

“And in the house,” etc. (Jerome.) The disciples did not question him first, etc., up to the point that bread strengthens the heart of man, as it is written: “If anyone wishes to come after me” (Luke 9), etc.

### Verse 11

“Whoever divorces,” etc. (Bede.) Matthew gives the fuller wording: “Whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, and marries another commits adultery” (Matthew 5). Therefore there is only one carnal cause: fornication; and one spiritual cause for sending away a wife: fear of God, as many are recorded to have done for the sake of religion. But no cause is prescribed by God’s law for marrying another while the wife who has been dismissed is alive.

### Verse 13

“But the disciples rebuked those bringing them.” Not because they did not want them to be blessed by the Savior’s hand and voice, but because, not yet having full faith, they thought that he would become weary, as human beings do, from the persistence of those bringing them.

### Verse 14

“For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.” He significantly says “such as these,” not “these.” As if he were saying: It is character, not age, that reigns. The kingdom of heaven is promised to those who possess a similar simplicity and innocence, to whom the saying addressed to the apostles applies: “Do not become children in your understanding, but be children in malice” (1 Corinthians 14).

### VERSE 15

“Whoever does not receive the kingdom.” Whoever does not persist in anger, does not remember an injury, does not lust when he sees a beautiful woman, and does not have one thing on his lips and another in his heart. It is as though he said: “If you are not such as these, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

“The kingdom of God”—that is, we are commanded to receive the teaching of the Gospel as little children: just as a child does not contradict his teachers, does not formulate arguments against them, but faithfully accepts what he is taught, obeys with fear, and remains quiet, so we too must receive the Lord’s words with simple obedience and without any contradiction.

### VERSE 17

“A certain man, running up and kneeling.” (Bede.) I believe that this man had heard from the Lord that only those who wished to be like little children were worthy of entering the heavenly kingdom. Therefore he desired to become more certain—not through parables, but openly—by what merits of works he might attain eternal life.

### VERSE 18

“Why do you call me”—(the same author)—because he had called him good as a teacher, etc., up to the point where he testifies that no one is good apart from God.

### VERSE 19

“Do not commit adultery.” (The same author.) This is the chastity of childish innocence, which is set before us for imitation if we wish to enter the kingdom of God. It should certainly be noted that the righteousness of the Law, when kept in its proper time, bestowed not only temporal goods but also eternal life.

### VERSE 20

“Teacher.” (The same author.) He should not be thought to have spoken from the intention of one who was testing him, etc., up to the point where he adds: “Go, sell whatever you have and give to the poor” (Matthew 5), etc.

### VERSE 21

“And come, follow me.” (The same author.) It is as though he said: “After despising riches, imitate the Savior”—that is, “Having abandoned evil things, do good.” A sack is more easily despised than desire or pleasure.

### VERSE 23

“How difficult it is.” (The same author.) Those who devote themselves to multiplying riches, etc., up to the point where they can enter the kingdom of God.

### VERSE 25

“It is easier for a camel.” How, then, did Matthew and Zacchaeus, Joseph, and very many rich men in the Old Testament enter? Perhaps because they regarded riches as nothing, or learned to despise them completely. Hence David says: “I am solitary and poor” (Psalm 24). And again: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” (ibid., 61). He does not say, “Do not receive them.”

### VERSE 26

“And who can?” Since there are more poor people than rich, they would not have said this unless they understood among the number of the rich all those who desired to acquire riches.

### VERSE 27

“With God.” He can turn a person from the desire for earthly things to the love of eternal things, and make the proud humble.

### VERSE 28

“Behold, we have left everything.” Great confidence: he was a fisherman, not a rich man; he sought his livelihood by his hands and by his trade, and yet he confidently says: “Behold, we have left everything.”

“And we have followed you.” Because it is not enough simply to leave things, he adds what is perfect: “and we have followed you.” It is as though he said: “We have done what you commanded; what reward, then, will you give?”

### VERSE 30

“A hundredfold.” (Bede.) On this occasion some establish the Jewish fable of a thousand years after the resurrection of the righteous, etc., up to the point where they enjoy the heavenly homeland, signified by the right hand, in the truest love of all the elect together.

### VERSE 31

“But many.” Because many begin but do not complete what they have begun, a terrifying sentence follows: “But many,” etc. The thief on the cross, a confessor, rejoices with Christ in paradise on the very day on which he was crucified for his sins by the grace of faith. Every day also we see many laypeople excel others in the merits of their life, while others, fervent in spiritual devotion from their earliest age, become sluggish in the end through idleness.

### VERSE 32

“And they were astonished.” This was because they remembered that he had foretold that he would suffer many things at the hands of the chief priests and scribes, and would be killed. They therefore feared either that they themselves would be killed with him, or that he—whose life and teaching they enjoyed—would be killed.

“And taking them aside.” (Bede.) Foreseeing that the minds of the disciples would be disturbed by his Passion, etc., up to the point where he approaches the place of death as one who is fearless.

### VERSE 35

“And they come.” Having heard of the resurrection, and forgetting the second coming, they think that he will reign in the human manner. Matthew says that their mother made the request, but Mark says that they themselves did so, wishing to disclose that their desire was the reason their mother asked.

### VERSE 38

“Or with the baptism.” The same as “the cup.” Hence elsewhere, concerning his Passion, he says: “I have a baptism with which I must be baptized, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished.”

### VERSE 39

“We are indeed able to drink the cup.” (Bede.) James was beheaded by Herod; John was thrown into a cauldron of boiling oil. From there Christ’s athlete proceeded to the crown of martyrdom and was immediately exiled to Patmos. Thus he did not lack the spirit of martyrdom, and he drank the cup of confession which the three youths drank in the furnace, although the persecutor did not shed his blood.

### VERSE 40

“But to sit.” It is as though he said: “Do you wish me to grant this to you?” But the kingdom of heaven does not belong to the one who gives, but to the one who receives. For “there is no partiality with God” (Acts 10); whoever is worthy will receive what has been prepared not for a person but for a life. “For you”—that is, for you who are still proud. It is as though he said: “If you wish to receive it, do not remain what you are. It has been prepared for others; become other than you are, and it will be prepared for you. First humble yourselves, since you already wish to be exalted.”

### VERSE 41

“And when the ten heard it, they began to be indignant.” They were indignant not at the mother but at the sons, who, ignorant of their own measure, were inflamed by immoderate desire.

### VERSE 42

“But Jesus, calling them.” The humble, pious, and gentle teacher neither rebukes the two for their immoderate ambition nor reproves the ten for indignation and envy. Rather, he teaches that the greater is the one who has become lesser, and the master is the one who is a servant. Therefore it is futile either for the former to sigh for higher positions or for the latter to grieve over their desire, since it is not power but humility that leads to the summit of the virtues.

Finally, he sets before them his own example, so that if they disregarded his words, they might at least blush at his deeds. “For the Son of Man also,” etc.

### VERSE 46

“And they come to Jericho.” (Jerome.) Jericho means “moon” or “anathema,” which is appropriate to the approaching Passion. The decline of Christ’s flesh is the preparation of the heavenly Jerusalem. Therefore, leaving Jericho, they approach Jerusalem—that is, the vision of peace.

“And as he was leaving it.” (Bede.) Because, as the Lord ascended into heaven and the faithful followed him, etc., up to the point where he scattered them throughout the world for the illumination of all peoples.

“Bartimaeus, a blind man.” (Jerome.) The blindness of the Jews, which will be illuminated at the end, at the coming of Elijah and Enoch.

### VERSE 47

“When he heard.” The people of the Gentiles, having heard the fame of Christ and seeking to become participants in him, were opposed by many—first by the Jews, and later also by the Gentiles—so that the world, which was to be illuminated and healed, might not invoke Christ. Nevertheless, the fury of those who opposed them could not prevent those predestined to eternal life.

“Son of David.” (Jerome.) Through the merits of the patriarchs the Jewish people are illuminated. To them the merciful and compassionate God is present, illuminating the blind and raising up those who are crushed.

### VERSE 48

“But he cried out all the more.” As the battle against vices grows heavier, hands must be raised with a cry to the stone of help—that is, to Jesus.

(Jerome.) The order of salvation is appropriate, etc., up to the point where he considers the apostles in the heights.

### VERSE 49

“And they call the blind man.” (Bede.) Allegorically, the Lord calls the blind man who is crying out when, through holy preachers, he entrusts the word of faith to the people of the Gentiles who desire knowledge of the truth. Those who call the blind man command him to be more courageous and to rise and come to him, when by preaching they order him to have hope of salvation, to rise from the sluggishness of vices, and to gird himself for the pursuit of the virtues by which he may deserve to be illuminated. It is as though they said: “Come to him and be enlightened” (Psalm 33); and, “Rise, you who sleep” (Ephesians 5), etc.

### VERSE 50

“And he, throwing off his garment.” That is, having cast aside worldly cares, he hastens to the giver of light with an unencumbered step of mind.

“Leaping up.” He rewards a ready will by granting its desire. Hence: “Whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you will receive it.”

### VERSE 51

“Rabboni, that I may see.” He does not seek gold, but light. A blind man may possess riches, but he does not see what he possesses. Following his example, let us not seek false riches, but the light which we can see with the angels alone, and toward which faith is the way. Hence it is said to the blind man who has been enlightened: “Go; your faith has saved you.”

### VERSE 52

“He saw and followed him.” (Bede.) He sees and follows who does what he rightly understands. To follow means to imitate. Hence: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John 12).

“In the way.” Let us consider by what way he walks, and follow through humility and labors—the way that says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). This is the narrow way that leads to difficult heights, from Jerusalem and Bethany to the Mount of Olives, which is the mountain of light and consolation.

## CHAPTER XI

### VERSE 1

“To Bethany.” (Bede.) Bethany is a village or town on the side of the Mount of Olives, etc., up to the point where there are two on account of knowledge of the truth and purity of works.

“Two of the disciples.” (Jerome.) They are called in pairs and sent in pairs, etc., up to the point where they may know the Lord between the two cherubim, singing psalms in spirit and mind.

### VERSE 2

“And immediately.” (Bede.) As preachers entered the world, they found the people of the nations, etc., up to the point where whoever is pure and holy belongs to God alone.

### VERSE 4

“A colt tied.” (Jerome.) The tied and untamed colt, which they loose and tame, is the people of the Gentiles. Before the door of faith, it stands at a crossroads in the bonds of its sins; in the freedom of its will it hesitates between death and life.

### VERSE 6

“And they let them go.” (Bede.) Those who objected to its being loosed, etc., up to the point where they cover it with fitting garments, so that it may be made worthy with Christ seated upon it.

### VERSE 7

“And he sat upon it.” (Jerome.) He began to reign, so that sin might not reign in mortal or wanton flesh, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.

### VERSE 8

“But many spread their garments.” Because many martyrs, stripping themselves of the clothing of their own flesh, prepare the way with their blood for the simple, so that they may walk unhindered toward the heavenly city to which Jesus leads.

(Jerome.) “Many,” etc. The feet are the last members, which the Apostle appointed for joining together; although they are not the back on which the Lord sat, they are nevertheless instructed by John along with the soldiers.

“But others.” (The same author.) “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree”: narrow at the roots, broad in flowers and fruits, because they are the good fragrance of Christ and spread along the way of God’s commandments through their good reputation.

(Bede.) Others cut branches or leaves from the trees; these extract from the books of the Fathers, in the teaching of truth, the words and sentences of the Fathers, and humbly submit them along the way of God to the mind of the hearer who is coming.

### VERSE 9

“And those who went before.” The Jewish people went before; the Gentiles followed. And because all who are faithful, or have been faithful, believed and believe in Christ, both those who go before and those who follow cry out “Hosanna,” which is rendered in Latin as “Save us.” For all the earlier generations also sought salvation from him.

### VERSE 10

“Blessed is he who comes.” Because there is one faith and one hope for all. They expected him and believed that he would come; we believe that he has come.

(Bede.) By the addition “Hosanna in the highest,” which means “salvation,” it signifies that the coming of Christ is not the salvation of human beings alone, but of the whole world, joining earthly things to heavenly things, so that every knee may bow to him—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Philippians 2).

(Jerome.) This agrees with Gabriel, who says: “He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High,” etc., up to the point where it is accomplished through the very word of supplication.

### VERSE 11

“And he entered.” (The same author.) With the Passion already approaching, he wished to be in the place appointed for the Passion before the ages, etc., up to the point where he had already begun the sacrament of the blessed sacrifice.

“Into the temple.” He gave us an example, so that wherever we might come, we should first turn aside to the house of prayer, if one is there. After commending ourselves to God through devotion to prayer, we should withdraw to carry out the tasks for which we came.

“And having looked around,” etc. He did not do this only once, but throughout all five days. By day he taught in the temple; at night he went out and remained on the Mount of Olives, as Luke says. By teaching he diligently performed the duty of correction toward unbelievers; by remaining among the faithful he graciously displayed the favor of his kindness.

“And when he had seen it.” (Bede.) Just as he speaks through parables, so he acts, etc., up to the point where, performing miracles, he found none; therefore he condemned it.

### VERSE 14

“Let no one ever eat fruit from you again.” (The same author.) You too, if you do not wish to hear Christ say at the judgment, “Depart from me, you wicked, into the eternal fire, because I was hungry and you did not give me anything to eat” (Matthew 25), beware of being a barren tree. Rather, offer to poor and hungry Christ the fruit of compassion that he needs.

### VERSE 15

“He began to drive out.” In the deed itself he showed what he had represented figuratively in the fig tree. The fig tree did not sin by having no fruit before its season; the priests did.

“Those who were selling.” (Bede.) Namely, the things that those who came from far away bought from the local inhabitants in order to offer them, etc., up to the point where they are always deprived of the priesthood.

### VERSE 16
