“And he would not permit.” He gives beforehand an example of the future judgment, when he will drive all the rejected from the Church and restrain them by eternal punishment, so that they may not enter again to disturb it.

“But you have made it.” They were in the temple for this purpose: either to persecute those who did not give bodily offerings, or spiritually to kill those who did give. The temple and house of God are the mind and conscience of the faithful. When they inflict injury upon their neighbor, they produce perverse thoughts, as though robbers were sitting in a cave and killing those who walk innocently. Thus the mind is no longer the house of God but a den of robbers.

### VERSE 20

“Dried up from the roots.” (Bede.) The fig tree was dried up from its roots to show that the impious nation was not to be chastised temporarily or in part by external attacks and released through repentance, as had often happened, but was to be struck with complete and eternal condemnation. Alternatively: it was dried up from its roots to show that it was to be deprived utterly not only of human support from outside but also of divine favor within; for it lost life in heaven and its homeland on earth.

### VERSE 21

“Peter remembered.” Peter recognizes the dried fig tree and the severed root, in whose place succeeds the most beautiful, fruitful olive tree called by the Lord. Hence what follows: “Amen, I say to you,” etc.

### VERSE 23

“Whoever says.” (Bede.) Some are accustomed to say that our people did not yet possess full faith, etc., up to the point where he laments that he has been expelled far from the injury of the pious.

(Jerome.) But this happened when the apostles said: “We are rightly transferred to the Gentiles, because you judge yourselves unworthy” (Matthew 21).

(Bede.) The distinction among those who pray must be noted, etc., up to the point where they nevertheless first forgive those who sin against them.

### VERSE 25

“And whenever you stand.” (Jerome.) Mark, according to his custom, has comprehended the seven verses of the Lord’s Prayer in a single prayer. For what more will the one from whom everything has been forgiven ask, except that he may persevere in what he has obtained?

### VERSE 28

“By what authority.” They doubt the authority of God and wish it to be understood that what he does belongs to the devil.

### VERSE 29

“I will ask you.” He could have refuted the slander of the tempters by an open answer, but he wisely asks them a question, so that they may be condemned either by their silence or by their judgment.

### VERSE 31

“If we say.” (Jerome.) They are darkened by the lamp of the world, of which he says: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ; I will clothe his enemies with confusion” (Psalm 131).

“Why then,” etc. It is as though he said: “The one whom you confess to have received prophecy from heaven bore witness to me, and from him you heard by what authority I do these things.”

### VERSE 32

“If we say.” Whichever of these they answer, they see themselves about to fall into a snare. They fear stoning, but still more they fear confessing the truth.

### VERSE 33

“Neither do I tell you.” (Bede.) For two reasons the knowledge of the truth is concealed from those who seek it: either the one who seeks understands too little, or, because of hatred or contempt for the truth, is unworthy that it should be revealed to him.

For the first reason it is said: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.” For the second: “Do not give what is holy to dogs.”

## CHAPTER XII

### VERSE 1

“A pit, or a winepress, or an altar,” or those winepresses whose titles appear at the head of certain psalms.

“He went away to a distant country.” He grants freedom of choice in action—not by a change of place, since God is everywhere and fills all things.

### VERSE 6

“Because they will reverence him.” He did not say this through ignorance, since he knows all things, but God is always said to deliberate so that free will may be preserved for human beings.

(Bede.) We ask Arius and Eunomius: Behold, the Father is said not to know, and he moderates his judgment; and, insofar as it depends on us, he is said to have lied. Whatever they answer on behalf of the Father, let them understand that the same applies to the Son, who says that he does not know the day of the consummation.

### VERSE 7

“But the tenants.” (The same author.) He proves that the leaders of the Jews did not crucify Christ through ignorance, etc., up to the point where they strove to prefer their own righteousness, which comes from the Law.

### VERSE 8

“And they threw him out.” He indicates their obstinacy: even after the Lord had been crucified and raised, they did not wish to believe the preaching of the apostles, but threw him out like a worthless corpse. For, insofar as it depended on them, they excluded him from their own borders and handed him over to the Gentiles to receive.

(Bede.) To any one of the faithful, the mystery of baptism, etc., up to the point where he will rejoice in crucifying the Lord and making a spectacle of him.

### VERSE 10

“The stone which the builders rejected.” (Jerome.) The rejected stone, borne by the corner, joining the Lamb with the bread at the supper, bringing the Old Testament to an end and beginning the New—this is the one who performs wonders in our eyes.

### VERSE 13

“And they send to him.” (Bede.) They feared the crowd and, what they could not do by themselves, etc., up to the point where they preferred to lose both the kingdom and everything else rather than be tributaries.

### VERSE 14

“Teacher, we know.” This flattering and deceitful question provokes the one answering to fear God more than Caesar and to say that taxes ought not to be paid, so that the Herodians who heard him might seize him as the instigator of rebellion against the Romans.

### VERSE 15

“But knowing their craftiness.” Those who think that the Savior’s question expresses ignorance rather than a dispensation should learn from this passage that he could have known whose image it was. But he asks in order to answer their words appropriately.

“A denarius.” The denarius is a kind of coin counted as ten nummi, and it bears the image of Caesar.

### VERSE 17

“Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s.” He himself did this by paying the tax for himself and for Peter.

“And to God the things that are God’s.” He also did this by fulfilling the Father’s will.

Alternatively: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s”—the impression of his own image; “and to God the things that are God’s”—the soul illumined by the light of his countenance. Hence: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us” (Psalm 4), etc.

### VERSE 18

“The Sadducees,” etc. There were two sects among the Jews, the Pharisees and the Sadducees. The Pharisees preferred the righteousness of traditions and observances, which they call *δευτερώσεις* (*deuterōseis*, “second traditions”); hence they are also called “separated” from the people. But the Sadducees—that is, “the righteous”—denied the resurrection of both body and soul.

“The Sadducees,” etc. (Bede.) Those who deny the resurrection of bodies, or do not believe it, judging that souls perish together with bodies, rightly invent such a fable, one that exposes the madness of those who assert the resurrection of bodies. Yet it could also have happened at some time among their people.

### VERSE 20

“Now there were seven,” etc. (The same author.) They oppose the indecency of the story in order to deny the resurrection. Mystically, however, the seven brothers who died without children correspond to all the rejected: throughout their entire life—which revolves in seven days—they are sterile in good works. As each dies, worldly existence itself ultimately dies, that is, passes away, like an unfruitful wife whom they took without the fruit of good works.

Jerome: The barren woman, leaving no seed from the seven brothers, etc., up to the point where it is said that the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.

### VERSE 25

“They neither marry nor are given in marriage,” etc. (Bede.) Latin usage does not correspond to the Greek idiom. Properly speaking, women are said to marry (*nubere*), while men take wives (*ducere*). But let us understand the statement simply: men will neither marry nor will women be given in marriage.

### VERSE 26

“I am the God,” etc. (Bede.) Although he could have brought forward many clearer testimonies concerning the resurrection, etc., up to the point where they did either good or evil with their souls.

### VERSE 28

“He questioned him.” (Jerome.) What does this question mean, since all those learned in the Law know this? Yet the commandments are arranged differently in Exodus, Leviticus, and Deuteronomy. For by these two rich breasts raised over the bride’s chest our infancy is nourished.

“The first of all,” etc. The greatest thing, which before everything else we ought to establish in the heart as the sole foundation of piety, is the knowledge and confession of the divine unity together with the performance of the divine work, which is completed in love of God and neighbor. This is the faith that works through love.

### VERSE 32

“Well said, Teacher.” (Bede.) The scribe shows by this answer that among the scribes and Pharisees a serious question had long been debated, etc., up to the point where no one without faith and love—which this scribe declares to have been his position—can be saved.

### VERSE 34

“You are not far from the kingdom of God,” etc. (Isidore.) Although he came to test him, ignorance is farther away than knowledge, as it is said to the Sadducees: “You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God” (Matthew 22).

(Bede.) Matthew says that he asked in order to test him, etc., up to the saying: “One who believes too quickly is light of heart and will be diminished” (Ecclesiasticus 19).

“And no one.” Because they were refuted in their arguments, they no longer questioned him; instead, they openly seized him and handed him over to Roman authority. Hence it is clear that the poisons of envy can be overcome, but that envy itself is difficult to quiet.

### VERSE 36

“Sit at my right hand.” For by this he shows the weakness of the Son, but also that one works in the other. The Son subjects enemies to the Father and glorifies God the Father on earth.

### VERSE 38

“Beware.” (Bede.) Note that he does not forbid those who belong to this office, etc., up to the point where we are either deceived by hypocrisy or inflamed by rivalry toward the same thing.

### VERSE 40

“Who devour widows’ houses.” As though they were going to be patrons at the judgment, they do not hesitate to accept money from the weak and from those troubled by the consciousness of their sins, although the hand extended to give, not gathered to receive, commends prayer to God. To such people the saying applies: “Let his prayer become sin.”

### VERSE 41

“The treasury.” (Bede.) *Phylattein* (φυλάττειν) is Greek for “to preserve” in Latin. *Gaza* is Persian for “riches”; *gazophylacium* is the place where riches are preserved, and the chest in which the people’s offerings were gathered for the uses of the temple. Hence in the Book of Kings: “Jehoiada the high priest took one treasury, and opened an opening above it” (4 Kings 12), etc.; and also the porticoes in which they were kept. Hence: “Jesus spoke these words in the treasury, teaching in the temple.”

“And he watched how.” Just as he said that those seeking primacy and empty glory should be avoided, and foretold a longer judgment for those who pray hypocritically, so he also discriminates among those who make offerings by a just examination, so that he may repay each according to heart and works. He does the same today in the Church.

“The rich.” (Bede.) The rich are the Jews, lifted up by the righteousness of the Law, etc., up to the point where they surpass all the works of the proud Jews.

### VERSE 42

“A poor widow.” (Jerome.) This poor woman represents me and those like me, who put in what I can and desire to explain to you what I cannot. God considers not how much, but from how much one desires to give. Anyone can offer a *quadrans*. This is the bread-cake in Leviticus, which signifies a ready will. A *quadrans*, because it consists of three things: thought, word, and deed.

“A quadrans.” Calculators call a quarter of anything a *quadrans*, whether of a place, a period of time, or money. Perhaps, therefore, here it signifies a quarter of a shekel, that is, five obols.

### VERSE 44

“For they all.” (Bede.) The Jew gives from his abundance as a gift, etc., up to the saying: “My God, his mercy will go before me” (Psalm 58).

## CHAPTER XIII

### VERSE 1

“And as he was going out.” (Bede.) When the Lord withdrew from the temple, etc., up to the point where it was destined to suffer punishment and the buildings destined to fall.

“Do you see these things?” It was divinely arranged that, when the grace of evangelical faith had been revealed throughout the world, the temple itself, together with its ceremonies, would be removed. Otherwise, someone still small and nursing in the faith might see those things—which had been proclaimed by the prophets and instituted by the Lord—continuing to exist, and, admiring that holy worldly order, gradually relapse into Judaism. Therefore the shadow is removed, and the truth, proclaimed throughout the world, holds the victory.

(Jerome.) He foretells the disaster of the final age, that is, the destruction of the temple together with its people and its letter. Concerning this it is said: “Not one stone will be left upon another” (Luke 21)—that is, the testimonies of the prophets will remain upon those to whom the Jews applied them, such as Ezra, Zerubbabel, and the Maccabees.

### VERSE 3

“And when,” etc. (Bede.) He remains quietly among the holy while he detests the madness of the proud. For the Mount of Olives signifies the fruitful height of the Church: that mountain produces not unfruitful trees but olive groves, by which light is nourished, rest is granted to the weary, and weakness is relieved.

### VERSE 5

“And he answered.” (The same author.) From the time of the Lord’s Passion, among the Jewish people who chose a seditious robber and rejected Christ the Savior, neither the wars of enemies nor the uprisings of citizens ceased. But the apostles are warned not to be frightened when these things approach and not to abandon Jerusalem and Judea, because the end will not come immediately. For the desolation of the province and the final destruction of the city and temple were delayed until the fortieth year.

### VERSE 6

“For many will come.” As the destruction approached, many came pretending that they were Christs and that the time of liberty had already arrived. Many also, in the Church during the time of the apostles, threatened among other things that the day of the Lord was imminent. Many came in the name of Christ who were antichrists, the first of whom was Simon Magus. All in Samaria, from the least to the greatest, listened to him, saying: “This is the power of God which is called Great,” because for a long time he had driven them mad by magical arts.

### VERSE 8

“For nation will rise.” (Bede.) All these things occur before the final and most bitter pains, etc., up to the point where those who fight against one another bring about the victory of the Church.

### VERSE 9

“But watch yourselves.” (Bede.) He explains why all these things will happen when he says, “Watch,” etc. For the greatest—or even the sole—cause of the destruction is that, after the Lord’s death, they also persecuted with impious cruelty the preachers and confessors of his name and faith.

### VERSE 10

“And among all the nations.” (The same author.) Because the Lord knew that the hearts of the disciples would be saddened by the destruction of their nation, he consoles them in this way, so that they may know that, after the Jews had been lost, they would have companions in the heavenly kingdom from the whole world. As ecclesiastical histories testify, long before the destruction of Judea all the apostles were scattered throughout the entire world to preach the Gospel, except James son of Zebedee and James the brother of the Lord, who had earlier shed their blood in Judea for the word of the Gospel.

### VERSE 14

“But when you see the abomination,” etc. (The same author.) The abomination may be understood as either the Antichrist or the image of Caesar which Pilate placed in the temple, etc., up to the point where it always obeyed the authority of the Romans.

### VERSE 17

“But woe to those who are pregnant,” etc. Because, burdened either by the weight of the womb or by the load of their children, they will not be able to flee. Hence it is read in the Book of Histories that Jonathan’s wife, disturbed in flight, received her son after he had fallen from her lap, permanently lame.

### VERSE 21

“And then, if anyone.” (Bede.) Some refer this to the Jewish captivity, when many who claimed to be Christs led the deceived people after them. But at that time there was no faithful person whom God would exhort not to follow perverse teachers. All—both besiegers and besieged—were alienated from Christ and hardened. It is therefore better understood of heretics, who come against the Church and falsely claim to be Christs. Their first was Simon Magus; the last will be the Antichrist.

### VERSE 24

“But in those days,” etc. (The same author.) The stars will appear dark at the judgment, etc., up to the point where what the same prophet says elsewhere will occur: “The light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, like the light of seven days” (Isaiah 30).

### VERSE 25

“Falling.” They will fall from the light when the seed of Abraham, to which the stars have been compared, will nearly have disappeared.

“And the powers that are,” etc. (Bede.) What wonder if human beings tremble, when the angelic powers tremble at the sight of the judgment? Hence Job: “The pillars of heaven tremble and are terrified at his command” (Job 26). And what does the little branch of the desert suffer when the cedar of paradise is shaken?

“They will be moved.” (Jerome.) They will be moved to the anger of vengeance when they are sent by the Son of Man, coming in the clouds of heaven with power—the power which earlier descended like rain upon a fleece in humility.

### VERSE 27

“From the four winds.” From east and west, south and north—and not only from these, but from the summit of the earth to the summit of heaven; that is, from the farthest boundaries of the earth in a straight line to its ultimate limits, where, for those looking from afar, the circle of heaven appears to rest upon the earth.

### VERSE 28

“But from the fig tree.” It is as though he said: Just as, when the tender shoots are on the fig tree and the bud breaks into blossom, you understand the coming of summer, spring, and the west wind, so, when you see these things that have been written, do not think that the end of the world has already arrived. Rather, understand that they are coming as forerunners, showing that it is near.

(Bede.) The fig tree is the Synagogue, which, because it had no fruit of righteousness when the Lord came to it, etc., up to the point of the summer of true light and peace.

(Jerome.) The parable of the fig tree is a prophecy. The leaves that have appeared are present words; summer is the approaching day of judgment, in which each tree will reveal what it has held within: whether it is dry and destined to be burned, or green and destined to be planted in Eden with the tree of life, whose leaves are for the healing of the nations—that is, the words with which it will be said: “Come, blessed of my Father,” etc.

### VERSE 31

“Heaven and earth will pass away.” The aerial heaven—from which come the birds of heaven and the clouds of heaven—concerning which Peter says: “The heavens that now are and the earth have been stored up by the same word, reserved for fire” (2 Peter 3). He clearly teaches that the heavens that will perish by fire are different from those destroyed by water—that is, the empty and cloudy heavens. For the water of the Flood, which rose only fifteen cubits above the mountaintops, did not reach beyond the boundaries of the air and ether.

Ecclesiastes (chapter 1): “One generation passes away, and another generation comes; but the earth remains forever.” Thus heaven and earth pass away according to their appearance, but remain forever according to their essence.

### VERSE 32

“Neither the Son.” For in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. They are hidden because it is not useful for us to know them. Hence he says: “It is not yours to know the times or moments which the Father has set in his own authority” (Acts 1). By this he shows that he knows, but that it is not useful for the apostles to know, so that, always uncertain about the coming of the Judge, they may live each day as though they were to be judged on the next. The Son therefore knows for himself, but not for us, so that we may always be watchful. Hence: “See, watch,” etc.

(Hilary.) The Son and the Holy Spirit, because they are not from themselves, do not know that day from themselves. But the Father, because he is from himself, knows it from himself.

### VERSE 34

“And to the doorkeeper,” etc. (Jerome.) To the one who preaches. To him it is said: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezekiel 3).

“Therefore watch.” Having given the example of the master of the household, he explains why he conceals the day of the consummation, saying: “Therefore watch.” One who sleeps does not see bodies but fantasies; when he awakens, he has nothing of what he saw. Such are those whom love of the world carries away in this life and abandons after this life.

### VERSE 36

“But what I say to you.” We are commanded not only as leaders of the Church but all of us to watch, guarding the doors of our hearts, lest the evil suggestion of the ancient enemy enter, and lest the Lord find us sleeping. Hence Paul says: “Watch, righteous ones, and do not sin.”

## CHAPTER XIV

### VERSE 1

“Now it was Passover.” (Jerome.) Passover is interpreted as “passing over,” while *phase* means “sacrifice,” etc., up to the point where we eat armed with virtue, saying: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (Matthew 26).

(Bede.) Passover, which in Hebrew is *phase*, comes from “passing over,” not from “suffering,” etc., up to the point where it admonishes us to undertake the path of the virtues.

“And the chief priests were seeking.” (Jerome.) Iniquity proceeded from the leaders, who ought to have prepared the temple and the vessels and purified themselves according to the Law for eating the lamb.

### VERSE 2

“Not on the feast day.” (The same author.) They avoid the feast day, which suits them: there is no festivity for those who have lost life and mercy.

### VERSE 3

“And when he was in Bethany.” (The same author.) The young deer always returns to its bed—that is, the Son, obedient to the Father unto death. He asks obedience from us. For Simon means “obedient.”

“Of Simon the leper.” Simon the leper signifies the unbelieving world at first, and afterward the faithful world.

“And as he reclined, she came,” etc. While he himself reclined—that is, humbled himself—the faith of the sinful woman came to touch him. It rose from the feet to the head and descended from the head through faith—that is, from Christ to his members.

“The woman.” (Bede.) Mary Magdalene, sister of Lazarus whom the Lord raised, etc., up to the point where, as Matthew and Mark testify, she anointed him with holy oil.

“An alabaster jar.” Alabaster is white marble marked with various spots; it preserves uncorrupted perfumes.

“Spikenard.” *Pistica nard* is so called because it was mixed—not composed only from the root, but also from the spikes and leaves—and was therefore more precious.

And when it was broken. (JEROME.) The house filled with the fragrance is heaven and earth. The broken alabaster is carnal desire, which is broken at the head, from which the whole body is joined together. (BEDE.) Mary’s devotion signifies the faith and piety of the Church, etc., up to the point where she venerates him with pious preaching and devoted service.

**VERSE 4.—** Now some were indignant. (ID.) By synecdoche he used the plural for the singular, etc., up to the point where he took care to disclose Judas’s habit of stealing for this reason. Why this waste? (JEROME.) The one lost from salvation found perdition, so that in the fruitful fig tree he might encounter the snare of death.

**VERSE 5.—** For this ointment could have been sold. (ID.) Under the pretext of greed he speaks the mystery of faith, etc., up to the point where “we may divide the spoils at evening.”

**VERSE 6.—** She has done a good work. (ID.) Whoever believes in God, it is reckoned to him as a work of righteousness. For it is one thing to believe him and another to believe in him—that is, to commit oneself wholly to him.

**VERSE 7.—** But me you will not always have. (BEDE.) Joined to you by bodily presence and familiarity, as now. Hence the Apostle says: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer” (II Cor. V). Spiritually, however, he is always with us; hence: “Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the consummation of the age.” (JEROME.) It is to be understood thus: “You will not always have me in bodily presence,” as previously, in companionship and familiarity.

**VERSE 8.—** What she had. What you think to be the waste of the ointment is an act of burial. Nor is it surprising that she gave me the good fragrance of faith, since I am about to pour out my blood for her.

**VERSE 9.—** Amen I say to you. (BEDE.) Observe in Christ knowledge of future things: after a few days he foreknew that the Gospel would be preached throughout the whole world. It should be noted that, just as Mary, throughout the whole world over which the Church is spread, deserved glory for the pious service that she devotedly rendered to the Lord, so Judas, who reviled her, is everywhere widely disgraced by the mark of his treachery. But the Lord rewards the good with pious praise and leaves unmentioned the future insults of the impious.

**VERSE 10.—** One of the twelve. (JEROME.) One in number, not in merit; in name, not in divinity; in body, not in spirit. Hence the Bridegroom says to the bride: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, with one of your eyes and with one hair of your neck” (Song IV). The eye and the hair are wisdom and virtue, since he says to Judas along with the others: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God” (Matt. XIII), and: “I have given you authority” (Luke X), etc.

He went to, etc. He went to the rulers; and after he had gone out, Satan entered into him. Here night announces knowledge to night. Each creature is joined to its like (Matt. XXVIII). Mary runs to the apostles, so that day may pour forth the word to day; Judas runs to the Jews, so that night may announce knowledge to night.

**VERSE 11.—** And he sought how he might betray him, etc. (JEROME.) He promises to hand him over, as his master had earlier said: “I will give you authority over all this.” BEDE. Many today abhor Judas’s crime, yet do not guard against it, etc., up to the point where, after removing witnesses, they exchange truth for falsehood and virtue for crime.

**VERSE 12.—** And on the first day of Unleavened Bread. (ID.) On the fourteenth day of the moon, when, after the leaven had been removed, the lamb was killed toward evening, etc., up to the point where he consecrated the beginning of the sacrifice itself, that is, of his passion.

(ISIDORE.) The unleavened bread, which is our redemption, is eaten with bitterness. For bitterness is the Lord’s passion.

**VERSE 13.—** Go into the city. (BEDE.) This is an indication of the foreknowledge of his divinity, etc., up to the point where the baptism of the life-giving fountain is consecrated for taking away the crimes of the world. (JEROME.) The city is the Church, enclosed by the wall of faith. The man who meets them is the primitive people; the jar of water is the law of the letter. A man [carrying] a flask of water. (BEDE.) The bearers of the water and the master of the house are deliberately left unnamed, so that it may be signified that all who wish to celebrate the true Passover—that is, to be imbued with the sacraments of Christ and to receive him as a guest in the dwelling of their minds—are to be given the opportunity.

Follow him. (JEROME.) He leads upward, where Christ’s refreshment is found. Hence Rahab commands the spies to go not through the low places but by the heights.

**VERSE 15.—** A large upper room. (ID.) The great Church, which proclaims the Lord’s name, spread with the variety of virtues and tongues. Hence: “Clothed round about with variety” (Ps. XLIV), that is, with virtues. In it the Passover is prepared for the Lord. The master of the house is the apostle Peter, to whom the Lord entrusted his house, so that there might be one faith under one shepherd. (BEDE.) The upper room is the spiritual law, which, emerging from the narrowness of the letter, receives the Savior in a lofty place, etc., up to the point where it recognizes that all the mysteries of Passover and the other decrees of the law are his sacraments.

**VERSE 17.—** Now when evening came. (JEROME.) The evening of the day signifies the evening of the world. For the last come around the eleventh hour; they are the first to receive the denarius of eternal life. Before the cross Abraham was in the underworld, and after the cross the thief was in paradise.

**VERSE 18.—** Amen I say, etc. Just as he had foretold his passion, so he foretells the betrayer, giving him an opportunity for repentance, so that when he understood that his thoughts were foreknown by God, he might repent of his deed. Yet he does not identify him by name, lest, openly rebuked, he become more shameless. He casts the crime into the number, so that the guilty man might repent. One of you. While falsehood is rebuked, truth is confirmed and fulfilled: “The one who ate my bread has magnified his treachery against me” (Ps. XL). All are touched so that harmony may arise on the lyre. All the strings, properly stretched, answer with a harmonious voice: “Surely it is not I, Lord?” One, lax and swayed by love of money, said: “Surely it is not I, Rabbi?”

**VERSE 19.—** To be sorrowful. Like the eleven, because they had conceived no evil against the Lord; but they trusted the teacher more than themselves and, fearing their own frailty, sorrowfully asked about their sin, of which they had no consciousness.

**VERSE 20.—** One of the twelve. (JEROME.) The wolf separates the sheep it desires. The sheep that leaves the fold lies exposed to the wolf’s bites. The one who dips his hand. (BEDE.) The Lord’s remarkable patience. First he said: “One of you will betray me”; the betrayer persists in evil. He accuses him more openly, etc., and yet does not identify him personally. Judas, while the others were sorrowful and withdrawing their hands from the food, with the recklessness and shamelessness with which he betrays the Lord, also dips his hand with the master into the dish, so that audacity might counterfeit a good conscience.

**VERSE 21.—** But woe. (ID.) Eternal woe to that person who approaches the Lord’s table unworthily, etc., up to the point where punishment is announced, so that the one whom shame does not restrain may be corrected by fear.

**VERSE 22.—** While they were eating. (ID.) After the old Passover, which was celebrated in memory of the deliverance of God’s people from Egypt, had ended, etc., up to the point where, therefore, he was to be raised from death more swiftly. He took. (JEROME.) Signifying his body in the bread, etc., up to the point where the enemies are extinguished, which are the mysteries of the Church of Christ. (BEDE.) The bread that strengthens the human heart, etc., up to the point where we might otherwise be saved without his passion.

**VERSE 23.—** He gave thanks. He gave thanks and blessed, already near to his passion, the one who accepts the punishment of another’s wickedness, though he had done nothing deserving punishment, to show how calmly each person ought to endure the scourges of his own guilt.

They had drunk. (JEROME.) A blessed drunkenness, a saving satiety, etc., up to the point where the blood of the New Testament, which is poured out for many, does not cleanse everyone.

**VERSE 25.—** I will no longer drink. (ID.) Here he changes the sacrifice but does not change the time, so that we should never celebrate Jesus’ supper before the fourteenth day of the moon. Whoever celebrates the resurrection on the fourteenth celebrates the Lord’s supper on the eleventh—something never found either in the New or in the Old Testament. The fruit of the vine. (BEDE.) The vine or vineyard of the Lord is the Synagogue, etc., up to the point where I may be filled with new joy with you over the salvation of that same people, regenerated through baptism.

**VERSE 26.—** And after singing a hymn. (ID.) The hymn may be understood as the one he sang in thanksgiving to the Father according to John, etc., up to the point where the gifts of the Holy Spirit, with which we are anointed in the heart, ought to rise up. To the Mount of Olives. (JEROME.) Jesus is seized on the Mount of Olives, and from there he ascends into heaven, so that we may know that from the place where we keep watch, pray, and are bound, without resisting, on earth, we shall ascend into heaven.

You will all be scandalized. (BEDE.) He foretells what they will suffer, so that when they have suffered it they may not despair but repent.

**VERSE 27.—** On this night. Those who are drunk are drunk at night (I Thess. V), and those who are scandalized are scandalized at night—that is, with their minds darkened. (JEROME.) All fall, but not all remain lying. “Because he sleeps, will he not continue so as to rise again?” (Zech. XIII.) To fall is carnal; to lie prostrate is diabolical. “I will strike the shepherd. Strike the shepherd.” The prophet asks for the Lord’s passion; the Father answers: “I will strike the shepherd.” Through the prayers of the saints the Son is sent by the Father—that is, he is incarnated, struck, and suffers—and the sheep are scattered when the shepherd is seized. Resurrection is promised so that hope may not be extinguished.

**VERSE 29.—** But Peter. (ID.) A bird without wings strives to fly upward, but the body weighs down the soul, so that, through fear of human death, fear of the Lord is overcome.

**VERSE 30.—** Before the cock crows twice. (BEDE.) Others understand it simply: “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times,” etc., up to the point where this is like the saying: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her” (Matt. V). (JEROME.) The cock crows; Peter denies three times, etc., up to the point where he washed away the filth of his threefold denial with tears.

**VERSE 32.—** Gethsemane. (ID.) That is, the valley of the fat ones, where fat bulls surrounded him and many calves encircled him. Sit here. (ISIDORE.) Those who are separated in prayer are separated in the passion, because he prays while they sleep, weighed down by the fatness of their hearts. Until I pray. (BEDE.) When the Lord prays on the mountain, etc., up to: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death.” And: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (Phil. II; John XV).

**VERSE 33.—** And he began to fear. (JEROME.) We are taught to be troubled and sorrowful before the judgment of death, since of ourselves we cannot say anything except through him: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV).

**VERSE 34.—** My soul is sorrowful, etc. (BEDE.) He is not sorrowful because of death, etc., up to the point where they are roused from the sleep of unbelief and the torpor of the mind.

**VERSE 35.—** And he prayed. (ID.) This voice is the sound of our weakness, etc., up to the point where, since it cannot happen otherwise: “Not what I will, but what you will.”

(JEROME.) This is directed against the Eutychians, who say that Christ has only one operation and one will. Here, however, he displays the human will, which through the weakness of the flesh rejects the passion, and the divine will, which is ready to accomplish the dispensation.

**VERSE 36.—** But not what. (JEROME.) To the very end he does not cease to teach us to obey our fathers and to place their will before our own.

**VERSE 37.—** And he said to Peter, etc. He had said: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you; even if all are scandalized, yet not I” (Matt. XXVI). Now, however, because of the greatness of his sorrow, he cannot overcome sleep.

**VERSE 38.—** So that you may not enter. He does not say, “so that you may not be tempted,” but “so that you may not enter into temptation”—that is, so that temptation may not overcome you or hold you within its snares.

(JEROME.) The one who neglects to pray enters into temptation. The disciples sleep three times; three times the Lord, while praying, awakens them. Their threefold sleep signifies the three dead whom the Lord raised: the first in the house, the second at the tomb, the third from the tomb. The Lord’s threefold watch teaches us to pray for forgiveness concerning the past, the present, and the future. But the flesh is weak. (BEDE.) For by its own weight the flesh always drags downward.

**VERSE 42.—** Rise. After praying for the third time, he taught that the apostles’ fear must be corrected through repentance. Secure, he proceeds to the passion, saying: “Rise, let us go.” As if he were saying: Let them not find us afraid, but let us go of our own accord to meet them, so that they may see joy and confidence in those who are about to suffer.

**VERSE 44.—** A sign. (JEROME.) He gives the sign of a kiss together with the devil’s poison, just as Cain offered a crafty and rejected sacrifice; hence they place wine mixed with vinegar on the cross.

**VERSE 45.—** Rabbi. (BEDE.) With shameless and criminal confidence he calls him “teacher,” etc., up to the point where he also fulfills the saying: “With those who hate peace” (Ps. CXIX), etc.

**VERSE 47.—** One. (ID.) According to John, Peter acted with the same ardor of mind as in the other things. For he knew that Phinehas, by punishing sacrilegious men, had received the reward of righteousness and an enduring priesthood. Luke says: “The Lord touched his ear and healed it” (Luke XXII). For he never forgets mercy and does not permit even his enemies to be wounded. Mystically: He teaches those who, by consenting to his death, have incurred a wound of the soul that, if they repent worthily, they can merit salvation.

**VERSE 48.—** As against a robber. (ID.) As if he were saying: It is foolish to seize with swords and clubs one who hands himself over to you of his own accord, and to seek him at night as though he were hiding, through a betrayer, when he teaches daily in the temple. But you gather against me in darkness for this reason: your power is in darkness.

**VERSE 50.—** Then, etc. (ID.) What he had said is fulfilled, that all would be scandalized, etc., up to the point where they learned to give themselves to their adversaries and to be recalled by God.

**VERSE 52.—** But he, etc. Just as Joseph, leaving his cloak behind, escaped naked from the hands of the shameless woman. Whoever wishes to escape the hands of the wicked should leave behind in his mind the things of the world and flee after Jesus. From them. From those whose presence and deeds he detested—not from the Lord, whose love he preserved firmly in his mind even while absent in body.

**VERSE 53.—** The high priest, etc. Namely, Caiaphas, who according to John was high priest that year. Josephus records something corresponding about him: that he had purchased the high priesthood from the Roman ruler without deserving the dignity. What wonder, then, if an unjust priest judges unjustly?

**VERSE 54.—** From a distance. (BEDE.) Since he was near denial; if he had been near Christ, he would not have denied him. Yet he is admirable in this: he did not abandon the Lord, even though he was afraid. His fear belongs to nature; what follows belongs to devotion; his denial belongs to sudden weakness; his repentance belongs to faith. Courtyard. (JEROME.) The courtyard is the circuit of the secular world. The servants are demons. The fire is carnal desire; whoever remains with them cannot weep for his sins. And he warmed himself. (BEDE.) This is the fire of charity, concerning which it is said, etc., up to the point where he immediately inflamed the hidden places of his heart with the coals of love.

**VERSE 56.—** False testimony. (ID.) A person gives false testimony when he does not understand words in the sense in which they are spoken, etc., up to the point where it appears that he had spoken specifically about the Jewish temple.

**VERSE 60.—** And rising, etc. Angry because he found no basis for accusation, he demonstrates the madness of his mind by the movement of his body. Not answering, etc. He provokes a response so that, from any occasion for speech, he may find an opportunity for accusation. But Jesus did not answer, because he foresaw that whatever he answered would be turned into an accusation.

You are the Christ. (JEROME.) The one whom he awaited from afar he did not see near, just as Isaac, with dimming eyes, did not recognize Jacob beneath his hands, but afterward sang from afar of what was to come concerning him.

**VERSE 62.—** And you will see. The priest asks about the Son of God; Jesus answers concerning the Son of Man, so that we may understand that the same person is both Son of God and Son of Man, lest we make a quaternity in the Trinity, and so that man may be in God and God in man. At the right hand of Power. Because “he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (Phil. II).

With the clouds of heaven. (JEROME.) He ascended in a cloud; with a cloud he will come. That is, he ascended with the body alone that he assumed from the Virgin, and he will come to judgment with the manifold Church, which is his body and fullness, as Matthew says: “When the Son of Man comes, and all the angels with him,” etc.

**VERSE 63.—** Now the high priest. (BEDE.) The same fury that had previously driven him from his seat, etc., up to the point where, when they were honored as gods in Lycaonia, they did this. He tore his garments, etc. (JEROME.) This means that they lost the ephod in which the Jews possessed their honor, etc., up to the point where, nevertheless, its chastity remains inviolate in those whom the lot of election finds, unto the consummation of the age.

**VERSE 64.—** They all, etc. (JEROME.) By this guilt he would dissolve our guilt, etc., up to the prophet’s words: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. CXV).

**VERSE 65.—** To cover his face, etc. Not so that he might not see their crimes, but so that, as they had once done to Moses, they might hide from themselves the grace of knowing him. This veil remains over their heart to this day, but it has been removed from those who believe in Christ. Hence, when he died, the temple was torn as though in two, and the mysteries of the holy of holies were revealed.

They struck him with slaps. (BEDE.) He who was then struck with blows is now struck by the blasphemies of false Christians. He who was consumed by the spittle of unbelievers is now dishonored by the mad insults of believers.

**VERSE 68.—** But he, etc. Observe that the one who denies himself to be Christ’s disciple denies Christ. For the Lord did not say, “You will deny that you are my disciple,” but “You will deny me.” Thus he denied him when he denied himself to be his disciple.

And he went outside, etc. (JEROME.) Peter, without the Spirit, yielded to the voice of a servant girl, etc., up to the point where we go outside, beyond what we had been.

**VERSE 70.—** For he is also a Galilean. (BEDE.) Galileans and inhabitants of Jerusalem speak the same language, yet every province and region has its own particular sound of speech, which it is difficult to change, etc., up to the point where that name was pronounced one way by the inhabitants of Jerusalem and another way by the Galileans.

**VERSE 72.—** And he remembered. (ID.) Peter denies at night and repents at the cockcrow. In the daytime, on the day on which he had denied him three times, he professed three times that he loved him. For what this means, etc., up to the point where, as the other Evangelists relate, he went outside, so that, separated from the impious, he might more freely wash away the guilt of his denial with tears.

# CHAPTER XV

**VERSE 1.—** And immediately, etc. It follows: “Binding Jesus.” It was the custom among the Jews that the one whom they had condemned to death should be handed over to the judge bound. It should be noted that they did not bind him for the first time then, but immediately after seizing him at night in the garden, as John says: “And so they led him first to Annas” (John XVIII).

(JEROME.) Samson is present, bound by Delilah. Samson is interpreted, etc., up to the point where he opens for us, who thirst, the fountain of everlasting life—that is, his body.

**VERSE 2.—** Are you the king of the Jews? Since Pilate asks nothing criminal except whether he is the king of the Jews, the impiety of those who could find no accusation against him, not even a false one, is exposed. You say so. He moderates his answer so that he speaks the truth without submitting to the accusation. Observe also that he gave Pilate, who pronounced sentence unwillingly, some answer, but refused to answer the priests and rulers, judging them unworthy of his words.

**VERSE 4.—** See, etc. The Gentile condemns Jesus but refers the cause back to the Jewish people. Consider in how many ways, etc.

**VERSE 11.—** But rather Barabbas. (BEDE.) The petition they obtained through all their efforts clings to the Jews to this day. When the choice was given them, they chose a robber instead of Jesus and a murderer instead of the Savior. Rightly, therefore, they lost salvation and life and subjected themselves so completely to robberies and seditions that they lost kingdom and homeland, and never again recovered liberty of body or soul.

**VERSE 14.—** But Pilate. Pilate gave many opportunities for releasing the Savior. First he offered them a robber in comparison with the just man; then he asked: “What then do you want me to do with the king of the Jews?” When they answered, “Let him be crucified,” he did not immediately consent, but, following the suggestion of his wife, who had sent him a message—as Matthew says—“Have nothing to do with that just man” (Matt. XXVII), he answered: “For what evil has he done?” By saying this, he absolved Jesus. But they cried out the more, etc. David says: “Many dogs have surrounded me” (Ps. XXI), etc. Isaiah says: “I waited for him to execute judgment, and behold, iniquity; and for righteousness, and behold, a cry” (Isa. V). Jeremiah says: “My inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest; it raised its voice against me” (Jer. XII).

**VERSE 15.—** Barabbas, and he handed him over, etc. (JEROME.) These are the two goats: one is *apompeius*, that is, the scapegoat, released into the desert of the underworld with the people’s sin; the other is killed as a lamb for the sins of those who have been released. The Lord’s portion is always sacrificed; the devil’s portion, which is their master, is driven headlong, unrestrained, into Tartarus.

Jesus he scourged. So that he might free us by scourges; hence: “The scourge will not come near your dwelling” (Ps. XC), whereas earlier it was said: “Many are the scourges of the sinner” (Ps. XXXI).

(BEDE.) Jesus scourged. He was scourged by Pilate himself; hence John says: “Pilate took Jesus and scourged him.” Then he adds: “And the soldiers, plaiting a crown of thorns” (John XIX), etc. He also presented him to the soldiers to be mocked. He did this so that, satiated with his punishments and insults, they would not thirst for his death as well.

**VERSE 17.—** And they clothe him. (BEDE.) Matthew has it thus: “And stripping him, they placed a scarlet cloak around him” (Mark XXVII). The meaning is the same. For it was given in place of royal purple, etc., up to the point where he is clothed in purple or scarlet when he glories in the triumph of the glorious martyrs.

**VERSE 19.—** And they struck him, etc. God is Christ’s head. Therefore they strike Christ’s head who deny that he is God. Those who defend their error by the authority of Scripture—for Scripture is customarily written with a reed—strike his head, as it were, with a reed. They spit in his face who, through words conceived in the inner madness of a blind mind, reject and curse the presence of his grace and deny that he came in the flesh.

They worshiped him. As though he had falsely called himself God. But today—which is a still graver madness—some worship him with firm faith as the true God, yet by their perverse actions immediately despise his words as though they were fables and place the promises of his kingdom after temporal enticements.

And they lead him out. (JEROME.) Here Abel is led into the field by his brother to be killed. Here Isaac is present, etc., up to the point where Jonah is cast out from the ship’s wood into the sea and into the whale’s belly for three days.

**VERSE 20.—** To crucify him. (JEROME.) What is the very form of the cross except the shape of the square world? The east shines with power; the north is held on the right; the south stands on the left; the west is fixed beneath the feet. Hence the Apostle says: “That we may know what is the breadth, length, height, and depth” (Eph. III). Birds fly through the air in the shape of a cross; a person worships and swims in the shape of a cross; a ship is driven across the seas by a yardarm resembling a cross. The letter tau displays the sign of salvation and the cross.

**VERSE 21.—** And they compel. (BEDE.) The Lord himself first carried his cross, as John says; afterward came this Simon, of whom the others also speak, and this fits the order of the mystery very well. For Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps (John XIX; I Pet. II).

(JEROME.) Simon, who carries the cross under compulsion, is the one who labors for human praise. People force him into this labor, which neither fear nor love of God compels him to undertake.

The father of Alexander. This Simon appears to have been a man of great reputation, since his sons too are identified by name as though known to everyone.

(JEROME.) Some are remembered through the merits of their fathers, others through the merits of their sons. This Simon, however, etc., up to the point where it is said through Jeremiah to Judea: “The Lord called your name a luxuriant, beautiful, fruitful, and splendid olive tree.”

**VERSE 22.—** The place of Golgotha. (JEROME.) The Jews report that at this place on the mountain the ram was sacrificed in place of Isaac (Gen. XXII), so that there Christ might be shorn—that is, separated from his flesh, namely, from carnal Judaism.

(BEDE.) The heads of the condemned were cut off outside the gate, and the places of the beheaded were called “skull places.” Therefore the Lord was crucified there, so that where the field of the condemned had been, the banners of the martyrs might be raised. And since he was made a curse of the cross for us, scourged and crucified for the salvation of all, he wished to be crucified as though guilty among the guilty.

**VERSE 23.—** And they gave him. (BEDE.) Matthew says, “mixed with gall” (Matt. XXVII), which is the same thing. For he used gall to signify bitterness. Wine mixed with myrrh is extremely bitter, although it is possible that they made the wine extremely bitter with both gall and myrrh.

(JEROME.) And they gave him, etc. By this vinegar the poisonous juice of the fruit is wiped away. And he did not accept it—that for which he suffers. Hence it is said of him: “What I did not seize, then I repaid” (Ps. LXVIII).

And he did not accept it. Matthew says: “When he had tasted it, he would not drink.” Matthew indicates that for our sake he tasted the bitterness of death, but on the third day he rose again.

**VERSE 24.—** And crucifying him with them. (JEROME.) Here salvation is fastened to the wood. At first death was fastened to wood: the first wood was that of the knowledge of good and evil; the second is for us the wood of good alone and of life. The extension of the first hand toward the wood grasped death; the extension of the second found the life that had been lost. By this wood we cross the surging sea to the land of the living.

His garments. (BEDE.) Christ’s four-part garment, corresponding to the number of soldiers, signifies the Church equally and harmoniously distributed throughout the four parts of the world.

(JEROME.) The Lord’s garments are the commandments with which his body, the Church, is clothed. They are divided among the soldiers of the nations, so that there may be four orders while there is one faith: the married, widows, rulers, and the separated. They cast lots for the undivided tunic, which is peace and truth in all things, like a royal garment or ring. Casting lots. (ID.) Over the tunic, which was seamless. Here it was allotted, etc., up to the point where the lot comes or yields only by God’s judgment.

**VERSE 25.—** Now it was the third hour. (JEROME.) This is properly found in Mark, for at the sixth hour darkness covered the earth, so that no one could move his head. For from the thirtieth, etc., up to the point where they should rather be said to have crucified him, although they strive to conceal this, than the soldiers, who obeyed their commander according to their duty.

**VERSE 26.—** And there was an inscription. (BEDE.) The inscription shows that, even by killing him, they could not bring about the result that he should not be their king; hence: “Yet I have been established as king by him,” etc. It is fitting that he should be both king and priest, since he offered the exceptional sacrifice of his flesh to the Father on the altar of the cross and displayed the dignity of a king in the inscription, so that he might make clear to all that through the cross’s gallows he had not lost but confirmed his rule.

**VERSE 27.—** And with him they crucify. (BEDE.) As the Apostle says: “Our old man was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and sin might no longer rule over us.” Therefore, as long as our works are being carried out so that the body of sin may be emptied, as long as, etc., up to the Apostle’s words: “Rooted and grounded in love, you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth” (Eph. III).

Two robbers. (ID.) The robbers crucified with the Lord signify those who, through faith and confession of Christ, through the struggle of martyrdom, or through any strict form of continence, undergo hardship. Those who do this for eternal glory are signified by the merit and faith of the robber on the right. Those who do it for human glory or any less worthy intention imitate the mind and actions of the robber on the left.

(JEROME.) Truth is counted among the wicked: it leaves one on the left and takes another to the right. So it will be on the day of judgment: from a similar crime, they receive dissimilar paths. One precedes Peter into paradise; the other follows Judas into hell. A brief confession acquires a long life, while blasphemy, once ended, is punished with eternal penalty. Here Judah’s foal is bound to the vine *ἀναβόλαιον*, that is, the cloak is dipped in the blood of the grape; here the kids ravage the vineyard.

**VERSE 29.—** Shaking their heads. (JEROME.) The death of the wicked is released when the bonds of the underworld are raised as far as the neck, which is the neck of the human race.

**VERSE 31.—** He saved others. (JEROME.) Even unwillingly they confess that he saved others, and they condemn themselves by their own sentence, because, having saved others, he could have saved himself if he had wished.

**VERSE 32.—** Let him now come down. It is a greater thing to rise from the tomb, and yet they did not believe. “They have all turned aside; together they have become useless” (Ps. XIII).

And those who were with him. (BEDE.) According to Luke (Luke XXIII), one robber blasphemed, saying: “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us.” The other, etc., up to the point where those who seek heavenly things undoubtedly attain them through Christ, by his mediation and mercy.

**VERSE 33.—** And when the sixth hour had come. (BEDE.) It should be noted that he was crucified at the sixth hour, when the sun was about to withdraw from the center of the world, and that he rose at dawn, when the sun was rising, etc., up to the point where, at the hour when the first Adam by sin brought death into the world, the second Adam by dying destroyed death.

Darkness. (JEROME.) Here Noah is present, drunk and stripped, covered by heaven and earth with a drunken cloak and mocked by man; here blood trickled from the wood.

**VERSE 35.—** And some, etc. Not all. Perhaps the Roman soldiers, not understanding the precise character of the Hebrew speech, thought from the word *Eloi* that he was calling Elijah. Or the Jews, corrupting the Lord’s words in their customary speech, were defaming him in his weakness by saying that he was calling for Elijah’s help.

**VERSE 36.—** But one ran, etc. (BEDE.) John says more fully: “Afterward, knowing that all things had been accomplished,” etc. It is as though he said: You have done too little; give what you are. For they were, etc., up to the point concerning which it is said: “The Lord planted a vineyard of Soreth; and how have you been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine? I waited for you to produce grapes, and you produced thorns” (Isa. V).

**VERSE 37.—** But Jesus, etc. (BEDE.) Luke explains what he said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit”; and saying this, he expired (Luke XXIII). John says: “When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said: ‘It is finished’; and bowing his head, he gave up his spirit” (John XIX). Between the words “It is finished” and “he bowed his head and gave up his spirit,” that loud cry was uttered which John omits but the others record: “Into your hands,” etc.

(JEROME.) For when the flesh had grown weak, divine power immediately prevailed, saying: “Open to me the gates of righteousness” (Ps. CXVII), etc. We, who are from the earth, die with no voice or with only one; but he who descended from heaven expired with a raised voice.

**VERSE 38.—** And the veil of the temple. So that the ark of the covenant and all the mysteries of the law that had been covered might appear and pass to the Gentiles. Formerly it was said: “God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. LXXV). Now, however: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God” (Ps. LVI), and throughout all, etc. And earlier in the Gospel: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. X); after the passion: “Go and teach all nations” (Matt. XXVIII).

**VERSE 39.—** Now when the centurion saw, etc. It is shown why the centurion marvels: because he saw him expire in this manner, that is, give up his spirit. For no one has power to give up the spirit except the creator of souls.

Truly, etc. (JEROME.) Observe that the centurion, before the cross and amid the scandal of the passion itself, truly confesses him to be the Son of God; whereas Arius, etc., up to the point where he confirms him truly to be the Son of God while the Synagogue remains silent.

**VERSE 40.—** There were also. (ID.) Just as the female sex is not excluded from salvation through the Virgin Mary, so it is not excluded from knowledge of the mystery of the cross and resurrection through Mary Magdalene, a widow, and the other mothers.

Of James the younger and Joseph. (BEDE.) By James the younger he means James of Alphaeus, who is also the brother of the Lord, because he was the son of the Lord’s maternal aunt. Of her John says: “There stood beside the cross of Jesus his mother” (John XIX), etc. He appears to call her Cleophas either from her father or from her kinship.

**VERSE 42.—** And when evening had already come, etc. (ID.) *Paraskeuē* is Greek; in Latin, “preparation.” The Jews living among the Greeks called the sixth day of the week by this name, because on it they prepared what was necessary for the Sabbath, according to what, etc., up to the point where, when the eighth age arrives, the bodies themselves, glorified by the resurrection, receive incorruption together with their souls as an eternal inheritance.

**VERSE 43.—** Joseph came. (JEROME.) Joseph came in the evening of the preparation from Arimathea, which is interpreted as “the one who takes down,” in order to take down Christ’s body, etc., up to the point where the elect, who are the stars of the sea, look on from afar, when, if possible, even the elect will be scandalized.

**VERSE 46.—** Now Joseph, etc. (BEDE.) From the Lord’s simple burial the ambition of the rich is condemned, since they do not even in their tombs, etc., up to the point where he celebrates it with earthly linen, just as the Lord’s body was buried in a clean shroud; so it was established by Pope Sylvester.

Which had been hewn out. (BEDE.) It is said that the Lord’s tomb was a round chamber cut from the underlying rock, of such height that a person standing upright could scarcely touch its roof with an outstretched hand. It has an entrance, etc., up to the point where the color of the monument and the burial chamber is said to be a mixture of white and red.

**VERSE 47.—** Now Mary, etc. (ID.) Luke says: “All his acquaintances stood at a distance, and the women who had followed him” (Luke XXIII). But while the others returned home after his body had been laid down, the women alone, etc., up to the point where, if perhaps they can imitate them in pious attentiveness, they consider in what order his passion should be embraced.

# CHAPTER XVI
**VERSE 1.—And when it had passed.** (BEDE.) Luke says that, returning from the tomb, they prepared spices and ointments, and on the Sabbath they kept silence, because it had been commanded [Col. 0241A] that the Sabbath’s rest, etc., should continue up to offering the Lord the fragrance of good works and the sweetness of prayers, with the face illuminated after the darkness of vices had been cast off.

**(JEROME.)** Now they run with the bride and the maidens, fragrant with spices; after her we sprinkle the book, that is, the bridal chamber, etc., up to the Lord rising within it in triumph and saying: “This is the day which the Lord has made,” etc. (Psalm CXVII).

**VERSE 2.—And very early.** (JEROME.) Another says “at dawn.” Dawn is the interval between the darkness of night and the brightness of day, in which salvation is to be revealed in the Church after the manner of the sun. When it rises, it sends before it a rosy dawn, so that such great splendor may be seen by eyes prepared for it, when the time of the Lord’s resurrection has shone forth. Then the whole Church of the holy women sang Christ’s praises, when he bestowed life and infused the light of faith.

**VERSE 3.—And they said to one another.** (JEROME.) Eagles gather around the body; martyrs and apostles see the stone rolled away, which is the law of death, as though it said: “Where is your sting, O death?” (1 Cor. XV).

**VERSE 4.—The stone rolled away.** (BEDE.) How the stone was rolled away by an angel, Matthew relates. Allegorically, however, the rolling away of the stone signifies the resurrection of Christ’s mysteries, which had been concealed beneath the veil of the letter of the law. For the law was written on stone; when its covering was removed, the glory of the resurrection was revealed, the abolition of ancient death was proclaimed, and throughout the whole world hope of perpetual life began to be preached.

[Col. 0241C] **VERSE 5.—A young man.** (JEROME.) Not an old man, not an infant, but one cheerful in age, as it is said: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth” (Eccles. XI), which is not truly present here when mixed with old age.

**(BEDE.)** The women who came with spices see angels, because those minds behold the citizens above which come to God with virtues and holy desires.

**Sitting on the right.** (BEDE.) On the southern side of that place where he had been laid, etc., up to their entering the tomb and finding two angels standing there.

**(GREGORY.)** By the left is understood the present life, by the right eternal life, etc., up to his restoring them to the number of the angels and repairing the losses of the heavenly homeland.

[Col. 0241D] **VERSE 6.—Do not be terrified.** (GREGORY.) As though he said: Let those be afraid who do not love the Lord’s coming or that of the citizens above, who, oppressed by vices, despair of their fellowship. But you, why are you afraid when you see your fellow citizens? Hence Matthew, describing the angel’s appearance, says: “His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow” (Matt. XXVIII).

**Jesus.** “Jesus” means “Savior.” But since many were called by this name not substantially but merely by designation, he identifies him by the place, “the Nazarene,” and adds the cause: “Crucified.” He also adds: “He has risen; he is not here.” He is absent in the presence of his flesh, yet nowhere absent in the presence of his majesty. “Behold the place.” Mortality is shown to mortals so that they may offer the gratitude that is due [Col. 0242A] and understand what we are and have been, and know what we shall be.

**VERSE 7.—And Peter.** (BEDE.) Peter is named, so that he should not despair because of his denial. For unless, etc., up to the one who was to become the Church’s shepherd learned through his own fault how he ought to show mercy to others.

**And Peter.** (JEROME.) He had shown himself unworthy of discipleship when he denied the Master three times. But past sins do not harm when they no longer please us.

**He goes before you.** This is rightly said of our Redeemer, for “Galilee” is interpreted as “migration.” He had already migrated from suffering to resurrection, from death to life, from punishment to glory. And rightly, after the resurrection, he is seen by the disciples in Galilee, because we shall see the glory of his resurrection joyfully [Col. 0242B] if now we migrate from vices to the heights of virtues. Therefore he who is announced in the tomb is shown in migration; and he who is recognized in the mortification of the flesh is seen in the migration of the mind.

**(BEDE.)** Note that Mark says: “He goes before you into Galilee,” etc. Yet he did not report that he was seen there. Matthew, however, etc., up to as he will be known in that eternity to which he will lead us because of the form of a servant, so that, as free persons, we may contemplate the form of the Lord.

**VERSE 8.—They fled.** (JEROME.) Of the future life it is said: “Pain and sighing will flee away.” Before the resurrection of all, the women imitate what they will do afterward: they flee from death and terror.

**And they told no one.** (JEROME.) For only those who have deserved it see the mystery of the resurrection. Hence, according to John: “Peter, rising, ran to the tomb to see what he had heard.”

**VERSE 9.—But rising.** He rose in the morning and was buried in the evening, so as to fulfill this: “In the evening weeping will remain, and in the morning joy” (Psalm XXIX). He was therefore buried on the sixth day of the week, called Parasceve, toward evening; during the following night and the day of the Sabbath he remained in the tomb; on the third day, that is, very early on the first day of the week, he rose. And rightly he lay in the tomb for one day and two nights, because he joined the light of his single death to the darkness of our double death. For we were held in the death of soul and spirit; therefore he brought to us his own death, that is, the death of the flesh [Col. 0242D], and dissolved our twofold death. He joined his single death to our double death and, by dying, took away our double death.

**He appeared first to Mary Magdalene.** He first showed himself to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons, because prostitutes and publicans precede the Synagogue into the kingdom of God, just as the thief preceded the apostles. The apostles weep and mourn because they have not yet seen him, but they will soon be comforted.

**(BEDE.)** In the beginning, woman was the cause of guilt for man, while man was the executor of error, etc., up to so that she might proclaim the resurrection to the evangelists and apostles themselves.

**VERSE 11.—And when they heard.** (BEDE.) The disciples’ late belief in the resurrection is not so much their weakness as our firmness; for the resurrection was shown to those who doubted by many proofs, through which we too are made more securely steadfast.

**VERSE 12.—To two of them.** (BEDE.) Luke relates this more fully (Luke XXIV): “Their eyes,” etc. Afterwards they recognized him in the breaking of bread. And as Luke says: “Rising at that same hour, they returned to Jerusalem,” etc.

**As they were walking.** (JEROME.) Here faith labors in the active life; there it is contemplative, etc., up to, having forgotten his flesh, he asks in this life for what we hope for in the future one.

**VERSE 14.—Finally, etc.** (BEDE.) On the fortieth day, when he was already about to depart from them into heaven, he especially said these things to them, etc., up to: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel.”

**The hardness of heart, etc.** (JEROME.) So that a heart full of charity might follow [Col. 0243B]; hence the crowds of martyrs willingly embrace death in this age, because they know that through temporal destruction they will live forever.

**VERSE 15.—To every creature.** To every nation of the Gentiles. For it had previously been said: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. X), so that the preaching first rejected by the Jews might then become assistance to the Gentiles.

**(JEROME.)** To the whole human race, which has something in common with every creature: with angels, cattle, trees, stones, fire, and water; with what is hot and cold, moist and dry—for man is called the lesser world.

**VERSE 16.—Whoever believes, etc.** Through others, infants believe, just as from others they drew the sins that are forgiven them in baptism [Col. 0243C].

**VERSE 17.—And these signs, etc.** Surely, if we do not perform signs, do we not believe? But these were necessary at the beginning, so that faith might be nourished by miracles; once the faith of the Church had been confirmed, they were no longer necessary.

**They will cast out demons, etc.** The Church does this spiritually today when, through the grace of exorcism, it lays hands on believers and drives out evil spirits.

**They will speak in new tongues.** This happens when the faithful abandon the worldly words of their former life, utter the holy mysteries, and exalt the praises and power of God as far as they are able.

**VERSE 18.—If they drink anything deadly, etc.** When they hear poisonous persuasions but do not carry them through into action, they are not harmed by them, even if they drink something deadly.

**They will lay hands on the sick, etc.** When they strengthen those near them who are established in good works by the example of good action, they lay hands on the sick, and they will be well. These miracles are greater insofar as they are spiritual; through them souls, not bodies, are raised.

**VERSE 19.—Into heaven.** (AUGUSTINE.) Note that sometimes “heavens” is used in the plural and sometimes “heaven” in the singular, etc., up to where the believers’ faith is instructed more by actions than by words.

**And he sits at the right hand.** (BEDE.) Now judging all things, he will come at the end as Judge of all. Stephen, however, saw him standing, because in the contest he had him as his helper.

**VERSE 20.—But they, etc.** (BEDE.) Note that the later Mark began his Gospel, the more, etc., up to the place where the apostles sowed the same word of the Gospel throughout the whole world.

[Col. 0243]

## THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE. (G)*

### PROLOGUE OF JEROME

*(See among his works.)*

## LUKE’S PREFACE TO HIS GOSPEL

**VERSE 1.—Since indeed, etc.** (BEDE.) Luke, concerning all that Jesus did and taught, etc., up to arranging the narrative more than weaving the truth of history.

[Col. 0243D] **VERSE 3.—All things.** (ID.) Not everything that he had attained, but everything that he considered suitable for confirming the faith of his readers. For deliberately he omits many things that the others relate, so that a different grace might shine forth in the Gospel and so that the individual books might each display their own particular mysteries of deeds and miracles.

**Theophilus.** “Theophilus” means “lover of God,” etc., up to he ought to know the order of the faith of his eternal divinity and his temporal dispensation.

## CHAPTER I

**VERSE 5.—There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea.** (AMBROSE.) The calf is a priestly sacrifice. Therefore this Gospel is represented by the calf: it begins with priests and is brought to completion in the calf, that is, in Christ, who is sacrificed for the life of the world.

**A certain priest.** He followed a proper order: by naming the king and the region in which he lived, he indicates the priest, his people, and his wife.

**Zechariah.** “Zechariah” means “remembering the Lord.” The angel appears to him at the right side of the altar, because the mystery is shown to one who remembers the Lord.

**Of the division of Abijah.** (BEDE.) “Abijah” means “the Father is Lord,” etc., [Col. 0244D] up to as the Old Testament is declared through the sevenfold Testament.

**Elizabeth.** “Elizabeth,” “fullness of my God,” signifies Mary, who was full of God.

**VERSE 6.—And they were both.** (BEDE, AMBROSE.) This is complete praise, embracing noble ancestry, upright conduct, priestly service, obedience to the commandments, and judgment in acts of justification.

**Just before God.** (AMBROSE.) Not everyone who is just before human beings is just before God. Human beings see one way, God another: human beings look at the face, God at the heart. Therefore it can happen that someone appears just to me because of a goodness sought for popular approval, yet is not just before God, if his justice is not formed from sincerity of mind but merely feigned through flattery.

[Col. 0245A] **VERSE 7.—And they had no.** (BEDE.) It was divinely arranged that John should be born from parents advanced in age and long deprived of the fruit of marriage, so that the unexpected birth of offspring might both make God’s gift more pleasing to them and prepare the others, through the astonishment of the miracle, to hear the future prophecy. Hence it is later added: “All who had heard it laid it up in their hearts, saying: ‘What, then, will this child be?’”

**VERSE 8.—And it happened.** Since, according to Moses’ command, when one priest departed another was ordered to succeed him, it was established in David’s time that those ministering in turn should serve for eight-day periods, from Sabbath to Sabbath, during their assigned rotation, each observing chastity and meanwhile not entering his home.

**VERSE 9.—By lot.** (BEDE.) He was not chosen by a new lot at the time when the incense was to be burned, etc., up to he is foretold while the one who is to be his forerunner is promised.

**VERSE 12.—And Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him, etc.** (AMBROSE.) We are accustomed to become troubled and to be taken out of our customary state when we are struck by the encounter with a higher power. But just as it belongs to human weakness to be terrified, so it belongs to angelic kindness to comfort the frightened by soothing him with its appearance. Demons, on the contrary, if they perceive that someone has been terrified by their presence, shake him with even greater horror.

**VERSE 13.—For your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you will call his name.** It has been heard more fully than you asked. You prayed for the liberation of the people, and a forerunner has been given to you.

**(AMBROSE.)** Many divine benefits are gathered here. First, the fruit of prayer; then, the birth from a barren woman; next, the joy of many and the greatness of his virtue. Even a prophecy from the Most High is promised. Moreover, so that there might be no doubt, the name of the future child is specified. Since such blessings flowed beyond his request, disbelief was justly punished by the penalty of silence.

**VERSE 14.—And he will be joy, etc.** (BEDE.) It is a sign of exceptional merit whenever God either imposes a name upon people or changes one, etc., up to because this one proclaims salvation to many, whereas the other gives it to all.

**(AMBROSE.)** “Joy and exultation.” Parents are admonished to give thanks no less, etc., up to mothers, because they are honored with the rewards of marriage.

**VERSE 15.—Wine and strong drink, etc.** (BEDE.) It is a great virtue before God to proclaim heavenly joys in the wilderness, etc., up to and the spirit of grace was already present.

[Col. 0245D] **VERSE 16.—And he will turn many of the children of Israel.** (ID.) Since John, bearing witness to Christ and baptizing in the faith of Christ, is said to have converted the children of Israel to God, it is clear that Christ is the Lord God of Israel.

**VERSE 17.—He will go before.** (ID.) Just as Elijah is the herald of the Judge, etc., up to the Judge is manifested with him in glory.

**In spirit and power.** (AMBROSE.) Spirit and power are rightly joined. For there is neither spirit without power nor power without spirit. Elijah had the power of abstinence and patience, and of turning the minds of the people from faithlessness to faith; he had the spirit of prophecy.

**He will turn, etc.** (BEDE.) He turns the hearts of fathers toward their children, etc., up to nearly the same words that the angel spoke concerning John, which Malachi had foretold concerning Elijah.

[Col. 0246A] **VERSE 18.—Therefore, etc.** (ID.) If the one who made the promise had been a human being, it would have been permissible to ask for a sign without penalty, etc., up to and it would have been the punishment of the disbelief he deserved.

**VERSE 19.—Before God.** (BEDE.) When angels come to us, they fulfill their ministry outwardly in such a way that inwardly they nevertheless stand before God in contemplation. For although an angel is a circumscribed spirit, the highest Spirit, who is God, is uncircumscribed; the angel runs within him wherever it moves or is sent.
