**VERSE 22.—And he was making signs to them and remained mute, etc.** He was trying to indicate bodily actions without a voice, yet could not express his will. The Jewish people resemble him, being unable to give an account of their deeds.

[Col. 0246B] **VERSE 23.—When the days were completed, etc.** Because, during the time of their assigned service, the priests devoted solely to the temple offices abstained not only from the embrace of their wives but also from entering their homes. But our priests, for whom not carnal succession but spiritual perfection is sought, and who must be present daily at the altar, are commanded to perpetual chastity.

**VERSE 24.—She hid herself.** (AMBROSE.) She conceals it because she is ashamed of the age at which she has given birth, etc., up to for she who would not be ashamed of intercourse in old age would not be ashamed of giving birth.

**VERSE 25.—For thus he has done.** (BEDE.) These things happened, John Chrysostom says, etc., up to because through him the affliction of repentance was to be preached.

**VERSE 26.—But in the sixth month.** (JEROME.) Just as the angel Gabriel was sent by God in the sixth month to a city of Galilee, so in the sixth millennium Christ was sent.

**Gabriel.** (BEDE.) Angels are sometimes identified by name so that their names may show what service they come to perform. “Gabriel” means “strength of God,” because he announces the one who came to defeat the devil.

**VERSE 27.—To a virgin.** Woman, seduced by the devil, brought death; in contrast, woman, instructed by an angel, brought forth salvation.

**VERSE 28.—The Lord is with you.** By a new love of chastity he lifted her to heavenly things and afterward, through human nature, consecrated her with the entire fullness of divinity.

**Blessed are you among women.** She is virgin and mother without precedent among women, and she bore God.

**VERSE 29.—She was troubled, etc.** Because she did not know whether what the angel said referred to the past or the future.

**VERSE 30.—And the angel said to her: Do not be afraid, Mary.** He calls her by name, as one more familiarly known, since she was troubled by the unusual greeting. He commands her not to fear and explains more fully why he called her full of grace.

**VERSE 31.—Jesus.** Jesus is called “savior” or “salutary.” For he will save not the people of Israel but his own people, whether from the uncircumcision or from the circumcision, gathered into one fold under one shepherd.

**VERSE 32.—The throne of David his father.** (BEDE.) That is, the Israelite people, etc., up to in those who, cut from the wild olive, have been grafted into the good olive.

**VERSE 35.—He will be called holy, the Son of God.** Jesus is born holy, overcoming the condition of corruptible nature; he was not conceived through the union of carnal intercourse [Col. 0247A]. We, bound by the condition of corruptible nature, can be sanctified through grace. And it is fitting that she who conceived contrary to custom as a virgin should, beyond the custom of human nature, give birth to the Son of God.

**VERSE 36.—And behold, etc.** (BEDE.) So that the virgin might not despair of giving birth, etc., up to she might also learn that the forerunner would be born from a barren old woman.

**Your kinswoman.** Because she was of the tribe of Levi, that is, of the tribe of God.

**(BEDE.)** We read that Aaron, who was of the tribe of Levi, etc., up to they were not without the fellowship of spiritual kinship according to God.

**VERSE 38.—Behold the handmaid of the Lord.** She does not exalt herself because of the singularity of her merit, but, mindful in every respect of her condition and of her divine kinship, confesses that she is the handmaid of him whose mother she is chosen to be; with great devotion she desires the angel’s promise to be fulfilled.

**VERSE 39.—But Mary rose in those days and went into the hill country with haste, to a city of Judah.** (AMBROSE.) Not disbelieving the oracle, etc., up to when it is added: “And it happened, as she heard.”

**VERSE 40.—And she entered the house of Zechariah.** From this holy women should learn what diligent care they owe to pregnant relatives.

**And she greeted Elizabeth.** (BEDE.) She greets first, because the more chaste a woman is, the more humble she ought to be.

**VERSE 41.—She exulted, etc.** Since he could not yet greet with his tongue, he greets with an exultant spirit and begins the service of his own forerunning. Behold, what the angel had said appears: “He will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.”

[Col. 0247C] **VERSE 42.—Blessed are you.** (BEDE, AMBROSE.) The words of the Gospel agree with the words of the psalm in which David is promised: “From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne” (Psalm CXXXI). Mary is blessed by Elizabeth with the same words with which she was blessed by Gabriel, so that she might be shown worthy of reverence by angels and human beings and preferred to our women.

**VERSE 43.—The mother of my Lord.** I perceive the miracle; I recognize the mystery: the mother of the Lord, pregnant by the Word, full of God.

**VERSE 44.—When it happened.** At the very moment when the voice enters the ears of the body, spiritual power enters the heart of the hearer, and kindles with love of the coming one not only the mother but also her offspring.

**He exulted.** (BEDE.) When the Spirit with which he had been filled revealed it, etc., up to the virgin believed, whereas the priest denied.

[Col. 0247D] **VERSE 46.—My soul magnifies the Lord.** (ID.) First she confesses the spiritual gifts granted to her, etc., up to I devote myself to observing his commandments.

**VERSE 47.—And it has exulted.** (ID.) (ID.) Because I do not care for earthly things; prosperity does not soften me, adversity does not break me, but only the memory of him delights me, from whom eternal salvation is hoped. I rejoice in the divinity of him whose temporal conception causes my flesh to bear fruit.

**VERSE 48.—Because he has regarded.** (ID.) Behold how lowly she considers herself, etc., up to and from the small and weak he makes the great and strong.

**Because he has done great things for me.** Because he took flesh in me, cleansed me from sins, and bestowed upon me the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0248A] **And mercy.** (BEDE.) From particular gifts she turns to God’s universal judgments, etc., up to he adds what the despisers deserve.

**VERSE 53.—He has filled the hungry with good things.** (ID.) Those who desire eternal things with their whole effort will be satisfied when Christ appears in glory. But those who rejoice in earthly things will finally be sent away empty of every blessing. Even in the present we see the humble filled by divine grace and the proud deprived of the light of truth.

**VERSE 55.—As he spoke to our fathers.** Recalling the fathers to whom this salvation was revealed, she names Abraham in particular, to whom the Incarnation itself was first made manifest.

**And to his seed forever.** Not so much to those born according to the flesh as to those who followed the traces of faith, to whom the Savior’s coming was promised forever [Col. 0248B], because the promise itself of inheritance will be enclosed by no limit. For believers will not cease even to the end of the age, and the glory of blessedness will be everlasting.

**VERSE 56.—And Mary remained.** (BEDE.) She remained until she saw the birth of the forerunner, which was chiefly why she had come. Nor did she remain so long merely because of family affection, but so that during such a prolonged stay the progress of both Elizabeth and John might increase. For if they were filled with the Holy Spirit at Mary’s first arrival, much more was added to them by such a long stay.

**VERSE 59.—On the eighth day.** The Lord’s resurrection is represented through circumcision, because it also occurred on the eighth day, that is, after the Sabbath. And just as circumcision used to free from the guilt of death, so the resurrection displayed in our Author the birth of immortal life and showed that it is to be hoped for in us.

**And they were calling him.** (BEDE.) John’s celebrated birth is the beginning of the grace of the New Testament, etc., up to it expresses the grace of the Gospel if rightly understood.

**VERSE 62.—And they were making signs to his father, etc.** Those who make signs to the father concerning the child’s name signify those who endeavor to establish the grace of faith by the testimony of the law.

**VERSE 67.—And he prophesied, saying.** (BEDE.) Great is the generosity of divine mercy. Behold, speech—which alone had been taken from the doubter—was restored to the believer together with the spirit of prophecy.

**VERSE 68.—Blessed.** While he asked God’s goodness, the forerunner was granted for his liberation.

**He has visited.** What he knew was soon to happen, he narrates in prophetic fashion as though it had already happened.

**VERSE 69.—A horn of salvation for us.** (BEDE.) By the horn, which rises above the flesh, since all bones are covered with flesh, Christ’s kingdom is signified, by which the world and the joys of the flesh are overcome. As a figure of this, David and Solomon were consecrated to the glory of the kingdom with the horn of oil, as previously was Saul with a vessel of oil.

**VERSE 71.—Salvation from our enemies and from the hand, etc.** He raised up salvation for us from our enemies; this explains the preceding verse, in which he had briefly said the same thing beforehand: “He raised up a horn of salvation for us.”

**VERSE 72.—To show mercy to our fathers [Col. 0249A] and to remember the covenant, etc.** He spoke and raised up salvation for us in order to show mercy, so that he might fulfill in us the mercy he promised to our fathers and complete in us through Christ the oath he made to our fathers concerning our liberation.

**VERSE 76.—And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare, etc.** (BEDE.) It is not surprising that he addresses an infant of eight days, etc., up to the things he recognized that he had received into sonship.

**VERSES 79, 80.—To guide our feet into the way of peace. And the child grew, etc.** So that the steps of our works might in every respect agree with the grace of our Illuminator, until we enter the dwelling of everlasting peace.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0249B] **VERSE 1.—An edict went out from Caesar.** (AUGUSTINE, BEDE.) Augustus reigned in peace for twelve years around the birth of Christ, etc., up to here Judea was first made tributary to the Romans.

**VERSE 2.—The first.** (BEDE.) At different times many regions of the earth are read to have been registered, but this was the first of those registrations that included the whole world; it is an enrollment of minds, because no one is excluded. Or certainly it first began when Quirinius was sent by Caesar into Syria to become the assessor of property.

**VERSE 4.—Nazareth.** (ID.) Every day the Lord is conceived in Nazareth, etc., up to the diligence of the speaking teacher is of no value unless it receives an increase of heavenly assistance so that it may be heard.

**VERSE 6.—And it happened.** The Lord willed to be conceived in one place and born in another, so that he might more easily escape the fury of the plotting Herod. Christ’s humility is commended, because he willed not only to become incarnate but also to be born at a time when, immediately after his birth, he would be subjected to Caesar’s census for our liberation.

**VERSE 7.—She wrapped him in swaddling clothes.** He is clothed in humble rags so that we might receive the robe of immortality. His hands and feet are bound so that our hands may be directed to good works and our feet into the way of peace. He became a little child so that we might be perfect.

**VERSE 8.—And shepherds.** (BEDE.) When the supreme Shepherd had been born, shepherds were kept from the snares of night, etc., up to those upon whom divine grace shines more abundantly.

[Col. 0249D] **VERSE 9.—And behold, an angel of the Lord.** (ID.) The citizens of heaven bear witness both to the Lord who was to be conceived, to him who was conceived, and to him who was born, so that they might sufficiently instruct mortals and render service to their Author.

**VERSE 12.—An infant wrapped in swaddling clothes.** (ID.) The infancy of the Savior is repeatedly impressed upon us through the testimonies of angels and evangelists, so that it may be fixed more deeply in our minds what he became for us. His humility is commended by this: “Though he was rich, he became poor for us, so that by his poverty he might enrich us” (2 Cor. VIII).

**VERSE 14.—And peace on earth.** When, by sinning, we were strangers to God, the angels counted us strangers as well. But because we recognized our king, the angels recognized us as their fellow citizens [Col. 0250A]. And the angel fears being worshiped by the human nature that he sees in his king.

**Men of good will.** (BEDE.) These are those who receive the Christ who has been born, not those who were troubled when they heard of his birth and persecuted him. “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isa. XLVIII).

**VERSE 16.—And they came in haste.** (BEDE.) Christ’s presence must not be sought with laziness, etc., up to they would find him as though in a manger.

**VERSE 17.—And when they had seen.** To see or know God is life, and the sole life of human beings is to know the true Father and that Jesus Christ, whom he sent, is the one God.

**VERSE 18.—They marveled.** They marvel both at the mystery of the Incarnation and at the great testimony of the shepherds, who would not know how to fabricate what they had heard but proclaimed the truth with simple eloquence. Yet the Lord sent not rhetors but fishermen to evangelize. Likewise, in the Old Testament he appointed shepherds as messengers of his dispensation. Therefore the testimony of the shepherds must not be despised.

**VERSE 20.—And they returned, etc.** (BEDE.) Thus spiritual shepherds, while others sleep, are now carried upward by contemplating heavenly things, etc., up to when they say: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will.”

**VERSE 22.—They brought him.** Infants who were brought to the temple from throughout the kingdom of Judea, if they belonged to the tribe of Levi, were retained permanently for the service of the house. If they belonged to another tribe, they were redeemed by a payment made by their parents and taken back home.

[Col. 0250C] **VERSE 23.—As it is written.** (BEDE.) It is written in the law: “The woman who, after giving birth, etc.,” up to she enters into the joys of heavenly blessedness with the fruits of good works.

**VERSE 24.—A pair of turtledoves.** (ID.) This was the offering of the poor, who were unable to offer a lamb, so that the Lord’s humility might be evident in every respect.

**VERSE 25.—And behold, a man.** Not only angels but every age and sex bear witness to the child who has been born. And just as he was foretold by the faithful of every generation, so, when he came, he was proclaimed by the praise of all the saints.

**VERSE 27.—The child.** Since childhood begins after seven years of infancy, Jesus is frequently called a child, [Col. 0250D] not so much because of his age as because of his service; hence the Prophet: “Behold my servant,” because the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve (Isa. XLII).

**VERSE 29.—Now dismiss your servant.** (AMBROSE.) Whoever wishes to be dismissed should come to Jerusalem, etc., up to then he will be dismissed so that he may not see death, because he had seen life.

**VERSE 34.—Behold, this one is appointed.** For the ruin of those who had stood and the resurrection of those who had fallen; or for the ruin of vices and the resurrection of virtues. He was appointed not only in himself but also in his preachers for ruin and resurrection. Hence the Apostle: “We are the good odor of Christ to God, among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing. For by the good odor, some are saved and others perish” (2 Cor. II).

[Col. 0251A] **VERSE 35.—A sword.** (BEDE.) The sorrow of the Lord’s Passion, etc., up to she sees the weeds sprouting.

**So that the thoughts may be revealed.** Previously it was uncertain which Jews would receive Christ’s grace and which would spit upon him. But when his birth was heard, their thoughts were revealed: Herod and others were troubled, while some approached Christ’s teaching.

**VERSE 36.—And there was Anna, etc.** Because the life of the whole world was lost through a man and a woman, Anna is joined to Simeon in bearing witness to the life restored through Christ. This accords with the mysteries of the Church: “Anna” is interpreted as “grace”; she was the daughter of Phanuel, whose name means “face of God.” Hence the psalm: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Psalm IV).

**Of the tribe of Asher.** That is, “of the blessed.” She was descended from Asher, who is eighth in birth-order among the twelve patriarchs, because of the mystery of the resurrection. There are five Annas: the first, Samuel’s mother; the second, Raguel’s wife; the third, Tobiah’s mother; the fourth, the daughter of Phanuel; the fifth, Mary’s mother.

**She had advanced in days.** (BEDE.) According to the historical account, Anna, devoted to a religious way of life, etc., up to they multiply because of apostolic teaching.

**VERSE 38.—To all who, etc.** To all the faithful who, weighed down by the yoke of the foreign Herod, awaited the liberation of the city and people, she promised that, through Christ’s coming, redemption from the tyranny of the foreigner was near.

**VERSE 40.—But the child.** (BEDE.) Insofar as he was a child, etc., up to when he had begun to become human, he was perfect as God.

**VERSE 41.—And his parents went, etc.** (ID.) Luke is rightly compared among the four living creatures to the calf, etc., up to he concludes his Gospel with the Lord’s disciples praising him in the temple at the end.

**VERSE 45.—And when they did not find him.** (BEDE.) If it is asked how he could have been left behind by his parents through forgetfulness, etc., up to he returned with the other parent.

**VERSE 46.—In the midst.** (ID.) Like a fountain, he sits in the midst of the teachers; but, as an example of humility, he first asks and listens before instructing, lest the young be ashamed to be taught by their elders or the weak presume to teach.

**VERSE 49.—Why were you looking for me?** (ID.) He does not reproach them because they sought him as a son, but intimates who his true Father is [Col. 0251D] and compels them to raise the eyes of their minds toward what he ought rather to do for him whose eternal Son he is. Since he is both God and man, he now presents the exalted things of divinity and now the weakness of humanity. As the Son of God, he remains in the temple; as the Son of Man, he returns with his parents wherever they command.

**VERSE 51.—And his mother kept all these words in her heart.** Everything she learned concerning the Lord or from the Lord—whether she understood it or could not yet understand it—she stored in her memory, so that when the time came to preach or write about his Incarnation, she could adequately explain everything to those who asked, exactly as it had happened. In the same way, through frequent meditation on the Lord’s deeds and words, let us drive away intrusive thoughts and labor to instruct others.

**VERSE 52.—He advanced in wisdom.** (BEDE.) Just as there is advancement in the age of the flesh, etc., up to both might be saved together.

## CHAPTER III

**VERSE 2.—The word came, etc.** (BEDE.) As the Son of God was about to gather the Church, he first acts in his servant, etc., up to thus he spoke one thing and declared everything.

**VERSE 3.—Preaching a baptism of repentance, etc.** (ID.) John preached a baptism of repentance and also administered it to some, etc., up to he would be preceded by his baptism, through which sins cannot be loosed.

**VERSE 4.—The voice of one crying.** “Voice,” because he is the herald of the Word.

**In the wilderness.** Because he announces the consolation of redemption to Judea, which had been deserted and abandoned. No word is heard without a voice, nor is a voice effective without understanding of the word.

**Prepare the way of the Lord, etc.** Whoever preaches faith and good works does nothing other than prepare a way for the coming Lord into the hearts of his hearers, so that the power of grace may illuminate them and make straight paths for God, while forming pure thoughts in the mind through the sermon of preaching.

**VERSE 5.—And the crooked places will be, etc.** (BEDE.) “Crooked places,” that is, the hearts of the wicked, distorted by injustice, will be directed toward the rule of justice.

**VERSE 6.—And will see.** (ID.) In this life no human being could see Christ, but on the day of judgment, in the seat of majesty, both the elect and the reprobate will see him alike, so that [Col. 0252C] the righteous may be rewarded and the wicked mourn forever. Hence it is also added:

## Verse 7.—“Who showed,” etc.? (AMBROSE.)

Who showed this in the prudence infused by the mercy of God, etc., up to the point where he prophesies that it would be transferred to the Gentiles.

## Verse 8.—“For I say to you.”

(ID.) He who, having lost the sense of reason, etc., up to “they are filled with fruits and clothed with foliage.”

## Verse 11.—“Whoever has two.”

(BEDA.) A tunic is more necessary for one’s own use than a cloak, etc., up to “but let him share with the poor what he has.”

## Verse 12.—“Tax collectors.”

(ID.) Those who collect public taxes, etc., up to the point where they would finally reach the sharing of their own possessions with their neighbors.

## Verse 15.—“But while the people were thinking.”

Not only were they thinking, etc., up to “they do not believe that he came through a virgin.”

## Verse 16.—“But he will come.”

I baptize with water because he has come who will baptize with the Spirit, and it is necessary that the way be prepared for him.

### “Of whom I am not worthy.”

(BEDA.) I am not worthy to investigate the mystery of the Incarnation, etc., up to the evangelical preaching with which the apostles were shod.

## Verse 19.—“Herod.”

Before Luke narrates anything about Jesus’ deeds, he says that John was seized by Herod, in order to show that he would describe only those events that took place in the year in which John was either arrested or punished.

## Verse 21.—“And when Jesus had been baptized.”

(BEDA.) The Lord is baptized, although he had no need to be cleansed, etc., up to the point where he, now instructed, openly proclaims the Son of God.

## Verse 22.—“In you I am well pleased.”

It is not another’s glory that is praised in the Son, but his own, as though he were saying: “Whatever you have is mine.”

## Verse 23.—“About thirty years old.”

(BEDA.) That he was baptized at the age of thirty, etc., up to “as in Jeremiah and Daniel.”

## Verse 26.—“Who was the son of Mattathias, who was the son of Amos, who was the son of Nahum, who was the son of Esli.”

(BEDA.) Mattath, who descended through Solomon, etc., up to the one who is shown by carnal generation to have become the Son of Man.

## Verse 29.—“Who was the son of Levi.”

These four who are introduced here were not sons of Jacob, but they shared in their names.

(BEDA.) As though alluding by their names to what was prefigured in them, etc., up to the point where various kinds of virtues would go before.

## Verse 31.—“Nathan.”

(ID.) That Matthew traces the genealogy through Solomon, etc., up to the one to whom judgment is entrusted by God the King: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

## Verse 37.—“Methuselah.”

(AMBROSE.) Methuselah’s years are counted beyond the Flood; this signifies Christ, whose life knows no age-limit.

### “Who was the son of Enoch.”

(BEDA.) From the baptized Son of God, ascending to God the Father, he places Enoch at the seventieth degree, etc., up to the point where he shows that they are to be joined for all ages in contemplating the unchangeable wisdom of God in the resurrection.

## Verse 38.—“Seth.”

Seth, Adam’s later son, is not passed over in silence, so that, since there are two generations of the peoples, he may signify that Christ is to be reckoned in the later rather than in the earlier generation.

### “Who was the son of God.”

The generation begins from the Son of God and ends in the Son of God. He goes before as one created in figure, so that he may follow as one born in truth; he goes before as one made in the image, so that for his sake the Image may descend.

# Chapter IV

## Verse 1.—“And he was led.”

(AMBROSE.) He was led into the desert with this purpose: to challenge the devil; for unless the devil had fought, this one would not have conquered for me; in mystery, to free Adam from exile; by example, to show us that the devil envies those striving toward better things.

### “Into the desert.”

Historically: into that desert which lies between Jerusalem and Jericho, where he had said figuratively that Adam was overcome by the devil.

## Verse 2.—“He was hungry.”

(BEDA.) It is not written of Moses or Elijah, etc., up to “but he hungers not so much for bodily food as for the salvation of the soul.”

## Verse 3.—“If you are the Son of God.”

(AMBROSE.) He knew that the Son of God would come, but he did not think that he had come through the weakness of the body, etc., up to “whoever does not feed on this word does not live.”

## Verse 4.—“It is written.”

He teaches that one must fight by teaching rather than by miracles, by humility rather than by power, and that nothing should be done at the devil’s prompting or merely for the display of power.

## Verse 5.—“And he led him.”

Luke follows the course of events as they happened, placing greed in the middle and pride last, in accordance with the character of the present age, because pride rages after all the other virtues. Matthew does not follow the historical order, but the order of Adam’s temptations.

## Verse 6.—“I will give you.”

He says this out of arrogance, not because the whole world belongs to him—for there are some who are good. “It has been handed over to me.” Power does not come from the devil, although it is nevertheless exposed to the devil’s attacks. Nor is the ordering of powers therefore evil, because the powers are subject to evil.

## Verse 7.—“You, therefore.”

(BEDA.) When the devil says to the Savior, “If you fall down and worship me,” he hears in return that he himself ought rather to worship him, his Lord and God.

## Verse 8.—“If you are the Son of God.”

In all the temptations he is trying to discover whether he is the Son of God. But Christ shapes his answer in such a way as to leave the matter ambiguous: “Throw yourself down.” The one whom neither gluttony nor greed overcame is tempted by vainglory, to see whether perhaps even the boastfulness of his victory might cast him down. “Throw yourself.” This voice suits one who strives to cast everyone down. In this he is shown to be weak, since he can harm no one unless that person first throws himself down.

## Verse 9.—“It is written.”

Because he had brought forward an example from the Scriptures, he is defeated by examples from the Scriptures. The devil uses testimonies from Scripture through heretics, not to teach but to deceive.

## Verse 10.—“Angels.”

(BEDA.) This prophecy is not about Christ, but about a holy man. Even if it were about Christ, he ought also to have remembered what follows: “You will tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample upon the lion and the dragon” (Psalm 90). But he speaks of the angels’ assistance as though to a weak man, while, as a deceiver, he is silent about his being trampled underfoot.

## Verse 13.—“And when it was completed.”

(ID.) Having conquered the three temptations, he says that every temptation was completed, etc., up to the point where he nevertheless fears to press on, lest there be more frequent triumphs.

## Verse 14.—“And his fame went out.”

He was honored not only by those who were present because of the miracles they had seen, but his fame was also spread among those who were absent.

## Verse 15.—“He was teaching.”

After the miracles, behold the wisdom by which he teaches, and by which his teaching magnifies the miracles that preceded it.

## Verse 16.—“And he rose to read.”

(BEDA.) He had not come to be served but to serve, etc., up to the point where he might correct them by the testimony of the reading of prophecy.

## Verse 18.—“The Spirit.”

(ID.) In the preceding passage of prophecy, the Savior speaks about the calling of the Gentiles and the confirmation of the Church, etc., up to “because the Spirit of the Lord is upon him.”

### “To proclaim the Gospel to the poor,” etc.

He understands the Gentiles, who were truly poor. For they possessed neither knowledge of God, nor the law, nor the prophets, nor anything else among good things, and they were deprived of all other spiritual riches.

## Verse 20.—“And when he had folded it.”

(BEDA.) After reading it to those who were present, etc., up to the point where he commits the word to the teacher to be dispensed according to the capacity of his hearers.

## Verse 23.—“Physician.”

Just as they call him the son of a craftsman, so, through the same madness of error, they call him a physician; but truth lies hidden in their error. For he truly was the son of a craftsman, the one through whom, in the beginning, all things were made; the one who works in the Holy Spirit and in fire; the one who makes vessels of various kinds in the great house of this world. He is also a physician, because through him all things in heaven and on earth have been restored. He says of himself: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matthew 9).

## Verse 24.—“Amen, I say to you.”

(BEDA.) Not only the Lord and head of the prophets, etc., up to the point where he turns away the miracles of his power.

## Verse 25.—“In the days of Elijah.”

(ID.) As though he were saying: “This is not contrary to the example of the prophets,” etc., up to “because there was no abundance of divine knowledge.”

## Verse 26.—“A widow.”

(ID.) The widow to whom Elijah was sent represents the Church of the Gentiles, etc., up to the point where the bread of eternal life is prepared for us in her.

## Verse 27.—“Naaman the Syrian.”

(ID.) Naaman, whose name is interpreted as “beauty,” signifies the people of the nations, etc., up to “because those who have been baptized must be strengthened by participation in the Lord’s body.”

## Verse 29.—“And they led him out.”

(ID.) The Jews, worse than disciples, with the devil as their teacher, etc., up to the point where they are preserved as though impressed by the hand of the divine Sculptor.

## Verse 31.—“And he went down,” etc.

(ID.) Neither moved by indignation nor offended by wickedness, etc., up to “nor is the law dissolved if there is a renewal of the fallen human being.”

[Col. 0255C] ## Verse 33.—“And in the synagogue.”

(ID.) In the synagogue there is a man who has an unclean spirit, because he had lost the Holy Spirit. The devil had entered, from where Christ had spiritually departed.

## Verse 34.—“I know who you are.”

The Son of God could be proved by his works. But did he not say to the apostles, “You will do greater works”? The answer is: by works—that is, by the manner of working. Others were saying, “In the name of Jesus,” etc.; he himself was saying, “I have commanded you,” etc.

## Verse 35.—“And when he had thrown him down.”

(BEDA.) He permits the man being healed to be thrown into the midst by the demon, so that, once his power has been revealed, it may invite more people to salvation.

## Verse 36.—“And with power.”

He does not work miracles like human beings who cast out demons by the word of God, but by his own power.

## Verse 38.—“Into Simon’s house.”

Peter’s house is the circumcision entrusted to his apostolate. The mother-in-law is the Synagogue, which in a certain way is the mother of the Church entrusted to Peter. She is feverish because she was suffering from the heat of envy while persecuting the Church. But Jesus, standing over her, heals her, because wherever the fear of God begins to exist, such feverish agitation usually withdraws.

## Verse 40.—“When the sun had set.”

(BEDA.) The setting of the sun signifies Christ’s Passion, through which more demoniacs are healed than he had previously healed sick people while living in the flesh, because while living in the flesh he taught only a few Jews, whereas after the resurrection he appeared to the Gentiles.

## Verse 41.—“You are the Son of God.”

(ID.) When the devil saw him wearied by fasting, etc., up to “because, if they had known the Lord of glory, they would never have crucified him” (Matthew 1).

## Verse 42.—“When it became day.”

Mystically: in the manifest light of the resurrection he is sought by the throngs of believers; and, found in the desert of the Gentiles, he is held back so that he may not depart.

# Chapter V

## Verse 1.—“And it came to pass.”

The crowd is restrained from its zeal for healing neither by time nor by place. Evening is approaching, yet it follows; a lake lies before them, yet the crowd presses on, and therefore he gets into Peter’s boat.

### “He was standing beside it.”

(BEDA.) The lake signifies the present age. But the Lord is now no longer in the lake, as though no longer in passible flesh, but beside the lake, because in the flesh in which he suffered he entered the stability of perpetual rest.

## Verse 2.—“He saw two boats.”

(ID.) Mystically, the two boats signify circumcision and uncircumcision. He saw them because he knows who are his in both peoples; their hearts, through merciful living, come from the waves of this age to the tranquility of the future life, as to a shore.

## Verse 3.—“He asked him.”

(ID.) The fact that he first asks for the boat to be moved back a little from the land, etc., belongs to the more distant nations to whom the preaching was later extended.

## Verse 4.—“Put out into the deep.”

(AMBROSE.) Although others are commanded to let down the nets, etc., up to the point where the Church is furnished and armed with gifts flowing from the Holy Spirit.

## Verse 5.—“At your word,” etc.

(BEDA.) Unless the instruments of disputation are let down by the word of grace, etc., up to the point where they do so even amid the scandals of their persecutors.

## Verse 7.—“And they filled.”

(ID.) This fullness increases until the end of the age, etc., up to the point where such humility merits the Lord’s compassionate consolation.

## Verse 10.—“From now on.”

(ID.) This applies particularly to Peter himself, to whom the meaning of the catch of fish is explained. But just as at that time he caught fish with nets, so at another time he will catch human beings with words; in this Peter is a type of the whole Church.

## Verse 12.—“In one of the cities.”

Here two visits to Capernaum are noted. The first was when John had been imprisoned, when he performed those three miracles in succession; the second was when he came down from the mountain with the chosen apostles, when this miracle of the leper took place.

[Col. 0256D] ## Verse 13.—“He touched him.”

Because of humility, to teach us not to despise anyone on account of any bodily blemish. He touches without disdaining, commands without doubting, and supplies the testimony of an action. “I will.” He says this because of Photinus, commands because of Arius, and touches because of Manichaeus.

## Verse 14.—“He commanded him.”

(BEDA.) He commands him to remain silent, yet he cannot remain silent. This is not because he wanted something and could not accomplish it, but because he gives an example: his own followers should wish to remain hidden in the great things they do; yet, so that they may benefit others, they should be revealed against their will.

## Verse 15.—“And the crowds were coming together,” etc.

(BEDA.) The healing of this man draws many crowds to the Lord. In order to show that he had been healed both inwardly and outwardly, he does not remain silent about the benefit he received, even though he had been commanded to do so. But Mark also says, fulfilling his evangelical duty: “Immediately he went out and began to preach and spread the report” (Mark 1).

## Verse 16.—“And he was praying.”

When he prays, he represents the contemplative life; when he heals, the active life.

(BEDA.) He heals as God and prays as a human being. In the city, etc., up to the point where he speaks silently through inward desires.

## Verse 17.—“And it came to pass,” etc.

(ID.) Luke passed over for the sake of brevity the place where he taught while seated, etc., up to the one whom he had made his own not by birth but by illuminating him with virtues.

### “And there were.”

(AMBROSE.) Among the remedies for the other infirm, as they gathered together, etc., up to the point where the limping traces of our actions may be restored by the remedy of the heavenly word.

## Verse 18.—“Men carrying.”

Allegorically: that is, raising the human mind toward higher things, although it may be sluggish because of the weakness of the outward person; through whose support he is taught more easily both to raise and to humble himself before Jesus, so as to be deemed worthy of the Lord’s gaze. For God regards humility.

### “And they were seeking,” etc.

(BEDA.) They desire to bring him forward, but are shut out by the intervening crowd, because often the soul, etc., up to the point where one descends to Christ’s humility through the devoutness of faith and arrives at knowledge of Christ.

## Verse 19.—“And through the roof tiles.”

(ID.) Jesus’ house is described as roofed with tiles, because beneath the contemptible covering of the letter, if there is a teacher who can open divine things, the power of spiritual grace is found. When he is lowered with the bed, this signifies that Christ must be known by a human being who is still established in this flesh.

[Col. 0257C] ## Verse 20.—“When he saw their faith.”

(BEDA.) Each person’s own faith is very powerful when, through another’s faith, a person is saved inwardly and outwardly.

(ID.) This healing of the paralytic signifies the salvation of the soul sighing toward God, etc., up to the virtues of prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice.

### “Man, your sins are forgiven,” etc.

You are a sinful human being; I am God, who forgives sins, and who, on account of the merit of others, releases you from your sins. Therefore, whoever is weighed down by sins should call upon the Church to pray for him.

Because the body had also become weak on account of the soul’s guilt, he first heals the soul in order to heal the body.

## Verse 21.—“Who can forgive?”

No one forgives sins except God, who also forgives through those to whom he has given the power of forgiving. Therefore, since Christ forgives, he is truly proved to be God. They give true testimony to God, but they err by denying Christ’s person. For unbelief can confess, but it cannot believe. Thus testimony is not lacking for the divinity, but faith is lacking for salvation.

Now God, wishing to save sinners, demonstrates that he is God both by his knowledge of hidden things and by the wonder of his deeds, answering them: “Why are you thinking evil in your hearts?” By the same majesty and power with which I see your thoughts, I can forgive sins to human beings. From yourselves understand what the paralytic receives. But because you do not recognize spiritual grace, nor believe what has been done inwardly, let what is not less powerful be proved by a visible sign, so that in the Son of Man you may recognize the hidden power of majesty by which, as God, he can forgive sins.

## Verse 22.—“But when he perceived,” etc.

(AMBROSE.) The great priest saw leprosy in the hearts of the Jews and showed them to be worse than that leper whom, after cleansing him, he commanded to present himself to the priest. But the high priest rejects these people, lest their leprosy also contaminate others.

## Verse 24.—“I say to you, rise.”

(BEDA.) To rise means to withdraw the soul from carnal desires. To take up one’s bed, etc., up to “understand the remission of guilt through the removal of punishment.”

## Verse 26.—“And amazement.”

(AMBROSE.) The unbelievers watch the man rising and marvel at him going away; they prefer to fear the miracles of divine work rather than believe them. For if they believed, they would not fear but love. “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4).

## Verse 27.—“Levi.”

(BEDA.) Levi is the same person as Matthew. But Luke, etc., up to the point where a tax collector was changed into an evangelist.

(BEDA, AMBROSE.) He left his own possessions—the man who had been seizing what belonged to others. He abandoned not only the profits of tax collection but also the danger that could come from the rulers of the age, because he had left the accounts of the taxes unsettled. And because he kept for himself no regard or thought whatsoever for this life, he deserved to become a faithful steward of the Lord’s talents.

(BEDA.) Through Matthew’s election, the faith of the Gentiles is expressed: those who had previously yearned after worldly things now diligently refresh themselves with devotion to Christ’s body. Through the pride of the Pharisees, the envy of the Jews is suggested, an envy tortured by the salvation of the Gentiles.

## Verse 30.—“Why,” etc.

(AMBROSE.) Every question arising from the law, which is tenacious of justice, does not have, etc., up to the point where walking and everything he did serve salvation.

(AMBROSE, BEDA.) Whoever receives Christ within the dwelling of his heart is nourished by the greatest abundance of overflowing delights. Therefore the Lord enters and reclines in the affection of the one who has believed. But the envy of the unbelieving is kindled again, and an image of future punishment is prefigured. For while the faithful feast and recline in the kingdom of heaven, unbelief will be tormented in hunger.

The difference between the rivals of the law and of grace is also shown: those who follow the law will suffer eternal hunger of mind. But those who receive the Word within, refreshed by the abundance of heavenly food and the fountain, cannot hunger or thirst. Therefore those who are fasting in spirit murmur, saying: “Why with tax collectors,” etc.? The sons of the devil spread the serpent’s poison. The serpent first uttered a voice, saying to Eve: “Why, indeed, did God say, ‘You shall not eat from every tree’?” (Genesis 3). These people imitate him.

## Verse 31.—“Physician.”

Christ is the physician who, by a wondrous method of healing, was wounded for our iniquities. By this medicine the serpent’s poison is expelled. Whoever uses this medicine does not remain hungry.

## Verse 32.—“To call the righteous.”

(BEDA.) He calls “righteous” those who, not knowing God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, are not subject to God’s righteousness; who presume upon the law and do not seek the grace of the Gospel. He calls “sinners” those who, considering their own evils and thinking that they cannot be justified through the law, submit themselves in repentance to Christ’s grace.

## Verse 33.—“Why do the disciples,” etc.

(BEDA.) Matthew says that the disciples themselves asked this. But it must be understood that both groups asked.

(ID.) Spiritually: the disciples of John and of the Pharisees fast, because those who perform the works of the law, etc., up to the point where you may understand grace and power.

## Verse 34.—“Surely you cannot.”

(ID.) As long as the bridegroom is with us and we are in joy, we cannot fast, etc., up to the point where the bridegroom’s sons will fast, longing for the Judge’s coming.

[Col. 0259B] ## Verse 35.—“But the days will come.”

(ID.) As though he were saying: “You will cause them to fast in mourning, because you are,” etc., up to the time when the Lord lived among the disciples in the flesh.

### “Then they will fast,” etc.

He answers concerning both kinds of fasting, that which occurs in tribulation and that which occurs in joy: “When the bridegroom has been taken away, then they will be in sorrow and mourning until consolation is given through the Holy Spirit.” Having received that gift, they will celebrate the fast that arises from joy, renewed now into spiritual life.

Here he first treats of the fast that belongs to the humility of tribulation. But the fast that belongs to joy of mind—when the mind is lifted toward spiritual things and is therefore separated from bodily foods—he indicates by the following comparisons, showing that this kind of fasting is not suited to those who are carnal and therefore still retain the old understanding.

## Verse 36.—“From a new garment.”

(BEDA.) The disciples are compared to an old garment, because they are still the old person. To them a new patch, etc., up to the words of the Apostle: “Put off the old person with his deeds, and put on the new” (Ephesians 4).

## Verse 37.—“Wine.”

By wine we are refreshed inwardly; by clothing we are covered outwardly. The garment, therefore, is the good works that we perform outwardly, by which we shine before human beings. The wine is the fervor of faith, hope, and charity, by which we are inwardly renewed in the presence of God through the newness of our understanding.

### “Into wineskins.”

(BEDA.) Those who are still old are also compared to wineskins; they are more easily burst by new wine—that is, by spiritual commandments—than they are able to contain it. They will be new wineskins when, after the Ascension, having received the Spirit, they are renewed through prayer by their desire for his consolation.

Another interpretation: sacraments of the new mysteries should not be entrusted to souls that have not yet been renewed but persist in the oldness of malice.

Another interpretation: the old wineskins are the scribes and Pharisees; the new patch and the new wine are the commandments of the Gospel, which the Jews cannot bear, lest a greater tear be made; with these the Galatians mixed the commandments of the law, putting new wine into old wineskins.

But these things suit the apostles, not those who, corrupted by the traditions of their ancestors, are unable to preserve the sincerity of Christ’s commandments. Hence he adds: “And no one,” because the commandments of the new grace seemed foul to Jews steeped in the saliva of their old life; burdened with the traditions of their ancestors, they could not perceive the sweetness of spiritual words.

## Verse 38.—“But new wine.”

The frailty of the human condition is revealed when our bodies are compared with the cast-off skins of dead animals. But new wines are suitable for renewed wineskins when we preserve inviolate the sacraments we have received. Grace preserves these wineskins when they are full; when they are empty, moth and rust consume them. Therefore let them always be full.

# Chapter VI

## Verse 1.—“And it came to pass,” etc.

(BEDA.) He says that the letter of the Sabbath had begun to be dissolved, etc., up to “after the second [Sabbath],” counted from the time when the preceding things were said or done.

[Col. 0260B] Through the grainfields, etc., mystically: the field is the world; the crop of the field is the fruitfulness of the human race; the ears of grain are the fruits of the Church, by which the apostles are filled, nourishing themselves on our progress.

### “His disciples were plucking,” etc.

Since the disciples had no opportunity to eat because of the crowds’ persistent demands, they were hungry as human beings; but by plucking ears of grain they comforted their hunger. This indicates a more austere life: not seeking prepared foods but simple nourishment.

Notice also that the apostles are already destroying the letter of the Sabbath against the Ebionites, who accept other apostles but reject Paul as though he were a transgressor of the law.

(BEDA.) Mystically: the disciples, hungering for the salvation of human beings, pass through the grainfields—that is, through regions which, etc., up to the point where he rebukes the teachers of the law for not knowing the law.

## Verse 2.—“They were saying to them,” etc.

Some say that these objections were made to the Lord himself. But it must be understood that they could have been made both to the Lord himself and to the disciples by different people; and whoever was addressed, the objection applies chiefly to him.

### “On the Sabbaths.”

The Sabbaths signify times of rest: either those observed in this age by people free from Jewish superstitions, or those that will be observed in the future, when in perpetual solemnity we shall eat the good things of the earth.

## Verse 3.—“Have you not read even this,” etc.?

(BEDA.) How can the Lord be accused of something that is not counted as a crime in a servant? The true King, etc., up to the point where all the sons of the Church are priests, anointed by the Holy Spirit so that they may offer themselves.

## Verse 4.—“He entered the house of God.”

Because of the great grace of hospitality, the priest’s spirit does not refuse a guest even when death is threatened. So we too ought to take upon ourselves the dangers of others. But the true David likewise enters the lodging of the mind, and the priests do not exclude him even at the danger of death.

## Verse 6.—“A man.”

(BEDA.) Mystically, this man signifies the human race, dried up in the fruitfulness of good works by the hand stretched out toward the tree in the first parent; the innocent hand stretched out upon the cross heals it. And fittingly the hand was withered in the synagogue, because where there is the greater gift of knowledge, there the transgressor is subject to greater guilt.

## Verse 7.—“They were watching.”

(ID.) Because he had excused by a credible example of the master the destruction of the Sabbath that they had criticized in the disciples, they now wish to accuse the master himself by watching him, so that if he does not heal, they may accuse him of cruelty or weakness, and if he does heal, of transgression.

## Verse 9.—“I ask you.”

(BEDA.) Anticipating the accusation they were preparing against him, he rebukes them, etc., up to the point where God is not the author of evil, although he is said to destroy those whom he does not save.

## Verse 10.—“Stretch out.”

(ID.) The fruitless weakness of the soul is healed by no better order than by the generosity of almsgiving. Hence it is said: “Do not let your hand be stretched out to receive and closed when giving” (Ecclesiasticus 4). For one who does not stretch out his hands to the poor according to his ability stretches them out to God in vain when asking for his sins to be forgiven.

## Verse 11.—“Folly.”

Because they were moved only by jealousy; for it was not a fault either for the man to stretch out his hand or for Jesus to heal him. It was great folly to plot the death of one whose benefits they greatly needed.

## Verse 12.—“He went out onto the mountain to pray.”

The mountain on which he chooses and teaches the apostles signifies the height of righteousness, because they were to be instructed and to preach, so that they would not remain among the weak but be raised toward heavenly things. Thus the law too was given on a mountain. He brings the apostles up more eminently, so that the mountains might first receive peace from the mountain and announce it to the people. Likewise Moses, alone understanding the law spiritually, ascended to the summit of the mountain where God was.

## Verse 13.—“The disciples.”

From among them he chose twelve, whom he called apostles—that is, those sent in his place. Hence: “As the Father sent me, so I send you” (John 20).

As he ascends the mountain, he calls them to himself and chooses whom he wills, because it was not their own effort but divine grace that caused them to be called to the apostolate. Hence: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (ibid., 15).

He did not choose the wise, the rich, or the noble, lest he seem to have drawn some to grace by wisdom, bought them by wealth, or attracted them by the authority of power and nobility.

## Verse 14.—“He surnamed.”

Not only at this point, but much earlier, when he is said to have been brought by Andrew: “You will be called Cephas,” which is interpreted as “Peter.” But because Luke wished to name the twelve apostles and necessarily had to mention Peter, he briefly indicated that he had not previously been called by that name. Rather, the Lord gave him the surname so that it would not be thought to have happened by chance, but so that the mystery of the rock might be commended to the hearers through the change.

[Col. 0261D] ## Verse 15.—“Matthew.”

Matthew places himself below his companion Thomas in the order, out of humility, although he is placed before him by the other evangelists.

## Verse 17.—“And coming down,” etc.

When the Lord was about to choose the apostles, he went up into the mountains; when he was about to teach the crowds, he returned to the level places. For crowds are capable of seeing Christ only in a humble place, and it is rarely found either that a crowd follows the Lord to higher things or that a weak person is healed on the mountain. Rather, once the fever of lust has been extinguished and the light of knowledge kindled, each person gradually climbs the summit of the virtues.

### “The seacoast.”

Not the nearby Sea of Galilee, because they do not place this event among the miracles occurring there, but it is named after the Great Sea. Tyre and Sidon could also be included in it. But because they are cities of the Gentiles, they are deliberately named, so that the extent of Christ’s power might be indicated—power that arouses even foreign cities.

## Verse 18.—“To hear.”

If we say that there were two sermons—he ascended the mountain and had the disciples there, and afterward descended and delivered this sermon to the crowd—then this is how it should be understood.

If we say that there was one sermon, it should be understood in this way: he ascended the mountain, and after a little while descended and delivered the sermon there, where there was level ground.

## Verse 19.—“To touch him.”

The person who faithfully believes in Christ touches him. The person who is strengthened in Christ is touched by Christ. Whoever both touches and is touched in this way is healed by the power of his spirit.

## Verse 20.—“And he, raising his eyes,” etc.

Although he speaks generally to everyone, he raises his eyes particularly toward the disciples, so that those who receive the word of God with the attentive ear of the heart may receive more abundantly the light of inward savor. To these he opens his mouth while seated on the mountain, so that he may utter great things; standing on the plain, he directs his eyes toward them, so that they may patiently understand what they have heard.

### “Blessed are the poor,” etc.

Those who cannot yet climb to the summit of perfected virtue should meanwhile be nourished by the blessedness of general perfection, so that, gradually progressing toward better things, while they willingly listen to the Lord standing on the plain, they may eventually ascend sublimely to him seated on the mountain.

For those whose hearts he is still laboring to subdue he addresses as though standing; those whom he finds trained by long discipline and already teachable he instructs in mysteries as though peacefully seated.

(BEDA.) What is said fully in Matthew through the eight beatitudes, in the sermon of perfection to the apostles on the summit of the mountain, is said in Luke, etc., up to the point where, because he excelled in faith, he deserved primacy above the others through faith.

## Verse 21.—“You who are hungry now.”

The one who hungers has compassion on the hungry; by having compassion he gives; by giving he becomes righteous. He presents himself as equal to those beneath him, excludes deceit, and seeks truth.

### “You who weep now.”

Whoever desires weeping, hunger, and poverty for the sake of the riches of Christ’s inheritance, the bread of eternal life, and the hope of heavenly joys is blessed; much more blessed is the one who does not hesitate to preserve these virtues amid adversity.

## Verse 23.—“Rejoice and exult.”

Amid hatred in people’s hearts, insults on their tongues, and the hands of persecutors, conduct yourselves with a more joyful heart, in view of the heavenly reward.

### “According to these things.”

He strengthens them by the example of the prophets, because those who speak the truth commonly suffer persecution.

## Verse 24.—“Nevertheless, woe,” etc.

Matthew describes on the mountain only the beatitudes of the good; Luke, however, also describes the woes of the wicked on the plain, because inexperienced hearers must still be compelled to good things by threats and terrors, whereas it is enough to invite the perfect by rewards.

### “Nevertheless, woe.”

Since above it is said that the kingdom of heaven belongs to the poor, it becomes apparent by contrast that the one who seeks consolation in temporal things alienates himself from this kingdom. It is not riches themselves but the love of riches that is at fault.

[Col. 0263A] Mystically: the rich man is the Jewish people, or the heretic, or the philosopher of the world. Delighting in an abundance of words and the support of eloquence, they have gone beyond the simplicity of true faith and stored up useless treasures, disputing according to worldly custom about the generation of Christ. In the future they will recognize the poverty of their faith and will know that the food of unbelief which they now belch forth, having been tormented by eternal fasting, is the cause of so great a punishment.

There will be a time when they will mourn their laughter. To them it is rightly said: “Woe to you when people bless you,” because, while they please the powerful here, they subject themselves to perpetual condemnation. For just as the poor, the hungry, and those who weep are tested by the wickedness of evil people, so those who devote themselves to riches, feasts, and laughter are nourished toward a greater punishment by the evil patronage of those who serve them.

## Verse 25.—“You who are filled,” etc.

You who abound more greatly among the rich, like the rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted lavishly, and who sought a drop of water from Lazarus’s finger.

### “Woe to you who laugh now,” etc.

Solomon says: “The heart of the wise is where there is sadness, and the heart of fools where there is joy” (Ecclesiastes 7), teaching that folly is to be attributed to those who laugh, and prudence to those who weep.

## Verse 26.—“When they bless you,” etc.

A great part of sinners’ punishment is that their crimes are not only left unrebuked but are even praised as though they had been well done.

## Verse 27.—“Love your enemies.”

Having stated what they might suffer from enemies, he next explains how they ought to conduct themselves toward those enemies. Here the Church is not nourished with milk but strengthened by the more solid food of charity. It is not enough not to hate; what is beyond human nature is commanded: to love.

Although the law commands reciprocal vengeance, the Gospel grants charity in place of enmity, kindness in place of hatred, prayers in place of curses, patience toward persecutors, and even the grace of reward to the hungry.

## Verse 28.—“Pray for those who slander you.”

What the prophets seem to invoke as curses are not the wishes of those praying, but predictions of what was to come; for they themselves prayed for their enemies.

## Verse 29.—“And whoever strikes you.”

Since charity is patient, it must endure the patience-testing act of the one who strikes; since it is kind, it must not answer curses with curses. If it does not seek what belongs to it, it must not resist the one who takes things away; if it is not jealous (1 Corinthians 13), it must not hate the enemy.

### “Offer to them,” etc.

The physician of souls, instructing them to heal their neighbors, commands them to endure everything that may contribute to their neighbors’ salvation. It belongs to mercy that, as with sick and delirious children, they should suffer many things if the salvation of those children requires it, until the illness passes.

What is so remarkable as to offer one’s cheek to the person who strikes? Rather, every impulse of indignation is broken and anger is calmed; through patience the other person is invited to repentance.

### “The garment.”

What is said about the garment and tunic is also to be done with other things that we claim are temporarily ours by some right. For if this is commanded concerning necessities, how much more are we commanded to despise what is superfluous.

[Col. 0264A] **VERSE 30.**—“Do not demand it back.” Because love is patient and kind (1 Cor. III), it not only bears the injuries of an enemy bravely, but also kindly anticipates the favor of a friend, so that others may be drawn by acts of kindness.

**VERSE 31.**—“And as you wish.” Lest he appear to abolish the law, he preserves reciprocity in benefits, though he sets it aside in injuries. He does not say, “As they do,” but, “As you wish that people should do to you, you also do to them,” so that the reciprocity may be more complete, when action is matched to desire. And extend works of love not only to friends, but also to enemies, so that they may begin to be friends; first extend the disposition of love, and afterward its works.

**VERSE 32.**—“And if you love.” The more distinguished your rank of profession is, the more abundant your care for virtue must be, so that you may embrace even those who do not love you in the bosom of charity.

There are two kinds of benefit: either when we give willingly what we give, or when we lend something to be repaid.

**VERSE 35.**—“Nevertheless,” etc. After rebuking the love and reciprocal benefit of sinners as though they were fruitless, he now shows how these things ought to be done fruitfully by the faithful, as though he were saying: Although such love and reciprocal benefit do not profit sinners, nevertheless you must love—not merely by the prompting of nature, as they love their friends, but at a higher level of virtue, your enemies. Philosophers divide justice into three parts: one toward God, which is called piety; another toward parents and the rest of the human race; and a third toward the dead, so that the proper funeral rites may be paid to them. But the Lord, surpassing the utterance of the law and the summit of prophecy, extended the duty of piety even toward those who had caused injury.

“Expecting nothing from it; and your reward will be great.” Do not place your hope of reward in a human being. Whether the person repays what you lent, God too will repay, since you acted at his command; or whether the person does not repay, your inheritance will be eternal.

**VERSE 36.**—“Therefore be merciful,” etc. He sends rain upon the wicked; he does not withhold the produce of the earth; the same sun illuminates the good and the wicked.

Mystically: he waters the Jewish people with prophetic rains, and the ray of the eternal sun has shone even upon those who did not deserve it. If, therefore, they believe, be merciful toward them by teaching and encouraging them; and do not judge rashly, lest someone conscious of his own sin be compelled to pass sentence upon another.

**VERSE 37.**—“Do not judge.” There are certain intermediate and uncertain actions, whose intention is not evident, because they can be done either well or badly. We do not even know what the person who now appears wicked will become. It is rash to despair of that person’s correction and to rebuke him as though he were rejected.

We are permitted to judge concerning manifest actions that cannot be done with a good intention.

**VERSE 38.**—“With the same measure.” This can be understood generally of everything done by thought, hand, or tongue, because God will repay each person according to his works.

[Col. 0265A] “With the same measure,” (AMBROSE). God will not repay with an unjust measure; but it is as though he were saying: The very rashness of judging and the unjust measure harm and punish you, and often do not harm the person against whom you act. Or, if you judge and measure rightly, it benefits and saves you, even if at times it does not benefit the person to whom you extend these things.

**VERSE 39.**—“He was saying.” By this he invites us to give alms and to forgive injury. “Can a blind man.” If anger has blinded you against an aggressive person; if you are avaricious toward someone who asks, can you, with your mind corrupted, cure that person’s vice? And not only will the one who injured you be guilty, but you too will be guilty if you do not know how to bear it. But if that person’s insolence finds you tranquil, both the offender will repent and you will be crowned for your patience, because you have taken care to lead the blind person to the light with a seeing eye—that is, with a serene heart.

**VERSE 40.**—“Like the teacher.” God does not avenge the injuries done to him, but by enduring persecutors he wished to make them gentler; disciples, who are human beings, ought to imitate this rule of perfection.

**VERSE 41.**—“But what do you see,” etc. A sinner truly cannot correct a sinner, because those who are forestalled by pride, hatred, or some other vice—judging these things slight or nonexistent—rebuke severely those whom they see disturbed in mind by anger or some minor sin. Such people prefer to censure and condemn rather than to correct and amend. “You do not consider.” An open eye sees badly—namely, its own self-display, while it wishes to heal others—but the blind person cannot look upon himself while falling into this condition still more disastrously.

[Col. 0265C] **VERSE 42.**—“Hypocrite.” If you wish to rebuke someone, first see whether you are like him. If you are, then groan together with him, and do not tell him to obey you; instead, urge him to strive together with you. If you are not like him, nevertheless, because you once were or could have been, show compassion, and rebuke not from hatred but from mercy. Rebukes, therefore, should rarely be employed, and never without great necessity; they should be used only with regard for God, after removing the beam from one’s own eye.

For these people undertake to accuse everything out of hatred or envy and wish to appear advisers, without providing an example of their own amendment. But first they must remove from the hidden recess of their heart the beam of envy, malice, or pretense, so that they may be able to cast from their brother’s eye the speck of anger or the fault of some envy.

[Col. 0265D] **VERSE 43.**—“There is no tree,” etc. The good or bad tree is not nature, which was created good by God in all things, but a good or bad will. The fruits are works, which cannot be good when the will is bad, nor bad when the will is good. “Nor does a tree.” If you wish to possess true and not counterfeit righteousness, which you display in words, fulfill it in deeds, so that you may be a good tree and be adorned with good fruits. For although a hypocrite may pretend, the one who does evil works is not good; and if he rebukes an innocent person, the one who does good works is not thereby evil. And note that this passage concerns manifest things.

**VERSE 44.**—“For each tree.” The wicked are recognized by their fruit, when they oppress the good and blaspheme God, if not with words, then by their deeds; and they are especially recognized by their impatience in adversity. Fasting, prayer, and things of this kind may be practiced by the false as well as by the good; but the sheep ought not to lay aside their fleeces even if wolves sometimes conceal themselves in them. “He is known.” They are known not by their clothing but by the works they perform. For just as a thorn does not produce a grape, so a good tree produces good fruit and a bad tree bad fruit, and not the reverse. “Nor do they gather figs from thorns.” From thorns—that is, the anxieties of the world—there is no fig, that is, the sweetness of resurrection; nor from a bramble, that is, the pricking of vices, is there a grape, that is, the fruit of the soul. As a grape, being close to earthly things, is corrupted, so it ripens in higher things. Or, from flesh that produces thorns and thistles we do not gather Christ, who hung upon the wood like a grape.

Thorn and bramble signify heretics, from whom no wise person can obtain holiness or virtue; instead, they tear and bloody those who draw near. Or thorns and brambles signify worldly cares and the pricks of vices. The grape and the fig signify the sweetness of a new way of life, for which Christ hungers in us, and the fervor of love that gladdens the human heart.

There is no grape or fig from thorns and brambles, because a mind still burdened by the habit of the old person can indeed pretend, but cannot bear the fruit of the new person. If at times the deeds or words of the wicked benefit the good, it is not the wicked who bring this about; rather, it happens through God’s plan concerning them.

**VERSE 45.**—“He brings forth what is good.” He loves his enemy, gives to everyone who asks, and things of this kind.

“He brings forth what is evil,” etc. He hates his friend, takes away what belongs to another, does not give what is his, and things of this kind; and God judges these according to the intention of the heart. Truly, because fruit proceeds from a good or evil heart, it ought to be judged good or evil, since from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks: that is, what lies within proceeds outwardly in effects, both in words and in deeds. This is with respect to the divine judgment, before which the mouth of the heart speaks, for God does not fail to know the intention from which words proceed. For he also judges words that appear outwardly good not to be good when they proceed from a bad root. Hence he adds: “Why do you call me ‘Lord’?” As though he were saying: Why do you boast that you are putting forth the leaves of right confession, when you display no fruits of good works? “From the abundance.” By the speech of the mouth the Lord signifies everything that proceeds from the heart in action or thought. [Col. 0266D] For “word” is also customarily used for “deed”; hence: “There was no word that he did not show them” (Isa. XXXIX).

**VERSE 46.**—“But why,” etc. This calling appears to be the fruit of a good tree, but because it does not proceed from the richness of charity, God does not judge it good. He sets forth the true distinction between good and bad fruits under another figure:

**VERSE 47.**—“Everyone who comes,” etc. After discussing at length those who are openly wicked and those who are truly or falsely good, he compares good hearers of the word to himself and the wicked to the devil. Just as Christ constructs, teaches, and governs one Church from people of various kinds, intending to lead it into eternal life, so the good hearer builds for himself, through various virtues, a heavenly dwelling in the future, where he will rejoice with Christ at its dedication. And just as the devil drags those who obey him from heaven toward earthly things and sins—where there is no foundation, because evil is without substance—and always hurls them into worse things, so the wicked hearer, whether initiated into the mysteries of Christ or entirely alien to them, is hurled as if into a bottomless pit. He finds nowhere to hold himself, and when he has come into the depth of evils, he despises.

**VERSE 48.**—“He dug deeply.” He digs deeply who, by the precepts of humility, completely removes all earthly things from the hearts of his own people, lest he serve God for the sake of anything transitory, so that God may have an unshaken dwelling in them. “He laid the foundation.” The foundations in the plural are the teachers; the foundation in the singular is Christ, the teacher of teachers.

Morally: the foundations of the house are the good intentions of a virtuous way of life, which the perfect hearer implants in himself through Christian humility, after clearing away the rubble of superfluous thoughts. In himself he spiritually carries out what Christ accomplishes generally in the whole Church.

“In the flood.” Elsewhere he calls this flood “the gates of hell”: “The gates of hell will not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI). This flood occurs in three ways, because each person is tempted either by his own desire, by the insolence of false brethren, or by open external attack. “And it was not shaken.” The danger of the final judgment may be understood through the force of the river’s assault, when the whole Church has been brought to completion. “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV). “Against that house.” Each of our houses is daily battered either by unclean spirits, wicked people, one’s own mind, or the unrest of the flesh. Insofar as they trust in their own strength, they are bent; insofar as they cling to the unconquerable rock, they cannot be shaken.

**VERSE 49.**—“Upon the earth,” etc. The devil builds the world, which is set in wickedness, upon the earth, because he draws people toward love of earthly things. He builds without a foundation because sin does not subsist in its own nature: evil is not a substance. Yet wherever it occurs, it grows together with a good nature—or it is “without a foundation,” that is, without a bottom. As, therefore, a person who is submerged in a pit is held at the bottom of the pit, so a fallen soul remains, as it were, in a certain place at the bottom if it restrains itself within some measure of sin. But when it cannot remain content with the sin into which it has fallen, being led daily toward worse things, it finds no bottom in the pit into which it has fallen by which it might be fixed.

“It fell, and its ruin was great,” etc. Every conscience that does not remain firmly fixed in hope in God cannot stand firm in temptations; and it is driven all the more violently the more it is separated from higher things into those belonging to the world. Truly, all the wicked, and all who are good only in pretense, become worse when any temptation assails them.

## CHAPTER VII

**VERSE 1.**—“When he had finished.” Beautifully, after completing the precepts, he teaches the pattern for carrying out his precepts. Immediately afterward the servant of a Gentile centurion is brought to the Lord to be healed; in him the Gentiles, who were sick under worldly servitude, are represented as destined to be saved by God’s favor. “He entered Capernaum.” “Of the centurion,” etc. He did not enter before he had finished speaking, even if he did not enter immediately after these words. For before he entered, during the interval, the leper was cleansed, as Matthew relates.

**VERSE 3.**—“He sent the elders,” etc. By divine providence the elders of the Jews are sent, and while they are present the sick man is healed, so that they may be without excuse if they refuse to believe.

The centurion sends friends, lest his own presence seem to burden the Lord’s dignity, and lest he appear to have provoked one office by another. This signifies that we who believe from among the Gentiles cannot ourselves come to the Lord, whom we cannot see in the flesh, but come to him who sits at the right hand of the Father. The Gentile people, like a centurion, are surrounded by the soldiery of virtues and by spiritual perfection, which is signified by the number one hundred. They are exalted, asking nothing earthly from the Lord for themselves or their own people, but only the joys of eternal salvation. And these people intercede for servants—that is, for those who are still oppressed by the spirit of slavery through fear—asking the Lord that, as they gradually advance toward higher things, perfect love may cast out fear (1 John IV).

Matthew says that the centurion himself approached; this is to be understood through faith. For it is through faith that one truly approaches God, and this faith is commended by the Lord in the centurion: “I have not found such faith in Israel.” Luke, however, follows the order in which the event occurred, so that we are compelled to understand how Matthew says that he approached.

**VERSE 5.**—“Our nation.” Mystically: the Gentile people, represented by the centurion, have Jesus not far from their house, although they do not dare invite him under their roof, because they fear him while they draw near to his salvation. Whoever uses the natural law rightly, doing the good things he knows, approaches him who is truly good. But to those whom the crimes of pagan error had bound, what is said elsewhere may be appropriately applied: “For some have come from far away” (Mark VIII).

**VERSE 6.**—“And Jesus was going.” Though he could powerfully heal by a word alone, he deigns to visit the sick man in order to commend humility. He who refused to go to heal the ruler’s son, lest he appear to have honored wealth, goes to a servant, lest he be thought to have despised servile condition. Faith shines forth in works when he heals, but humility works more greatly in the affections when he goes. “I am not worthy.” Because of his awareness of Gentile life, he thought himself more burdened by the Lord’s condescension than helped by it, and unable to have Christ as his guest, since, although endowed with faith, he had not yet been instructed in the mysteries. But because divine grace knows how to grant what human weakness does not presume, he deserved, as a figure of the Gentile people, to have his faith praised by the Lord while he was still unbaptized and to have his servant healed.

**VERSE 8.**—“For I too,” etc. If I, a human being under another’s authority, can command those beneath me, how much more can you, who have ministering angels serving above all things, through their ministry and without bodily presence say to illness, “Depart,” and it will depart, and to health, “Come,” and it will come.

**VERSE 9.**—“Not even in Israel.” This man’s faith is placed above that of the more privileged, even those who see God. In this one man the faith of the Gentiles is preferred to Israel.

**VERSE 10.**—“And when they returned.” Matthew explains more explicitly that when the Lord said, “As you have believed, let it be done for you,” the boy was healed (Matt. VIII). But blessed Luke customarily abbreviates what others have clearly explained, or deliberately passes over what others have briefly stated, while more carefully clarifying what they have omitted. “They found the servant.” The servant is healed when the Lord believes, because the merit of the master can also benefit servants, not only through the merit of faith but also through the devotion of discipline.

**VERSE 11.**—“And it happened,” etc. After healing the sick man, he raises the dead, because sickness precedes death.

“Which is called Nain.” Nain is a city of Galilee, two miles from Tabor toward the south, near Endor, which is a large village. Nain is interpreted as “wave” or “disturbance.”
