**VERSE 12.**—“When he drew near,” etc. (BEDE.) When the Word was made flesh, the Gentile people through the gates of faith, etc., up to the point where, meanwhile, he rules in the few Jews who have been converted and finally in their fullness.

“Behold, a dead man was being carried out,” etc. The dead man who is carried out before many people beyond the gate signifies one who sins criminally and does not conceal his sin in the chamber of his heart, but reveals it to others through the evidence of deed or speech, as though through the doors of his city. His mother, the Church, mourns him as her only son. Although the mother Church is gathered from many persons, she is nevertheless one virgin mother Church, while each individual is a son. The gate through which he is carried out is one of the senses by which a person falls into sin: the eye, when he looks in order to lust; the ear, when he listens to idle or shameful things; the tongue, when he lends it to quarrels.

“Her only son to his mother.” (AMBROSE.) Adam is carried from the earth by the four elements, from which the human being is constituted. “He touched the bier,” etc., up to the point when he thinks about avarice, or when he cannot be touched because of excessive fever.

**VERSE 13.**—“And the crowd.” Many were with the Lord, and many with the widow, so that, upon seeing the miracle, many might become praisers and witnesses of God.

**VERSE 15.**—“And he sat up.” The Lord raised three dead persons: the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue in the house, that is, in thought; the only son of his mother at the gate, that is, in speech; and Lazarus in the tomb, that is, in deed.

**VERSE 16.**—“He has visited.” He both ordained that the Word should once become incarnate and sends the Holy Spirit daily into human hearts so that they may be raised.

**VERSE 18.**—“And they reported.” (AMBROSE.) Not with a simple heart, but with envy urging them, etc., up to the point where [Col. 0270A] they may be corrected and believe in Jesus and, when the teacher asks, say to themselves: “Are you the one who is to come?”

(BEDE, GREGORY.) He does not say, “the one who has come,” etc., up to the point that the collapse of love does not impede faith; for such a collapse is religious.

**VERSE 22.**—“And in reply he said to them: Go and report to John what you have seen,” etc. Jesus knew that no one could believe fully without the Gospel, because just as faith begins from the Old Testament, so it is fulfilled in the New. When questioned about himself, he indicated by deeds rather than by any word that he was who he was; he did not answer the questions asked but addressed the scandal of the messengers.

**VERSE 23.**—“Blessed.” As though he were saying: I certainly perform marvelous deeds, but I do not disdain to suffer what is lowly; and people must beware of despising death in me while they venerate signs.

“Whoever is not.” (GREGORY.) Whoever has not doubted the power of his divinity. This is not directed against John, whom he soon praises so greatly, but recalls unbelievers from their faithlessness and explains to John what he was asking, because “God is the God of salvation, and the Lord God belongs to the Lord’s escape from death” (Ps. LXVII). After seeing so many signs and virtues, the faithful person could not doubt his death, but could marvel at it; yet the mind of unbelievers suffered scandal in him when it saw him dying even after the miracles.

**VERSE 24.**—“What.” After teaching that John’s disciples must believe in the Lord’s cross, he turns to the crowds and calls the poor to virtue, lest those lifted up in heart, unstable in mind, and weak in judgment prefer transient splendors to eternal goods, but rather take up the cross than the trappings of the world. Therefore he praises John, who, having set aside the love of life, did not change the pattern of righteousness even through fear of death. The world is compared to a desert because it is still uncultivated and barren; one must not advance into it in such a way as to think that people puffed up in their carnal minds, empty of virtue, and boasting of the glory of the fragile world are worthy of imitation.

“A reed shaken by the wind.” (BEDE.) The reed signifies the carnal mind, which, when touched by approval or slander, bends in any direction. But John is not a reed shaken by the wind, because neither favor made him flattering nor anyone’s anger made him harsh; prosperity did not lift him up, nor adversity bend him.

**VERSE 25.**—“Clothed in soft garments.” Through clothing the human body is understood. Therefore, by a prophetic example, he exhorts us to undertake virtue. “Behold, those in costly clothing.” Those whose limbs are loosened by the flowing softness of riches, strangers to the heavenly kingdom, grow old within the dwellings of this world under the power of demons, who are the rulers of darkness.

**VERSE 26.**—“More than a prophet.” Because he is an angel—not by nature but by office, since he is sent to announce the heavenly judge.

**VERSE 28.**—“But I say.” By this he is not placed above the patriarchs and all human beings, but is shown to be equal to the other saints. “But whoever.” Every saint who is already with God is greater than the one who is still in the world. Or: I, whom the opinion of many makes lesser, have been set above him in the Church of the saints. Or: the last angel of heaven is better than any human being.

**VERSE 29.**—“And all the people.” If this is understood to have been said by the Lord, the people are designated as those who, hearing John, understood. If it is said to have been inserted by the evangelist, then it remains to be understood as referring to those who heard the Lord himself discussing John’s greatness.

**VERSE 31.**—“To what, then,” etc. After praising John, he turns to rebuke those who were moved neither by John’s preaching nor by the preaching of Christ himself.

**VERSE 32.**—“They are like children.” The children are teachers humble in spirit. The marketplace signifies the synagogue, or Jerusalem itself, in which the ordinances of God’s commandments were established. There they were accustomed to reproach their fellow citizens because they had not been moved to praise God with devout hearts by psalms—which is signified by dancing, the agility of the limbs—nor had they been turned to repentance by dirges, that is, the lamentations of the prophets over destructions already accomplished or still to come.

**VERSE 34.**—“The Son of Man came eating and drinking.” He came then, and he comes now, but you reject both ways of salvation. “We lamented for John; we sang for Christ.”

**VERSE 35.**—“Wisdom has been justified.” He shows that the children of wisdom understand that righteousness consists neither in abstaining nor in eating, but in the equanimity with which one endures want and in temperance, so as not to be corrupted by abundance. “The kingdom of God is not food and drink” (Rom. XIV). It is not their use but their desire that is condemned. “Has been justified,” etc. Whatever you may think of me, I am nevertheless rightly understood by the apostles as the power and wisdom of God, to whom the Father revealed what he concealed from the prudent.

**VERSE 36.**—“He was asking.” As he had declared in words, so by deeds also he establishes that wisdom has been justified by all her children, including Mary after repentance from sin.

**VERSE 37.**—“In the house.” In whatever person’s inner house you recognize wisdom and righteousness reclining, hasten to the feet—that is, to the lowest part—of wisdom; seek with tears, confess your sins, spread out your hair—that is, lay all the dignities of your body before him—and kiss him, that is, speak of nothing except wisdom. “She brought.” As many forms of delight as she possessed within herself, so many holocausts did she find in herself.

(JEROME.) “An alabaster flask of ointment,” that is, the body with faith, etc., up to the point where it means the sins of the Jews.

**VERSE 38.**—“She began to bathe.” Mary, the sister of Lazarus, performed the same office twice: once in Galilee, when she first approached in humility and tears, where she received the forgiveness of sins; a second time in Bethany, no longer called a sinner but chaste, and therefore devoted. There she anoints the feet; here, the head.

**VERSE 43.**—“The one to whom more.” In human judgment, perhaps the one who owed more offended more. But through the Lord’s mercy the matter is changed, so that the one who owed more loves more, and yet obtains grace. “You have judged rightly.” The Pharisee is convicted by his own judgment, because, like a madman, he carries the rope by which he will be bound.

**VERSE 44.**—“I entered your house.” I entered the Jewish people in the flesh I assumed.

**VERSE 46.**—“You did not anoint my head with oil.” Even if that people confessed that they believed in God and not in a human being, nevertheless they neglected to proclaim with due praise the very power of the divinity that appeared through miracles. But the Gentile world, while believing the mystery of the Incarnation, proclaims with the highest praise even what is lowly in him.

**VERSE 47.**—“Her sins are forgiven.” In the house of the Pharisee—that is, within the custody of the law and the prophets—it is not the unbelieving Pharisee but the repentant sinner who is glorified, because the ardor of charity burned away the rust of sins in her.

**VERSE 49.**—“And those who were reclining together began.” Once the sick woman was healed, other sick people became concerned about her salvation.

**VERSE 50.**—“Your faith has saved you.” Faith saved her because she did not doubt that she could receive what she asked for; she had already received hope from the one from whom she sought salvation.

## CHAPTER VIII

**VERSE 1.**—“And it happened.” Like an eagle rousing its young to fly, the Lord gradually clothes his disciples with the feathers of virtues in the nest of faith, so that afterward they may be able to fly more loftily and instruct others. First he teaches in the synagogues, performs miracles, spreads his fame everywhere, receives, heals, and instructs the crowds; then he makes disciples, from whom he chooses twelve. At first he teaches them in the presence of the crowd and grants the customary benefits to the afflicted; but now he keeps them alone with him, so that they may hear him more intimately. To them alone he explains the more hidden mysteries, and finally, having strengthened them by the display of his virtues, as though by the protection of wings, he gives them power to heal and sends them to preach the kingdom of God.

**VERSE 2.**—“Mary who is called Magdalene.” When Mary traveled with the Lord and is remembered as ministering to him, he calls her by the familiar name Magdalene. When he describes her as the sinful woman, he reverently calls her “a woman” by the general name, lest the name of such great renown, which we venerate today, be stained by the mark of her former error. Mary means “bitter sea,” because of the inborn groaning of repentance by which she or we mourn our individual evils. “Seven demons.” The same Church from the Gentiles, cleansed from the filth of vices, is signified by Mary; it is also signified by Joanna, previously devoted to idolatrous rites but now redeemed by Christ’s mercy and filled with grace, having previously been, as it were, the wife of the devil.

**VERSE 3.**—“And Joanna,” etc. Joanna means “the Lord is her grace,” or “the merciful Lord,” from whom comes everything by which we live. “The steward of Herod.” When any wicked spirit labors to deceive for the kingdom of the devil, it exists as the steward of the most impious Herod. “From their resources,” etc. It was an ancient custom among the Jews, and was not counted as blameworthy, for women to feed and clothe teachers from their own substance. Because this could cause scandal among the Gentiles, Paul records that he abstained from it. They therefore ministered earthly things to the Lord, from whom they reaped spiritual things, so that he might give preachers the pattern that they ought to be content to receive food and clothing from the peoples.

**VERSE 4.**—“When a great crowd,” etc. Whenever the word “crowd” is inserted in the Gospel, just as a diversity of people is implied, so also a diversity of intentions is indicated. For they did not all follow Christ with the same intention, but for different reasons: some for good, some for evil. Nevertheless, the Lord grants benefits to all by teaching, feeding, and healing them. “The one who sows went out,” etc. The Son of God went forth from the bosom of the Father, to which no creature had access, in order to sow his seed; he came into the world to bear witness to the truth. Hence, according to the other evangelists, when he was about to speak this parable, he is remembered as having gone out from the house, approached the sea, and boarded a boat, indicating the same thing by the position of his body as by the progression of his discourse.

**VERSE 5.**—“Beside the road.” The road is the heart, worn down and dried out by the continual passage of evil thoughts, so that it cannot receive or germinate the seed of the word. The seed is trampled by wicked thoughts and snatched away by demons. They are therefore called “birds of the air” because they are of a heavenly and spiritual nature, or because they move through the air.

**VERSE 6.**—“Upon the rock.” The rock is an untamed heart, penetrated by no plow of true faith, in which there is neither true love nor the virtue of perseverance.

[Col. 0273C] **VERSE 8.**—“A hundredfold,” etc. Since the denarius is customarily understood as perfection—because observance is contained in the ten commandments of the law—the hundredfold, which arises through the multiplication of the denarius, signifies great perfection. The heart therefore produces a hundredfold fruit when, through love of neighbor, it attains the active life and, through love of God, the contemplative life, and is adorned with the perfection of spiritual virtues.

**VERSE 9.**—“This parable.” Note that this is the first parable presented together with its interpretation. And wherever the Lord, when asked by the disciples, explains his words privately, we must take care not to wish to understand anything other, more, or less than what he himself explained. He deigns to expound this parable himself so that he might make known that he speaks figuratively and teach that the meanings of things are also to be sought in what he did not choose to explain.

**VERSE 10.**—“Seeing.” The teachers of the Jews, who have deservedly been blinded because of their perversity, falsely imagine that they see.

**VERSE 12.**—“What was beside the road.” Those are sown beside the road who do not deign to receive the word with any faith, any understanding, or even the slightest opportunity for usefulness that might prompt them. Those sown upon the rock and among thorns hear, indeed, approve the usefulness of the word, and taste desire for it; but they are prevented from reaching what they desire, either by frightening them through adversity or by flattering them with prosperity. All who do not put the word they have heard into practice are designated by these three classes.

**VERSE 13.**—“They believe for a time.” Many who hear a discussion against avarice or lust say that those who despise the world and live chastely are blessed. But when desirable appearances are presented to their eyes, they immediately abandon whatever they had rightly considered.

**VERSE 14.**—“They are choked.” Pleasures and riches, through their intrusive thoughts, choke the throat of the mind, strangling the life-giving breath that would otherwise allow a good desire to enter the heart.

**VERSE 15.**—“Into good soil,” etc. This refers to good hearers who eagerly listen to the word, store it in the womb of memory, and thus bring forth the fruit of action at the proper time, patient amid the prosperity and adversity of the world. Good soil produces fruit with patience because it does good, bears the evils of others with equanimity, and, while humbly receiving the blows of discipline, is received into rest after those blows.

**VERSE 16.**—“No one,” however. These words are spoken according to the analogy of human custom.

**VERSE 17.**—“For nothing,” etc. As though he were saying: Let not the fear of worldly people hold you back, nor the bad opinion that unbelievers now have of you. For although you appear insignificant, your glory will eventually be revealed, when the Lord brings to light the things hidden in darkness. Then you will be crowned, and your adversaries will be punished.

[Col. 0274C] **VERSE 18.**—“For whoever has,” etc. These words appear to have been spoken especially to the apostles, who are granted knowledge of the mysteries through charity, and to the faithless Jews, who hear through parables what they do not understand. They may also be understood generally, because the gifted person, through neglect, deprives himself of true wisdom, while the simple and diligent person tastes it through labor. Whoever possesses love of the word will also be given the understanding to grasp what he loves. But whoever lacks love of hearing, even if through natural ability or diligent effort he thinks that he understands, will nevertheless taste none of the sweetness of true knowledge. “And whoever does not have.” The slothful person is therefore often given natural ability so that he may be punished more justly for his negligence, since he scorned to know what he could have attained without labor; and sometimes the diligent person is burdened by slowness of understanding, so that he may find greater rewards the more diligently he labors.

**VERSE 24.**—“And it ceased, and there was a calm.” Note that every creature senses its Creator. He commands and rebukes, and they sense the one commanding—not because, according to the heresy of certain people, they are living beings, but because things that are insensible to us are sensible to the majesty of their Creator.

**VERSE 25.**—“They said to one another in amazement.” It was not the disciples but the sailors and the others who were in the boat who were amazed. Hence Matthew says: “But the men were amazed, saying: What sort of man is this?” (Matt. VIII). If we say that the disciples were amazed, they too are rightly called men.

“To the region of the Gerasenes.” Gerasa is a city of Arabia near Mount Gilead, in the tribe of Manasseh, not far from the lake of Tiberias. It signifies the Gentiles whom the Lord visited through preachers after his Passion and Resurrection. Gerasa—or Gergesa—means “expelling the inhabitant,” that is, the devil, by whom the place had previously been inhabited; or “the approaching stranger,” who had been far away in time.

**VERSE 27.**—“Among the tombs.” What else are the bodies of unbelievers but certain tombs of the dead, in which the words of God do not dwell?

**VERSE 28.**—“Jesus, Son of God.” Arius contends that the one whom the demon confesses to be the Son of God is a creature. The Jews say, “He casts out demons by the prince of demons,” while the demons deny that he has anything in common with them. It is a torment to the devil to cease injuring a human being; and the longer he has possessed someone, the more difficultly he releases him. Therefore, let anyone injured by the devil beware and break his yoke quickly, because his dominion is avoided more easily the sooner it is escaped.

**VERSE 29.**—“He was bound with chains.” Chains and fetters are the harsh and heavy laws of the Gentiles, by which sins were restrained even in their commonwealth. Yet when these laws were broken, people were led by desire to crimes that exceeded ordinary custom.

**VERSE 30.**—“Because many demons had entered him,” etc. The many demons that oppress one person signify the many forms of idolatrous worship in one Gentile people. In contrast it is said: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV). Thus, rightly, the unity of languages was divided in Babylon and reunited in Jerusalem.

[Col. 0275C] **VERSE 31.—“And they begged.”** The demons knew that, at the Lord’s coming, they would eventually be plunged into the abyss—not because they themselves foretold the future, but because they recalled what the prophets had said about them.

**VERSE 32.—“A herd of swine.”** The swine are people deprived of speech and reason, devoted to filthy deeds, grazing on the mountain of pride. And unless someone has lived like a swine, the devil does not receive power over him—or receives it only for testing, not for destruction.

**VERSE 34.—“They fled and reported it in the city and in the villages.”** The herdsmen fled because neither the philosophers of the Gentiles nor the leaders of the Synagogue can provide medicine for those who are perishing; and although they flee the Christian law, they nevertheless proclaim its power in their astonishment and wonder.

[Col. 0275D] **VERSE 35.—“They went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man, etc.”** This signifies the multitude, delighted by his beautiful way of life, honoring it indeed but unwilling to endure the Christian religion, while saying that they cannot fulfill it. They marvel at the faithful people healed of their former manner of life, sitting at the Lord’s feet—that is, with sound judgment of mind, observing the footsteps of the Savior whom they are to follow—and clothed in the practices of the virtues which, when deceived, they had lost.

**VERSE 37.—“And they begged him.”** Conscious of their weakness, they judge themselves unworthy of the Lord’s presence, unable to grasp the word of God and unable, in a firm mind, to bear the weight of wisdom. Therefore he did not remain troublesome to them for long, but [Col. 0276A] returns, because he does not deign to heal the unwilling; rather, he quickly abandons the weak, for whom he sees that his presence is a burden.

**VERSE 39.—“Return to your house, etc.”** Allegorically: after the remission of sins, one must return to a good conscience and serve the Gospel, also for the salvation of others, so that afterward he may rest with Christ. Thus, when he already wishes to be near Christ, he must not neglect the mystery of preaching, which is directed toward the liberation of his brothers. Hence the Apostle says: “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. I), “but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake.”

**VERSE 43.—“To physicians.”** The physicians are the demons, who, as though advising human beings, demand to be worshiped in place of God; the Gentiles had served them.

[Col. 0276B] **VERSE 44.—“She touched the fringe.”** He touches the fringe who perfectly loves and believes the mysteries of the Incarnation, until he reaches the point of grasping greater things. If we consider how great our faith is, and understand how great the Son of God is, we see that, in comparison with him, we touch only the fringe; we cannot reach the upper part of his garment.

**“And immediately, etc.”** Since he was about to raise the dead girl, he returned in order to establish faith, but first healed the woman with the hemorrhage. Thus Elizabeth’s barrenness is shown to be about to give birth, so that the Virgin may be believed to be about to conceive.

**VERSE 45.—“Who is it?”** He does not ask in order to be taught something he does not know, but so that the woman’s faith might become evident.

**VERSE 46.—“For I also know.”** No one who touches him remains hidden: God does not need eyes in order to see, nor does he perceive bodily, but possesses within himself the knowledge of all things. Even the power that is gracious toward all our iniquities and heals all our infirmities proceeds not from us but from God.

**VERSE 47.—“But when the woman saw.”** This woman touches the fringe modestly, approaches faithfully, believes devoutly, and wisely recognizes that she has been healed. So the people of the Gentiles who believed in God were ashamed of sin in order to abandon it; they brought faith in order to believe; they displayed devotion in order to ask; they put on wisdom in order also to perceive their own healing; and they took courage in order to confess that they had snatched what belonged to another.

**VERSE 51.—“The father of the girl.”** The girl’s father is the assembly of the teachers of the Law, namely the scribes and Pharisees; if they should wish to believe, the Synagogue subject to them will also be saved.

[Col. 0276D] **VERSE 52.—“But they were weeping.”** They weep who see the Synagogue alienated from God, who is life, and grieve, thinking that it can no longer be brought to life. It has lost the presence of the bridegroom, by which it ought to live, and lies as though dead among those who mourn, without even understanding why it is being mourned. **“Do not weep.”** Let those weep for their dead who consider them dead; where there is faith in the resurrection, there is not death but the hope of rest. **“She is not dead, etc.”** The girl is dead to human beings, who cannot raise her; not to God, for whom the soul lives, while the flesh rests in readiness to be raised.

**VERSE 53.—“They laughed at him, etc.”** Rightly were they excluded, [Col. 0277A] who preferred to laugh rather than to believe and were unworthy to see the miracle of the resurrection.

**VERSE 54.—“Taking her by the hand.”** He takes her by the hand because, unless the hands of the Jews—which are full of blood—are first cleansed, the Synagogue will not rise. **“Girl, arise.”** Whoever recovers from the death of the soul, with Christ strengthening his hand, must rise from the filth of vices and, as Mark says, walk in good works; he must immediately be satisfied with heavenly bread, that is, with the word of God and the altar.

**VERSE 56.—“He commanded them.”** Just as public wrongdoing requires a public remedy, so slight sins can be removed by a lighter and secret penance. Hence the girl, lying in the house, rises before a few witnesses, and those same witnesses are forbidden to spread the miracle abroad.

# CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0277B] **VERSE 1.—“When Jesus had called them together.”** After first granting them the power to perform signs, he sends them to preach the kingdom of God, so that the greatness of their deeds might also bear witness to the greatness of the promises, that the power displayed might give credibility to their words, and that those who preached new things might perform new things.

**VERSE 3.—“Take nothing.”** In Mark it is written that they should take nothing on the journey except a staff (Mark VI). But it must be understood that both commands were given by the Lord: that they should carry nothing except a staff, and that they should carry not even a staff. Not carrying a staff means not being anxious about what is necessary for human sustenance, because such things are owed to preachers by those to whom they preach, when they can be received without scandal. Carrying nothing except a staff means making use of the power given to preachers to receive what is necessary. **“Two tunics.”** A simple garment is whatever is necessary for someone according to the character of the place or season. A double garment is what exceeds necessity. Allegorically, by the two tunics he forbids duplicity.

**VERSE 4.—“Remain there.”** Do not run from house to house and alter the inviolable rights of hospitality. Hence, according to Matthew, the house in which they are to remain must first be chosen, so that the need to change their lodging may be removed.

**VERSE 5.—“The dust of your feet.”** The dust is shaken off as a testimony to the labor they undertook when they entered the city and to the fact that the preaching reached even those people. Or it is shaken off so that they may receive nothing from those who despised the Gospel—not even the necessities of life.

**VERSE 8.—“John has risen.”** Those who said that John, concerning whom they had seen no sign, had risen, denied with the utmost malice that Jesus had risen, although they had seen many marvelous works and although many wondrous things had occurred at his Passion.

**VERSE 10.—“They reported.”** The apostles report to the Lord what they had done, how they had taught, and how John had suffered while they were teaching. Hence it follows: **“And taking them.”** He does not impart the nourishment of heavenly grace to the idle, nor to those sitting in the city of the Synagogue—that is, in worldly dignity—but to those seeking Christ among deserted places. Those who are not fastidious are received by Christ, and are healed spiritually and bodily, [Col. 0278A] even when they are in need. And note that, after the account of John’s Passion has been completed, Christ refreshes them, because after the decline of the Law, evangelical food begins. Finally, after the woman who bears the figure of the Church has been healed, and after the apostles have been sent to preach, the account of nourishment follows, because through the apostles true refreshment takes place in the Church.

**VERSE 11.—“They followed him.”** They followed not on animals or in vehicles, but by the labor of their own feet, in order to show the ardor of their minds. **“He healed.”** No one receives Christ’s food unless he has first been healed, because heavenly nourishment is granted after the remission of sins.

**VERSE 12.—“The day had begun to decline.”** When the day has declined, he refreshes them, because we have been saved from spiritual hunger either as the end of the ages approaches or when the sun of justice has set. And note the order of the mystery: first, medicine is given to wounds through the remission of sins; afterward, the nourishment of the heavenly table is supplied.

**VERSE 13.—“Unless perhaps.”** The apostles did not yet understand that the faith of the believing people was not for sale, but they knew that we rather were to be redeemed through his freely given provisions.

**VERSE 14.—“Five thousand.”** The five thousand signify those who, while still in a worldly manner of life, know how to use well, through the five bodily senses, the external things they possess. They are fed with five loaves because such people still need to be instructed by the precepts of the Law and restrained by legal fear. For those who wholly renounce the world are four thousand, because of evangelical teaching, and are refreshed by the grace of the seven loaves, that is, of the sevenfold Spirit.

**VERSE 15.—“And they all reclined.”** According to another Evangelist, the five thousand recline on the grass, because those who still possess bodily senses take pleasure in better things. For all flesh is grass. The four thousand recline on the earth, for pressing upon the earth is more than lying upon grass.

**VERSE 16.—“He distributed them to his disciples.”** He prompts the apostles to break the bread, so that, when they testify that they do not have any, the greatness of the sign may become more evident. He indicates that hungry hearts must be fed daily through their teaching.

**VERSE 17.—“And they were satisfied.”** The fact that the people are satisfied while eating signifies that hunger will be driven away from the elect forever, because whoever has received Christ’s food will not hunger. The fact that the apostles minister signifies the future distribution of the Lord’s body and blood. **“Twelve baskets.”** Why is more left over for the five thousand than for the four thousand? Because the four thousand were with Christ for three days, and therefore received a greater amount of heavenly nourishment.

**VERSE 18.—“And it happened.”** After the miracle, when the crowds wanted to make him king, he dismissed the crowd, withdrew, and went up the mountain alone to pray; and before the disciples entered the boat, they were with him. He himself, however, prays to the Father alone. The saints can be joined to the Lord by faith and love, can behold him as superior to human beings, and can follow his life in the flesh through the steps of humility; but he alone penetrates the incomprehensible mysteries of the Father’s position, and he alone prays what he knows ought to be prayed. He is not found praying with the disciples, but entreats alone, because human hearts do not grasp God’s plan, nor can anyone share the inner things with Christ.

**“Who do the crowds say that I am?”** He first inquires into the opinion of the crowd in order to test the disciples’ faith, so that the apostles’ faith might not appear to have been established by popular opinion but by recognition of the truth. The crowds are rightly so called because they express various opinions about the Lord; their speech and understanding are unstable and wandering. Distinguishing his own from them, he says: **“But you, who do you say that I am?”**

**VERSE 19.—“John the Baptist.”** The opinion concerning John perhaps arose because, while still in his mother’s womb, he sensed the Lord’s presence. They said Elijah because he was taken up into heaven and is believed to be destined to come. They said Jeremiah because he was sanctified in his mother’s womb.

**VERSE 20.—“But you.”** Whoever teaches must consider the persons of his hearers, lest he be mocked before he is heard. **“The Christ of God.”** He has embraced everything, expressing both nature and name. For in the name of Christ there is an expression of and faith in both divinity and incarnation and in the Passion. Even if a heretic does not deny the name of Christ, he nevertheless denies Christ if he does not confess everything that belongs to Christ.

**VERSE 21.—“He commanded them, etc.”** He orders the disciples to remain silent in order to deceive the prince of this world and, by avoiding boastfulness, to teach humility. At the same time, he does this so that the still inexperienced and imperfect disciples might not be crushed by the burden of a greater preaching.

**VERSE 23.—“But he was saying.”** Matters relating to faith in the Lord’s birth and Passion he disclosed separately to the disciples alone; this, however, he disclosed to everyone. **“Let him deny himself.”** Unless someone departs from himself, he does not draw near to the one who is above him; and he does not grasp the newness to which he is called unless he puts to death the old self in which he was born. When he ceases from vices, he must also seek virtues; hence it follows:

**VERSE 24.—“For whoever.”** (GREG.) Just as the soul must be surrendered in a time of persecution, so in a time of peace earthly desires must be broken, so that the more secure a person appears, the more vigilant he may be in guarding himself.

**VERSE 26.—“The Son of Man.”** A verbal profession is not sufficient as proof of faith, when a profession of generality shields it from shame.

**VERSE 27.—“There are some standing here.”** Whoever stands with Christ does not taste death, because he who has deserved Christ’s fellowship will not experience even the slightest sense of eternal death; not even in death is the order of his life interrupted. **“Until they see the kingdom.”** Because it was difficult to offer the soul to dangers and the body to death, he supports the weakness of the human mind by the reward of present things, so that it may not be broken by despair or weariness. Once eternal glory has been seen, even if only in passing and for a brief moment, they are nevertheless made stronger against the adversities of the world. Thus he promises that future glory will be seen in passing on earth, so that it may be hoped for more certainly in heaven as eternal glory. Or he promises that some of the disciples will see the expansion of the Church before they depart from the world through death, so that, raised up in the present against the glory of the world, they may be believed more certainly destined to reign in heaven.

[Col. 0280A] **VERSE 28.—“After these words.”** Those who count only six days signify that, after the six ages of the world, the saints must rest from labor. Luke, who counts both the first day on which the promise is made and the last on which the promise is fulfilled, suggests that we shall rise on the eighth day. For just as Christ rose on the eighth day after the sixth day of the week, on which he ascended the cross, and after the seventh day of the week, on which he rested in the tomb, so we shall rise in the eighth age after the six ages of the world during which we suffer and labor for the Lord, and after the seventh age, the rest of souls that takes place meanwhile in the other life.

**“He took Peter.”** [Col. 0280B] He mentions only three because “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX), and those who preserve the faith of the Trinity inviolate deserve to rejoice in the eternal vision. The knower of merits knew that these three apostles were more perfect than the others. They signify those who possess faith, hope, and charity. Or, through Peter, superiors or married people; through James, penitents or those engaged in active works; through John, virgins or contemplatives.

**VERSE 29.—“And he became.”** When he was transfigured, he did not lose the substance of true flesh, but displayed the glory either of his own resurrection or of ours. What he was then to the apostles, he will be after the judgment to all the elect. For at that very judgment he will appear to the good and the evil in the form of a servant, so that they may see the one whom they pierced.

**“And his clothing.”** The Lord’s garments are the saints who have put on Christ. The garment that, while the Lord remained on earth, appeared contemptible and like that of others shines when the Lord ascends the mountain, because what we shall be has not yet appeared; but at last we shall be like him when we see him as he is. Or the garments of the Word are the sayings of Scripture and certain coverings of divine understanding. Just as he himself and his garment appeared to those apostles in another form and his clothing shone, so already the meaning of divine reading grows bright to the eyes of your mind.

**VERSE 30.—“Behold, two men.”** It must be noted that the bodies or souls of Elijah and Moses did not appear, but that those bodies were formed from some underlying created substance. It may also be believed that this was done through angelic ministry, so that angels assumed their persons. A dead man and a living man appear to signify Christ who would die and afterward live, and so that we may live for Christ and die to the world. He also gives the apostles a sign from heaven, so that their faith may increase. But when the scribes were testing him, he refused to give them one, so that they might be hardened. **“They were Moses and Elijah who were seen.”** Through Moses, those destined to come from the underworld; through Elijah, those destined to come from heaven; and through the apostles, those destined to come from the earth are signified at the judgment.

**VERSE 31.—“They were speaking of his departure.”** Moses, that is, the lawgiver, and Elijah, the foremost of the prophets, appear with the Word in order to show that he is the one who spoke in the Law and the Prophets, and the one whom the Law and the Prophets promised. They are seen not in lowly places but on the mountain, [Col. 0281A] because only those whose minds are exalted perceive the majesty of Scripture, which has been fulfilled in the Lord.

**VERSE 32.—“They were weighed down by sleep.”** They are weighed down by sleep because the sense of the human body is overwhelmed by the splendor of the incomprehensible divinity. Or they are weighed down by sleep so that they might see the glory of the resurrection after the body’s rest; and the saints will see the Lord’s majesty all the more truly insofar as they rejoice in the immortality of their flesh, in which they conquered death. Then they will contemplate Moses and Elijah in glory, because they will understand better how not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law (Matt. V), and how the Lord did not abolish the Law and the Prophets but fulfilled them.

**VERSE 33.—“It is good for us to be here.”** He who had climbed to the heights does not wish to descend to earthly things, but wishes always to remain on high; and Peter represents those entering the kingdom of God. **“It is good for us to be here.”** It is good to be in the kingdom of God. It is as though he said: “Let us alone enjoy this light, not the envious Jews.” **“Three tabernacles.”** That is, words, thoughts, and deeds. **“One for Moses.”** How do they recognize those whom they had not previously seen? Through the majesty coming upon them, just as in the future resurrection each person will recognize another, and through charity one will understand the desired qualities in another.

**VERSE 34.—“A cloud came and overshadowed them.”** Although Peter, through weakness, does not understand, the devotion of his service is nevertheless pleasing. Hence the cloud also overshadows them: this is the overshadowing of the divine Spirit, which does not darken human affections but reveals hidden things. Its perfection is shown when a voice is heard saying: **“This is my Son.”** Because he sought a material tabernacle, he received the shadowing of a cloud, so that he might learn that in the resurrection the saints are to be protected not by the administration of houses but by the glory of the Holy Spirit.

**“And they were afraid.”** They are afraid because human weakness cannot endure the sight of a greater glory; and the more someone seeks greater things, the more he collapses into lower things if he does not know his own measure.

**VERSE 36.—“And the voice.”** The voice of the Father teaches Peter the truth once his terror has been removed. And note that, just as at the Lord’s baptism, so also at his transfiguration the mystery of the Trinity is declared, because the glory that we confess in baptism we shall see in the resurrection. The Spirit appeared in a dove, [Col. 0281D] here in a bright cloud, because whoever now preserves the faith with a simple heart will then contemplate in the open light of vision what he believed, and will be protected by the very grace by which he is illuminated.

**“Jesus was found alone.”** Not Elijah, not Moses: only the one whom you see must have a tabernacle fixed in your heart. Therefore they depart when the Lord begins to be designated, lest the Father’s voice be thought to have been sent to servants.

**VERSE 37.—“It happened on the following day, when they had come down from the mountain.”** According to the quality of their merits, the Lord ascends daily for some, glorifying the perfect—whose manner of life is in heaven—by raising them higher, and instructing them in eternal things that cannot be heard by the crowd. He descends for others, when he strengthens, teaches, and chastises those who are earthly and beginning their progress.

**“A crowd met them.”** On the mountain he prays, teaches, displays his majesty, and discloses the Father’s voice to the apostles; descending, he is met by the crowd, is assailed by the weeping of the wretched, reproves the sins of unbelief, and drives out evil spirits.

**VERSE 39.—“And behold, a spirit seizes him.”** Matthew describes him as epileptic; Mark describes him as deaf and mute. He signifies those who change like the moon, never remaining in the same condition but waxing and waning through various vices; they neither confess the faith nor wish to hear the word of faith itself.

**VERSE 42.—“And when he was approaching.”** While the boy is approaching the Lord, he is thrown down, because those who turn to the Lord are often struck more severely by the demon, either so that they may be led back to vices or so that the devil may avenge himself for having been expelled. So, at the beginning of the Church’s birth, he placed many [Col. 0282B] severe struggles in the way of those whom he saw being taken from his kingdom.

**VERSE 43.—“And he rebuked.”** It is not the boy, who suffers the force, but the devil, who inflicts the force, who is rebuked. For whoever wishes to heal a sinner must reprove and drive out the vice, while restoring the person with love until, once healed, he returns him to the spiritual fathers of the Church.

**VERSE 44.—“Put these words into your ears.”** You who cling to my discipleship, to whom I have disclosed my mysteries more openly, store in your minds the event of the precious blood by which the world is to be redeemed, while the others marvel at such deeds of divine greatness. **“The Son of Man is about to be handed over.”** Amid the great works of divine power he repeatedly brings up the despised matter of human suffering, so that it may not terrify them when it comes suddenly, but may be endured more lightly because it was anticipated.

[Col. 0282C] **VERSE 45.—“But they did not understand.”** This ignorance arises not so much from slowness as from love. Since they were still carnal and ignorant of the mystery of the cross, they could not believe that the one whom they had recognized as God would die. But just as they were accustomed to hear him speak through figures, so they thought that what he said about his being handed over signified something else figuratively.

**VERSE 46.—“A thought entered.”** They had seen Peter, James, and John led separately onto the mountain, and supposed that some secret had been entrusted to them. They also reasoned that the keys of the kingdom of heaven had earlier been promised to Peter and that the Church was to be built upon him; or that these three had been preferred to the others; or that Peter had been placed above all the apostles; or, because they had seen Peter made equal to the Lord himself in the payment of the tribute, they thought that he ought to be preferred to the others. But it must be understood that this question was raised both before and after the tribute was paid.

**VERSE 48.—“Whoever receives this child.”** Or, simply: he teaches that Christ’s poor are to be received by those who wish to be greater, for Christ’s honor. Or he teaches that they are to be children in malice, preserving the simplicity of childish innocence, so that they may deliberately follow, for Christ’s name, the form of virtue that a child observes under the guidance of nature. **“He receives me.”** Whoever receives an imitator of Christ receives Christ, and whoever receives the image of God receives God.

**VERSE 49.—“John said.”** John, who loved God and was loved by the Lord, thought that someone who did not render service ought to be excluded from the benefit. Therefore he is taught that no one is to be barred from the good that he possesses in part, but rather is to be encouraged toward what he does not yet possess. Such people also are considered admissible for the salvation of others. Therefore, among heretics or wicked Catholics, we must detest and prohibit not the common sacraments in which they are with us and are not against us, but the division opposed to peace and truth by which they are against us and do not follow the Lord with us.

**VERSE 50.—“Do not prohibit. For whoever …”** John is not reproved because he acted out of love, but is taught to understand the difference between the weak and the strong: although the Lord rewards the stronger, he does not exclude the weak.

[Col. 0283B] **VERSE 54.—“Lord, do you wish?”** (BED.) The apostles, still inexperienced and unaware of the proper manner of taking vengeance, etc., up to the point where such power was granted by God to holy men.

**“Shall we say that fire should descend from heaven?”** At their word, fire would descend from heaven, because they are sons of thunder. **“And consume them?”** **“And he turned and rebuked them and said.”** This is in the likeness of Elijah, who both by his own hand and by fire obtained from God inflicted death upon the priests of Baal. And in the fact that the apostles presume for themselves the power of such a prophet, it is shown that the merit of the prophets was present in them.

(AMBR.) The apostles do not sin, since they follow the Law, etc., up to the point where the one who does not fear does not seek vengeance.

**VERSE 55.—“You do not know of what spirit you are.”** Of whose spirit you have been marked, whose deeds you imitate: now you are acting with pious concern, but in the future you will judge justly.

**VERSE 56.—“The Son of Man did not come to destroy souls but to save them, etc.”** Perfect virtue has no desire for vengeance, and there is no anger where there is the fullness of charity.

(BED.) Vengeance is not always to be taken against those who sin, etc., up to the point where fire is kept away from them in this passage.

**VERSE 57.—“A certain man said.”** (ID.) Moved by the greatness of the signs, this man wishes to follow, etc., up to the point where he feigned the service of a disciple; this pretense is represented by the fox.

**VERSE 58.—“Foxes have dens.”** (ID.) The fox is a deceitful animal, intent upon ambushes and practicing predatory fraud; it also dwells in dens even among human habitations. So the heretic, having no house of faith, draws others into his own deceit and leads them away from the faith.

**VERSE 59.—“But he said to another.”** Observe that the Lord did not reject faults but deceit, because, while he rejected the deceitful man, he chose the innocent one; yet he chose the one whose father he knew to be dead—the father concerning whom it is said: “Forget the house of your father” (Ps. XLIV), etc.

**VERSE 60.—“Let the dead bury their own dead.”** (BED.) Mystically: the son is not recalled from his father’s duty, etc., up to the point where he must not bury the devil’s treacheries within himself.

**VERSE 61.—“To renounce these things.”** If a disciple who intends to follow God is reproved because he wishes to renounce his household, what will become of those who, often without any benefit, visit the homes of their relatives whom they have abandoned?

# CHAPTER X

**VERSE 1.—“After these things, etc.”** (BED.) Just as in the apostles there is the model of bishops, etc., up to the point where the sun customarily completes the circuit of its light in seventy-two hours over three days.

**“He sent them two by two.”** By sending them two by two, he indicates that no one ought to undertake the ministry of preaching who does not have charity toward another. Or they are sent in pairs according to the fact that pairs of animals were sent into the ark—that is, male and female—which were previously unclean in carnal generation but were cleansed by the sacrament of the Church through spiritual grace in the preaching of the disciples.

[Col. 0284B] **VERSE 2.—“The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few.”** The harvest is the crowd of believers; the laborers are the apostles and their followers. Although the harvest has been sown with the word of God, it nevertheless requires the labor of cultivation and the attentive service of the laborers, lest the birds of heaven scatter the seeds that have been sown.

**VERSE 3.—“Like lambs among wolves.”** Just as a wolf lies in wait for sheep, so the heretic lies in wait for the faithful. And just as a wolf circles the sheepfold at night, not daring to enter, watching for the dog’s sleep and the shepherd’s absence or negligence, so the heretic attempts by the night of his interpretation to deceive the faithful. He does not enter the Church, but strives either to avoid, kill, or send into exile the shepherds of the Church. The wolf is rigid by the nature of its body and cannot easily bend itself; so the heretic ordinarily does not turn the intention of his hardened heart back from error.

**VERSE 4.—“Therefore do not carry a purse or a bag.”** A preacher ought to have such confidence in God that, even if he does not foresee the expenses of the present life, he nevertheless knows with complete certainty that they will not fail him, lest, while the mind is occupied with temporal things, he preach eternal things less fully. **“Greet no one along the way.”** He commands them to hasten and press forward, lest conversation with anyone they meet turn them back from the journey entrusted to them. He does not simply say, “Greet no one,” since it is a human custom to greet others; rather, he adds, “along the way,” because it is not the diligence of greeting that is removed, but the obstacle that could hinder devotion, so that when divine commands are given, human concerns may for a little while be set aside.

**VERSE 7.—“And remain in the same house.”** If your peace is received, it is right for you to remain there, receiving material support from those to whom you offer heavenly things. Behold: the one who prohibited the purse and bag permits expenses to be received from preaching, but only so that they may be content with the food and drink offered. **“Remain.”** One must not move casually from house to house, so that constancy may be preserved in the love of hospitality and the bond of friendship that has grown up may not easily be dissolved. **“For the laborer is worthy.”** Note that two rewards are owed for the one work of preachers: one on the way, which sustains us in our labor; the other in our homeland, which rewards us in the resurrection.

**VERSE 8.—“And into whatever city.”** Having described the various arrangements for lodging, he teaches what they ought also to do in the cities: namely, to share in all things with the devout and to separate themselves entirely from association with the impious.

**VERSE 11.—“Even the dust.”** He commands them to shake off the dust, either as a testimony to the earthly labor that they undertook for them in vain, or to show that they seek nothing earthly from them to such an extent that they will not even allow dust from their land to cling to them.

**VERSE 12.—“For it will be more tolerable for Sodom in that day.”** Although the Sodomites burned with vices and were inhospitable, there were nevertheless among them no guests such as the prophets were among the Jews, or such as the apostles were found to be. Lot, although righteous, did not teach anything among them and performed no signs. Therefore, to whom much has been given, much will be required from him, and the powerful will suffer powerful torments (Wis. VI).

**VERSE 13.—“Woe to you, Chorazin.”** Chorazin, Bethsaida, Capernaum, and Tiberias are cities of Galilee on the shore of the lake of Gennesaret. The Lord mourns for them because, after so many miracles and works of power, they did not repent. They are worse than the Gentiles, who violate only the natural law, because, after disregarding the Law that had been set forth, they did not fear to trample upon the Son of God as well and reject grace with ingratitude.

**“And sitting in ashes.”** We see the Savior’s words fulfilled, because when the cities mentioned above refused to believe in the Lord’s presence, Tyre and Sidon—which had formerly been friends of David and Solomon—afterward, when Christ’s disciples preached, received the faith devoutly. But why preaching was given to those who would not believe, and not given to those who would believe, is known by the one who knows all things.

**VERSE 16.—“Whoever hears you hears me.”** Whether hearing or despising the preacher of the Gospel, let each person know that he is not hearing or despising insignificant persons, but the Savior himself, because in the disciple the teacher is heard, and in the Son the Father is honored.

**VERSE 17.—“Lord, even.”** They confess well, giving honor to Christ’s name. But because their faith is still weak, they rejoice in their powers and are elated by the performance of signs; they are terrified by an example and recalled to humility. For if the devil was cast down from heaven because of pride, much more will those who were raised from the earth be humbled if they grow proud.

**VERSE 19.—“Over serpents and scorpions.”** The serpents are evil people or demons who oppose the beginnings of virtue with the poisons of corrupt persuasion. The scorpions are those who strive to corrupt virtues as they are brought to completion.

**VERSE 20.—“Do not rejoice that the spirits are subject to you, etc.”** Casting out evil spirits and performing other virtues is sometimes not the merit of the person who performs them, but the invocation of Christ’s name accomplishes this either for the condemnation of those who invoke it or for the benefit of those who see and hear. Although people may despise those who perform signs, they nevertheless honor God, at whose invocation the miracles occur. He forbids them to rejoice at the humiliation of the devil, who fell because of pride, but commands them to rejoice in their own exaltation, [Col. 0286A] so that, from the place where those others fell, these may rise—having been humbled.

**“But rejoice.”** If someone has performed heavenly or earthly works, he is, as though adorned with letters through these works, eternally fixed in God’s memory.

**VERSE 21.—“In that same hour.”** While speaking of the subjection of unclean spirits and of names written in heaven, he shows by what means such great exaltation has been given to human beings: namely, through the humility of Christian faith. **“I confess to you, Lord.”** I give thanks because you have revealed to the apostles the mysteries of my coming, which the scribes and Pharisees, who consider themselves wise, do not know.

**“You have revealed them.”** He does not say “to the foolish and dull,” but “to little ones,” that is, to the humble, thereby proving that he condemned arrogance, not intelligence. **“Because it was so.”** He does not explain why he chose some and rejected others, but says that this was pleasing to God. Here we receive an example of humility, so that we may not rashly investigate heavenly counsels.

**“All things have been handed over to me, etc.”** Having commended humility, through which one comes to faith, he beautifully connects the subject with faith itself, when he says that all things have been handed over to him—not the elements that he himself created, but the little ones to whom the Father revealed the mysteries of the Son. When you hear “all things,” you recognize the omnipotent one, not one unlike or degenerate from the Father. When you hear “handed over,” you confess the Son, to whom, by the nature of one substance, all things rightly belong—not things bestowed by grace as a gift.

**VERSE 24.—“Many prophets.”** The prophets and righteous, from afar, saw the Lord’s glory through a mirror and in an enigma; but the apostles, having the Lord present and questioning him directly about what they wished, were not taught through angels or various forms of visions.

**VERSE 25.—“A lawyer stood up.”** The teacher of the Law, who lay in the Law without faith, rises in order to stand. He stands while calling him “Teacher,” but by standing he also tests God, concealing what he was.

**VERSE 27.—“He answered and said.”** He said what he had read, but did not fulfill what was written, because he had the Lord present, whom he ought to love, but called him “Teacher,” not God.

### Verse 29

“But he, wishing...” The lawyer, in order to appear to have answered wisely, first professes that he does not know the commandment of the Law, because, refusing to humble himself and wishing to justify himself, he cannot see the mysteries revealed to Christ’s little ones [Col. 0286D]. Christ accordingly shapes his answer so that everyone who shows mercy may be understood as a neighbor, while, in particular, the Son of God himself—who became our neighbor through his humanity—may be indicated. “Who is my neighbor?” No one is nearer to a human being than God, who knows what is within and without and can care for everything. But every unbeliever or tempter has neither God nor a human being as his neighbor.

“A certain man...” (AUG.) This man is understood as Adam in the human race, etc., up to the point where he was nearer than the priest or the Levite of the same people.

### Verse 31

“But it happened...” The priest announces God’s Law. The Law did indeed descend through Moses [Col. 0287A] into the world, but it brought no healing of this kind. The Levite descended, displaying the type of the prophets, but he too heals no one, because the Law reproves sins but passes by, since it does not bestow forgiveness.

### Verse 33

“Moved with compassion.” This is not said of the priest and Levite, because the Law possesses not mercy but judgment and vengeance.

### Verse 34

“He brought him to an inn.” He does not call it a house but an inn, by which name he signifies the miseries and foulness of this life, lest a person rejoice in this exile as though it were his homeland.

### Verse 37

“He who showed mercy.” Kinship does not make someone a neighbor, but mercy does; and this mercy is according to nature. For nothing is so consonant with nature as helping one’s fellow participant in nature.

[Col. 0287B] ### Verse 38

“It happened, while...” After discourse has been given about love of God and neighbor, an example of both kinds of love is supplied—not merely in word, but in the display of action. Through these two sisters, two spiritual ways of life are signified.

Through Martha is signified devotion active in works, by which we are joined to our neighbor in charity. Through Mary is signified the religious attention of the mind to God’s word, by which we sigh in love for God.

The active life gives bread either to one who is hungry in body or to one ignorant of doctrine; it corrects the erring, recalls the proud to humility, and distributes to each what is useful. The contemplative life retains love of God and neighbor but rests from external action; it clings to the desire of the Creator alone, and, trampling down every care, burns with eagerness to see the face of the Creator. It longs to be joined [Col. 0287C] to the citizens above, who rejoice in incorruption, eternal in the presence of the Lord.

“Into her house.” When Jesus enters the house, an evil life—if it had existed there—flees; two innocent lives remain, one laborious and the other at rest, while he himself, the fountain of life, stands between them.

### Verse 39

“Sitting at his feet.” The more humbly she sits, the more greatly she falls. Water flows into a valley from the swelling heights of a hill. Mary sits because the contemplative soul, after the disturbances of its vices have been quieted, enjoys the desired rest of mind already possessed in Christ. Martha stands because the active life, full of labor, sweats in the struggle.

### Verse 40

“But Martha...” Mary was intent on how she might be nourished by the Lord; Martha was intent on how she might nourish the Lord. The latter prepares a banquet for the Lord, while the former already delights in the Lord’s banquet.

[Col. 0287D] ### Verse 41

“And answering...” Mary does not answer, but, as one at rest, entrusts her cause to the judge. For if she had prepared a speech with which to answer, she would have relaxed her attentiveness to listening.

“Martha, Martha.” The repetition is an indication of affection, or perhaps of a warning meant to make her listen more attentively.

### Verse 42

“But one thing is necessary.” The one is preferred to the many. For the one does not come from the many; rather, the many come from the one. Nevertheless, many things are necessary for those advancing toward the one.

“Mary has chosen the better part.” Martha’s part is not reproved, since it too is good; but Mary’s part is praised, and why it is the better part is added immediately afterward.

## CHAPTER XI

### Verse 1

“And it happened.” After the account of the sisters [Col. 0288A]—who signify two ways of life—he introduces the Lord as praying and instructing the disciples in prayer. For the prayer he taught contains within itself the mystery of both ways of life, and the perfection of those ways is to be obtained not by our strength but by prayers.

“When he had ceased.” The Savior is often presented as praying in order to lead the disciples to devotion to prayer. Accordingly, when the prayer was finished, he questioned them, so as to teach how they ought to pray.

### Verse 5

“Which of you has a friend?” After he had set before those asking him the form of prayer, he also enjoined persistence and frequency in prayer, so that prayer might be offered not only during the day but also during the night. For whoever asks his friend for bread at midnight and persists in the earnestness of his request is not defrauded when he prays.

### Verse 7

“Do not trouble me.” He does not remove the hope of obtaining what is requested [Col. 0288B], but kindles the desire to pray more intensely by showing the difficulty of attaining it.

“The door is already shut.” The door which Paul asks to be opened for him to speak the mystery of Christ, and which John saw opened for himself, is understanding of the divine word. It is shut during a famine of the word of God, when understanding is not granted.

“And the children”—that is, those who, distributing evangelical wisdom as bread, preached throughout the world—“are already with the Lord” in eternal rest. Nevertheless, by praying it comes about that the one who prays receives understanding from the Lord himself, even when no human being is present through whom wisdom may be preached.

“I cannot rise.” (AMBR.) No one fears disturbing one whom he knows to be always praying and keeping watch.

### Verse 8

“Yet because of his persistence...” [Col. 0288C] There are many snares and a heavy sleep of the body, because if the mind begins to sleep, it loses the vigor of its virtue. Awaken your sleep, therefore, so that you may knock at Christ’s door; when you have entered, the treasures hidden and dark in Christ Jesus will be opened to you.

### Verse 9

“Ask, and it will be given to you.” If a human friend rises and gives, compelled not by friendship but by annoyance, how much more will God give, who, without annoyance, bestows most generously what is requested.

Therefore, lest the mind, turned away from the vanity of error, waste away longer in spiritual poverty, let us ask for the feasts of the word; let us seek the friend who will give; let us knock at the door where hidden things are kept. For he gives great hope who, by promising, does not deceive.

“For everyone who asks receives.” Perseverance is necessary for us to obtain what we seek. If what is asked is given, what is sought is found, and to the one who knocks the door is opened, it is evident why something is not given, why the seeker does not find, and why the door is not opened [Col. 0288D]: he has not sought, asked, or knocked rightly.

### Verse 10

“Seek, and you will find.” “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth, and he will do the will of those who fear him” (Psalm 44). James rebukes others who do not ask in this way, saying: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James 4), since you persist in sins.

### Verse 11

“Which father among you, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone?” etc. (BED.) Mystically: bread signifies charity because of its greater desirability and necessary use, etc., up to the point where it extends itself toward the things that lie ahead.

[Col. 0289A] ### Verse 13

“How much more...” The comparison is clear. If a sinful human being, still weighed down by fragile flesh, does not refuse to give temporal things to children who ask, much more will the heavenly Father bestow unfailing goods in heaven upon children endowed with fear and love of him.

### Verse 14

“And he was casting out...” After the words of preaching that he had set before the humble, he also performs miracles, so that those who do not believe the preacher may believe when they see the miracles. Matthew says that this demoniac was also blind.

In him the Lord performs three miracles: he sees, he speaks, and he is freed from the demon. What then happened carnally in one person happens daily in the conversion of the nations: first, when the demon and every pollution of idolatry have been expelled, they see the light of faith; then mouths that were previously silent are opened to the praise of God.

[Col. 0289B] ### Verse 15

“By Beelzebub.” Ninus, king and founder of Nineveh, dedicated a statue to his father Bel and instituted divine honors for him. The Chaldeans, adopting the likeness of this image, called it Bel. The Palestinians adopted it and called it Baal; the Moabites, Beel-peor.

The Jews, however, worshipers of the one God, called it Beelzebub in mockery of the Gentiles. For *Baal* is said to mean “man,” and *zebub* “fly”; hence *Beelzebub*, that is, “man of flies,” or “one who has flies,” because of the filth of the blood sacrificed in his temple.

The Jews also asserted that the prince of demons dwelt in this image, and they said that Jesus cast out demons by his power.

### Verse 18

“But he, seeing their thoughts...” The Lord reserved this as his own prerogative: to look upon and judge thoughts [Col. 0289C]. It is characteristic of the Jews to seek signs; hence Paul says: “Jews ask for signs, and Gentiles seek wisdom” (1 Corinthians 1).

“But he, seeing...” He answers not their words but their thoughts. In this he gives a sure sign of his power, by which he searches out the secrets of hearts.

According to the literal sense, it is clear that every kingdom which is solid and firm, if divided into parts, is reduced to desolation, emptied of its inhabitants; and house falls upon house when the inhabitants of one household are either crushed or punished by the family of another household.

He explains where these things tend spiritually when he adds: “But if Satan also is divided against himself.” If, as you say, I cast out demons by the prince of demons, then the kingdom of the devil is divided against itself, and thus the power of his wickedness [Col. 0289D] cannot stand.

But if one demon cannot cast out another, you falsely say that I cast out demons by the prince of demons. If he can, as you say, then look to yourselves, so that you may depart from his divided kingdom and not be involved together in its ruin.

That the Lord does not cast out demons as the prince of demons, but for another reason, let them attend to what follows.

### Verse 19

“But if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out?” He calls the apostles the sons of the Jews. Among the other miracles they had received from the Lord, they also cast out demons. They attributed this expulsion not to the devil but to God, since they knew that they had learned no evil arts from the Lord.

Therefore, choosing the lowly and despised things of the world, in which [Col. 0290A] there was no contrived wickedness, they will sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

Or, “sons” means the exorcists of that people, who, having invoked the name of the Lord, cast out demons. It is as though he said: If the expulsion of demons in their case is attributed not to the devil but to God, why should the same work in me not have the same cause? Therefore they will be your judges—not by authority, but by comparison, since they attribute the expulsion not to the devil but to God.

“But if...” It is as though he said: A divided kingdom cannot stand; but the kingdom of Satan is divided, as you say, if Satan casts out Satan. Therefore, and so forth.

### Verse 20

“But if I cast out demons by the finger of God...” The Son is called the hand or arm of the Father. The Holy Spirit is called a finger because of the distinction among the various gifts given to human beings through the Holy Spirit [Col. 0290B], just as fingers are distinct from one another; and the inequality of the members does no harm.

Although the arm is larger than the finger, the arm and the finger nevertheless constitute one body. By this finger the Law was written on the tablets. This finger the magicians confessed to be present in Egypt.

“Surely the kingdom of God has come...” That is, God’s judicial power, by which he separates the good from the wicked on the day of judgment. Or, “kingdom” means heavenly blessedness. It is as though he said: If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then without doubt you should know that the entrance to the heavenly kingdom has been opened to believers.

### Verse 21

“When a strong man, fully armed, guards his courtyard...” It is as though he said: If I cast out demons by Beelzebub, as you say, then I would in some respect agree with the devil’s works. But I agree with him in no way; rather, I hasten to overcome him and cast him out [Col. 0290C] from my faithful ones.

“When the strong man”—strong for harming, armed with many spiritual wickednesses—“guards his courtyard,” that is, the world, which lies in the power of the evil one. In it, until the coming of the Son of God, the devil ruled without opposition and exercised his wickedly peaceful dominion in the hearts of unbelievers.

### Verse 22

“But when one stronger than he attacks him...” He calls himself stronger because, not by a peaceful agreement and cooperation, as they falsely accused him, but by stronger power he cast the devil down and freed the world from his domination.

The devil’s weapons which he took away are the most subtle devices of spiritual wickedness. The spoils are the souls deceived by him, whom Christ the victor distributes. This is one of the marks of a triumphant conqueror: “When he had led captivity captive, he gave gifts to men” [Col. 0290D], some as apostles, others as evangelists (Ephesians 4), etc.

### Verse 23

“He who is not with me...” Truly my works do not agree with Satan’s works, because I myself agree with him in nothing; rather, we are wholly opposed. I am humble and kind, desiring to save souls; he is proud and envious, desiring to destroy them.

By my preaching I gather virtues; he scatters and separates from the unity of the Church. “And he who does not gather...” These words may, by extension, be understood of all heretics and schismatics, who are all excluded from the kingdom of God.

### Verse 24

“When the unclean spirit...” Because you withdraw yourselves from my kingdom by attributing my works to the devil [Col. 0291A], the devil dwells in you as in his own kingdom, more grievously than at the beginning.

“When he has gone out.” The devil went out from the Jews when that people received the Law and the worship of the one God. He then passed to the Gentiles, who were dry and barren, lacking the richness of the Holy Spirit and love of neighbor.

Among them he now finds no rest, because, once the faith of Christ has been received, he is expelled from the hearts of the Gentiles. Then he says: “I will return to the Jews whom I previously left.”

He finds that people swept clean—that is, cleansed of the Pharisees’ superfluous observances and of the ceremonies of the Law, which have no value after Christ’s coming. And, in order to possess it more firmly, he takes with him the whole company of demons.

The Israelites are now worse—blaspheming Christ in their gatherings—than they formerly were in Egypt before receiving the Law, because it is greater unbelief [Col. 0291B] not to receive the one who has come than not to believe in the one who was to come.

“Seeking rest, and finding none.” Because, having fed upon wicked thoughts and actions, he perceives that all his temptations have ceased in the minds of believers, he then says: “I will return to my house from which I came out.”

“I will return to that conscience from which I was expelled in baptism, and subject it to myself once more as my former possession under my customary domination.”

### Verse 25

“And when he comes, he finds it swept clean.” When, driven by his crimes, he returns to such a rejected person, he finds the sinner’s conscience cleansed of vices in baptism but filled with no good work.

### Verse 26

“Then he takes seven other spirits...” The fullness [Col. 0291C] of all vices. These spirits are called worse than the devil because, although the devil is evil, those who are handed over to vices under the pressure of their own merits are not only evil but also strive, through hypocrisy, to display an appearance of goodness by pretended virtues.

“And the last state of that person becomes worse than the first.” It would have been better to remain ignorant of the way of truth than, after acknowledging it, to turn back.

### Verse 27

“Blessed is the womb...” Here Mary, who carried the Lord, is praised. The perversity both of the Jews of that time and of future heretics who deny Christ’s true humanity is refuted, because the true Son of God is confessed against the blaspheming Jews, and the true son of man, consubstantial with his mother, is attested.

For unless he were one flesh with his mother, that virgin womb and those breasts [Col. 0291D] would be blessed in vain.

“And the breasts...” According to the physicians, from the same source come milk for nourishing children and semen for begetting them. Therefore he could be conceived from the virgin’s seed who could be nourished by her milk.

### Verse 28

“Rather...” It is as though he said: Mary is not to be praised only because she carried the Word of God in her womb; she is supremely blessed because she kept God’s commandments in her actions.

So too all are blessed who conceive the word of God through the hearing of faith and bring forth and nourish the keeping of good works in their own hearts or in the hearts of their neighbors.

“Those who hear...” This is said in praise of the Church. By contrast, the Pharisees are condemned, since they sought neither to hear nor to fulfill God’s word, but to blaspheme it.

[Col. 0292A] ### Verse 29

“He began to say...” Some had slandered his works, and he had answered them up to this point. Others, testing him, sought a sign from heaven, and he answers them here.

“This generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it,” etc. He gave the disciples a sign of his divinity: first, when he was transfigured on the mountain, and afterward, when they saw him lifted up into heaven. But to unbelievers: from the lowly suffering of his humanity.

### Verse 31

“The queen of the south will rise...” After the people of the Jews have been condemned, the mystery of the Church is expressed. It is gathered from the ends of the earth: in the Ninevites, through repentance—which abolishes sin; in the queen of the south, through the pursuit of wisdom—which avoids sin. Thus it gathers together to recognize the words of the true Peacemaker.

For the Church consists of two elements: either that you cease to sin, or that you do not know how to sin [Col. 0292B].

“In the judgment.” She will rise not a thousand years before the judgment, as the Jews imagine, but in the judgment itself.

“With the men.” (BED.) Behold, the common resurrection of both good and wicked is shown.

“And condemn them.” Not by the authority of judgment but by comparison with a better action, because, leaving her kingdom, she came to Judea to hear a man famous for wisdom, while the Jews do not hear the true Wisdom of God dwelling among them but blaspheme him.

“In the preaching.” Jonah preached for a few days; Christ for a long time. Jonah preached to foreigners; Christ to his fellow citizens. Jonah performed no sign; Christ performed many.

### Verse 33

“No one...” (BED.) He preferred the Church to the Synagogue in the figure of the queen and the Ninevites, etc., up to the point where they refuse to enter by believing through the open door of the light.

[Col. 0292C] ### Verse 35
