“See therefore that the light in you is not darkness.” After establishing right faith, he also instructs them concerning good works and a good intention, so that not only their works but also their thoughts and the intentions of their hearts may be cleansed.

It is as though he said: I light the lamp of faith in your understanding and place it in the Church. You, for your part, light your lamps as far as you can—that is, cleanse the intentions of your hearts—so that even your works may please God because of their pure intention.

Although these words were directed especially against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, who secretly sought signs, they instruct us generally according to the moral sense.

### Verse 37

“And while he was speaking...” He does not say, “while he was speaking these things,” but simply, “while he was speaking.” This suggests that he did not turn to the Pharisee immediately after these words had ended [Col. 0292D], but after other matters had intervened.

For while he was still speaking after this discourse had ended, behold, his mother and brothers were seeking to speak with him. After he answered the one who announced them, “The one who does the will of my Father is my brother, sister, and mother,” he then entered the Pharisee’s house for a meal.

“Why was he not baptized?” The Jews frequently wash their hands before eating, holding to the tradition of the elders; and when they return from the marketplace, they do not eat unless they have been baptized—that is, ritually washed.

### Verse 39

“Of the cup.” Mark reports that the Jews were accustomed to observe ritual washings of cups, jugs, couches, and bronze vessels.

The cup is a glass vessel; the bowl is earthenware made from clay. By this is signified the frailty of the human body. In it they outwardly display holiness [Col. 0293A] and pretend to righteousness: what was outside they washed, but within they were utterly wicked.

“But as for what is within you...” No one should think that fornication and similar bodily vices alone are serious, while spiritual vices—such as greed, anger, pride, and so forth—are trivial, as the Pharisees thought.

### Verse 41

“But give as alms what remains.” Now the good teacher explains how the pollution of the body should be cleansed. Here he expands what he had said briefly above about cleansing the eye of the heart.

This entire passage is directed toward inviting us to pursue simplicity and condemning the superfluities and earthly things of the Jews. Because they understand the Law according to the body, they are compared to glass and a bowl on account of their fragility.

Although they sin grievously in this matter, forgiveness of their sin is nevertheless promised to them [Col. 0293B] if they strive to show mercy.

“Give to the poor what remains after what is necessary for food and clothing.” Or: I give this counsel—what remains after such great crimes, give as alms.

The first almsgiving is to heal your souls by believing in me, who cleanse hearts. When hearts have been cleansed through faith, everything external will also be clean.

Whoever wishes to give alms in an orderly way begins with himself and first gives it to himself. For almsgiving is an act of mercy; hence it is said: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God.”

### Verse 42

“You neglect judgment.” Briefly he touched upon many of their vices. They devote themselves to tithing even the least things but do not possess fear of the coming judgment or love of God.

They neglect judgment because they do not refer everything [Col. 0293C] they do to judgment. They neglect charity because they do not love God from affection.

But again, lest he make you devoted to faith while neglecting works, he adds the perfection of the faithful person, so that after faith he may perform works.

### Verse 44

“You are like tombs.” Here he rebukes the superstition of those teachers, who outwardly display the appearance of sound doctrine but conceal the filth they carry within.

### Verse 45

“But answering...” Having heard the word of God, the Pharisee, because of an evil conscience, thinks that an insult has been directed against him. When the punishment of the faithless has been mentioned, he understands that he is being condemned.

### Verse 47

“Woe to you.” They are not reproved for adorning the tombs of the prophets, but because they imitate the prophets’ murderers [Col. 0293D]. By building the tombs, they accuse the crimes of their fathers.

But by persecuting Christ and the apostles they imitate their fathers’ crimes, and they turn upon themselves the sentence of condemnation that they had pronounced against their fathers.

### Verse 48

“Indeed...” You build them in order to win the favor of the crowd, as though you abhorred their crimes; but your very action shows that you agree with their faithlessness, because you do this good deed wrongly, for the sake of empty glory.

“But you...” Because you are their imitators, you fill up what was lacking in your fathers: namely, that you persecute me and my followers, just as they persecuted the prophets.

### Verse 49

“Prophets and apostles; and some of them they will kill and persecute” [Col. 0294A]. Heretics lie when they say that the Old Testament had one author and the New Testament another.

### Verse 50

“From the generation...” All wicked people are one generation, one city, and one body of the devil, just as all good people are said to be one generation and one body.

### Verse 51

“From the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah.” Why does he extend it to this point, when many were killed after him before Christ’s birth, and, once Christ had been born, the infants were immediately slain by this generation?

Because Abel was a shepherd of sheep and was killed in the field, while Zechariah was a priest and was killed in the temple court, the two signify the orders of martyrs: the laity and those devoted to the service of the altar.

[Col. 0294B] ### Verse 52

“Because you have taken away the key.” The key is the humility of Christ. Those who possess it understand the Scriptures.

The lawyers neither understand it themselves through the Law and the prophets nor wish it to be understood by others.

“To enter with the key” means not being content with the surface of the letter but penetrating to the understanding of the mysteries.

Or, if a teacher scandalizes by his example those whom he builds up by his word, he neither enters the kingdom of God himself nor allows those who could enter to do so.

### Verse 53

“When he said these things to them, the Pharisees and lawyers began...” How true were the accusations of their faithlessness, hypocrisy, and impiety that they had heard is shown by the fact that, although such a storm of thunder was crashing over them, they did not repent but attacked the teacher of truth.

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0294C] ### Verse 1

“Beware.” Everything that he discussed earlier in the Pharisee’s house belongs to this leaven. Hence the Apostle also says: “Not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice” (1 Corinthians 5), etc.

“Beware of the leaven.” This is a beautiful passage concerning the preservation of simplicity and the imitation of faith, so that, after the manner of the Jews, we may not express one thing in our hearts while pretending another with our voices, since we know that on the day of judgment there can be no hiding place for deceit.

### Verse 2

“Nor is anything hidden that will not be known.” Therefore do not imitate pretenders, because certainly a time will come on the day of judgment when both your virtue and their hypocrisy will be revealed to everyone. Hence it follows:

“Whatever you have said in the darkness will be said in the light.” Not only will everything be disclosed in the future, but even in the present age, throughout the whole Church across the world, what you have spoken in darkness—that is, in the shadow of persecutions and prisons—will be publicly preached [Col. 0294D], when your deeds are read aloud in the heights.

“Whatever you have said in the darkness will be heard in the light.” (AMBR.) What you have said in darkness—that is, in fear—will be spoken in the light, that is, in confidence in the truth, after receiving the Holy Spirit. And what you have spoken in the ear—that is, secretly—will be proclaimed upon the housetops, that is, after the dwelling of the flesh has been trampled down.

### Verse 4

“I say to you...” (ID.) Since there are two causes of faithlessness, etc., up to the point where courage is thus the foundation of faith.

### Verse 5

“But I will show you...” There are two kinds of persecutors: one openly persecuting, the other deceitfully flattering. Just as above [Col. 0295A] he armed them against hypocrisy, so here he arms them against executioners.

This entire passage instructs them to undergo suffering for confessing the Lord—whether through contempt for death, hope of reward, or steadfastness in the face of the announced punishment.

### Verse 6

“Are not five sparrows...” (AMBR.) The five sparrows are the five senses of the body; or, according to Matthew, the two are body and soul, etc., up to the point where the contemplation of the faithful will certainly prevail with him.

“They are sold for two pennies.” A *dipondius* is a weight composed of two *asses*. What is one in numbers is an *as* in weights; what is two is a *dipondius*.

“And not one of them...” He had inspired an affection for simplicity and raised the strength of the mind; only faith was wavering, and he strengthens it through things of lesser value.

As the Apostle says [Col. 0295B]: “Does God care for oxen?” (1 Corinthians 9). But care is one thing, and knowledge another.

### Verse 7

“But even the hairs...” This is not a matter of actual counting but of the capacity for knowledge, by analogy with money that is counted in order to be preserved. Here the great providence of God is evident: neither small nor insignificant words escape him.

### Verse 8

“Everyone who...” Lest anyone think that faith of the heart alone would suffice during persecution, he says: “Everyone who confesses me.”

A person confesses Jesus with that charity which works through love; he denies him who does not obey the commandments.

“The Son of man.” The Son confesses before the Father the one who, through the Son, has access to the Father. He is denied by the Son before the Father when the Son and the Father are not revealed to him in the power of their divinity.

And lest it be thought that the condition is the same for all who deny [Col. 0295C]—both those who deny deliberately and those who deny through weakness or ignorance—he adds: “Everyone who speaks a word against the Son of man will be forgiven.”

### Verse 10

“But to the one...” Even for the person who, having been scandalized by the weakness of my flesh, suspects me to be merely a human being or a glutton, there will be forgiveness.

But whoever, not recognizing the grace of the Holy Spirit—which inspires repentance and restores one to the assembly—remains with an impenitent heart, will be unforgiven. For this is no longer human but diabolical.

### Verse 11

“When they bring you into synagogues, before rulers and authorities...” The terror of such gatherings usually takes away freedom of speech.

“Do not be anxious.” Offer your will for Christ. Christ himself will speak on his own behalf.

[Col. 0295D] ### Verse 13

“Teacher...” While the one commending the grace of heavenly peace and unity wishes to introduce the disturbance of earthly division, he calls him “man,” that is, earthly.

For where there is such zeal and contention, people are earthly and walk according to human standards.

Among brothers, an inheritance should be divided not by a judge standing between them but by piety acting as mediator, although the inheritance of immortality is not something that human beings should seek through money.

### Verse 14

“Who appointed me...” I am not the God of dissension but of peace and unity. I came to reconcile human beings with angels, so that many may have one heart and one soul—not so that they may be divided, but so that they may have everything in common and no one among them may be in need.

The one who does not gather with me is a divider of brotherhood and an author of dissension.

[Col. 0296A] ### Verse 15

“From every kind of greed.” No one should think it a crime to divide an inheritance or gather produce into barns. The heavenly Judge also identifies this as greed, and therefore he adds: “a certain rich man.”

Just as above he argued against the Pharisees and hypocrites, so here, taking occasion from a foolish request, he argues against greed.

“Not in abundance.” A human being does not live by bread alone but by the word of God (Deuteronomy 8), nor is temporal life prolonged by an abundance of riches.

### Verse 16

“And he said...” After the commandment he adds an example for avoiding greed for temporal things.

“The land of a certain rich man produced abundant crops.” The rich man is not reproved for cultivating the land or storing the crops [Col. 0296B] in barns, but because he placed the hope of life in them and did not distribute them to the poor, so that he might receive them back in the eternal dwellings.

### Verse 17

“What shall I do?” Counting the crops and goods as his own, he does not distribute to the poor what remains but plans to reserve it for his own luxury in the future, unaware who will use what he has gathered.

### Verse 19

“My goods, and I will say...” (AMBR.) Goods are not truly a person’s if he cannot take them away with him. Mercy alone accompanies the dead.

“Rest.” Behold, the plague of laziness is joined to the plague of greed, so that he does not even call upon God for temporal things.

### Verse 20

“But God said...” God’s speaking means that, by a sudden act of judgment, he restrains a person’s wicked schemes.

“Fool!” Because you were promising yourself long periods [Col. 0296C] of wealth, tonight your life will be taken from you, and you will leave to others what you gathered.

“They demand it...” In the night the soul is taken away—one that, in the darkness of its heart, refused to foresee what could happen to it.

### Verse 21

“So is the one who is not rich toward God.” A person is rich toward God when, despising transitory things, he distributes them to the poor; his expectation is the Lord, and his substance—that is, the possession of his conscience by which he is sustained and nourished—is with God, not in earthly purses.

### Verse 22

“And he said to his disciples...” He confirms the apostles through faith in the hope of eternal things, because many are made sluggish by love of present things and despair of the future.

“Do not be anxious.” It would be more perfect to give everything to the poor and make friends from unrighteous mammon. But because devotion to faith is often recalled by weakness [Col. 0296D], he does not forbid providence, through which bread is prepared in the sweat of one’s face; rather, he forbids anxiety, which disturbs the mind and recalls it from eternal things.

### Verse 24

“Consider...” The saints are rightly compared with birds. Possessing nothing in the world and not laboring, they seek eternal things by contemplation alone, already resembling angels.

“How much more...” If God’s providence generously supplies necessities to birds that do not labor and do not claim common fruits for themselves by any special dominion, then it is true that the cause of our poverty is greed: we claim common things as though they were our own and begrudge them to others.

### Verse 26

“If therefore you cannot even do what is least...” If you cannot work even for the increase of your bodily stature [Col. 0297A]—an operation that is small for God in comparison with spiritual creation—why are you anxious about the other, greater things, that is, about the preservation of the soul?

### Verse 27

“Consider the lilies.” The comparison is clear. Lilies, unlike other plants, do not require any cultivation by farmers.

The lily also commonly signifies heavenly blessedness, to which the Lord invites us. Lilies grow not in forests but in gardens; so we too ought to be born in gardens of virtues.

“Not even Solomon...” (AMBR.) Solomon is said here to have been clothed, and elsewhere to have been covered with glory. He clothed the weakness of bodily nature, as though covered by a certain virtue of mind, with the glory of works.

“He was clothed like one of these.” What purple of kings, what design of weavers [Col. 0297B], can be compared with flowers? The color itself is called the flower’s clothing, as it is said: “Redness covered him.”

### Verse 28

“Tomorrow into the oven.” In Scripture, “tomorrow” signifies the future, as Jacob says: “Tomorrow my righteousness will answer for me” (Genesis 30).

### Verse 29

“Do not seek what you will eat or what you will drink.” He does not simply say, “Do not seek or be anxious about food or clothing,” but more explicitly, “what you will eat or what you will drink.”

In this he appears to rebuke those who, rejecting common food or clothing, seek provisions or garments more luxurious or more austere than those used by the people with whom they live.

“Do not seek to exalt yourselves.” Having forbidden anxiety about food and clothing, which are matters of necessity, he also forbids the pride that usually follows from an excess of these things [Col. 0297C]. Therefore do not seek them, because such anxiety makes you resemble unbelievers.

### Verse 30

“And all these things...” Because everything belongs to children, all these things will be added to you even when you do not seek them, so that neither in the present nor in the future will any grace be lacking to the faithful.

If these things are withheld from them, it is for testing; if they are given, it is for thanksgiving, because all things work together for good for those who are good.

### Verse 32

“Do not be afraid.” Seek the kingdom, and do not despair of the kingdom, because the Father, in his gracious goodness, will give you the kingdom—not according to your merits.

“Little flock.” Either because of the greater number of the reprobate, or rather because of the devotion of humility, through which the Church grows and through which the kingdom is reached.

[Col. 0297D] **VERSE 33.**—“Sell.” Do not merely fear that those who are serving on behalf of the kingdom will lack the necessities of life; also sell what you possess for almsgiving, which is the way to the kingdom, since through it sins are redeemed. Do not merely share your food with the poor; also sell your possessions, so that, having once renounced all your goods for the Lord, you may afterward work with your hands for the means of living and for almsgiving. “Give alms.” Let the one who despises all worldly things for heaven sell what he has and distribute it; let the one who does not possess such great virtue give alms from what he has. “A treasure that does not fail.” Temporal things either fail because of their own frailty, or, if something durable remains, such as precious stones, it can be taken away by thieves. But things given for Christ confer an eternal fruit in heaven.

**VERSE 34.**—“For where your treasure is.” This is said universally, both of money and of all pleasures. The glutton’s treasure is his belly, and there his heart is; so it is with other things. For if the treasure is on earth, the heart is below; if it is in heaven, it is fixed in Christ. It is necessary that wherever the treasure of love has gone before, there the affection of thought should follow.

**VERSE 35.**—“Let your loins be girded,” etc., “and your lamps.” God is not pleased with one without the other: either when someone does good works while luxury has not yet been restrained, or when he lives chastely without exercising himself through good works. And so that you may be removed from love of temporal things, and may perform the good works you do with a pure intention toward eternal things, “gird your loins”—that is, restrain the movements of carnal desires—and “have burning lamps,” so that in your activity you burn with the love of God alone and offer an example to others.

**VERSE 36.**—“Waiting.” Whether you avoid evils or do good works, you are not made clean by these things; instead, you must await only the Redeemer’s coming. “When he returns.” The Lord went to the wedding when, after the resurrection, the new man joined to himself the multitude of angels; he returns from them when he is revealed to us through judgment. Thus he appropriately adds concerning those who are waiting: “So that when he comes, they may immediately open to him.” He does not wish to open to the judge who knocks—the one who, fearing to see in anger the one he despised, dreads leaving the body. The person who gladly and confidently receives the judge opens to him, and rejoices at approaching death; hence it is added: “Blessed are those servants whom, when he comes,” etc.

**VERSE 37.**—“Watching.” The person watches who keeps his eyes open in the true light, so that he may avoid the darkness of negligence; who also puts into practice what he has believed; who is diligent in caring for the flock entrusted to him. What is owed to those who watch he adds: “Amen, I say to you.”

**VERSES 38, 39.**—“And if he comes in the second watch,” etc. He calls them “watches” by comparison with sentries. In the night of this world we must always be vigilant against the enemy and await the coming light, that is, the judge’s arrival. The first watch, therefore, is the vigilance of childhood; the second, of youth; the third, of old age. If someone has neglected to keep watch in childhood, let him nevertheless not despair, but let him come to his senses in youth, or at least finally in old age, because the merciful judge patiently awaits our delays. To shake the slothfulness of the mind, he introduces the analogy of those condemned in worldly affairs, so that through it the mind may be roused to guard itself. Hence: “But know this: if the master of the house had known.” When the master of the house does not know, the thief breaks into the house, because while the spirit sleeps, neglecting its own custody, unexpected death breaks into the dwelling of the flesh and drags it to punishments. He would resist the thief if he were watching, because, anticipating the judge’s secretly approaching arrival, he would meet it through repentance.

**VERSE 40.**—“At an hour when you do not expect it, the Son of Man will come.” The Lord always wished the final hour to remain unknown, so that it would always be feared and preparation for it would always be made.

[Col. 0299A] **VERSE 41.**—“But Peter said to him.” Since the Lord had set forth two matters—namely, that he would come suddenly and that they ought to be prepared by waiting—Peter asks whether those exalted institutions of heavenly life, which are necessary for those preparing themselves, concern the apostles and those like them alone, or all who are to be saved.

**VERSE 42.**—“But the Lord said.” In response to the questions, the Lord says that the first and the second judgment will come upon everyone, and that each person will either be rewarded or condemned according to his merits. Then he adds what Peter had chiefly asked: namely, that the grace of virtues which he had brought to the world should be pursued by each person as far as possible. This is expressed in the words: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth.” “Who, do you think, is the faithful steward?” As if he were saying: This concerns you more particularly, you who have been appointed stewards, regarding vigilance and preparation, so that you may prepare both yourselves and others for the judge’s coming, because few administer well the stewardship entrusted to them. “And the prudent one whom the Lord appointed over his household,” etc. How rare is the person who serves the Lord for the Lord’s sake, feeding Christ’s sheep not for profit but from love of Christ, prudent with regard to the future and providing for himself, whom he appointed—that is, how rare is the person who has been called by God like Aaron, rather than thrusting himself forward, and who does not feed himself more than the sheep!

**VERSE 43.**—“Blessed.” As if he were saying: There are few faithful people. But the one who is found faithfully distributing the provision of the word and keeping watch over the care of the flock will be glorified with eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0299C] **VERSE 44.**—“Over all that he possesses.” As great as the difference in merits between good hearers and good teachers, so great is the difference in their rewards. He makes the good hearers recline and, passing by, ministers to them; but he appoints the stewards over all that he possesses—not so that they alone may have eternal things, but so that they may have them before the others, both on account of their own life and on account of their care of the flock.

**VERSE 45.**—“But if that servant should say.” Notice that among the servant’s vices is reckoned the fact that he thinks his master’s return is delayed. Among the virtues of the good servant, however, it is not reckoned that he expected him soon, but only that he ministered faithfully. Nothing, therefore, is better than patiently accepting that we do not know what cannot be known, while nevertheless laboring to be found worthy.

“And to eat.” That is, to become occupied with all the crimes and enticements of the world, which cause the mind to wander; or, literally, if he is devoted to gluttony and drunkenness.

**VERSE 46.**—“And will assign him his portion.” The wicked will be punished with the unbelievers, but differently. Those who sin knowingly will be punished more severely; those who sin out of ignorance, less severely. And among the unjust, each person will have a condemnation as much more tolerable as his iniquity was less.

**VERSE 48.**—“With few.” The mildest punishment of all belongs to those who, apart from original sin, have added no further offense.

**(AMBROSE.)** Many who think they will be beaten less if they do not know, etc., up to “but they are judged despisers.”

[Col. 0300A] “But everyone.” The wicked person who knows more will rightly be beaten more, and the one who does not know, less, because more was entrusted to the former and less to the latter; and from everyone to whom more is entrusted, more is required.

**VERSE 49.**—“Fire,” etc. As if he were saying: You were asking whether I warn everyone, with loins girded and lamps burning, to await the Lord’s coming. But I, who came into the world for this very purpose—that I might kindle human beings from the desires of the world toward heavenly things—want nothing other than that the radiance of this conflagration should illuminate every part of the world until the end of the age, and that it should burn so intensely in the hearts of the faithful that it could not be extinguished by any surge of waves or blast of wind.

“But I have a baptism with which to be baptized,” etc. So that this fire may be kindled in the hearts of the faithful, enabling them perfectly to despise all temporal things [Col. 0300B] and themselves, I must first be baptized with a baptism—that is, drenched with the anointing of my own blood. For the Spirit would not be given unless Jesus were first glorified. “And how.” The Lord’s condescension is so great that, in order to pour devotion into us, bring perfection in us to completion, and mature the passion undertaken for us, he testifies that he has this purpose within himself. Although he had nothing in himself from which he might suffer grief, he was nevertheless distressed by our troubles, and at the time of his death displayed sadness—not from fear of his own death, but because of the delay of our redemption, which he assumed. “Until it is completed.” Whoever is distressed until perfection is secure regarding perfection; he is not distressed because of perfection itself. Rather, the death of the body is the release of anxiety, not an accumulation of pain.

[Col. 0300C] **VERSE 51.**—“Do you think?” Since, after the baptism of the Passion and after the coming of the fire, the earth would be burned, he says this because the whole world was divided against itself on account of the faith of Christ: every household had believers and unbelievers, the latter fighting against the faith and the former on behalf of the faith.

**VERSE 52.**—“In one house.” Every human being is one house, either of God or of the devil. Thus the spiritual person is a spiritual house. “Divided.” The first cause is religion toward God; the second is piety toward one’s neighbor. For divine things must be placed before human things. One must not, therefore, renounce one’s own relations, but God must be preferred to all. Indeed, relations by nature are gifts of God, and the gift that is received ought not to be loved more than God, by whom the received gift is preserved. “Three against two.” That is, son and daughter and daughter-in-law against father and mother; and two against three, that is, father and mother—where the mother-in-law is also understood—against son, daughter, and daughter-in-law.

**VERSE 54.**—“He was also saying.” After he had instructed the apostles concerning his first coming, indicating what had happened in it, and had admonished them about the future, teaching how they ought to await him, he turned his discourse to the crowds, among whom were Pharisees, as Matthew indicates. Since they neither believed that the first coming had occurred nor awaited the second properly, they were testing him by seeking a sign from heaven. He therefore rebukes them, because, if they wished to pay attention, they could have a sure indication of both comings from the words of the prophets. “When you see.” Mystically, a cloud rising from the west signifies Christ’s flesh rising from death, from which time the rain of evangelical preaching has been poured upon all lands. The south wind blowing before the heat signifies lighter tribulations before the judgment.

“A cloud comes.” Literally, the meaning is clear: those who can foresee the condition of the winds from changes in the elements could also know the time of both comings, both from the sayings of the prophets and from the magnificence of the works.

**VERSE 56.**—“Hypocrites,” etc. And so that certain uneducated people in the crowd, flattering themselves because of their ignorance, might not excuse themselves by saying that they did not know the Law and the Prophets, he adds that they could discern by natural reason either that the one who performed works which no one else had performed was above humanity and was God, or that, after so many injustices of the world, the just judgment of the Creator was going to come.

**VERSE 58.**—“When you are going.” When in this life you prepare yourself to see the judge’s face appeased, although the word of God is opposed to your flesh, nevertheless use it as a guard given to you on this journey, lest contempt accuse you. “With your adversary.” Our adversary on the way is the word of God, contrary to our carnal desires in the present life. The person is freed from it who humbly submits to its commandments; otherwise, guilty because of contempt for the word, the sinner will be held in the judge’s examination, and the judge will hand him over to the exactor—that is, the devil. For he will permit the devil to drag his soul to punishment, and the exactor himself, who demands punishment for the offense he suggested, will thrust it back into Gehenna.

[Col. 0301C] “Take pains,” etc. These words also concern trampling down the enticements of the world and awaiting the judge’s coming. As if he were saying: Since it is certain that the strict judge will come, live here in such a way that you will not be condemned in that judgment.

**VERSE 59.**—“Until you repay.” He continually repays by suffering punishments for his sins, but he never obtains pardon.

# CHAPTER XIII

**VERSE 1.**—“There were present.” While the Teacher of truth was instructing those present about how they ought to prepare themselves for the judge’s coming, and how those who do not prepare themselves must be condemned, word was brought to him about the Galileans, as though they had therefore suffered this because they had not prepared themselves well. The Lord answers that they truly had been sinners and had perished justly, and that other sinners would likewise perish if they did not attend to the fact that they were sinners. “Those who reported it.” As if they were saying: It is evident that these men were sinners and destined for eternal condemnation, since they were killed by an impious governor in so criminal a death amid their sacrifices. “Of the Galileans.” The Galileans paid the penalties for their crimes by an impious and criminal death; nevertheless, it was not death itself that harmed them so that they would be sent into the second death, but their wicked life. They were punished either for the correction of the living, so that “when a pestilent person is scourged, the foolish become wiser,” or as an example for those unwilling to be corrected, and therefore destined to perish most miserably.

**VERSE 3.**—“All,” etc. This was fulfilled after the Lord’s Passion, when the Romans, beginning from Galilee, so devastated the unrepentant Jews [Col. 0302A] that they defiled not only the courts of the Temple but also the inner parts of the house, where the Galileans had no access, with human blood.

**VERSE 4.**—“Those eighteen.” These inhabitants of Jerusalem, like the Galileans, were not the only sinners, but they were punished as a terror to the rest. Crushed by the fall of the tower, they signify the Jews who refused to repent and who were destined to perish with their walls. Nor is it without reason that there were eighteen: among the Greeks this number is expressed by iota and eta, that is, by the same letters with which the name “Jesus” begins. It signifies that those Jews would perish above all who refused to receive the name of the Savior. That tower signifies the one who is the tower of strength; it is rightly associated with Siloam, because Siloam, interpreted as “sent,” signifies him who, sent by the Father, came into the world and will crush all upon whom he falls.

**VERSE 6.**—“A fig tree.” At the origin of the human race, after Adam and Eve had sinned, they made themselves coverings from fig leaves. The fig leaves therefore signify sins. They were under the fig tree, as if under the shadow of death, concerning which it was said: “Light has arisen for those who were sitting under the shadow of death” (Isaiah 9).

**VERSE 7.**—“Seeking fruit.” The vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel, in which the Synagogue was established, just as a fig tree is in a vineyard. But he who allowed the sinful one in the vineyard to be plundered by passersby also commanded that this fig tree be cut down. In seeking fruit from it, he was not ignorant that it was present, but showed figuratively that the Synagogue ought already to have fruit. Nor does he seek it prematurely, since he came for three years. The one who established the Synagogue through Moses, appearing in the flesh, teaches frequently in the Synagogue and seeks the fruit of faith, but does not find it in the Pharisees.

“And he said to the gardener of the vineyard.” The gardener of the vineyard is the teachers and apostles, through whose prayers and admonitions the continual care of God is commended. The Lord often complains to them about the fruitless people of the Jews, who during the three years of his visitation—that is, in the legal decrees, the prophetic testimonies, and the grace of the Gospel—had proved negligent.

“Why does it also occupy the ground,” etc. The Jewish people may be signified by the ground occupied by the barren fig tree. It is oppressed by the harmful shadow of its leaders, so that it does not see the light of truth, and is hindered by their example from being warmed by the sun of love. Hence (Matthew 23): “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees,” etc. The person occupies the ground who does not exercise the place he holds in good works, who by an evil example provides an impediment to others.

**VERSE 8.**—“Until I dig around it,” etc. Until, by instilling fear of present afflictions and eternal condemnation, I humble the root of the unfruitful mind. A pit is low, and reproof humbles the mind when it shows it its own condition. The gardener knows how to cultivate the ground who knows how to rebuke vices. He understood that the hardness and pride of the Jews were the cause of their barrenness. He therefore promises that hard hearts will be dug with apostolic mattocks and that the proud will be recalled to humility.

“I will spread manure.” That is, I will bring back to the mind the abomination of the evils it has committed, and, as if from the richness of manure, I will awaken the grace of compunction together with the fruits of good works. The sins of the flesh are called manure. They are placed at the root of the tree when the memory of the thought touches the conscience of wickedness; and when the person repents of it, he returns to the fruitfulness of action, as if through contact with manure.

**VERSE 9.**—“And if indeed.” Since the order of repentance required that he should add something such as “it shall be preserved,” he nevertheless added nothing of the kind, but left the sentence suspended.

“But if not”—namely, if it does not produce fruit—he immediately appended the judgment of coming condemnation, because he saw that they were more inclined to deny than to believe.

**VERSE 10.**—“He was teaching.” The Lord is said to have taught this comparison concerning the fig tree in the Synagogue, so that it might be indicated that the parable pertained to the Synagogue itself. The fact that he seeks fruit on the fig tree and does not find it signifies that he offers the word to the Synagogue, but it does not receive it. Nevertheless, understanding that it was not to be uprooted entirely, but that its remnants were to be saved through faith, he immediately presents there the healing of the primitive Church under the figure of the bent woman. The reserved fig tree, therefore, signifies the same thing as the woman made upright. “On the Sabbaths.” He teaches on the Sabbaths and makes the bent woman upright because, through the word of preaching, he leads those raised from temporal things to eternal things into the rest of the resurrection.

[Col. 0303C] **VERSE 11.**—“Behold, a woman,” etc. This woman could not be made upright until after eighteen years, because human nature cannot lay aside this corruption and be raised to put on the incorruption of eternal blessedness unless it has first fulfilled the Law contained in the ten commandments and the grace in which Christ’s resurrection took place and ours is awaited.

“Years,” etc. The number six, in which the creation of the world was perfected, signifies the perfection of works. Multiplied by three, it produces eighteen, and signifies those who have perfection of works in the three periods of the Lord’s visitation—namely, before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. At that time, therefore, Judea was bent away from the uprightness of its mind, and worked at things that were more earthly than heavenly.

[Col. 0303D] **VERSE 14.**—“Because it is the Sabbath.” God rested from the works of the world on the Sabbath. Hence Moses also commanded that one should rest on the Sabbath from servile and harmful activity, prefiguring the time when our secular works, but not religious works—that is, the praising of God—would cease. As a sign of this, the Lord also heals on the Sabbath. The ruler of the synagogue, not understanding this, is deceived and deceives others, because the Law prohibited not healing a human being on the Sabbath, but doing servile works—that is, being burdened by sins.

**VERSE 15.**—“Hypocrites.” He rightly calls them hypocrites, that is, pretenders, because, although they desire to appear as teachers of the peoples, they do not hesitate to postpone the healing of a human being to the care of an animal. “Does he not untie his ox?” Mystically, the ox that knows its owner and the donkey that knows the manger of its lord signify the Jewish and Gentile peoples. Both, freed from the bonds of sin, laid aside the thirst and heat of this world by drinking from the Lord’s fountain. In these two animals the Lord foretells the calling of the two peoples, despite the opposition of the Jews.

**VERSE 16.**—“And ought not this woman,” etc. The daughter of Abraham—and every faithful soul is a daughter of Abraham—the Church gathered from both peoples to the faith, after the time of the Law and of the Lord’s resurrection had been fulfilled, broke through the bonds of its long captivity by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. Thus, for the daughter of Abraham to be raised from the bond of a harmful inclination is the same as for the ox or donkey to be untied from the manger and led to drink.

**VERSE 17.**—“All his adversaries were ashamed.” Those who are ashamed of the Savior’s words show themselves to be like the barren fig tree. Those who rejoice in the miracles, therefore, belong to the daughter of Abraham—that is, to the Church—which glorifies God for her being made upright. “His adversaries.” The scribes and Pharisees could neither openly contradict the truth nor, because of envy, were willing to believe. “All the people were rejoicing.” The simple and humble, who love the words of truth and the miracles, are a figure of the nations who, after the Jews have been blinded, are to be gathered to the faith through humility. Hence the Savior also commends their faith by comparison with a grain of mustard seed.

**VERSE 18.**—“He was therefore saying.” Since those who were rejoicing and glorifying were present, he spoke for the commendation and instruction of those who were to be exalted in the Church through humility and the fervor of faith.

[Col. 0304C] **VERSE 19.**—“It is like,” etc. The mustard seed is a lowly and simple thing, but when it is crushed, it releases its power. The kingdom of heaven, therefore—that is, the faith by which one comes to the kingdom—is compared with a mustard seed, because at first it is humble and almost despised, and bitter in taste because of the weakness of Christ and the scandal of the cross. But when crushed by adversities, it pours forth the grace of its power and fills those around it with its fragrance, since even after death it proclaimed throughout the whole world the glory of the resurrection and ascension. Alternatively, the mustard seed is Christ’s body, which Joseph took and buried in a garden, and which afterward grew through the resurrection and ascension. “It spread out its branches,” sending preachers throughout the whole world, in whose words and consolations the faithful breathe again after the weariness of the world.

[Col. 0304D] **VERSE 21.**—“Which a woman took,” etc. The woman is the Church, whose flour we are—all of us who are crushed through the practice of fear and hope as though between the upper and lower millstones, so that we may be one bread, many in Christ. The Church therefore hid the leaven of love in three measures of flour, because she commands us to love God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength.

**VERSE 22.**—“And he went,” etc. He preached everywhere without distinction, not discriminating among persons, but seeking salvation for believers.

**VERSE 24.**—“Strive to enter,” etc. As if he were saying: Truly there are few, and they attain it with great labor, because unless the mind’s purpose burns fervently, the wave of the world cannot be overcome, through which the soul is always dragged downward.

[Col. 0305A] **VERSE 25.**—“But when,” etc. Christ is the master of the house. Although he is everywhere present through his divinity, he is said to be already inside for those whom his present vision gladdens in heaven, but he is as though outside for those whom, while they struggle in this pilgrimage, he secretly assists. He will enter, therefore, when he leads the whole Church to contemplate him. He will shut the door when he takes away from the reprobate the opportunity for repentance. They will stand outside and knock—that is, separated from the just, they will plead in vain for the mercy they despised. “You will begin to stand outside.” Strive now, in the time of mercy, because at the time of judgment the opportunity for repentance is taken away from the reprobate, though it is now open to all who devoutly seek it.

“I do not know you.” The light does not know the darkness, that is, it does not look upon it; for if it did look upon it, it would not be darkness.

[Col. 0305B] **VERSE 26.**—“We ate,” etc. The eating of feasts does not help when the piety of faith does not commend it. Knowledge of the Scriptures does not make someone known to God when the wickedness of his works shows him to be unworthy. Alternatively, this may be understood simply of the Jews, who, rejecting the mysteries of the faith, think themselves pleasing to God because they feast in the Temple before the Lord after offering sacrifices and listen to the reading of the prophets. Or, mystically: the one eats and drinks before the Lord who eagerly receives the nourishment of the word.

“In the streets,” etc. Scripture is food in its obscure passages, because it is broken as if by exposition and swallowed by eating. It is drink in its clearer passages, where it is absorbed just as it is found. Those who complain, when reproved by the judge, about what they have eaten testify that they have understood both hidden and open things.

[Col. 0305C] **VERSE 28.**—“There will be weeping,” etc. Weeping is usually produced by heat, and the gnashing of teeth by cold, because there they will pass from waters of snow to excessive heat. Or the gnashing reveals the feeling of one who is indignant because he repents too late of what he stubbornly committed. Or they will gnash their teeth—those who here rejoice in gluttony. The eyes that here wander through lusts will weep. Note through the weeping of the eyes and the gnashing of the teeth the true resurrection of the wicked.

**VERSE 29.**—“And they will come.” Many are fervent at first and afterward grow sluggish. Many are cold at first and suddenly become ardent. Many who are despised in this world will be glorified in the future. Others who are honored among human beings will be condemned in the future. Alternatively, the Gentiles, who had long lived without faith, are to be called to the faith, while the Jews are to be rejected.

[Col. 0305D] **VERSE 32.**—“Tell that fox,” etc. The fox is a deceitful animal, lying in a den for ambush, foul-smelling, and never walking on straight paths. All these characteristics correspond to heretics, whose type Herod represents, who attempt to extinguish Christ—that is, the humility of Christian faith—in believers. “Behold, I cast out demons,” etc. As if he were saying: Neither Herod nor the heretics, of whom he is a figure, will be able to disturb what I intend to do. I intend to cast demons out of human hearts, so that, after abandoning vanities, they may believe in me; and to complete healings, so that they may live according to my commandments. Afterward I will be completed in my body, which is the Church, and on the day of the resurrection I will lead it, glorified, into fellowship with the angels.

**VERSE 33.**—“Nevertheless, I must.” Herod will not be able to disturb me so that I do not act and am not brought to completion in this way; nor will he be able to bring about my bodily death, which must take place in Jerusalem, where he himself does not rule but Pilate does. “Today and tomorrow,” etc. The first day is renouncing vanities through the grace of God. The second is agreeing with the truth in conduct and life. The third is final glorification.

**VERSE 34.**—“Jerusalem,” etc. Where my prophets are, there I, the head of the prophets, must be sacrificed. For this crime it will rightly be destroyed, and, like a merciful father, I grieve over its destruction. “How often I wanted to gather.” As if he were saying: I wanted to, but you did not; and all whom I gathered by my will, which was always effective, I gathered despite your unwillingness, because you were always ungrateful. “Your children.” In saying, “How often I wanted to gather your children,” etc., he testifies that all the prophets of old had been sent by him. “As a bird,” etc. Beautifully, the one who had called Herod a fox because he was plotting his death compares himself with a bird, since the deceitful fox always sets ambushes for birds.

**VERSE 35.**—“Your house.” The Temple or the city, because, after killing the Lord, the Romans, plundering it like an empty nest, took away both the place and the nation. “You will not see me,” etc. Unless you repent and confess that I am the Son of the omnipotent Father, you will not see my face at the second coming. “When you say,” etc. The crowd did indeed say this to the Lord when he came into Jerusalem. But since Luke does not say that the Lord later returned to the Galileans so that this might be sung to him by them, it compels us to understand this mystically as referring to the coming of glory.

# CHAPTER XIV

“And it happened,” etc. **Ὕδωρ** means “water”; from it comes *hydrops*, a watery subcutaneous disease arising from an affliction of the bladder, with swelling and foul breath. It is characteristic of the person suffering from dropsy that the more he drinks, the more he thirsts. Thus he is compared with the person weighed down by an overflowing stream of carnal pleasures, and he is also compared with the avaricious rich man.

**VERSE 3.**—“Is it lawful,” etc. Jesus teaches and acts especially on the Sabbaths, not only on account of the spiritual Sabbath but also because the people’s gathering is larger, seeking the salvation of all.

[Col. 0306D] **VERSE 4.**—“But they were silent.” They rightly remain silent, since they see that whatever he says will be directed against them. If it is lawful, why do they observe the Sabbath? If it is not lawful, why do they care for animals? “But he.” He therefore heals the man with dropsy before the Pharisees and immediately argues against avarice, so that he may convict them of the avarice by which they violate the Sabbath and misinterpret the Law. On the Sabbath one must rest not from good works but from evil works, as it is said: “You shall do no servile work on it” (Leviticus 23)—that is, sin. Thus, in eternal rest, one will rest only from evil things, not from good.

**VERSE 5.**—“Which of you.” He resolves the question with an appropriate example, showing that those who accuse him of violating the Sabbath in an act of charity violate it themselves in an act of greed. “An ox or a donkey into a well.” He aptly compares the man with dropsy to an animal that has fallen into a well, because he was perishing from harmful moisture. He rightly names an ox and a donkey, signifying either the wise and the foolish, or both peoples: the Jew pressed under the yoke of the Law and the Gentile not subdued by any discipline, but dull and brutish. He draws them all out of the well of desire: “For all have sinned and lack the grace of God” (Romans 3:23).

**VERSE 7.**—“He was also saying.” After convicting them of avarice and violation of the Sabbath, he begins to teach those present who were capable of receiving it about evangelical grace, inviting them to humility against the pride that the Pharisees possessed in the Law, or intending through his teaching to show how they ought to choose their places at table in the Church.

**VERSE 8.**—“When you are invited.” When, called by a preacher through the grace of faith, you have joined yourself to the members of the Church, do not exalt yourself by boasting of your merits, as though you were superior to the rest. “Lest someone more honorable.” He gives the place to one who was invited later and is more honorable. The person who has become too confident because of his manner of life is quickly surpassed by the alacrity of those who have followed him in Christ. “And with shame you take the last place,” etc. When, recognizing better things in others, he humbles whatever high opinion he had held of his own works, saying with the Prophet: “When I was exalted, I was humbled and confounded” (Psalm 87:16).

**VERSE 9.**—“And then you begin,” etc. Then, ashamed that you once presumed greater things about yourself, you will begin to humble yourself in repentance and recognize that your merit is lesser. Do not now begin to seek what is reserved for you at the end, because the inheritance toward which one hastens at the beginning will fail at the final blessing.

**VERSE 10.**—“Then glory will be yours,” etc. Every day, when the Lord visits and judges his guests, he grants such great gifts of his Spirit to the humble that the gathering of the faithful glorifies them with admiration. In astonishment, it bursts forth in praise of its creator, saying: “But to me, your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored” (Psalm 138:17).

**VERSE 12.**—“He was also saying.” According to the literal sequence: After warning those who are invited how they ought to recline, he also warns the one who invites whom he ought to invite, lest the temporal expenditure of goods that he makes come to nothing or perhaps increase his sin. Rather, he should spend temporal things in such a way that through them a way to eternal things is opened. “And to the one who had invited him.” He speaks to the ruler of the Pharisees, who perhaps could become proud because he had invited so many to the banquet as though out of mercy; or, as may be inferred from the Lord’s words, he had invited them chiefly so that he might in turn be invited by them, and thus no special recompense would follow. “Do not invite your friends.” He does not forbid brothers, friends, and rich people to celebrate banquets with one another as though it were a crime, but shows that this does not contribute to the rewards of life. There are also certain banquets of such rich people that receive not only repayment in the present but condemnation in the future. Hence the Apostle says: “Not in revelries and drunkenness” (Romans 13:13)—that is, in luxurious banquets, which are either celebrated through the contributions of all or customarily provided in turns by companions, where no one is ashamed to do or say anything dishonorable. “Lest perhaps.” As if he were saying: If you intend to invite so that you may be invited, you can be deceived there; but if you distribute to the poor, you will not be deceived regarding your reward.

**VERSE 13.**—“Invite the poor.” The person who invites the poor will receive a reward in the future. The person who invites friends, brothers, and rich people has received his reward. But if he does this for God’s sake, following the example of Job’s sons, then, as with all the other duties of brotherly love, the one who commanded it himself grants the reward. The person who invites the dissolute for the sake of wantonness will not escape punishment.

**VERSE 14.**—“At the resurrection.” Although all will rise, the resurrection of the just is spoken of as singular and, as it were, proper to them, because they will be transformed in it.

**VERSE 15.**—“When one of those reclining had heard these things,” etc. Captivated by the sweetness of the resurrection he had heard about, he bursts forth in its praise and asserts that those who attain it will truly be blessed, although he does not understand well by what merits one can reach that blessedness. “Blessed,” etc. “If anyone eats from this bread, he will live forever” (John 6:51). If anyone, perfectly incorporated through the sacrament of the Incarnation, merits to enjoy the vision of the divine majesty, he will rejoice in eternal blessedness. But because many receive it only in faith, as if in prayer, while they disdain truly to attain its sweetness, their sluggishness is rebuked.

**VERSE 16.**—“A certain man,” etc. The incarnate Word prepared for many a fullness of inward sweetness, but few come, because many who submit to him through faith immediately contradict him by their evil lives. “A great dinner.” This banquet is called not a meal but a dinner, because after the meal of which Matthew speaks, dinner remains, whereas after dinner no banquet remains; many are cast out from the meal, but no one from dinner.

**VERSE 17.**—“And he sent his servant.” The hour of dinner is the end of the age. Hence the Apostle says: “We know those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10:11). At this end the servant—that is, the order of preachers—is sent to those invited through the Law and the Prophets, so that, rejecting their disdain, they might prepare themselves to taste the dinner, because everything is already prepared. For after Christ has been sacrificed, the entrance to the kingdom stands open.

**VERSE 18.**—“And they began,” etc. They make excuses because no one is excluded from the kingdom except the one whom his own profession excludes. Everyone makes an excuse who loves earthly things more than heavenly things, even if he says that he is striving toward heavenly things. “I have bought a villa.” A villa, that is, earthly substance. The person goes out to see the villa who thinks only of external things for the sake of possessions; and this is what the lovers of the world seek first, namely, bodily substance.

(AUG.) In the purchased estate, domination and pride are signified. For to possess an estate, etc., up to: love of earthly things is the glue of spiritual wings.

[Col. 0309A] “I ask you.” When he says, “I ask you, excuse me,” humility sounds in his voice while he scorns to come; pride appears in his action.

**VERSE 19.**—“Five yoke of oxen.” The five yoke of oxen signify the five bodily senses, which are rightly called yokes because they are doubled in both sexes. Since they know and touch not inner things but only external ones, curiosity is rightly represented through them: while it investigates the life of one’s neighbor externally, it does not know its own inner life. The more a curious person is skilled in what belongs to another, the more ignorant he is of himself. Nor do the words of the one making excuses differ from the meaning of his vice, when he says, “I am going to test them.” For testing ordinarily belongs to curiosity.

**VERSE 20.**—“I have married a wife.” Because many marry wives not for the sake of offspring but for carnal desires, carnal pleasure is signified by this matter; on account of it, a person disgusted with God’s supper refuses to come.

**VERSE 22.**—“It has happened,” etc. “We have gathered many such people from the Jews to your supper, but they do not fill the place at your banquet; there remains a place where the multitude of the nations may be received.”

**VERSE 23.**—“Go out into the roads and hedges,” etc. Observe that in this third invitation it is not said, “Invite,” but “Compel them to enter.” Those who, broken by the adversities of this world, return to the love of God and are corrected away from the desires of the present life, enter only when compelled. Some are called and despise the call: they receive the house of understanding but do not fulfill it in their works. Some are called and come: they fulfill in their works the understanding they have received.

**VERSE 25.**—“Now great crowds were going,” etc. The crowds following Jesus as he journeys toward Jerusalem signify those who, invited or compelled to come to the supper, imitate Jesus with complete devotion as he goes before them toward the vision of eternal peace. He therefore instructs these people that they ought to desire that homeland with sincere love and, for its sake, renounce the affections of carnal kinship.

**VERSE 26.**—“If anyone comes.” We can both hate and love: we love those joined to us by natural relationship in accordance with the divine command, while we do not know as friends those whom we endure as adversaries on the way of God, hating and avoiding them. “Even.” We rightly hate the soul when we do not yield to its carnal desires but resist and break them.

[Col. 0309D] **VERSE 27.**—“And whoever does not carry.” The cross is carried in two ways: either when the flesh is afflicted through abstinence, or when the spirit is distressed through compassion for one’s neighbor. “And comes after me.” Someone may lacerate his flesh for empty glory, or show carnal compassion toward his neighbor in order to favor sin. He appears to carry the cross, but he does not follow God.

**VERSE 28.**—“For which of you.” After the Lord had given those following him to Jerusalem lofty commands concerning contempt for the world and rejection of the body, he adds a command concerning perseverance, for which patience together with humility is necessary. He teaches this through the example of a builder. “To build a tower.” Since he had given lofty commands, he appends a comparison with the building of something lofty. “He calculates the expense.” The one who calculates the expense discerns that temporal money must be spent, the heart must be turned away from the desires of the world, and the soul must be prepared against the adversities of the world.

**VERSE 29.**—“All who see.” As the Apostle says: “We have become a spectacle to the world, to angels and to human beings” (II Cor. IV). In everything we do, we ought to consider the hidden adversaries who lie in wait for our works; unless we watch against them, we suffer the mockers whom we have as persuaders to evil.

**VERSE 31.**—“Or what king,” etc. After the comparison concerning the tower to be built, he adds a comparison concerning a greater matter, a king about to go to war. By this it is shown that, even through the fulfillment of the preceding commandments, no one can attain glory unless the sentence of the severe Judge is tempered by mercy. For in God’s sight every human being is imperfect. “If he can.” The one who comes to meet God with ten thousand is like someone offering the works of the Ten Commandments that he has performed outwardly. But God comes against him with what is, as it were, double the number, since he examines the person prepared only in works with respect to both work and thought. Therefore, while he is still far away through the postponement of judgment, we must attend to the insufficiency of our weakness and send ahead, to obtain peace from the severe Judge, an embassy of tears, good works, and devout affections.

[Col. 0310B] **VERSE 33.**—“So therefore,” etc. He draws the conclusion from the preceding comparisons. Since the one who does not calculate the expense cannot build well, and the one who does not send an embassy ahead cannot meet the king safely, neither can anyone be my disciple who does not renounce everything.

**VERSE 34.**—“Good.” Truly, whoever wishes to be my disciple must renounce everything, because then he will be good salt—that is, worthy to be placed among the apostles for seasoning the spiritual hearts of his hearers with spiritual wisdom.

**VERSE 35.**—“Nor into a dung heap.” Salt makes the earth sterile. Hence the anger of conquerors used to sow destroyed cities with salt so that no shoot might arise in them. In the same way, the apostles, after destroying the kingdom of sin, restrain the growth of vices. Salt seasons food and dries meat. Preaching preserves human nature, unharmed by the worms and decay of vices, for its Creator.

# CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0310D] **VERSE 4.**—“Which of you,” etc. In the preceding passages you had learned to reject negligence, avoid arrogance, embrace devotion, not be held captive by worldly occupations, and not prefer things that perish to things everlasting. But because human frailty cannot keep a firm foothold amid so great a slipperiness of the world, the physician also shows a remedy against error there: the Judge does not deny hope of pardon. “A hundred sheep.” Since the number one hundred is perfect, God possessed a hundred sheep—that is, the perfect number—when he created the substance of angels and human beings. But one perished when humanity abandoned the pastures of life through sinning. Therefore, because the number of rational creatures had been diminished by the loss of the human being, he seeks a human being on earth so that the total might be restored.

“Does he not leave them?” It is as though he said: “You murmur because I receive sinners, but I came only to gather the wandering, just as each of you labors to bring back a wandering sheep.”

**VERSE 5.**—“He places it on his shoulders.” He placed the sheep on his shoulders who, taking on human nature, himself bore our sins. Hence Christ’s shoulders are the arms of the cross: there he laid down our sins and rested upon the neck of that noble instrument of execution.

**VERSE 6.**—“And when he comes.” After humanity has been restored, the shepherd returns to heaven and finds there the choirs of angels. They are friends because in their steadfastness they continually guard his will; they are also neighbors because they enjoy the clarity of his vision. Observe that he does not say, “Rejoice with the sheep that has been found,” but “with me,” because his joy is our life.

**VERSE 7.**—“I say to you.” In the ninety-nine, the number of the righteous is understood; in the one sheep, that of sinners. “Joy.” Because the angels are rational, they rejoice over the human being reconciled to them; this kindles us toward uprightness. Let us do what is pleasing to them, whose protection we ought to seek and whose offense we ought to fear. “More than over.” If the angels are understood in the ninety-nine righteous who did not go astray and do not need repentance, it seems greater to justify the ungodly than to create and preserve the righteous. Although both acts belong to equal power, the former involves greater mercy and greater joy.

[Col. 0311C] **VERSE 8.**—“Or what woman.” The woman—that is, the wisdom of God—had ten drachmas when she created human beings and angels in her image. But she lost one when humanity departed from the likeness of its Creator. Yet God’s wisdom lights a lamp to search for it when it appeared in the flesh, because the lamp is light in a vessel of clay—that is, the Word in flesh. When this became radiant among human beings, it overturned the house, because it disturbed human consciences concerning their guilt; thus the drachma is found when the likeness of the Creator is restored in a human being.

“Having ten drachmas.” The Lord created the nature of angels and human beings, which he willed to endure unto eternity, in his own likeness. Therefore the woman had ten drachmas when humanity was added to the nine orders of angels, so that the tenth number of the elect might be completed. Humanity did not perish from the Creator even after its fault, because the wisdom of God, shining with miracles through the flesh, restored it from the light of the vessel of clay.

“She calls.” The friends and neighbors are the heavenly powers, who are so close to God because they contemplate him more intimately. She calls them when, through the manifestation of the grace bestowed upon human beings, she kindles them more intensely to love herself.

**VERSE 11.**—“A certain man.” Through the two preceding parables he indicates how greatly he himself rejoices with the angels over the salvation of penitents. In this third parable he not only displays joy but also rebukes the murmuring of the envious.

**VERSE 12.**—“And he said,” etc. Just as God has no other from whom he might be formed or by whom he might be ruled, so this person wishes to use his own power and live without anyone forming or governing him. “Father, give me.” Half the inheritance is given to those who ask for it, and the father is not at fault for giving it to the younger son. There is no weak age in the kingdom of God, nor is faith burdened by years, unless a person himself judges that he is unfit when he asks. If this son had not withdrawn from his father, he would not have known the hindrance of age; but, having gone far away, he deservedly wastes his inheritance. “And he divided.” To the faithful he imparted the protection of his grace, which they desired; to unbelievers, however, he granted only the natural gift of understanding, with which they were content.

**VERSE 13.**—“Not many days later.” Not long after the creation of the human race, the soul chose to carry free will with it as a certain power of its nature and to abandon the one by whom it had been created, trusting in its own strength. It consumes these powers all the more quickly the more it abandons their giver. This is the prodigal life, which loves to squander itself and spread out in external spectacles, leaving the one who is inward to it.

**VERSE 14.**—“And he began.” Since nothing is enough for prodigal pleasure, because pleasure always hungers for itself, the one who abandoned the treasures of wisdom and the height of heavenly riches is deservedly in need.

**VERSE 15.**—“To one of the citizens.” That citizen is the one who, having been deservedly placed over earthly desires because of his wickedness, is called the prince of this world. He sends the son into the estate because he subjects him to the desire for worldly substance. He feeds pigs when he does those things in which unclean spirits rejoice.

“To feed pigs.” The pig is an unclean animal that delights in filth. So too is the devil, who is nourished among idols by the blood of cattle and by the death of the human being himself. He therefore sent him into the estate—that is, made him his servant—to feed pigs, sacrificing his soul to the devil.

**VERSE 16.**—“And he desired.” The food of demons is drunkenness, fornication, and things of that kind, which are alluring and entice people to use them. The luxurious have no other concern than to fill their belly, whose god is their belly (Phil. III). Yet he cannot be satisfied by them, because pleasure always hungers for itself.

“No one gave him anything.” When the devil makes someone his own, he no longer provides further abundance of vices, knowing that the person is already dead.

**VERSE 17.**—“How many hired servants.” Those who strive to perform worthy deeds with a view to the reward to come are daily refreshed by the nourishment of heavenly grace. But the one who lives outside the father’s house—that is, without faith—and seeks the blessed life in empty philosophy perishes from hunger.

**VERSE 18.**—“Father, I have sinned.” Although God knows everything, he nevertheless awaits the voice of confession. Without danger, reveal what you know is already known: you have a reason for Christ to intercede for you, so that he may not have died for you in vain; and the Father has a reason for forgiving, because what the Son wills, the Father also wills.

**VERSE 19.**—“Make me,” etc. He does not presume to aspire to the affection of the Son, who does not doubt that everything belonging to the Father is his; instead, he desires the status of a hired servant, intending already to serve for wages. Yet he testifies that he cannot even earn this except by the father’s gracious favor.

[Col. 0313A] (AMBR.) There is a difference among a servant, a hired servant, and a son. A servant, etc., up to: after the father’s kiss, he most nobly disdains it.

**VERSE 20.**—“But while he was still far away,” etc. Before he understood God, yet once he was already seeking him devoutly, though he was not yet worthy to return through his works, the incarnate Word anticipated the son’s return. He came to earth before the son came to the house of confession, not abandoning the Word itself but, in the Word, condescending to our exile. He humbled the arm—that is, the Son—for the embrace of the one returning. The Father fell upon the son’s neck when he imposed upon him the easy yoke of his love, and he kissed him, so that what is said elsewhere might be shown: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song I). “Returning.” The one returning receives from the Father the kiss of charity when, through grace, he is assured of pardon.

[Col. 0313B] **VERSE 22.**—“Quickly bring out,” etc. “The first robe” is the garment of innocence in which the first human being was created, but after the fault discovered himself naked and took on a garment of skin—that is, a mortal garment.

“The ring.” This is the seal of faith, by which promises are sealed in the hearts of believers.

“On his hand.” That is, in his works: so that faith may shine through works and works may be strengthened through faith.

“And shoes.” That is, fortify yourself with the examples of those who came before in the office of preaching, so that the work may be adorned by right living and the course toward eternal things may be prepared.

**VERSE 23.**—“Bring the calf.” Preach Christ and make his death known, so that one may believe in the heart and, by imitating the slain Christ, receive with the mouth the sacrament of his passion for amendment.

**VERSE 24.**—“And they began to feast.” Not only is the son for whom the calf was killed refreshed, but also the father and his servants, because the refreshment of God and of the saints is the salvation of sinners. Observe that after the robe, ring, and shoes have been given, the calf is sacrificed: unless someone puts on the hope of the first immortality, unless he fortifies his works with the ring of faith, and unless by confessing he proclaims that faith itself, he cannot share in the heavenly mysteries.

**VERSE 25.**—“Now his elder son was,” etc. The son—that is, the people of Israel—had not gone far away to worship idols. Nor was he in the house, because he did not penetrate the inner meanings of the law: content with the literal sense, he performed earthly things and expected earthly things.

This is the one who bought the field, the five yoke of oxen: pressed down by the burden of the law, he enjoys earthly senses and married a wife in carnal affection.

“And when he came.” The son approaches the house when someone among that people understands the law spiritually, rejects the labors of servile work, and considers the freedom of the Church. He hears the symphony and the choir—that is, the Gospel preached by those filled with the Spirit in harmonious voices. He calls one of the servants when he takes one of the prophets to read. He questions him when he searches in that prophet to discover what these celebrations of the Church are, in which he does not see himself participating.

**VERSE 26.**—“He asked.” Israel now also asks why God rejoices at the admission of the nations; through envy it does not know the father’s will and stands outside, although it is invited by heralds.

**VERSE 28.**—“He became angry.” The Jews were angry and complained because Jesus was feasting with the nations. They are still angry about the salvation of the nations and do not wish to enter. But when the fullness of the nations has entered, the father will go out to plead with Israel, when the calling of the Jews becomes manifest.

**VERSE 29.**—“Behold, for so many years.” (HIER.) Having followed the righteousness of the law, he is not subject to the righteousness of God. For what righteousness of God is greater than forgiving those who repent?

“Your commandment,” etc. As though it were not transgression to envy another’s salvation or to boast of one’s own righteousness.

**VERSE 30.**—“You have killed the calf for him.” They confess that Christ has come, but through envy they do not wish to be saved. This may be understood of the Jew and the Gentile; in general, however, it may be understood of the righteous person and the sinner.

“He has devoured your substance,” etc. The prostitutes are the superstitions of the nations. The one who abandons the marriage of the Word of God and fornicates with the demon through shameful desire dissipates his substance with them.

“Son, you are always with me,” etc. He does not rebuke him as a liar; rather, he approves his perseverance with him and invites him to enjoy a greater exultation.

“All that is mine,” etc. In eternal blessedness, each thing belonging to all belongs to each, and all things belonging to each belong to all.

# CHAPTER XVI

**VERSE 1.**—“To the disciples.” Because the proud and greedy Pharisees denied forgiveness to those who asked for it just as they denied money to those in need, the Savior speaks now to them and now, with them listening, to the disciples concerning compassion.

“A certain man.” Properly, a steward is the keeper of an estate, but here the term is used for an administrator—that is, a dispenser—who distributes the entire substance of a household. We must not take everything in this steward as something to imitate, namely, that we should act fraudulently toward God. On the contrary, these comparisons are given so that we may understand that if the Lord could praise one who was committing fraud, how much more is God pleased by the one who performs such works according to his command.

**VERSE 6.**—“A hundred measures.” A *cadus* is called an *amphora* in Latin; it contains three urns. A *chorus* is filled with thirty *modii*. This may be understood simply in this way: whoever relieves a poor person’s need by either half or a fifth should be rewarded with the payment of mercy.

**VERSE 8.**—“And the Lord praised.” If the steward of unrighteous mammon is praised by the Lord’s voice because from an unrighteous possession he prepared righteousness for himself, and although he suffered loss he nevertheless praised the steward’s prudence—not because he had acted fraudulently against his lord, but because he had acted prudently for himself—how much more will Christ, who can suffer no loss and is inclined to mercy, praise his disciples if they have been merciful toward those entrusted to them.

“The sons of this age.” Everyone is called the son of the one whose works he performs. Hence “the sons of this age,” that is, of darkness, and “the sons of light,” that is, of eternal life.

[Col. 0315A] **VERSE 9.**—“Make friends for yourselves.” *Mammon* means “wealth” in the language of the Syrians; it is called unrighteous because it has been gathered through unrighteousness. If, therefore, unrighteousness, when well administered, is turned into righteousness, how much more do the banquets of the divine Word, in which there is no unrighteousness, raise a good steward to heaven.

**VERSE 10.**—“He who is faithful.” In sharing money with the poor. “And in what is greater.” By clinging to the Creator and becoming one spirit with him. But whoever does not administer well the temporal things he possesses empties for himself the glory of eternal things, of which he boasts.

**VERSE 11.**—“Therefore, if,” etc. Whoever does not give his brothers for their use what God created for everyone will be unrighteous in distributing spiritual money, dividing the Lord’s teaching not according to need but according to persons.

**VERSE 12.**—“And if you have not been faithful in what belongs to another.” If you have not administered well the carnal riches that pass away, who will give you the true and eternal riches?

**VERSE 13.**—“No servant.” Rebuking greed, he says that lovers of money cannot love God. Therefore whoever loves God despises money; for it is not possible to love both transitory and eternal things at once.

“Or he will cling to one.” (AUG.) He will not indeed love. For no one loves, etc., up to: and flatters himself concerning his goodness and impunity.
