“You cannot,” etc. He did not say that one may possess riches, but that one may serve them. A person serves when he guards riches as a servant; but whoever has shaken off the yoke of servitude distributes them as a master. Whoever serves mammon serves the one who, because of his perverse character, is deservedly called by the Lord the prince set over these possessions.

**VERSE 14.**—“Now the Pharisees were listening.” The Lord was warning the scribes and Pharisees not to think proudly, not to presume upon their own righteousness, but to receive repentant sinners and redeem their own sins, should any have fallen upon them, through almsgiving. But they ridicule the teacher of mercy, humility, and frugality, as though the guilty man were commanding things of little use and never to be done, or, if useful, were unnecessarily imposing things they had already completed.

**VERSE 15.**—“And he said,” etc. You despise sinners as weak and hopeless, and believe yourselves perfect in all things and free from every frailty, needing no remedy through almsgiving. But the one who enlightens the hidden things of darkness and reveals the counsels of hearts sees how justly this height of swelling pride must be condemned.

**VERSE 16.**—“The law and the prophets.” They ridiculed him as he argued against love of money, as though he were contradicting the law and the prophets, since many rich people pleased God in the law and the law promises the good things of the earth to those who observe it. He counters this by teaching that there is a difference between the law and the Gospel: in the law, lesser things are commanded to carnal people on account of the earth; in the Gospel, greater things are commanded to spiritual people on account of heaven.

“And everyone.” Great is the power when what is born from the earth seeks to possess heaven through virtue, though it could not hold it by nature, and disregards even the tongues of those who mock, just as the Lord is disregarded by the Pharisees. Everyone who uses force hastens with vehement zeal and does not grow sluggish through a torpid disposition. There is therefore a religious violence of faith and a criminal sluggishness. Let us therefore do violence to nature, so that it may not sink toward earthly things but raise itself toward heavenly things.

**VERSE 17.**—“It is easier.” Although I say, “The law and the prophets were until John,” I do not preach the destruction of the law. For it is easier for the greatest elements of the world to pass away than to transgress the smallest commandments of the law, since even those things that seem insignificant or superstitious are not without spiritual mysteries, when everything is recapitulated in the Gospel.

**VERSE 18.**—“Everyone,” etc. (AMBR.) Not every marriage is from God. For Gentiles are not joined to Christians, since the law forbids it. Where there is an unequal marriage, the law of God is not present.

**VERSE 19.**—“A certain man.” Against the avaricious mockers he establishes by an example what he had proposed: namely, that the rich man is tormented in hell because he did not make Lazarus his friend, by whom he might have been received into eternal dwellings. It appears to be a narrative rather than a parable.

“Who was clothed in purple,” etc. (GREG.) Purple is the color of royal attire, obtained from sea-shells, etc., up to: because he did not know the inward parts of compassion, since he did not wish to redeem the commandments at a price.

**VERSE 20.**—“And there was a certain man.” If we see anything blameworthy in the poor, we must not despise them, because perhaps those whom weakness of character wounds are healed by the medicine of poverty.

“Full of sores.” The disdainful rich man recoils from this man’s sores, unwilling to endure the stench of sores among precious foods and perfumed guests, while dogs lick them.

**VERSE 21.**—“Desiring.” In one matter two judgments of God are fulfilled: from seeing the poor man, the rich man’s failure to show mercy brings upon him an accumulation of condemnation; and, in turn, from seeing the rich man, the poor man, tested daily, is proved. Poverty and sickness afflict him for the sake of his greater testing, as do the rich man’s visible abundance and the absence of any consolation offered to him.

“Dogs.” In the language of dogs, the tongues of flatterers may be signified: they lick wounds when they praise with wicked favor the evils that we condemn in ourselves.

**VERSE 22.**—“Into Abraham’s bosom.” Abraham’s bosom is the rest of the blessed poor, whose is the kingdom of heaven and in which they are received after this life. The burial in hell is the depth of punishments that devours the proud and the merciless after this life.

“And he was buried.” In the law, not stinginess but robbery is condemned; in the Gospel, the rich man is tormented because he did not give what was his.

**VERSE 23.**—“But lifting up his eyes.” The unbelievers see from afar when, placed below before the day of judgment, they observe the faithful above them in rest; afterward they cannot contemplate their joys. What they see is far away because they cannot reach it through merit.

“He saw Abraham.” (GREG.) It must be believed that before the retribution of the final judgment the unrighteous are in a place of rest, etc., up to: and they are tormented by the punishment of those whom they uselessly loved.

[Col. 0317A] **VERSE 24.**—“That he may dip.” The one who did not give Lazarus the crumbs falling from his table desires that water be dripped into his mouth from the tip of Lazarus’s finger; and the one who did not give the smallest things in life seeks the smallest things in hell.

**VERSE 25.**—“Because you received.” (AUG.) Observe that this rich man possessed something good, from which he received transitory good in this life; and Lazarus possessed something evil, but the fire of poverty purified him.

**VERSE 26.**—“And in all these things.” Just as the reprobate wish to pass from punishments to the glory of the saints, so the righteous, through mercy, wish in their minds to go to those placed in torments in order to free them. But they cannot, because although the souls of the righteous possess mercy according to the goodness of their nature, they are now joined to the justice of their Creator and are constrained by such uprightness that no compassion for the reprobate moves them.

**VERSE 27.**—“Therefore I ask.” After hope for himself has been removed from the one burning, his mind turns to his relatives, because punishment eventually teaches the mind of the reprobate, though uselessly, to love, so that even then they may love their own spiritually—those whom, while they loved sins here, they did not love.

Thus the rich man is preserved for punishment with both knowledge of the poor man whom he despised and memory of the brothers whom he left behind, so that he may be tormented more intensely by seeing the glory of the despised man and by the punishment of those whom he loved uselessly.

“That you may send.” This rich man begins to be a teacher too late, when he has neither time to learn nor time to teach.

**VERSE 31.**—“If they do not listen to Moses.” Those who despise the words of the law will fulfill with even greater difficulty the commandments of the Redeemer who rose from the dead, since they are more subtle; and those who refuse to fulfill his words will plainly refuse to believe him.

# CHAPTER XVII

**VERSE 1.**—“And he said to the disciples.” It must be understood that, while the Lord was speaking about mercy, the avaricious Pharisees persisted in mockery and thereby caused scandal for weak hearers, so that they would not pay attention. He therefore rebukes them while speaking to the apostles: by their own vice they caused scandals to arise, which could not fail to occur in a world full of hardships and errors.

**VERSE 2.**—“If a millstone,” etc. This refers to the custom of the province in which such a punishment for crimes existed: the guilty were bound to a stone and sunk into the depths. Truly, it is more useful for an innocent person to end life through the gravest punishment than to mourn eternal death after injuring a brother.

“Of the little ones.” Not in age but in faith and disposition: they seek opportunities for how they may be scandalized. Therefore you must take care of them, lest through an occasion provided by you they depart from faith and salvation.

**VERSE 3.**—“Pay attention to yourselves.” He indicates the order by which we can avoid scandals and escape perpetual woe. If we take care not to injure anyone, if we rebuke the repentant out of zeal for righteousness, and if we forgive the penitent from the heart, we are not commanded to forgive everyone indiscriminately who sins, but the one who practices repentance. The first step, therefore, is to rebuke the sinner, so that afterward we may forgive the penitent. For the one who sees someone sinning and remains silent sins in the same way as the one who does not forgive the penitent.

“And if he repents.” We are commanded to grant forgiveness differently to a repentant brother and to an enemy who persecutes us. When forgiveness is granted to a brother, we share fellowship with him through charity; toward a persecutor who wishes us evil—or does it if he can—we wish and do whatever good we are able.

**VERSE 4.**—“Seven times.” Universality is customarily signified by the number seven. We are therefore commanded to forgive all sins, or to forgive the one who is always repentant.

**VERSE 5.**—“Increase.” Since he had said above (Luke XVI), “He who is faithful in what is least,” etc., the apostles, who had been faithful in what belonged to another and in what was least—that is, in contempt for earthly things—ask that faith be increased in what belongs to them and in what is greater. They already possess the beginnings of virtue through faith and ask to progress in the same faith until they reach perfection.

[Col. 0318B] **VERSE 6.**—“To a mulberry tree.” Through the mulberry’s blood-red color, since its fruit and branches are red, the Gospel of the cross is expressed. Through the faith of the apostles, it was uprooted from the Jewish people, in whom the word of preaching was held as though in the stock of a lineage, and transplanted into the sea of the nations. The following parable concerning the ministers of the word also suits this interpretation.

The leaves of the mulberry, when applied to a serpent, bring death; so the word of the cross, while bestowing every beneficial thing, removes every harmful thing. The fruit of the mulberry is white in its blossom, glows red when formed, and becomes black when ripe. So the devil, beginning with the blossom of an angelic nature and the power of shining splendor, became a terror through transgression; he is excluded through faith.

**VERSE 7.**—“But which of you,” etc. The servant plowing or feeding is the teacher of the Church, of whom it is said: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke IX). The Lord also says to Peter: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI).

This servant returns from the field when, having interrupted the work of preaching, he returns, as it were, to the tribunal of his conscience and examines his words or deeds. The Lord does not immediately command him to pass from this life and be refreshed by eternal rest; instead, he commands him to prepare something at home for the meal—that is, after the labor of open preaching, to display humility in his own conduct. For God feasts in such a conscience.

**VERSE 8.**—“And serve me.” The one who considers the Creator’s nature and fears his judgments serves the Creator by humbling himself concerning his own virtues. For *minister* derives from a lesser status.

**VERSE 10.**—“So you also.” After exhorting them to the perfection of faith, through which marvelous works are performed—even against the nature of things—he also warns them not to boast about their works. The more faith surpasses outwardly through virtues, the more humble the conscience should be inwardly, because we rightly owe obedience to the Lord.

“Unprofitable servants.” If one human being requires from a human servant not a single but many services and shows no gratitude, how much more should you, who can do nothing without me, not perform merely one kind of work or labor but continually increase what came before with new efforts. Nor should you boast because you serve well.

“What we were obliged to do.” The one who came to serve rather than to be served made us his debtors, so that, trusting not in our works but fearing his examination, and having fulfilled everything that was commanded, we may recognize ourselves as imperfect for as long as we live in exile from God.

**VERSE 11.**—“And it happened.” After the parable that invites us to kindness and perseverance in the various services of God, those ungrateful for the benefits bestowed are rebuked.

**VERSE 12.**—“They met,” etc. The lepers are heretics, who, like people having various colors in one body, mix various sects—now falsehood, now truth—within the same preaching. Because they are avoided and removed from the Church, they must call out from afar with a loud cry.

“Who stood,” etc. Those who sinned against the Decalogue, neither loving God, concerning whom they think wrongly, nor their neighbor, from whom they are divided, cry out to God beneath the denarius and are healed when, within the fellowship of the Church, they obtain an integral and true doctrine, discuss everything according to the rule of the Catholic faith, and are free from the variety of falsehoods as from leprosy.

But one gives thanks—that is, the one who remains in the unity of the Church through humility. Those who, lifted up by pride, are ungrateful to their purifier are nine, because through their lack of unity they fall short of the perfection of the denarius.

**VERSE 13.**—“And they lifted up their voice.” Recognizing from the Savior’s words that they had gone astray, they call him the teacher of salvation and, through knowledge of the teacher, return to the form of salvation.

**VERSE 14.**—“Go,” etc. Whoever has been cleansed by God’s grace from heretical wickedness, pagan superstition, Jewish unbelief, or fraternal schism must come to the Church and display the true color of faith, like that of the others.

**VERSE 15.**—“But one.” The one who returned signifies the devout humility of the one Church in Christ. Falling at his feet and giving thanks, he sees, after suppressing thoughts of presumption, how weak he is; he attributes no virtue to himself but understands the good he does as coming from mercy.

**VERSE 16.**—“And he fell on his face.” He falls on his face who is ashamed of the evils he has committed. A person falls where he is confounded. The one who falls forward sees where he falls; the one who falls backward does not see. Thus the good fall on their face, humbling themselves in visible things so that they may be raised toward invisible things; the wicked fall backward, because they fall into invisible things and do not see what follows them.

[Col. 0319D] **VERSE 19.**—“Rise.” The one who, recognizing his weakness, lay humbly before God is commanded by divine consolation to rise to stronger works and to go on increasing until he reaches more perfect things.

“Your faith.” The faith that inclined him to give thanks condemns, by contrast, those who are ungrateful for the benefits they have received.

“Has saved you.” In the preceding parable it is determined that faith must be increased through humility. In this one, the matter itself clearly shows that it is not merely the acknowledged reasoning of faith but the operation carried out by faith that saves the believer.

**VERSE 20.**—“Having been asked.” They ask because, as Luke explained below, they supposed that, when the Lord came to Jerusalem, his kingdom would immediately be revealed.

“The kingdom of God does not come,” etc. When it will come, it cannot be observed either by angels or by human beings, unlike the time of the Lord’s incarnation, which had been fixed by the prophecies of the prophets and made known by the proclamations of angels. Indeed, from the moment he was conceived, born, baptized, preaching, dying, rising again, and ascending into heaven, it was continually declared by signs—whether of angels, human beings, or certainly miracles.

**VERSE 21.**—“For behold, the kingdom.” It cannot be observed because my kingdom is not corporeal, as you suppose, but spiritual; it has already begun through faith.

**The Kingdom of God.** Or the Lord’s answer may be understood in this way: [Col. 0320B] “The kingdom of God is within you,” for he who will one day come as Judge of all is even now reigning in the hearts of the faithful. But when heretics disturb the Church with wicked doctrines, the faithful desire that the Lord, returning to earth on a single day if this were possible, should declare the truth of the faith openly. Yet they will not see this, because what has once been manifested by the radiance of the Gospel does not need to be confirmed by the Lord’s bodily appearance.

**VERSE 22.**—**The days will come.** He did not wish to say when he would come, but said that he would come, in order to instill in all the terror of the imminent judgment and not provide the security of delay.

**You will desire.** After my ascension, when you, groaning in this exile of the world, will desire to see me in my glory—a desire worthy of praise, though not to be fulfilled in this world. **One day.** He rightly says “one,” because in that glory of which the prophet says, “One day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. LXXXIII), there is no interruption of darkness, nor even any memory of misery or pain. It is good to desire the presence of this day, but not, because of the magnitude of our desire, to fabricate dreams for ourselves as though the day of the Lord were imminent, which he predicts that some will do.

**VERSE 23.**—**And they will say, etc.** There were some who, calculating the courses of the ages, claimed to have discovered the exact year, day, and hour of the consummation of the age.

**VERSE 24.**—**For just as, etc.** Do not believe them, because the second coming will be sudden and so manifest that no one beneath the sky will be able to remain unaware of it; for the ordeal of judgment takes place beneath the sky, that is, in the midst of the air.

**VERSE 25.**—**But first, etc.** While speaking of the glory of his coming, he also inserts the subject of his passion, so that when they saw dying the one whom they had heard would reign, the sorrow of the passion might be mitigated by hope of the promised glory.

**VERSE 26.**—**And just as it happened.** He establishes by several examples the suddenness of the day of his coming. The one whom he had compared to lightning, which swiftly traverses everything, he compares with the days of Noah and Lot, when sudden destruction overtook mortals.

**VERSE 27.**—**They were eating, etc.** Marriages and food are not condemned, since in the former the means of succession and in the latter the means of nature are established; rather, the immoderate use of permitted things is censured. Because they gave themselves wholly to these things and despised God’s judgments, they perished by fire or water. **Until the day.** Allegorically: Noah builds the ark when the Lord gathers the faithful into the Church. He enters it when it has been completed, when he illuminates it with his presence on the day of judgment. But while the ark is being built, the wicked indulge themselves; and when it is entered, they are punished with eternal damnation.

**VERSE 28.**—**Likewise, etc.** Omitting the great crime of the Sodomites, he recalls only those things that they might think trivial or even harmless, so that you may understand with what punishment unlawful acts are struck, if even lawful acts—and those without which life cannot be lived—when carried out immoderately, will be punished with fire and sulfur.

**Lot.** Allegorically: Lot, whose name means “one who turns aside,” is the people of the elect. While he dwells in Sodom—that is, among the reprobate—as a resident alien, he turns aside from their crimes as far as he is able. When Lot goes out, Sodom perishes, because at the consummation of the age the angels will go out and separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous, and cast them into the furnace of fire (Matt. XIII).

**VERSE 30.**—**The Son of Man.** He who meanwhile sees everything when he appears will then judge everything, when he sees all who have forgotten his judgments and surrendered themselves to this age, so that they rightly deserve to be destroyed together with the world they inhabit.

**VERSE 31.**—**On that day.** Up to this point he has spoken of the fact that the kingdom—that is, Christ—comes not with observable signs but unexpectedly; now he shows what kind of people ought to await his coming. The one who is on the roof is he who, rising above carnal things, lives spiritually as though in the free air. His vessels in the house are the carnal desires that he formerly loved but had left behind in the world while seeking things above; when judgment approaches, he must not return to them.

**And the one in the field.** Having said that the one who is in the field must not turn back, lest this appear to have been said only of those who would openly return from the field—that is, openly deny the Lord—he shows that there are many who seem to keep their faces turned forward but nevertheless look backward in their hearts.

**VERSE 32.**—**Remember.** Lot’s wife signifies those who, in tribulation, look backward and turn away from hope in the divine promise. Therefore she became a pillar of salt, because, by warning people not to do likewise, she seasons their hearts so that they may not be foolish.

**VERSE 33.**—**Whoever.** Whoever wishes to save carnal life in this world by denying Christ will lose it in the future; or whoever seeks the soul’s eternal salvation must not hesitate to give it over to the death of this present age.

**VERSE 34.**—**On that night.** That is, in that tribulation so dark that, if possible, even the elect will be led into error (Matt. XXIV). **Two in one bed.** Namely, those who choose leisure and are occupied neither with secular nor ecclesiastical affairs.

**VERSE 35.**—**The one will be left.** He is the one who abandons the state of life in which he has been formed, whether through human praise or through some corruption. Concerning him Jeremiah says: “The enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lam. I). **There will be two, etc.** These are two classes of those who follow the changing course of worldly affairs. They are designated by the feminine gender because they are governed by the counsel of greater powers, as women are by men; nevertheless, they work together insofar as they devote their affairs to the uses of the Church. Some act solely for the sake of eternal things, possessing as though they did not possess; others act for temporal things, placing their hope in the uncertainty of riches (1 Tim. VI).

**VERSE 37.**—**He said to them.** To the two who were asking one question he gives one answer: he indicates that the saints will be taken up with him, and by adding something else he suggests that the wicked, rejected by him, will be condemned with the devil. **Wherever, etc.** Wherever the Lord is bodily, there the elect will be gathered, those who, by humbly imitating his passion, are nourished as though on his flesh; through the resurrection their youth will be renewed like the eagle’s.

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0322B] **VERSE 2.**—**A certain judge.** This parable exhorts us to pray and believe, and not to presume upon ourselves but upon God.

**VERSE 3.**—**But a widow.** This widow may resemble the Church, which appears desolate until the Lord comes, though even now he secretly cares for her. **Vindicate me.** Although the righteous are instructed to pray for their persecutors, they nevertheless seek this vengeance upon the wicked without compromising justice: that all the wicked may perish, either converted to righteousness or deprived through punishment of the power that they can now exercise against the good, as long as this itself benefits the good or they retain any temporal power. When the righteous desire this end to come, although they pray for their enemies, they are not absurdly said to desire vengeance.

[Col. 0322C] **VERSE 8.**—**Nevertheless.** I say that I will avenge the righteous, but they will be very few; for when I appear on the day of judgment in the form of the Son of Man, there will be such a scarcity of the righteous that the ruin of the whole world will already have to be hastened, not so much because of the cry of the faithful unjustly condemned as because of the torpor of those who will rightly be condemned. **Do you suppose?** In this word the unbelief of doubt is rebuked, not the opinion of the Divinity. He knows all things through whom all things exist, but by questioning he rebukes the hearts of unbelievers.

**VERSE 10.**—**Two men.** Since he concluded the parable by which he invited people to pray by saying that, when the Judge comes, faith will scarcely be found on earth, he shows more carefully in this parable that God examines not the words of faith but its works, so that no one might flatter himself with a superfluous knowledge or even confession of faith. Among these works humility holds the chief place. Because the proud, who presume upon their own righteousness and despise the weak, do not possess it, they are as though empty of faith and are not heard when they pray.

[Col. 0322D] **VERSE 11.**—**God, I give thanks, etc.** There are four kinds of swelling pride: when someone thinks that he possesses the good he has from himself; or, if he believes it was given by God, thinks it was given on account of his merits; or when he boasts of possessing what he does not possess; or when, despising everyone else, he seeks to appear uniquely to possess what he possesses. The Pharisee suffered from this disease. He therefore went down unjustified, because he attributed the merits of good works uniquely to himself and placed himself above the tax collector.

[Col. 0323A] **VERSE 12.**—**I fast twice.** Behold, the Pharisee has an eye for displaying abstinence, obtaining mercy, and giving thanks to God, but not for guarding humility. And what does it profit if an entire city is guarded while one opening through which the enemies may enter is left open?

**VERSE 13.**—**And the tax collector.** As a humble man, he does not dare to approach, so that God may approach him; he does not look up, so that he may be looked upon. He presses down his conscience but raises up hope; he beats his breast and exacts punishment from himself so that God may spare him; he confesses so that God may forgive. God forgives what the man acknowledges. **God, be merciful.** The tax collector, praying humbly, belongs to those of whom it is said: “God will not fail to avenge his elect who cry out to him.” The Pharisee, boasting of his merits, belongs to those of whom it is added: “When the Son of Man comes, do you suppose he will find faith on earth?”

**VERSE 14.**—**Because everyone, etc.** After the dispute between the Pharisee and the tax collector has been set forth, the judge’s sentence is given, so that pride may be avoided.

**VERSE 15.**—**But they were bringing.** After the dispute just mentioned and the sentence given to the humble teacher, infants are brought forward, to show that an innocent and simple age belongs to grace. The apostles rebuke them, not because they did not want the infants to be blessed by the Savior’s hand and voice, but because, not yet perfect in faith, they thought that he, like other human beings, was wearied by the importunity of those bringing them.

**They were rebuking.** Perhaps they did this because previously they wanted the Jewish people, from whom they were descended according to the flesh, to be saved; yet they also pleaded for the Canaanite woman. [Col. 0323C] They therefore knew the mystery: that both peoples were called. But perhaps they did not yet know the order.

**VERSE 16.**—**Let the children come.** Let no one prevent the sick from coming to the physician. These have not yet committed anything on the branch, but they have perished in the root. Those who cannot act on their own behalf have entrusted their cause to their elders. Let the physician touch them and bless the little ones together with the elders (Ps. CXIII). **For of such is the kingdom.** He does not say “of these,” but of those who deliberately possess the innocence and simplicity that these have by nature, because it is not age that reigns but conduct. For it is not a virtue to be unable to sin, but to be unwilling to sin. Just as a child does not persist in anger, does not remember an injury, does not desire a woman, and does not think or speak evil, so you will not enter the kingdom of heaven unless you possess such innocence and purity of heart.

**VERSE 17.**—**The kingdom of God.** That is, we are commanded to receive the teaching of the Gospel as a child receives it. A child, while learning, does not contradict his teachers. He does not construct arguments and words to resist, but faithfully receives, obeys, and remains at rest.

**VERSE 18.**—**And he asked him.** *(BEDA.)* This ruler had heard that those like children were worthy, etc., up to the point where he adds to those who wish to be perfect: “Sell everything and give to the poor” (Mark X).

**Good Teacher.** Because he called him a good teacher and did not confess him as God or the Son of God, he says that although a holy human being may be called good, he is not good in comparison with God. Christ, however, does not reject the testimony to his goodness, but excludes goodness from a teacher who is considered apart from God.

**VERSE 19.**—**But he said.** *(AMBROSE.)* A crafty question, and therefore an incisive answer. For the tempter, etc., up to the point where it is defined by these words that a rich man who is merciful is contrary to nature.

**You know the commandments.** This is the purity of childlike innocence, which is offered to us for imitation if we wish to enter the kingdom of God.

**VERSE 23.**—**He was rich.** No rich man—that is, no one who trusts in his riches—will enter, as Jesus explains according to Matthew. Therefore it is not the rich who remain rich who will enter, but those who have ceased to be so.

**VERSE 25.**—**For it is easier.** Mystically: it is easier for Christ to suffer for those who love the world than for those who love the world to be converted to Christ. Christ is called a camel because, willingly humbled, he bore the burdens of our weakness. The needle signifies the piercing through which he indicates the narrowness of his passion; by that passion, like a needle, he deigned to mend the torn garments of our nature—that is, to restore them after the Fall. Alternatively: it is easier for a Gentile people, deformed by the hump of sins, to enter by the narrow way of life than for a Jew who glories in his merits and refuses to humble himself in order to bear Christ’s light burden.

**VERSE 26.**—**Who can?** They understand that all who love riches are to be counted among the rich, even if they do not possess them; otherwise, since the multitude of the poor is greater, they would not say: “Who can be saved?”

**VERSE 29.**—**No one.** Whoever has abandoned carnal things for the Lord will receive spiritual things. Mark says: “A hundredfold now,” etc. (Mark X), that is, in this life full of persecutions they taste the joy of the kingdom and enjoy the sincere love of all the elect.

**VERSE 30.**—**Will receive, etc.** Whoever has abandoned all riches for the Lord and despised the affections of the flesh will receive much more in the present life; from brothers and sisters spiritually bound together by the bond of their purpose, he will receive in this life a far more gracious love.

**VERSE 31.**—**He took aside.** Foreseeing that his disciples would be disturbed by his passion, he foretells both the suffering of the passion and the glory of the resurrection, so that when they saw him dying they would not doubt that he would rise again. **And they will accomplish.** By this he shows that whatever the prophets foretold was directed toward the mystery of his dispensation. In this he strikes at the heretics who say that Christ preached against the Law and the prophets, and that the God of the Old Testament is one and the God of the New Testament another. He also refutes the madness of the pagans, because they deride his cross, even though he shows himself, as one foreknowing the future, to be aware of his approaching passion and, as one who does not fear death, goes to the place of it.

**VERSE 34.**—**And they, etc.** The disciples cannot understand the Lord’s discourse about his passion, repeated so many times, because they most desire to see the one whose death they cannot bear to hear of; and although they know him not only as an innocent human being but also as the true God, they do not think that he can die.

**VERSE 35.**—**A blind man.** The blind man signifies the human race, which, excluded from the light above, suffers the darkness of its condemnation; but it is healed by the Lord as he approaches Jericho. Jericho is interpreted as “moon,” by which the decline of mortality is understood. Thus, when the Word of God assumes the weakness of our flesh, the human being returns to knowledge. The blind man sits beside the road when he begins to believe in the one who says: “I am the way” (John XIV). He begs when he prays.

**VERSE 39.**—**And those who went before, etc.** Those who go before Jesus as he comes signify the throng of carnal vices. These scatter a person’s thoughts and disturb the voice of prayer, preventing Jesus from coming to illuminate the human heart. But when the blind man already feels himself weighed down by the phantoms of former vices and finds the voice of his prayer hindered, so that he cannot obtain intercession for himself, he cries out more fervently.

**VERSE 40.**—**But standing, etc.** While passing by, he hears the blind man; while standing, he gives him sight. Through his humanity he sympathizes with the voices of our blindness, but through the power of his Divinity he pours into us the light of grace. **To be brought to him.** The man, who had sensed the one passing by to some extent while suffering the crowds of phantasms in prayer, applies himself more intensely to prayer and is brought to the one who stands. He receives light because God is fixed in a steadfast heart, and thus the lost light is restored.

**VERSE 41.**—**What do you want, etc.** He does not ask out of ignorance, but in order to be asked, so as to stir the mind to prayer. Understanding this, the blind man adds: “Lord, that I may see.” The blind man does not ask for gold or anything temporal, but only for light. Let us therefore imitate him whom we have heard to have been healed in mind and body. Let us ask the Lord for the light of eternal vision, and he will say to us: “See; your faith has saved you.”

**VERSE 43.**—**And immediately he saw.** He sees and follows who does the good that he understands and imitates Jesus, whether present or passing by. Such a person not only makes progress before God on account of the gift he has obtained, but also kindles others to praise God. **And all the people.** The people praise God not only for the gift of light that has been obtained, but also for the merit of the faith of the one who obtained it: they praise him not only because he powerfully and mercifully gives light, but because he hears the cry of firmly crying faith.

## CHAPTER XIX

**VERSES 1–2.**—**And entering, etc.** Behold, the camel, having laid aside the burden of its hump, passes through the eye of the needle, when, despising the wealth obtained by fraud, it ascends the narrow gate that leads to life. And because, through the devotion of faith, he supplies by climbing the tree what he lacked by nature in order to see the Savior, he rightly receives the blessing of the Lord’s hospitality, which he did not dare to ask for but desired. Mystically, Zacchaeus, whose name means “justified,” signifies believers from the Gentiles, who had been weighed down by their involvement with temporal things and were small, but were sanctified by the Lord.

**And he himself was rich.** Who should despair of himself when this man came to God, whose wealth came from fraud? Through him it becomes clear that not every rich man is avaricious.

**VERSE 3.**—**Because of the crowd.** What crowd but the ignorant confusion of the multitude, which cannot see the summit of wisdom? Zacchaeus therefore looks upon the Messiah whom he desires not in the crowd but after surpassing the people.

**VERSE 4.**—**A sycamore.** The sycamore is a tree resembling the mulberry in its leaves but surpassing it in height. It is interpreted as “foolish fig,” that is, the cross. It nourishes believers like a fig tree, but is mocked by unbelievers as foolish. The small man climbs it when any humble person, conscious of his own weakness, glories in the power of the cross. Through this praiseworthy foolishness he sees the Lord passing by, because, although not yet as firmly as he now does, he nevertheless swiftly and as though in passing directs his attention toward the light of heavenly wisdom.

**Because he was going to pass that way.** *(ISIDORE.)* By that place where the sycamore stood, or where he would come to believe, etc., up to the point where it stood out as though in the fruitful height of its work.

**VERSE 5.**—**And when he had come.** Through the heralds of his word, in whom Jesus was present and spoke, he came to the people of the nations. This people, already exalted by faith in his passion, burns also to acknowledge his divinity. Looking up, it sees that the one who has been raised above earthly things by faith has chosen the one who chooses him and loves the one who loves him. **Come down.** The command to come down from the sycamore and thus prepare a dwelling in the house means what the Apostle says: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer. For if he died through weakness, yet now he lives through the power of God” (2 Cor. V, XIII). **To remain.** Once the Lord remained in the house of the leader of the Pharisees—that is, he taught in the synagogue of the Jews.

**VERSE 7.**—**They were murmuring.** It is clear that the Jews always hated the nations or failed to understand their salvation. Hence it is also said against Peter: “Why have you entered among Gentiles who have the foreskin?” (Acts IX).

**VERSE 8.**—**But standing, etc.** While others accuse the man as a sinner, he and Zacchaeus, standing—that is, persisting in the truth of the faith he had begun—not only prove that he had been converted from a sinner, but also that he had lived among the innocent. Although he had lived innocently even before his conversion, he who before conversion could give half may after conversion give even the whole. **If I have defrauded anyone, etc.** First comes repayment according to the Law; then what remains is to be distributed to the poor. From the sycamore, through wise foolishness, the tax collector learns this fruit of life: he returns what he has stolen, abandons what is near, despises visible things, and desires to follow the footsteps of the one whom he does not yet see.

**VERSE 9.**—**Let him be a son.** Not by flesh but by faith. Just as Abraham, at God’s command and in hope of the future inheritance, left his homeland, so did this man, who acquires a treasure in heaven through hope.

[Col. 0326D] **VERSE 10.**—**He came, etc.** Even though they murmured, he did not disdain to explain his mysteries: he had come into the world chiefly for the repentance of sinners to be regarded, and he calls himself the Son of Man to reveal to us the dispensation of his mercy.

**VERSE 11.**—**While they were hearing these things, etc.** Having accepted and commended the repentance of the wealthy tax collector, he teaches through a parable that he prefers the repentance of sinners to the righteousness of the proud. He also shows that he will reign more widely among humble Gentiles who are ignorant of the Law than among Jews who boast of the righteousness of the Law.

**Because.** Not only those who persevere as righteous, but also those who turn from unrighteousness belong to the children of promise.

[Col. 0327A] **VERSE 12.**—**A nobleman went away.** This is the nobleman to whom the blind man cried: “Have mercy on me, Son of David,” and to whom the trumpets cried: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.” He was appointed king by the Father, the king to whom the nations were given as an inheritance. **Into a distant country.** Leaving the blinded Jews, he passes over to illuminate the nations. They cry to the Lord from far away—that is, from the ends of the earth—or because salvation is far from sinners (Ps. CXVIII). God is present everywhere and far from those who worship idols, yet even they have been brought near by the blood.

**VERSE 13.**—**And calling ten servants.** He calls ten servants when he chooses disciples instructed in the letter of the Decalogue. He gives ten minas when, having risen after the resurrection, he opens their understanding so that they may understand the words of the Law spiritually. A mina weighs ten drachmas. And because every word of Scripture suggests the perfection of heavenly life, it shines as though with the weight of the number one hundred. **Trade with these.** Offer the words of the Law, examined through mystical interpretation, to the peoples, and receive from them a confession of faith and uprightness of conduct.

**VERSE 15.**—**And it happened.** Every day Christ returns after receiving the kingdom from the Father, because he continually observes the condition of the Church as she journeys on earth. To one servant he lends money for trading; in another he examines the measure of completed work. He grants greater grace to the one who labors wisely, but deprives the one who follows a luxurious life even of what he had given. At the judgment, many who seemed fit to teach will, because of their negligence, be counted among the unlearned. Some who devoted themselves to a simpler observance will receive the highest rewards among the apostles. “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward” (Matt. X).

**VERSE 16.**—**But the first came.** The first servant is the order of teachers sent among the circumcised. He received one mina to trade because he was sent to preach one God, one faith, and one baptism. But he acquires ten when, by teaching, he associates with himself the people established under the Law.

**VERSE 17.**—**You were faithful in a very little.** Whatever gifts we receive in the present is little in comparison with future things. “We know in part and we prophesy in part” (1 Cor. XIII). **Ten cities.** The ten cities are souls that, through the words of the Law, reach the grace of the Gospel. Over these the one who has faithfully entrusted the money of the word to God will then be placed in glory. Hence the Apostle says: “What is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you before the Lord Jesus?” (1 Thess. II).

**VERSE 18.**—**And another.** A fitting order: he who was going to call the nations and send the Jews to be killed, because they did not wish Christ to reign over them, first introduced this comparison, lest it be said that he had given the Jewish people nothing by which they could become better: what could be demanded from one who had received nothing? He makes five from one mina who possesses moral virtues on account of the five senses.

**VERSE 20.**—**And another, etc.** The one sent to the uncircumcised was entrusted by the Lord with the same one mina—the same faith that had been entrusted to the circumcised—for preaching. It makes five minas because he converts the nations, enslaved to the five bodily senses, to the grace of evangelical faith. **In a cloth, etc.** He places the money in a cloth who, being fit to preach, either refuses to undertake the ministry of preaching or does not carry out what he has undertaken well, but hides the gifts he has received with himself in the idleness of time, saying: “It is enough for me to give an account of myself; why should I preach to others, or be forced to give an account of others?” Yet even before God those are inexcusable to whom the Law was not given and who did not fall asleep after hearing the Gospel, because through creation they could recognize the Creator.

**VERSE 21.**—**You reap where, etc.** God reaps where he did not sow—that is, he holds even those guilty of impiety to whom he did not provide the word of the Law or the Gospel. Therefore, fearing the danger of judgment, I will rest from administering the word.

**VERSE 22.**—**You knew, etc.** What he thought he had said as an excuse is turned into guilt. If you knew me to be so harsh and cruel, why did this thought not instill fear in you, so that you would know that I would seek my own more carefully?

**VERSE 23.**—**The money.** That is, you did not make evangelical preaching known to the prepared hearts of the faithful. **Mine on the table.** Not yours. Hence the Apostle says: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God” (1 Pet. IV). **With interest.** Whoever purchases the money of the word from a teacher by believing must repay it with interest by acting. Or he pays interest on the loan of the word when, from what he hears, he also strives to understand other things.

**VERSE 24.**—**Take it away, etc.** He loses the grace entrusted to him who neglects to share it with others through preaching. But it is increased for the one who has labored in it. So the royal anointing that Saul lost through pride David earned through obedience. For the Spirit of the Lord, who departed from Saul, was directed to David from that day forward.

**VERSE 26.**—**And it will be given abundantly.** Mystically: when all Israel has been saved, then the fullness of spiritual grace, which we now exercise sluggishly, will be bestowed abundantly upon the teachers of that time.

**VERSE 28.**—**And after saying these things.** When the parable was finished, he went to Jerusalem, to show that the preceding parable had concerned the fate of that great city, which shortly afterward would kill him and, because of hatred for his kingdom, would perish in hostile disaster.

**VERSE 29.**—**To Bethphage.** Bethphage was a village of priests on the Mount of Olives, and its name is interpreted as “house of the mouth.” Bethany was a village or town on the side of the same mountain and is called “house of obedience.” As the Lord was about to come to Jerusalem, he exalted these places by his presence, because before his passion he filled many, through teaching, with the gifts of devout confession and spiritual obedience. They are appropriately situated on the Mount of Olives—that is, in the Lord himself, who refreshes us with the anointing of spiritual chrism and with the light of conscience and piety. And because he does not wish a city set upon a mountain to be hidden, he sends disciples into the village opposite them, so that through them he may penetrate the fortifications of the whole world set against them.

**VERSE 30.**—**As you enter, you will find.** As preachers enter the world, they find the people of the nations entangled in the bonds of unbelief, free and wanton. **Which no one, etc.** That is, no rational teacher had placed upon it the bridle of correction—one who would either restrain its tongue from evil or compel it to go along the narrow way of life. No one had given it the garments of salvation by which it might be warmed through useful exhortation. No one sat upon it, because no one had corrected its foolishness by restraining it. **Tied up.** Bound by the chains of unbelief, it served the Lord in error, being enslaved or constrained by him, but could not claim dominion for itself. It had made him its lord not by nature but by guilt. Therefore, when the Lord is named, one is recognized. For although there are many gods and lords, generally there is one God and one Lord.

**VERSE 33.**—**When they were untying, etc.** Do not despise this little donkey, because just as ravenous wolves may be found in sheep’s clothing, so beneath the outer covering of the body—which we share with beasts—a mind full of God may be vigorous. **They said.** It had many masters, because, devoted not to one superstition, it was dragged according to the will of unclean spirits into various errors. **Why are you untying it?** Those who had opposed the untying of the colt fall silent when they hear the name, because the teachers of error who resist the teachers coming for the salvation of the nations defend their darkness until, with miracles bearing witness, the power of the true owner shines forth. But once the power of the Lord’s faith appears, the complaints of the adversaries give way, and a congregation that bears God in its heart is brought forward.

**VERSE 35.**—**The garments.** The garments of the apostles are the teaching of virtues, or the discernment of the Scriptures, and spiritual grace. With these they first cover the hearts of human beings, previously naked and cold, so that they may deserve to have Christ as their rider. **They placed them.** While the people of the nations carry Christ, the disciples spread their garments on the road, because, stripping off the covering of their own bodies, they prepare the way for the simple with their blood, so that with an unimpeded step of mind they may advance toward Jerusalem, where Christ leads them—that is, toward the true vision of peace.

**VERSE 37.**—**At the descent.** As the Lord descended from the Mount of Olives—that is, humbled himself to the weakness of our flesh, though he was in the form of God—the crowds descended with him. That is, those who need his mercy are humbled so that they may be exalted by him. **Rejoicing.** He had often entered the city of Jerusalem, but he had not been called king, a title he had always avoided, except now, when he ascended in order to suffer. This happened so that he might arouse their envy against himself more intensely, because the time of his passion was already approaching. **Concerning.** Especially concerning the resurrection of Lazarus, which had recently taken place. Indeed, the crowd also came to meet him because they had heard that this sign had been performed by him. They also praise him for the signs and teaching that he performed when he went up for the day of the Feast of Booths, as John relates.

**VERSE 38.**—**Blessed.** The crowd, which would shortly crucify him, calls him king and declares that the son of David expected according to the flesh has come, so that testimony may be forced from them against their will. **Peace.** Just as, when the Lord was born, the heavenly hosts of human beings and angels sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men,” so human beings sing to the one who was soon to triumph: “Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest.”

**VERSE 39.**—**Teacher.** What astonishing madness in those who were envious! They knew him to teach the truth, yet when they heard him called “Teacher,” they judged that his disciples should be rebuked, as though they themselves had been better instructed—disciples whom the one who, through miracles, was manifestly God had trained.

**VERSE 40.**—**The stones.** When the Lord had been crucified and the apostles were silent through fear, the rocks that were split, with the tombs opened, openly cried out that he was God and Lord of the world.

Mystically: if blindness should come upon Israel so that it falls silent in praise of God, the people of the nations, their stony hearts softened, will believe in and proclaim their Creator.

**VERSE 44.**—**And they will not leave.** The perverse person, when he adds perversity to perversity, builds as though one stone upon another. But when the soul is seized for vengeance, such a construction of thoughts is scattered. This happens because you did not recognize the time. God visits the perverse soul sometimes through a command and sometimes through a miracle. But because, in its pride, it despises him and is not ashamed of its evils, it will finally be handed over to its enemies, with whom it will be joined in the fellowship of condemnation at the eternal judgment. **For peace, etc.** While you give your flesh over to pleasures and do not foresee the evils to come, you possess present goods that can provide temporal peace. And why is this so? He adds: because you do not foresee the evils that will come upon you. If you had foreseen them, you would not have rejoiced in present prosperity.

**VERSE 45.**—**And entering.** After enumerating the evils, he entered the temple and drove out those who were buying and selling. By this he indicated that the ruin of the people arose chiefly from the guilt of the priests. For when he strikes the sellers and buyers, he shows from where the root of destruction proceeded.

**VERSE 47.**—**And he was teaching.** The house of God is the conscience of the faithful. A person makes it a den of thieves when, abandoning the simplicity of holiness, he considers how to do something by which he can injure an innocent neighbor. But, conversely, the Lord teaches the minds of the faithful to avoid evils. **They were seeking to destroy him.** They could not destroy him because they feared the disturbance of the people; or they wanted to destroy him because, having neglected their own teaching authority, they saw the whole people flocking to his instruction.

## CHAPTER XX

**VERSE 2.**—**By what authority.** They doubt God’s authority and imply that what he does belongs to the devil. Hence they add: “Or who is it, etc.?” In this they plainly deny the Son of God, believing that he performs signs not by his own powers but by those of another.

**VERSE 3.**—**I will ask you, etc.** He could have refuted the slander of his tempters with a direct answer, but he wisely asks them a question, so that they may be condemned either by their silence or by their own answer.

[Col. 0331A] **VERSE 4.**—**The baptism of John, etc.** He whom you confess to have received prophecy from heaven bore witness to me, and from him you heard by what authority I act. Understanding this, they are uncertain what they ought to answer.

**Neither will I, etc.** For two reasons truth must be hidden from those who ask: either because they are less capable of hearing it—hence it is said, “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John XVI)—or because they ask out of hatred and contempt, hence it is said, “Do not give what is holy to dogs” (Matt. VII).

**VERSE 9.**—**But he began.** After refuting the chief priests and scribes through their own question, the Lord continues what he had begun. While they listened, he addressed the people, who heard his words more willingly, introducing a parable by which he both accused them of impiety and showed that the kingdom of God would be transferred to the nations.

**A vineyard.** Morally: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. V). The tenants are the workers who were hired to cultivate it at the first, third, sixth, and ninth hours. **And he himself went abroad, etc.** He who is everywhere is more present to those who love him and absent from those who are negligent. He remained away for a long time so that the demand might not appear improper. For the more indulgent the generosity, the less excusable the obstinacy.

### VERSE 10

**And in due time.** The first servant who is sent is Moses, the lawgiver. For forty years he sought from the cultivators the fruit of the law that he had given, but they beat him and send him away empty-handed.

### VERSE 11

**And he added, etc.** The second servant is David the prophet, who, after Moses, invited the cultivators of the vineyard to the practice of good works through the melody of psalmody and the sweetness of the harp. But they too treated him with insult and sent him away empty-handed, saying: “What share have we in David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse?” (1 Kings 12). Yet on behalf of this vineyard, lest it be utterly uprooted, he pleads: “Lord God of hosts, turn and look down from heaven, and see and visit this vineyard” (Psalm 77). The third servant is the chorus of the prophets. They rebuked the people and foretold the evils that threatened the vineyard, but they too were persecuted and killed.

### VERSE 14

**When they saw him.** He plainly proves that the Jews crucified the Son of God not through ignorance but through envy. For they understood that he was the one of whom it had been said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 117). And so, taking counsel for themselves, they say: “Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12), etc. Therefore the inheritance of the Church—which the Father did not leave behind by dying, but which Christ himself, having purchased it by his death, possessed by rising again—the Jews wish to seize, while they attempt to extinguish the faith that comes through him. They are not subject to the justice of God, but wish to establish their own. **This is the heir:** Christ is the heir because he survived his own death and receives, as hereditary gains in our progress, the benefits of the testaments that he himself established.

### VERSE 15

**And having cast him out.** Mark changes the order: “They killed him and cast him outside the vineyard” (Mark 12). In this their obstinacy is indicated: after the resurrection they were unwilling to believe the apostles who preached, but, throwing him away like a useful corpse, they gave him to the Gentiles to receive.

### VERSE 16

**Let it not be so.** They contradict the judgment that they recognize as having been spoken against their own faithlessness. For they understand that what they were harboring in their minds is contained in the parable. Since the Jews deny that it would be just for the law of divine knowledge—which they themselves despised—to be transferred to the Gentiles, listen to what the Savior replies.

### VERSE 17

**What is this, etc.?** How will this prophecy be fulfilled? Unless it is because Christ, rejected by you, must be preached to the Gentiles who will believe, so that in himself, the one cornerstone, he may join two walls.

**The builders.** Those who above are called cultivators are here called builders, because those who were commanded to cultivate the people so that they might bear fruit were also commanded to establish that people as a house worthy of the Lord who would dwell in it.

### VERSE 18

**Everyone who falls.** Whoever believes and yet sins falls upon the stone. He is not crushed but broken, because he is preserved for salvation through patience. But upon whomever the stone falls—that is, whoever utterly denies him—he is crushed, so that not even a potsherd remains. Or, one falls upon him who now despises and insults him: such a person is not yet utterly destroyed, but is shattered, so that he does not walk upright. The stone falls upon him whom, when he comes in judgment, it crushes.

### VERSE 19

**And they sought, etc.** They seek to kill him as though he were a liar, in whom the things he had said are proved true. For he is the heir, while they are the wicked cultivators, restrained only by human fear until his hour should come.

### VERSE 20

**And watching him.** What they could not accomplish by themselves because of fear of the people, they wish to achieve through empty devices, so that they might appear free from responsibility for his death.

### VERSE 22

**Is it lawful for us, etc.?** Since Judaea had recently become tributary to the Romans under Augustus, the Pharisees—who prided themselves on their justice, who gave tithes and firstfruits to God—denied that tribute should be paid to a human being. Because of this revolt, the kingdom and the entire homeland were later destroyed.

### VERSE 24

**Whose image does it bear, etc.?** One is the image of God, another that of the world. If, therefore, Christ did not bear Caesar’s image, why did he pay the tax? He did not give what was his own; he returned to the world the things that belonged to the world. And you, if you do not wish to be subject to Caesar, do not possess the things that belong to the world. If you possess riches, you are subject to Caesar. If you wish to owe nothing to an earthly king, abandon all that is yours and follow Christ. And rightly he first determines that the things belonging to Caesar must be returned. For no one can belong to the Lord unless he has first renounced the world.

### VERSE 25

**Return, therefore.** Just as Caesar demands the impression of his own image, so God desires the soul marked with the light of his countenance.

### VERSE 27

**Some Sadducees also approached, etc.** There were two sects among the Jews: the Pharisees, who preferred the justice of traditions and observances, and were therefore called “separated” from the people; and the Sadducees, who likewise claimed for themselves what they were not—that is, righteousness.

### VERSE 28

**Teacher.** Those who do not believe in the resurrection of bodies and think that souls perish with the bodies invent a shameful story, which exposes as delirious those who affirm the resurrection. Yet it may be that something of this kind once happened among their people.

**So that he may take, etc.** Under the law of the letter, a man was compelled to marry during his lifetime. But under the law of the Spirit, chastity is commended.

### VERSE 35

**But those, etc.** Since all, both good and evil, will rise and remain without marriage, the Lord nevertheless speaks only of the elect in order to stir them toward the glory of the resurrection. But if in the resurrection they will neither marry nor give in marriage, then bodies capable of marrying and giving in marriage will rise. This is said of those who possess sexual members but will not be bound by either pleasure or necessity to marry.

And observe that although he speaks of hidden mysteries with plotters and those who trample upon them, he nevertheless does not give what is holy to dogs. Many suitable hearers were present, and they ought not to be neglected because of the uncleanness of others.

**Neither will they marry, etc.** Marriage exists for children, children for succession, succession because of death; where, then, there is no death, neither is there marriage.

### VERSE 37

**But that the dead rise.** After answering the question that had been proposed concerning the condition of the resurrection, he addresses the resurrection itself against their unbelief.

### VERSE 40

**And they no longer dared, etc.** Confuted in argument, they no longer question him, but openly hand him over to Roman authority. From this we understand that the poisons of envy can indeed be overcome, but with difficulty become quiet.

### VERSE 41

**How do they say, etc.?** As he brings his commandments to completion, the Lord concludes the faith of his testament, so that we may believe that the Lord Jesus is true God and true man, seated at the right hand of the Father.

### VERSE 43

**Until I place.** The subjection of the enemies by the Father signifies not the Son’s weakness but the unity of nature, whereby one acts differently in the other. For the Son also subjects the enemies to the Father, because he glorifies the Father upon the earth.

### VERSE 46

**Beware of the scribes.** We are commanded to beware of those who desire empty glory for two reasons: lest we be deceived by their hypocrisy, or be inflamed by their example to love temporal things.

**And they love greetings in the marketplace.** He does not forbid greetings in the marketplace, nor the first seats to those to whom they are due according to the order of their office, but to those who love them without deserving them. He reproves the mind, not the rank. Nor is a person free from blame if he wishes to take part in the disputes of the marketplace while desiring to sit in the chair of Moses.

**Who devour, etc.** Mark says: “Under the pretext of lengthy prayer”—those who pray at greater length so that they may appear more religious—“they receive, as though they were patrons, praises and money from the weak and from those troubled by the consciousness of their sins.” Their prayer becomes sin, so that they are unable to intercede for others and cannot even benefit themselves unto salvation; indeed, they will be condemned more severely because of those very prayers.

**They will receive greater condemnation.** By this he indicates that those also who pray standing in corners so that they may be seen by people certainly deserve condemnation, but that these men will receive the greater condemnation.

## CHAPTER XXI

### VERSE 1

**And looking up, etc.** He had warned that those who sought primacy and empty glory should be avoided. He also carefully distinguishes those who bring gifts into the house of the Lord, so that he may repay each according to the intention of the heart.

### VERSE 4

**From their abundance.** The Jew gives from his abundance, presuming upon his righteousness, and so prays within himself: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of mankind” (Luke 18). The Church gives its entire livelihood as an offering to God. It understands that whatever it possesses comes not from its own merit but from the divine gift, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”

### VERSE 5

**And to some, etc.** After the widow’s offering, in which the Church from the Gentiles is signified, the destruction of the temple is introduced, so that, through the veil of the letter that conceals it, the hidden mysteries of the Church may begin to be revealed. For God took care to overturn the city, the temple, and all the things belonging to the figures, so that after Christ’s coming no one would return to them.

### VERSE 7

**They asked him.** Because he had foretold that everything would be destroyed, while they were praising the temple’s buildings, the disciples—as Mark says, Peter, James, John, and Andrew—ask him privately about the time and the signs of the foretold destruction.

### VERSE 8

**For many will come.** As the fall of Jerusalem approached, there were many leaders who said that they were Christs and that the time of liberty was near. In the times of the apostles also many founders of heresies appeared, who, among their other falsehoods, preached that the day of the Lord was at hand; the Apostle also rebuked them.

### VERSE 9

**Wars and revolts.** These abounded in Judaea from the Lord’s passion onward. The apostles are warned not to be terrified by them and abandon Jerusalem and Judaea, because the end would not come immediately, but after the forty-second year.

### VERSE 10

**Then he said.** Some of these things come from heaven, others from the earth, others from the elements, and others from human beings.

**Mystically.** “Nation will rise against nation,” and the pestilence of those whose speech spreads like a cancer, and famine—the hunger to hear the word of God—and the shaking of the earth, meaning separation from the true faith among heretics, are to be understood. They fight among themselves and thereby bring victory to the Church.

**And great signs.** These too are found to have been fulfilled at that time in Josephus, who relates that a star resembling a sword hung over Jerusalem for a year, that armed chariots and horsemen battled in the air for forty days, and that a heifer gave birth to a lamb among the hands of those sacrificing it.

### VERSE 13

**But it will happen, etc.** This concerns those who either persecute or do not change their lives. The death of the righteous is a help to the good, but a testimony of condemnation to the wicked, so that the perverse perish without excuse precisely where the elect receive an example by which to live.

### VERSE 16

**By parents, etc.** The torment is greater when someone suffers at the hands of those on whom he had relied, because, together with bodily harm, the evils of lost love cause anguish. And because the things foretold concerning the affliction of death are harsh, consolation concerning the joy of the resurrection is added.

### VERSE 18

**And not a hair.** It is as though he were saying: Why do you fear that what hurts when it is cut off will perish, when not even that which does not hurt when it is cut off can perish from you? For cut flesh hurts; a hair does not.

### VERSE 19

**By your patience.** Patience is the root and guardian of all virtues. Through it, therefore, we possess the souls that possess the body, when by reason we govern those souls toward endurance. True patience is to endure the evils of others with equanimity and to be moved by no grief against the one who inflicts them.

### VERSE 21

**And those who are in the regions.** Ecclesiastical history relates that the Christians who were in Judaea were warned by an angel, as the destruction approached, and lived across the Jordan in the city of Pella until the desolation of Judaea had been completed.

### VERSE 23

**For there will be great distress, etc.** This distress and wrath continue even to the present day for that people scattered throughout all the nations. Yet they will not last forever.

### VERSE 24

**Until the times of the nations are fulfilled, etc.** That is, until the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, and so all Israel has been saved (Romans 11), and, as though rejoicing at the throne of its own birth, returns. The Lord sets out in order what will follow when the times of the nations have been fulfilled and all Israel has been saved. For according to Matthew, the apostles asked about these things—not only about the time when the temple would be overthrown, but also about the sign of his coming and the consummation of the age.

### VERSES 25–26

**And there will be signs.** These things concern the coming itself, when all the wise and foolish virgins, roused by an unfamiliar cry, trim their lamps—that is, reckon up the works they have with them—and with the greatest fear await the outcome of the eternal judgment that already approaches.

As the final judgment draws near, the sound of the sea and of the waves becomes confused, and the whole earth is afflicted by inhabitants pressing upon it from every side. The greatest lights of heaven, struck by a new terror in their rays, veil their troubled appearance, because, as their end approaches, the elements, as though trembling with fear, sway and roar.

### VERSE 27

**And then they will see.** They refused to hear him when he was placed in humility, so that they might then feel his power all the more severely, the more they now refuse to incline their hearts toward his patience. But because these words have been spoken against the reprobate, he immediately adds what follows for the consolation of the elect.

### VERSE 28

**When these things begin to happen.** That is, when the plagues multiply and the terror of judgment is revealed through the powers that are shaken.

**Raise your heads.** Cheer your hearts, because, while the world to which you do not belong is coming to an end, the redemption that you seek is near. The fact that the world ought to be despised is made clear by a careful comparison.

### VERSE 29

**See the fig tree.** He compares the kingdom of God to summer, because then the clouds of our sorrow will pass away and the eternal days of life will shine under the brightness of the sun. Just as summer is recognized as near from the fruit of the trees, so the kingdom of God is recognized as near from the world’s ruin. These words show that the fruit of the world is its ruin. For it grows for the purpose of falling; it sprouts for the purpose of consuming in calamities whatever it has produced.

### VERSE 33

**Heaven and earth.** Nothing in the nature of bodies is more durable than heaven and earth. Nothing passes more swiftly than speech. As long as words are incomplete, they are not words; when they are complete, they are no longer there at all. For they can be completed only by passing away.

He therefore says: “Heaven and earth will pass away.” It is as though he were saying: Everything among you that is durable and unchanging is not durable unto eternity; and everything that is seen to pass away with me is held fixed and without passing away, because my speech, which passes away, expresses abiding judgments.

**But my words will not pass away.** And since my words will undoubtedly be fulfilled, take care that you are not, contrary to the warning of my words, devoted to gluttony, drunkenness, and worldly cares, as some will be at the time when judgment approaches. Concerning them it is said: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ sudden destruction will come upon them” (1 Thessalonians 5).

### VERSE 37

**And he was, etc.** What he taught by word he establishes by example. He had warned that, before the universal judgment and the uncertain departure of each individual, people should renounce the pleasures and cares of the world, keep watch, and pray. As his own passion approaches, he himself persists in teaching, watching, and praying; he urges by word those for whom he was about to suffer and commends them to the Father in prayer.

So too, when we conduct ourselves justly and piously amid prosperity, let us not despair of divine mercy amid adversity. We teach in the temple by day because we offer the faithful a model of good works; we remain on the Mount of Olives by night because, in the darkness of affliction, we breathe again through the consolation of spiritual joy.

## CHAPTER XXII

### VERSE 1

**The feast of Unleavened Bread was approaching, etc.** It is called Passover, etc. Passover is named not from “passion” but from “passing over,” because on that day the destroyer passed through Egypt, or because the Lord passed over while liberating his people. By this name it was signified that the Lamb would pass from the world to the Father on this day.

There is this distinction between Passover and Unleavened Bread: Passover refers only to the day on which the lamb was killed in the evening, that is, on the fourteenth day of the first month. The days of Unleavened Bread extended from the fifteenth day through the twenty-first day of the same month.

But the evangelists use the terms interchangeably, calling the day of Unleavened Bread Passover and Passover the days of Unleavened Bread. Thus Luke says here: “The feast of Unleavened Bread, which is called Passover” (Luke 22), because the day of Passover was also commanded to be celebrated with unleavened bread.

And since we make Passover perpetual, we are always commanded to pass from this world. One day on which the lamb was sacrificed in the evening is followed by seven days of Unleavened Bread, because Christ, having suffered once for us in the fullness of time, commanded us to live throughout the entire age of the world—which is ordered by seven days—in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

### VERSE 2

**And they sought, etc.** Matthew testifies that this occurred two days before Passover, when the chief priests and scribes had gathered in the courtyard of Caiaphas.

### VERSE 3

**He entered.** John says that after the morsel had been handed to Judas by the Lord, Satan entered him. But Satan had already invaded him before the morsel: the one whom Satan had first entered in order to deceive, he later entered in order to possess more fully, since he had now been handed over to him.

### VERSE 7

**The day came, etc.** Although he was crucified on the following day—that is, on the fifteenth day of the month—yet on this night, when the Lamb was sacrificed, he entrusted to his disciples the mysteries of his flesh and blood to be celebrated. Having been seized and bound by the Jews, he consecrated the beginning of that very sacrifice, namely, his passion.

### VERSE 10

**Behold, as you enter, etc.** As God, who knows all things beforehand, he speaks with the disciples about what is happening elsewhere. And appropriately a man carrying a jar of water meets those preparing the Passover, so that it may be shown that the mystery of this Passover is to be celebrated for the cleansing of the world through the water of baptism. There, the typological fervor at the threshold is removed from the true worshipers of Passover, and baptism in the life-giving fountain is consecrated for the removal of sins.

The jar signifies the full measure of completed time, at which it was fitting that these things should occur.

**A man carrying a jar.** He is designated without a name, so that he may be regarded as poor and insignificant, yet he is chosen by the Lord. His holiness appears in this: on his couch the Lord rests with his disciples, delighting in the lofty virtues.

**Follow him.** The names are deliberately omitted—both that of the water-carrier and that of the master of the house—to indicate that the opportunity is given to all who wish to be imbued with Christ’s mysteries, which is to celebrate the Passover, and who seek to receive Christ as a guest in the lodging of their minds.

### VERSE 12

**A large upper room.** This is the spiritual law. Emerging from the narrowness of the earth, it receives the Savior in a lofty place. One who remains in the letter celebrates the Passover in an inner chamber; but one who follows the water-carrier—that is, the herald of grace—into the house of the Church, rising above the surface of the letter, prepares a place of refreshment for Christ on the throne of the mind, understanding that all the mysteries of Passover and all the other decrees of the law are written concerning him.

### VERSE 15

**I have earnestly desired, etc.** He first desires to eat the typological Passover and thus reveal the mysteries of his passion to the world, so that he may show himself to be both the one who approved the ancient Passover and the one who demonstrates that it belonged to the figure of his dispensation. When the truth has now arrived, the shadow must cease.

As a figure of this, the manna ceased after the children of Israel had eaten from the produce of the land and no longer used that food.

### VERSE 16

**I will not eat.** I will no longer celebrate the Mosaic Passover until what is spiritually understood in the Church as the kingdom of God has been fulfilled. In this kingdom Christ continues to eat even to the present day, when he spiritually practices in his members what Moses commanded the unformed people to observe bodily.

### VERSE 17

**And taking the cup.** This cup belongs to the old Passover, which he was bringing to an end. After taking it, he gives thanks, specifically because the old things had passed away and all things new were about to come.

**He gave thanks.** He shows what each person ought to do under the scourge of his own guilt, since he himself bore with equanimity the scourges belonging to another.

### VERSE 18
