**For I tell you.** Just as he denies that he will eat the typological food of the lamb, so he denies that he will drink the typological drink of the Passover until, after the glory of the resurrection has been revealed, the kingdom of God—that is, the faith of the world—arrives. Through the transformation of these two sacraments, he teaches that the remaining sacraments and commands of the law are to be transferred to spiritual observance.

It may also be understood simply: from the hour of the supper until the time of the resurrection, when he would come in the kingdom of God, he was not going to drink wine. After the resurrection, he ate and drank with the disciples.

### VERSE 19

**And taking, etc.** When the solemnities of the old Passover were finished, he passed to the new Passover, which he desired to be celebrated continually in the Church in remembrance of his redemption. In place of the flesh and blood of the lamb, he substituted the sacrament of his own flesh and blood under the figure of bread and wine.

He breaks and distributes it to show that the breaking of his body would not occur without his own will. He gives thanks for the completion of the old things and the beginning of the new.

**With bread, etc.** Because bread strengthens the body, while wine produces blood.

### VERSE 21

**Nevertheless, etc.** Just as he foretold the passion, so he foretold the betrayer, so that, seeing that he could not remain hidden, he might repent of his deed. He does not identify him by name, lest, being openly corrected, he become more shameless. He therefore assigns the guilt to the group, so that the guilty man might repent; and he foretells the punishment, so that the one whom shame had not convicted might be restrained by the announced penalties.

**The hand of the one betraying me.** Following Judas’s example, the Son of Man is betrayed by anyone who dares to violate that inviolable sacrament of the Lord’s body. He sells him who, neglecting fear and love of him, is proved to love passing and criminal things.

### VERSE 24

**And there arose, etc.** (Bede.) We do not know the cause of the dispute, but it is not incredible, etc., down to: let us see what the spiritual teacher commanded.

(AMBROSE.) Let us therefore beware with the greatest care, etc., down to: so that the contest may not be about boasting of precedence, but about humility.

### VERSE 25

**He said to them.** The pious teacher does not rebuke the dispute that had begun but describes the form of humility that they should follow, as though he were saying: You wish, after the manner of worldly people, to reach possession of the kingdom through precedence; but one does not attain the summit of the virtues through power, but through humility.

It is necessary, however, that a subordinate display correction as a mother and discipline as a father, lest strictness become harsh or piety lax.

### VERSE 27

**For which is greater, etc.?** To complete his words of exhortation, he sets forth an example from himself. Hence John writes: “If I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet,” etc. All the things that the Lord did in the flesh may also be understood in the word “serve”: not only preaching or working miracles, but also laying down the soul that he received for us, so that we too may learn to lay down our souls for one another.

### VERSE 28

**You have remained with me.** My weakness did not disturb you; rather, you persevered in the good work you had begun. Therefore, just as the Father gave me, who persevered unto death, the name that is above every name (Philippians 2), so I will lead you, who persevere with me, into the eternal kingdom.

It is to be understood that Judas had already withdrawn, and that many others had already gone back, after hearing the words of the incomprehensible sacrament, when the Lord said these things.

### VERSE 30

**And you will sit upon thrones.** This is the transformation wrought by the right hand of the Most High: those who now humbly rejoice to serve their fellow servants will then be exalted and nourished at the Lord’s table with everlasting banquets. Those who, having been unjustly judged during temptations, remain with the Lord will there come with him as just judges over their tempters. For the more despised they are here, the higher the summit of their power will rise there.

**Judging the twelve.** By “twelve” is signified not twelve persons but a multitude of judges, because of the two parts of the number seven, by which universality is signified—namely, three and four, by which twelve is multiplied.

### VERSE 31

**But the Lord said.** So that the Twelve would not boast that they alone, out of so many thousands, were said to have remained with the Lord during the temptations, he warns them that they too could have been crushed by the same storm unless they had been protected by divine grace.

When Satan seeks to tempt and to shake them as one cleans wheat by winnowing, we are taught that no one is tempted by the devil unless God permits it.

**Behold, Satan, etc.** Satan asks to sift the good when, burning to afflict them, he breathes out the heat of his malice. The more enviously he seeks their temptation, the more he asks—as though pleading for their testing.

### VERSE 32

**But I have prayed.** Not that you may not be tempted, but that your faith may not fail, so that after the fall of denial you may rise again through repentance to your former state.

It is useful for the saints to be tested by temptations, so that either their strength may become evident when they are tempted, or, having learned their weakness through temptation, they may learn to become stronger. Thus, when they have been tested, they may receive the crown of life.

### VERSE 33

**He said to him, etc.** Because the Lord had said that he had prayed for Peter, Peter, conscious of his present affection and ardent faith but unaware of his future fall, did not believe that he could fail him.

But the one who knows what is in a human being, so that no one may carelessly trust in his own state or rashly despair after a fall, foretells the manner, time, and number of his denials, and, as the merciful one, promises the help of his protection.

### VERSE 35

**When I sent you.** He does not instruct his disciples according to the same rule of life in a time of persecution as in a time of peace. When he sent the disciples to preach, he commanded them to take nothing on the road, ordering that the one who announces the Gospel should live from the Gospel.

But when the moment of death was at hand, and that entire people was persecuting both the shepherd and the flock, he established a rule appropriate to the time, permitting them to carry what was necessary for life until the madness of their persecutors subsided and the time for evangelizing returned.

### VERSE 36

**But now, etc.** Here an example is also given to us, that sometimes, when circumstances require it, we may without guilt relax certain aspects of the strictness of our purpose. For example, if we travel through inhospitable regions, we are permitted to carry more provisions for the journey than we would have at home.

**And whoever has none.** He commands them to take a sword or a cloak, or, if they have neither, to buy one, so that readers may understand that the disciples lacked not the means of resistance but rather possessed a love for their teacher that preferred to suffer.

Even if there had been no other reason for drawing the sword, this alone would have been sufficient: after the servant’s ear was cut off, the Lord healed it by his touch. By this we are warned not to retain anger against one who has been struck, but, having risen again, to receive faith.

### VERSE 38

**Behold, two swords.** Two swords are brought forth: one of the New Testament and the other of the Old Testament, by which we are armed against the snares of the devil.

And it is said: “It is enough.” The two swords are sufficient as a testimony to the Savior who suffered willingly. One teaches both the apostles’ boldness in fighting for the Lord and the Lord’s possession, even while about to die, of the piety and power to heal the ear severed by the sword’s blow. The other, which was by no means drawn from its sheath, showed that they had not been permitted to do everything they could in his defense.

### VERSE 39

**And he went out.** Since the Lord was to be handed over by a disciple, he went to his customary place, where he could easily be found, lest anyone think that he feared death.

And rightly he leads to the Mount of Olives the disciples who had been imbued with the mysteries of his blood and body, signifying that all would be baptized in his death and strengthened by the highest gift of the Holy Spirit.

### VERSE 40

**Pray.** It is impossible for a human being not to be tempted. He does not say, “so that you may not be tempted,” but “so that you may not enter into temptation.” Pray—that is, so that temptation may not overcome you and hold you within its snares.

### VERSE 41

**And he himself, etc.** After giving the apostles the command to pray, he withdrew from them. He prays alone for all, who alone was about to suffer for all, indicating that his prayer differs from ours as much as his passion differs from ours.

**He was about a stone’s throw away, etc.** Mystically, by this he intimates that they should direct the stone toward the very same place—that is, bring the intention of the law, which was written on stone, all the way to him. For that stone can reach him, since “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10).

### VERSE 42

**Praying, he said.** He prays not so much from fear of suffering as from mercy toward the former people, lest he drink the cup offered by them. Hence he pointedly says: “this one”—that is, the cup of the Jewish people, who have no excuse of ignorance for my death, because I am announced to them daily in the law and the prophets.

If it is possible for the multitude of the Gentiles to believe without the destruction of the Jews, I refuse the passion. But if they must be blinded so that others may see, let not my will but yours be done.

**Father, if you are willing, etc.** (Ambrose.) He grieved for me, although he had nothing for which he himself needed to grieve. For he took upon himself my sadness in order to bestow on me his joy. Therefore I confidently call it sadness, while I proclaim the cross.

**Nevertheless, etc.** As the Lord approached his passion, he took upon himself the voice and fear of the weak in order to draw them away from it. Again, through obedience he showed strength of mind, so that when something we do not wish to happen threatens us, we may ask through weakness that it not happen, yet through strength remain prepared to fulfill the will of the Creator rather than our own.

### VERSE 44

**And his sweat became, etc.** As death approached, he expressed in himself the struggle of our minds. It is rightly the case that we suffer a certain force of terror when, after a little while, we are to encounter what will endure forever.

**Like drops of blood running down upon the earth.** The earth watered with blood declares that he was already obtaining the effect of his prayer: namely, that he would cleanse with his blood the faith of the disciples, which was still burdened by earthly weakness; that whatever scandal they suffered from his death, he would entirely remove by dying; and that he would raise the whole world, dead in sins, back to life.

### VERSE 47

**To kiss him.** The Lord accepts the kiss, not to teach us to feign, but so that he would not appear to reject even the betrayer and might affect the betrayer more deeply by refusing him none of the duties of love. Hence it is said: “With those who hated peace I was peaceful” (Psalm 119).

### VERSE 49

**Lord, shall we strike with the sword?** The order is as follows: After they had asked, saying, “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?” he then replied, “Allow this much.” That is: Let what is about to happen not disturb you. They must be permitted to proceed this far, so that they may seize me and the things written about me may be fulfilled.

But in the interval between the words of those asking and the response, Peter, moved by an even greater eagerness to defend the Lord, struck on his behalf. What could happen simultaneously could not be said simultaneously. Therefore “Allow this much” is not said as though the Lord approved Peter’s deed, since Matthew records him as saying: “Return your sword to its place,” which Jesus evidently said after the deed had been done.

### VERSE 50

**The servant, etc.** Mystically, the servant is the Jewish people, improperly enslaved to the rulers. In the Lord’s passion it lost its right ear—that is, spiritual understanding—while its left ear, content with the baseness of the letter, remained; Peter did not remove it, but divine judgment revealed that it had been taken away. This ear is restored by the Lord’s mercy in those among them who have preferred to believe.

### VERSE 52

**They had come out against him, etc.** According to the other evangelists, the chief priests and officers had not come to Jesus but had waited in the courtyard of Caiaphas.

But because they arranged the Lord’s death in such a way as to appear innocent—as though he had been handed over by a disciple, seized by the tribune and the crowds, condemned by the governor, crucified by the Romans, and with even the people choosing Barabbas—the evangelist, wishing to show that those whose counsel directed everything were especially guilty, says that they came to seize the Savior, coming with the authority of their own command.

**As against a robber, etc.** It is foolish to seek with swords and clubs one who voluntarily offers himself to their hands, and to search at night, through a betrayer, for one who supposedly lies hidden and avoids their eyes, although he teaches daily in the temple. But for this reason you gather against me in darkness: the power by which you arm yourselves against the light is itself in darkness.

### VERSE 54

**The high priest’s house.** Caiaphas, who had purchased the high priesthood for the price of one year from the Roman ruler. Yet he was first taken to Annas, as John says.

**He followed from a distance.** Appropriately from a distance, since he was about to deny the one who had been near him. This signifies that the Church would imitate Christ’s passion in a very different way: the Church suffers for itself, while Christ suffers for the Church.

### VERSE 55

**A fire in the middle.** The fire kindled by the impulse of desire through the malign spirit armed the tongues of the faithless in the courtyard of Caiaphas, so that they might deny and blaspheme God. What the malign council was doing inside the high priest’s house was symbolically displayed by the fire kindled outside amid the cold of night.

Stiffened for a time by this cold, Peter wished to warm himself as though at the servants’ coals, because he was seeking the comfort of temporal advantage through the company of the faithless. But when the Lord looked upon him, he abandoned this faithlessness. After the resurrection, when he saw the coals laid out and the fish placed upon them, he inflamed his heart with the coals of love.

### VERSE 56

**A certain servant girl.** Why does a servant girl expose him first, when men could more readily have recognized him? Unless it is to show that this sex had sinned in the Lord’s death, although it would be redeemed through his passion. For this reason a woman first received the mystery of the resurrection and guarded the command, so that she might abolish the ancient error of transgression.

### VERSE 57

**But he denied.** Peter does not deny him on the mountain, in the temple, or in his own house, but in the Jews’ praetorium, in the house of the high priest, where there is no truth, where Christ has been seized and bound.

What else could have happened but that he should go astray when a Jewish doorkeeper admitted him? Eve brought Adam in badly; a woman brought Peter in badly.

### Verses 59–60

“Man, I do not know what you are saying.” A person denies Christ not only when he says that he is not the Christ, but also when, though he is one, he denies that he is a Christian. Thus what the Lord says is fulfilled: “You will deny me.” “He is a Galilean.” The inhabitants of Jerusalem and the Galileans are equally Hebrews and speak one language, but each province has its own peculiarities, and one cannot change the familiar sound of one’s speech.

“And immediately.” After the third denial the cockcrow follows. The mysteries of events are indicated by the succession of times. At midnight he denies; at cockcrow he repents. After the resurrection, in the daylight, he professed three times that he loved the one whom he had denied three times, because the one who had wandered in the darkness of forgetfulness corrected his error by remembering the light already hoped for, and in the presence of that same true light fully raised up whatever he had thought.

### Verse 61

“And the Lord, turning.” By his gaze he summoned him to tears, as though recalling to his mind how many times he had denied what the Lord had foretold to him; nor could the one whom the Light of the world regarded remain in darkness.

### Verse 62

“And going out.” Separated from the council of the impious, he washes away his guilt. He was not permitted to hesitate within, for this reason: so that a remedy of repentance might be established in the foremost figure of the Church, and no one might dare to trust in his own strength.

### Verse 63

“They mocked him,” etc. The prophecy was fulfilled: “With a rod the cheek of the judge of Israel will be struck.” And likewise: “I gave my cheek to those who struck me.” But he who was then beaten with the fists of the Jews is now struck by the blasphemies of false Christians.

“They covered his face,” not so that he might not see their crimes, but so that they might hide from themselves—as once they did from Moses [Col. 0343B]—the grace of knowing him. “For if they believed Moses, they would also believe the Lord” (John VIII). This veil remains upon their hearts to this day, but it has been removed from believers: when he died, the veil of the temple was torn.

### Verse 64

“Prophesy.” This was an insult directed against one who called himself a prophet. But heretics and Jews, who to this day deny Christ, and wicked Christians, who provoke him by their evil deeds, also say, as though mocking him, “Prophesy: Who is it that struck you?” They do this because they suppose that their thoughts and works of darkness are not seen by him.

### Verse 66

“If you are the Christ.” They do not desire the truth but prepare an accusation. They understood the Christ to be a mere man who would be born from David. [Col. 0343C] Accordingly, they ask this so that, if he were to say, “I am the Christ,” they might accuse him of arrogating royal power to himself.

### Verse 67

“If I tell you.” He had often said that he was the Christ. He had also asked them how they could say that the Christ was the son of David when David calls him Lord, thereby urging them to believe that he was God. But they were unwilling either to believe him when he spoke, to answer him when he questioned them, or to release one who was innocent.

### Verse 69

“But from now on it will be.” Those who sought to accuse him as David’s offspring hear something still greater: that he will come to glory through contempt.

### Verse 70

“You say that I am.” He so moderates his reply that he both speaks the truth and does not expose his words to accusation. He preferred to prove himself Christ, the Son of God, rather than to say it in such a way as to remove from those who acknowledged his claim the grounds on which they could condemn him.

### Verse 71

“For we ourselves have heard it.” When he said, “The Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God,” they condemn themselves by their own sentence: they hand him over to death even though, by the testimony of their mouth and deeds, they recognize him to be God.

## Chapter XXIII

### Verse 1

“They led him away.” They handed him over to Roman authority, so that in this way the Jews might show that they were not responsible for his execution. In this, however, not their innocence but their madness is revealed.

### Verse 3

“But Pilate,” etc. Since two charges had been brought forward—namely, that he forbade the payment of tribute and that he called himself Christ—Pilate could have recalled what he had said about taxes: “Give to Caesar what belongs to Caesar.” Regarding this as an obvious falsehood and making light of it, he asked only about what he did not know.

“You say so.” By the same expression with which he answered the chief priests, he also replies to the governor, so that both may be condemned by their own statement.

### Verse 4

“I find no guilt.” On the day before he suffered, the Lord said to his disciples: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (Luke XX). But since the ruler—that is, Pilate—acquits him in whom he finds nothing deserving condemnation, consider what the Jews are doing: they do not investigate the truth out of love for justice, but, driven by envy, strive to condemn the righteous.

### Verse 5

“He stirs up the people.” They accuse not him but themselves. For teaching the people and stirring them from their former bodily sluggishness by his instruction, and by such action passing from Galilee to Judaea—that is, through the whole land of promise, from end to end—is not a crime but evidence of power. Accordingly, Pilate did not even think the Savior should be questioned about this; rather, taking the opportunity, he wished to declare him free by judging him innocent.

### Verse 7

“And when he learned.” So that he would not be compelled to pass sentence against an innocent man whom he knew had been handed over through envy, he sent him to Herod to be heard, so that he might either be acquitted or condemned by his own tetrarch. Yet, so that the Jews might have no excuse remaining, Herod too—who was a Jew both by birth and by religion—was allowed to show what he thought about Christ. Thus it might be demonstrated that both regions, Judaea, in which Christ was born, and Galilee, in which he was raised, had conspired in his death.

“But he answered nothing.” He was silent and did nothing, because Herod’s unbelief did not deserve to see divine things, and the Lord was avoiding ostentation. Herod signifies all the impious who do not believe the Law and the Prophets and cannot see the works of Christ in the Gospel. Therefore, while the chief priests accuse him, he answers little before Pilate and nothing before Herod, lest, having dispelled the charge, he should be released by the ruler and thus delay the benefit of the cross.

### Verse 11

“And he mocked him.” The fact that he is despised and mocked in a white robe signifies that the Lamb, sacrificed in chaste flesh for the sins of the whole world, suffered and was buried. That here he is mocked while clothed in white, but according to the other Evangelists in a purple or scarlet robe, signifies the twofold kind of martyrdom by which the Church is adorned in her sufferings, so that she may be white in action and red with blood. For he himself, blooming with the flowers of his members, produces lilies in peace and roses in war.

“And he sent him back to Pilate.” He is sent to Herod, sent back to Pilate; and although neither declares him guilty, each nevertheless complies with the promptings of another’s wickedness.

### Verse 12

“And they became friends.” The unspeakable alliance that Herod and Pilate made in killing Christ is preserved by their successors as an inherited right, while Jews and Gentiles, divided in mind as they are by race and religion, nevertheless agree in persecuting Christians and destroying the faith of Christ.

In the figure of Herod and Pilate, who became friends through Jesus, the pattern of the Jews and the nations is preserved, so that through Christ’s passion the future concord of both peoples might be established. Yet the Gentile is to receive the kingdom of God first and transmit devotion to the faith to the Jew, so that they too may clothe the body of Christ with the glory of his majesty—Christ whom they had formerly despised.

### Verse 14

“You brought him to me.” Observe how earnestly Pilate seeks to release Jesus. First, when they accuse him, he says that he has found no charge against him. Then, when they persist in their undertaking, he sends him to Herod to discover whether Herod can find any crime in him or decide that he should be released. Finally, after learning Herod’s judgment and finding no offense in Jesus, [Col. 0345B] he asks for the verdict of the crowd, since one person had to be released at Passover. Wishing to release him a second and even a third time, he questions them again. But the more carefully he seeks to release him, the more criminally they demand his death.

### Verse 15

“But neither did Herod.” To reproach the Jews’ or the Gentiles’ hardness, Pilate acknowledges that neither he nor Herod had found anything deserving death or mockery in Christ, but that he had yielded to the shouts of another’s cruelty.

### Verse 16

“Therefore, after chastising him,” etc. Pilate acquits Jesus, whom he has proved innocent; but, so that the Scriptures might be fulfilled, he acquits by his judgment the one whom he nevertheless crucifies in the mystery.

### Verse 18

“Take this man away,” etc. Because they chose a robber instead of Jesus, a murderer instead of the Savior, and a destroyer instead of the giver of life, they rightly lost both salvation and life. They subjected themselves so completely to robberies and seditions that they lost both the homeland and kingdom they had preferred to Christ, and to this day they have not recovered the freedom of soul or body that they had sold.

“Barabbas,” etc. Barabbas, whose name is interpreted as “son of the teacher” or “son of their father,” is Antichrist, whom those will prefer to Christ to whom it is said: “You are from your father the devil.”

Pilate is interpreted as “the mouth of the hammer.” He signifies the devil, who is the hammer of all matter, through whom God permits vessels to be tested and whom he finally crushes when he breaks him in the final condemnation.

### Verse 21

“Crucify him, crucify him.” Great is their cruelty: they seek not merely to kill him but to crucify him, so that, with his hands and feet fastened to the wood, he might be killed by a prolonged death, lest his pain end too quickly, and so that he might remain visible for a long time on the cross.

### Verse 22

“I will chastise him,” etc. He offered this chastisement—mocking and scourging him—to the desires of the wicked, so that they would not rage as far as crucifying him. The words of John the Evangelist bear witness to this, as does the very column to which the Lord was bound, which to this day displays to those who look upon it sure signs of the Lord’s blood.

But although Pilate does this, the insatiable fury of the sacrilegious does not cease. Rather, it presses on more intensely, because they had seen that the accusation they had brought against the Lord had been nullified by Pilate’s careful examination. At last the shameless turn to prayers alone, so that what they had been unable to accomplish by accusation or something resembling argument, they now accomplish by asking, shouting, and carrying the matter through.

### Verse 25

“But he released,” etc. The author of sedition and murder is released to the Jews—that is, the devil, who, having been expelled from the homeland of light because of his guilt, had been sent into the prison of darkness. Therefore they cannot have peace, because they did not choose the author of peace.

### Verse 26

“They seized a certain man,” etc. At first the Lord carried the cross, but afterward it was laid upon Simon, whom they encountered as they went out. This was fitting: “Christ suffered for us so that you might follow in his footsteps” (I Peter II). Whoever wishes to follow him must take up his cross and follow.

Since Simon was not an Israelite but a Cyrenian, the Gentiles are signified through him. Formerly strangers and guests with respect to the covenants, they are now, through faith, fellow citizens and members of God’s household and co-heirs with Christ. Hence Simon is interpreted as “obedient heir of Cyrene.”

Simon came from a village—that is, from a *pagus*, from which “pagans” derive their name: those alienated from the city of God and ignorant of its civic way of life. But Simon, coming out from the village, carries the cross behind Jesus, when the peoples of the Gentiles, abandoning pagan rites, obediently embrace the footsteps of the Lord’s passion.

### Verse 27

“He was followed,” etc. But not everyone follows the cross with the same intention. The wicked follow so that they may look joyfully upon the dying man. The women follow so that they may mourn the one whom they desired to live, but who was about to die, dying, and dead.

The lamentation of the women is not introduced because many men were not also grieving, but because the female sex, being regarded as more contemptible, could more freely display before the chief priests what it thought against them. Since the Lord knows who are his (II Timothy II), he passed over the raging crowd and turned his eyes and face toward the women who loved and mourned him.

“Who were lamenting.” They were grieving over mortal life, which was destined to end in death, not over the blind men who were killing the physician.

### Verse 28

“Daughters of Jerusalem.” Notice that when he calls them daughters of Jerusalem, it means that not only the women who had come with him from Galilee but also many women who were citizens of that city had joined themselves to him.

“Do not weep.” Do not lament me as one who is about to die, whose resurrection can soon undo death, whose death will destroy both death and death’s author. Rather, wash yourselves and your offspring with fitting fountains of tears, lest you be condemned with the faithless as punishment for my crucifixion.

### Verse 29

“Behold, the days are coming.” These are the days of Roman siege and captivity. When captivity is imminent and hostile destruction rages through fields and cities, it is natural for all who can escape to seek high or hidden places in which they may conceal themselves.

### Verse 30

“Fall upon us.” This may, by way of excess, be understood of those of either sex who castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.

### Verse 31

“For if they do this in the green wood.” The green wood is Christ and his elect; the dry wood is the impious and sinners. Hence he says: If I, who committed no sin and who rightly am called the tree of life, producing twelve fruits of grace in each month, do not leave this world without the fire of suffering, what torments await those who are empty of fruits and who are not afraid to give even the tree of life to the flames?

“And if it is time for judgment to begin with the household of God,” and all who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution, “what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel?” (I Peter IV; I Timothy III).

### Verse 32

“They were also led away.” What was said is fulfilled: “He was reckoned with the transgressors” (Isaiah LIII). He is reckoned among the wicked in death, so that in the resurrection he might give life to the wicked—he who, having become man for the sake of human beings, gave human beings the power to become children of God.

### Verse 33

“The place of the Skull.” Outside the gate of Jerusalem were places where the heads of condemned persons were cut off; these were called places of the Skull, that is, of the beheaded. He is crucified there so that, where there had been the execution ground of the condemned, the banners of martyrdom might be raised.

“And the robbers,” etc. The Jews’ iniquity is execrable in deed: they crucify, as though he were a robber, the Redeemer of all. Yet the robber is good in the mystery: he lay in wait for the devil in order to seize his vessels.

Through the one signified on the right is the mortification of the flesh for heavenly glory; through the one on the left, the mortification of the flesh for some worldly purpose.

### Verse 34

“But Jesus,” etc. Since Luke intended to write of Christ’s priesthood, it is right that the Lord should intercede before God for his persecutors according to the law of priesthood, and open paradise to the confessing robber. Nor does he pray in vain, but obtains this for those who believed after his passion.

He does not pray for those who, through envy and pride, understood that he was the Son of God, denied him, and crucified him; rather, he prays for those who had zeal for God but not according to knowledge, and who did not know what they were doing.

“Dividing.” John treats this more fully. The four-part garment signifies the Church throughout the whole world, which consists of four parts and is spread everywhere, equally distributed among all its parts—that is, in concord.

“The tunic, for which they cast lots,” signifies the unity of all the parts, which is held together by the bond of love.

“Lots.” God’s grace is commended through the casting of lots. In this way it comes to everyone in the one garment when the lot pleases all, because God’s grace also comes to everyone in unity. When the lot is cast, the matter is entrusted not to anyone’s person or merits but to the hidden judgment of God.

### Verse 35

“He saved others.” They condemn themselves by their own statement, since, even unwillingly, they confess that he saved others. He could indeed have saved himself, but because Christ was God’s chosen one, he did not wish to descend from the cross. For he came in order to be crucified for us, and therefore neglected to save himself from the cross, because by dying he sought to save, along with the other sinners, even those who crucified him.

### Verse 36

“The soldiers also mocked him,” etc. Notice that the Jews mock the title “Christ” and “Son of God,” which had been handed down to them by the authority of Scripture. The soldiers, ignorant of the Scriptures, insult not God’s chosen Christ but the King of the Jews.

“And offering him vinegar.” The Jews were vinegar, degenerating from the wine of the patriarchs. With this vinegar the soldiers give drink to the Lord, whom they hand over to death at the Jews’ instigation.

### Verse 38

“There was also,” etc. These three languages stood out above the others: Hebrew, because of the Jews who gloried in the Law; Greek, because of the wisdom of the Gentiles; Latin, because of the Romans who ruled.

Therefore, whether they wish it or not, every kingdom of the world, all worldly wisdom, and all the mysteries of the divine Law testify that Jesus is the ruler of believers and confessors.

“This is the King of the Jews.” The inscription that bears witness that Christ is king is placed not below but above the cross. Although on the cross he suffered in the weakness of a human being, above the cross he shone with the majesty of a king. Therefore, after he had been sacrificed, the inscription was placed above him so that it might be evident to all who wished to read—that is, to believe—that through the cross he did not lose but strengthened his dominion.

### Verse 40

“He rebuked him.” This rebuke also reveals the future scandal of the cross among believers, some of whom are on the right and others on the left.

### Verse 42

“Lord, remember me.” Great grace shines forth in this robber. He has no limb free from punishment except his heart and tongue, and he offers everything that remains free. He believes with his heart and confesses with his mouth.

He had faith, since he believed that the one whom he saw dying with him would reign. He had hope, since he asked for entrance. He firmly held charity, since he both rebuked the robber for his wickedness and proclaimed to him the life he had come to know.

Great is his virtue: he confesses the one whom he sees dying in human weakness, the one whom the apostles had denied, the one whom they had seen performing miracles by divine power.

### Verse 43

“Amen, I say to you.” This is a most beautiful example for aspiring to conversion: forgiveness is granted to the robber so quickly, and grace is more abundant than the prayer. For the Lord always gives more than is requested. The robber said, “Remember me,” etc.; the Lord said, “Today you will be with me,” etc. The Lord forgives quickly because the robber converts quickly.

### Verse 44

“And darkness came,” etc. The sun withdrew its rays, either so that it might not look upon the hanging Lord or so that the impious, while blaspheming, might not enjoy its light.

Notice that he is crucified at the sixth hour—that is, when the sun was about to withdraw from the center of the world—and rises at dawn, when the sun rises, because “he died for our sins and rose for our justification” (Romans XVIII).

After Adam sinned in the afternoon, when the light of faith had begun to decline, the voice of the Lord was heard. At the same hour, therefore, at which the Lord had then closed paradise to the sinning Adam, he now opens it to the repentant robber.

### Verses 45–46

“The veil of the temple,” etc. This happened as the Lord expired, but Luke anticipates it because he wishes to join the miracle of the sun to the miracle of the veil.

The veil is torn so that the ark of the covenant and all the mysteries of the Law that had been covered may appear and pass over to the Gentiles.

Josephus says that the angelic powers who had formerly guarded the temple then cried out together: “Let us flee from these dwellings.”

“Father,” etc. By invoking the Father, he declares himself to be the Son of God. By commending his spirit, he indicates not a failure of power but his assurance, together with a share in that same power. For he loves to give glory to the Father, instructing us in this to give glory to the Creator.

### Verse 47

“Now when the centurion saw.” Seeing that he possessed such power as to send forth his spirit—a power possessed only by the creator of souls—the very man who had crucified him, amid the scandal of the passion itself, confesses him to be the Son of God, while the Jews refused to believe after so many miracles.

Thus the centurion signifies the faith of the Church. When the veil of the heavenly mysteries has been opened through the Lord’s death, the Church immediately confirms him as righteous and the Son of God, while the Synagogue remains silent.

### Verse 48

“Beating their breasts.” Their beating of their breasts as a sign of repentance and mourning can be understood in two ways. Either they were grieving because the one whose life they had loved had been unjustly killed, or they trembled because they remembered that they had brought about the death of one who, in death, had been glorified even more.

Whatever cause compelled them to beat their breasts, let us observe the difference between nation and nation. The Gentiles, fearing God as the Lord died, glorify him with the voice of open confession. The Jews, merely beating their breasts, return home in silence.

### Verse 50

“Named Joseph.” Joseph is worthy, through the nobility of secular power, to receive the body, and through the justice of his merits, to bury it.

### Verse 52

“This man approached,” etc. It is not the apostles but Joseph, a just and steadfast man, and Nicodemus, in whom there was no deceit, who bury him. Such too is the burial of Christ: it contains no fraud or wickedness, and by it the Jews’ evasiveness is blocked. For if the apostles had buried him, they would have said that the one whom they claimed had been stolen had not been buried.

### Verse 53

“In a linen cloth.” From the simple burial of the Lord, the ambition of the rich is condemned, since they cannot be without riches even when dead.

Mystically: He who receives Jesus with a pure mind wraps him in a clean linen cloth. Hence the Church also has the custom of celebrating the altar’s sacrifice not in silk or dyed cloth but in pure linen.

“And he laid him.” Christ is therefore rightly placed in the tomb of a righteous man, so that the Son of Man might have a place to rest his head and might rest in the dwelling of righteousness. He is rightly placed in a new tomb, so that whoever receives Christ may walk in newness of life. No one buries Christ except one who believes in Christ.

“In a hewn tomb.” The Lord alone is enclosed in the tomb, so that his burial and resurrection may be shown to differ from the frailty of our nature. He was buried, but for as long as he wished; he rose, but when he wished.

“Where no one had yet been laid.” If he had been placed in a tomb where someone else had been laid, it might be claimed that someone else had risen.

“In a tomb hewn from rock.” This was so that, if it had been built from many stones, he might be said to have been carried away by removing the foundations of the tomb.

### Verse 54

“And it was the day of preparation,” etc. Humanity was made on the sixth day, and God rested on the Sabbath. Therefore, crucified on the sixth day, he fulfilled the hidden meaning of the day of preparation. Resting in the tomb on the Sabbath, he awaited the event of the resurrection.

Thus we must suffer for the Lord in the sixth age of the world. In the seventh age—that is, when we die—the body remains in the tomb and the soul with the Lord in rest after its works, until the bodies rise in the eighth age.

### Verse 55

“The women.” While others who had observed these things concerning Jesus departed after the body had been laid down, only the women, who loved him more closely, attended to the funeral service so that they might offer the ministry of their devotion at the proper time. They waited for what Jesus had promised, and therefore they were the first to see him.

### Verse 56

“And returning.” After inspecting the Lord’s burial, they returned and prepared spices and ointments. Having read, heard, and remembered the Lord’s passion, they turn themselves toward works of virtue that please Christ, and they keep silence on the Sabbath.

After the Sabbath, they are to come to the Lord with their gifts. When the preparation of the present life has ended, they joyfully await the time of resurrection in blessed rest, when they will meet Christ with the fragrant spices of their deeds.

“And on the Sabbath,” etc. It had been commanded that the silence of the Sabbath be observed from evening to evening. Therefore, after the Lord had been buried, the women occupied themselves with preparing ointments for as long as work was permitted, from the day of preparation until sunset. When the Sabbath had passed and the sun had set, they came in the morning to anoint him, since on the evening of the Sabbath, with night already approaching, they could not go to the tomb.

## Chapter XXIV

### Verse 1

“On the first day of the week,” etc. “One of the Sabbath” means the same as “the first day of the Sabbath,” that is, one day counted from the day of the Sabbath or Sabbaths; this day is now called the Lord’s Day.

The fact that the women came to the tomb very early shows the great ardor of their love in seeking and finding the Lord.

Mystically: An example is given so that, with faith illuminated and the darkness of vices dispelled, we may approach the sacred body of the Lord. The tomb is a figure of the altar, on which the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood is celebrated. The spices they bring signify the fragrance of virtues and the sweetness of prayers with which we ought to approach the altar.

### Verse 2

“The stone rolled away.” The rolling away of the stone signifies the opening of Christ’s mysteries, which had been covered by the veil of the letter. The Law was written on stone; when its covering is removed, the Lord’s dead body is not found, but the living one is proclaimed, because “even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, now we know him no longer” (II Corinthians V).

He could leave the tomb while it was closed, just as he came forth from the womb while it was closed.

### Verse 4

“Perplexed in mind.” They were troubled in mind because they were astonished that a stone of immense size had been rolled away, and they grieved that the body, so worthy of reverence, had not been found.

Just as, when the Lord was tempted in the wilderness, the angels ministered to him after his victory had been completed, so now, after death had been conquered, the angels came. They announce the glory of the triumphant one not only by their words but also by their shining appearance.

And just as they stood by the body in the tomb, so they also stand daily by the consecrated body on the altar.

### Verse 5

“They lowered their faces.” Notice that neither the holy women are said to have fallen to the ground nor any of the saints at the Lord’s resurrection to have prostrated themselves on the ground in worship. Hence the custom arose in the Church of not kneeling in prayer during the Easter season, but of praying with the face inclined toward the ground.

### Verse 6

“Remember.” As we learn from this passage, while still among the disciples the Lord foretold even to the women who followed him that he would rise on the third day. He expired at the ninth hour on the day of preparation and rose in the morning of the first day of the week.

It is fitting that he lay in the tomb for one day and two nights, because he joined the light of his single death—which was only in the flesh—to the darkness of our double death, which was in both body and soul, and healed both aspects of our condition. For if he had taken upon himself both deaths, he would have freed us from neither.

### Verse 8

“And they remembered.” Just as the women standing at the Lord’s tomb remembered the words that he had spoken beforehand about his dispensation, so we, while celebrating the mysteries of the Lord’s passion, must remember not only the passion but also the resurrection.

### Verse 9

“They announced it.” Just as at the beginning a woman was the author of guilt for a man, and a man the executor of the error, so now the woman who had first tasted death saw the resurrection. So that she might not bear among men the disgrace of perpetual guilt, she who had transmitted guilt to the man also transmitted grace.

And because the inferior sex is not considered strong enough for the steadfast proclamation of the Gospel, the ministry of evangelizing is entrusted to men.

### Verse 11

“And they did not believe them.” The disciples’ slowness to believe was not so much their weakness as the foundation of our future firmness. While they doubted, the resurrection was shown by many proofs. When we recognize these as we read, what else happens but that we are strengthened by their doubt?

### Verse 12

“But Peter, rising.” John records that he and Peter ran together, and that when Peter entered the tomb and saw the linen cloths and the sudarium, John, bending down, saw the linen cloths but did not enter.

It must be understood that Peter first stooped down and saw what Luke records and John passes over in silence. Then he entered, so that he might inspect the interior more carefully, though he entered before John.

### Verse 13

“Named Emmaus.” Emmaus is the distinguished metropolitan city of Palestine. After the conquest of Judaea under the emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, it was restored, and when its status changed, its name also changed.

### Verses 15–16

“While they were talking.” As they spoke about him, the Lord approached and accompanied them, both to kindle belief in the resurrection in their minds and to fulfill what he had promised to do: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matthew XXVIII).

“Approaching,” etc. “Their eyes,” etc. He appeared indeed in his own form, but he did not show them the form by which they would recognize him. Just as they loved him inwardly and yet doubted, so he was present outwardly but did not reveal who he was.

To those speaking about him he offers his presence, but to those doubting about him he removes the appearance by which he could be recognized.

### Verses 18–20

“Are you the only stranger,” etc. “To whom,” etc. They suppose that he is a stranger because they do not recognize him. And truly he was a stranger to them: by the glory of the resurrection he already stood far removed from their frailty, and, since they did not know the resurrection, he remained foreign to their faith.

“A prophet, mighty in deed,” etc. “And how they handed him over,” etc. They acknowledge him as a prophet and a great man, but remain silent about the Son of God, either because they do not yet believe perfectly or because, if they do believe, they fear that they will be handed over into the hands of the Jews, not knowing with whom they are speaking.

### Verse 21

“But we had hoped,” etc. In a certain way they reproach themselves for having hoped for redemption through the one whom they had seen dead and did not believe would rise. They grieve especially that the one whom they knew to be innocent had been killed without guilt, and for this reason they walked sadly.

### Verse 22

“They terrified us,” etc. They are rightly said to have terrified them, because, by reporting that the body had not been found, they added more sorrow than they brought joy through announcing the resurrection by which they might have been comforted.

### Verse 24

“Some of our people went,” etc. Since he had said above that Peter ran to the tomb, but now Cleopas says, “Some of our people went to the tomb,” etc., it must be understood that the two went together. He mentioned Peter alone at first because Mary first announced the matter to him.

### Verse 25

“O foolish ones and slow of heart.” A twofold necessity of humiliation presses upon us: we are neither instructed in the Scriptures as much as we ought to be nor attentive enough to fulfill what we know.

For if Moses and the Prophets spoke about Christ and foretold that he would enter through suffering and glory, how can one glory in being a Christian who neither investigates in the Scriptures how things pertain to Christ nor desires to attain through sufferings the glory he wishes to possess with Christ?

### Verses 28–29

“And he himself,” etc. “Remain with us,” etc. He presented himself bodily as he was in their minds. They were being tested to see whether they would love him whom they did not yet love as God at least as a stranger.

But those with whom the truth was walking cannot be strangers to glory. They invite him into the lodging—or rather, they compel him. From this example it is gathered that strangers are not only to be invited into lodging but also drawn in.

### Verse 30

“He broke,” etc. They did not recognize him in the exposition of Scripture, but they recognized him in the breaking of bread, because it is not hearers of the Law but doers who will be justified, and the truth is understood better by doing than by hearing.

### Verse 31

“Their eyes were opened,” etc. The appearance of weakness is withdrawn from bodily eyes, so that the glory of the resurrection may begin to appear to their minds.

### Verse 32

“And they said,” etc. Mystically: Another appearance was shown to them in Christ so that they would recognize him only in the breaking of bread, so that all might understand that they do not recognize Christ unless they become participants in his body—that is, in the Church. The Apostle commends the unity of the Church in the sacrament of bread when he says: “One bread, one body are we, though many” (I Corinthians X).

Therefore, when he offers the blessed bread, their eyes are opened so that they recognize him, and the obstacle that Satan had placed in their eyes so that Jesus would not be recognized is removed. The Lord permits this obstacle to remain until they come to the sacrament of bread. But once they have shared in the unity of the body, the enemy’s obstacle is taken away, so that Christ can be recognized.

“Burning.” (Gregory.) After hearing his words, the heart that had previously been cold with the numbness of unbelief and fear was kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that it now burns with heavenly desire and stretches itself toward believing the truth. As many commands as a person receives, so many torches, as it were, set him aflame.

### Verse 34

“The Lord has risen.” The report that Jesus had risen had already been made by the women, and he had appeared to Simon Peter; these two found the disciples discussing these things. But they too had previously heard that he had risen and were afraid to say on the road when the women had reported only that angels had been seen.

Since they did not know the one with whom they were speaking, they could fear that they might fall into the hands of the Jews if they openly said anything about Christ’s resurrection.

### Verse 36

“Jesus stood among them,” etc. This is the appearance of which John speaks (John XX): “When it was evening on that day,” etc., and he said to them, “Peace be with you.”

Although John says that Thomas was not with them, while Luke says that these two found the eleven gathered together, together with those who were with them, it must be understood that Thomas had gone out before the Lord appeared to them while they were speaking these things.

### Verses 37–38

“To see a spirit.” “And he said to them.” The disciples knew that he had been a true human being, but after he died they did not believe that true flesh could rise from the tomb on the third day. Therefore they thought they were seeing the spirit that he had released in his passion, but the Lord removes this error.

“Why are you troubled?” (Ambrose.) The apostles believed, but nevertheless were troubled, etc., up to the point where the Lord unexpectedly entered through closed doors with his body.

“Thoughts,” etc. These thoughts are not descending from above but rising in the heart like bad weeds. I demand the faith that I planted in you; I condemn what has arisen from you if the resurrection is not true, for then the fruit of the passion is lost.

### Verse 39

“Touch me and see.” By many proofs he persuades them of the resurrection, offering himself to be seen by their eyes and handled by their hands. By allowing them to touch him and showing his bones and flesh, he signifies the condition of his resurrection and of ours: in it our body will be subtle through the effect of spiritual power and tangible through the reality of its nature.

After the resurrection the Lord displays two apparently contrary qualities in his body: it is tangible and of the same nature, so that he may form us in faith, and incorruptible and possessed of another glory, so that he may invite us to the reward.

### Verse 40

**He showed them his hands, etc.** He did this so that, by displaying the scar of his wounds, he might heal the wound of unbelief. These [Col. 0354A] scars he preserved then and will preserve at the judgment. First, to establish faith in the resurrection; then, as he intercedes for us with the Father, to show forever what kind of death he endured for humanity; third, to indicate to those redeemed by his death how mercifully they were helped, by presenting the proofs of that same death. Finally, he preserved the scar he received from them so that at the judgment he might declare how justly the wicked are condemned. He did not therefore preserve the scars because he lacked the power to heal them, but so that he might carry forever the triumph of his victory.

### Verse 41

**Do you have anything here?** To make the truth of the resurrection evident, he wished not only to be touched but also to eat with them—not because either he or we ought to require food after the resurrection, but to manifest that he was a body [Col. 0354B] and not a spirit. He ate by power, not by necessity. In one way thirsty earth absorbs water; in another way a hot ray of the sun does so: the former through need, the latter through power.

### Verse 42

**A piece of broiled fish.** The broiled fish is himself, the suffering Mediator, caught in the waters of the human race by the snare of death and roasted in the time of his passion. In the resurrection he is also the honeycomb for us: the honeycomb in wax, that is, divinity in humanity. His eating of this honey signifies that he receives into his body for eternal rest those who, while experiencing tribulations for God, do not depart from the love of inward sweetness. Those who are roasted here will there be satisfied with true sweetness.

### Verse 43

**And when he had eaten.** He removes every ambiguity [Col. 0354C]: he was seen, he was touched, he ate. And lest he seem in any respect to have deceived the human senses, he turns to the Scriptures, so that even if, as the pagans say, he might appear to have been able to do what he wished by magical arts, at least they might see that he could not have prophesied before he was born.

### Verse 45

**Then he opened.** After being seen, after being touched, and after the law had been recalled, he opened their understanding so that they might understand what they saw and read. Then, after commending the truth of his body, he commended the unity of the Church: **“And that it be preached in his name.”**

### Verse 46

**It was necessary, etc.** It was necessary that the ministers who were to preach repentance and forgiveness [Col. 0354D] to all the nations should begin from Jerusalem. This was so not only because the utterances of God had been entrusted to them, and because theirs are the adoption of sons, the glory, the covenants, and the giving of the law; but also so that the nations, entangled in various errors and crimes, might be summoned to hope for pardon by this greatest indication of divine compassion: that he grants forgiveness to those who crucified the Son of God.

### Verse 49

**But you remain seated.** After he had fully instructed the disciples concerning the power of preaching, although he could have strengthened them suddenly if he had wished, he delayed, saying: **“But you remain seated.”** He did this to provide an example for those who would follow, so that the imperfect might not presume to preach before the proper time. One remains seated in the city when one confines oneself within the enclosures of the mind, lest one wander outward through speech; then, when one has been perfectly clothed [Col. 0355A] with divine power, one goes forth, as it were, from oneself, instructing others.

### Verse 50

**But he led them out.** Passing over in silence everything that had taken place during the forty days, he quietly joins the final event of the day of the resurrection, when he ascended into heaven, to the first day. And fittingly, when he is about to bless the disciples, he leads them out to Bethany, which means “house of obedience,” because the one who descended on account of the disobedience of the perverse ascended on account of the obedience of those who were converted.

### Verse 53

**In the temple.** He did this so that, in the place of prayer, amid devotions of praise, they might await the promised coming of the Holy Spirit with hearts prepared in every respect. Thus [Col. 0356A], after celebrating in Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of peace—the solemn observances of the passion and resurrection, let us, with the Lord as our guide, seek Bethany, so that with a peaceful mind we may be imbued with the sacraments of his body and blood and take care to be a house of obedience.

**Praising and blessing.** Luke, who undertook to expound Christ’s priesthood more fully than the others, and who therefore began his Gospel with the ministry of the temple through the priesthood of Zechariah, fittingly completed it with devotion in the temple. There he concludes with the apostles, who were to become ministers—that is, ministers of the new priesthood—not in the blood of victims but in the praise of God and in blessing.

[Col. 0355]

# THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN (G)*

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0355B]

Among all the pages of divine Scripture, the Gospel excels, because what the law and the prophets foretold as future, the Gospel declares to have been fulfilled. Among the writers of the Gospels, however, John stands out for the depth of the divine mysteries. From the time of the Lord’s Ascension, he preached the word of God for sixty-five years without the aid of writing, up to the final years of Domitian. But after Domitian was killed, when, with Nerva’s permission, he had returned from exile to Ephesus, he was compelled by the bishops of Asia to write against the heretics concerning the co-eternal divinity of Christ with the Father. These heretics had invaded his churches while he was absent and denied that Christ existed before Mary.

Hence, in the figure of the four living creatures, he is rightly compared to a flying eagle, [Col. 0355C] which flies higher than the other animals and gazes upon the rays of the sun with unblinking eyes. The other evangelists, who sufficiently expound Christ’s temporal birth and the temporal deeds he performed in humanity, and who said little about his divinity, walk with the Lord on earth like walking animals. But this evangelist, expounding little about his temporal deeds while contemplating the power of his divinity more sublimely, flies with the Lord toward heaven.

For he who reclined upon the Lord’s breast at the supper drank, more excellently than the others, a draught of heavenly wisdom from the fountain of the Lord’s breast itself. He had indeed read the Gospels of the three evangelists and approved their faith and truth. In them he saw that some history of the deeds was lacking, especially those things the Lord did at the beginning of his preaching, namely, before John the Baptist was shut up in prison. Therefore, as if those matters had been left aside by the others, John writes what Jesus did before John was handed over, but he took particular care to commend the divinity of Christ and the mystery of the Trinity.

For the other three evangelists, following more fully the Lord’s temporal words and deeds, which are especially useful for forming the conduct of the present life, devoted themselves to the active life. In that life one labors so that the heart may be cleansed for seeing God. John, however, relates few of the Lord’s deeds, but records more carefully the Lord’s words [Col. 0356B] that reveal the unity of the Trinity and the blessedness of eternal life. Thus he directed his intention and preaching toward commending the virtue of the contemplative life, in which one is free for the purpose of seeing God.

This is that John whom the Lord called from the stormy, wave-tossed tempest of marriage and to whom he entrusted his virgin mother to a virgin.

## CHAPTER ONE

### Verse 1

**In the beginning was the Word.** Against those who, on account of Christ’s temporal birth, said that Christ had not always existed, he begins by speaking of the eternity of the Word: **“In the beginning was the Word.”**

### Verse 3

**All things were made through him.** (AUG.) The one through whom every creature was made is not a creature, etc., [Col. 0356C] up to the point where all agree concerning the power of the divinity.

**And without him nothing was made.** (ORIG.) He distinguishes it in this way: **“And without him nothing was made.”** The order is: “There is nothing that was made without him.”

### Verse 4

**What was made was life in him.** (AUG.) John Chrysostom: **“And without him nothing was made. What was made.”** Hilary: **“Without him nothing was made that was made in him.”**

### Verse 6

**There was a man sent.** After ascending in sublime flight beyond all nature to the heights of theology, because he had contemplated that the Word had always been with the Father, he immediately descends to the lowliness of human nature, and especially to the forerunner of the Word, against those who said that human nature had been entirely lost and reduced to nothing [Col. 0356D] in its first parent.

**A man sent.** A man, not an angel, as the heretics maintain, sent by God. Therefore he was able to speak of God.

### Verse 9

**He was the true light.** Every human being is said to be that nature in humanity which was made according to the image and likeness of God. Everything else that exists in a human being consists of the lower parts of humanity and is, in a certain sense, outside the human being. In that nature—namely, in the soul, as though in a higher world—the true light shines, and it illuminates those who come into that world [Col. 0357A] and are reborn through grace, because those whose life and conduct are in heaven are, as it were, in another world.

### Verse 11

**And his own did not receive him.** From the beginning of the world there was no time in which there were not people who received the divine Word. Hence he adds: **“But as many as received him.”**

### Verse 12

**To become children of God.** What marvelous power: those who were sons of the devil are called, through him who liberated them, sons of God and brothers of Christ. The order by which they become sons of God, and how this generation differs from carnal generation, is then added: **“Who were born not of blood.”**

### Verse 14

**And the Word became flesh.** So that we may confidently believe that human beings are born from God, he adds that God was born from a human being. Through this assumption of weakness our weakness is healed, so that we may become children of God. [Col. 0357B] This is what is meant by: **“And the Word became flesh.”** What was above descended below. Why should it be surprising if what was below ascended into what is above? Nor is it surprising that human beings are born from God, since God was born from a human being.

**Full of grace and truth.** The man Christ was full of grace because, without any preceding merits, from the moment he was conceived, the divinity in him filled that man with every overflowing fullness, for the benefit of all the saints. Hence his mother is called not only the mother of a man but also the mother of God. Nor is it surprising that he is called man and also God, since God is also called man. This grace is called both grace and truth because it was formerly promised and has now been manifested—namely, that God should be in humanity, filling him with every good thing, and through him filling his own people.

[Col. 0357C]

### Verse 15

**This was he of whom I said.** The demonstrative pronoun indicates that Christ was present in that place. For the Lord himself often used to come to John while he was still unknown, before he had been baptized and begun to preach.

**He who will come after me.** He who was born after me, who would preach after me, baptize after me, and die after me. This does not mean that he had not already been born when John said these things, since he had also been baptized; rather, he was to come in preaching and in death, though not in the resurrection.

**He was made before me, because he was before me.** From the Greek: “He was made in front of me,” that is, “He appeared to me,” namely because he was before me.

### Verse 16

**And from his fullness.** After setting out the testimony of the forerunner, the evangelist returns to the testimony [Col. 0357D] of his own assertion. It is as though he said: “The Word became flesh; we saw his glory, full of grace and truth, and from his fullness we have all received.” We received grace so that we might believe in him, and truth by which we might understand him.

**We have received.** (AUG.) Not only grace, which is plainly given freely and not according to merit, such as faith working through love, by which the righteous live; but, in addition to this, grace—that is, eternal blessedness, which is called both the reward of righteousness and grace, because merit itself comes from grace.

**Grace for grace.** Grace is given in the conception of what is good through grace. Grace in the strict sense, which is not given on account of merit, is granted first; if afterward we work with it and become accustomed to good works, then grace is given in return for the earlier grace.

[Col. 0358A]

### Verse 17

**Through Moses.** Through Moses, the servant, came the foretelling; through the Lord Jesus came the fulfillment of salvation.

### Verse 18

**No one has ever seen God.** That is, no pure human being living in this body has seen God as he is. Hence it was said to Moses: **“No man shall see me and live”** (Exod. XXXIII), that is, no one living in a body shall see my divinity.

For this reason God added to Moses: **“Stand in the cleft of the rock, and when I pass by you shall see my back”** (ibid.). The rock is Christ; the cleft is the gallows of the cross; “when I pass by” means “when I pass from the world to the Father.” The “back” signifies his birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension, through which, by faith, we reach his blessedness and vision.

When we read that God appeared to human beings, whether visibly to bodily eyes [Col. 0358B] or invisibly in prophetic visions through a created medium, we must understand that the visions of the prophets were made through a certain spiritual creature, by which they are said to have seen God.

**The only-begotten Son, etc.** He briefly adds what the fullness of grace and truth is: namely, knowledge of the Trinity itself. Hence: **“This is eternal life, that they know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.”** This knowledge is not complete in the present life, because no one in the flesh has seen God as he is.

Therefore even Moses, although grace had not yet been given through him, said after all that he had seen, in the figure of God: **“Show me yourself”** (Exod. XXXIII). But the Son, who is in the Father’s secret presence, narrated him, because **“no one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him”** (Luke X). He explains to his own people what must be believed concerning the Trinity of the Godhead, how one must reach it, and he leads them into it.

### Verse 19

**And this.** This testimony and the other testimonies that follow are John’s [Col. 0358C], given after Christ had been baptized, when Jesus was already coming to invite the disciples whom John, through his testimonies, sends to him.

This testimony is given against the idea that Christ was hidden: hidden because he was humble, humble so that he could be despised and killed, in order to redeem the world.

**Who are you?** The Jews thought that John was the Christ who had been promised in the law. Others thought that he was Elijah, because of his extreme abstinence and chastity, his solitary life, his exceptionally severe rebuke of sins, and his harsh terror concerning future vengeance. Others said that he was one of the prophets [Col. 0358D] raised from the dead, because of the gift of prophecy.

### Verse 20

**He confessed.** He confessed, as he says afterward, not that he was the Christ. He did not deny what he was—that is, that he was the forerunner—as he says when questioned later: **“I am the voice of one crying.”** The order of the words is: “He confessed and did not deny,” when they sent to him.

### Verse 21

**Are you Elijah?** Since everyone knew the name of Christ, they also knew that Elijah would precede him. But Elijah was to precede the one who would judge in power, while John was figuratively Elijah, preceding the one who was to be judged. Thus there are two heralds, corresponding to his two advents.

Hence: **“I am not Elijah,”** that is, “I am not the herald who points to his power”; rather, I show the humility [Col. 0359A] over which you stumble, as though saying: “Serve the humble one before the exalted one judges.” Behold, I am neither the Christ nor the judge in respect of power.

### Verse 23

**I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness.** He does not say, “I am a man,” or “John,” or “the son of Zechariah.” He does not consider human substance or descent; rather, having been exalted beyond all these things as the forerunner of the Word, he leaves behind everything contained within the world. He ascends on high, having become the voice of the Word, and confesses no substance in himself except the abundance of grace by which he surpasses every creature, so that he may be the voice of the Word.

The voice is the interpreter of the mind; the mind—that is, the understanding of all things—is the Son of God. John, therefore, is the voice and interpreter of this mind, because he first showed him to the world: **“Behold, the Lamb of God.”**

Isaiah prophesied this concerning [Col. 0359B] John: **“I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness,”** in which the Word resounds—that is, prophecy, manifestation, and the lamp of the present Word.

### Verse 24

**From the Pharisees.** That is, from the leaders of the Jews, who do not seek instruction but envy. Nevertheless, they come to John because they hear that he preached the common resurrection of all, which they too believed; hence they also agree with Christ in many matters. They likewise listened to the apostle Paul in many things.

### Verse 25

**Why then do you baptize?** The Pharisees heard in the prophets that Christ would come and baptize. They knew that the Jordan had prefigured baptism, and that Elijah and Elisha had crossed it with dry feet. Nor did they doubt that a figure of baptism had [Col. 0359C] preceded them in Elijah and Elisha. Hence they thought that these men had now risen and baptized.

Therefore they do not ask, “Are you one of the prophets?” but simply, “Are you the prophet?”—namely, the one who prefigured baptism.

### Verse 26

**I baptize with water.** Let no one charge me with presumption for what I do, because I wash bodies with water but do not take away sins. Just as I am the forerunner by birth and preaching, so also I am the forerunner by baptizing. But this one, who takes away sins, stands among you.

### Verse 27

**Whose sandal I am not worthy, etc.** He does not say, “I am not worthy to unfasten.” He does unfasten it, since he revealed him and disclosed many things about both his divinity and his humanity. But he says, **“I am not worthy,”** because he considers himself unworthy to undertake such a task; in this the meaning is simply humility.

[Col. 0359D]

### Verse 28

**These things took place in Bethany.** There are two Bethanies: one beyond the Jordan and another near Jerusalem, where Lazarus was raised.

The Bethany beyond the Jordan signifies human nature under the natural law, before the streams of grace [Col. 0359D]. That grace became abundant after Christ’s incarnation. This nature had been created for obedience to the law of nature, and John baptizes in it because he does not free from sin. He baptizes beyond the streams of divine gifts, which had not yet begun in Christ to descend into human nature.

The Bethany on this side of the Jordan signifies the same human nature obedient under the law of grace. It is near Jerusalem—that is, near the vision of peace—through love [Col. 0360A]. In it Christ raises the dead, because he frees from sin.

### Verse 29

**The next day John saw Jesus.** Figuratively, John—that is, the people of grace—on the next day, meaning after the law, recognizes the Lamb by whom he is redeemed.

**Coming toward him, and he said.** He came not only in bodily steps but also through the approaches of inward contemplation, because he deigned to be recognized by John according to both his divinity and his humanity.

**Behold the Lamb of God, etc.** The Lamb provides three things to those who possess him: the milk of simple doctrine, by which little ones are nourished; wool, that is, the growth of virtues; and the food of his flesh.

**The sin of the world.** The sin of the world is called original sin, which is common to the whole world. Through it the entire human nature, created all at once and as one, transgressed the divine laws through disobedience [Col. 0360B] in paradise. Grace removes this original sin, as well as each additional sin.

### Verse 30

**A man comes after me.** Christ is a man in whom he is like us and paid the debt on our behalf; he is the Son of God in whom he is like the Father and reconciles us to him by forgiving sins.

### Verse 31

**That he might be revealed.** This is the Lamb who takes away sins—not I, although I now know him better. For this reason I baptize, so that he may be revealed to Israel. Otherwise, because of arrogance, they might be baptized by Christ less readily. By the practice of baptizing he prepared the way for him. Hence, after they have come to him who is the way, his baptism ceases.

In John’s baptism the humility of Christ is also revealed, and this humility is the fulfillment of all righteousness. For just as it is necessary for Christ [Col. 0360C] to be born and to die, so also it is necessary for him to be baptized. If he who has no need is baptized by a servant, then however wise and holy they may be, let no one disdain to be baptized by the Lord, without whom they remain in sins.

**Baptizing.** Christ is baptized by John so that all humility, which is the whole of righteousness, may be indicated. But he is not baptized by John alone, lest John’s baptism appear holier and greater than Christ’s baptism, in which God as man was baptized, while in Christ’s baptism human beings are baptized. Others are baptized by John so that the practice of baptizing may prepare the way for Christ’s baptism.

### Verse 32

**And testimony.** Just as John said that he had come to reveal Christ, so he bore witness, namely, that he had seen the Spirit. Through this he learned what he had not previously known. He had also come to preach repentance [Col. 0360D]—that is, to prepare for Christ’s preaching—but he mentions only the preparation of baptism in particular because Christ’s baptism is the supreme sacrament among the others.

**The Spirit descending.** This does not mean that the Spirit descended for the first time then, but that through this descent it might be shown that he remains in those baptized with water and not otherwise, and that John might understand Christ more excellently through him.

### Verse 33

**And I did not know him.** (AUG.) Having seen the dove, John says that through it he learned what he had not previously known, etc., up to the point where the Apostle says: “They differ in labor and intention, but are not different in operation.”

(HIER.) He shows that John did not know through Christ’s baptism—that is, he did not know that the world had been redeemed. For he knew [Col. 0361A] that Christ was the Son of God and had been born in the flesh.

Augustine says that John was ignorant only of this: whether Christ retained the power to baptize for himself or would bestow it on one of his own.

**And remaining.** (AUG.) Spiritually, the Spirit is said to remain in Christ because he never departed from him through sin; in Christ he always lived and acted wondrously. He comes upon the saints and departs through sins. Yet he always remains in them for some purpose, as Christ promised them—namely, so that they may always devote themselves to good things.

He does not remain in them for every purpose, namely, so that they might prophesy through him or perform miracles. Therefore what John says here is the first sign by which Christ is recognized.
