**Who baptizes.** Christ baptizes in the Spirit, not only by forgiving sins in water, but also afterward by cleansing, kindling love, and filling people with gifts.

[Col. 0361B]

**This is the Son of God.** Here John bears witness to the Son of God whom earlier he had called a man, so that testimony might be given to both natures.

### Verse 35

**The next day John was standing again.** Figuratively, John stands and the law ceases, yet he continues to bear witness to Christ. Jesus walks—that is, grace gathers people from every direction.

### Verse 37

**They followed Jesus.** They followed him so that from then on they might listen to him rather than to John, though they did not yet adhere to him completely. They followed in order to see where he lived, so that they might come to him continually and be instructed by him. Later they followed him perfectly, when he called them from the boat. Two followed, because those who follow must be inflamed with a twofold love.

### Verse 38

**Turning around.** They had seen him, as it were, from behind, but [Col. 0361C] he presented his face to them when he descended from majesty so that he could be seen, displaying the light of the Gospel in place of the shadow of the law.

**What are you seeking?** He asks not because he is ignorant, but so that those who answer may receive a reward. They ask about the matter, not the person—“what,” not “whom”—lest he appear to point to himself; they answer him concerning the person.

**Where are you staying?** Mystically, they wish to be shown in whom Christ dwells, so that they may conform themselves to him. Or, seeing the incarnation, they devoutly ask to be shown how the eternal dwelling is with the Father.

### Verse 39

**Come.** As though it could not be explained in speech but must be demonstrated by action: come by believing and doing, and you will understand; come through John’s testimony and depart from the law, and you will receive grace.

**That day.** He indicates the New Testament, or the present life.

**It was about the tenth [Col. 0361D] hour.** Because they had come from the law, the Decalogue sent them to Christ. At the tenth hour they seek to be taught by him, because no one teaches the law except the one who gave it. He teaches with mercy, and the things they were unable to fulfill are fulfilled. Alternatively, the tenth hour signifies the evening of the world.

### Verse 40

**The brother of Simon Peter, one of the two who had heard John and followed him.** The younger brother by birth believes first [Col. 0362A]; the order of faith is not meaningless. Perhaps Andrew is called Peter’s brother in relation to dignity, because the Church was to be founded upon Peter—that is, upon his faith.

### Verse 41

**He first found.** True piety immediately announces the treasure it has found to a brother, so that he may be a brother in faith just as he is by blood.

**We have found the Messiah, etc.** “Christ” in Greek, “Messiah” in Hebrew, “Anointed” in Latin. For he truly was anointed by the Holy Spirit in a special way, and from this anointing Christians receive their name.

After his vision Jacob raised the stone as a monument and anointed it by pouring oil over it. Through that stone, the future rock—namely Christ—he already understood figuratively, by divine inspiration, that Christ would be anointed by the Holy Spirit. In that rock he prefigured that the Church would be founded, etc.

### Verse 42

**You are Simon, son of.** He first gives the name he has from his parents, so that the change may be signified when he calls Simon “Peter.” In the change the vitality of the mystery is indicated, but the former name is not without significance. Simon means “obedient,” “son of grace,” or “dove,” when he comes to Jesus, following his brother [Col. 0362B]. Hence, from the rock Christ, he is called Peter: weak in him, in the figure of the Church founded upon the rock.

**You are Simon.** (CHRYS.) He changed his name to show that he himself is the one who gave the Old Testament and changed names, because he called Abram Abraham, Sarai Sarah, and Jacob Israel. Thus he imposed names on many from birth, such as Isaac and Samson; on others, after the naming they received from their ancestors, such as Peter and the sons of Zebedee. For those whose virtue was to shine from their earliest age received their names at that time; but for those whose virtue was to increase later, the naming was given later.

**Son of Joanna, etc.** “Jona” and “Joanna” are used indifferently. “Jona” is interpreted as “dove,” and “Joanna” as “grace.”

[Col. 0362C]

### Verse 43

**Into Galilee, and he found Philip.** Galilee means “transmigration” or “revelation.” A human being migrates from vices to virtues and afterward from virtue to virtue, and thus revelation comes to him, so that he may see the God of gods in Zion.

Therefore, when he goes out into Galilee to call a disciple to follow—that is, to imitate—he indicates by the place itself that, just as he advanced in wisdom and entered into glory through sufferings, so should his followers.

### Verse 44

**From the city of Bethsaida.** The city is not named without reason, nor is it without reason said to be the city of Philip, Peter, and Andrew. Its name means “house of hunters,” which indicates the disposition and office of these men. They are hunters in capturing souls. Hence Philip, before he becomes an apostle, freely calls Nathanael.

[Col. 0362D]

### Verse 45

**Philip found, etc.** Nathanael, highly learned in the Scriptures, understands what others do not: that a unique Nazarene could come from Nazareth. But because he was extremely learned, he was not chosen as an apostle; for all the apostles were chosen first from among the unlearned, so that the wise might be confounded.

**Whom Moses wrote about.** Like a cautious hunter, he establishes the truth for his brother by many arguments, namely, that Jesus is the one foretold in the law and the prophets.

**The son of Joseph.** Joseph is of the house of David, so that through him—not because Jesus was born from him, but through Mary his mother, whom he knew from the prophets to have given birth as a virgin—the fact that Jesus is from David may be indicated.

### Verse 46

**And Nathanael said to him.** He either asks in doubt or makes an assertion as a learned interpreter of the law: could anything good, or an outstanding teacher, or the supreme Savior come from a city of such a name?

Nazareth is interpreted as “flower,” “bud of purity,” or “holiness.” The response fittingly follows both interpretations: **“Come and see,” etc.**

### Verse 47

**Behold, truly an Israelite.** “Deceit” means pretense. If he has sins, he confesses them. He does not therefore deny that he is a sinner, but praises his confession. The Pharisees, however, are deceitful: they proclaim themselves good although they are evil.

### Verse 48

**How do you know me?** Knowing that the Lord was speaking about his conscience, Nathanael does not ask out of indignation but with wonder: from where, and by what power, did he know him?

**I saw you under the fig tree.** (AUG.) Nathanael, whose name means “gift of God,” is the true people of Israel, the gift of God, who was hidden under the fig tree—that is, subjected to the habit of sinning and the shadow of death. The first parents likewise covered themselves with fig leaves. Nathanael had been seen and sought by the Lord before he saw and sought the Lord, and even before he was called through the apostles.

### Verse 49

**Rabbi, you are the Son of God.** Nathanael recognized that Christ, though absent, had seen what he himself had done elsewhere—namely, how and where he had been called by Philip. This is an indication of divinity. Therefore he confesses him not only as teacher but also as the Son of God and king of Israel—that is, Christ, in whom he is proved to be an Israelite, which means “one who sees God.”

### Verse 51

**You will see heaven opened.** Nathanael, the Israelite, is said to be going to see heaven opened and the angels of God descending and ascending, just as the patriarch Jacob formerly saw the ladder and the angels ascending and descending. Through a blessing he was called Israel.

**Angels of God.** This miracle often appeared: angels ascended and descended upon Christ.

**Upon the Son of Man.** Christ calls himself the Son of Man, affirming what is lesser—namely, humanity. Nathanael and Peter affirm the Son of God, which is greater—namely, divinity. Behold the confirmation of both natures in Christ.

Those who confess his divinity are worthy to ascend; the one who asserts his humanity bears witness that he came to redeem. He confirms that he is a man, lest some err by believing that he is only God, as Peter also did when he said: **“Far be it from you, Lord.”**

# CHAPTER TWO

[Col. 0363D]

### Verse 1

**And on the third day.** (AUG.) After Christ had been manifested through John’s testimonies, he manifested himself by a miracle.

**And on the day.** This signifies the third day, that is, the time of grace, after the time before the law and under the law, when Christ came in the flesh to the wedding of the Church.

### Verse 2

**And he was invited.** By this he shows that the marriage he made should not be despised, and he intimates the sacrament of marriage.

### Verse 3

**When it failed.** The wine fails so that, when wine is miraculously made from water, the power of the hidden divinity may appear.

(AUG.) Greater power is present in the creation and governance of heaven and earth, etc., up to the point where the power that also works in greater things is brought back to remembrance.

### Verse 4

**What is this to me?** (ID.) In these words he does not deny his mother, as the heretics say, etc., up to the point where he understands entry to God and drinks the wine.

### Verse 6

**Two or.** (ID.) This is the statement of one making an estimate, so that he might say that they were two and also three, etc., up to the point where they were disseminated through the three sons of Noah.

### Verse 7

**And they filled them.** The fact that the jars were filled at his command signifies that this Scripture too is from the Lord. But while Christ lies hidden in it under a veil—that is, under the covering of the letter—it tastes like insipid water. When the veil is removed, it is intoxicating wine.

He could indeed have filled empty vessels with wine, since he creates all things from nothing; but he preferred to make wine from water, to teach that he did not abolish the law but fulfilled it, and that in the Gospel he neither does nor teaches anything other than what prophecy foretold.

### Verse 9

**When the steward tasted.** The *triclinium*—that is, three rows of reclining guests, differing from one another in rank—signifies teachers, the continent, and the married. The master of the feast is some learned interpreter of the law who drinks the spiritual sense of the law.

Thus to open the spiritual sense in the Scriptures to the disciples is to change water into wine. When, after the resurrection, he opened their understanding, they understood the Scriptures.

**Water made wine.** Through the water, John’s baptism; through the wine, Christ’s passion. Hence the wine is first brought to the master of the feast—that is, to John, who drinks the passion before Christ does.

[Col. 0364C]

### Verse 11

**This he did.** (HIER.) At the beginning of the signs which, as a mortal, he was to give to mortals, he changed water into wine. Just as, already immortal, he opened the understanding to his disciples so that they might understand Christ in the law and the prophets, so he first imbued carnal minds with the flavor of wisdom, and afterward, when they had been raised, he would fill them with greater glory.

### Verse 12

**After this, etc.** After the first sign involving wine, he adds another indication of divine majesty in driving the sellers from the temple.

Figuratively, the Son of God, as humble, descends to Capernaum—that is, into the world—according to what he has from his mother and brothers.

### Verse 13

**And the Passover was near.** We celebrate Passover when we pass from vices to virtues. Jesus came for this purpose when he visits the Church daily, considers the conduct of each person, and drives out those who, among the saints, do good either hypocritically or do evil openly.

The oxen that plow signify preachers of heavenly doctrine. Those who sell them preach not out of love for God but for temporal profit.

Sheep, being innocent, provide their fleeces to clothe others. They signify works of purity and devotion, which are sold when they are performed for human praise.

The Spirit appeared in the form of a dove; hence the Spirit is received through the dove, which the Simonians sell.

Those who lend money in the Church do not serve heavenly things hypocritically but earthly things openly.

All these are driven out from the portion of the lot of the saints: those who do good hypocritically or evil openly. They are scourged with cords of sins for correction; [Col. 0365A] if they remain uncorrected, they will be bound at the end.

He also drives out the sheep and oxen because he shows the life and teaching of such people to be rejected. He overturns the tables because in the end the very things they loved will be destroyed.

**And he went up.** If the one who gave God’s decrees also keeps them, he teaches how carefully human beings ought to devote themselves to prayers and the solemn observances of God.

He is read as having gone up to the Passover twice: once in the first year of his preaching, before John had been imprisoned, which is the occasion described here; and a second time when he went to his passion. On both occasions he drove the sellers from the temple.

### Verse 14

**And he found in the temple.** If, in the figurative temple that is the house of prayer, he forbids commerce that is considered respectable, although it concerns things offered in the temple, how much more does he forbid drinking and other more serious offenses?

### Verse 15

**From cords.** The cords with which they are driven out are the growth of evil actions. Hence Isaiah: **“Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity”** (Isa. V). And Solomon: **“Each person is bound by the cords of his sins”** (Prov. V).

### Verse 16

**Those who sell doves.** Not only those who sell doves, but also all others who make the house of God a house of commerce—that is, all who seek their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ.

### VERSE 17

**“The zeal of your house.”** (AUG.) Good zeal is the ardor of the soul by which the mind, having cast aside human fear, is enkindled for the defense of truth. He is consumed by it who strives to correct whatever wrongs he sees; if he cannot, he endures it and groans.

[Col. 0365C]

### VERSE 18

**“What sign do you show us, since you do these things?” He answered:** Why do they ask for a sign, since he drives the customary commerce from the temple? And he says, **“Destroy this temple.”** As though he were saying: Because this temple signifies the temple of his body, in which there is no blemish, I rightly cleanse this figurative temple, since by divine power I am able to raise up that temple after it has been destroyed by men’s death.

### VERSE 20

**“Then the Jews said.”** They understood carnally what was spoken spiritually; the Evangelist discloses this to us: **“But he was speaking about the temple of his body.”**

**Forty-six.** (AUG.) *Anatolē* in Greek means “rising” or “east,” *dysē* means “setting” or “west,” and *arkt os* means “north,” and so on, up to the statement that they have the number six forty-six times.

**“Built.”** (AUG.) Solomon’s building was completed in seven years, and so forth, up to the statement that the elect are to be gathered from the four winds.

### VERSE 23

**“When he was in Jerusalem at the Passover.”** He went among the gathering in order to convert many by words and signs. Since some who were moved only by the signs believed in him—truly, but in such a way that afterward they could be scandalized by his Passion—and since they had not yet been reborn of water and the Spirit, they were not worthy for Jesus to entrust himself to them or dwell familiarly with them. For he knew what was in them better than a person himself knows what is in him.

This faith is appropriate to catechumens, who believe in him; but because they have not been reborn, the communion of Christ’s body and blood is not entrusted to them. Nicodemus was one of these. Believing, he says that Jesus came from God on account of the signs he had seen; but he had not yet been reborn. Therefore he came by night, not by day, because he had not yet been illumined by heavenly light.

## CHAPTER III

### VERSE 1

**“Now there was a man,” and so forth.** He was one of those who had believed through the signs.

**“Nicodemus by name.”** Nicodemus means “victory of the people,” or “one bearing the figure of the victor of the people”: all those who, believing in Christ from the Jewish people, conquer the world through faith.

### VERSE 2

**“This man came,” and so forth.** Night signifies the letter of the Law, or ignorance of the heart, or fear. Perhaps he came by night because, being a teacher in Israel, he was ashamed to speak openly, or because he feared the Jews.

Because he had prudently observed the manifest signs, he sought more fully the mysteries of faith. Therefore he deserved to be taught about Christ’s deity and his twofold birth, about his Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension, about the second generation, the entrance into the kingdom of heaven, and many other matters.

### VERSE 3

**“Amen, amen, I say.”** He explains the second birth to one who was not asking about it, lest Nicodemus should think that faith alone—which he had acquired through seeing the signs and believing in Jesus—was sufficient for salvation without the power of spiritual regeneration and without the sacraments.

Moreover, because Nicodemus understood him to be merely a man, like John the Baptist or one of the prophets, Jesus therefore began to instruct him concerning the second regeneration, by which he would understand him to be the Son of God and that he himself could become a son of God.

**(AUG.)** The second birth about which Jesus teaches is spiritual: it is from God and the Church unto life. But Nicodemus understands only the carnal birth, which is from Adam and Eve unto death. Yet just as he says that carnal birth cannot be repeated, so spiritual birth, once effected by anyone, cannot be repeated. For they have been born from the seed of the true Abraham, whether through the free woman or through the slave woman.

**“Unless someone.”** The visible sacrament of water is necessary for the cleansing of the visible body, just as the invisible teaching of faith is necessary for the sanctification of the invisible soul.

**“Has been reborn.”** (CHRYS.) This means: If you have not been born from above and have not received certainty concerning the doctrines somewhere, you are wandering outside and are far from the kingdom of heaven. Here he shows and indicates that reality is not merely what appears, but that other eyes are needed in order to see God.

### VERSE 5

**“Of water.”** Of visible water as sacrament, and of the Spirit in invisible understanding, so that he may visibly receive the symbol of baptism and fulfill the spiritual understanding of that symbol. Or: of visible water and the Holy Spirit.

### VERSE 6

**“That which is born.”** He distinguishes this spiritual birth from carnal birth, saying: **“That which is born of the flesh.”** That is, what is born from the first man through the succession of the flesh is carnal. By the name “flesh” he signifies not flesh alone but the whole carnal person. Conversely, the whole spiritual person, soul and body, is called “spirit.”

**“And that which,” and so forth.** Through the word and sacrament, the Spirit is invisibly present, so that the one born from Adam unto death is born as a son of God unto life. He is called not merely spiritual but “spirit,” because just as the substance of spirit is invisible, so through the visible sacrament he is invisibly made a son of God.

**“The Spirit is.”** Do not be surprised if I call one born in this way “spirit.” For just as the Spirit breathes where he wills, and you do not know from where he comes or where he goes, so is everyone who is born of the Spirit.

### VERSE 8

**“The Spirit breathes where he wills.”** He has power over whose heart he illumines. You hear his voice in the Scriptures, or when someone filled with the Holy Spirit speaks. Although you hear it, you do not know from where it comes—that is, how it entered that person’s heart—or how it returned, because its nature is invisible.

So it is with everyone who is born of the Holy Spirit: through the Spirit’s invisible action he begins to be what he was not, so that the unbeliever does not know from where he comes or where he goes—that is, by what grace he comes into the adoption of sonship and goes into the kingdom of God.

Since these things are unknown to the carnal person, he asks again: **“How can these things happen?”** Lacking spiritual understanding in the letter of the Law, he thinks that what is said about birth through the Spirit is impossible. Therefore the Lord rebukes him: **“You are a teacher,”** and so forth.

**“And you hear his voice,” and so forth.** The voice of the Spirit is the voice of Christ, which Nicodemus heard. But because he had not yet been born of the Spirit, he did not know from where it came or where it went—that is, on what occasion Christ wished a person to be born in the Spirit, or toward what perfection he said that one born from the Spirit should proceed. For the one born from him becomes, by grace, one spirit with him, just as the Spirit himself is one by nature.

### VERSE 10

**“You are the teacher,” and so forth.** He does not insult him, as though he wished to be regarded as superior to the one who is over all. Rather, because he wishes Nicodemus to be born of the Spirit—which can happen only to one who is humble—he humbles the man puffed up by his teaching office.

It is as though he said: Proud ruler, you know nothing. Humble yourself, so that, like the one who emptied himself and was born of the Spirit, you may learn what you do not now know.

### VERSE 11

**“What we know we speak.”** That is, because he himself is the knowledge, utterance, and speech of the Father.

**“And what we have seen we testify.”** Because he himself is the vision, the true testimony, and the truth of the Father. The plural form intimates the mystery of the Trinity.

### VERSE 12

**“If I have told you earthly things.”** (AUG.) Since you do not receive earthly things, how can you receive heavenly things—that is, the heavenly birth of the Spirit? You not only fail to believe but do not even understand earthly things: what I said about the temple of my body, which I received from the earth, being destroyed by you and raised by me.

### VERSE 13

**“No one has ascended.”** This pertains to the second birth in the Spirit, because no one ascends in Christ to the Father unless he is born of the Spirit. No one is saved through Christ’s death unless he is born of the Spirit; and no one is born of the Spirit except in Christ’s death.

When he says **“the Son of Man,”** he gives us assurance of ascending, since we are sons of men.

### VERSE 14

**“And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness.”** He introduces his own death, which is the origin and cause of possessing the realities mentioned above, and by faith in it he instructs Nicodemus.

Since Nicodemus was carnal and familiar with the Law, Jesus brings forward a portion of the Law, showing that it was a figure and sign of his death. Thus it may also become clear concerning the other parts of the Law that they are figurative.

Because death is signified by the serpent, and Christ, having died, is called a serpent, whoever looks upon him in faith is freed—just as, by looking upon that figure, those who were afflicted by fiery serpents were freed. The fiery serpents signify the incitements of vices.

**“So must the Son of Man be lifted up,” and so forth.** He invites the teacher of the Law to the significance of the Law. Since he had spoken of the Son of Man, lest Nicodemus think that he was only this, he adds that he is also the Son of God.

**“For God so loved.”** He discloses the cause of human salvation, namely the love of God the Father, from whom all restoration comes through his Son in the Holy Spirit.

### VERSE 16

**“The world.”** *Cosmos* in Greek, which is translated into Latin as *mundus*, means “ornament” or “adornment.” Therefore “the world” signifies human nature—not because, in bodily terms, it consists of the four elements, but because, in the soul, it has been adorned by God and made in the image of God. God loves it in order to make it eternal.

**“That he should give his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes,” and so forth.** Here he says of the Son of God the same thing he said above of the Son of Man: through the one by whom we were created in deity, we are restored in humanity.

### VERSE 19

**“Now this is the judgment.”** Why is the one who does not believe judged? Because the light has come, awakening people and urging them to recognize their evils, in which all are involved. Some hate the light that admonishes them and flee, lest the evils they love be exposed. Others, admonished by the light, accuse their own evils; this is to practice the truth, and thus they are illumined.

**“For their works were.”** The one who is in darkness but loves the light is not evil. Rather, the person is called evil, and his works evil, when, after the light has come, he hates the light and loves evil.

This is what he says: **“For their works were evil.”** Their works are impiety, unbelief, hatred of eternal light, unwillingness to look upon it, and the desire to remain in the darkness of sins.

### VERSE 21

**“But whoever does.”** Having shown by what justice the one who does not believe is condemned, he shows by what justice the one who believes is saved.

**“But whoever does.”** That is, the one who is displeased with his evils and accuses himself—who does not forgive or spare himself—but comes to the light.

He begins to act with God when he accuses his evils, because the beginning of good is the accusation of evil. Therefore his works—namely, that he accuses himself as God accuses him—are made manifest, because they have been done in God. For unless God’s light shone upon him, he would not be displeased with himself.

### VERSE 22

**“After these things.”** Not immediately after the discussion with Nicodemus that took place in Jerusalem, but after an interval of time he returned from Galilee to Judea.

**“Into the land of Judea, and there he remained,” and so forth.** Morally: Wherever there is confession of sins or of divine praises, Jesus comes there, together with his disciples—that is, his teaching and illumination. There he remains, cleansing from offenses; hence what follows: **“And there he remained and was baptizing.”**

**“Now John was also.”** Although Christ was already baptizing, John continued to baptize, because the shadow still remained. The forerunner ought not to cease until the truth is manifested.

### VERSE 24

**“For John had not yet been thrown into prison.”** Here he plainly marks the deeds of Christ before John was imprisoned, which the other Evangelists passed over. They begin with what happened after John was sent into prison, when, with the forerunner’s baptism having ceased, Christ’s baptism openly began.

### VERSE 25

**“Now a dispute arose among John’s disciples,” and so forth.** While John preaches and his school continues, Christ preaches and works secretly but baptizes openly, so that a question may arise concerning John’s baptism and Christ’s baptism and be resolved by John’s testimonies.

### VERSE 26

**“And they came to John and said to him: Rabbi,” and so forth.** They wished to accuse Christ, whom shortly before they had seen baptized by John.

### VERSE 27

**“John answered and said,” and so forth.** Because I was born from parents of advanced age, beyond the ordinary course of human nature, you think that I am something beyond human. But know that I am merely a man, while he is God, from whom I have whatever I have. From me comes weakness; from him, the sublimity of grace.

Do you suppose that I would say anything contrary to my testimony? I do not baptize for the remission of sins, but he does.

**“He cannot.”** It is as though he said: I am merely a man; I have nothing except what has been given by God. That is, I baptize unto repentance, not unto remission, because I am not the Christ, but he is, as you know I have testified to you. Therefore run to him.

### VERSE 28

**“I am not the Christ.”** I am not anointed by the Father with the fullness of the Spirit, but I have received from his fullness in order to go before him.

### VERSE 29

**“This joy of mine.”** My joy is complete in this: that I have become the bridegroom’s friend, and that I stand and rejoice.

### VERSE 30

**“He must increase.”** I rejoice at the bridegroom’s voice. The bridegroom will increase—that is, he will be found to be the Christ, although he was thought to be a prophet. I will decrease, because I will be found to be his prophet, although I was thought to be the Christ.

**“He must increase.”** That is, he must be exalted: while he forgives sins and gives grace, his glory—which is always perfect in itself—increases in human beings, as a person sees and possesses more of it. The person who formerly gloried in himself decreases when he confesses his sins and receives what Christ gives.

The Passion of both bears witness to this: Christ is exalted on the cross, while John is diminished by the loss of his head. Creation also bears witness: John was born as the days were decreasing, but Christ as they were increasing.

### VERSE 31

**“I must decrease.”** John is a figure of the Law; Christ is the truth. The Law decreases when the truth appears.

**“He who comes from above is above all,” and so forth.** (ALC.) That is, from the height of human nature before the sin of the first parent, and so forth, up to the second point: according to the height of the Father, to whom he is equal.

**“Of the earth.”** That is, the one who was born of earthly parents, from whom he contracted sin and the punishment of sin, is of himself nothing but earth.

**“And what he has seen.”** Since he himself is the Word of the Father, he does not hear or testify to human beings any word other than the Father’s Word. He knows and indicates that he himself is the Word the Father spoke—that is, brought forth and begot from himself—and that he is from the Father. The Evangelist says this as he is able, although it cannot be fully stated or understood.

### VERSES 33–34

**“He has set his seal that God is true.”** This means that he has placed a sign in his heart, as though marking something special: namely, that the one who was sent for the salvation of human beings is the true God.

**“He is truthful. For the one whom God sent.”** Every human being is a liar of himself; no one can speak the truth unless illumined by God.

The one whom God the Father sent speaks the words of God. What does this mean? The one whom God sent is God; therefore he speaks the words of God. Thus the Son’s words, bearing witness about himself that he is God, are the words of God.

**“He speaks the words of God.”** In this he distinguishes himself from Christ. But because he was sent and speaks the words of God, he adds more openly: **“For God does not give the Spirit by measure.”**

The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand. He gives to human beings by measure; to the Son he does not give by measure. Just as he wholly begot his Son from himself, wholly, so he gave his whole Spirit to his incarnate Son—not piecemeal, not by divisions, but generally and universally. He gives for no other reason than that the Father loves the Son.

### VERSE 36

**“Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; but whoever,” and so forth.** It is as though he said: Whoever believes in the Son has the Son himself, and through this has life.

**“But the wrath of God remains upon him.”** The wrath with which he was born remains. Therefore he does not say “comes” but “remains,” because through the Son who was sent, who is life, the effect of that wrath is not removed—namely, death, corruption, and the rest—all of which remain.

## CHAPTER IV

### VERSE 1

**“When Jesus therefore learned.”** Jesus knew their knowledge and envy: they had not learned about him in order to follow him but in order to persecute him. Therefore he fled, teaching his people to yield to evil persons, not because he was afraid or unable to escape them.

**“And he baptizes.”** This is rightly said. He himself always cleanses invisibly in the Spirit and by grace, but his baptism also takes place bodily. It consists of two things: water and the word of life. Hence Paul says: **“He cleanses her by the washing of water and the word of life”** (Ephesians 5).

### VERSE 2

**“But his disciples.”** In their baptism the Spirit was given, although not as manifestly as it was given after the Ascension, in an ineffable and inconceivable manner.

### VERSE 3

**“He left Judea.”** That is, he left the unbelieving Pharisees, who were considering persecuting him because his baptism was increasing and because, through his teaching, they understood that the Law was being nullified.

**“And he departed.”** After he had received a few from the Jewish people, he left the unbelievers who followed the letter of the Law, which leads no one to perfection.

**“And he departed into Galilee.”** That is, into the spiritual understanding of the letter itself.

**“Into Galilee.”** The Lord is believed to have been transfigured in Galilee; this signifies the transformation of human nature into its original glory. In Galilee he gave the disciples on the mountain the teaching by which believers are to pass into life.

### VERSE 4

**“He had to pass.”** Samaria lies between Judea and Galilee. That is, between the letter of the Law, signified by Judea, and the divine laws revolving around God, whose figure is Galilee, there is the natural law placed in the middle.

Therefore, since he took the foundations of the Church from the Law, he had to pass to the nations established under the natural law, so that, having joined both together, he might return to Galilee, the blessedness of eternity.

### VERSE 5

**“So he came.”** He came so that the Samaritans might recognize him and be converted to him, claiming for themselves the inheritance of the patriarch Israel.

**“Which is called Sychar.”** Sychar means “conclusion” or “branch”: that is, the Gentile people confined under sin, a branch cut from the wild olive tree and grafted into the olive tree.

### VERSE 6

**“Now there was,” and so forth.** Since natural reason arises from no other source than the cause of all good things, it is beautifully said that this is Jacob’s well: that is, reason proceeding from the infinite height of the Father.

**“Jesus therefore, being wearied,” and so forth.** Allegorically: Jesus’ journey is the assumption of flesh, in which there is weariness—that is, weakness—while his power raises up the human being whom he created. Sitting signifies humility.

The sixth hour signifies the sixth age, in which he came. The well signifies the depth of this age. The Samaritan woman signifies the Church, which comes from the Gentiles, no longer already just but destined to be justified.

The water of the well signifies the will of this age, which is drawn up from the depths by people who submit and incline themselves toward it, with desire already placed beforehand as the water jar.

**“He was sitting.”** As though he were relieving his weariness, this indicates the teacher who is about to instruct those who approach and to possess them.

**“Above.”** A spring is called such wherever water flows from the earth. If it is on the surface, it is simply called a spring; if it is in the depths, it is also called a well.

### VERSE 7

**“She came.”** In the figure of the Church from the Gentiles, which previously drew water—that is, pleasure—from the depths of the age. Jesus thirsts for her faith and asks to drink from her.

**(GREG.)** Or the woman signifies the Synagogue, which comes to draw water, and so forth, up to the primitive Church.

**“Give me.”** Jesus, sitting above the spring, asks the primitive Church, which he had chosen from the Gentiles, for a drink of faith by which one believes in him. He asks from human nature a drink of reason by which the Creator and Redeemer may be sought.

The apostles, sent into the city—that is, into the world—to buy spiritual food—that is, faith, action, and knowledge—are the things by which the teachers of the Church are satisfied.

**“Give me.”** Although Jesus could have been thirsty after his weariness, he does not demand this drink. Rather, he desires that the heart of the Church from the Gentiles become a drink for him through its recognition of his labor.

### VERSE 8

**“For his disciples.”** The disciples went into the city, namely to the Jews, who are fortified by the valley of the Law and armed with the weapons of prophecy, in order to buy food from them—that is, preparing their hearts for God through the preaching of faith.

### VERSE 9

**“Therefore she says.”** Not knowing what drink he was asking from her, she thought that he was speaking about water. She objected that she herself belonged to the foreign people whose vessels the Jews did not even use in their daily intercourse.

But Jesus, who was asking for faith, desired to give her the Spirit and admonished her to ask. The Spirit is both the gift of God and living water.

**“For the Jews,” and so forth.** The Jews curse the Samaritans and call them “supplanters,” because they had deprived them of the inheritance of their father Jacob by abstaining from their foods and vessels.

### VERSE 10

**“Jesus answered.”** He instructs her gradually and in simple words, so that at last she may receive the gift of God, namely the Spirit.

### VERSE 11

**“The woman said to him.”** “Living water” means no other water than that which is collected where it springs forth. Understanding carnally, the woman said: **“Since you have no vessel for drawing, and the well is deep, how do you have living water?”**

Lest he seem to promise another spring, she adds: **“Are you greater?”** That is, can you be greater than Jacob, who used this well with his household?

Against this, Christ openly shows that he is speaking not carnally but spiritually, saying that the one who drinks his water will not thirst.

### VERSE 12

**“Are you greater?”** The foreign woman calls Jacob her father because she had lived under the Law of Moses and possessed the estate that Jacob had given to his son.

**(AUG.)** The vessel is desire; the water is pleasure. It is refreshed, not extinguished.

**“And he himself drank from it.”** Human beings and cattle drink from a well. Similarly, reason, as though from a well corrupted and darkened, is dug out and exercised with great labor.

Some drink as human beings, using reason for good, like the saints. Others drink as cattle, using it for evil, like philosophers.

### VERSE 13

**“But whoever.”** Whoever gives his heart to my preaching and recognizes the gift of grace will have faith born in him, faith that works through love; thus at last he will pass into eternal life.

### VERSE 14

**“Water.”** Bodily water flows downward; spiritual water leaps upward and carries with it those who drink it into eternal glory.

### VERSE 16

**“Go, call your husband,” and so forth.** In order that, under his guidance, you may ascend to contemplation of spiritual understanding:

**“Go, call your husband.”** You, who are sensual, call your rational understanding, by which you may be ruled as by a husband. You, who now understand carnally, I—the light and head of the husband—will illumine.

It is as though he said: What I say is not to be understood carnally, as you, an animal person, understand it, but spiritually and under the guidance of reason. Therefore prepare your understanding for me and come, by understanding these spiritual things that I say.

### VERSE 17

**“The woman answered.”** In fact, this woman at that time had no husband, but she was living with someone illegitimate. Understanding carnally, she answers from that relationship; she had not yet called her husband, that is, her understanding.

**“Jesus said to her.”** Gradually raising her up, he continues to speak mysteries, so that little by little he might lead her to recognize who was speaking with her.

He does not praise the woman’s answer as a good or prudent answer; rather, he praises her confession of the truth.

### VERSE 18

**“For you have had five husbands.”** The five husbands are the five laws given to human nature.

The first was given in paradise before sin, in the prohibition concerning the tree. The second was given after transgression and expulsion from paradise, concerning the multiplication of human offspring. The third was given to Noah before the Flood, concerning the construction of the ark. The fourth was given after the Flood, concerning the divisions of the nations. The fifth was given to Abraham, concerning circumcision and the sacrifice of his son.

Human nature was subject to these five laws, as to five husbands, from the beginning of the world until Moses. Afterward the letter of the Law was given, which brought no salvation. Hence it is said: **“The one whom you now have is not your husband.”**

Abandon the letter; go to the Spirit of the letter, to the New Testament, by which you may conceive spiritual offspring of virtues.

**(AUG.)** The five husbands are the five bodily senses that ruled you. Now, in the time of discernment, a husband does not rule you—that is, the understanding of wisdom—but an adulterer, error, corrupts you, while you receive carnally what I say. Therefore call your husband, so that you may understand spiritually, as I say.

The five senses are called husbands in the earlier age because they are legitimate. After the fall of the human being and by God’s decree, that age is naturally governed not toward eternal things but toward the pursuit of temporal things when they please, and their avoidance when they offend.

### VERSE 19

**“You are a prophet.”** The woman, progressing through what she had heard, had already begun to possess some understanding. Therefore she calls him a prophet, but not yet fully, because she does not believe that Christ has come.

### VERSE 20

**“Our fathers worshiped,” and so forth.** You are a prophet, and therefore judge this dispute that troubles me.

The Jews placed themselves above the Samaritans because of the temple Solomon had built, in which they worshiped. Conversely, the Samaritans opposed the Jews on account of the mountain on which their fathers, who pleased God, had worshiped rather than in the temple.

Thus the patriarchs worshiped on mountains, while the Jews worshiped in the temple, prefiguring the manner of right prayer.

### VERSE 21

**“Woman.”** Here the Lord restrains the boastfulness of the Samaritans, who thought that they were no less religious than the Jews.

He therefore speaks in the person of the prophets and of all who believe in Christ. Hence he says: **“You worship the Father whom you do not know,”** because no one worships the Father unless he worships the Son, through whom one comes to knowledge of the Father.

But we know the Son, and through the Son the Father. Hence what follows: **“For salvation is from the Jews,”** and so forth. That is, because Christ, who is salvation, is from the Jews—not only in the origin of his flesh, but also because faith and the primitive Church arose from them.

**“Believe me.”** The husband who can believe is already within you; therefore believe. **“For unless you believe, you will not understand”** (Isaiah 7).

**“When neither on the mountain.”** Behold, both your mountain and the temple of the Jews will alike be rejected. Yet you are unequal in this respect: you Samaritans worship what you do not know, whereas we Jews—not all, but the elect—worship what we know, because to us belong the knowledge of God, the covenant, the promise, and prophecy; Christ is from us.

This is what it means that salvation is from the Jews. Yet although we differ in this way, I do not prefer the place of the Jews to the place of the Samaritans. This is what follows.

### VERSE 23

**“But the hour is coming, and now is, when.”** Before I came in the flesh, no one could worship the Father in spirit and truth except the patriarchs and prophets, to whom my incarnation had been revealed. Through my presence in the flesh, true worshipers will come to be.

**“In spirit and truth.”** The Father is to be worshiped not in the temple and not on this mountain, but inwardly, in the innermost temple of the heart, and in the truth of knowledge.

### VERSE 24

**“God is spirit.”** Since God is spirit and not a body, he does not seek a bodily place—a mountain or temple—in which to be worshiped. Rather, pure spirit is his temple, in which he is to be worshiped, not concerning visible things that pass away, but concerning eternal things that are truth.

### VERSES 25–26

**“I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called,” and so forth.** Now more advanced through the words of the teacher, she knows from whom she ought to receive perfect instruction: from the Messiah.

**“He will announce all things to us.”** Jesus says to her: He will show us how to worship in spirit and truth, setting aside the temple and the mountain, and how, when the shadows have been cast away, we may be illumined by the truth.

**“I am, the one who speaks.”** Recognize that the one whose coming you await has come. Bring with you the husband who rules you, and labor to learn what is necessary for faith.

Since he knew that she was now capable of being taught by the one whom, although he was already teaching her, she did not recognize, she was worthy that he should reveal himself to her. Hence he says: **“I am the Messiah.”**

After receiving this revelation, she has nothing more to ask. Hence what follows: **“Then she left her water jar,”** and so forth. But the Evangelist inserts an account of the disciples.

### VERSE 27

**“And they marveled that,” and so forth.** They did not marvel that he was speaking with a woman, since he was accustomed to speak with women, but that he was speaking with a foreign woman. They did not understand the mystery of the future Church from the Gentiles.

They suspect nothing evil; rather, they marvel at his clemency, because he teaches an erring Gentile, like one who came to seek what had been lost.

### VERSE 28

**“Then she left.”** Having heard **“I am he,”** and now understanding Christ as the head of her husband, the woman left her water jar—that is, desire—and ran to evangelize.

Let those who are about to evangelize learn here that they must first lay aside concern for and the burden of this age.

### VERSE 29

**“Come and see.”** She leads those inexperienced people gradually toward the truth. She does not immediately assert that he is Christ, lest they become angry and indignant.

### VERSE 33

**“Has someone brought him something to eat?”** They did not dare to question the Lord, fearing that he might rebuke them if they asked carelessly.

### VERSE 34

**“My food is.”** They did not understand “food,” just as the woman above did not understand “water.” Therefore the teacher instructs them, not indirectly as he instructed her, but now openly, saying: **“My food is to do,”** and so forth.

**“His will.”** The Father’s. The Father’s will is that people believe in him—that is, in the Son whom he sent. The Father’s work is our salvation. Therefore Christ’s food is our faith and our salvation.

He does the Father’s will by teaching people to believe in him; he accomplishes the Father’s work by bringing the mystery of redemption to maturity.

### VERSE 35

**“Do you not say?”** Since he seeks the faith and salvation of the peoples, he burns with zeal for the work and prepares to send laborers.

**“Lift up your eyes.”** Consider with the understanding of your mind that, once winter—that is, unbelief—has passed, the warmth of faith is present and hearts are ready, so that you may gather from them the works of righteousness.

It is as though he said: Help to fulfill the Father’s will. And you can do so, because the harvest is ready. That is: See the Gentiles readily believing.

### VERSE 36

**“So that both the one who sows.”** Both the sower and the reaper were necessary. This makes the saying credible, because one sows and another reaps. For unless they had been prepared by the prophets, they would not have listened to the apostles.

### VERSE 38

**“I sent you.”** I make you reapers where others have sown—that is, in Judea, where the first harvest was gathered. From there, some went out and sowed throughout the whole world; from those seeds another harvest arises, to be gathered at the end of the age by the angelic reapers.

**“They have labored, and you have entered into their labors.”** Great were the labors of the patriarchs and prophets, in all of whom there was prophecy concerning Christ. They suffered much, as though in the cold of sowing.

### VERSE 40

**“When they had come.”** First they heard his reputation; afterward they saw him present. Even this was not enough for them, but they made him remain with them so that they might be instructed by his own words, which they preferred to the woman’s words.

In all these matters, by contrast, the hardness of the Jews is reproved: they do not believe even the miracles.

**“And he remained there two days.”** Morally: Every day Christ is announced among those who are outside through the woman—that is, through the Church—and they believe through this report.

Then he remains among them for two days, without mention of night, so that their light may be instructed by the two commandments of love.

### VERSE 42

**“And they said to the woman.”** After the Lord, through the presence of his flesh, had poured the grace of knowledge upon Jews instructed spiritually, they said to the woman—that is, to the Law: **“We no longer believe because of your speech.”**

### VERSE 43

**“For we ourselves have heard.”** Because he had first remained among these people and performed miracles for them, yet only a few believed in him—hence, after seeing the sign, his disciples believed in him, not the others—he now returns from the Samaritans, who believed easily without seeing any sign, to these people, so that those who had not believed through the earlier signs might now believe.

This signifies that, at the end of the age, he will return from the Gentiles, who were easily converted, to the Jews, his own homeland, because previously he had not received honor among them.

### VERSE 44

**“Because a prophet.”** Allegorically: Christ’s homeland is the Jewish people, among whom he lacks honor, because few of them believe. This is what is said concerning Christ’s fellow citizens from Galilee.

The Church of the Gentiles, which believes easily, is like the Samaritans. The former believe through the miracles, and they are few; the latter believe through the word of preaching alone, and they are many.

Behold why he comes: he returns because he testified that a prophet has no honor in his homeland. Otherwise, it would seem that he ought not to return to those among whom he has no honor, but to remain among those who received him well.

### VERSE 46

**“Now there was a certain royal official whose son.”** This royal official can signify a teacher from the Jewish people who, after the complete conversion of the Church from the Gentiles—toward which the Lord migrated through his disciples after being expelled by the Jews—prays for his son, the Jewish people.

He knows that this son will receive faith only at the end of the age, and he asks that he be healed from the long illness of unbelief.

### VERSE 47

**“And he was asking.”** He already believed that Jesus could heal his son. But because he did not believe that Christ, through his divinity—which is everywhere present—was with his son, he asked him to come down and heal him bodily by being physically present. Hence he is rebuked for unbelief: **“Unless you see signs and wonders,”** and so forth.

By contrast, the centurion is praised, for he says: **“Speak the word, and my boy will be healed”** (Matthew 8). Hence: **“I have not found such faith in Israel.”**

Or perhaps the royal official wished to test what kind of person Christ was; hence he is rebuked: **“Unless you see signs and wonders.”**

For the salvation of his son, he himself and his entire household believed.

### VERSE 48

**“Unless you see signs.”** In this he is reproved for unbelief: he did not believe that Jesus was present everywhere. Through this hardness his people—the Jews—are signified, since they do not believe even after seeing miracles.

By contrast, Samaria signifies the faith of the Gentiles, who believed through the word alone. Allegorically, this hardness will endure among the unbelieving Jews from Christ’s first coming until after the reign of the Antichrist.

**“And wonders.”** A *prodigium* is so called as though from *porro dictum*, “something spoken beforehand,” because it signifies something. Or *prodigium* may be understood as “far from the finger,” because it prefigures something remote and future.

[Col. 0376C] **VERSE 49–50.**—“Come down.” As though he could not heal in any other way unless he were physically present. Therefore the Lord, showing that he is not absent wherever he is invited, heals by a command alone: “Go; your son lives.” He does not go to the royal official’s son, lest he seem to honor riches; he promises to go to the centurion’s servant, who does not despise human nature—in this destroying the pride that does not weigh human nature in people, but only what is outwardly apparent.

“He himself believed.” The other citizens did not, signifying the small number of the Jews who had faith, although they had seen signs. Hence he adds: “This was again the second sign that Jesus performed.” In the Samaritans, as above, the great multitude of the Gentiles who would be converted by the word alone was signified.

**VERSE 54.**—“This was again the second sign that Jesus performed” [Col. 0376D] “when he had come from Judea into Galilee.” Of all the miracles Jesus performed in the year before John’s death, John mentions only these, along with Christ’s dispute with the Jews, which is set out above. For the other Evangelists clearly reported what he passes over here.

## CHAPTER V

**VERSE 4.**—“But an angel.” Behold two miracles: one performed invisibly by an angel in the pool, the other visibly by the Lord. In both cases one person was healed, so that unity might be commended. Otherwise, in terms of power it was not great, nor in kindness small, that one among so many should be healed by him who could raise them all by a single word. [Col. 0377A] But in these bodily matters he directs his attention more to the eternal salvation of souls.

**VERSE 5.**—“Thirty-eight.” That is, two short of forty. This number consists of four times ten and signifies the perfection of works in the ten commandments of the Law and the four Gospels. The one who lacks love of God and neighbor is two short of this number.

**VERSE 6.**—“Do you want to become well?” He does not fail to know what the man wants, but kindles in him a desire for the health of which he had already despaired. Hence the man was already complaining that he had no one to put him into the water.

**VERSE 8.**—“Take up your mat.” Love your neighbor by bearing his weakness, just as he patiently bore your weakness; and be concerned not only with your own restoration, but also with the salvation of your neighbors. Behold the angel of the great counsel, hidden in the flesh, made one man well when the water of the Jews had been stirred. [Col. 0377B]

**VERSE 9.**—“And he was walking.” By loving God, hasten toward his vision; neither abandon your brother because of love for the one to whom you are journeying, nor cease seeking him because of your brother.

**VERSE 10.**—“Therefore they were saying.” The Jews, observers of the letter and ignorant of the grace by which the Law is fulfilled, did not understand that the Law commands one to cease from every servile work—that is, from sin. Hence it says here: “Take up your mat,” and so forth. “It is not lawful.” They do not accuse him concerning the healing, since they themselves heal animals on the Sabbath, but concerning the carrying of the bed.

**VERSE 11.**—“He answered them.” He does not yield to those who object; rather, obeying the command of the healer, he sets the authority of his healing against his accusers.

[Col. 0377C] **VERSE 13.**—“He did not know who it was.” Standing among the crowd, he did not recognize Jesus, but afterward he recognized him in the temple. Here we are taught that whoever wishes to arrive at the vision of God must flee the crowd of his passions and the wickedness of men and approach the temple of inward prayer.

**VERSE 14.**—“In the temple.” Not in the crowd but in the temple, because if we wish to recognize the grace of the Creator, we must flee gatherings and become a temple. “Do not sin.” He indicates that the man had been ill because of his sins; but Jesus healed him inwardly just as he had healed him outwardly. Therefore he warns him lest, by sinning again, he be judged more severely.

**VERSE 16.**—“Because he was doing these things on the Sabbath.” As though he were acting as a breaker of the Law against God, who rested on the Sabbath after working first for six days. Against this Jesus says: God did not work only for six days, as you think, but works even now. For he who created new things in six days and rested from them on the seventh day afterward continues to work until the end by governing, sustaining, renewing, and propagating them, so that what has been created may endure. Since God is always at work, it is clear that the passage concerning the Sabbath rest contains a sacramental meaning. [Col. 0377D]

**VERSE 17.**—“But Jesus answered.” As though he were saying: Blind men in the Law, why are you jealous of me if I make a man well on the Sabbath? I, God, work always with the Father.

**VERSE 18.**—“Therefore Jesus answered.” Since they were disturbed by hearing of the equality with God the Father of one whom they considered a mere man, he adds that he is the Son equal to the Father, of the same will, the same power, [Col. 0378A] and the same operation. In explaining these matters he uses a manner of speech capable of stirring the minds of the immature—even if it does not fill them—and of exercising and nourishing the minds of the mature. For he speaks concerning the Son’s divinity: “The Son cannot do anything from himself except what he sees the Father doing,” and “the Father shows him” all things. These statements are not to be understood literally, as they would be among human beings, but mystically. He speaks these secrets either so that they may be disturbed, or perhaps so that, once disturbed, they may seek a physician. He also speaks them for our sake, so that they might be written for us—things which, if poorly understood, lead into error, but if well understood, lead into truth.

**VERSE 19.**—“Amen, amen, I say to you.” Here he treats of his identity with the Father, his lesser status according to his humanity, and what he does in these respects—namely, both resurrections, of the body and of the soul. “The Son cannot.” I am so equal to the Father that I do not exist from myself, but I am from him. The one who is not from himself neither does nor can do anything from himself; rather, he does and can do from him from whom he is. “The Son also does these things.” The whole body appears to do whatever the mind does, but not in the same way, since the mind commands the body. The Father and the Son, however, work the same things in the same way, because the Father and the Son have one nature, one substance, one will, one power, and one operation. [Col. 0378B]

**VERSE 20.**—“He shows him all things.” For the Father to show all things to the Son means that he performs all things through the Son, so that the Father and the Son may be held equally in our faith. And lest the Son be regarded as in any way lesser, he adds: “He will show him greater works than these”—that is, he will do greater works through him. [Col. 0378C] What works? “For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life.” It is greater to raise the dead than to heal the sick, which was the matter under discussion. “Greater works than these.” The Father raises souls through the Son, so that souls may live from the substance of the Father and the Son; and to the Son made man in time he will show greater works, namely, the resurrection of bodies, so that you may marvel that it is accomplished through the Son.

**VERSE 21.**—“For just as the Father raises.” He begins to show what the Son does insofar as he is equal to the Father: namely, he raises souls from death. This is the first resurrection, from vices. In what follows he also shows the resurrection of dead bodies, insofar as he is the Son of Man, and the Father has given authority to him—that is, to the Son.

“Thus also the Son.” *(Augustine.)* Because the Father and the Son are the same life. “He judges and raises bodies,” and so forth, up to the point where this reason is given: because he is the Son of Man. [Col. 0378D]

**VERSE 23.**—“So that all may honor.” He honors God who commends the Creator as omnipotent and eternal. He honors the Father who believes that the Father has a Son equal to himself. He honors the Son who believes that the Son is equal to the Father.

“He who does not honor.” *(Augustine.)* For if the Son were believed to be lesser, the Father would be dishonored: either because, through envy, he would not have wished to beget him equal, or because, through weakness, he could not have done so. In either case he would be shown not to be God, since he would be powerless.

**VERSE 24.**—“For whoever,” and so forth. Since I am equal to the Father and to be honored with him by one honor, whoever hears my word—that is, whoever believes that I am the Son and believes that he is the Father—has eternal life. For this is eternal life, as he will say later: that they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.

“Hears and believes.” Why does he say, “hears my word and believes,” not “in me,” but “in the one who sent me”? Because his word is in me; indeed, I am his Word. Whoever therefore believes in him believes in his Word—that is, in me.

“But has passed over.” Here he passes from the death of unbelief to the life of faith and righteousness, and afterward from corruption to eternity. Concerning the first resurrection he adds more explicitly: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming and now is,” and so forth.

**VERSE 25.**—“For the hour is coming.” I said that the Son raises and gives life, which is true, because the hour is coming, and so forth—and this is a manifestation of his Father. [Col. 0379B] Here the raising of the soul from sins is under discussion.

“The voice of the Son.” This applies only to the righteous, who hear concerning his incarnation in such a way that they believe he is the Son of God.

“Just as the Father.” *(Augustine.)* The life which is itself the Father and the Son pertains to the soul, not to the body, and so forth, up to the point where it says that life itself is also the life of the body.

“In himself.” Not from another, but he himself is life. Thus the Son also is life in himself. Yet they differ: the Father is life without being born, while the Son is life by being born from the Father. Hence he says, “He gave”—not that the Son once existed without life, but that life is born from him. Therefore “he gave” means that life begot life. [Col. 0379C]

**VERSE 27.**—“And authority.” After speaking of the resurrection of the soul, he adds what concerns the resurrection of the flesh. The Father gave the Son the authority which the Son possesses with the Father in secret, because he is the Son of Man; in that form he will be seen judging the good and the wicked. For the vision of the form of God is promised only to the pure in heart: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5).

*(Augustine.)* Christ, insofar as he is the Son of God, and so forth, up to the point where he says that through the Word made flesh the resurrection of bodies becomes the work of the Son of Man.

**VERSE 28.**—“For the hour will come.” Just as above he is the author of the resurrection of the mind into eternal life, so here also he is the author of the resurrection of the flesh; otherwise no one would believe it.

**VERSE 30.**—“I cannot do anything from myself.” The Father gave me authority to judge; nevertheless I cannot act from myself—that is, the one who is not from himself does not act from himself. Thus whoever accuses him concerning his work on the Sabbath accuses the Father.

“But just as.” I hear through the unity of substance—that is, I know that hearing is nothing other than knowing or existing. Or: I, the Son of Man, can do nothing from myself; but just as I hear from God, I judge. My judgment concerning anyone is just because I do not seek my own will—that is, the will of the man—but the Father’s will, which concerns the salvation of human beings; for this he sent me, that is, caused me to become incarnate.

“I do not seek.” He now speaks insofar as he is equal to the Father, so that his true divinity may be proved; now insofar as he is lesser, so that his true humanity may be proved.

**VERSE 31.**—“If I bear witness.” I have spoken of the identity of his essence with the Father, from which not bodies—which do not perceive—but rational souls, intermediate between God and bodies, live. I have also spoken of the lesser status of his humanity, in which he dies, rises again, raises bodies, and judges. He now proceeds to speak of his testimonies, which he does not need to receive from a human being, since he has them from the works that the Father gave him and from the Father himself. [Col. 0380A] Yet he also has them from human beings, as from lamps: namely, from John and Moses. Although they cannot unite souls to God, they can nevertheless refute his enemies.

**VERSE 34.**—“But these things.” Nevertheless I introduce John’s testimony, so that through John you human beings may be led to truth itself and, by believing, may be saved.

**VERSE 35.**—“He was,” and so forth. He presented me outwardly as visible to human eyes and inwardly kindled human hearts to know me. All the prophets and apostles are also lamps; Christ is the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world.

**VERSE 37.**—“You have neither heard his voice.” Even if you think that you heard his voice and saw his appearance on Sinai.

**VERSE 41.**—“Glory.” I do not say this because I seek my own glory, but because I grieve for you in your error. You do not possess the love of God, and I wish to lead you back to the way of truth.

**VERSE 42.**—“Because you do not have love.” The love of God is not in you because you do not receive me—that is, you do not believe—because I have come so that the Father may be glorified through me.

**VERSE 43.**—“If another comes.” The Antichrist, who seeks his own glory and not God’s, will come in his own name. [Col. 0380C] This is what the Apostle says: that they may believe the lie, because they did not believe the truth.

## CHAPTER VI

**VERSE 1.**—“Across the sea.” Tiberias and Capernaum are on the same shore, on our side; the place where this miracle occurred is across the water, on the opposite shore. It is not properly called a sea, but a great reflux of the Jordan.

**VERSE 2.**—“And a great crowd was following.” Having seen this miracle, a great crowd of the Gentiles follows him. For just as he healed those whom he cured of bodily illness by restoring them inwardly in spirit, so he healed these people from the disease of unbelief.

**VERSE 5.**—“When he had lifted up.” By his example he admonishes us to raise the eyes of our hearts, so that, if perhaps under his guidance we are permitted to ascend to the height of action and knowledge, the crowd of following carnal thoughts may not disturb us or cast us down from the height of contemplation. Rather, we should take care to feed that crowd with spiritual food, as much as it is able to receive.

**VERSE 7.**—“Two hundred.” The number one hundred doubled signifies the perfection of good action and rational knowledge. These are not sufficient for instructing people in faith unless the height of theology is added. Theology leads souls, purified through good works and enlightened through knowledge of created things, to the consummate fullness of spiritual nourishment.

**VERSE 9.**—“There is one boy.” This boy is Moses the lawgiver, whose Law brought no one to perfection. [Col. 0381A] “One,” because he prefigured the future vanity of the Church. “Here,” that is, in the Old Testament, which, although it is already growing obsolete as the New Testament shines forth, has nevertheless not yet entirely disappeared.

“But these things,” and so forth. As though he were saying: What use are the letter of the Law or bodily perceptions for the multitude of believers in you who are going to seek spiritual nourishment—things that surpass every letter and every bodily perception?

**VERSE 10.**—“Have the people sit down.” The Teacher of truth first instructed his hearers in the simplicity of the letter, as though in lowly places, and in the simplicity of visible creation, so that they might thereby be raised to the height of contemplation.

**VERSE 14.**—“When those people had seen what Jesus had done,” and so forth. At that time they were progressing toward faith, but not yet with complete faith; therefore they did not know how to call him God. We, being more certain than they, say: [Col. 0381B] This is the Word, without whom there is neither prophet nor angel.

**VERSE 15.**—“Therefore Jesus.” Those who wish to seize him and make him king signify the disciples and other believers who wish to anticipate the time of his kingdom, thinking that he came in such a way that he would already reign. But during this time the kingdom is being gathered; at the end it will be revealed when he says: “Receive the kingdom prepared for you.”

Therefore he fled, not because he feared being seized—for afterward he spoke with those same people—but because he wished to signify that his height cannot be understood. He fled to the mountain, that is, he ascended into heaven, alone as priest interceding for the people who remained outside. Meanwhile the people were tossed by waves, and so he adds: “When evening came.”

The evening of the world is after Christ’s ascension, when the disciples descend into the labors of the world [Col. 0381C] and steer the ship, that is, the Church.

**VERSE 19.**—“They were afraid.” The disciples, who bore the figure of all who would later exist in the Church, saw the Lord coming toward them over the waves of the sea and were afraid. As another Evangelist says more explicitly, they thought he was a phantom. This is not without mystery. Even today many in the Church, when they hear themselves urged to abandon present and perishable goods for the sake of whatever eternal goods are to be possessed, are afraid and think that they have been deceived. To them the Lord says: “Do not be afraid; it is I.”

**VERSE 22.**—“The next day.” The crowd was given to understand that Jesus had walked upon the water, because there had been only one boat, Jesus had not entered it with the disciples, and there was no other way for the crossing to have taken place unless he had walked upon the water.

[Col. 0381D] **VERSE 25.**—“When they had found him.” Behold, he is present with those from whom he had fled lest they make him king. Why, then, had he fled, except because of the sacrament mentioned above? Again, present among them, he speaks so that he may fill the minds of those whose stomachs he had satisfied, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you.” He teaches those whom he appointed as teachers to flee praise and earthly power, yet nevertheless to persist in preaching.

**VERSE 26.**—“Amen, amen, I say to you.” After treating of his divinity, by which he is the same as the Father and is to be honored with the same honor, and of his humanity, by which he frees from death and raises up and is worthy of great honor, he now wishes to treat of the food of life, that is, the word of God.

This is the connection according to the meaning. Literally, however, it is as follows: You seek me not because of me, but because of the loaves that perish. Therefore work—that is, seek me because of me, not because of something else. For he is that food which remains unto eternal life, as he will state openly later. Similarly, many seek Jesus every day, not because of Jesus, but so that they may prosper in this present life.

**VERSE 27.**—“God the Father has sealed him.” He distinguished him from the others by his own seal, because the one who is the Son of Man is also the Son of God. Therefore do not despise me, the Son of Man, but ask me for spiritual food.

**VERSE 29.**—“This is the work of God.” Faith working through love is a work, because if ability is lacking, only the will is sought. Faith that works through love is rightly called a work, for it is the beginning and the end of every good thing.

[Col. 0382B] **VERSE 32.**—“Therefore he said.” By their preference of Moses’ work to his own, he showed that Moses’ work was lesser. It was not bread from heaven, but only a figure of that bread; his own work is greater, for he is the bread from heaven that gives life. This is the food that he said above remains unto eternal life.

**VERSE 33.**—“For the true bread.” The angels eat the pure Word as solid food; we eat the Word converted into milk. For if we cannot eat it, we can suck it. Unless he were made flesh, he could not be known or tasted by us.

**VERSE 34.**—“Lord, always give us this bread,” and so forth. When the Samaritan woman heard, “Whoever drinks from this water will never thirst,” she understood it bodily and, wishing to be free from labor and need, said: “Give me [Col. 0382C] this water.” In the same way these people seek bread that will refresh them and never fail, and for this reason they wished to make him king.

But Jesus calls them back to himself and explains more clearly what bread he meant: “I am the bread of life.” I can give life because I am life-giving bread, baked and formed by the fire of the Holy Spirit in the oven of the virgin womb, and given to the world to drive away the hunger of ignorance of God.

**VERSE 36.**—“But I told you.” As though he were saying: I did not speak of this bread because I knew you would be satisfied, but to rebuke your unbelief, because you see and do not believe.

**VERSE 37.**—“Everything that the Father gives me,” and so forth. That is, whatever the Father draws to me, the Father gives to the Son. The Father draws to the Son those who believe in the Son because they believe that he has God as Father. [Col. 0382D]

“He will come.” The humble person is united to me, who am humble, and therefore he is not cast outside. Being cast outside belongs only to the proud, who possess no interior good, either here or in the future.

**VERSE 39.**—“For this is the will of the Father who sent me,” and so forth. It is not God’s will that one of the little ones should perish. The swollen perish; from the little ones there is no loss.

“I should lose nothing,” and so forth. That is, because he sees me and believes in me, and I am life just as the Father is, he already has life now—not life belonging to him alone—and I will also raise him up.

**VERSE 40.**—“That everyone,” and so forth. Above he said: “Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me.” Here he says: [Col. 0383A] “Whoever sees the Son and believes in him.” He does not say: “Whoever believes in the Father,” because to believe in the Son is also to believe in the Father. For just as the Father has life in himself, so the Son also has life in himself.

**VERSE 41.**—“They were grumbling.” They did not know this bread or his heavenly Father. Inflated by their own righteousness, in which they presume on their own strength, they did not hunger for the righteousness of God that comes from heaven.

**VERSE 43.**—“Do not grumble.” As though he were saying: I am not bread that came down from heaven, as if I were not truly that bread; but no one can come to me unless drawn by the Father. Therefore you do not believe that I am the Father, because you have not been drawn by the Father.

**VERSE 44.**—“Unless the Father.” *(Augustine.)* The Father draws to the Son the one who believes in the Son because he thinks in this way, and so forth, up to the point where the great grace is commended.

“And I will raise him up,” and so forth. I, being equal to the Father, will make him see what he believes, eat what he hungers for, and possess what he has loved and desired. This cannot exist in the present, where he is only being drawn.

**VERSE 45.**—“It is written.” Truly no one comes to me unless the Father teaches him, because the prophecies bear witness to this. All the people of that kingdom—that is, of the Christian faith—will be taught by God. For although human beings speak outwardly, God alone opens the understanding inwardly and instructs it in the knowledge and love of truth. Thus everyone who hears and learns from the Father comes to me.

“In the prophets.” He says “prophets” in the plural because all the prophets, filled with one and the same Spirit, although they prophesied different things, nevertheless aimed at the same end.

[Col. 0383C] **VERSE 46.**—“Not that anyone has seen the Father,” and so forth. That is: I know the Father because I am from him. Therefore believe, because whoever believes in me has eternal life.

He could have said, “has me,” but instead he reveals that he himself is eternal life. The Word is the life of human beings; and to the flesh he had assumed—flesh through which death intervened so that he might remove death—he gives life in the resurrection, and he gives life to others who believe in him.

**VERSE 48–49.**—“I am the bread of life. Your fathers,” and so forth. The manna in which you boast, given to grumbling fathers whose sons you are, was not the bread of life, because they did not understand spiritual food in it. So also you, who hear me, do not understand spiritually. Moses and the other elect lived from the manna because they ate it spiritually. The same is true of those who now receive my words spiritually. [Col. 0383D]

“I am the bread of life.” Behold, he veils the sacrament in words, so that the Jews—and also some disciples—who did not believe his words might be scandalized, while the humble apostles, believing humbly, might be proved. Hence Peter says: “You have the words of eternal life.”

**VERSE 52.**—“And the bread,” and so forth. He determines how he is bread, not only according to the Word by which all things live, but also according to the flesh assumed for the life of the world.
