Human flesh was subject to sin and therefore dead; united and incorporated with his pure flesh, becoming one with him, it lives from his spirit, just as the body lives from its own spirit. Whoever is not of Christ’s body does not live from Christ’s spirit. [Col. 0384A]

Because the Jews did not belong to this unity, they argued. It is not explained to such people how the Lord gives his flesh to be eaten; rather, they heard what would stir them still more.

**VERSE 54.**—“Unless you eat the flesh,” and so forth. *(Augustine.)* He wishes this food and drink to be understood as fellowship, and so forth, up to the point where he says that from many grains there is one bread and from many grapes wine flows together.

**VERSE 55.**—“Whoever eats.” Some saints explain this as eating at the altar, and they speak well; but they ask how it becomes eternal life, since some receive it unto death, as the Apostle says. If someone eats at the altar with the kind of eating discussed here—that is, with faith working through love—he eats unto eternal life. If someone eats otherwise, it is unto death.

[Col. 0384B] **VERSE 56.**—“For my flesh.” The soul and the body will truly live from this food, because my flesh truly is food. It alone makes people immortal, so that they neither hunger nor thirst. No other food grants this, even if this is what one seeks from it.

**VERSE 57.**—“Whoever eats.” He now explains how what he has said comes about and what it means to eat the flesh and drink the blood: it means to remain in Christ and to have Christ remaining in oneself. Whoever does not remain in Christ, and in whom Christ does not remain, does not eat spiritually; thus he receives the sacrament bodily to his judgment.

**VERSE 58.**—“As the Father sent me.” The Father sent me, who am equal to him—that is, made me human—and therefore I refer my life to him as to one greater. “He himself will live.” [Col. 0384C] That I may live from the Father is brought about by my self-emptying; that a human being may live from me is brought about by participation, through which he eats me.

**VERSE 59.**—“This is the bread.” Thus it is established that this is truly the bread from heaven, not manna. Those fathers who ate manna, people like you, died forever; but the human being who eats this bread, though he did not possess life, will live forever.

Above he said: “I am the bread that came down from heaven.” Here he says: “This”—that is, the Son of Man, whose flesh I invite you to eat—is that bread which came down from heaven. Therefore the Son of Man and the Son of God are one and the same.

**VERSE 61.**—“Therefore many.” Many who think carnally suppose that he was promising to distribute among them, piece by piece, the flesh with which he was clothed. They consider it contrary to nature for him to give human flesh as human food.

[Col. 0384D] “This is a hard saying,” and so forth. *(Augustine.)* It had to be said in such a way that people would not understand it, but that God’s secret would be concealed in words. God’s secret ought to make people attentive, not hostile.

**VERSE 63.**—“If therefore,” and so forth. The sentence is interrupted, as though he were saying: Then you will understand that I do not offer my body in the same way you suppose, and that this grace is not consumed by bites. Rather, by giving myself to them through spiritual grace, I transform them into my body.

Here he plainly resolves what had disturbed them. They thought he would distribute his body, but he says that he will ascend into heaven, certainly whole and entire. What, then, should be held? He adds openly:

**VERSE 64.**—“It is the Spirit who gives life.” The flesh, as you understand it—as flesh purchased in the market, like any other food—does not profit. Yet the flesh itself, as a vessel of the Spirit who works salvation in it, profits greatly. So too knowledge alone puffs up, yet knowledge itself is not evil; through love it builds up. [Col. 0385A]

“The words that I have spoken,” by which I said that I must be eaten, that I must remain in them and they in me. For someone to remain in Christ as a member, and Christ in that person as in a temple, unity is required. Unity comes from love, and love comes from the Spirit. Therefore the Spirit who gives life does not separate the members joined together.

**VERSE 65.**—“But there are some,” and so forth. “Prophet: Unless you believe, you will not understand.” Through faith we are joined together; through understanding we are given life.

“And who will betray him.” Judas withdraws among those who were scandalized, but remains in order to plot against him. The Lord neither keeps silent about him nor openly identifies him, so that all may be afraid while one perishes.

**VERSE 66.**—“For no one can,” and so forth. He adds the reason why some do not believe: it has not been given by God. Faith does not arise from human beings as something their own, but from God as grace.

**VERSE 67.**—“From this point,” and so forth. Learn to speak cautiously. Yet if someone is scandalized by your words, he has consolation in the fact that many were scandalized by the saying of the one whose example is offered to you.

**VERSE 71.**—“Did I not choose you?” The number twelve is sacred and remains, even though Judas perishes from it. He chose eleven to remain; he chose Judas so that through him the divine dispensation of mercy might be fulfilled for the salvation of the world, using evil for good, just as evil people use God’s good things for evil.

## CHAPTER VII

**VERSE 1.**—“After these things.” While remaining in the flesh, the Lord frequently walked in Galilee, so that those who wish to imitate him may learn to pass from vices to virtues, which Galilee signified. Or it was so that the holy people of that time might await the passage of the word of God from Judea to the Gentiles.

**VERSE 2.**—“The feast.” It is not called this because it was one day, for there were seven days; but, according to their custom, all the days together are called as one because of the one feast. The feast of Tabernacles was so called because in the seventh month the Jews lived in tabernacles, in memory of those in which their fathers had lived in the desert. [Col. 0385D]

**VERSE 3.**—“So that your disciples also.” The works known to true disciples should be proclaimed with divine praise, not with popular favor.

**VERSE 4.**—“No one.” They are concerned for his glory. As though they were saying: You do marvelous things, but in secret; make yourself known so that everyone may praise you.

**VERSE 6.**—“My time.” Therefore my time is not now, but your time is, because I am not a lover of the world as you are, but its accuser. Therefore the world does not listen to you, its false witnesses, who call good evil and evil good.

[Col. 0386A] **VERSE 8.**—“For I am not going up.” *(Augustine.)* Some say that this refers to the Passion, because he did not ascend the cross at the Feast of Tabernacles, but at Passover, when the lamb is customarily killed.

**VERSE 10.**—“Not openly,” and so forth. Typologically: Christ went up secretly to the feast because he was hidden in all those figures, although he is now manifest to us. His being hidden provides an example of avoiding the wicked; his speaking openly and not being seized by those who sought him reveals his power.

**VERSE 16.**—“He answered them: My teaching is not mine.” The teaching is not that of a human being, but of God. Or: it is not the word of no one, but the teaching of someone—namely, of him who is the Word. His teaching is not his own, but that of the one from whom he is. This means: “I am not from myself.”

Because he saw that not everyone would understand this profound matter, he gave them counsel: “If anyone wishes to understand, let him believe.” That is: If someone believes that I am the Son of God, he will recognize concerning the teaching—that is, he will understand—that my teaching is not mine.

**VERSE 18.**—“Whoever speaks from himself.” The Antichrist is not truthful, and injustice is in him because he seeks his own glory, not God’s. He was not sent by God, but permitted to come.

“But whoever,” and so forth. That is: I, although equal to the Father, nevertheless seek the Father’s glory, not my own, in the form of a servant. In this he gives an example of humility, so that we may attribute every good thing to God.

**VERSE 19.**—“Did not Moses give you the Law?” I speak from God and seek his glory; I am truthful and just. But you, who boast in the Law, seek to kill me contrary to the Law, which forbids killing.

[Col. 0386C] **VERSE 20.**—“You have a demon.” They seek to kill him and, what is worse, say that he has a demon, although he drives out demons.

**VERSE 21.**—“I performed one work.” You marvel at one work; what would you do if you saw everything? The one work was that he healed the whole man on the Sabbath. Therefore the foolish observers of the Sabbath were disturbed, but Moses convicts them by commanding circumcision on the eighth day, which sometimes falls on the Sabbath.

This is the point: no one should be disturbed if salvation is always accomplished, even on the Sabbath. Let everyone know that acts of salvation must always be performed.

**VERSE 22.**—“Circumcision.” *(Alcuin.)* Circumcision was given for three reasons. First, and so forth, up to the point where it says that the heart is stripped of desires.

[Col. 0386D] **VERSE 23.**—“If a man receives circumcision,” and so forth. As though he were saying: You who boast in the Law are dealing with my death contrary to the Law that announces me. Yet it is not contrary to the Law that I, the Lord of the Sabbath, made the whole man well on the Sabbath.

The observance of the Sabbath, like everything else, exists for human salvation. Thus, when you yourselves circumcise on the Sabbath because it pertains to salvation, you do not believe that you are breaking the Sabbath.

**VERSE 24.**—“Do not judge,” and so forth. You ought not to be angry with me for saving a man on the Sabbath, just as you are not angry about circumcision on the Sabbath. One must not judge according to appearance—that is, according to the actions of persons—so that what was permitted to Moses may not be permitted to me. Rather, judge with a just judgment, that is, according to the truth of things. [Col. 0387A]

Once you know this truth, you will condemn neither me nor Moses, nor say that I oppose him. In this he rebukes them and instructs us not to show partiality when judging cases—not that we should fail to honor persons differently according to differences of rank.

**VERSE 25.**—“Therefore they were saying.” Although he had gone up to the feast secretly, he speaks openly, and the power that had been thought to be timidity appears. Some marvel that the one whose death was so earnestly sought is not seized by force. Since they do not yet fully understand that the power is his, they suppose it is the rulers’ knowledge, for they had learned that he was the Christ.

Therefore they say to themselves that this cannot be the Christ, since no one knows where the Christ is from. For although the prophets speak of the place of his birth and matters of this kind, his eternal birth is from the Father. Hence the Prophet says: “Who can recount his generation?” (Isaiah 53). Christ therefore answers both points: his weakness and his majesty.

**VERSE 28.**—“You know me, and you know where I am from.” That is, you know the appearance of my face, and you know my birth and parents. You know me according to the flesh, but not according to divinity, because I did not come from myself.

They did not know that he was the Son of God or that he had been sent by the Father. They did not know God the Father, who is the true begetter of Truth himself. But how can they know? He adds: “I know him.” Therefore seek me and believe in me, because no one knows the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him (Mark 11).

**VERSE 29.**—“But I know him.” I know him because I am from him, and so forth. In brief, he embraces both points: “I am from him,” because the Son is from the Father, while the Father is not from another; and “you see me in the flesh,” because he sent me. Here the authority of the begetter and the nature he shares with human beings are both affirmed.

**VERSE 30.**—“His hour.” This does not mean that the event was compelled by necessity, but that it awaited the opportunity determined by his will. He wished to be born at the proper time, after a long succession of heralds. Likewise, the preacher of the Gospel wished to die at the proper time.

**VERSE 32.**—“The Pharisees heard.” The enraged rulers heard the murmur by which the crowd glorified Christ and sought to kill him. Yet, since he did not yet wish to be seized, they could not apprehend him; they merely heard him teaching.

[Col. 0387D] **VERSE 33.**—“For a little while longer.” As though he were saying: What you now wish to do, you will do afterward, but not now, because I am still with you for a little while, during which I must fulfill my dispensation. Then I am going to the one who sent me; then I must suffer.

You who now do not wish to hear me, present and performing miracles, will seek me after the resurrection and ascension, when great miracles will be performed through the apostles by my power and when a great multitude will believe. Then, pierced by remorse for the great crime of Christ’s death, they said to Peter: “What shall we do?”

“I am with you, and I am going.” He does not say, “I will be,” but “I am,” because although, as a human being, he changes places, as God he does not change, since he is everywhere. Hence elsewhere: “The Son of Man who is in heaven”—as though he were saying this while speaking on earth.

### Verse 34

“You cannot come.” He does not say, “You will be able,” but “You can.” For such were they then that they could not, just as elsewhere he says to Peter: “You cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward” (John 13). Thus no despair is expressed concerning these people either.

### Verse 35

“To themselves,” etc. Hence they did not know what they were saying to the Lord, and yet, without knowing what was going to happen, they foretold it. For although he is not going to the Gentiles through the apostles who were then present, he is nevertheless going to the Gentiles who will believe.

### Verse 36

“Who is this?” While they had unknowingly prophesied the truth, by repeating the same question they show that they prophesied out of ignorance, so that they may seem rather to have been ignorant than to have prophesied.

### Verse 37

“But on the last day.” After the Jews’ disputes about Jesus, and after the words he spoke by which some would be condemned and others instructed, on the last day of the Feast of Booths he calls out—not merely by speaking but by crying aloud—so that whoever thirsts may come to him.

“If anyone thirsts.” Let him drink the Spirit, as he explains afterward; and when he has drunk, rivers of living water will flow from his belly. The belly is the conscience of the heart, which, cleansed by drinking the Spirit, lives and possesses a spring. And it itself is the spring or river that flows through benevolence, when one wishes to benefit one’s neighbor. Whoever thinks that his own goods are sufficient for himself alone was not that spring.

(JEROME.) I boldly and with complete freedom declare that from that time onward, etc., up to the point where, when Jesus was led to his Passion, they deny him and swear that they do not know Christ.

### Verses 39–40

“For the Spirit had not yet been given,” etc. Although the prophets had received the same Spirit, as had John and others before Christ’s resurrection, a different, more open and fuller manner of giving was still to come. After the resurrection, when he first appeared to the apostles, he breathed upon their faces—the one who by his first breath had given life to the first man and raised him from the clay. Thus, signifying that he himself was the same one, he breathed the Spirit upon the apostles so that they might rise from the mud.

Then, after the Ascension, he sent the Spirit more fully in tongues of fire, so that they might teach all nations, just as at that time they spoke in all languages. So now the unity of the Church speaks in all languages; whoever is cut off from that unity does not have the Spirit.

“Because Jesus had not yet been glorified,” etc. “From that crowd,” etc. But after they had been baptized in the Holy Spirit and the grace of the Holy Spirit had been poured out upon them, they then spoke freely to the rulers of the Jews: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5). They raised the dead, rejoiced amid scourging, shed their blood, and were crowned with other punishments. Therefore the Spirit was not yet in the apostles, nor were spiritual graces flowing from their belly, because the Lord had not yet been glorified.

### Verse 45

“So they came.” Sent to seize him, they returned free from guilt and filled with wonder, bearing witness to the divine teaching.

### Verse 47

“Have you also been deceived?” They had been commendably deceived: having abandoned the evil of unbelief, they had passed over to faith.

### Verse 48

“Has any one of the rulers believed in him?” Those who teach the Law despise the one who sent the Law; but those who did not know the Law believe in the one who gave the Law, so that what is said might be fulfilled: “That those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9).

### Verse 51

“Does our Law?” Because those wicked men wanted to be condemners before they had become informed, whereas this man thought that, if they patiently listened to him while he was present, they might perhaps become like the officers who preferred to believe rather than to seize him, he wishes to lead them by the authority of the Law to be willing first to hear him.

### Verses 52–53

“And you are a Galilean,” etc. “And they returned,” etc. Jesus was called a Galilean because his parents were from Nazareth.

## Chapter VIII

### Verse 1

“But Jesus.” Since it was his custom to teach in the temple by day and return in the evening to Bethany, which is on the Mount of Olives.

Mystically: This signifies the height of mercy, from which we receive chrism, that is, anointing. In the morning he returns to the temple. Morning is the rising of new light after the darkness of the Law, at which he comes to reveal and give mercy to the faithful, that is, to those who are in his temple. Sitting signifies the humility of the Incarnation, through which he has mercy and teaches. Hence the people come to him more willingly, but the hostile Pharisees test him concerning justice, to see whether he says anything against it.

They knew that he was meek and a preacher of mercy, and therefore that he pleased the people. Thus they supposed that he would say that the adulterous woman should be released; and in that case he would be called an enemy of the Law, opposed to Moses and to God its author, and guilty of death together with the adulteress. But if, according to the Law, he said that she should be stoned, they would mock him as though he did not possess the meekness that he preached and for which he was loved.

He is not ensnared by either accusation. Preserving meekness, he answers with what belongs to true justice: “Let him who is without sin cast the first stone at her.” Yet he does not immediately judge; instead, bending down, he writes with his finger on the ground.

### Verse 3

“They bring her.” Mystically: The woman caught in adultery signifies the Synagogue, which committed adultery against the Law of Moses by following the traditions of the fathers. Or she signifies one who, having abandoned the Law of Moses, now follows the faith of Christ; hence the Jew now accuses her as though an adulteress. Or she signifies the Church, which, having abandoned God, had fornicated with demons; the Jew accuses her for approaching Christ and regards her as a new kind of idolatry.

### Verse 6

“But Jesus, bending down.” What he wrote on the ground—whether their words or something else—has not been determined. He bends down and writes with his finger. Nevertheless, he teaches that before judgment is rendered we ought to bend down, that is, to condescend in judgment or to exercise discernment when acting.

### Verse 8

“And bending down again.” Having delivered the sentence of justice by which those conscious of their evil were struck, he again writes on the ground, as was his custom, turning his face away, so that those whom he foresaw would leave more quickly than they would ask further questions might be free to depart. He teaches us that, just as before correcting another we should examine ourselves humbly, so also afterward, lest the same or something similar be found in us.

### Verse 11

“Neither will I condemn you.” Because she could fear that this man, who was without sin, would punish her, he says to her, as the merciful one who forgives past sins: “Neither will I condemn you,” while, as the just one, forbidding her to sin any further.

### Verse 12

“Then Jesus spoke again.” After the tempters had been driven away and the woman’s guilt had been healed, he adds more openly what he can do by his divinity, so that they may not be uncertain whether he, as a man, can forgive sins.

“I am the light of the world.” This light is covered by the cloud of flesh and is thereby made bearable to human beings. Hence I can both forgive sins and illuminate the human being.

### Verse 13

“Testimony.” They think that he should not be believed. As though they said: “He testifies about himself alone,” forgetting the lamps mentioned earlier and John the Baptist himself, who clearly bore witness about him.

### Verse 14

“My testimony is true.” My testimony must be regarded as true because I know where I come from—that is, because it is confirmed by the Father’s testimony. I came, sent by the Father, yet without abandoning him; and when my ministry is completed I return to the Father, yet I do not leave the world.

### Verse 15

“You judge according to the flesh.” Because you do not know this, you judge according to the flesh: that is, you think I am a human being whose claim to honor should not be believed, and you even condemn me.

“I judge no one.” I do not judge according to the flesh, as you do; or, at this first coming, I do not judge at all, but save. Yet because he will judge at his second coming, he adds: “And if I do judge,” etc.

### Verse 16

“Because I am not alone” (AUGUSTINE). It is true because I am not alone, but I and the Father. Behold, then, two in persons, although one in substance. This means: My judgment is true because I am the true Son of God; and it is proved that I am the Son because I am not alone, but the Father is with me.

### Verse 17

“And it is written in your Law.” (IDEM.) Having spoken about judgment, that his and the Father’s testimony is true, he proves it by the authority of the Law. For it is said, etc., up to the point where the accused Susanna had it.

### Verse 19

“Then they said to him.” Judging according to the flesh, they understood Christ’s Father carnally. But the man was visible openly, while the Father’s Word was hidden.

“Where is your Father?” As though they said: “We see you, but not the Father with you.” In response they are told: “You know neither me nor my Father.” For if you do not know what I am in secret, although you see the man, then you do not know the Father either. But if you knew me—which comes first—you would know me, and thus you would know the Father, because we are one.

“Perhaps the Father also,” etc. He does not doubt; rather, he mocks and rebukes their doubt, as a master might say to a servant, “Perhaps I am your master.”

### Verse 20

“These words,” etc. *Gaza* means riches; *phylassein* means to guard.

Typologically: The treasury is the mysteries of Scripture, which are in the temple, that is, in Christ. He opened these secrets to the apostles after the resurrection, but at this time he speaks in parables to the Jews who do not understand.

“And no one seized him.” That is, while he was speaking about his divinity.

### Verse 21

“I am going away.” As though voluntarily, and therefore you labor in vain. He is going to the place from which he had come and from which he had never departed.

“You will seek me,” because you will pursue him after he has been taken up into heaven, not desiring to have him as friends. Hence he foretells their punishment: “You will die in your sin.”

### Verse 22

“Will he kill himself?” These are foolish words, as though, if he were speaking about death, they could not follow him to death. He was speaking not about death but about the glory to which he was going through death. Therefore he adds to those carnal people:

### Verse 23

“You are from below.” And therefore you have earthly thoughts; like the serpent, you eat the earth.

### Verse 24

“Therefore I said to you.” Here he explains what it means to be from the world: to be sinful unbelievers who think earthly thoughts. He explains this to them.

“For if.” In contrast, he gives hope to those who will believe.

“You will believe.” He says, “You will believe,” not “You will perceive,” because no one now grasps the immutable essence.

“I am,” and “you will die,” etc. He does not say what he is—whether Christ, the Son of God, or something of that kind—but he uses toward them the expression of eternal essence, just as formerly toward Moses, whom he was sending to liberate Israel. It is as though he said: “I who sent Moses to liberate the children of Israel have come in my own person to liberate the lost.” Everything else that is sent is not truly what it is.

### Verse 25

“Principle” (AUGUSTINE). Believe that I am the Principle, etc., up to the point where he himself is the right hand, strength, wisdom, and Word of the Father.

(IDEM.) Behold what “being” means: the Principle remains in himself, renews all things, and cannot be changed.

“I speak to you.” I have many things to say to you: teaching if you believe, accusing if you do not believe. Though I do not now judge but save, I will afterward judge.

“I have,” I say, but everything comes from the Father, who is true in himself. From him I am the truth whom he generated from himself; therefore I speak true things and judge. Behold how he gives glory to the Father, to whom he is equal, so that he may teach us, who are lesser, to give glory to God.

### Verse 27

“And they did not understand.” When he says, “The one who sent me is true,” they did not understand that he was speaking about the Father, because their eyes were still closed. Therefore he adds to them: “When you have lifted up the Son,” etc. There he shows that some among them would believe after his Passion and would recognize who he was.

### Verse 29

“Because I am.” Being is the immutable substance of divinity. But lest the speaker himself be understood to be the Father, he adds: “I do nothing of myself,” because I am not from myself but from the Father.

“Because I,” etc. Equality itself is eternal. It is always so—not from some beginning and thereafter, but without beginning and without end. For God’s generation has no beginning in time, because through the Only-Begotten the ages were made.

### Verse 30

“Many believed in him.” Faith is believing what you do not see; truth is seeing what you believed. We do not know in order to believe; we believe in order to know. Therefore Christ, as man on earth, plants faith, and afterward will grant that he may be seen; that is the reward of faith.

### Verse 31

“True disciples.” You will reach this height through faith, which is humble, despised, and is a mustard seed.

### Verses 33–34

“Free.” The Lord used this word to refer to freedom, not in the sense in which Latin commonly speaks of someone being freed from weakness. The Lord had not said, “You will be freed,” but “The truth will free you.” Yet by this statement they understood only carnal freedom.

“He answered them,” etc. Not those who believed, but others in the crowd who did not believe were indignant when they heard, “It will free you,” because they thought he had spoken about carnal freedom.

“We have never been slaves.” They are lying. Joseph served in Egypt; their fathers served in Egypt in the mud; and these very people served through Caesar’s taxes.

“Amen, amen, I say,” etc. *Amen* is Hebrew and means “true” in Latin. No translator changed it, lest, once stripped bare, it become cheap; rather, it should retain the honor of a secret word. It is like an oath. Hence Jerome, commenting on Isaiah, says: “The Lord swears by himself, because he does not render void the sentence of his mouth and the word that he has once uttered”—that is, he swore by himself.

### Verse 35

“But the servant,” etc. In this he terrified us. What hope, then, is there of freedom for those who are not without sin?

### Verse 37

“I know,” etc. After the Lord had exposed those who gloried in the empty freedom of the flesh and in the true slavery of sin, and had granted that these people were children of Abraham according to the flesh, he shows that such people are not children of Abraham through imitation of his faith and justice. Rather, they are children of the murderous devil, seeking to kill him and thus truly being slaves.

### Verse 39

“They answered and said to him.” Because he accused them of doing the works of their father, they confess that their father is Abraham and provoke him to say something against Abraham, so that they might have an opportunity to do what they wanted. But the Lord praises Abraham and condemns these degenerate descendants, saying: “If you were children of Abraham,” etc.

### Verse 40

“But now you seek,” etc. He does not say—as he could have—that he is Abraham’s Lord, lest this provide an occasion for accusation; nor does he say that he is the Son of God. Rather, he speaks of what they envy and of what they are able to kill.

### Verse 41

“You do the works,” etc. He now indicates another father, whose children they are not by nature but by imitation.

“We,” etc. Now understanding that the Lord was not speaking about the origin of the flesh but about life, and knowing from the usage of Scripture that fornication is spoken of spiritually when the soul is subjected to false gods, they change their answer. They now remain silent about their father Abraham, lest it be said to them, “Why do you glory in one whose life you do not imitate?” They call God their father, wishing to see what he could say to them about this.

### Verse 42

“Then Jesus said.” Just as he previously showed that Abraham was not their father, so now he shows that God is not their father, because they do not recognize the Son whom he sent, nor do they love him.

“For I.” His procession from the Father is eternal; in it the Only-Begotten Son is equal to the Father. He came as a man made flesh, and in this respect he is a brother to human beings.

### Verse 43

“Why do you not understand my speech?” The matter is as I say, but you cannot understand what I say, because you cannot hear when you are unwilling to be corrected through believing.

“And why is this?” Because you are from the devil; you have chosen to remain children of the devil.

### Verse 44

“You are from your father,” etc. He now determines who their father is. They are his children not by being born from him, as the Manichaeans say, but by imitating him. Hence it is also said to the Jews: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite” (Ezekiel 16).

“And the desires.” You are children of the devil because you wish to do the desires of your father and to kill me in the flesh, since you cannot kill me in the mind.

“He was a murderer.” Note that a murderer is not only one who kills with a sword, but also one who kills by a word, as the devil did to the first parents. Hence in the Psalm: “Their tongue is a sharp sword” (Psalm 56).

“And he did not stand in the truth.” Why did he not stand? Because there is no truth in him—that is, the Word and wisdom of the Father. When it is said that truth is in Christ, it is said in such a way that he himself is the truth. Therefore, if the devil had stood in the truth, he would have stood in Christ; but he did not stand in it, because it is not in him.

“He speaks from his own,” because he is a liar. But this is not enough, since a human being also is a liar, and does not possess what is his own, but began from what was another’s, namely, from the devil. Therefore he added: “And he is its father,” namely, the father of the lie that he invented.

“From his own.” Because he has it from nowhere else but from himself, after he fell from the truth. Hence it is added that he is the father of the lie, which he generated from himself, just as God generates truth from himself.

### Verse 46

“Which of you,” etc. He does not disdain to demonstrate through reason that he is not a sinner, etc.

### Verse 48

“Do we not say,” etc. Because they had been convicted of not being children of Abraham or of God but of the devil, they hurl insults, since they could not resist him.

### Verse 49

“I honor.” I do not make much of myself (lest I seem arrogant to you); I do what I ought, but you do not do what you ought, because you have not honored me. If you knew me, just as I honor the Father, so you would honor me.

### Verse 50

“But I.” Having heard the insult, “You have a demon,” he says in response concerning his glory only this: “I honor the Father,” attributing everything to him. I do not seek my own glory as human beings do, who return something when insults are inflicted upon them; rather, I reserve it for the Father, and there is one who seeks and judges.

There are two kinds of testing. One is the testing of examination, concerning which it is said: “God is testing you” (Deuteronomy 13). The other is the testing of deception, concerning which it is said: “God is not a tempter of evil” (James 2).

So too there are two fears: one which charity casts out, and another which remains forever and ever.

There are also two judgments: one of condemnation, in which the Father does not judge, but has given all judgment to the Son; the other of discernment, concerning which it is said: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause” (Psalm 42).

In this sense he says: “There is a Father who seeks my glory and distinguishes it from your glory,” because you glory according to the world, whereas I do not. Rather, I glory in the glory that I had with the Father before the world existed, which is distinct from human vanity.

### Verse 51

“Amen, amen, I say to you.” It is not I but the Father who seeks my glory. I, however, say to you: Although you say, “You have a demon,” I call you to life. From this let the human being learn to return good, not evil.

“He will not see.” When Scripture says “see” or “taste,” it means nothing other than “experience.”

### Verse 52

“Now we know.” Just as a good person becomes better when insulted, so an evil person becomes worse through a benefit.

### Verse 53

“Whom do you make yourself?” According to them, he was making himself the Son of God, equal to God, as though he were not so. But he was not making himself so; rather, he truly was. Hence the Apostle says: “He did not regard it as robbery to be equal with God” (Philippians 2). Therefore they do not ask, “Who are you?” but, “Whom do you make yourself?”

### Verse 54

“Jesus answered.” In response to their question, “Whom do you make yourself?” he refers his glory to the Father, from whom he has what he is as God.

### Verse 55

“He is my Father.” He openly says that his Father is the God who was announced to the Jews: “I am not announcing to you a new God, but the one whose knowledge you customarily boast of.”

“He who glorifies.” The Father’s voice glorifies the Son at his baptism, on the mountain, and in other such events.

“And you have not known him.” You have not known him spiritually, while you have served earthly things. Behold, he sees them openly resisting him, yet he does not cease to preach himself to them.

“And if I say,” etc. Lest he appear to glory arrogantly in this, he adds, “And if I say.” Arrogance must be avoided in such a way that truth is not abandoned.

### Verse 56

“Abraham.” Believing, he rejoiced in hope, so that by understanding he might see so great a mystery.

“My day” (AUGUSTINE). It is uncertain whether this refers to a temporal day, etc., up to: “and that the very same was made flesh?”

### Verse 59

“And he went out.” Going out of the temple—that is, out of the figures of the Jews—let us see what he did in the temple of the Gentiles.

## Chapter IX

### Verse 1

“And passing by.” He was not standing in the way of sinners, but beside the way of our mortality.

“A blind man.” The blind man signifies the human race, in which blindness is natural, because, when the first human being sinned, a defect grew within nature. Hence, according to the mind, every human being is born blind.

### Verse 3

“Neither did this man sin.” They did indeed sin, but he was not born blind because of that sin. Rather, the cause is that the works of God might be manifested in him. By illuminating him, and by signifying through him what the Son of God would do in the blindness of the human race, the Son of God is manifested. Hence he adds: “I must work.”

### Verse 5

“As long as I am in the world.” Christ was not light in the world only at that time, but is always with the elect through faith until the consummation of the age, and this is the time for working.

That night is the infernal night, in which no one is permitted to work, just as the rich man in the flames was not permitted to work. It is only the time for receiving.

### Verse 6

“And he made clay.” Just as he formed the first man from the clay of the earth, so through the same kind of clay he reformed the human race.

He made clay from saliva because the Word became flesh. Saliva is the wisdom that proceeded from the mouth of the Most High. The earth is Christ’s flesh.

“He anointed his eyes.” That is, he made him a catechumen, one who believes that the Word became flesh. The anointed man does not yet see, but he is sent to wash—that is, to be baptized in the One who was sent, namely, in Christ. For this reason the name of the pool is interpreted accordingly. After being baptized, he received light from his sins.

### Verse 7

“And he came back seeing,” etc. The question arises how he healed this man without faith, since it is written that no one whose interior healing was absent was healed outwardly. But this is said of those who were sick because of sins. This man was not afflicted because of sin, but for the glory of God.

### Verse 16

“This man is not from God,” etc. The one who keeps the Sabbath spiritually is without sin; those who are slaves of sin do not keep it.

### Verse 17

“What do you say about him?” They seek an accusation so that he might be expelled from the synagogue, but be found by Christ.

“But he said,” etc. He is still anointed in the heart; he confesses, yet does not lie.

### Verse 18

“Until they called,” etc. Mystically: The parents signify the devil or vices, who say: “He is of age; let him speak for himself.” They do not wish the human being to confess Christ.

“Give glory to God. We know,” etc. To give glory to God is to speak the truth about someone as though God were present; that is: “Confess, as we do, that this man is not God but a sinner.”

### Verse 27

“Why do you want to hear it again?” (AUGUSTINE.) He becomes angry at their hardness: the blind man has become seeing, and he can no longer endure the blind.

### Verse 28

“Then they reviled him.” According to their hearts, this was a curse. But what is said is desirable for everyone: that they should be Christ’s disciples.

### Verse 29

“We do not know where this man is from.” Earlier they had said, “We know this man.” Hence here they say that they do not know him. But we say that we do not know what we reject.

He is unknown because he is concealed by humility; he is revealed by the power of signs. They do not know where he is from, yet as God he illuminates the blind.

### Verse 33

“If this man were not from God,” etc. Disregarding their anger, he freely confesses the truth. For these things could be done only by the Lord; nor could they be done by the disciples unless God were in them.

### Verse 34

“You were born entirely in sins.” That is, with closed eyes. They say that this is because of the sins of his parents, but Christ heals the whole person: outside, the eyes; within, he opens the heart.

“And are you teaching us?” And they expelled him. By questioning him so often in order to learn, they had made him a teacher; but, ungrateful, they expelled the one who was teaching. Yet because he was expelled, he became more truly a Christian.

### Verse 36

“Who is he?” Still un-anointed, by these words he shows that his heart had long been prepared to believe, but that he did not know in whom he ought to believe.

### Verse 37

“And you have seen him.” Now the Lord washes the face of the anointed man; now he illuminates the eyes of his heart, and he confesses not only the Son of Man but also the Son of God.

### Verse 39

“That those who do not see.” That is, those who think they see seek to see; and those who see—that is, those who think they see—do not seek the physician. This is judgment, that is, discernment, which distinguishes the cause of believers from that of the proud.

He will not now make the judgment of condemnation, but he will make it at the end. Hence: “I judge no one.”

## Chapter X

### Verse 1

“Amen, amen, I say to you.” Because the Pharisees boasted that they could see, which they could have done if they had been Christ’s sheep, the Lord sets forth a comparison concerning his flock and the gate by which one enters the sheepfold, against their arrogance.

He shows that neither wisdom, nor observance of the Law, nor a good life has any value except through him. Without him they are nothing, whether among Jews or Gentiles, among philosophers or Pharisees who teach how to live happily, or among heretics under the name of Christ. Yet they do not preach Christ; all of them, without him, seize and kill.

“Through the gate.” That is, through me, as he explains afterward. This gate is humble. Whoever wishes to enter through it must humble himself, lest, if he is upright and exalted, he stumble against the lowly gate.

“A thief.” Because he calls what belongs to another his own—that is, he makes God’s sheep his own.

“A robber.” Because he kills what he has stolen.

But all who hold and teach the truth in Christ the shepherd are one shepherd.

### Verse 2

“The shepherd of the sheep.” Christ is properly the shepherd according to the office of feeding the sheep, as he himself explains afterward: he enters the sheepfold through the gate.

But because others share with him in the pastoral office, what is properly said of him also applies to them in their own manner. The gate is the means by which one enters. Therefore Christ is shepherd and, by himself, the gate; and every shepherd under him enters the hearts of the sheep through that gate. If he preaches something else, the sheep do not listen; if he preaches Christ, Christ’s sheep recognize the voice.

### Verse 3

“To him the gatekeeper opens.” The gatekeeper is Christ, who opens himself; or Scripture, which leads to Christ; or the Holy Spirit, who teaches all truth.

“And the sheep,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) Some are true sheep because the Lord knows them, etc., up to the point where no one of his own despises this voice and no outsider hears it.

### Verse 6

“But they did not understand.” The predestined sheep do not know themselves for a time, nor do they hear the shepherd’s voice, but they persevere at the end. Conversely, wolves hear for a time, but they persevere at the end.

### Verse 8

“All,” etc. A thief is one who enters against Christ through simony or in some other way; after entering, he kills by a bad example, and thus is openly a robber.

Such a person should not be called a hireling merely because, when the wolf comes, he does not resist but yields for the sake of his payment. If he does not resist when the wolf violently drags the sheep away, he receives this payment: he is not dragged away with the sheep, but afterward, by living badly, corrupts them and, having fallen away to another side, becomes a thief or robber, losing the name of hireling.

### Verse 9

“If anyone.” Here he clearly shows that not only the shepherd but also the sheep enter through the gate.

“And he will enter.” He will enter by thinking good thoughts within and go out by doing good deeds as an example to others. Or he will enter the Church so that he may live here by faith. Hence he later says: “That they may have life.”

And he will go out from this life so that he may live forever. Hence afterward he says that he will have life more abundantly, and that, entering and going out, he will find pasture.

### Verse 10

“Except that he may steal,” etc. He steals by appropriating another’s property for himself; he slaughters by withdrawing someone from the faith; he destroys by leading him into eternal condemnation.

### Verse 12

“But the hireling,” etc. A hireling is one who seeks what belongs to himself, not what belongs to Christ; one who serves God not for God’s sake but for some reward. He is blameworthy and is not a son, yet he is necessary and must be tolerated.

A thief, however, must always be avoided. The superiors who are sons are also shepherds, yet there is one shepherd, because they are all members of the one whose sheep they are as his own.

“And the wolf seizes.” The wolf is either a violent person who ravages bodily or the devil who destroys spiritually. Whoever seeks not the souls of the sheep but his own interests does not confront him by resisting or rebuking evil; this is to flee, because fear is the flight of the soul. He flees lest he lose what he loves. Hence, giving the reason for his flight, he adds: “Because he is a hireling and does not care for the sheep,” but for his own interests.

Shepherds, however, are not said to flee if they yield to persecution while preserving themselves for the benefit of the sheep. Even when bodily absent from them, they are present to them in spirit.

### Verse 14

“I am the shepherd.” After exposing the fault of the false shepherd, he again sets forth the form of the true shepherd.

“I am the good shepherd, and I lay down my life for the sheep.” He alone did this, yet not as though he were separate from all his own, since he and they are one. He could do this without them; they cannot do anything without him.

### Verse 15

“And I.” The Son knows the Father by himself; we know the Father through him, as it says elsewhere: “No one has ever seen God, except the Only-Begotten who is in the bosom of the Father; he has revealed him” (Matthew 11).

Likewise: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matthew 11; Luke 10).

“And I lay down my life.” This is proof of love for the Father and for the sheep. So Peter, confessing his love three times, is commanded to feed the sheep and to die for them.

“For the sheep.” For the sheep of the house of Israel who had perished, to whom he was sent bodily. They are not unlike those who are from the Gentiles. Hence he says:

### Verse 16

“I must.” Although he does this through his own people, because he himself is in them.

“And my voice.” He does not say “the voice of my people,” because he himself speaks in them.

### Verse 17

“Because I,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) The Word by whom he assumed a human being—that is, flesh and soul, etc., up to the point where it is said that this happened not by his own power but by the power of the divinity dwelling in the flesh.

### Verse 22

“Now the Feast of Dedication took place,” etc. *Caenon* means “new”; hence *encaenia*, that is, initiation or dedication. The *encaenia* were the festival of the dedication of the temple, which was carried out by Judas Maccabaeus in winter.

Winter is mentioned here to signify the coldness of the Jews, who do not approach the fire—that is, who do not believe in Christ.

Solomon dedicated the temple after its construction in autumn (1 Kings 8). Zerubbabel and the priest Joshua dedicated the temple rebuilt after the captivity in spring (2 Esdras 6). Judas Maccabaeus dedicated it in winter after Antiochus’s profanation (1 Maccabees 4).

### Verse 23

“In the portico.” The porticoes that surrounded the temple are commonly signified by the name “temple.”

### Verse 24

“So the Jews surrounded him.” While the Lord patiently preached the truth amid insults, they did not submit but tested him: “How long will you take away our life?” They accuse the one who saves of taking away their lives. They thought he was merely a man, although one destined to reign above all.

“If you are the Christ, tell us openly.” They do not desire the truth but prepare an accusation, so that, if he says he is a king, they may hand him over to the authorities as one acting against Augustus.

But the Lord moderates his response so that there may be no room for accusation against them, and so that it may plainly appear to the faithful, for whose sake these things are reported, that he himself is the Christ—not merely a man, as they suppose, but the Son of God.

### Verse 29

“And no one can snatch them from the hand of my Father.” Because, by virtue of what I am from the Father, I am greater for protecting than they are for attacking.

### Verse 30

“I and the Father are one.” By these words he not only resolves the Jews’ question—they had approached in order to test him—but also condemns the madness of future heretics.

### Verse 31

“So they took up stones.” Those who had endured everything else could no longer endure this, but, hard-hearted, they ran to stones. Yet because Jesus suffers only what he wills, he continues to speak.

### Verse 33

“You make yourself.” They understood that the words “I and the Father are one” could not be said except where there is equality between the Father and the Son—something Arius did not understand. But Christ, seeing that they were slow and unable to endure the brilliance of the truth, moderated it in these words: “Is it not written,” etc.?

### Verse 34

“Because I.” God is spoken of in three ways: by nature, by adoption, and falsely—as demons and idols are called gods.

### Verse 35

“If he called them gods.” If human beings become gods by participating through the word of God, how is he not God through nature, through whom they participate?

### Verse 38

“Believe the works.” Give faith to the works, so that, through the merit of faith, you may come to know the works more fully and proceed to faith in his divinity.

### Verse 39

“Because the Father is in me.” The Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father, as one equal is in the one to whom he is equal. Hence he can also say: “I and the Father are one.”

“And whoever sees me sees the Father.” This belongs properly to him. But for a human being it is a gift through participation to be said to be in God, who contains him, and God in him, as in a vessel.

### Verse 41

“And many came to him.” These people seize hold of the one who remains, not as the wicked wished to seize the one who was departing.

“Because John,” etc. He did no sign in Jerusalem as this man did; and whatever he said bore witness to him, as though we came through the lamp to the day.

## Chapter XI

### Verse 1

“Now there was a certain man.” While he remained beyond the Jordan, Lazarus became ill, and his sisters sent to him there.

These sisters of Lazarus signify the Jews already received into eternal blessedness, who intercede with the Lord for the healing of their brother—that is, for the remaining Jews who still wander in the darkness of ignorance—through a well-known action.

“Lazarus was sick.” Lazarus signifies the Jews who were weak in faith in Christ. Martha and Mary signify the teaching of good Jews.

### Verse 3

“Behold, the one whom you love,” etc. Lazarus signifies the sinner, who is loved by the Lord because he came not to call the righteous but sinners.

The sisters of the sinner are good thoughts, which pray that sins may be dissolved.

### Verse 4

“For the glory of God,” etc. That is, so that the Son of God may be glorified. Behold, he calls himself God, against those who say that the Son of God is not God.

### Verse 5

“He loved.” The Savior of the sick and the raiser of the dead loved Lazarus because he was sick and dead.

### Verse 6

“For two days.” So that the four days might be completed. On the first day, when the message was brought to him, the sick man died beyond the Jordan. He remained there for two days—there are three—and on the fourth day he came.

### Verse 7

“Let us go into Judea.” Mystically: This signifies that faith will return to the Jews at the end through Elijah and Enoch.

### VERSE 8.—“The disciples say to him”

Terrified, and wishing to give their Teacher advice so that he might not die, just as Peter does elsewhere: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall never happen to you.” But just as Peter is praised for what came from another—“Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because the Father has revealed this to you”—yet blamed for what came from himself—“Get behind me, Satan, for you savor not the things of God but those of men”—so he rebuked these disciples also, saying that they should walk during the day in which they ought to walk, lest they stumble, and that those who walk without him stumble; for at that moment they were unwilling that he should die who had come to die for human beings. He says that the hours are those that follow the day, not that the days follow them, but that the day illumines them. Twelve is a sacred number that remains complete: for when Judas, who did not shine among the hours, had been cast out, another was substituted in his place.

### VERSE 9.—“Are there not twelve hours?”

(HIER.) Christ is the day, and in another sense the apostles are the day; how Christ [and so forth], up to the point where the twelve apostles are understood.

### VERSE 15.—“That you may believe”

Not that they were then beginning to believe, but that they might believe more firmly. For their faith was always increased by miracles.

### VERSE 17.—“And he found him”

(AUG.) Mystically: There are four days of death. A human being is born [and so forth], up to the point where mercy does not abandon even such people.

### VERSE 22.—“But even now I know”

I know this: that you can raise him if you wish. I leave that to your judgment. I do not presume, however, nor do I ask you to raise him, since I do not know whether it would be useful for him to be raised.

### VERSE 25.—“Even if he has died”

Jesus raised three dead persons: one in a house, that is, in the heart; a second at the gate, that is, in the mouth; a third in a tomb, that is, in the act and habit of sinning.

“He will live.” Thus Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob live, of whom God is said to be the God as of the living. The believer, even when dead, lives; just as the unbeliever, even when living, is dead.

### VERSE 28.—“Secretly”

Because if the Jews had heard that she had been called by Jesus, they would not have followed her, and thus would not have seen the miracle. But because they thought that she was going to her brother’s tomb, they followed her.

“And he is calling you.” For the sake of brevity, Martha’s words show that this had not previously been stated—namely, that the Lord had called Mary.

### VERSE 31.—“They followed”

The evangelist took care to relate this so that we might see what occasion caused the resurrection of one who had been dead four days to have more witnesses.

### VERSE 33.—“He groaned in spirit”

Notice his power: he himself groaned and troubled himself, though no one else could trouble him, just as he accepted all such things because he willed to do so. It also signifies how much a human being ought to be troubled when oppressed by such a great mass of sin. When a sinner, reckoning up what good things he has received from God and what evil things he has repaid, groans in spirit and is troubled, Christ groans and is troubled within him, because faith in Christ is Christ in the heart. Faith groans in a person when it rebukes him for his sins.

### VERSE 34.—“Where have you laid him?”

He who, while absent, knew that Lazarus had died also knows where he has been buried. Yet by speaking in this way, as though he did not know, he signifies the lost human being; hence it is said: “I do not know you” (Matt. VII), and: “Where are you, Adam?” (Gen. III).

### VERSE 38.—“Jesus therefore…”

He shows the difficulty of bringing such a sinner back to life.

“But it was a cave.” Morally: Every sinner, weighed down by the mass of his sins and burdened by his own law, already stinking through his evil habit, openly corrupts others by his bad example. The sisters are certain thoughts, because at times, when a person considers that he has acted wickedly, he grieves.

### VERSE 39.—“Lord, by now he stinks”

She feared that, when the stone was removed, a stench would be released rather than that her brother would be raised.

### VERSE 42.—“But because of the crowd…”

By these words he shows that he seeks the Father’s glory, as he also showed in his other works. For because, according to his humanity, he was less than the Father, he asks him to raise Lazarus, and therefore says that he has been heard. He says this on account of those standing around, so that they might thereby believe that he is the Son of God.

### VERSE 43.—“With a loud voice”

He groaned, wept, and cried out, because one whom the mass of an evil habit oppresses rises with difficulty. Yet after the loud voice he rises—that is, he is brought to life by God’s great grace when he repents.

### VERSE 44.—“And immediately he came out”

While the sinner remains contemptuous, he lies buried. When he repents, he rises; when he confesses, he comes forth, as though emerging from hidden places into manifestation.

“Unbind him.” Christ himself gives life inwardly; to his ministers he grants the power of unbinding.

### VERSE 48.—“They will believe in him”

“And the Romans will come.” Because they sensed that his teaching was opposed to the temple and to the ancestral laws, they feared that, if everyone believed in Christ, no one would remain to defend the city of God and the temple against the Romans.

“And they will come to Rome.” They fear temporal things, not eternal ones, and they lost both. The place was Jerusalem, which they lost; they lost their own nation, being scattered everywhere.

### VERSE 51.—“He did not say this of himself”

(AUG.) Notice that even wicked men, through the spirit of prophecy, foretell future events [and so forth], up to the point that this is permitted only to the high priest, as is read concerning Zechariah.

### VERSE 52.—“For the nation”

That is, for the Jewish nation, in which the sheep were found—this much was all that Caiaphas understood. But because the evangelist knew that there were other sheep, he added: “But also to gather together into one the children of God who were scattered abroad.” They are children by predestination, just as the sheep are in Israel; for they did not yet exist, since they had not yet believed.

### VERSE 55.—“Now the Passover was near”

As the figurative Passover was approaching, at which the true Lamb was already to be sacrificed, there was among the Jews a plan to kill him; and he himself was approaching the place of his passion.

## CHAPTER XII

### VERSE 1.—“He came to Bethany”

He came to Bethany first so that the raising of Lazarus might be more deeply impressed upon everyone’s memory, and so that the Jews, who were plotting the death of so great a raiser of the dead, might be confounded as inexcusable.

### VERSE 3.—“Mary therefore…”

Precious ointment is made chiefly from nard, especially from its spikes; here, however, it is called *pisticus* because of the place from which it came. The term is interpreted as “faithful,” not corrupted by any other admixture.

“Then one said…” Judas, although wicked, is nevertheless numbered among the apostles, so that we may be taught to tolerate the wicked, lest we divide Christ’s body, and that we may learn that the wicked do not harm the good.

### VERSE 6.—“Not because…”

As far as his intention was concerned, the poor were no concern of his, because he did not care about them—not because he had been entrusted with distributing funds to the poor.

“He had the money box…” He whom angels serve had a money box for the expenses of the poor, accommodating himself to the weakness of human beings.

### VERSE 7.—“Leave her alone”

He knew the thief but did not expose him, teaching us to tolerate the wicked. He commends Mary’s devotion so greatly that he shows he was going to die and be anointed with spices for burial. Therefore Mary, who was not permitted to anoint him when dead, was granted the service of honoring the living man with a burial rite. Hence, according to Mark, it is said: “What she had”—that is, what she was able to do—“she did; she anticipated anointing my body for burial.”

### VERSE 8.—“You do not always have me”

In bodily presence. Or: “You will not have me”—you, Judas, and those like you—because although the wicked now share in the sacraments, afterward they do not have the Lord as the good do.

### VERSE 9.—“And they came”

Curiosity, not charity, brought them. We, by contrast, if we learn that Jesus has found a house in an obedient soul in which he may dwell, should come there in contemplation—not merely because we see a human being raised in the soul, but so that we may imitate a good life and thereby attain to the vision of Jesus.

### VERSE 10.—“They planned”

Because they could neither conceal nor deny the miracle, they foolishly wished to kill Lazarus, as though the one who had raised the dead could not raise someone who had been killed.

### VERSE 12.—“On the next day”

Behold, the sheep from Israel come to the shepherd. The branches are praises signifying victory over the devil and death.

### VERSE 13.—“They cried out”

(AUG.) “Hosanna” is the voice of one beseeching, indicating feeling more than signifying any particular matter, like the interjections.

“King of Israel.” He is not a king in the earthly manner—which would be a small thing—but because he rules, leads minds and kingdoms to heaven, and is a king of mercy, not of indignation.

### VERSE 15.—“Do not fear, daughter”

Within the rejected people there was a daughter of Zion—that is, Jerusalem—namely, the sheep who devoutly go out to meet the one who is coming. To them it is said divinely: “Recognize the one whom you praise, and do not fear when the one who is your redemption suffers.”

The colt on which no one had sat is the people of the Gentiles, who had not received the law of God.

### VERSE 19.—“Behold, the whole world…”

Through his passion and resurrection he redeemed the whole world, and it followed him. And what is surprising if the world follows the one through whom the world was made?

### VERSE 21.—“These therefore approached”

He shows that the Gentiles were converted through the preaching of the apostles.

### VERSE 23.—“But Jesus…”

They were Jews who were crying out, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord”; now Gentiles seek to see him. Behold, the two walls coming together. Therefore he is called the cornerstone.

“The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” This glorification is not spoken on account of these people who wished to see him, but on their occasion he announces the future fullness of the Gentiles, when he has been glorified in heaven. But the height of this glorification is preceded by the humility of the passion; hence: “Amen, amen, I say to you,” and so forth. There he says that he is the grain destined to die and multiply. Having already encouraged them to this passion, he adds: “He who loves his life,” and so forth.

“Unless a grain of wheat…” (AUG.) He himself is the grain by which the faithful soul ought to live, the grain from which the spiritual harvest must arise. Although there are many grains of seed, he compares himself to none but wheat. Hence the custom began in the Church of making the Lord’s body from this grain alone.

### VERSE 25.—“He who loves…”

(AUG.) Whoever loves his life in this present life loses in the future what is more fitting; hence he adds: “He who hates his life,” and so forth. A person does not love but hates his life in this world when, by loving God, he chooses to be killed rather than to sin against him.

### VERSE 26.—“If anyone serves me”

The reward of the work by which he serves Christ is to be with him: apart from him, being is nowhere good; with him, being is nowhere evil. Hence he adds more clearly: “If anyone serves me…”

### VERSE 27.—“Now my soul is troubled”

“And what shall I say?” After predicting the passion and exhorting them to it, he gives voice, as it were, to his own strength and then adds the feeling of our weakness, which he truly assumed, though he assumed it voluntarily for our sake, so that we might not despair because of this weakness. Here he also teaches what we ought to say and to whom we should flee.

It is as though he said: “My soul is troubled; what shall I say? Where shall I flee? Whom shall I invoke? In whom shall I hope? In the Father who saves, to whom I present my will, because for this reason—that I should suffer these things—I have come to this hour.” Thus glorification also comes to him in this way, and in his members.

### VERSE 28.—“Father, glorify…”

“I seek salvation, but I do not refuse the passion. Because of this passion, glorify me”—that is, make me the glory of your name.

### VERSE 30.—“This voice was not for me”

He shows that this voice did not declare to him something he did not know, but declared it to those to whom it was necessary that it be made known.

### VERSE 31.—“Now is the judgment”

That is, the judgment of discernment, which precedes the final condemnation. For now, through the passion, the devil’s legal claim having been destroyed, many will be freed. Hence, in explaining this, he adds: “I suffer, I am troubled, and through these things…” He will be cast out: he will be driven out from the redeemed. Through the preaching of the apostles he will be fully driven out; formerly, even when he was allowed to tempt a few, he did not harm them inwardly.

### VERSE 34.—“And how can you say…”

“How will he die on the cross?” They thought that this was what he had said, because this was what they were planning to do.

“The Son of Man.” They remembered that he had often said that he was the Son of Man, not that he had said here, “If the Son of Man is lifted up.” “Who is this Son of Man? For if he is the Christ, he remains forever. If he remains forever, how will he be lifted up from the earth”—that is, die on a cross?

### VERSE 35.—“Walk”

That is, understand everything: Christ will die in order to redeem, yet will live forever in heaven, where he will lead you. Or: while you have Christ with you, walk, lest the darkness of ignorance and perpetual death overtake you.

“He does not know where he is going.” Whoever does not believe in Christ’s death does not know where he is going, but stumbles against the rock of offense, which is Christ, as the Jews despise and mock him as one who died.

### VERSE 36.—“While you have the light”

That is, while you understand something true concerning Christ’s eternity, believe in the truth, adding the truth of his humility, so that you may be reborn in the truth.

“He departed from them.” Not from those who had begun to believe, but from those who were envious. By hiding himself, he took thought for our weakness; he did not diminish his power.

### VERSE 38.—“That the word of Isaiah might be fulfilled”

It must be fulfilled in every respect, yet not by a necessity that forces it to happen, but voluntarily. For God foreknew and foretold that they would not believe and would sin; nevertheless, he did not compel them to this. He foreknew and foretold it because it would happen.

### VERSE 39.—“They could not believe”

(AUG.) This does not mean that human beings cannot be changed for the better, but that, so long as they remain such as they are, they cannot believe.

### VERSE 43.—“The glory of God”

For this reason the cross is fixed on the foreheads of believers, where the seat of shame is, so that no one may be ashamed of the name of Christ and so that he may seek God’s glory rather than that of human beings.

### VERSE 44.—“Jesus”

While some did not believe and others did believe—some openly, with palms and praises, others secretly, as his passion was already approaching—Jesus cries out. He had remained hidden for as long as the passion had not yet been completed.

“He who believes in me.” Because he appeared as a human being while God was hidden in the human being, lest they think that he was only what they saw, he wishes them to believe him to be such and so great as the Father is.

### VERSE 45.—“And whoever sees me sees him who…”

There is so little difference between me and him that whoever sees me sees him. This vision is not bodily but intellectual, belonging to the pure in heart.

“Whoever sees me…” He does not say, “does not see me,” but “sees him who sent me.” Likewise he said, “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me, but in him who sent me.” He said the former so that, because he appeared as he did, he would not be believed to be merely the Son of Man; he said the latter so that he would be believed equal to the Father.

No other person who was sent—that is, an apostle, who is only a servant—would say either of these things. He can, however, say other things that are common to the Son, such as: “Whoever hears or receives me hears and receives the one who sent me,” because the Lord is honored in the servant and the Father in the Son.

### VERSE 46.—“I am light”

This is not said of another: “The light came into the world,” except of the one who illumines. The others are light insofar as they have been illumined, because their life shines before human beings.

“The word that I have spoken.” He plainly says that he will judge on the last day, because he is the Father’s Word, who has spoken himself and announced himself.

### VERSE 49.—“Commandment”

The Father did not give the Son a commandment through an angel or any other creature, nor did he give him a commandment of which he had previously been ignorant. Rather, when he begot the Word and Wisdom in which all commandments exist, he gave him the commandment. Just as he gave life to the Son who is life by begetting life, so, by begetting life, he gave him the being of life, which was without defect.

### VERSE 50.—“And I know…”

When he says that the commandment is eternal life, and he himself is eternal life, he plainly says that he is God’s commandment.

“Whatever I speak, therefore, just as the Father has told me, so I speak.” For understanding minds, truth is born from the Father; thus truth speaks inwardly without sound, just as the Father told him. But so that human beings might believe what they are not yet able to understand, words sounded forth from the mouth of flesh. Once expressed and fixed in writing, they raise us, to some extent, toward truth itself.

## CHAPTER XIII

### VERSE 1.—“That he should depart”

The evangelist explains to us the name of Passover—namely, “passing over”—and its significance: just as Israel passed over from Egypt, so Christ passes over from the world. So do we, marked with the blood of the Lamb, pass from vices to virtues and from the world to heaven.

“He loved them to the end.” “To the end” means to Christ, who is the consummating end: that, through love of him, they may pass over to where he himself passes. Or “to the end” means to death—not that his love is terminated by death, but that he loved to such an extent that love led him all the way to death. In this he gave an example, so that all might remain in God’s truth to the end.

### VERSE 2.—“And supper having taken place”

The supper signifies the passion. For just as there is no meal after supper, so, after Christ had suffered once, he does not suffer again.

“He rises from supper.” After the passion he lays aside his garments; in the same flesh, now immortal, he girds himself with a linen cloth according to his former weakness. He pours water into a basin—that is, the grace of baptism—washes the feet and wipes them from sins in baptism. He takes up his garments—that is, the Jews at the end of the age, whom he had previously set aside in their blindness.

### VERSE 4.—“He rises from supper”

From that heavenly refreshment by which he was refreshed with the angels, he lays aside his garments, the glory of eternal blessedness.

“And he puts on his garments.” He set aside his exalted status in order to assume his humility. Humility is thereby perfectly commended to human beings, since one so exalted humbled himself so far as even to wash the feet of his betrayer.

### VERSE 5.—“Then he pours…”

He poured his blood upon the earth in order to cleanse the footsteps of believers, which had been soiled by earthly sins.

### VERSE 8.—“Peter says to him…”

Because of the greatness of the mystery promised, he does not yet permit this to happen; terrified by fear, he cannot yet endure God’s humbling himself at his feet.

“He answered.” Whoever is not washed through baptism and the confession of repentance has no part with Jesus.

### VERSE 9.—“Simon says to him…”

Peter’s error benefited us. He erred so that we would not err. He erred when he offered himself to God to be washed entirely, and God corrected him, showing that one who has been baptized once should not be baptized again.

### VERSE 10.—“The one who has been washed…”

From these words we understand that the apostles had been baptized, although we do not read where or when.

“The one who has been washed…” By baptism he has been washed and is clean. But because he is again defiled by the dust of earthly dwelling, it is again necessary to wash the feet. The Lord washes them by interceding for us, and we ourselves wash them by praying.

Even the person who studies truth in leisure, while continuing to open to the bridegroom who knocks in others, soils his feet, because truth is heard humbly but cannot be preached without danger. Yet the Lord washes these feet through his disciples.

### VERSE 12.—“And when he had reclined again, he said to them: ‘Do you know what I have done to you? You call me…’”

Just as earlier he instructed them by example, so now he instructs them by word, as the teacher of truth. What he says about himself is not arrogance but truth that benefits his hearers, as Paul also does.

(GREG.) The humble are unwary when, while avoiding arrogance, they entangle themselves in falsehood, because they rise up against the truth that they abandon. For whoever, compelled by necessity, speaks true and good things about himself is joined to humility all the more as he is joined to truth.

### VERSE 18.—“Not about all of you”

You will not all do this by which you may be blessed; but whoever eats my bread, not so that he may profit but so that he may conceal himself, will lift up his heel against me—that is, he will trample me—so that Scripture may be fulfilled, which foretold this. It does not compel him, but it did not remain silent about what was going to happen.

### VERSE 19.—“From now on I tell you”

It is as though he said: “Until now I have tolerated and kept silent, but now I identify the betrayer before what is soon to be done, so that when it has happened you may believe that I am the one of whom that Scripture foretold.”

### VERSE 20.—“Amen, amen, I say to you”

After teaching them by his example about humiliation and the suffering of the heel, he adds the honor by which he may console them: that both he and the Father are received in them.

### VERSE 21.—“When Jesus had said these things…”

Our weakness was truly troubled in him, not his power, just as he truly suffered. Yet he voluntarily accepted this disturbance, so that the servant who is troubled by necessity would not despair.

That he is troubled signifies that spiritual people are to be troubled out of charity when an urgent cause compels them to separate the weeds from the wheat before the harvest.

### VERSE 26.—“And when he had dipped the bread…”

The dipping of the bread signifies Judas’s hypocrisy, for he came to the supper as a feigned friend. Things that are dipped are not cleansed but stained. If the dipping signifies something good, damnation nevertheless followed him not inappropriately, since he was ungrateful for that very good.

“He gave it to Judas, Simon Iscariot’s son,” and so forth. Judas did not, as some think, receive Christ’s body only at this moment. For it must be understood that the Lord had already distributed the sacrament of his body and blood to everyone, among whom Judas also was. Then, through the dipped morsel, the betrayer himself was pointed out, and so forth.

### VERSE 27.—“What you are doing, do quickly”

He did not command Judas’s evil but foretold it—good for us—because he wished it to happen quickly, not so much hastening toward Judas’s punishment as toward the salvation of the faithful.

### VERSE 29.—“Because he had the money box”

In it they examined what had been offered for the needs of their companions and of other needy people. In this an example is given to the Church for preserving what is necessary. The Church is commanded not to worry about tomorrow, lest it serve earthly things or, through fear of poverty, abandon justice.

### VERSE 30.—“And it was night”

The night corresponds to the sacrament. For the son of darkness had gone out, doing the works of darkness.

### VERSE 30.—“Now the Son of Man has been glorified”

(AUG.) When Judas went out, concerning whom it had been said, “You are not all clean,” and so forth, up to the point as though what was soon to happen had already happened.

### VERSE 33.—“Little children”

(ID.) Because he had said that God would soon glorify him, and so forth, up to the point where this cannot be understood, because what follows would not agree with it.

“Where I am going, you cannot come.” At that time the apostles, not yet strengthened by the Spirit, could not follow the Lord—that is, die for the Lord and for justice—or come to immortal life, to which he was going. They were to follow afterward. He then teaches how they may become fit and proceed where he goes before them.

“I give you a new commandment.” (AUG.) Not that this commandment is absent from the ancient law—“You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” and so forth—up to the point where this love causes one to die to the world.

### VERSE 34.—“That you love one another as I have loved you”

Let no one think that the love of God, which is present in love of one’s neighbor, has been omitted. In one’s neighbor, no one is loved except God. Likewise, Christ loves God in us. He does not mean that we already possess this love, but that we should possess it, just as a physician seeks in a sick person not illness but the health that he has come to give.

### VERSE 36.—“Lord, where are you going?”

Having heard “Where I am going” and understood the way by which he can follow—that is, love—Peter says that he is ready to follow.
