And because the Lord knew his state of mind, he said that he could not follow immediately, not removing hope of the future but confirming it: “You shall follow afterward.”

### VERSE 37.—“I will lay down my life…”

He presumes greatly who promises to lay down his life for the one who had not yet given his life for Peter, as though he could go before him.

(AUG.) He knew his will but not his strength. As a weak man, he boasted of his will, but the physician was looking at his weakness. Peter was promising; Christ foresaw. The one who did not know was listening; the one who foresaw was teaching.

### VERSE 38.—“The cock will not crow…”

Peter begins his threefold denial before the first cockcrow, but completes it before the second cockcrow.

## CHAPTER XIV

### VERSE 1.—“Let not your heart be troubled…”

(AUG.) So that they would not fear death as though he were merely human and therefore become troubled, and so forth, up to the point where one glory belongs to the moon and another to the stars.

### VERSE 2.—“In my Father’s house…”

The house of God, the temple of God, and the kingdom of God—the kingdom of heaven—are righteous people, among whom there are many differences. These are the dwelling places of that house.

(AUG.) At present the righteous are the kingdom of God and the kingdom of heaven, and so forth, up to the point that what you possessed in hope you may possess in reality.

“If it were not so…” That is, if I had not predestined a dwelling place—which is inconceivable with respect to God, who predestined all good things before all ages—then I would now prepare one, that is, predestine one. But this too is inconceivable with respect to God, as though he were predestining something in the present.

(ID.) He confirms that they exist, because if they did not exist he would have said, “I will go and prepare,” and so forth, up to the point that this multitude is the multitude of dwelling places.

### VERSE 3.—“And if I go…”

(ID.) He went away by hiding himself, he comes by appearing, but he remains by ruling, so that we may advance by living well; and in this way the place is prepared.

(ID.) Faith believes what it does not see; for if it saw, and so forth, up to the point where the desire of love is the preparation of the dwelling place.

### VERSE 4.—“And where I am going…”

This was said according to those who knew both the Son and the Father. Thomas, however, although he thought that he did not know, is convicted by the fact that he knew him himself, and therefore knew both the way and the life—that is, the Son and the Father.

Of those who know, it is said below: “From now on you will know him through me; and you have seen him in your heart, since you have seen me wholly like him.”

### VERSE 5.—“Thomas says to him…”

He said that they knew where and by what route one goes, because he does not lie. But Thomas says that they know neither, not realizing that they know. Christ, however, proves that they know: if they knew him, and he is the way, they knew the way; and if they knew him, and he is the truth and the life, then they knew the truth and the life to which he goes.

Therefore he goes by himself as the way, to himself as the truth and the life, and to the Father, because he is one with the Father.

### VERSE 7.—“If you had known me…”

Because he had said that no one comes to the Father except through him, who is inseparably the same with the Father, he shows that the Father is known through knowledge of himself, lest they ask who the Father is. Some had not yet understood this, and he rebukes them, saying: “If you had known,” and so forth.

“And you have seen him.” As it is said of two who are wholly alike, “If you have seen this one, you have seen that one,” so they had seen the Son who was wholly like him. But they had to be instructed to understand that the Father also was such, and not unlike him.

### VERSE 9.—“How can you say…”

“And though he is wholly like him…” It is as though he said: “I see the spirit in which you speak. You are not seeking another who is like me, but think that he is better.”

“From myself.” I am not from myself, I who speak. He attributes what he does to the one from whom he himself is.

### VERSE 12.—“Whoever believes in me…”

The Father and I work without distinction. And whoever believes in me—not that this should be understood of the apostles alone—will do the works that I do through myself; that is, I do them in him or through him, and he will do even greater works.

“The works that I do.” Yet he will not do them from himself, but from me. “The servant is not greater than his lord.” For Christ himself does many things without them; they can do nothing without him, except sin.

“Greater than these.” (AUG.) Because if Christ healed through the fringe of his garment, Peter healed through his shadow. Or, “his work,” and so forth, up to the point that, if both possessed equal power, this would nevertheless be the greater mercy.

### VERSE 15.—“If you love me…”

How does he exhort them to love and keep the commandments so that they may receive the Spirit, when they cannot love and keep them unless they have the Spirit? But what they had in a lesser and hidden manner they were to receive more abundantly and openly, so that what they possessed might become known to them.

### VERSE 16.—“And I will ask the Father”

(THEOPH.) “I will ask”—that is, I will beseech the Father—and he will send you another Paraclete, and so forth, up to the point that the Spirit the Paraclete and his grace may wholly come upon them, condescending to them. To them he says, “I will ask the Father.”

### VERSE 17.—“Because it does not see…”

Those who love the world do not have spiritual eyes with which to see the Holy Spirit. Nor can they see him with bodily eyes, because the Holy Spirit did not appear clothed in human nature.

“And he will be in you.” He will be in you; he will not merely remain in order to be present, because existing somewhere precedes remaining there. Let no one therefore think that he remains as a guest visibly with another. He can be recognized in them, not by others.

### VERSE 18.—“I will not leave you orphans”

The Spirit will not be given in my place in such a way that I am not also with you.

*Orphani* is Greek; in Latin, the term is *pupilli* (“orphans”).

### VERSE 19.—“A little while, and the world…”

The world that now sees with bodily eyes will shortly no longer see, because the risen Christ did not show himself to it. Yet the whole span of time is a short while. When it has ended, the wicked will be taken away so that they may not see the glory of God, which the righteous will see.

“Because I live, you also will live.” He uses the present tense because his resurrection is soon to occur. He uses the future of those whose resurrection will take place at the end.

### VERSE 20.—“And you in me, and I in you”

This is so now and is understood in a certain way through faith. But then it will be understood through sight, when this union—which is now begun—is perfected.

### VERSE 21.—“Whoever has…”

Not only will you apostles live and know, but also whoever keeps the commandment in memory and observes it in life. Or: he has it by doing and keeps it by persevering. Or: he has it in words and keeps it in conduct. Or: he has it by hearing and keeps it by doing.

“And I will love him.” I will love him for this purpose: that I may manifest myself to him. He loves him now also, but not for this purpose; rather, he loves him so that we may believe and keep the commandments, and thereby deserve to receive what comes afterward.

“And I will manifest myself to him.” Whoever has my commandment knows me, and this is what is meant there: “I will manifest myself to him.” But he first states the cause related to the commandment: “Because he loves me; and whoever loves me, my Father will love him.” And because the Father loves him, then I too will love him, and from this comes the manifestation.

### VERSE 22.—“Judas says to him…”

Having heard that the world would not see him then, but that they themselves would see him, Judas asks on behalf of everyone for the reason for this distinction. According to the Lord’s answer, the reason is love, by which alone, and by nothing else, the holy nation is distinguished from the unholy.

### VERSE 23.—“We will come to him”

God comes to a human being when the human being comes to God. The human being comes by believing, obeying, gazing, and receiving; God comes by helping, illuminating, and filling.

“And we will make our dwelling…” Charity causes God to dwell in the house in which the Father and the Son make their dwelling. Thus he will also grant the manifestation about which Judas had asked.

### VERSE 25.—“I have spoken these things to you”

These things concern the dwelling among those who love him, signifying the future spiritual Church, among whose blessed members he does not depart.

“Remaining with you.” This signifies the present bodily Church, in which he visits by delivering, and then returns.

### VERSE 26.—“The Paraclete”

Although consoling when there is need is the work of the Trinity, it belongs especially to the person of the Holy Spirit, because in Scripture the Holy Spirit is designated by the name of goodness. Through goodness, therefore, God consoles us; through it he grants us all his good things.

“He will teach you…” Although the Son teaches us and reveals the Father, he does all this through his goodness.

“He will teach you all things.” He will teach what I have said—not that the Son speaks and the Spirit teaches, as though the Son did not teach, because what the Son says and teaches, the entire Trinity says and teaches. But because the Trinity exists, the individual persons must be indicated distinctly; we must hear them distinctly but understand them inseparably. Therefore, when we say “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit,” we do not say that they exist separately, since they cannot exist separately.

### VERSE 27.—“I leave you peace”

He is going to the Father.

“Peace…” Repeating the same point, he says: “My peace I give you.” This is what the Prophet says: “Peace upon peace” (Isa. XXVII).

There is peace in this world, in which, while remaining, we conquer the enemy, love one another, and do not judge one another concerning hidden things. There will be peace in the future, when we shall reign without an enemy, where one person will not be able to disagree with another, where everything will be open and each person will receive praise (I Cor. IV).

In him and from him there is both kinds of peace. For he himself is our peace (Eph. II), and we believe in him because he exists, and we shall see him as he is. Therefore, when he says “my peace,” what follows should also be understood with respect to what precedes.

Or: the peace in this world is ours; it is something, but not complete. In the future, peace will be his, where nothing resists in the manner in which he possesses it.

“Let not your heart be troubled.” Because I leave you in peace, let your heart not be troubled by what I said—“I am going”—as though a wolf were to attack in the shepherd’s absence. For although I go as a human being, as God I am present.

### VERSE 28.—“If you loved me…”

(AUG.) This was the meaning of his going to the Father and departing from us, and so forth, up to the point that incorruptible dust might sit at the Father’s right hand.

“You would rejoice…” Human nature should rejoice because it is raised to the Father’s right hand, in which the rest also place their hope.

### VERSE 28.—“That you may believe”

Not that you should believe because you have seen what happened—for there is no praise or merit in faith concerning what is seen; indeed, faith does not concern what is seen but what is not seen.

Believe that I am the Son of God—not with a new faith, since they had believed this previously, but with faith increased and renewed. For when he said these things, their faith was small, and when he died, it was nothing.

### VERSES 30–31.—“And in me…”

The Lord did not wish to possess anything that he could lose; he came poor so that the devil would have nothing to take away.

## CHAPTER XV

### VERSE 1.—“I am the true vine”

You ought to follow me as I go before you toward the passion, because I am the vine—that is, your head, of the same nature as you—so that human nature may bear fruit in me.

“And the Father…” I too am the farmer with the Father, because I am the cleanser of the branches, which is the farmer’s work, not the vine’s. He also makes the branches into workers, although not from their own resources, nor through themselves, but through me.

### VERSE 3.—“Because of the word…”

He does not say, “Because of the water of baptism,” because water by itself, without the word, is merely water; through the word it becomes a sacrament.

### VERSE 5.—“I am…”

Whoever thinks that he bears fruit from himself is not in the vine. Therefore, repeating and explaining what came before, he adds: “I am the vine; you are the branches.”

“You are attached to me as branches to the vine.”

“Whoever remains in me.” Therefore whoever—not only you—remains in me by believing, obeying, and persevering.

“And I in him.” By illuminating, helping, and granting perseverance.

“He bears…” Although Christ, according to his humanity, is the vine, he would not grant this grace to the branches unless he were also God.

### VERSE 6.—“If anyone…”

Branches cut off are more worthless than other pieces of wood, because they are assigned to no use except the fire. They are either in the vine or in the fire.

### VERSE 7.—“And my words…”

God’s words are said to remain in us when we do what he commands and love what he promises. Whoever does not do this touches but does not adhere; therefore the words are not for his benefit but for testimony to his condemnation.

“You will ask…” If a believer asks for something and it does not happen, he is not asking for what has a dwelling in him, nor for what has his words dwelling in him, but for what the desire and weakness of the flesh possess.

[Col. 0411A] **VERSE 8.**—“By this he is glorified,” etc. Whoever remains in me bears much fruit, which comes from the grace of God; thus it is his glory, not man’s. This is the meaning of “By this,” etc. “That you may bear very much fruit.” He does not thereby show equality between our nature and his, but the grace by which he is Mediator. For the Father loves us, but in the Son. “You may become.” How? “If you love me.” From what kind of love? From observance of the commandments. “If you love me as the Father loved me”—not “as much as.” For equality is not being indicated, but likeness, granting them eternal eternity.

**VERSE 11.**—“That my joy.” God’s joy concerning us, whom he foreknew and predestined, is always complete. In us it begins from faith, grows, and indeed will be perfected in the resurrection.

**VERSE 12.**—“This is my commandment,” etc. Above he also spoke about love of neighbor, but the repetition is a confirmation. There, however, he says, “I give a commandment,” as though it had not existed previously; here, “This is,” as though it were not something else. There he says “new,” so that we may not remain in the old; here, “my,” so that it may not be despised.

**VERSE 13.**—“Greater than this.” He defines the fullness of mutual love that he commands them to possess.

**VERSE 15.**—“I will no longer call you.” Having commended love, he adds something expressing condescension: he calls good servants—those who know by doing what he commands—friends, and removes from them the name “servant,” which is associated with fear, by casting fear out. The servant does not know what his master is doing. For when he does something, he is puffed up as though he himself were doing it, and not the master.

[Col. 0411C] **VERSE 17.**—“These things I command,” etc. Here he shows what the fruit he had mentioned is, for the sake of which the Father will also give what we ask, and who also gave this—that we should love.

“That you may love.” (AUGUSTINE.) He rightly commends love so often, as though it alone were to be commanded, without which the other things cannot be done, although it cannot be possessed without the others. For its sake we must patiently endure all the adversities of the world. Hence he adds:

**VERSE 18.**—“If the world.” The name “world” sometimes designates the good and sometimes the evil, because it is one mass that wholly perished in Adam; from it there are some vessels for honor and others for dishonor.

**VERSE 19.**—“The world would love what is its own.” If the wicked punish the wicked person’s crime, the world partly hates what is its own; when it punishes, it partly loves, because the wicked person favors the wicked.

**VERSE 20.**—“My word.” Namely, this: “It is not.” And also the preceding statement: “Know that it hated me before you.” He then adds the reason: “A servant is not greater,” etc. By his own example—which could not be surpassed—he urged them to bear the world’s hatred; he adds why they ought to imitate him in this: because he is the Lord, and they are servants.

**VERSE 22.**—“If I had not come.” Here he points more explicitly to the Jews, to whom he came, and of whom he had spoken above under the name “world.” Since he came to them, he shows here that they are inexcusable concerning all their evils. “They would not have sin,” etc. Those to whom he did not come or speak have an excuse—not for every sin, but for this: that they did not believe in Christ. But those to whom he came and spoke through the apostles are not excused. “Those who sinned without the law will also perish without the law” (Rom. 2). “Concerning sin.” Namely, that they do not believe me but hate me, and will persecute me in my own person and in mine. Yet this sin against me also redounds against the Father, because whoever hates me also hates my Father. And what is most serious is that I not only came and spoke, but also performed works; when they saw them, they hated both me and the Father.

**VERSE 24.**—“The things that no one else did,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) That he fed so many thousands with a few loaves, that he walked upon the waters, etc., up to “and because he himself did it by himself, no one [did it] without him.”

“They hated,” etc. The Jews say that they love God, and yet, without knowing it, they hate him, because those who wish to be wicked do not wish to have the truth by which they are condemned. Just as they hate their punishment, so they hate the truth that inflicts the punishment, not knowing that he is the truth. And if they hate the truth, they hate him from whom the truth was born; thus, without knowing it, they hate the Father, from whom the truth was born.

**VERSE 25.**—“They hated me without cause.” He hates without cause who seeks no advantage from hatred or escape from any disadvantage. Thus the wicked hate Christ. Thus the righteous love without seeking anything else, but for his own sake.

**VERSE 26.**—“But when.” Now, seeing his works, they hate both me and the Father without cause. But when the Paraclete comes, he will convict by clearer testimony those who saw and hated; he will also bring some of them, pierced by remorse for so great a crime, to conversion. “Whom I will send.” On Pentecost the Holy Spirit came upon the one hundred and twenty people assembled, among whom were all the apostles, in the house where the supper had taken place. “Who proceeds from the Father.” The Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, but the Son is said to proceed from the Father because he is accustomed to refer to the Father even what belongs to him and comes from him. Therefore, from the one from whom the Son has his being, the Father has it that the Spirit proceeds from the Son.

# CHAPTER 16

[Col. 0412C] **VERSE 1.**—“I have said these things,” etc. After he taught by his own example that they should bear hatred—teaching them what they ought to do, though they could not do it—and after he also promised the Spirit, through whom they would be able to resist, he adds, “I have said these things,” etc. This is an example concerning the Spirit, who will strengthen them, so that, with love poured into their hearts, they may have great peace and not be scandalized.

**VERSE 2.**—“But the hour is coming.” As though he said: If, after being driven out by them, you gain so many for me—which ought to make you rejoice—it will not be enough for them to drive you out. But they will not allow you to live, lest you win everyone and turn them away from Judaism, in which they believe that the God of Israel and his holy things are being abandoned.

**VERSE 4.**—“But I have said these things.” After he said that their sufferings would come and that the Spirit, the Comforter, would be given to them, he adds: “I did not tell you these things,” etc. If we understand this as referring to the sufferings, he had foretold them not only after the supper but also before the approaching Passover and from the beginning of the mission of the twelve apostles. But he had not foretold the consolation of the Spirit that was to come, because he himself was their Advocate or Comforter through his bodily presence. Since he is now about to depart, however, it was necessary for him to say that the one who would strengthen them against those who rejected and killed them was going to come.

**VERSE 5.**—“I am going to him.” He said this so openly that no one asked what they saw with their bodily eyes: they saw him ascending in a cloud, certain of the glory of the one whom, after his passion had first been foretold, they had asked, “Lord, where are you going?”

**VERSE 7.**—“For if,” etc. This does not mean that, while he was present on earth, he could not give the Spirit, but that they were not fit to receive him unless they ceased to know him according to the flesh.

“But if.” When your minds have thus been snatched up toward heavenly things, the Spirit, together with the Father and the Son, will be present. For once they had been changed from carnal to spiritual, they would possess the Trinity with greater capacity, as had been promised.

[Col. 0413B] **VERSE 8.**—“He will convict.” This does not mean that the Son does not convict, but that the Spirit will give them love and drive out fear, so that they may have the freedom to convict.

(AUGUSTINE.) The world is convicted concerning sin because it does not believe in Christ. “It is convicted,” etc., up to “lest they be judged with the prince of the world, whom they imitate after he has been judged.”

“And concerning righteousness.” The world is not convicted concerning his righteousness, but concerning the righteousness of believers, in comparison with whom it is condemned. Hence he does not say, “The world will not see me,” but, “You will not see me,” you apostles. This is directed against unbelievers who say, “How shall we believe what we do not see?” It is true righteousness to believe what is not seen, so that those who saw the man might believe that he was God. And when, through the ascension, the form of the man was removed from their sight, then the statement was fulfilled in every respect: “The righteous person lives by faith.”

[Col. 0413C] **VERSE 10.**—“And now,” etc. That is, you will never see me as you see me now—as one destined to be judged and mortal—but as the glorified judge. This is the righteousness of faith, concerning which the Apostle says: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him” (2 Cor. 5). Since the world does not wish to accept this from them, it is convicted.

**VERSE 11.**—“Concerning judgment.” Since, if they follow him who has been condemned, they are condemned with him, they are frightened by the punishment of that proud one, lest they think that they themselves will be spared.

**VERSE 13.**—“All the truth,” etc. He promises that the Spirit will accomplish everything—not that everything will be completed in this life.

“From himself,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) Because he is not from himself, since the Father alone [is so], etc., up to “he always knew, knows, and will know.”

**VERSE 14.**—“He will glorify me.” By making you spiritual, he will declare how the Son is equal to the Father—the one whom they had known according to the flesh as a man. Or, by removing fear, he will make you announce my glory to the whole world, so that it may benefit not me but human beings.

“From what is mine.” This does not mean that the Spirit is less than the Son. Why, then, did he say this? He explains: “All things whatsoever the Father has are mine.” Therefore I said, “He will take from what is mine.” The Spirit receives from the Father what the Son receives, because in this Trinity the Son is born from the Father and the Spirit proceeds from the Father. But the one who is born from no one proceeds from no one: the Father alone is such.

[Col. 0414A] **VERSE 15.**—“All things,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) Christ speaks of the Spirit. “The Spirit of the Father,” etc., up to “thus it is plainly shown that the Spirit belongs to the Father and the Son.”

**VERSE 16.**—“A little while.” That is, a short time remains until I suffer and am shut in the tomb, and then another short time until you see me risen. Or the first short time is the three days during which, shut in the tomb, I will not be seen; and the second short time is the forty days during which, risen, I will be seen. “Because I am going.” This means that the time has come for me, having laid aside mortality, to bring human nature into heaven.

**VERSE 20.**—“Because you will weep.” After I have been killed, concerning which the enemies will rejoice. Similarly, all good people weep amid the troubles of this age, while lovers of the world rejoice. The good, however, are compared to a woman giving birth, who has given birth in labor but rejoices over the fruit, and rejoices more over the arrival of the future child than she is saddened by the present pain.

**VERSE 23.**—“If you ask anything.” (AUGUSTINE.) This should certainly be understood in the sense that when he says, “He will give you,” the benefits signified are those that properly pertain to those who ask. The saints are heard for themselves, but not for all other friends or enemies.

“He will give you.” In the future you will not ask, but now ask, and what pertains to you will be given to you—even if it is not granted in every matter for which you ask. For this reason he says “to you.”

**VERSE 25.**—“I have spoken these things in proverbs.” What I have said up to now I have said, as it were, in proverbs—things that people are accustomed to hear but not understand—because you are natural persons. A natural person, however, does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God (1 John 1). Whatever is said concerning incorporeal and immutable substance is, as it were, a proverb to such a person. “But the hour is coming.” When the Spirit has been given, I will make you spiritual, so that with the most certain understanding of mind—though not yet as in the future—you may see God. Then I will openly announce the Father, so that you may understand that he and I are of the same substance. Then, “Ask in my name.” For then you will truly know and understand that, although as man I ask the Father, as God I hear together with the Father. Hence he says, “I do not say to you that I will ask the Father.”

**VERSE 27.**—“For the Father himself.” The Father loves us because we love the Son, although we have received from the Father and the Son the ability to love the Father and the Son. Once love has been given through the Spirit—whom we also love together with the Father and the Son—the one who loves first causes us to love him.

**VERSE 28.**—“Again, I leave the world.” He left the world in bodily presence. He goes to the Father because he led humanity into the invisible realities of the Father’s majesty. He left the world because he removed from the sight of those who love the world what they had seen. He returns to his homeland because he taught his lovers to believe that he is equal to the Father.

**VERSE 29.**—“His disciples say to him.” Since the hour he promised had not yet come, they say: “Behold, now he speaks openly.” The things that the Lord knows to be proverbs to those who do not understand, they understand so thoroughly that they do not even understand that they do not understand. Therefore, warning them about their weakness, he replied: “Now you believe,” etc.

[Col. 0415A] **VERSE 30.**—“Now we know that you know all things.” They plainly show that, when he spoke about them, he was addressing especially what pleased them to hear; and the questions they themselves wished to ask, he anticipated and brought forth of his own accord. Therefore, because he knew their thoughts, they confess that he knows all things, as God and the Son of God. “And you have no need,” etc. Since you know all things, you do not need to ask anyone from whom you might learn something. Nor do you need to be asked by anyone, since you know beforehand what he wishes. If he sometimes asked or was asked, this was necessary not for him but for others.

**VERSE 31.**—“Now you believe.” Like little children, to whom all lofty things are still proverbs, you believe; but the hour of the passion is coming, and is already near. In it you will be so disturbed that you will abandon what you now believe—not only bodily, but also in the faith of your minds. Hence: “We were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel.”

**VERSE 32.**—“And I am not,” etc. Behold, they have made progress, but he wishes to extend them toward something greater. When they say, “You came from God,” he says, “The Father is with me,” lest they think that he came forth from God in such a way that he also departed from him. “Because the Father is with me.” He had said, “I leave the world and go to the Father”; now he says, “The Father is with me.” To the one who understands, this is a saying; to the one who does not understand, a proverb. Even if it is not food for him, it is nevertheless nourishment of milk. From this comes the fact that they knew he knew all things.

# CHAPTER 17

[Col. 0415C] **VERSE 1.**—“Jesus said these things.” Not only the things spoken at the supper, but also those spoken from the beginning. Yet he especially says that these things were spoken at this supper so that they might have peace in him. This is the peace for which we are Christians, for which we are instructed in the sacraments, for which we are taught in every way, for which we received the Spirit as a pledge, for which we believe in him, hope in him, and are kindled with love for him. This is consolation and liberation amid tribulations.

“Father, the hour has come.” He could have prayed in silence, but in praying he is also a teacher, and he makes known a prayer that is an edification both for those present and for those to come. “The hour has come.” Not because fate compelled it, but because God ordained it—he who, outside of time, arranged in fitting order all things that take place in time. “Glorify your Son.” Humility began in the passion, and glory in the resurrection. The hour of the passion has come, the sowing of humility; do not delay the glory of the resurrection, so that your Son may glorify you. The Father’s glory in itself can neither increase nor diminish. Among human beings he was less known while he was known only in Judea, but through the Son’s resurrection he became known everywhere.

“That your Son may glorify you.” In the knowledge of human beings, as you granted, until they know you and the one whom you sent. For the Father cannot be glorified by human knowledge unless he is known through the one by whom he is glorified—that is, unless he becomes known to the people. This is the Father’s glorification, which is to take place not only among the apostles but also among all believers.

**VERSE 3.**—“This is eternal life,” etc. The order is: “That they may know you and the one whom you sent,” that is, Christ, together with the Spirit, who belongs to both, to be one and the only true God. If, then, the Son glorifies you in the way in which you gave him authority over every creature—and you gave it in such a way that everything you gave him he might give them eternal life—“this is eternal life: that they may know you.” Thus the Son glorifies you: he makes you known to all whom you gave him.

“That they may know you.” What is here from the Father will be complete in the future. Therefore, whoever advances in knowledge tends toward greater life. When knowledge is complete, praise will be without end. That is the glorification in question; but here he is glorified first, when he becomes known to the faithful. Hence: “I have glorified you on earth.”

**VERSE 4.**—“I have completed the work.” That is, if he were openly speaking of the future, he would say, “I will glorify you by preaching to the nations.” “I will complete the work,” because it has already been accomplished in predestination; and what will certainly happen is to be regarded as already accomplished. He makes this predestination more clearly manifest in his own glorification when he says: “Which I had with you before the world existed”—that is, just as then, in predestination, I had it with you before the ages, so now accomplish it in reality in the world and in time.

“You gave me,” etc. Grace is indicated here. For there is nothing in a human being that he has not received.

[Col. 0416B] **VERSE 5.**—“To human beings.” All these things can be said concerning all future believers. This is the glorification by which the glorified Son glorifies the Father on earth, with the past being used for the future.

**VERSE 6.**—“They were yours.” (AUGUSTINE.) These belonged to the Father, as all things do, etc., up to “because the human being did not yet exist.”

**VERSE 7.**—“They have known.” Lest it be thought that this knowledge had already taken place through direct vision, he adds: “They have truly believed.” This is not in the sense in which he said, “Now you believe; the hour is coming when you will be scattered.” Nor were they yet such, but he foretells what they will become once they have received the Spirit, without whom they did not even keep the word he had spoken.

**VERSE 9.**—“I pray for them.” The first prayer was: “Glorify the Son, so that the Son may glorify you.” He carried this out concerning them and concluded with the faith of believers. Now he prays that the Father may preserve those whom he has left bodily behind.

**VERSE 10.**—“And all my things are yours.” The Father did not lose what he gave to the Son, since the Son adds: “All my things are yours, and your things are mine.” Everything that belongs to the Father belongs to the only-begotten Son, because he is also God, born from the Father, and equal to the Father.

[Col. 0416D] **VERSE 11.**—“Keep them.” So that they may be one in their nature, just as we are one in ours. Therefore he does not say, “That they may be one with us,” or “That we and they may be one as we are one,” because they are not of the same nature as God, as the Son, according to his divinity, is one with the Father.

**VERSE 12.**—“While I was with them.” We must not understand that the Father and the Son preserve them alternately, as though one preserved them after the other. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who is one God, preserve them together. But Scripture does not raise us up unless it first descends to us. When it speaks in this way, we should understand that it distinguishes the persons, not that it separates the nature.

“The joy” that he expressed above—“that they may be one as [lacuna]”—this is that peace and blessedness in the future age for the sake of which all things take place, and for the sake of which he says that he spoke in the world.

**VERSE 17.**—“Sanctify.” Just as sanctification began from your grace, through which they are no longer of the world, so by the same grace make them more holy, so that they may persevere in the truth, of which the ancient sanctifications were a shadow—that is, in me, who am the truth. He makes this clear by adding: “Your word is truth,” which means, “I am the truth.” In Greek, *logos* (λόγος); in Latin, “word” or “speech” (*verbum* or *sermo*), who is the only-begotten Son of the Father.

**VERSE 19.**—“And for their sake I sanctify myself.” That is, so that it may benefit them, I will sanctify myself as man in the Word who has existed from the beginning of his incarnation, when the Word became flesh. It benefits them in this way because I also sanctify in myself those who are myself, since head and body are one Christ. Hence he adds: “So that they themselves may also be,” sanctified in the truth and in me, as I am.

**VERSE 20.**—“I do not pray for them alone.” He now begins to speak not only of the apostles, but also of the other members. He does not pray for those who have already died in his faith, but for those who are in temptations. “But also for those who.” Until the end of the world, or for those who already believe wherever they are, though not yet as perfectly as they will believe after the resurrection.

“Through their word.” Through the word of the Gospel, which belongs to them—not because it was preached only through them, but also through Paul and any others, but because it was entrusted to them first and principally for preaching. This is the word of faith, the word of God, through which the thief believed, Paul believed, and everyone believes.

[Col. 0417C] **VERSE 21.**—“That they all may be one.” He does not say, “We are all one,” but “that they all may be one,” just as you, Father, are in me and I am in you—understand, “we are one.” Thus the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, so that they may be one because they are of one substance.

We, however, can be in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; or the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit can be in us. Yet we cannot be one with God, because we are not of one substance. God is in us as in a temple; we are in him as a creature is in the Creator.

“That they also may be.” He says “in us,” so that they may attribute to God’s grace the fact that they are one in faith and love, just as now they are “light in the Lord.”

“That the world.” Here “world” is understood to mean all those who are one. The fact that they are one does not cause them to believe; rather, by believing they become one. Although they were one by nature, through disagreement with the One they were not one. Yet he prayed that the world might believe, just as he prayed that all might be one—as though the third clause were understood: “I pray that the world may believe.”

**VERSE 24.**—“Those whom you gave.” That is, you drew them to me, and so I also chose them from the world. The others were not given to him; they are not his, although he has authority over all.

“I desire.” What the Almighty wills cannot fail to happen. But this is the human will concerning which he says: “Not as I will” (Matt. 26).

“Let them see.” When they see him judging good and evil in the glorified form of a servant, the wicked will be removed so that he may not see the glory of God as God. Only the pure in heart will see it, and for them it will be eternal life.

[Col. 0418A] **VERSE 26.**—“So that the love.” The love with which the Father loves the Son is in all the righteous, because they are his members and are loved in him, who is loved in his entirety. Therefore he adds: “And I am in them.” As though he said: Because I am in them, it is differently that I am in us as in a temple and that we are in him; for we are that one, since, according to his humanity, we are the body of the head.

# CHAPTER 18

**VERSE 1.**—“Where he was.” He is seized in a garden so that he might destroy the sin committed in the garden of delights. Passing through the torrent of this age, he led his disciples into it.

**VERSE 3.**—“A cohort.” Not a cohort of Jews, but of soldiers, kept by the governor in accordance with the order of legitimate authority, so that, while they held him, no one would dare resist—or, if anyone did dare, would be unable to resist so many.

“He came there.” He is handed over at night so that he might be found without the crowds that were frequently present during the day.

**VERSE 5.**—“I am.” With this single utterance, by the power of his hidden divinity, he cast down so many fierce and powerful men, though he was about to die. For he wished to be seized, but only when he wished it.

**VERSE 6.**—“They went backward and fell to the ground.” In this way Christ now says everywhere through the Gospel, “I am”; and the Jews, awaiting the Antichrist, go backward and fall upon the earthly things they love.

**VERSE 8.**—“Let these go.” (AUGUSTINE.) They do what he commands: they allow those whom he does not wish to perish to go—not that they would not later die, but because at that time they did not yet believe in the way those who do not perish believe.

[Col. 0418C] **VERSE 11.**—“Put it away.” As though he said: “Let vengeance cease.” Or: “Return the sword to its place,” that is, direct the word of preaching toward the nations, where, according to Paul, a great and open door is found.

Or, after the fullness has entered, he says to Peter—through whom the whole order of preachers is signified: “Send the word of preaching to Israel.” For all who take up the sword will perish by the sword (Matt. 26). By what sword? By the one that turns with fire before paradise, and by the sword of the Spirit, which is written among the armor of God.

**VERSE 12.**—“The cohort, then.” It was customary among the Jews that the person whom they judged worthy of death should be bound and handed over to the governor.

**VERSE 13.**—“And they led him away.” At that time there were two chief priests, as Luke says, Annas and Caiaphas, who held office in alternate years. But that year belonged to Caiaphas, and by his will Jesus was first led to Annas—not because he was his colleague, but because he was his father-in-law. Or perhaps their houses were situated in such a way that Annas could not be passed by those going through.

**VERSE 15.**—“And another disciple.” Since it is not stated here who this person is, let no one determine it rashly. Yet John usually signifies himself in this way.

**VERSE 17.**—“He says: ‘I am not.’” (AUGUSTINE.) Not only does the person who says that Christ is not the Christ deny Christ; the person who denies that he is a Christian also denies him. Thus what the Lord said is fulfilled: “You will deny me three times” (Matt. 26).

**VERSE 21.**—“Why do you ask me?” That is: from one whom you do not wish to hear the truth. Ask instead those whose statements you will not resent. He moderates his answer so that he neither conceals the truth nor appears to defend himself.

**VERSE 22.**—“But when he had said these things.” The question is raised why he did not do what he taught: he ought to have answered in no other way, but to have offered the other cheek. Yet he answered truthfully, gently, and justly; and he prepared not merely his cheek but his whole body for the one striking him. In this way he shows that the commandments concerning patience are to be fulfilled not by displaying the body but by preparing the heart. For someone can visibly offer his cheek while angry. It is better, therefore, to answer when truly at peace and calmly prepared to endure greater things.

[Col. 0419B] **VERSE 23.**—“If I have spoken wrongly.” He speaks wrongly who speaks against the truth. “If I have spoken wrongly, give testimony proving that I am a liar.”

**VERSE 25.**—“Now Simon Peter was standing.” (AUGUSTINE.) After saying that Annas sent Jesus to Caiaphas, he returns to the point in the narrative where he had left Peter, so that he might explain what occurred in Annas’s house concerning Peter’s threefold denial.

**VERSE 28.**—“Into the praetorium.” That is, where the governor Pilate lived. But if they brought him to Caiaphas, how did they enter the praetorium? Perhaps, because some matter required it, both had come from Annas’s house to hear Jesus. Caiaphas went to the governor’s praetorium and left Jesus with his father-in-law to be heard; or Pilate had established a praetorium in Caiaphas’s house, and the house was so large that the master lived in one part and Pilate in another.

“So that they would not be defiled.” During the days of Unleavened Bread, they considered it a defilement to enter the dwelling of a foreigner.

**VERSE 31.**—“It is not lawful for us,” etc. They say this because of the holiness of the feast day. The Law commands that they not spare evildoers, especially those leading people away from their God, as they said this man was. And they speak against themselves, because they were killing the one whom they handed over to be killed, just as Pilate killed him, though not with his own hands.

When Pilate wished to hand Jesus over to the Jews so that they might judge him according to their law, they refused to receive him, saying: “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone.” Thus Jesus’ prediction concerning his death is fulfilled: that the nations would kill him after he had been handed over by the Jews. They act as though they were strangers to the crime, although they sin more greatly; this reveals not their innocence but their madness.

**VERSE 34.**—“Do you say this from yourself?” Jesus knows both what he is asking and what the other will answer. Nevertheless, he wished this to be said not so that he himself might know, but so that what he wished to be known might be written down.

**VERSE 35.**—“What have you done?” As though he said: If it is not a fault that you called yourself king, what else have you done? It would not be surprising if you were handed over to the judge for punishment, since you call yourself king. But if this were not the reason, perhaps another would have to be sought—as though he said: Confirm whether this is the charge brought against you, or whether there is another.

[Col. 0420A] **VERSE 36.**—“Kingdom.” This is what he wished us to know. But first, by asking in turn, he wished to show what human beings—Jews or Gentiles—thought about his kingdom. Once this had been shown, he answered both groups more appropriately: “My kingdom is not of this world.” As though he said: You are mistaken. I do not obstruct your domination in this world, so that you need not fear in vain and serve it; rather, come to the heavenly kingdom by believing.

**VERSE 37.**—“You say that I am.” He is not afraid to confess that he is king, but his answer is framed so that he neither denies that he is king nor admits that he is of this world, as the one who said, “So you are a king?” understood. He answered him: “You say that I am a king.” As though he said: You speak carnally, as a carnal person.

**VERSE 38.**—“Again.” He does not wait for an answer, lest delay arise when he wished to release him. For the custom by which someone could be released at Passover suddenly came to mind.

**VERSE 39.**—“Now it is your custom.” Because they had been freed from slavery at Passover, they had this custom of releasing someone at Passover.

**VERSE 40.**—“Now Barabbas was a robber.” That is, a son of a master—the devil—who was a master to the Jews in their crime and faithlessness. Or Barabbas means “son of the father,” that is, of the devil.

# CHAPTER 19

[Col. 0420C] **VERSE 1.**—“Then Pilate took Jesus.” Pilate did this—that is, he permitted the soldiers to do it, or even ordered them to do it—in the hope that the Jews, satisfied with the punishments, would desist from killing him.

**VERSE 2.**—“They placed a crown of thorns.” In the crown of thorns is signified the taking upon himself of our sins, for which he wished to become mortal. Hence the Forerunner says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” Thorns are placed as a sign of sins. Hence the Lord says: “Your earth will produce thorns and thistles” (Gen. 3)—that is, your conscience will not cease producing the pricks and barbs of vices.

**VERSE 4.**—“Then Jesus came out.” Behold, the things Jesus had foretold about himself are fulfilled through hidden power. His patience is commended, by which the martyrs are formed.

[Col. 0420D] **VERSE 5.**—“And he says to them.” Here it becomes clear that Pilate did not fail to know that these things had been done by the soldiers, whether he ordered or permitted them, so that they might suffice for the Jews once they had been satisfied. But they become even more inflamed and cry out: “Crucify him, crucify him.”

**VERSE 7.**—“The Son of God.” Behold another and greater cause of envy: the unlawful aspiration to kingship seemed a small matter there, yet Christ was truly both king and Son of God.

**VERSE 9.**—“But Jesus.” Here and elsewhere Christ is read to have remained silent so that the prophecy might be fulfilled: “Like a lamb before its shearer, he was silent; so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53). This comparison with a lamb was given so that, in his silence, he might be regarded not as guilty but as innocent.

[Col. 0421A] For he is not convicted as one conscious of guilt, but as the gentle one he is sacrificed for others.

**VERSE 12.**—“And from then on.” That is, for this reason, lest he incur the sin of killing an innocent man—though even less on account of those envious men—he sought to release him. This does not mean that he sought to do so only then; if he had wanted to do so earlier, he was now seeking to do so.

“If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend.” Above they proposed the law according to which he ought to die, because he had made himself the Son of God. But since Pilate does not fear the law of a foreign nation, and fears more the killing of the Son of God, they frighten him with Caesar, whom he cannot disregard as the source of his authority.

**VERSE 14.**—“Now it was the day of Preparation.” (AUGUSTINE.) “Preparation,” which is interpreted as “readiness,” etc., up to “and it is the sixth day of Preparation.”

**VERSE 15.**—“Shall I crucify your king?” He still attempts to overcome the terror they had instilled concerning Caesar, saying: “Shall I crucify your king?” He wishes to break those whom he could not move by the disgrace inflicted upon Christ by appealing to their own disgrace.

**VERSE 16.**—“Then he handed him over.” Since they declare that Caesar is openly against Pilate if, by releasing with impunity the one whom they had handed over to be killed for this claim, he wishes to set another king over them, Pilate is overcome by fear. Therefore, overcome by fear, he handed Jesus over to them to be crucified.

“He handed Jesus over to them to be crucified.” “To them” does not mean that they themselves took him in their hands, since they had earlier excused themselves from this. Rather, they appear implicated in the crime from which they attempt to distance themselves, since Pilate did this only for their sake. Hence he does not say “so that they might crucify him,” but “so that he might be crucified” by Pilate’s judgment and authority.

**VERSE 17.**—“Bearing.” Jesus carried his own cross. A great mockery for the impious, but a great mystery for the pious, who glory in it as in a scepter of kingship. The cross is also a lampstand for the lamp that was not to be placed under a bushel. At first the Lord carries the cross because he suffered first; afterward it was placed upon Simon of Cyrene, because we must follow his footsteps.

**VERSE 18.**—“And with him.” The robber who remained in faithlessness signifies the Jews; the one who confessed signifies the nations.

**VERSE 19.**—“And it was written.” These three languages stood out above the others: Hebrew on account of the Jews who gloried in the law of God; Greek on account of the wise among the nations; Latin on account of the Romans, who at that time ruled almost all nations.

**VERSE 23.**—“When the soldiers had crucified him.” Here are the events that took place beside the cross, after he had already been crucified.

“Four.” The fourfold garment signifies the Church spread throughout the whole world, which consists of four parts, distributed equally—or concordantly—throughout all its parts. The tunic, allotted by lot and consisting of a single piece, signifies unity, which is held together by the bond of love.

“From above.” Love surpasses everything throughout the whole Church, because no one who appears to belong to the whole is without a share in it. From this whole, as the Greek language indicates, the Catholic Church receives its name; it is commended in the lot of God’s grace.

[Col. 0422A] **VERSE 26.**—“When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple standing whom he loved.” Although he was about to perform divine deeds and had seemed to reject his mother as unknown, he now showed that the hour had come which he had foretold, in which he acknowledged the one from whom he had been born mortally. He teaches that pious children should care for their parents. Hence the Apostle says: “If anyone does not care for his own, he has denied the faith” (1 Tim. 5), etc.

**VERSE 27.**—“And from that hour the disciple took her into his care.” Although he no longer possessed private property, he had received her a hundredfold in that community where everything was held in common—possessing nothing and possessing all things.

# CHAPTER 20

[Col. 0422B] **VERSE 4.**—“They were running.” John signifies the Synagogue, which came first to the tomb but did not enter, because it heard the prophecies concerning the incarnation and passion but did not wish to believe that he had died. Peter signifies the Church, which recognized that he had died in the flesh and believed that he was the living God; after him, at the end, it too will enter in Judea.

**VERSE 7.**—“It is separated.” The mysteries of divinity are incomprehensible and removed from the knowledge of our weakness. In what is wrapped up, neither the end nor the beginning is seen. So the loftiness of divinity neither began to exist nor ceases to exist.

“Into one place.” God is not in division of minds but in unity. Or, the cloth around the head signifies the passion of Christ, whose mysteries are separately hidden from unbelievers, because they are far removed from ours: he suffered voluntarily and without guilt, whereas we suffer unwillingly and with guilt.

[Col. 0422C] **VERSE 9.**—“For they did not yet understand.” Namely, to such an extent that, even when it was openly said by the Lord himself, because of their habit of hearing parables from him, they did not understand.

### Verse 11

**Weeping.** She now weeps more over him who has been taken away than over him who was killed, because no memory remained of so great a teacher, whose life had been taken from her, and this grief held her there. **While, therefore, etc.** Although she knew that he was not there, because she was overcome with grief she thought she could trust neither her own eyes nor those of the two believing men. Or rather, this happened by divine prompting.

### Verse 12

**He saw two.** The angels, that is, messengers, signify that the Gospel of Christ must be proclaimed from head to feet, that is, from beginning to end. He was also to be proclaimed from his Passion, because he is God before the ages and man at the end of the age. Thus the angel sits at the head when he says, “In the beginning was the Word”; at the feet, when he says, “The Word was made flesh.” Or the two angels signify the two Testaments, one preceding and the other following. They are joined because with equal meaning they proclaim him incarnate, dead, and risen.

### Verse 13

**Why are you weeping?** As though he were saying: “Do not sin.” In a certain way they forbid her tears by announcing joy. But she, thinking that they were asking because they did not know, reveals the cause of her tears: “Because they have taken away my Lord,” that is, the body of my Lord.

### Verse 14

**And she did not know that it was Jesus, etc.** She had her back turned toward the one whom she believed had not risen; because she loved and doubted, she saw him but did not recognize him.

### Verse 15

**Whom are you seeking?** Thinking that he was the gardener, she says to him. This is not because she is uncertain whom she was seeking, but because she does not know the one whom she is seeking. For she is not seeking Christ, but the one whom she thinks has been carried away.

**Lord.** She calls him “Lord” because she thinks him the gardener, in order to honor the man from whom she was requesting a favor. Yet she does not call him “Lord” in the same sense as the one whom she was seeking, who had been taken away.

Recognizing Jesus, she calls him “Teacher,” because she remembers him as the one from whom she was learning to distinguish human things from divine things.

**If you have taken him away.** She does not say “whom,” because the force of love makes her think that the one whom she is always considering cannot be unknown to anyone else.

### Verse 16

**Mary.** Turning, she says to him: “Rabboni,” which means “Teacher.”

**Jesus says to her.** After he had called her by a common name and was not recognized, he calls her by name, as though saying: “Recognize the one by whom you are recognized.”

### Verse 18

**Mary Magdalene came announcing to the disciples that she had seen the Lord, etc.** There the fault is cut off from which it had arisen. A woman brought death to a man; now a woman announces life to men. She who then recounted the serpent’s words now tells the words of the Life-giver, as though God were saying through the very events: “From the hand by which the drink of death was brought, receive the drink of life.”

### Verse 19

**When therefore, etc.** This happened on the very day of the Resurrection, on which Jesus appeared five times: first to Mary Magdalene; second to her again while she was running with the others who wished to announce it to the disciples; third to Peter; fourth to Cleopas and his companion; fifth to the disciples, with the doors shut, after the two mentioned above had already returned.

### Verse 20

**He showed them his hands and his side.** After the Resurrection, the Lord showed two contrary things in his body: that it was tangible and of the same nature, to establish them in faith, and that it was incorruptible and possessed of another glory, to invite them to the reward.

### Verse 21

**Then he said to them again: “Peace be with you,” etc.** He offers peace who came on account of peace; he repeats the greeting to show that through his blood the things in heaven and the things on earth have been reconciled.

### Verse 22

**Receive the Holy Spirit.** *(Augustine.)* The Spirit is given on earth so that one’s neighbor may be loved; the Spirit is given from heaven so that God may be loved.

### Verse 23

**Whose sins you forgive.** Here is the charity that is poured into their hearts through the Holy Spirit. To those who share in him, he forgives sins; from those who do not share in him, he retains them. Therefore, after he said, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” he immediately added: “Whose sins you forgive.”

### Verse 24

**But Thomas, one of them.** Thomas was absent, and did not believe what he heard, not by chance but by divine arrangement. Therefore the Lord offered himself to be touched by him, because through his doubt and the proof given to him no one is now left any reason to doubt.

**Who is called Didymus.** Didymus means “twin,” because Thomas was doubtful; that is, he was an abyss, since through doubting he came to know more deeply.

### Verse 28

**He answered.** He saw and touched the man, and beyond this, with doubt now removed, believed him to be God; he confessed the one whom he did not see.

### Verse 29

**Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed.** He did not say “because you have touched me,” but “because you have seen me,” since sight is, in a certain way, the general sense by which the other four are commonly designated. Perhaps he did not dare to touch him; but he believed merely by looking, or perhaps also by touching.

**Blessed.** He commends the faith of the nations, but uses the past tense, because he already knew as accomplished in his predestination what was still future.

## CHAPTER XXI

### Verse 1

**After this he manifested himself.** They had left everything and followed Jesus. If, after Jesus’ death and before he was restored to them alive, they had resumed their former occupation, they might have seemed to have done so out of despair. But after he had been restored alive, after they had received the Spirit of his breathing, and after his words, “As the Father sent me, I also send you,” they suddenly become what they had been: fishermen, not of men but of fish.

It must be understood, however, that they were not forbidden to seek their livelihood through their lawful trade, while preserving the integrity of their apostleship, when they had no means by which to live. Thus, while they labored, God added the necessities he had promised them. Here, however, their poverty was arranged so that, through the fishing, such great mysteries might be displayed.

### Verse 14

**This is now.** This does not mean that he was manifested only three times, but refers to the days: first, the day on which he rose; second, eight days later; and this day, when he performed this deed concerning the fish. The manifestations are therefore counted according to the days. The first, however often it occurred, took place on one day, the day of the Resurrection. The second was eight days later, and this is the third. With this third manifestation the Gospel ends.

### Verse 15

**When therefore they had eaten.** Jesus knows what he is asking—whether Peter loves him more; Peter says what he knows about himself, namely, that he loves him. Since he does not know how much the others love him, he is silent about whether he loves him more than they do. Behold, he teaches that hidden matters must not be defined rashly, and he answers more cautiously about himself after the danger of his earlier denial.

**Feed my lambs.** If you love me, feed my lambs. Do not seek your own glory in them as though they were yours, but mine; seek my gain, not yours, because love of God is proved by love of one’s neighbor. Whoever refuses the work of piety toward his neighbors loves God less.

This charity, however, is given by divine grace. John subtly indicates this when, in asking about love, he says here what he does not say elsewhere: “Simon, son of John,” that is, obedient through the grace of God. For the fact that he loves and obeys more ardently than the others is nothing but the grace of God.

### Verse 17

**He says to him a third time.** He asks what he knew not once but again and a third time; and a third time he hears from Peter that he is loved, and a third time commands him to feed the sheep. A threefold confession is returned for the threefold denial, so that the tongue may serve love no less than it served fear. And just as it was the judgment of fear to deny the shepherd, so it is the duty of love to feed the Lord’s flock.

**Peter was grieved.** *(Augustine.)* Even when sins have been forgiven, a human being endures the misery into which he came through sin. The punishment is longer than the guilt; nor would the guilt seem small if the punishment were removed together with it. Thus, either to demonstrate the misery that is due, or to correct a life prone to fall, or to exercise necessary patience, punishment temporarily holds a person—even one whom guilt no longer holds as guilty. This is the condition of these days: to be mourned, but not condemned.

**Feed.** To feed the sheep is to strengthen believers so that they do not fail; to provide earthly support for those subject to one’s care, if necessary; to offer examples of virtue; to resist adversaries; and to correct sinners.

### Verse 18

**When you grow old.** He foretells that Peter will suffer, just as he had foretold that he would deny him. Once strengthened by the Resurrection, Peter could now accomplish what, while weak, he had promised prematurely. He no longer fears the destruction of this life, because, when the Lord rose, he provided an example of the life to come.

### Verse 19

**And when he had said this.** After saying these things, Jesus began to depart. Peter, not yet understanding what he had heard—“Follow me”—began to follow him with his feet; and John also followed, the one who knew that he was loved.

### Verse 20

**Whom Jesus loved.** Jesus loved the others also, but he honored this one with a more intimate sweetness of his love, because he was chosen as a virgin and remained a virgin. For this reason he also entrusted his mother to him.

*(Augustine.)* John is distinguished from the others by the suppression of his name, etc., until: John, who is a virgin, is suited to the future life, where they neither marry nor are given in marriage.

**Upon his breast.** In the breast of Jesus are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. The disciple who reclined upon it was endowed with a greater than ordinary gift of wisdom and singular knowledge; by him was signified how many divine mysteries he would write beyond the others.

### Verse 21

**Lord, but what about this man?** Because Peter had heard that he would be crucified, he also wished to know the end of his brother.

### Verse 22

**So I want him to remain until I come.** I do not wish to bring him to completion through martyrdom, but to have him await the peaceful release of his flesh, when I, coming, will receive him into eternal blessedness.

### Verse 23

**And he did not say to him.** This is not to be understood as meaning that John did not die in the flesh, but that, whatever he suffered earlier, he would end his life in peaceful old age. For it was not a great thing to grant the beloved one immunity from death, since to be dissolved and to be with Christ is far better.

### Verse 24

**This is he, etc.** Here he openly identifies his own person by his office, whereas he had not wished to identify it by name.

### Verse 25

**I do not think that the world itself.** *(Augustine.)* It is not to be believed that the world could not contain the books because of the extent of places, etc., until: as with other tropes, that is, other modes of expression.

**Not even itself.** He does not say that it could not be contained because of physical space, but because of the capacity of the readers, although, with the truth of the events preserved, words often seem to exceed the truth through hyperbole.

# ACTS OF THE APOSTLES *(G)*

## PROLOGUE OF BLESSED JEROME

See among his works.

## CHAPTER I

### Verse 1

**I composed an account.** That is, I wrote, because to write is to work. Or he says this because, by his deeds, he deserved to be the writer of the Gospel.

**I composed.** The entire book of the Gospel is called one discourse because it has one meaning; or the singular is used for the plural. The Gospel is good news, by which rest after labor, a kingdom after service, and life after death are announced.

**Concerning all things.** Concerning Christ’s words and deeds that he judged worthy or suitable to his office of administration.

**Theophilus.** Theophilus means “friend of God” or “lover of God”; and if you are a friend of God, this is written to you.

**The things that Jesus began to do.** From the baptism of John, by which Jesus was baptized, until the day on which he was taken up into heaven, because Luke composed discourses concerning that entire period. At the end of the Gospel he wrote: “When he had blessed them, he departed from them and was carried up into heaven.”

**To do.** He establishes or instructs as a good teacher the one who does what he teaches.

### Verse 2

**Giving commandments to the apostles to preach the Gospel through the Holy Spirit.** The Gospel was preached through the Spirit, because he inspired the words and granted confidence.

Or: **commanding through the Holy Spirit**, that is, what the Son commands, the Holy Spirit also commands.

Or: **he commanded because of the Spirit**, because he would not have commanded unless the Spirit were going to come.

**He chose.** This is turned into praise of the apostles, whose deeds he proposes to write.

**Taken up.** Taken up by the Divinity, or taken up by a cloud, as a true human being.

### Verse 3

**Alive.** A living and genuine body, not a phantom body, which the apostles recognized as something perfectly familiar. Or “alive,” because he lived after death. Or “alive,” that is, no longer destined to die.

**Over the course of days.** He did not appear to them continuously for forty days. For John says that four other days intervened after the day of the Resurrection. After those days he appeared again for forty days: because he had been dead for forty hours, he confirms that he lived for forty days.

The number forty may also be understood as a figure of the present age, during which Christ dwells in the Church; or because the human being, composed of four elements, is instructed against transgression of the Decalogue.

### Verse 4

**Eating together with them.** He announces the signs of a true body, because he proved that he had risen not through one bodily sense only, but through sight, hearing, touch, appearing, speaking, and eating together with them.

**The promise that he had promised.** Through Joel, as is found below. Although the promise was made by Christ, it would nevertheless be fulfilled by the Father. Or it is called the Father’s because it is promised in his Word, that is, in Christ.

### Verse 5

**For John.** *(Bede.)* When the Lord said, “For John baptized with water, but you, etc.,” until: which did not take place in John’s baptism.

Baptism is given in two natures, namely, bodily and spiritual, because the person who is baptized consists of two parts, body and soul. Yet there is one baptism, just as there is one human being.

**But you, etc.** When Peter denied the Lord, the apostles had not been baptized—not with water, but with the Spirit. For after the Resurrection it was said: “But you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit.” They had not yet been strengthened by Christ’s Resurrection and by the sending of the Spirit.

Just as circumcision was not necessary for the righteous before it was commanded to Abraham and his descendants, so, after the sacrament of the New Testament—that is, baptism—was given by the Lord in place of circumcision, when he said, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit” (John 3), etc., it is certain that no one belongs to the body of Christ unless baptized, except those to whom martyrdom is reckoned in place of baptism.

It is likewise written when Paul was baptized, but it is not written when the other apostles were baptized. We must nevertheless understand that they were baptized because of the saying: “Unless someone is born again,” etc.

### Verse 7

**It is not yours to know.** He does not say, “It will not be yours,” but “It is not yours,” indicating that they are still weak and therefore unfit to know the secret. When he says, “It is not yours to know,” he shows that he himself knows, since all that belongs to the Father belongs to him; but it is not beneficial for them to know. Rather, they should live as though they were to be judged every day.

**Which the Father has.** The time of that kingdom, he says, is so secret that it is disclosed only to the Father’s knowledge. But you will receive the power of the Holy Spirit, so that what you cannot do because of the weakness of the flesh, you may be able to do through the power of the Holy Spirit.

**In his own power.** He said this excusably as a true human being, but the power of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one. The Son too is the power of the Father.

### Verse 8

**But you will receive.** Knowledge of the times is taken away, but the divine help they need is supplied. In this way, when something is taken from children, something else is given so that they are not entirely saddened.

**When the Holy Spirit comes upon you.** When the Spirit comes upon you, he will not bring the kingdom of Israel, or the kingdom of God in Israel, as you suppose; rather, he will give you the power to testify about me. The time of that kingdom is so far distant that, before it comes, the fame of the Gospel will travel not only through Jerusalem but through all the boundaries of Judea and Samaria, and even to the ends of the world.

**In Jerusalem and throughout all Judea.** The sequence of order has been preserved in the names of the places. Jerusalem is followed immediately by the province of Judea; Samaria is joined to it by location; thereafter the commonality of the whole earth is added.

**In Jerusalem.** Mystically: in the vision of peace; in the confession of the true faith; in the keeping of God’s commandments. Through those who would make themselves strangers to the earth, he foretold that they would preach; through them, as though the spokes of a wheel extended from the center of the earth, where he worked salvation, spiritual grace and saving doctrine flowed throughout the whole world.

### Verse 9

**And when he had said these things.** Mark recalls the matter differently, saying: “And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven” (Matthew 28). But because Luke more significantly added, “When he had said these things, he was lifted up,” he shows that, when those discourses had been completed, the Lord ascended into heaven.

### Verse 11

**Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven?** Their understanding ought to have been more discerning, because the Galileans excelled the other Jews in wisdom.

Or: **Galileans**, that is, “turning about,” because through the instability of their understanding they would forget God’s commandments.

### Verse 12

**Then they returned, etc.** The apostles’ return from the Mount of Olives to Jerusalem signifies the Church, which, ascending from the active life to the contemplative life, descends again into active conduct.

The Mount of Olives was called by the ancients the “mountain of three lights”: the lamp shining from the temple, the sun rising on the other side, and the natural light of the olive oil on the mountain itself. These three correspond to perfection: the light of the divine Word shining from the Church, the radiance of the Sun of Justice, and the brightness of a pure conscience.

### Verse 13

**And when they had entered.** In Greek it is arranged as follows: “When they had entered the city, they went up into the upper room, where Peter was staying,” etc.

In Greek the order of the names is: Peter and Andrew, James and John, Simon the Zealot and Judas of James.

**The upper room, etc.** *(Bede.)* It is a place above, signifying that, lifted up from the earth, they ascend to the heights of knowledge and virtue.

The upper room is so called as a third roof, a figure of charity built upon faith and hope. Charity, moreover, has been poured into our hearts through the Spirit.

**Peter and John.** Peter is placed first because he is prince and shepherd. Peter and John are rightly placed first because they ran together to the tomb, since they loved more than the others. The first, if it is permissible to say so, loved more than the others; the other was loved greatly by Jesus.

The catalog of the apostles is included so that no false persons might be received in addition to these. Their places are also listed in pairs, with the degrees of their merits distinguishing them.

These are the twelve sons of Jacob; the twelve springs in the desert that Israel found at Elim; the twelve loaves of the Presence; the twelve stones on the high priest’s vestment; the twelve signs of the zodiac; the twelve stones of the altar; the twelve stones lifted from the Jordan; the twelve oxen beneath the bronze sea; the twelve stars in the bride’s crown; the twelve foundations; the twelve gates; the twelve months of the year; the twelve hours of the day; and the twelve fruits of the tree of life.

**The Zealot.** *(Bede.)* The Zealot is the one who in the Gospels is called the Cananaean. “Chana” means “zeal.” He was from a village of Galilee where the Lord changed water into wine. After his brother James, he governed the Church of Jerusalem.

With the son of perdition perishing, the number of the apostles remained incomplete. For, in the likeness of the moon, the Church waxes and wanes; but old things pass away, and new things come to be.

### Verse 14

**Mary, etc.** The Virgin is distinguished from the women, although a virgin is sometimes called a “woman” not because of corruption but because of sex. Behold, the beginning of the Church’s birth is adorned with the flower of virginity.

**Among the brothers.** That is, among the sons, whose Father is one in heaven.

Peter is said to have stood in the midst, as though condescending through common compassion. This example should be adopted by the pastors of the Church.

This number, one hundred and twenty, corresponds to the age of Moses. Just as, under this number, after Moses died, Jesus succeeded him and led the people into the promised land, so in the Church the leadership of Christ succeeded the ancient law, leading the true Israel into the kingdom of heaven.

### Verse 18

**He acquired a field.** Not because he himself possessed a field, but because the price of the field belonged to him who sold the Lord of life. Having lost the land of the living, Judas possesses a field of blood and death, with the everlasting memory of his crime and his name.

Yet he did not possess the potter’s field bought with the price of blood, since he immediately punished himself for the crime of betrayal; rather, “he possessed” is said for “he caused to be possessed.”

Some foolishly interpret the field possessed by Judas as hell. Others think that he possessed that field because he was buried there together with foreigners.

**The entrails.** The entrails, which are the seat of deceit, torn open by so great a crime, were unable to contain themselves. It is rightly through the seat of deceit that the entrails are poured out—not through the place of the kiss, that is, the mouth with which he kissed Jesus, although with a false outward appearance, but through another place in which the poison of hidden malice lay.

### Verse 19

**Of them,** that is, of those living in Jerusalem. Although both groups spoke Hebrew, the distinctive speech of the people of Jerusalem differed from that of the Galileans, from whom the apostles came. This is shown during the Lord’s Passion, when Peter himself, unwillingly betrayed by his speech, was shown to be a Galilean.

### Verse 20

**Let it be desolate, and let there be no one, etc.** Until Matthias is chosen and appointed in his place.

Or: Let Judas himself not be the one who dwells in it; instead, another should be appointed in his place, since he was judged unworthy of repentance.

### Verse 23

**Two.** Clement reports that these two, who were appointed for the apostolic lot, had been among the number of the seventy disciples.

**Who was surnamed.** He dwells on Barnabas’s praise, because in the case of Matthias it is enough to say that he was chosen by lot. Barnabas’s praise is increased so that he might not seem to have been rejected as unworthy. This was later made clear, because he was appointed an apostle of the Gentiles together with Paul and reserved for that office.

**Justus.** This is either Latin or Hebrew, and means “sparing” or “raised up.”
