**And Matthias.** This means “given” or “gift of God”; the gift of the apostleship was bestowed upon him by the Lord. Or it means “cloth of God.” Rightly, the one who was just, as Arator says, is surpassed by the praise of men in his smallness.

## CHAPTER II

### Verse 1

**In the same place.** That is, in the upper room into which they had ascended. Whoever desires the Spirit transcends and tramples underfoot the dwelling of the flesh through contemplation of the mind.

### Verse 2

**From heaven.** The Spirit is given from heaven so that God may be loved; he is given on earth so that one’s neighbor may be loved. For he was given twice after the Resurrection to commend the two commandments of charity.

**Sound.** It may be said that the speech of tongues sounded from the mouths of the apostles.

**The Spirit.** Before the Passion, the Spirit was given to the apostles for the grace of teaching and healing. After the Resurrection, Jesus breathed the Spirit upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven” (John 20), etc.

He had first given this gift to Peter alone. But, as is believed, it was then given to him by anticipation; now it was granted to Peter together with the others in completion. The power of forgiving was also given to those whom he was sending to the office of preaching.

**Mighty.** By comparison with what preceded, the grace of the apostles is called mighty; or the Spirit came in the likeness of a mighty wind.

**The whole house.** The Spirit is poured into those sitting in one house so that the unity of the Church may be commended, when the third law begins in the upper room. At the giving of the law, the people stood far away out of fear; here, when the Spirit came, they had been gathered together in unity out of love.

**Sitting.** So that what had been said to them might be fulfilled: “Sit here in the city.” Sitting is an indication of humility and stability. By these qualities a seat is prepared for the Holy Spirit, who rests upon the humble.

*(Gregory.)* The Spirit appeared in fire, but through himself, etc., until: and hearts were taught by voice or sound.

### Verse 3

**Divided.** The division of languages took place at the tower, but what pride scattered, humility gathers together. In pride there is dispersion; in humility there is concord.

Behold, the Lord’s statement is fulfilled: “I will not leave you orphans, but I will send the Paraclete Spirit” (John 14). As their advocate, he spoke for all of them in every language.

He who came on account of the Word brought tongues, for the tongue has a kinship with the word, so that they cannot be separated from one another. Thus the Word of the Father, that is, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are inseparable, indeed of one nature.

**As of fire.** The Spirit came in fire because he purifies sinners, enlightens them, kindles them, and burns them. Fire has four properties: it burns, purifies, warms, and illuminates. Similarly, the Spirit consumes sins, purifies hearts, shakes off sluggishness, and enlightens ignorance.

Fire is incorporeal and invisible in its own nature, but when it assumes some material body it becomes visible, appearing in different colors according to the materials in which it burns. Thus the Spirit cannot be seen except through the creatures in which he works.

### Verse 4

**And they began.** Here is the sign of fullness: a full vessel bursts forth. Fire cannot be hidden in one’s bosom.

**In various tongues.** Either they spoke in all tongues, or, speaking in their own tongue—that is, Hebrew—they were understood by everyone as though they were speaking in the native languages of each person, according to the saying of the prophet: “In other tongues and with other lips I will speak to this people,” etc.

### Verse 5

**From every nation, etc.** *(Rabanus.)* As though it were said: “Wherever they were born.” Captivity caused the Jews to be born among all nations; this captivity took place under Antiochus not many years earlier.

### Verse 6

**Confused.** This confusion is set against the confusion of languages from which Babel received its name. Thus the humility of the apostles responds to human pride.

**Each one.** All the languages are said to have numbered seventy-two. Therefore the disciples of the second rank were also chosen under this number, so that the number of preachers might correspond to the number of languages.

### Verse 8

**We have heard.** This signified that one Church would speak in the languages of all nations.

*(Bede.)* It is asked whether those who were speaking, etc., until: the miracle seemed rather to belong to the hearers than to those who were speaking.

### Verse 9

**Cappadocia, etc.** These five provinces, which are listed after Judea, do indeed speak Greek; but, because of their native customs, there is a difference in pronunciation. Therefore the grace in the apostles was marvelous: it not only taught them the differences, but also caused the distinctive variations within each language, corresponding to the number of provinces, to be expressed in their speech.

### Verse 10

**Roman visitors.** In Greek: “Romans who were living abroad,” that is, Jews who were leading the life of foreigners in Rome.

### Verse 14

**Men of Judea.** There are two causes of their prudence: namely, that they were Jews and that they lived in Jerusalem, a place suited to sobriety.

### Verse 17

**I will pour out.** Through this word he shows the abundance of the gift, because the Spirit was to be given not merely, as formerly, to prophets and priests, but freely to persons of both sexes.

**Of the Spirit.** In saying this, he refers to different gifts, not to any diminution of the substance.

**Upon all flesh.** He explains what “all flesh” means in what follows: “And your sons shall prophesy,” etc.

*(Rabanus.)* “Upon all flesh”: males and females, or the circumcised and the Gentiles, according to the saying: “There is neither male nor female, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free” (Galatians 3).

**And they shall prophesy.** The Law and the Prophets lasted until John; from that time the kingdom is proclaimed in the Gospel. But it is one thing to prophesy about Christ and another to foretell and teach future events.

### Verse 19

**And I will give.** Mystically, wonders in heaven are labors in the Church; signs upon the earth are punishments for earthly people; blood signifies martyrdom; fire signifies the Gospel or the Holy Spirit; the vapor of smoke signifies contrition of the soul or heart.

**Wonders in heaven.** For when Christ was born, a new star appeared; when he ascended the cross, the sun was darkened and the sky was covered with darkness.

**Blood.** This signifies not only the blood of a wound but also that of sweat, when in prayer his sweat became like drops of blood. This is counted among the signs of his divinity, because such a thing is not found in human nature.

Therefore it signifies that the whole world is to be washed in Christ’s blood. Just as the tabernacle had been consecrated by the blood of victims, so the faithful people would be dedicated by his blood; and so that Jerusalem alone would not be a place of prayer, but in every place under his dominion the elect would lift their hands to the Lord in prayer.

**The vapor of smoke.** The vapor of contrition and tears. For just as smoke comes from fire, so contrition comes from the ardor of the Holy Spirit.

**The sun will be turned, etc.** This was partly fulfilled in Christ’s Passion and is partly believed to be destined to occur before the day of judgment. At that time the sun was darkened, but the moon could not appear to human beings as turned into blood, because, since it was then the fifteenth day—at Passover—it had been hidden from human sight during the daytime by the earth’s interposition.

### Verse 23

**By the determined counsel.** *(Rabanus.)* In this alone the Jews were blameworthy: they acted without an obedient mind.

**And by the foreknowledge of God, etc.** *(The same.)* In Greek it is arranged as follows: “Having received him as one delivered according to foreknowledge.” For he was delivered by the governor into their power, so that they might choose either him or the robber; but, when life was granted to the robber, they killed Jesus through the hands of the soldiers.

### Verse 24

**He raised him up.** This was not the ordinary resurrection shared with others and deferred until the end, but the resurrection celebrated on the third day, so that the testimony of this Resurrection might be an assertion of his divinity.

*(Rabanus.)* “He raised him up” according to his humanity, which the Jews hated most of all.

**Having loosed the pains.** The sense of this statement seems to be that, when the Lord descended to the underworld, the pains of punishment were loosed because they could not touch him. But according to the Greek, where it is written, “Loosing through him the pains of death,” and according to the statement that it was impossible for him to be held by death, it is clear that through his descent the saints were freed from the regions of the underworld.

Although they were in Abraham’s bosom, that is, in the consolation of rest, they had not yet been wholly freed from the pain of death or the underworld, because they had not deserved to enter the joys of heaven until the prophetic saying was fulfilled: “By the blood of the covenant you brought out your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water” (Zechariah 9). They were prisoners before they were led out.

### Verse 25

**I foresaw the Lord.** This is the voice of Christ exulting after the Resurrection at the right hand. The left signifies the present life; the right, eternal life.

**That I may not be moved.** After the Resurrection everything will be immovable.

**And my tongue exulted.** Because rest was given after labor. He labored in hope of eternal life.

**You will not abandon.** I will not again be shaken by the corruption of a second crucifixion and death.

**You have made known to me.** I know that I will always live.

**You will fill me with complete joy.** That is, I will not die again.

**Because at the right hand.** The reason he is not moved is that the Lord assists at his right hand, with the left unable to prevail. For if he is not at the right hand, the devil occupies that side, as it is said concerning Judas: “And let the devil stand at his right hand” (Psalm 108).

### Verse 26

**And he exulted.** During the Passion he said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26), and he began to be afraid and troubled, so that he might show himself to be truly human in soul and body and truly capable of suffering.

But afterward his soul and tongue exulted, because through his Passion the human race was to be saved.

### Verse 27

**In the underworld.** It is clear that his soul was not abandoned in the underworld: after taking away those for whom he had descended, he immediately returned to the heights. Nor was his flesh corrupted, but it was glorified through a swift Resurrection.

### Verse 28

**You have made known to me.** These words are understood not only of him who, once he had received the fullness of divine power and wisdom, destroyed death by himself and rose to life, but also of the righteous, who, having found through him the way of truth, will return to life and rejoice when they see his face, because that sight surpasses all things and is perfect blessedness.

### Verse 33

**Having received the promise of the Holy Spirit.** Christ received it as a true human being, and as God pours out the Spirit, as Joel says: “I will pour out,” etc.

The apostles likewise receive from him the promise of the Spirit, who is said in the Gospel to be sent by the Father.

**He poured out this, etc.** Earlier Peter said that Jesus had been raised by God; now, lifting the faith of his hearers higher, he identifies him as the Lord and confirms that he poured out the Spirit. For this is the sign.

Beautifully, he uses the word “pouring out,” which he had recalled above that the prophet Joel used, so that from this also it might be established that Jesus himself is the Lord. Before assuming flesh, he customarily spoke in the prophets; he gives signs and wonders in heaven and on earth; he saves all who call upon him. He fulfills, as true God, the other things that the prophet describes.

### Verse 34

**Sit at my right hand.** *(Rabanus.)* From this psalm Peter clearly teaches that Christ’s kingdom is not earthly but heavenly, etc., until: in the other, he is the Lord of the same.

### Verse 36

**The Lord.** By placing the name of majesty and power, he shows that Jesus is the one to whom every creature must be subject.

**Christ.** This is the name of royal or priestly dignity. In the Law, kings and priests were anointed as a figure of him.

**And Christ.** He is truly Christ, anointed with the complete fullness of the Holy Spirit, and from that same Spirit he gave powerfully to whomever he wished.

**Jesus whom, etc.** Jesus is Lord and Christ, one person existing in two natures: eternally born from the Father in his divinity, temporally made in his humanity, when he was incarnate in the Virgin’s womb through the working of the Holy Spirit.

### Verse 37

**They were pierced.** Joel’s prophecy is fulfilled, because after the fire of the Holy Spirit comes the vapor of contrition. Smoke commonly drives out tears. Those who had mocked begin to weep; they beat their breasts and offer prayer to God as a sacrifice, so that they may be able to taste that blood by which they are to be saved—the blood they had previously invoked against themselves and against their children.

### Verse 38

**In the name.** Either in honor, or in this form, because the faith of the Three is contained in the One.

### Verse 39

**And to all.** This refers to the final statement of the prophecy, namely: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.” This pertains especially to the calling of the Gentiles, who, having been made far from the children of Israel, were to be saved through calling upon the name of the Lord.

Verse 40.—“He testified,” etc., that is, testimony and exhortation. “Be saved.” This is the character of the testimony and exhortation; but Luke has compressed Peter’s many words into a brief sentence. “From this generation.” There are two generations: one of the good, the other of the wicked.

## CHAPTER III

Verse 2.—“The temple gate,” etc. King Jotham, son of Uzziah, king of Judah, built this gate exceedingly high. For all the temple gates were on the ground, except the Beautiful Gate, which was suspended; it is called by the Hebrews the Gate of Jotham.

(BEDA.) The Beautiful Gate of the temple is the Lord, through whom, etc., up to “the keys of heaven have been given.”

[Col. 0434B] Verse 6.—“Silver,” etc. Peter remembered that commandment: “Do not possess gold and silver.” The money that was placed at the apostles’ feet they did not store away for themselves, but kept for the needs of the poor, who had abandoned their patrimonies.

Verse 8.—“And leaping up he stood,” etc. The order of perfection is this: first he who had been lying down rises; then he undertakes the path of virtues; and thus he enters the gate of the kingdom with the apostles.

Verse 10.—“With astonishment and ecstasy,” that is, with fear and an excess of mind. Ecstasy is also said to occur when the mind is not alienated by fear, but is taken up by the inspiration of revelation.

“And he ran,” etc. (BEDA.) Israel having been saved through the apostles, the whole world ran, etc., up to “he alone holds dominion throughout the peaceful world.”

Verse 13.—“The God of Abraham,” etc. (RAB.) Three are mentioned, with no wicked person intervening, either because of the primacy of righteousness, or, etc., up to “which is likewise observed in spiritual generation.”

Verse 15.—“You killed him,” by will and by word, and this against the law, which says: “Whoever kills a man willingly shall himself be killed.”

Verse 16.—“Complete healing,” in the two things stated above.

Verse 17.—“Through ignorance.” Two things cooperated: your ignorance and God’s foreknowledge.

Verse 18.—“Through the mouth of all,” etc. It therefore had to be fulfilled, because not one alone but all had prophesied.

[Col. 0434D] Verse 19.—“So that sins may be blotted out.” Sins will then be completely blotted out when, through the power of the resurrection, death—the last enemy—has been destroyed.

Verse 20.—“So that when the times come,” etc. These words are stated continuously with what precedes: namely, “so that when times of refreshment come from the presence of the Lord, then your sins may be blotted out.”

Verse 21.—“Whom it is necessary,” etc., that is, [for him to receive] the Church through faith, or to sit in heaven at the right hand of the Father.

Verse 22.—“Moses indeed.” He gives examples, not of everyone who spoke, nor of everything they said, but only of certain persons and matters.

[Col. 0435A] “For a prophet,” etc. The Son of God assumed flesh from the people of Israel, appearing in the likeness of Moses. Just as Moses brought carnal Israel, instructed and purified by ceremonies and sacred laws, into the promised land, so Jesus led spiritual Israel to heaven through the grace of the Gospel. And just as despisers of the law of Moses were expelled from the promised land by their enemies, so those who despise the teaching of the Gospel will be driven from the assembly of the saints by avenging spirits.

“From your brothers.” (RAB.) God raised Joshua from Ephraim and Jesus from Judah.

Verse 23.—“He shall be exterminated from the people,” that is, from the lot of the saints, and shall be made an outcast. Or, he shall be cast beyond the boundaries of blessedness.

[Col. 0435B] (RAB.) Those who resisted Joshua were cast out from the carnal people; those who resist Christ are exterminated from the spiritual people. Disobedience in either case is followed by death, whether carnal or spiritual.

“From Samuel onward.” Under Samuel the period of the kings began in Judea.

Verse 25.—“Of the covenant.” (BEDA.) From that covenant which was made with Moses, etc., up to “in your seed all the nations shall be blessed.”

“Fathers.” He used the plural “fathers,” not the singular “father,” because the promise was made not to Abraham alone but also to Isaac and Jacob. “In your seed,” etc. (BEDA.) The seed of Abraham is Christ; in faith in him, blessing was promised to all families, that is, to Jews and Gentiles.

[Col. 0435C] “All the families.” Not that all are blessed, but because none is blessed except in him, just as it is said: “He enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1).

“They shall be blessed.” Cursed in Adam’s sin, they were blessed in Christ. In him even those who preceded the Incarnation are blessed, because the same man who is God opened the gate of heaven and at the end will say to all the elect: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matthew 25), etc.

## CHAPTER IV

Verse 1.—“The priests and magistrates,” etc. These appeared to be the teachers and judges of the people. “Sadducees.” They denied the resurrection, and therefore were distressed by the apostles’ teaching, which proclaimed the resurrection.

[Col. 0435D] Verse 2.—“Being distressed,” because the multitude was gathering to hear the apostles.

“Resurrection.” This was especially directed against the Sadducees. Both groups, however, were distressed because the apostles affirmed that Jesus—whom they had killed as a man—had been glorified by God the Father.

Verse 4.—“And it came to pass,” etc. If the five thousand people whom the Lord fed in the wilderness are understood as representing the people of the law liberated by Christ, then the five thousand instructed by the apostles here may also signify the people of the Gentiles, who were to follow spiritually the mysteries of the same law. They are rightly given this heavenly gift in the evening, because when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son into the world, etc.

[Col. 0436A] Verse 11.—“This is the stone.” (RAB.) In answer to the questions about Christ, he preaches about him, and especially about David, in whom they believed above all others as their patriarch.

“Rejected.” (AUG.) There is no historical account concerning the rejected stone.

Verse 13.—“Uneducated,” etc. This was said not because they were wholly ignorant of letters, but because they did not possess expertise in the grammatical arts. “Unlearned.” They were called unlearned because they had not developed their natural ability through instruction. Greek ἰδίωμα, Latin proprietas, means “distinctive character” or “particularity.”

(BEDA.) The unlearned are sent to preach so that believers might not think that faith was produced by eloquence rather than by God’s power, according to the saying: “Not in the wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power” (1 Corinthians 1).

[Col. 0436B] Verse 19.—“But Peter,” etc. (RAB.) You who are judges, perform your office—not by uttering a perverse sentence, but by judging justly. Behold, full grain is found in the ear: what previously bent like grass now stands upright.

Verse 20.—“For we cannot.” That is, “we do not wish to,” or the expression has been transformed into the condition of not sinning, as happened with the confirmed angels.

Verse 21.—“They glorified.” In Greek: “All were glorifying for that which had been done”; it does not contain “for that which had happened.”

Facts or words are glorified when, as rumor spreads, they are brought to the knowledge of many. God, however, is glorified in human deeds; this is characteristic of Christian piety and humility, since he himself says: [Col. 0436C] “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5).

Verse 22.—“For he was more than,” etc. From this it became clear that the glory or grace of the miracle was greater; therefore he speaks not of the man’s age but of the duration of his infirmity.

Verse 24.—“With one accord,” etc., “without sound.” Or, with the perfection of unanimity, according to the saying: “If two or three have gathered together in my name, whatever they ask concerning anything, it shall be done for them.”

Verse 25.—“The nations raged.” The roar is the voice of a lion. Hence Jeremiah says: “My inheritance has become for me like a lion in the forest; it raised its voice against me” (Jeremiah 12). “They meditated on vain things,” either concerning the coming Christ or concerning keeping him in death.

Verse 26.—“They gathered together.” Herod and Pilate gathered together in friendship.

Verse 27.—“You anointed.” They explain the name “Christ.” “Christ” comes from chrism, that is, anointing, according to the saying: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44).

Verse 29.—“With all boldness.” They ask God that they may be able to speak the word of God with complete confidence.

Verse 30.—“Through the name.” In Greek: “Through the name of your child Jesus.” This accords better with the apostles’ prayers, since they were striving that the man crucified by the Jews might be made glorious through miracles and that, through the name of the one who had been taken up into heaven, he himself, the Son of God, might become known.

Verse 31.—“The place was shaken.” The great power of the prayer of the faithful; this was done to raise up their minds.

[Col. 0437A] Verse 32.—“One heart.” Those who had abandoned the world did not exalt themselves above others by boasting in the nobility of their lineage. Rather, as born from the womb of one and the same mother, the Church, they rejoiced in the same love of brotherhood. “Nor did anyone of them.” The virtues possessed by the righteous they do not regard as their own, but as belonging to those for whose benefit they administer them.

“Common.” In Greek κοινά, whence “coenobites,” that is, people living communally. “Coenobia” are their dwelling places.

Verse 33.—“The apostles gave testimony.” He distinguishes the order of teachers and hearers. The multitude of believers, having rejected temporal possessions, were joined to one another by the bond of charity. The apostles, however, shining with power, [Col. 0437B] disclosed the mysteries of Christ.

Verse 36.—“Joseph.” (RAB.) “Barnabas,” interpreted as “son of consolation,” means “increased” or “made fruitful” through the growth and progress of spiritual good.

“What is interpreted.” Whenever Scripture gives the names of things or persons together with their interpretation, it signifies that a more sacred meaning is contained in them. He is rightly called “son of consolation,” who, having despised present things, consoles himself with hope of the future. The Holy Spirit is also called the Paraclete for this reason: by infusing himself into those who suffer distress in the world, he grants paraclesis, that is, consolation. Likewise Peter, because of the grace of the Spirit, was called Barjona, that is, “son of a dove.”

“Son of consolation.” (RAB.) Either because he consoled the poor by his almsgiving, or because of the consolation of the reward that he deserved to receive from God, or because he was considered worthy to console the apostles for Judas.

## CHAPTER V

Verse 3.—“He tempted.” (RAB.) He uses the past tense, “he tempted,” because the temptation had been completed. Temptation operates in three ways: suggestion, delight, and consent. All three were fulfilled in Ananias. “And to defraud.” (ID.) His lie seems to have consisted in this: he had vowed the whole amount. It is better not to make a vow than not to fulfill it after making it, to the Holy Spirit.

Verse 4.—“But to God.” Above he had said, “to the Holy Spirit”; therefore it is clear that the Holy Spirit is God.

Verse 5.—“He fell.” (RAB.) The beginnings of laws are always commended by punishments. The two sons of Aaron were consumed when they offered strange fire; Uzzah died while supporting the ark. He fell so that the other transgressors might be terrified by his example.

“And great fear came,” etc. (BEDA.) This is anticipation: for only a few had heard of the man’s death before his wife’s death, although it could have been said of the few that they were afraid.

Verse 7.—“About three hours,” etc. (RAB.) A short time for repentance is granted to the wife, whose guilt is more pardonable than that of her husband, since she consented to the head.

Verse 8.—“Tell me,” etc. (ID.) By questioning the wife, he discloses her guilt from her own confession, just as the husband had revealed his guilt by his action.

[Col. 0438A] Verse 9.—“Why indeed,” etc. Is this spoken as a rebuke? Or should it be punctuated as follows: “What?” as if he were saying, “What is this?” Then he answers himself: “Indeed, was it agreed between you to tempt the Spirit of the Lord?”

“To tempt,” etc. (RAB.) The temptation of the Spirit consisted in their testing how great his knowledge was.

“They buried her.” (ID.) From this many derive the example that wives should be buried beside their husbands. Others consider it unworthy to draw examples from transgressors, since their equal partnership in the crime, death, and burial had made their deserts equal.

Verse 11.—“And great fear came.” Ananias died before Sapphira, quickly in the sight of the Church, so that the authority of the apostles might be shown, and so that it might be demonstrated how great a sin it was to take back from the Church what had been offered; the others were also to be corrected by their example.

Verse 12.—“Of the apostles.” The word “apostles” is used in the plural because this was not done by the hand of Peter alone. Although the others are silent out of respect for him, their deeds are not thereby denied.

Verse 13.—“Of the others,” etc. The example of Ananias and his wife—the punishment of the two who had fraudulently joined themselves to them—provided an example for the others.

Verse 14.—“They increased,” etc. (RAB.) The multitude of believers was so great that, as the strength of faith increased, a shadow alone was sufficient. Or: so many sick people were brought by the believers that they could not all be touched.

Verse 17.—“Heresy.” (RAB.) “Heresy” is interpreted as “division,” because a heretic, rejecting the statements of others, chooses what he thinks should be followed.

“Filled with the sect of the Sadducees,” etc. The Sadducees are interpreted as “righteous,” being named after Zadok the priest, either because of their lineage or because of their customs. Yet, while justifying themselves, they claimed for themselves what they did not possess. Denying the resurrection of bodies, they said that souls perished with the flesh. They also believed that neither an angel nor any spirit existed. They rejected all the Scriptures except the books of Moses. For this reason they especially agreed with the rulers in persecuting the apostles, who by their power and signs bore witness to Christ’s resurrection.

Verse 20.—“The life of this one.” (RAB.) Either Christian life or eternal life. This is not added because the Christian sect was notorious, and it was on account of it that they had been handed over to prison.

[Col. 0438D] Verse 23.—“We certainly found the prison,” etc. The insane Jews—stirred by envy—say that Jesus was stolen from the tomb by the apostles, while claiming that the apostles themselves had been taken out of a locked prison by theft.

Verse 24.—“The magistrate.” According to the Greek, “magistrate” should be read in the singular, as also in what follows, where it says: “Then the magistrate went away with the attendants.” “They were perplexed.” Even so they do not believe; inner wickedness hardens the faithless heart against signs that are plainly evident.

Verse 28.—“By commanding,” etc. In Greek: “Did we not strictly command you?” This manner of speaking is more appropriate to someone asking a question. “You have filled Jerusalem.” Jerusalem is the chief of the cities, in which we also dwell. In this they unwittingly praise the apostles, who, though terrified by threats, do not cease preaching.

“Upon us the blood.” (RAB.) It is clear that this was said by antiphrasis: “His blood be upon us.”

The high priest’s rash question is refuted by a prudent answer.

(ID.) They ask, for words can contain uncertainty even when a firm judgment is held in the heart.

Verse 30.—“The God of our fathers.” (RAB.) He is not a new God, nor one recently invented by us. He says this so that their disobedience may be inexcusable.

Verse 32.—“The Holy Spirit.” The Holy Spirit strengthened us so that, even though you resist, we may firmly proclaim the great works of God, with him speaking within us and shaping the words that you hear.

“To all.” (RAB.) Not only to us, but to all who obey—including you, if you are willing to receive it. By this he summons them to repentance.

Verse 34.—“Gamaliel.” He was thought to have been a disciple of the apostles, remaining among the Jews by the apostles’ counsel so that he might destroy their most wicked plans and calm their fury.

Verse 36.—“Theudas.” (BEDA.) Theudas persuaded many, after removing their possessions from the city, to occupy the banks of the Jordan. Since he was a magician, he claimed to be a prophet and promised to provide them a passage by dividing the river. By order of the procurator Fadus, a troop of cavalry came upon him; after many had been killed or captured, they carried his head back to Jerusalem.

Verse 37.—“Judas the Galilean,” etc. Josephus says of him that he compelled the people not to lose their liberty by paying tribute to the Romans, arguing from the law that one must serve God alone and that those who paid tithes ought not to pay tribute. This sect grew so greatly that the Pharisees and a large part of the people asked Christ whether it was lawful to pay tribute to Caesar.

Verse 40.—“After being flogged,” etc. (RAB.) Here the strength of faith is evident: it could be restrained neither by words nor by scourges. First they were forbidden by speech; now they were beaten with scourges.

Verse 41.—“Because they were worthy.” They did not think they were suffering hardship, but receiving the greatest gift, because: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for God” (Matthew 6).

Verse 42.—“Every day,” etc. Such brief sections are often inserted, gathering together many matters in summary, so that they may serve as a conclusion to the preceding discourse and establish a foundation for what follows.

## CHAPTER VI

Verse 1.—“Of the Greeks.” (RAB.) Either Gentile newcomers living in the city, or, etc., up to “they were burdened by the daily ministry.”

“They were being neglected.” Because of their deficiency, they were burdened more heavily.

Verse 2.—“It is not right for us,” etc. The apostles show that bishops and teachers of the Church ought not to be entangled in bodily and material affairs.

Verse 3.—“Consider,” etc. (BEDA.) From this point the apostles already decreed, etc., up to “not without the mystery of the number seven.”

[Col. 0440A] Verse 4.—“But we,” etc. They do not ask about themselves; they make a judgment.

Verse 5.—“And they chose,” etc. (RAB.) This order is to be observed in ordinations: let the people choose, and let the bishop ordain.

“Stephen.” He is placed first and praised alone, either so that all may be praised in one person, or so that the honor of martyrdom may be assigned to the first.

Verse 6.—“And praying.” The common administration required ministers to be chosen. When they were found worthy, as the providence of the saving plan gradually increased, it pleased the Church to ordain these same men as ministers of the sacred altar and of the Lord’s blood, as well as of the common meal and table. This is demonstrated by the statement: “Praying, they laid their hands upon them.” This is proper to those who are advanced to the office of the most sacred altar. Following this example, prayers are offered at ordinations, although the apostles’ prayer itself is not written down.

Verse 7.—“And the word,” etc. (RAB.) This appears to be a recapitulation, because he had said: “Every day they did not cease teaching,” etc.; then he returns to the same point, saying: “And the word of the Lord increased.”

(ID.) In this book, and also in the Gospel, such brief sections are often inserted, etc., up to “because earlier, as the people increased, zeal had been aroused.”

Verse 8.—“Stephen,” in Greek; in Latin, “crown.” What he was going to accomplish in deed he anticipated through the omen of his name, because after Christ’s cross he was the first to be crowned sublimely by martyrdom, though he was humbly stoned. In Hebrew, Stephen is interpreted as “our standard”; having suffered first, he became a model for the martyrs who followed in dying for Christ.

Verse 13.—“This man.” Out of contempt, they do not call him by his proper name, but call him “a man,” as though he were merely carnal and insignificant.

## CHAPTER VII

Verse 2.—“Men, brothers and fathers.” Since Stephen was accused of blaspheming Moses and God, at the beginning of his speech he addressed their slander, saying that the God who spoke to the fathers and prophets was the God of majesty and glory. He also praises Moses, but proves that they were rebellious and always disobedient. Yet he used an artful manner of speaking toward rebels, beginning as though he feared them: “Men, brothers and fathers.” Gentle and kindly speech wins over the hearer and commends the speaker. He began graciously so that he might be heard for a long time; and although he refused to speak against God and the law, he preaches the true God at the beginning of his address. He also expounded the law in such a way that he appeared to be the preacher of the very one whose destruction he was accused of seeking. As his speech proceeded, he refuted their errors and demonstrated the strength of his spirit and his freedom from fear of the enemy.

“God of glory,” etc. Stephen remembered that commandment: “Love your enemies” (Luke 6), etc., and proclaimed salvation to his persecutors.

“In Mesopotamia.” Mesopotamia lies at the northern head of Syria.

[Col. 0441A] (RAB.) Mesopotamia and Harran are in Chaldea; he migrated from Mesopotamia to Harran.

Verse 3.—“And he said,” etc. In Genesis it seems to be stated that after the death of his father the Lord spoke to Abraham, whose father died in Harran, where Abraham lived with him. But before he lived in the city, while he was in Mesopotamia, he was told:

“Go out from your land,” etc. He calls the land and kinship of Abraham the homeland and race of the Chaldeans, from which he had already departed, now dwelling in Mesopotamia. Yet he was still held by the hope and desire of returning, and therefore he hears: “Go out from your land and from your kinship”—not so that he might remove his body, which he had already done, but so that he might tear out the love of his heart.

(RAB.) Stephen omitted the third phrase, namely, “and from your father’s house,” either because of the people’s excessive knowledge or their ignorance.

Verse 4.—“Then he went out,” etc. (RAB.) Abraham went out from Ur of the Chaldeans. “Ur,” etc., up to “after his father’s death he was told: ‘Go out from your land,’ etc.”

“His father,” etc. (ID.) He returns to the origin of Israel’s lineage and to the beginning of divine friendship, so that he may omit nothing in which he might appear to blaspheme.

“You dwell.” He says “you,” not “we,” because the apostles had already, in a certain sense, abandoned the land; and Stephen, who was already as if placed in death—

Verse 6.—“For your seed shall be,” etc. (BEDA.) This should not be understood as though they were to be treated badly, etc., up to “whether in the land of Canaan or in Egypt.”

“Four hundred years.” (RAB.) It should be joined as follows: “A sojourner,” etc., up to “was completed for the distribution of the promised land.”

Verse 7.—“I will judge.” (ID.) “Judgment” sometimes signifies discernment, as in: “Judge me, O God, and discern my cause” (Psalm 42). Sometimes it signifies punishment, as in: “Judge them, O God” (Psalm 5).

Verse 8.—“The covenant of circumcision.” (ID.) The covenant or sign was made so that the people of Israel, etc., up to “it signifies that boasting in spiritual circumcision must be avoided.”

“On the eighth day.” (RAB.) The mystery of our circumcision is displayed through eight days. By the eighth day of the New Testament—which is contained in the Lord’s resurrection and in the eight beatitudes—we are circumcised from vices.

[Col. 0441D] Verse 9.—“They sold him into Egypt.” Narrating briefly, he passes to the conclusion. Joseph was not first sold to the Egyptians, but to Ishmaelite merchants and Midianites, and they sold him in Egypt to Potiphar the priest.

Verse 14.—“In persons.” This is said according to the edition of the Septuagint translators. In the Hebrew text only seventy persons are found.

(RAB.) If Jacob and Joseph, together with his two sons, are not counted, etc., up to “than to make his statement suspect in relation to the Hebrew truth.”

Verse 15.—“And he went down.” According to the situation of the places, the movement from the promised land into Egypt is a descent; and because slavery followed upon freedom, Jacob is said to have gone down into Egypt with his descendants.

Verse 16.—“They were transferred.” (RAB.) By synecdoche they are said to have been transferred on account of Joseph, to whom Jacob, etc., up to “Carry my bones away from here with you” (Genesis 50).

(BEDA.) Scripture testifies only concerning Joseph that his bones, etc., up to “the twelve patriarchs were not buried at Arbe but at Shechem.”

“And they were placed,” (RAB.) Genesis teaches that Abraham bought the field from Ephron, son of Zohar the Hittite, etc., up to “they were unwilling to serve either Moses or the Lord.”

“In the tomb,” etc. This concerns Jacob alone. His sons carried his body out of Egypt and buried it in the double cave, where Abraham was buried with Sarah, and Isaac with Rebekah; Leah was also buried there. Hence that city is called Hebron, that is, “union,” because the fathers were buried there with their wives. He confuses two histories and entangles one with the other. Abraham did not buy the field from the sons of Hamor, the sons of Shechem; Jacob bought Shechem from them. Therefore it should be joined as follows: “They were transferred to Shechem by the sons of Hamor, the sons of Shechem”—as if it said, “to that Shechem which Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor, the sons of Shechem.” In Genesis, Shechem is read as having been the son of Hamor. Hence some think there were two men named Shechem: one whom Luke calls the father of Hamor, and another whom Genesis calls his son. Others join the beginning and end of the statement, saying “from the sons of Shechem,” and then adding “Hamor’s sons,” so that this passage agrees with Genesis.

Verse 18.—“Another king.” This king is the devil, who loves the effeminate and hates the manly.

[Col. 0442C] Verse 19.—“Our race,” etc. He means “our fathers,” and says “our race” so that he may not seem to blaspheme the fathers.

Verse 20.—“Pleasing to God,” etc. Blessed Stephen shows that Moses did not blaspheme.

Verse 22.—“Moses.” (RAB.) Moses has the same meaning as “aquatic,” because he was taken from the water, or “one who wipes,” because he was found in a basket smeared with bitumen. Moses is a type of the Savior, who, after striking down the devil, liberated his own people.

Verse 24.—“He defended him,” etc. He shows that the man who was committing the wrong was not of Moses’ own people.

Verse 26.—“He appeared to them.” (RAB.) Thus Christ appeared after the Ascension through the apostles to the Jews who were quarreling and to the unbelievers who resisted the apostles.

[Col. 0442D] Verse 27.—“Who appointed you,” etc. It is as though Moses answered: “No one—but God alone.” “There is no authority except from God.” Someone had earlier received a similar answer from Christ: “Man, who appointed me judge or divider over you?” (Luke 12). By asking, “Who appointed you,” etc., he reproves them in their dispute, since even then they were opposed to the law and to Moses.

Verse 28.—“Do you perhaps,” etc. Some think that the man who had been defended spoke the words in anger.

Verse 29.—“He fled.” Moses was in Midian, that is, Christ was among the Gentiles.

Verse 30.—“In the flame of fire,” etc. The fire in the bush is the Holy Spirit; the sins of the people are like thorns, because the ardor of the Holy Spirit did not consume the sins of that people, which opposed dense thorns of wickedness to God’s benefits.

(RAB.) For this reason the form of fire—which cannot be imitated—was shown to them, lest any, etc., up to “how readily a man removes his sandal.”

Verse 32.—“I am.” “I am” is the proper word of God, according to the saying: “I am who I am,” etc.; “He who is has sent me to you.” Serpents are not to be feared where God speaks as present.

Verse 33.—“Take off your sandal.” This admonishes us that, while standing in the Church—which is holy ground—we should renounce dead works.

Verse 34.—“Seeing,” etc. (RAB.) God is entirely sight and entirely hearing; he sees everything and hears everything. Yet he is said to see and hear when he has mercy.

[Col. 0443B] “I have seen the affliction.” (ID.) Although I permit someone to be tested, it should not therefore be thought that I am unaware.

Verse 35.—“Whom they denied.” This is synecdoche. Many are said to have denied him when one spoke, or perhaps because several agreed with the one who denied him.

“Ruler.” It is great praise that he is called the ruler, redeemer, and liberator of the people.

Verse 37.—“This is Moses.” He turns back upon them the guilt which they, being disobedient and unbelieving, were casting upon Moses.

Verse 38.—“Words of life.” (RAB.) That is, the two tablets containing the Decalogue and the remaining commandments, concerning which it is said: “Whoever does them shall live by them.”

Verse 40.—“To Aaron.” (ID.) As though to a ruler. They speak as if ignorant of divinity. The true God was not made, but made all things; he is not a creature, but the Creator of all.

“Make gods for us.” (ID.) They call them gods because of the two pillars, etc., up to “the pillar of fire went before the people at night.”

Verse 42.—“The host of heaven.” The host of heaven sometimes means the army of angels, but in this passage he calls the stars the host of heaven, since he immediately adds, “the star of your god.” In the Book, etc. Although there are many prophets, it is nevertheless called one book; among the Hebrews it is one book.

“Did you offer victims?” (RAB.) Although they offered sacrifices because they were obliged to serve God, in their minds, nevertheless, etc., up to “they were always returning to Egypt in their hearts.”

The question arises how they did not offer them to God, since we read that they did offer certain things to God—not willingly, but from fear of punishments. God, however, accepts not what is offered but the will of those who offer.

Verse 43.—“Images,” etc. (RAB.) “The star of your god” is Lucifer, to whom they assigned images. The same gods were worshiped in images and in stars.

(ID.) Some interpret “the star of your god” so that the phrase belongs to God, because they received not the Lord himself but his star.

“And I will transfer you.” Because of these sacrileges you will be led captive beyond Babylon. The first martyr should not be thought to have erred when, instead of what is written in the prophet—“They were led beyond Damascus”—he said, “beyond Babylon.” He supplied the meaning rather than the exact wording, because they were led beyond Damascus into Babylon, or beyond Babylon.

Verse 44.—“The tabernacle.” Since they said that he acted against the holy place, he shows that he did not speak blasphemy against the holy place.

“According to the pattern.” (RAB.) The pattern that he had shown him on Sinai; because the tabernacle was made according to that pattern, it is shown to have itself been a pattern.

(ID.) Historically, when it is said “with Jesus,” this is because Moses was dead.

Verse 46.—“To find a tabernacle.” That is, the true temple, of which the former was a figure, which would not be moved from its place—that is, the Church, which he foresaw would be firm and unchangeable. Concerning it the Apostle says: “The firm foundation of the Lord stands” (2 Timothy 2:9). And elsewhere: [Col. 0444B] “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians 3).

Verse 48.—“But the Most High does not dwell.” (RAB.) By Solomon’s statement he convicts the Jews, etc., up to “that he does not dwell in the temple of the Jews alone.”

“As the prophet says,” etc. He first spoke of the original tabernacle, which was a shadow and not the reality; afterward he introduced testimony concerning the tabernacle that was more real. “If I enter into the tabernacle of the Lord,” etc. He placed God at the end of the statement, so that every word might be established “on the testimony of two or three witnesses.”

Verse 49.—“Heaven is my throne.” In this way he shows that he surrounds everything. Elsewhere he declares that he measures heaven with a span and encloses the earth in a handful.

“But the earth.” By the example of the earth he signifies every creature of the Creator.

[Col. 0444C] Verse 51.—“Stiff-necked.” (RAB.) Having been cleansed of the crime of which the false witnesses accused him, he begins to accuse the Jews, because one who is without guilt is worthy of the office of teacher.

“And uncircumcised,” etc. He shows that circumcision—which they vaunted against the grace of the Gospel—has no power to save those whose thoughts and hearing are unclean.

Verse 52.—“Your fathers.” (RAB.) Above he said “our fathers,” speaking persuasively; now, while rebuking them, he calls those alone their fathers whose wickedness they imitate.

“And they killed.” (RAB.) He sets out three stages of their wickedness: first, that they resisted the Spirit; second, that they persecuted the prophets; third, that, as their wickedness increased, they killed them.

Verse 55.—“Standing.” Immovably, because he would not fall again; or the posture signifies one who helps, judges injuries, and fights on behalf of his servant.

“I see the heavens.” (RAB.) As he was about to depart from earth, he saw the heavens opened, so that he who had despised earthly life for Christ might deserve heaven’s inheritance. Thus, in the very midst of his passion, he sees the reward.

“The Son of Man.” Although Christ is the Son of God, he preferred to call him the Son of Man, so that the unbelief of the Jews might be confounded: they had crucified him as a mere man, refusing to believe that he was God.

[Col. 0445A] Verse 57.—“And they drove him out.” (RAB.) In this they gloried as fulfilling the law. For Moses said concerning the blasphemer: “Take him outside the camp, and let the people stone him” (Leviticus 24).

Verse 58.—“Lord Jesus, receive my spirit,” into the heaven that I see opened. Christ said to the Father: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.” Stephen, as a servant addressing his Lord, says: “Lord,” etc.

“For they do not know.” (RAB.) Many of them thought that by killing Stephen they were fulfilling the law, because they believed him to be a blasphemer. Christ had also foretold this: “The hour will come,” he said, “when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God” (John 16).

Verse 59.—“He fell asleep.” It is beautifully said, “He fell asleep,” and not “He died,” because he offered the sacrifice of love and fell asleep in hope of the resurrection. The saints do not die, because they are changed for the better, and temporal life is transformed into eternity.

“Saul, however,” etc. He did not stone him himself, but consented to those who stoned him. He would have perished had God’s grace and repentance not come to his aid. For those who do things and those who consent to them are worthy of death.

## CHAPTER VIII

Verse 1.—“On that day.” (RAB.) The day on which Stephen was killed—not because persecution happened only then, but because from that day a great persecution began, after one of the leaders of the Church had been killed.

“Church.” This means collection, assembly, or calling. “They were scattered.” This is what the Lord commanded: “When they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matthew 10). It happened by his will, so that through the occasion of tribulation a seedbed of the Gospel might arise.

Verse 2.—“Devout men cared for Stephen,” that is, men who feared God; either Christians, who were later scattered, or Jews who feared God although they were not yet Christians.

Verse 3.—“Saul.” (RAB.) He was named after Saul the persecutor, who was king of Israel from the tribe of Benjamin, as Paul also was. For according to the custom of the ancients, descendants derive their names from their ancestors.

“He ravaged.” (ID.) Like a wolf ravaging the flock, in accordance with Jacob’s prophecy: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he will devour the prey, and in the evening he will divide the spoils” (Genesis 49).

“Dragging.” He dragged them away but did not kill them, because perhaps the Lord guarded his hands so that they would not be stained with the blood of the innocent.

“Those who were scattered.” (RAB.) Although they were scattered through fear, they remained steadfast in preaching the Gospel.

Verse 5.—“Philip.” He was among the number of those who were scattered and was the first to preach Christ in Samaria. He was the second deacon after Stephen. He is narrated as second after Stephen, as though he were his successor and belonged to the same rank.

Verse 6.—“They paid attention.” (RAB.) Those who heard believed the words and saw the signs. There are two causes of faith: the words of preaching and the signs of miracles. From the present passage and the story of the Samaritan woman, Bede says, it is proved that the minds of this people were ready to believe.

[Col. 0446A] **VERSE 11.**—**Magicians.** (RAB.) Magicians philosophize about individual things: the nature of the world, the course of the stars, and their movements. **Deceiving.** Leading people away from the truth, or turning them through their tricks toward excess, bewilderment, and astonishment. **He had bewitched.** To bewitch is to drive away the rational mind.

**VERSE 12.**—**Philip.** (RAB.) Some say that this Philip was the apostle, one of the Twelve, but this does not seem true according to the sequence of this book.

**Jesus Christ.** (ID.) Of whom they were ignorant; or—as has been stated—he preached the Trinity in the name of Jesus, and whoever perfectly believes only one person of the Trinity cannot lack belief in the other two.

[Col. 0446B] **VERSE 13.**—**Then Simon.** (ID.) Either he believed in the Lord through Philip’s words and power, [and so on, up to] those who fraudulently entered the Church and stole baptism.

**VERSE 14.**—**They sent.** Peter associates John with himself, because the virginity of the Church is pleasing and welcome.

**VERSE 16.**—**In the name.** It should not be read as “baptized only in the name of Jesus,” as though the other persons were excluded, but rather: “they had only been baptized,” and so on—that is, they had not yet been confirmed. **Jesus.** Nevertheless, beforehand they believed in the Father and in the Holy Spirit, as did the other Jews. Or: the full faith of one person confirms faith in the Trinity.

**VERSE 17.**—**They laid hands.** (BEDA.) Philip, who was evangelizing in Samaria, one of the seven, [and so on, up to] when he hands over the Paraclete Spirit to the baptized.

**VERSE 19.**—**Authority.** (RAB.) Not merely the authority to baptize in water, to preach, or to perform the miracles that Philip possessed, but to lay hands on anyone, [and so on].

**VERSE 20.**—**Your money.** Not ours—for we do not desire it—but yours, which you compare to the Spirit, so that you may sell it for him and purchase the Spirit with it. He therefore wanted to buy the Spirit so that, selling him to others, he might receive more.

**Money.** (RAB.) From this one learns that alms should not be accepted from the condemned.

The apostles, unwilling to accept money, say: “May your money be with you”—that is, “Keep what is yours”—“and this, for your destruction,” so that, having gathered money unjustly, you may suffer eternal punishment.

**VERSE 22.**—**Repent.** Repent of the greed and wicked understanding by which you thought that commerce could be conducted concerning the Spirit.

(RAB.) “So that all may see what you are.” Peter does not say this because he is unaware that Simon will not repent, but because it is right for everyone to preach; he performs his duty so that Simon may be without excuse. He is also rebuked publicly so that others may no longer be deceived by him.

**Pray to God.** His heart is open before God; concerning him the Prophet says: “How good is the God of Israel” (Psalm 72). No one can deceive him, because “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wisdom 1).

**VERSE 24.**—**Pray.** Because of despair he himself does not dare to pray, but asks the apostles to pray for him; he does not dare to pray for himself because he does not believe that he will be heard. He also speaks deceitfully to the apostles. [Col. 0447A] **What you have said.** Not “what I have believed,” but, as an unbeliever, he attributes to them the things that are going to happen.

**VERSE 26.**—**But an angel.** After the apostles’ return, the narrative concerning Philip is woven in. **Toward the road,** and so on. For the road descends, and one travels downward along it because of the nature of the place.

**VERSE 27.**—**An Ethiopian.** By nature and by merit. For an Ethiopian is a dark-skinned person. Hence: “Ethiopia shall stretch out its hands to God” (Psalm 68).

**Powerful, and so on.** (BEDA.) Sending ahead the treasurer of the queen of the Ethiopians, [and so on, up to] “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear” (Psalm 45), and so forth.

**Of Queen Candace.** It was the custom of that region to be ruled by women, and for them to be called Candaces.

**VERSE 28.**—**He was returning.** He was beginning to return while reading Isaiah. Wherever the beginning of salvation is recounted in the New Testament, testimony is taken from Isaiah, whose name means “salvation of the Lord.”

**VERSE 30.**—**Do you think you understand, and so on?** (RAB.) They recognize one another’s languages, either through the eunuch’s instruction or through Philip’s spirit.

**VERSE 31.**—**How, and so on?** Here he censures the audacity of those who think that they can understand divine Scripture without a teacher.

**VERSE 33.**—**In his humiliation.** (BEDA.) Indeed, although he was the judge of all, he found no truth of judgment against himself; without any fault of his own, he was condemned through the sedition of the Jews and Pilate’s sentence.

**Humiliation.** (RAB.) The Passion by which he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death (Philippians 2).

[Col. 0447C] **He will be taken away.** The second man, heavenly and from heaven, separated from earthly things by holiness; or, he will pass from life into death.

**VERSE 35.**—**He opened.** (RAB.) He opened the treasury of knowledge. Or, he opened his mouth so that the Spirit might speak in him, according to: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 81).

Mystically, Philip opened the mouth of the Church, so that through it he might be preached to the Gentiles, who had previously not known him.

**He evangelized.** He solved the question of the one asking, “Of whom did the prophet speak?” He demonstrated that the prophecy had been spoken about Jesus.

**VERSE 36.**—**To some water.** The preaching had led to this point, so that he needed the water about which he had heard on the road in connection with baptism.

[Col. 0447D] **VERSE 37.**—**If you believe.** (RAB.) He was not ignorant of the eunuch’s faith, but wanted an open confession, so that an example of questioning and confessing might be given to those who baptize and to those who are baptized.

**VERSE 39.**—**The Spirit of the Lord.** (RAB.) Or, the Spirit violently rushed upon him, just as upon the apostles, [and so on, up to] those upon whom the Spirit had descended.

**VERSE 40.**—**He was found.** He was found by the people, who had not found him during the rapture, because he had traveled through the wilderness or because he had moved with extraordinary speed.

**Caesarea.** (BEDA.) He means Caesarea of Palestine, where he is later described as having a house, which is still shown today, as is also the room of his four daughters, who were virgins and prophesied.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0448A]

**VERSE 1.**—**But Saul.** He returns to what he had said above: “Saul was still ravaging the Church.” **Threats, and so on.** By threats he terrified those present and subjected them to slaughter. It is uncertain whether he killed them or scourged them, or did both. **Breathing.** He breathes like fire: not kindled by another, he himself set others ablaze.

**VERSE 4.**—**And falling.** Terrified, he fled to the ground; or, as though worshiping, he fell upon his face.

**Why me, and so on?** (BEDA.) He does not say, “Why are you persecuting me?” and so on, [up to] “Whatever you did to one of the least of these, you did to me” (Matthew 25).

**VERSE 5.**—**I am Jesus.** He does not call himself God or the Son of God, but says in effect: “Receive the weakness of my humility, and lay aside the scales of your pride.”

[Col. 0448B] **VERSE 7.**—**Rise.** Work diligently like an ox, and become a teacher of the Church. It is written in the Law: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing” (1 Corinthians 9).

**Enter.** (RAB.) As he is about to enter the city, he is terrified lest he bring sorrow upon the holy; thereafter the Lord commands him to enter, so that he may learn the faith he had attacked.

**And it will be told.** An example of learning is given, and pride is rebuked, so that no one may consider another unworthy to teach him what he does not know.

**VERSE 8.**—**With his eyes opened.** (RAB.) It is shown in his body what he had previously suffered in his soul. For just as an opened eye is useless without sight, so the Law is useless without faith in Christ.

(BEDA.) He could not see well again unless he had first been blinded and, excluding his own wisdom, which was thrown into confusion, entrusted himself to faith.

[Col. 0448C] **VERSE 9.**—**And he was.** (RAB.) Here a pattern is given for penitents: they should begin with three days. The rank of catechumens is also consecrated by this three-day period.

**For three days.** It appears that, blinded for three days, he awaited the light of grace—not sluggish in idleness, but enlightened by God and searching out heavenly things. It is believable that during this time he was also taught the dispensation of the Gospel.

**Not seeing.** Because he had not believed that God would conquer death by rising on the third day, he is instructed by his own example: the darkness of three days was changed when the light returned.

**He did not eat.** (RAB.) This had happened to his soul, which had possessed neither inward food nor drink. Through the body’s hunger and thirst it is shown that the needy soul must be satisfied.

[Col. 0448D] **VERSE 10.**—**Ananias.** (ID.) Calling someone by his own name indicates intimacy.

**VERSE 11.**—**Into a village.** (ID.) Villages are fields, or places near cities, or places situated within a city close to one another.

**VERSE 15.**—**Go, and so on.** He is not to be feared as a persecutor, but embraced as a brother, because he is ready to endure the evils he inflicted upon the saints.

**VERSE 17.**—**He entered.** The prophecy of Isaiah was fulfilled: “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb”—that is, Saul with Ananias.

**VERSE 18.**—**The scales fell, and so on.** (BEDA.) The serpent’s body is covered with scales, [and so on, up to] the light that he received in his mind.

(RAB.) The falling of the scales is an image of the renewed inner vision, freed from the veil of the Law.

**VERSE 20.**—**And immediately.** He fulfilled the Lord’s saying: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke 9), and so forth.

**VERSE 21.**—**Is this not?** (RAB.) He gives an example of not being ashamed where truth can change its judgments.

**VERSE 24.**—**They were guarding.** Not the Jews, but the citizens together with their king, Aretas, as he himself writes to the Galatians. For the Gentiles were joining the Jews in persecuting Christians.

**VERSE 26.**—**When he had come.** He did not come to Jerusalem to the apostles as soon as he was baptized; rather, as he writes to the Galatians, he first went away to Arabia and from there returned to Damascus. Then, after three years, he came to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and so forth. Afterward, as Luke testifies, he came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia.

**VERSE 27.**—**Barnabas.** (BEDA.) He was a Cypriot by birth, a Levite, who is mentioned above as having brought the price of a field and laid it at the apostles’ feet.

**VERSE 29.**—**With the Greeks.** Jews are called Greeks because they were born among the Greeks during the Dispersion.

**VERSE 30.**—**Caesarea.** Caesarea Philippi is a city of Syria. Tarsus is a city of Cilicia.

**VERSE 31.**—**The Church.** Such statements, as was said above, are often inserted at the end of narratives and at their beginning, for the praise of the apostles and of ecclesiastical faith. **And consolation.** Consolation is given amid labor; hence it is clear that the Church was being tested.

[Col. 0449C] **VERSE 33.**—**A man named Aeneas.** (RAB.) Aeneas signifies the human race lying sick, [and so on, up to] the one who is weakened by the pleasure of the flesh and the delight of the world.

**VERSE 34.**—**Rise.** He whom he had cured of paralysis he commanded to rise and make his bed, implying that the one who had received faith in his heart should not merely shake off his torpor but also prepare works in which he might rest.

**VERSE 35.**—**Lydda and Sharon.** Two cities were converted to God; for this reason miracles were performed in them.

**VERSE 36.**—**Named Tabitha.** (RAB.) Tabitha is translated from Hebrew into Latin as Dorcas, or “doe,” as is found in some copies.

**Dorcas.** Allegorically, Dorcas is a doe or a gazelle; [Col. 0449D] it signifies a soul exalted by devotion to virtue but despised in human opinion. By giving the interpretation of the name, Luke indicates that a mystery is present. These animals live in the mountains and see sharply; hence in Greek they are called *dorkades* because of the sharpness of their sight. Thus those exalted by the merits of their works look upward and keep watch over themselves attentively. They live simply, with a discerning measure of conduct; they walk as though with a cloven hoof; and they ruminate on the word of God through constant meditation.

**VERSE 39.**—**In the upper room.** (RAB.) She is placed in an upper room either because of the height of her merit or because of the sublimity of the miracle that was to be performed upon her.

**VERSE 40.**—**Having put them out.** (ID.) This was done according to Christ’s example when he raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, [Col. 0450A] either to avoid exaltation or lest the unworthy should see the sign.

**He opened.** (BEDA.) The order of those rising again is correct: first he opens the eyes of the mind; then, recognizing Peter’s voice, she sits up and recovers the light of her discernment, so that she may live for the teaching of those who assist. **He opened her eyes.** These are the three stages of resurrection.

**VERSE 41.**—**Then, giving.** Touched by Peter’s hand, Tabitha rises, because a soul weakened by sins is restored by no better means than by the examples of the saints.

## CHAPTER X

**VERSE 1.**—**Now there was a man, and so on.** (RAB.) By the merit of perfection and by his manly work, this centurion is called a man, according to: “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job.”

**Cornelius.** (BEDA.) He did not reach faith through virtues, but reached virtues through faith. (GREG.) Cornelius, whose almsgiving before baptism was attested by an angel, [and so on, up to] being strengthened in faith through works.

**VERSE 2.**—**Devout, and so on.** (RAB.) All these things arise from the goodness of nature, [and so on, up to] he may be believed to have conceived without the seed of a man—that is, without the teaching of a master.

**VERSE 3.**—**He saw.** (RAB.) Not at night and not in a dream, because the Gentiles, with their gross understanding, [and so on, up to] as was previously shown in the example of Peter and John.

**An angel of God.** (ID.) Not of Satan. By this the apostles who preached to and baptized the Gentiles are defended: how could a human being be jealous of what was revealed by an angel? **Entering,** perhaps toward him, and calling him; this also provides Peter with an opportunity to answer the Jews who argued against him and said: “Why did you enter among men who have foreskins?” (Acts 11), and so forth. **Cornelius.** Familiarity is shown, by which the name of a Gentile man is included in the knowledge of angels.

**VERSE 5.**—**And now send men, and so on.** (RAB.) Here recompense begins: God, who is merciful, shows mercy to the merciful, because “blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy” (Matthew 5).

**Joppa.** (ID.) It is a city in the Promised Land, near the Tyrrhenian Sea and situated on its eastern shore. Jonah descended there and entered a ship in order to flee.

**VERSE 6.**—**He is lodging, and so on.** Peter is lodging in the house of Simon, that is, “the obedient one,” who is a tanner, because the teacher of the Church gladly dwells where there are obedient people who chastise the body and subject it to servitude, having crossed the waves of the world through freedom of mind. For the steadfastness of faith despises the world’s fleeting glory and terrors.

**VERSE 7.**—**And when he had departed.** (RAB.) He does not say, “When Cornelius had awakened,” because the angel appeared to him neither in a dream nor in an ecstasy, but openly.

**A soldier.** (ID.) He does not say “servants who feared the Lord,” because at the beginning he had said that Cornelius was devout and feared the Lord with all his household.

**VERSE 9.**—**As they were approaching, and so on.** Another reading has: “When they appeared”—namely, those sent by Cornelius; [Col. 0451A] that is, they were approaching closely enough to be seen from the house of Simon the tanner.

(RAB.) Instead of “into the upper places,” another reading has “into the upper room,” and rightly so: for the Gentile people are like an upper house, whereas the Synagogue is below, because it is immersed in the world.

By saying “into the upper places,” he signified that the Church, having abandoned earthly desire, would have its way of life in heaven. At the sixth hour Peter becomes hungry amid his prayers—indeed, hungry for the salvation of the world, which Jesus came to seek and save in the sixth age of the world. He indicated this when, at the same hour, he sat beside the well of Samaria.

**VERSE 10.**—**When he was hungry.** (RAB.) He hungers through compassion for the salvation of the Gentiles, which is now shown in a vision. It appeared at the sixth hour because it took place in the sixth age of the world.

**VERSE 11.**—**Heaven opened.** (BEDA.) The opening of heaven is the revelation of the heavenly mysteries soon to come to the Gentiles. It signifies here that heaven has been opened to the Gentiles and that entry is to be made available.

**A certain vessel.** (ID.) That vessel signifies the Church, [and so on, up to] through whom the Church, filled with a heavenly gift, is exalted.

**Linen cloth.** It signifies the Church, the brightness of holiness, and the mortification of the flesh. **From heaven to earth.** (RAB.) From this we are warned that, where our head and root are—and we are its branches—there our anchor of hope must penetrate.

**VERSE 12.**—**All four-footed animals.** All the nations that would believe and be incorporated into the unity of Christ’s body, so that all might become his members.

[Col. 0451C] **VERSE 13.**—**Kill.** Cleanse, mortify, and sacrifice them, so that you may make them offerings to God, so that those rescued from oldness may pass into newness.

**VERSE 14.**—**I have never eaten anything common, and so on.** (BEDA.) Whoever eats food placed outside brings it into his own body. Therefore he commanded that the Gentiles, placed outside through unbelief, be incorporated into the fellowship of the Church, which Peter signifies.

(ID.) Peter considered the Gentiles unclean, [and so on, up to] but bind them by the love of God alone.

**VERSE 21.**—**Coming down.** (BEDA.) He is commanded to descend from the roof and go to preach, [and so on, up to] “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3).

**Here I am, and so on.** He shows that he knows of their arrival, while also giving an example of humility by avoiding a circuitous answer.

**What is the reason, and so on?** The Spirit said that the soldiers were present but kept silent about why they had come, because, in order to preserve humility, the spirit of prophecy sometimes touches the mind in part and sometimes does not touch it.

**VERSE 22.**—**He received an answer.** The Lord answered him through an angel because of his almsgiving and prayers. **Into the house.** By this they persuade him, because the angel had ordered them to enter his house, even though he was a Gentile.

**VERSE 23.**—**Bringing them in, and so on.** Here the apostles’ fellowship with the Gentiles begins, because he had come down to them, who had heard from the angel the command to enter the house of a Gentile; therefore he received the Gentiles as guests.

**VERSE 24.**—**Having summoned his relatives, and so on.** There were two reasons for the summons: the closeness of kinship and friendship.

**VERSE 27.**—**And speaking, and so on.** (BEDA.) The holiness of his conduct earned the fellowship of equality, just as the zeal of his punishment revealed his authority in the fault of Ananias and Sapphira.

**VERSES 30–31.**—**And behold, a man, and so on.** He does not say “an angel,” so free was he from arrogance, and he says: “Cornelius, your prayer has been heard, and your almsgiving has been remembered before God.”

**In the sight of God.** (RAB.) In Greek: “In the sight of God we are present.” This is rightly said by one who was ready to obey God, believing that he is present everywhere.

**VERSE 34.**—**God is not a respecter of persons, and so on.** [Col. 0452B] (BEDA.) It is clear that God is not a respecter of persons, [and so on, up to] but that he might receive all who believe.

**VERSE 37.**—**You know, and so on.** (RAB.) It should be read this way: “You know Jesus as John preached: Jesus of Nazareth, how he anointed him,” and so on. Or: “John preached this: that he anointed him”—not, indeed, in an earthly manner, but with the Spirit and the power of signs.

**VERSE 38.**—**Who went about, and so on.** In Greek, “for forty days” is added—not that they ate and drank with him every day, for that would conflict with John, who inserts eight days during which he did not appear to them, so that he might reveal himself a third time; and he fasted for the same number of days before his death, needing food, whereas after the resurrection he ate when he no longer needed food. He fasted before his death so that we might abstain from the desires of this age. He ate, teaching by this that he is with us until the consummation of the age. Fasting belongs to combat, because the one who is in the contest abstains from everything. Food belongs to the hope of peace, which will be perfected when this mortal nature has put on immortality. When we take up the way of the Lord, we fast from the vanity of the world and are refreshed by the promise of what is to come.

(RAB.) “For forty days” does not mean continuously, but on certain occasions occurring within that forty-day period.

**VERSE 41.**—**And we drank.** (BEDA.) Here Peter explains what is left unspoken in the Gospel: that after the resurrection he drank with Christ—unless perhaps we understand it to be indicated where he says: “Until I drink it with you in the kingdom of my Father” (Matthew 26).

[Col. 0452D] **VERSE 45.**—**The Spirit.** The Spirit is the house of God insofar as he is given to those who love God through him; but in himself God is present, even if he is given to no one, coeternal with the Father and the Son. Nor, because they give him and he is given, is he lesser than they. For he is given as God’s gift in such a way that he gives himself as God: “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3).

**VERSE 47.**—**Can anyone forbid water, and so on?** It is as though God, who is greater, had given the greater thing first and reversed the order: can what is lesser be forbidden? You have come so that you may be witnesses; therefore judge.

**VERSE 48.**—**In the name of Christ.** Although the Church’s rule is that baptism is administered in the name of the Trinity, Luke nevertheless testifies that it is administered in the name of Jesus Christ. Ambrose resolves this by saying that through the unity of the name the full mystery is accomplished: whoever says “Christ” also designates the Father, from whom the Son comes, and the Holy Spirit; whoever says “Father” also indicates the Son and the Spirit; and whoever names the Spirit names the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds, and the Son, whose Spirit he also is. Therefore, so that authority may be joined to reason, one is also baptized in the Spirit, according to: “You shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit” (Acts 11), and the Apostle: “In one Spirit we were all baptized” (1 Corinthians 12).

## CHAPTER XI

**VERSE 6.**—**The four-footed animals of the earth, and so on.** (RAB.) I am astonished that some interpret this as referring to foods, [and so on, up to] he explained the mystery of this vision.

**VERSE 18.**—**Then God has also granted to the Gentiles, and so on.** This is what is read in Job: “Gold will come from the north, and fearful praise to God,” because the splendor of faith first arose in the cold breast of the Gentiles, and, because of this unexpected faith, Judea glorifies God in fear.

**VERSE 19.**—**Now those who had been scattered, and so on.** He returns to what he had said: therefore those who had been scattered traveled about preaching the word. The narrative concerning Philip, Peter, John, and Paul has been inserted between these statements.

**VERSE 20.**—**But there were some.** (RAB.) Not of those who had been scattered from Jerusalem, but, [and so on, up to] who lived among the Greeks in the Dispersion.

**VERSE 21.**—**And a great number.** (BEDA.) After the revelation of the evangelical linen cloth—in which the holy animals rested in heavenly hope—the Church began to grow, when the Gospel was preached through foreign provinces, islands, and cities, [Col. 0453C] not only to Jews but also to Gentiles.

**VERSE 22.**—**And they sent Barnabas.** (RAB.) Barnabas means “a man in goodness.” Barnabas is often praised in this book, lest anyone believe that he lacked the merit for the apostolate; afterward he was ordained by the apostles as an apostle of the Gentiles.

**VERSE 23.**—**And he exhorted them, and so on.** He changed or added nothing, but taught perseverance, because true and full faith was present in them.

**VERSE 25.**—**Tarsus.** It was said above that the brothers brought him by night to Caesarea and sent him on to Tarsus. **To seek Saul.** Behold Barnabas’s goodness: he does not presume to teach the people alone, but seeks an associate in the apostolate.

[Col. 0453D] **VERSES 26–27.**—**Disciples, Christians.** In this, [and so on,] the disciples appear not to have kept God’s command: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow” (Matthew 6). But it is clear that he does not disapprove of someone making such provisions in a human manner; rather, he disapproves of serving God for their sake, so that in his work he looks not to the kingdom of God but to temporal things. This command is therefore reduced to the following rule: in providing for these matters, we should attend to the kingdom of God; but in the service of God we should not think about such things.

**Prophets.** (RAB.) Those of whom it is said: “Your sons shall prophesy” (Joel 2). This is praise of Antioch, where many perfected people gathered.

## CHAPTER XII

**VERSE 4.**—**Four squads of four.** A *quaternion* is the commander of four soldiers. For just as a centurion has one hundred men under him, so a quaternion has four soldiers under him.

**Wishing, and so on.** (RAB.) The grace would have been greater if the Jews themselves had killed him, because he was a ruler, rather than Herod himself, just as with James.

**VERSE 6.**—**Soldiers, bound, and so on.** (RAB.) Four difficulties reinforce the guard: soldiers, chains, the prison, and guards.

**VERSE 7.**—**Light.** A sign of the presence of God’s angel. His presence provided light for Peter alone and did not shine upon the others.

**And having struck him.** (RAB.) The angel could have made bodily contact by assuming a body formed from air.
