**VERSE 11.**—**Coming to himself.** He returned from the height of contemplation to what had previously been within ordinary understanding.

**VERSE 13.**—**The girl came out, and so on.** And a woman was the first of all to announce to the disciples that the Lord had come forth from the tomb, so that where sin abounded, grace might abound all the more.

**VERSE 15.**—**It is his angel.** (HIER.) Great is the dignity of souls: each person, from the beginning of birth, has an angel assigned to guard him.

(ID.) As for the fact that each of us has angels, [and so on, up to] these are the ones who ascend and descend upon the Son of Man.

**VERSE 17.**—**That they should be silent, and so on.** Until he had recounted the miracle; or he commanded silence so that the shouting of those rejoicing would not make his arrival known in the city.

**VERSE 23.**—**Immediately, and so on.** While he did not recoil from the impiety of unlawful flattery, looking up shortly afterward he saw an angel looming over and pressing upon his head, and immediately recognized him as the agent of his destruction—the one he had previously known as the provider of good things. Thereafter, afflicted continuously for seven days by abdominal pain, he violently ended his life.

## CHAPTER XIII

**VERSE 1.**—**Now there were in the Church, and so on.** They were the same people who were prophets and teachers. Or, some of them were prophets and others teachers.

**Niger.** (RAB.) “Black,” if it is Latin. Or “ascending,” if it is Hebrew.

**VERSE 4.**—**Sent by the Holy Spirit.** (RAB.) Sent away by human beings, they are immediately sent by the Holy Spirit to Seleucia. He was their guide on the journey, the one who separated them from the others.

**They went to Seleucia.** (ID.) In some copies one finds: “They went to Seleucia, which is Salamis”; these are two names for one city.

**VERSE 7.**—**Sergius Paulus.** These are two names belonging to one person: Sergius and Paulus.

**VERSE 8.**—**Elymas.** (RAB.) According to some, Elymas means “the measure of my God,” or “magician,” and for this reason he resisted.

**To turn away.** (ID.) He wanted to turn the one who had begun to convert away from faith toward transgression, in accordance with his name.

**VERSE 9.**—**Saul.** (ID.) Saul means “the temptation of one who looks back,” or “security,” or “wonderful.”

[Col. 0455A] **Who is also Paul.** (BEDA.) He received the name Paul from the proconsul Sergius Paulus, whom he brought under the authority of faith.

It was fitting that the apostle of the Gentiles should receive his name from a Gentile.

(RAB.) He was called the apostle Paul by Sergius Paulus, [and so on, up to] “I am the least of the apostles” (1 Corinthians 15).

**VERSE 11.**—**And now, and so on. You will be blind, and so on.** Paul had to perform miracles for the completion of the apostolate to which the Lord had appointed him, after he had long kicked against the goads.

**VERSE 14.**—**Antioch of Pisidia.** (RAB.) It is thought to distinguish it from another Antioch; but many think them to be the same.

**They sat down.** (ID.) As though they were going to hear the Law, not preach it. Behold an example of humility.

[Col. 0455B] **VERSE 19.**—**The land of Canaan, and so on.** (RAB.) That is, the land of promise, which, as most people think, was given to Israel, [and so on, up to] and for this reason he deserved to be cursed.

**VERSE 20.**—**He gave, and so on.** The period of the judges passes by, to test God’s patience.

**VERSE 26.**—**To you.** (RAB.) To the Jews. “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15). Or “to you” means to you who are scattered, because, as follows, the inhabitants of Jerusalem rejected it.

**VERSE 27.**—**Judging.** (ID.) Judging Jesus to be guilty of death. Or “judging the words of the prophets,” that is, not believing them. For whoever slanders his brother slanders the Law and judges the Law; how much more do those who slander Christ?

**The holy and faithful things of David.** (BEDA.) Isaiah, tasting in advance the mysteries of the New Testament, says: “I will make with you an everlasting covenant, the holy and faithful things of David.” In Hebrew: “I will make with you an everlasting covenant, the faithful mercies of David.”

**VERSE 35.**—**You will not give, and so on.** (ID.) After the resurrection he does not die; death will no longer rule over him. Therefore it says “holy and faithful things,” that is, things incorruptible and destined to remain eternally.

**VERSE 41.**—**Look, you despisers.** In Greek: “Hear, you despisers, and look, and be destroyed.”

**Marvel.** (RAB.) Join the words this way: “Marvel and be scattered by the Assyrians and Chaldeans, and finally by the Romans,” because I am carrying out the work of both forms of vengeance. “You will not believe,” and so on. Or, because of the magnitude of both forms of vengeance, they are said not to believe until they have been completed.

[Col. 0455D] **VERSE 43.**—**And those who worshiped.** (ID.) It is rightly read “those who worshiped God,” as it appears in Greek. It signifies those who were Gentiles by nature but Jews by religion, called in Greek *proselytes*.

**VERSE 46.**—**First.** (ID.) Jesus first came to heal the ruler’s daughter, but the woman suffering from the flow of blood forestalled him and received healing. **Of eternal life.** The apostles did not speak because they knew that the life they were rejecting was eternal, but according to their own understanding and faith.

**VERSE 47.**—**For thus, and so on.** (ID.) The prophecy is an unchangeable command for us. First the command is stated; then the prophet’s testimony is introduced, spoken in the person of the Father addressing the Son.

**I have appointed you.** He does not say, “I have appointed you all,” because what is said to Christ also pertains to the apostles, who are his members. **I have appointed you as a light to the Gentiles.** (BEDA.) This was said specifically to Christ, yet the apostles consider it said to themselves because they are his members. Thus, because of the unity of the same body, it was said: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” and so forth.

**VERSE 48.**—**Predestined.** The order is this: after present labors and the mortification of the flesh, life follows.

**VERSE 50.**—**Devout women.** (RAB.) Either Jewish women who observed the religion of the Law, or Gentile women who were beginning to embrace the religion of salvation.

**VERSE 51.**—**Having shaken off the dust, and so on.** In accordance with the Gospel command, the dust is shaken off as a testimony that they had made the labor fruitless.

[Col. 0456B] (RAB.) The dust is rightly shaken off, because at the judgment they will be cast out by Christ like dust driven from the face of the earth by the wind (Psalm 1). But if they had received the apostles, they would have freed their feet—that is, their senses—from dust, that is, from vices.

## CHAPTER XIV

**VERSE 6.**—**They fled for refuge.** (RAB.) The apostles’ flight arose no more from fear than from love of the word of God. **And throughout, and so on.** The following is found in Greek: “But God made peace”; some Latin copies lack this.

**VERSE 10.**—**They raised.** (RAB.) This indicates impudence. Or, his thought was higher than his barbarous tongue, which did not know the one God.

**VERSE 12.**—**Garlands.** (ID.) Either to adorn the front of the temple according to the Gentile custom, or to place them upon the apostles as though about to sacrifice to them as gods. It was the custom of the Gentiles, when sacrificing in honor of their gods, to take garlands, the victims being garlanded at the same time.

**VERSE 16.**—**Filling with food, and so on.** (ID.) He is speaking of bodily things, because there is joy in food and wine, which gladdens the human heart.

**VERSE 18.**—**They dragged him.** (ID.) To stone him as though he were a corpse. Concerning this he himself says to the Corinthians: “Once I was stoned” (2 Corinthians 11), and so forth.

**VERSE 21.**—**To remain in the faith.** (ID.) Despite many tribulations, because an abundance of tribulations demands perseverance in faith. **Because through many tribulations.** Labor is placed first; afterward entry into the kingdom is preached, because the hope of reward is the consolation of labor.

## CHAPTER XV

**VERSE 2.**—**Dissension.** Caused by Paul and Barnabas against those who were saying these things.

**They determined.** (RAB.) Namely, those who had come down from Judea, [and so on, up to] that he had come to faith.

**VERSE 6.**—**The apostles gathered.** (ID.) Here an example is given of holding assemblies to discern the matters necessary for the faith.

**VERSE 7.**—**Through my mouth.** (ID.) Not through that of another apostle, as though he were saying: “I who first preached to the Gentiles will be the first to remove the yoke of the Law from them.” For none of the apostles preached to the eunuch; rather, Philip the deacon did so, and the eunuch was freely endowed with the gift.

[Col. 0457A] **VERSE 9.**—**Purifying by faith.** (CHRYS.) “By faith alone,” he says, “they attained this, and not through works or circumcision.” For they are not saying this merely while giving an account on behalf of the Gentiles, but also because they wish to draw those people away from the Law; nevertheless, they do not yet say this explicitly.

**VERSE 12.**—**The whole multitude was silent.** The order of the speakers, or of speaking, should be noted: they are silent as each person speaks, beginning with Peter.

**VERSE 13.**—**And after, and so on.** (CHRYS.) He was the bishop of the Church of Jerusalem, [and so on, up to] where he also brings the works to an end.

**VERSE 16.**—**I will return and rebuild, and so on.** “I will return” to the Gentiles, whom he had previously said were entering their own ways; James introduced this testimony to confirm that interpretation. [Col. 0457B] This testimony plainly agrees with Simon’s words.

(RAB.) The shadow of the Law, corrupted by the traditions of the Pharisees, was raised up by grace when the Lord revealed himself—that is, when the Lord appeared in the flesh—so that not only Jews but also Gentiles might seek his name.

**VERSE 17.**—**Upon whom it has been invoked.** (ID.) According to: “The priests shall invoke my name upon the children of Israel” (Numbers 6); and elsewhere: “Moses and Aaron among his priests” (Psalm 99), and so forth.

**It has been invoked.** The future is expressed in prophetic fashion.

**VERSE 19.**—**I judge.** (RAB.) The judgment was rightly made, being confirmed by the testimony of three: two apostles and the prophets.

**VERSE 20.**—**And from what has been strangled.** A strangled animal is a carcass, concerning which Ezekiel says: “The priests shall not eat any carcass or anything seized by a wild beast, whether of birds or cattle” (Ezekiel 44). This command is fitting for those anointed with spiritual oil to observe: they must not eat an animal whose blood has not been poured out, which the apostles’ letter decreed should be avoided.

**And from blood.** (RAB.) From the shedding of human blood, [and so on, up to] but so that they might be chaste and abstain.

**VERSE 22.**—**Then it seemed good.** (ID.) With Peter speaking, Barnabas and Paul giving their account, and James, bishop of Jerusalem, judging, the decision rightly seemed good. **It seemed good to send to Antioch.** Envoys sent by Christ may send their own envoys.

**VERSE 23.**—**The apostles and elders.** The common title of the apostles is placed first, so that no opportunity for disagreement might remain.

[Col. 0457D] **To the brothers from the Gentiles.** (RAB.) The first benefit of the writing is that the apostles call the Gentiles “brothers,” that is, sons of the one God. **Greetings.** This is an ellipsis: the breadth of charity is too great for any single word, and therefore no one word is supplied, so that they may be understood to wish them every good thing all at once.

**VERSE 24.**—**Overturning your souls.** In Greek: “Overturning your souls by saying, ‘You must be circumcised and observe the Law,’ although we gave them no such command.”

**VERSE 28.**—“It seemed good,” that is, “it pleased us.” “To the Holy Spirit,” who, as arbiter of his own power, breathes where he wills and speaks what he wills.

[Col. 0458A] “To the Holy Spirit.” (RAB.) And to us—not indeed according to merely human judgment, but according to sound judgment.

“And to us.” Yet not by our will alone, but by the prompting of that same Spirit.

“How necessary these things are.” (RAB.) These things are necessary, without which there is no salvation; circumcision, however, is not necessary. Rather, whatever you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to others.

**VERSE 29.**—“That you abstain from these things,” etc. (TERT.) Therefore, since both kinds, etc., up to “whose purity pertains more to God than to that of the intestines.”

**VERSE 34.**—“But it seemed good.” (RAB.) This is the subject of what follows: “But Judas alone went away to Jerusalem.”

**VERSE 39.**—“Dissension.” They were not sinning in this, because not every disturbance is sin, but only one that is irrational and does not arise justly. “They took Mark.” He was related to Barnabas, and thus they are also said to have been cousins. After Barnabas was dismissed by Paul, he returned to his native island and nevertheless continued the evangelical work entrusted to him.

**VERSE 40.**—“Having chosen Silas.” (RAB.) The Lord caused him to remain for this purpose, in accordance with the statement: “But it seemed good to Silas to remain there, so that he might cooperate with Paul, just as Mark did with Barnabas.” For there was divine counsel in this.

## CHAPTER XVI

**VERSE 1.**—“The son of a widow.” (RAB.) Or, “of Judaea.” That she was Jewish by descent is evident from the statement that his father was of Gentile origin.

[Col. 0458C] **VERSE 3.**—“And he circumcised him.” (ID.) He circumcised Timothy because of the Jews’ scruple, so that he would not appear to condemn the law of Moses, but rather not to impose it upon the Gentiles as unnecessary. He did not circumcise Titus, lest the Gentiles should take from him an opportunity for circumcision. And what is the meaning of his statement: “But because of the false brothers who had slipped in,” etc.?

**VERSE 4.**—“To observe the decrees that had been.” (ID.) They did not preach what they themselves had done, but what the apostles had decreed in accordance with God’s will. This is an example of teaching rightly even what one has not done oneself. In a figurative sense, the priests wore breeches, as though they were sowing the work, not as though they were going to perform it.

**VERSE 5.**—“And the churches indeed,” etc. (ID.) This has often been explained in the preceding chapters, when we said that a statement of this kind closes the preceding narrative and begins the following one.

**VERSE 7.**—“They attempted to go.” (ID.) The apostles are permitted to wish, but not to go, etc., up to “Luke in Bithynia,” etc.

**VERSE 9.**—“A Macedonian man.” An angel of that people appeared in the likeness of a Macedonian man, whether by the particularity of his language, a distinctive appearance, or the force of his words.

“Help us.” (RAB.) This is spoken from the human point of view; angels do not need human assistance. Or the angel says this on behalf of those over whom he presides, so that they may be baptized and saved.

“Help us.” He shows that the Macedonians—or the angels—were inspired by God, or that certain teachers had begun to be instructed.

**VERSE 11.**—“Samothrace.” Thrace, Neapolis, and Philippi are cities.

**VERSE 12.**—“Some days, conferring.” In certain books it is found as: “Conferring the word of the Lord on the Sabbath.”

**VERSE 14.**—“A seller of purple.” A queen clothed in royal purple, or a weaver of purple cloth, or a seller of purple, signifies the Church, which sells purple when it pours out its blood for Christ, so that life may be purchased. Purple rightly signifies blood by its color and nature, because it is made from the blood of shellfish. Lydia compelled the apostle and his companions to enter her house, because the Church received with devoted heart the preaching that had been rejected by the Jews.

[Col. 0459B] **VERSE 15.**—“She compelled us.” (RAB.) Here one example is given, or two: one concerning compelling guests to enter, and the other concerning entering the homes of those newly converted.

**VERSE 17.**—“Having followed Paul.” (ID.) Although she had met him, the woman did not call out to his face but behind them, preserving her modesty.

**VERSE 23.**—“They threw them into prison.” (ID.) By this, the power of the one who delivers them is made greater. The same point is indicated by what follows: “He threw them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks.”

**VERSE 25.**—“But about midnight,” etc. One must pray at midnight and maintain diligence in prayer amid dangers.

**VERSE 26.**—“There was a great earthquake,” etc. The devotion of those praying and the power of prayer are expressed: while they were singing hymns in prison, their praise moved the earth, shook the foundations of the prison, opened the doors, and loosed the prisoners’ chains.

[Col. 0459C] **VERSE 29.**—“He fell down,” etc. (RAB.) Because of power and knowledge: power, because the doors had been opened by the earthquake; knowledge, because Paul understood why he wished to kill himself. Therefore, above all, he fell at the feet of Paul and Silas.

**VERSE 33.**—“He washed their wounds.” (BED.) A beautiful variety of events: by washing their wounds, he lost through them the wounds of his sins. “Immediately.” (RAB.) The speed of obedience is signified. The grace of the Holy Spirit knows no slow deliberation.

**VERSE 34.**—“And having brought them in, he set food before them,” etc. (ID.) An excellent example of both things: entering the house and setting food before them.

## CHAPTER XVII

**VERSE 4.**—“And from those who worshiped, and from the Gentiles.” That is, both from those who had exchanged the Gentile rite for Judaism and from those who had remained Gentiles, many were coming to Christ.

(RAB.) The first cause of their wickedness was that they were from the common people; the second, that they were worse than the common people.

**VERSE 6.**—“They dragged Jason.” (BED.) In Greek: “Jason and certain other brothers.” Hence it is to be understood that Jason was a brother and a faithful man.

**VERSE 7.**—“Another king.” (RAB.) Besides Caesar. This was contrary to Caesar’s decree; hence the Gospel says: “Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar” (John XVIII). The apostles, however, proclaimed that Christ was king of the Jews—that is, of those who confess—and for this reason the Jews also accused Christ himself.

[Col. 0460A] **VERSE 13.**—“By Paul.” He was the leader in proclaiming the word; therefore afterward he alone was sent away, so that he might go from Macedonia to the sea.

**VERSE 15.**—“Those who had set out.” (RAB.) The brothers who had escorted Paul from Athens set out. Some think that this was said of Silas and Timothy, who set out from Macedonia to Paul.

**VERSE 18.**—“Epicureans.” (ID.) They were called this after their founder, who is said to have defended pleasure. The Stoics are called in Greek *Stoics*, and in Latin *elementa*; they argued that sins were equal, that is, that every sin was uniform.

[Col. 0460B] “What does this babbler wish to say?” A *seminiverbius* is one who sows words; or *seminiverbius*, that is, a speaker of words, because the word of God is seed. Hence: “If we have sown spiritual things among you,” etc.

(AUG.) We read that the Apostle Paul was called a sower of words. This was said by mockers, but should not be rejected by believers. For he was a sower of words but a reaper of conduct. And we, although little ones and not to be compared with him in God’s field—which is your heart—sow the word of God, awaiting abundant grain, or fruit, from your conduct.

“But others.” (RAB.) They had heard from the Jews that the name of demons was abominable, and therefore they compared Paul’s teaching to this abomination. Or the Jews are the ones who say this—that is, the Sadducees.

[Col. 0460C] **VERSE 19.**—“To the Areopagus.” (RAB.) This is the name of the council at Athens, called after the idol Mars, who is called *Arios* among them.

**VERSES 22–23.**—“Men of Athens,” etc. “What you worship without knowing, this I proclaim to you.” He responds to what they had said or implied: “You are bringing in some new things,” as if to say, “The new things I am bringing in are already among your ancient traditions.” He says this to persuade them, so that they would not reject his words as though they were new.

“An unknown god.” (RAB.) That is, the true God, whom no one knows as he is, etc., up to “which is passed over in silence,” or it was simply written: “To an unknown god.”

**VERSE 24.**—“The God who made the world.” Observe the order of this argument: first he teaches that there is one God, the creator of all things, in whom we live, move, and exist, and whose offspring we are. Thus he shows that God is to be loved not only for light and life, but also for our kinship of origin.

**VERSE 26.**—“From one he made every race of mankind.” In Greek: “from one blood,” because blood designates the propagation of the flesh, and by “flesh” the human being is understood.

**VERSE 28.**—“For in him we live.” (AUG.) Because he works in us the fact that we live, move, and exist, etc., up to “for what does not come from him of whom it is said: ‘From him and through him and in him are all things’?” (Rom. XI).

“Just as some of your own poets have said.” To those who did not accept the prophets, he gives the testimony not of Moses, Isaiah, or any of the prophets, but of their own authors. By inserting a verse of Aratus, he preserves and confirms his own truth through their false writings, which they could not contradict. “For we are indeed his offspring,” etc. This testimony is taken from the poet Aratus, not from the divine Scriptures, so that he would not appear to be introducing something new.

[Col. 0461A] **VERSE 29.**—“Being therefore offspring,” etc., “we ought not.” (RAB.) Man stands between these things, having God above him, and gold, silver, and other such things below him; these must not be compared with him.

**VERSE 30.**—“God, overlooking.” (ID.) That is, forgiving them as matters that could be pardoned; and then “overlooking,” that is, judging them unworthy of his knowledge.

**VERSE 31.**—“Giving assurance to all.” (ID.) By the example of his resurrection. Or the sense is: he has appointed him to judge, and then this should be joined to it: “giving assurance to all that they will rise.”

**VERSE 34.**—“Dionysius.” (BED.) This is the Dionysius who was later ordained bishop of Corinth and governed the Church well. He also left many volumes for its benefit, taking his surname from the place over which he presided. The Areopagus is the council of Athens, deriving its name from Mars, who is called *Arios* in Greek; *pagus* means “village.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

**VERSE 2.**—“Because Claudius had ordered everyone to depart.” (BED.) Josephus reports that this happened in the ninth year of Claudius. Suetonius says that Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome.

**VERSE 3.**—“Of the craft of tentmaking.” (ID.) As exiles and foreigners, they build tents for themselves to use on the road, etc., up to “and by word and deed he protects them from the winds of ambush.”

**VERSE 6.**—“Your blood be upon your own heads.” (CHRYS.) He does this so as not to frighten them by words alone, and he argues more forcefully, since many had been persuaded.

**VERSE 7.**—“The house of Titus Justus, a worshiper of God.” Titus Justus was either the man’s proper name, or he was so called because of the merit of his justice. This was not the Titus who was Paul’s disciple, to whom Paul wrote the Epistle and whom he ordained bishop of Crete. With that Titus, Barnabas also went up to Jerusalem and discussed the Gospel with the apostles, inquiring at their council whether he was rightly preaching that the Gentiles could be saved through faith and baptism without circumcision—not because he himself doubted this, but so that the minds of the doubting apostles might be strengthened by apostolic authority.

[Col. 0461D] **VERSE 15.**—“But if they are questions about a word.” Now, plainly, the matter has been explained and narrated—that is, the Gospel—and also the names “Jesus” and “God,” or “God the Father.” In Greek: “When all the Greeks seized Sosthenes,” etc.

**VERSE 18.**—“Who had his hair cut.” (RAB.) It is uncertain who had his head shaved; it may have been Paul or Aquila, either through fear of the Jews or from eagerness to convert them. The statement is ambiguous, but according to Jerome it should be understood of Paul.

**VERSE 22.**—“Caesarea.” (ID.) Caesarea is the metropolis of Cappadocia. For he had not yet come into Syria Phoenicia.

**VERSE 27.**—“He contributed much.” Another translation: [Col. 0462A] “He benefited those who believed greatly, through grace.” This is what the Apostle writes: “I planted, Apollos watered” (1 Cor. III), etc.

## CHAPTER XIX

**VERSE 4.**—“John baptized.” (BED.) John did not remit sins by his baptism, but taught repentance. For just as circumcision among the patriarchs was a seal of the faith they possessed, so this washing was received by the penitent people as a seal of their devotion; it prefigured Christ’s baptism, in which remission takes place.

(RAB.) It is not baptism unless it is given in the name of the Trinity. Those baptized by Judas are not rebaptized, because they were baptized in the faith of the Trinity; but those baptized by John are, because John baptizes only in water, whereas Christ baptizes in the Holy Spirit. Therefore, whether a good or wicked minister baptizes, if faith in the Trinity is complete, the Lord baptizes. Those baptized by John in water alone were baptized by Paul.

(BED.) The question is whether someone who, perhaps through ignorance, was baptized by one who was not baptized himself but nevertheless possessed the right faith ought to be rebaptized. I think this chapter explains the matter. For what difference is there between being baptized then, before the beginning of Christ’s baptism, and being baptized now by someone without receiving that same baptism? John proclaimed that those whom he baptized in faith and in the name of the coming Christ were to be baptized again, saying: “I baptize in water; he will baptize in the Holy Spirit.”

**VERSE 7.**—“There were about twelve men in all.” (RAB.) “The judgments of God are a great abyss.” Behold, Asia, which had been unworthy of the apostles’ visitation, is now consecrated by the apostolic number and exalted by the gift of prophecy. It should also be noted that here the Holy Spirit displayed the signs of his coming upon twelve disciples, and above upon one hundred and twenty—the number completed by ten times twelve: the former in Jerusalem, the latter in Ephesus, which is a Greek city. This shows that only those—whether Jews or Gentiles—who are in Catholic unity are filled with the Spirit.

**VERSE 9.**—“Arguing every day in the school.” (BED.) From the fifth hour until the ninth and tenth hours, as some report: he gave five hours to work, another five to teaching, and two to food and prayer. This, however, is supported by no authority. “In the school of Tyrannus.” (RAB.) The name Tyrannus is used as a title of rank, or it is a proper name meaning “one who holds them” or “one who confirms.”

[Col. 0462D] **VERSE 10.**—“For two years.” During this period Paul wrote the First Epistle to the Corinthians at Ephesus.

**VERSE 12.**—“Half-girdles” (*semicinctia*). (RAB.) Garments hanging down on one side, or belts or night garments, or a kind of cloth that the Hebrews wear on the head.

**VERSE 13.**—“Exorcists.” Solomon devised and taught his people methods of exorcism—that is, adjuration—by which expelled unclean spirits did not dare to return to human beings. This is done through the wicked to their condemnation and for the benefit of those who see and hear, because although they despise those who perform signs, they nevertheless honor God, at whose invocation the signs occur.

**VERSE 14.**—“Seven sons,” etc. (BED.) Since Satan disguises himself as an angel of light, etc., up to “he shows which guardians of the Church are meant by the command: ‘Catch for us the little foxes that ravage the vineyards’” (Song II).

**VERSE 19.**—“Many of those who had practiced curious arts.” (BED.) The skill of magical art. Its practitioners rightly burn their books, even though those books are valued at a high price, because the demons whom they had served are seen to invoke Jesus and honor his apostles.

**VERSE 21.**—“When these things had been completed,” etc. (CHRYS.) Having spent a sufficiently long time in the city, etc., up to “thus everywhere he wove together his works.”

[Col. 0463B] “To see Rome.” (RAB.) Perhaps he had not seen it before, or perhaps he considered the tribulation he would suffer there to be slight. He says only “to see,” not that he would suffer many things.

**VERSE 22.**—“Into Macedonia.” (RAB.) He wanted to cross from Asia, where Ephesus is, into Europe, where Macedonia and Achaia are, and then return to Asia—that is, to Jerusalem—with the collection about which he wrote to the Corinthians.

**VERSE 28.**—“Great is Diana of the Ephesians.” (BED.) Demetrius said that Diana was going to perish; they, in contrast, marvel that she is great.

**VERSE 32.**—“Some were shouting one thing, others another.” The “other thing” they were shouting was either that they should be dragged into the theater, or that another god was great, or that another idol was involved; they were also hurling insults at Paul.

[Col. 0463C] **VERSE 34.**—“One cry arose from them all, as they shouted for about two hours: ‘Great is Diana of the Ephesians.’” The Jews rightly drag Alexander the secretary out of that crowd, which was entirely worshiping Diana.

**VERSE 37.**—“Neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of your goddess.” (RAB.) They are called sacrilegious because of profane zeal. For *sacred* signifies what is pure, and *profane* what is impure.

**VERSE 40.**—“And when he had said these things.” He speaks as though he were a Jew, unwilling that Jews should be killed by idol worshipers; or he spoke as a Christian.

## CHAPTER XX

[Col. 0463D] **VERSE 2.**—“To Greece.” Greece is the province of Achaia. Paul came there after Macedonia, since he had planned this, as was said above. He intended to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem.

**VERSE 4.**—“Sopater.” In Hebrew, *Sopater* is interpreted as meaning “one who recounts the dispersion” or “one who saves the dispersed.”

**VERSE 7.**—“On the first day of the week.” The name of the day is mentioned so that it may be understood as preparation for the virtue that was to be practiced and proclaimed.

(BED.) “The upper room”: the height of spiritual gifts. “Night”: the obscurity of the Scriptures, etc., up to the statement: “These are the two Testaments.”

**VERSE 9.**—“Eutychus,” etc. (ID.) In Hebrew this means “mad,” in Greek “fortunate,” etc., up to “so that even the memory of the teacher who was about to depart might be fixed more firmly in the mind.”

[Col. 0464A] **VERSE 10.**—“When Paul had gone down, he leaned over him.” (ID.) He went down and leaned over him, embracing him, etc., up to “and, as the Sun of righteousness breathed upon him, he was brought back to life.” “For his soul is in him.” (RAB.) That is, it had not wholly departed, or it had returned. He said this for the sake of unbelievers, as in: “The girl is not dead but sleeping.” Thus despair is removed.

**VERSE 16.**—“Pentecost.” It is established that the time of Passover and Pentecost was observed in the time of the apostles.

**VERSE 31.**—“Keeping it in memory.” (RAB.) He wants them to retain in memory what he had told them, for remembrance of a divine command is no small safeguard.

[Col. 0464B] **VERSE 35.**—“It is more blessed.” (ID.) This is not read in the Gospel, for not everything was written down. Perhaps Paul heard it from the apostles or received it from the Holy Spirit. Or it may be said that, even if Jesus did not use these words, he indicated this meaning when he said: “Give to everyone who asks,” and elsewhere: “Do not acquire gold,” etc.

(BED.) He does not place the rich who give alms above those who left everything and followed the Lord. Rather, he especially glorifies those who renounce all that they possess and nevertheless labor with their hands so that they may have something with which to give to the person suffering need. You bishops, therefore, be diligent in feeding orphans, etc.

## CHAPTER XXI

**VERSE 1.**—“And when it happened,” etc. “Cos, Rhodes, and from there Patara.” (RAB.) Cos and Patara are islands.

**VERSE 8.**—“Philip the evangelist.” He deserved to be called an evangelist because of his promptness in the ministry of preaching.

**VERSE 9.**—“Now he had four daughters.” (RAB.) Elsewhere the daughters of the apostle Philip are said to have been prophetesses, but the truth of this passage must not be contradicted, unless perhaps it is understood that both men had prophetess daughters.

**VERSE 11.**—“Thus says the Holy Spirit.” (BED.) He imitates the ancient prophets, who used to say: “Thus says the Lord God,” because the Holy Spirit, equally with the Father and the Son, is Lord and God. Nor can the activity of those whose nature and will are one be separated.

**VERSE 21.**—“Saying that they ought not.” (BED.) As if they were saying: “In Christ’s teaching you condemn the legal observances as sacrilegious,” etc., up to “but the Jews were not prohibited.”

“Nor according to.” At that time Jews who believed in Christ were not prohibited from living according to the law, while the temple and their religious observance still stood, although they were to obtain salvation through the sacraments of the New Testament. Believers from the Gentiles, however, were forbidden to turn to the law; nevertheless, they were commanded carefully to observe the law’s precepts concerning conduct and bodily purity, such as “You shall not covet,” etc.

Four councils were held at Jerusalem. The first concerned the election of another apostle in place of Judas; the second, the election of the seven deacons; the third, the decision that circumcision should not be imposed upon those from the Gentiles who believed; the fourth was this one, concerning the Jews of that time not being prohibited [Col. 0465A]—where necessity required it—from being initiated into the legal ceremonies, because of the scandal of those who thought that the apostles condemned the law of Moses as they condemned the doctrines of idolaters.

**VERSE 24.**—“For the things that concern you,” etc. He was not rejecting the legal observances in the manner stated. If he celebrated them for the purpose of concealing his real opinion through a simulated action, James would not have said this.

**VERSE 27.**—“When the seven days were nearly completed,” etc. They had not yet been completed, but their course was still underway, etc., up to “lest the Romans should come and take away both the place and the nation.”

**VERSE 35.**—“And when he reached the steps.” The steps do not signify the descent from the temple but the ascent into the fortress.

[Col. 0465B] **VERSE 37.**—“Do you know Greek?” (RAB.) This is either a question or an assertion, because, as is thought, the tribune spoke Greek; or he said it so that the Jews would not understand.

**VERSE 39.**—“From Tarsus,” etc. (ID.) He had moved there with his parents when he was captured.

## CHAPTER XXII

**VERSE 3.**—“Born in Tarsus.” (BED.) Paul was born in the town of Gischala in Galilee, etc., up to “thus Christ, born in Bethlehem, was called a Nazarene.”

“A zealous defender of the law.” In Greek: “a zealous defender of the law of God as it exists,” in accordance with the statement: “I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. X).

[Col. 0465C] **VERSE 7.**—“Saul, Saul.” (RAB.) Some copies have “Saul, Saul,” so that it may be shown that *Saulus* was named after Saul.

**VERSE 9.**—“They heard.” (ID.) They perceived only the sound of Paul’s voice, or of the one who was speaking to Paul.

**VERSE 10.**—“And there.” (ID.) This is an example of humility: not disputing with teachers and not presuming upon ourselves as though we had been taught by God.

**VERSE 13.**—“Brother Saul, regain your sight.” (ID.) There were two things in Paul’s eyes: blindness and illumination; therefore he rightly believed.

**VERSE 14.**—“He appointed you beforehand.” (ID.) The order is fitting: first, he was appointed beforehand in God’s foreknowledge; then he comes to know the truth, sees the Just One, and hears from his own mouth; afterward he becomes a witness of what he has known, seen, and heard.

**VERSE 17.**—“I fell into a trance.” He does not recount this out of self-exaltation but from necessity, so that he might appear fit to evangelize the Gentiles.

**VERSE 20.**—“I was consenting.” By confessing that he consented, he indicates that he did not kill, unless “striking” is taken to mean “killing,” or unless he is understood as arranging the killing.

**VERSE 28.**—“I acquired this citizenship at great cost.” Another edition makes the tribune’s meaning clearer. The tribune said: “You say this so easily—that you are a Roman citizen? I acquired this citizenship for a considerable price.”

“Citizenship.” That is, social fellowship among citizens, or participation in the administration of the state. It was not impossible for the tribune to be a citizen of Rome; rather, he had purchased membership in the citizen body so that he might share in its privileges. Paul was even more truly a Roman citizen, since he possessed this status not by purchase but by birth.

## CHAPTER XXIII

**VERSE 3.**—“God will strike you.” (RAB.) He does not say, “May God strike you,” because this is prophecy, not a curse, etc., up to “but the Apostle spoke by divine inspiration.”

**VERSE 5.**—“I did not know, brothers.” That is, “I did not know that he was Ananias.” Or he subtly says that he does not acknowledge him as ruler, because the Jewish priesthood had been rejected.

**VERSE 9.**—“What if it is a spirit?” (RAB.) Here it appears, according to Jerome, that the Sadducees did not confess the existence of spirit or angels. Therefore the Pharisees mention spirit and angel, because they knew that this was contrary to the Sadducees.

[Col. 0466B] **VERSE 10.**—“Lest Paul should be torn apart by them.” (ID.) This was because the Sadducees wanted to seize him, or because both groups were contending together.

**VERSE 12.**—“They bound themselves by an oath, saying.” In Greek, *anathematized*: those who are alienated from the fellowship of Christ and the Church by a priestly anathema know how much authority this word possesses.

**VERSE 23.**—“Prepare two hundred soldiers,” etc. (RAB.) He orders this so that the Jews would not carry him off and the tribune himself be accused before the governor of the crime of accepting money from the Jews as the price of Paul’s death.

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Col. 0466C] **VERSE 14.**—“The Father and my God.” (RAB.) He is shown to be his son, not his servant, as it appears in other manuscripts.

**VERSE 21.**—“Except concerning this one matter.” (ID.) He speaks by antiphrasis, for he knew that this pleased them. It is as if he said: “I have committed no offense except that I preached what they themselves also believe.”

**VERSE 23.**—“To have his own people minister to him.” (ID.) His disciples and companions. Alternatively, he ordered that no one be prevented from ministering to him from his own possessions or resources.

**VERSE 25.**—“He trembled,” etc., “and hoped.” (ID.) Join the words in this way: “trembling and hoping.” On account of these two things he placed him in relatively free custody: fear of God and hope of money.

[Col. 0466D] **VERSE 27.**—“He left Paul in chains.” (ID.) It is uncertain whether Felix left Paul while still alive or at his death. Nevertheless, it seems better that he did so while alive, in order to gain favor with the Jews.

## CHAPTER XXV

**VERSE 1.**—“When Festus had come into the province,” etc. (RAB.) Understand this as the province of Palestine, just as Roman governors were continually sent to Palestine, each succeeding another.

**VERSE 18.**—“Concerning which,” etc. (ID.) These causes, matters, or words: “concerning which I was expecting,” that is, expecting them from the accusers; or, “the evils about which I had suspicions.” Alternatively, “concerning which”—that is, concerning the accusers—“I suspected evil,” because they were bringing no charge worthy of death.

**VERSE 19.**—“About their own superstition.” (RAB.) He called the law of both parties—that is, of Paul and the Jews—superstition.

**VERSE 23.**—“With much pomp.” (ID.) That is, with a great crowd surrounding them, or with a great desire to hear Paul. In Greek, *phantasia* is used instead of “pomp,” meaning the elaborate display and royal magnificence of office, by which she was surrounded on every side.

## CHAPTER XXVI

**VERSE 8.**—“Why is it judged incredible?” (RAB.) Or read it this way: “King, what do you say? Is it judged incredible among you?” He asks this as though saying: “It is not incredible.” He did indeed raise the dead previously as an example of what was to come, or he raises them now.

**VERSE 10.**—“When they were being killed, I cast my vote.” (ID.) Another edition reads: “And when they were to be killed, I cast my vote,” that is, “I gave the sentence concerning how they were to be killed.” “I cast my vote”: I judged that they should be killed. He does not say “I killed them,” unless the following is considered to pertain to the killing: “Punishing them,” etc., and “being exceedingly enraged,” etc.

**VERSE 14.**—“Against the goad.” (ID.) Until now you have resisted without a goad, but now, if you resist, you will kick against the goad, which is very difficult. The goad is correction itself.

“You are mad, Paul.” (BED.) He thinks it madness that a man in chains, having been given the opportunity to defend himself, etc., up to the Prophet’s words: “He did not turn toward vanities and false insanities” (Psalm XXXIX).

**VERSE 24.**—“Your great learning is driving you mad.” (RAB.) The philosophers of the Gentiles changed their sects by reading many things. “To madness”: understand, “of changeability.” Or he calls the resurrection of the dead, which Paul proclaims, madness.

## CHAPTER XXVII

**VERSE 1.**—“When it had been decided that he should sail,” etc. In Greek: “When it had been decided that we should sail to Italy, they handed Paul and certain other prisoners over to a centurion.”

**VERSE 2.**—“Adramyttian.” (RAB.) That is, according to some, a ship sailing to Rome; but it is better derived from the name of the African city called Adramyttium.

[Col. 0467D] **VERSE 5.**—“We came to Lystra.” (BED.) In place of Lystra, Smyrna is written in Greek. Jerome, however, gives Myrrha.

**VERSE 9.**—“The fast.” (RAB.) Great hunger at sea made the sailors weaker. Some say that this was the forty-day fast before the Lord’s birth, but that is not probable. It is better to understand it as the seventh-day fast, on which Gedaliah was killed; or the fast of the tenth month in January, when the captives in Babylon learned that the temple had been destroyed.

**VERSE 12.**—“The harbor,” etc. (ID.) The harbor of Crete is said to be in Phoenice, opposite Crete. They were seeking the harbor of Crete because they were sailing toward Crete.

[Col. 0468A] “Toward the southwest wind,” etc. The southwest wind lies between the southern and western quarters, inclining more toward the west. The northwest wind lies between the northern and western quarters, deflected farther toward the west. The province of Phoenice had Crete to the west.

**VERSE 13.**—“Asson.” (RAB.) This is the name of a place so called because from there ships were released to proceed into the sea.

**VERSE 14.**—“A typhonic wind.” Another translation: “a stormy wind.”

“Euroaquilo.” (RAB.) That is, Boreas, the wind between the north and the east. This wind was contrary to the ship sailing toward Phoenice.

**VERSE 17.**—“The Syrtis.” (ID.) Syrtis means straitness or tribulation.

[Col. 0468B] **VERSE 21.**—“Indeed, we ought,” etc. (ID.) It is as if he said: “You did not obey God,” since Paul had urged them above; or, “I ought to have been heard,” that is, “so that you would have heard me.”

**VERSE 26.**—“We must run aground on some island.” (ID.) It is as though he said: “The prophecy concerning an island is a sign of the truth, so that when they reach it they may be certain of their safety.”

**VERSE 27.**—“In the Adriatic.” This is the region toward which they were sailing; or the name of a certain strait in the Tyrrhenian Sea; or, more likely, the name of the land from which the Adriatic Gulf takes its name. Alternatively, *Adria* is understood in the plural as “reefs,” and therefore the sailors thought that land was appearing. In the *Book of Hebrew Names*, Adria means “containing evils,” or “a place of evils.”

**VERSE 34.**—“To take food.” (BED.) No one escapes the storms of the world except the one who is nourished by the bread of life and who, amid the nights of tribulation, relies upon wisdom, fortitude, temperance, and justice. With the Lord’s help shining forth, such a person reaches the harbor of salvation, seeking freedom from the world and the flame of love by which the inner parts are warmed.

**VERSE 37.**—“We were two hundred and seventy-six souls.” (RAB.) He does not say “men,” because perhaps women were also present; or, because of the mixture of Christians, soldiers, and sailors, this expression is used.

**VERSE 41.**—“A place between two seas.” (BED.) The Greeks call the sea *Thalassa*, etc., up to “and the sea is called *Thelasson* by the Greeks.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Col. 0468D] **VERSE 2.**—“A fire.” (RAB.) Some say that *pyra* is the name of a kind of wood.

**VERSE 8.**—“Dysentery or *dysin*.” (BED.) This is a disease of the intestines. “He healed him.” Why does Paul heal an unbelieving sick man by prayer, when he treats Timothy and Trophimus, faithful men who were sick, in such a way that he cures one and leaves the other? The reason is that the man who was not alive inwardly had to be healed outwardly by a miracle; those who were living healthfully within did not need this.

**VERSE 13.**—“Puteoli.” Puteoli is a place beyond Rome where Virgil built medicinal baths, each, as is said, bearing its own inscription against the particular illness it was supposed to cure. Hence the people of Salerno, driven by envy, later attacked them with armed force, destroyed the inscriptions, and mutilated the buildings.

**VERSE 15.**—“When the brothers had heard.” (RAB.) The Christians living in Rome—whence did they come? It is evident that Paul had not preached to the Romans previously.

[Col. 0470A] **VERSE 30.**—“In rented quarters.” That is, in the unrestricted custody in which he was being kept, or in his own assembly where he argued against the Jews.

**VERSE 31.**—“Without hindrance.” (RAB.) In the twenty-fifth year after the Lord’s Passion, etc., up to “Peter and Paul were crowned with martyrdom.”

[Col. 0469]

# THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED PAUL TO THE ROMANS (G)*

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0469A]

The Romans are a people of Italy. They had been led astray by false apostles and, under the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, had been brought under the law and the prophets. The Apostle recalls them to the true evangelical faith, writing to them from Corinth.

## CHAPTER I

**VERSE 1.**—“Paul.” (BED.) In the second year after Christ’s Passion and resurrection, he says that Paul came to the faith according to the apostolic Acts, etc., up to “in accordance with the apostles’ decree, he departed to teach the Gentiles.”

(AUG., *On the Spirit and the Letter*, ch. 7.) He chose this name for no other reason, etc., up to “Saul is interpreted as ‘restlessness’ and ‘temptation.’”

(AMB.) Moreover, he is reported to have done this according to the custom of the holy apostles, who, progressing in virtue, were called by changed names, so that even by their names they might be new—just as Cephas and the sons of thunder were.

(HIER., *Commentary on the Epistle to Philemon*.) Paul took this name from the first spoil that he brought to the Church, namely Sergius Paulus the proconsul, whom he converted in Cyprus.

“Servant.” From a servant and a humble man, God made an apostle and one exalted. So you also should be humble: “For everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV).

(AUG.) By placing both names, he testifies that there is one person of God and man. He places one name for the Jews and the other for the Gentiles. For “Christ” is a name known to the Jews, by which they see and hear the Son of God designated and promised in the law; even if you proclaimed another to them, they would not believe. To the Gentiles, however, since they had not read of him anywhere, he first presents “the Savior,” that is, Jesus. Although “Christ” is not a proper name but the name of a sacrament, like “prophet” and “priest,” it is rightly placed first for the Jews because they knew it. Although these names were given to many, this was only figuratively; he alone is the true King and Priest.

“Called.” Not by himself, but by God; or “called,” that is, named by human beings through the privilege of the name. “Apostle.” Behold, one who was lowly has become exalted. “Set apart.” From the teaching of the scribes and Pharisees—this is directed against the Jews—or from the other apostles in body but not in mind, as in: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have called them” (Acts XIII).

“Gospel.” (HAYM.) It is good news, etc. “Of God.” It was not invented by a human being.

[Col. 0470B] **VERSE 2.**—[Note: Whatever Walafrid has incorporated here from the exposition of Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt, on the Epistles of Paul, the reader should seek among Haymo’s own works in volumes CXVI, CXVII, and CXVIII of Migne’s *Patrologia*. EDITOR.] “Which he had promised beforehand.” It did not come as something sudden upon its completion, but had been promised long before. Hence the saying is true in this matter: “One is the sower and another the reaper.”

### Verse 3

**“Who was made for him.”** Who was made according to the flesh—through the work of the Holy Spirit, from a virgin—that is, who was born. This counters the impiety of heretics who, understanding this passage with dulled minds, accept Christ as merely human. By adding “according to the flesh,” therefore, he preserves the dignity proper to his divinity, in which Christ is the Word of God, through whom all things were made.

**(AUG.)** “Who was,” etc., up to “so that he might suitably appear to the carnal, clothed [with flesh].”

**(ID., Commentary on this Epistle.)** Christ, therefore, is one person of two substances; yet neither God nor man can be called a part of this person. Otherwise the Son of God, before he assumed the form of a servant, was not whole, and he would have become greater when humanity was added to his divinity.

### Verse 4

**“Who was predestined.”** **(AUG., Treatise 105 on John.)** This elevation of human nature was predestined to be so great, so exalted, and so supreme that, to whatever height it might be raised, it could have none higher—just as, for our sake, divinity itself had no lower point to which it could humble itself than the nature of man, assumed with the weakness of flesh, even unto the death of the cross.

**(AUG., Book I, On the Predestination of the Saints, chapter 15.)** The mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, is also the most splendid light of predestination and grace itself, etc., up to “so that he who was to be, according to the flesh, the son of David might be the Son of God in power.”

**“Of the dead, Jesus Christ.”** He uses “of Christ” in place of “of him” or “of his,” employing a proper name as a pronoun according to Hebrew usage. This manner of expression is especially common in the ancient Scriptures, as in: “Moses did as the Lord commanded Moses.”

**(CHRYS.)** This means that we did not attain the dignity of being apostles through our own power; nor did we obtain it through our many labors and exertions. Rather, we found grace.

### Verse 5

**“Among all the nations.”** Not only among the Jews, with whom—because they were called without the law—they ought not to act under the law.

**“For his name.”** For his glory, not ours, as you do.

### Verse 6

**“Called by Jesus Christ.”** That is, called by him, namely Jesus Christ. The genitive is used for the ablative, according to Greek usage.

### Verse 7

**“Called saints.”** They were not called because they were saints; rather, they were made saints because they were called. And they were called because they were loved.

### Verse 8

**“I give thanks.”** To give thanks is to recognize that all things have been given by God, and to praise him for this in heart, voice, and deed.

**“To my God.”** **(AUG., On the Sheep.)** This expression can belong only to the saints, whose God he is said to be, as “the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” Although, by nature, there is one God of all, he is nevertheless said to belong particularly, by grace, to those who are shown to be his worshipers by the merit of faith and righteousness.

**“For all of you.”** When praying for others, he prays first for you, from whom great benefit comes through Christ the mediator, through whom God has given you every good thing.

**“Because your faith.”** **(AMBR.)** He rejoices with them over the good beginning they have made, by which he shows his love toward them, and he urges them to advance. He says that he does all these things because their faith benefits many.

### Verse 9

**“Witness.”** I attribute to the Lord the faith that you possess. For I pray that it may be possessed from him; or he explains when he gives thanks: in his prayers—how? “Without ceasing.”

### Verse 11

**“For I long.”** So that what he could not persuade them of by words, his presence might persuade them of through the power of miracles.

### Verse 12

**“To be comforted.”** Now I am desolate, as are you; even if you do not feel it, nevertheless we might be comforted together.

### Verse 13

**“Brothers.”** Because they have been reborn, and some are upright; see above: “called saints.”

### Verse 14

**“To Greeks.”** He says nothing about the Jews, because he is the teacher of the nations.

**“To Greeks.”** He places the Greeks first because all worldly philosophy had its beginning among them.

**“To barbarians.”** He calls barbarians those who are, as it were, outside the law—those who are neither Hebrews, nor Greeks, nor Latins. This preaching is owed to no one more specifically than to them. He is a debtor because he was sent to all.

### Verse 16

**“For it is the power of God,” etc.** Because the unbelievable preaching is confirmed by signs, which is not the case with false heralds.

### Verse 17

**“For the righteousness of God.”** **(AMBR.)** It is that which freely justifies the ungodly through faith without the works of the law, etc., up to “those who deny that this is the Christ whom God promised.”

**“Is revealed.”** **(AUG.)** He approaches the Gentiles according to their former condition, etc., up to “who, puffed up by themselves, fell into idols.”

**“From faith,” etc.** **(AMBR.)** From the faith of God who promises, to the faith of the human being who believes him, etc., up to “to the faith of realities and of the form.”

**(AUG.)** Faith is that by which things not seen are believed, etc., up to “to the faith of the realities that we shall obtain once they have been believed.”

**“As it is written.”** In Habakkuk, chapter 2, it reads: “But the righteous person shall live by his own faith.” Yet this and many similar testimonies that he cites appear to differ from the translation of the Hebrew truth that we now use. For sometimes he takes wording from the Seventy translators, and sometimes, speaking in the same Spirit by whom the prophets spoke, he takes only the prophet’s meaning, using his own words and arrangement.

### Verse 18

**“Against all ungodliness.”** Ungodliness is sin against God; wickedness is sin against human beings. Or, the ungodly person is the unbeliever, such as an idolater; the wicked person is one who, through the perversity of his conduct, departs from justice.

**“Of those who suppress the truth.”** As if he were saying: Why should wrath fall upon them for their ungodliness, since they did not know God? He answers: They could indeed have known him, but they themselves are unwilling, preferring to remain unjustly in their own pleasure.

**“They suppress the truth of God.”** For, as it is said, “what can be known of God is manifest among them.” As if he were saying: They possess within themselves the means by which they may know him, namely natural reason.

**“They suppress it in wickedness.”** What they hold is good, but the place in which they hold it is evil. They hold the truth, but in wickedness. Have you found God? You have found the truth, and you hold it in wickedness. What you came to know through God’s works, you have lost through human works.

### Verse 19

**“What is known of God.”** **(GREG., Book X of the Morals, chapter 4.)** What is known of God is what we can attain from the ordering of this world and from the natural order. What is unknown of God is what is hidden from every creature, such as the account of his substance or nature and the mystery of human liberation.

**“Is manifest among them.”** **(AUG.)** Not only did natural reason contribute to this, but God also helped them daily, lest nature alone should appear sufficient.

### Verse 20

**“From the creation.”** **(GREG., Book XXIX of the Morals, chapter 8.)** “From the human being” by excellence, because the human being excels among the other creatures; or because of the relationship human beings have with all creatures. For a human being is locally in a place with bodies, senses with animals, and understands with angels. Hence: “Preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16).

**“Although they knew,” etc.** **(AUG., Sermon 55 on the Words of the Lord.)** They saw where they ought to come, etc., up to “for what God had freely given, they took away from those who were ungrateful.”

### Verse 21

**“Was darkened.”** **(AMBR.)** A cloud of error covered their hearts. Although, from the beautiful things he had made, they ought to have honored the Creator all the more, they became dull and abandoned him.

### Verse 22

**“They became fools.”** This shows how the heart was darkened, which is punishment: wise in the nature of things, but fools concerning God.

### Verse 23

**“And they exchanged.”** **(AUG., Letter 119, chapter 6, to Januarius.)** Here he condemns the images of the ungodly. Some worshiped the earth, others the sun, and others things of this kind.

**“Into the likeness of an image.”** He intensifies their foolishness in order to display the height of their stupidity.

**“Of human beings and birds,” etc.** It was an ancient custom among the Romans to worship images of human beings, such as Romulus, Jupiter, and others, especially from the arrival of Aeneas in Italy. They worshiped birds, four-footed animals, and serpents from the time when Alexandria was conquered by Augustus and subjected to Rome.

**(AMBR.)** For the Babylonians were the first to call the image of Bel a god, etc., up to “and birds, because pagans have raven rites.”

**(AUG., Book VII of the City of God, chapter 33.)** Through this one true religion of Christ it could be revealed that the gods of the nations are utterly unclean demons, who, under the pretext of departed souls or the appearance of worldly creatures, desire to be thought gods.

### Verse 24

**“He handed them over,” etc.** **(AUG., Book on Grace and Free Choice, chapter 21.)** It is clear that God works in human hearts to incline their wills either toward good, according to his mercy, or toward evil, according to their merits—by his judgment, sometimes hidden, sometimes manifest, but always just.

**“May be affected.”** **(GREG., Homily 11 on Ezekiel.)** A sin that is not washed away by the lament of repentance, etc., up to “God permits the blinded mind to fall into something else as well.”

### Verse 25

**“Because they exchanged.”** He elaborates more fully, part by part, on the guilt and punishment, so that he may set them side by side.

**“Because they exchanged.”** He shows that they changed the glory of God in these respects: they thought that something was God which was not God, and they worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator. He then sets out the aspects of their impurity: females with females and males with males. In these matters he compares the punishment with the guilt, so that just as they sinned against the Creator contrary to nature, they might be punished in their own nature. Hence he concludes: “And the recompense.”

**“They exchanged the truth.”** **(AMBR.)** They gave the name of God, who is true, to those who are not gods.

**(AUG.)** The truth of the creature comes from God, but the creature is not God. They turned this truth into a lie, worshiping creatures as though they were the Creator.

**“And worshiped,” etc.** But lest they say, “I do not worship images, but the things represented by them, such as the sun,” he adds: “And served the creature.” Here he condemns what they understood by the images.

**“Amen.”** As if he were saying: It is true that blessing belongs to the true God forever; but, for a time, ungodliness gives honor to the gods of the nations. Therefore what they say is false.

### Verse 26

**“Passions.”** That is, pleasures which, although they delight, are nevertheless passions of a nature not to be named.

**“Natural use.”** **(AUG., Book III Against Julian the Pelagian, chapter 20.)** Do you suppose, Julian, that the Apostle praised lust on this account, etc., up to “it is contrary to nature and disgraceful.”

### Verse 27

**“And the recompense,” etc.** **(AUG.)** But few see these punishments, etc., up to “they are both sins and punishments.”

**“It was necessary.”** Here the reason for which they were handed over is shown without any ambiguity.

### Verse 28

**“And just as,” etc.** Because they still do not repent, they fall into other things on account of the same guilt. By “just as,” he assimilates the punishment to the sin: just as they sinned in their knowledge of God, so they were punished in their own understanding.

**“They did not approve.”** Because they did not recognize, as reason showed, that God ought to be held in knowledge; or because they thought that God was ignorant of and indifferent to evils.

**“He handed them over,” etc.**

### Verse 29

**“With every wickedness.”** He enumerates the parts in order to accuse their evil more openly, especially when someone plots harm against another.

Wickedness (*nequitia*) is rashness, when someone dares what he cannot do, or a lack of self-restraint.

Contention is an attack on the truth through the confidence of shouting.

Malignity is an evil will, either when one can go no further or when one fails to return thanks for benefits.

Detractors are those who deny or distort the good qualities of others.

**“Hateful to God.”** Lest whispering or detraction seem insignificant because they are expressed in words, he adds concerning them: “hateful to God,” so that they may understand that through whispering and detraction alone they can incur eternal condemnation.

**“Arrogant.”** The arrogant are those who refuse to endure someone who came before them or who is their equal.

### Verse 31

**“Without order.”** Disorder in the body indicates the quality of the mind.

### Verse 32

**“Worthy of death.”** Lest they be thought to suffer only the punishments in which they delight, he adds the final punishment: eternal death.

**“Those who approve of those who do these things,” etc.** To approve is to remain silent when one is able to rebuke, or to encourage error.

## Chapter II

### Verse 1

**“Therefore,” etc.** This is said generally of both Gentiles and Jews. The Jew judged the Gentile because of his former condition; the Gentile judged the Jew. Both were human beings, not spiritual beings.

If the Jew judges the Gentile for idolatry, the Jew himself is also an idolater. If the Gentile judges the Jew for transgressing the law, he himself is a transgressor of the natural law.

**“Inexcusable.”** Because you yourself are a witness to your condemnation when you judge another. Why is this so? Because you do the same things.

**“You who judge.”** In this he shows himself to be what he is not—that is, righteous.

**“You do the same things.”** By his authority the Apostle destroys the empty excuse of Gentiles and Jews. A Jew could say in defense of his sin: “Even if I do the same things, my Jewish lineage and the law defend me; the Gentile is defended by ignorance.” Against this the Apostle says: “You who judge,” etc.

**(THEOD.)** It is clear to those who understand that those who behave wickedly are punished by divine judgment.

### Verse 3

**“But do you suppose?”** This chapter is commonly read as directed against Jews and Gentiles, but it may also be read specifically against any arrogant prelate of the Church.

**“That you will escape.”** You sin more seriously when you promise yourself impunity, because you despise God’s goodness, and do not understand that you are despising it—and you do this? This is a rebuke, as if he were saying: It is astonishing.

### Verse 4

**“Or the riches of goodness.”** **(AMBR.)** His goodness is abundant, because it gives many things to many people, etc., up to “but he turns it into impunity.”

### Verse 5

**“But according to,” etc.** There are some who are displeased by the evils they commit and, moved by repentance of heart, labor to escape from them insofar as they are able; he is not speaking about such people here.

There are others who take pleasure in evils and, presuming excessively upon God’s mercy, persist stubbornly in them. In this they display his patience and heap up their own burden by sinning still more grievously.

There are also others who are indeed displeased by evils, but because they understand them to be serious, they think that they can no longer be forgiven, like the one who said: “My iniquity is greater” (Genesis 4), etc.

The former, through excessive hope, judge God not to be just; the latter, through despair, consider God not to be good. Therefore both groups will perish, being endangered by both hoping and despairing, troubled by contrary realities and contrary affections.

**“Of just judgment.”** **(CYPR.)** He said that God’s judgment is just, etc., up to “repentance cannot benefit the sinner.”

### Verse 6

**“Who will repay each person.”** At present he does not repay those whom he liberates, because his goodness is now generous toward the wicked. In the future, however, he will repay evil for evil, because he is just; and good for evil, because he is good and just. He will not repay evil for good, because he is not unjust.

**(GREG.)** It belongs to justice that those whose mind, etc., should never be free from punishment, up to “that a human being should be punished eternally.”

### Verse 8

**“Indignation.”** Lest he appear to become angry without taking vengeance; hence come tribulation and distress.

### Verse 9

**“Tribulation and distress.”** In the meantime, in the soul alone, before the judgment; but after the judgment, wrath and indignation.

**“Upon every.”** Above he spoke indefinitely: “upon those who”; here he speaks universally, so as to include both Jew and Gentile.

He says “soul” because he is speaking about the unbeliever, whose soul will be constricted by spiritual punishment on account of its unbelief.

**“Of the Jew first.”** **(AMBR.)** He always places the Jew first because, just as the believer is more honored on account of Abraham, so the unbeliever must be treated more severely because he rejected the promise made to the fathers.

### Verse 11

**“For there is no,” etc.** He makes Jew and Gentile equal in punishment and glory, because God judges not according to persons but according to merits, condemning both according to the measure of their sin.

**(AMBR.)** God does not follow the privilege of lineage by receiving an unbeliever for the sake of his ancestors, nor does he reject a believer because of the unworthiness of his parents. Rather, he rewards or condemns each person according to that person’s own merit.

### Verse 12

**“Without the law.”** **(AUG.)** The Apostle called the Gentiles “without the law” because they had not received the written law of Moses, which the Jews gloried in having received.

**“In the law.”** **(ID.)** Those who knew the divine commandments have their excuse taken away, etc., up to “or by the addition of their own will.”

**“Will be judged.”** Not so that they might be saved as if through fire, as some say, but they will perish completely. For Christ says that it will be more tolerable for Sodom in the judgment than for Jews who do not believe in Christ. He also says that they will have no excuse for the sin of unbelief, because he came and spoke to them. Those to whom he spoke neither personally nor through his own people do have an excuse; nevertheless, they will not escape condemnation, because “those who are without the law,” etc. They will nevertheless suffer lighter punishments, because from the one to whom more is entrusted, more is required.

### Verse 13

**“For it is not the hearers.”** Does the law alone save? No, because it does not make people righteous. This is what he means: not those who hear, but those who do will be justified—whoever they are, and this indeed occurs through grace.

But “those who do,” that is, those who believe in Christ, whom the law promised—whoever they may be—are justified, and this occurs only through grace.

**(AUG., Book on the Spirit and the Letter, chapter 26.)** “The doers of the law will be justified,” that is, they will be counted righteous or made righteous. It does not mean that those who were already doers will be justified, since the Gentiles also are included.

### Verse 14

**“For when,” etc.** Above he had said that the Gentile would be condemned if he acted badly and saved if he acted well. But since he does not possess the law, as though he did not know what is good or evil, he seems to himself not to be accountable for either. The Apostle responds: Even if he does not possess the written law, he nevertheless possesses the natural law, through which he understands and is conscious within himself of what is good and what is evil.

For vice is contrary to nature, and grace certainly heals it. The image of earthly affections has not so completely worn away from the human soul that no outlines of it remain. What was impressed there through the image of God when the human being was created has not been entirely erased.

Therefore, once the vice has been healed by grace, people naturally do the things belonging to the law. This does not mean that grace has been denied through nature; rather, nature has been restored through grace. By this grace, in the inner human being renewed, the law of righteousness is rewritten—the law that guilt had erased.

### Verse 15

**“The work of the law.”** It is the faith that they voluntarily possess in their hearts, that is, in their inmost affection, where faith works through love.

### Verse 17

**“But if you are called a Jew,” etc.** Here he attacks the Jews, accusing them more severely of their sins because they possessed more helps.

### Verse 19

**“To be guides of the blind.”** He calls the Gentiles blind and existing in darkness, since they are blind because they have been deprived of reason; and even if they know something, they are nevertheless in darkness.

### Verse 20

**“Having the form.”** So that you may be an example to others of knowledge of the law and of truth.

Some people possess knowledge and understanding of a particular book and think as its author thought, but nevertheless do not possess the truth derived from it, because they do not know how it is true, or even that it is true. But the Jew boasts that he possesses the meaning of the law and knows that this meaning is truly the meaning of the law, so that he may be an example to others who wish to know.

### Verse 24

**“For the name of God.”** Among the nations the name of God is blasphemed because of the Jews, since the Jews tried to persuade believers that Christ should not be called God.

Or it is because, in former times, the nations did not recognize that the Jews had been handed over to them on account of their offenses, but gave the glory for their victory to their own idols, as though they had conquered the God of the Jews through the Jews.

### Verse 25

**“Circumcision indeed.”** Above he showed that the law does not help them; now he shows that circumcision does not help them in obtaining righteousness.

**“It is beneficial if you keep the law,” etc.** By obeying God, it makes the sign a sign of truth, while the inexperienced people are kept under the fear of God.

**“It is beneficial.”** It is asked how he can say here that circumcision is beneficial, when later he says: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing.” The answer is that this is to be understood according to the circumstances of different periods.

In the period of the old law, circumcision was once beneficial, but it was not beneficial for salvation without spiritual observance of the law; this is what is meant here. Now, namely in the time of grace, after the truth has been manifested, it is not merely unbeneficial but harmful; this is discussed later.

### Verse 26

**“Will not.”** Does not the Gentile, by comparison with himself, show you, O Jew, to be condemnable—you who have known through the law, not through nature or circumcision, what he has known through nature, namely Christ?

### Verse 27

**“Will judge,” etc.** **(ORIG.)** Circumcision is in the flesh. To circumcise is to cut from the genital member, etc., up to “in whom there is not circumcision of the flesh but observance of the law.”

### Verse 28

**“For he is not.”** As if he were saying: A Jew can rightly become a Gentile, and a Gentile a Jew, as has been said.

**“A Jew.”** The word is interpreted as “one who confesses.” For the person who truly believes and rightly confesses is truly a Jew.

### Verse 29

**“Circumcision of the heart.”** **(ORIG.)** It is that which purifies the soul and cuts away the stains of vices.

**“Whose praise.”** **(AMBR.)** God praises the believer, etc., up to “which appeared before human beings in his works.”

**“Not from human beings.”** **(AUG.)** By circumcision of the heart he means a will that is pure from every illicit desire. This does not come about through the letter, which teaches and threatens, but through the Spirit, who helps and heals.

## Chapter III

### Verse 1

**“What, then, is greater?”** He raises the objection that he sees could be raised, in order to resolve it.

Since a Jew becomes a Gentile and a Gentile a Jew, what advantage does the Jew have, who is called God’s particular people, over the Gentile, who is called an unclean dog? Or what did he gain from circumcision?

He answers: It was indeed beneficial formerly, but this does not make them more worthy in faith. This is what he means: According to the former condition, the Jew has much more than the Gentile, and this in every respect.

“Every respect” means either in the administration of temporal things or in the revealing of spiritual things. In both respects God did much for the Jews that he did not do for the Gentiles, and thus, according to their former condition, they were more worthy.

### Verse 2

**“First, indeed,” etc.** As if he were saying: To omit the other, lesser matters concerning temporal things, I place this first and most important: the words of the Lord—that is, the law and the prophets—were entrusted to them as to friends, through which they might understand the redemption that was to come.

But you will say: This did not give them greater privilege, since some of them did not believe the words and therefore did not receive the promised Christ.

The answer is that this nevertheless did not make them less beneficial to those who believed. This is what he means: Although some did not believe, faith was not thereby nullified.

### Verse 3

**“What if some were unbelieving?”** **(AMBR.)** He says: No. Because some were unwilling to believe, will the others among the Jews be prejudiced, so that they are not considered worthy to receive what God promised to the faithful? Certainly not, since the promise was made in such a way that it would benefit those who believed.

**“Faith.”** **(ORIG.)** We understand this as the faith that God has with those to whom he entrusts his words, or as the faith by which some believe God.

### Verse 4

**“But God is true,” etc.** He adds this so that it may appear that God’s promise was made and fulfilled not on account of any human dignity, but on account of mercy, so that grace might be given to the unworthy and might therefore be more highly commended.

God is called truthful, that is, unchanging, both in essence and in promise. The human being is called a liar, that is, neither possessing the truth by nature nor remaining steadfast because of sins.

**“Every human being is a liar.”** This refers to the person who denies that God fulfilled his promises—especially the Jew, whom God overcomes when he grants the promises.

**“Every human being.”** This includes the Jew as well, so that the Jew may not appear more worthy than the Gentile in the new condition.

### Verse 5

**“But if our iniquity,” etc.** He has said that God is truthful and every human being a liar, and that God gives good things to the unworthy; in this his justice and grace appear more commendable. Therefore the carnal person, saying that God uses evils as an instrument for his own glory, takes the matter so far as to call God unjust because he punishes sins that benefit him. The Apostle removes this objection by saying:

**“Is God unjust?”** God is truthful and the human being is a liar. If this is so, and if our iniquity commends God’s justice, what seems to follow? That God is unjust. But is God unjust when he inflicts evils?

### Verse 7

**“For if the truth.”** After inserting this removal of the charge against God, the Apostle returns to the argument of the carnal person who attempts to prove that God is unjust if he punishes the wicked, since he is thereby glorified.

Why, then, am I still judged as a sinner, as though I were not one? Or: “Still,” that is, after conversion, after he has given gifts to the unworthy. For when I previously deserved punishment because of my own deeds, he was not more glorified.

It is as if he were saying: What might have seemed true before remission ought not to seem true afterward—namely, that I should be judged a sinner. In other words: It is certain that the truth of forgiveness would not have abounded to God’s glory unless I had sinned.

### Verse 8
