**“And not as,” etc.** As if he were saying: If this is what you mean—that God’s truth abounds through sin—why do we not do evil so that good may come, as people slanderously claim that we teach and ascribe to us on the basis of words such as: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more”?

Or it may be joined more closely to the preceding wording:

How will God judge? As if he were saying: Not rightly, because even now he would not justly judge me as a sinner, since I am not one—and in truth I am not.

### Verse 9

**“What then?”** As if he were saying: God did more for the Jew in the former condition, and because he fulfilled good things for them not on account of any merit of theirs, what follows? Do we surpass them?

Certainly not. Therefore we Jews do not surpass the Gentiles in the present condition of grace, although in the former condition we surpassed them in every respect.

**“Not at all.”** For God shows no partiality, but in every nation the person who fears God is acceptable to him (Acts 10).

### Verse 11

**“There is no one seeking.”** From their works they could have sought and discovered that Christ was God.

### Verse 12

**“All have turned aside,” etc.** He does not mean the entire people without exception, but another part of the people. For there are always two peoples within one people. Hence Jeremiah says: “Then everyone rose up against the prophet of the Lord, wishing to kill him.” He adds: “But all the people did not permit them” (Jeremiah 38).

He said that “everyone” rose up, meaning the wicked; and that “all the people” did not permit it, meaning the good.

**“There is not even one.”** For Christ alone makes good, both in himself and in his own people.

### Verse 15

**“Their feet are swift.”** He speaks of those concerning whom the Lord says: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets” (Matthew 23). And again: “An evil and adulterous generation” (Matthew 16). And Isaiah says of them: “Woe to the sinful nation, the wicked seed” (Isaiah 1), etc.

### Verse 16

**“Destruction.”** They do such things that they are crushed in this age, through Titus and Vespasian; and in the future they will be wretched, punished in soul and body.

### Verse 19

**“In the law.”** The law is sometimes called, in general, the Old Testament, as in: “The Lord opened the minds of the disciples so that they might understand the things written about him in the law, the prophets, and the psalms” (Luke 24; John 10; Psalm 81).

Sometimes the psalms are called the law. As the Lord says: “It is written in your law: ‘I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.’” And elsewhere: “That the word written in their law might be fulfilled: ‘They hated me without cause’” (John 15; Psalm 34).

**“So that every mouth may be stopped,”** including the mouths of the Jews who boast of their glory and claim to have come to faith through their own merits; or, the mouths of the Jews may be stopped in the same way as those of the Gentiles mentioned above, who boasted of their good nature.

### Verse 20

**“Because from the works.”** Just as he took away their glory in circumcision, so he also wishes to take it away from the other works of the law. This is a new statement, although it is joined to what precedes by the words: “Because from the works of the law,” etc.

The works of the law are those established and defined in the law, such as the ceremonial and figurative works. These were never able to cleanse the conscience, even when performed with love and devotion, because they were not instituted for justification but to signify future things and to reveal the weakness of sin. For the law did not come to remove sins, but to show and punish them.

**“No flesh will be justified,” etc.** Understand this with reference to ceremonial works, not moral works, which certainly do justify and are brought to perfection in the Gospel.

**“Before him.”** Before the one who sees what is hidden within—namely, whether something is done out of love of righteousness or out of fear of punishment, which human beings do not see.

**“Through the law.”** Here he begins to speak about the law, to show that righteousness does not come from it.

**“Through the law comes knowledge of sin.”** He does not say this because sins were previously unknown, but because through the law it became known that all sins would not go unpunished before God.

Some sins were known before the law, as when Joseph, accused of adultery before Pharaoh, was sent to prison. His brothers said: “We suffer these things deservedly, because we sinned against our brother” (Genesis 39).

Other sins became known through the law that had previously been unknown, such as concupiscence and original sin. Certain sins were also recognized through the law as more serious than they had previously been thought.

### Verse 21

**“Witnessed to,” etc.** Because the law represented it through many sacraments, it thereby bears witness to God’s righteousness, since no one is justified by it. The prophets bear witness by foretelling it, which the coming of Christ fulfilled.

### Verse 22

**“But the righteousness,” etc.** This is not the righteousness by which he is essentially righteous, but the righteousness with which he clothes the ungodly when, in his mercy, he makes the unbeliever a believer.

It is called God’s righteousness, although it seems more properly to be called mercy, because it originates in a promise. When God’s promise is repaid, it is called God’s righteousness. It is righteousness because what was promised has been paid; and when God receives those who flee to him, it is called God’s righteousness, because not to receive them would be injustice.

### Verse 23

**“They lack glory.”** That is, indulgence and forgiveness of sins.

### Verse 24

**“Justified freely.”** Not through the law, not through one’s own will, but through the grace of Christ—though not in such a way that it occurs without our will. Rather, the law reveals that our will is weak, so that grace may heal the will, and the healed will may fulfill the law, no longer placed under the law or in need of the law.

**“Freely.”** That is, without any preceding merits of works. Otherwise grace would no longer be grace, since it is given not because we have performed good works, but so that we may be able to perform them.

### Verse 25

**“God set forth,” etc.** He did this to show himself truthful in his promises. This manifestation was necessary not only for the remission of present sins but also for those that preceded, through God’s forbearance—God being patient and not punishing them.

He also did this to show, in the time of Christ, what could not have occurred at any other time: that he might be just and the one who justifies the person who is of the faith of Jesus.

**“Faith in the blood.”** That is, faith in the Passion; or, through faith and through the Passion, for neither is effective without the other.

**“For the remission.”** The effect of remission is twofold: freedom from punishment and enjoyment of glory. The righteous possessed the first before Christ’s death, since they did not experience actual punishment. But after Christ’s death they were given the glory of the divine vision, from which they had been delayed while God endured their sins.

### Verse 26

**“In forbearance.”** God patiently endured the sins of those who lived before the law and under the law. He neither punished nor remitted them in such a way that they would possess glory, until the one came who would absolve, by the price of his blood, the sins both of those who preceded him and of those who followed.

### Verse 27

**“It has been excluded.”** If he means the praiseworthy glorification that is in the Lord, he says that it has been excluded not so that it might depart, as something driven away, but so that it might stand forth and be made manifest. Hence artisans who work in silver are also called “excluders”; hence the Psalmist says: “That those who have been tested may be excluded” (Psalm 67), etc.

Or, if he wishes to recall defective boasting, he says that it has been excluded through the law of faith—that is, expelled and rejected—because through the law of faith each person recognizes that, if he lives well, he has this from God’s grace.

### Verse 28

**“A person is justified.”** This does not mean that a believer ought not afterward to work through love, as Abraham also wished to sacrifice his son. Works follow the justified person; they do not precede the person who is to be justified.

A person becomes righteous by faith alone, without preceding works, so that those who performed the works of the law out of fear are not more righteous, since faith works through love in the heart even if it does not emerge outwardly in a deed.

Thus one does not come to the righteousness of faith through the merits of earlier works, in which the Jews placed themselves ahead. For the good works said to precede faith are empty, so that they appear to possess great strength and to run with great speed—but off the road.

Where faith was absent, there was no good work. For intention makes the work good, and faith directs the intention.

**“Without works.”** Without preceding works, not without subsequent works, without which faith is empty, as James says: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2); and Paul himself says: “If I have all faith” (1 Corinthians 13), etc.

**“Through faith.”** **(AUG., Enchiridion, chapter 107.)** This is the faith of Christ that the Apostle commends, the faith that works through love.

### Verse 31

**“By no means.”** The law is not destroyed when, having been fulfilled according to the spirit, it ceases according to the letter.

**“We establish.”** We establish it because we have shown that what the law says has been completed; or “we establish,” that is, we confirm it, because this is the grace of faith by which the law is fulfilled—the law which would be weak without faith.

The status of the law is confirmed because its mystical and ceremonial elements are fulfilled spiritually, and what was lacking in moral matters is added in the Gospel. What the law promised was to come, the faith of the Gospel testifies has arrived. Thus the mystical and promissory elements have been fulfilled in the Gospel according to spiritual understanding, while the killing letter is removed.

## Chapter IV

### Verse 1

**“According to the flesh.”** That is, from the works of the law.

As if he were saying: Shall we say that he was righteous because of these works? No. For if he is righteous through carnal observance, he has the eternal glory that follows righteousness; but he has it from himself, not from God.

Or this justification exists in human opinion and not before God. He has glory before God; therefore he was not justified by works.

If, then, he was not justified by works, from where was he justified? The text follows and says from where, etc.

**VERSE 3.**—“He believed.” Believing was a sufficient cause of righteousness for him, and it is so for others as well. Nevertheless, for one who has time to perform works, the reward will not be given solely according to grace, but also according to the debt owed for his works. But for one who does not have time to perform works, if he believes, faith alone is sufficient for righteousness and thus for salvation, according to the grace proposed to all, or according to what God established beforehand in the Law.

**VERSE 4.**—“But to him who works,” etc. As if he were saying: Abraham is righteous by faith; but for one who performs those carnal works, or any good works, in order to merit grace, if a reward is given him, it is not from grace but from the debt owed on account of his merit. But for one who does not perform these carnal works or any good works, but merely believes, faith is sufficient for righteousness. Thus he attributes to others what he said about Abraham: namely, that if he is righteous by works, he has glory, but not before God, and therefore he is righteous by faith.

“According to grace.” If it is grace, it is given freely, or is freely bestowed. You have done nothing good, and the forgiveness of sins is given to you. Your works are examined, and they are all found to be evil.

“But according to debt.” (AUG.) Do not flatter yourself about merits, etc., up to “let us act by his own gift and generosity.”

**VERSE 5.**—“But to him who believes,” etc. He does not say “to him.” For one believes him who believes that the things he says are true; the wicked do this as well. To believe him is to believe that he is God; the demons do this too. But to believe in him is to love him by believing, to cherish him by believing, to go toward him by believing, and to be incorporated into his members.

“According to the purpose.” As if he were saying: The ungodly person is justified without preceding works, and this according to the purpose of God’s grace—that is, according to God’s grace proposed to all who believe, or according to what God established long beforehand.

**VERSE 7.**—“Forgiven.” “To forgive,” “to cover,” and “not to impute” are words of the same meaning and force. “Iniquities.” Original sin is understood by “iniquities,” namely, the tinder of sin, which is called concupiscence or concupiscibility, or the law of the members, or the weakness of nature, and by other names. Before baptism this is both guilt and punishment; after baptism, however, it is punishment and not guilt. It makes the little child capable of desiring, but not desiring [as printed; the repeated word may be corrupt]; the adult, however, it also makes to desire. In baptism this is forgiven and passes away with respect to guilt, but remains with respect to its activity. It is called “original” because it is drawn from the corrupt condition of our origin, and because we were conceived through the corrupt law of generation, which arose from the sin of the first man—that is, through the concupiscence of the flesh. Therefore we are liable to the sin called original sin.

“ Sins have been covered.” (AUG.) Do not understand what he says—“sins have been covered”—as though they were there and alive. He says “covered,” therefore, so that they would not be seen; but for God to see sin is to punish it.

**VERSE 9.**—“In circumcision,” that is, at the time of circumcision, Abraham’s faith was reckoned as righteousness.

**VERSE 10.**—“But in uncircumcision,” that is, at the time of uncircumcision.

**VERSE 13.**—“For the promise was not through the Law.” Other promises were made to Christ than to Abraham. The promises made to Abraham were made in such a way that those who imitated him in this manner would be blessed by Christ. They were not made to Christ in this way, but so that he would not merely be an example and model for the establishment of morals and works; rather, he would bless those who imitated him with an eternal blessing. “To his seed.” That is, to all believers who are Abraham’s seed, not by flesh but by imitation. Or, to Christ, to whom the promise is said to have been made because it was to be fulfilled in him.

**VERSE 14.**—“For if,” etc. As if he were saying: Truly, Abraham is not heir of the world through the Law, because his children through the Law are not those who are called heirs—namely, those who possess what he himself possesses. For if this were so, the following contradictions would result: faith would be frustrated, although it is established that Abraham was righteous; and the promise would be abolished, that is, left unfulfilled, so that there would be no heirs. For the Law makes no heirs; rather, it produces wrath, and thus transgression. For transgression arises from it, since without it there is no transgression. Therefore, because these consequences would follow if it were from the Law, the heirs are from faith, and thus the promise is firm.

**VERSE 15.**—“The Law produces wrath.” It produces wrath by making offenders liable—not as an efficient cause, but because grace does not assist—or it produces wrath by making them liable to temporal punishments; for it produces transgression. How this happens he explains by saying:

“For where there is no law,” etc. (ORIG.) He shows that transgression cannot exist unless there has been a law. Yet it does not follow that, whenever there is a law, transgression will exist in every case. It can happen that there is a law and no transgression, but not the reverse.

“Nor is there transgression.” He does not say, “There is no iniquity.” Everyone who goes beyond the Law is unjust, but the reverse is not true. Those who have not received the Law can be called unjust, but they cannot be called transgressors.

**VERSE 16.**—“Not to him who is of the Law.” Since such a person has fallen away from grace, one must depart from the Law for the sake of faith, so that the promise may be firm. For the Law without the grace of the promise not only does not take away sin; it also increases it.

**VERSE 18.**—“Who, contrary to hope.” He begins to commend Abraham’s faith, so that we may imitate him, who received righteousness through faith and received such a promise.

“Thus shall your seed be,” etc. It should be known that Abraham first came to know God as three and one, and through this merit of faith obtained forgiveness of all sins. After his justification, he received from God the promise that he would become the father of many nations. Then the promise was made to him again that his seed would be like the stars, and so forth.

**VERSE 19.**—“He was not weakened.” Some, puffed up by worldly reasoning, neglected God. Therefore God did what is impossible for the world, so that believers might be saved through these things.

**VERSE 20.**—“In the promise.” Isaac, promised contrary to the nature of human generation, was a sign that the Son of God would be born from a human being contrary to human nature, and that through the Spirit of regeneration the sons of human beings would be generated from sinners as sons of God, and from mortals as immortals.

**VERSE 24.**—“In him who raised Jesus,” etc. He appropriately began to speak about the Lord and said that he did not die on account of his own sins—for in that case he ought not to have risen, just as no one before him had risen—but on account of our sins, in order to free us from them. In the same way, he restored Abraham and Sarah’s womb, already dead from old age and barrenness, to life and to the begetting of children.

**VERSE 25.**—“Who was delivered up.” Christ’s death alone signifies the destruction of the old life, while the new life is signified only in the resurrection. It begins with justification and will be perfected in immortality.

**CHAPTER V**

**VERSE 1.**—“By faith.” Above he said that we were justified freely by grace, so that faith itself would not become proud. Let the believer not say, “I have faith so that I may merit justification.” For the answer is given to him: “What do you have that you did not receive?” Let us have peace, since we have been reconciled to him through Christ, the minister of grace.

**VERSE 2.**—“Through whom.” He enumerates the benefits that are received from Christ.

**VERSE 3.**—“Tribulation.” Charity, which is the proper gift of the Holy Spirit, causes tribulation not to destroy patience.

“Hope.” That is, certainty of the future glory, which appears futile to human reasoning; but it is strengthened by the testimony of virtue—that is, of patience or miracles.

**VERSE 5.**—“But hope.” It is in God, who does not deceive, not in lying man. The pledge of this hope is the Spirit. For it is written: “Let the fountain of your water be your own, and let no stranger share it with you” (Ecclesiasticus 5). The Spirit is himself this fountain; the wicked cannot receive him, and no one can possess charity and remain wicked. But someone can bear the name of Christ and baptism, receive the body of the Lord, and possess the other sacraments while remaining wicked. Charity, therefore, is the proper gift of the Spirit and the unique fountain.

“God’s charity.” Or: God loves us abundantly, and through the Spirit, who makes us understand God’s love toward us, we have this love in our hearts.

**VERSE 6.**—“For why, then?” Since God loves us, or since we love him through the Spirit, hope will be fulfilled. For unless this were so, Christ would have suffered in vain. This is why Christ died for the ungodly—that is, out of love for the ungodly or in their place—not for those who had once been ungodly but were not so then, but for us when we were weak in sins.

“According to the time,” that is, for three days only, so that you would not despair of the power of one whose benevolence is displayed in death. From him we receive such pledges: he gave his death to the ungodly, while he preserves his life for the righteous. He died for you, mortal human being, so that you might live with him. He took upon himself our death so that he might give us his life; he received from you that by which he would die for you. He clothed himself with what would enable him to die for you; he will clothe you with what will enable you to live with him. He clothed himself in mortal flesh through the virginity of his mother; he will clothe you with everlasting life in equality with the Father.

**VERSE 7.**—“Scarcely.” He is speaking of the righteous. Perhaps he means “for the good person.” He shows that both are difficult and rare, but that one is more difficult and rarer than the other.

“For the righteous,” etc. The righteous person is righteous through discipline and is also good. Yet there is also a good person who is not righteous—that is, one who was born in simplicity: an innocent person who has not yet labored to increase himself in good works, such as little children cleansed in baptism. Although the righteous person is better, the condition of innocence is nevertheless more pitiable than that of righteousness, because such righteousness does not exist without severity.

**VERSE 8.**—“While we were still.” Behold: while he hated us with respect to our sins, he loved us with respect to the work of his creation; and this he did before the foundation of the world. It was necessary to say how greatly he loved us, so that we would not despair, and what sort of people we were, so that we would not become proud. Another way was possible for God, who can do all things, but none was more fitting for healing our misery. What raises us so greatly and frees us from despair of immortality more than the fact that he esteemed us so highly that a human being would die for us?

**VERSE 9.**—“Much more, therefore.” It is a more serious matter to die for sin and take away sin than to save those who are already righteous and cooperating with grace.

“In his blood.” In this way the devil is overcome by justice, not by power. By justice, because the devil killed Christ, who was undeserving; therefore he rightly loses others as well. Not by power, because the devil is a lover of power and a deserter of justice, and in this human beings imitate him more readily. It therefore pleased God that the human being should be delivered not by power but by justice, which conquers, so that the human being might imitate him. Afterwards power followed in the resurrection, because the dead man came back to life, never again to die.

**VERSE 10.**—“We were enemies.” Not merely sinners in some general way. “We have been reconciled.” For previously, because of our nature corrupted by sin, we were justly under the power of the devil.

**VERSE 12.**—“Therefore.” He said that righteousness and life exist through Christ. He intends to prove that they can exist through him by means of a lesser analogy.

“Through one.” Namely, Adam. The Apostle did not say “through one Eve,” following the customary manner of speech by attributing the succession of human posterity—which succumbs to sin and the death arising from it—not to the woman but to the man. For posterity is ordinarily named from the man, not from the woman. Or this is because the woman is from the man, and the two are one flesh. Therefore, whether it is attributed to Eve or to Adam, both pertain to the first man. Through this the Apostle wished original sin of propagation to be understood, whose originator was Adam, not sin by imitation, whose originator was the devil. Hence: “Through the devil’s envy death entered this world.”

“To all human beings.” This is because even before the Law, when it did not seem so—since the Law had not taught it—sin was indeed imputed among human beings, but not before God, as sinners supposed. They thought that it would go unpunished because they did not know that he would judge. But when the Law was given, they learned that God cared about human affairs and judged them. Before this, sin was not imputed, but death reigned securely, possessing human beings through the impunity they believed in, until Moses, through whom knowledge of the one God returned. Death therefore reigned—as another reading has it—not, however, in everyone, but in those like Adam the transgressor, who, having neglected God, served the creature, just as Adam consented to the devil in place of God. Nearly everyone was like this until the Law. A very few, such as Abraham, served the one God; death did not reign over them. Rather, they were preserved in hope of being saved and liberated at Christ’s coming.

**VERSE 13.**—“Until the Law,” etc. That is, because neither the Law could take away sin, but increased it, whether the natural Law or the written Law. Yet sin was not imputed—that is, it was unknown. Nevertheless, it reigned until Moses, that is, until the Law, because even the Law could not remove the kingdom of death. Death reigns insofar as it does not allow the guilt of sin to come to eternal life but drags it to Gehenna. The grace of Christ alone destroyed this kingdom even among the ancients; apart from them it reigned over everyone, including those who did not sin by their own will as Adam did, but were held by original fault, as children are.

**VERSE 14.**—“But death reigned.” Sin was not imputed, but its effect made this evident, because bodily death reigned daily through various sufferings, finally bringing about dissolution, even until Moses, when this seemed less apparent.

“Who is a type.” Adam is a type of Christ, because just as Adam is the father of all according to the flesh, so Christ is the father of all according to faith. And just as Eve was formed from Adam’s side, so from Christ’s side flowed the sacraments by which the Church is saved. Therefore, just as Adam was able to communicate sin and death to his children, so Christ communicates his righteousness and life to his. Indeed, Christ confers more good on his own than Adam inflicted evil; therefore Christ is more able to save than Adam was to destroy.

**VERSE 15.**—“But not as,” etc. The likeness consists in this: one person sets things right, and one person sinned. But Adam’s case is not like Christ’s, because Adam’s one trespass caused many—that is, those who transgressed in the same way—to die, whereas Christ’s grace extends to many because it reaches both those who transgressed similarly and those who did not.

**VERSE 17.**—“For if.” (AMBR.) “Death reigned,” not “it reigns,” because those who are through the Law, etc., up to “for there is not a general condemnation or justification in everyone.”

“Through one he reigned,” etc. The powers that death possessed in Adam it exercised over all who came afterward, for Adam was their source, just as the guilt—which belonged to him alone—was transmitted to all. “Much more,” etc. This is because death reigned in them temporarily and with an end, whereas Christ’s grace reigns eternally.

**VERSE 18.**—“Through the righteousness of one,” etc. This does not mean that everyone born from Adam is regenerated through Christ, but just as no one has a carnal generation except through Adam, so no one has a spiritual regeneration except through Christ. If anyone had been generated apart from Adam, or regenerated apart from Christ, he would not say “all” and “all.” Just as no human being exists apart from that first generation, so no righteous person exists apart from this regeneration. Later he calls the same people “many.”

**VERSE 19.**—“For just as,” etc. He defines the trespass of one and the righteousness of one, so that, just as Adam deservedly lost us through sin, Christ might appear to have liberated us through righteousness.

“Thus also through one,” etc. He says “of a human being,” not “of God” or “of the Word,” lest you think that the righteous of old were liberated by faith in the Word of God alone—that is, by faith in the Word without faith in the incarnation.

**VERSE 20.**—“But the Law entered,” etc. He had shown that Christ removes all sins, both original and actual. Here he adds that Christ also frees from the sin of the Law—that is, from transgression—so that the Jews might be more indebted to Christ. As if he were saying: Justification came first; the Law entered secretly afterward.

(AMBR.) Here the Apostle says what resulted from the giving of the Law, etc., up to “God forgave everything.”

“But the Law entered.” The Law was given to those born in sins in order to subdue pride, as if to say: “One who commands is not lacking, but one who fulfills is lacking,” because a person born in sin cannot fulfill it. Therefore Christ was born—that is, grace was born—which would heal. “So that the trespass might abound.” Namely, so that the one who was already in filth might become even filthier by transgressing; so that the ordinary person might have a pedagogue, the perfect person a sign, and the hard-hearted person might feel the scourge.

“It abounded all the more.” For the grace of Christ benefits even those whom the devil could not overcome; and because sin reigned for a time, grace reigns forever.

**VERSE 21.**—“Just as sin reigned in death.” He does not add “through one” or “through Adam,” because he is not speaking only about what human beings derived from Adam, but also about what they added by their own will. But when he says, “Let grace reign,” he adds “through Jesus Christ,” etc., because through him not only original sin but also voluntary sins are forgiven.

**CHAPTER VI**

**VERSE 1.**—“Shall we remain?” Perverse people derive this from the statement: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more.” To say this is to be ungrateful toward grace. And because grace is powerful where sin abounded, one must not remain in sin, as some suppose, in order to obtain greater grace. Grace did not abound where sin abounded because of the merit of the sinner, but through the assistance of the one who came to help. Therefore we must not remain in sin; rather, through that same grace we ought to be able—and are able—to be as dead and buried to sin, and to rise into righteousness and afterward into eternal life.

**VERSE 2.**—“We have died.” That is, we have been freed from sin through baptism, so that by grace it no longer rules in us. To die to sin is to be freed from sin. “How shall we still,” etc. Since grace has granted that we should die to sin, what else do we do if we live in it except show ourselves ungrateful to grace?

**VERSE 3.**—“Or do you not know?” Having died to sin—which takes place in baptism—we must not live to it again, so that it would be necessary to die to it a second time. For we have died “in the death of Christ,” that is, in the likeness of Christ’s death, so that just as he died once in the flesh and lives forever, so we, having once died to evil through baptism, may live forever in the good. Or he says “in death” because death is the cause of this purification.

**VERSE 4.**—“Buried with him.” Everything that took place in Christ’s crucifixion, burial, resurrection, ascension, and sitting at the right hand was arranged so that Christian life would be conformed to these things mystically, not only through words but also through actions. Consider each aspect of Christ, who lived as the old human being with respect to punishment, hunger, thirst, and the like, but not with respect to guilt. In this way he brought the old life to an end and ordered it: bearing the pain of the cross, he had his limbs stretched out and fixed so that they would not move toward their former actions. Then, buried and withdrawn from human sight, he rested, requiring us to lay aside the oldness of sins with the pain and groaning of repentance; to have our limbs fixed through self-restraint and righteousness, so that we would not return to our former evils; and to rest from them so completely that neither their sight nor their memory would remain. He requires this of us not only in the sacrament of his passion, but also makes it possible if we wish to imitate him.

“He rose from the dead.” The death and resurrection of Christ are also sacraments.

**VERSE 6.**—“The old human being.” That is, the former deeds have been crucified—that is, they have died. Our oldness and our curse consist in two things: guilt and punishment. Christ, through his single oldness, consumed our double oldness. For he rested in the tomb for one day and two nights. His single oldness is signified by the one day, while our twofold oldness is signified by the two nights. Hence: Christ destroyed our present, past, and future guilt: the past by forgiving it, the present by drawing us away from it, and the future by granting grace so that we might avoid it. Likewise, he consumed punishment: he entirely destroyed punishment in Gehenna, so that those who truly repent will not experience it. But he did not remove temporal punishment completely; hunger, thirst, death, and the like remain. He did, however, overthrow its kingdom and dominion, and at the end he will utterly destroy it.

**VERSE 9.**—“Knowing that Christ.” (AUG.) One person has risen, never again to die. Lazarus rose, but he was going to die; the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue rose, but she was going to die; the widow’s son rose, but he was going to die. Christ rose, never again to die. Hear the Apostle: “Christ, rising,” etc. Hope for such a resurrection, and for this reason be a Christian—not for the prosperity of this earthly life.

**VERSE 10.**—“For the death that he died to sin.” (AUG.) The Apostle commends the sacrament of baptism: just as Christ is proclaimed to have died once, in the likeness of sin, so whoever has been baptized into him should die to the reality of which that death was the likeness—that is, to sin—and should live by being reborn from the washing, just as Christ rose by rising from the tomb.

**VERSE 11.**—“So you also.” Whatever he said above is granted to human beings through the grace of Christ; here he attributes it to the Romans.

**VERSE 12.**—“Therefore, do not let sin reign.” Since he said above that we had died to sins and ought not to live in them, although no one is without sin, he now specifies what must be avoided above all, as though he were concluding the question raised earlier: “Shall we remain in sin?”

“Obey its desires [concupiscences].” “Concupiscence” sometimes denotes the tinder of sin, namely, innate vice; sometimes it denotes an interior act, which occurs in the first movement and is called *propassion*, in the second movement and is called delight, and in the third and is called consent. Here he does not prohibit the concupiscence that exists in the first movement, because it is not within our power to determine when it arises. But by God’s grace we can restrain it so that it does not proceed to delight and consent; it is this progression that he prohibits.

**VERSE 15.**—“What then?” Since the Law is from God, the person who sets it aside in favor of grace sins.

“What then? Shall we sin?” Since we are not under the Law, which terrifies, but under grace, which makes good promises—what then? Shall we sin? Some say this because they preach that the Law is to be maintained as though it were joined to us or restrained us.

**VERSE 16.**—“Do you not know that,” etc. He warns us not to profess God in words while becoming servants of the devil in our actions. We are the servants of the one whose will we do.

**VERSE 17.**—“But thanks be to God,” etc. He shows their transformation and discloses how pleasing it is to God, offering him a hymn: “For you were,” he says, “slaves of sin; but by your own free and voluntary disposition you shook off its dominion and embraced spiritual teaching.”

“The form of teaching.” Our teaching is a form that restores the image of God after it has been disfigured.

**VERSE 19.**—“Human,” etc. Up to this point the Apostle has shown that one must not sin. Here he says what must be done from now on—namely, that one must serve righteousness. No one can excuse himself from this, because there is no one who cannot act well, at least by willing to do so; and this itself is through grace.

“For just as you presented,” etc. (AUG.) If not more, then at least as much as before, so that faith would not be fled from as harsh and unbearable.

“Just as then no fear compelled you, but the desire and pleasure of sin led you, so now the delight of mature righteousness,” although it is not yet perfect. Hence he said: “Human.”

“So now.” Righteousness ought to be loved even more than iniquity was loved then, so that for righteousness a person may endure pains and despise everything, even death.

**VERSE 20.**—“Free.” A slave’s freedom exists when he takes pleasure in sinning; this arises from free choice. He serves freely when he willingly does his master’s will. In the same way, he freely serves righteousness when he loves it and rejoices in it.

**VERSE 21.**—“What fruit, then?” This recollection makes them recoil from their former deeds and makes them more indebted to grace.

“You are ashamed.” There is a certain temporal shame: the disturbance of the soul that looks back upon its sins, recoils at the sight of them, blushes in horror, and corrects itself through that shame.

“Their end,” etc. Death is the fitting repayment for sin. But eternal life, which is the end of the righteous, is given solely by grace through Christ, because merits themselves arise from grace, and grace is given in return for grace.

**VERSE 22.**—“But now, having been freed.” (AUG.) He called them “free from righteousness,” not “freed”; now, concerning sin, he does not call them “free,” lest they attribute this to themselves, but accordingly calls them “freed,” in keeping with the Lord’s saying: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8).

“Wages.” It is rightly called wages, because eternal death is paid as a debt to the service of the devil. To whom would the just Judge give a crown, if the merciful Father had not first given grace? How could those debts be paid unless that grace had first been freely given?

(AUG.) Since sins had separated the human race far from God, it was necessary that we be reconciled through the mediator, who alone was born, lived, and was killed without sin, so that human pride might both be reproved and healed through the humility of God, and so that it might be shown to humanity how far it had departed from God, etc.

**CHAPTER VII**

**VERSE 1.**—“Do you not know?” Up to this point he has spoken of the power of grace; now he says that the Law is no longer to be retained, and discusses the end of the Law and its former uselessness. Therefore the Romans should not wonder that the Apostle says, “You are not under the Law but under grace.” Above it was said that the Law does not justify; here, that it ought to cease, because it was given until Christ.

The order is: “Do you not know this, namely, that the natural law rules in a person as long as he lives?”—which you ought not to be ignorant of, because you know the Law, and I speak to those who know the Law. What I say is made plain in it if it is understood spiritually. Or: the Mosaic Law rules in a person, so that he obeys it; for you too know the Mosaic Law, for I speak to those who know the Law, etc. Thus the wording may be read in two ways, either of the natural law or of the Mosaic Law. “Lives.” For the Law is said to be dead when its authority ceases.

**VERSE 2.**—“For the woman who is under a husband.” To strengthen their minds, he uses an example from human law. The Romans know the Law because they are not barbarians, but have apprehended natural justice, in part from the Greeks, like the Greeks and Hebrews.

**VERSE 3.**—“Therefore, while her husband lives,” etc. If one who observes the dead Law wishes to belong to faith, he is an adulterer with respect to both, and Christ does him no good. But if the husband has died, then, with the Law ended, one who passes to Christ after abandoning the figures does not transgress.

**VERSE 4.**—“Through the body of Christ.” For Christ was the fulfillment and truth; the legal observances were figures and shadows of Christ and of those things fulfilled in Christ.

**VERSE 5.**—“For when we were.” Here he sets out four states of the human being: before the Law, under the Law, under grace, and then in the other life, where there is no conflict.

**VERSE 6.**—“But now,” etc. (AUG.) In the preceding comparison there are three things: the husband, etc., up to “that they may not conquer him.”

“From the law of death.” For concupiscence was increased when the Law prohibited it where faith was absent, and to the accumulation of sins the crime of transgression was added; for where there is no law, neither is there transgression.

“In the newness of the Spirit.” This means the works of the new human being, which we attain not by our own powers or by the Law, but by grace—that is, by the Spirit. We must remain in these in such a way that nothing is added from the works of the Law, which are old.

**VERSE 7.**—“What then shall we say?” Since the Law is a law of death and increased the powers of sin, holding us back from good action, the Law seems therefore to be sin—that is, to teach sinning—or to be such that its giver sinned because of it, as though it were an evil thing. No; rather, it is good. It made sin known, because before this some things were not known either to be sins, or to be so grave, or to be punishable. “By no means.” But sin [did this]. He shows that the Law is not sin but an indicator of sin, so that the soul, through anxiety over guilt, might turn to receive grace.

(AUG.) “By no means.” With one word he acquits the Law, etc., up to “great is the authority of the Apostle in its defense.”

(THEOD.) The words, “I did not know” and “I was unaware,” do not here signify complete ignorance; rather, he says this: “Through the Law I received a more exact knowledge of natural discernment.”

“For I would not have known concupiscence.” The Apostle read this as a general statement, from which everything follows. The Law is good: while it prohibits this, it prohibits everything. “Concupiscence.” Some understand it generally; others as that spoken of in the Decalogue: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property or wife” (Exod. 20). Generally, because every evil comes from it. “I did not know.” In his own person he treats a general case.

**VERSE 8.**—“But sin, taking an occasion.” Such is our carnality that it desires prohibited things more ardently; when these are not brought to mind, it lies as though dormant. And the devil, seeing that the Law had been given as an aid to human beings, burned more fiercely and pressed harder to turn it to their ruin, whereas before, possessing them almost securely, he tempted them less; or sin takes occasion from the things themselves, as when a woman or gold is seen.

(AUG.) Concupiscence was less when before the Law you sinned securely, etc., up to “it is complete when it transgresses the Law.”

(AMBR.) In saying “every concupiscence,” he signifies all sins. For sin existed before, but not every sin, when the crime of transgression was still absent. But now every sin has been added, because transgression too has been added.

(AUG.) Concupiscence was increased by the prohibition of the Law, while the grace that liberates was still absent.

**VERSE 9.**—“But I was once alive.” It is clear that he speaks not in his own person but generally in the person of a human being. “But I was once alive.” Note the two human beings in the same person: the inner and the outer, that is, reason and the tinder of sin, which is in the flesh. He says that the inner person agrees with the Law and, by its testimony, approves the Law as good. But the outer person fights against the inner person and against the Law, takes captive, and through the Law has greater power to sin. “But when [the commandment] came,” etc. Here is the second state, under the Law—that is, here the Apostle speaks in the state of a person placed under the Law. “It revived.” It began to appear and rebel. He says, “It revived,” not “it lived.” For it had once lived in paradise, when what was committed against the given command clearly appeared. But when people, born sinners, lived without a command, it lay hidden as though dead, without being known because it was unchecked. Once the Law was given, it revived in human awareness, though it had once lived in the awareness of the first human being.

**VERSE 10.**—“And the commandment was found.” Previously he was a sinner unknown to himself, but now he was made manifest to himself as a transgressor.

“For,” as if he were saying, “How was that which was given to me for life found to lead to death?” Because through it he was deceived by false sweetness. “Taking an occasion,” etc. What is desired becomes sweeter while it is forbidden; thus sin deceives through the commandment. For where charity fails, desire for evil grows through prohibition; once the deed is done, what was forbidden becomes sweeter, and so sin deceives by false sweetness. For deceptive sweetness is followed by more numerous and greater bitter punishments. “It deceived.” It drew him from good to evil, and thereby led him to eternal condemnation.

“It killed.” (AUG.) “With your sword which you carried,” etc., up to “therefore be humble and you will be able to conquer.”

**VERSE 12.**—“Therefore the Law indeed.” The Law itself is holy, teaching soundly; and the commandment is what it prescribes through the Law.

“Holy,” in itself; “and just,” that is, making the sinner righteous; “and good,” that is, useful, procuring life. Since it is clear to me that the Law is good, and yet death comes to me through it, as was said above, has what is good become death—that is, has it been given me by God so as to be an efficient cause of death? No; the tinder of sin is the efficient cause, turning a good thing into evil.

**VERSE 13.**—“So that sin might appear.” I do not say “so that it might exist,” for it also existed when it did not appear, as above. “I did not know concupiscence.” He did not say, “I did not have it.”

“Through what is good”—the Law. It does not, of course, cause sin, but rather reveals and prohibits it.

“So that it might become beyond measure.” For through the Law it did not diminish, but increased beyond its customary desires.

**VERSE 14.**—“But I.” Up to this point he has excused the Law, showing that guilt ought not to be laid upon it. Here he says that it should not be laid upon the principal nature either—that is, reason, insofar as it is from God—and thus not upon the Creator, but upon human beings, who are corrupted from themselves so that they are unable to resist depraved impulses. “I am carnal.” The Apostle says this of himself without impropriety as well, according to the flesh, as long as he lives here, because of the movements of the flesh. Every saint rightly says this. “Sold under sin.” This too is from the fault of the first human being, who, for the pleasure of forbidden food, sold himself and all others. Or, “under sin” means that they are slaves of sin. Or each person has sold himself by the habit of his own will.

**VERSE 16.**—“For what I do.” He proves that he is a slave of sin: because what I do according to the outer person—by neglecting good or doing evil—I understand according to the inner person ought not to be done. I truly do what I do not understand, because I both neglect the good that I will and do the evil that I do not will. “I do not understand,” because I see myself knowing one thing through the Law and doing another. “For I do not do the good that I will, but [the evil that I do not will].” Subject to sin, he does what he does not will. “I do.” “I desire”: this is not because the Apostle follows concupiscence and it draws him to evil; he struggled, he was not overcome. He sets this before you concerning himself, so that you may not despair of it in yourself.

**VERSE 17.**—“But now.” Now redeemed, now having received the grace of Christ—he who had formerly been sold under sin. “Not I.” The mind is free; the flesh captive. Although he does not consent to it, sin dwells [in him], while he lives by faith. There are desires, but if they do not reign, he himself does not act; he would act if he consented. “But that which dwells in me.” How does it dwell, since it is not a substance but a privation of good? Behold, the body of the first human being was corrupted through sin. That very corruption remains in the body by the condition of the offense, retaining the force of the divine sentence given in Adam; through participation in it the soul is stained by sin.

**VERSE 18.**—“For to will.” Not [to accomplish]: because to will the good lies close to me, since it lies and rests beside the flesh, unable to rise to do good. “Beside”: because in a certain way it is natural for reason to will the good; but this willing is such that it is always overcome by the force of the flesh. God’s willing, however, overcomes the flesh. “To will.” The things commanded by the Law are good, so much so that one naturally loves and wishes to do them, but the power to accomplish them is lacking.

“To will.” (AUG.) The good person always wishes entirely not to feel concupiscence, but never accomplishes this in the present life.

To complete. He does not say “to do,” but “to complete,” because he does accomplish something. He does good, because he does not consent to concupiscence; but he does not complete it, so as not to covet at all. Likewise the enemy does evil when he stirs desire, but does not complete it, because he does not drag one through to evil.

**VERSE 19.**—“For I do not do what I will.” I do not find the power to complete the good, because I do not even find that good which I will. He demonstrates this from the aspect where it might seem less evident, but conversely he speaks of the evil, since he also does what he does not will, and so forth. Or, “I do not find the good,” because it is not there. For many foolish people do not find the good in something, although it is nevertheless there.

**(AUGUSTINE.)** It is one thing not to covet, and another not to follow one’s covetous desires. Not to covet at all belongs to the perfect; not to follow one’s covetous desires belongs to one who is fighting, to one who is struggling. Where the battle is raging, why despair of victory?

**VERSE 20.**—“But if I do what I do not will,” and so forth. He concludes the preceding statement: therefore I do not perform that—namely, the evil—from which the earlier question is concluded, namely, that he consents to the law of God. But it is “sin that dwells in me.” Pressed by sin, the human being does its will; yet this is the human being’s fault. He says this in order to indicate from how great evils God delivers the human being.

**VERSE 21.**—“I find, therefore.” He had called the law good, and nature good, since nature wills the same thing and consents to it. Here he adds that the good law is an aid to good nature; and yet the external human being overcomes those two joined together, so that, seeing that he cannot escape through either of them, the human being may be subject to grace.

“To the one who wills.” Only so far: because I cannot complete it, since evil is near to reason, lying in ambush in the flesh as though at the doors of the soul, and compelling a person to do something other than what the person and the law will.

**VERSE 22.**—“According to the inner.” **(AMBROSE.)** Because the flesh is transmitted from Adam and has sin within it; if the soul too were transmitted, sin would dwell within it also, because Adam’s soul sinned. But if the soul itself had sin within it, the human being would not recognize himself.

**VERSE 23.**—“But I see.” **(AUGUSTINE.)** It belongs to the body of death that the law of the members should oppose the law of the mind, while the flesh lusts against the spirit. But the law of sin does not reign when its desires are not obeyed.

“The law in my members.” The tinder of sin is rightly called a law, because it was lawfully established that the one who did not obey his superior should not be served by his inferior—that is, by the flesh.

“Captive.” From the flesh, and only in part, because the mind resists and delights together with the law of God. Thus it is read concerning the Apostle himself: “The mind does not consent to sin; death contends; the mind does not consent.” There is in me something dead and something alive: what, then, may be hoped for from this?

**VERSE 24.**—“Wretched man.” Not in the mind, but in the flesh.

“Who will free me?” He will be freed when this mortal body puts on immortality, where no concupiscence will remain.

**VERSE 25.**—“Therefore I myself.” Here is the third activity in the law of the spirit. But because he says that he has been freed by grace, lest anyone grow sluggish in false security, as though sin could no longer do harm, he specifies how liberation exists—namely, if he remains in grace. Otherwise sin will seize him again.

“I myself.” I in the flesh, I in the mind: not two, but one composed of both. With the mind I do not consent; with the flesh I covet.

# CHAPTER VIII

**VERSE 1.**—“There is therefore now no.” Although formerly there was condemnation, there is none now: when one is in Christ.

“No condemnation.” Through the grace of baptism and the washing of regeneration, both the guilt with which you were born and whatever you previously committed have been removed.

**(AUGUSTINE.)** Although they have desires of the flesh to which they do not consent, and so forth, up to “but regeneration has accomplished this good.”

**VERSE 2.**—“For the law of the Spirit.” Here he shows by what means grace frees: namely, through the Holy Spirit, because it is the law of the Spirit. The Holy Spirit teaches what must be done and what must not be done; he is the giver of life. This occurs through Christ, who gives the Spirit. He explains how it occurs in Christ.

**VERSE 3.**—“For what was impossible.” He shows how liberation has been accomplished in Christ.

“Through the flesh.” Through carnality, which rebelled and, upon hearing the law, was stirred up even more. Thus the law of the letter was weakened through the flesh, and for that reason it was unable to free from the law of sin and death.

“Sending his own Son.” **(AUGUSTINE.)** Not to a place where he was absent—for he is everywhere—and so forth, up to “because he appeared visibly to the world.”

“In the likeness,” and so forth. Not in sinful flesh, because his mother conceived him not through concupiscence but through grace. That flesh, therefore, was not sinful: he was neither conceived in the concupiscence of lust, nor did it have the cause of sin within it, nor did he sin in it. He was therefore like us in punishment, not in the quality of sin.

**[Col. 0495A]** “And concerning sin.” **(ORIGEN.)** This means: through the sacrifice of his flesh, which he offered on the altar of the cross, he condemned sin and reduced it to nothing in his flesh.

“He condemned.” That is, he destroyed the devil, namely, on account of the sin that he commits in Christ’s flesh. Or “sin,” that is, the tinder proceeding from Adam’s sin: he condemned it, that is, weakened it.

**VERSE 4.**—“So that the justification.” Sin is so condemned through Christ that the righteousness promised by the law of Moses might be brought to completion.

**VERSE 5.**—“For those who are according to the flesh.” One who walks according to the flesh is not righteous, because neither is the one who belongs to the flesh. Why not? Because he covets carnal things as supreme goods, and this conflicts with righteousness.

**VERSE 6.**—“For the wisdom.” One who savors the things that belong to the flesh is not righteous; for the wisdom of the flesh is death.

“Life and peace.” “Life” refers to what follows, namely, that the inclination of the flesh is death; “peace” refers to what follows thereafter: the inclination of the flesh is hostility toward God.

**VERSE 7.**—“Because the wisdom of the flesh.” By enumerating these things he deters people from obeying the flesh.

“Is hostile.” It considers God unable to do anything beyond what is seen in the natures of things.

**VERSE 9.**—“If indeed.” He speaks ambiguously, because their faith is not yet perfect, but there is hope of attaining perfection.

“The Spirit of God.” The Spirit of Christ, because the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ are the same Spirit.

**VERSE 10.**—“The body indeed.” By the name “body” he signifies the whole human being, just as Ezekiel, conversely, uses the name “soul” when he says: “The soul that has sinned,” and so forth. The meaning is this: if the Spirit of Christ is in you, although the body is dead—that is, although the human being has died on account of sins, that is, in sins—the spirit, that is, the soul that had been impious, nevertheless lives, because it is joined to God, who is life. This occurs on account of justification, that is, the remission of sins, which comes from the Holy Spirit.

He says “dead,” not “mortal.” Before sin, the animal body—that is, the mortal body—was capable of dying. But it was not necessary for it to die. Now it is called dead on account of sin, that is, because it is necessary for it to die. This weakness is retained in order that sin may be avoided, so that the person may consequently fear sinning more.

**VERSE 11.**—“But if the Spirit.” **(AUGUSTINE.)** Note that the Holy Spirit, and so forth, up to “just as no one can declare the generation of the Son.”

“He will give life even to mortal bodies.” **(IDEM.)** Behold the fourth activity. In the first activity, and so forth, up to “because we had abandoned God, who is superior to us.”

“Mortal.” Not “dead,” because in the resurrection, when this mortal body puts on immortality, not only the necessity of dying—which it now has on account of sin—but also mortality, which the animal body possessed before sin, will remain no longer.

“On account of the one dwelling.” It appears most clearly that the human being merited not only the death of the spirit but also the death of the body on account of sin, and that through the Holy Spirit both have been freed by Christ.

**VERSE 13.**—“But if by the Spirit.” Either by the Holy Spirit or by our own spirit—which, nevertheless, is not possible except through the activity of the Holy Spirit.

**VERSE 14.**—“They are led.” He says “they are led,” not “they are governed.” For being led is more than being governed. We say that someone is “led” as though he scarcely does anything himself; but we say that someone is “governed” as though he is already doing something and is governed so that he may act rightly. They are therefore “led” not because they do nothing by themselves, but because, in order to do something, they are impelled by the force of grace.

**(AUGUSTINE, *On Rebuke and Grace*, ch. 2.)** Let those who say, “What use is it to us?” and so forth, not deceive themselves, up to “may rejoice that they have received it.”

**VERSE 15.**—“For you have not received,” and so forth. You ought to be sons, not servants, because you have not received a spirit of servitude that makes unwilling people serve through fear of punishment.

“But you have received the spirit of adoption.” It is the same Spirit, but he is called differently on account of his different works.

The Egyptians are said to have received the Spirit of wrath, because the water, divided by the Spirit, harmed them. The children of Israel are not said to have received the Spirit of wrath, because the divided water benefited them.

It is the Spirit of fear for those who, through the law, having been convicted of their sins and their own weakness, did not understand the grace of the Spirit. It is the Spirit of freedom through his work in those to whom regeneration unto eternal life and faith—which works through love—have been imparted.

There is therefore one Spirit who produces two fears, and these also produce two kinds of servants. There is a servant who is also a son, who fears the Lord and honors his father; hence Malachi: “If I am Lord, where is my fear? If I am Father, where is my honor?” (Malachi 1). And there is a servant who fears punishment but does not love righteousness.

Since fear is mentioned, it should be known that, apart from the natural fear present in everyone, there are four fears: worldly fear, which is evil and not from God; servile fear, which is good and from God but is not sufficient; initial fear, which is good and sufficient; and chaste fear, which is good and brings to perfection. The present passage concerns the last of these, for it generates us as sons of God.

“In whom we cry out.” This too comes from the gift of the Spirit, which makes us cry out, “Abba”—Hebrew for “Father” in Latin.

“Abba, Father.” The Apostle used both expressions on account of the mystery. In his passion Christ also said, “Abba, Father,” because the Church comes from both peoples. By sharing in their suffering, he showed in himself that his sons—namely, the martyrs—should not despair if, during the time of passion, sadness should intrude through human weakness.

**VERSE 16.**—“That we are sons of God.” The Holy Spirit causes us to recognize this when the remission of sins takes place in the Church. Although the entire Trinity accomplishes it, it is nevertheless understood to belong to the Holy Spirit because he is common to the Father and the Son, and is the union of both. Through him the fellowship and unity occur by which we become one body of the one Son of God.

Unity binds us together, and charity creates this unity; charity comes only from the Holy Spirit. These things are said so that we may love unity and fear separation.

**VERSE 17.**—“Heirs.” Although God does not die, this expression is taken from human laws. Or he will “depart,” so that he will no longer be seen through a mirror in a riddle, as now, but face to face.

It may also be said that Christ, our head, departing into his passion, left us possession of ecclesiastical peace, just as he himself said: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14). Christ is also our inheritance. Hence: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Psalm 15), and so forth.

“If indeed we suffer together.” No one can put to death the deeds of the flesh, from which life will come, without distress; patience is necessary for this.

**VERSE 19.**—“For the expectation of creation.” “Creation” means the good, who remain in God’s creation, or because they are the cause of all things. “Corruption” is vanity, to which creation has been subjected. For all things that are born are weak and corruptible, and thus vain, because they cannot maintain their proper state.

**(AUGUSTINE.)** What he says, “for the expectation,” and so forth, must be understood in such a way that neither sense, and so forth, up to “labors and is subject to corruption.”

**VERSE 20.**—“Not willingly,” and so forth. It sinned voluntarily, but it does not bear its punishment voluntarily; it has been subjected to deception, yet this occurred on account of the justice and mercy of the one who both punishes sin and intends to heal.

**VERSE 21.**—“Because creation itself.” **(AUGUSTINE.)** At present creation is only creation, since the form of the sons has not yet been perfected, and so forth, up to “for the human being, having lost the seal of the image, remained merely creation.”

“It will be liberated.” It will be revealed: “it awaits revelation”; then he adds, “it will be liberated.” All these things occur through the Spirit.

**VERSE 22.**—“Every creature.” **(AUGUSTINE.)** The human being. “Every creature” is either bodily, and so forth, up to “even if not in all human beings.”

“Every creature.” **(AMBROSE.)** All the elements fulfill their functions with labor, and this is for our sake. Therefore they will rest when we have been taken up; for this reason we should prepare ourselves diligently.

“It groans.” It is always becoming new in this respect, which is indicated by the inchoative verb, and this is on account of the longing for the heavenly homeland.

“It is in labor.” That is, it suffers.

“Until now.” **(AUGUSTINE.)** Although someone who is in Abraham’s bosom has ceased to suffer, nevertheless all creation still groans in those who have not yet been liberated.

**VERSE 23.**—“Not only,” and so forth. **(AUGUSTINE.)** That is, not only in the human being with respect to the body, but we too, within ourselves and apart from the body, except for bodily troubles.

“Not only.” **(AUGUSTINE, *Exposition of the Propositions in the Epistle to the Romans* 53.)** Not only creation itself, which is called merely creation in human beings, and so forth, up to “or when distress troubles us.”

**[Col. 0497D]** “The firstfruits of the Spirit.” That is, those whose spirit has already been offered to God as a sacrifice, and kindled by the divine fire of charity.

“Adoption.” So that the body too may receive the benefit of adoption, and they may be sons of God in every respect.

**VERSE 24.**—“For in hope.” He says this so that the greater merit of hope may be apparent, and so that hope should therefore save.

“The Spirit helps our weakness.” **(AUGUSTINE.)** Because we groan and ask to be liberated; but, lest we ask either before the proper time or in a contrary manner, the Spirit helps us. What prayer obtains is clearly a gift of God, but the ability to pray also comes from grace.

**VERSE 26.**—“With inexpressible.” How could that be expressed when what is unknown is desired? Yet it is not entirely unknown. For if it were wholly unknown, it would not be desired. And again, if it were seen, it would not be sought through groans.

“He searches.” **(AMBROSE.)** Not as though he were seeking something he did not know—for nothing is hidden from him, and the prayer of all spirits is known to him.

**VERSE 28.**—“But we know that for those who love,” and so forth. It is as though he were saying: The Holy Spirit not only does this, but also causes all things to result in good for those who love him, whether prosperous or adverse things. For such a God consoles through prosperity and exercises through adversity.

Thus the evils that the faithful endure piously are beneficial, either for correcting or removing sins, for exercising and testing righteousness, or for demonstrating the misery of this life. Although the death of the flesh originally came from the sin of the first human being, its good use nevertheless made the most glorious martyrs. Therefore not death alone, but all the evils of the age, ought to remain after sins have been forgiven, so that the human being might have things against which to struggle for the truth, and through which the virtue of the faithful might be exercised.

“According to the purpose.” It is as though he were saying: Their being called comes from nowhere other than God’s predestination. Hence all things cooperate for good—not because of merit.

**VERSE 29.**—“For those whom God predestined,” that is, whom he prepared through the grace he applied so that they might believe the word of preaching, “he foreknew,” that is, knew long beforehand that they would become conformed to the Son, who is the image of the Father, wholly the same with the Father. Hence it is said: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14).

“Of the image.” So that we may bear the image of the heavenly one, just as we bore the image of the earthly one.

Or “firstborn,” because before all creation he was not made but born, and because he was the first born without sin and the first to rise impassible, in whom he has brothers.

**VERSE 30.**—“He called.” External calling occurs through preachers and is common to the good and the wicked. Internal calling, however, belongs only to the elect. Of the external calling it is said: “Many are called, but few are chosen.”

Predestination is fulfilled through calling. To call is to assist someone’s knowledge of faith, or to pierce the heart of one whom it causes to hear; and this belongs only to the elect.

“He glorified.” This concerns those who were foreknown, not the others. Although the others may believe for a time and appear good, because they do not persevere they are not glorified.

“He glorified,” or “he will glorify.” This is future, but it is spoken of as past because God is said to have done what he determined from eternity to do. Hence Isaiah: “He has done the things that are to come” (Isaiah 44).

For such people all things work for good, even their deviations, so that they may thereby become more cautious and not place confidence in themselves.

Four things are mentioned here: predestination, calling, justification, and glorification. One is in God, and three are in us. Predestination does not exist in us but secretly with him, in his foreknowledge. The other three exist in us.

**VERSE 31.**—“If God is for us.” **(AUGUSTINE.)** God is for us: he predestined us before we existed, called us when we were turned away, justified us when we were sinners, and glorified us when we were mortal.

**VERSE 32.**—“He handed over.” This is said because the Father handed over the Son, although the one who drank this cup is himself also its author. Hence the Apostle says: “Christ loved us and handed himself over for us” (Ephesians 5).

If the Father handed over the Son, and the Son handed himself over, what did Judas do? The Father did well in handing over the Son; the Son did well in handing himself over; Judas did evil in handing over his teacher out of greed. What was provided for us through Christ’s passion will not be attributed to Judas’s wickedness: he will have the reward of wickedness, while Christ will have the praise of grace.

“All things.” It is less to give us all things than to hand Christ over to death for our sake. Therefore all the things mentioned above—namely, the triune God—are ours, for seeing and enjoying.

“Equal things,” namely, the angels, with whom we will be equal in the future for fellowship, although now we are inferior to them.

“Lower things” are also ours, for ruling over them. Likewise, certain higher things—such as the exalted angels and all the heavenly ministries of God—are ours, not for domination but for use, just as the possessions of the Lord belong to servants, for nourishment, adornment, or some similar purpose.

**VERSE 34.**—“At the right hand of God.” In the honor in which he is God, whose petition cannot be disregarded.

“He intercedes.” Each day he presents before the Father’s face both the human being whom he assumed and the grievous kind of death that he endured for us.

**VERSE 35.**—“Who will separate us,” and so forth. **(CYPRIAN.)** None of these things can separate believers, and so forth, up to “so that we too may suffer on his account. But in all these things we conquer.”

**VERSE 38.**—“Neither angels, nor rulers, nor powers.” These orders are understood as referring to evil angels, and to good angels if such a thing could occur.

**VERSE 39.**—“Neither height nor depth.” That is, neither prosperity nor adversity. Hence Solomon: “Do not give me riches or poverty, lest, when filled, I become a liar, or, when poor, I steal and swear falsely by the name of God” (Proverbs 30).

Many sin through elevation; many through necessity. Against this is set Ahaz in Isaiah, who did not want to ask for a sign either in the height or in the depth.

The remedy is found in Christ, who was neither exalted by the power through which he is equal to the Father, nor disturbed by death’s casting down. He is the sign in the height and in the depth, so that he would neither be lifted up by royal power nor troubled by affliction, as occurred at that time because of the war against the Assyrians.

# CHAPTER IX

**VERSE 1.**—“I speak the truth.” Now nothing can separate me, but formerly I was separated; hence I now grieve, and thus the evils are already turned toward good.

“I speak the truth.” **(AMBROSE.)** Because he seemed to be speaking against the Jews, and so forth, up to “Job, however, was fifth from Abraham, namely a descendant of Esau.”

**VERSE 3.**—“For the sake of my brothers.” For the Jews, or even for those who are now brothers in the faith but are being drawn back; they are also my relatives, and thus I was sinning more grievously.

**(AUGUSTINE.)** Here the excellence of the Son is declared with such perfection, and so forth, up to: “The mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2).

**VERSE 6.**—“Not, however, that the word has failed.” The Apostle consoles his grief. For who would grieve over people who were formerly considered dead? God did not, in his foreknowledge, decree their salvation, nor is he a respecter of persons. For he condemns no one before the person sins, and crowns no one before the person conquers. But by his foreknowledge he has determined what each person’s future will is to be, and on that basis the person is condemned or crowned.

Because he was grieving over the Jews, he consoles himself by finding it written that not all are to be saved, but only those who resemble Isaac. In them he shows that the grace of God alone makes sons of God.

“Not, however, that the word of God has failed.” Because he had said that the promise of the eternal inheritance was made to the Jews, although most of them themselves did not believe, it seemed that the word of God had not been fulfilled. To this he responds: although it was not fulfilled in some, it was nevertheless fulfilled in others—namely, in the believing Gentiles, who are now the true sons of Abraham.

“Not that it has failed.” It is as though he were saying: Although it has labored in this way, and although not all believe, the word of God has not failed. Or: I am not saying that it has failed. For the word of God “to fail” means that the promises are not fulfilled.

**VERSE 7.**—“In Isaac.” That is, they are gathered together in Christ, who calls through grace. They were prefigured in Isaac by the promise—not those who make themselves righteous, but those whom God makes righteous. These are the sons of the free woman who is above, who is our mother.

The sons of the flesh are the earthly Jerusalem, which is in servitude with her children. Just as Isaac did not merit that his birth should be promised, so neither did they; but by grace alone the promise was made to them and the adoption of sons was given to them.

**VERSE 10.**—“And not only that one.” Sarah had a promise, but Rebecca also had a promise, having two sons from one intercourse with Isaac, our father. He says “from one intercourse” so that people may not suppose that the merits of the parents differed in those born from them, but rather that of the father—that is, of our founder, whom we should imitate if we wish to be sons of God.

The promise made to Sarah shows that no one is saved on account of lineage. The promise made to Rebecca shows that no one is chosen on account of any merit of his own or of his parents, but by grace alone.

**VERSE 11.**—“For when they had not yet been born.” Rebecca received this promise: “The elder will serve the younger.” That is, Esau, by persecuting Jacob, would benefit him.

**VERSE 12.**—“Not from works.” From future works that would not have been future as good or evil unless grace had been added or withdrawn.

**(AUGUSTINE.)** If it is said that divine judgment distinguished their future conduct, and so forth, up to “for how can things be called future that will not exist at all?”

**VERSE 13.**—“The elder will serve the younger.” Literally this is true, because the Idumeans, who descended from Esau—who is also called Edom—were subjected to the children of Israel. But the prophecy intends more particularly that the Jewish people, the elder—that is, first in the worship of the one God—would serve the younger, that is, the later Christian people.

“Jacob I loved,” and so forth. In Jacob he found nothing lovable except the gift of his mercy; in Esau he hated nothing except original sin. But how is this right, since they had done nothing? Because the matter is astonishing, he raises the objection against himself: “What, then, shall we say?”

To be willing and to run come from mercy. This is apparent in others from the same mass to which perdition is owed.

**VERSE 14.**—“What, then?” Because he chose this one and rejected that one without merit, will God be called unjust? No. He chose this one through mercy and rejected that one through justice. In neither case is there injustice: he chose this one through mercy, as Moses says; he rejected that one through justice, as Scripture shows when it introduces God speaking to Pharaoh.

“Far be it.” It is established that no one is liberated except by gratuitous mercy, and no one is condemned except by the most equitable justice. But why he liberates this person rather than that person—let whoever can search out so deep a judgment do so; nevertheless, let him beware of the precipice.

**VERSE 15.**—“I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy.” That is, on the one on whom I foreknow mercy is to be bestowed and who will remain with me. This means giving to the one to whom it ought to be given, and not giving to the one to whom it ought not be given; calling the one whom he knows will obey, as David did, who persevered so well after receiving pardon.

Saul, when his prayer was not heard, did not persevere but turned to idols; hence he appears justly rejected by the one who foreknew this.

**VERSE 16.**—“Therefore it depends not on the one who wills,” and so forth. It is as though he were saying: The human will alone is not sufficient unless there is also the mercy of God.

Conversely, it is said: The mercy of God is not sufficient unless there is also the human will. Therefore, if the former statement is rightly made, why should the converse not also be rightly said: “It is not of God who has mercy, but of the human being who wills”?

It remains, then, that this statement should be understood correctly, so that everything may be attributed to God. He both prepares the human being’s good will so that it may be helped and helps it once prepared. He precedes the one who wills so that the person may will, and follows the one who wills so that the willing may not be in vain.

**(AUGUSTINE.)** Who is so impiously foolish as to say that God causes the evil wills of human beings, and so forth, up to “just as he grants grace through his mercy.”

**VERSE 17.**—“I raised you up.” Or “I aroused you,” or “I preserved you.”

**(AMBROSE.)** “For this very purpose I preserved you,” and so forth, up to “but so that, with you hardened, I might display my power through signs in Egypt.”

**VERSE 18.**—“Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills.” There is no merit that precedes mercy; the merit of hardening is the sin of the entire condemned mass. He does not harden by imparting wickedness, but by not imparting mercy, just as they are not worthy of it.
