He does this through a hidden equity removed from human judgment, because the Apostle does not explain it but marvels: “O the depth of riches.”

“He hardens.” **(AUGUSTINE, Letter 105.)** Not as though he compelled anyone to sin, but because, when some people sin, he does not bestow upon them the mercy of his justification. For this reason he is said to harden them: because he does not have mercy on them, not because he drives them to sin. He judges, through a most hidden equity, far removed from human understanding, that grace should not be given to those on whom he does not have mercy.

**VERSE 19.**—“Why does he still?” Once it has been established that this proceeds from the will of God, why is it asked how one person is good and another evil? There is no need, because each person will be what God wills that person to be, and therefore he unjustly condemns one and saves another.

Or “what is being sought?” That is, why does anyone strive to act well when he can do nothing except what God wills?

**VERSE 20.**—“O human being.” This is not because he lacks a reason to give, but because he calls the human being back to himself.

**VERSE 21.**—“From the same lump.” The whole mass of the human race is justly corrupted and made claylike. If a vessel is made from it for honor, that is mercy; if for dishonor, that is just, because this is what it was by nature.

Behold justice in those who do not have time to act. Concerning those who do have time, he adds: “What if God,” that is, what will you answer to God?

“Another for dishonor.” A vessel made for honor, but placed in dishonor: if it is vile, it has the clay from itself, not from the potter.

“What if God,” and so forth. **(AUGUSTINE, *Book I to Simplicianus*, Question 2.)** It is as though he were saying: It has already been shown that, even if God gives nothing good, he is nevertheless not unjust, and so forth, up to “but they abused this grace.”

**VERSE 22.**—“He endured.” God endures the wicked in order to destroy them in an orderly manner, and he uses them as an instrument for the salvation of the good. For God would not create any angel or human being whom he foreknew would become evil unless he likewise knew to whom he would make them useful for good purposes.

**VERSE 23.**—“In order to show.” It is as though he were saying: He endures the wicked for this purpose, and displays his wrath beforehand and brings it to knowledge of himself, so that he might show, in the vessels of mercy—that is, in those elected through mercy—the riches of glory, that is, how rich, how great, and how glorious mercy is.

For this reason he gives so many good things to the wicked: to prove that they are justly condemned, and to make the faithful love him more, since he has preserved grace itself for them.

**VERSE 25.**—“As he also says in Hosea.” Once it has been shown that the sons exist by grace alone, he begins to prove through the prophets that they come from both peoples.

**VERSE 27.**—“If there should be.” Thus the salvation of the Jews is described, so that the greater part is blinded.

**VERSES 28–29.**—“For the word.” The prophet adds by what means they are saved: namely, through the word of the Gospel, so that the glory of works of the law may be excluded.

The word of the Gospel, which is called “completing,” leads to perfection and abbreviates all the legal prescriptions in the one Christ. Nevertheless, it is equitable with respect to the earlier word of the law; hence “in equity” is added—that is, so that nothing necessary for righteousness may be lacking among all the things prefigured.

Or it is “in equity” because it retains what is equitable, such as moral commandments, and cuts away what justice requires to be removed, such as figures.

“And abbreviating in equity.” He saves through the concise means of faith by grace, not through innumerable observances.

But lest anyone doubt, the prophet adds:

“Unless the Lord of hosts.” The Lord made the word, which was so necessary that, unless there were a seed—that is, the word—and so forth.

Or by “seed” are understood the remnants who were to be saved, namely, the apostles and other good people. Unless the word of God had been preached through them, the Gentiles would have perished. This is the meaning: Unless the Lord of hosts, when he blinded others, had left us—that is, for our benefit—a seed, namely the apostles, from whom Christ’s harvest grew.

“And like Gomorrah.” He included both, to indicate the similarity of guilt and punishment. It is as though he were saying: We would be equal in punishment because we would be alike in guilt.

**VERSE 31.**—“Israel.” Israel followed the law as though from behind, because it never attained spiritual understanding.

“Pursuing righteousness.” The law of Moses is the law of righteousness if it is rightly understood.

Or “pursuing the righteousness of the law,” that is, the righteousness that comes from fear of punishment and not from love of righteousness, Israel did not attain it, and so forth.

**VERSE 32.**—“Because it was not from faith.” It was not seeking to be justified by faith. Since it did not seek righteousness from God, it did not believe in the one who justifies the ungodly, not believing that God works in the human being to produce justification. He next indicates why it happened that they did not believe.

“They stumbled.” Christ was like a small stone over which one does not take care, hidden in humility. Isaiah bears witness to this (chapter 8): “Behold, I set before you”—that is, I cause to be born—“in Zion,” that is, among the Jews, “Christ, a stone of stumbling,” a small stone of which no one takes care, “and a rock of scandal,” that is, one that will utterly crush and distress the wicked in the future.

Christ is called the stone of stumbling according to the condition in which he appeared here to the wicked. He is called the rock of scandal according to what he will do to the wicked in the future.

**VERSE 33.**—“And a rock of scandal.” A “rock” is what exists before polishing, and a “stone” what exists after polishing. The polishing of Christ was his passion, through which he laid aside the misery of weakness.

Before his passion, therefore, Christ was the rock of scandal. At that time the Jews were scandalized, becoming angry and indignant because he made himself the Son of God.

Through polishing, he became the stone: Christ in his passion, when those same Jews stumbled most severely and were blinded, believing that the one whom they saw dead was not God.

“He will not be put to shame.” **(AUGUSTINE.)** Whoever believes in him will not have his own righteousness, which comes from the law, although the law is good; rather, he will fulfill the law itself, not through his own righteousness but through righteousness given by God. In this way he will not be put to shame.

# CHAPTER X

**VERSE 1.**—“And supplication.” The will, when it is moved to believe what is true, is not sufficient for itself unless God assists it through grace. Hence: “No one comes to me unless it has been given by my Father” (John 4).

**VERSE 2.**—“For I bear witness concerning them that.” **(AMBROSE.)** He speaks of those who did not receive Christ out of envy but through error. To them Peter says: “I know that you did this through ignorance” (Acts 3).

“Not according to knowledge.” For it is foolish to venerate the law and persecute the God of the law.

**VERSE 3.**—“For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God.” Not the righteousness by which God is just, but the righteousness that exists in the human being from God.

“They were not subject to the righteousness of God.” This is the righteousness of God, established not in the commandment of the law, by which fear is instilled, but in the assistance of Christ’s grace.

**VERSE 4.**—“The end.” Not consuming, but perfecting. He therefore perfects righteousness through faith without the works of the law.

“Christ.” Righteousness comes from Christ. For if it came through the written or natural law and not through faith in Christ, then Christ would have died for nothing.

“For righteousness.” Not human righteousness, but divine righteousness. There is both human and divine righteousness. The passage about the human is: “Moses”; the passage about the divine is: “But the righteousness that comes from,” and so forth.

“Scripture.” In Numbers and Leviticus it is written: “Whoever does these things will live by them.”

**VERSE 5.**—“He will live in it.” It has this reward: namely, that he not be punished by this death. Yet it is not great righteousness to fear, nor does such fear have merit before God.

**VERSE 6.**—“That is, to bring Christ down.” That is, to deny that Christ ascended.

**VERSE 8.**—“The word is near.” That is, it is useful; or, there is nothing inappropriate either in saying or believing it.

Or “near,” because it is not far from the nature of souls and from the manner of speaking in which it is addressed to us for belief.

“This is the word.” **(AUGUSTINE, *Treatise 80 on John*.)** Concerning this the Lord says: “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you,” and so forth, up to “for even in the word itself one thing is the passing sound and another the enduring power.”

**VERSE 9.**—“For if you confess.” **(AUGUSTINE.)** Behold the praise of faith and its reward. The praise of faith is that you believe that Jesus is Lord, and so forth, up to “who precedes it in the resurrection appropriate to it—that is, in justification.”

**VERSE 10.**—“With the heart one believes.” A person can do other things unwillingly, but cannot believe unless willing.

“Confession.” **(AUGUSTINE, Sermon 3 on Psalm 30.)** To confess is to say what is in the heart, and so forth, up to “because just as one believes, so one ought also to speak with the mouth, so that one may preach accordingly.”

**VERSE 12.**—“Those who call upon him.” One who prays calls upon him, but certainly cannot do so unless he first believes. Therefore those who call upon him not only believe but also pray, so that after a person has believed, the person does not cease to ask for what God promised to those who watch with their whole heart.

For believing grants the remission of sins; calling upon God obtains his promises.

### Verse 14

“How, then, will they call upon him?” and so forth. Having established that what is assumed comes from both peoples, he shows by what means it comes—namely, through the mission made to both peoples; whoever does not receive it is without excuse. Calling upon him saves; therefore one must believe: “For how,” and so forth. Or: “How will they believe?” and so forth. It is as though he says: They will not believe unless they hear. For no one in former times believed without hearing in some way, whether inwardly or outwardly. He says that believing comes from hearing, hearing from preaching, and preaching from God’s sending, so that everything descends from the fountain of grace. Preaching truly comes from a mission, because God also sent false preachers who announce well, since he knows how to use evil for good. At times he also sends wicked men to wicked men in anger—that is, he permits the wicked to preach to the wicked for their punishment, so that each may perish through the other, as is just.

**(Augustine.)** When the Apostle says, “How will they believe in him whom they have not heard?” he is speaking of the Gentiles, and so forth, up to the point where he says that preachers of Christ must be sent.

### Verse 15

“How, then, will they preach unless they are sent?” Here it becomes clear that preachers were also sent to the Gentiles. “How beautiful.” Because they illuminate the world; by this it is evident that they were sent by God, since otherwise they could not do this. “Peace.” Reconciliation between people and people: the barrier of legal observance among the Jews and of idolatry among the Gentiles having been destroyed. And reconciliation between God and the ungodly through justifying faith, and between human beings who believe in him. “Those who announce good things.” Peace upon peace, because the kingdom of God is also peace.

### Verse 16

“For Isaiah says,” and so forth. God, who foreknows, foretold the Jews’ unbelief, but did not cause it; nor would he have foreknown their evils unless they possessed them. Likewise, he blinds them by abandoning them, not by causing their blindness—and this is what their will deserved. If it is said that the Jews cannot believe because Isaiah foretold it, I reply that they cannot because they do not wish to. What God foreknew, he foretold; he did not cause it. They cannot believe while they remain proud, while they are such as to attribute everything to their own powers and deny that divine assistance is necessary for right action.

### Verse 17

“Faith comes from,” and so forth. Although God teaches inwardly, the herald still proclaims outwardly. “Through the word.” That is, through the grace of Christ, who sends us teachers of the evangelical word. For unless something is said, it can neither be heard nor believed.

### Verse 18

“And indeed.” Or *equidem*, that is, “certainly”; and therefore they are without excuse, as David shows in the Psalms, saying: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth.”

**(Augustine, Letter 80, addressed to Hesychius.)** This was not fulfilled in the time of the Apostles, and so forth, up to the statement: “You will be my witnesses to the end of the earth” (Acts 1).

### Verse 19

“But I say: Has Israel not known?” He proved that everyone had heard, and therefore that the Jews had heard. But since they could have heard without understanding, he affirms that they also understood.

“He knew.” Israel is said to have understood the teaching of the Gospel and the coming of Christ because it could not contradict them by reason or authority; yet Israel did not truly understand them in such a way that they would settle rightly in its mind.

“Unto jealousy.” The Jews are envious when the Gentiles call their God their own and claim that their promises, law, and prophets belong to themselves.

“Into a not-a-nation.” The Gentiles were not previously called a holy nation because they were without the law; or, now they are “not a nation” because they do not live as Gentiles.

“Into a foolish nation.” That is, against a foolish nation: against the Gentiles who did not know the true God.

### Verse 21

“All day long.” Throughout the whole period in which I dwelt among them and illuminated the world, I openly displayed works and affections to the Jews; or, during part of the whole day, I stretched out my hands upon the cross, and so forth.

“I stretched out my hands.” It is as though he says: I showed the Jews even greater things. For he denied them no benefit: he raised their dead and healed their various illnesses. He is said to stretch out his hands who generously bestows benefits upon those who ask.

## Chapter XI

### Verse 1

“I say, then.” Since he had refuted the Jews with so many authoritative testimonies, the Gentiles might have mocked them, saying that they had been completely rejected.

### Verse 2

“He foreknew.” In place of “he predestined,” he says “he foreknew.” This must be understood as is clear from what follows. He said “foreknew” so that the Jews would not again become proud because he had said that they were not rejected and were God’s people.

**(Augustine.)** Will anyone dare to say that God did not foreknow whom he would grant to believe, or whom he would give to his Son so that he would not lose any of them? If he foreknew these things, he certainly foreknew his own benefits, by which he deigns to save us. The predestination of the saints is nothing other than foreknowledge—namely, the foreknowledge and preparation of God’s benefits, by which all who are saved are most certainly delivered.

“Do you not know?” It is as though he says: The Lord did not reject the remnant at this time, but saved it, just as in the time of Elijah he reserved many for himself, when Elijah alone seemed to remain. If Elijah did not know that others besides himself had been reserved, it is not surprising if these people do not know.

### Verse 4

“Seven thousand.” The number seven signifies totality; the number thousand signifies perfection.

### Verse 5

“So, then.” It is as though he says: At that time there were many, although Elijah did not know it. Therefore, “so” means secretly in the same way; or “so” means by the same grace.

### Verse 6

“But if it is by grace, it is no longer by works.” That is, if they were saved in another way—which cannot happen except by the grace of God—then grace itself would no longer be grace but a debt.

### Verse 7

“What, then?” Having heard that the remnant was saved by grace and not by works, what should be said? “The elect obtained it.” Election belongs to grace, not to merits. Blindness, however, belongs to merits. For they were blinded because they did not wish to believe, just as the others believed because they wished to. Thus mercy and judgment were enacted by God in their very wills: to some he added grace through mercy, while through judgment he permitted others to be blinded. For whoever, after understanding, refused to believe ought to receive what he wills—namely, that thereafter he should not be able to believe. They were therefore helped in their will, not by the insertion of evil, but by grace withdrawing, so that, because they knowingly called the truth false, they would thereafter not understand what is true. This is what the envy of an evil will deserves; it is not so with those who act in this way through error.

### Verse 8

“God gave them a spirit of compunction.” This signifies an evil compunction, because it often happens that even something good is burdensome to a person, as Christ’s teaching was to the Pharisees. Thus he calls a spirit of compunction the envious mind with which they envied Christ’s teaching.

**[Col. 0507A] “To this very day.”** That is, for as long as the present day can be called “today”—namely, until the present day of all those to whom this writing will come.

### Verse 9

“The table.” That is, Scripture: “their table,” meaning the table first offered to them and placed before them, because they delight in its carnal observances; or “before them,” because if they wished to attend to its reasoning, they could understand.

“Into a snare,” and so forth. Just as they offered me vinegar, so may iniquity become a snare for them, because they knew iniquity and persisted in it.

“Into a snare,” and so forth. Scripture, which is bread to those who understand, ensnares when it is misunderstood and Christ’s preaching is rejected on its account. Again, the Scripture of the law was the cause of their captivity when, through zeal for it, they killed Christ; and in that captivity it became for them the cause of stumbling and disgrace. Later it will be the cause of eternal condemnation, which is specifically called God’s retribution.

### Verse 10

“Let their eyes be darkened.” Because they did not see without cause, let it happen to them that they not see.

“Let their eyes be darkened.” These words are spoken not as the wish of one making a petition, but in the capacity of one making a prediction.

### Verse 11

“I say, then: Have they stumbled?” Since I say that they were blinded by the authority of the prophets, do you think that they fell irrecoverably and without benefit? He answers as though saying: No. Their fall is beneficial, and they can be restored, so that no one may despise them.

“Have they stumbled so as to fall?”

**(Augustine.)** He does not say this because they did not fall, and so forth, up to the point where he warns them rather to beware lest, while they become proud, they fall.

“Salvation.” While they are scattered throughout the world as a testimony that the prophecies about Christ were not fabricated.

“That they might envy them.” This may be understood as meaning that the Jews should imitate the Gentiles in what is good. This has often happened, and it will happen more fully at the end of the age, when the Jews will follow Christians at the end of Christ’s work. Then Moses’ hand will be withdrawn into his bosom; then our Moses will return to his mother and to his brothers.

It may also be understood as meaning that the Gentiles should envy the Jews—that is, believe as the Jews themselves believed. Or it may mean that the Gentiles are stirred by jealousy of God concerning the Jews’ evil works.

### Verse 12

“But if,” and so forth. It is as though he says: I said that the Jews’ transgression is beneficial; if that is so, then their conversion will be even more beneficial.

“How much more.” That is, if God turned their evil into good—into the riches of the world—then their good will much more enrich the Gentiles through teaching and example when, at the end, their fullness is converted. By this he shows that their fall is neither useless nor irrecoverable.

### Verse 13

“As long as.”

**(Anselm.)** Although I am an apostle of the Gentiles, I will nevertheless honor my ministry by adding something beyond what I owe, so that I may also labor concerning the Jews, making the attempt. If this path does not succeed, I will undertake another. I would not do this if I despaired of their salvation.

**(Chrysostom.)** Again he strives to free himself from an evil suspicion. He seems indeed to rebuke those who were from the Gentiles and to humble their minds; yet, little by little, he pricks the Jew.

### Verse 16

“But if the first portion is holy.” I said that their acceptance would be very beneficial. Lest you Gentiles say that their acceptance cannot occur, as though the whole race had been rejected, I say that if the first portion—that is, a few taken from them, such as the apostles and the other disciples—is holy, then the whole lump can be sanctified.

“And if the root.” That is, the patriarchs, from whom the saints derive the sap of faith.

“And the branches.” Those who sprang from their race, established upon their faith.

### Verse 17

“But if you, being a wild olive, were grafted in,” and so forth.

**(Anselm.)** Let us see how the Lord himself also foretells the grafting in of the wild olive and the breaking of the branches, and so forth, up to the point where he says that what the Lord foretold would be done.

“A partner.” In the hope of the promise; this is contrary to the usual practice. For ordinarily a good tree is grafted into a bad one; here, the bad is grafted into the good.

### Verse 18

“Do not boast,” and so forth.

**(Anselm.)** The Gentiles who already believed in Christ were raising themselves up against the Jews because they had crucified Christ, even though from the Jews themselves another wall would come to the cornerstone. Therefore the Apostle restrains them: “Do not boast,” he says, and so forth. That is, you are not secure if you destroy those through whom you stand.

### Verse 19

“You will say, then: Branches were broken off.” It is as though he says: If it is not permissible to boast against those who stand, perhaps it is permissible to boast against those who were rejected in order that I might be grafted in. The Apostle removes this thought as follows: You speak well, because it is true that they were broken off on account of unbelief. You stand by faith—that is, not by your own merit but by God’s grace. Therefore do not become proud, lest you too be broken off through pride, as they were through unbelief. You are not secure if you destroy those through whom you stand. The person who rejoices in another’s evils is easily deceived.

### Verse 20

“You stand by faith.” It is God’s gift that you stand, not your merit.

“But be afraid.” Fear lest you lose the benefit of such great grace and fall into punishment. For reverent fear is present when the soul takes care lest God abandon it after it has abandoned him.

### Verse 22

“If you remain in goodness.” If you have acted in a way worthy of God’s kindness—for you need not have faith alone.

“But God’s severity.” This means that he did not spare them because he found them unworthy of their fathers’ virtue.

### Verse 24

“Contrary to nature.” That is called contrary to nature which is contrary to nature’s custom, as when a shoot bears the fruit of the root. God, however, does nothing contrary to nature, because whatever he does is nature.

“An olive tree.” By the olive tree the faith of the Fathers is understood here.

### Verse 25

“For I do not want you to be ignorant,” and so forth.

**(Augustine.)** The defenders of the law, interpreters of the law, teachers of the law, and understanders of the law crucified the author of the law. O blindness! This is what has happened in part to Israel: Christ was crucified so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter.

### Verse 26

“Ungodliness.” That is, unbelief, or the practice of legal observance. For the worship of the Jews, once Christ’s coming has been recognized, is ungodliness.

### Verse 27

“When I have taken away.” This will happen at the end, when the Jews are converted through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch. Hence Malachi says: “I will send you Elijah the Tishbite, who will turn the hearts of the fathers toward the children and the hearts of the children toward the father” (Malachi 4), so that the children may understand as the fathers did—that is, as the prophets understood.

### Verse 28

**(Augustine.)** “According to the Gospel,” and so forth. Or it may be understood in this way: Then they will be converted; but now they are enemies of Christ and, indeed, our enemies as well. Again, they are enemies from themselves—that is, because of their own fault. But this is “according to the Gospel” and “for your sake”—that is, for the advancement of the Gospel and for your benefit.

“Enemies for your sake.” He shows that this proceeds from God’s arrangement. Of themselves they can become enemies, and this benefits the Gospel, since God uses evil for good, so that, although they act against God’s will, God’s will—which wisely orders all things—is fulfilled.

“But beloved for the sake of the fathers.” They are elect and beloved for the sake of the fathers to whom these promises were made. For they were not called with the calling by which many who are not foreknown are called, although they perish—concerning which it is said: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 22). Rather, they were called with the calling by which the elect are called, which is without change: whoever hears from the Father comes to the Son, and the Son loses nothing of all that has been given him. Whoever perishes was not of that number. Hence: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2).

“According to election and for the sake of the fathers.”

**(Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 16.)** They are to be saved because the gifts—that is, the promises—and so forth, up to the statement that they do not see them with sorrow.

### Verse 30

“For just as.” That is, for the same reason God formerly permitted you not to believe: so that, after your conversion, you would not have a cause for boasting.

### Verse 31

“That they also.” Having learned that salvation comes not through the law but through grace, they will likewise obtain mercy through humility.

### Verse 32

“He confined.” That is, he permitted them to be confined. Here he seems in some way to explain the mystery. For God confined all people in unbelief so that, repenting of the bitterness of their unbelief and turning through faith to the sweetness of God’s mercy, they might remain more humble; thus the grace of the gift would be all the more precious, and they would cry out: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord” (Psalm 31).

“Of all.” That is, of Jews and Gentiles—not meaning that he will condemn no one, as some have falsely thought.

### Verse 33

“O the depth,” and so forth. He had stated a matter of astonishing profundity. Struck, as it were, by the dread of that profundity, he exclaims: “O the depth,” and so forth. For our understanding is exceedingly small when it comes to examining the justice of God’s judgments and the gratuitous grace bestowed without preceding merits. We are less moved by the fact that grace is granted to the unworthy than by the fact that it is equally denied to other unworthy people.

**(Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 36, toward the end.)** I know that just as there is no impossibility with God, so there is no injustice, and so forth, up to the point where he says that God first permitted them to be confined in unbelief.

**(The same.)** At times God’s grace is granted to the children of unbelievers, and so forth, up to the statement that, if not in this life, certainly in the next.

“His ways.” That is, the fulfillments of his plan, because even when the plan is carried out, what he had arranged cannot be understood.

“Counselor.” His only-begotten Son is the Counselor of the Father, and he is also called the Angel of Great Counsel. But no human being or angel was his counselor.

### Verse 35

“Or who first gave,” and so forth. Although we cannot know God’s judgments, at least this is certain: he gives good things solely by grace and not because of preceding merit.

**(Augustine.)** God became a debtor, not by receiving something from us, and so forth, up to the statement: “And this you did, who helped those who were laboring,” and so forth.

### Verse 36

“For from him,” and so forth. The words “from,” “through,” and “in” indicate distinctions of persons; the repeated pronoun “he himself,” however, indicates identity of substance. And because glory belongs to such a one, it does not belong to the righteous as such.

**(Augustine, *On the Nature of the Good*, chapter 27, “From Him.”)** All things are not from him in the sense of being made from his substance, and so forth, up to the statement that he wished each of these three expressions to be referred to one of the three persons.

“All things.” When we hear that all things are from God, we must certainly understand all natures and everything that exists naturally. For sins, which corrupt nature and arise from the will of sinners, are not from him.

## Chapter XII

### Verse 1

“I appeal to you.” Up to this point he has sufficiently humbled both parties and annulled their glorying in their former condition. Now, as though the matter were concluded, he proceeds to moral instruction.

“I appeal to you.” Previously, he was warning one side not to become proud against the other; from this point onward, he urges each to labor for the benefit of the other.

“I appeal through,” and so forth. That is, through the apostolate mercifully entrusted to me by God, or through the mercy shown and granted to you by God.

“A sacrifice,” and so forth.

**(Augustine, *The City of God*, book X, chapter 6.)** The true sacrifice is every work that is performed, and so forth, up to the statement he adds: “But be transformed in the renewal of your mind,” and so forth.

### Verse 2

“Do not be conformed.” This is a general prohibition.

“But be transformed.” This is a specific command. The former concerns self-restraint, the latter justice. The former concerns not coveting, the latter loving; the former concerns turning away from evil, the latter doing good. By not coveting we strip off the oldness; by loving we put on the newness.

“Be transformed.” Because in Adam the image of God was partly lost, it must begin to be restored by the one from whom it was formed. For it cannot restore itself, just as it was able to deform itself.

### Verse 3

“For I say.” This is the sacrifice of Christians: that many should be one body in Christ. This is demonstrated to the faithful by the sacrament of the altar, in which the Church is signified through the thing that it offers. For just as bread is made from many grains, so the holy Church consists of the many members of the faithful, who rejoice together through participation in their Creator. By his gift they are holy and one. This is also shown in what follows, where he says: “We, though many, are one body in Christ” (1 Corinthians 10). This cannot happen unless they think with sobriety, which is commanded here.

“To think with sobriety.” That is, one’s thinking should not go beyond the limits of justice; it should concern what is useful to us alone and harmful to no one.

**[Col. 0511A] “According to the measure of faith.”** According to the faith that God distributes in due measure. This is faith working through love, without which no one’s works are to be considered anything. The Spirit was not given to Christ according to measure, but to all others he is given, and what is given is added to them. Hence John says of Christ: “God does not give the Spirit according to measure”; to the others he is divided—not the Spirit himself, but his gifts.

### Verse 4

“For just as in one body.”

**(Augustine.)** No one can be righteous as long as he is separated from the unity of this body, and so forth, up to the point where he says that they should possess piety for good use.

### Verses 5–6

“But individually we are members of one another, having,” and so forth. We have good things for this purpose, with their differences. Or: we are individually members; therefore let this be carried out through differing gifts. What those graces are, from whose diversity we are called members, and how we ought to serve one another through them, he explains by saying: “Whether prophecy according to the proportion of faith, or service,” and so forth.

“Having,” let us be members of others, so that we may prophesy to them. I say “having according to the proportion of faith,” because prophecy is given according to what their faith, or the faith of the hearers, requires.

Note that in his enumeration of the graces he begins with prophecy, because the first proof that our faith is rational is that believers, after receiving the Spirit, prophesied.

### Verse 8

“He who shows mercy.” This mercy is daily medicine for daily wounds, even if the wounds are minor. Yet “judgment without mercy will be upon the one who has not shown mercy” (James 2). It is entirely just that forgiveness be granted to the one who forgives and that a gift be given to the one who gives.

Whoever, as though excessively righteous and secure, awaits judgment without mercy provokes wrath against himself. This mercy is manifold: forgiving the sinner, assisting the oppressed, and so forth. Therefore he adds the phrase “with mercy,” assigning one of its members, since another member had been mentioned previously: “the one who gives, with simplicity.” Simplicity excludes hypocrisy; cheerfulness displays joy and confidence in the hope of what is to come.

### Verse 11

“Not slothful.” Cursed is the one who does God’s work negligently. The slothful person is without hope in the divine way of life. Therefore, so that the coldness of sloth may be driven away: “Be fervent,” and so forth.

“Fervent in spirit.”

**(Theodoret.)** He called grace “spirit,” and so forth, up to the point where he explains this statement.

“Devoted to prayer.” That is, doing this continually.

“Serving the Lord,” and so forth. It is as though he says: Although I told you to be fervent in spirit, do not thrust the words of God upon people indiscriminately and inopportunely. Rather, be fervent at the appropriate time, so that you may speak words of faith in suitable places, to suitable persons, and at a suitable time.

“Fervent.” The Spirit is fire, by which love burns. Hence the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12).

### Verse 12

“Rejoicing in hope.” Those who are certain about future things rejoice, and therefore they are patient in tribulation.

### Verse 16

“Being of one mind.” This is not accomplished by the mouth alone. True humility exists only when it is not merely on the tongue, so that those who presume upon themselves may not fail to grieve with others but instead reproach them.

### Verse 19

“Give place.” He does not command the saints to refuse to be avenged by God, for the saints cry out in the Apocalypse—not indeed to satisfy hatred, but because it is written: “The righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance.” Rather, he commands them not to avenge themselves, but to give place to God’s wrath, since God says: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.”

If a good person wishes God to punish an enemy, this is not returning evil for evil. When a righteous person and an evil person both wish God to avenge them against their enemies, how are they distinguished? The good person desires that the enemy be corrected rather than punished. When God punishes, he does not delight in the enemy’s punishment; rather, he is pleased by what pleases the Lord, because he loves him, and God is the one whom he follows in this matter: “He rains upon the righteous and the unrighteous” (Proverbs 25). Yet even in this age God chastises the stubborn more harshly, and at the end he will condemn them. Vengeance should therefore be left to him.

He gives place to the anger of his adversary who allows the adversary to do what he wishes.

### Verse 20

“But if he is hungry.” Note the force of the conjunction “but.” The passage should be read as though the two conjunctions had not been interposed. Or it may be read in such a way that neither conjunction is superfluous, as though he said: Not only should you not defend yourselves, but if, and so forth.

## Chapter XIII

### Verse 1

“Every soul.”

**(Augustine, *Exposition of Proposition 720 from the Epistle to the Romans*.)** What the Apostle says here gives the most correct admonition, and so forth, up to the statement that every person should be subject to the one superior to him.

“For there is no authority.” Authority is from God; but the things that are from God have been ordered. Therefore authority is ordered. Accordingly, whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance. This is clear concerning good authority, since God perfected it. It can also reasonably be understood concerning bad authority, since through it the good are purified, the wicked are condemned, and authority itself is driven toward something worse.

Know also that the term “authority” sometimes means the authority itself, which is given to someone by God, and sometimes the person who possesses authority. The careful reader should distinguish these meanings.

“And those that exist have been ordered by God.” That is, they have been rationally arranged by God. Hence: “God does not reject the powerful, since he himself is powerful” (Job 36).

**(Gregory.)** The person who desires to imitate God imitates him who holds the summit of power, and so forth, up to the point where he says that it is not just authority but wicked action that is condemned.

### Verse 2

“But whoever resists.”  

**(Augustine.)** What if a ruler commands what is unlawful? In that case one must set aside that authority, out of fear of the greater authority. Therefore, if the emperor commands one thing and God another, the heart must obey God.

### Verse 3

“Rulers.” The Apostle calls those rulers who are established to correct conduct and prevent wrongdoing. They bear God’s image so that all others may be subject to one authority.

“They are not a terror to good conduct,” and so forth. If the ruler is good, he does not punish the one who acts well, but loves him. If he is bad, he does not harm the good person but purifies him. The evil subject ought therefore to fear, because rulers have been established to punish evils.

“You will have praise from it.” If the authority is just, it praises you itself; if unjust, it provides you with an occasion for praise.

### Verse 4

“For he is God’s minister.” Rulers have been given so that evils may not be committed.

“An avenger for wrath.” That is, an avenger for the purpose of exacting God’s wrath, or an avenger for showing God’s wrath, because this punishment indicates that those who persist in evil will be punished more severely.

### Verse 6

“For this reason.” You ought to be subject because, for this very reason—that is, to display your subjection—you pay taxes, which are a sign of subjection. He does not say “you pay” but “you render,” as though you were returning something; for you render them while they fight for the fatherland and administer judgments. You render them as those who serve God. Through the fact that you give them taxes, you serve God, because they are God’s ministers.

Or: you render taxes because they are God’s ministers, so that the good may be praised and the wicked punished.

### Verse 7

“Tax.” Or, the tax that is paid to lords.

“Revenue.” That which is carried to the lord’s household.

### Verse 8

“Owe nothing to anyone.” Peace toward all, love among brothers. Otherwise they are not truly brothers.

“You should love.” Love is mentioned here because it contributes to this humility. For love alone, even when repaid, always retains the person as a debtor. It is repaid when it is bestowed, but it remains owed even after it has been repaid, because there is no time when it ought not to be bestowed. Nor is it lost when it is repaid; rather, by being repaid it is multiplied. It is repaid by possessing it, not by lacking it, unlike money, which cannot be repaid unless it is possessed, nor possessed unless it is repaid. Indeed, when love is repaid by a person, it grows within that person, and the more it is repaid to others, the greater it becomes.

“He who loves his neighbor.” Although there are two commandments of love, one is often given for both, because neither God can be loved without one’s neighbor, nor one’s neighbor without God. Love of neighbor appears more openly in deeds; love of God is more hidden. Therefore he gives special mention to the former, about which the Lord says: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another,” where the greater commandment of love for God seems to have been omitted.

Yet both are found in each commandment by those who understand rightly. Whoever loves God cannot despise the one whom God commands to be loved; and whoever loves his neighbor in a holy and spiritual way—what does he love in that neighbor except God?

“He who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.” Every human being must be understood by “neighbor,” because no one exists with whom we ought to work evil. Therefore, whoever loves human beings ought to love them either because they are righteous or so that they may become righteous. He ought to love himself in the same way: either because he is righteous or so that he may become righteous. Whoever loves himself otherwise loves himself unjustly, because he loves himself in order to be unjust and therefore in order to be evil. Thus he no longer loves himself; for “whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul.”

### Verse 11

“And this, knowing.” Namely, knowing that it is the hour—or, as some books read, “this time,” meaning the time of grace.

“Since we have had love.” It is the hour—that is, the opportunity—but it is brief.

“To rise from sleep.” Sleep is negligence or ignorance.

“For now.” The reasons are inserted here why we ought to rise.

“It is nearer.” The person who does good is near to eternal life. Baptism is for forgiveness; a good life is for the crown. Or “nearer,” because we are closer to death.

### Verse 12

“The night has passed.” The reason why they ought to rise is again shown: the night of unbelief and ignorance has passed—that is, it existed—but now it does not. Its memory warns you to beware.

“But the day has drawn near.” The day—that is, eternal blessedness—has drawn near, since sins have been forgiven and you are righteous through grace.

“The night.” The old human being, who passed away in baptism.

“The day.” Christ, the sun of righteousness, by whose light they learned the truth, so that they might know what must be done.

“Works of darkness.” Evil works that came from the darkness of ignorance, or that love darkness and lead to darkness.

### Verse 13

“Not in revelries.” Note that the Romans are being addressed in these matters, and therefore they have no right to boast.

**(Augustine.)** Pride is the mother of these diseases, as is the greed of the human mind, which often also generates hypocrisy. This cannot be resisted unless fear and love are impressed upon us through frequent testimonies from the divine books.

## Chapter XIV

### Verse 1

“But the one who is weak.” Perfect faith is shown by discriminating against no food and considering none unclean, because “all things are clean to the clean.” But certain weak people thought that one ought to abstain from certain foods, and thus there was contention among the Romans. Therefore he commands that such people be received, not rejected, but raised toward faith by patience, example, and word. If it is unknown with what intention someone acts, one must not dispute about it.

“Not for disputes.” A person whose thought is not disclosed, or whose future condition we do not know, must not be condemned.

### Verse 2

“The weak person.” The weak person is one who distinguishes among foods, thinking some clean and others unclean because the Jews were forbidden to eat them. He says that such a person should be left to his own judgment, lest he eat with scruple.

Or, although perfect faith believes that all things are permitted, a person who is weak and prone to falling—easily overthrown by the impulse of desire—should eat vegetables, that is, light and dry foods that do not nourish vices, and abstain from those by which lust is aroused. For the richness of meat and luxurious banquets incite the body to lust.

### Verse 3

“Let the one who eats.” Above he commanded that one should not dispute about the thoughts of others; here he commands that one should not despise them.

“Let him not judge.”

**(Augustine, *Book II of the Sermon on the Mount*.)** One should judge what is manifest, not what is hidden, and so forth, up to the statement that all kinds of human food may be taken without distinction.

### Verse 4

“He stands or falls before his own master.” You have no right to judge the unknown heart of another’s servant. His own master is the one for whose honor the person who stands does so. The fall of the one who falls also belongs to that master, who can raise him up or judge him.

“He stands or falls.” He says this because it is uncertain: perhaps the one who is thought to be falling is standing. “He stands or falls.” By this he shows that he does not know with what intention the person acts in doubtful matters.

“But he will stand.” Here he hints that we should turn doubtful matters toward the better interpretation, desire the salvation rather than the death of the guilty, and retain hope of good in the future, even if the present situation is otherwise.

“But he will stand.” For he is not guilty either if he eats or if he does not eat, provided that he does so out of devotion.

### Verse 5

“For one person.” Above he said that some eat everything and others do not eat everything; there he was speaking about kinds of food. Here he says that some abstain at all times, while others abstain at a particular time, and he says that both practices can be rightly followed.

“In his own judgment.” That is, let him be left to his own counsel, lest, having suffered scandal, he withdraw from love, which is the mother of all virtues.

### Verse 6

“The one who regards the day.” I say, let him abound in his own judgment, because whoever regards the day—whether every day or an intervening day—regards it for the Lord.

“And the one who eats, eats for the Lord.” That is, for the Lord’s honor, since he believes that all things created by the Lord are clean and is sustained by them in order to serve him.

### Verse 7

“For none of us lives for himself.” Whoever is restrained by the law lives not for himself but for God, who gave the law. If there were no law, each person would live for himself.

“For himself.” Rather, for the Lord, by whose judgment he is condemned or crowned; or “for himself,” meaning for his own praise, but in relation to God. For just as there is no end to God’s greatness, so there will be no end to our praise. When we have died in this flesh, we will not cease to praise God. In this interpretation he is speaking only about the faithful.

Or “for himself,” meaning judged by himself, but by the Lord; in this sense the statement concerns both the good and the wicked.

### Verse 10

“Before the tribunal.” This is said by comparison: a tribunal is the seat of a judge, placed on high so that the judge may be seen by everyone and may himself observe all from an elevated position. In the same way Christ will sit, as it were, on a tribunal, because he will be seen by everyone; he himself will see the consciences of all and will judge their cases.

### Verse 13

“Therefore let us no longer.” Let us not claim for ourselves what does not belong to us. Let us not criticize matters whose intention we do not know; or, even when they are manifest, let us not criticize them in such a way that we despair of the person’s health. In both matters judgment is rash, arising either from pride or from lack of insight. Hence it is said: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged” (Luke 6).

### Verse 14

“I know and am confident.” It is as though he says: I tell you not to place a stumbling block before your brothers. I do not mean that I call food a stumbling block or scandal because it is unclean, since I know this through the confidence that is in Jesus: after he came, he released us from the law.

He uses “common” for “unclean,” either because the term was taken from vessels that formerly were common to every use, some of which, after being dedicated to sacrifices, were no longer called common but holy; or because the term was taken from the Jews, since the Jews themselves were called God’s particular people, while all others were called common and unclean.

### Verse 16

“Therefore let what is good not be blasphemed.” When a person who has good works is criticized over a minor matter, his good is obscured, and his good begins to be blasphemed through evil. Hence Ezekiel says: “The righteousness of the righteous will not benefit him if he goes astray” (Ezekiel 33).

“Therefore let what is good not be blasphemed.” Eating, which is good in itself, becomes liable to blasphemy when it harms others. Since it harms them, abstain; for food is not the cause of the kingdom of God.

### Chapter 14

**Verse 17.**—For the kingdom of God is not food and drink. It is not the use of foods, but desire that must be restrained. It does not matter what food, or how much, a person takes according to what is appropriate for human beings, for his own person, and for the necessity of his health; what matters is how readily and cheerfully he can do without these things when it is proper or necessary to do without them.

Joy in the Holy Spirit. For whoever, and so forth. This joy certainly arises not from banquets, as many are accustomed to do, but in the Holy Spirit, from fraternal peace; just as anger arises in dispute, where there is no Spirit, since he is present only among peacemakers. Moreover, by his grace these three things—righteousness, peace, and joy—are in a person; but they were not present in these Romans.  
[Col. 0516B]

**Verse 18.**—He is pleasing to God and approved by human beings. This is according to the fact that there is joy in the Holy Spirit. A person is considered approved by human beings according to righteousness, and also according to peace, because dispute produces discord. Therefore, after laying aside rash judgments, let us pursue what belongs to peace, not discord, and what belongs to edification, so that the others may be built up, or so that those already built up may be mutually preserved—the Jew in relation to the Gentile, and the Gentile in relation to the Jew.

**Verse 21.**—He is offended. He is disturbed, not knowing what he should hold. He is offended who departs from the right faith.

**Verse 22.**—Blessed. He calls blessed the person who does nothing except what he judges useful; but he considers the person worthy of condemnation by his own judgment who does not do what he says he ought to do.

[Col. 0516C]

**Verse 23.**—But whatever is not from faith. Yet not everything done with faith is good, because ignorance arising from fault is harmful. The whole life of unbelievers is sin, because everyone who lives or acts unbelievingly sins grievously, and nothing is good without the highest good, when recognition of eternal truth is absent. Even among the best moral practices there is a false virtue. Works that appear commendable, apart from faith, are like great strength and a very swift course outside the road. It is not from faith. Our faith requires a person to do what he understands well to be necessary; and it is sin when something is done otherwise than it has been judged.

## Chapter 15

**Verse 5.**—To think the same thing. As if he were saying: Unless you think the same thing, you will not be able to honor God.

[Col. 0516D]

**Verse 8.**—Of circumcision. That is, of the Jews, to whom he came bodily; hence: “I was not sent except to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel” (Matthew 15). For the sake of truth. He did not reject the Jews, to whom truth properly belonged, and mercy to the Gentiles, to whom no promise had been made. The promises. For he had promised Abraham: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 22). And to David: “From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne” (Psalm 131). Jacob also said: “A star shall arise from Jacob” (Numbers 24).

**Verse 9.**—I will confess. Confession is not only of sins, but also of praise.

**Verse 12.**—There shall be the root of Jesse. And from this root there shall be the one who will arise, and so forth. Jesse is the root; David the tree, which through the branch—that is, Mary—produced the fruit, that is, Christ.  
[Col. 0517A]

**Verse 13.**—And peace. So that you may rejoice, may he grant peace and concord to one another; and this will happen if the faith is sound. That you may abound. That is, so that through these things, once possessed, you may become more certain of eternal blessedness, and abound in the power of the Holy Spirit—that is, in the strength of good works, which is given through the Holy Spirit.

**Verse 14.**—I am confident. Lest the Apostle seem to regard everyone as discordant and to be correcting the foolish, he removes this impression, explaining that he begins in order to admonish the more perfect concerning the correction of those who are less advanced. He therefore sets himself forward as an example, since he labors on behalf of others; and these people ought to do the same, since he himself is prevented from coming to them because of his work on behalf of others. Filled with all wisdom. Through this praise he urges them toward better things, in the manner of one exhorting. Hence he does not say “to teach,” but “to admonish,” as if to say that what is known nevertheless slips away from the mind. What is known is ordinarily admonished when it sometimes slips away from the mind or is held negligently.

**Verse 15.**—Because of the grace. He does not write rashly; rather, the Apostle of the Gentiles dares to write to all the Gentiles by the authority entrusted to him through grace.

**Verse 17.**—I have therefore. So should you also act if you labor for your brothers. He says this to show that he is no less capable than the apostles who had been with Christ.

**Verse 20.**—Not where Christ has already been named, and so forth. Because he knew that false apostles and others were teaching falsely under the name of Christ, something which later required the greatest labor to correct, he was therefore eager to forestall this and to hand on the truth intact where Christ had not yet been proclaimed. He proves this by the testimony of the prophet.  
[Col. 0517C]

**Verse 21.**—And those who have not heard, and so forth. So that understanding of the word of God might be true and inviolable, he hastened to imbue the Gentiles with the truth.

**Verse 26.**—For they were pleased. Paul invites the Romans to works of this kind, because one who lives through the mercy of God ought to be devoted to a fellow believer. For the poor. These people had given themselves wholly to divine service, caring nothing for worldly matters; they were an example of good conduct to the faithful.

**Verse 30.**—That you may help. Many very small people, when gathered together in unanimity, become great, and it is impossible that the prayers of many should not obtain their request. If, therefore, they desire to see him, let them pray that they may receive him, once he has been delivered, with the joy of charity; hence it follows: “that I may be delivered.”

[Col. 0517D]

**Verse 31.**—Accepted. So that, having understood his affection toward them, they may give thanks to God unanimously with him. For it is a great gain for one through whose ministry many have become joyful and praise God.

**Verse 33.**—Now the God of peace. Christ, who said: “I give you my peace, and I leave you my peace” (John 14), who is with his own until the consummation of the age—so may he also be with you. For he himself is the one who said: “I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28).

## Chapter 16

**Verse 1.**—I commend to you. From this point the Apostle puts forward many righteous people whom those in Rome ought to trust, as if to say: Do as I have said, and imitate these people. Phoebe. Phoebe was evidently a very wealthy and noble woman who supported the Church at the place called Cenchreae from her own resources. At that time she had gone to Rome on some business, and perhaps he sent this Epistle through her.

**Verse 2.**—That you may receive her worthily. Or, as other manuscripts read, “with great honesty and honor.”

**Verse 3.**—Prisca and Aquila. Aquila is the husband of Priscilla. These people had come to Rome to assist Paul in strengthening the Romans. Thus all the others whom he greets are also understood to have been in Rome.

**Verse 4.**—The churches of the Gentiles. For they labor for the advancement of the Gentiles by exhorting them in the faith of Christ; they also did not refuse to undergo dangers on behalf of the Apostle.  
[Col. 0518B] Therefore the Romans too ought to obey them.

**Verse 10.**—Apelles. Through temptations he was found faithful in Christ, although he was not his personal friend or partner in the work.

**Verse 11.**—Those of Aristobulus. This Aristobulus was accustomed to gather brothers in Christ, whom the Apostle greets, thereby approving his action. Those of Narcissus. Narcissus is said to have been a presbyter, as is read in other manuscripts; by traveling about he strengthened the holy brothers. Since he was not present at that time, he greets his own people; and because he did not know the merits of all of them, he makes a distinction by adding: “who are in the Lord”—that is, those whom you know to be worthy.

**Verse 12.**—She labored. The labor of which the Apostle speaks so frequently consists in exhortation, in the ministry of the saints, and in distress and poverty endured for God.  
[Col. 0518C]

**Verse 13.**—And my mother. Because of her holiness he calls her his mother, whose son he placed in charge of ecclesiastical service.

**Verse 15.**—And all. He commands all those to whom he writes and whom he names to greet one another with a holy kiss—that is, in the peace of Christ—so that their kisses may be religious, not carnal.

**Verse 16.**—Of Christ. That is, those who place their trust in Christ, not in anything else.

**Verse 17.**—That you may watch. He is referring to the false apostles, whom throughout the Epistle he warns them to avoid.

**Verse 19.**—For your obedience. I therefore warn you to avoid them because your faith and obedience are praised everywhere. For you are at the head of the world, and by your example others could already be corrupted. Or: I ask you to avoid them because you have readily obeyed what is good, and I rejoice in this; but I want you to be wise in discerning what is good and to be without any share in evil.  
[Col. 0518D]

**Verse 20.**—But the God. You should be wise; but may God crush Satan—that is, the false preachers, or any person opposing you, or the devil. Under your feet. So that you may despise the head, that is, the first movements of suggestions; and, if it is the devil, may you crush his head, as was said of Eve in the figure of the Church, or of sensuality. Grace. He now wishes for them the grace that he promised at his coming.

**Verse 21.**—Greets you. As if to say: So many and such important people rejoice with you in your undertaking; therefore it is fitting that you persevere.  
[Col. 0519A]

**Verse 23.**—And the whole. Above he had spoken of all the churches; here, however, he speaks of the church of another province, from which Gaius came.

**Verse 25.**—Now to him. Thus I admonish you. To him who is able to strengthen you, let glory be given—from whom alone, who is good, are all good things. Here the central point of the Epistle is indicated, because the Apostle chiefly intends to admonish them to attribute everything to the grace of God.

According to the revelation. He means by “the mystery” the incarnation of Christ and the other things that had been hidden for eternal ages. For although they had been known in some respect to the ancient fathers, they had nevertheless been fully known by no one until they were revealed in their own time through Christ himself.  
[Col. 0519B; Col. 0520A]

**Verse 26.**—Through the Scriptures of the prophets. They had been opened by him and give testimony to this preaching. Made known among all the Gentiles for obedience, that is, so that they may obey the faith by doing good. Silent to others, but known to God alone. For although it has now been revealed to human beings, it was nevertheless known to God alone, because he alone knows why it was done in this way. Here he restrains those who inquire, asking: Why did God delay so long? Why did he permit so many nations to perish?

**Verse 27.**—To him be honor. (AUGUSTINE.) What is added—“To him be glory,” and so forth—continues until: “because through him God the Trinity became known to human beings,” which is the mystery.  
[Col. 0520B]

# First Epistle to the Corinthians (G)*

## Argument

The Corinthians are Achaeans. They likewise heard the word of truth from the Apostle, and they were subverted in many ways by false apostles. Some were led astray by the verbose eloquence of philosophy, others by the sect of the Jewish law. The Apostle recalls them to the true faith and evangelical wisdom, writing to them from Ephesus through his disciple Timothy.

## Chapter 1

**Verse 1.**—Paul, called. That is, called an Apostle of Jesus Christ by all through the privilege of his name. Here he does not call himself a servant, because authority and commendation were rather necessary against the pride of the Corinthians, among whom he had become despised. And Sosthenes. See how, through the person who was living among them, he implies that he had learned of their faults. A brother. By this he removes the possibility that he had informed him with an evil intention, but shows that he had done so out of charity and a desire for correction.  
[Col. 0519C]

**Verse 2.**—With all. He also writes to all the fellow Corinthians who were struggling with the same vices.

**Verse 3.**—Grace. He first puts forward what is good, so that others may conform themselves to it. And to the Lord Jesus Christ. He is distinct from the Father by personal property, but is one God with him by unity of substance.

[Col. 0519D]

**Verse 5.**—In all things. He assumes that there are particular forms in every word—that is, in every kind of language—or in every manner of preaching, namely, to the less advanced, the moderately advanced, and the perfect.

**Verse 10.**—I appeal. Up to this point he has praised the good. After praising these people, he invites others to resemble them.

**Verse 11.**—Those of Chloe. This is the name of a place or of a person. Some think it is a place, as if he were saying: “from those who are in Antioch.” Others think that she was a woman devoted to God, with whom many people worshiped God.

**Verse 12.**—Now I mean this. Here he begins to act against those who baptized, in whom they were boasting. I indeed. By placing his own name and those of the apostles among them, he indicates the false teachers, lest, if he said “in the name of this one or that one,” they might think that he begrudged them something and wished to attribute it to himself. Or he named the good apostles in order to show that if one must not glory in the name of the great, neither should one glory in the name of those whose doctrine is corrupt.  
[Col. 0520B]

**Verse 13.**—Is Christ divided among you? As if he were saying: You make many Christs—that is, givers of graces. Or: the one who works the same thing in everyone is divided when it is believed that he works more in one person and less in another. Or: because you say this, Christ is now divided by you, that is, separated. Was Paul crucified for you? By means of the truth that the Corinthians held, he makes them ashamed of the falsehoods; just as by Christ’s resurrection, which they believed, he proves the resurrection of the dead, which they denied.

**Verse 14.**—I give thanks to God, and so forth. (AUGUSTINE.) Paul gives thanks to God that he baptized none of them, since, as though they had forgotten in whose name they had been baptized, they were dividing themselves according to the names of human beings. Since baptism given through a contemptible human being has the same power as baptism given through an Apostle, it is understood to belong not to that person, but to Christ, and so forth.

**Verse 17.**—But to evangelize. Even the less learned can baptize perfectly. But to evangelize perfectly is much more difficult and a rarer work. Therefore the teacher of the Gentiles, superior to many others, says that he was sent to evangelize, not to baptize. Nevertheless, when necessity required it, he sometimes did this also. Not in wisdom. That is, not according to worldly wisdom. Not in the wisdom of speech. By “wisdom” he means the wisdom of the philosophers, which is called wisdom, although it is not truly so. Nevertheless, it is the wisdom that makes people verbose, through which the cross—that is, the death of Christ—is emptied of its meaning, and it is judged contrary to nature that the immortal God should die. Of speech. Verbal composition is sought where, as the power itself testifies, truth does not commend itself.

**Verse 18.**—To those who are perishing. That is, to the wise of the world, whose wisdom also perishes and is shown to be false, and they themselves are to be condemned.

The power of God. By being killed he conquered the devil and freed humanity; or he gives power to believers, through which miracles are performed when circumstances require it.

[Col. 0521A]

**Verse 19.**—For it is written. He therefore did not send me in wisdom because he had foretold that he would not receive it in evangelical preaching, but would destroy it and reject it from the company of his preachers; and so it happened.

**Verse 21.**—God was pleased through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. That is, through faith in the cross, immortality comes to mortals, so that salvation is found where foolishness is believed.

**Verse 26.**—For consider. Truly, what is foolish and weak in God is wiser and stronger than human beings. You can test this in yourselves. For they called you foolish and weak; among the foolish and weak things of God such people as those who called you are numbered, and yet they confound the wise and the strong. And they truly are such, because they are not many.  
[Col. 0521B] He does not say “none,” perhaps on his own account: he alone among the apostles was skilled in secular literature, rich in earthly possessions, and distinguished by a family of Roman rank; nevertheless, he considered these things worthless and did not use them.

**Verse 27.**—But the foolish things. See how they openly act against God’s ordering, because they boast of worldly wisdom while God puts forward humility. For the humble God came, seeking the humble, not the exalted. Although he first chose the poor, the unlearned, and the weak, he does not therefore abandon the wise, the rich, and the noble. But if he chose such people first, they would rightly seem to have been chosen because of those qualities, and pride—the cause of humanity’s fall—would thus be present in them. Unless a fisherman went before faithfully, a humble orator would not follow. Hence Nathanael, although learned, was not chosen as an apostle.

[Col. 0521C]

**Verse 29.**—So that no one may glory. He should glory not in himself but in God, as is shown there: “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord.”

**Verse 30.**—But from him. No one should glory in himself; nevertheless, there is another glory, because you are from him.

## Chapter 2

**Verse 2.**—For I judged not. Whoever speaks lofty things to someone less capable is seeking not his benefit but his own display.

**Verse 6.**—The perfect. Not those who possess knowledge and are teachers, for they have no need of it, but hearers who are already capable of receiving it.

**Verse 7.**—In a mystery. By explaining the mysteries of the Old Testament in which Christ was signified, as in the offering of Abel or of Abraham. Things that were hidden.  
[Col. 0521D] They were hidden not in words but in power: they could not be grasped by human reasoning, but were believed through the efficacy of the Spirit.

**Verse 8.**—For if they had known. Either if the lesser rulers had known that he was the Messiah promised in the Law, or if the greater rulers had known that he was God, or the Son of God, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

**Verse 9.**—Nor into the human heart. What rises into the heart is beneath the heart; what is eternal, to which the heart rises, is above the heart. Or: it is not a human being but the Spirit who knows. He has ascended. A thing is said to ascend into the heart when, having been well understood, it pleases.

**Verse 10.**—He searches, and so forth. The Spirit of God is said to search all things, not so that he may find what he does not know, but because he leaves absolutely nothing unknown; or because he causes you to search. For whatever you do by his gift, he is said to do, because without him you would not do it.

**Verse 12.**—But the Spirit who is from God. The Holy Spirit certainly belongs to the Father and the Son, and also to us. For what has been given is referred both to the one who gave it and to those to whom he gave it. Thus the Holy Spirit belongs not only to the Father and the Son who gave him, but also to us who received him. This is not our spirit in which we exist, because that spirit of ours in which we exist is the spirit of the human being, who exists in it. Nevertheless, we have received that spirit which belongs to the human being. But one thing is what we receive in order to exist, and another what we receive in order to be holy. In Scripture, the human spirit is understood as the soul itself or as the rational power of the soul. For he gave us nature so that we might exist, a soul so that we might live, and a mind so that we might understand. So that we may know. Many possess God’s gifts and, because they do not know from whom they have them, boast of them in impious vanity. No one is blessed by God’s gifts who is ungrateful to the giver. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “To the one who has, it will be given.” To have fully is to know from where one has received. Therefore, “from the one who does not have”—that is, who does not know from where he has received what he has—“even what he has will be taken away from him” (Luke 8).  
[Col. 0522B]

**Verse 13.**—Spiritual things. This is what you Corinthians are not; and therefore it is your fault, not ours, that we have not spoken greater things.

**Verse 14.**—But the natural person. A person is called natural in his life when he is carried along by the unrestrained wantonness of his soul, which the ruling spirit does not contain within the limits of the natural order, because he himself does not subject himself to be governed by God. In the judgment of his mind, a person is called natural when he judges concerning God according to bodily images, the letter of the Law, or philosophical reasoning. Because he is examined spiritually. The natural person cannot understand spiritual things because he is examined—that is, examination and testing of those spiritual things takes place only spiritually, by the spiritual person; and the text is read personally: “he is examined.” Or it may be understood this way: The natural person does not understand spiritual things because he is examined spiritually—that is, by spiritual things alone it is proved what the natural person is, since he rejects what he hears, and these things are proposed to him for no other reason than that he may be examined.

**Verse 15.**—But the spiritual person. This may refer either to life or to knowledge. A person is spiritual in life when, having the Spirit of the Lord as his ruler, he governs his soul. A person is spiritual in knowledge when, although he sees partially and through a mirror, he does not understand according to bodily images, the letter of the Law, or human philosophy, but, subject to the Spirit of God, judges with complete certainty and faithfulness. All things. Not absolutely everything contained in divine knowledge, but all things sufficient for righteousness and life—that is, everything that must be judged.

## Chapter 3

**Verse 2.**—For you are still carnal. He rebukes those who complained that they had not previously heard spiritual things, although they were still unworthy to hear them.

His ministers. (AUGUSTINE.) A human being ministers outwardly as a servant, and so forth, continuing until: “because God works both willing and accomplishing.”  
[Col. 0523A]

**Verse 8.**—They are one. It might seem that, although they give nothing from themselves, God nevertheless works more through one than through another.

**Verse 9.**—Co-workers. In cultivating the Lord’s field, not corrupters, as some say. This is clear from what follows: “You are God’s agriculture.” Agriculture. Because he cultivates you for fruit. Building, because the one who cultivates dwells in you. Thus the field and the building are the same thing, though not in visible objects. We cultivate God by worshiping him, not by adorning him. He cultivates us in such a way as to make us better.

**Verse 11.**—For no one can lay another foundation. (AUGUSTINE, *On Faith and Works*, chapter 15.) The faith of Christian grace—that is, the faith that works through love—and so forth, continuing until: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the test of tribulation tests human beings” (Sirach 27).

Christ. That is, the faith of Christ, which works through love, through which Christ dwells in hearts. There is no other foundation. This foundation does not allow anyone to perish.

**Verse 12.**—But if anyone. Gold, silver, and precious stones signify excellent doctrine; in the other three, vain doctrine is signified. If it deceives now, it will appear in the fire, because it will burn while the good remains, and there will be a reward for him—namely, eternal life for good doctrine. Wood, hay, stubble. These should not be understood as evil works, as though faith without works saves; that is not the case.

[Col. 0523C]

(AUGUSTINE, on Psalm 30.) Let no one who has wicked works promise himself the kingdom of God, and so forth, continuing until: “the smallest and lightest sins, which the fire can easily consume.”

**Verse 13.**—For the day. Here “day” is the day of a person acting according to his own will; but at the judgment, or at each person’s death, it is the Lord’s day, according to the merits of the judge—or rather, judgment already begins here, in the house of God. That is, punishment begins with those who are to be saved, and will be completed in the reprobate. The elect are punished for this reason: so that they will not be punished there. On that day there is the fire of tribulation, by which love of temporal things is burned away while people grieve over what they have lost. Hence it is also said: “Such people will have tribulation in the flesh.” The fire of the final judgment will last until those who are to be saved have been purified. The fire will test.  
[Col. 0523D] We read that there will be two fires. One is eternal, by which the reprobate will be punished eternally; it will follow the judgment. The other will precede it, and by it the face of this world will be burned away; it will correct those who have built upon the foundation with wood, hay, and stubble. Those who have built with gold, silver, and precious stones are secure from both fires.

**Verse 14.**—A reward. He has rest for his soul, which despises all things, not only after the end but also in this life.

**Verse 16.**—Do you not know, and so forth. He said this beforehand in order to prick those who, living shamefully, violate their own bodies—especially the man who has his father’s wife. Here he is speaking about those who build upon the foundation.

**Verse 17.**—But if anyone. This person is saved through fire; but if anyone wishes to destroy the temple that you are, God will destroy him. And you do not know this?

The temple. (AUGUSTINE.) Those in whom God dwells through faith are the temple of God, and so forth, continuing to explain how they are also now the temple of God’s angels.

(AUGUSTINE.) Such an assembly is the building of God’s temple. Such an assembly is produced not by carnal generation but by spiritual regeneration. God therefore dwells in individuals as in his temples, and in all gathered together as in his temple. God is therefore present everywhere, and wholly present everywhere; yet he does not dwell everywhere, but in his temple, toward which he is gracious and favorable through grace. Among some he is received as dwelling more fully, among others less fully. He dwells in natural human beings and in little ones not according to the age of the flesh but according to the mind, because he secretly works in them so that they may be his temple; and in those who advance and persevere in advancing, he brings this to completion.  
[Col. 0524B]

(IDEM.) But someone might say: Before God made heaven and earth, before—and so forth—continuing until: “But those are most blessed for whom having God means knowing him.”

For the wisdom of this world, and so forth. (AMBROSE.) “Wisdom” is used improperly for cunning.

**Verse 21.**—Let no one, and so forth. He is speaking of baptizers or teachers. No one. Because they are yours: all things have been given for your service, and one must glory only in superior things. In human beings. For they are not givers of graces, whether they are good or evil, but only ministers.

[Col. 0524C]

**Verse 22.**—For all things. Let individual teachers or baptizers not claim people for themselves, since everyone makes use of them. The world is ours if we place its course within God’s will. The present life is ours if it is lived modestly and to the glory of God. Death is ours if, in hope of what is to come, we willingly die for Christ.
