Present things are ours if we use them in such a way that we do not give offense. Future things are ours if, believing in them, we desire them more greatly.

Whether life, and so forth. Both the life and the death of teachers ought to serve the edification of their subjects. Or understand “life” as holy human beings and angels, who strive for the advancement of the faithful, and “death” as the devil and his members, who, while persecuting them, serve the benefit of God’s servants.

**Verse 23.**—But you are Christ’s. Just as these things belong to us, so we should be subject to Christ. And Christ is God’s. He is his proper Son, doing his will, so that we too may do the Father’s will. Why, then, do you hope for something from human beings to the injury of Christ?

## Chapter 4

**Verse 1.**—Thus let us regard us. Up to this point he has spoken about the glory of the false teachers; here he deals with his own contempt. Thus let us regard us. The Apostle says this because they thought little of him; but a person should think of him as God does, who chose him.

And stewards. (AUGUSTINE.) Not only the good but also the evil are stewards, and so forth, continuing until: “to be a participant in that one.”

**Verse 2.**—Here it is now required. We should be judged in this way concerning ourselves, but here among you in a way unlike elsewhere. Already in the present, although one ought to wait until God judges.  
[Col. 0525A]

**Verse 3.**—Myself. It is dangerous for you to judge what is hidden in my heart or in the hearts of others. For one must believe that there is such great depth in a human being that it is hidden even from the person in whom it exists. Thus in Peter the depth of his weakness was hidden when he rashly promised that he would die with the Lord. Since, therefore, each person can scarcely, or not at all, give a true judgment about himself, how can he judge another, when no one knows what is happening in a human being except the human spirit? From human judgment. That is, from human beings while they are living in their own day, and it is not yet the Lord’s day. Human. For there is a day of the Lord, on which he will judge, when each person will give an account for himself, and then the secrets of hearts will be revealed.  
[Col. 0525B]

**Verse 4.**—For I am conscious of nothing. (AMBROSE.) Do not say: “We have not sinned.” Saint Paul said: “Although I am conscious of nothing against myself,” yet he added: “But by this I am not justified.” You also, if you are conscious of nothing, nevertheless confess to the Lord, lest there be something that escapes you.

**Verse 5.**—Until the Lord comes. Otherwise an injury is done to the judge, because it is an injury to the judge if a sentence proceeds from a servant before his judgment. He will bring to light. That is, he will make the hidden things of darkness—that is, sins—manifest. Then each person will receive praise. This applies to the one who acts or thinks well; here, however, it is not known who is worthy of praise.

**Verse 6.**—Me and Apollos. I have offered an example for everyone, so that all may shun such behavior as they shun it in us. So that no one, and so forth, may go beyond what is written. From the one—that is, from someone better than that person—as though he were someone other than the one who does not exist, whether with respect to himself or with respect to the ministry.

**Verse 7.**—For who distinguishes you? From the mass of the lost? No one except God. Or, if you were baptized by Peter, how are you distinguished from the one baptized by Paul? He has nothing from the baptizer, and neither do you. Or he rebukes those same people who were boasting of the teaching of the false apostles. As if he were saying: You glory on their account, but what do you have from them that you did not have from me? And if you received it from me, why do you glory against me, as though you had not received the same thing from me?

[Col. 0525D]

But what do you have, and so forth. He seeks to remove another kind of arrogance: that a person should not become proud because of some grace given to him by God, imagining that he has it from himself or from the minister.

But if you received it. He says this against those who, although hearing the same things from the Apostle, gloried in the teaching of the false apostles. By commending themselves through eloquence, they turned glory toward themselves, whereas the Apostle had made himself appear contemptible in order to give glory to God. Therefore the Apostle speaks to them ironically, as though granting what they thought about themselves, when he adds:

**Verse 8.**—Already you are filled. As if he were saying: I ask you, “Why do you glory?” and so forth; but it seems that I am not right to do this, because you are already filled and already rich. This is irony, as if he were saying: It is not so. These are the words of someone who is angry, not of someone confirming them.

That you might reign. To reign truly is to be secure in the hope and promises of God and to rejoice in adversities.

**Verse 9.**—For I think. As if he were saying: This must in no way be thought. He speaks ironically. I say “without us,” because through the evils we suffer God shows that we apostles are last, people for whom no concern is taken, as though destined for death—that is, reserved for no purpose but death. This is apparent from the fact that people gather to see us as though we were a spectacle or a monster; through this we are proved all the more to be friends of God. Or you ought to reign with us for this reason: because I think, and am certain, that in our tribulations we are like the last ones—Elijah and Enoch.

[Col. 0526B]

And to angels. Good angels and good human beings praise; evil ones mock. These are the right and the left. We use both to strike the enemy, that is, the devil; neither do the former exalt us, nor do the latter break us.

**Verse 10.**—For Christ’s sake. We preach his cross, while you, remaining silent, appear wise in Christ.

**Verse 13.**—As refuse. Through all these things we are proved wise and strong in Christ.

**Verse 14.**—Not to shame you. Like a healing physician, he softens harsh things with gentle ones.

**Verse 15.**—Guardians. By calling them guardians, he signifies children. Through the Gospel. He added “through the Gospel,” lest what belongs to God be thought to belong to him. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not call anyone your father on earth; one is your Father, God” (Matthew 23). He does not remove this name from everyone else, but prevents the grace of God by which we are begotten for eternal life from being attributed to the nature, power, or even holiness of any human being.  
[Col. 0526C]

**Verse 19.**—If the Lord wills. He says this to show that, if he did not go, God had not willed it, plainly because of their unworthiness.

**Verse 20.**—In power. He uses words of terror so that those who were inflated might be humbled and prepare themselves to receive him. But may it never happen that pious children say: “If you are coming with a rod, do not come.” For it is better to be disciplined by a father’s rod than to perish through a robber’s flattery.

## Chapter 5

[Col. 0526D]

**Verse 1.**—It is everywhere reported. He begins to deal with fornication and rebukes the fornicator who was keeping his father’s wife, as well as those who tolerated him. For they too were participants, since they allowed a person guilty of so great a sin to meet with them without correction. He therefore showed that not only the one liable to death, but also those who adhered to him, were not free from the crime.

**Verse 2.**—You are inflated. By the wind of pride, which drives out mercy; for if one member suffers, the others also suffer with it.

**Verse 4.**—In the name of the Lord. I have judged in this way: that when you are gathered together as one, without any disagreement, with my authority and the power of Christ cooperating, you should hand such a person over to Satan.  
[Col. 0527A]

**Verse 5.**—To hand him over, and so forth. The Apostle is said to have possessed this power: when he could not turn someone away from folly, he handed him over to be tormented by the devil until, professing repentance, he ceased from evil.

So that the spirit may be saved. In this way the Apostle hands him over to Satan not cruelly but lovingly. Moses likewise judged a few of those who worshiped idols, terrifying them in the present and establishing discipline for the future. So too did Elijah and other good men, because in this way fear is instilled in others and the sin of the offenders is diminished. Hence Christ did not rebuke this example of Elijah in his disciples, but because they desired the vengeance of fire against those who had not offered them lodging out of hatred rather than love of correction. Peter too is read to have taken vengeance on Ananias and his wife. Or he hands him over so that the Holy Spirit, by whom those who have been defiled are stripped bare, may be saved for them and not lost on the day of judgment.  
[Col. 0527B]

**Verse 6.**—The whole lump. They were participants because they tolerated the guilty person. But if someone lacks the authority to expel a person whom he knows to be guilty, or is unable to prove the charge, he is free from guilt. Nor is it the judge’s role to condemn without an accuser, just as Christ did not cast out Judas.

**Verse 7.**—A kneaded mass. It is flour joined together by water without leaven—that is, unleavened bread. He therefore wants these people to be one through love, pure from the corruption of sin, having put on the new person, just as they were made in baptism. *Zyma* in Greek, *fermentum* in Latin: “leaven.”

Passover is a sacrifice, not a passage, as some think. For first there is Passover, and then passage, because first there is the example of the Savior, and then salvation.

(AUGUSTINE.) This renewal of our life is a kind of passage from death to life, and so forth, continuing until: “because Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.”

**Verse 8.**—Of sincerity. Of new life and truth, without any deceit, so that sincerity may produce a pure life and truth exclude every fraud.

**Verse 10.**—Otherwise, and so forth. They could not win such people for Christ if they avoided their conversation and their meals; hence the Lord also ate with tax collectors and sinners.

**VERSE 11.—“But now.”** Then I wrote to you, and you did not receive it well; but now I am writing specifically. **“Is named.”** The Apostle intended that naming to be understood as that which is brought against anyone together with a sentence, in due judicial procedure, and with integrity. For if any kind of naming were sufficient, many innocent people would have to be condemned, since crimes are often falsely attributed to someone by name. By saying “is named,” he shows that the wicked are not to be removed from communion with the Church rashly or by any means whatsoever, but through judgment; or, if they cannot be removed through judgment, they should rather be tolerated, lest, by perversely avoiding the wicked, someone should depart from the Church and send to Gehenna those whom he appears to be fleeing.

## CHAPTER VI

**VERSE 1.—“Does anyone dare?”** Taking this kind of judgment as his occasion, he begins to discuss judgments, in which the Corinthians were sinning in many ways: for example, they despised the faithful and resorted to unbelieving judges, or appointed foolish judges, and litigated, defrauded, and committed other things of this kind.

**VERSE 2.—“Because.”** Because by the example of their faith such unbelief will be condemned.

**VERSE 4.—“Therefore, secular judgments.”** Since the Apostle had said that they could judge matters of the smallest importance, he determines who should be appointed to settle such affairs—namely, those who are despised within the Church. For the greater ought to devote themselves to spiritual matters.

**(AUG., *On the Work of Monks*, chapter 20.)** “Therefore, the wise men who remained faithful in those places,” etc., up to “or by intervening to cut them short.”

**VERSE 5.—“To your shame.”** Let those who have acquired wisdom in external matters examine earthly cases. But those endowed with spiritual gifts ought not to become entangled in earthly affairs, so that, while they are not compelled to arrange inferior goods, they may be able to serve higher goods. Nevertheless, care must be taken that those who shine with spiritual gifts do not entirely abandon the affairs of their weaker neighbors; rather, they should either entrust them to others who are suited to handle them or manage them personally.

**VERSE 8.—“To the brethren.”** Those whom you ought to help—and thus you lose the kingdom, and worse still because you do so knowingly.

**VERSE 9.—“Or do you not know?”** Notice that he repeats “Do you not know?” so often, as though saying: “By following me, you ought to know this; but by following false apostles, you have become fools.”

**VERSE 11.—“But you have been sanctified.”** Notice that the conjunction “but,” repeated here, gives considerable weight to the statement.

**VERSE 12.—“All things are lawful for me.”** Since he had said that it was preferable to endure wrong rather than to litigate wrongly, lest anyone should think that he should in no way reclaim what was his, he adds: “I am permitted to reclaim all my possessions, but I will not reclaim them, because not everything is beneficial for my course; rather, such things hinder it.” Likewise, he demonstrates the same point by another argument, as though saying: “They are lawful, but I will not reclaim them, because, although I am free, I do not wish to be brought under the power of a judge; or I do not wish to be under the domination of anything, so that I might offend a brother on its account.”

**VERSE 13.—“Food is for the stomach.”** On account of these considerations, such things should not be reclaimed; nevertheless, food is owed to the stomach. By this he indicates things necessary to nature, and therefore lawful to reclaim. But one should not labor greatly for them, because they will be destroyed; therefore judgment may be made concerning them, or they may be disregarded.

**VERSE 15.—“Bodies.”** The body used by the sanctified Spirit cannot fail to be holy. **“They are members,”** etc. Just as all the members governed by one and the same soul constitute one body, so all who are given life by the same Holy Spirit become one body in Christ. **“Of Christ.”** Because he received a body and is the head of bodies.

**VERSE 16.—“One body.”** Physicians report that these are united to such an extent that, if their blood were mingled, they would be completely joined together.

**VERSE 17.—“But whoever is joined,”** etc. Not by identity of substance but by participation: he approaches and clings to him through faith in such a way that he becomes a sharer in his blessedness. This will then be complete when his desire is satisfied with immutable goods—namely, in the Trinity itself, his Lord, whose image he is.

**VERSE 18.—“Flee fornication.”** With other vices, conflict may be awaited; but this one you must flee, so that you do not approach it, because it cannot otherwise be overcome more effectively. **“For every sin.”** No sin so dishonors and defiles the body as that one does. **“But whoever commits fornication.”** This is not said on account of the magnitude of fornication, as though it alone were in the body and other sins outside the body. Many other sins are just as great as fornication, or greater. Rather, it is said on account of its quality, because it defiles the body more shamefully than other sins.

**VERSE 19.—“A temple.”** From this it is clear that the Holy Spirit is God. For if he were not God, we would certainly not be his temple. Yet not only the Holy Spirit, but also the Father and the Son have us as their temple. Therefore the temple of God—that is, of the whole Trinity—is the holy Church.

**VERSE 20.—“And glorify God.”** To glorify God is to display the image of God through good actions. **“In your body.”** If you do not spare yourself for your own sake, spare yourself at least for God’s sake, who made you his dwelling. If you overthrow it, you sin against God, which is a grave kind of sin; another kind is sinning against a human being.

## CHAPTER VII

**VERSE 1.—“Concerning the matters.”** Taking as his occasion the fornication that he forbids, he continues with marriage, about which they had asked him. He treats it in three ways: according to counsel, according to concession, and according to command.

**VERSE 6.—“But this,”** etc. Someone might say: “If the Apostle granted this as a concession, then marriage is a sin; for to whom is a concession granted except to a sinner?” Clearly, when the Apostle granted this concession to weakness, he was referring to the intercourse of married people, where there is the evil of lack of self-control. The evil of lack of self-control is that a man knows his wife even beyond the necessity of begetting children; yet even there there is the good of marriage. For the fact that there is an evil of lack of self-control does not mean that the marital union, when it goes beyond the intention of procreation, is not good. Indeed, this good is not culpable because of that evil; rather, that evil becomes venial because of the marital good. The Apostle does not condemn this good of marriage, but the evil of lack of self-control. Intercourse necessary for procreation is without blame, and it alone is properly marital. But the intercourse that advances beyond necessity serves not reason but lust.

**VERSE 7.—“Let each one,”** etc. No one should be compelled, lest, being forbidden what is lawful, he admit what is unlawful; rather, let each person choose what he should pursue. Nevertheless, it is better to be more inclined toward this state.

**VERSE 9.—“To burn”** means to be driven or overcome by desires. Therefore he does not say that it is better as though burning were good and marrying better; he has followed the customary expression.

**VERSE 11.—“But if she departs.”** To depart is one thing; to abstain by mutual agreement is another. The former is evil; the latter is good.

**(AMBR.)** For this reason he does not add anything about the husband as he does about the wife: it is permitted to a husband to take another wife, because the inferior party does not altogether come under this law; the phrase “the superior,” however, is said to have been added by falsifiers [the text is corrupt].

**“And the husband must not.”** A husband ought not dismiss his wife, because he would cause her to commit adultery. But if she is an adulteress, he does not cause her to commit adultery; rather, he dismisses an adulteress. The reason that Christ excepted is passed over here because it is well known, namely, fornication.

**VERSE 12.—“But to the rest.”** Where both parties are faithful, the Apostle gives this command of the Lord. But to the rest, where both are not faithful—which happened at the beginning of the Church, when the Gospel began to be preached—“I say,” etc. **“If any brother,”** etc. Idolatry and every harmful superstition are fornication. The Lord permitted a wife to be dismissed on account of fornication, but he did not command it; thus he left the Apostle room to advise that whoever wished should not dismiss an unbelieving spouse, since that person might perhaps become faithful.

**VERSE 14.—“Has been sanctified.”** This often happens: one person is converted to the faith through the other. Or the unbelieving husband is clean with respect to the believing wife, and the believing wife suffers no uncleanness from her union with him. **“Otherwise.”** If you dismiss one another, refusing to live together and joining yourselves to others, you are adulterers, and your children are illegitimate and therefore unclean. But now they are holy, because they are born from lawful marriages and under reverence for the Creator.

**VERSE 15.—“For not.”** A marriage without devotion to God is not fully a marriage; therefore the person who dismisses a spouse for God’s sake does not sin if that spouse has joined himself or herself to another. But if both have believed, the marriage is confirmed through knowledge of God. **“In peace.”** One ought not quarrel with the person who departs, because that person departs through hatred of God.

**VERSE 16.—“For how do you know?”** Above, he exhorted them by means of what had already happened; now, because the same things may happen again, he exhorts them to the same course. These things are done not by command of the law but through free love.

**VERSE 17.—“The Lord has assigned.”** God has given each person the time at which he will be saved—that is, he knows when each will believe and sustains him until he believes. So you too should wait.

**VERSE 18.—“Was anyone circumcised?”** The Apostle nowhere removes a custom that, when observed, does not hinder salvation. He warns that hope of salvation should not be placed in such matters, since they are observed only for the sake of avoiding offense to the weak. Hence he says that they are nothing, adding: “Circumcision is nothing.”

**VERSE 20.—“Let each one remain in the condition.”** This concerns those conditions or ways of life that do not harm faith and good morals. For just as a married person is called to the faith of Christ, so also is a thief. But the former remains in marriage, not away from marriage; the latter is called not in theft but away from theft. It is not necessary for married people to cease being married on account of the faith of Christ, just as it is necessary for thieves to cease being thieves.

**VERSE 21.—“A slave,”** etc. Above he gave one example concerning a manner of life; here he gives another concerning a condition of service. **“Use it rather.”** The more despised a person is in this world for God’s sake, the more he will be exalted in the future.

**VERSE 22.—“A freedman.”** Because he has been rescued from sins, which make people slaves. Therefore neither should a slave be despised because of his condition, nor should a freedman who has been rescued exalt himself and place himself above a slave.

**VERSE 23.—“You were bought.”** Repay the favor, so that you may be servants of Christ, not of human beings. Those are servants of human beings who subject themselves to human superstitions. **“Servants of human beings.”** This happens to you if you say, “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” and so on.

**VERSE 25.—“Concerning virgins.”** Taking the case of that fornicator as his occasion, he teaches concerning the avoidance of every kind of fornication.

**VERSE 26.—** By “necessity” he means the poverty of this world, which married people often suffer. To the weak he offers a weak argument. For he could have given a more worthy account of virginity by commending its excellence more fully. Virginity surpasses the condition of human nature, by which human beings are made like angels. Yet the victory of virgins is greater than that of angels. Angels live without flesh, but virgins triumph in the flesh.

**VERSE 29.—“This therefore I say.”** Here he exhorts them to self-restraint, as though saying: “When you marry, so that this may be done without sin, I give you this counsel: let those who have be as though they did not have.” He does this who, having a wife, pays the marital debt and does not demand it; who takes a wife because of his own weakness, grieving rather that he could not remain without a wife than rejoicing that he married, and especially when they preserve abstinence by mutual agreement. Those marriages should certainly be pronounced more blessed which, whether after begetting children or after renouncing offspring, have been able by mutual agreement to preserve abstinence.

**VERSE 34.—“She is concerned,”** etc. Since she does not fear condemnation and is secure regarding salvation, she thinks only about the things of the Lord. **“That she may be holy,”** etc. A married woman does this too, but an unmarried woman does it more fully: being free from worldly necessities, by which a married woman is bound, she devotes herself more intensely to heavenly commandments.

**VERSE 35.—“Not as a snare.”** Rather, I am aiming at what is honorable: that a person may be chaste in body and spirit. This is not because marriage is shameful, but because this state is more honorable and offers greater freedom to pray to God.

**VERSE 36.—“But if anyone,”** etc. Just as he made a determination concerning virgins, so he makes one concerning their guardians.

**VERSE 38.—“He does better.”** Because he assigns her merit before God and frees her from worldly anxiety. Therefore he rightly says: “For it is better to do what is lawful and beneficial than what is lawful and not beneficial.”

**VERSE 39.—“A woman is bound.”** He had said that a woman who leaves her husband because of fornication should remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband, but he had not said whether she should remain so for her entire lifetime or only for the lifetime of her husband. He therefore determines this point. Thus a virgin may always marry whom she wishes; but a woman—that is, a married woman—even if dismissed and separated from her husband because of fornication, is bound by the law while her husband lives, etc. **“But if he has fallen asleep.”** He does not say whether it is the first, second, or subsequent marriage; for we ought not define what the Apostle does not define. Therefore I must neither condemn any marriages nor impose shame upon them because of their number. The Lord does not condemn a woman married seven times, nor does he say that such a woman cannot be in the resurrection. He says only: “They neither marry nor are given in marriage.” Therefore I do not dare to say, contrary to the sense of human modesty, that they may marry as often as they wish, nor do I condemn from my heart any marriages whatsoever. What is said of women married once applies to every widow.

**VERSE 40.—“Happier,”** etc. He clearly shows that a faithful woman who marries again after her husband’s death is blessed, but that she is happier if she does not marry. **“I think, however.”** The Apostle does not doubt, but rebukes those who despise him, just as the Lord does when he says: “If you knew me, perhaps you would know my Father also”; or, “Do you suppose that he will find faith on earth?” By using a word of doubt, he reproves unbelief.

## CHAPTER VIII

**VERSE 1.—“Concerning these things.”** As though he were saying: “You know as well as I do that it is lawful to eat them, because we all possess knowledge.” He says this concerning those who, possessing knowledge, ate with offense to others. He first reproves them and says that they do not possess knowledge sufficiently. Others, however, who were ignorant, ate under the worship of the idol.

**“Knowledge puffs up.”** Knowledge is useless in itself, but useful when joined to love. In itself it puffs one up into pride, like the demons, who are named in Greek from knowledge: *daimones*. To restrain the arrogance of knowledge, a goad was given to Paul. It is better to know our weakness than the natures of things; whoever adds this knowledge adds the sorrow of pilgrimage arising from desire for the homeland.

**VERSE 3.—“But if anyone loves God.”** He loves God who, for the sake of love, moderates knowledge so that it may benefit the brother for whom Christ died.

**VERSE 4.—“Concerning foods.”** Having criticized their knowledge, he finally discloses what true knowledge is. **“An idol is nothing in the world.”** That is, among the creatures of the world. God formed the material, but human folly gave it its form. For whatever exists among creatures was made through the Word. But the human form in an idol was not made through the Word, just as sin was not made through the Word. Therefore it is nothing, and human beings become nothing when they sin. **“Except one.”** He says this so that no one may suppose that God is in an idol.

**VERSE 5.—“For although there are many gods.”** That is, many among the nations: our God terrifies them—namely, the demons, who, wishing to appear to be gods, demand for themselves what is owed to the true God: altars, sacrifices, and other things. But our God makes human beings into gods.

**VERSE 6.—“God.”** God is spoken of in three ways. He is called God substantially: the Trinity. He is called God adoptively: the saints, who are gods by the grace of adoption. He is called God nominally: demons and idols. **“From whom.”** All things were created from the Father but through the Son. It is not that some things were created through the Son and others through the Father, but the same things through both; otherwise not all things would be through the Father, nor all things through the Son. But if all things are through the Father and all things are through the Son, then the same things were made through the Father as through the Son. Therefore the Son is equal to the Father, and the operation of both is inseparable. **“And one.”** He adds this concerning Christ according to his humanity; it was not necessary to add it concerning the Holy Spirit.

**VERSE 7.—“Is defiled.”** This occurs through those who possess knowledge of the one God but not together with love. Through them the weak were led into this error; it is not their food that is defiled, but their conscience.

**VERSE 12.—“Against Christ.”** To sin against Christ is to deny Christ.

## CHAPTER IX

**VERSE 1.—“Am I not free?”** He begins to set himself forward as an example, so that just as he himself abstains from lawful things for fear of offending the brethren, so they may do likewise. As though he were saying: “Abstain from this lawful thing, because I have the freedom to receive support, and yet I do not receive it.” Although this is the immediate point, he also intends to prove himself an apostle, because the Corinthians had formed a diminished opinion of him on account of the false apostles.

**VERSE 4.—“Do we not have,”** etc. **(BEDA.)** “For the Lord permitted it, he did not command it,” etc., up to “therefore it is the Lord’s permission, not his command, to receive expenses.”

**“A believing sister as a wife.”** The Lord had women in his company so that they would not appear to be excluded from salvation; they also ministered to him. The apostles did the same.

**VERSE 6.—“To work.”** The expression “to work” is more honorable than “to receive.”

**VERSE 7.—“Who serves as a soldier?”** Lest, because he abstains, he should appear to have reproved his fellow apostles, he adds: “Who serves as a soldier?”

**(CHRYS.)** “Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit?” By the first example he shows dangers; by this one he shows great labor, misery, and care; and he adds a third example in these words.

**“Who feeds a flock,”** etc. **(ID.)** He displays the great diligence owed by a teacher toward those under him. This is clear from the following: the apostles were soldiers, farmers, and shepherds—not of wars, earth, or irrational animals, but of rational souls and of that army which is armed against demons. **“And from the milk.”** The milk of the flock means whatever is given by the people to their leaders.

**VERSE 8.—“Do we not,”** etc. **(ID.)** This means: “Do I confirm my case merely by human examples? Or does the law not say this as well?”

**VERSE 9.—“Is it about oxen?”** They are indeed a matter of concern, but not in such a way that he should establish a law concerning them.

**VERSE 12.—“So that there may be no obstacle.”** That is, so that it may not be said of us that we preach the Gospel for the sake of gain and temporal profit rather than for the salvation of souls and eternal reward, and that the Gospel is being treated as merchandise.

**VERSE 13.—“Do you not know?”** He returns again to what he had begun, showing that it is lawful for him, yet that he does not do it. Natural reason also teaches that a person should live from the place where he labors.

**VERSE 15.—“But I.”** The Apostle abstains from receiving support so that he may not become an example to the rapacious false apostles.

**“It is good,”** etc. For whoever does not wish to use what is owed to him contributes more to the Church. Thus the Apostle had the greatest glory before God: he did not demand support from the weak but obtained his daily livelihood through his own labors. **“Glory.”** The glory I have before God by showing compassion to the weak.

**VERSE 16.—“For if,”** etc. **“For a reward.”** Or, if I preach in this way, I have no glory, because then I would be doing it out of necessity, since “woe”—that is, poverty—would be present, as with the false apostles. **“Necessity.”** The necessity of sustaining this life. **“Woe.”** Because I have nothing from which to live.

**VERSE 17.—“For if willingly.”** Since reward comes from willingness, let us see how: namely, if I do this out of such love that I prefer to suffer poverty rather than abuse my authority. **“But if unwillingly.”** If I benefit others because I am compelled by necessity, it will benefit them, not me. **“A stewardship has been entrusted to me.”** Here stewardship is understood in the sense that a servant administers another person’s revenue, receiving nothing himself except provisions. Elsewhere he is called a steward who, as a son, ministers the Gospel to fellow heirs. We ought not to preach so that we may eat; rather, we ought to eat so that we may preach, so that food may not be the good that is desired but the necessity that is added.

**VERSE 19.—“From all.”** From the affairs of human beings, taking nothing from them. **“Of all,”** with “people” understood: I made myself the servant of all, supporting everyone, just as a good steward supports the weak—especially you, Corinthians—through my patience. I did this not through the cleverness of trickery, but through compassionate affection, so that I might win more people for Christ.

**VERSE 20.—“As a Jew.”** **(HIER.)** Not truly a Jew, just as he was not truly a Gentile, in matters of food, etc., up to “how he would wish to be served if he were sick.”

**VERSE 21.—“To those under the law,”** etc. To the Samaritans, who accept the books of Moses, though the Jews have no dealings with them. They are descended from the Persians; after Israel had been removed, the king of the Assyrians—or of the Persians—placed them in order to inhabit the regions of Samaria.

**VERSE 22.—“All things to all.”** He yielded to everyone, but he did not go beyond religion.

**VERSE 24.—“Do you not know,”** etc. He shows how great is the usefulness of our law, in which the palm is promised not to one person but to all; the one who arrives first waits to be crowned together with the one who arrives later. **“The prize.”** This is the reward of the race.

**VERSE 25.—“Everyone who,”** etc. Many comparisons are drawn from things that are not themselves praiseworthy, as in the Gospel from the unjust judge who did not want to hear the widow, and from the lazy man who lent bread not out of friendship but out of annoyance. Likewise here, athletic contests and games are not being commended.

**VERSE 26.—“Not as though.”** The person who does such things runs into uncertainty, so that he can hope on the basis of some things and despair on the basis of others.

**VERSE 27.—“I discipline my body.”** The Apostle frightened us by his own fear. For what will the lamb do when the ram trembles? **“Lest perhaps,”** etc. This could happen quickly; therefore others should be more careful, lest by giving offense they become rejected.

## CHAPTER X

**VERSE 1.—“For I do not want.”** Whoever wishes to attain the goal must act in this way. Baptism and the sacraments are not sufficient, as some think; nor did God’s benefits profit the Jews when they later sinned. **“Our fathers.”** By the example of the Jews, who offended through their negligence, he makes them vigilant. **“Under the cloud.”** Because all those things happened to them as figures of us.

**VERSE 2.—“Baptized into Moses.”** They were purified under Moses’ leadership through those visible signs. Or they received a sign of baptism, which had the same effect for believers. They were baptized because they were delivered from death and through it cleansed from ignorance of God, which oppressed all the nations, and prepared to receive the law. Or they are called baptized because they bore the form of our sacrament. Moses signifies Christ, the cloud the Holy Spirit, and the sea baptism.

**VERSE 3.—“The same food.”** That is, the same in faith, though different in time and different in form. **“Spiritual.”** That is, signifying something spiritual. By calling it spiritual, he shows that it is to be understood spiritually in Christ, and he intimates this concerning all the elements while explaining one: “The rock was Christ.”

**VERSE 4.—“The rock following them.”** That is, satisfying their desire, because wherever they went, overflowing waters followed them; so Christ accompanies his own in the wilderness of this world. Or “following,” that is, signifying the truth that would follow. **“But the rock.”** It is customary for a thing that is signified to be named by the name of the thing it signifies. **“The rock.”** That is, Christ, followed them because, whenever human assistance failed, he was present.

**VERSE 7.—“Nor idolaters,”** etc. He touches upon those who feasted in an idol temple, thinking themselves free from guilt. **“The people sat down.”** By recalling their example, he points out what exists among the Corinthians, showing how severely such things were punished among the Jews. **“To play.”** That is, to worship, because it resembles children’s play. Childhood is naturally inclined to play. What is more like children’s play than worshiping idols?

**VERSE 9.—“Nor let us test Christ.”** Notice that Christ is the God whom the Jews tested, and therefore they perished from the serpents until the bronze serpent was raised up; those who looked at it were healed from the bites.

**VERSE 10.—“As a figure.”** Here he shows why those signs are no longer observed: since the reality has become manifest for our correction.

**VERSE 11.—“They were written.”** They were not written for us alone. Through these examples we are summoned to a more corrected life, so that, if obedient, we may deserve a reward, or, if disobedient, a more severe punishment. **“The ends of the ages.”** Because we are in the final age, and we ought to be corrected all the more by the many examples of those who came before. Or, the ends of the age have come upon us: worldliness is coming to an end in us, and therefore it is more shameful if we sin.

**VERSE 12.—“Let him who thinks he stands take care lest he fall.”** This applies to those who, presuming on their knowledge, ate sacrificial food with offense to their brethren, and, boasting about the false apostles, judged the Apostle even though they themselves were guilty.

**VERSE 13.—“Temptation has seized you,”** etc. He urges that they be subject to human temptation and no other. Human temptation is this: that, in necessity or distress, a person does not lose confidence in God while seeking human help. Therefore to suffer for Christ is a human temptation, through which one progresses before God.

**“You may be able to endure.”** This comes through humility. For he guards the humble in every temptation, so that those who do not possess the wind of pride do not crack in the furnace.

**VERSE 14.—“Therefore,”** etc. Since sacraments alone do not save, since the one who falls is punished, and since God’s help is not lacking, flee from the worship of idols. Or, let those who are knowledgeable not eat sacrificial food with offense to the weak, to whom they would appear idolaters. Or, let the weak themselves not become idolaters; and when I tell you to flee, I am speaking of something profound, as to the prudent, and therefore judge carefully. Or, now I am speaking to the weak, as above to the prudent.

**VERSE 16.—“The cup of blessing.”** Therefore one must flee the worship of idols, because just as the person who eats sacrificial food becomes one with the demon, so through the body of Christ one becomes one with Christ.

**“The bread that we break.”** **(BEDA.)** When Christ is eaten, life is eaten. But who would dare, etc., up to “he remained whole with the Father, so that he might feed the angels.”

**VERSE 17.—“Because there is one,”** etc. One bread through the unity of faith, hope, and love. It is the body through the administration of love, because we are one and ought to have one mind. He says this so that one faith may have one understanding and one work.

**VERSE 18.—“Consider.”** This is a comparison for understanding what was said above. He added “according to the flesh” because there is also an Israel according to the spirit: those who no longer follow the ancient shadows but the truth that follows—the truth signified beforehand by those shadows—and who offer to God in the body of Christ a sacrifice of praise, from which the God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting.

**VERSE 19.—“What then?”** Since I said, “Flee from the worship of idols,” I may seem to be saying that something great was sacrificed to idols. But this is not what I am saying. Rather, I say that what the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons, because the devil is worshiped in the idol—and he is worse than the idol.

**VERSE 20.—“To become partners of demons.”** **(AUG., *On Christian Doctrine*, book II, chapters 20–21, etc.)** Consultations and agreements also belong to this category, etc., up to “those who attempt to predict the outcomes of actions are called astrologers.”

**VERSE 22.—“Are we provoking the Lord to jealousy?”** Those who eat with offense to their brethren appear to vie with and envy the Lord, whose kingdom they diminish.

**VERSE 23.—“All things are lawful for me.”** By the power of free choice and the teaching of natural law. This does not mean that everything, including unlawful things, is permitted; but let us suppose that everything is permitted.

**VERSE 25.—“Everything that is sold in the market.”** Since such things are lawful, yet should not always be used, he determines how it is permissible to eat or not to eat them.

**VERSE 28.—“On account of that person.”** Because the person who serves idols will boast through this and be confirmed in his error, while a bad example is given to the brethren.

**VERSE 29.—“For why,”** then? As though saying: “What need is there for me to be thought to eat for the sake of reverence? For I am judged not to differ from an idolater.”

**VERSE 31.—“Therefore, whether you eat.”** Therefore let not only your voice resound with the praises of God, but let your actions also agree with your voice. When you sing with your voice, your life will at some point be silent. But sing in such a way that you never become silent. If you cry out with your mouth while thinking deceitfully, you have fallen silent in the praise of God; and, what is more serious, you have proceeded into blasphemy. When God is praised because of your good work, you praise God; and when God is blasphemed because of your evil work, you blaspheme God. Therefore, if you take food and drink for the refreshment of the body and the restoration of the limbs, giving thanks to him who has granted you these supports and consolations for your mortal and fragile condition, your food and drink praise God. But if you exceed the measure owed to nature through excessive greed and gorge yourself with drunkenness, however many praises of God your tongue may utter, your life blasphemes.

**VERSE 32.—“The Church of God.”** This refers to the weak, who are offended when, by your example, they cling to things hostile to God.

**VERSE 33.—“I please everyone.”** Whoever pleases people for the sake of truth is no longer pleasing them personally; rather, truth pleases them. If a person pleases for his own sake, that is pride. This is what he says elsewhere: “If I were pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ” (*Galatians* 1). But did he please his persecutors? He pleased every kind of person whom he gathered into the Church of Christ, whether those already within it or those who were to be brought into it.

## CHAPTER XI

**VERSE 1.—“Imitate.”** There are ranks in the Church, of greater and lesser, so that the former may go before by example and the latter follow by imitation. But those who go before will also err if they follow no one; therefore they follow someone—namely, Christ.

**VERSE 2.—“I praise you,”** etc. Here he begins to discuss veils, in which he reproves them for not observing his traditions: some of their men prayed or prophesied with covered heads, while some women did so with uncovered heads. Therefore the Apostle is angry with them, because, although he was their Apostle, they were forgetful of his traditions. It is as though he were saying: “Although I blame you for other things, I praise you for this”—an irony.

**VERSE 3.—“The man,”** etc. Here “man” may be understood as the spirit—not the Holy Spirit, who remains immutable with the Father and the Son and is given immutably to worthy souls, but the human spirit, which, like the husband of the soul, governs the animal affection as a wife. **“Christ is the head.”** The human spirit is governed by the wisdom of God, which is Christ. In Christ, as in the head, are all spiritual senses—that is, the fullness of graces—from which this man receives. Through this the man is the head of the woman, that is, the ruler of the animal nature, which is governed by the spirit as a woman is governed by a man.

**“Praying.”** In other circumstances he may veil himself; but here he presents himself to his judge and enters into conversation with him, where it is necessary for him to acknowledge his condition.

**VERSE 7.—“Since he is the image.”** “Image” and “likeness” are used interchangeably, but properly speaking the soul’s likeness to God consists in this: that it is unbounded, wholly and simultaneously everywhere.

**(AUG., *On the Trinity*, book XII, chapters 7–9.)** A human being is called the image of God and made according to the image, because he is not equal, etc., up to “so that those who live wickedly may conceal their shame by speaking well.”

**VERSE 11.—“Nevertheless.”** Although in the first creation the man is not from the woman but the woman from the man, this is not so in the subsequent generation. **“In the Lord.”** That is, in the Lord’s operation, in which neither is created without the other.

**VERSE 12.—“But all things.”** After speaking of each separately, in order to subject all things to one God as their single source, he adds that all things are from God, so that neither should the woman grieve over her subjection nor the man become proud of his exaltation.

**VERSE 13.—“Judge for yourselves.”** Because the Corinthians had not observed his tradition—for which he rebukes them—he now persuades them not by the authority of tradition but by nature. Nature teaches us that if a man grows his hair, etc. Hair is a woman’s glory because she naturally has it as a veil; hair is an indication of a veil, so that the will of nature may be supplemented. Therefore a man is not naturally long-haired, because he is not to be veiled, and the law forbids a man to wear long hair.

**VERSE 14.—“If he wears long hair,”** etc. The long hair of Samuel and the prophets, serving as a veil of the Old Law, is removed at the revelation of the Gospel. Therefore, when you pass over to Christ, the veil will be taken away.

**VERSE 17.—“But in giving this instruction.”** What is required is not the skill of one who abandons the matter, but attention to the authority of the one who commands. **“I do not praise you.”** He begins to speak about the Lord’s Supper, in which they were sinning greatly.

**VERSE 19.—“There must also be factions,”** etc. The Apostle neither wants nor desires there to be factions, but because it will happen, he says so. He then adds what benefit this has: not only will the rejected—those who say, “I belong to Paul”—be made manifest, but also those who are approved. He calls “factions” those who doubt the resurrection. There were divisions concerning spiritual gifts, and these, through their own evil, benefit Catholics. For all the enemies of the Church, whether blinded by error or corrupted by malice, benefit the Church. If they receive power to afflict it bodily, they exercise its patience; if they oppose it through holding evil opinions, they exercise its wisdom.

**VERSE 20.—“The Lord’s Supper.”** He calls the reception of the Eucharist the Lord’s Supper. They ought not to receive it after eating or mingle it with their ordinary meals, as those whom the Apostle rebukes did, but should receive it fasting, in honor of so great a sacrament. Although he gave his body and blood to his disciples after supper, the universal Church should not therefore be criticized for always receiving it while fasting. For the Savior, wishing to commend the greatness of this mystery all the more forcefully, wanted to impress this final act upon their hearts and memory. The order in which it was thereafter to be received he left to be taught by the apostles, through whom he was going to organize the churches.

**VERSE 21.—“For each one,”** etc. He is referring to those who, after completing the sacrifice, took back for themselves the offerings they had brought to the altars for the sacrifice and did not allow them to be shared with others who had nothing, but consumed them alone, so that they even became drunk while others were hungry.

**(AMBR.)** The offering that has been made becomes the possession of the whole people, etc., up to “he repeats the form given by Christ in such matters.”

**VERSE 22.—“The Church.”** The Church consists of the faithful, concerning whom it is said: “That he might present the Church to himself in glory.” Yet the Apostle also testifies that the house of prayer itself is called by this name when he says, “Or do you despise the Church of God,” etc. **“Do I praise you?”** Or distinguish it in this way: “Do I praise you in this?” Certainly I do not praise you.

### Verse 23

Source column references: 1 Cor. 11:24 [Col. 0539C], 29 [Col. 0539D], 32 [Col. 0540A]; ch. 12:1 [Col. 0540B], 3 [Col. 0540C], 6 [Col. 0540D], 8 [Col. 0541A], 11 [Col. 0541B], 13 [Col. 0541C], 17 [Col. 0541D], 23 [Col. 0542A], 25 [Col. 0542B], 28 [Col. 0542C], 31 [Col. 0542D]; ch. 13:2 [Col. 0543A], 4 [Col. 0543B], 8 [Col. 0543C], 12 [Col. 0543D]; ch. 14:6 [Col. 0544A], 7 [Col. 0544B], 14 [Col. 0544C], 16 [Col. 0544D], 21 [Col. 0545A], 26 [Col. 0545B], 29 [Col. 0545C], 37 [Col. 0545D]; ch. 15:2 [Col. 0546A], 8–9 [Col. 0546B], 14 [Col. 0546C], 21 [Col. 0546D], 24 [Col. 0547A], 25 [Col. 0547B], 27 [Col. 0547C], 29 [Col. 0547D], 32 [Col. 0548A], 34 [Col. 0548B], 36 [Col. 0548C], 39 [Col. 0548D], 42 [Col. 0549A], 44 [Col. 0549B], 45 [Col. 0549C], 50 [Col. 0549D], 51 [Col. 0550A]; ch. 16:1 [Col. 0550C], 6 [Col. 0550D]; introduction to 2 Corinthians [Col. 0551, 0551A].

“For I received…” He shows that the mystery of the Eucharist was celebrated during the meal but was not itself a meal. For it is spiritual medicine and a memorial of redemption, so that we may obtain greater things, because we have been set free by Christ’s death. In eating and drinking this, we ought to remember him, having thereby received the New Testament, because the blood is the witness of the divine benefit; hence we receive it for the protection of body and soul: Christ’s flesh for the salvation of the body, and his blood for our soul. Therefore the Law previously forbade the eating of blood. “On the night…” He suffered during the night and came to the light of the resurrection.

### Verse 24

“He broke it.” That is, in the sacrament, according to what was seen and was believed by the faithful to remain whole. He gave one portion to all, so that they might remain in unity; but when he broke it, he showed his voluntary suffering.

### Verse 26

“Whenever…” He explains what remembrance of Christ is intended: namely, remembrance of his death. “Until he comes.” For this will not be changed, as the sacraments of the Jews were.

### Verse 27

“Unworthily.” It is not because someone eats without attaining salvation that what he receives is any less the body and blood.

### Verse 29

“Eats judgment upon himself.” It is asked how this can be so, when the Lord says: “Whoever eats me will live because of me.” But there are two ways of eating: one sacramental, by which both the good and the wicked eat; the other spiritual, by which only the good eat. And this is not merely to eat Christ and receive his body in the sacrament, but to remain in him and have him remain in oneself. For the one who eats spiritually is the person who remains in the unity of the Church, which the sacrament itself signifies. Whoever is at variance with Christ neither eats Christ’s flesh nor drinks his blood, even though he may daily receive the sacrament of so great a reality to his condemnation.

### Verse 30

“Therefore among you…” This happens for the correction of others.

### Verse 32

“While we are judged…” For those who suffer, their own punishment is sometimes also a purification, as in the case of the prophet Addo, who ate what he had been forbidden to eat. He was able, while alive, to be terrified or grieved by what he would not have felt after death. For it was said to him: “Your corpse shall not be brought into the tomb of your fathers” (1 Kings 13). Through this the prophet’s disobedience could be punished, lest his soul be carried away to the punishment of Tartarus. “We are chastened.” The correction of all is contained in a few, so that others may be corrected through fear of our punishment.

### Verse 33

“Wait for one another.” So that the offering of many may be celebrated together and served to all.

## Chapter XII

### Verse 1

“Concerning spiritual things.” The Apostle now begins to discuss the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Some were becoming proud because of the greater gifts, while others envied and despised them because of the lesser gifts, as though they themselves would never possess them.

### Verse 2

“You know.” Before handing on spiritual matters, he recalls earlier things, so that just as they were then the image of idols, so now they may be the image of God.

### Verse 3

“Therefore I make known…” Because in the individual charisms they gave greater glory to human beings than to God, not knowing that these gifts were administered by the Holy Spirit, he shows in every case that praise and grace belong to God. Thus, just as then the whole evil of the idol’s image came from human beings, so now all good is to be believed to come from the Spirit of God.

“No one speaking in the Spirit…” That is, by thinking, speaking, and acting. He says this in three ways—namely, in heart, mouth, and deed: “Anathema to Jesus,” that is, some separation from Jesus, meaning any sin. It is as though he said: Through the Spirit one is kept from evil.

“Except in the Holy Spirit.” As though he said: To act well and to do every good thing comes through the Holy Spirit. Therefore the greater person should not despise the lesser, because no one has anything except from the Holy Spirit.

### Verse 4

“Varieties.” This is common to all; but graces are divided so that the lesser person may not despair and the greater person, when he hears of the graces, may not become proud.

### Verse 6

“But it is the same God.” He says this so that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit may not seem to perform different works separately, because he had attributed graces to the Spirit, ministries to the Lord, and works to God. Referring everything to the one God, he adds: “Because God works.” “All things in all.” He does not attribute everything to one person, but works all things in all, so that what someone does not possess in himself he may possess in another, and thus charity and humility may remain.

### Verse 7

“To each one.” The gifts are divided, and they are not given individually for anyone’s merit, but for the benefit of building up the Church. We too have received the Holy Spirit if we love the Church, if we are joined together in charity, and if we rejoice in the catholic name and faith. Let us believe, brothers, that each person possesses the Holy Spirit in proportion to his love for Christ’s Church.

### Verse 8

“Wisdom.” Wisdom consists in the contemplation of eternal things; knowledge consists in action concerning temporal things. Hence in Job: “Behold, piety”—that is, the worship of God—“is wisdom,” which in Greek is *theosebeia* (“godliness” or “worship of God”). And what is his worship except love and knowledge of him? To abstain from evil, however, is knowledge; and evils belong to temporal matters, amid which one must act carefully and prudently.

The person to whom wisdom is given is like the sun; the person to whom knowledge is given is like the moon in the night of this age; those to whom the other gifts are given are like stars, because these are necessary in the night.

### Verse 9

“To another faith.” Faith also belongs among God’s gifts and endowments. Therefore it is not charity alone, but charity together with faith, that comes to us from God.

### Verse 10

“Utterances.” Utterances are allegorical declarations that appear in the Prophets and in the Gospels.

### Verse 11

“One and the same Spirit.” What he previously said was performed by three, here he attributes to the Spirit. Because they are of one nature, what one performs, three perform. “One and the same,” he says, lest they be thought to be as numerous as the works; this does not mean that the Spirit works without the Father and the Son. The operation of the Trinity is inseparable.

“Dividing to each.” Therefore neither should this person grieve nor that person become proud. “As he wills.” He alone knows what is fitting, and he gives freely, not according to human merit.

### Verse 12

“So also is Christ.” Christ is called the head and the body because of the ineffable unity of the head and the members. One Spirit does everything in the members of Christ’s body, just as one soul sees in the eye, hears in the ear, and performs everything in all the other members.

### Verse 13

“For indeed…” He shows how Christ’s body is one: all of us who have been baptized—that is, washed and led by one Spirit—have been brought into this purpose, that we should be one body, that is, of one mind through that one Spirit, so that the whole human body may be animated by one soul.

And because we have all drunk in the reception of the various gifts of the Holy Spirit, we have drunk in one Spirit, because he directs all the gifts toward producing one thing. No person is to be despised or preferred, nor is God’s glory to be given to human beings, because one and the same Spirit works all things in all.

### Verse 14

“For the body also…” Through the likeness of the human body, he shows that the unity of Christ’s body, that is, the Church, possesses a variety and diversity of functions, and that this diversity does not remove unity. The unity of the human body does not consist in singularity but in many members, so that they may render to one another what they owe.

### Verse 17

“If the whole…” It is as though he said: If everyone in the Church had one and the same function, how would the needs of the body be fulfilled, when its governance requires different functions?

### Verse 18

“The members, each one of them, as he willed.” So that nothing might be lacking to it. Thus also in the Church he has established different persons, to whom he has assigned different gifts.

### Verse 19

“But if all were one…” Not only would the multitude of the senses perish, but the body also. So if everyone in the Church had one function and one dignity, the members would not be distinguished, nor would there be a body.

### Verse 21

“Or again, the head to the feet…” Dignity itself is contemptible without those subject to it. For function is what makes dignity stand. A great emperor needs an army.

### Verse 23

“Those that are dishonorable.” Far be it that there should be any disgrace among the members of the saints. They are called “dishonorable” because they do not have the visible appearance of beauty possessed by those members that are publicly displayed.

Alternatively, this may refer to the law of the members that arises from sin: the illicit use of the members is shameful, not the members themselves.

It may also refer to certain brothers who, although honorable, are poor in possessions and clothing, yet are sometimes more upright in life. Or it may refer to those who have become dishonorable in the Church through some sin and are more abundantly assisted with consolations and prayers, so that they may become honorable.

### Verse 24

“But our honorable members…” It is as though he said: In the brothers whose zeal for learning and conduct has been adorned with honor, there is nothing that needs to be added by us. “But God has tempered the body.” Removing what is harmful, he places in its stead what is beneficial, namely, mutual proportion.

### Verse 25

“But [let them be] in the same [concern] for one another.” It is as though he said: Let the members be concerned to strive toward the same thing—that is, toward the same object of care—so that each may care no less for another than for himself.

### Verse 26

“And if one member suffers…” This is plainly true of the members of the body: if the eye or foot is seized by some illness, the whole body suffers with it. So we too ought to suffer with our brothers if any adversity arises, and rejoice if things turn out well.

### Verse 27

“Now you are the body…” “A member” may refer either to Christ or to me, by whose preaching you were instructed.

### Verse 28

“And some indeed…” Here he distinguishes the gifts of God, identifying which are higher and which lower. For the Corinthians thought that what was less was greater and what was greater was less.

“First.” In dignity and time, the apostles, preaching in Christ’s place and judging all.

“Second, prophets.” That is, those revealing the mysteries of Scripture or future events.

“Third, teachers.” Those who give instructions for living, or who instruct children in letters.

“Varieties of tongues.” (CHRYS.) Behold, knowing many languages is a gift of God. And notice that he places last what they were placing first.

### Verse 29

“Are all apostles?…” Whoever does not possess these gifts in himself should love them in others; and in them he already possesses what he does not have in himself.

### Verse 31

“A more excellent way.” Charity, because it is a greater gift than all those mentioned above. Hence at the end, to those who say, “Lord, in your name we prophesied, cast out demons, and performed mighty works,” the Lord will say: “Depart from me; I do not know you, workers of iniquity” (Matthew 7).

## Chapter XIII

### Verse 1

“If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels…” Here he proves that charity is more excellent, because the other gifts are of no value without it, while it is of great benefit without them.

“Charity.” Charity is the proper and singular source of good things, with which the outsider does not share. Like oil, it cannot be pressed down below but rises above; if it is absent, the rest are possessed in vain; if it is present, everything is possessed.

“Like sounding bronze…” Just as bronze resounds only when struck by something and not by itself, so the one who speaks in tongues does not speak by himself, since he does not know what he is saying, but through the power of the Spirit he utters things with which he delights his hearers.

### Verse 2

“And if I have prophecy…” As Balaam, Caiaphas, and Saul did.

“And know mysteries…” As Judas did with the apostles, and the devil, who, as Ezekiel says, knew divine mysteries.

“And knowledge…” As the scribes and Pharisees did, hence: “You have taken away the key of knowledge; you did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering” (Matthew 23).

The wicked certainly possess these things too; they will confess them at the judgment, where they will not dare to lie. They will not be told, “You did not possess them,” but “I do not know you,” because they possessed them without charity.

### Verse 4

“Charity is patient…” These are the weapons with which Christ’s soldier is armed. As the principal weapons of this armor, he placed patience and kindness first.

(ORIG.) Patience bears calmly the evils inflicted by neighbors; kindness desirably bestows its own good things upon neighbors. “It does not envy,” because another’s happiness does not grieve it. “It is not puffed up,” because its own happiness does not exalt it.

### Verse 5

“It does not seek its own…” It is not a lover of money.

### Verse 7

“It believes all things.” He does not say that it believes everyone, because it believes God alone.

“It hopes all things.” This appeared in the fathers, that is, in the people of Israel, who hoped to receive what God promised.

“It endures all things.” This appeared in the Head, that is, in Christ, who patiently awaited the glory of the resurrection and ascension.

### Verse 8

“Charity.” It is more excellent also in this respect: it does not end either in this age or in the age to come, even though some of its works cease. “It never fails.” If we love through believing and hoping what is not yet seen, how much more when it is seen?

### Verse 10

“That which is imperfect will be abolished.” The destruction of imperfection occurs when what is imperfect is brought to complete fulfillment.

### Verse 12

“Now…” Through faith, images of the truth are seen.

“But then face to face.” That is, the realities themselves will be seen openly.

“Then I shall know.” That is, I shall see the promises as he is, namely, as present with God, where Christ is. Or, I shall know in the same way that I have been foreknown to know what is now hidden.

“A mirror.” The soul is a mirror, through which we know God in some manner, but obscurely.

“An enigma.” An enigma is not every allegory, but an obscure allegory. Thus, just as “through a mirror” signifies an image, so by the name “enigma” he understands a likeness, though an obscure one and difficult to grasp.

### Verse 13

“Faith, hope, and charity…” Knowledge and prophecy serve these, without which the life of no righteous person in this age is perfect.

“But the greatest of these is charity.” Charity is such that faith and hope cannot be absent from it, although faith and hope can exist without charity.

## Chapter XIV

### Verse 2

“For the one who speaks in a tongue…” This happened when the person speaking in a tongue did not understand himself, so that he knew the utterance of some language but not its meaning.

### Verse 6

“But now…” I said that the one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in a tongue. In myself you can see that a tongue is of no benefit, whereas prophecy is beneficial.

“But now…” If I come to you now, while you are believers, speaking in tongues, what benefit will I give you? Nothing, he says. What benefit, then, did a tongue give when you were unbelievers? Nothing, he says.

“Either in revelation.” So that I may explain a revelation. Revelation occurs when certain mysteries are shown through figures, as in the Apocalypse.

“Or in knowledge.” So that I may explain matters belonging to knowledge. These are things that illumine faith, such as the nature of the Godhead.

“Or in prophecy.” So that I may explain the Scriptures that concern future things.

“Or in teaching.” So that I may explain the Scriptures that shape conduct.

### Verse 7

“Nevertheless, lifeless things…” Through myself I have shown that a tongue is useless without an interpreter. I say that I have shown this through myself, who am rational; nevertheless, I can show the same thing through lifeless objects.

### Verse 8

“For if it gives an uncertain sound…” Again, he uses another comparison. “For if it gives an uncertain sound…” Among the Jews, trumpets were used at festivals and in war, with different sounds.

### Verse 10

“And there are so many kinds of voices…” There are many languages, but they have their own meanings of words, so that they may be understood.

### Verse 11

“If therefore I do not know…” Since others would not understand without an interpreter, I shall be a barbarian.

### Verse 12

“So also you…” Or under a single division: “So.” And for this reason, so that you may not be barbarians, seek also, as I do, to abound.

### Verse 14

“My spirit prays.” The spirit is called the lower power of the soul, below the mind, where likenesses of bodily things are imprinted. The mind is the soul’s other, higher power, as stated above.

The spirit of Pharaoh was shaped so that he might see images; the mind of Joseph was illumined so that he might understand.

“Without fruit.” This is what happens when someone speaks in an unknown tongue or utters signs of certain things without understanding, as Latin speakers are accustomed to sing in Greek, taking pleasure in the sound of the words while nevertheless not knowing what they are saying.

### Verse 15

“I shall pray with the spirit.” That is, I approve of speaking in such a way that signs of things are formed in the spirit and their understanding shines forth in the mind. Or: “I shall pray with mouth and mind.”

### Verse 16

“Amen.” Note that the word *amen* is neither Greek nor Latin but Hebrew, and it is interpreted as “truly.” Although “truly” could have been said, he nevertheless said *amen*. Neither the Greek nor the Latin translator dared to alter it, lest it become cheapened by being exposed, but so that it might retain the honor of being veiled in secrecy.

### Verse 18

“I thank God…” He offers himself as an example: they ought not to speak in tongues except for edification, just as he does, who knows all languages.

### Verse 20

“But be children in malice.” Be removed from malice like children, applying yourselves to what is beneficial; this is perfection of understanding.

### Verse 21

“In the Law…” The reason why he ought not to seek tongues is that they are a sign for unbelievers, which they are no longer, and not for the edification that believers now require.

“With other tongues…” This does not refer to the Sabbath, new moons, circumcision, or similar matters, but to the New Testament.

Or: not in revelation, of which they are unworthy, but the Gospel is spoken to them in parables.

“And even so they will not listen.” He said this beforehand concerning those whom he foreknew would not believe, for whom the truth is not evident or pleasing because of their sins.

### Verse 22

“Therefore tongues are for a sign…” That is, the words of God in an unknown and foreign language are obscure, so that they may not be seen by the faithless. When they are heard, this is a sign that, because of their faithlessness, it has been made impossible for the hearers to understand. This happens to unbelievers, whose senses are covered; prophecy, not an unknown tongue, is appropriate for believers.

### Verse 23

“If therefore the whole church comes together…” Another reason is given here why they ought not to speak in tongues. It is as though he said: Since tongues are for a sign and not for edification, they ought not to speak in them.

### Verse 26

“What then…” He now begins to determine how tongues are to be used. It is as though he said: Since these things arise from speaking in tongues, what must be done with them? He answers: Use tongues for edification, as all the other things that must be done are also to be used.

“Each one has…” Therefore no one should excuse himself.

“A psalm.” The praise of God through song.

“A teaching.” Spiritual understanding through prudence.

### Verse 27

“Or at most three.” No more than three, lest the one speaking in tongues occupy the entire day and leave no place for the prophets to explain the Scriptures.

### Verse 28

“But let him speak to himself.” The person speaks to himself who is moved to compunction by what he says. And he does this for the honor of God, whom he praises or addresses in prayer.

### Verse 29

“Let two prophets speak.” For the speech of so many people is sufficient, and “in the mouth of two or three every word shall stand.”

### Verse 30

“But if something is revealed to another…” What was not given to the greater is given to the lesser.

### Verse 33

“For God is not a God of disorder.” God would be a God of disorder if he compelled those whom he fills to speak all at once.

“As in all the churches…” Let women be silent, as I teach in all the churches.

### Verse 35

“It is shameful.” For this is contrary to ecclesiastical discipline.

### Verse 37

“If anyone thinks that he is a prophet…” He certainly is not one if he does not recognize that these things are so. For the person who truly is a prophet recognizes them in this way; and the one who is ignorant of these matters will be ignored—that is, rejected.

The little ones, who glory in the cross, may be ignorant of what is discussed with the greatest subtlety, yet they attain glory, because not one of the little ones for whom Christ died will perish.

“Let him acknowledge.” In saying this, he indicates that the words of the epistles are difficult, since he commands that they be recognized by a prophet or spiritual person.

### Verse 38

“But if anyone is ignorant…” If anyone is ignorant of these matters and refuses to believe that they are commands of God, he will be ignored, as in the Gospel: “I do not know you,” that is, “I do not know you to be mine,” or among the predestined.

## Chapter XV

### Verse 2

“Through which also you are saved.” If you retain that Gospel—that is, the resurrection of the dead—in the manner in which I confirmed it to you, namely, through the resurrection of Christ.

“Unless you believed in vain.” This means: if you do not hold to the resurrection of the dead. Faith that is not received under the hope of resurrection is vain.

### Verse 4

“He rose on the third day.” I also said this according to the Scriptures. For Hosea says: “After two days he will revive us; on the third day we shall rise in his sight” (Hosea 6). If the one who died and was buried rose again, do not doubt that the dead who have been buried will rise again.

### Verse 5

“He appeared to Cephas.” He appeared to Cephas before the other men to whom he is read to have appeared in the Gospel; otherwise this would contradict the statement that he first appeared to the women.

### Verses 8–9

“To one born prematurely.” He is called “premature” because he was born outside the proper time, that is, before he should have been born—or because he received the apostleship after the time, later and belatedly, after Christ had already been taken up.

Or he is like one born prematurely because he is the least, whether in time and calling—not in dignity, labor, and preaching.

He truly said this out of humility, and he proves it by saying: “I am not worthy.” Why, then, is he an apostle? “But by the grace of God…” At first, grace alone was involved, since there were no preceding merits except evil ones. But afterward merits begin through grace.

### Verse 10

“More abundantly.” This was fulfilled more fully because he lived by the work of his hands and did not do less for the Gospel. And lest it be thought that human will can accomplish anything without God’s grace, he adds: “Not I, but the grace…”

### Verse 11

“And so you believed.” He rebukes them because, although this faith was evident among all the churches, they had nevertheless departed from it.

### Verse 14

“But if Christ…” Up to this point he has shown that Christ rose. Now, through Christ’s resurrection, he proves the resurrection of the dead. The false apostles denied that Christ had truly suffered, been buried, or risen, and even denied that he had come in the flesh.

### Verse 15

“We are also found…” These and other consequences are introduced so that the Corinthians may be ashamed to follow the error of the false apostles. Such absurdities follow from it, and he himself condemns them. Therefore, lest they remain in this error, he says: “We are found…”

“Against God.” It is perhaps not a lesser but a greater crime for falsehood to be praised in God than for truth to be condemned.

### Verse 17

“And if Christ has not been raised…” If Christ has not risen, Christ remains in death. And if he remains in death, he remains in sin, which is the cause of death. If he is held in sin, he could not forgive your sins. Thus you are still in your sins, which you believed had been forgiven; and so your faith is vain.

### Verse 21

“For since by a man…” Behold the first fruits: man and man, one man unto life and one man unto death; yet that one is merely man, whereas this one is God and man.

### Verse 22

“And just as…” By the word “just as,” both likeness and cause are indicated: just as death came through Adam’s corruption, so life comes through Christ’s Spirit.

### Verse 23

“Each in his own order.” He explains the sequence, treating the matter as certain: the times when it happened and when it will happen, so that the dead may rise.

“Then those who belong to Christ…” Another reading has: “Then those who are Christ’s at his coming,” namely, they will rise.

Thus those who believe in Christ but are less worthy of him will rise later in time and lower in dignity. He explains who belongs to Christ by adding: “Those who believed at his coming…”

### Verse 24

“Then the end.” He introduces this to commend the resurrection, after which the end of the world and the completion of all things will occur.

“When he has abolished…” While the world lasts, angels rule angels, demons rule demons, and human beings rule human beings, either for the benefit of the living or for their deception. But when human beings have been gathered, all precedence among angels and human beings will cease; that disagreement between rulers and subjects will no longer exist.

Then it will be known to all that none of these beings, whether earthly or heavenly, possessed anything from themselves, but received it from the one from whom all things exist.

### Verse 25

“For he must reign…” The meaning is: His kingdom must be manifested for the time being, until all his enemies confess that he reigns. By saying “until,” he excludes a greater manifestation, not a longer continuation of the kingdom.

Hence elsewhere: “Our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy,” and so forth. This does not mean that they will then turn away, but that they will seek nothing more.

### Verse 26

“The last enemy to be destroyed is death.” Among other things, it is clear that Christ also possesses the power to raise the dead, when he adds: “The last enemy to be destroyed is death.”

Christ reigns now, and he will reign then; but finally—that is, after everything else—death will be destroyed, because human beings will no longer be dissolved, as the heretics suppose.

“Last.” Because there will be nothing left to destroy after this mortal nature has put on immortality.

“Enemy.” Either the one against whom we are hostile, or the one that is hostile to us. This is again a commendation of the resurrection.

### Verse 27

“Except the one who subjected all things to him.” Just as he exists from no one, so he cannot in any way be subject to anyone. For he himself is the beginning of all things.
