“So that God may be all.” When he says that every creature has Christ as its head and God is Christ’s head, there will be not merely one God in all things—that is, in the confession of all—but every creature will confess that he is the one from whom all things exist.

### Verse 28

“So that God may be all.” He is the end that he has so often placed above by way of conclusion. He now explains piece by piece what the future consummation will be.

“All things.” Everything that can be desired.

“In all.” In his members, because the reward of virtue will be the one who gave virtue, since God himself will be the source from which they are satisfied.

### Verse 29

“For the dead.” That is, for the removal of sins.

Or, for those who make themselves dead in imitation of Christ’s death: what will they do if they are not going to have life?

“If the dead are not raised at all…” As though Christ himself had not risen? Why are they baptized if sins are not forgiven, if Christ has not risen?

### Verse 31

“By your glory…” Or: “Through your glory.”

“Because of your glory.” Or: “Through your glory.”

Behold, the Apostle swears, so that we may know that truthful swearing is not a sin. Nevertheless, this does not mean that one should swear in doubtful matters; it is safer not to swear than to perjure oneself through the habit of swearing. To swear falsely, however, is a very grave sin.

An oath is not contrary to the commandment: it does not arise from the evil of the one who swears, but from the unbeliever or the weak person who otherwise does not believe.

### Verse 32

“If, according to human judgment…” That is, acting rationally, since it belongs to a human being to believe, not to die like an animal—I fought, that is, I argued.

“Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.” This concerns those who, as though nothing were to come after death, devote themselves only to their bellies like cattle, saying: “Who has come from there? I have not heard the voice of anyone coming from there.”

They are answered: “Fool, if your father rose, would you believe?” The Lord of all has risen, and you do not believe. He wished to die and rise again so that we might all believe in one person and not be deceived by many.

Would you believe a father who would die again, and not believe one who is already immortal—one who, finally, has testimony in heaven, testimony on earth, testimony from the angels, and testimony from the underworld?

### Verse 33

“Do not be deceived…” By the false apostles, who seek a wound from medicine and attempt to twist a bond from the Scriptures, from which they may cast upon you the noose of death.

“Bad company corrupts good morals.” (THEODOR.) Here he called the good “simple,” that is, those who are easily deceived.

### Verse 34

“Awake.” Do not do this, but awaken from the body; and thus you will be righteous.

And afterward: “Do not sin,” by consenting to them, because they are ignorant of God.

### Verse 35

“But someone will say…” Until now he has proved the resurrection of the dead by arguments; now he shows that it can occur through the very nature of things.

It is as though he said: These arguments prove it; nevertheless, someone depraved might speak as though the resurrection of the dead could not occur according to nature.

“And if they rise, with what kind of body?” As though he said: It cannot be anything other than what it is now—that is, subject to suffering and mortal.

The Apostle answers: “Fool”—that is, you who do not pay attention to what you see every day in a grain.

### Verse 36

“Foolish man, what you sow…” Thus what has died will be able to live, and with a better body, so that what you sow may rise in a better form.

### Verse 38

“But God gives…” Just as a bare grain is sown and, by God’s will, rises clothed, as it were, carrying with it much increase, so the dead person will be able to live by God’s power and rise with a better body.

“To each kind of seed.” So also he will restore our ancient bodies, as Job says: “Whom I myself shall see, and not another.”

There will nevertheless be a difference in glory and dignity, although they will be of the same nature. Just as not all flesh has the same dignity, though it comes from the same elements, so also this is what he says:

### Verse 39

“And the same flesh…” Every flesh is a body, but not every body is flesh, as wood is a body.

### Verse 40

“Heavenly bodies.” The bodies of those who rise are heavenly; before they die, they are earthly, because they come from Adam.

And because Christ is heavenly, bodies are called heavenly through him, and are no longer called merely flesh. Because Adam is earthly, earthly bodies are named from him.

### Verse 41

“For star differs from star…” “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places,” even though the same denarius—that is, eternal life—belongs to all.

There is one blessedness, which the righteous receive, but the quality of the recompense differs. Although those who rise will possess unequal brightness, nevertheless God is all in all, because God is charity, and this will come about through charity, so that what each person possesses may belong commonly to all.

### Verse 42

“It is sown…” Although a human being, from conception until dissolution, is in corruption, and afterward swarms with worms, he will nevertheless rise in incorruption.

### Verse 44

“A natural body.” That is, a body that receives nothing from the soul except that it is given sensation through it, as animals do.

“It will rise a spiritual body.” It will pass into the nature of spirit, that is, it will possess certain spiritual qualities, because it will be agile and light and will not require food.

When he said that the body would pass into incorruption, he mentioned corruption so that the greater dignity of the resurrection might be shown.

“If there is a natural body…” Truly it will rise a spiritual body, because if it exists now, it is natural—that is, it certainly exists; at some time it will be spiritual.

For just as we are natural because our carnal father was made into a living soul, so in the resurrection we shall be spiritual, because our spiritual Father was made, in his resurrection, into a life-giving spirit.

### Verse 45

“Man.” The whole human race is, in a certain sense, those two men, the first and the second: born from the first, reborn from the second.

Christ is called Adam because he comes from the same material; he is called the last because no other human being follows him who might be the head or author of the human body.

“But not first the spiritual…” He said that our future bodies would be spiritual. But lest anyone doubt whether a natural body can become spiritual, he proves it by the likeness of Christ. It is as though he said: He was made a life-giving spirit.

But what is spiritual was not first in him; what was natural came first, and afterward what was spiritual. The same can happen to us.

### Verse 47

“The first man…” He truly was first as a living soul, because he was formed from the dust of the earth and was natural and subject to suffering.

“The second man, from heaven…” Since the divine nature was united to human nature, he is therefore heavenly—that is, spiritual in the resurrection.

And because the first father was earthly, all such people are earthly.

“Heavenly.” Christ is called heavenly because he was conceived and born not by human custom but by divine will.

### Verse 50

“Now this I say…” The Jews believed that there would be a future resurrection, but according to the manner of this life, so that people would marry and beget children. Hence some of the Sadducees could not answer concerning the woman who had had seven husbands; they were thinking of the resurrection in a carnal way.

But the Apostle removes this understanding, saying:

“Flesh and blood…” By flesh and blood he signifies the belly and lust, that is, the works of the flesh, which will not exist there.

“Nor will corruption possess incorruption.” Lest you think that this is said according to the substance of the flesh, he makes the matter clear. He therefore said that flesh would not possess the kingdom of God because the corruption of mortality, which is indicated here by the name “flesh,” will not possess incorruptibility.

### Verse 51

“All indeed…” Or, according to Jerome, who asserts in his letter to Marcella that those found alive will not die: all the dead will rise, but not all who are found alive will be changed—only the saints will be.

### Verse 52

“At the last…” That is, at the last sign, which will be given so that these things may be fulfilled.

This trumpet is the cry of which it is said: “At midnight there was a cry: Behold, the bridegroom is coming.” By the name “trumpet” some evident and glorious sign is meant. Elsewhere it is called the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God; in the Gospel it is called the voice that the dead in the tombs will hear, and they will come forth.

“We shall be changed.” He explains how this will happen, or what kind of change it will be.

### Verse 54

“Death has been swallowed up.” That is, it has been destroyed in Christ’s victory; or, death exceeded the usual manner of conquering by attacking Christ.

Alternatively, death is the delight of sin together with consent, and it has been swallowed up because God’s servants will conquer the desires of their flesh.

### Verse 55

“Where is your victory, O death?” These are the words of the prophet—or of the Apostle rejoicing and mocking death—in the person of those who rise, so that the resurrection may be more certain.

It is as though he said: You conquered in those who were dying; you have been conquered in those who rise. Your victory, by which you had swallowed the bodies of those who died, was temporary; the victory by which you have been swallowed up in the bodies of those who rise will be eternal.

## Chapter XVI

[Col. 0550C]

### Verse 1

“Concerning the collections.” After the other matters, he briefly gives instructions about collections to be made for the saints who were in Jerusalem.

This is not contrary to the saying, “Do not worry about tomorrow.” It is not worrying about tomorrow if someone thinks about these matters in a human manner; it is so if someone serves God for their sake, looking in his works not toward the kingdom of God but toward acquiring these things.

“So also you…” (AMBROSE.) The Apostle commands the whole congregation to assemble on the Lord’s Day, and so forth, up to the point where he says that it is not burdensome and that much is found.

### Verse 2

“On…” That is, on the Lord’s Day. Among the Jews this day is called one day of the Sabbath, or the first day of the Sabbath; we Christians call it the Lord’s Day.

### Verse 6

“I shall remain, or even spend the winter…” There, like a physician, he stayed where many were sick.

### Verse 15

“I appeal to you, brothers: you know the household of Stephanas and Fortunatus…” The order of this letter looks forward and extends as far as the words: “that you also may be subject to them.”

### Verse 18

“My spirit and yours…” “Mine” means joy; “yours,” charity.

[Col. 0551]

## The Second Epistle to the Corinthians

(G)*

## Argument

[Col. 0551A]

After the Corinthians had performed their penance, the Apostle writes them a consolatory Epistle from Troas through Titus; and, praising them highly, he exhorts them to better things, showing that they had indeed been saddened, but had amended their ways.

## CHAPTER I

**VERSE 1.—“Paul, an apostle.”** He first places the customary greeting in the usual manner. Then, speaking to those who are mature, he gives thanks to God for the benefits bestowed by grace. Next, by his own example, he invites them to endure suffering; afterward, by humbling the false apostles, he rebukes them and exposes their deceitfulness. He also commends himself in many ways. Finally, a moral exhortation is added, together with a repeated blessing. Thus, prefacing the greeting, against false pride he calls himself “Paul,” and against presumption of heart, “an apostle,” saying: “Paul,” and so forth. [Col. 0551B]

**VERSE 2.—“Blessed.”** First he speaks to the mature about tribulation, setting himself forth as an example of patience and of the consolation received from God, and counting as praise what others regarded as disgrace. **“God.”** The Creator of all. **“The Father of the Lord.”** Through whom he is also a Father to us. **“The Father of mercies.”** A fatherly giver of forgiveness for sins, of good works, and of steadfastness in tribulation. **“And God.”** The giver of every perfect consolation, such as it is fitting for God to give to those who suffer for Christ. That God is the God of consolation is clear from the fact that he consoles.

**VERSE 4.—“By which we are comforted.”** That is, which God gave for this purpose, not only that he might console, but also that he might exhort. Thus our consolation also serves to exhort others, so that we may truly be able to console them. [Col. 0551C]

**VERSE 9.—“We ourselves.”** Not only did others despair concerning us, but despair existed within us also, and so forth, because our nature promised nothing but death or failure. He signifies that such an insolence of the wicked had risen against the preachers of the faith that they had death before their eyes. They had been so afflicted that they despaired of the present life. But because God does not withhold his protection from those placed in despair, especially from his own people, he delivered those who despaired of themselves and trusted in God. For they confessed that they would fail under the excessive pressure unless God were present.

**VERSE 10.—“And he delivered.”** God does not withhold his protection from his own who are placed in necessity. [Col. 0551D]

**VERSE 12.—“For our glory.”** Therefore both you and others ought to pray for us. Or, therefore your prayers will be able to help us, because that in which we glory is so honorable, namely: **“Testimony.”** These are good works, which outwardly testify to what exists in the conscience. **“Testimony,”** that is, a conscience that does not reproach but bears witness that we have acted in simplicity, and so forth.

**“In the sincerity of God.”** Just as conscience is a great punishment for the wicked, so it is joy for the righteous. This does not mean that they boast proudly of it, but that they attribute everything to God. Therefore he rightly does not say, “Our glory is the testimony of another’s wickedness or of lesser grace,” but “of our conscience.” Since it is hidden, it is not subject to another’s judgment; therefore no one should presume either to think or to pronounce a judgment against it. **“Not in carnal wisdom.”** Carnal wisdom consists in loving pleasures, avoiding hardships, or preaching according to the nature of things rather than against it, as the false apostles did; he rebukes their embellished preaching. [Col. 0552A]

**VERSE 13.—“But I hope.”** He hopes that they will progress, because they had begun to become better after learning the Apostle’s affection toward them, and they gloried in him.

**VERSE 14.—“Because we are your glory.”** You will recognize that you ought to obtain eternal glory through us—that is, that we are your glory—and that we obtain it through you, properly instructed; this would not be so if we received occasions of offense from you. [Col. 0552B]

**VERSE 15.—“With this confidence.”** Because the life of some was pure or amended, he wished to see those whom previously it had been unworthy to see. If, then, he did not go, he wished it to be understood that there were some among them on account of whom the Apostle did not fulfill his intention, and that they ought now to labor to cleanse themselves. **“I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second grace,”** and so forth. “First,” because in the earlier Epistle he had promised that he would come but had not come; and therefore he seemed deceitful and fickle, which he now excuses. He did not do this except because of their fault. A person who says what is false but believes it true should not be judged a liar, because, so far as he is concerned, he does not deceive but is deceived. On the other hand, he lies who says what is true but believes it false; he is not free from lying: unknowingly he speaks the truth with his mouth, but knowingly, since he does not believe it true, he lies by his will. [Col. 0552C]

**VERSE 17.—“That there might be with me ‘yes and no.’”** That is, that I should place my will before usefulness. It is as though he said: “It is not so, because usefulness must be placed before will; and this is what I did.”

**VERSE 18.—“But God is faithful, because our word which was among you is not,”** and so forth. It is as though he said: “You should not believe that I lie in this matter, since I have lied to you in no other matter.” This can be believed because God is faithful, and he promised teachers of the truth.

**VERSE 20.—“For our glory.”** Through this we are proved to preach the truth. I say “ours,” but I do not attribute it to ourselves alone; rather, I attribute it to God, because it is God who confirms us. [Col. 0552D]

**VERSE 21.—“With you in Christ.”** If you are firm in Christ, then our position is established all the more, since you were confirmed through us.

**VERSE 23.—“But I,”** and so forth. It is as though he said: “I did not stay away because of fickleness or earthly advantage, but in order to spare you.” A spiritual person does not fulfill a plan already made when, with greater foresight, he considers something beneficial for salvation.

[Col. 0553A]

**VERSE 23.—“Not that we lord it over.”** So that they would not be indignant as though he were exercising dominion, because he had said, “to spare you I did not come,” he adds: “Not that we lord it over,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER II

**VERSE 1.—“But I determined.”** I did not come in order to spare you, but I determined this very thing that I had promised when I sent the first Epistle—namely, that I would not come again—or that there would again be sorrow, as there had been when I heard of their sins.

**VERSE 2.—“For if I cause you sorrow.”** Whether by correcting, rebuking, or in any other way, whether through a letter or through my presence.

**VERSE 4.—“Not that you might be made sorrowful.”** The Apostle corrected them for this purpose: to show with what love he loved those whose sins grieved him more than they themselves were grieved. One who corrects without this affection causes sorrow. For he insults who does not grieve with his brother. [Col. 0553B]

**VERSE 5.—“But if anyone has caused sorrow.”** He commands that the fornicator whom he had previously judged should be handed over to Satan be received again, because he had been corrected. **“But in part, so that I might not burden you,”** and so forth. I do not impose the burden of sorrow upon everyone, because some had grieved over the sins.

**VERSE 6.—“This rebuke, which is administered by the majority, is sufficient,”** so that, on the contrary, much more should follow. Although, in view of the length of time or for some other reason, the punishment may not seem sufficiently severe, it must nevertheless not be considered slight, since it is imposed by the majority of those among whom he was assembled and handed over to Satan. Certainly, he suffers great pain when he sees many people abhorring his offense. Thus it is sufficient that he be rebuked by the majority. [Col. 0553C]

**VERSE 7.—“You should forgive and console.”** He rightly commands that one afflicted on account of sin be forgiven and helped through consolations. If a corrected person grieves in his heart, he immediately bears fruit. For this is true penance: to cease from sin.

**VERSE 9.—“For this reason I also wrote.”** Since I wrote that he should be received, I wrote for this further reason: so that, having tested whether you were obedient to me in expelling him, I might know whether you would be obedient in everything.

**VERSE 11.—“So that we may not be outwitted.”** We ought to forgive so that we are not deceived by Satan through excessive harshness. Often, because of harsher punishments, a weak person is plunged into despair.

[Col. 0553D]

**VERSE 12.—“When I had come to Troas,”** and so forth. After inserting the matter concerning the reception of the fornicator, he returns to them, showing that just as their fault was responsible for his not coming to Corinth, so also his failure to make progress in Troas resulted from Titus’s being detained among them. Without Titus he could not make progress there, because perhaps Titus was able to use their language more expressively.

**VERSE 13.—“Because I did not find.”** He could not instruct the faithful alone and at the same time resist the tumultuous unbelievers.

**VERSE 14.—“The fragrance of knowledge,”** and so forth. This means Christ, who, like a fragrance proceeding from the Father, makes the invisible Father known. Just as something unseen is recognized by its scent, and its location is understood, so Christ makes the Father known. Or understand by “fragrance” the miracles or words of teaching through which one comes to knowledge of him. [Col. 0554A]

**VERSE 15.—“A good fragrance.”** Just as formerly the lawful sacrifice was a fragrance, so now true preaching and the sincere reputation of the apostles are a fragrance. Christ is the fragrance of God the Father; the apostles are the fragrance of Christ, in whose life and preaching Christ is revealed, not blasphemed. As it is said of the wicked: “Through you the name of the Lord is blasphemed among the nations.”

**VERSE 16.—“The fragrance of death.”** From our preaching death proceeds for those who fall from it into eternal damnation.

**VERSE 17.—“As many do.”** Here he touches upon the false apostles, who violated the truth by corrupt teaching. Isaiah speaks of them: “Your merchants mix water with wine.”

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0554B]

**VERSE 1.—“We begin again.”** He knew that they took his commendation in a hostile sense, as in the first Epistle, as though he were seeking his own glory. He therefore begins, against their opinion, to show that he seeks not his own glory but God’s.

**VERSE 3.—“Written not.”** You are a representation of Christ and of me; but this is firmly written in our hearts, not in a way that can be erased, as what is written with ink is erased; or not with the dark marks of heretical depravity, by which heresies are inserted. **“Not on tablets.”** Stone signifies only a most hardened will, inflexible against God. **“Fleshly.”** That is, possessing understanding, not like senseless stone.

[Col. 0554C]

**VERSE 4.—“Confidence.”** He had said that he did not need letters of recommendation; now he says that he does not commend himself, but Christ. It is as though he said: “You are the letter of Christ and of us, but we refer the confidence to speak such things not to you but to God.”

**VERSE 5.—“Not that we are sufficient.”** (Augustine, *Book II Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 8.) Who does not see that thinking comes before believing? No one believes anything unless he has first thought that it ought to be believed. Indeed, believing itself is nothing other than thinking with assent. Therefore, if thinking what is good does not come from us, neither does believing.

**“But our sufficiency.”** Let those who think that the beginning of faith comes from us and its completion from God attend here and weigh these words. He commends grace, which is not given according to certain merits but produces every good merit. [Col. 0554D]

**VERSE 6.—“Who also made us fit.”** Here he commends himself through the dignity of his office, namely, the Gospel, placing himself not only above the false apostles who preach carnal observances, but even above Moses himself, the minister of the Law.

**VERSE 9.—“Abounds much more.”** That is, it abounds more in honor than the old covenant, because God’s glory is greater in salvation than in death. Although he justly condemns what was done under the Law, it contributes more to his praise if he forgives, so that the guilty person may be able to correct himself; this is granted through grace in the New Testament.

**VERSE 10.—“For not even.”** It truly abounds, so greatly that, in comparison with it, the former glory should not even be called glory.

[Col. 0555A]

**“What was glorified.”** This refers to Moses in the part mentioned above, that is, in his face. Or, “it is not glorious in this respect,” that is, in comparison with our glory. For the former glory was as great as should be believed of a servant; but the latter is as great as belongs to the begetter of Christ. For Christ is in the glory of God the Father. Thus the difference between the glory of Moses and that of Christ is as great as that between an image and the reality.

**VERSE 12.—“Having.”** Having shown the dignity of the New and Old Testaments, he shows the use of both. **“Great confidence.”** Through practice we exercise ourselves in good works, from which confidence grows in us. For we shall see as much as we believe; and because the glory has been revealed, we do not conceal our understanding as Moses did, but speak openly.

**VERSE 14.—“The same thing.”** They understand it now in no other way than before Christ’s coming. **“Which is annulled in Christ.”** Hence, at Christ’s Passion, the veil of the Temple was torn, signifying that through Christ’s Passion the mysteries of the Law and the Prophets were revealed. He calls it a veil in relation to prophecy, because it was not understood.

**VERSE 15.—“But until this day,”** and so forth. It is annulled for those who are in Christ; but over their heart there is a veil, that is, blindness weighing down their reason, when—that is, although—Moses is read to them, that is, explained. Thus two things prevent their understanding: the veil, meaning obscurity in the reading, and blindness over their hearts. This remains to the present day. [Col. 0555B]

**VERSE 16.—“But when it has turned.”** That is, when their mind has been converted through faith, having laid aside the hardness and blindness of their hearts. **“The veil will be removed.”** Then, as wine is understood to lie hidden in water, every prophecy without an understanding of Christ is something tasteless and foolish.

**VERSE 17.—“Now the Lord is the Spirit.”** The order of the words is: “The Holy Spirit is Lord,” that is, he can do whatever he wishes; therefore he illuminates whom he wishes and leaves whom he wishes in darkness. Wherever the Spirit of the Lord—that is, of the Son, through whom the Holy Spirit is given—is present, there is freedom. Therefore the Jews, who do not have the Spirit, cannot understand freely as we do. Or: the Lord to whom they are converted is Spirit, that is, a spiritual essence, and thus he causes them to understand spiritually.

[Col. 0555D]

**VERSE 18.—“We, with unveiled face.”** The veil is upon the Jews. In a mirror one sees only an image. Therefore we strive through this image—that is, through the reason that we possess—to see, in some manner, him by whom we were made, as through a mirror. **“Into the same image.”** The same image is the glory of God, as above: “The man is the image and glory of God.” **“Are transformed.”** We pass from one form into another, from an obscure form into a luminous one. For that obscure image of God itself is present in human beings, in which they were created and by which they rule over animals. When this excellent nature is justified by God, it is changed from a deformed form into a beautiful form. Nature is good even amid vices. Or this may be understood as passing from the glory of creation into the glory of justification. Or from the glory of faith, in which we are children of God, into the glory of appearance, in which we shall be like him when we see him as he is. [Col. 0556A]

## CHAPTER IV

**VERSE 2.—“Commending ourselves.”** “So that your light may shine before human beings.” **“Before God.”** Not so that they may be seen by human beings.

**VERSE 4.—“Among whom.”** The order of the words may be: “Among those who are perishing, the true and just God has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age.”

**“The god of this age.”** That is, God, who rules not only the good but also drives the wicked headlong according to their deserts, giving them what they want—that is, not to believe. He does not do this through malice but through justice. Or “the god of this age” means pride, gluttony, or the devil, the prince of the world, who rules over worldly people. [Col. 0556B]

**VERSE 5.—“For we do not.”** It is as though he said: “I rightly speak of the glory of Christ,” or, “We have commended ourselves before God in the manifestation of truth, and we do all such things,” and this is for Christ’s sake.

**VERSE 6.—“To make the light shine.”** This occurred in the separation of the elements. Darkness began when the confused mass of heaven and earth first came into being; afterward, when light was added, what had been made became more excellent. This signifies the progress of the human soul, concerning which it is said: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians V). **“Into the face of Jesus.”** The meaning is this: Since the divine nature cannot fall under sight, it is seen through the assumed humanity, radiant with divine light and emitting flashes of light, insofar as this is possible. From this it is also clear that God did not instill unbelief, since he abundantly offered the splendor of understanding light to all. They themselves loved unbelief; but because they did not wish to look, he did not offer them the ray.

**“Of the knowledge of glory.”** The knowledge of the glory of God is that by which we know the light through which our darkness is illuminated.

**VERSE 7.—“We have.”** Up to this point he has spoken of the height of knowledge; here he speaks of the frailty of the flesh, which contributes to glory, even though the opposite might seem to be the case. **“A treasure.”** He affirms that the mystery of God, dispensed to the faithful and hidden from unbelievers, is a treasure.

**VERSE 10.—“Always carrying the dying,”** and so forth. There is no doubt that Christ is killed in the martyrs, and that, in those who suffer for the faith, whether their departure, imprisonment, or scourging, the sufferings of Christ are present, so that his life may also be made manifest in their body. These sufferings reveal the merit that leads to the future life promised by Christ. Hence he says elsewhere: “When I am weak, then I am strong,” and again: “Through tribulations,” and so forth. **“May be manifested.”** For some were doubting the resurrection.

**VERSE 12.—“Therefore death,”** and so forth. Because through death we obtain the life of Jesus, death is not useless but accomplishes something great in us. But the life in which you delight amid earthly things brings eternal death upon you. Or take “therefore” passively: because of the hope of Jesus’ life, death operates—that is, it is brought about in us by the sufferings mentioned above; we allow it to be brought about. But through this, life is brought about in you, that is, faith is planted. [Col. 0557A]

**VERSE 14.—“With you.”** You are not to be beneath us, as though inferior to us, but equal to us, if you are willing. And I rightly assert this about you, because we do all these things to instruct you by our example. Thus everything concerns you: so that the grace of God, abundant in us, may abound in you, and through you in others, and through you may abound in many by thanksgiving, so that both you and they may give thanks to God. **“For the glory of God,”** that is, to show that God is glorious.

## CHAPTER V

**VERSE 1.—“For we know that if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have a building,”** and so forth. That is, we shall have an immortal body if the body is dissolved through tribulations; and this is why it will be dissolved, so that the condition and cause may precede. **“Not made with hands, but eternal.”** That is, not constructed by human joining, produced not through human generation or increased by human nourishment, but ineffably fashioned by God. **“Eternal.”** Because one will remain in it forever.

**VERSE 2.—“For.”** We groan not only because of our present dwelling but also in this respect—that is, in contemplating such great glory. We groan because desire is delayed, which we would not do unless we were certain. As a figure of this, Achsah, the daughter of Caleb, asked for the upper and lower springs, so that we might pour out tears not only because of the misery of our present sojourn but also because of the delay of heavenly glory. We groan because we desire, in addition to the soul’s calling, which we have already received, something more. **“From heaven.”** That is, we desire to have an immortal and impassible body, like the heavenly bodies.

**“For indeed we who,”** and so forth. It is as though he said: “We who are more perfect groan because of the delay, since even the less perfect groan—those who cherish the flesh.” The Apostle includes himself among these so that they would not think less of themselves.

**VERSE 3.—“If indeed, once clothed, we shall not be found naked.”** The saints desire this: that, when they rise and receive their bodies, they may not be found naked—that is, deprived of the promised glory. For this is what must happen: that, clothed with the body, they may be clothed over with glory, which is a transformation in splendor. **“Burdened by this body.”** Yet we do not wish death to be removed from us, but to be clothed over—that is, to be clothed by God with the garment of immortality, which destroys mortality rather than allowing it to supervene. [Col. 0557D]

**VERSE 4.—“We who are in the tabernacle.”** We who love the dwelling of this body, which ought not to be cared for, since it is a tabernacle only for a time, groan with desire for the heavenly dwelling. I say that we are burdened, as though he said: “It is not surprising that we groan, because we are separated from blessedness.” We also groan because of this lesser matter, since we are stripped of this body. **“Because of it.”** That is, for this reason we groan. We would not wish to be stripped, if this could be avoided. Or: we groan with desire for the heavenly dwelling. But God has brought this about. Or: we do not wish to be stripped, yet God has caused us to desire immortality. **“So that it may be swallowed up,”** and so forth. In such a way that mortality exists nowhere: neither below nor above, neither within nor without. “Death has been swallowed up in victory.”

[Col. 0558A]

**VERSE 6.—“Being confident.”** God makes us desire immortality, and through the Spirit he also makes us certain; therefore we are confident. **“We are away from the Lord.”** How can this be, when it is written elsewhere: “In him we live and move and are” (Acts XVII)? Because, although God is everywhere, he is not seen here as he is in heaven. Thus we are away from him not in faith but in sight.

**VERSE 10.—“So that each person may receive.”** This includes children, who, if they did not act through themselves, acted through others, when through them they believed or did not believe. They are judged according to what they did, not according to what they would have done if they had lived longer. For he says, “according to what he did in the body,” not according to what he would have done if he had lived. Therefore a person foolishly promises himself after this body what he neglected to acquire here in the body. **“We persuade.”** The apostles persuade those who live rightly to believe and to provide for themselves, because through the perverse speech of some the day of the Lord has been called into doubt.

**VERSE 11.—“But we are manifest to God.”** We are manifest because we preach what God commands.

**VERSE 13.—“Whether we are beside ourselves.”** It is as though he said: “You may rightly glory in us, because whatever we do is either for the honor of God or for the benefit of our neighbor.” **“Whether we are beside ourselves,”** that is, if we commend ourselves, in which we are thought foolish, it is for God—that is, for the honor of God, who has exalted us in this way. **“Whether we are sober,”** so that we do not speak highly of ourselves; this is for your benefit.

**“Whether we are beside ourselves.”** The Apostle speaks of a certain ineffable contemplation and rapture, in which he heard what is not permitted a human being to speak. It is for God, not for you, who cannot comprehend it. [Col. 0558C]

**“Whether we are sober.”** By accommodating ourselves to you. **“For you.”** Because we speak in such a way that you can understand. These are the angels of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “You will see heaven opened, and the angels ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.” Jacob saw these same angels ascending and descending on the ladder.

**VERSE 14.—“For the love of Christ,”** and so forth. Since Christ died for us out of love, it is clear that all died in Adam; Christ died for them in order to free them from death. So that this grace might not be useless to human beings, the apostles necessarily commend themselves in order to attract them. For through the glory and merit of the apostles the grace and benefit of Christ are recognized. [Col. 0558D]

**“If one died for all.”** That is, if Christ died for all as far as he was concerned, although he did not benefit all, then all human beings ought also to die for his honor.

**VERSE 15.—“Those who live in the body should no longer live for themselves, but for the will of God.”** They certainly ought to do this. Although Christ was weak and subjected to insults even unto death, he is no longer so after the resurrection; rather, he appears to be what he was understood to be. Hence: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he” (John VIII). Therefore they should repay him as God, not merely as a human being who suffered for them.

**VERSE 16.—“We know no one.”** That is, we do not praise anyone. **“According to the flesh.”** That is, one who seeks his own interests rather than those of Christ—temporal things rather than eternal things. No one ought to do this. Even if Christ was mortal as I am, and for this reason, while I was an unbeliever, I thought him merely human, he is now immortal, and therefore we are certain of the reward.

If anyone, therefore, has been reborn in Christ, he is already new; for him mortality has passed in hope, and it will pass in reality, and a new immortality will be given. Or, if anyone is new, the old Law has passed away for him, and he possesses the new.

**“We know no one according to the flesh.”** He holds the future life with such certain hope as though it were already present. This has been fulfilled in Christ’s rising, and it is not according to the flesh—not because we shall not rise in the same substance of flesh, but because we shall not rise in the same quality of corruption, which is signified by the word “flesh.”

**“And if we have known Christ according to the flesh.”** Although, while he was an unbeliever, he understood that Christ had been promised in the Law according to the flesh, so that he observed and commanded the observance of legal practices, nevertheless, after his conversion he no longer believes that this remains so; the shadow has entirely ceased. [Col. 0559B]

**VERSE 17.—“The old things.”** Entirely the Old Testament and everything belonging to the old man—thus it is. **“The new things.”** The New Testament and everything belonging to the new man have come. **“The old things.”** Such as the error of idolatry, which was succeeded by knowledge of the one true God.

**VERSE 19.—“God was.”** This signifies that the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, because their substance is one. There is unity where there is no difference; therefore the one is in the other, because their image and likeness are one.

**VERSE 20.—“Be reconciled.”** We are reconciled by confessing our sins and doing penance to him who reconciles us to himself.

**VERSE 21.—“He made him sin for us.”** It is the usage of the Old Testament to call sacrifices for sins “sins.” Or “sin” means the likeness of sinful flesh. Hence it is said: “From sin he removed or condemned sin,” that is, from the likeness of sinful flesh, because God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh.

Likewise, “curse” is understood as death, which came from God’s curse, so that what is truly said in the Law may be understood: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deuteronomy XXI). What does “cursed” mean? “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis III). What does “everyone” mean? Christ, who hung on the tree, although he was true life, died a true and not fictitious death.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0559D]

**VERSE 1.—“Not in vain.”** The grace of God is the forgiveness of sins. A person receives it in vain if he does not wish to exercise himself in good works, or if he trusts in legal observances.

**VERSE 2.—“Now is the time.”** Not in the old Law, or now rather than tomorrow or next year, because salvation is given immediately at the believer’s death.

**VERSE 3.—“So that it may not be reviled.”** This would certainly happen if we did not exhibit by the example of our works what we teach in words.

**VERSE 4.—“As God’s ministers.”** These do not flatter people, as the false apostles do in their pursuit of profit. **“In great patience, in tribulations.”** Amid so many hardships, Christ’s burden and rest are light: inwardly, the Holy Spirit gives life, and the hope of the future softens everything. Love makes every savage and monstrous thing easy and almost nothing. In this sense understand what is said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew XI). And again: “Take my yoke upon you, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy” (ibid.), and so forth. [Col. 0560A]

**VERSE 6.—“In purity of life, in knowledge.”** So that they may know how to act chastely in all things and mix in nothing of adulterated opinion. **“In gentleness of life, in the Holy Spirit.”** That is, so that, according to God, they may be gentle and approachable, not like those who by sweet speech deceive the hearts of the innocent. **“In unfeigned love.”** Love is feigned when it abandons someone in adversity. [Col. 0560B]

**VERSE 7.—“In the power of God.”** We should not place our hope in human beings or in goods; if there is anything good, let us attribute it to God. Or he says this because the person who possesses the qualities mentioned above performs miracles for the conversion of unbelievers.

**VERSE 8.—“Through glory and dishonor.”** Let us present ourselves as ministers of God. **“Through glory.”** Whether we are honored among human beings or dishonored and despised, let us neither become conceited because of the former nor collapse or grieve because of the latter. Likewise, whether we are disgraced because of some crime or have a good reputation because of some deed, let us present ourselves to God as regarded by some as deceivers, although this is false.

He does not simply say, “regarded as deceivers,” but adds “as,” and from this comes the disgrace. By others we are regarded as truthful. It is as though he said: “This is true; nevertheless, let us neither become proud of a good reputation nor grieve over a bad one.” Likewise, by some we are regarded as disciplined, and so forth. [Col. 0560C]

**VERSE 10.—“As sorrowful.”** Their enemies thought that the apostles would not escape the threats of the wicked. By God’s help they are safe from present and future death.

**“Possessing all things.”** Such are those who, having rejected earthly riches, already possess heavenly riches through faith. They possess everything while having nothing, because, retaining earthly goods for use or works of mercy, they hope one day to possess heavenly riches. The apostles’ glory consisted in possessing absolutely nothing and being free from anxiety; yet they possessed both things and the owners of those things, because everything was placed at their feet.

**VERSE 11.—“Our mouth.”** It is as though he said: “I have said many things about you, but all these things, spoken fully and at length, concern correcting you, Corinthians, and not my own pride. Therefore you are foolish to have rejected me.” [Col. 0560D]

**VERSE 14.—“Do not be unequally yoked,”** and so forth. The reason is that you are righteous while they are wicked; therefore you should share with them in nothing.

**VERSE 15.—“What agreement does Christ have?”** Just as Christ and Belial do not agree, so a Christian and any unbeliever do not agree. Likewise, the temple of God has nothing in common with idols. Since you are the temple of God, you should not share with those who are the temple of the devil.

**VERSE 16.—“With idols?”** He prohibits the worship of idols because they separate people from the one God. In all these ways he shows that the fellowship of the false apostles must be avoided. [Col. 0561A]

**“For I will dwell.”** This may be understood of the bodily life that Christ lived among human beings. Christ says: “I will dwell among them and walk among them” (Baruch III), that is, “I will live bodily among them.” Hence elsewhere: “He was seen on earth and lived among human beings”; and, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I). Here, too, Christ is our God, and the Church is his people; therefore the Apostle wishes them to be separated from every contamination.

## CHAPTER VII

**VERSE 1.—“From every iniquity.”** Namely, of the mind. This occurs when we follow the fear of God, because one who acts without God’s involvement is holy according to the world, not according to God.

**“From every defilement of the flesh.”** That is, from carnal observance; and perfecting sanctification, which belongs entirely to the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0561B]

**VERSE 3.—“To die together.”** Either so that you may suffer with me, or so that you may be crowned with me.

**VERSE 4.—“I am filled with consolation.”** Through those who had already been corrected, he invites the others to correction. **“I abound,”** and so forth. This happens to the Apostle when he sees those for whom he suffers making progress.

**VERSE 5.—“Our flesh.”** He says “flesh” because, amid adversities, the soul that is in the suffering body rests in hope of the future. **“Outwardly.”** This refers to open enemies; “inwardly” refers to false brothers, who are harder to endure. Or tribulation comes from those who are outside, while from those who are inside—that is, the faithful within the Church—there are fears that they may be shaken. Or “those who are inside” means those who are in the Church bodily but not in mind, in name but not in person—that is, false brothers, as above. [Col. 0561C]

**VERSE 7.—“By which he was consoled in you.”** Because I saw Titus consoled by you, and I too was consoled.

**VERSE 8.—“And if I had previously regretted it.”** He says this so that he might not seem inhuman, as though he rejoiced at another’s sorrow. **“Seeing.”** It is as though he said: “I do not regret it, but I rejoice.” I see that the Epistle caused sorrow; hence at first I was grieved and regretted it.

**VERSE 9.—“You were made sorrowful.”** Not with anger, which makes people worse, but with shame, which corrects.

**VERSE 10.—“Repentance unto salvation.”** The satisfaction of repentance consists in cutting away the causes of sin and not allowing access to their suggestions. [Col. 0561D]

**“Of the world,”** and so forth. This occurs when the sinner is grieved that he has been exposed.

**VERSE 11.—“For behold.”** Godly sorrow produces repentance unto salvation, because the things that lead to salvation produce earnest concern.

**“What earnestness among you.”** One who repents is concerned lest he sin again. He does not excuse himself but confesses, thereby defending himself from hell. He desires to be restored because he knows that sin has deformed him; he possesses zeal for good works and takes vengeance upon himself for what he has done.

**“You have shown yourselves,”** and so forth. That is, by punishing the man who had committed incest, you showed yourselves to be undefiled by the affair—that is, by his grave sin, since he had his father’s wife, and by consenting to him you had been defiled. [Col. 0562A]

**VERSE 12.—“The one who did the wrong.”** This means the man who committed incest. Or he refers to those whom he mentioned earlier in the first Epistle as having committed wrongs and frauds against their brothers. He shows that he wrote asking for pardon not more on behalf of those who had sinned than on behalf of the Church, which sympathizes with and is indignant at anyone who suffers insult or fraud.

This is what he says: “Therefore, although I wrote to you, it was not only because of the one who did the wrong”—that is, committed fraud against his neighbor—“nor because of the one who suffered the fraud, but to make manifest our earnest concern,” and so forth. He shows that he has the concern of the entire people, namely, that the unjust may be corrected, the polluted sanctified, and they may be reconciled to the Church.

[Col. 0562B]

**VERSE 13.—“Much more abundantly.”** It is as though he said: “We rejoiced over both matters”—that is, over your correction and over Titus’s joy. But we rejoiced much more abundantly over Titus’s joy, because the Apostle rejoiced not only over those who had been corrected but also over the others whom he hoped would be corrected.

**VERSE 14.—“But as everything,”** and so forth. In correction, the truthfulness of the one who rebukes becomes evident when those who are rebuked amend themselves. When corrected people amend their ways, they bear witness to the one who rebuked them. Thus, showing that his preaching was true through its effectiveness among them, the Apostle says: “But just as everything was in truth,” and so forth.

**“And his inward affections,”** and so forth. This refers to holy affection in every good matter.

### Verse 8

“Not as commanding,” etc. I did not merely ask Titus, but I myself say that you should abound—not as though commanding, that is, not as though imposing penance, since in that case the Corinthians would be bound as if by a vow.

### Verse 9

“He became poor.” He does not say, “He became poor although he had been rich,” but “although he was rich.” For he assumed poverty without losing his riches: rich within, poor outwardly; God hidden in riches, man appearing in poverty.

“That through his poverty.” Through his poverty, we cast off the rags of iniquity so that we may be clothed in the robe of immortality. [Col. 0563A] All, therefore, have become rich by believing in the poor Christ. Let no poor person, then, despise himself in his cell, rich in conscience. He sleeps more securely on the ground than the rich man in gold and purple. Therefore do not be afraid to approach him in your poverty: clothed in our poverty, he impoverished himself and enriched us.

### Verse 10

“But also to will.” As though he were saying: Some of yours had wished, while others had begun; now, however, let both groups bring it to completion.

### Verse 13

“But by equality.” Let each person divide with the saints whatever he has, since no more is demanded than he ought to retain for himself. Thus Zacchaeus gave half of his possessions to the poor.

### Verse 14

“That there may be equality.” Not that they do not differ in glory, [Col. 0563B] but because there is, and there will be, sufficiency for everyone. “As it is written.” This concerns the manna, as a sign of this matter.

### Verse 15

“He who had much did not have too much.” The saints have more in hope of the future, while those who are rich in the present have less; nevertheless, there they will be made equal. Just as here they support the poverty of the saints, so there they will be supported by them and will become rich in eternal good.

“He who had much did not have too much.” Thus the rich person who gives much and the poor person who gives little have an equal reward if their willingness is equal.

### Verse 18

“But we sent.” The Apostle sent two brothers with Titus, but he does not name them; perhaps the Corinthians did not know them and had not yet had any experience of them. Since the abundance of collected money is enough to give the wicked an opportunity for suspicion, it provides security. Therefore, he says, we sent such men—not one alone, but two and three. He commends them not only on account of the Gospel or merely on account of their election, but also because they had been tested and therefore chosen, so that they might arouse no suspicion.

### Verse 19

“For this grace.” That is, for the preaching to the Gentiles, to which I have been appointed and which I desire.

### Verse 20

“Avoiding this.” The Apostle does not wish to appear to act carelessly in caring for the saints, and therefore he gives advance notice so that his concern may appear as prudent provision.

“In this matter.” In the matter of doctrine and miracles, so that it might be said: “He preaches well, but he does not remember the saints,” as the other apostles did and as he himself had been commanded.

### Verse 21

“Before God.” On our account, our conscience is sufficient for us; on your account, our reputation must not be polluted but must carry weight among you. There are two things: conscience and reputation. Conscience is for oneself; reputation is for one’s neighbor. Whoever trusts in his conscience and neglects his reputation is cruel.

### Verse 22

“Confidence.” As though he were saying: Did he go because of his confidence in you? And because of Titus and Luke, with whom he gladly went.

### Verse 23

“Whether.” Or, whether through your fathers, the apostles of the churches, to the glory of God—that is, because they themselves are apostles of the churches, which means to the glory of God in Christ, that is, to the glory of Christ. For in them there is not the glory of human beings but of Christ.

### Verse 24

“Manifestation.” That is, now show your charity, which you have shown to others, and our glory, which you have likewise shown to be genuine, by receiving these men well—and do this before the churches, so that others may take an example from you.

## Chapter IX

### Verse 2

“And your eagerness.” Through the eagerness of the Corinthians, other churches were stirred to good works when they heard that the Corinthians, although previously entangled in errors, had afterward become people of good will.

### Verse 4

“We may be put to shame.” For if what the Apostle testified about them is not found to be true, he himself will be ashamed, and they will be put to even greater confusion.

### Verse 6

“He who sows sparingly.” The person who has little and gives little does not sow sparingly if his mind is ready to give more should he have more.

### Verse 7

“Not from sadness.” Whoever gives unwillingly because of present embarrassment receives no reward. The cheerful giver who gives in order to be rid of the annoyance of the person asking, rather than to refresh the needy person’s inward being, loses both the merit and the substance of the gift. He gives generously who possesses the disposition to give, even if he has nothing that he can give.

### Verse 8

“To abound,” etc. Although what a person with little contributes may be small, he nevertheless abounds because it is done with right judgment: the question is not how much is given, but with what disposition it is given.

### Verse 9

“For righteousness.” The righteous person is one who regards the goods of this world as common property for the sake of an eternal reward.

### Verse 10

“Increases of fruits.” Righteousness is holiness and a good life; from these come fruits, that is, eternal [Col. 0564C] reward. The increase of almsgiving is such that, in return for it, both virtues here and glory in the future will be increased.

### Verse 11

“Which produces.” That is, the giving itself is the reason why thanks are offered to God, whose giving we administer.

### Verse 15

“Thanks be to God.” He gives thanks to God for the mutual need and mutual supplementation of the need of Christ’s provincials and Christ’s soldiers. Here he dealt with material things in relation to the former, and after dealing with spiritual things in relation to the latter, he exclaims as though full of joys: “Thanks be to God,” etc.

## Chapter X

### Verse 1

“Now I myself, Paul.” He begins to deal with those who were not corrected, who followed the false apostles and thought that the Apostle was harsh. It is as though he were saying: “I invite those who have been corrected to almsgiving. I, Paul, am truly humble, not proud, although I urge others to give alms. To you, just as to them, I appeal and say,” etc.

### Verse 3

“We do not wage war according to the flesh.” We do not exercise the warfare given to us by God according to the flesh—that is, for earthly advantage.

### Verse 4

“For the destruction of strongholds.” So that the plans fortified by the various cunning devices of human beings or demons may be destroyed.

“Strongholds,” etc. Strongholds are the hearts of unbelievers, which the devil possesses and fortifies with various errors, so that the word of God cannot enter through faith. This may also be understood by comparison with fortifications. The weapons of the Apostle’s warfare are powerful for conquering these things, [Col. 0565A] and he identifies the parts of that stronghold, namely, the plans.

### Verse 6

“And being ready.” Nothing weighs on our conscience that would prevent us from acting boldly.

“To avenge,” etc. A person avenges disobedience when he condemns it through obedience. He destroys it when he leads those who resist to faith. This is a worthy vengeance: that unbelief should be condemned by those whom it had defended.

### Verse 7

“Those things which are according to appearance.” I have said many things by which I showed you that you ought to follow us rather than the false apostles. It is as though he were saying: If what I have said is not enough for you, why should you follow me rather than the false apostles? Look at these things that are “according to appearance,” that is, things as evident as those placed before the eyes.

[Col. 0565B]

### Verse 8

“I shall not be ashamed.” For it is true, and it is not said for my glory but for your benefit.

### Verse 9

“So that I may not seem.” Here he says that when he is present, he fulfills by deed what he threatens by word when absent. He says this because of the statement, “ready to avenge every disobedience.” Thus, he says, I do not wish to seem merely to frighten you with words and not fulfill in action what I threaten in words. You should know that what I threaten in words I will fulfill in deeds.

### Verse 11

“Let such a person consider,” etc. (Jerome.) Let no one think that I am threatening those things, etc., up to: “and toward sinners I show myself strong through severity.”

“Such.” For if we were to flatter your vices, we would not build up but destroy.

[Col. 0565C]

### Verse 12

“For we do not dare,” etc. We will be such in deed, because we are not like the false apostles, who arrogate authority to themselves and flatter vices. This is what he means: We do not insert ourselves among certain people—that is, among the false apostles who commend themselves, or rather arrogate authority to themselves. That is, we do not place ourselves among them so as to usurp authority; instead, we have received it from God. Or, we do not compare ourselves with them so that, like them, we might flatter you and your vices—a thing that even someone possessing authority could do.

### Verse 13

“But we,” etc. We do not, like those who glory by usurping authority, glory beyond the proper measure.

“But according to the measure.” By God’s will he was instructed to evangelize the Corinthians. A portion was assigned to each person, indicating to whom each was to be directed in preaching, so that each might have certain peoples of his own whose faith he could make the ground of his glory. Yet all those whom he had founded in the faith belonged to the Apostle’s rule: he had been sent by God to all.

[Col. 0565D]

### Verse 15

“Not in the labors of others.” To do this would be to glory beyond the proper measure. But we have hope in you—that is, hope of being magnified through you before others and of evangelizing according to our rule, that is, according to what has been entrusted to us by God, without hoping to glory in another person’s rule.

### Verse 17

“But whoever glories.” I will not glory in another person’s rule. Likewise, whoever glories—that is, whoever wishes to exercise authority—should glory “in the Lord,” that is, in the measure given by God.

[Col. 0566A]

### Verse 18

“But the one whom God.” God commends, and that person is approved, whom he considers worthy and sends to preach his gift. He does not commend the person whom he does not send, because such a person preaches without having been sent.

## Chapter XI

### Verse 1

“I wish that you would bear with me,” etc. As though he were saying: I glory in my administration, which appears foolish. But I wish that you would bear with me, etc. He calls the glorying according to the flesh “foolishness,” lest in this matter he appear inferior to them—something he himself does not care about, but which benefits the Corinthians to discuss. “Foolishness.” For it has been said: “Let not your own lips praise you, but those of your neighbor.” “Bear with me.” As though he were saying: Even if I am burdensome, bear with me patiently.

[Col. 0566B]

### Verse 2

“I am jealous.” Jealousy is a movement of the mind caused by another person’s condition, either toward good or toward evil. Here it is a matter of love, not envy, because he is jealous for them with the jealousy of God—that is, with the jealousy inspired by God’s Spirit. Through this he shows that he will say what follows out of love for them, not so that these things may advance his own praise, but for their advancement.

“For one.” He descends from the plural to the singular, wishing it to be understood that the whole Church is a virgin and that, in all her true members, she preserves virginity of mind, even if not of body. Virginity of the flesh is an untouched body; this virginity belongs to few. Virginity of the heart is an incorrupt faith; this belongs to all the faithful.

### Verse 3

“But I fear.” (Jerome.) The serpent deceived Eve by lying about God, etc., up to the point where he asserts that it does not exist at all or that it is not eternal, contrary to the authority of all the Scriptures.

### Verse 4

“For if the one who comes.” One who has not been sent.

“You would rightly bear with him.” If something greater came to you through them than through us, you would rightly bear with them. He declares the Galatians accursed if they should receive something else—something that would certainly not be greater but contrary.

### Verse 5

“I consider.” Above he dealt with the false apostles; now he deals with the true apostles, in comparison with whom Paul seemed inferior because he had not lived in Jesus’ company.

### Verse 6

“For even if I am unskilled.” This does not refer to the apostles, since they were not eloquent, but to the false apostles, who composed elaborate speeches. Therefore, being unskilled in speech is not a fault before God; lacking the knowledge of God, which pertains to salvation, is.

[Col. 0566D]

### Verse 7

“Because I preached the Gospel freely.” I did not do less, but more: freely, which is why you are angry with me and prefer others to me, even though this is not a matter of sin but of glory.

### Verse 10

“The truth is.” (Jerome.) Just as Christ once established it and did not deny it, so it is necessary that I too, without lying, act in this way.

“So that in what they glory.” They glory in receiving, but since I do not receive, they will not receive.

“For such men,” etc. “Let them be found to be as we are.” That is, like us. “In what,” that is, in this: that they glory in being like us.

### Verse 13

“Transforming themselves.” They do this in order to test those whom it is necessary to instruct in this way, or in order to deceive, as is fitting. Great mercy from God is necessary for this, lest someone who thinks that he has good angels as friends actually have wicked demons, false friends, and endure them as enemies all the more harmful because they are more cunning and deceitful.

### Verse 15

“Whose end.” That is, the retribution given at the end of life will correspond to their works. Just as the false apostles sought things that perish, so they too will perish; and just as they are ministers of eternal righteousness, so they too will be eternal.

### Verse 17

“What I am saying.” He speaks in this substance of glory—that is, in the glory of the flesh, which they consider a substance, loving it as though they believed that they subsisted through it.

“But as in foolishness.” These things appear to belong to the swelling of the flesh, in which there is foolishness. For it is foolishness for someone to praise himself. But because the Apostle does this not for himself but for God, he therefore says, “as in foolishness.”

[Col. 0567B]

### Verse 20

“He strikes.” That is, he deceives. A person is struck in the face when an injury is inflicted upon his mouth. Certain Jews did this: because they belonged to Abraham’s lineage, they disparaged those who were uncircumcised and exalted themselves, claiming nobility of the flesh. The Corinthians tolerated them and preferred them to the Apostle.

### Verse 22

“Hebrews.” Hebrews are so called from Heber, who alone retained the natural language amid the confusion of tongues. Since there are many Hebrews who are not Israelites, such as proselytes, he adds: “They are Israelites, and so am I.”

### Verse 23

“As though less wise.” (Ambrose.) He shows that he was compelled to burst forth into praise of himself.

“In labors.” Finding an opportunity, he also touches upon the true apostles, whom he surpassed in labor, so that he would not appear to have received less grace.

[Col. 0567C]

### Verse 24

“Five times from the Jews.” It was customary among the Jews to beat those who acted against the law in the synagogue for the sake of correction. Thus they beat Paul, who opposed the law, five times, giving him thirty-nine blows at each correction and pardoning the fortieth out of mercy.

“One less.” On the last occasion one strip of the whip was withheld; or, at each beating, one blow was omitted.

### Verse 26

“Dangers from robbers,” etc. When the devil could not have him killed in the city, he stirred up robbers against him on the road, even though he carried nothing that the robbers desired.

[Col. 0567D]

### Verse 27

“In hunger.” Where, then, is God’s promise: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Luke XII)? But the physician to whom we have once entrusted ourselves knows when to add these aids and when to withdraw them.

### Verse 28

“Anxiety.” The greater the charity, the greater the wounds caused by the sins of others. Hence: “Whoever adds knowledge also adds sorrow.”

### Verse 29

“Am I not burned?” All tribulations burn, but not to destruction; rather, to purification. This feeling purifies because it comes from charity. All who suffer scandal are the frying pan of those who possess charity—that is, of the bones that bear the flesh: of the perfect, who carry and govern the carnal. Hence: “And my bones were burned in the frying pan.”

[Col. 0568A]

### Verse 31

“I do not lie.” For God bears witness to me through signs and wonders.

## Chapter XII

### Verse 2

“I know a man.” He speaks as though about another person; thus the event is described and boasting is avoided.

“Whether in the body, or,” etc. The Apostle did not know whether, when he was snatched up, his soul had been in the body or had entirely left the body, so that the dead body lay there; or whether, in some other condition of a living body in which the soul remained, his mind had been taken up to see or hear the unspeakable things of that vision. Since this was uncertain, he perhaps said, “whether in the body or outside it.”

“Caught up.” Raised above nature.

“Up to the third heaven.” That is, to knowledge of the divine nature. The first heaven is the airy region; the second is the firmament; the third is spiritual, where angels and holy souls enjoy the contemplation of God.

### Verse 4

“He was caught up.” (Theophylact.) Observe his profound self-abasement and humility: how he recounts these things as though they concerned another person. For concerning this, he says, “I will glory.” But for what reason would you glory if someone else had been caught up? Therefore, he is speaking about himself.

“Secret words.” An intimation concerning the hidden essence of God, as though conveyed through words.

### Verse 6

“Beyond what,” etc. For if I were to report great things and more of them, perhaps some would think that I was not a weak human being but an immortal man or an angel, etc.; therefore I speak sparingly about myself.

[Col. 0568C]

### Verse 7

“And lest the greatness.” I refrain from glorying too much, lest I be considered something else. Therefore, a thorn was given to me, piercing the flesh. What was it? A wicked angel sent by Satan to buffet me—that is, to restrain every movement of pride by provoking tribulations or by tempting me, as some say, through lust. A temptation to which one does not consent is not sin, but material for the exercise of virtue.

### Verse 9

“He said to me.” Through inspiration or through an angel.

“For power is perfected in weakness.” The perfection of virtues is that which has a contrary weakness with which it may lawfully struggle. Therefore I will glory in weaknesses, not unwillingly but willingly.

[Col. 0568D]

### Verse 11

“I have become foolish.” In all these commendations I seem foolish, but this is your fault, because you ought to have commended me against the false apostles.

### Verse 12

“With all patience.” He mentions patience first, which pertains to conduct, because he bore with them for a long time, as with impatient sick people, so that by applying the power of signs he might heal their wounds as though with medicine.

“And with powers.” Power is the general category of signs and wonders, that is, every miracle. A sign is something that signifies something at whatever time it occurs, and it is a type of wonder. A wonder concerns the future. Or, sign and wonder refer to things contrary to nature, while power refers to things that are not contrary to nature, [Col. 0569A] such as freeing someone from illness through the laying on of hands and prayer.

### Verse 14

“For children ought not,” etc. Carnal fathers gather possessions for their children, but it is fitting that spiritual fathers receive support from their children. Here he proves to such an extent that he does not wish to receive anything that he transfers the cause of the carnal father to the spiritual father, saying that he is ready not only to spend himself for their salvation but also to die.

### Verse 15

“And I will be spent,” etc. Perfect charity is indeed this: that someone be ready even to die for his brothers. But does this happen as soon as charity is born? When it is born, it is nourished; when nourished, it is strengthened; when strengthened, it is perfected; when it has reached perfection, it says: “I desire to depart and be with Christ.”

[Col. 0569B]

### Verse 19

“You have long been thinking,” etc. As though he were saying: Perhaps you have long thought that I would speak as though I were a defendant, for the sake of making an excuse, saying that I did not burden you. But I say, with God as witness, who knows, that I did not deceive you, and that I did not act proudly, but in Christ, for your advancement.

### Verse 21

“Lest when I come again,” etc. (Chrysostom.) It is glory to punish, reproach, and exact penalties, etc., up to: “but because of his command.”

“And they have not repented.” It is not enough to change one’s conduct for the better and withdraw from evils unless satisfaction is made to the Lord for the things that have been done: through the sorrow of repentance, the groaning of humility, and the sacrifice of a contrite heart, with almsgiving cooperating.

## Chapter XIII

### Verse 2

“I will not spare.” After so many corrections, if some do not amend themselves, they ought not to be spared.

### Verse 3

“Whether you seek proof.” It is customary in divine Scripture to attribute to the person of God what he does in us, just as the Apostle attributes the speech itself to the one by whose gift he spoke, namely Christ. Christ is not weak in you but appeared powerful when he gave gifts. Having experienced this, they should not doubt that they can be punished by him.

### Verse 4

“For we also are weak.” Christ lives, although he had previously been weak. For we too, though greatly inferior, are weak in him—that is, although in imitation of him we suffer many things from the faithless, nevertheless we will live, that is, through him we will have power to judge you.

Or, “we will live with him,” that is, we will share a similar blessedness with him. And this is from the power of God, which is present in you—that is, in your consciences.

“In you.” That is, toward you. Death inflicted by the faithless is life toward believers, because those who rise again through the power of God will live with Christ.

[Col. 0570A]

### Verse 7

“But we pray,” etc. The Apostle prays that, if they act well, we may find nothing in them requiring correction, and that we may thus appear rejected. For approved people appear so when they judge sinners. Therefore, if there are none for him to judge, when his authority ceases he appears, as it were, rejected.

“May we be rejected.” That is, may we appear rejected, having nothing for which we can exact vengeance or make a judgment.

### Verse 9

“For we rejoice,” etc. (Jerome.) We rejoice if it is not necessary for our power to appear, as Peter’s appeared in the case of Sapphira and Ananias.

[Col. 0570B]

### Verse 10

“According to the authority.” Again he shows that he does not desire to misuse authority among them, adding that he received it not for destruction but for building up. Hence he adds: “Not for destruction.” Those who are corrected are not destroyed; rather, once corrected, they are built up.

### Verse 11

“Rejoice, brothers.” That is, act well so that you may be able to possess true joy.

“And the God of peace will be with you.” From this you will have peace through love of him, and from this the removal of all evils. This peace preserved the world, ended a prolonged war, joined heaven and earth, and made human beings angels. Let us imitate this peace. For love is the mother of innumerable goods. Through it we have been saved, and through it we attain all unspeakable goods.

[Col. 0570C]

### Verse 13

“Grace.” He wishes the whole Trinity to bless them. He assigns to each what is appropriate: grace—that is, forgiveness—to the Son; charity to the Father, who sent the Son out of love; and communion to the Spirit, through whom union takes place.

“And the charity of God.” The love of God sent Christ, whose grace saves. And so that we may possess this grace of salvation, may the communion of the Holy Spirit—or the Holy Spirit himself—be with you in such a way that he communicates and grants you both the grace of Christ and the love of God. As though he were saying: May the whole Trinity be with you, granting grace for your sins and love through the Spirit.

[Col. 0569]

# Epistle to the Galatians (G)*

## Argument

[Col. 0569D]

The Galatians are Greeks. They first received the word of truth from the Apostle. But after his departure they were tested by false apostles, so that they might turn toward the law and circumcision. The Apostle recalls them to faith in the truth, writing to them from Ephesus.

## Chapter I

### Verse 1

“Paul, an apostle.” By the title of his office he inspires fear.

“Not from human beings.” Understand: from apostles, such as certain men chosen and sent by the Jews, the false apostles.

“Nor through a human being.” But through Jesus, who had already been raised. He taught not gradually, as a human being teaches human beings, but everything at once through the Spirit. Thus he is greater precisely in what made him appear lesser. The other apostles appeared greater because they were earlier; this one was least because he was last. But for that reason he appears more worthy: the earlier apostles were established through Christ while he was still partly human, that is, mortal. Paul, however, the last, was established through Christ who was already wholly God, that is, immortal in every respect.

### Verse 2

“Who are with me.” The Christian brothers grieve over your seduction; they are witnesses to my truth, and you ought to believe them—not a few, but all of them.

### Verse 3

“And the Lord Jesus Christ.” You dishonorably equate him with the law when you assert that he is not sufficient for salvation without the law, just as you assert the law is sufficient without him. But from him, apart from the law, come grace and peace.

[Col. 0571A]

### Verse 4

“Who gave.” That is, he offered himself willingly, because no one else could open the book except the Lion from the tribe of Judah.

“His very self.” Because there was no other offering worthy of wiping away our sins; this is the beginning of salvation. What place, then, does the law have? As though he were saying: None whatsoever.

“From the age.” That is, from conformity to the world, which entices us.

“The present evil age.” It has greater power because eternal things are not visible.

“Evil age.” He says this not because the world created by God is evil, but because evils are done in it. In this sense it is said: “The days are evil,” “the world is placed in the evil one,” and “perilous times.” [Col. 0571B] A forest full of robbers, a sword by which blood is poured out, and a cup in which poison is prepared are called evil because not only times but also places and instruments have acquired infamy from the evils committed in them.

### Verse 5

“To whom be glory.” As though he were saying: The good who are present bear witness to these things, and those who will be present in the future will also bear witness. In this salvation he has already offered a foretaste of his own commendation, of what the grace of God can do, and of the fact that the law contributes nothing.

### Verse 6

“I marvel.” The Apostle proceeds logically to the destruction of the law. He reproves them for their fickleness, because they passed indiscriminately from the Gospel to the law. Since *Galatian* means “transferred” or “removed,” he appropriately takes the occasion for his reproach from the very name. Since these good things mentioned above come from Christ, I marvel that, after first being so well instructed, you are being transferred so quickly, so violently, and in so short a time, etc.

[Col. 0571C]

### Verse 8

“But even if we,” etc. A good angel may be understood here—not because this will happen, but because he is so certain of the truth of his Gospel that, even if an angel were to announce something else, he would not believe him but would anathematize him.

“Other than what.” (Augustine.)
