Take note: he does not say, “More than what you received.” For if he had said that, he would have prejudiced his own position, since he wished to come to certain people to whom he himself was writing, such as the Thessalonians, in order to supply what was lacking in their faith. But the person who supplies adds what was lacking; he does not take away what was already present. Whoever goes beyond the rule of faith does not advance along the way but withdraws from the way.

“Let him be accursed.” Why this? Because someone who proclaims another gospel wants it to flow from a private source, not from the common one. If a human being, obstructed by a carnal mist and led from the common fountain back to his own falsehood, can do this, then what of an angel? Indeed, if an angel flowing from his own source had not been heard in paradise, we would not have been plunged into death. The water was placed in the midst, and God’s command was given to all. The water was, in a sense, public, flowing without fraud, stain, or mud. But an angel came down from heaven, having become a serpent, because he already wished to scatter poison by stealth, and he released his poison. He spoke from his own source, from what was his own: “Taste, and you will be like gods” (Genesis III). And desiring to be what they were not, they lost what they had received.

“Accursed.” This word is used in place of a curse, and in ordinary speech it is called a dedication or consecration. For scarcely anyone is said to devote himself except by cursing himself. Hence: “And he anathematized him and his cities, and the name of that place was called Anathema” (Numbers XXI). From this it came to be understood that anathema is something detestable and abominable, so that the victor would take nothing from it for his own use but would devote the whole thing to punishment. This was to anathematize, which in ordinary speech is called to devote or condemn.

The origin of this word is in the Greek language, from those objects that, once vowed and paid—that is, promised and given back—were placed on high in temples. The expression is derived from **ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀναθῆναι**, meaning “to place above” or “to set up.”

[Col. 0572A]

### Verse 9

“As we said before.” He infers from the greater: Since we would excommunicate even an angel, the false apostles must all the more be excommunicated.

### Verse 10

“Now.” He says “now” because earlier, when he said that a human being was justified by the law, he proclaimed human glory useless and the grace of God. Here he also indicates that those seducers do this so that they may be praised by the Jews. Paul does not fear offending them for the sake of the glory of Christ, with whose coming the law ceases.

“If I were still.” From this some think that conscience is sufficient, so that they should care little what another person thinks of them. But conscience is necessary before God, while conduct before one’s neighbor is necessary as well; if it is carried on carelessly, it harms by example. Hence elsewhere: “Please everyone in all things, just as I also please everyone” (2 Corinthians X). Likewise: “Be without offense to Jews and Greeks and to the Church of God” (2 Corinthians VIII). Likewise: “We provide what is good not only before God but also before human beings” [Col. 0572C] (Matthew V). Likewise: “Let your works shine before human beings,” etc.

Therefore, against rash judges, detractors, whisperers, and murmurers—those who seek to suspect what they do not see and even seek to publicize what they do not suspect—conscience is sufficient. Nor should we seek our own glory from those whom we wish to please, but their salvation, so that they may praise not us but God, who made us such. Hence: “Do not do your righteousness before human beings,” where he reproves those who display their works in such a way that they make human praise the goal of their works and count that same praise as the reward of their works.

### Verse 14

“And I was advancing in Judaism.” As though he were saying: I had previously been powerful in those legal practices alone, but now I have abandoned them; therefore, follow my example and withdraw from them.

[Col. 0572D]

### Verse 15

“But when it pleased.” As though he were saying: Then it becomes clear that I did not learn from human beings—and not afterward either.

“He separated me from my mother’s womb.” Hence it is written of Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jeremiah I). Therefore, he who knows beforehand those who will exist before they exist causes whomever he wishes to be born, and calls those whom he wishes, once born, by grace so that they may be righteous. Thus he called Paul by grace to announce Christ.

“From the womb.” The mother is the Synagogue; its womb and its secret chambers are the Pharisees, from whose number he was separated.

## Chapter II

### Verse 1

“Then after fourteen years.” From the Passion of the Lord, when he had been converted to the faith, he came, as Bede demonstrates in his commentary on the Acts of the Apostles.

### Verse 2

“And I conferred with them.” He shows that he did not regard the Gospel as secure unless it had been strengthened by the authority of Peter and the others.

“Privately,” etc. I conferred separately with these men, not publicly, so that no scandal concerning the faith would arise among the believers from Judaism, who thought that the law had to be observed. At that time, when Peter had come to Antioch—although this is not recorded in the Acts of the Apostles—Paul opposed him to his face.

### Verse 4

“Brought in secretly.” By Jews. What unbelievers could not do on their own, they attempted through false brothers whom they had introduced under the appearance of religion, in order to investigate what freedom we have in the faith of Christ—not so that they might retain it, but so that through some dispute they might reduce it from freedom to slavery under the law. If the truth of the Gospel existed among the Gentiles, they would not remain but would all become Judaizers. Therefore, here, where he was presenting the defense of his preaching, he did not wish to yield in any way. Elsewhere, where it did not cause harm, he circumcised Timothy because of the scandal of the Jews. In all these matters he both commends himself and proves that the law is not to be observed.

[Col. 0573B]

### Verse 5

“Not even for an hour.” He did not yield even for an hour, because he never yielded. But if he yielded at some point, how can it be said that he did not yield even for an hour? And why would he yield to false brothers if he intended to act on his own? He therefore yielded on their account, something he would not have done on his own: he humbled himself before the law by circumcising Timothy, so that the deceit and scandal of the Jews would cease. They were ready to stir up tumult and rebellion if he received as a son of Judea someone uncircumcised and ordained him bishop.

[Col. 0573C]

### Verse 6

“Whatever they once were.” I do not return to earlier matters, because what exists now is sufficient. But those who seemed to be something contributed nothing to me. In this it becomes clear that he is not inferior to them. God is shown not to accept persons, because if he did, I, Paul, who was previously impious, would not have been someone to whom such men contributed nothing.

Or, “it makes no difference,” but they added nothing to me.

“Those who seemed to be something.” That is, of some authority, because they had walked with the Lord and had been present at his Transfiguration. I say that they seemed to be such to these false brothers. For those who seemed to be something seemed to be something only to carnal human beings; [Col. 0573D] in themselves they are nothing. Even if some are good ministers of God, Christ is something in them, not they by themselves. For if they were something by themselves, they would always have been something.

### Verse 9

“Pillars.” The Church is called the firmament of truth. Wisdom also built it, that is, established it on seven pillars. This number signifies either the whole company of preachers, since it is customarily used for the whole, or the sevenfold working of the Holy Spirit.

“They gave the right hands.” How did he confer with them and receive their right hands? Because he shared the same word with them. The very conference displayed the unity of doctrine; otherwise the Church would not have believed one who had not been with the Lord.

“That we should be among the Gentiles.” So that I might be first in preaching to the Gentiles, just as Peter was among the circumcised. And just as the apostles were associated with Peter, so Barnabas was associated with me.

[Col. 0574A]

### Verse 11

“I opposed him.” Paul would not have dared to do this unless he considered himself his equal.

### Verse 12

“For before certain men came,” etc. Certain people were zealous for the law, honoring Christ and the law with equal right. Fearing them, he did not associate with the Gentiles. If that were all, it would not be blameworthy, just as Paul himself sometimes yielded because of scandal. But the error consisted in this: that he compelled the Gentiles to Judaize.

### Verse 14

“How do you compel the Gentiles?” Not by the command of a teacher, but by the example of his conduct.

### Verse 15

“We.” Having commended his authority, he now begins to argue that carnal observances [Col. 0574B] are not to be observed after Christ. As though he were saying: The Gentiles ought not to Judaize, because we, who were powerful in the law, know that it does not justify. Therefore, having abandoned it, we flee to Christ.

### Verse 16

“Except through faith,” etc. He does not say “by faith” because good works are useless, since God will repay each person according to his works. Rather, he says this because good works come from grace, whereas grace does not come from works. For faith working through love would accomplish nothing unless the love of God were poured out in us through the Holy Spirit; nor would faith itself be in us unless God gave it.

### Verse 17

“But if, while seeking,” etc. If we have truly recognized that we cannot be justified unless we pass over to Christ, can Christ possibly permit us to fall back into what we were? If he permitted this, he would certainly be a minister of sin for us—that is, of our former state—just as he would have been a minister of righteousness for those who passed over to him.

VERS. 19.—“For through the law.” That is, understood spiritually. “I died.” So that I might not live carnally. “That I might live for God.” Not for myself, but so that I can now live for God, because I am with Christ. “I have been crucified.” That is, Christ’s cross has extinguished in me the ardor of sin, so that I no longer reach out toward it—as though I had my hands fastened by nails.

VERS. 20.—“I live.” I possess strength in the virtues for doing good. “Now it is no longer I.” That sinner whom I formerly was. “But Christ lives in me.” That is, Christ’s newness appears in me. “What, then, is the purpose of the law?”

CHAPTER III

[Col. 0574D]

VERS. 1.—“O foolish Galatians.” (AMBROSE) The words of one who is angry. The Galatians were foolish because they did not even recognize that they had been deceived by the false apostles. “Who has bewitched you?” Bewitchment (*fascinus*) occurs when, through magical illusions, certain things are shown to human eyes otherwise than they are. In common usage, one also calls *fascinus* that which harms infants. For certain people are said to have eyes that burn by their gaze; thus their action here is also called bewitchment. It may even happen that demons serve this sin. Likewise envy burns like bewitchment. For the envious person harms not only himself but also those in whom some good begins to arise. Hence Solomon says: “The bewitchment of wickedness obscures good things” [Col. 0575A] (Wis. IV). Thus it happened that the envious, as though bewitching them, harmed the Galatians, recently reborn in Christ, so that these same Galatians, with their stomach of faith nauseated, vomited out the food of the Spirit. “Before whose eyes.” They were truly bewitched, because before your eyes—that is, in your presence—he, who is so great, “Jesus Christ, was publicly portrayed.” That is, disinherited. And this occurred among you; elsewhere you ought not to tolerate anyone’s losing his kingdom and inheritance, much less among yourselves.

VERS. 2.—“This alone I wish to learn from you.” Having admonished them by reproach, he proves that the law ought not to be observed, because everything necessary—the Spirit, righteousness, and blessing—comes not from the law but from faith. It is as though he were saying: “Although you have been bewitched and are foolish, nevertheless I wish to learn this from you, because it is so evident that even fools can teach it. If there were nothing else, this alone would suffice for proof, since it is certain that you received the Spirit. But did you receive him from works in which you never labored, or from faith, which comes through the ease of hearing?”

[Col. 0575B]

VERS. 4.—“In vain.” He says this because they had already endured much for the sake of faith and, amid their sufferings themselves, had conquered fear through love. They had therefore suffered so much in vain if they wished to fall away from the love that had endured so much in them and return to the law.

VERS. 5.—“He who therefore supplies.” Since you received the Spirit not from works, which you never possessed, but from faith, you can see that I, who possessed the works of the law, received the power of giving the Spirit and working miracles not through those works but through faith. There could have been doubt concerning what had been under the law; but through the likeness of these examples everything is clear.

[Col. 0575C]

VERS. 6.—“For righteousness.” Here he calls the remission of sins and the practice of a good life “righteousness.”

VERS. 8.—“Foreseeing.” Not only righteousness from faith but also blessing, because Scripture says: “In you all nations shall be blessed”—that is, in conformity with your faith. “Because from faith.” Not from works, and so forth. “He proclaimed beforehand,” that is, he showed. Or, “he proclaimed beforehand,” that is, he showed that it had been foretold that they would be blessed in eternal blessedness. “In you.” In imitation of your faith, and so forth.

VERS. 10.—“For whoever,” and so forth. [Col. 0575D] This should be understood not of works pertaining to moral conduct but of the works performed in those observances. The law written on tablets is useful; the rest is a burden. He proves this by the authority of Scripture, saying: “It is written.” Those who are from the works of the law are accursed, because, as it is written by Moses in Deuteronomy (Deut. XXI), “Cursed is every man,” and so forth. It is as though he were saying: “I commanded many things, none of which anyone will be able to fulfill completely; but they were given as a burden, and therefore all are accursed.” Here he suggests that the Savior ought to be desired, the one who would put an end to these things and free people not only from other sins but also from the curse of the law. Why, then, do the Galatians pass from grace to the curse?

VERS. 11.—“Is justified before God.” The person who worships him freely—that is, not from desire to obtain anything from him besides him, nor from fear of losing something. For in him alone is our true blessedness, and it is perfect.

[Col. 0576A]

VERS. 12.—“But the law,” and so forth. Righteousness and life come from faith, but the law is not from faith. It might indeed seem that the works of the law were performed from faith, so that eternal things might be hoped for in return for them. But this is not so, since the Jews observed them from fear of punishment. “He will live in them.” He does not say, “Whoever does them will live by them,” although he had first said, “The law is not from faith,” so that you may understand that in this passage “law” refers to the works themselves that were performed in those observances. Those who lived by these works certainly feared that, if they did not perform them, they would suffer stoning, crucifixion, or something of that kind. Therefore, “whoever does them will live in them”—not before God, that is, he will receive a reward, but so that he will not be punished by this death. But whoever lives by faith, when he departs from this life, will then possess the most immediate reward all the more. Therefore, whoever desires or fears present things that are seen does not live by faith, because the faith of God concerns invisible things.

[Col. 0576B]

VERS. 13.—“Made for us,” that is, reckoned not only accursed but also as a curse. Or, he was truly made accursed, that is, mortal. “Cursed is everyone who hangs.” It is as though he were saying: “Let it be sufficient punishment that a guilty man dies suspended, and that he remains there until evening, so that he may then be taken down and buried; otherwise, if he remained there longer, it would be a greater disgrace and a stain upon his family. ‘Every man’—even Christ, so that future heretics might not deny his true death.”

VERS. 17.—“Now this is what I say.” God made this promise to Abraham; and I say and affirm that this covenant, confirmed by oaths, is not annulled by the law—something that ought not to be thought of the law, because it was given only for a time. For the law was given long after the promise had been made to Abraham. If the blessing came through the law, then Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the men of that earlier time, would not have possessed it. “The law does not annul it.” That is, it does not make it false; it would do so if the blessing were given through it. For that promise did not say that the blessing would come through the law but through the seed. But if the blessing came through the law, then he promised the seed in vain, and the seed itself came in vain. The law does not annul the promise—as though it now had power to empty it of its force—for then the promise would be false and God a liar.

[Col. 0576C]

VERS. 19.—“Because of transgressions.” [Col. 0576D] The law was placed in the middle, between the promise and the seed to whom the promise was made—that is, between Abraham and Christ—in order to educate God’s people under the fear of God, so that they might become worthy to receive the promise, which is Christ. “Ordained through angels.” I say that the law was ordained through angels—that is, through Moses and the other ministers of God—or that it was given to human beings through the ministry of angels, among whom were certainly the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. At times God was represented through them without any distinction of person. Observe that he does not say “given” but “ordained,” as though it had been given in an orderly way between the time of the natural law—by which they were convicted that they could not be helped—and the time of grace, before they were to be convicted concerning the law. Whoever, therefore, now brings it back acts against the order of the angels. “In the hand.” That is, in Christ’s power, so that the law might stand for as long as he wished and cease when he wished. Therefore, you act against the one who destroyed it. He is mediator between two extremes, and for this reason it might seem either that Christ was not God or that there were two gods. To this he replies that although a mediator is not mediator of one but of two extremes, nevertheless he is one God with God the Father according to the divine nature, while he mediates through the human nature.

[Col. 0577A]

VERS. 20.—“The mediator.” The law possessed by the mediator belongs only to one people; yet the mediator himself does not belong only to one people—that is, to the Jews, who possessed the law—but also to the Gentiles. Therefore, do not seek the law in order to possess the mediator. “The mediator is not of one, but God is one.” He is sufficient for reconciling everyone to God, because he is God; therefore, do not add anything else to him.

VERS. 21.—“Is the law therefore,” and so forth. [Col. 0577B] Since the law exists because of transgression, is it therefore opposed to the promises, so that through it the promise is fulfilled in a different way from that in which it was made? It is not that life—that is, eternal blessedness—does not come from the law. For if life came from it, then righteousness would also come from it. But righteousness does not come from it; rather, it condemns and confines people under sin. This is what is said:

“But Scripture shut everything up.” The law itself completely shut the Jews under the dominion of sin and showed that all human beings were shut up under sin, as is also said in Romans: “God has shut up all things in righteousness, that he might have mercy on all.” Through the sins made known by the law they were shut up, so that they could not excuse themselves but would seek mercy.

VERS. 23.—“Before.” [Col. 0577C] Before the coming of faith, the law was useful to the Jews. “Faith should come.” Faith is spontaneous, summoned by no merit. “We were guarded.” Not free, but slaves. “Shut up.” So that, having been accustomed in this way, we might be led. “Into it.” That is, into such a good faith. “Which.” It existed in the time of Christ. “To be revealed.” In Christ’s time many things were opened that had previously been obscure. Behold the honor of the law: it guarded us like a pedagogue. But this is not something great, because it belongs to children, not to adults.

VERS. 24.—“Our pedagogue was in Christ Jesus.” [Col. 0577C] Through Christ’s instruction: he instructed us for this purpose, so that, coming to faith in this way like children, we might be justified unto perfection. Or, “in Christ,” that is, in carrying out Christ’s commandments.

VERS. 26.—“You are all sons of God through faith.” [Col. 0577D] We Jews, in the time of faith, have abandoned the pedagogue, because all of you Gentiles, who did not possess the law, are sons. What we abandoned by your example, do you receive? As though he were saying: “You ought not to do this.” “In Christ Jesus.” In Christ’s instruction and in conformity with his death.

VERS. 27.—“You have put on.” That is, you have been made conformed to him; this is for you both an honor and protection against heat. Elsewhere the Apostle makes clear that Christ is a garment, saying: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ.” People put on Christ sometimes as far as participation in the sacrament, and sometimes even as far as sanctification of life. The first is common to the good and the wicked; the second belongs properly to the good.

VERS. 29.—“Therefore you are Abraham’s seed.” [Col. 0578A] Christ is called the seed of Abraham, where it is read that the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. Here, however, the children of Christ—that is, all believers—are called Abraham’s seed. Whenever Christ is called Abraham’s seed, it should be understood bodily: namely, that he was generated from Abraham’s stock. Whenever we who believe in him are called Abraham’s seed, we should understand the seed spiritually, as the seed of faith.

CHAPTER IV

VERS. 1.—“Now I say,” and so forth. At present you Gentiles and we Jews belong to Christ, and are Abraham’s seed and heirs. But formerly we Jews were under the law while we were children, like a future heir who has been appointed by his father.

VERS. 3.—“Under the elements.” [Col. 0578B] By “elements” he means new moons—that is, lunar days—and the Sabbath; not that they hoped in the elements as the pagans did, but that they worshiped God through these things. “Of the world.” Because the law promised not heavenly but earthly things—or transitory things, as the world is.

VERS. 4.—“The fullness of time came.” That is, after the whole period had been completed during which the law was destined to last, God then sent his Son, and so forth. “The fullness of time.” He knew when he ought to come and even when he ought to suffer, and so forth. For neither his hour nor ours exists except according to his will. Before this, however, a long succession of heralds had to be sent ahead.

“God sent his Son.” Hence: “I came forth from the Father and came into this world” (John XVI). And yet the Evangelist John says of him: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him” [Col. 0578C] (ibid. I). Then he adds: “He came to his own.” He was therefore sent to the place where he already was. Hence the Prophet also says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII). We must therefore ask how this sending is to be understood. If, then, we think soberly about the Son of God in a manner worthy of him, we ought to understand him as having been sent because, from that incomprehensible and ineffable secret of profound majesty, the Word of God gave himself to be grasped by our minds—not only when he emptied himself but also when he dwelt within us.

“Born of a woman.” In accordance with Hebrew usage, he calls women not those who are unchaste but females. “Born under the law.” This was so that he might appear circumcised, as Abraham’s son, bearing the sign of the one to whom he had been promised; in him circumcision was fulfilled, and therefore the sign should now cease. [Col. 0578D] For Abraham believed that he would have a son in whom all the nations would be blessed; we believe that this has now taken place.

“That we might receive adoption.” That is, so that we might become participants in divine glory. For just as he participates in it by nature, so he adopts us for the purpose of seeing it. We receive adoption from the fact that the only Son of God did not disdain participation in our nature, being born of a woman, so that he might be not only the only-begotten Son but also the firstborn among many brothers. He says “adoption” so that we may understand distinctly the unique Son of God.

VERS. 6.—“God sent.” To prove that we have been adopted [Col. 0579A] by God as sons, he gave us his Spirit, who displays the Father’s sign in his sons, so that, because our weakness and unworthiness would not dare to say this ourselves, he may prompt us to dare to say it. “The Spirit of his Son.” Note that the Spirit is also the Son’s Spirit. Note also the Trinity here. (AUGUSTINE) If someone should perhaps ask whether the Spirit proceeds from the Son, and so forth, up to the words: “He has from him that the Holy Spirit should also proceed from him.”

“Crying out.” It should be noted that in Scripture “crying out” does not mean the emission of a loud voice but is understood as knowledge and the greatness of doctrines.

“Abba, Father.” He elegantly placed two words signifying the same thing because of the whole people, called from Jews and Gentiles into the unity of faith, so that the Hebrew word might pertain to the Hebrews and the Greek word to the Gentiles. The identical meaning of both words pertains to the unity of the same faith and Spirit.

[Col. 0579B]

“Who by nature are not,” and so forth. He shows that there is one nature of the true God—namely, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. But what is it to be God by nature except to be the true God? Hence the Apostle says elsewhere: “You turned to serve the living and true God” (1 Thess. I; the printed citation reads “I Peter II”).

VERS. 9.—“Rather, you have been known.” Scripture frequently uses this kind of expression. Hence: “In the holy place I appeared to you, that I might see your power and your glory” (Ps. LXII), that is, “You saw me, so that I might see you.” God knows us—that is, he grants us knowledge of himself. It is not from us that we know him; he knew us from eternity. But he is said to know us at the time when he causes us to know these things.

“Weak.” The law is truly a poor element, because it does not justify perfectly.

[Col. 0579C]

“Poor.” Because whatever help it gives, it gives not by itself but in relation to grace. Elements are called poor when they need one another to govern the world.

VERS. 10.—“Days.” Those observe days who say, “Nothing should be begun today.” “Months.” Those who scrutinize the course of the moon and say, “Nothing should be begun under such a moon”; they observe and venerate such months. “Seasons.” As when they say, “Now is the beginning of spring.” “And years.” When they say, “It is the new year.” There ought, however, to be no suspicion concerning these things, because anything done simply in devotion to God can turn out favorably.

VERS. 11.—“I fear for you, lest perhaps,” and so forth. [Col. 0579D] Those observe these things who wish or refuse to begin something on particular days, months, or years, as though certain times were favorable and others unfavorable.

VERS. 12.—“Become as I am.” I too, who possessed the law, am now without the law, just as you ought to be without it. I mean, I who, although born a Jew, now reject these carnal things by spiritual discernment. “Because,” and so forth, “as you are,” and so forth. I am a man who was corrected from error, and so you too can be corrected.

“Brothers, I beg you.” After correcting them harshly, he refreshes them by recalling their good works. “You have done me no wrong.” He excuses himself, because the false apostles had said that Paul was an enemy of the Galatians and had not wished to teach them what he preached in other churches.

VERS. 13.—“Your temptation.” [Col. 0580A] They were tested when the Apostle was suffering bodily affliction, to see whether they would abandon him through fear or embrace him through love.

VERS. 14.—“But you received me as an angel of God,” and so forth. He says this because God speaks in his saints, and Paul wanted not himself but God in himself to be loved. Therefore he testifies concerning them that they had received him as an angel of God and as Christ Jesus. In all his saints, then, the one who said, “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. XXV), is to be loved. So great is the love of the head for his body.

VERS. 15.—“Where, then, is your blessedness?” Admiring their spiritual work, he commends them so that, looking upon this, they may not fall into carnal fear. And because they had changed for the worse, he reproves them. Although they had received him as an angel, he nevertheless does not spare cutting and burning, because he seeks not his own interests but those of Christ. [Col. 0580B] He does not seek milk and wool from the sheep—that is, the advantage of satisfying his needs and the favor of honor—but the salvation of all.

“If it were possible.” Could what the Apostle says have been done? What is not done justly cannot be done. He said that he was unable to do what, without doubt, he could do by power, but could not do by justice.

VERS. 16.—“By telling you the truth.” No one wants to be reproved when he is in error, and everyone who reproves appears to be an enemy.

VERS. 17.—“They are zealous for you.” “I am not an enemy, but they are zealous for you,” and so forth. Those who are not seeking so much that the Galatians should become better as that they should become worse and be dragged backward through perverse zeal are not zealous for them in a good way.

VERS. 19.—“Until Christ.” [Col. 0580C] Until the beautiful Christ whom you deform has been formed in you. Or, so that he may appear beautiful to others through you. This is more forcefully expressed than if he had said that they were to be formed in Christ.

VERS. 20.—“I wish.” Knowing that speech addressed to those who are present has greater force, the Apostle wishes to exchange the apostolic voice, contained in letters, for his personal presence. For divine Scripture builds up when it is read, but it is much more beneficial when it is changed from writing into a voice. A living voice, resounding from the mouth of its author, has great force; it is uttered and distinguished with that pronunciation because it has been generated in the human heart.

VERS. 21.—“Tell me,” and so forth. Answer me. For the sentence remains suspended up to this point. The statement “you who are again in labor,” and so forth, is inserted in the middle. “You who wish to be under the law, have you not read the law?” Whichever alternative they choose, they are shown to be foolish. If they have not read it, they ought not to accept what they do not know. If they have read it, the law itself proves that it should be abandoned. If they do not understand it, they are foolish.

VERS. 22.—“It is written,” and so forth. Abraham had several sons, but Scripture specifically develops the cases of only two, hinting that something remarkable was prefigured in them: one from a slave woman and one from a free woman. Nor did it make this distinction without reason. Both were born from Abraham, but through different operations. The one born from the slave woman was according to the nature of the flesh, by which a young woman ordinarily conceives from an old man. The one born from the free woman was not according to the power of the flesh—for she was an old, barren woman and he an old man—but through the operation of God, who had promised. Custom therefore produced the first, showing nature; the promise gave the second, signifying grace. In the first, human practice is displayed; in the second, divine beneficence is commended.

[Col. 0581A]

VERS. 24.—“By allegory.” Something is said “by allegory” when the words appear to sound like one thing but signify something else in their meaning, as here Abraham signifies God the Father, for he is the father of many nations. “Abba” means “father,” and “am” means “many”; “nations” is understood. “At Mount Sinai.” By mentioning such a place, the Apostle signifies that the Jews were proud against the Gentiles because of the commandment, or that they themselves were proud and swollen against the commandment itself, which is Hagar—that is, which is signified by Hagar. For Hagar means “alienation,” because she alienates from the inheritance.

VERS. 25.—“The mountain.” [Col. 0581B] It is connected and similar in every respect with the Jerusalem that now exists—that is, with the Jewish people who now exist and serve temporarily. The whole people is the mother; individuals are her children, or proselytes, all of whom serve through fear of punishment. Through all these things it is clear that the old law is not to be retained, but the new law, which is above and free.

“Arabia,” and so forth. Humility or affliction, because they were afflicted under the carnal observances.

VERS. 26.—“But the Jerusalem above.” The city of the saints is heavenly, although in certain people whom it gives birth to here it is still a pilgrim. Sarah, the barren woman, signifies that human nature, corrupted by sin and therefore condemned, deserved no true happiness in the future. Isaac, born according to the promise, signifies the children of grace. And because this was to occur not through regeneration but through generation, circumcision was therefore commanded [Col. 0581C] at the time when Sarah’s son was promised. Circumcision signifies nature renewed after its oldness has been stripped away. By commanding all sons and servants to be circumcised, he testifies that this grace pertains to everyone.

“Who is our mother.” Because individuals, instructed by her word and example, serve out of love.

VERS. 27.—“It is written.” He proves by the authority of Isaiah that she is free and a mother, adding: “Rejoice.” To rejoice, burst forth, and cry out belong to freedom. “You who do not give birth.” He says this because at that time she seemed to have borne no one. “You who do not labor in childbirth,” because she had not yet experienced the effort. “Rejoice in your heart.” “Burst forth.” Display the joy of your mind outwardly. “Cry out.” Proclaim your joy to others. “Because she who was deserted has many children.” This pertains to the mother. Isaiah, looking toward the time of Christ, addresses the Church [Col. 0581D] of the Gentiles, formerly barren but then fruitful, saying: “O barren Church, which in the time of the law gives birth to no one even through the power of a miracle,” and so forth.

“She who was deserted.” The Church, formerly deserted, has more children than the Synagogue that meanwhile gives birth. Isaiah would have said this needlessly concerning the ancient Sarah; therefore he should be understood as speaking about the Church. The Church was barren among all the Gentiles before this offspring, whom we see, arose.

“Therefore the one who has a husband” is the Synagogue, which has the law as its husband. “The deserted woman,” living in the wilderness and wandering without any power of a husband, is the multitude of the Gentiles, which was barren and produced no offspring from any legitimate word. Nature, corrupted by sin, does indeed give birth to citizens of the earthly city; but grace, freeing nature from sin, gives birth to citizens of the heavenly city.

[Col. 0582A]

“She who has a husband.” The Synagogue had a husband, namely, the law, and was once fruitful in children. The barren Church, however, without a husband—that is, Christ—and without any address from the bridegroom, lay for a long time in the wilderness. But after the Synagogue received the writ of divorce and turned all the husband’s adornment into the adornment of an idol, then the husband, while the former girdle rotted away, wove another belt for his loins, another loincloth from the Gentiles. As soon as she was joined to her husband, she conceived and gave birth. Hence Isaiah cries out: “Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out your ropes” (Isa. LIV).

VERS. 28.—“Isaac.” “Laughter,” that is, those who serve in joy, not from sadness or necessity.

VERS. 29.—“Was persecuting.” [Col. 0582B] I do not think we can easily find where Ishmael persecuted Isaac; rather, only that, when the son of the Egyptian woman was playing with Isaac, Sarah became indignant.

VERS. 31.—“With what freedom.” The freedom by which we have been freed by Christ is the remission of sins and justification through faith working by love.

CHAPTER V

VERS. 2.—“If you receive circumcision.” [Col. 0582C] Circumcision and the other legal observances are not harmful to those born and instructed in them, although they are unnecessary; it would be more harmful to prohibit them as though they were harmful. Gentiles, however, must not be compelled to observe such things. But if they wish to conform to them, as Timothy did, they should not be prohibited. If they place their trust in them, however, they are lost. The Jewish observances may therefore be retained so that they may not appear to have been rejected rather than brought to an end. They must not be imposed upon the Gentiles, lest they appear either not to have been instituted for the sake of the one who made the promise of Christ, or still to make a promise. By their cessation it is now clear that they were signs of what was to come; they were gradually to be buried honorably by being abandoned, not avoided as though they were the sacrileges of the Gentiles.

VERS. 3.—“He is a debtor.” He says this so that, out of fear of the innumerable observances written in the law, they might refrain from those things to which some wished to subject them, lest they be compelled to fulfill them all—something that neither the Jews themselves nor their fathers were able to do, as Peter says.

VERS. 4.—“You have fallen from grace.” Grace came for this purpose: that, when the burden ceased, it might justify. Whoever brings the burden back loses grace.

[Col. 0582D]

VERS. 5.—“For we.” Whoever trusts in the law loses grace. This can be seen by contrast, because righteousness and hope—that is, future blessedness—come from faith. We accomplish this through the Spirit, who can neither be deceived nor deceive.

“The hope of righteousness.” That is, what righteousness hopes for—namely, eternal life—or that which is itself hoped for, righteousness. For faith, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, hopes to be renewed and advance in it. Or, the hope of righteousness is Christ, from whom righteousness itself is hoped for.

VERS. 6.—“For in Christ.” Those who wish to live piously in Christ Jesus must seek virtues and flee vices. Things that lie between virtues and vices are neither to be sought nor avoided, such as circumcision and uncircumcision, which have no value in Christ.

[Col. 0583A]

“But faith.” Faith without love is empty. Faith accompanied by love is Christian faith; another kind belongs to the demon. For “the demons also believe and tremble” (James II). Those who do not believe are slower and worse than demons. Yet it makes a great difference whether someone believes that he himself is Christ or believes in Christ. The demons believed that he was the Christ, but they did not believe in Christ. For the person who believes in Christ is the one who hopes in Christ and loves Christ.

VERS. 7.—“You were running well.” Here he praises the Galatians and blames those through whom they were induced to wish to Judaize; he warns them not to agree with them.

VERS. 10.—“I have confidence.” [Col. 0583B] He says that he has confidence concerning them because they were led astray not willingly but through deception. Therefore, now that the true way has been shown, he readily believes that they will return.

“He who troubles you.” That is, he troubles you so that, the order having been changed, you become carnal instead of spiritual. Some say that he is secretly attacking Peter, concerning whom he wrote above that he resisted him to his face because he had not walked with a straight foot toward the truth of the Gospel. But Paul would not speak with such insolent abuse against the head of the Church, nor would Peter be worthy to bear the judgment of the Church. Therefore, it should be judged that these words concern someone else—either someone who had been with the apostles, or someone who had come from Judea, or someone who had believed from among the Pharisees, or some important person regarded among the Galatians as possessing the judgment of the disturbed Church.

VERS. 11.—“But I, brothers.” The false apostles alleged that Paul preached circumcision elsewhere but did not wish to reveal his own opinion easily to them.

[Col. 0583C]

“Why am I still being persecuted?” (JEROME) He suffered very frequent persecutions from the Jews because he taught that those from the Gentiles who had believed in Christ ought not to be circumcised.

“The scandal of the cross.” The preaching of the cross was a scandal to the Jews because it nullified the Sabbath and circumcision. If he had admitted circumcision, it would not have been a scandal to them, and they would have been at peace.

VERS. 12.—“Would that they were cut off.” They trouble you, but would that they were cut off—not bodily, but that they might lose the power of begetting in you, or accomplish nothing in others; not merely circumcised but completely cut off, so that they might possess no power at all to beget. And rightly do I wish this, lest they reduce you to slavery under the law. For you have been called by God into freedom.

VERS. 13.—“Do not turn freedom.” [Col. 0583D] The meaning is: “Take care that, when you hear the name ‘freedom,’ you do not think that you may sin with impunity. But serve through the love of the Spirit.” Love must be possessed not through a carnal affection but through the Spirit.

VERS. 14.—“For the whole law.” [Col. 0584A] Both those commandments that pertain to good moral conduct and those that concern the sacraments—when they are rightly understood by free people and are not observed carnally by slaves—must be referred to love.

“You shall love your neighbor.” This is written in Leviticus (Lev. XIX). He rightly says that the whole law is fulfilled in this, although there are two commandments of love on which the whole law and the Prophets depend, because love of God is contained in love of one’s neighbor. Therefore the perfection of salvation lies in this commandment, because God cannot be loved without one’s neighbor: “For whoever does not love his neighbor whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John IV). Since, then, the two commandments are so constituted that neither can be kept without the other, it is sufficient to mention one of them.

“As yourself.” No one can love his neighbor who does not love himself. But the person who loves iniquity does not love himself. “Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X).

VERS. 15.—“You bite.” [Col. 0584B] Or, “you accuse,” that is, by laying accusations against one another. “Lest you be consumed by one another.” Through schism in the Christian religion and through empty glory and empty victory, the opportunity having been changed from love, he touched upon this vice of theirs, because disagreement is hostile to love. Their contention, envy, and destructive quarrels were nourished especially by this vice; through them fellowship and life are consumed.

VERS. 16.—“But I say in Christ,” and so forth. He shows how sufficient the faith of Christ is without the law, because through it they overcome the flesh and its works and follow the Spirit. It is as though he were saying: “Do not give freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but serve through the love of the Spirit.” I say that this can be yours in Christ, and never otherwise.

“You will not fulfill.” He does not say, “You will not do them” or “You will not have them,” because they could not avoid having them. Rather, “you will not fulfill” means that you will not complete their works by the consent of your will.

[Col. 0584C]

VERS. 17.—“For the flesh desires,” and so forth. The flesh is said to desire because the soul acts according to the flesh, just as the ear is said to hear and the eye to see, although it is rather the soul that hears through the ear and sees through the eye. The flesh desires nothing except through the soul, but it is said to desire when the soul, through carnal desire, resists the Spirit. The cause of this carnal desire is not in the soul alone; it arises from both, because without both no pleasure is felt.

VERS. 18.—“But if you are led by the Spirit,” and so forth. From this it is evident that the person under the law does not possess the Holy Spirit—not merely dispensationally, but truly. “You are not under the law.” This benefit is already yours; therefore this part should be chosen. He says that those are damnably under the law whom the law makes guilty—those who do not fulfill the law while, ignorant of grace, they presume upon themselves. Moreover, the person who abstains from evil through fear rather than love is under the law and is guilty in his will. This law produces fear, not love.

VERS. 21.—“They will not inherit the kingdom of God.” [Col. 0584D] There is no intermediate place, so that the person who will not be in the kingdom will not be in punishment.

VERS. 22.—“Love.” He placed the head first, from which the members follow. No one rejoices well who does not love the good from which he rejoices. No one has true peace with another unless he loves him. No one is patient in persevering expectation unless he burns with love. No one is kind unless he loves the person whom he helps. No one is good except through loving. No one is healthfully faithful except with the faith that works through love. No one is gentle if love does not regulate him. No one restrains himself from what dishonors him unless he loves what makes him honorable. [Col. 0585A] Therefore he rightly commends love so frequently, as though it alone were to be commanded, although it cannot exist without the other qualities by which a person becomes good.

“Joy.” Purity of conscience. Hence: “There is no rejoicing for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isa. XLVIII).

VERS. 24.—“But those who belong to Christ.” [Col. 0585B] As though he were saying: “The law was imposed against the wicked; the cross, however, was imposed for the good.” This is what he says: “Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified their flesh,” and so forth. It is fitting for our devotion that, while we celebrate the passion of the crucified Lord, we should make the cross of the restraint of carnal pleasures for ourselves. In this cross the Christian ought always to hang during this life, fixed to the nails and commandments of righteousness, just as Christ was fastened to the cross by nails.

VERS. 25.—“If we live by the Spirit.” What he said generally above he now applies to those to whom he is writing, including himself among them. By this he shows that he is not telling them to do what he himself is unwilling to observe. It is as though he were saying: “I am not telling you anything that I myself do not also wish to do.”

VERS. 26.—“Empty glory.” [Col. 0585C] Empty boasting is the desire to win where there is no reward.

“Envying one another.” It should be understood that, although the poison of the ancient enemy is infused into the human heart through every vice, in the zeal of envy the serpent shakes his whole inward being, and in impressing this malice has, as it were, moved a doorpost. This zeal has no limit; it remains continually without end, whereas other crimes come to an end. The more successfully the person who is envied advances, the more the envious person burns with the fires of resentment and is kindled into a greater blaze. Hence come the threatening face, the grim expression, pallor in the face, trembling lips, gnashing teeth, rabid words, unrestrained insults, and hands ready for violence; and, even if he is meanwhile without a sword, his frenzied mind is nevertheless armed with hatred.

CHAPTER VI
### Chapter VI

**Verse 1.**—Brothers, and if. Up to this point he has addressed the whole Church, rejecting the law and commending grace; now he turns to the prelates, instructing them how they should treat their subjects—namely, gently, because they too are brothers, even if superior.

In some offense. An offense (*delictum*) is turning aside from what is good; sin (*peccatum*) is doing evil. Or, an offense is what is done ignorantly, while sin is what is done knowingly [Col. 0585D]. Nevertheless, the terms are used indifferently. Being overtaken is when, even for a moment, one does not see what ought to be done; or when someone who has seen it is overcome, so that evil is done while the truth remains hidden; or when weakness compels him.

Of gentleness. Otherwise, if you act differently, he may refuse to accept the rebuke and begin to defend himself, lest he appear dishonorable.

Considering yourself. Nothing inclines one so greatly toward mercy as reflection on one’s own danger.

**Verse 2.**—And thus you will fulfill the law of Christ. That is, love; for out of love Christ bore our sins, and he also commanded us to love one another.

**Verse 3.**—Nothing. In comparison with the spiritual person, who attributes everything to grace.

**Verse 4.**—Let him test. Let him examine carefully.

But his own work [Col. 0586A]. Not another person’s sin, as the Pharisee did who said, “I am not like the rest of humanity” (Luke XVIII); he was just not in reality, but deceitfully.

In himself. That is, inwardly, in his pure conscience.

He will have glory. That is, he will glory and rejoice.

And not in another. That is, not in another person’s praise, namely, when another praises him. For whoever has a conscience of good works ought not to glory in this before another or pour his praise outward, but to glory humbly in himself.

Or understand it this way: “And thus,” that is, if he considers his own actions, knowing that no one ought to glory in possessing a pure heart, “in himself,” and so forth.

And thus in himself. That is, if we consider our own actions, we will set ourselves before no one, nor will we judge anyone. The truly just person puts another before himself, because he knows his own faults better than another’s; knowledge of these faults is his glory [Col. 0586B]. For he rejoices when he recognizes his own sickness, which he desires to heal.

**Verse 5.**—For each person. No one is defiled by another’s sin.

Burden. Some works concern sharing in weakness, about which he said above, “Bear one another’s burdens”; others concern rendering an account to God, which is what he means here.

Against those who think that a person is defiled by the sins of others, he says: “For each person,” and so forth. Against the negligent, who take care to correct no one, secure in the belief that they are not contaminated by another’s sins, he says: “Bear one another’s burdens.”

We bear one another’s burdens of weakness when, through gentleness, we endure another’s anger, and when we forgive the one who has injured us if he asks. Or by “burden” a good or evil work is understood. In Scripture, “burden” is taken both in a good and in a bad sense; thus: each person, whether good or evil, will bear his own burden—that is, he will receive the reward of his works [Col. 0586C].

**Verse 6.**—Let him share. Let him make his own goods common to the teacher, and let him not make excuses, because God cannot be deceived. It is a customary command that the person to whom the word of God is preached should provide the preacher with what is necessary; this is rightly indicated by the word “good.” So also the Lord, speaking with his disciples in the Gospel, says: “Though you are evil, you know how to give good things to your children.” Foreseeing, however, that some would plead poverty and wish to evade the command, he added:

**Verse 7.**—Do not be deceived. As if he said: Let no one make a vain excuse, because God cannot be deceived. He knows your hearts and is not ignorant of your resources. A plausible excuse may placate a human being, but it cannot deceive God [Col. 0586D].

**Verse 8.**—He who sows in the flesh adds “his own.” But when he says “in the spirit,” he does not add “his own,” because carnal seed is from a human being, whereas spiritual seed is from the Spirit of God.

The harvest is promised here at the end. Therefore perseverance is necessary in sowing.

“In the flesh, in the spirit.” (AMBROSE.) A Christian consists of spirit and flesh. In comparison with the Holy Spirit, the human being is flesh.

But he who sows. That is, he who renders obedience to the Spirit through faith, serving righteousness with love and understanding the law spiritually—he will reap from the Spirit, and so forth. [The printed *offensum* is contextually uncertain; *obsequium*, “obedience,” is likely intended.]

**Verse 9.**—Let us not grow weary. If a person does not put an end to his work, God does not put an end to his reward [Col. 0587A]. As much as we sow in works, so much will we reap in fruits. And as far as the eagerness of the seeker extends, so far will the hand of the one who repays open itself in reward, because each person will receive according to what he does; for whoever is strong in sowing will be strong in reaping.

For at the proper time. God does not immediately do everything that is prayed for unto salvation; nor does he deny it because he delays it, but at his own time—that is, at the fitting time—he grants it.

**Verse 10.**—While we have time. The time for sowing is the present life through which we are running. In it we are permitted to sow what we wish. When it has passed, the time for working is taken away; hence: “Work while it is day; night will come when no one can work” (John IX).

Toward all. Mercy must be shown to everyone. Yet the just, who are of the faith, are to be given precedence [Col. 0587B]. The Lord bears witness to this even concerning all our enemies who are wicked and persecute the Church: “Do good to those who hate you. Love your enemies” (Luke VI), because they too are human beings, for whom the Lord makes his rain fall and gives his sun.

**Verse 11.**—See, however. After exhorting them to moral works, he returns to the subject with which he had previously been dealing—namely, that they should not be held by legal observances. But lest anyone deceive the unwary under his name, he takes precautions by completing the end of the letter with a note in his own hand. From this point to the end he wrote in his own hand.

**Verse 12.**—These people compel. These were false teachers who preached Christ in such a way that they also taught that the law had to be observed. They preached the cross so that they might profit from the faithful, and the law so that they might please the Jews.

So as to avoid the persecution of Christ’s cross, and so forth. Perhaps he says this because the Roman emperors Gaius Caesar, Octavian, and Augustus promulgated laws allowing Jews, wherever they lived, to live according to their own rite and observe the ceremonies of their ancestors. For whoever was circumcised, even if he believed in Christ, was regarded among the nations as a Jew; but whoever was uncircumcised and proclaimed by his foreskin that he was not a Jew became liable to persecution by both Gentiles and Jews [Col. 0588A]. Those, therefore, who had corrupted the Galatians, wishing to avoid these persecutions, persuaded the disciples to accept circumcision as a defense. For neither could the Jews persecute them, nor the Gentiles, who saw them circumcising proselytes and themselves observing the legal requirements.

**Verse 14.**—The world has been crucified to me. It often happens that a person does not hold the world in his mind, yet the world nevertheless binds him in its occupations; the person is dead to the world, while the world, as though alive, sees him and strives to carry him away, intent on other things, into its own activities. But Paul neither desires the world nor is desired by the world, so that, the two being dead, neither sees the other.

Since Paul neither sought the glory of the world nor was himself sought by the world’s glory, he therefore glories that both he has been crucified to the world and the world to him [Col. 0588B].

And I to the world. I desire nothing in the world, nor does the world recognize anything of its own in me. As the Lord says: “For the ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV).

**Verse 17.**—Henceforth. He does not wish turbulent disputes to make him weary of a matter that has been sufficiently explained. Or, as it is read in Greek: “Henceforth let no one cause or impose labor upon me,” namely, so that I should again have to labor among you. For a student imposes labor on a teacher when he thinks differently from what he has taught.

The marks. A mark (*stigma*) is a puncture or sign made with some instrument of iron. He therefore calls the wounds he suffered in persecutions “marks,” as though they were the signs of his punishments. The meaning is: I ought not to be troubled, because I have other conflicts and struggles, which contend with me in the persecutions that I endure.

**Verse 18.**—The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. The conclusion of the letter, and almost a subscription, which he also uses in certain other letters. It is as though he were saying: May you hold fast what has been said—grace, not dissent; not slavery to the law; not quarrel or strife; and so forth.

---

### The Letter to the Ephesians (G)*

### Argument

[Col. 0587C]

[Col. 0587D] The Ephesians are Asians. Having received the word of truth, they persevered in the faith. The Apostle praises them highly, writing to them from the city of Rome, from prison, through Tychicus the deacon.

## Chapter I

**Verse 1.**—Paul the Apostle. As is his custom, he places the greeting first. Then he gives thanks to God, initially setting forth the benefits granted to the human race, and afterward those specially bestowed upon the apostles; then also those bestowed upon the Ephesians themselves, showing by whom and for what purpose they were called.

Next he demonstrates Christ’s dignity and preeminence; afterward he invites them to patience and love, commending the unity of faith and the Church and enumerating the gifts of grace. Finally, exhorting them to battle against the rulers of darkness, he describes the armor of Christian warfare [Col. 0588C].

To all the saints. To the perfect, and not only to them, and so forth.

The faithful. Those who, even if not holy, are at least sound in faith [Col. 0588D].

Saints, through the practice of virtues. And faithful, through the right faith that is in Christ Jesus. He rightly placed these two terms: a good life is useful and believed only when faith is in Christ Jesus. They are truly saints if they are faithful in Christ.

Or distinguish between “saints” and “faithful,” so that “saints” means the greater and more perfect, and “faithful” the less perfect.

**Verse 3.**—Blessed. Having prefaced the greeting, he begins with thanksgiving, indicating that everything comes from God.

He blessed. There is one word of blessing, but it must be understood in different ways according to the suitability of the persons. God is blessed by a human being when he is exalted with worthy praises. A human being is blessed by God when God bestows on him the gifts of his grace—not because of his merits, but because of his mercy.

[Col. 0589A] **Verse 4.**—As he chose, and so forth. Therefore no one should think that souls were eternal with God and had then earned something, according to the error of those who say that before these visible things there were certain holy souls and that they were therefore chosen at that time.

**Verse 5.**—Who predestined. After mentioning the predestination that pertains to the righteousness and holiness of the present life, another predestination is now set forth, one that pertains to eternal life, whose effect he noted above.

**Verse 6.**—To the praise of the glory of his grace, and so forth. As if he said: The glory of grace is eternal adoption.

In which he graced us. The effect of the first preordination, which is directed toward righteousness.

In the beloved Son. God the Father, loving his only-begotten Son, gives the Son’s divine gifts to those whom he loves and to whom he wills to give them.

[Col. 0589B] **Verse 7.**—In whom we have, and so forth. He shows a twofold grace: for he both redeemed us and did not impute our sins.

**Verse 8.**—Which abounded exceedingly. Up to this point he has spoken of what he gave to the whole human race; now he speaks of what he gave particularly to the apostles.

**Verse 10.**—In the dispensation. That is, in the fullness of the time dispensed by God—in this time of grace, in which divine providence rationally arranged that what had been promised or prefigured in earlier times should be fulfilled. For if human beings had been entirely ignorant, without prior instruction, they would not have received Christ; and unless they had first been convicted of pride by the natural and doctrinal law, they would have thought little of Christ’s coming.

[Col. 0589C] To restore. (AUGUSTINE.) “The things in heaven are restored,” and so forth, up to: “They are renewed from the oldness of corruption.”

All things that are in heaven. That is, the angels; or “to restore,” that is, to complete.

Those that are on earth. That is, human beings, who had been corrupted by sin.

In him. That is, through Christ.

**Verse 11.**—In whom we also. Lest the apostles, in whom grace abounds, appear to have earned more than others, he shows that they too were called freely, not through merits, just as the others were.

By lot. “Lot” signifies grace, because election does not belong to human choice but to God’s will. Hence the Lord’s tunic, woven from above, which signifies love, came by lot.

He accomplishes all things. Even the willing of what is good, and the beginning of our believing, so that no one may glory in a human being because of our example. For this is true: “You did not choose me, but I chose you,” and so forth. The praise of God’s glory consists in many being brought to the faith, just as the glory of a physician consists in healing many.

[Col. 0589D] **Verse 13.**—In whom you. Now he comes to what he gave to the Ephesians.

When you had heard. Here he indicates both the cause and the time.

**Verse 15.**—Therefore. After enumerating the benefits bestowed upon the human race, the apostles, and the Ephesians, the Apostle adds what he thinks about their benefits: namely, that he gives thanks and asks that more be added, so that they may not become proud but may press onward.

**Verse 17.**—That God, and so forth. As if he said: In seeking to obtain this, I do not put forward merits, but rather that God and Father of Christ, and so forth.

[Col. 0590A] **Verse 18.**—The eyes of the heart. Therefore recognize the author in his image, since he cannot be reached by bodily sensation. Do not think, then, that God is reached by bodily sensation, but by the eyes of the mind; listen to him himself.

In the body, where the members are distinct, you hear in one place and see in another. But in your heart, where distinct members are not found, you hear where you see.

For this purpose may he enlighten the eyes. So that you may know, and so forth. He says this so that they may be more eager; for when they fully know what fruit belongs to believers, they will become more eager in cultivating religion.

Or understand it this way: “That hope” is to be taken properly. The meaning is: that you may know what his will is—namely, how great is the value of the hope of eternal life to which he calls you. And that you may know what is the fulfillment of that hope. He explains this when he says: “And what are the riches.” Here he reveals what he understands by the name “hope”: he takes hope to mean the thing hoped for.

[Col. 0590B] **Verse 19.**—What is its surpassing greatness. The highest teachers will have a certain increase of glory beyond what all will commonly have. For all will have the same denarius; yet “star differs from star in glory” (1 Corinthians XV). And “there will be different dwelling places in the Father’s house” (John XIV).

**Verse 20.**—Raising him, and so forth. The example of the glory of the saints consists in the Savior’s resurrection, so that in it the faithful may recognize what has been promised to them.

At his right hand. The right hand is eternal blessedness, which is given to the saints; the left is misery, which is given to the impious. God is not bounded or enclosed by any bodily form.

**Verse 21.**—Above every, and so forth. He says this because of the incarnation of the Son of God, so that even as a human being he may be said to be above all the heavens and above every creature, possessing his name by nature, not by adoption.

**Verse 22.**—Under his feet, and so forth. Complete submission is signified by the feet, and everything is rightly subject to him because it was made through him. Or the feet signify humanity, because just as the foot is the lower part of the body, so in Christ the lower nature is humanity, which even the angels adore.

And him, and so forth. After recalling Christ’s dignity, he returns to us, showing that Christ’s dignity concerns us. It is as though he said: God exalted Christ in such a way that his exaltation concerns us, because he is the head and we are the body, so that we may share in him.

The head. According to his divinity, because all were made through him; and also according to his humanity, to which the Church is joined by nature and grace. For “we have all received from his fullness” (John X).

[Col. 0590D] **Verse 23.**—His fullness. Because he is filled through them, while nevertheless he is “all things in all things,” here and in the future.

Again. When those entering into the confession bend the knee to Christ, he is fulfilled, because those who depart appear to empty him.

All things in all. Because the members contribute nothing to him, but he contributes everything to the members; for by his power they are what they are.

## Chapter II

**Verse 1.**—And you, when you were, and so forth. He recalls their former condition so that they may be humbled in the midst of good things, and so that it may be certain that, if these things were given to enemies, they will more surely be given to friends [Col. 0591A]—things which the Apostle desires for them. It is as though he said: He is the head of the whole Church and of you, because he made you alive together with him, although you were dead.

Or: We who have believed possess the hope of the inheritance, and you also have believed. But God made us alive together, or raised Jesus, and so forth.

**Verse 2.**—The prince. Namely, Beelzebub, who is the prince of evil spirits; or “the prince of spirits,” understood intransitively.

The prince of error. He calls the spirit of the air the prince of error, because he rules in the air.

Of the air. The darkened air is the underworld of demons.

Spirit. That is, “of spirits”; the singular genitive is used for the plural.

He works in the children of unbelief. What does he work, if not his evil deeds? And above all in this: through that very distrust and unbelief by which they are enemies of the faith—though he knows that they can be cleansed through him [Col. 0591B].

**Verse 3.**—And we too were by nature, and so forth. As if he said: Since these things just mentioned were once in us, let the Gentile not despair that he can become equal to the Jews.

Children of wrath. Mortals are born under God’s wrath, because, when Adam sinned, vice took root in place of nature. The human race was held under a just condemnation, and all were by nature children of wrath.

**Verse 5.**—He made us alive together. Or: he made us Jews and Gentiles alike alive together. This is what he means: by whose grace you Gentiles have been saved. And he raised both groups together.

**Verse 6.**—He made us sit together, and so forth. He does not recklessly count as already accomplished what he does not doubt will be future; he does so faithfully. Certainly Christ already sits in the heavenly places, whereas we do not yet; but we hold this by certain hope.

[Col. 0591C] **Verse 7.**—Abounding in the ages to come, and so forth. In the future age the gift of God will appear in the reward of believers—what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard.” These are the abounding riches: so much will be given that the mind cannot investigate it.

**Verse 8.**—And this is not from yourselves, and so forth. Lest you say: “I earned it; therefore I received it.” Do not think that you received it by earning it. Grace preceded your merit: it is not grace from merit, but merit from grace. For if grace came from merit, you bought it and did not receive it freely. Grace precedes all merits, so that my merits may receive God’s gifts.

**Verse 9.**—Lest anyone should boast. He does not say this because good works done with devout intention are rendered fruitless—since God repays each person according to his works and the glory of God belongs to the one who does good—but because works come from grace, not grace from works.

It is therefore good for a human being not to presume upon the powers of his own free choice. For the one who thought that he could preserve what had been given without God’s help went into a distant land and, living prodigally, consumed everything. Worn down by misery and returning to himself, he said: “I will rise and go to my father” (Luke XV). He would not have had this good thought unless the most merciful Father had secretly inspired it in him as well.

[Col. 0591D] **Verse 10.**—For we are his, and so forth. No one ought to boast, because we have been created in faith and in works; we are his workmanship—that is, his work—or we have been created through workmanship, that is, through his operation. Thus even of works there is no boasting through faith, since faith and everything else come from grace.

**Verse 11.**—Therefore. So that you may know that everything comes from God’s grace. He had compared Jews and Gentiles, since both had been under sin; now he shows that the Gentiles had been more unworthy and had endured the reproaches of the Jews, so that, now made equal to the Jews, they might be more indebted to God’s grace.

At one time you. In some manuscripts it is found written “who” rather than “you.” According to this reading, the sentence is understood without pause up to: “But now in Christ,” and so forth; the meaning, however, remains the same.

**Verse 12.**—Guests. A guest is so called as though from “foot of the doorway,” because when someone was received into a house, the master of the house placed his foot over the threshold, and the one received placed his foot upon it; after they had given one another their right hands, he swore that he had entered peacefully.

[Col. 0592B] **Verse 14.**—Who made both one. For he himself is the cornerstone, in whom the two peoples, like walls coming from different directions toward the corner, are joined to one another as though in a kiss of peace.

The wall. That is, the obstacle: on one side arising from the law, on the other from idolatry.

**Verse 15.**—Making peace, and so forth. He makes peace between them in order to reconcile both to God the Father.

In himself. In no other way than through the cross—that is, through death—did he destroy the hostility between God and human beings, namely, sins. For the Savior’s death benefited everyone.

**Verse 17.**—You who were far away, and so forth. If you love God with affection, you are near; if you hate him, you are far away. No one is far from God by geographical distance, but by affection.

**Verse 19.**—You are not guests. That is, you are not inferior in faith, as those once received under the law were.

And strangers. That is, foreigners from God.

But you are citizens. That is, of the same right and dignity in the house of God.

Of the saints. Not of carnal Israel.

And members of the household. That is, household members.

Of God. Those to whom he reveals his hidden things.

**Verse 20.**—With Christ himself as the supreme cornerstone, and so forth. (AUGUSTINE, on Psalm LXXXVI.) Lest the apostles or prophets, upon whom the city was founded, rely upon themselves, he follows by saying: “With Christ Jesus himself as the supreme cornerstone.” For the whole building rests upon Christ as upon its first foundation. This foundation is above, not below, unlike a physical building.

**Verse 21.**—It grows into a holy temple in the Lord. No one is so perfect that he cannot grow.

## Chapter III

[Col. 0592D]

**Verse 1.**—For this reason, and so forth. Having shown that peace and reconciliation were accomplished through Christ, he now sets forth through whom they themselves were built together: God revealed that salvation belonged also to the Gentiles, sent him to preach to them, and caused him to suffer for them, so that they might be more grateful to God.

**Verse 2.**—If indeed you have heard. That is, if you have understood grace—namely, the apostleship entrusted by God, who knows why he chose me for this office.

Or “apostleship” means the office through which we weigh out different things to different people. By this he wishes them to know that he was sent by Christ at God’s command to preach to the Gentiles the mystery of God’s grace.

**Verse 3.**—As I wrote above, and so forth. Namely, “He himself is our peace.” There he summarized, in a brief statement, the substance of the mysteries revealed to him, not bringing forth everything he knew, but showing it from a small portion [Col. 0593A].

**Verse 5.**—And to the prophets. The earlier prophets indeed knew long ago that the Gentiles would be called and would become participants in God’s gift; but it was hidden from them that salvation would come to them without the law, through faith in Christ.

**Verse 6.**—Through the Gospel, and so forth. Through preaching, the gift of God became known—the gift that God gives to the Gentiles according to the operation of his power, by which he raised Christ, in whom all are saved without the works of the law.

**Verse 7.**—A minister. For this is not mine but God’s; therefore no thanks are owed to me, but to God.

**Verse 8.**—Unsearchable. Unsearchable by nature, that is; but through grace and the revelation of the Holy Spirit they are made searchable to the faithful.

**Verse 9.**—Hidden from the ages. In the world, the rational causes of all things that occur naturally are hidden, just as Levi was hidden in Abraham’s loins when he paid tithes. In God, however, the causes of those things that occur through grace are hidden, as are the causes of those things that occur wondrously and not naturally in order to signify this, and which were accomplished through the ministry of angels.

In God. God has hidden within himself the causes of certain deeds, which he did not implant in created things. He fulfills them not by the work of providence through which he established natures so that they might exist, but by that work through which he administers them as he wills—having created them as he willed. There too is the grace by which sinners are saved. For the human being is restored not through nature corrupted by vice [Col. 0593C], but through God’s grace.

**Verse 10.**—So that it may be made known. I was given the task of evangelizing and enlightening. See how great this is: through it something was added even to the angels, who learned many secrets through these events.

In the heavenly places. Because the Church was first there, and this Church too is to be gathered there after the resurrection, so that we may be equal to the angels of God.

**Verse 11.**—According to the determination. Wisdom, which in its own nature is simple, is multiform according to the things done in the age—things which God determined, that is, preordained—because it varies in many forms.

And lest the teachers of sacred Scripture appear to contradict one another in the statements mentioned above, what was said can be distinguished in this way: those who possess greater dignity, and through whose ministry these things were announced, knew them in part—for example, those attendants and messengers; but those of lesser dignity were ignorant of them [Col. 0593D].

**Verse 14.**—For this reason. I ask and entreat God for you, that grace may cooperate with you. This is what he adds: “For this reason.” Here he shows that they possess the power of their own will. But lest they think that this is sufficient, he adds: “I bend my knees to the Father.”

Only this much is found in the Greek. What has been added in the Latin manuscripts—“of our Lord Jesus Christ”—fits well, since he was praying that we might obtain through the merit of the one who is properly and naturally his Father, not adoptively.

**Verse 15.**—Fatherhood, and so forth. Neither angel nor human being is truly a father as God is, who is the Father of all by creation and of the faithful by recreation, having adopted them as sons.

Or “is named” means “is capable of being named.” For from the one who is Father of all, the angels in heaven and human beings on earth received the ability to call others fathers.

Note also that Christ, the only-begotten Son of God by nature, indicates that by the benefit of adoption he is himself a father when he says: “Son, your sins are forgiven you” (Matthew II). The Holy Spirit likewise is a father, through whom the righteous are adopted as sons.

A human being is called father either by nature, by the authority of example, or by reason of benefaction.

**Verse 17.**—In love. I also pray that, having been rooted—that is, firmly planted, after the likeness of a tree, which grows and produces more abundant fruit the more deeply it is fixed in the earth—
