[Col. 0594B] **Verse 18.**—With all the saints. This is the fellowship of the heavenly commonwealth. These people do not seek their own interests but those of Christ; that is, they do not pursue private advantages, but in the common fellowship they seek the welfare of all.

What is the breadth. Of love, which ought to extend even to enemies and to do good cheerfully, because whoever gives sadly loses what he gives. Breadth of love is therefore necessary, lest whatever good you do perish. But because, when iniquity abounds, the love of many grows cold, length is also necessary.

And height. Of love. This means that the heart is directed upward, so that God is awaited as the reward. If you do good even to your enemies and give cheerfully, you have breadth; and if you persevere in these things to the end, you have length. But if you do all this not for the sake of the heavenly reward, you do not have height; and then you have neither breadth nor length.

To possess height is to think of God, to love God, and to love the helper freely; finally, it is to regard him himself as the one who crowns, and at last as the reward itself, expecting nothing other than him. If you love, love freely. If you truly love, let the one whom you love himself be the reward.

And depth. Of love; that is, so that you may understand God’s hidden judgment—why he gives to this person but not to that one. Everything we can do proceeds from the depth of God’s judgments, which we cannot search out or contemplate. I see what I can do; I do not see from where I can do it, except that I know it is from God. Why he gives to one and not to another is far beyond me: it is an abyss and a depth [Col. 0594D].

Now, then, love itself is exercised in good works to help others and extends even to enemies; this is breadth. It now endures adversity with long-suffering and perseveres in what it has truly held; this is length. It does all this for the sake of attaining the eternal homeland promised to it on high; this is height. That love, however, arises from what is hidden; and this is depth.

**Verse 19.**—So that you may be filled. A Christian lacks nothing when he knows the Father and the Son in this way. Otherwise the confession of the deity is not complete, because faith is complete neither in the Father alone nor perfect in the Son alone.

With all the fullness of God. Not so that they may be “full God,” as certain misguided people have wished, but so that they may be perfectly full of God.

Or understand it this way: in confession and thanksgiving, honor should be reserved for the Son just as for the Father, and everything that comes from God the Father should be believed to have been made and restored through the Son, so that the believers may possess a full confession of divinity [Col. 0595A].

**Verse 20.**—He is able to do all things, and so forth. Among these things are certain matters that no one would otherwise ask for or understand—for example, that God, having become human, should die for human beings, and other such things.

## Chapter IV

**Verse 1.**—I beseech you. Up to this point he has shown that everything must be attributed to grace; from here he gives moral instruction, first to everyone generally and afterward to the individual orders.

**Verse 2.**—In love. (AUGUSTINE.) For this is the action of the right path, always keeping its eyes upon God [Col. 0595B]. Such action is neither broken by business nor turbulent, neither weak nor bold, neither fugitive nor hasty, nor lying prostrate.

**Verse 3.**—In the bond of peace. That is, preserving peace. Peace exists when we endure until the final harvest those sins that cannot be uprooted without damage to the grain or without hope of correcting those who are to be saved.

**Verse 5.**—One Lord. You ought to preserve unity because we have one Lord, not three, whose different wills would require you to disagree. You are also commanded to believe the same thing and to act in the same way.

And you have one God, the Creator of all, and Father, who provides for all; therefore no one can place himself above another [Col. 0595C].

Who is God. He is above all, that is, he surpasses all creatures; his dignity should summon you, and he is diffused through all because he is everywhere and therefore to be feared, since he cannot be avoided anywhere.

And in us all. Through grace, in those who preserve unity. Thus this is understood not individually of one person, but collectively of all—that is, of the Trinity.

One faith. Not numerically one, but one in kind, because it is similar in everyone.

**Verse 8.**—He led captivity captive. That is, those whom the devil had taken captive from paradise and made his own, as well as the world’s and hell’s, Christ again made captive when they were led back to heaven.

**Verse 11.**—Prophets. (AMBROSE.) In the New Testament, prophets are called interpreters of the Scriptures. Nevertheless, there were certain prophets at the beginning of the faith who foretold future things, such as Agabus and the seven daughters of Philip [Col. 0595D].

Evangelists. They are also deacons, because, although they are not priests, they can nevertheless evangelize.

**Verse 12.**—For the work of ministry. He gave these people for the work of ministry, so that each might fully perform the work of ministry entrusted to him. For if one person had everything, he would not perform each task perfectly.

For completion. That is, so that he might perfect those who are already holy.

And for the building up. That is, so that they might build up in the body of Christ those who are still alienated.

**Verse 13.**—Until. That is, until the day of judgment.

All. We who are in one faith without disagreement, and in one unity of the knowledge of the Son of God without difference.

Or: in the virtues by which the Son of God is known in us, or by which we shall know him in the future [Col. 0596A].

Let us meet. Either meeting one another from the various regions of the world, or running toward Christ himself with desire, toward joy.

Into a perfect man. So that each person may be a perfect man and possess the same age, which is the measure and limit of human age, beyond which a human being does not naturally increase. Christ possessed the fullness of years and bodily development at this age, in which he departed from this world. For all will rise at the same age at which Christ died and rose again, whatever their age was when they died.

**Verse 15.**—Christ. He is called “anointed.” In the Old Testament, kings were anointed.

**Verse 17.**—This, then. He warns them to avoid the custom of their former paganism. As if he said: Since God has given so many aids for preserving unity, and since you can grow and meet him, I tell you—I do not merely beseech you—as I did before [Col. 0596B].

**Verse 18.**—Darkened. Not slightly; therefore it is less surprising if they walk in vanity rather than you, who have been enlightened and possess the hope of life.

From the life of God. There are two lives: one of the body and the other of the soul. Just as the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul; and just as the body dies if the soul departs, so the soul dies if God departs.

When the soul withdraws from the light of righteousness, the more it seeks what it may find against righteousness, the more it is driven away from the light of truth and plunged into darkness.

**Verse 19.**—Despairing. Or “without pain,” a term derived from the Greek; that is, not grieving over sin.

[Col. 0596C] **Verse 21.**—As the truth is. He says this because there are some in the Church who, under the name of Christ, do not follow the truth that Christ taught.

**Verse 22.**—Put off. He does not command that the body be put off, but that one’s life be changed for the better.

The old. Some think that the old human being is the body and the new human being the soul. But the body is the outer human being and the soul the inner; this oldness and newness take place in the inner person.

**Verse 23.**—In the spirit of your mind. The Apostle did not intend two things to be understood here, as though the mind were one thing and the spirit of the mind another, but because the mind is spirit.

A similar expression is: “In the putting off of the body of the flesh,” that is, of the flesh which is the body. The mind, therefore—or reason or understanding—is the image of God, by which the human being rules over the rest. Created in the knowledge of God, after it became foolish through sin it is renewed in that same knowledge, so that the image may begin to be reformed by the one by whom it was formed [Col. 0596D].

**Verse 24.**—Which was created according to God. He was conceived in a virginal womb by the work of the Holy Spirit, from the seed of a woman without the seed of a man. This was something new; hence Jeremiah: “The Lord will make a new thing upon the earth: a woman will encompass a man in the womb of her body” (Jeremiah XXXI).

**Verse 25.**—Therefore. He explains the parts of the old and new human being.

With his neighbor. Even a Gentile is a neighbor, because every human being is a neighbor by the condition of the first birth; or, in the hope of conversion, everyone ought to be regarded as a neighbor.

### VERSE 26

**“Be angry.”** That is, be indignant with yourselves so vehemently that you cease to sin, because when this anger is present the sun of righteousness does not set upon it, but rather shines upon it. Anger is the natural movement of the soul against those who sin; but do not sin by exceeding the proper measure in reproving too harshly. Hence Solomon says: “Do not be excessively righteous, lest righteousness destroy you” (Eccl. VII). Righteousness must therefore be tempered; for this reason God also tolerates the wicked, so that some of them may be corrected.

**“Let not the sun go down.”** He wishes anger not to continue, because if it persists, an opportunity is given to the devil. An angry person thinks evil thoughts, and thus the devil inserts himself so that he may carry out evil. **“Let not the sun go down.”** Christ must not abandon the mind, for he never dwells with anger.

### VERSE 27

**“Do not,” etc.** There are two gates by which the devil enters: desire and fear concerning earthly things. When these are turned in the opposite direction, God enters by the same gates. The former must be closed, and the latter opened.

### VERSE 29

**“Every word,” etc.** In God’s servant all things ought to appear good, and his purity ought not to be stained in any respect.

### VERSE 30

**“And do not grieve.”** By disobedience, grieve the Holy Spirit—that is, the preacher of truth—thereby grieving the Holy Spirit with respect to yourselves. You ought not to do this, since you have been sealed, as it were, like wax, with his image left upon you; or you have been sealed, that is, distinguished from the wicked.

### VERSE 31

**“All bitterness.”** Even if these things arise when causes are present, they must nevertheless be restrained.

**“Blasphemy.”** Blasphemy is speech by which false things are said about God himself. Thus it is worse to blaspheme than to swear falsely: by swearing falsely, God is made a witness to a false matter; but by blaspheming, false things are said about God himself.

## CHAPTER V

### VERSE 2

**“For an odor of sweetness.”** If Christ’s death was a sweet odor to God, then he willingly accepted his death. Did those who crucified him therefore not sin? But this is not so, because they unjustly killed the righteous one, who was offered by the will both of the Father and of himself. What does Judas have, likewise, except sin in betraying Christ? Yet unless Christ had handed himself over, Judas would not have handed him over. Judas handed Christ over; Christ handed himself over. But the former was conducting the business of Christ’s sale, while the latter was accomplishing our redemption. Therefore the former acted wickedly, whereas the latter acted mercifully.

### VERSE 5

**“The greedy person.”** He equates greed with idolatry because he signifies one whose god is money; or because he appropriates and stores up for himself the things of God which God wishes to be used in serving the needy, and prefers them to God, just as idolatry does the honor due to God.

### VERSE 6

**“With empty words.”** All their arguments are empty words, devoid of fruit and drawing people toward punishments.

### VERSE 9

**“For the fruit,” etc.** Works of this kind are the fruit and work of light.

**“And righteousness,” etc.** Righteousness and truth are parts of goodness. The meaning is: “In all goodness, righteousness, and truth”—that is, speak appropriately what is righteous and true.

### VERSE 11

**“Reprove.”** With a gentle spirit, as the Apostle says elsewhere. Do this so that the rebuke may resound outwardly with severity, while inwardly the love of gentleness is maintained. He joins two things together, namely, that they should neither participate by consenting nor fail to reprove. In these two ways the wicked person does not stain you: if you do not consent, and if you reprove.

The Apostle embraces both when he says: **“Do not participate,” etc.** That is, do not consent, praise, or approve. And because it is not enough merely not to consent, he adds: **“But rather reprove,”** that is, criticize, correct, and restrain. The meaning is: Do not be consenting to evil by approving it, nor negligent by failing to reprove it, nor arrogant by reproving it insultingly.

### VERSE 13

**“But all things,” etc.** As if he said: Although it is shameful to speak of the things they themselves do, they must nevertheless be reproved, because they are often made manifest through confession and repentance. Therefore they must be reproved, because what is thus made manifest is turned into light; or the wicked are made aware that they themselves are wicked, and therefore must be reproved, because in this way they begin to become light.

**“Everything that is made manifest.”** That is, the wicked person, when he comes to know that he is wicked, becomes light.

**“Is light.”** That is, through repentance he begins to be converted to goodness.

### VERSE 14

**“Rise.”** Through confession.

**“And arise.”** Through satisfaction.

### VERSE 16

**“Redeeming the time.”** That is, restore at another time what you did less of at one time, dividing up the days which the impious do not divide. Some divide their days, others fill them, and others do not even begin them—that is, some die in Egypt, others in the desert, and others in the holy land. It is not surprising if you have done less, since the days are evil and not everything can be done according to one’s will.

### VERSE 21

**“Submitting to one another.”** Not only hearers to prelates, but also prelates to their subjects, serving them in charity and humbly caring for them. For although the dignity of superiors is greater, it is nevertheless administrative; hence the Apostle says: “I have made myself the servant of all” (1 Cor. IX). It is therefore proper to superiors—while preserving their dignity—to serve, just as it is proper to inferiors to obey humbly. This ordered submission of both superiors and inferiors ought to exist in the chaste fear of Christ, who commanded humility.

### VERSE 22

**“Wives.”** Up to this point he has spoken generally about conduct; now he gives certain exhortations to the individual orders.

### VERSE 27

**“Not having spot,” etc.** Through good action she is clean from stain, and through hope she is stretched toward heavenly things. Therefore her garment shone on the mountain, whitened like snow, signifying the Church cleansed from every stain of sin. Through Christ’s extension upon the wood of the cross, she has been stretched free from wrinkle and toward heavenly things by desire.

**“Not having now spot or wrinkle,”** but in order that she may be holy: here, through good works; and undefiled, through abstinence from evil. Or this will occur in the future: then the Church will be holy through glory and undefiled through the removal of corruption.

Just as Christ shed his blood to wash away the Church’s stain and stretched himself upon the cross to remove its wrinkle, so men, if necessary, ought to die for the sake of saving their wives and instruct them with the word of life, so that they may present them to God.

### VERSE 29

**“For no one ever,” etc.** Whoever therefore prefers to be without a body does not hate the body, but its corruptions and burden.

**“As Christ also does the Church.”** So let a husband act toward his wife, who is his flesh. For in this way Christ also nourishes the Church with the food of his body and cherishes it with the spiritual garments of commandments, virtues, and good works.

### VERSE 32

**“This is a great mystery.”** Lest anyone think that the matter concerns a man and a woman according to the union of their natural sexes and bodily intercourse, he adds: **“I speak of Christ,”** etc. Therefore, in accordance with what exists in Christ and the Church, what was said—“They are no longer two, but one flesh”—is understood; and just as they are called bridegroom and bride, so they are called head and body. Whether, then, one says “head and body” or “bridegroom and bride,” understand one thing.

For from two there comes, as it were, a single person: namely, from head and body, and from bridegroom and bride. Isaiah commends this remarkable and excellent unity when Christ, speaking in him, says: “As a bridegroom he bound a turban upon me, and as a bride he adorned me with an ornament.” That spiritual unity was foreshadowed by what is said literally in Genesis about the union of marriage.

## CHAPTER VI

### VERSE 2

**“First.”** Namely, among the commandments that concern human beings in the second table. For the Decalogue belongs to the two commandments of love: love of God and love of neighbor.

Three strings belong to the first commandment, concerning God—that is, three commandments—because God is Trinity. To the other commandment, concerning one’s neighbor, belong seven strings, that is, seven commandments. Those three concerning God were written on the first table, while the other seven concerning one’s neighbor were written on the second table.

Among these, this commandment is rightly first because, just as God is principally the beginning of man, so the father is secondarily his beginning. A promise is added to this commandment, which is not added to the others.

### VERSE 5

**“Slaves, obey.”** Slavery began from sin. The first cause of slavery was sin, so that one human being might be subjected to another by the bond of condition. This occurred only because God judged it so; with him there is no iniquity, and he knows how to distribute different punishments according to the merits of sinners.

**“In simplicity.”** He makes slavery free: not through deceitful fear, but through faithful love, until iniquity passes away and all power is brought to nothing.

### VERSE 10

**“Finally.”** After the particular commandments by which he admonished the individual orders, he now admonishes everyone in common. It is as if he said: Up to this point I have helped you by word and deed; henceforth, in the future and for the remaining time, do so by faith and love.

### VERSE 12

**“Rulers of the world.”** They are not called this because they rule the world consisting of heaven and earth. Rather, he calls sinners “the world,” concerning which John says: “And the world did not know him” (John I). They rule such a world, against whom we have perpetual warfare, because they also cause us to suffer at the hands of troublesome people. They incite and inflame them, move them as their vessels, and touch them as instruments.

Against them we have an unseen struggle, for which the Apostle arms us.

**“Of darkness.”** Lest anyone think that demons rule this visible world, he explains what he means by “world”: **“of this darkness,”** that is, of sinners. As if he said: Demons do not rule the world consisting of heaven and earth, but sinners.

**“Against spiritual forces.”** As if he said: They are enemies to be feared because they are spiritual, invisible, and wicked; and they fight not over a small matter, but to take away the heavenly inheritance.

By “heavenly places” he means the powers in which we suffer the demons’ assault; or the wicked spirits are in the heavenly places, that is, in this lower air. They fight like horsemen upon human horses. Let us therefore kill the horsemen and possess the horses.

### VERSE 14

**“Girding your loins,” etc.** That is, restraining carnal desires with the belt of chastity, not hypocritically but in truth, or through charity.

**“Having put on the breastplate of righteousness.”** Righteousness is rightly compared with a breastplate because, just as a breastplate is woven from many rings, so righteousness consists of many virtues.

Alternatively, righteousness may be compared to a breastplate because, just as a breastplate guards the chest, tightens the belly, and protects the thighs, so righteousness drives away the superfluous thoughts that usually revolve in the chest, restrains the gluttony of the belly, and suppresses lust as well.

### VERSE 15

**“Having your feet shod.”** Mark says that the apostles were shod with sandals or soles, so that the foot would be neither straight nor bare upon the ground—that is, so that the Gospel would neither be concealed nor rest upon earthly advantages.

**“Feet.”** That is, let the affections be fortified with virtues, lest they be pierced by vices, so that they may be ready to preach the Gospel which announces peace between God and man; or so that they may be ready to fulfill the commandments of the Gospel.

### VERSE 16

**“The shield of faith.”** Faith is a shield under which righteousness is safe, as under the protection of all the virtues. It is extended before all the weapons, and the devil attacks it before everything else.

### VERSE 17

**“And the helmet.”** The helmet is eternal salvation, the memory of which envelops the mind so that it does not fail.

**“And the sword of the Spirit.”** The word of God is a two-edged sword, teaching about temporal and eternal things. It promises consolation concerning the former in the Old Testament, and perfection concerning the latter in the New Testament. What was promised to us temporally belongs to one edge of the sword; what is promised eternally belongs to the other edge. The two Testaments are therefore also called such because the Old promises earthly things, while the New promises eternal things.

Concerning this sword the Lord says: “I have not come to send peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matt. X). This sword is truly sharp, because it divides from the world the one whom it has made.

### VERSE 18

**“In the Spirit.”** He prays in the Spirit who prays with a pure conscience and an undivided faith. He prays in the flesh who, with a polluted mind, sins again—not by accident, but deliberately.

### VERSE 19

**“For an opening,” etc.** That is, so that I may be able openly to disclose the mystery of the Gospel, namely, the secrets of the Incarnation and the Passion. As if he said: May the pressure of tribulation, through fear itself, not blunt the sharpness of doctrine.

### VERSE 23

**“Peace to the brothers.”** He wishes them peace, which is the gate of love.

# EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS (G)*

## ARGUMENT

The Philippians are Macedonians. After receiving the word of truth, they persevered in faith and did not accept false apostles. He highly praises this in writing to them from prison at Rome through Epaphroditus.

## CHAPTER I

### VERSE 1

**“Paul.”** In his customary manner he places the greeting first; then he gives thanks to God for them, asking greater blessings for them, so that, growing in virtues, they may also reach perfection. Next he exhorts them to patience in tribulations by the example of himself and Christ; afterward he warns them to beware of the cunning of the false apostles. Finally he inserts a moral exhortation, and near the end says that he rejoices in the grace they had sent him at Rome through Epaphroditus.

**“Timothy.”** He adds Timothy because he was going to send him to them. In this way he commends him to some extent, so that they may receive from him the same things he writes.

**“Servants.”** He called them servants so that they too might endure hardships for the Lord.

**“Of Christ.”** So that they might stand against the false apostles.

### VERSE 3

**“I give thanks to my God.”** As if he said: Continue doing what you are doing, because your actions are such that I praise God for them.

### VERSE 5

**“Participation.”** Through this you made your possessions common by advancing the Gospel.

### VERSE 6

**“Confident.”** As if he said: I pray that you may stand firm, and I am confident that what I ask is indeed being done by you, and not something else; but see to it that my confidence is not in vain.

**“He will perfect.”** He himself works in us to will by beginning the work, and cooperates with those who will by bringing it to completion.

### VERSE 7

**“As it is right for me.”** Thus I give thanks, pray, and have confidence, as it is right to think—that is, to will. He explains the reason: because I have you in my heart, I desire what is good for you, whether I am imprisoned, knowing that you too are bound, or whether I am defending the Gospel, which you also do.

### VERSE 8

**“I long for you all,” etc.** That is, I long for you with the intimate love of Christ, so that you may be perfectly loved by him, or so that you may love God and your neighbors with the affection with which Christ loved, he who laid down his life.

Or this refers to what he said above, that he desired them to be companions in his joy. He specifies how: with the love of Christ, not human love, so that he may have them as participants in God.

### VERSE 10

**“So that you may approve what is better.”** That is, so that your love may increase in knowledge, enabling you to test and discern not only what is evil and good, but also, among good things, which are better. Thus, after testing, you may be sincere in yourselves, without works of corruption, and, with respect to your neighbor, without offense.

### VERSE 11

**“Filled with the fruit,” etc.** That is, with the reward of righteousness, so that you may be the glory and praise of God, so that it may be said of you: “Wonderful is God in his saints” (Ps. LXVII).

### VERSE 12

**“But I want you to know,” etc.** Up to this point he has spoken generally; now he sets forth specifically what encourages endurance, namely: “I give thanks for you”; “I am confident.” But I want you to know, etc. It is as if he said: Since you are so perfect, persevere and take care that the tribulations pressing upon you do not diminish this perfection of yours, but look to my example.

### VERSE 13

**“So that the bonds,” etc.** Since I patiently endure every kind of evil, it is clear that I am not guilty of a false crime for which a just punishment would strike me, but that I possess a certain virtue of truth, which the strength to endure magnifies.

### VERSE 14

**“Dared,” etc.** His steadfastness so encouraged many that they were not afraid to preach the Gospel.

### VERSE 17

**“But some,” etc.** Having been convinced by me in a dispute, they preach as I convinced them that they ought to preach.

**“From contention.”** From private hatred, which they had at some time brought against me and in which they were refuted. And lest they seem to have been corrected, he adds: **“Not with a pure intention.”**

### VERSE 18

**“What then?”** He does not prohibit the hirelings, but permits them, because they too are useful for certain purposes.

**“But I will also rejoice.”** I rejoice either in my evils or in the progress of the Gospel, because through it there is salvation for me.

### VERSE 21

**“For me to live is Christ,” etc.** As if he said: I rightly magnify Christ, whether by life or by death, because Christ is life for me—life here through faith and hope, and in the future through direct vision. For the sake of this life he surrendered his mortal body, so that he might receive it immortal for eternity. Hence he adds: **“And to die is gain.”**

### VERSE 22

**“But if to live,” etc.** Christ is life for me, so that I may magnify him. If this is so, then I do not know what to choose, whether to die or to live. As if he said: If there were no fruit here, there would be no doubt that I would choose to die in order to have Christ as my reward. Therefore, do not hesitate to die for Christ.

### VERSE 24

**“But to remain,” etc.** Behold, he chooses not what is better for himself, but what is useful for many, because of charity, which must be preferred to everything.

### VERSE 25

**“And the joy of faith,” etc.** That is: so that we may rejoice in your faith, or so that you may rejoice in faith as you advance in it. This exists only where there is a pure conscience.

### VERSE 28

**“And this is from God,” etc.** Even what you suffer does not come from yourselves, but from God, because on account of the merit of Christ, who obeyed the Father, this was granted to you among his other gifts.

### VERSE 29

**“Not only,” etc.** Both therefore belong to the grace of God: the faith of believers and the endurance of those who suffer, because he said that both had been granted.

### VERSE 30

**“The kind of struggle you saw in me.”** When I was stripped and beaten for the sake of the pythoness from whom I had driven out the evil spirit, and who brought great profit to her masters.

## CHAPTER II

### VERSES 1–2

**“If there is any consolation,” etc.** If you wish to have consolation in the things of Christ—that is, in the forgiveness of sins and in his other gifts—or, alternatively, if you wish to console me; if there is any comfort of charity among you—that is, if you wish the charity of the churches, which pray and do good works for their brothers, to be your consolation and strengthening in your adversities.

**“If there is any fellowship of the Spirit.”** Because of this fellowship, those upon whom the Holy Spirit first came spoke in the languages of all nations.

**“If there is any affection.”** That is, if you have an affection of compassion toward me. I do not mean compassion itself, that is, the giving of mercy.

If, I say, you wish these things to benefit you, **“complete my joy,”** that is, be humble and united. You will be so if you have the same mind, etc.

### VERSE 3

**“Nothing through contention.”** Note that there were contentions among them.

**“Considering others superior,” etc.** This must truly be considered, because there may be something hidden in another by which he is superior, even if our own good—which makes us seem superior—is not hidden.

### VERSE 4

**“Not looking to his own things.”** Here he teaches how they should avoid contention and empty glory, and how they should regard others as superior: namely, if they consider not their own good things but those of others.

### VERSE 5

**“Have this mind,” etc.** As if he said: Let each person seek not his own advantage but that of others, as Christ did. I invite you to patience and humility. You ought to have within yourselves what was in Christ. Just as Christ did not seek his own things but ours, so let us bear one another’s burdens.

### VERSE 6

**“Who, being in the form,” etc.** He first sets forth lofty things about Christ, so that those in whom there is a place of lowliness may not disdain to humble themselves.

**“Not robbery.”** That is, by usurping what would not be his, as did the devil and the first man.

Or he did not consider himself equal to God according to his humanity; to do so would be to commit robbery, that is, to presume upon what was not his. **“But emptied himself.”** Having shown his exalted status, he then speaks of his humility.

*(Augustine, Enchiridion, chs. 35–36.)* **“He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,”** etc., through the passage ending with: Christ, having become man, could have no sin.

**“The form of a servant.”** He did not lose the form of God: the form of a servant was added, not the form of God removed.

**“He emptied himself.”** To empty himself means to show himself visible from the greatness of his invisibility.

### VERSE 7

**“Having become.”** According to the form of a servant, whereas according to the form of God he was uncreated, and likewise in his habit—that is, in his manner of life.

### VERSE 8

**“He humbled himself,” etc.** *(Chrysostom.)* The Son willingly obeyed the Father, not as though into servitude, etc., through the passage ending with: by this he honored the Father above all things.

### VERSE 9

**“Therefore.”** Having shown the humility of Christ, which appeared most clearly in his Passion, he now demonstrates his glory and what, and how much, humility deserves.

### VERSE 10

**“So that at the name.”** Here he reveals to whom the name of God was given, before whom every creature bends the knee—namely, to God.

But someone might say that the man was God by adoption, and thus Christ was God truly in one respect and adoptively in another. Yet creation does not bend the knee to an adoptive god, but to the true God. It is therefore established that Christ is true God, before whom the knee is bent, not an adoptive god.

### VERSE 11

**“Because the Lord,” etc.** Some deny this, saying: How can it happen that a man should be in the glory of God the Father? But if he is adoptive, a man who is God cannot be in the glory of God the Father.

### VERSE 13

**“For God.”** God did not wish his saints to glory in their own strength even with respect to the perseverance of good, but in him. He gives them not only the kind of assistance he gave to the first man—without which they cannot persevere if they wish—but also works in them the will itself. Since they will not persevere unless they both can and will, the possibility and the will to persevere are granted to them by the generosity of divine grace.

Their will is so kindled by the Holy Spirit that they can because they so will, and they so will because God works in them the will to will.

### VERSE 14

**“But all things.”** He adds patience to humility.

### VERSE 15

**“A crooked generation,” etc.** That is, of the wicked, who corrupt and pervert the right order. They are called a “generation” because they have not been reborn from water and the Holy Spirit.

**“As lights.”** He rightly compares the saints with lights. For just as night does not extinguish the stars of heaven, so worldly iniquity does not obscure the minds of the faithful who cling to heaven through the sacred Scriptures.

### VERSE 20

**“For I have no one,” etc.** At this time many are hirelings together with the Apostle, but there are no true sons or shepherds except Timothy.

### VERSE 21

**“For all,” etc.** These are the hirelings, who must be tolerated because they have in their mouths the same things as the shepherds, who must certainly be loved. But thieves, who preach falsehoods, and robbers, who kill, must be avoided.

## CHAPTER III

### VERSE 1

**“Finally.”** As if he said: Up to this point I have instructed you how you ought to stand in battle against tribulations. Finally, I warn you against the false apostles, so that you do not receive legal observances from them, but believe that faith in Christ alone is sufficient.

He begins with the sincerity of faith.

**“To write.”** So that the writing might remain longer than spoken words.

### VERSE 3

**“For we,” etc.** That is: We have circumcision. This is what the Apostle wished to say: We are righteousness. For circumcision is righteousness. He commends this more strongly by saying that we are circumcision—that is, righteousness—than by saying that we are circumcised—that is, righteous; yet when he says that we are righteousness, we are to understand that we are righteous.

**“Who serve by the Spirit of God,”** or “God,” etc. He indicates the Spirit of the Lord, to whom *latria* is offered, although that service ought to be offered to the Creator alone. There is another kind of service by which we are commanded to serve one another through charity, called in Greek *doulia*.

**“And do not put confidence in the flesh.”** He serves the flesh who hopes to please God through carnal things. But when the flesh itself is subjected to the spirit through good works, we serve God in the spirit, who subdues the flesh so that the spirit may obey God.

### VERSE 4

**“Although I myself,” etc.** Lest the Apostle seem to despise in others what he does not possess, and to be unable to place confidence in the flesh, he adds: **“Although,”** etc.

### VERSE 5

**“Of the tribe of Benjamin.”** The tribe of Benjamin remained attached to Judah, not withdrawing from the Temple when the division occurred under Solomon’s servant. At that time the tribe of Judah, which was royal, the tribe of Benjamin, and the tribe of Levi, which was priestly, remained together, not withdrawing from Jerusalem and the Temple.

### VERSE 7

**“For the sake of Christ.”** So that I might not show the coming of Christ to be either not yet accomplished or superfluous. For all these impediments were empty and futile, preventing access to grace.

### VERSE 8

**“Nevertheless I consider.”** I did not judge these things to be worthless only for the sake of possessing Christ, but even if I could not attain Christ himself.

**“For this one thing,”** namely, for the sake of the surpassing knowledge that we have of Jesus, above all other knowledge.

**“As refuse.”** As if he said: They are not merely losses of good things, but things that defile one who already observes them. And this is so that in the future they may have Christ as their reward, and here may be a member in him. This cannot happen unless I regard those things as refuse.

### VERSE 9

**“My own righteousness,” etc.** If righteousness is from the law, how is it yours? Did you impose the law upon yourself? God gave and imposed the law. God commanded you to obey his law. Yet it is also yours, because you presume upon the law, judging by your own will that you are able to fulfill it.

*(Chrysostom.)* He rightly said: **“Not having my own righteousness,”** etc., through the passage ending with: which proceed from our own effort.

**“But that righteousness,” etc.** *(Augustine.)* This is the righteousness that obtains from God, which removes fear, etc., through the passage ending with: it must be entirely removed according to the shadow of legal figures.

**“The righteousness of faith.”** Righteousness, namely, exists in faith; and just as it is born from faith, so it cannot exist except in faith.

### VERSE 10

**“To know him.”** He adds a commendation of faith through the many things it accomplishes. In the other life it enables us to know God perfectly, who is believed in here. It also enables us to possess the resurrection, which is our resurrection through the power and efficacy of Christ’s resurrection.

In this life it gives us fellowship in suffering; for no one would suffer so much except through faith. It also gives conformity to his death—that is, that we may die as he did, if necessary.

### VERSE 11

**“I may attain.”** Giving to God what he has given to me, through this I shall come to the resurrection.

Or: **“I may meet Christ”** at the judgment, which belongs only to the saints, coming first to the true and glorious resurrection, which is not merely a rising among the dead but a rising far out from the dead. For although all will rise on the day of judgment, only the righteous will be gloriously changed and will meet the Lord, carried by angels into the air. The impious, however, will remain on the earth until they receive the judge’s terrible sentence.

**“Not that I have already received.”** He says this about himself so that those whom he praises may not be exalted as human beings, but may add labor, as he does, who is so great.

**“But I pursue,” etc.** Not with bodily steps, but with the affections of the mind and the habits of life, so that I may be able to become a possessor of perfect righteousness. By advancing day by day along the right path through spiritual renewal, I am already a perfect traveler on the way of that righteousness. For he was a perfect traveler, but had not yet reached the perfection of the journey itself.

**“If somehow I may apprehend.”** He says this because it is difficult. And lest it seem superfluous to suffer so much when he already possesses faith and other good things, he adds: I rightly labor so much for that glory, because I do not say that I have already received anything; for if I have received any glory, it is nothing in comparison with what is to come. Or, if I have received anything—as in the knowledge of Christ—I do not say that I am perfect in it. And if this is so concerning me, what should I say concerning others?

### VERSE 13

**“Those things that are behind.”** He does not leave former deeds behind because they were evil, but because they were small in comparison with the reward. He stretches toward greater things so that he may always advance toward what is better.

### VERSE 14

**“I pursue.”** Until I come to the appointed good.

**“The upward calling.”** That is, eternal life, to which God calls; and therefore it is a worthy thing, etc.

### VERSE 15

**“We are perfect.”** It must be understood that the righteousness by which the righteous person lives from faith is true righteousness. Although it may rightly be called perfect in certain righteous people, insofar as this life permits, it is nevertheless small in comparison with that great righteousness which the equality of the angels has attained.

The person who did not yet possess that greater righteousness called himself perfect because of the righteousness already present, and imperfect because of the righteousness still lacking. This lesser righteousness produces merit; the greater produces reward. Therefore whoever does not pursue the former does not attain the latter.

**“And if you think anything differently.”** That is, if you have devised anything better for the worship of God, know that this too is God’s gift, because he will reveal it to you.

But lest presumption arise from this, he adds: **“To what we have attained, let us think the same.”** That is, let us not think outside the rule of discipline, but hold what is common and modest in evangelical truth.

**“Nevertheless, where we have attained,” etc.** Now we are imperfect; now we think differently. Nevertheless, it is necessary that we all think the same about that to which we have attained in faith and knowledge, and that we remain in the same rule—that is, that we complete it in action.

### VERSE 18

**“Enemies of the cross.”** Those who introduce observances of the flesh assert that the cross was superfluous.

### VERSE 19

**“Whose god is the belly.”** As though salvation consisted in food, so that the belly is made a god. They glory in circumcised private parts, which is to set one’s mind on earthly things; and whatever they do, they do for the belly.

Or they make foods that belong to the belly into a god, when they say that these foods justify people, and their glory is in such things—things over which they can be confounded and ashamed—when they claim to be justified through temporal matters. Thus their temporal glory will lead them to eternal confusion.

### VERSE 20

**“Our citizenship.”** That is, by living and understanding, let us be like the angels. Hence also—that is, in addition to the benefits we already possess—we await the Lord.

## CHAPTER IV

### VERSE 1

**“Joy and consolation.”** That is, through whom I rejoice in the present and will be crowned in the future. For a teacher will be worthy of a crown on account of disciples victorious in the contest.

### VERSE 2

**“I urge Euodia,” etc.** I admonish everyone, but especially Euodia and Syntyche, because these devout women were accustomed to receive preachers.

### VERSE 3

**“Names.”** Those who are distinguished by their merits will have different dwellings in the eternal house. Hence: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John XIV).

**“The book of life.”** Predestination, in which all who are to be saved have been predestined. As if he said: Do not, Philippians, take it badly that I have not named all of you individually in my letter. Even if you are not written in it, you are nevertheless contained in the book of life.

### VERSE 4

**“Rejoice,” etc.** Having rejoiced in their faith and works, the Apostle wishes them, so that they may be more eager, to rejoice in the Lord as they advance in this pursuit. He repeats it to show that he truly rejoices in them.

### VERSE 5

**“Moderation.”** That is, a proper measure, so that all joy may be in the Lord, and so that others may learn this through you.

Or let your moderation be known to all believers and unbelievers, so that they may imitate you and be unable to find fault.

**“The Lord is near.”** That is, he is ready to give whatever is necessary, whether spiritual or temporal. Do not be anxious or fearful about anything, but present petitions concerning the things you wish to obtain.

### VERSE 6

**“But in every prayer.”** Prayer and supplication are used generally, whether for oneself or for others, and concerning any matters; petition, however, is made concerning specifically named necessities.

**“Let them be made known.”** This knowledge is produced by persistence and watchfulness in prayer. Then peace guards the hearts in Christ. He says this because whoever is at peace with God does not fear an adverse mind.

**“Before God.”** Or before the angels, who offer them to God. Hence: “When you prayed, I offered your prayer before God.”

Or let them be made known before God through endurance, not before human beings through boasting.

### VERSE 7

**“And the peace of God”**—that is, God, who is supreme peace, which cannot even be conceived; and therefore nothing outside him is needed.

**“Surpasses all understanding.”** Our understanding, not that of those who always see the face of the Father.

Or the peace with which God himself is at peace surpasses all understanding except his own, because neither can we know it in this way nor can any angel.

### VERSE 8

**“Finally, brothers,” etc.** Up to this point he has warned them against persecutors and false preachers. Finally, in his conclusion, he explains what belongs to perfection.

**“Whatever is just.”** This concerns one’s neighbor.

**“Holy.”** This concerns one’s own life.

And, to say less, **“whatever is lovely,”** that is, worthy of being loved, such as modest conduct, humble speech, and similar things.

**“Of good reputation.”** *(Augustine.)* Our life is necessary for us, but a good reputation is necessary for others. Therefore whoever guards his life from accusations of disgrace benefits himself; but whoever guards his reputation is also merciful toward others.

### VERSE 10

**“I rejoiced,” etc.** Here he recalls that they had often sent him what he needed, and he shows that his own eagerness had become greater because, after having been negligent in this matter, they had applied diligence and repeated their action, so that, having remembered their apostle, they might send forth fruit to be stored in the heavenly granary.

**“At some time,” etc.** At some point, because they were not able to do so at every time.

**“You have blossomed again.”** By ministering what I needed.

This ministry is called a blossom because from it the fruit of eternal life proceeds.

**“For me.”** Because your compassion benefits me.

But lest they seem to have stopped for some evil reason, he adds: You have blossomed again now, but previously you were occupied and hindered by various adversities.

### VERSE 11

**“Not as though,” etc.** He rejoices not for his own sake, but for their progress.

### VERSE 12

**“I know how to be brought low.”** Whoever is not broken by poverty is not withdrawn from thanksgiving. Whoever is not inflamed by desire for temporal things knows how to be brought low—that is, to endure want.

**“To abound.”** Whoever is not exalted by the things he has received, who does not turn them toward the use of empty glory, and who does not possess alone what he has received but mercifully divides it with the needy, knows how to abound.

Whoever, after receiving food, does not use it to gorge the belly and does not give more to the flesh than necessity demands knows how to be satisfied.

Whoever endures the lack of food without murmuring and does nothing for the sake of obtaining necessary sustenance by which the soul might fall into the snare of sin knows how to hunger.

## VERSE 17

“Not because I seek [a gift].” The thing given is presented as a gift—food, drink, and the like. But the fruit is good works and the giver’s upright intention. Thus the Lord in the Gospel does not simply say, “Whoever receives a righteous man or a prophet,” but adds, “in the name of a righteous man or a prophet.” To receive a prophet or a righteous man is the gift; to do this in the name of a righteous man or prophet is the fruit. Elijah is read to have been fed both by a raven and by a widow. But through the raven, who fed him without doing so in the name of a righteous man, he was fed by a gift; through the widow, by fruit, because she knew that she was feeding a man of God. “But fruit”—that is, a good and upright intention joined to a good work. [Col. 0608D] For he does not rejoice so much that his own need has been relieved as he rejoices in their fruitfulness.

## VERSE 18

“In an odor.” What was sent by you pleases God as a most fragrant odor. It is also compared with prayer, which is God’s incense. Hence it is said: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11).

## VERSE 19

“May he fill all your desire.” Not with earthly things, but with glory. Or, the desires of the saints are fulfilled by the glory of Christ, so that Christ himself may thereby be glorified.

[Col. 0609]

# THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS (G)*

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0609A]

The Colossians, like the Laodiceans, are Asians, and they too had been approached beforehand by false apostles. The Apostle himself did not visit them, but corrects them by letter. For they had heard the word from Archippus, who had also received the ministry among them. Therefore the Apostle, already imprisoned, writes to them from Ephesus through Tychicus the deacon and Onesimus the acolyte.

# CHAPTER ONE

## VERSE 1

“Paul.” As usual, he places the greeting first. After giving it, he gives thanks for their virtues, commends their faith and love, and prays that they may be perfected in Christ. He then commends Christ’s benefits and primacy according to both natures; afterward, recalling the dignity of his ministry, he warns them not to withdraw from Christ after being deceived by prophecy or by the ceremonies of the Law. Finally, he instructs all together morally according to their sexes, ages, and conditions, and at the end admonishes Archippus to be diligent concerning the ministry he has undertaken. “The Apostle,” etc. Observe that he rightly calls himself an apostle here before everyone, since he was an apostle even to those to whom he had preached through his disciples.

## VERSE 3

“We give thanks.” He shows the good things they have received by giving thanks for them.

## VERSE 6

“As also,” etc. That is, purely and truly, just as it came through me and others into the whole world and still remains in it—as though he were saying: What has happened to you is no less than what has happened in the other churches. While the Gospel is in the world, it bears fruit there through good works, and grows through an increase of knowledge and in the number of the faithful. By this the others do not possess more than you do; rather, God acts in you as he does in them, and therefore you ought to add nothing further.

[Col. 0609C]

## VERSE 7

“For you,” etc. Desiring their salvation, he began to assist Archippus.

## VERSE 8

“In the Spirit.” Because you love for spiritual rather than carnal reasons.

## VERSE 9

“Be filled in all.” It is a great thing to know fully what God wills in all matters of the active and contemplative life.

## VERSE 10

“In knowledge.” So that they may not be ignorant of the substance of their faith—that is, of the thing hoped for—and may therefore be firm.

## VERSE 11

“In all strength.” I mean: strengthened by God in every virtue, namely chastity and the others. [Col. 0609D] The one who is the Father’s radiance, that is, the Son, can accomplish this well. Or, it may mean: according to the clear knowledge he has given you.

## VERSE 12

“Giving thanks.” He now begins to say that the Law is not beneficial but harmful, while Christ is sufficient for all good things. This can be known from the fact that he himself and the other apostles—who had been involved with legal observances—abandoned them and fled to Christ. As though he were saying: We pray for you, giving thanks to God because he makes us worthy, something the Law could never do.

[Col. 0610A]

“He made us worthy.” Not in the Law, but in the light—that is, through God, who is light from light and by whose grace we are illuminated. Or, “in the light,” that is, in clear knowledge; whoever turns away from it falls into darkness. “Of the lot.” God’s will is a lot among the human race, with whom there is no iniquity, but who does everything through justice, even if that justice is hidden.

## VERSE 13

“He delivered us from the power.” That is, from hell, where we were held by the devil, both through our own sin and through Adam’s transgression. “And transferred,” etc. When he lifted us from the depths of Tartarus, he brought us into heaven with his only Son. For believers who are devoted with steadfast mind already depart from the world and, under the guidance of the angel of the Father’s right hand, are brought into heaven. “The kingdom of the Son.” Concerning it he himself says: “My kingdom is not of this world.” [Col. 0610B] He does not say, “It is not here,” but “It is not from here,” because although he sojourns in the world, he is not of the world. For concerning his kingdom he says: “You are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world.” They were of the world when they belonged to the ruler of the world.

## VERSE 14

“Redemption.” After the devil’s power was destroyed, the possibility of freedom was given to us through the pouring out of the blood of the one who had no sin. Since the devil rightly held those whom the condition of death had bound as guilty of sin, he would rightly release them through the one whom, although guilty of no sin, he unjustly subjected to the punishment of death.

## VERSE 15

“Who is the image.” The image of a king is one thing on a coin and another in a son. We are the coin, and Christ the Son is the image of God in us. No image of God ought to be worshiped except that one which is what he himself is—not worshiped in place of him, but together with him.

## VERSE 18

“The head of the body, the Church.” For he stands in relation to the Church as the head does to the body. Since the Church began with Abel, how can he be their head? Properly, because he is the beginning of the Church—that is, its founder. “Who is the beginning.” Of the Church according to his divinity—that is, the founder of the Church—because by the power of his divinity and the gift of his mercy he illuminated all the righteous who were generated from Abel to the last righteous person. According to his humanity also he may be called the beginning of the Church, because it was founded upon faith in his humanity. And rightly he is both head and beginning, ruler and founder, because he is the firstborn, etc. “Firstborn,” etc. Just as, being born from God before all things, he was first so that he might create all things, so as man he is the first to rise again, so that he might restore them, and thus always remain first and chief.

## VERSE 19

“Fullness.” Because he can do all things from himself. Hence: “As the Father has life in himself, so also the Son,” who raises and gives life to whomever he wills. In this way he is shown to be perfect God.

## VERSE 20

“To reconcile through him.” It pleased God to reconcile through him, and he himself made peace—not without cost, but through blood—between heavenly and earthly things. Thus the way into heaven is opened to humanity. All things made through him live in their author.

## VERSE 21

“Alienated and enemies.” They were alienated and enemies by the disposition of his will, which amounts to the same thing, because they did not receive what God commanded through Moses, since they were devoted to their idols.

## VERSE 22

“He reconciled in the body.” If a mortal and dead man could reconcile, now that he is immortal he can do all things.

## VERSE 23

“If indeed you remain.” He had said so many and such great things about Christ so that they might place their hope in him alone, in whom all things exist, and might not think that they should subject themselves to any of the elements or angels. He alone is to be worshiped, and no one is to be esteemed in comparison with him. “In the whole.” The new creation which is now beneath heaven is still a pilgrim, but it will come to glory.

## VERSE 24

“I complete.” I complete what remains of the sufferings that Christ endured, or that he now commands to be endured—that is, I am ready to suffer.

## VERSE 25

“I was made.” He says that he was made a minister of the Gospel by God through Christ, so that the ministry begun by God might be fulfilled through a suitable servant, a ministry that had been hidden from the ages. “It was given to me.” So that I might fulfill what God ordained concerning you—namely, that you should be saved through the Incarnation. He says this so that salvation might not appear not to have been promised to the Gentiles. Or, “it was given to me in you”: what is sought from my people is as great as what would be sought from me personally.

## VERSES 28–29

“Admonishing.” We admonish those who contradict, and overcome them; we teach those who obey. “In all wisdom.” True wisdom exists when Christ is recognized. “That we may present,” etc. “In whom.” As though he were saying: God adds miracles to my labor for confirmation.

# CHAPTER TWO

## VERSE 1

“I wish,” etc. It follows: “For you.” The Apostle was no less concerned for those whom he had not seen than for those whom he had seen.

## VERSE 2

“Built up in love.” The love that God had for us, since he handed over his Son for us. “Into all riches.” That is, into the full resources of understanding, where they may possess perfect knowledge of human and divine things, such as the soul and the heavenly spirits. Otherwise no one ascends to the knowledge of God.

[Col. 0611D]

“Of God the Father,” etc. So that you may know that the Father is a different person from the Son, although he is one in substance with him. If you seek to attain knowledge, turn only to Christ, because in him are all the riches, though hidden. Therefore do not be surprised if you are in Christ and have not yet found them, because they are not revealed to everyone, but to those who ask and knock.

## VERSE 4

“But this.” I say this not only so that you may strive toward what you do not yet possess, but also so that no one may deceive you and, by means of worldly matters, draw you away from the hope that is in Christ.

## VERSE 5

“But also in spirit.” The saints have been given the ability in spirit to see distant things. Let those therefore be on their guard whose actions are not hidden from their teacher.

[Col. 0612A]

“Rejoicing.” By this he makes them more ready concerning the Gospel, because he says that he rejoices in the ordered character of their conduct and the stability of their faith, so that, knowing how they please God in this, they may become firmer.

## VERSE 7

“Rooted.” The lesser members in the active life. “Built upon others in him.” That is, you who are greater and are engaged in contemplation.

## VERSE 8

“Deception.” What the false preachers say about the Law. “And empty.” Because this falsehood has no usefulness, although false things sometimes possess some usefulness. “According to the elements.” He touches on those who explain idols more subtly, saying, “Juno is air, Neptune is the sea.” Therefore, after saying “according to philosophy” and “empty,” he adds, “according to the elements of the world,” as though warning that not only ordinary worshipers of images, but also those who present themselves as learned teachers and interpreters of signs, must be avoided.

[Col. 0612B]

## VERSE 9

“Bodily.” Not because God is corporeal, but he uses a metaphorical expression. In a temple made by human hands he dwelt not bodily but in shadow—that is, through signs that prefigured him. “Bodily,” because God dwells in Christ’s body, which he assumed from the Virgin, as in a temple. He does not dwell in the saints in the same way, because Christ is the head in whom all the senses are present, whereas the others, as though possessing touch alone, have received the Spirit according to a measure. Of them it cannot be said, “The Word became flesh” (John 1), nor is any one of them called the only-begotten of God.

## VERSE 12

“Buried with him.” That is, baptized in the likeness of his burial. “Through faith in the operation.” That is, by believing in the works of God. He explains one of God’s works which those who wish to rise again especially need to believe: namely, that God raised Christ, and that by Christ’s example he will raise them also. Hence he adds: “Who raised,” etc.

## VERSE 14

“Blotting out.” God not only forgave you Gentiles, but also us Jews, releasing us from transgressions arising from the Law. And this is what “blotting out” means.

“Handwriting.” He means Adam’s sin, which Christ took away and fastened to the cross, though not that alone. For unless he removed both this and the other sins, we would not be freed from death and hell. When the innocent one is killed, sin is crucified. “Decree” is the adverse sentence against all human beings, expressed in the words: “You shall surely die,” and so forth.

[Col. 0612D]

“Fastening it.” So that it might now cease, since all sacrifices have been fulfilled in the offering of the true Lamb.

## VERSE 15

“Stripping principalities and powers.” By taking away Abraham, Isaac, and the other righteous. “He led them away in triumph”: he led them far from this kingdom into heaven. “Confidently”: that is, with the hope of victory. “Triumphing”: that is, conquering them on the cross, not secretly but openly. For if one considers the perfection of the Church, the ancient enemy is plainly seen to have been defeated. Or, “he led principalities and powers away in triumph,” that is, he expelled them from the Church. “Triumphing over them in himself”: by his death. For by offering one wholly true sacrifice for us, he extinguished whatever guilt existed—guilt by which principalities and powers held us captive for the endurance of punishment. Thus, from the place where the devil received outward power to kill the Lord’s flesh, his inward power, which held us captive, was itself killed.

[Col. 0613A]

## VERSE 17

“These are a shadow,” etc. At that time such precepts existed, and failure to observe them was sin; now they are testimonies and confirmations of the truth. I, Scripture, which was then an exactor of symbolic works, am now a witness to the things signified. What was then observed as a foreshadowing is now recited as confirmation. “But the body.” That is, Christ is the truth of this shadow; it pertains to Christ. Or, all those things are the body of Christ—that is, they signify Christ’s body, whether the body he assumed from the Virgin or the Church, which is his body.

## VERSE 18

“Willing.” That is, loving what he has not seen. Or, “willing,” namely, attempting to persuade others concerning what he has not seen—that is, the ceremonies of the Law, whose rationale he does not understand. “Puffed up.” He understands nothing by “puffed up” beyond what sensuality grasps.

## VERSE 19

“Constructed,” etc. They are joined into one through connection, because they believe the same things and do the same things. “And supplied in service.” “Through bonds,” that is, through love, without which the members do not cohere, serve one another, or live. “Into the increase of God.” God is increased by those who return, just as he is diminished by those who depart.

## VERSE 20

“If then you have died.” Until now he warned those who were standing firm not to be led astray; now he addresses those who were already observing some things from the Law. As though he were saying: Take care not to be deceived, but tell others why you observe the Law. He calls the elements the creatures of this world. “If,” he says, “when you received the faith of Christ, you were separated from sin and from the elements of the world”—that is, from abstinence and every superstition concerning the creatures of the world—“why,” etc. This can be understood as “with Christ” and “just as Christ.”

[Col. 0613C]

## VERSE 22

“All these things perish with use,” etc. If anyone uses them according to the Jewish rite—abstaining from some things and using others, believing that he is justified by this—they lead to death. I speak of things that now exist according to the commandments and doctrines of human beings, etc., not of God. For after the truth came, God no longer commands these things; rather, the Pharisees command them by their authority and teach them through arguments.

[Col. 0613D]

## VERSE 23

“In humility,” etc. This does not refer to the humility that is a virtue, but, as is understood from the Greek, to that by which the mind regards lowly things—that is, useful and earthly things—and to the abasement of the soul. Such observances are “not for sparing the body,” because they involve much labor, which is empty; nor are they “in honor of God,” since his purpose is said to be rendered void, nor in honor of the saints, whose faith is destroyed; nor are they “for the satisfying of the flesh,” because they take away many things. “In superstition,” etc. Religion is feigned so that false things may appear true. It humbles the mind toward the earth, so that it may not rise to heavenly things, and it harms the body, whose head is Christ. It is not “in honor,” because, with Christ the head severed, they fulfill the mind of the flesh. For the fattening of the flesh is human tradition, since it says that what the prudence of the flesh teaches is sufficient.

[Col. 0614A]

# CHAPTER THREE

## VERSE 1

“Those things that are above.” Not in place, but in the excellence of their merit.

## VERSE 2

“Those things that are above.” Spiritual things, which were signified by carnal observances: eternal glory and the things that lead to it.

## VERSE 3

“Your life is hidden.” This means that your time has not yet come, because summer has not yet arrived—that is, Christ’s advent, when fruitful trees will be distinguished from barren ones. But the time of those who love earthly things is always ready. When Christ appears, that will be our time.

## VERSE 5

“Put to death,” etc. After the arguments concerning the fullness of Christ, a general exhortation concerning conduct is given to all, so that they may not return to their former way of life. “Your members.” That is, the parts of the old person, or the desires of the members. “Fornication,” etc. He describes the sins which he calls members, so that after receiving knowledge of the truth they might devote themselves to a good life. It is greatly harmful to know the truth and not carry it out in one’s deeds. For “the servant who knew his master’s will and did not do it will be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12). “And greed.” Under one name he forbids two very serious things: idolatry and greed. Their wickedness is not different, since greed is the root of all evils, and both are fulfilled in nearly the same act. Just as idolatry seeks to take glory away from the one God, so that he alone may not possess the name of deity, so the greedy person extends himself into God’s possessions, seeking to usurp for himself what God made for all. Both are enemies of God, because they deny God what belongs to him.

[Col. 0614C]

## VERSE 7

“In which you also walked.” This makes them rejoice that they have escaped and warns them to be cautious thereafter.

## VERSE 8

“But now.” Above he forbade the more serious sins; now he forbids the lesser ones, so that these may not be thought harmless. There are people who are not habitually drunk but who sometimes become drunk. Likewise, there are people who are not habitually deceitful and yet sometimes lie; the same occurs with other sins. He therefore forbids lying even occasionally, and especially habitual lying.

## VERSE 10

“Who is renewed.” The renewal of the mind is said to be “according to God,” as is read in the Epistle to the Ephesians, or “according to the image of God,” as it is read here. It is therefore “according to God,” so that it may not be thought to take place according to some other creature.

[Col. 0614D]

## VERSE 14

“Love.” For it is the more excellent way, surpassing knowledge and all commandments. This is the Lord’s seamless garment, woven from above. It is seamless so that it may never be torn apart; it reaches toward unity, because love gathers everyone into one.

## VERSE 15

“Peace.” This is necessary for the unity of the body, which peace itself has created. “The peace of God.” Peace can be said to exist without love, but love always has peace with it.

## VERSE 16

“Teaching and admonishing.” He says this so that instruction may be given to those who do not know, and admonition to those who do know.

[Col. 0615A]

## VERSE 17

“Whatever you do.” Since above he commanded that God be praised in the heart, he now urges that God’s name be praised and exalted in words and deeds as well. Our words and works should be free from blame, so that the Lord may be magnified, whose teaching makes his disciples blameless. “All things.” Not only what you do in word or deed, but everything, including thoughts and whatever else there may be. Or, “whatever you do, do all”: that is, do it perfectly, attributing it to God. And this is what follows: “doing it in the name.” “Giving thanks.” We truly give thanks to God through Christ if we observe the measure of his commandments.

## VERSE 21

“Fathers.” He commands fathers to be moderate toward their children, so that the children may not be discouraged by them and sin against them, thereby offending God. For anger is an inconsiderate thing, so much so that the person who becomes angry sometimes spares not even himself.

[Col. 0615B]

## VERSE 23

“Work from the soul, as for the Lord.” God approves that innocence by which a person becomes innocent not through fear of punishment but through love of justice. For whoever does not sin out of fear, although he does not harm others, nevertheless harms himself greatly. Simulated equity is not equity, but doubled sin. In it there are both iniquity and pretense.

[Col. 0616A]

# CHAPTER FOUR

## VERSE 3

“Door.” That is, may he make my mouth open; it was given for this purpose, so that the word might come forth from it. It is open when he says many great things.

## VERSE 5

“Redeeming the time.” That is, preparing opportunities to preach to them by various means.

## VERSE 8

“So that he may know what concerns you and may console your hearts,” etc. The person who sees that he is known is more careful than the person who sees that he is unknown.

## VERSE 10

“You received him,” because he returned to me, and therefore, if he comes.

[Col. 0616B]

## VERSE 16

“See that it is also read in,” etc. From this passage we understand that the Apostle’s instructions are general and that his epistles were written for the benefit of all people.

## VERSE 18

“Remember,” etc. Before giving the greeting, he first offers an exhortation, saying: “Remember,” etc.

[Col. 0615]

# THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS (G)*

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0615B]

The Thessalonians are Macedonians. After receiving the word of truth in Christ Jesus, they persevered in the faith, even during persecution by their fellow citizens. Moreover, they neither received false apostles nor accepted what was said by the false apostles. The Apostle praises them highly, writing to them from Athens through Tychicus the deacon and Onesimus the acolyte.

# CHAPTER ONE

## VERSE 1

“Silvanus and Timothy.” The greeting is prefaced with their names, but the sense and words of this epistle belong to the Apostle alone.

## VERSE 2

“Grace to you and peace.” As is his custom, he places the greeting first. After it, he gives thanks for their virtues, recalling not only their faith and works but also the manner of their conversion and their endurance of evils.

[Col. 0615D]

## VERSE 3

“Before God.” They are so certain as though you were already seeing them, and in this way he encourages them.

## VERSE 5

“In the Holy Spirit.” Because through me you received the gifts of the Spirit—not sparingly, but in fullness. “What kind of people we were,” etc. The fact that we ourselves suffered as an example for you also makes it clear that God loved and chose you.

# CHAPTER TWO

## VERSE 1

“For you yourselves know.” You know this about it: it did not come in secular prosperity, which is empty, but amid great anxiety because of adversity. Therefore we placed our confidence not in ourselves, who are fragile, but in the Lord.

[Col. 0616B]

## VERSE 2

“In Philippi.” He suffered the oppression mentioned here because of the python spirit which he had driven out of the girl.

[Col. 0616C]

## VERSE 3

“Exhortation.” Here he seems to begin speaking against the false apostles, recalling first the truth of the Gospel and then his prudent conduct among them. “In deceit.” Even truth is involved in deceit when it is not preached out of love for the truth and for the benefit of the hearers, but in order to acquire glory or some other gain.

## VERSE 4

“Not as pleasing human beings.” Unless he himself works this in us, we cannot avoid it. No one feels how much power the love of human glory has to do harm unless he has declared war against it. For although it is easy for someone not to desire praise when it is denied him, it is nevertheless difficult not to take pleasure in it when it is offered.

## VERSE 5

“Neither.” Here he touches upon the false apostles, who wanted themselves rather than God’s teaching to be commended. The Apostle, however, who sought glory not in the present but in the future, humbled himself so that God’s preaching might be exalted. “In an occasion.” I do not say that I acted for greed; I did not do or say anything in which there might be an occasion for greed. “God is witness,” who knows the heart, for this is not so evident to human beings.

[Col. 0615D]

## VERSE 7

“We could have been,” etc. He presses the case against the false apostles so strongly that he says he refused support, although he was entitled to seek it, in order to restrain those who had neither the means nor the shame to ask. He calls the obligation of apostolic authority a burden because the false apostles, usurping it improperly, demanded it importunately from the common people. “His own children.” A woman sometimes raises another person’s children for payment, not out of love; but she raises her own out of affection.

[Col. 0617A]

## VERSE 12

“He called.” With the calling that accords with his purpose.

## VERSE 13

“Therefore.” Because he called you, we give thanks. I say that he called you, and this is apparent from the fact that you quickly and firmly received the word, etc. “Heard from God.” That is, what we heard from God, or in which God is heard. “As it truly is, the word of God.” They received the word with such devotion that they proved themselves to understand that its teaching was from God.

## VERSE 14

“For you became imitators,” etc. He has said much against the false apostles; now, so that they may not be shaken by his own tribulation or that of the apostles, he exhorts them.

## VERSE 16

“It has come upon.” They are always filling up their sins because God’s wrath has come upon them so that they may be blinded. “To the end.” Because at the end of the world some of the Jews will be converted.

[Col. 0617B]

“By word, presence,” etc. Word and presence ceased because the Apostle could not address them face to face; but his heart and concern did not cease.

## VERSE 18

“But Satan hindered us.” The fact that God permitted him to be hindered serves to increase their crown, because they stood firm in his absence.

## VERSE 19

“What is,” etc. (CHRYSOSTOM.) How great is this ardor! Never could a father and mother, even if they had come together and joined their desire, have displayed a desire equal to Paul’s. “I rejoice,” he says, “more because of you than because of the crown.” Consider, then, how great it is for the Church planted by Paul to be present whole and to have put down roots.

[Col. 0617C]

“Or a crown of glory.” If it is glory now, what will it be before the true Judge?

# CHAPTER THREE

## VERSE 2

“To strengthen you.” For this reason he himself had desired to come.

## VERSES 6–7

“As we also do you; therefore.” Because he announced these things, we were comforted, even without his presence.

## VERSE 9

“For what thanksgiving,” etc. Nothing is so worthy that it could suffice as compensation for the salvation of the Gentiles that has been gained.

## VERSE 13

“Without blame.” So that you may not complain about evils, or may be so innocent that no one can complain about you, and so that you may also be “in holiness.” [Col. 0617D] That is, existing before God through the perfection of virtues, not merely before human eyes.

# CHAPTER FOUR

## VERSE 1

“Finally.” Until now he urged those who were mature to have patience amid their own tribulation or that of others; now he urges the lesser ones concerning purity, exhorting them to continence. “Just as.” By hearing and understanding from us—that is, from me and Silvanus—“how you ought to walk,” etc., so also walk by conducting yourselves rightly. “And to please God.” The person who pleases God is the one who adorns the right faith he possesses through the practice of virtues and perfect works. “So also walk.” The order is: “We ask you to walk as you received.” [Col. 0618A] “That you may abound more.” This is not altered in the arrangement of the wording.

## VERSE 2

“For you know what commandments,” etc. (JEROME.) Sanctification withdraws the Christian from all incontinence. It is not fitting for the incontinent person to touch Christ’s holy body, especially since Moses, wishing to sanctify the Jews, commanded the whole people to abstain from every woman so that they might be worthy to enjoy God’s presence.

## VERSE 4

“His own vessel.” That is, let him possess his wife by ruling her, and let him do so “in sanctification,” abstaining from intercourse on feast days, and “in honor,” not abusing her shamefully.

## VERSE 8

“He who also gave,” etc. He gave you the Spirit to accomplish these things. Therefore do not despise such a great helper, who does not dwell in a body subjected to sins. Or, he gave him to us apostles so that we might have greater authority to preach and rebuke.
