“Now concerning brotherly love,” etc. This exhortation is not contrary to the laws mentioned above. For it happened that some generously supplied the needy, while others, because of their generosity, neglected to work. He therefore rightly praised the former and gave the latter useful counsel.

## VERSE 11

“Make it your aim.” As though he were saying: It is difficult to abandon a habit, but compel yourselves. “And work with your hands.” Work must be done; one must not remain idle. It is honorable, like a light to unbelievers, and you will not desire another person’s property, much less ask for or take it.

[Col. 0618C]

## VERSE 12

“We do not want you to be ignorant.” After the exhortation concerning continence and the correction of curiosity, he confirms that the dead will rise again, both through Christ’s resurrection and by his own authority.

## VERSE 13

“Through Jesus he will bring with him.” They always went on, following him, until they came to the sleep of death. Hence it is also written in another Epistle: “We who are alive.”

## VERSE 14

“Them.” Not only those who will be found alive, but also the dead, concerning whom you are doubtful. “Who have fallen asleep.” He calls Christ dead but the faithful sleeping, so that they may believe more firmly in the resurrection. He calls Christ dead so that, when we hear that he died and rose again, we too may hope to rise through the power of his divinity.

[Col. 0618D]

## VERSE 15

“For the Lord himself.” In his own person.

“In the trumpet of God.” (ANSELM.) This trumpet will awaken everyone and terrify the enemies; it will summon his own to battle, so that they may conquer their adversaries, while the enemies flee from the face of the Lord and are cast into Gehenna. Again, just as the trumpet once summoned the Hebrew people to their festivals, so this trumpet will summon the people of the saints to the celebration of eternal joy. “At the command of God,” he says, “and when the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God sound.” “He will descend.” Not in humility as before, but commanding by his own voice, or by that of the archangel or the angels, through which he will raise the dead. It is called a trumpet because it will be manifest, or because it will be like one used for battle; it will belong to God and Christ, to whom God will grant efficacy.

## VERSE 16

“In the clouds.” Because a cloud will receive them, just as it received Christ at his ascension. Hence another interpreter says: “With clouds as bearers.”

# CHAPTER FIVE

## VERSE 1

“Concerning the times.” That is, whether in summer or winter, by day or by night. “And seasons.” Namely, at what hour of the day or night Christ will come.

## VERSE 2

“The day of the Lord.” The present day belongs to human beings according to their own will, but then it will be the Lord’s day. “Like a thief.” He will come unexpectedly upon the wicked, as also happens at each person’s death. “Like a thief,” I say—not by day but by night, when he comes more secretly and people are asleep, and then he takes everything away, so that the person who thought himself rich, awakening, finds nothing. Thus many who are now secure will then discover that they possess nothing good. For this reason he began with the times: to warn them to be on their guard, lest they be caught in this way.

[Col. 0619B]

## VERSE 3

“For when they say.” For, as is found in the words of Daniel, the Antichrist and his ministers will reign for three and a half years, and Elijah and Enoch will be killed by him, as is also found in the Apocalypse: “Then there will be such tribulation as has not been before and will not be afterward.” Afterward he will be killed by Michael together with the greater part of his followers.

## VERSE 5

“Children of light.” Faith is the light that makes the day—that is, the character of the virtues. Conversely, unbelief is darkness, and the character of vices is night. “We are not of night or of darkness,” etc. That is, let us not grow sluggish in the present, but let the mind keep watch, attentive to these fleeting things, and let us use them soberly, not as our own goods but as things given for support. Truly, we who are not of night ought not to sleep. For the one who sleeps sleeps because of night: that is, their vices and sins have drawn them to this state, so that, forgetting eternal life, they rest in these things. Those who are drunk have this condition from the night of vices, through using these things immoderately.

“Having put on the breastplate,” etc. Just as a breastplate protects the vital organs, so faith and love protect us against the desire for earthly things.

## VERSE 13

“So that you may hold them.” By supplying what they need and showing reverence for their dignity. For what good is it to possess honor without fruit? Just as riches produce neglect of salvation, so poverty, while seeking to be satisfied, turns away from justice. Therefore in another epistle he commands that presbyters be honored with double honor.

[Col. 0620A]

## VERSE 15

“Evil for evil.” Evil is repaid with evil when the person who ought to be rebuked is not rebuked but neglected through wicked concealment. “Toward all,” etc. Toward everyone without exception. “Without ceasing.” That is, live justly always and desire eternal things. The just person never ceases to pray unless he ceases to be just. Whoever always acts well always prays. For the good desire itself is prayer; and if the desire is continuous, the prayer is continuous.

## VERSE 18

“In Christ.” The will of God has been shown, because these things existed in Christ, in whom nothing displeased God. “Do not quench the Spirit.” Since it is God’s will that you do all these things, you who are greater and possess through the Holy Spirit the gift of understanding must not hide it, lest you deservedly lose it. You who are subject to them must not despise their prophecies. Nevertheless, do not accept everything indiscriminately; test them—that is, examine them by reason—and hold fast to what is found good. “Do not quench the Spirit,” that is: If the Holy Spirit reveals something to someone’s ear, do not prevent him from speaking what he perceives. We quench the Holy Spirit who has been given to us—not as he is in himself, but as he is in us—when we drive him away by sinning.

[Col. 0620B]

## VERSE 23

“May the God of peace himself sanctify you in every way,” etc. That is: I admonish both those set over others and those subject to them in this way, but God himself is the one who can accomplish it. “Your spirit.” Let reason be preserved whole, by not consenting to the flesh. “And soul.” That is, let sensuality be preserved whole by serving reason. “And body.” So that you do nothing through its instrumentality about which anyone might complain. Sometimes the soul is defiled by an evil thought while the body nevertheless remains clean. Therefore he says that the spirit in a person ought to be whole. If an evil life or thought intervenes, the spirit will not be whole. The spirit, soul, and body are what constitute a human being: the part by which we understand, the part by which we live, and the part by which we are visible and tangible. These are again spoken of as two, because the soul is often named together with the spirit. “Without blame.” It is one thing to be without sin, which in this life is said of the Only-begotten alone; it is another to be without blame, which could be said of many righteous people even in this life. For there is a certain manner of good life concerning which no just complaint can be made even in this present conduct. “At the coming.” That is, until the end of life.

## VERSE 24

“Faithful.” As though he were saying: I pray that he may sanctify you, so that he may preserve you once sanctified. There is no reason to doubt this, because the one who called you to be holy is true to his promises.

[Col. 0619]

# THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS (G)*

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0619D]

The Apostle writes a second epistle to the Thessalonians and makes known to them the events of the last times and the overthrow of the adversary. He writes this epistle from Athens through Titus the deacon and Onesimus the acolyte.

# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0620D]

### Verse 3

**“To give thanks,” etc.** Here he gives thanks to God for their virtues, lest perhaps they become elated over so great a good, which they possessed from God, as though they possessed it from themselves. **“To one another.”** Namely, so that the one who is loved may love others, and may show charity through mutual services.

[Col. 0621A] **Verse 5. “As an example of the just,” etc.** For if he punishes sins so severely in those who repent, what will he do with the hardened? He says this so that it may be understood that he does not spare the impious, since he does not spare the just. **“Just,”** if indeed what is established is just. For “if indeed” is not placed here to express doubt, but affirmation; hence another translator says: “Since he is just,” etc.

**Verse 7. “At the revelation.”** He begins to show how horrible the future tribulation will be for the former, and how delightful the future rest will be for the latter.

**Verse 8. “Of the Lord Jesus.”** Who comes in a flame of fire—not that he is surrounded by flame, but in its effect, because he will burn up his enemies. **“Those who did not know God.”** For there are others who do not know the law.

**Verse 9. “Who will pay the penalties.”** That is, they will endure them. For *dare* (“to give”) is sometimes used for “to endure,” and so here. And appropriately: for the one who suffers gives penalties to the one whom he has offended, as though they were welcome. **“In eternal destruction.”** As though he were saying: They will always feel the punishments, though they will not always perish.

**“When he comes to be glorified,” etc.** For he himself will appear glorious and wondrous in believers, but severe toward unbelievers, when he constrains them with eternal punishments. The brief sense of these words is: He will come to punish the wicked and glorify the good.

**Verse 10. “Because our testimony.”** He gives rest to you who are troubled with us because you believed the testimony—that is, whatever we said concerning that day of judgment—about the glory of the good and the punishment of the wicked.

**Verse 11. “For which.”** The order of the words is: “On which day we pray that he may deign”—that is, may judge you worthy—“we always pray.” Or, “for which,” that is, “on account of which,” or “to avoid the danger of whose day one must always pray.” **“The work of faith.”** That is, the confession which is properly the work of faith in power, so that they may in no way be turned away from confession. Or, “the work of faith” means every good deed that faith demands, and without which faith is dead. **“In the power of perseverance,”** namely, so that he may grant you perseverance to the end.

## Chapter II

**Verse 1. “Now we ask you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ,” etc.** Up to this point he had said that he gave thanks and prayed for them; here he speaks definitively about the day of judgment, entreating them not lightly and readily to accept or fear the opinion that the Lord’s coming was near at hand.

**Verse 2. “Do not be quickly shaken.”** As though he were saying: If you are shaken, it is quickly, for nothing lasting is being brought upon you. **“Nor by a spirit.”** That is, if an evil spirit, appearing in a vision as an angel of light, should persuade you of this. Or, if someone should say that through the Holy Spirit, revealing it, he has learned that the day of judgment is imminent, do not believe him. **“Nor by a letter.”** Deceivers commonly fabricate a letter in the name of some distinguished man in order to mislead, so that the authority of the name may commend what could not be accepted on its own. **“As though the day of the Lord were imminent.”** He does not say this in such a way that he does not wish them to have their loins girded and their lamps burning in their hands, waiting for when the Lord will return from the wedding feast.

[Col. 0622A] **Verse 5. “For unless he comes.”** He speaks obscurely about the destruction of the Roman empire, lest he provoke them to persecute the Church. Or he says this about the spiritual empire of the Roman Church, or about falling away from the faith. **“Unless the deserter comes first.”** Some manuscripts read this way. There is no doubt that he is speaking of the Antichrist, whom he calls the deserter—certainly a deserter from the Lord God. For if this can rightly be said of all the impious, how much more of him! **“The son of perdition.”** The Antichrist, not by nature but by imitation.

**Verse 4. “In the temple.”** Or, “the temple.” Some wish this passage to be understood not merely of the ruler himself, but of his entire body—that is, the multitude of people belonging to him, together with the ruler himself. They think it more correct to say, as it is in Greek, [Col. 0622B] not “in the temple,” but “into the temple of God he takes his seat,” as though he and his followers together were the temple of God, which is the Church. Thus one says, “He takes his seat into a friend,” meaning “so as to be a friend.”

**Verse 6. “You know.”** He says that they know what restrains him, but he does not explain it openly; therefore we do not know, except that some suspect that this was said about the Roman empire, until it is taken away or removed from the midst. For this reason they think that the Apostle did not wish to write it openly, lest he incur the charge of having wished evil upon the Roman empire, which was expected to be eternal. **“In his own time.”** When the accession to the Roman empire and to obedience to the Roman Church has been completed, there will be a falling away from both empires. When this has been fulfilled, that wicked one will appear, once the time of mercy has been completed, during which the fullness of the Gentiles enters into the faith. The falling away will be revealed, and thus the day of the Lord will be at hand.

**Verse 7. “For the mystery,” etc.** From the very beginnings of the accession, iniquity is found, but mystically—that is, concealed under the name of piety—so that they wish to be regarded as ministers of Christ although they are false ones. The devil secretly killed the martyrs through Nero and others, just as through him he will then do so openly by killing Elijah and Enoch and very many others. Nero and the others are shadows of the future Antichrist, just as David and Abel are shadows of Christ. **“Until it is removed from the midst.”** That is, until the power of the Roman empire is removed from the midst of the world, because people from everywhere were converging upon Rome as upon a head. Or, let the one who holds the faith hold it until that faith itself grows cold. Or, let the one who restrains him—that is, accession to the faith—restrain him until that accession itself is removed from the midst. Or, until the iniquity which now exists mystically becomes public—that is, as though it were among ordinary things—so that a person is no longer ashamed to commit adultery or theft, just as he is not ashamed to walk or speak. **“It is removed from the midst.”** Namely, the falling away—that is, it appears openly. And then, once the falling away from the true God has been revealed and charity has grown cold because of the abundance of iniquity, he will be revealed, etc.

**Verse 8. “By the breath of his mouth.”** That is, by the power of the Holy Spirit, who is called the breath of the mouth because he proceeds from it.

**Verses 9–10. “With lying signs and every deception.”** Those signs are called lies either because they will not be real as they appear, but fantastic, or because, even if real, they will draw people into falsehood by God’s permission.

**“Therefore God will send them.”** *(Augustine, Book XX of* The City of God, *chapter 19.)* God will permit the devil to do these things, etc., up to “judged most unjustly by others.”

**Verse 12. “As first fruits for salvation.”** Namely, so that we might believe in Christ and confess the faith not in that final and dangerous time, but in the primitive Church. Or, we apostles are the first fruits of all believers, because the apostles believed first, and this was for the salvation of all the nations.

**Verse 13. “For the acquisition of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.”** Or, so that you may be an acquisition in which God is glorified.

**Verse 15. “And gave consolation.”** By promising the kingdom of heaven. **“In grace.”** That is, through the grace he gave, we hope for eternal things. Or, he gave all these things not according to our merit, but in his grace.

## Chapter III

**Verse 1. “Finally, brothers, pray.”** He urges them to pray, so that God may deign to direct and pour forth his teaching in an unwearied course through the mouths of the apostles into the ears of those who hear, and from their ears into their hearts, so that the disturbances of the wicked may be restrained.

**Verse 2. “That we may be delivered.”** From false apostles, lest they deceive our people or lay ambushes for us. Or, “that we may be delivered from the unreasonable,” that is, from unbelievers who resist the word of God and do not remain in the harbor of peace. **“And from evil men,”** who persecute unbelievers. I say “that we may be delivered” because not all who will receive the faith have yet received it through me. **“For faith is not possessed by all.”** That is, even while you pray, not everyone will believe, but only those foreordained to adoption as sons.

**Verse 6. “We announce.”** He begins with the inquisitive and idle, warning the good to correct them.

**Verse 7. “You know how you ought to imitate us.”** Since they do not do these things, you ought to avoid them. Or, “they do not walk according to the tradition.” For you know how I conducted myself, which you do not see in them—as though he were saying: There is no need for me to explain this tradition to you, because you know that we were not troublesome, like those who concern themselves with other people’s business, wandering here and there.

**Verse 9. “But that we might make ourselves [an example].”** It must be noted that the Apostle taught not only by words, but also exhorted by deeds. For it is the mark of a capable teacher to fulfill by actions what he teaches by words.

**Verse 10. “For if anyone does not wish to work.”** Some say that the Apostle commanded this concerning spiritual works; otherwise, if he were speaking of bodily labor, in which farmers and craftsmen work, he would seem to hold an opinion contrary to the Lord, who says in the Gospel: “Do not be anxious about what you will eat” [Col. 0624B] (Matthew 6), etc. But they needlessly attempt to cast darkness over themselves and others, so that what charity usefully commands they not only refuse to do, but refuse even to understand, although in many other passages of the letters the Apostle teaches most plainly what he means here. For he wants the servants of God to work bodily for their living, so that they may not be compelled by poverty to ask for what is necessary. Nor is this contrary to what was stated above: “Do not be anxious about what you will eat,” etc. For this was not said so that they should not procure, by honorable means, as much as is sufficient for their need, but so that they should not fix their attention upon these things, nor do for their sake whatever they are commanded to do by the proclamation of the Gospel.

**Verse 11. “Conducting themselves inquisitively.”** This behavior is contrary to the Lord’s discipline; for their god is their belly, those who provide for their needs through shameful concern.

**Verse 13. “Do not grow weary.”** For even if they work, they may nevertheless lack certain necessities. Therefore he warns that those who had the means to provide the servants of God with what was necessary should not, on this pretext, become lazy. For the one who is humane in giving does not come under condemnation; rather, the one who, although able to endure labor, wishes to live idly does.

[Col. 0623]  

# The First Epistle to Timothy (G)*

## Argument

[Col. 0623C]

He instructs Timothy and teaches him about the ordering of the episcopate, the diaconate, and the whole of ecclesiastical discipline, writing to him from Laodicea through Tychicus the deacon.

## Chapter I

**Verse 2. “Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father.”** In this greeting he names three things that he desires, whereas in the others he named only two. Here “mercy” is understood as what is called “grace” in the other epistles, that is, the remission of sins. Peace is tranquility of mind, a foretaste of eternal peace. These things are customarily desired for everyone alike. But the grace that he adds here is desired for bishops, namely, the gift of the Holy Spirit, by which God’s ministers are armed.

**Verse 3. “As I urged you.”** After the greeting, he first begins here to reject the false apostles and those who were still teaching that the law had to be observed.

**“I urged you.”** *(Ambrose.)* He says “I urged you” in order to display the affection of charity and the form of humility.

**“Myths and genealogies.”** *(Augustine, Book II against the Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets, chapter 1.)* A certain heretic, an enemy of the law and the prophets, thinks that the Apostle here called the divine utterances myths, etc., up to “which sacred Scripture nowhere relates.”

**Verse 4. “Genealogies.”** Genealogies were accounts by which certain Jews claimed to be descended from the family of Abraham and David, as though something were owed to them on that account; or accounts by which they claimed that Christ did not originate from David.

**Verse 5. “But the goal.”** The building up of God is in faith, because from faith comes hope, and from hope charity, which is the fulfillment of the law. Or arrange it this way: Certain people teach and devote themselves to myths and genealogies, but the goal and fulfillment of the law is charity; therefore there is no need for other things. **“Of the commandment.”** “Of the commandment” is said in place of “of the commandments,” whose fulfillment is love of God and neighbor. Hence: “On these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets” (Matthew 22).

*(Augustine, on Psalm 31.)* The goal is called an end, etc., up to “therefore let desire be restrained and charity be stirred up.”

**“A good conscience.”** “Conscience” is used for hope. For the person in whom there is the scruple of a bad conscience despairs of reaching what he loves. **“And an unfeigned faith.”** Or, not a faith made of clay and fragile; or, one in which each person invents whatever he wishes for himself, but only the catholic faith.

**Verse 6. “From which.”** Here he condemns the adversaries who were handing on legal observances.

**“Not understanding,” etc.** For whenever they begin to be reproved and convicted concerning their perverse and false opinion, they pronounce many words from the holy books in defense of what they had said with the lightest recklessness and the most obvious falsehood, wishing to be teachers of the law, although they do not understand either what they are saying or about what they are speaking.

**Verse 8. “Now we know.”** Lest he seem to accuse the law, he adds: “Now we know,” etc. But lest he again seem to introduce it, he adds: “Knowing this, that the law is not established for the just,” because the just person is not from the law but from faith. What need, then, does he have of the law? It was given either to punish the guilty or to restrain one who wishes to sin. Yet the just person, although he does not need it, uses it, so that he may thereby have authority over others and bear witness to the future by his deeds. **“Use it lawfully.”** The person who knows that the law was given for a time and abandons it under Christ. Those who have been justified through remission no longer need the law, from which they have been freed through Christ. There are, however, many ways of using the law lawfully, so that a person can rightly be said to use the law lawfully in one respect as just, and in another respect as unjust. The unjust person uses it lawfully when, understanding why it was given, he is led by its threat, as by a tutor, to grace, through which he becomes just. The just person likewise uses it lawfully when, by holding to it, he imposes it upon the unjust, so that when the disease of ingrained desire begins to increase in the unjust through the stimulus of prohibition and the accumulation of transgression, they may flee to justifying grace and, delighted by the sweetness of righteousness through it, escape the punishment threatened by the letter.

**Verse 12. “I give thanks to him who,” etc.** Here he shows that he had evils under the law. But the good things are these: that he was forgiven, that he is faithful, and that he has been placed in the ministry, and hence is strong. Through these he shows that after the Gospel the law is uselessly retained.

**Verse 13. “But I received God’s mercy.”** Those who sin knowingly also obtain mercy, like David, as do those who sin unknowingly, for whom forgiveness is easier. “I received mercy because I acted unknowingly.” Or, ignorance is given as the reason for mercy, although not strictly, since the ignorance was evil whereas the mercy was gratuitous.

**Verse 14. “It abounded exceedingly.”** It abounded beyond the greater evils of former times. For he not only forgave sins, but also gave faith and love. Concerning these things no one should doubt: “Jesus Christ came into this world to save sinners.” And this saying is faithful—that is, true and worthy of acceptance—because it is useful.

**Verse 15. “Worthy of all acceptance,”** because he saves body and soul. Or, “this saying is human.” Another reading has: “Not to say divine; for if a human being who receives another human being as a guest is called humane, how much more humane is the one who receives a human being in himself?” **“Because Christ Jesus.”** Christ had no reason for coming except to save sinners.

**“First.”** That is, worse, because he was a persecutor, and there was no one before him in this respect. For no one was more violent among persecutors; therefore no one was first among sinners. He was first not in order of time, but in the magnitude of his iniquity.

**Verse 16. “But for this reason I received mercy,” etc.** He judges that he received mercy for this reason: so that no sinner, oppressed by any crimes, would now despair of himself, but rather, following this example, would presume that he too would receive the same forgiveness. This is a very great and truly immense gift. **“In me.”** God appointed him a preacher to the Gentiles, and in him displayed so great an example of his mercy.

**Verse 17. “Invisible.”** Because the other gods are visible. He is not called “the only invisible one,” because there are also certain invisible creatures, such as the soul, which nevertheless can be grasped by the senses: all its powers can be known, but it is not God for us. God is therefore invisible to human beings in his nature, according to the saying: “No one has ever seen God.” He is seen when and as he wishes, not as he is, but as though he wishes to appear in a form. In the future, however, the children will see him as he is. **“To God alone.”** He is God alone by nature—that is, he alone creates—which is understood of the Trinity itself, not of the Father alone, as some wish; for he does not say “to the Father alone,” but “to God alone.” We proclaim one and only God: the Trinity itself. The Only-begotten, insofar as he is God with God, and the Holy Spirit in his own nature, is also immortal and invisible.

**Verse 18. “This commandment.”** After recalling how many and how great the benefits of the Father and of Christ toward sinners are, he shows how he should imbue the people with ecclesiastical discipline.

[Col. 0626D] **Verse 19. “Conscience.”** He calls their thoughts “conscience,” in which humility must be preserved above all. When it was despised, certain people fell into great errors, as was shown at the beginning of the Epistle to the Romans.

**Verse 20. “Whom I handed over.”** The Apostle excommunicated both of them, so that in this way the kingdom of Satan might be excluded from Satan. For no creature—whether one that remains in the truth, giving glory to God, or one that has not remained in charity, seeking its own glory—fails to serve the divine providence, whether it wishes to or not. The former does what is good with that providence willingly. With regard to the latter, what is just is done. Yet what is justly done to it is not reckoned to it, but rather the disposition with which it acts; for God did not deny rational creatures free will, but retained for himself the power by which he justly orders the unjust. **“I handed over.”** Yet not in such a way that they should perish, because Satan can do nothing unless permitted. He torments those handed over to him; hence: “Now do not sin any longer, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5). Thus the apostolic power used Satan for the correction of human beings. For the transgressing angels, together with their prince the devil, are rightly called administrators or agents of divine providence. The devil is called the magistrate of this world, but a magistrate under God the emperor does only as much as is permitted to him; and the administrators and agents of this world do nothing except insofar as the Lord allows it.

## Chapter II

[Col. 0627B] **Verse 1. “I urge.”** Up to this point he has spoken about false apostles; here he speaks about prayers. **“First of all.”** That is, supplications must be made before everything else. Here the order of the Mass is shown, which is a particular kind of prayer. **“Supplications.”** Either the prayer that is made near or before the consecration. **“Prayers.”** That is, the consecration itself. **“Petitions.”** Or intercessions, as though from an obligation, so that what is performed here may be perfected in eternal life, as when the people are blessed by the bishop. **“Thanksgivings.”** For things done, which conclude everything, as though everything came from God: “Let us bless the Lord.” **“For all.”** So that we may follow God’s clemency, because God wishes all people to be saved, even though according to justice he rejects some. **“So that we may have peace from persecution.”**

**Verse 3. “For this.”** Lest anyone think that these things should not be done for those whom the Church suffers, he adds: “For this is good.” And lest anyone think that salvation could be attained through the worship of one God and a good life without participation in the body of Christ—that is, without faith in the Church—he says: “One God, and one mediator,” so that the salvation of all people never takes place except through the mediator, God the Word, who always existed but, according to the flesh, was made human.

**Verse 4. “Mediator of God,” etc.** This is that arbiter whom Job desires when he says: “Would that there were an arbiter for us.”

*(Augustine, Book IX of* The City of God, *chapter 15.)* The mediator between God and human beings had to possess something similar to God, etc., up to “another who is good, Jesus Christ, who reconciles enemies.”

**Verse 7. “And in truth.”** The future truth is the reality and reward of faith. Do you seek the reward? Let faith come first. For we believe in order to know; we do not know in order to believe. What is faith, then, except believing what you do not see? Faith, therefore, is believing what you do not see. Truth is what you believed you would see.

**Verse 8. “Therefore I wish men,” etc.** *(Augustine, Sermon 93 on the Time of the Year.)* Christ raised his hands for us on the cross, etc., up to “so that your deeds may come to mind.”

**“Anger,”** toward one’s neighbor; **“dispute,”** toward God.

**Verse 9. “Not in elaborate adornments,” etc.** He does not want them to devote themselves, beyond what suits their station and customs, to things that provide an occasion for stirring up desire, but rather to be in all things proclaiming and displaying good works outside the devotion of the heart.

**Verse 11. “A woman in silence.”** He has said that the duty of prayer belongs to everyone, and how, for whom, why, and that one must pray everywhere. Now he says that the duty of teaching belongs only to men, and he determines what sort of men should be appointed to it.

**Verse 12. “To teach,” etc.** Behold, he not only taught the woman to have humble and respectable attire, but also denied her the authority to teach and commanded her to be subject to the man, so that both in dress and in obedience she might be under the authority of the man from whom she derives her origin.

**Verse 14. “Adam was not deceived.”** *(Augustine, Book II of* The Literal Meaning of Genesis, *final chapter.)* Since the Apostle calls him a transgressor in comparison with Adam’s transgression, etc., up to “I think that he could in no way have been deceived.”

**Verse 15. “She will be saved.”** Although the woman was the cause of sin, she will nevertheless be saved—not only a virgin and one who practices continence, but also a married woman, even if she never ceases from the work of marriage, provided that she departs from this world while bringing forth children. If she remains in faith, love, and sanctification, so that she knows no man other than her own husband. **“With sobriety.”** That is, with moderation, so that she also uses her own husband temperately.

## Chapter III

**Verse 1. “He desires a good work.”** A work, not a dignity; labor, not pleasures; not to increase in elevation, but to decrease in humility, so that he may become the servant and minister of human beings for Christ’s sake. Thus, setting aside Rachel—beautiful in face, yet not abandoned—he enters with Jacob to Leah, bleary-eyed; and with Moses he descends from the mountain to the plains, from the leisure of contemplation to the labor of action.

**Verse 2. “Blameless.”** The same as “without accusation” in the Epistle to Titus. It is almost contrary to nature to be without sin; nevertheless, one should be chosen in comparison with whom the rest of the flock might be called blameless. **“The husband of one wife,” etc.** That is, monogamous after baptism. For if he had a wife before, who died, this is not counted against him; since he is entirely new, neither fornication nor any other things that occurred before now harm him. **“Sober,”** etc. Ministers of the temple are forbidden to drink wine and strong drink, lest their hearts be weighed down by drunkenness, and so that their understanding may remain vigorous and continually clear.

**Verse 3. “Not greedy.”** Seeking nothing beyond food and clothing.

**Verse 6. “Lest he fall into pride.”** A priest of only a moment’s standing does not know humility or the proper measure of persons, nor has he learned to despise himself: he has not fasted, wept, corrected himself, or distributed anything to the poor. Those who, in an hour’s instant, while not yet disciples, become teachers fall into arrogance, which is the devil’s ruin.

**“It is also necessary,” etc.** This conclusion corresponds to the beginning: he must be blameless not only before those in his household but also before outsiders—Jews, Gentiles, and heretics—so that those who disparage the religion may not dare to disparage his authority.

**Verse 10. “No crime,” etc.** A crime is a serious sin, most deserving of accusation and condemnation.

**Verse 15. “The Church.”** The gathering of many for the worship of one God. **“The pillar of truth.”** It holds the truth firmly within itself so that it does not collapse, even though it suffers tribulation.

**Verse 16. “Appeared to angels.”** What was hidden is not made known to angels only in God, but also appears to them here when it is brought about and disclosed. Therefore he is said to have appeared to angels—not now in the form of humility, but in power. Thus the one who was previously seen as humble appeared in majesty after conquering death, so that the angels, recognizing the mystery that had previously remained hidden and had been revealed in the flesh, might bend their knee before him as though giving thanks to God, because they had learned the truth. **“In the world.”** So that the world’s unbelief could not obtain forgiveness for its error. As the Lord says concerning the Jews: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin,” etc. (John 15).

## Chapter IV

**Verse 1. “Now the Spirit plainly says.”** He does not conceal what the Holy Spirit revealed would happen for the instruction and caution of the Church. He says that men of destructive teaching will arise, so that the Church, forewarned, may be watchful lest it be deceived by such men—as though he were saying: The house of God is indeed worthy, but the Spirit plainly says this. Therefore, on account of its exalted dignity, do not lay aside your care for it.

[Col. 0629C] **Verse 2. “Seared.”** A cautery is an iron instrument; the word is derived from *cavere*, “to guard against.”

**Verse 3. “Which God created.”** This is the doctrine of the saints; the other is the doctrine of demons.

**Verse 5. “Is sanctified.”** Food becomes holy and health-giving, not harmful to soul or body. The word sanctifies; prayer obtains; but the devil tempts through food.

**Verse 8. “For bodily exercise.”** It is indicated here that Timothy exercised himself in vigils, fasts, prayers, and good works, but was not equally intent upon works of mercy. **“Piety,”** which performs good works for the brothers and is effective for winning God’s favor.

**Verse 11. “Command these things.”** He urges him to make his progress an example to others in every respect, so that he might appear admirable in a young man, and so that his discipline might be respected; so that his actions might excuse him—and so that he would be regarded not as a youth but as an elder, and older people would be ashamed if they did not show themselves serious in conduct and morals according to his example.

**Verse 14. “Prophecy.”** He called the inspiration of the Holy Spirit “prophecy,” through which he knew in advance what he would do concerning this matter and others. Therefore he says: “Which was given to you through prophecy,” because, through revelation by the Spirit, the Apostle knew Timothy to be worthy of episcopal honor. **“The presbytery.”** In place of “the presbyters,” because there cannot be fewer than three. And he calls the presbyter a bishop; or perhaps one person laid hands on him with the others agreeing.

## Chapter V

[Col. 0630A] **Verse 1. “Do not rebuke an elder.”** Lest, offended that he has been corrected by a younger man, he become more exasperated than improved.

**Verse 2. “As sisters.”** So that, seeing that they are admonished out of love, they may correct themselves more readily. **“In all chastity.”** In addressing young women, a young man is rightly admonished concerning chastity.

**Verse 3. “Honor widows who are truly widows.”** That is, those who are deprived of the help of all their own people and cannot work with their hands, whom poverty weakens and age exhausts; for them God is hope, and prayer is their entire work.

**Verse 4. “Parents.”** Parents are the same persons previously called sons and grandsons. Hence even in secular law a parent is commanded to succeed to a parent by degree. We repay them in kind, since we were raised by our fathers and nourish others according to the same law.

**Verse 5. “Desolate, let her hope.”** Seeing that she has no support from any side, she is devoted to God with her whole heart, hoping from him alone for the help of life and salvation.

**Verse 6. “She who lives in luxury.”** It is a kind of hypocrisy to wish to possess the honor of a widow but not to obey God, doing one thing while professing another, when she professes religion.

**Verse 8. “Does not provide.”** Care must be given to parents, just as Jesus entrusted his mother to John.

**Verse 10. “Washing the feet.”** *(Augustine, Tractate 58 on John.)* Let us do these things for one another in humility, as the exalted one did humbly, etc., up to “the effect of humility is confirmed.” [Col. 0630C] **“Of the saints.”** Whom do I mean? Those who are in tribulation, not saints in general. For they may be saints and may be cared for by everyone with the greatest service. Do not pursue those overflowing with an abundance of possessions, but the afflicted and those unknown to many. Do not assign these things to the bishop of the Church for distribution; serve them yourself instead, so that you may receive the reward not merely of expenditure but of service. Give with your own hands; sow the furrow of piety.

**Verse 11. “Avoid.”** That is, do not be so concerned with their vows of chastity that you undertake to support them from the Church’s provisions.

**Verse 12. “Having,” etc.** *(Augustine,* On the Good of Widowhood, *chapters 8–10.)* If chastity is preserved within the marriage bond, condemnation need not be feared, etc., up to “everyone of this kind is like Lot’s wife, who looked back.”

**“They have made void.”** Even if they have not married, they have done so by their will: not because marriage is condemned, but because the deceitfulness of the intention and the broken faith of the vow are condemned. The will that turns away from its resolve is condemnable, whether marriage follows or not.

**Verse 15. “They have turned back after Satan.”** By looking back, they fell away from and perished after abandoning that excellent purpose of widowhood or virginal chastity.

**Verse 17. “Those who rule well.”** Here he speaks about the honor of presbyters, as though he were saying: Observe what I said about widows, and also command this concerning presbyters, so that presbyters [Col. 0631A] who rule well in life and teaching may be regarded as worthy of honor.

**Verse 19. “Do not accept an accusation against a presbyter,” etc.** The person who corrects is usually not loved, and therefore, when an opportunity arises, he is easily accused. Against this he warns that an accusation against a presbyter should not readily be accepted.

**Verse 20. “Before everyone,” etc.** *(Augustine, Sermon 16 on the Words of the Lord.)* Sometimes you must correct the sinner privately, between yourself and him alone, etc., up to “but when sin is committed publicly, it must be rebuked publicly.”

**Verse 21. “I testify before God.”** That is, let God be my witness that I have saved my soul for you; take care.

**Verse 23. “Do not continue drinking only water,” etc.** Because he had admonished him concerning chastity, on this occasion he prohibits excessive abstinence, which Timothy himself had undertaken.

**Verse 24. “The sins of some people,” etc.** Since he had said that nothing should be done without prior judgment, he determines where prior judgment is necessary and where it is not, dividing good and evil things into manifest and hidden. It is as though he were saying: Examination is necessary because, just as some things are manifest and need no examination, so some things are hidden, concerning which judgment cannot be made without prior examination. **“Made manifest.”** He says this of those whose intention is clear; these precede judgment, because if judgment follows them, it is not rash. **“They follow.”** Just as hidden evils will not remain hidden in their own time, when the time of Christ arrives in which they will be revealed, so it is also with good things. Let us therefore judge concerning these; let the others be left to God’s judgment.

## Chapter VI

**Verse 1. “All who.”** It must be understood that certain people preached a freedom common to all in Christ. This is certainly true of spiritual freedom, but not of bodily freedom, as they understood it. Therefore the Apostle speaks against them here, commanding servants to be subject to their masters. They should not demand the release spoken of concerning the Hebrews, that they serve for six years and then be sent away free without payment; this is mystical.

**Verse 4. “Proud.”** Pride leads him, not reason, when he bursts into conflict in search of approval—a thing avoided by the gentle and good. **“Sick.”** For he does not die by wholly rejecting the faith, nor does he recover strength for knowledge of the truth; rather, as though suffering repeated attacks, he languishes around questions and disputes over words. **“Questions.”** The question was whether he was a slave, since all were born from the same fathers and Christ redeemed them all.

**Verse 9. “For those who wish,” etc.** This is said to those who wish to be rich but are not, so that they may not desire it. A different instruction is given to those who already are rich: they should not be proud in mind, but should give to the poor. **“They fall into temptation and the devil’s snare, because the root of all evils,” etc.** There is no kind of evil that does not at some time arise from desire, because desire is the root of all evils.

**Verse 10. “Desire.”** In Greek there is *philargyria* (φιλαργυρία), “love of money.” [Col. 0632A] If avarice is understood as what properly means love of money, it is placed as a species in place of the genus, which is desire.

**“With many pains.”** For the greedy endure proportionately greater anxiety and torment the more they desire things that either pass away once possessed or that they cannot possess.

**Verse 11. “But you, man,” etc.** He does not say that he fears this concerning Timothy, but he knew that this would come into the hands of the churches. **“Flee these things.”** Nothing is so harsh and pernicious as for a churchman, especially one who holds a high position, to devote himself to the riches of this age, because he harms not only himself but also others, for whom he provides a contrary example. **“Piety.”** Piety consists in having compassion on the needy, which the greedy person does not do. [Col. 0632B] **“Faith.”** Whoever has true faith in God does not desire to become rich amid miseries, nor does he value the world more highly than God.

**Verse 13. “I command you.”** In Timothy the Apostle speaks to all his successors. **“And Christ Jesus.”** He exhorts them by the example of Christ.

**Verse 15. “Blessed and alone,” etc.** He does not say this of the Father alone, but of God, who is the Trinity itself.

**Verse 16. “Who alone possesses immortality.”** He possesses it by nature; others possess it from him by grace. **“Inaccessible, whom no human being.”** No one approaches it from himself; whoever is granted access receives it as a gift from him. The Prophet understood this when he said: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Psalm 33), etc.

### Verse 17

**The rich of this world.** Above he dealt with those who wish to become rich, saying that they fall into temptation and the devil’s snare; here he deals with those who are rich, warning them not to place their hope in riches. And because he said that evils arise from covetousness, and argued against it, lest the rich should seem rejected, he defines the matter.

**Not high-minded.** The Apostle did not fear riches, but the disease associated with them, namely pride, which is the worm of the rich. Great is the spirit that is not tempted by this disease amid riches. Great is the person who does not therefore consider himself great because he is rich. But whoever considers himself great for that reason is proud, needy, swollen in the flesh, bursting with arrogance in his heart, begging, puffed up, not full.

**For enjoyment.** God gives temporal things in this life for use, eternal things for enjoyment: the former so that we may do good with them; the latter so that we may become good.

### Verse 19

**To lay up treasure.** For this purpose riches that will not perish are set before them.

### Verse 20

**O Timothy.** Timothy means “precious to God”: *Τίμιος* means “precious,” and *Θεός* means “God.”

**Profane.** Such as *hypostasis*, a term used both of person and of substance. Hence heretics also wished, through the multiplication of this term, to introduce the idea that there are three substances. Understand “profane words” as words opposed to religion; other words are not to be avoided.

### Verse 21

**Promising it, they have fallen away from the faith, etc.** For these people love nothing so much as promising knowledge and mocking, as ignorance, the faith in true things—which children are commanded to believe.

[Col. 0633]

## THE SECOND EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY

*(G)*

### Argument

[Col. 0633A]

He writes again to Timothy concerning the exhortation to martyrdom, the whole rule of truth, what will happen in the last times, and his own passion, writing to him from the city of Rome.

## Chapter One

### Verse 1

**Paul, an apostle.** First the Apostle offers a greeting; then he gives thanks for the good that Timothy possesses, where he shows his desire to see him. Afterwards he urges him to preach and to endure martyrdom, both by his own example and in other ways. From there he says what people will be like in the last days; finally, he speaks of the time of his own imminent departure.

**By the will of God.** Not by my own merits—as though he were saying: You too have been sent freely, [Col. 0633B] and therefore are all the more bound to preach grace.

### Verse 3

**I give thanks.** He gives thanks for Timothy’s goodness, commending the grace of faith that is in Christ.

**Remembrance.** Timothy wept when he was sent away from Paul, ready to accompany him into every danger. Therefore, let him retain in his absence what he possessed while present, also receiving the remembrance of the faith that may remind you, since that faith was firm even among women.

### Verse 6

**For which reason.** Having commended his faith, Paul exhorts him to preach it without fear or shame.

**Through the laying on of hands.** That is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, which you received for the establishment of the Church, for performing miracles, and for every service of religion.

[Col. 0633C]

### Verse 7

**Of fear.** Troubled by fear, Peter denied Christ. Hence: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. XXVI). We have not received the spirit of this fear, but of that fear concerning which the Lord says: “Fear him who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna.” For the Holy Spirit gives fear not of the world, but of God, who can destroy in the fire of Gehenna.

### Verse 8

**Therefore do not be ashamed.** He teaches that steadfastness is required and that one must not be ashamed in one’s confession. There is no reason to be ashamed of it, because although Christ appeared as a human being, his deeds showed that he was God. Even though he was crucified, he nevertheless rose from the dead, and, with many watching as a cloud received him, he ascended into heaven. Thus, where weakness is thought to be present, power appears.

### Verse 9

**Who delivered us.** It is fitting to repay the one who has delivered us. Since we are unable to respond worthily to his benefits, let us at least faithfully and earnestly carry out his embassy.

### Verse 10

**Who destroyed.** Death, having been conquered, is not to be feared for the sake of Christ’s faith.

**But has enlightened.** He explains there what these things refer to:

**Having the form. Through the Gospel.** God has revealed immortal life, which was previously unknown; I say, he revealed it through the preaching of the Gospel, whose preacher Paul is.

[Col. 0634A]

### Verse 11

**For which I was appointed.** Here he exhorts by his own example.

**A preacher, an apostle, and a teacher, etc.** What, then, is the reason that he continually calls himself the teacher of the nations? He wishes to persuade us that the nations too have been called to God’s inheritance and therefore must not be excluded from sharing in the faith.

### Verse 12

**For I know.** As though he were saying: For this reason I am not ashamed—that is, I do not fail, nor do I suffer in vain—because he has promised, and he is truthful and powerful; and therefore I have believed in the very one who will repay me.

**Because he is powerful.** He is secure through hope in and the magnificence of the Savior, because what he entrusts to him is safe. He entrusts his salvation to him so that, suffering here on his behalf, he may find salvation with him when he begins to judge, so that, punishing the unfaithful, he may pronounce this man worthy of eternal life.

[Col. 0634B]

### Verse 13

**Having the form.** Here he shows what the preceding words about himself refer to. As though he were saying: Thus I labor in the office entrusted to me; therefore you too, having the form, etc.

**Among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes.** These men were with the Apostle deceitfully, in order to find an accusation against him; but after they saw that they had been exposed, they withdrew from him.

## Chapter Two

### Verse 4

**No one serving as a soldier.** As though he were saying: If you wish to be a good soldier, do not entangle yourself in worldly affairs, because no one, etc.

**Affairs.** Worldly affairs arise when the mind is occupied with gathering money without bodily labor, as with merchants and people of that kind. He forbids Timothy to do this because, being weak, he could not labor.

### Verse 6

**The farmer who labors.** As though Timothy were asking: How, then, shall I live, since I cannot dig and would be ashamed to beg? He adds: “the farmer who labors.” As though he were saying: Even if you do not entangle yourself in worldly affairs, there is nevertheless a means by which you can live:

**For it is necessary, etc. First to partake.** That is, to take.

**Of the fruits.** That is, the necessities provided by his hearers, because “the laborer is worthy of his wages.” Just as a farmer or vinedresser tastes the first fruits of his labor, so the Apostle commands him first to take what is his, and then distribute the rest to others. For he must first satisfy his own need from what he has received and afterwards minister to others from what remains.

[Col. 0634D]

### Verse 8

**Remember.** Labor as I do, and do so in hope of eternal life. He recalls these things not on Timothy’s account, but on account of the heretics whom he foresaw would arise and deny them.

### Verse 9

**As an evildoer.** Here he notes the insult inflicted upon him.

**But the word of God is not bound.** As though he were saying: Although I am bound in body, the word of God is not bound; for I do not cease teaching those who are present by speech and those who are absent by letters.

[Col. 0635A]

### Verse 10

**Salvation, etc., with glory, etc.** As though he were saying: You have been justified so that you may obtain salvation here and, after this life, heavenly glory.

### Verse 11

**A faithful saying.** This is the saying: they will obtain salvation and glory, because we have died to the world, just as Christ died to the old human being, and because we endure—that is, because we are martyrs.

### Verse 14

**Remind them of these things.** I remind you of these things already mentioned, so that you may suffer. Or: Remind your people of these things.

**For it is useful for nothing.** Contention, being less stable, often generates scruples. In disputes, people commonly bring forward such arguments, having polished them with malice, in order to disturb the minds of foolish brothers. Nor can it happen that contention does not force something to be said against one’s conscience, so that one loses inwardly while appearing outwardly as the victor. No one tolerates being defeated, even when he knows that what he hears is true. Therefore, there should be discussion among God’s servants, not quarrelling.

[Col. 0635B]

### Verse 17

**Among whom are Hymenaeus and Philetus.** He disclosed their names so that Timothy might spiritually avoid them; he designates them as profane and impious, and as straying from the truth.

### Verse 18

**Saying that the resurrection has already taken place.** There are two resurrections. The first takes place in the soul through faith, when someone who was dead in unbelief and other sins is brought to life through faith and baptism. The other will be the resurrection of bodies, which will occur on the day of judgment.

It is of the resurrection that takes place in the soul through faith that the Apostle speaks here, when he says: “Saying that the resurrection has already taken place”—namely, that the resurrection of minds has taken place in baptism, and that there will be no future resurrection of bodies.

All sects that promise a religion acknowledge the resurrection of minds in faith. Otherwise they would not appear worth hearing. Therefore, since all who established a sect of some false religion wished to be believed, they could not deny this resurrection of minds; they all agreed about it. But many denied the resurrection of bodies, like those whom the Apostle names.

### Verse 19

**The Lord knows those who are his, etc.** That is, he loves and defends those whom he has foreknown. Here the foreknowledge is noted by which he foreknew those who would become conformed to the image of his Son—that is, he predestined, called, justified, and glorified them.

[Col. 0635D]

### Verse 20

**Vessels of gold and silver.** Just as wooden and earthen vessels are useful for cleansing vessels of gold and silver, so the wicked contribute to the advancement of the good.

Therefore, the great house is the Church, in which there are vessels of gold and silver—that is, good, faithful, and holy servants of God, scattered everywhere yet bound together by spiritual unity, living in the same communion of the sacraments.

There are also wooden and earthen vessels—that is, those who are in the house without being part of the structure of the house or of its peaceful fellowship, and yet still bodily together with the good.

### Verse 23

**Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions.** Not all questions are to be avoided, but useless and undisciplined ones.

[Col. 0636A]

### Verse 24

**The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all.** Those who contradict make enough noise already. Therefore, let the servant of God not make noise against himself through a zeal for disputation. He did not wish us to be lacking in correcting our brothers, nor to devote ourselves to combat. Many people, when awakened from sleep, want to quarrel and then sleep again when they are forbidden to quarrel.

### Verse 25

**Lest perhaps God grant them repentance for the recognition of the truth.** Correction does no good unless the heavenly physician looks upon the person—that is, unless he causes each person to repent of his sin. Such repentance is sometimes obstructed by shame and fear of displeasing others, when a person takes more delight in the opinion of others than in justice, by which each person humbles himself through repentance.

Therefore, God’s mercy is necessary not only when repentance is being carried out, but also so that it may be carried out. For, so that Peter might weep bitterly, the Lord looked upon him. Hence the Apostle says here: “May God grant them repentance” (Matt. XXVI).

[Col. 0636B]

## Chapter Three

### Verse 2

**Lovers of themselves.** Not lovers of the Lord, like Peter, who, when questioned three times by the Lord, three times professed that he loved him, saying: “You know that I love you.” Therefore the Lord entrusted his sheep to him to feed, because true love is shown in feeding the sheep, if one seeks there not one’s own interests but the things of Christ.

From the fact that they love themselves and not God, the evils that follow arise as from a root.

**Ungrateful.** Those are ungrateful who repay evil for good to those who correct them.

[Col. 0636C]

### Verse 5

**Having the appearance.** Because they possess the same sacraments as the godly.

**But denying the power.** Power is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith.

### Verse 6

**Who penetrate.** For they entered women’s houses and deceived them.

### Verse 7

**Always learning and never coming to knowledge, etc.** Let us always walk on the road until we come to the place to which the road leads; let us never remain on it until it brings us to where we will dwell. Thus, by seeking we press forward, and by finding we arrive at something.

### Verse 8

**As Jannes and Mambres, etc.** As though he were saying: Such people lead others astray, but they always resist the truth. This is what he says: “As Jannes and Mambres, etc.”

Jannes and Mambres were two brothers who were magicians of Pharaoh. The Apostle did not find their names in the divine books, but in apocryphal writings, from which this account is taken. They resisted Moses up to the third sign, at which they failed, saying: “This is the finger of God.” Just as they resisted Moses, so these people—that is, the heretics—resist me.

[Col. 0636D]

### Verse 13

**But evil people, etc.** Such are those who fear offending the people before whom they speak. They do not prepare people for temptations, but promise the happiness of this world, which God himself did not promise to the world.

He predicts that labors will come upon the world until the end; you promise prosperity. He came to strengthen your heart by suffering, dying, being smeared with spittle, crowned with thorns, bearing reproaches, drinking gall and vinegar, and being fastened to the wood. He endured all these things for you.

He strengthens the weak so that, once they have believed, they will not hope for the prosperity of this world. Hence: “Son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptations.”

### Verse 15

**You know the sacred writings, which are able to make you, etc.** This indicates how greatly knowledge of the Old Testament benefits us, since there the person and incarnation of Christ are intimated, and these are effective for the salvation of human beings.

## Chapter Four

### Verse 2

**Be persistent.** You act at an opportune time, but you appear intrusive to someone who does not willingly listen, although what you say may at some point benefit him. Yet, knowing that what appears intrusive to him is in fact opportune, keep concern and love for his health in a gentle and moderate spirit.

**Reprove in every way.** He advises Timothy to show more severe patience. To Titus, who was excessively patient, he commends firmness.

### Verse 3

**They will heap up teachers for themselves.** That is, teachers who will teach what they wish. This is a prophecy of the holy Apostle, who, foreseeing the future, commands steadfastness in doctrine so that the Church may be prepared against what was to come.

For he says that there will be people who wish to be taught according to their desires, turning from steadfast and truthful teachers to those who will teach them what they are glad to hear, because the truth will seem harsh to them. Thus, having abandoned true doctrine, they will devote themselves to fables.

[Col. 0637C]

### Verse 5

**Do the work of an evangelist.** Demonstrate by your deeds what you preach with your mouth, so that the mouth of the turtledove may be turned back toward its armpits, and that there may be pomegranates and bells at the edges of the blue robe.

### Verse 6

**I am already being poured out.** We use *libare* to mean “to taste,” “to pour,” and “to sacrifice.” Hence *delibare*, which here is used for the sacrifice itself: he calls his passion a libation. For the one who suffers for justice is sacrificed to God.

### Verse 7

**I have kept the faith.** Faith is the foundation of the Christian religion. It cannot be possessed except by God’s mercy, because it is God’s gift. Hence he says elsewhere: “I obtained mercy, not because I was faithful, but so that I might become faithful.”

We find that the Apostle obtained God’s grace without any good merits—indeed, with many vices—when God returned good for evil. Now, as his passion approaches, he recalls his good merits, after which he will receive the crown, although it was after his evil merits that he received grace. Unless grace had first been given freely, the crown would not be repaid.

Therefore, his merits are not his as though they had been acquired from himself; they are gifts of God.

[Col. 0638A]

### Verse 8

**He will repay.** If faith is grace, and eternal life is, as it were, the reward of faith, it appears that God will repay eternal life as a debt to the faithful person to whom he owes it, since that person merited it through faith. But because faith is grace and eternal life is grace, he will therefore repay it through grace.

**The just judge.** Certainly he is just in repaying good for good; yet because he is first merciful in repaying good for evil, the very justice by which good is repaid for good is not without mercy.

### Verse 13

**The cloak.** *(Chrysostom.)* Here he calls the cloak a *paenula*, etc., up to the point: “so that it may not be necessary to receive it from others.”

### Verse 14

**Alexander.** This is the man whom he earlier said had returned to apostasy. He made buildings for Diana at Athens and stirred everyone up against the Apostle.

**He showed me many evils.** *(Chrysostom.)* Whoever is oppressed by some great person, etc., up to the point: “so that the weaker too may receive consolation from this side.”

### Verse 16

**At my defense.** He calls the pressure and tribulation inflicted upon him a defense. Tribulation is a defense for Christians, because it defends them on the day of judgment.

**May it not be charged against them.** He does not pray for Alexander, who had sinned by attacking the brotherhood out of envy, but for those who had broken off the love and had succumbed through fear; he prays that they may be forgiven. There is a great difference between those who sin in this way and those who sin in that way.

### Verse 17

**From the lion’s mouth.** From Nero, whose hands the Lord rescued him from when he came to Rome, brought there by those in charge of Judaea because he had appealed to Caesar. For when he came to Rome, he remained for two years in unrestricted custody; afterwards he went on to other nations that were in the vicinity of Rome.

[Col. 0637]

# THE EPISTLE TO TITUS

*(G)*

### Argument

[Col. 0637D]

He admonishes and instructs Titus concerning the establishment of the presbyterate, spiritual conduct, and the avoidance of heretics who believe in Jewish traditions, writing to him from Nicopolis.

## Chapter One

### Verse 1

**Paul, a servant, etc.** A servant by condition, though not by the miserable servitude of sin, but of God. Some are called servants because of their nobility, as Moses and David are called servants, and Mary is called a handmaid.

**According to the faith of the elect.** That is, the faith which God’s elect hold or by which they are saved, and therefore one must labor all the more through it.

[Col. 0638D]

### Verse 2

**In hope of eternal life.** This is the substance and fruit of the apostolic office. Through this he commends the apostolic office as something not to be pursued lukewarmly.

**Before the times, etc.** It is not a recent promise, but one made before the times of all the ages.

### Verse 3

**He manifested.** This took place at the appropriate times, namely the Word—that is, the Son. “This is eternal life.”

[Col. 0639A]

### Verse 4

**To Titus, his true son according to the common faith.** That is, according to the catholic faith, not the private faith of some individual. In Greek, *catholic* means “common” or “universal” in Latin.

**For this reason.** First he says what Titus must do and what sort of presbyters he must appoint, beginning in this way: “For this reason.” Recalling these matters, he urges him to carry out what he had arranged for him.

### Verse 5

**Presbyters.** He says “presbyters” in the plural, not in the singular, so that the burden of pastoral care might be more easily borne by being divided among many.

### Verse 6

**Without accusation.** If he had said “without sin,” no one in the Church could rightly be ordained as a minister. Many baptized believers are without accusation; but I would say that no one in this life is without sin—not because anything remains of the sin that is not forgiven in baptism, but because, while we remain in the weakness of this life, the sins that occur daily do not cease to be forgiven daily for those who pray faithfully. However just a person may be found to be in this life, he is nevertheless not without sin.

**The husband of one wife.** *(Jerome, Letter to Oceanus.)* After baptism, etc., up to the point: “because it is to apostatize from the one God and turn to the superstition of another.”

**Having faithful children.** That is, children not even accused of sexual immorality, or of being disobedient to him. Otherwise there is no hope that he can correct others, nor does he have the standing to address others who live with such people.

### Verse 7

**For it is necessary.** Such a person must be appointed; for in the administration of the office he must be without accusation—that is, an irreproachable bishop.

[Col. 0639C]

Here he openly shows that those previously designated by the name “presbyters” were bishops.

### Verse 9

**To refute those who contradict.** Those who contradict are not to be understood in only one way. Very few contradict us by speaking, but many by living badly. For who dares to contradict the truth openly in speech? Many do not contradict with their tongue but with their life. To refute them is a good work, a great burden, a steep ascent.

### Verse 12

**One of them said.** *(Augustine, Book II Against an Adversary of the Law and the Prophets.)* This was Epimenides of Crete, in whose books this statement is found, etc., up to the point: “must be appointed to the ministry of the house of God.”

### Verse 14

**Commandments.** Because, after the truth had been manifested, the commandments of the law were already commandments of human beings, not of God.

### Verse 15

**All things are clean to the clean.** They deny this because in the law Moses prohibited certain things and distinguished the clean from the unclean. But he did not wish this to be understood according to the natures that God created, but according to their meanings.

Thus all things are clean to the clean according to nature. Hence in Genesis: “God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good.” According to their meanings, certain things are unclean to Jews; nor are all things suitable for us, either for the health of our bodies or for the customs of human society.

### Verse 16

**But by their deeds.** If denial is made not only with the tongue but also by deeds, certainly we find many Antichrists, who confess Christ with their mouth but disagree with him in their conduct. Whoever denies Christ by his deeds is an Antichrist.

Such are all wicked Catholics, who deny him not in words but in deeds. Therefore, do not be secure as though your faith alone were sufficient; join a right life to right faith, so that you may confess Christ both by teaching what is true in words and by living well in your deeds. For if you confess in words but not in deeds, your faith is merely, properly speaking, the faith of demons.

## Chapter Two

### Verse 1

**But speak what is fitting for sound doctrine.** These are the things that pertain to good morals.

### Verse 2

**That older men be sober-minded.** *(Chrysostom.)* Old age has certain vices of its own and ailments from which youth is free. Old age itself is also an illness; yet it contains, in addition, a certain sluggishness and slowness, deep forgetfulness, dulling of the senses, and irritability. For there are many things that can scarcely be endured at such an age.

[Col. 0640B]

### Verse 3

**In holy behavior.** That is, their walk, movements, appearance, and speech should display holiness.

**Not enslaved to much wine.** For there are some who, when the bodily vigor of sexual desire grows cold, have surrendered themselves to wine because of their lust.

### Verse 4

**So that they may love their husbands.** They naturally love them with natural affection; let them also love them with chaste affection, so that, with modesty, they may render what is owed to their husbands rather than demand it.

### Verse 5

**So that the word may not be blasphemed.** This can refer to older men, older women, and all the preceding instructions, as though he were saying: Exhort the old men, the old women, and the young women to conduct themselves as I have said, because they ought to do this so that the word may not be blasphemed, etc.

[Col. 0640C]

### Verse 7

**In all things, etc.** For everyone who lives badly in the sight of those over whom he has been placed, so far as it depends on him, kills them; even if they live, they live by God’s mercy.

### Verse 10

**So that they may adorn the doctrine of the Savior.** This refers to all the preceding groups, namely old men, old women, and slaves, as though he were saying: Exhort all those mentioned above to conduct themselves as prescribed, so that by their actions they may adorn the doctrine of the Savior, etc.

**Adorn.** The adornment of a teacher is the honorable life of the disciple.

### Verse 11

**For the grace has appeared.** As though he were saying: Everyone must be admonished, because Christ was born for everyone; he excluded no one.

Or: “Grace,” that is, Christ, who is the grace of God.

Or: “The grace of God and our Savior,” etc.—that is, God and our Savior, namely the Son of God. Although he is invisible in the form of God, he appeared through grace in the form of a servant.

[Col. 0640D]

### Verse 13

**And the appearing of the glory of the great God, etc.** He will come not in weakness as before, but in glory and power, to give rewards according to merits. In his first coming he was so humble that he not only instructed us but also gave himself.

**A zealous follower of good works, etc.** For Christ redeemed us for this purpose: so that, pursuing a pure life and being filled with good works, we might be able to be heirs of God.

### Verse 15

**Reprove with all authority, etc.** So that the admonition may not be received harshly when it is known to be given for salvation.

## Chapter Three

[Col. 0641A]

### Verse 1

**For every work, etc.** As though he were saying: Admonish them to be slow to do evil but ready to do good, knowing that each person must receive what is due, because what is due is prepared for each person.

### Verse 3

**For we too were once.** Although some of us were philosophers, we nevertheless lacked true wisdom.

### Verse 4

**Kindness, etc.** Through which he abundantly bestows spiritual gifts upon us.

### Verse 10

**A heretical person.** A heretic is one who attacks the law through the words of the law. He constructs his own meaning from the words of the law in order to confirm the perversity of his mind by the authority of the law. Such people must be avoided, because, after being corrected repeatedly, they would become more practiced in evil.

[Col. 0642A]

### Verse 11

**By his own judgment.** He condemns himself who praises error and censures truth.

### Verse 13

**Zenas, the lawyer.** He says this not because Apollos was less learned, but because Zenas belonged to this profession in the synagogue.

**Apollos.** He was the bishop of the Corinthians. Because of the sedition stirred up against him by false apostles, he had withdrawn with his companion Zenas to Titus, the Cretan bishop. But once the Corinthians had been pacified through Paul’s letters, Paul instructed Titus to send them on ahead to Nicopolis before he came, in such a way that they would lack nothing for their journey.

**So that they may lack nothing, etc.** He commands that their necessary expenses be provided because it was right that those who supplied spiritual things should not lack material necessities.

[Col. 0641]

# THE EPISTLE TO PHILEMON

*(G)*

### Argument

[Col. 0641B]

He writes a familiar letter to Philemon on behalf of his slave Onesimus, writing to him from prison in the city of Rome through the aforementioned Onesimus.

## Single Chapter

### Verse 1

**Paul, a prisoner.** He does not say “an apostle,” which is a title of dignity, but “a prisoner,” which is a title of humility, because he does not command but entreats. Here there is an intercession on behalf of Onesimus; therefore he recalls what belongs to humility, beginning with his own injury, so that he might lend authority to his letter.

For just as being bound because of sin is a disgrace, so, conversely, enduring the bonds of imprisonment for Christ is the greatest glory. At that time, therefore, he was in custody. For this reason he says that he is a prisoner.

### Verse 5

**Which you have.** Because Philemon believed in Christ and loved him, he believed in and loved the saints also; thus, through the works of faith and charity, he served Christ and the saints.

### Verse 6

**That the sharing.** As though he were saying: You have faith and charity in Christ and in the saints, so that the sharing of your faith may become evident—that is, so that your faith, sharing in our faith, may become evident; or so that it may be evident what you share with others from your faith.

**And this, in the recognition of every good thing.** That is, so that it may become evident, and so that by this merit it may be recognized that every good thing is in you through Christ—that is, the sufficiency of all good things.

Or understand it this way: I remember you and give thanks in my prayers for this purpose, so that the sharing of your faith—that is, the working of faith by which you serve Christ and the saints—may become evident in the recognition that is in Christ Jesus.

That is, it should be accompanied by the knowledge of eternal good, so that this may be awaited as a reward. For the Apostle prays that Philemon’s work may be carried out with knowledge of goodness—that is, that he may work with such a mind that he awaits from it a future reward, Jesus Christ, and not merely the repayment of temporal things.

[Col. 0641D]

### Verse 7

**The hearts of the saints.** That is, the most beloved children of the saints; or, the affection of the saints directed toward you found rest in you. It was comforted and refreshed by you, because they found you good in every respect.

### Verse 10

**I entreat you.** It is a great thing when someone, not inferior but superior, lowers himself and entreats. The elderly ought to be obeyed all the more because of the similarity of age.

[Col. 0642B]

### Verse 11

**Who once was useless to you, etc.** *(Chrysostom.)* See how prudently he confesses the offense of Onesimus himself, so that by this very means he may extinguish the master’s anger. He does not say, “He will now be useful to you,” lest Philemon fail to believe it; rather, he also introduced his own person, so that Philemon might thereby more readily hope for better things.

For if Onesimus will be useful to Paul, who demands such diligence in virtue and perfection, how much more will he be useful to his master?

### Verse 12

**That is, my own heart, etc.** When the Apostle was in custody, Onesimus, a fugitive returning to divine aid, was baptized by him. Seeing in Onesimus a hope of usefulness, Paul commends him in such a way as to signify that he is receiving his own heart in him.

[Col. 0642C]
