### Verse 15

**For perhaps.** He says “perhaps” because human matters are uncertain, and there could have been another reason why God arranged things in this way.

### Verse 16

**Especially to me.** To me, your teacher: Onesimus, having offended his own master, fled to the Apostle so that, with his sins blotted out, he might return useful. He became so useful that he was not only made equal to his master in merits, but became a brother to his own teacher.

And lest Philemon, because he was the master, become arrogant against his slave, Paul humbles him by saying: “A brother also in the flesh,” because all descend from one Adam, and “in the Lord” through faith.

[Col. 0642D]

### Verse 18

**Charge this to me.** Now he removes every excuse by saying that anything Onesimus may have done to injure Philemon, or anything he may owe, is to be charged to Paul.

**Yes, brother, let me have joy from you in the Lord.** That is, I will rejoice over you in the kingdom of God if you do what I ask. He then adds what that is: “Refresh my heart,” etc.

**Confident in your obedience.** By flattering him in this way, he prompts him not merely to do what is asked, but to do even more. For it often happens that someone who sees that others think well of him makes himself better.

### Verse 22

**At the same time.** To make him more concerned and more ready to obey, he indicates that he will come to him. This itself may move him toward granting pardon, since absent people are often despised.

[Col. 0643]

# THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS

*(G)*

### Argument

[Col. 0643A]

First it must be considered why the Apostle Paul, in writing this epistle, did not follow his usual practice of giving either his name or the dignity of his office. The reason is this: writing to those who had believed from circumcision, and knowing that they were proud, he did not wish to place before them the merit of his office as the apostle of the Gentiles and not of the Hebrews, while himself demonstrating humility.

In a similar way, the Apostle John, because of humility, did not place his name first in his epistle, for the same reason. This epistle, written to the Hebrews, is said to have been sent by the Apostle in the Hebrew language; Luke the Evangelist, preserving its meaning and order, composed it in Greek [Col. 0643B] after the death of the blessed Apostle Paul.

## Chapter One

### Verse 1

**Long ago.** This is not something new. God, who is unchanging, was then as he is now.

**Speaking.** He says “speaking” in the present tense because what happened then also happens now.

**To the fathers.** That is, to those who are our fathers both in the flesh and in the worship of God.

**In the prophets.** For it was not they who spoke, but God in them.

**At many times.** That is, many times to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the others, and often to the same individuals.

**In many ways.** Sometimes through dreams, as to Daniel; sometimes with an audible voice, as to Moses; sometimes through inward inspiration, as to David.

### Verse 2

**In the Son, who is greater than the prophets.** For he is the Lord of the prophets, their fulfiller and sanctifier. Thus he is a prophet and also the Lord of the prophets. [Col. 0643C] Likewise Christ is an angel and also the Lord of the angels.

**He appointed immutably.** He appointed him heir of all things—that is, possessor of the whole creation. For Jacob is no longer the Lord’s portion, nor Israel his inheritance, but absolutely all the nations of the world.

### Verse 3

**Who, being the radiance of glory, etc.** Here he commends Christ according to his divine nature, showing that he is coeternal and coequal with the Father and of the same substance as he, but distinct in person.

**The figure of his substance.** Here he indicates personal distinction, as a figure is distinct from the one whose figure it is. Yet he is equal, because he is not unlike the Father, as he himself says: “The Father is in me”; and: “Whoever sees me sees my Father also” (John XIV).

Observe that these names—namely, light and glory—are sometimes referred to the divine nature and sometimes to a person. When they are referred to a person, they are sometimes referred to the Father and sometimes to the Son.

For we say: The Father is light, and the Son is light. Similarly, the Father is glory and the Son is glory; and these two are one glory and one light, not two. The Son is also called “glory from glory,” just as “light from light,” “beginning from beginning,” and “God from God”—yet not two gods, but one; not two beginnings, but one.

“Radiance” and “figure,” however, as also “image,” properly refer to the person of the Son and are said relatively.

[Col. 0644A]

**And sustaining all things, etc.** It was said above that he made all things through him. Here he attributes to him the highest authority, because he governs and preserves all things with authority.

For just as all things were created by him, so they are preserved unchanged through him. The omnipotence of the Creator is the cause of every creature’s continued existence; if this power ever ceased to govern what it had created, the form and nature of all things would collapse together.

**Purification.** Having shown the excellence of the one through whom he created and governs all things, he now commends his kindness in humility. He reminds us of the cross, resurrection, and ascension when he says: “He sits,” etc.

**In the heights.** By saying this, he does not confine God to a place, but shows that the human Christ is higher and more eminent than all things. Likewise, by speaking of the right hand, he did not deform God but demonstrated a likeness of honor. For his sitting with the Father demonstrates nothing other than equality of honor.

### Verse 4

**So much better.** Yet in the psalm he says: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. VIII). Here he is said to be better than those same angels. Just as the former statement can be understood according to his human nature, so the latter could be understood according to his divine nature, unless the effect were added, by which it becomes clear that he is speaking here of Christ according to the flesh.

For according to that by which he is acknowledged to be consubstantial with the Father’s substance, he was not made but born. The discussion, therefore, concerns his human nature, according to which he was lower than the angels in his passion, yet greater and better also in the fullness of grace, [Col. 0644C] from which the angels themselves receive according to measure.

A more excellent name. While he was mortal, he had a more excellent name, because angels ministered to him. After he became immortal, it was still more excellent. And because this could have been said of him without implying superiority over them, he adds “more excellent than theirs,” that is, very different from the name of angels: the name that is above every name, namely, God, or Son—which is truly more worthy than the name by which they are called angels, that is, messengers. For the name “Son” indicates natural possession, not adoption; unless he were the proper Son, the Apostle could not assert from this the greatness of his honor. A proper Son, however, is begotten from the Father himself. But if he were a son by adoption, he would be inferior not only to the Father but also to the angels.

[Col. 0644D] **VERSE 5.—Today.** So that the generation might not appear to belong to the past, he said “today.” Although that day may also be understood as the day on which Christ was born according to his humanity, nevertheless, because “today” signifies presence—and in eternity nothing is past, as though it had ceased to exist, nor future, as though it did not yet exist, but only present—for whatever is eternal always is, it is more divinely understood of the everlasting generation of the Wisdom of God, which the most sincere and catholic faith proclaims.

[Col. 0645A] **I will be his.** That is, I will be his honor, or the honor of that man who was to be born from a virgin. Yet this may also be understood as spoken according to the flesh, for the flesh shares in higher things, just as divinity shares in humble things.

**VERSE 6.—Again he introduces** him who was visible after assuming flesh, although previously he was invisible in the world. This assumption is called an exit from the Father; the introduction into the inheritance is where he is commanded to be adored.

**And let them adore.** And again the Father speaks of the same Son: “When he introduces.” That is, when he shows that he is to be led inward, as far as the hearts of human beings, through faith. What does he say? “And let them adore.” The angels adore because they obey his command and reverence him.

**VERSE 7.—Angels.** “Spirit” is the name of a nature; “angel,” of an office. Those whom God created as spirits he makes angels by sending them as messengers. He uses all of them according to the unchangeable determination of his judgment, whether the good, through his grace, or the evil, through their own will. Thus the will of God is the first and highest cause of all bodily forms and movements. Nothing visible occurs that is not either commanded or permitted from the inner, invisible, intelligible court of the supreme ruler, according to his ineffable justice. Or those spirits are called angels when they are sent to announce light things; but when they are sent for vengeance, as in Sodom, they are called burning fire. So too ministers of the Church are fire when our vices are burned away, but angels when they announce the word of God.

**VERSE 8.—To the Son.** Here he commends Christ both through dignity [Col. 0645C] and through power. **Forever.** Because he will always reign, and the final judgment will always stand; hence: “These will go into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. XXV).

**VERSE 9.—God has anointed you.** According to his humanity, since the Godhead had no need of this. “Anointed” signifies a king or priest. “God” is repeated because of the greatness of the love. Or, according to Augustine: one occurrence is vocative, the other nominative, so that the sense is: “O you, God the Son, your God has anointed you,” namely, the Father. In Latin the cases appear to be identical, but in Greek the distinction is completely clear: the nominative is understood one way and the vocative another.

**VERSE 10.—And you.** After the excellence of his humanity, he returns again to the eternity of the Son. **In the beginning.** Because the Creator exists before created things, without any beginning. **Of the hands.** The power of a command—that is, the power of the will—is called “hands,” because all things were made as he willed.

**VERSE 11.—They will perish.** They will perish with respect to what they are, while creatures are changed for the better. **But you will remain.** Just as he was eternal before all things, so, because he remains, he will be the same after all things have been changed. **They will grow old.** That which is consumed in the manner of clothing is said to grow old, as does human flesh, although it too will be changed for the better.

**VERSE 12.—And like a garment.** This signifies the change of heaven. Hence: “I saw a new heaven and a new earth” (Rev. XXI). **You will change them, etc.** Because God’s works will stand under eternity, so that they will not return to corruption. **But you** are wholly unchangeable.

**VERSE 13.—To which of the angels.** He begins to speak [Col. 0646A] about the glory of Christ’s humanity. **Sit.** The Father, acknowledging him, offers it to the victorious Son. **Of your feet.** By the feet eternal stability is signified, that is, stability in eternity, where he stands, as though his footprints had been set there, by the power of omnipotence.

**VERSE 14.—Are they not all, etc.** As if he said: Certainly. Understand, therefore, how great an honor exists for us, that God appoints his angels as ministers for us, as for friends. Although there is a great difference between angels and human beings, he nevertheless made them close to us, because they care for our salvation, hasten about on our behalf, and perform their office for us. This is the angelic work, the duty of angelic service: that everything be done for the salvation of those near them. Yet this is even more truly the work of Christ, because he commanded the angels, who are superior to us, to provide their ministry for our salvation.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0646B] **VERSE 1.—Therefore.** After saying many things about the Son of God that serve to commend him, he exhorts those to whom he writes to attend carefully to and preserve what was announced to them through him. All the preceding arguments tend toward this: they proved that Christ was greater than the prophets and angels. **More abundantly** than the things spoken through the Law, the prophets, or the angels. The Apostle omitted the name of the Law because in the argument he develops later he also makes this clear.

**Let us drift away.** We flow onward through the punishments of mortal nature; by adding sins we flow away, and we drift completely into eternal condemnation. From this he urges that the words of Christ be heard, because of the punishment that will come upon the negligent.

**VERSE 2.—And every transgression.** He says “every” so that there may be a punishment for each individual sin; for it is not only the transgressor who is guilty of many things who will pay the penalty. **A just reward.** He speaks this way so that no one may think justice is destroyed by mercy. When he says “retribution,” he refers to the measure of the punishment, which will be equal to the sin: just as the sin is greater or lesser, so the punishment will be greater or lesser. When he says “reward,” he refers to the quality of the punishment: whoever has perished in the fire of lust will be tormented by the fire of eternal burning.

**VERSE 4.—And by distributions of the Spirit.** By this he indicates an abundance of graces that was not present among the ancients—not such great signs, nor such varied wonders—through which he shows that they were not believed in a simple manner, but through signs and wonders. Therefore, when we believe, it is declared that we believe not in them but in God.

**VERSE 6.—What is man?** This may be read as an exclamation of wonder, so that by “man” and “son of man” Christ as man is understood. God remembered him in his conception by granting him immunity from sin, and visited him in the resurrection by granting him the glory of immortality. It may also be read with contempt, referring to the earthly: Adam was a man, but not a son of man, as human beings are called who bear his image. Those who bore the image of Christ, however, are rather called sons of men. The former is called the old man; the latter, the new. “Man,” therefore, in this passage is earthly, whereas “son of man” is heavenly. The former is far separated from God, but the latter is present. Thus God remembers the former as one placed far away, while he visits the latter, whom he illumines by his countenance, that is, by the presence of his grace. “You visit him”: the Father visited man through the Son of man, as a physician visits a sick person.

**VERSE 7.—Glory.** Honor through the brightness of immortality, because every knee is bent in this way. **Above the works of your hands.** The more excellent works, namely angels and human beings, which are called “works of the hands” because of their excellence.

**VERSE 8.—But in subjecting everything.** He explains David’s meaning. David says (Ps. VIII): “You subjected all things.” In the statement that Scripture subjected, that is, showed all things to be subject, it left nothing—that is, it excluded nothing from among all things.

**VERSE 9.—But we see Jesus, etc.** Angels may be called greater than man because they are greater than man in body. They are also greater in mind, but only insofar as the merit of original sin burdens the body and thereby the mind itself; this, however, is not so in Christ. If it seems to you that nothing great is said about God the Father if the form of a servant is greater, since the angels too appear greater than it, you are not thinking correctly, nor are you considering what place human nature has among created things, since it was created in the image of God. Yet no injury was done to it when Christ said: “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV). He placed God the Father above not only his flesh but also the human mind that he bore. This is undoubtedly recognized as the form of a servant, since every creature serves the Creator.

**Because of the suffering.** Here he begins to show that the words of Christ must be heard not only because of his power or vengeance, but because of the love with which he loved us, so that he might die for us.

**VERSE 10.—Author.** Christ. **Of their salvation, that is, of the sons.** He himself is Son by nature; we will be his heirs, who are sons by adoption. See how great he is among us: he is Son, and we are sons. Yet the difference is that he saves, while we are saved; he sanctifies, while we are sanctified. Scripture sometimes joins us together and sometimes separates us. “Many sons,” it says: here it joins them; “author of their salvation”: here it distinguishes him.

**Through suffering.** Unless Christ died, man would not have been redeemed, and, not being redeemed, would have perished. If this had happened, everything would have been made in vain. For all other things serve man, and man serves God. Nor would God be glorified in anything, since everything was made for this purpose. The predestination concerning the bringing of sons would also be false. **To perfect.** He began this in the resurrection, when he was exalted in the glory of immortality. It was increased in the ascension, when he ascended to the right hand of the Father. It will be completed in the judgment, when everything is subjected to him and he will be “all in all” (I Cor. XV).

**For he who, etc.** (AUG.) He proves that it was fitting for Christ to suffer for our deliverance, etc., up to the point where it is established that he knew both natures through himself.

**All from one.** But he is the proper Son, whereas we are adopted. When he says that he “is not ashamed to call them brothers,” he shows that our brotherhood with him is not a matter of nature but of mercy. He proves this through the prophet, so that it may not be thought to be something new.

**VERSE 14.—Therefore, since.** Since all were from one, and since the children who were to be sanctified had shared in flesh—that is, since they were human beings composed of soul and body, which is received through blood, and therefore corruptible—for this reason he too, Christ, shared in the same things as the children, or in the same things, namely flesh and blood, and likewise, that is, as one capable of suffering and mortal, so that he could die and thus destroy the devil, and by death abolish the Law, making the Jews free through grace, who had been slaves of the Law through fear of punishments. **Through death.** What a wonder! Death was the weapon by which the devil conquered, and through it the devil was conquered by Christ.

[Col. 0648B] **VERSE 16.—Nowhere.** He shared in these things in order to sanctify human beings. This reason is rightly added, because if he had not intended to free them, he would not have shared in their condition. This is evident concerning angels, because nowhere—that is, in no Scripture—is it read that he took hold of angels. **He took hold.** The Apostle said “he took hold,” not “he assumed,” as though to say: He overtook one fleeing far away. Here the dignity of human nature may be understood, as well as the mercy and grace by which he did this, and the care he had for us. Human nature was fleeing beforehand, and fleeing far away—for we were far away—and he pursued and seized it. This dignity was granted not to angelic nature but to human nature: that God should be joined to it in one person.

**VERSE 17.—In all things.** Because he was born, brought up, and grew; suffered and died. He was earlier called the imprint of the Father’s substance.

**VERSE 18.—For in that.** That is, in the flesh he assumed, he suffered many savage things. Through experience he knows what this affliction of those who suffer is. **Those who are tempted.** God tempts in order to test; the devil, in order to deceive; man, in order to know what he does not know.

## CHAPTER III

**VERSE 1.—Therefore, brothers.** He infers this from everything said above, as if to say: Because he is powerful, because he suffered for us, and because he can help.

**VERSE 2.—Who was faithful.** He begins to compare Christ with Moses, just as above he compared him with the prophets and angels, so that Christ is faithful beyond Moses because he sought not his own glory but the Father’s, and concealed none of his commands. Christ is faithful to the Father, as Moses was, in the whole house of the Jews and Gentiles.

**VERSE 3.—Greater.** As if he said: The fact that he was faithful is shown by the result itself, because he is worthy of glory, as Moses was—and indeed of greater glory than Moses, that is, existing above Moses in merit.

**VERSE 4.—For every house, etc.** “He built,” I say, for a house cannot come into existence by itself but must be built by someone. Was it therefore built by Christ? Truly, because God is the one who makes the house and all things. The one who created all things, including the house, is God. For God is the maker of both houses: both the one that Moses governed and the one that Christ established.

[Col. 0649A] **VERSE 5.—And Moses.** He shows that Christ is worthy of greater glory than Moses because Christ is the builder of the house, whereas Moses is not. Here he also gives another reason: Christ is the Son, while Moses is a servant. Moses handed over carnal things to carnal people, but Christ handed over spiritual things.

**VERSE 7.—Therefore.** After commending Christ in many ways as superior to angels and prophets, he implied that we ought to observe what we heard from him. So now, having commended Christ as superior to Moses, he begins to terrify them, lest they be unbelieving toward Christ, by recalling the example of their ancestors; and, lest they lose rest, he encourages them through the opportunity of the time. **Today.** Now he speaks through himself, whereas previously he spoke through heralds: if you were hard then, be soft now.

[Col. 0649B] **VERSE 8.—Do not harden your hearts;** that is, do not be rebellious and obstinate toward God, but obedient.

**VERSE 9.—They tested;** that is, they investigated out of curiosity.

**VERSE 10.—Offended.** Very greatly and implacably angered. **Angry.** Or, close at hand in order to apply the scourges of correction.

**VERSE 11.—In my anger.** God is said to become angry by the figure of anthropopathy. **If they will enter into my rest.** This is aposiopesis, that is, an incomplete statement: “They will not enter.”

**VERSE 12.—An evil heart of unbelief.** So that you think Christ is not sufficient without the Law. This is evil, because in this way a person falls into many sins. Nor is this a small matter, since this is a heart that departs from the living God.

[Col. 0649C] **VERSE 13.—While it is called today;** that is, the time of grace, concerning which the prophet said earlier in the Psalms that grace is now granted to believers for salvation no less than when Christ was bodily present. **The deceitfulness of sin,** that is, of the devil, who is the cause of sin.

**VERSE 14.—For we are partakers of Christ.** You ought to exhort one another and not be obstinate, because through grace we have become what we were not, sharing with Christ in the inheritance. Yet this is on the condition that we hold firmly to the beginning of our substance—that is, of faith, which is the beginning of good things, through which God exists in us, through which we are deified, and through which we share in the divine substance—until the end.

**VERSE 16.—For some, when they heard.** He says this so that no one may think it sufficient merely to hear about rest, since all those people also heard; but not all who heard reached it.

## CHAPTER IV

**VERSE 2.—It did not profit, etc.** After leaving Egypt, when they had traveled a long way and received many indications of God’s power in Egypt, at the Red Sea, and in the wilderness, they decided to send spies who were to examine the nature of the land. **What they heard.** They did not believe the spies, who brought back an evil report; or punctuate it this way: “the faith derived from what they heard.”

**VERSE 3.—And indeed.** Here he discusses what the first rest signifies. **From the works.** Since he had said that an announcement had been made concerning rest, he says when it was announced: namely, before the Law, after the completion of the works of the seven days, through the rest of the Sabbath; under the Law, when it was signified through the promised land; and in the time of grace, when the Holy Spirit said through David: “Today,” etc. It was as though that rest had been announced, although the completion of this true rest had not yet been signified, because no one had yet possessed rest. **Completed.** This took place when man was made, for whose sake all things were made, and he himself was made to glorify God.

**VERSE 4.—And he rested on the seventh day.** He made everything in six days, so that afterward nothing would be made except from the matter then created and in the likeness of what had been made. On the seventh day he rested, and for this reason it signifies rest. So too, in the sixth age, Christ the man was born into the world for labor; he suffered on the sixth day and at the sixth hour of the day, and rested on the seventh. Thus also, while we live under the works of the six days, we labor; leaving them, we rest—provided that our works are found to be very good.

**VERSE 5.—And in this one.** He speaks of the second rest, which is signified figuratively by the rest of the promised land.

**VERSE 7.—He establishes a certain day, “Today.”** This concerns the third rest that was signified and the time when it is given, although obscurely: it was promised through Christ to believers. **After so long a time.** Here it becomes clear that this is another rest, the one of which David says “today,” distinct from the rest to which Joshua led them. For if it were the same, David would not speak of another. Therefore it is certain that there is another rest to which Christ leads, and that Palestine signified it through the earlier rest.

**VERSE 8.—To them, the children of Israel, to whom rest was first announced** by a sign, namely, the promised land, he would never have granted rest—that is, at no time—afterward, that is, in the subsequent age, he would speak of another day, namely, the time of grace, in which it was to be given. Or: afterward he would never have spoken of another rest apart from the promised land. By saying “on this day,” he means the same thing as he had said above: “today,” etc.

**VERSE 9.—A Sabbath-rest;** that is, the true rest signified by the Sabbath—that is, the festal joy of complete repose—in which the Lord rested and which was observed under the Law. Then we shall be perfectly free from labor, refreshed by greater grace and filled with God. And we shall know perfectly that he is God. There we shall be free, see, and love. We shall love and praise: this is what there will be at the endless end. For what other end is ours except to arrive at the kingdom whose end there is not?

**VERSE 11.—Into the same example.** Or, into a punishment like the one they received through unbelief. He calls it an example so that we may direct our minds there, lest we likewise fall away.

**VERSE 12.—The word of God.** It came from royal seats. **Living.** Although unbelievers think it dead. **Penetrating.** Reaching, through complete examination, to the separation of soul—that is, sensibility—and spirit—that is, reason. **The division of soul.** We live through the soul with beasts; through the spirit we understand with angels. Therefore “soul” signifies carnal sins, that is, those committed through bodily action, such as lust. “Spirit,” however, signifies spiritual sins, that is, those of the mind, such as pride. The word of God distinguishes between carnal and spiritual sins: who does what, and with what intention.

**And of spirit.** The word of God penetrates by inseparable knowledge, because it knows how sensibility is divided from reason, and how each is divided within itself: whether sensibility, more devoted to lower things, is inferior, or whether, recalled from them, it is more worthy. Thus it also sees how spirit is divided within itself: whether it strains toward God while thinking about the divine vision; whether, at a lower level, it considers heavenly things; whether, lower still, it deals rightly with worldly affairs on earth; or how spirit—that is, reason—is separated from sensibility, when what is lower in reason rises above what is higher in sensibility.

**And of the joints as well.** “Joints” refers to the joining of sensibility and reason itself, which the Son of God sees: namely, how they cohere with one another in some respect, or how this and that—that is, reason and sensibility—agree with one another in their differences, when the higher difference of sensibility, by consenting, agrees with the differences of reason. Or the lower difference of reason, pressed down and captive, sometimes consents to the lower difference of sensibility.

**Of the marrow.** Marrow, because it is what is inward, here signifies whatever is more interior and subtle in the soul or spirit, which the Son of God also sees. For he distinguishes thoughts—that is, what different people think differently—and he distinguishes the intentions of those thoughts, toward what each is directed, whether good or evil. And, to say more, no earthly or heavenly creature is invisible to him; everything is naked and exposed, because it is fully seen from every side. Likewise, “joints” means the conjunctions of thoughts; “marrow,” their intentions.

**VERSE 14.—Therefore, since we have.** Here he begins to speak about Christ the high priest: how he is sufficient, and how he is more worthy than the former priest; how he changes both that priest and the Law subject to him through his better Law, and how he is necessary for us for righteousness and salvation.

**VERSE 15.—For we do not have, etc.** As if to say: We must hold fast, and we ought to hold fast, because although he is powerful, he is also merciful, having experienced our weakness. **Who cannot, etc.** It is impossible for a person who has not experienced affliction and endured everything bodily and perceptibly to know the afflictions of those who suffer. Christ knows them not only because he is God, according to which he knows all things, but because he is man and endured similar things.

**VERSE 16.—At a fitting time of help.** Now is the time of help; now is the time of gifts, when those who sin after baptism can find repentance through grace. But when the bridal chamber has been closed, when the king has entered to see those reclining at table, and those worthy of it have come to the bosom of the patriarch, then it will be the time of despair for the wicked. Now, however, while the contest still continues and the prize hangs in the balance, one must not despair, but approach with confidence—that is, without doubt—so that through grace one may approach and find help at the proper time. For there is also a time that is not suitable.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0652A] **VERSE 1.—For every high priest.** Since spiritual things do not introduce the weak in the same way as bodily things, he begins with these matters, wishing to show that the New Testament is better than the Old. He attributes some things in common to Christ and the priests, some higher things to Christ alone, and still other, humbler things to those priests alone.

**VERSE 2.—Since he himself also.** Here he removes the occasion for exalting himself above others.

**VERSE 4.—Nor does anyone, etc.** He strikes at the ambitious, who are not called but thrust themselves forward.

**VERSE 5.—He did not glorify himself.** The Son was glorified by the Father when he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III). [Col. 0652B] This glorification had long before been foretold through the Prophet: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. II).

**VERSE 6.—You are a priest.** Christ is a priest, not according to the fact that, born from the Father as God with God, he is coeternal with the one who begets him, but because of the flesh he assumed and because of the victim he offered for us. **According to the order of Melchizedek.** Melchizedek was not temporal, since Scripture is silent about the beginning and end of his life; he is therefore a figure of Christ, who has neither beginning nor end. And just as Melchizedek offered bread and wine once, so Christ, under the appearance of bread and wine, gave his body and blood to his disciples.

**VERSE 7.—Prayers and supplications.** He speaks of Christ’s action and life, whose every action is instruction for the faithful and prayer to God. Whatever Christ did consisted of prayers and supplications for all. The pouring out of blood was a powerful cry, through which he was heard because of his reverence in that passion. Reverence consists in this: he suffered without sin and solely out of love. **He was heard.** From this it is clear that through him we can obtain mercy, since he is already at the right hand of the Father.

**VERSE 8.—He learned, etc.** That is, he voluntarily accepted obedience even to death.

**VERSE 9.—For all who obey him.** His suffering is so effective that it is sufficient for the salvation of all. This salvation can rightly come through him because he himself was called, etc. He became the cause of salvation—not of just any salvation, but of eternal salvation; not for a few, but for all—on this condition, however, that they obey him. Otherwise they cannot attain salvation. And he can rightly be the cause of salvation for others, since he was called by God a high priest, as he also showed in reality through his works that he was such. Because he fulfilled the office of a high priest, was obedient to the Father in all things, and in himself attained such a consummation of every good thing that he was sufficient even for the salvation of others, he was therefore called by God a high priest—and this according to the order of Melchizedek, namely, so that the entire order of divinity might be considered in him, insofar as it could be considered in Melchizedek.

**VERSE 11.—Difficult to interpret.** The discourse concerning the incarnate Son is difficult to interpret because you are weak in understanding the profound mysteries.

**VERSE 12.—For although you ought to.** He inserts a rebuke concerning their weakness, so that they may struggle to understand the lofty things about Christ. **What are the elements of the beginning.** The beginning of teachings is simple doctrine. Its elements are the subject matter of which he speaks, such as birth and suffering.

**VERSE 13.—For everyone, etc.** Whoever cannot grasp the statement “the Word became flesh,” how will he grasp “in the beginning was the Word”? Every discourse on this subject, by which the aim is not merely to believe but also to understand and know what is being said, is burdensome: it weighs them down more easily than it nourishes them. Consequently, spiritual people do not keep these things entirely silent before carnal people, because the catholic faith must be preached to everyone. Yet neither should they abandon them by trying to lead them to an understanding incapable of receiving them, thereby making the discourse more readily despised in its truth than making the truth perceived through the discourse.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0653B] **VERSE 1.—Therefore.** After rebuking and blaming them severely because they wished always to learn the very same things, he again encourages them by numbering himself among them and urging them toward perfection. **The discourse of Christ’s beginning.** This is the teaching with which beginners are to be catechized, such as the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer. **Not again,** that is, not as before, so that, having fallen once, they may fall again. Or: not laying again, but laying it now in such a way that there will be no need to lay it again. **Foundation.** What he earlier called “the discourse of the beginning,” he here calls the foundation, because it is first proposed to those coming to the Christian religion, so that what belongs to perfection may be built upon it. This foundation is divided into six things: beginning, or repentance; faith; the teaching of baptisms; the laying on of hands; resurrection; and judgment. Whoever converts someone to faith first causes that person to repent, believe in God, be baptized for remission, be confirmed through the laying on of hands, and await the resurrection and the day of judgment.

**VERSE 4.—Impossible.** So that no one may think that a second or third baptism can take place after sins, he adds: “Impossible,” not merely difficult, so that no one may place confidence in this. **Those who,** that is, even those who possessed these good things. How much less those who were thoroughly evil.

**VERSE 6.—To be renewed,** through baptism, whose power rests upon the cross of Christ. Hence he adds: “Crucifying again.” In baptism we are conformed to his death and burial. Whoever thinks he can be baptized a second time crucifies Christ a second time, insofar as it lies with him. This is to expose him to contempt and mockery: just as he died once, so we die to sins once in baptism, not a second or third time.

**VERSE 7.—Often receiving.** He says “often receiving” because if it were rare, it would not suffice; if constant, it would become cheap. **Rain.** Holy teaching, the dew of heaven, which the heavens pour upon thirsty earth—that is, preachers of the word of truth. **Producing vegetation.** He signifies those who have often drunk the word of heavenly teaching through the Law and the prophets, yet were not thereby ready to produce the shoots of faith. **By whom it is cultivated.** The cultivators of the earth are those who cut down thickets with the spiritual plow and prune away harmful growth with the sickle of God’s word. Or, “by whom it is cultivated” refers to those same people who cultivate themselves through good works, imitating their predecessors, according to the saying: “And they produced the fruit of their origin,” because they imitate their fathers, who begot them in faith.

**VERSE 9.—We are confident.** Since the Apostle has no basis for praising them in the present, he raises them up through hope in future things. Through their past he draws them toward these things, revives and strengthens their spirits, recalls ancient matters to their minds, and makes them believe that God has not forgotten the good things they did. For just as their earlier good works had been rendered dead and void by subsequent evils, so those same works will come back to life through repentance and subsequent good works.

**VERSE 10.—Work.** He has borne great witness to them. He commends three good qualities in them: namely, that they made all their possessions common to the saints. This is the work; and it arose from love, which gives shape to actions. This is their eagerness; and it was directed toward the glory of God. This is their pure and upright intention.

**VERSE 11.—We desire.** He shows great love toward them, demonstrates the same care for each individual, cares equally for the greater and the lesser, and loves them all.

**VERSE 13.—For when God made the promise to Abraham, etc.** He says three things: that the promise was made, that it was confirmed by an oath, and that it was fulfilled in Abraham.

**VERSE 14.—Unless blessing, etc.** This is aposiopesis, that is, an omission. As if to say: If I do not do this, let me not be believed about anything.

**VERSE 17.—In which he desired more abundantly.** As if he said: If an oath makes a human being, who is a liar, believed, how much more must God be believed, who cannot lie?

**VERSE 18.—We have fled for refuge.** One flees to hope who, because of the hope of blessedness, disregards tribulations.

**VERSE 19.—Which, like.** Just as an anchor holds a ship, so hope holds the soul, lest it sink in the sea of this world by consenting to iniquity; and it holds it firm, so that it does not even waver.

**(AUG.) Cast your care upon God, etc.,** up to the point where he says that if hope fluctuates for a time, it is its anchor.

**VERSE 20.—Forerunner.** Christ ran ahead for this purpose, so that we might follow. He is rightly called a runner because no fault impeded him, according to the saying: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Ps. XVIII). [Col. 0654D] And elsewhere: “He did not stand in the way of sinners” (ibid. I). He is also called a forerunner because he ran before us and on our behalf.

## CHAPTER VII

**Priest of the Most High God.** (CHRYS., Homily 35 on Genesis.) Perhaps he was a priest appointed by himself, for that is how priests were appointed at that time. Or, because he was advanced in age, he was honored by his own people. Or because he too was zealous to offer sacrifice, as were Noah, Abel, and Abraham when they offered sacrifices.

**VERSE 3.—Without beginning, etc.,** and without having an end of life. Christ absolutely had neither beginning nor end. **Forever.** He says this because Scripture is silent about anyone succeeding him. Or he speaks mystically of Christ’s priesthood.

[Col. 0655A] **VERSE 4.—Consider, however, etc.** He dwells upon commending the dignity of Melchizedek and the excellence of his priesthood, placing him above Abraham himself, the father of all, and above all the Levites.

**VERSE 5.—And indeed, concerning the sons of Levi, etc.** As if to say: From this also consider how great he is, because certain descendants of Levi, by receiving sacrificial offerings—for otherwise they would not dare to do so—have a commandment in the Law, and without its authority they would never presume to take tithes.

**VERSE 8.—He bears witness.** “I,” or, “the same person,” in many passages. **He lives.** He bore the type of our high priest, whose excellence of power is shown through his likeness. Through Melchizedek, in whom the figure came beforehand, the priesthood of Christ is distinguished from the priesthood of Levi; in the figure of Christ, however, Melchizedek is said to live. Hence Christ is called a priest forever, because he offered himself not from any necessity but by the will of his own power.

**VERSE 11.—Under it.** Because the Law is in the hand of the priest, and through him the Law that is said to bring perfection is fulfilled. This transfer was prefigured in Samuel, who was chosen as priest by the Lord from the tribe of Ephraim, while the sons of Eli were rejected, the Lord saying: “Whoever honors me, I will honor; and whoever dishonors me, etc.”

**VERSE 12.—For when the priesthood is transferred, etc.** He subsequently proves that another has arisen, both through tribe and through rite. Through tribe, in the passage: “For the one concerning whom these things are said, etc.” Through rite, in the passage: “And still more, etc.” **For when the priesthood is transferred.** Since the Law and the priesthood were likewise given by the same person and under the same promise, what is said of one must necessarily be understood also of the other.

**VERSE 14.—For it is evident, etc.** The priesthood was transferred from tribe to tribe, from the priestly to the royal, so that the priestly and royal offices might belong to the same person. Observe the mystery: at first he was royal; afterward he became priestly. So Christ was always king, but he became priest when he assumed flesh and offered the sacrifice.

**VERSE 16.—Not according to the Law.** That is, not according to the carnal understanding of the Law, as though he were to act according to carnal observances, but according to the power of the Law itself—that is, its spiritual understanding. Those who carry this out have eternal life. There is a difference between priesthood and priesthood: the former is carnal, the latter spiritual; the former temporal, the latter eternal.

**VERSE 22.—By so much.** From praise of the priest he draws a commendation of the Law. **A better one.** Because it promises better things, that is, eternal things; the Old Testament, however, promised temporal things.

### Verse 24

“But this one…” Just as Christ remains, so also does the law which he brought, in which there is true remission of sins and perpetual grace. Because the old law could not provide this, it was excluded. He shows that it remains forever by referring to the high priest, who is one; this would not be so unless he were immortal, just as there were many priests under the law because they were mortal.

### Verse 25

“Therefore he is also able to save…” Having shown that through Christ’s priesthood the old priesthood and the law are destroyed, he commends Christ’s work by disparaging, through contrast, the operation of the old priesthood. [Col. 0656A]

### Verse 26

“Holy, inwardly”: innocent. “Undefiled,” in his hands and body. “Separated from sinners,” that is, free from every sin.

### Verse 27

“Who does not have…” Since he is such, he has no need to offer every day. The Apostle did not say this as though Christ ever had need of such an offering, but in order to remove from him what applies to others. He did this once, by offering himself. So great is the sacrifice that, although offered once and only once, it nevertheless suffices for eternity.

### Verse 28

“For the law appoints men…” Those priests have need to offer every day because they are weak; Christ, offering himself once, suffices for all because he is perfect. [Col. 0656B]

## Chapter VIII

### Verse 1

“Summary.” (CHRYS.) The Apostle Paul mixes lowly things with exalted things, always following his Master, and so forth, up to “the one who must perform the priestly office.”

“We have such a one.” Here the chapter begins and ends at “God and not man.” “In the heavens,” or above the material heavens, or above thrones and dominions.

### Verse 2

“A minister of the holy places.” Because he ministers an increase of virtues and eternal life to the saints. Alternatively, in heaven he ministers the glory signified by the Holy of Holies.

“A minister of the true tabernacle.” That is, of the truth which the ancient tabernacle prefigured—namely, righteousness in the present Church and glory in the future. God established this true tabernacle so that it might remain forever; the shadowy one, however, was not fixed but portable. “And not man”: he adds this because God also established the old tabernacle, but through a human minister. [Col. 0656C]

### Verse 3

“That he may have something to offer.” Since it is necessary for him to have something to offer, it must be either earthly or heavenly. But it cannot be earthly, for if it were, he would not be a priest. Therefore what he offers is heavenly.

### Verse 4

“If he were…” If, then, he were such a priest… Anyone who offers, if there were some earthly person capable of cleansing the human race, would not be a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, because the priests who offered the legal sacrifices would be sufficient. But because they were mortal and sinful, and therefore unable to cleanse the human race, Christ came, one who would suffice. [Col. 0656D]

“Now, however”—that is, in the final age—Christ has received a better priestly ministry, by as much as his law is better. He now passes from priesthood and sacrifice to the distinction between the Covenants.

### Verse 5

“It was answered…” Not when he was beginning, since he had already expressed many things through figures, but when he was unable by himself to bring them to completion, he consulted the Lord, who instructed him concerning the figures, just as he instructed him concerning the reality.

### Verse 6

“And of a better Covenant…” He now passes from sacrifice and priesthood to the distinction between the Covenants, preferring the New to the Old because the New was ratified by better promises.

### Verse 7

“For if that first one…” He proves that Christ’s Covenant is better than the Old: the former is not free from fault, whereas this one is. For if it had been free from fault, a second would not have been given; but a second was given. Thus it appears that the former was imperfect and this one perfect.

“If it had been free from fault, certainly not.” He speaks as though the Old Covenant itself possessed fault. This appears to be the case because it commands without grace and makes people transgressors. It would be asked of the Lord, who first gradually instructed and educated them, so that afterward he might give what was perfect. [Col. 0657A]

### Verse 9

“Which I made with their fathers.” Since he had made a special covenant with certain people, he specifies it.

“Which I made in the day”—that is, in the time of the law, which was given after the exodus from Egypt. What he therefore said earlier to Abraham, before the law—“In your seed all the nations will be blessed” (Gen. XXII)—he later fulfilled in the Gospel. For that promise was spiritual and specifically concerned grace. [Col. 0657B]

“They did not remain in the Covenant.” He attributes their failure to remain in the Covenant to their own fault, so that the law they then received would not appear blameworthy. It is the law which Christ did not come to abolish but to fulfill. Nevertheless, it does not justify without grace, because of the offense of the old humanity. Since that offense is not healed by the letter that commands and threatens, the former is called “Old” and the latter “New,” because of the newness of the Spirit, which heals the defect of old age. He clearly explains this by saying: “This is the Covenant,” and so forth.

### Verse 10

“By giving my laws into their minds.” Not on stone tablets, and not with ink, but through the Spirit. When the Spirit is present—he is the finger of God—love is poured into hearts, and love is the fullness of the law. For the righteous are not terrified from without but love righteousness inwardly. [Col. 0657C]

“By giving my laws”: behold the Covenant.

“I will write them above.” As though he said: “The things that ought to remain above them and rule over them.”

“And I will be their God.” That is, they will live from me and for me, and in the future they will see me. This is perfection, so that one person will not teach another.

This is the distinction between the Old and the New: the former was written on stone, the latter in the heart; there the reward was earth, here it is the vision of God.

### Verse 11

“He will not teach.” What was hidden in the letter, and what the people learned through the traditions of their teachers, the Spirit, when he came, taught the apostles. This is what the Prophet says: “They will not teach one another, because all will know” (Jer. XXXI). Likewise it is said in the Gospel: “Then he opened their understanding” (Luke XXIV), and so forth.

“The greater.” Understand “greater” either in time—for example, those who came before us and awaited us before receiving the denarius—or in knowledge or virtue: those who were able to understand the incorporeal and unchanging light, insofar as this is possible in the present life, although the lesser were nevertheless able to believe it.

When what is perfect has come and what is partial has been abolished, then the one who appeared in the flesh, having assumed flesh, will show himself to those who love him. Then all will know him, from the least to the greatest, because even the least will then know perfectly, when he is instructed by himself rather than by someone greater.

## Chapter IX

### Verse 1

“He had.” Up to this point he has shown the distinction between the Covenants, that the New surpasses the Old and transforms it. He now demonstrates the same thing from the structure of the tabernacle itself.

“Holy,” not spiritual, but “worldly,” because it was considered holy by human beings. And indeed it had a worldly sanctuary, because there was a first and a second tabernacle.

### Verse 2

“For a holy tabernacle was made.” Inside the first tabernacle there was the altar of incense; outside, before the entrance and under the open sky, was the altar of burnt offerings. Alternatively, what is outside signifies the Old Covenant and is a figure of a figure; what is inside signifies the New.

### Verse 5

“Cherubim.” By the Cherubim the fullness of knowledge is signified; by the mercy seat above the ark, Christ is signified, because it was given especially to Christ by God the Father that he should be the propitiation for our sins. [Col. 0658B]

### Verse 7

“Once a year.” The fact that entrance was made every year signified that perfection had not yet come.

“For his own ignorance and that of the people.” Christ offered for his people, but not for himself, except insofar as he did so in his members. Hence he himself says: “The words of my offenses” (Ps. XXI). He calls our offenses his own because he took them upon himself—not in order to possess them, but to erase them.

### Verse 8

“Not yet made manifest.” Heaven is still inaccessible to mortals according to the condition of the body, and previously it was inaccessible even according to the soul. But the resurrection must be awaited patiently; in it, through Christ, access to heaven will be opened also to bodies.

“The way of the holy places.” The way of the saints is Christ; alternatively, it is the spiritual understanding of the law, through which one ascends into the inner regions of heaven. [Col. 0658C]

### Verse 9

“Which is a parable.” He makes clear that these things were spoken figuratively concerning the sacrifices to be completed either in the first or in the second tabernacle, adding: “which is a parable,” and so forth.

### Verse 10

“Until the time of correction”—that is, until the time of grace, when those who had previously been under a pedagogue were to be corrected for the better. The law could not make them perfect, but it nevertheless was not to cease at that time.

### Verse 11

“Through the greater.” Christ entered the tabernacle, that is, heaven. By the name of the sign—“tabernacle”—the Apostle designates the thing signified—heaven. It is rightly called “greater,” because it contains more than that earthly tabernacle, and “more perfect,” because perfect blessedness is there. [Col. 0658D]

### Verse 12

“Into the holy places.” He explains what he had said: “A tabernacle not made with hands,” namely, the Holy of Holies, that is, the heavenly places.

### Verse 13

“For if the blood…” He proves from the lesser that redemption could be accomplished through Christ, because through those legal rites bodily purification was effected.

“Of goats.” The goat signifies Christ through the likeness of sinful flesh.

“The bull.” Christ is called a bull because, with the horns of the two Covenants, he drives away his enemies.

“For the purification of the flesh”—that is, so that the flesh might be purified because of the commandment of the law. But in Christ there is perfection.

### Verse 14

“He offered himself.” Christ, mediator between God and human beings, is the giver of the New Covenant. [Col. 0659A] He is, as it were, our high priest and the giver of the new law.

“Undefiled.” His blood is undefiled.

“And from dead works”—that is, sins. Whoever touches them is polluted, just as one who touched a dead body was polluted; nor does he enter heaven, just as the unclean person did not enter the temple.

“To serve the living God.” Nevertheless, Christ’s death was necessary for the redemption not only of the Gentiles but also of those transgressions which the law exposed without removing. Our sin was so great that we could not be saved unless the Only-Begotten of God died for us, who were debtors to death. Yet in this way he made us worthy of the Covenant and of the promised inheritance, and thus the Covenant was made firm.

### Verse 15

“By means of an intercession.” Between the Old Covenant and the New—among which not only the sacraments but also the promises are divided—the distinction is Christ’s passion. By his death it is established that earthly things are not promised, but eternal things. For at the death of the Only-Begotten, great things must be hoped for. [Col. 0659B]

### Verse 16

“For where there is…” Christ is the giver of the New Covenant, with death intervening. Now, for the confirmation of the Covenant, Christ could die, as he proves from the custom of human law.

### Verse 19

“Wool.” Christ’s love is wool for us, from which we may make a garment.

### Verse 22

“And without the shedding of blood…” This qualification is added because through the water of sprinkling made from the ashes of a red heifer, remission of sins was sometimes effected when blood was not shed. Nevertheless, blood had been shed in the sacrifice of the heifer. [Col. 0659C]

Although those sacrifices were more suitably imposed upon a perverse people than offered to God as something he desired, they were nevertheless figures of the truth, which is Christ. By his blood we have been redeemed and cleansed, because our purification and God’s propitiation for us are impossible without blood.

### Verse 23

“But the heavenly things themselves…” Christ, who was signified in certain things, did not need to be cleansed, but all his members do. Nevertheless, the signs of him which served the ministry in the tabernacle were cleansed with blood.

### Verse 25

“Nor that he should offer himself repeatedly…” He has proved that Christ cleansed the heavenly things through his sacrifice. He now proves that he did so by better sacrifices—that is, that his sacrifice was more worthy and effective than all the others. Those sacrifices, repeatedly offered, brought no completion; this sacrifice, offered once, leads us back to our homeland. [Col. 0659D]

### Verse 26

“Otherwise…” If, when offered once, he had not been sufficient to exhaust the sins of all who believe in him, he would have had to suffer repeatedly from the foundation of the world. To prevent this, he suffered once at the consummation of the ages.

“At the consummation.” That is, in the final age, in which everything that had previously been imperfect has been completed. Therefore it was not necessary for him to begin suffering from the foundation of the world.

### Verse 27

“And just as…” The natural law demonstrates this, and the point is proved by what would otherwise be incongruous.

“To die once.” This is not to be understood as though Christ were offered even once by necessity arising from his own sin; rather, he was offered solely by his will. But just as a human being who has died once does not die again by necessity and the law of nature, so Christ, offered once under that same law, cannot die again.

“After this, judgment.” After dying once, judgment remains, in which all will receive according to what they have deserved. It does not remain for them to rise again and die a second time.

### Verse 28

“He will appear without sin.” Thus, at that time there will be no sacrifice for sin, but righteousness in rewarding or condemning. If there will be no sacrifice even on the day of wrath, much less will there be one at other times.

Alternatively, “without sin” means without the likeness of sinful flesh, but rather in glorified flesh.

## Chapter X

### Verse 1

“For the law, having a shadow…” He proved that Christ died once. But why—or why only once? Because the law could not make people perfect; therefore a spotless lamb had to be offered.

“Not the very image.” That is, the truth. In a painting, until someone applies the colors, there is a kind of underpainting. This underpainting is something like a shadow and not yet an image; but when someone has applied the colors themselves, then it becomes an image.

“Those who approach.” Although the high priests entered the Holy of Holies every year, continually offering the same sacrifices, they were never able to be perfected by their sacrifices. [Col. 0660B]

### Verse 2

“Once cleansed, would they not have ceased…” Christ’s one sacrifice makes people perfect. Even if thousands sin, they do not need another sacrifice, because it suffices for everything and washes every conscience from sins. The old sacrifice could not do this; for if it had, there would have been no need to repeat it.

It is like a medicine which, if it is powerful, effective for health, and capable of driving away every illness, accomplishes everything when applied once. If it is always being applied, this is clear evidence that it has not brought health. Therefore, because no one was healed by those sacrifices, they were offered frequently. [Col. 0660C]

### Verse 3

“Remembrance, not absolution; an accusation of weakness, not a display of power.” Because God wished to reveal their weakness and establish a remembrance of sins, he commanded those sacrifices always to be offered.

### Verse 5

“You did not desire…” From the time of the passion, in which the completion of all sacrifices took place, those sacrifices began to displease God. Before then he had never abolished them, but subjected himself to them, being presented in the temple with the sacrifices.

“But you prepared a body for me.” The signs were removed because the truth had been presented. Then it was time for those signs to be taken away and for the truth to come. The Lord was never pleased by those fragrances except through the faith and desire of the one offering them. Nevertheless, he commanded that they be offered to him rather than to idols, and subjected them to servitude, not to justification, so that they might be figures of what was to come. [Col. 0660D]

### Verse 6

“You took no pleasure.” In those figures the truth was foretold. They celebrate the figures, many knowing the reality of the figures, but more remaining ignorant that they ought to cease once the reality has been presented.

### Verse 7

“Then.” When I saw that all those things displeased you and that a body suitable for this purpose had been given to me, I said: “Behold, I come to offer myself, to do and fulfill your will, because you are my God.”

Therefore I come to fulfill your will because it is written and prefigured concerning me in the counsel of the Godhead, which is my head. I am the liberator of the human race according to my humanity, in whom human beings may read everything necessary for themselves; therefore there is no need of the law. [Col. 0661A]

### Verse 8

“After saying above…” As though he were saying: This passage not only indicates that the ancient sacrifices did not make anyone perfect, but also that Christ’s one sacrifice did so. It also indicates the removal of the Old Covenant and the establishment of the New, if the words are carefully considered. For after saying above, “You did not desire them,” he adds, “Then I said.”

Thus he removes the first sacrifice and with it the Old Covenant, and establishes as lasting the new sacrifice and with it the New Covenant.

### Verse 10

“By which we have been sanctified…” Once the cleansing of sins had been accomplished, we were reconciled to God. [Col. 0661B]

### Verse 11

“And every priest…” Lest it appear that the blood offered once a year by the high priests had been of little benefit, or that the sacrifices performed daily by the priests made people perfect, he adds this, as though saying: The high priest, offering every year, did not attain completion; likewise every priest always offers, and yet no one is ever perfected through those sacrifices.

### Verse 12

“But he sits at the right hand.” One who has deserved to be exalted in this way can rightly bring things to completion.

### Verse 13

“From now on.” That is, as regards what remains: the glory of the good and the punishment of the wicked.

“A footstool.” Even if they now resist him and do not appear to be subjected to him, then all will be shown to be subject to him, under whose command they will be given over to punishments.

### Verse 15

“But the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us…” The Holy Spirit testifies that he has perfected forever those who have been sanctified, and that in the New Covenant God will remember sins no more.

“Afterward.” As though he were saying: After saying what does not suffice for our proof, he added other things that confirm both points we are making: “by giving laws,” which pertains to completion; and “I will no longer remember their sins and iniquities,” which pertains to sanctification.

### Verse 16

“I will write them above.” He does not say “I will write,” but “I will write above,” because those laws surpass human strength, and no one will be sufficient for their fulfillment except through the help of grace. In these words he says that he perfects people through virtues; then he speaks of sanctification.

[Col. 0661D] ### Verse 18

“Where there is forgiveness…” It can be seen not only from this passage that Jesus sanctifies and perfects, but also that after the time of grace no offering for sins is to be made, since forgiveness has been accomplished.

### Verse 20

“Through the veil.” Our faith is veiled, because faith has no merit when human reason supplies proof by experience.

### Verse 22

“In the fullness of faith.” Our faith is perfect because none of these things is now visible: neither priest nor sacrifice.

“Having our hearts sprinkled.” This shows that not faith alone is sought, but also life accompanied by virtue.

“Washed with water,” that is, by baptism.

### Verse 23

“For he is faithful.” Just as God is faithful in his promises, so he wants us to be faithful to him in our promises. Let us therefore hold fast to faith and confession, as far as concerns us.

### Verse 24

“And let us consider…” The perfect person exhorts others; the lesser imitates the perfect person. Accordingly, the Apostle exhorts them to those things that are appropriate to faith.

### Verse 25

“As is the custom…” He blames those who divide the unity of love, as though they could not live among others because of their holiness, when rather they ought by their example to have consoled them.

“But comforting…” One who persists equally in labor comforts the person who is laboring, because the effort—or exertion—of a fellow laborer is a relief from labor, as happens on a journey.

### Verse 26

“For if we sin deliberately…” That is, if we remain in the will to sin, Christ, who is the sacrifice for sins, does not profit us even in the present life. From this it is clear that he will not profit us in the future either.

“After receiving knowledge of the truth”—that is, although we had come to the faith, on account of which some are secure as though they could never perish.

He does not say “for those who are willing,” but “for those who sin deliberately,” because one who is deliberate persists in something, whereas one who is merely willing may do so for a time. Alternatively, this may also mean: even if we sin in intention, let alone in action.

“No sacrifice for sins remains,” just as under the old law sacrifices for sin were repeatedly offered. Christ is not to be sacrificed again for sins: it was done once, and a second time is not necessary. Rather, it is necessary to remain in faith and truth. If one does not do this, judgment awaits him unless he is renewed through repentance. [Col. 0662B]

### Verse 28

“By two or three witnesses.” Convicted. [Col. 0662C] What, then, will happen to those against whom angels, saints, and their own conscience bear witness?

### Verse 29

“Has trampled underfoot…” He tramples Christ who sins freely, without fear or repentance. The one who participates unworthily treats the blood as defiled if, after being cleansed by it, he returns to his vomit and neglects to repent.

“He has insulted the Spirit.” He insults the Spirit when he does not gratefully receive its benefit.

“Has treated as polluted.” Such is the person who believes that sins are forgiven through carnal observances, whereas Christ’s blood draws us away from those observances. He is therefore polluted, and he pollutes us, if he draws us away from the source of forgiveness.

“And has insulted the Spirit of grace.” That is, the Holy Spirit freely given; or, he insults the one who gives grace. He attributes the forgiveness accomplished by the Spirit itself to carnal observances; alternatively, he casts the Spirit away from himself by living badly. [Col. 0662D]

### Verse 30

“Vengeance is mine…” This was said concerning enemies who do harm, not concerning those who suffer harm.

Here he also consoles them, saying that God remains forever and lives. Therefore, even if tyrants do not now receive what has been promised to them, they will receive it afterward. They, not we, ought therefore to share in the groaning.

For it is not the one who suffers who suffers something evil, but the one who does evil; nor does the person who is helped receive the benefit, but the one who provides the benefit. Knowing these things, let us therefore become patient in enduring evils and ready to do good.

[Col. 0663A] ### Verse 31

“Remember.” He invites them by recalling their former deeds.

(CHRYS.) Just as the best physicians, when they have healed others, and so forth, up to “so that you may not fall into the hands of God: remember,” and so forth.

“Formerly…” If those who were beginners endured, it is shameful if they now fail.

“A great contest…” Their sufferings arose both from their own pains and from the pains of others, with whom they sympathized.

### Verse 33

“And at another time…” As though he were saying: You endure a contest of sufferings, both in your own sufferings and in your compassion for others; these are the two forms of suffering that contend against us.

“A spectacle.” It is a serious reproach; it is more serious when someone is made a spectacle to human beings and is reproached publicly rather than privately.

[Col. 0663B] ### Verse 38

“He lives.” (AUG.) “Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous and upright, for praise befits you,” and so forth, up to “he raises up the one who is failing and crowns the victor.”

### Verse 39

“But we…” That is, we are not children of pagans but of faithful prophets.

## Chapter XI

### Verse 1

“Now faith is.” Here is praise and commendation of faith, of which he gives a definition. In it he notes three things: what it accomplishes in us, namely that it is the foundation of all good things, and that it concerns things not apparent. It has been treated more fully in the Epistle to the Romans: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for,” that is, the cause which will at some time make the hoped-for things subsist in us; that is to say, it will make us attain future goods. Faith is properly called “substance” because it underlies things hoped for and makes them exist in believers in another life. It is the foundation of all good things, which no one can alter and without which there is no good building; or, it already makes things hoped for exist in the heart of the believer.

“Evidence,” that is, certainty concerning things which do not appear; and, if anyone doubts about it, proof while the future resurrection is still being proved, because the patriarchs, the apostles, and other saints believed thus. Faith is the cause of things hoped for because it is the cause of righteousness, through which they are to be hoped for. This is the meaning of: “In this they received testimony”—testimony of righteousness—because on account of faith God testified that they were righteous.

“The elders”: this is said not because they were old in age, but because they were the predecessors of these people. Thus it is plain that faith is not new, but is to be maintained, since the ancients maintained it. [Col. 0663C]

### Verse 3

“By faith we understand.” He uses examples to commend faith, showing that faith concerns things not apparent.

### Verse 4

“By faith, a more abundant…” He shows that the ancient fathers obtained testimony of righteousness through faith, giving another example for the commendation of righteousness.

“Though dead, he still speaks.” That is, he gives us matter for speaking, so that we may offer an example from his faith. For death did not extinguish the renown of his faith. From the faith and patience of those before them he consoles these people. Abel still speaks because by his example he admonishes others to be righteous. Death indeed killed him, but it did not kill along with him his glory and remembrance.

(AUG.) “Neither Enoch nor Elijah withered away through old age over so long a time, nor yet …,” down to “before he deserved to depart from there because of sin.” [Col. 0664A]

### Verse 6

“Because he is.” Being properly belongs to God, because he is unchangeably.

### Verse 7

“By faith Noah, etc.” “And of righteousness, etc.” That is, he was righteous by faith, like his fathers; for unless he had been righteous, God would not have commanded this of him.

### Verse 8

“By faith he who lives.” Here he comes down to the fathers of the Jews and shows in them, as in those before them, that all righteousness had its origin in faith. He gives the example of Abraham.

“He obeyed” God saying to him: “Go forth from your land and from your kindred.” He had already done this. For this was said when he had already left the land of the Chaldeans and had already settled in Mesopotamia. Therefore the Lord turned not his body but his mind away from his land, lest he wish to return. For he had not left it in mind, but was held by a desire to return; this desire, by God’s command and help and by Abraham’s obedience, had to be cut off. [Col. 0664B]

### Verse 11

“Because he considered him faithful.” At first she laughed, even if from joy, yet not with full faith; but afterward, by the angel’s words, she was established in faith. Abraham also laughed when a son was promised to him, but that laughter was of wonder and joy, not of doubt.

### Verse 12

“From one.” From a dead womb, or from Abraham as good as dead. He calls Sarah’s womb dead with respect to conception by an elderly man; or he calls Abraham himself dead with respect to begetting by an elderly woman.

“As the stars.” This refers to the good, that is, those who are compared to stars by the light of virtues and by multitude.

“And as the sand.” This refers to the wicked, that is, those who are compared to sand in instability and number. The sea is the Gentile world itself; its shore is its rite. Some Jews were made near to it, though not among the Gentiles. [Col. 0664C]

### Verse 13

“And greeting them.” He uses a word transferred from sailors, who see from afar the cities they desire and greet them before entering them. Therefore, from the metaphor of sailors, he says, “And greeting them”: that is, rejoicing over and desiring them, as sailors do when they see cities from afar. Thus they confessed that they were themselves strangers, who possess nothing in a foreign country.

“Guests.” These are not of their native land; and they confessed that they were not of the world and had nothing in the world. Therefore they confessed this. Those who say this make it understood that they seek another homeland, which was what they wished to signify. And lest anyone suppose that they sought the land from which they had departed, it follows: “And indeed, if …” [Col. 0664D]

### Verse 17

“When he was tested.” God did not test Abraham as one ignorant of his faith, but so that Abraham himself and the world might know the truth and firmness of his faith.

### Verse 19

“And as a parable.” Abraham offered by faith not only in reality but also in signification. For he understood that Christ was signified, whose divinity does not die; but the ram caught by its horns among the brambles—that is, flesh suffering among the Jews upon the horns of the cross—could be offered to God, having first been crowned with Jewish thorns. [Col. 0665A]

### Verse 20

“Isaac.” Here he had faith not only that the one blessed was better, but he also believed that the Christian people would supplant the blessing made and promised to the Jews.

### Verse 21

“He worshiped the top, etc.” Perhaps he had taken a staff from his son when his son was swearing faith to him; and while holding it, immediately after the words of the oath, he worshiped God. For he was not ashamed to bear for a little while the emblem of his son’s power, where a figure of a great future event and of Christ’s future kingdom among the Gentiles was prefigured.

### Verse 22

“He gave command concerning his bones.” He adjured the children of Israel to carry them into the land of promise and lay them in the tomb of their fathers, namely in the double cave, in which Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other fathers were buried, where Adam and Eve also rested. They wished this because they foresaw that Christ would be born in that land, so that they might rise again with him. [Col. 0665B]

### Verse 26

“The reproach of Christ.” This is said either because Moses suffered for Christ, or because he signified Christ’s future reproaches; or because Moses endured from his brethren, whom he wished to free, what Christ endured from his own people, whom he had come to redeem. They said to Christ: “You have a demon” (John VII); and these men said to Moses: “Do you wish to kill us as you killed the Egyptian?” (Exod. II). Yet he endured this patiently, as Christ did also.

### Verse 27

“Not fearing.” His earlier flight into the land of Midian was not fear but faith, because he believed that God would deliver him. He did not wish to remain there, lest it become a cause for boasting if he threw himself into open danger and tested God, which is devilish. For as long as saints have something to do, they ought not to test God; thus the Lord made way for the Jews and commanded his own: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. X). [Col. 0665C]

### Verse 28

“By faith he celebrated the Passover.” Certainly by this faith, because he thus believed that the people would be saved: they from Pharaoh, we from the devil.

### Verse 29

“They crossed the Red Sea, etc.” Thus the faithful cross through baptism, their sins forgiven, as though the Egyptians, with the devil the prince of darkness, had been drowned.

### Verse 30

After a circuit of seven days, with the Levites carrying the ark of God and sounding bronze trumpets. [Col. 0665D]

### Verse 31

“Receiving the spies with peace, etc.” As though saying: Thus you too ought to receive in faith the two Covenants, sent from Christ through the apostles as spies; and thus you will not perish with the unbelievers.

### Verse 32

“Of Gideon.” Having received the sign of the fleece from the Lord, he went against the Midianites with three hundred men and defeated them by night.

“Samson.” As is read in the book of Judges, he severely afflicted the Philistines.

“Jephthah.” When going to battle against his enemies, he vowed to the Lord that, if he obtained victory over them, on his return he would offer to God whatever first met him; his daughter met him, and he sacrificed her. [Col. 0666A]

### Verse 33

“Who through faith.” Although he declines to say what each individual did, he nevertheless says what some accomplished through faith.
