“Promises.” The Apostle says “promises” again, not merely “promises,” because many promises were made to David, as to Abraham. He wisely avoids recounting histories lest he prolong his discourse, touching briefly on certain matters. For he neither passed over everything in silence nor became tiresome by speaking; he avoided density and length, lest he weary the hearer.

### Verse 35

“But others were stretched out, etc.” Among those fathers of the Old Testament, though rare, there were nevertheless examples of patience, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah. The Lord says that their blood would be required of those who persisted in the iniquity of their fathers, by whom those men were killed. And in the New Testament there were not lacking persons abounding in temporal prosperity, in which we experience God’s mercy. [Col. 0666B]

### Verse 38

“Of whom the world was not worthy.” That is, the world was not worthy of their manner of life, lest they be considered contemptible because of the tribulations they endured; or, they were so contemptible to human beings that they were thought unworthy to stand or dwell among them. Both they and those before them did not immediately receive the promised life until Christ. Why is it not added:

### Verse 40

“God having provided something better for us.” Inasmuch as he would assume our nature and rejoice with us more gloriously. If they held fast to faith, though they waited so long for rest on our account, much more should we hold fast, since immediately upon death we receive it.

## Chapter XII

[Col. 0666C]

### Verse 1

“Therefore we also.” After commending faith, he returns to what he had begun, exhorting to patience in many ways and especially by Christ’s own example.

“A cloud.” That is, a multitude of saints who are witnesses of faith; like a cloud, by their example they refresh us in the heat of tribulation and water us with teachings.

### Verse 2

“Who, with joy set before him, etc.” Thus, with eternal joy set before us, we ought to run, setting shame aside; or, with the joy of a temporal kingdom set before him, when the crowds wished to seize him and make him king, he refused, because it was the way of humility.

### Verse 3

“Fainting.” To faint is to deny faith through fear of tribulation. Therefore you ought not to faint, for you have not forgotten the consolation, nor ought you to forget it. [Col. 0666D]

### Verse 6

“Every son.” Even the only Son, who was without sin. Therefore, if you are exempt from the suffering of scourges, you are exempt from the number of sons. That only Son, born from the Father’s substance, equal to the Father in the form of God, the Word through whom all things were made, had no place in which he could be scourged. But he clothed himself with flesh for this purpose, that he might not be without scourging. Would he who scourges the only Son without sin leave unscourged the adopted son who has sin? The only Son was without sin, yet not without scourging; in his sufferings he set before us an example. Therefore we ought not be troubled when any saint suffers grievous and unworthy things, if we have not forgotten what the Just One of the just and the Holy One of the holy endured. Observe here God’s justice and mercy: justice in his scourging, mercy in his receiving. [Col. 0667A]

### Verse 8

“Then [you are] illegitimate children.” Note that one who begets through adultery is not rightly called a father, because those begotten by him are not called legitimate children.

### Verse 9

“We showed reverence.” To show reverence is to render honor with fear.

### Verse 10

“And they indeed.” Here another reason is shown why God must be obeyed: for what is useful, namely, in receiving his sanctification.

### Verse 11

**Discipline.** In Greek this is called *παιδεία* (*paideia*), that is, instruction through hardships, when someone suffers evils on account of his sins so that he may be corrected, as it is understood here. [Col. 0667B] There is also a discipline that is called knowledge, taking its name from learning, and in Greek is called *ἐπιστήμη* (*epistēmē*).

### Verse 12

**Hands.** That is, the affection of charity with which you once embraced God: raise them upward again toward God. And your knees—that is, your strength, which has been loosened by charity growing cold—raise them likewise.

### Verse 13

**Steps.** So that your faith may walk rightly, confessing what it believes, even if suffering is required. Faith is rightly called a foot, because it carries everything. Have straight steps, so that no one may turn aside from the true way of faith, as does the one who accepts carnal observances; for this is to go astray. And let it not limp, as one who falters through fear of suffering; rather, let him be healed if he has gone astray or been afraid. Alternatively, “straight steps” are a right intention in one’s works.

### Verse 14

**Holiness.** That is, purity of mind [Col. 0667C] and body; hence: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5), and so forth. “Without which no one will see God.” See how he terrifies the lover of the good—that is, of the vision of God. He did not say, “He will be cast into the fire,” or “He will be handed over to unwearied torturers”—although these things are true—but, wishing you to be a lover of the good, that is, of the vision of God, rather than a fearer of evil, he says: “Without which no one,” and so forth. By the very thing you desire, he terrifies you.

### Verse 15

**“Watching,” and so forth.** Do not doubt that you can be so patient, because God’s grace is present; but lest you withdraw from it, you can retain grace in this way. “Lest any root,” and so forth. The delight of sin is rightly called bitterness, and therefore must be avoided. The root of bitterness is an evil thought, which produces not sweet fruits—that is, works—but bitter ones, by which the way to heaven is obstructed.

[Col. 0667D] ### Verse 16

**“Lest there be any fornicator,” and so forth.** Here he shows in detail how they ought to watch, lest any root of bitterness sprout, by identifying some among them. **Firstfruits.** Or, “his birthright.” Here he calls the birthright the honor and dignity of the priesthood, because before Aaron’s priesthood all the firstborn were priests, as Shem was. This was a great dignity, since the firstborn also received the larger portion of their father’s substance and inheritance. He shone more splendidly in the richness of his clothing, and the blessing was given to him. See how far Esau was from religion, when for the sake of his belly he gave away the blessing. He recalls Esau’s deed in order to dissuade them from imitating him.

### Verse 18

**“For you have not come,” and so forth.** He had said that no one [Col. 0668A] should fall short of grace in the ways he had just indicated. Grace is ready, and this is what he means: You have not approached the harshness of the Law, which he describes, so that by contrast the sweetness of grace may be understood. You have come not to fire, but to the Holy Spirit, who is a fire consuming sins; and one approaches him not by bodily movement but in spirit.

**Whirlwind.** A whirlwind is the force of winds accompanied by hail and rain, and it signifies the assault of vices, which were more severely condemned through the Law. But now, through the grace of the Spirit, one comes to calmness.

**Darkness.** He says this because the Law was obscure; now there is clear understanding.

**Storm.** A storm is greater than a whirlwind, and is a tempest that drives things wherever it will. This is the slavery of sin according to the activity that dragged human beings along through the Law; but now there is rest from imperfect vices.

[Col. 0668B] ### Verse 19

**“The sound of a trumpet.”** A trumpet is a sign summoning people to war; it is also the movement of desire, which is extinguished not by the Law but by grace.

**“The voice of words.”** Such a voice is the Law’s command and threat, which the people considered burdensome and intolerable because it was command alone, without assisting grace.

### Verse 20

**“For they could not bear,” and so forth.** Without grace they were insufficient for observing the commandments.

**“And if even an animal,” and so forth.** The mountain is divinity; the animal is the failure of reason, as when a word of blasphemy is uttered against God. To touch is to offend. Thus the animal touches the mountain when someone offends God by blasphemy; the Law commands that such a person be stoned without mercy. But in the Church, if he wishes to return, he is received mercifully.

[Col. 0668C] ### Verse 22

**“But you have come,” and so forth.** These words depend on what precedes, where he says to what they have come after those things have been removed. He does not set down their opposites, which are understood by contrast, as was indicated above, but first states what follows from them, so that he may more strongly persuade them to hold fast to grace.

**“To Zion.”** That is, to those who contemplate God on high; and contemplation is a great reward.

**“And to the city of God.”** He says this because God dwells in them when he justifies them.

### Verse 23

**“Who are enrolled.”** It is as though he said: Do not doubt that you will reach the angels, because your predecessors have reached them. This is what he means: “Who are enrolled,” that is, enrolled with those who are in heaven, meaning that they belong to their order.

### Verse 26

**“Yet once more,” and so forth.** It is as though he said: They have already been shaken, but [Col. 0668D] I will shake them once more. By “once more” he indicates that they will not be shaken again.

He also speaks of the lower heaven, namely the aerial region; hence birds are called “birds of heaven.” Nearly all this windy air, which Scripture calls heaven or heavens, is meant here—not the highest heavens, where the sun, moon, and stars are established. Scripture says that these lower heavens will be shaken, and elsewhere that they will perish, on account of the great transformation they will undergo.

### Verse 27

**“The things that are immovable.”** It is as though he said: They truly are immovable, because whatever they may be—whether in their principal essences or in the outward forms they have assumed—they will be immovable in that respect.

### Verse 28

**“Therefore, receiving an unshakable kingdom.”** Since God [Col. 0669A] promises an unshakable heaven and earth, it is clear that we possess grace, without which we could not reach that promised realm. Through grace we receive the unshakable kingdom, so that no one may therefore fall short of grace.

**“Let us have grace.”** That is, let us have faith, hope, and charity in holy action. Or: “Let us have grace,” meaning, let us give thanks for everything, murmuring about nothing, because in this way God is served well.

### Verse 29

**“Our God is a fire.”** That is, the Holy Spirit, who is that gift and grace because he has been given to us freely.

## Chapter XIII

### Verses 1–2

**Charity.** From this point the Apostle gives moral instruction, as though he were saying: Since charity must be possessed, let it remain among you, and do not forget hospitality. [Col. 0669B] Through hospitality some have unknowingly sheltered angels, as Lot did, while nevertheless knowing who was present in them.

### Verse 3

**“As though you were bound together with them.”** That is, as you would wish assistance to be given to you if you were bound, or if you were suffering.

### Verse 5

**“Let your conduct be,” and so forth.** After the Hebrews had lost their possessions, they wanted to gather them again; the Apostle forbids this. But lest they say, “What if necessities should fail?” he adds consolation.

**“Without avarice.”** An avaricious person is grasping in giving and covetous in receiving.

**“I will not abandon you.”** God says this to everyone who hopes in him, as he said to Joshua. He is with us, so that we may say confidently, and so forth.

**“Nor will I forsake you.”** Someone would be forsaken if he perished from hunger; but since this does not happen, a person should not be covetous.

[Col. 0669C] ### Verse 6

**“I will not fear,” and so forth.** Every human adversary is meant, including the devil, who is called “human” because he deceives human beings.

### Verse 7

**“Remember,” and so forth.** Since it would take too long to speak of each person individually, he urges them to follow their teachers.

### Verse 8

**“Jesus Christ,” and so forth.** This belongs to the preceding statement, where he testified that God had said: “I will not abandon you, nor will I forsake you.” They might have thought that this promise applied only to Joshua. He answers that God will help us as he helped Joshua. It is as though he said: There is no doubt that the one who helped Joshua yesterday—that is, in the past—helps us today—that is, in the present—and will help those who come in every age.

### Verse 10

**“We have an altar,” and so forth.** We must not be concerned [Col. 0669D] with foods, because we have an altar—that is, the body of Christ. Through faith in him, prayers and works that have been offered are acceptable to God. Those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat from it, and so forth.

**“The tabernacle,” and so forth.** This means the observances of the Law. Those who distinguish foods and observe other legal practices of this kind are signified by the name “tabernacle,” because these practices were imposed for a time. Alternatively, our body is rightly called a tabernacle, because we must dwell in it only for a time; therefore it should not be served by indulging its desires.

### Verse 11

**“For the bodies of those animals,” and so forth.** Through a twofold allegory—one belonging to the Old Testament and the other to the New—he proves that the body of Christ must not be eaten by those who serve the tabernacle. For this reason [Col. 0670A] the bodies of animals are burned outside the camp, and Christ suffered outside the gate, so that we, who wish to be cleansed from sins by his body and blood, might abandon the pleasures of the tabernacle and endure reproaches and hardships.

**“Animals.”** Christ was signified by those animals.

### Verse 12

**“The gate.”** The gate of the city is the sense of the body; Christ sinned in none of these senses, and therefore suffered outside. Let us too, with the gate of the senses closed against vices, suffer outside.

### Verse 15

**“Through him, therefore,” and so forth.** Since he is the way for us and from him we take our example, let us hasten toward martyrdom.

**“Of those who confess.”** (Augustine.) “Therefore, you who fear the Lord, praise him,” and so forth, up to the point where he says that the visible sacred sign was a sign of that invisible sacrifice.

[Col. 0670B] ### Verse 16

**“Beneficence.”** Having dismissed the argument of the wicked concerning gluttony, he returns to conduct.

**“Beneficence,”** that is, generosity toward others. Even if your possessions have been taken away, give alms from what you have. He had said this above: “Do not abandon the gathering.”

### Verse 17

**“So that they may do so with joy.”** Let us do these things with joy when we see people advancing in the words of God. The worker in the fields labors with joy when he observes the trees and sees fruit; when he observes the crop and sees its abundance. Then he understands that he has not labored in vain, has not bent his back in vain, has not worn out his hands in vain, and has not endured cold and heat in vain.

**“It is not expedient for you.”** I do not say, “It is not expedient for them,” because even for them it is beneficial to grieve over your condition. For those rulers, when they grieve over your evils, [Col. 0670C] benefit from the grief itself—but you do not. Therefore, in the Lord’s field, let rulers and subjects alike work for what is good, so that together we may rejoice in the reward.

### Verse 18

**“Pray for us.”** He rebukes the pride and arrogance of mind shown by certain bishops, who disdain to ask their subjects to pour out prayers for them.

**“We have a good conscience.”** That is, our conscience does not accuse us, nor are we aware of having plotted against you. We have said nothing deceitfully and have done nothing for the sake of gain. Therefore, do not form any unfavorable opinion.

**“In all things.”** The Apostle was accused of neglecting his own people, but he shows that he has affection for all Jews and [Col. 0670D] Gentiles. He rejoices in their past virtues and wishes them better things in the future.

### Verse 21

**“Making,” in you, and so forth.** You can possess no good unless he goes before you and follows after you.

### Verse 22

**“For indeed, with very few words,” and so forth.** It is as though he said: No one can reject the length of this discourse. This was what his opponents were doing, and therefore he touches on it discreetly.

**“Greet all your leaders.”** Just as he writes generally to everyone, so he generally wishes peace to all leaders and subjects. To greet is to wish salvation.

[Col. 0671]

# Prologue of Saint Jerome to the Seven Canonical Epistles

[Col. 0671] See Jerome’s *Divine Library*, the letter to Paulinus, and the book *On Illustrious Men*.

[Col. 0671]

# The Canonical Epistle of Blessed James (G)*

## Argument

[Col. 0671A]

The Apostle James instructed the holy clergy in the cultivation of heavenly commandments, the rule of Catholic observance, the majesty of unconquered patience, the revelation of many things, and the instruction of teachers.

## Chapter I

### Verse 1

**“James.”** After the apostles had been sent to preach, this man assumed the care and governance of the Church of Jerusalem.

**“To the twelve tribes.”** It belonged especially to the twelve apostles to show concern for these people, since they served as ambassadors for the Lord among the circumcised. Hence Paul also says: “James, Cephas, and John, who were regarded as pillars, gave the right hand,” and so forth. For this reason he writes chiefly to them, [Col. 0671B] and also because he himself had been appointed bishop over them by the other apostles.

### Verse 2

**“Consider it all joy.”** Do not be indignant if the wicked flourish in the world while you suffer, because it is not characteristic of Christian truth to be exalted in temporal matters, but rather to be humbled. The wicked possess nothing in heaven; you possess nothing in the world. In hope of the good toward which you are striving, whatever may happen along the way, you ought to rejoice.

**“When you fall into trials.”** He begins with the more perfect, speaking of external trials.

### Verse 3

**“The testing of faith,” and so forth.** The same statement, but in reversed order, is found in Paul, and so forth, up to the point where he says that faith is thereby proven perfect.

### Verse 6

**“But whoever doubts.”** Whoever, weighed down by the consciousness of sin, doubts the heavenly rewards, easily abandons the steadfastness of faith when the winds of temptation arise. Carried according to the will of the tempter by the wind, he is swept through various errors of vice.

### Verse 10

**“But let the rich man.”** He calls rich the person who places all his hope in riches. It is not harmful to possess riches, but to love them.

**“But let the rich man glory.”** This is said ironically. It is as though he said: He ought not to glory in the glory by which he is proud and oppresses others, because that glory will end and be humbled in hell. Or, let him glory in his humility—that is, not in pride, but by humbling himself and serving others with his riches.

**“Because like the flower of grass.”** The righteous flourishes like a palm tree; the unrighteous like grass, because the former remains while the latter quickly passes away. The flower of the righteous is hope, which awaits its fruit; the root of the righteous is charity, which remains immovable. The root of the wicked is greed; the flower is delight in temporal things.

### Verse 11

**“The rich man in his journeys.”** The rich man’s roads are temporal things, by which he seeks to be made blessed; they will quickly be destroyed.

**“The heat of the sun.”** This is the arrival of the severe Judge, either unexpectedly at each person’s death or universally at the judgment.

In that judgment the righteous will remain like a fruitful tree.

### Verse 12

**“Blessed is the man.”** Since it is difficult to exhort people to despise the world, he adds a statement about the greatness of the reward: “Blessed is the man,” and so forth. [Col. 0672A] You must endure not only blows and prisons, but also the loss of temporal possessions, which are worthless and transient, and whose lovers will be punished.

### Verse 13

**“Let no one, when he is tempted,” and so forth.** (Bede.) Up to this point he has spoken of external temptations; now, and so forth, up to the point where he says that a person sins as though by necessity.

**“Because he is tempted by God.”** God sends external temptation for the testing of his own people; but he does not send the interior temptation by which theft, adultery, or murder is often conceived.

### Verse 14

**“Each person is tempted.”** There are two kinds of temptation. One tests, as when God tested Abraham. The other deceives, and God tempts no one in this way.

When we build wood, hay, and straw upon the foundation, the devil places fire upon it. Let us build with gold, silver, and precious stones: he will not dare to tempt us. Yet he does not desist entirely; he sits in hiding in order to kill the innocent.

**“It gives birth to death.”** Just as the person who overcomes temptation receives the rewards of life, so the person who is overcome after being enticed by desires rightly incurs the ruin of death.

### Verse 17

**“Every good gift,” and so forth.** (Bede.) After teaching that vices come to us not from God but from ourselves, and so forth, up to the point where he says that “perfect gift” may be understood.

**“Nor of alteration.”** No shadow obscures his light in such a way that he might send some evil. The things of light are always good in God, but his gifts in us are sometimes overshadowed by sins that come upon us.

[Col. 0672C] ### Verse 18

**“Of his own will.”** Every good thing is from God. You have attained it not through your merits, but solely through the grace of the divine will.

**“So that we might be a beginning,” and so forth.** Through this birth we should not think that we are what he himself is; rather, by adoption he has granted us a certain primacy among creatures. Hence another translator says: “So that we might be the firstfruits of his creatures.”

### Verse 19

**“Slow to anger.”** No one should become angry rashly or without cause—whether against sinful subjects, against any brothers, or against the prosperity of the wicked—for the maturity of wisdom is perceived only with a tranquil mind. Whoever judges while angry, even if he judges what is just, cannot imitate the justice of divine judgment, in which no disturbance has a place.

[Col. 0672D] ### Verse 21

**“Therefore, putting away,” and so forth.** He urged them to seek instruction. In order to receive it and advance in it, he now exhorts them to purity of body and soul. For whoever does not turn away from evil cannot do good.

**“The implanted word.”** This is the word that we impose upon your hearts by preaching; or, it is the word implanted and sown on the day of redemption, when God gave you birth. Now receive it more perfectly and fulfill in works what you hold in mystery.

### Verse 23

**“Considering his face.”** The person who proposes in his mind to contemplate in Scripture, as in a mirror, the face of his birth—how human beings were born, how fragile they are, what they are destined to become, how brief their life is, and in how many miseries they are placed—acquires great remorse and a desire to repent. But immediately, seduced by some temptation, he forgets his remorse and returns to sins. He compares to this instability the person who gladly hears the word but neglects to fulfill it. There is a likeness between the person who applies himself to Scripture voluntarily, without a teacher, and the person who hears Scripture from another, when neither fulfills it.

When a child is born, he cries. This indicates the soul’s pain and the fact that he enters life into the miseries of the flesh. The soul accustomed to the enticements of the flesh later forgets this pain.

### Verse 26

**“Not restraining his tongue,” and so forth.** (Augustine, *Sermon 3 to the Brothers in the Desert.) What else is verbosity? and so forth, up to the point where he says: “And you should attend carefully: Whoever does not restrain his tongue, his religion is vain,” and so forth.

### Verse 27

**“And to keep himself undefiled from this age.”** By “age” he understands the world, or everything that is in the world, such as the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life.

## Chapter II

[Col. 0673C] ### Verse 1

**“Do not.”** It is as though he said: The Lord does not invite the rich to faith while despising the poor; rather, he chose the poor in this world and endowed them with faith. The world casts out the poor and honors the rich; the faith of Christ, by contrast, teaches that all the glory of the rich is like the flower of grass, while mercy toward the poor flourishes forever.

**“Of the Lord of glory.”** He calls him the Lord of glory so that obedience may be given to his commands, since he rewards with eternal glory what is given to the poor for love of him.

### Verse 5

**“Listen.”** (Bede.) Pay closer attention, because it is not those who are richer in this age, and so forth, up to the point where he says that he nevertheless made these people distinguished and noble through their expectation of the future kingdom.

**“Has not God?”** (Bede.) God chose the poor, saying elsewhere: “Do not fear, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom.” He also chose poor parents to care for and nourish him.

### Verse 6

**“But have not the rich?”** He shows more clearly whom he had previously called rich: namely, those who prefer riches to Christ. They themselves are strangers to the faith, oppress believers through their power, and drag them before the tribunals of the powerful. This is another reason why they must not be chosen: they inflict evils upon the faithful.

### Verse 7

**“They blaspheme.”** In the time of the apostles, many Gentiles and Jews are found to have done this, especially the richer among them.

### Verse 8

**“If, nevertheless, you fulfill the law.”** Because he had spoken harshly and seemingly contemptuously about the rich, and had in a certain sense appeared contrary to the divine Law, which commands that everyone be loved, [Col. 0674A] lest the rich be thought altogether deserving of contempt, he adds: It is as though he said: They must not be chosen for the reasons stated; but if you fulfill the law that says, “You shall love your neighbor” (Matt. 22), you do well. For although the rich are not to be chosen because of their riches, they are not for that reason to be loved less for God’s sake.

**“Royal.”** That is, excellent; or because it is common to all and embraces everyone. Or it is the law that says: “You shall not show partiality to the poor, nor honor the face of the powerful” (Lev. 19), and elsewhere: “There shall be no distinction of persons; you shall hear the small as well as the great, because judgment belongs to God” (Deut. 1).

### Verse 10

**“But whoever,” and so forth.** Lest they think that transgressing the Law in this one matter is a contemptible sin, he adds: “But whoever,” and so forth.

**“But if he should offend in one thing, he has become guilty of all.”** It is truly the case that whoever offends in one matter is a transgressor of the whole Law, because whoever sins acts against the author of the Law, whom he neglects in his own law, and against charity, which is the cause and mother of the whole Law.

Let us consider this statement by analogy. If someone offended me, he would offend all my brothers and friends in offending me, and in a certain sense would sin against them all. In the same way, whoever neglects one commandment renders the other commandments—which seemed to be helping because they had been fulfilled—useless to himself.

### Verse 12

**“So speak,” and so forth.** (Bede.) Since it is evil to choose the rich because of their riches, and so forth, up to the point where he says that it calls the willing to repentance and forgives sins.

It is as though he said: Speak well and act well. If you neglect this, you will be condemned more severely than those who lived in the time of Moses, because from the one to whom more has been entrusted, more is demanded. The more mercy a person receives from the Lord, the more unjustly he denies mercy to his needy neighbor, and the more justly he pays the penalty for impiety.

### Verse 13

**“But mercy triumphs.”** (Bede.) Just as the person who has not shown mercy will grieve at the judgment, so the person who has shown mercy will rejoice and exult when rewarded.

### Verse 14

**“What good is it,” and so forth.** Here he discusses works of mercy more extensively, so that he may console those whom he had terrified in the preceding statement, teaching by what remedies daily sins—without which human life is not conducted—may be expiated. He does this so that those who offend not merely in one matter but in many may not be found guilty of all at the judgment.

[Col. 0674D] ### Verse 18

**“But someone will say.”** You ought to be stirred to good works not only for the reasons given above, but also so that you may not suffer reproach from others. Someone, confidently relying on his own works in order to show that faith alone is insufficient, will say reproachfully: “You have faith,” and so forth.

[Col. 0675A] ### Verse 19

**“You believe,” and so forth.** He has proved that those who lack works do not possess true faith. Now he discloses what sort of faith they have, so that they may not think highly of such faith.

**“The demons also believe, and tremble.”** (Bede.) It is written, and so forth, up to the point where he says that they must be considered slower and more insolent than demons.

### Verse 20

**“Do you wish to know, O empty man?”** (Bede.) Having proved that faith without works is dead, and so forth, up to the point where he says that they should imitate them in temptation and in action.

### Verse 21

**“Abraham our father,” and so forth.** (Bede.) That Abraham is said to have been justified by faith without works, and so forth, up to the point where he says that both are set forth as examples.

**“Offering his son Isaac upon the altar.”** It was a great temptation when he was commanded to kill his son; great faith when he believed that even from a dead man he could receive offspring; and a great work when he did not hesitate to offer his beloved son.

### Verse 22

**“You see that faith cooperated with his works, and by works,” and so forth.** Because he offered the one in whom he had received the promise, the great power of faith is evident. Even though he offered him, he believed that the promise would be fulfilled, because he believed that God was powerful enough to raise the dead.

[Col. 0675B] **“Likewise also Rahab the prostitute.”** (Bede.) Lest they make the excuse that they cannot imitate the works of so great a father, and so forth, up to the point where he says that she is also counted among the generations of the Savior.

## Chapter III

### Verse 1

**“Do not.”** Just as I urged you to perform works, so I urge you to avoid foolish teaching.

**“Do not become many teachers.”** In the time of the apostles there were many who came down from Judea to Antioch. Insufficiently instructed in the law of faith, they taught that Gentile converts ought to be circumcised and introduced other errors. They imposed considerable labor in debate upon the true preachers. He therefore removes such people from the ministry of the word, lest they impede [Col. 0675C] the true preachers.

**“A greater,” and so forth.** (Bede.) Whoever, being uneducated, usurps the office of teaching and does not sincerely proclaim Christ deserves greater condemnation than if he alone perished through his own crime. Conversely, whoever ministers well acquires for himself a good standing.

### Verse 2

**“In many things.”** It is truly dangerous to wish to preside over others, because not only you, who are less instructed, but all of us who preach—even those who are greater—offend in many things: some by teaching badly, others by living badly, and others in still different ways. The blessed Apostle includes himself among them so that he may rebuke more freely.

The righteous person offends in one way, the wicked in another. The righteous offend through the weakness of the flesh, yet do not cease to be righteous. Hence Solomon says: “The righteous man falls seven times and rises again.” Just as offense is daily, [Col. 0675D] so the remedy of prayers and good works is daily. But the ungodly fall into evil.

**“If anyone.”** He wishes to show that offense through speech is unavoidable, in order to deter the inexperienced from desiring authority. Whoever wishes to preside over others must be more perfect than they are, so that he may not offend when he ought to benefit them. But the inexperienced cannot avoid offending in preaching.

**“Does not offend in speech.”** (Bede.) This refers to speech whose offense human frailty can avoid: deceit, detraction, pride, boasting, and also idle and superfluous talk. Such a person is perfect.

### Verse 3

**“If we put bits into horses’ mouths.”** (Bede.) We ought much more [Col. 0676A] to put them into our own mouths.

Some books read: “But as bits to horses,” and connect this with what follows: “So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things.”

### Verse 5

**“And it boasts of great things.”** (Bede.) It raises up rewards when the one directing it guides it well; when he guides it badly, it raises up great destruction for himself and his own. Hence Solomon says: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. 18). It raises up life when it teaches the Church well, and death when it teaches badly.

He speaks against those who, lacking both life and knowledge, presumed to teach. The tongue therefore boasts of great things when, despising the words and judgments of others, it boasts that it alone is wise and eloquent. Against this it is said: “Do not multiply lofty words while boasting.”

**“See how great a fire.”** In the same way, an uncontrolled tongue causes a great store of good works to perish. Therefore, since it is almost impossible even for the perfect to avoid the sin of the tongue, not everyone should seek the office of teaching.

[Col. 0676B] ### Verse 6

**“A world of iniquity.”** He calls it a world because through it nearly all crimes are either contrived—such as robberies and sexual violations—or committed—such as perjuries and false testimonies—or defended, as when some impure person, excusing the crime he has committed, pretends to possess the goodness he has not practiced.

**“Which defiles the whole [Col. 0676C] body.”** Because the tongue is such, it defiles the whole body and causes it to be regarded as unclean in God’s sight. It is therefore a serious matter to undertake the office of teaching, because the tongue is set among our members and is one of our members, excessively close to us.

**“It sets the wheel of life on fire,” and so forth.** (Bede.) It contaminates the whole course of temporal life, and so forth, up to the point where he says that it compels the other members to bring its purpose into effect.

### Verse 7

**“For every kind of beasts,” and so forth.** (Bede.) We read in Pliny that in Egypt a very savage asp was tamed by a certain head of household, leaving its cave every day and accustomed to receive food from his table. We read in Marcellinus that a tiger was domesticated and sent from India to the emperor Anastasius.

### Verse 10

**“From the same mouth proceeds.”** Others, seeing what we do, are led by our example to bless and curse in the same way.

**“This ought not to be.”** Truly, it ought not to be that with the same mouth we bless the Head and curse the members, because the sweetness of blessing is consumed by the bitterness of cursing.

[Col. 0676D] ### Verse 11

**“Does a fountain,” and so forth.** A preacher must sometimes employ bitter preaching, withdrawing people from evil and rebuking them. It is sufficiently difficult for him to do both, using different words directed toward the same end.

### Verse 12

**“Can a fig tree, my brothers,” and so forth.** It cannot happen that a teacher should be a fig tree, possessing the sweetness of the blessedness to which he exhorts and using sweet words, while also being a vine that makes people forget all temporal things, for which harsh words must be used. This is therefore difficult.

Likewise, a salt spring cannot produce sweet water. That is, a preacher who sharply censures the conduct of others cannot, in that same teaching, be sweet to those same people.

[Col. 0677A] ### Verse 13

**“Who is wise and disciplined among you?”** Having refuted those who possess neither holiness of life nor restraint of tongue, he urges those who seemed wise—or even were wise—to show their wisdom more by living in a disciplined manner than by teaching others. Whoever is more inclined to teach than to act sometimes falls into boasting or contentiousness, or into envy of other teachers, as well as many other evils.

### Verse 14

**“And be liars against the truth.”** Do not lie to God, to whom in baptism you promised to renounce the pomps of the devil. You do not fulfill this promise when you wish to become proud of your good works.

### Verse 17

**“But the wisdom from above.”** This is the gentleness which he earlier commanded them to possess, opposed to bitter zeal and contentions.

[Col. 0677B] **“First of all pure.”** Unless purity first takes its seat in the mind, no perfection will follow in action.

**“Open to persuasion, agreeing with what is good.”** If it does something deficiently, whether through ignorance or negligence, it gives assent to the persuasion of good people.

### Verse 18

**“But the fruit.”** After distinguishing wisdom according to its individual virtues, he adds its fruit in order to invite them more easily to pursue it.

**“Is sown in peace.”** It does not seek to appear more learned or holier than it is, nor does it tear apart its neighbor to commend itself; contentious wisdom does that. Such wisdom should be desired not only for the reasons already given, but also because it is sown by those who make peace, as though they were casting this seed, and because the fruit of eternal blessedness—that is, the reward [Col. 0677C] of righteousness, which is repaid for righteous works—is prepared in peace.

Whoever therefore strives for peace here and sprinkles the soil of his heart with works of peace as with seed ought rightly to possess eternal peace as the fruit of this seed.

## Chapter IV

### Verse 1

**“From where are wars,” and so forth.** (Bede.) He had prohibited zeal and contention; therefore he discusses the matter more extensively, adding the other vices that follow from them: from contention comes desire, and from desires come wars and quarrels. Whoever desires to be preferred or to abound in temporal goods hates, envies, and kills.

### Verse 2

**“For this reason.”** Because of these things—that is, because you do not ask God worthily. If you asked him with pious intercession, he would grant you not only eternal things but also the temporal necessities of use.

### Verse 4

**“Adulterers, do you not know?”** (Bede.) He had spoken above about the manifest enemies of God, and so forth, up to the point where he says that by this they are made enemies of God.

### Verse 5

**“Or do you think?” and so forth.** You ought not to quarrel. The spirit that is in you does not desire in order to produce envy, but rather makes you harmonious. Scripture says: “The spirit that dwells in you desires unto envy.” [Col. 0677D]

Or: “The spirit desires unto”—that is, against—“envy”; it desires that envy be removed.

Or, it desires that you should envy the world and not love it.

Or, the spirit of any human being desires temporal things unto envy, because it envies others what it does not possess.

### Verse 6

**“But he gives greater grace.”** The Spirit of grace does not make people envious; rather, he gives grace—that is, free gifts—greater than the riches of this age. [Col. 0678A]

**“Therefore,”** that is, so that we may know whom he gives to and whom he does not, Scripture says: “He resists the proud but gives grace to the humble,” and so forth.

God punishes all the wicked, but he is said especially to resist the proud because they are struck with a greater punishment: they neglect to submit to God through repentance. But he gives grace to the humble, who submit themselves to the hands of the true physician in the wounds of their vices.

### Verse 11

**“He speaks evil of the Law; he judges the Law.”** The Law prohibited detraction. It is as though he said: The Law did not do this.

Or, whoever speaks evil of a brother who is fulfilling the Law also speaks evil of and judges the Law, asking why it gave such commands as require people to forget injuries done by their brothers.

### Verse 13

**“But you,” and so forth.** You must avoid detraction not only so that you may not be judged by God as a transgressor, but also because perhaps you excel in nothing over those whom you condemn.

**“Come now, you who say.”** After rebuking [Col. 0678B] detraction, he censures the rashness of those who, possessing no certainty about life, promise themselves life and profit in the future out of desire for temporal things.

**“We will spend a year there and trade,” and so forth.** He identifies the manifold folly of those who both plan an increase in profits, suppose that they will live for a long time, and consider it within their own power to spend a year there, while in all these matters refusing to recall the judgment of the heavenly Judge.

### Verse 15

**“For what is your life?” and so forth.** He does not agree with those who say that after death there is nothing, or that death itself is nothing. Rather, he speaks in such a way as to teach that the life of the wicked is brief in the present, and that eternal death will follow it in the future.

## Chapter V

[Col. 0678C] ### Verse 1

**“Come now.”** In the acceptable time and on the day of salvation, redeem future punishments through tears and almsgiving.

### Verse 3

**“And rust.”** (Bede.) Not only will visible fire of Gehenna torment the merciless rich, and so forth, up to the point where he says that they will therefore be punished more severely.

*[The supplied source ends here.]*
As a Testimony. That is, for the increase of punishments: namely, so that, by gazing visibly upon this, you may endure greater torments.

It shall eat the flesh. That is, the bodies or carnal desires; for the flame raging outwardly will torment the lustful souls, while the pain piercing inwardly will accuse them of their tenacity. Just as fire consumes metals and other things, so rust will consume your flesh.

[Col. 0678D] **VERSE 4.—Behold, the wages.** (BEDA.) Great is the wickedness of those who refuse to receive the poor; but it is greater still when they refuse to pay laborers and servants the wages due for their work. Hence Job: “If my land cries out against me, and its furrows weep? If I have eaten its fruits without payment?”

**VERSE 5.—You have feasted.** (ID.) You have sinned not only by gathering excessively, etc., up to and including the other crimes that the Jews had committed.

**VERSE 7.—Be patient.** (ID.) He rebukes the proud and unbelieving, etc., up to and including the Apostle’s words: “You have your fruit in sanctification, but the end is eternal life” (Romans 6).

**VERSE 10.—The prophets.** (ID.) The prophets, who were so holy that the Spirit of God spoke its mysteries through them, etc., up to and including what concerns the Lord in relation to the outcome of death.

**VERSE 11.—The endurance of Job.** He does not say, “the end of Job,” to whom temporal goods were restored, but “the endurance of Job.” And “the end of the Lord,” because he invites us to suffer by Job’s example, yet not so that we may receive temporal things, as Job, the old man, did, but eternal things, as Christ, the new man, did.

And the end of the Lord. (BEDA.) You heard in the reading and saw with your eyes the Lord patiently suffering on the cross; but through the Gospel proclamation you have also learned of the glory of his resurrection and ascension.

**VERSE 13.—Let him pray.** Let him not murmur or criticize God’s judgments, but let him run to the Church on bended knees, [Col. 0679B] so that God may send consolation.

**VERSE 15.—And if he is in sins.** (BEDA.) Many are punished with the death of the body even because of their sins, etc., up to and including the words that rightly follow: “Confess,” etc.

**VERSE 17.—He prayed with prayer.** He establishes by example how powerful the continual supplication of a righteous person is: Elijah, by praying only one prayer, held back the heavens for so long, kept the rains from the earth, and denied its fruits to mortals.

And again. (BEDA.) When Elijah perceived the appointed time, etc., up to and including: “Why, then, do many faithful people offer many prayers?”

**VERSE 19.—If anyone among you.** Having demonstrated the efficacy of prayer, he shows how meritorious it is to pray for one’s brothers and restore them to salvation. Thus, having removed malicious and idle speech from our tongues in the earlier part, he shows at the end of the Epistle what we ought to say. Let us pray and sing psalms whenever we are struck by adversities; let us confess our sins; let us pray for one another so that we may be saved—not only for temporal salvation, but rather for eternal salvation. For if it is a great merit to rescue from death a body that will one day die, how great a merit is it to free from death a soul that will live forever in the heavenly homeland?

**VERSE 20.—He will save.** Some manuscripts read: “He will save his soul from death.” And truly, whoever corrects one who is wandering thereby acquires for himself the greater joys of heavenly life.

[Col. 0679]

# THE FIRST EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED PETER (G)*

## Argument

[Col. 0679B]

Simon Peter, son of Jonah, of the province of Galilee, from the village of Bethsaida, brother of the Apostle Andrew, shows that the disciples of the unconquered Savior, scattered throughout the whole world and strangers in this age, should repent of their former life and advance into a new life; and he urges them with every concern.

## CHAPTER ONE

**VERSE 1.—To the resident aliens.** (BED.) In Latin *advenae*, in Greek *proselytoi*—that is, converts, etc., up to and including: “Beloved, I appeal to you as resident aliens and pilgrims.”

Of the Dispersion. In the year of the Ascension, Stephen was killed, and many were scattered through fear.

Of Pontus. All these provinces belong to the Greeks in Asia, but there is also another Bithynia in Europe; from it those Bithynians who are in Asia originated. The Bithynia that is in Asia is called Greater Phrygia, and the Hiera River separates it from Galatia.

[Col. 0679D] **VERSE 2.—Grace.** Without the grace of Christ, one never comes to the peace of his reconciliation; we can have nothing peaceful except through his grace.

And may peace be multiplied. That is, let no adversity draw you back from the praises of God; let every tribulation invite you to praise, because all things are multiplied for blessedness, so that you may complete perfectly what you have begun well.

**VERSE 3.—He regenerated us.** (BED.) Since we had been born through our merits for death, etc., up to and including: “so that through purity you may be heaven and the dwelling-place of God.”

**VERSE 4.—Incorruptible.** By nature the soul is not incorruptible; but by God’s grace, through faith and righteousness, it is perfected into incorruptibility in understanding.

In you. He who gave you believers the power to become children of God placed in you that perseverance by which you may receive an inheritance in heaven, because whoever does not keep the Father’s discipline does not deserve his inheritance.

**VERSE 5.—By power.** No one can be kept in goodness by the power of his own freedom unless the one from whom you received the beginning of good action brings it to perfection. Labor through faith and in faith, destined for eternal salvation, which, even if it is not now visible, is nevertheless prepared to be revealed if we are prepared.

**VERSE 6.—Now, if it is necessary.** “If” means “although it is necessary.” Or: if it is necessary to suffer grief, let us not fail.

**VERSE 7.—So that the testing, etc., may result in praise.** When the Judge praises your faith, he will say: “And you gave me food,” etc. (Matthew 25).

More precious than gold. (BED.) The patience of the saints is compared with gold, etc., up to and including: “so that he also adds: ‘May it be found,’” etc.

[Col. 0680D] In praise. So that through steadfastness you may be praiseworthy and glorious at the revelation—that is, on the day of judgment, when it will be revealed how great God’s power is.

And honor. So that it may be said to you: “Come, you blessed of my Father” (Matthew 25).

**VERSE 9.—The salvation of souls.** This salvation is greatly to be loved, because they earnestly sought to know when, or in what order, eternal salvation would come into the world. Hence it is said: “Many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Matthew 13).

**VERSE 10.—They prophesied.** They spoke openly to human beings and explained what they themselves had learned secretly through inward contemplation.

**VERSE 11.—Into what or what sort of time, etc.** They asked what time—that is, in what year—or under which ruler. What sort: whether warlike or peaceful; or in what manner—through the birth of a virgin, or by some other means.

The Spirit of Christ. He calls archangels and those near to him “spirits,” through whom the Lord works, because they are subject to Christ.

The later glories. There are two glorifications of the Lord according to the form of the humanity he assumed: one by which he rose from the dead, and another by which he ascended into heaven before the eyes of the Apostles. A third remains, and it will take place in the sight of human beings when he comes in majesty to repay each according to his works.

**VERSE 12.—They were ministering to you.** He says this to urge them to take care of the salvation offered to them, which the saints of earlier times loved so greatly.

By the Holy Spirit. (BEDA.) The Spirit in the prophets and the Spirit in the Apostles appear in this way: the prophets and the Apostles announce the same salvation—the former as future, the latter as fulfilled. Thus there is one Church, one part of which preceded Christ’s coming and the other follows it.

**VERSE 13.—Therefore.** Since such great grace has been promised to you, so that you may see revealed what the angels now see, take care to become all the more worthy of receiving it.

Hope. Await it confidently in mind and chastely in body. For whoever does not know how to please the Lord, rightly deprived of hope in good things, fears that their arrival may be hastened.

**VERSE 14.—Children.** So that you may safely await it, be obedient children of the Father who corrects you.

**VERSE 15.—Holy.** That is, sanctified and sanctifying you, so that you may be holy in all your conduct. Hence: “Be perfect, you also,” etc.

**VERSE 17.—In fear, etc.** (HIER.) “I, polluted by every filth of sin, wait day and night with trembling to render the final penny. And I await the time when it will be said to me, ‘Jerome, come forth.’”

Of your sojourning. So that you may be holy, conduct yourselves in fear during the time of your sojourning, as long as you are in the exile of this world. Blessed is the one who is always afraid. I say this if you call upon God—as though he were saying: You do not truly call upon God unless you are concerned and fearful.

**VERSE 19.—But with precious blood.** The order of the wording is: “but with the precious blood of Christ, as of an undefiled and immaculate lamb.” Here he touches upon the Levitical and priestly celebrations. He signifies the soul cleansed through righteousness, which is offered to God.

## CHAPTER TWO

**VERSE 1.—Therefore, laying aside all malice.** What is malice, except the love of doing harm? What is deceit, except doing one thing while pretending another? What is flattery, except seduction through deceptive praise? What is envy, except hatred of another’s happiness? What is detraction, except criticism that is more spiteful than truthful? Malice delights in another’s evil. Deceit divides the heart. Flattery the tongue. Detraction wounds reputation.

**VERSE 2.—Like newborn infants.** (BEDA.) Since you have been reborn and made children of eternity, become through the pursuit of good conduct what infants recently born according to the nature of their age are.

Rational. Be infants by removing malice, yet rational through wisdom. Let no reasoning draw you toward the cunning of the world; be without deceit. Hence: “Be wise as serpents” (Matthew 10), etc.

Desire milk. (BEDA.) He touches upon those who come reluctantly to hear sacred readings, ignorant of that thirst and hunger of which the Lord says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matthew 5). Therefore they reach the perfection and growth of salvation more slowly, by which they could be nourished with the solid food of the word—that is, learn divine mysteries or perform greater good works.

So that you may grow in it. So that, by learning well through the sacred matters of the Lord’s Incarnation, you may arrive at the contemplation of divine majesty.

**VERSE 3.—If indeed you have tasted.** (ID.) Once the malice of the heart has been cleansed in this way, desire the life-giving nourishment of Christ, if you understand how great divine sweetness is. For whoever tastes nothing of his sweetness should not be surprised if he fails to avoid defiling himself with earthly desires.

**VERSE 5.—Like living stones.** Through unbelief they are hard and senseless; but through disciplined understanding they are made alive and fitted to be joined together by charity in God’s building.

You are being built up. To offer good works, alms, prayers, and yourselves.

Through Jesus Christ. This applies to everything: you are being built up, you are priests, you offer, and all of this is through Jesus Christ, whose grace gives you everything.

**VERSE 6.—For this reason, to confirm that the Lord is rightly called a stone because of his firmness, etc.**

**VERSE 7.—Therefore, for you who believe there is honor; but for those who do not believe, etc., “the stone that the builders rejected.”** He was rejected by these people just as by those others; and that stone—here, for believers—became the cornerstone, while for unbelievers it became a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.

**VERSE 8.—And a stone of stumbling.** Since Christ is the stone on which the good rest securely and are supported, he will be a cause of stumbling for unbelievers in the present, because they do not believe in him and therefore fall from vice into vice. In the future he is a rock of offense, because their feet will strike against that stone, Christ, whom they trampled as though he were lowly, and they will fall into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

They stumble by the word. One stumbles by the word when, having heard the word, one is offended by it; one stumbles in mind when one does not believe what one has heard. He heightens their foolishness. Nor do they believe in the one in whom they have been placed: by nature human beings were made for this, to believe God and obey his will.

**VERSE 9.—But you are a chosen race.** The Apostle applies to the Gentiles who believe in Christ this testimony of praise, once given through Moses to the ancient people. Like a cornerstone, Christ united the Gentiles to the salvation that Israel had in him.

A royal priesthood. United to the body of the High Priest, they ought to hope for the kingdom and offer God sacrifices of blameless conduct.

A people of acquisition. Redeemed by the blood of Christ’s redemption, just as the people of Israel were once redeemed from Egypt by the blood of the lamb. Hence, in the following verse, he mystically recalls the ancient history and teaches that it has been specially fulfilled in one people.

You may proclaim. (BEDA.) Just as those who had been freed from Egypt sang a triumphal song to the Lord, so we, after the darkness has been dispelled and remission has been received through Christ, who leads us to the homeland of heavenly glory, ought to return worthy thanks to God for heavenly benefits.

**VERSE 10.—Who once were not a people.** (ID.) From this it is proved that he writes this Epistle to those who had come to the faith from the Gentiles. These verses are taken from the prophecy of Hosea, where the calling of the Gentiles is discussed.

**VERSE 11.—Beloved.** (ID.) Up to this point he has instructed the Church generally, etc., up to and including the statement that the freedom of a more relaxed life endures greater dangers from enticing temptations.

As resident aliens. Place your minds on earthly things all the less because you remember that you have a homeland in heaven. The reprobate have their homeland here, and they hunger after its desires; therefore they will be banished into perpetual exile, deprived of its pleasures.

**VERSE 12.—Observing your good works.** (ID.) It often happens that pagans who criticized the faith of Christians later, observing their good conduct, begin to praise Christ.

[Col. 0683C] **VERSE 13.—Therefore be subject to every human institution for God’s sake, whether to the king, etc.** So that your conduct may please everyone, do not resist any human authority, any person, or any principality to which God has willed you to be subject, because “there is no authority except from God, and whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance.” He explains the institution in its parts when he says, “whether to the king,” etc.

**VERSE 14.—As sent by him.** God often permits someone to exercise an evil tyranny, so that the wicked may be confounded and the good tested more fully.

For vengeance. (BEDA.) He says this, not because it always happens, but because he simply describes what the ruler’s action ought to be. Even if he condemns the good, what he does nevertheless contributes to their praise if the good patiently endure his wickedness and wisely resist his cunning.

**VERSE 15.—But the praise of the good.** Since this is so, the godly truly receive praise whatever rulers may do, because this is God’s will; he even uses the wicked for good. Therefore you too should use them for good, whether they are good or evil, causing the ignorance of foolish people to fall silent. Use them for good in whatever way you can, and merit praise through them; nor will they themselves find anything in you to criticize, while you honor and endure even them, although they are impure.

**VERSE 16.—Not as a covering.** (BEDA.) Do not use your freedom as a covering for malice, etc., up to and including: “Hence he adds: ‘But as servants of God.’”

**VERSE 17.—Love the brotherhood.** (ID.) Among all others, love even those who are subject to you in temporal condition as brothers in Christ.

**VERSE 18.—Servants, be subject.** Up to this point he has urged free people to submission; now he speaks to servants, so that they too may be subject to their masters.

Not only to the good. Another translation has: “Not only to the good and moderate, but also to the more difficult.”

To the harsh. That is, to the undisciplined. *Schola* is Greek; in Latin, “a place” where people gathered to hear teachers of the liberal arts. Hence *schola* is interpreted as “leisure,” because there they devoted themselves to studies. The *scholastici*, therefore, are educated people. The harsh are unlearned and rustic. See how above he urged submission to every human institution for God’s sake.

**VERSE 19.—If because of consciousness of God.** If, for the sake of God, who knows the good intention, someone is unjustly beaten by his master while serving him well and enduring—that is, considering his sorrows light—this is grace; by it he becomes pleasing to God, and this is demanded by the grace of faith.

Suffering unjustly. If you suffer unjustly, you acquire God’s grace. For if you patiently endure punishments inflicted by masters—though I mean that you sin by refusing to obey them and are struck by those same masters, that is, frequently corrected by them so that through blows you may be brought to obedience—what grace will you receive from this? None; for this reason you will receive nothing from God.

**VERSE 21.—For you were called to this.** He greatly dignifies the condition of servants, affirming that those who do good and are beaten without fault by cruel and wicked masters are imitators of the Lord’s passion.

Because Christ also. (BEDA.) Having addressed servants specifically above, he now instructs the whole Church, recalling to masters what its author endured for their salvation or liberation.

**VERSE 23.—But while they judged unjustly, he handed himself over.** They judged according to an unjust law, although he was righteous. Or: he entrusted to God the Father those who judged unjustly—that is, those who most wickedly condemned him and pressed for his death—so that, by receiving punishment, they might be corrected. He touches upon the Gospel parable in which it is said that the merciful shepherd, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the desert, came to visit the one that had perished.

[Col. 0684D] **VERSE 25.—And bishop.** Or “visitor,” which is the same thing. For a bishop is an overseer, because “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers.” And: “He visited us, the dawn from on high.”

## CHAPTER THREE

**VERSE 3.—Whose adornment should not be.** The order of the words is this: “Their adornment should not be hair-braiding, or gold surrounding them, nor should it be the adornment of clothing”—that is, festive garments in which they dress. Rather, let your adornment be the person of the heart within, known to God alone, in the incorruptibility of the spirit. I mean a spirit at rest from the assault of vices and modest, so that it does not become proud. Although such a spirit is not evident to human beings, it is nevertheless rich in the sight of God.

[Col. 0685A] **VERSE 7.—Husbands.** It is as though he were saying: Just as I commanded wives, through their holy conduct, to win their husbands and serve them, so likewise I command you, husbands, to win the women through your conduct and to care for them—you, I mean, living with them and rendering what is owed. Do this with understanding, not in the passions of desire, but as we understand God’s will: namely, that you beget children for the worship of the one God. I mean that you should show honor to the female vessel as the weaker one, providing them with clothing and other necessities; and if at times they wish to abstain from intercourse, show them honor, because they are weaker.

Show them honor also as co-heirs of the grace given in the present and of the life to be given in the future—or of the life to be given as a reward for grace.

[Col. 0685B] **VERSE 9.—Not returning.** Do not merely refrain from returning evil for evil; instead, give a blessing in return for a curse.

Because to this. (BEDA.) Since he had forbidden returning evil for evil, etc., up to and including the statement that we too will receive a crown for their salvation, which we prayed for.

So that you may inherit a blessing. When the Judge says: “Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom” (Matthew 25). Or “blessing” may be understood as the blessing by which the saints will bless God in the future life. Therefore, whatever each person desires to receive in the future, let him strive to contemplate and do this in the present: let him bless the Creator and his brother, and make himself worthy of a brother’s blessing.

**VERSE 13.—And who is he?** (BEDA.) You ought to turn away from evil and do good because no one can draw you away from goodness or from the crown if you wish to persevere; indeed, they benefit you while intending to harm you.

**VERSE 14.—But do not fear their fear.** In the future you will be blessed; in the present, do not fear their fear—that is, those things in them that may appear fearful, such as royal power and similar matters.

**VERSE 15.—But sanctify the Lord.** Behold the holiness of Christ; contemplate inwardly with the affection of your heart how incomprehensible his glory is, and thus sanctify Christ himself within you, so that he may depart neither from your memory nor from your love. Whoever does not consider this holiness falls before the enemy’s snares.

To everyone who asks. Let us not refuse those who wish to receive a reasonable account. Hence Paul says: “Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, knowing how it is necessary to answer each person.” Those who are outside—that is, not yet believers—wish to learn something about the hope that is in you. Therefore, whoever presides over ecclesiastical teaching should instruct those who are patient and silence those who resist.

[Col. 0685D] **VERSE 16.—But with modesty.** In the very knowledge of teaching he urges that the manner of teaching be observed, so that humility may be shown both in life and in speech.

**VERSE 17.—It is better.** (BEDA.) Thus you ought to endure and confound your accusers, etc., up to and including the statement that he is removed and prepared for eternal punishment.

**VERSE 18.—That he might offer himself to God.** (ID.) For even then, if any wished to believe in the Lord’s preaching—which he displayed through the life of the faithful—he rejoiced to offer them to God the Father. But if any reviled the good as though they were evildoers, they were confounded when the flood approached.

**VERSE 19.—In prison.** (ID.) Those whose understanding has been darkened by darkness are rightly said even in this life to be confined in prison; in this inner prison of the mind they are burdened by unjust works until, released from the flesh, they are cast into the outer darkness of eternal condemnation. The righteous also have a prison here, but it is one of tribulations; the reprobate have one of vices.

**VERSE 20.—When they were awaiting God’s patience.** God’s patience invited them to repentance, sparing them for the hundred years during which Noah built the ark, through which it was shown what would happen in the world. They therefore did not use God’s patience for repentance, but waited for it as though it would last forever.

Noah. Noah is interpreted as “rest,” and signifies Christ, who gives rest to the souls of his faithful.

When the ark was being built. (BEDA.) Just as the ark was constructed from smoothed wood, so the Church is constructed from the gathering of faithful souls. And just as, when the world perished, a few were saved through water, so, in comparison with those who perish, the number of the elect is small, because narrow is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it.

**VERSE 21.—Which also saves you in a corresponding form.** Baptism saves; I mean baptism corresponding in form, that is, entirely assimilated to that ark, because whatever happened there carnally happens here spiritually.

Not the removal of the filth of the flesh, etc. I do not mean that baptism saves where there is only the removal of the filth of the flesh—that is, where the flesh alone is washed externally, as the heretics had—but where there is the appeal of a pure conscience: that is, where the baptized person’s good conscience is questioned and required by the baptizer. Such baptism saves; the other kills. The appeal is directed toward God, so that through a good conscience one may become united with God.

**VERSE 22.—Swallowing up death.** (BEDA.) What we swallow, we cause to be taken into our bodies so that it nowhere appears again. In this way the Lord utterly consumed death, so that it had no power against him; while the appearance of a true body remained, the former stain of frailty was absent. This is also promised to us, as he adds, so that we too might be made heirs of eternal life.

Angels being subjected to him. We do not doubt that the angels were always subject to the Son of God; but here he mentions their subjection in order to show that the humanity he assumed was so exalted in the resurrection that it was placed above the power of every angelic dignity. Hence: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet” (Psalm 8).

## CHAPTER FOUR

**VERSE 1.—Since the one who suffered.** (BEDA.) Whoever extinguishes carnal desires in the mind through fear of heavenly judgments is already like Christ crucified, as one dead to sins. He lives only for the service of God.

**VERSE 4.—Blaspheming.** (ID.) Even if they blaspheme you because you have separated yourselves from their unbelief, nevertheless, seeing works of righteousness and piety in your conduct, they marvel and in some way revere the faith.

**VERSE 6.—For this reason the Gospel was preached even to the dead.** (BEDA.) God takes such care that we be put to death in the flesh, etc., up to and including the statement that their judgment condemns the evil in the ungodly.

**VERSE 7.—Of all things.** Since he had said that the living and the dead would be judged in the judgment, lest anyone flatter himself because of the remoteness of the future judgment, he prudently warns that, although the time of the final crisis is uncertain, it is nevertheless certain for everyone that we cannot remain long in this life.

Be watchful in prayers. (BEDA.) Let the mind think of nothing except what it is praying for. When we stand to pray, let every carnal thought withdraw; let the sincere intention of the heart pray to God not through the sound of the voice but through the mind’s understanding.

**VERSE 8.—Having continual charity.** (ID.) Whoever admonishes and rebukes his neighbor through charity, etc., up to and including the statement that charity, although it is not always displayed publicly, can nevertheless do this.

**VERSE 11.—If anyone speaks.** If anyone possesses the knowledge of speaking, let him attribute it not to himself but to God. Let him fear teaching his brother contrary to God’s will, the authority of the Holy Scriptures, or usefulness; nor should he remain silent about what ought to be said.

If anyone ministers. (BEDA.) When you have done everything well and according to his will, attribute it not to your own merits but to his grace, so that others, seeing your good works, may glorify your Father who is in heaven.

**VERSE 12.—Beloved, do not be surprised.** If you suffer the heat of tribulations inflicted irrationally for your testing and glory, do not therefore think yourselves exiles from the members of Christ. Do not marvel at the evils inflicted, so that through them God may test and prove you, because it is ancient and customary for God’s elect to suffer adversity in the present for eternal salvation.

**VERSE 14.—You will be blessed, etc.** Whoever suffers for Christ’s name is blessed. You must not believe that you suffer without reward, like those who suffer for their own crimes and are punished unwillingly.

His Spirit rests upon you. Because it will rest upon you who suffer: in the present, partly for good works, and in the future, perfectly for reward.

[Col. 0687D] **VERSE 17.—For the time has come, etc.** (BEDA.) Therefore one must suffer for Christ’s name, etc., up to and including: “But the reprobate now spend their days in their own goods, and in a moment they will descend into hell” (Job 21).

**VERSE 18.—And if the righteous, etc.** (ID.) This is taken from Proverbs according to the Old Edition. In our edition, which follows the Hebrew truth, it reads as follows: “If the righteous receives recompense on earth, how much more the ungodly and the sinner?” That is, if mortal life is so frail that even the righteous—who will be crowned in heaven—do not pass through it without tribulations because of the innumerable stain of corrupted nature, how much more do those who have no share in heavenly glory await the certain outcome of their perpetual condemnation?

[Col. 0688A] (AUG.) You ask why the righteous can scarcely be saved in God’s judgment. Why, except because it is certain that God’s justice is so great that sometimes what appears just to us in human beings is found unjust in God’s judgment, according to the saying: “Man looks at the face, but God looks into the heart” (1 Samuel 16).

(BEDA.) It is not difficult for God to free the righteous; but, in order to show that the whole of human nature has justly been condemned, God himself does not wish to free it easily from so great an evil. Hence sins are easy and righteousness laborious—except for those who love it. But the charity that makes people lovers comes from God.

**VERSE 19.—Let them commend their souls, etc.** Since judgment begins from the house of the Lord, and it is necessary to enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations, this remains for those who are going to suffer: when they suffer according to God’s will—that is, on account of righteousness—let them commend their souls to God, presuming nothing about themselves, so that he may cleanse them here according to his will and glorify them in the future, because he is faithful in giving good things to those whom he created. I mean that they suffer while doing good, not because of sins.

## CHAPTER FIVE

**VERSE 1.—The elders.** Having previously instructed free people and servants, men and women, separately, and having inserted a general exhortation, he now addresses the old and the young.

**VERSE 2.—Not under compulsion.** Do not preach the Gospel so that you may live from the Gospel, but willingly according to God—that is, solely with regard to the heavenly reward.

**VERSE 5.—Likewise, young men.** (BEDA.) After explaining how the elders should preside, etc., up to and including the following general admonition:

“But all of you, show humility toward one another: the elders by teaching, and the young by following.”

**VERSE 6.—Humble yourselves.** (BEDA.) What grace God confers upon the humble, etc., up to and including the fitting reward of exaltation that follows.

**VERSE 8.—Like a roaring lion, etc.** Just as a lion’s roar blocks the ears so that they do not receive another sound, so the devil, terrifying the minds of the faithful and suggesting unlawful things, turns them away from the way of truth so that they do not hear Christ’s voice.

**VERSE 9.—Knowing.** (BEDA.) Have all the greater confidence, etc., up to and including: “Let you be ashamed to be the only ones among all who are unable to suffer.”

[Col. 0688D] **VERSE 12.—I have written.** “I have written to you,” he says, “not as one commanding, but as one entreating and testifying by the authority of the Scriptures that this is the true grace that I proclaim by writing, because there is salvation in no other, by whom you must be saved.” Or: “I entreat you to make the grace in which you stand and with which you have been instructed your true grace, and to hold fast to it as something that benefits you.” Whoever despises grace does not diminish grace, but makes this grace—not his own, that is, not useful to himself.

**VERSE 13.—In Babylon.** (BED.) He calls Rome Babylon because of the confusion of its manifold idolatry, etc., up to and including the statement that it cannot be free from the devil’s oppression.

[Col. 0689]

# THE SECOND EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED PETER (G)*

## Argument

[Col. 0689A]

Simon Peter declares that the wise are dead to this world through faith, and makes clearer than daylight to those same people how great the magnitude of piety is.

## CHAPTER ONE

**VERSE 1.—Simon.** (BEDA.) He writes this Epistle to the same people to whom he wrote the first, etc., up to and including the statement that they did not yield and should not yield to heretics.

A servant and Apostle. The identity of the writer is commended.

Equal. (BEDA.) He recognizes them as equal to himself, not on account of circumcision, but because they had received the same grace and faith of Christ that he had received, and exercised it through works.

In righteousness. Human prudence did not discover this righteousness, nor did the institution of the Law teach it; rather, our Savior displayed it in the Gospel: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5).

**VERSE 2.—Grace to you.** (BEDA.) In the First Epistle he wrote, “May it be multiplied”; in this one, “May it be fulfilled,” because he writes the former to beginners and the latter to those who are more perfect. Grace is multiplied for those who progress well in this life through faith; it will be fulfilled for those who arrive in the other life through vision. Hence he adds, “in the knowledge of God,” that is, so that we may know the one true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent.

**VERSE 3.—How all things.** (ID.) Thus the grace of Christ may be fulfilled, etc., up to and including the statement that he restored the weak and inglorious by his power and glory.

[Col. 0689C] **VERSE 4.—He has given us the greatest and precious promises.** That is, eternal life, which we attain through knowledge of him. Or, he has given us what he promised concerning the conversion of others through us, or concerning the coming of the Holy Spirit, or concerning the power of miracles.

**VERSE 5.—Minister in faith.** (BEDA.) Do not merely flee the desire of the world, etc., up to and including: “so that you may not be soft and dissolute.”

**VERSE 6.—And in knowledge, self-control.** (ID.) Once you have learned to do good, immediately abstain from evil in hope of eternal life, both in thought and in action, lest knowledge of heavenly things prove fruitless if someone does not restrain himself from the world’s enticements.

**VERSE 7.—And in piety.** (ID.) Do not bestow works of piety upon your adversaries with regard to anything other than fraternal love: pray for them so that they may be converted, although they refuse conversion through your teaching or rebukes.

**VERSE 8.—For if these things are with you, etc.** Therefore hold to these things and minister them to others, because if all these things are present in you in the affection of your heart and even abound—that is, if they prevail against the battles of vices—they will not make you empty of virtues in this age or without fruit in the future.

[Col. 0690A] **VERSE 9.—He is blind and gropes with his hand.** (BEDA.) The eye signifies knowledge and the hand action, etc., up to and including: “He could not foresee it and fell into it.”

Receiving forgetfulness. When a person falls from sin into sin, he appears to have forgotten the covenant he made with God in baptism.
