Namely, all the mysteries of the Church have been revealed to everyone who wishes to enter, but these people, through their own evil merit, cannot understand them.

“The temple was opened,” that is, the mysteries of the Church were revealed. In it God dwells, and in it they serve God’s honor.

**VERSE 6.**—“And they came out.” And because these things had been so opened, preachers will come forth and rebuke those who act wickedly.

**VERSE 7.**—“And one.” What they preach they will possess from the instruction of the fathers who came before them. They are all called “one” because they teach one thing. “Of wrath,” that is, of anger: for they correct and rebuke, threaten sinners with God’s anger, and sometimes even excommunicate them.

**VERSE 18.**—“Smoke from the majesty,” etc. Although at that time everything will be so open to the faithful, it will nevertheless be closed and obscure to unbelievers [Col. 0737D]. “To enter,” that is, to understand that hidden judgment of God—why he chose some and rejected others—until the saints recognize it openly at the end of the world. Or, in the meantime, “to enter” means to enter the Church until the complete condemnation of the wicked has taken place in the judgment, since afterward it is certain that they will not enter.

## CHAPTER XVI

**VERSE 2.**—“A wound.” Disobedience is the reason why that wound is inflicted.

**VERSE 3.**—“And it became blood.” That is, their condemnation was inflicted because of the blood they shed. “Blood,” that is, that condemnation will be like the condition of the dead, namely, irrevocable. For just as the dead person does not return to life, so that sentence of condemnation will not be revoked [Col. 0738A]. “Every living soul.” All who consent with them, who seem to live—not because they openly persecute, but because of their consent—will be condemned.

**VERSE 4.**—“Upon the rivers,” etc. Because these people likewise will be condemned for the blood they shed, whether bodily or spiritually.

**VERSE 5.**—“I heard.” That is, I understood that the preachers who will carry out this vengeance attribute it not to themselves but to the Lord, and affirm that it is justly done. “Who are and who were.” He does not add “who will come,” because he understood that his coming was near.

**VERSE 6.**—“And you gave them blood to drink.” That is, eternal punishment for the shedding of blood, in the shedding of which they took delight and thereby earned it.

**VERSE 7.**—“And I heard.” What the teachers say, the disciples confirm. “Indeed, Lord God almighty,” etc. Out of great devotion they turn their speech toward God. “Just.” For it is just that whoever shed blood should drink the vengeance of blood.

**VERSE 9.**—“And they were scorched.” Or, while afflicted, they will affect their tormentors with the heat of anger when they are found inseparable; and thus they burned with envy and anger. “Nor did they repent.” Within, they grieved in repentance; outwardly, they did not dare to confess.

**VERSE 10.**—“Upon the throne of the beast.” He says this because these are bodies only, and not spirits. He will sit upon them because he will give them bodily things, not spiritual ones. “They gnawed,” etc. They will all feed themselves through mutual slander.

**VERSE 12.**—“That its way might be prepared.” When the world has ended, there will be the resurrection of the faithful, who will come from the rising of the sun, that is, from Christ, when he begins to shine, that is, to reveal himself [Col. 0738C].

**VERSE 13.**—“I saw.” He saw the bowl poured out upon these people and saw that they were not corrected but driven into greater blindness. “Spirits going out.” That is, all the ungodly, who because of their excessive wickedness are to be called unclean spirits; or the demons themselves, whom they generate in the hearts of others. For just as the faithful, through their teaching, generate faith in Christ in the hearts of others, so these people generate the devil through their wickedness. “Of frogs.” Frogs dwell in mud, are noisy, and deprive others of rest; so do these people.

**VERSE 14.**—“They go forth,” etc. The demons go forth, and the devil will gather them, because they are all one.

**VERSE 16.**—“And he will gather them.” That is, they will make them place their confidence in Antichrist, who is a refuge for all who wish to steal the saints’ faith from them; or to whom all the wicked of the various sects will boast of belonging [Col. 0738D].

**VERSE 17.**—“And the seventh angel.” Having shown over whom the angels pour out their bowls, he adds what happens to those wicked people through this pouring out: namely, that here they will resist as much as they can, as though they had received strength from the very infusion, but at last they will be thrust into hell.

**VERSE 18.**—“And the city became.” Because of this condemnation and because of the sins they themselves add, the city itself was condemned, and punishment was divided among each according to merit—namely, among Jews, Gentiles, and false Christians. “The cities of the nations fell,” that is, all gatherings of the wicked who remain in the first generation will be condemned: in the carnal generation, not in the second, spiritual regeneration [Col. 0739A].

**VERSE 19.**—“It came into remembrance.” That is, God remembered each of their sins, of which he had previously seemed forgetful. “To give her the cup.” So that God himself might give them punishment measured according to the pleasures they had enjoyed. God repays the wicked according to their merits, that is, what they deserved, but not as much as they deserved, so that in the very retribution, where justice is evident, mercy may also be present. For “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.” He also gives the good according to their merits and more than they deserved, so that mercy there may prevail over justice [Col. 0739B].

**VERSE 20.**—“And every island fled.” He saw that all who, afflicted for God in the world and distinguished by virtues, had avoided the company of the wicked during their life in view of these punishments, and therefore were not found among their punishments.

**VERSE 21.**—“A talent.” There are three kinds of talent: the great, of one hundred and twenty pounds; the middle, of seventy-two; and the small, of fifty. Here he speaks of the middle one, because sinners will not escape this vengeance in the seventy-two languages.

“And they blasphemed.” That is, although placed in hell and knowing that they are being punished according to merit, they will nevertheless grieve that God possesses such power that he can inflict plagues upon them; and this is blasphemy.

## CHAPTER XVII

**VERSE 1.**—“And one came,” etc. Having described the plagues that preachers will inflict in the time of Antichrist and the eternal condemnation that the wicked themselves will suffer, he urges attention to the causes of that condemnation. As though he were saying: I have shown you what will happen in that future time; now beware, you who are powerful, because the same devil who will then deceive so openly deceives secretly every day and will lead you to the same destruction as he will lead them.

“Angels.” Here the angel takes the role of a teacher, while John takes the role of a learner. “I will show you the condemnation,” that is, the cause of the condemnation of the wicked, who, having abandoned the Creator, fornicate with the demon by worshiping idols, loving earthly things, and serving uncleanness [Col. 0739D].

“Of the harlot.” This great harlot is Antichrist and the wicked who will exist in his time. She already sits upon the waters, that is, already reigns over wicked and powerful people, whose head he is. “Who sits upon many waters,” that is, who reigns over many peoples whom she draws to herself through lust.

Thus the Lord says to Job: “His strength” (Job XL), namely, the devil’s, is “in the loins,” when he deceives men, whose seed is in the loins; “in the navel,” when he deceives women, whose seed is in the navel. Hence the Prophet (Ezek. XVI) speaks to Jerusalem as to a harlot: “On the day of your birth,” that is, in this age of the world, “your navel was not cut off,” that is, you did not restrain your lust [Col. 0740A].

**VERSE 2.**—“They became drunk,” etc. Just as a drunk person fears nothing, so those who cling to earthly things will be so blinded by love of the earth that they will neither love God nor fear punishments.

**VERSE 3.**—“A woman sitting.” That is, those effeminate people who conform themselves to Eve, from whom sin began. They have the devil as their foundation, who is bloodstained both in himself and in his own; or because they shed the blood of the saints and misunderstand the words of God.

“Seven heads.” The five bodily senses, followed by error, and finally Antichrist: through these seven the devil leads human beings to sin.

“Ten horns.” That is, the ten kingdoms that will exist in the time of Antichrist, through which other things are signified.

**VERSE 4.**—“Surrounded with purple.” That is, with royal clothing: they will claim to be kings in order to deceive [Col. 0740B]. “With gold.” Because they will appear to be enlightened by divine wisdom. “A golden cup,” that is, divine Scripture, from which the faithful drink for salvation. “Abomination.” That is, things which, according to those interpretations, ought to be rejected by human beings because they teach bodily uncleanness and fornication against God.

**VERSE 5.**—“And upon her forehead.” Although she is so well suited to deceive, nevertheless, faithful people, do not despair: she has upon her forehead, that is, openly, a sign which is a mystery to the uneducated. Through it she gives an example of committing sins, on account of which earthly people will be driven away from the salvation of the faithful.

**VERSE 6.**—“Drunk.” That is, weighed down by the vengeance for the shedding of blood, so that because of her excessive sufferings she does not know where she is. “And I was astonished.” Here John represents those who, when they see the wicked exalted in the world, are astonished when they hear of the punishments promised to those wicked people, and ask why God permits them to be exalted when they are destined to be punished in this way. But they are taught to understand that this exaltation was granted for their greater blinding, and that eternal condemnation will finally be justly inflicted [Col. 0740C].

**VERSE 7.**—“I will tell you.” That is, why these wicked people—and the devil who caused them to sin—are punished; this is unknown except to the learned.

**VERSE 8.**—“The beast that carries her.” The beast, that is, the devil, carries—that is, rules—the woman, that is, all wicked and effeminate people. For whoever rules others is said, as it were, to carry the burden of rule.

“He was.” Before Christ’s coming, the devil possessed the greatest power; but afterward, although he did not lose it entirely, he possesses it in a considerably weakened form [Col. 0740D]. “He is about to ascend.” In the time of Antichrist he will receive power again, for through those who are in the depths of sin he will ascend into exaltation. “And he will go into destruction.” When Antichrist has died, he will no longer have a place from which to tempt.

“They will marvel.” When the wicked see their power so completely destroyed, they will grieve—not as repentant people, but merely in astonishment. “Seven heads.” Through these seven the devil raises human beings to pride, and unbelievers rely upon them.

**VERSE 10.**—“Five have fallen.” If Adam had persevered in obedience, the bodily senses would not have been turned toward any pleasure, certainly not toward evil pleasure. But through sin they were so corrupted that it is now natural to seek things smooth to the touch, tasty to the palate, fragrant to the nose, and beautiful to the sight [Col. 0741A].

These are the five kings through whom the devil rules in childhood, because he himself was the cause of their corruption. These are the five husbands of the Samaritan woman.

In youth, error follows. Once a person possesses discernment, if he sins, the fault is attributed not to the senses but to error. Concerning this the Lord says: “The one whom you now have is not your husband” (John IV).

**VERSE 11.**—“He is of the seven.” Because he sins in the same way and will be punished in the same way; and he is himself the eighth, because he surpasses all others both in wickedness and in punishment.

**VERSE 15.**—“They are peoples,” etc., that is, the wicked of the present, gathered from every diversity of human beings.

**VERSE 16.**—“They will make her desolate.” The destruction of the wicked is the devil’s consolation; he will destroy them when the number of the ungodly has been completed. “And naked.” The devil has the power to perform signs in order to deceive; he will lose this power when the number of the good has been completed, because afterward temptation will have no place.

“Flesh.” The flesh of the harlot is said to be eaten because they will take delight in inflicting punishments.

“With fire they will burn.” That is, they will be tormented because of the pleasures of the harlot that they followed.

**VERSE 17.**—“Until the words are fulfilled.” This refers to the promise of rewards or punishments.

## CHAPTER XVIII

**VERSE 1.**—“And after these things I saw.” In this sixth vision he deals with the final punishments that the wicked will suffer in hell for their individual sins. First he speaks of Babylon, afterward of the beast and the false prophets, and finally of the devil himself, in whom the end becomes apparent: when he is condemned, the end will have come. As he is about to pursue this condemnation, he says that it was also preached by Christ, so that it may receive greater credence [Col. 0741C].

**VERSE 2.**—“Fallen, fallen.” This is said twice because of the twofold condemnation of soul and body, or because she will be punished eternally. “A dwelling-place of every unclean spirit.” The demons are unclean in wicked hearts because of the enticements of the flesh; through the arrogance of the mind they are birds, or because they roam through this air.

**VERSE 3.**—“From the power.” That is, from the sins through which riches are acquired, because every rich person is either wicked or the heir of a wicked person.

**VERSE 4.**—“And I heard.” Having declared that this condemnation was destined for the future, he adds an admonition for those living in the present. “Come out,” because little time remains, after which they will receive their reward according to merit [Col. 0741D].

**VERSE 5.**—“For her sins have reached,” etc. Sins reach as far as contempt of God through impenitence.

**VERSE 6.**—“Repay her.” Just as she exercised my vengeance against you who are being purified, so you should avenge my injury upon her. “Repay her double double,” that is, inflict upon soul and body greater punishments than she inflicted upon you.

**VERSE 7.**—“As much as she glorified herself,” etc. This is rightly said, because some receive more and others less. To explain the reason for this distinction, he repeats what he said above. “And she says, ‘I am not a widow.’” Because she has consolation in temporal things [Col. 0742A].

**VERSE 8.**—“Death.” The absence of life, that is, of God, because his presence is life.

**VERSE 9.**—“And they will weep.” Others, however, will have perpetual joy. “The kings of the earth.” Even those who ruled their earthly realm well; but because at some time they fornicated with this woman, they will grieve that they were never like them. “When they see the smoke of her burning,” that is, when riches have failed, which is a sign of the eternal fire of judgment; or when they see the punishment raised beyond measure.

**VERSE 11.**—“And the merchants of the earth will weep.” Because they will grieve over the loss of those things in which they had placed their prosperity [Col. 0742B].

**VERSE 12.**—“Gold and silver,” etc. Gold signifies wisdom; silver, divine words. Christ is signified by the precious stone; the apostles by pearls; by white linen, the justifications of the saints; by purple, martyrdom; by silk, virginity; by scarlet, charity; by imperishable thyine wood, unfailing constancy; by ivory, the beauty of virtues; by bronze, strength and long-suffering; by iron, the sharpness of exaltation; and by marble, unconquered humility.

**VERSE 13.**—“Cinnamon.” In cinnamon, the fragrance of the virtues they feign is to be understood. “Fine flour and wheat,” that is, the flesh of Christ, by which the faithful are truly satisfied and the reprobate are provoked.

“Of slaves and souls.” He distinguishes them because some become slaves only in body, as Joseph did; others also in mind, as when an Egyptian is sold to a Jew and circumcises himself according to their custom, or worships the idols of the pagans [Col. 0742C].

**VERSE 20.**—“Rejoice over her.” After predicting that this condemnation would come upon the wicked, he urges the good to rejoice, so that they may agree with the divine judgment; or because, once these people have been condemned, the reward of the good follows.

**VERSE 21.**—“And he lifted up.” God raises up the wicked so that he may punish them more severely, or so that they may fall. “A stone like a millstone.” Literally, all these things were also seen. “With this force.” After the individual punishments have been described, the manner of condemnation is shown, as though he were saying: What I saw foretold, I also saw already fulfilled, as you see in this figure; or: the more greatly they were exalted, the more grievously they will fall.

## CHAPTER XIX

**VERSE 1.**—“After these things I heard.” That is, I saw the condemnation of the wicked completed, just as I had heard from Christ that it would be completed. He now adds that the saints rejoice over this condemnation, just as they had been instructed to rejoice in the verse: “Rejoice over her, heavens.” Through this, the much greater punishment of the wicked is understood.

“Hallelujah,” etc. We say “hallelujah” because it is praise of our God; and because he has done such things for us, we ought to praise him by antonomasia.

**VERSE 4.**—“And the elders fell,” etc. Not only the lesser saints praised God for this condemnation, but also those greater ones who had been judges and teachers of others in the Church [Col. 0743A]. “Amen.” God is to be praised especially for this: that he punishes our enemies in this way.

**VERSE 5.**—“And a voice,” etc. After the condemnation of the wicked and the rejoicing of the saints, he adds an admonition for those living now, as though saying: You have seen the rejoicing; now take care for yourselves, for your salvation. “Little ones.” Those who cannot penetrate higher mysteries or fulfill God’s purpose—“Sell everything and follow me”—are understood by the name “little ones.”

**VERSE 6.**—“And I heard something like the voice,” etc. Having shown the joy that the saints had over the destruction of the wicked, he adds another joy that they will have over their own salvation, which he is about to describe.

**VERSE 7.**—“And his wife,” etc. It is fitting that the Church should be joined to Christ, because the Church herself has made herself fit to be received [Col. 0743B].

**VERSE 10.**—“And I fell,” etc. Because I understood him to be greater than I and was ready to obey him, so you also obey me. “See that you do not do this.” In the Old Law he did not forbid himself to be worshiped; but after the Ascension, seeing a human being exalted above him, he feared being worshiped by a human being.

“For the testimony,” etc. Whatever the prophets said bears witness to Christ.

**VERSE 11.**—“And I saw heaven opened.” Having described the condemnation of Babylon and the rejoicing that the saints will have over it, he adds the condemnation of Antichrist himself and his apostles, expressed in the words: “And the beast was seized.” Why will these people be condemned? Because they fought against Christ as much as they could. Yet Christ will be able to conquer, since he possesses such power according to both his divinity and his humanity that no one can resist him; therefore we ought to imitate him.

Hence he also inserts an admonition: “And I saw one angel.” I saw those who were called to the wedding; I also saw those who are able to come. For they have a good helper and good admonishers. “A white horse,” that is, the flesh of Christ carrying the Word of God into battle against the devil.

**VERSE 12.**—“Like a flame for the woods.” Because it burns away vices, kindles, and illumines. All these things are said without reference to any particular person, so that we may note only what he is like and how great his power may be.

**VERSE 13.**—“The Word of God.” That is: “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. XXXII). Through him the Father made all things, and through him the Father announced himself to the world [Col. 0743D].

**VERSE 14.**—“Clothed in white and clean linen.” That is, in clean bodies, restraining themselves from illicit things and being urged toward good deeds—namely, toward righteousness—by the stimulus of charity.

**VERSE 15.**—“A sword sharp on both sides.” That is, the divine sentence, cutting through the wicked thoughts of the mind and the illicit movements of the body; or the Old and New Testaments. “He will rule them.” He will advance the saints from virtue to virtue, while allowing the wicked to slip from vice into vice.

**VERSE 16.**—“And he has upon his garment.” Or, in the hearts of the faithful, who are the Son’s garment, it is written: “King of kings.”

**VERSE 17.**—“And I saw one angel.” Having shown Christ’s dignity, by which he will be able to conquer the devil, he adds an admonition concerning the present, as though saying: You ought to cling to one such as this. “To all the birds.” To all the faithful who are agile and swift in advancing good works. “Come,” etc. Come by doing good works, in the same faith, not following various heresies as the wicked do; or: come to me from the various regions of the world.

“And be gathered.” As though saying: You ought to be very concerned to be able to come to this banquet, because unless you fight well, you will succumb to the devil. He is exceedingly ready to harm you, yet with God’s help you will be able to overcome him.

**VERSE 20.**—“These two were cast alive.” Namely, Antichrist and his chief apostles will suffer greater punishments than the others, like one who is burned alive [Col. 0744B].

**VERSE 21.**—“And the rest were slain.” That is, their followers will be punished with a lesser penalty; or the others, if they are converted to him, will die to the world and live to God. “And all the birds,” that is, all the saints, took delight in their punishment and in the advancement of their brothers.

## CHAPTER XX

**VERSE 1.**—“And I saw an angel.” Having stated the condemnation of Babylon, Antichrist, and the pseudo-apostles, he adds the condemnation of the devil himself. He first gives the reason why, and the time when, he will be condemned; and who will be able to conquer him: namely, he who in his humble coming was able to bind him as much as he wished will, when glorified, be able to destroy that same enemy altogether.

“Of the abyss.” The dark hearts of the wicked are called the abyss; or it is the devil himself, whom the Lord permits to rage and restrains when he wishes [Col. 0744C].

**VERSE 2.**—“He seized.” That is, he showed him to have sinned when that devil killed one who was free from sin. “He bound him.” It should be understood that the devil was bound in Abraham and the other faithful in the same way as in those now present; but in the former, hope in the future Christ bound him, whereas in the latter Christ himself, having come, bound him.

**VERSE 3.**—“And he cast him,” etc. Cast out from the faithful, he began to rule more cruelly among the wicked; thus we read in the Gospel that he entered into the swine. “He sealed over him,” etc. That is, he placed a seal upon him, namely the sign of the cross, which so overcomes him as to repel him from the faithful. “And after this he must,” etc.: that he may recover the power which he had before Christ’s coming [Col. 0744D].

**VERSE 4.**—“And I saw thrones.” With the devil bound, I saw the faithful set free, the lesser members ready to obey their prelates, and the prelates judging their subjects. During the time of the binding I saw the Church thus freed for good works; and at that same time I saw those who die for Christ immediately enter glory, never descending to hell, as Abraham and the other prophets descended, though they were righteous.

“And the souls of those beheaded.” And I similarly saw the souls of those who had not worshiped. “And they lived.” And I do not say that they will live and reign in the future, but that even in this present time—that is, from the moment they were killed—they lived and reigned with Christ.

[Col. 0745A] **VERSE 5.**—“But the rest of the dead did not live,” that is, they will suffer eternal punishments, even in this present time, because they die immediately. “This is the resurrection.” The fact that the devil is thus bound, that people rise from sins, and that the souls of those who have died immediately enjoy eternal rest, is the first and greatest resurrection.

“First.” This is called first in contrast with that resurrection which will take place at once in soul and body.

“He who has a part.” Since not all can be perfect, neither will all be in the same brightness. The second death, that is, eternal condemnation, which will be in the body and soul of the reprobate, will not seize the elect, who are never increased in anything. But they will be priests, that is, offering eternal praises to the Divinity and the humanity.

[Col. 0745B] **VERSE 7.**—“Out of the prison.” That is, out of the hearts of the reprobate, in which he is now bound so that he may not rage as he wishes. “Magog.” That is, the uncovered: all persecutors concealing the devil within themselves and finally proceeding to open persecution. Or, literally, he will first deceive these two nations, and through them proceed to the others.

“And they surrounded the camp of the saints,” that is, those same saints, fortified in virtues and united in this battle.

**VERSE 10.**—“Day and night.” He says this in comparison with the glory of the saints, which is day, and their own punishments, which are night.

**VERSE 11.**—“And I saw a throne.” Having stated the destruction of the devil and his members, he adds the destruction of the world, for the greater punishment of the wicked. For it is fitting that, when the wicked have been destroyed, the world should be destroyed according as it had been corrupted by them. Although he had often spoken of the glorification of the saints and the punishments of the wicked, he had made no mention of bodies—whether they were to be glorified or punished; therefore here he shows this openly [Col. 0745C].

**VERSE 12.**—“And books were opened.” The books are the divine commandments, which those who neglected them will know to be the reason they are punished according to merit; or the books are the consciences of individuals, which will be open to all. “Another book.” That is, Christ, who will then appear powerful to all and will give life to his own. Or, the book is God’s foreknowledge, because then the wicked will openly know that they were not predestined to the life which, while in the world, they promised themselves. “From the things written.” By comparison with the saints the wicked will be condemned, for in the saints themselves the wicked will read what they refused to do [Col. 0745D].

**VERSE 13.**—“And the sea gave up its dead.” He wishes openly to show that the bodies of the dead, however much they have been cut to pieces, will be made alive at that judgment—a fact which some do not believe.

**VERSE 14.**—“This is the second death.” As though saying: Beware of the first death, because this second follows from that first.

## CHAPTER XXI

**VERSE 1.**—“And I saw.” In this seventh vision he treats of the renewal of the elements and the glorification of the saints, describing the merits through which the saints were so glorified. “A new heaven and a new earth.” There is no doubt that the transformation of the air and earth will take place through fire [Col. 0746A]. But there is doubt about the water, for it is believed to have purification within itself.

**VERSE 2.**—“Like a bride adorned.” Just as a bridegroom sends gifts beforehand to his bride before taking her, so Christ gives the Church faith, virtues, and good works before he receives her into glory.

**VERSE 3.**—“A loud voice from the throne.” Having said that he saw the renewal of the elements and the glorification of the saints, which was unknown, he adds the authority of the holy Fathers who foretold it, lest it seem unbelievable. “Behold the tabernacle.” That is, it is evident that the humanity of Christ, in which he served, and the people who imitated him and used it well, will be in that same glory.

[Col. 0746B] “And they, his people.” That is, offending in nothing—which cannot be while they are in mortal flesh.

**VERSE 4.**—“And death.” Truly there will be no tears there, because there will be no cause of tears.

**VERSE 5.**—“And he said.” As though saying: Write down whatever has been shown to you concerning this renewal. This was done for the benefit of those now living, for whom I was commanded to write these things. “Write: because these,” etc. Having commanded him to write and announce these things to others, he adds an exhortation that all may strive to belong to this renewal.

**VERSE 6.**—“And he said to me.” Having set forth the authority of the saints concerning this renewal, he sets forth the authority of God himself. “It is done.” Lest anyone ask what will happen after that renewal, he is told that nothing remains to be done.

[Col. 0746C] “Alpha and Omega.” As though saying: I shall be able to bring about this renewal, because I created all things and all things will be consummated in me. “To the thirsty.” I will not give to one thirsty only for a time, but to one who perseveres.

**VERSE 7.**—“He shall possess these things.” That is, myself, who am the beginning of all blessedness.

**VERSE 8.**—“To the fearful.” That is, those who through fear of punishments avoid receiving the faith, or abandon it after receiving it, will have eternal condemnation.

**VERSE 9.**—“Come and I will show you.” Having described the glory which the saints will possess, he states by what merit, or with what aid, they are to receive it.

**VERSE 10.**—“Upon a great mountain.” Christ is the mountain because he is a great protection to his own, because he fills the whole world, and lofty because insuperable. “He showed me the city.” And upon that mountain he showed me the foundation of the Church [Col. 0746D].

**VERSE 11.**—“Light.” The heavenly Jerusalem, shining according to its measure, is like Christ, who was steadfast in purpose and radiant in virtues. “Of jasper.” This stone is hard and green; thus the Church shines in faith and is made firm in it.

**VERSE 12.**—“A wall.” That is, Christ the defender, who is great in Zion and lofty with the Father. Or understand defenders of others, who are great in overcoming others, so that others may not be overcome: namely, apostles, prophets, or angels who are messengers of truth. “Twelve gates.” That is, the patriarchs, by whose example others are brought into the faith. Or the gates are the apostles, who introduce others into the Church.

[Col. 0747A] “Angels,” that is, subjects who, perfectly instructed, have been appointed in the place of angels. The number of twelve gates, which is comprised under three through the four parts of the world, pertains to the mystery of the twelve apostles, through whom faith in the Trinity is spread throughout the fourfold world. “Names inscribed,” etc. That is, the remembrance of the holy Fathers of the Old Law is in the apostles, because what those men foretold as future, these teach as fulfilled. Or all nations are placed in the faith and love of the apostles. Hence: “You are our letter, written in our hearts” (II Cor. III).

**VERSE 13.**—“Three gates from the east.” The east is the Jews, from whom the sun of righteousness rose; and among them are three gates, because among them faith in the Trinity was first proclaimed by the apostles and prophets. The north is the cold nations, which believed after the Jews. “From the south,” that is, from the brightness of faith, which is from Christ’s coming. “From the west,” that is, from the final age of the world, which through Elijah and Enoch will receive faith in the Trinity [Col. 0747B].

**VERSE 14.**—“The wall.” That is, the faith of Christ by which he fortified the city. It has twelve patriarchs, through whom it is founded, because they first held this faith, and all who come to faith rely on them. “And in those twelve.” The faith which these hold, those understood as future and foretold.

**VERSE 15.**—“And he who spoke with me.” I saw this city so fortified and adorned, yet I did not see everyone there equal to another; rather, each was perfect according to his measure. “A golden measuring rod.” That is, divine Scripture composed by God’s wisdom, which touches and illuminates the hearts of the faithful. “That he might measure the city and its gates.” That is, that according to their measure he might give even the lesser ones understanding of the Scriptures themselves [Col. 0747C].

“It is laid out square.” The four sides are faith, hope, charity, and action; and they are equal, because as much as one believes, so much one hopes; as much as one hopes, so much one loves; and as much as one loves, so much one acts. It is square, therefore, because it has steadfast faith, long-suffering hope, ample charity, and effective action. Or the four sides are the four principal virtues, none of which ought to exceed another. In a human being, therefore, there is prudence in seeking good and avoiding evil, followed by temperance, by which one withdraws from pleasures. After this is fortitude, so that one may do what one understands; then justice, so that one may so regulate one’s actions as not to seem excessively righteous or wise in one’s own eyes.

[Col. 0747D] “By stadia.” A stadium is a place, a course, and a measure; eight make a mile, and it denotes those striving for the prize.

“Twelve thousand.” These are perfect in faith in the Trinity from the four parts of the world.

**VERSE 17.**—“The measure of a man.” According to the letter, Saint John shows that the angel appeared to him in the form of a man, plainly indicating that he whom the angel signified was a true angel, that is, the Son of God, and a true man.

**VERSE 18.**—“And it was.” He had said that this city had walls, gates, and foundations, and that among them some were greater and others lesser. Here he explains what the wall, the city itself, the foundations, and the gates are like. “The structure of its wall was of jasper stone.” That is, if anyone is instructed to be a defender of others, he has this from the faith which he firmly holds and preaches, signified by green jasper, so that he may be a defender of others.

[Col. 0748A] “Gold.” Gold denotes wisdom; glass, however, the purity of faith, by which one promises with the mouth what one believes with the heart.

**VERSE 19.**—“Jasper.” This stone is green and therefore signifies the unfading verdure of faith. Or jasper is the unfading faith of the saints, always persevering in the verdure of its work.

Sapphire. It resembles a clear sky which, struck by the sun’s rays, sends forth a blazing radiance; but it signifies the height of the saints’ hope, whose way of life is in heaven, who, renewed by the true sun, seek eternal things more ardently and teach others to seek them, saying: “Our way of life is in heaven” (Phil. 3). Chalcedony. (Bede.) This stone has the color of a pale lamp: it shines, etc., up to “and they draw sinners and the weak to themselves and unite them to themselves.”

Emerald. (Id.) The fourth is of such intense greenness above all grasses and foliage that even, etc., up to “it is called fourth because of the four Gospels.”

**VERSE 20.**—Sardonyx. (Id.) The fifth is three-colored, black at the bottom, white, etc., up to “what is accomplished through the five senses is called fifth.”

Sardius. The sixth, of a uniform blood-red color, signifies the glory of martyrdom. It is sixth because Christ was crucified on the sixth day. Or, sardius, having the appearance of red earth, signifies the saints who, although lofty in understanding of mind, nevertheless remember their frailty, considering themselves sons of Adam, who is called red earth and was made on the sixth day; hence sardius is also introduced as the sixth.

Beryl. (Bede.) The eighth is the activity of preachers. Beryl shines, etc., up to “returning to the pallor of the active life through the care of earthly administration.”

Topaz. This stone is placed ninth because it is rarer and more precious. It has two colors, from gold and an ethereal brightness; it shines most intensely when touched by the sun’s splendor, surpasses the brightness of all gems, and singularly draws observers to gaze upon it. If you polish it excessively, you darken it; if you leave it to nature, it is brighter; and among royal treasures nothing is more precious. It signifies the contemplative life, which the holy kings prefer to all the riches of works and gems of virtues and toward which they direct their gaze most intently, and all the more so the more frequently they are enlightened by divine grace. Its golden color comes from inward charity, its ethereal color from the sweetness of contemplation. This latter is continually darkened by the friction of the world, for scarcely can anyone be touched by sorrows and at the same time contemplate the joys of heaven with a tranquil mind. Or, “if you polish it”—that is, if you honor and adorn them with worldly dignities—you darken it, because they devote less time to contemplation or become lesser in merits. And just as the eighth is the active life, so the ninth is the contemplative life, which belongs to the angels, whose orders are nine.

Some say that it has the colors of all stones, and hence its name, because *pan* means “all.” It is found on an island of Egypt called Topazon, and signifies the saints, radiant with every color of virtues.

Chrysoprase. It grows in India, a mixture of green and gold. Some also say that it is purple with golden spots. It signifies those who, through charity, merit the greenness of the eternal homeland and display another, purple color of martyrdom. Because they follow the Lord’s example, they are in India—that is, near the rising of the sun—and await reigning with Christ. They are contained in the number ten: the Decalogue is fulfilled through love, which has no end. Thus, in chrysoprase the work of martyrdom and its reward are signified. *Chryson* means “gold”; *prasos* means “leek.”

Hyacinth. This stone is the eleventh. As it changes with the air, it is transparent in clear weather and dark in cloudy weather. It signifies highly discerning teachers, adapting themselves to every condition—manners, ages, and understandings.

Amethyst. The twelfth stone is purple, mingling the colors of violet and rose and emitting from itself certain little flames. The purple color signifies the character of the heavenly kingdom and the primacy of the angelic society to which the saints will come. Violet signifies the saints’ humble modesty together with the fragrance of good works. Rose signifies the precious death of martyrs, who emit flames of charity not only among themselves but also toward enemies and persecutors. Amethyst therefore signifies the perpetual remembrance of the heavenly kingdom in the hearts of the humble, and that outstanding virtue by which they even pray for their enemies and care for their salvation, which is the virtue of virtues. The variety of colors signifies the multiplicity of virtues.

**VERSE 21.**—And twelve gates. It is as though he said: “I said that there were twelve gates”; these twelve gates are the prophets, who introduce people from the four regions of the world into faith in the Trinity. Through the instruction of each there are pearls, that is, their imitators, who, called from whatever part of the world to faith in the Trinity, are radiant with virtues. “Each gate,” etc. It is as though he said: In order for them to be gates, it was necessary that they be pearls.

The street of the city was gold. That is, they were full of wisdom or brightness, cleansed from criminal stain. Transparent glass. That is, concealing no impurity within themselves. Or, because the wicked can recognize their wickedness in their deeds as in a mirror.

**VERSE 23.**—It does not need the sun. Here the saints need the sun and moon for service; there they do not, for God will illuminate them completely. Or, it does not need the sun or the moon—that is, greater or lesser preachers.

**VERSE 24.**—And they will walk. There will be such light in the future that, even to the end of the world, the nations will walk—that is, they will advance from good to better—in the light, in the hope of this light, or through the light, or through the rays of its knowledge. The kings of the earth. That is, those greater ones who rule their own earthly nature and that of others.

**VERSE 25.**—And its gates. In the present, preaching is sometimes withdrawn, lest thieves enter and trample it while it is night—that is, a place of ambush. But because there the day is perpetual, all fear will be removed.

**VERSE 26.**—They will bring. In the manner of conquerors who carry spoils into their cities.

**VERSE 27.**—Nothing unclean will enter it. Having spoken of the city’s holiness, lest any false brother presume to attain one of these ranks, he determines who will enter and who will not.

# CHAPTER XXII

**VERSE 1.**—And he showed me. After showing the city’s situation, its dignity, its walls, and its foundations, he describes the refreshment that God provides for the city, both in the present and especially in the future: in the presence of the Godhead or through imitation of the life of the Lamb, who set before us in himself an example.

A river. That is, flowing water, namely, eternal blessedness. Under the appearance of water, the washing of baptism is indicated, through which this blessedness is reached.

From the throne of God. That is, from those in whom God will principally sit, because he is especially in them, and through their instruction lesser ones will be crowned.

**VERSE 2.**—And on both sides. Around the river—that is, in this life—we have the tree of life, namely, the body and blood of Christ, by which we are refreshed; beyond the river—that is, in the future—we will have him himself present. Or, by “around the river” let us understand the time before baptism, and by “beyond” what occurred after baptism, so that we may indicate that the faithful in both the old and the new law are saved through Christ. This was signified by Moses, who led the children of Israel as far as the Jordan River, and by Joshua son of Nun, who led them from the Jordan River into the land of promise.

The tree of life. It is as though he said: He himself gives refreshment; he also gives those who will prepare the people to whom he himself will give it.

Fruit. That is, the prophets and apostles bearing fruit in faith in the Trinity throughout the four regions of the world.

And the leaves of the tree. It is as though he said: Christ will produce fruit in this way: the apostles, and after them others also, will spread the leaves of Christ himself.

**VERSE 6.**—And he said to me. Just as at the beginning he commended the vision, so now, at the end, he does the same.

The Lord. And rightly you ought to believe, because it is he who has authority over the gifts of the Holy Spirit, through whom all the prophets spoke the things they said.

His angel, etc. Just as the angel commended these things to John, so John commends them to his disciples. It is as though he said: This announcement was not made to me for my sake, but so that you might believe me.

**VERSE 8.**—And after I had heard and seen. Here he makes us understand that we ought to hold him in veneration for these things, but not him alone: we ought to worship God and, through observance of the words of the book, attain purification like that of the angels.

**VERSE 9.**—And your brothers, etc. Those who possess the grace of interpretation should not be thought alien to the prophetic office, such as Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, Gregory, and others.

**VERSE 11.**—Let the one who does harm continue to do harm. Since it could be objected that it was wrong to prophesy to the wicked, because they would thereby be punished more severely, he is told not to cease on that account, because it is just.

**VERSE 14.**—Blessed are those who wash, etc. Because he had said, “Let the one who does harm do harm; let the one who is filthy remain filthy,” lest some wicked person say, “Since I am wicked, why should I repent?” he says that not only are those blessed who refuse the greater persecution, but also those who have defiled the garments they received in baptism, if afterward they wash them and repent that they sinned.

**VERSE 16.**—I, Jesus. John commended the book through the angel and through his own dignity; now he also commends it through the authority of Christ himself. It is as though he said: Let all who hear know that I, Jesus, sent my angel to testify these things to you.

The bright star. A radiant star, that is, great charity, announcing the day—that is, future blessedness—through my resurrection, which occurred in the morning.

[Col. 0752A] **VERSE 17.**—And the Spirit, that is, the Trinity, which is called spirit because of the excellence of its purity: “And the Spirit and the bride say,” etc. Here he also adds the testimony of the Trinity and of the faithful, as though he were saying: “For this reason you ought to receive it, because the Spirit and the bride,” etc.

And let the one who thirsts come. Yet not just anyone: let only the one who thirsts come—that is, who desires to believe.

Let the one who wishes take the water of life freely. And there is no labor involved, because willingness alone is sufficient.

**VERSE 18.**—For I testify, etc. After commending the book through himself, through the angel, through Christ, through the Trinity, and through the faithful, knowing that there were certain people in Asia who, to promote their errors, would add something or take something away, he adds an excommunication.

[Col. 0752B] **VERSE 21.**—The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. The apostle’s conclusion in the word of Christ.

[Col. 0751]

# WALAFRID STRABO, FULDA MONK: EXPOSITION OF THE FIRST TWENTY PSALMS

*(Pez., Thesaurus Anecdotorum novus, vol. IV.)*

# PEZ’S PRELIMINARY NOTICE

[Col. 0751C]

“Among our monks of Reichenau there came to light Walafrid the abbot’s Exposition of the seventy-six psalms, beginning with the first in the following manner: ‘All Scripture divinely inspired, of the Old and New Testament, invites the faithful to imitate the Mediator of God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ,’ etc.; the second volume appears to have been lost.” Thus far Jean Mabillon, vol. IV of the *Analecta*, p. 633.

Following his authority, I spared no effort among our distinguished Reichenau monks to persuade them to share with me this exposition by their Walafrid, a man exceedingly renowned in the ninth century for learning and virtue, brought forth from darkness. In this matter I found learned and diligent men all the more indulgent and ready to assist me because they conceived the more certain hope that their labor might contribute something to the advantage of the Catholic Church.

Accordingly, they sent me the complete exposition of all seventy-six psalms, skillfully and accurately transcribed under the care of the distinguished and most learned D. P. Apronian Hueber, prior of Mehrerau. I had promised my friends its prompt publication in my *Thesaurus*. I should never have changed my judgment had I not, after carefully examining the work, discovered that the kernel and marrow of Walafrid’s commentary had long ago been presented to scholars in the *Ordinary Gloss*, which likewise has Walafrid Strabo as its author.

Therefore, lest I become burdensome to learned men who would like me to be somewhat more sparing elsewhere in presenting theological material, I decided to insert in my *Thesaurus* only the exposition of the first twenty psalms, as a specimen of the remainder of the work. If any learned men, from this specimen, perceive a greater difference between Walafrid’s exposition of the psalms and the *Ordinary Gloss* on the same psalms than I have perceived, and should judge that it would be worthwhile for an explanation of the remaining psalms also to be published in the same manner, I shall comply with their wishes in subsequent volumes all the more readily, since it is only fair that the great labor of our friends at Reichenau, intended for the common benefit and use, should not perish altogether.

# ON THE FIRST PSALM

**VERSES 1–2.**—“Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, and has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the seat of pestilence. But his delight is in the law of the Lord,” etc.

Every Scripture divinely inspired, of the Old and New Testament, invites the faithful to imitate the Mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, so that through imitation we may deserve to attain likeness to him. As he himself says: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also will my servant be.” Thus also the apostle and evangelist John says: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.”

Thus this first psalm also teaches believers to follow the author and giver of true blessedness, turning away from evil and doing good, so that they may attain likeness to him and become like a tree planted beside the streams of waters.

He turns away from evil perfectly who neither delights in it in his heart, nor does it in deed, nor teaches others to do it. This is not going in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standing in the way of sinners, nor sitting in the seat of pestilence, but rather meditating on the law of the Lord—not out of necessity but willingly, without ceasing—which is signified by “day and night.”

Or, as Scripture commonly does, let “day” stand for prosperity and “night” for adversity, so that neither the joy of temporal circumstances nor the adversity of passing things may turn the mind of one who follows the Lord away from meditation on the divine law. How necessary this is is also shown where the Lord commanded Joshua, the servant and confidant of the lawgiver who had first learned the law, not to depart from the book of the law but to meditate on it day and night, so that he might direct his way and understand all that he said.

[Col. 0753B] But if someone asks more plainly what the counsel of the ungodly is, Scripture speaks of it in many places, especially the book called Wisdom, where it says: “The ungodly said among themselves, thinking incorrectly.” And shortly afterward: “Come, and let us enjoy the good things that exist, and let us use creation as though we were in the swiftness of youth.” And again: “Let us oppress the poor righteous man, and let us not respect the gray hairs of great age,” etc.

The way of sinners is the one about which the psalmist elsewhere adds after such words: “This is the way of those who are a stumbling block to themselves.” And the Lord says: “Broad is the way that leads to destruction.”

The seat of pestilence signifies perverse doctrine, which arises in two ways: either by openly inviting people to criminal deeds, as Solomon shows in Proverbs, saying: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them. If they say, ‘Come with us; let us lie in wait for blood; let us hide snares for the innocent without cause,’” etc.; or by leading people into error, as follows there after a little while, where he also calls this seat a chair, saying: “The foolish and clamorous woman, full of allurements and knowing nothing at all, sat at the doorway of her house on a chair.” And shortly afterward: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant.” These undoubtedly signify perverse doctrine. For the wicked pursue all these things to such an extent, and by pursuing them reject and detest meditation on the divine law, that, according to the Prophet, they hate the one who rebukes at the gate and abhor the one who speaks rightly, saying to God: “Depart from us; we do not want to know your ways.”

[Col. 0753D] Sacred Scripture observes this order, which the first psalm presents here in the briefest form, setting out what evils are to be avoided and what good things are to be done, in many passages. One similar passage is that of the blessed apostle James, who says: “Putting away all uncleanness and the abundance of wickedness, receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.” And again: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you; draw near to the Lord, and he will draw near to you.”

The Church also most prominently observes this order in the sacraments of those reborn from water and the Holy Spirit: first they renounce the devil and all his pomps or works, and afterward profess that they believe in God the almighty Father, in Jesus Christ his Son, in the Holy Spirit, in the Catholic Church, and in the forgiveness of sins. Thus they are immersed in saving water, incorporated into the Church—for outside it, even if someone should do the things mentioned above, he will not be able to be saved—and, made members of the tree of life, they begin to advance toward its likeness.

The blessed Paul, harmonizing with this in the words that follow, shows this when he says: “All of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death. For we have been buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be planted together in the likeness of his resurrection.”

**VERSE 3.**—“And he shall be like,” etc. During his passion, this tree said of itself: “If they do these things in the green wood, what will happen in the dry?” If the transgressor stretches out his hand to this tree and takes from its fruit, he will live forever. In the Apocalypse also he promises this to the victor, saying: “To the one who conquers I will grant to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God.”

By the streams of waters, understand either the Holy Spirit, as the Evangelist records the Lord saying: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” Explaining this, he adds: “He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were going to receive.” By the Spirit’s work the Savior’s incarnation itself took place, according to what the angel Gabriel says to Joseph about the blessed mother of God, Mary: “Do not fear to take Mary your wife, for what has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit.”

Or understand the sayings of Scripture, which foretold the coming of the righteous one, the future sufferings in Christ, and his later glories, as the righteous and justifying Lord himself says to the apostles after his resurrection: “These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you: that everything written in the law of Moses and the prophets and the psalms about me must be fulfilled.” And again: “Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures,” so that from them they might draw the life-giving moisture which they would distribute to believers, according to what the Prophet promises them: “You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Savior.”

That the divine sayings are signified under the name of waters is also testified by the same Scripture in many places. One such passage is: “Deep water is the word from the mouth of a man, and an overflowing torrent is a fountain of wisdom.”

The fruit and leaves of this tree are the things that Jesus began to do and teach. Concerning him, one of the disciples said: “He was a prophet, mighty in deed and word before God and all the people.”

As for the words “in his season,” the Apostle explained them, saying: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.” These are the fruit of the tree.

And what follows—“and its leaf shall not fall”—signifies the unchanging firmness of his words. Thus he himself says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.”

Concerning the prosperity of his works, the Father also promises through Isaiah: “My word, which goes forth from my mouth, will not return to me empty, but will do whatever I have willed, and will prosper in the things for which I sent it.”

**VERSE 4.**—“Not so the ungodly,” etc. The ungodly are not like those who, through imitation, advance so far toward the likeness of the tree of life that, seeing its blessedness and eternity, they themselves become blessed and eternal, according to what God promises through the prophet Isaiah: “For as the days of the tree shall be the days of my people.”

Rather, like dry and barren dust, because they are strangers to the moisture of the waters mentioned above, they are thrown from the solidity and stability of the earth into the wind of the present age—that is, of the present and future Church—and, once thrown out, become food for the serpent, of whom it is written: “And dust shall be the serpent’s bread.”

The wind itself is understood as the devil, as it is written: “The north wind is a harsh wind.” The one called “the right-hand one” is also called a spirit, and in the prophet is called the spirit of fornication; by the Apostle he is named the spirit who now works in the sons of disobedience.

**VERSE 5.**—“Therefore the ungodly shall not rise,” etc. If some distinction is to be understood here between the ungodly and sinners, the ungodly are to be understood as those of whom the Lord says: “Whoever does not believe in the Son has already been judged.” Sinners, however, are those to whom the Judge will say: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire.”

They will indeed rise in judgment, but not in the assembly of the righteous, just as the Lord threatens certain people through the prophet Ezekiel, saying: “They shall not be in the assembly of my people, they shall not be written in the writing of the house of Israel, and they shall not enter the land of Israel.”

**VERSE 6.**—“For the Lord knows,” etc. “Knows” means approves, and, praising them, rewards the deeds of the righteous. Thus through Solomon he promises that he will say in the universal judgment of the Church: “Give her the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates.”

In the gates—that is, at the entrance of the heavenly kingdom—the gates are closed to the foolish virgins, who will remain among those whose path will perish. For the Lord also says that he does not know what perishes, and what the Lord does not know perishes. Thus he says that he will answer the foolish virgins mentioned above and those who will say, “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name?” and so forth: “Amen I say to you, I do not know you,” or, “I never knew you.”

# ON THE SECOND PSALM

**VERSE 1.**—“Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate on vain things,” etc. This is an interrogative rebuke. The prophet reproves the peoples: Why did they rage against the Lord and Savior when they had no grounds for anger? He says that they meditated on vain things because they did not accomplish what they wished—that Christ should be destroyed.

[Col. 0756A] **VERSE 2.**—“The kings stood,” etc. This is said about the Lord’s persecutors, who are also mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles. “Stood” does not signify presence but intention.

**VERSE 3.**—“Let us break their bonds,” etc. Although it can be understood otherwise, it is more suitably taken as spoken from the perspective of those whom he said had meditated on vain things, so that “let us break their bonds” means: Let us take care that they do not bind us and that Christian religion not be imposed upon us. “Their bonds” may refer either to God the Father and his Christ, or to Christ and the apostles.

**VERSE 4.**—“He who dwells in the heavens,” etc. The thought is repeated. For in place of “He who dwells in the heavens,” “the Lord” is subsequently placed; in place of “he will laugh,” “he will mock” is subsequently placed.

None of this should be understood carnally, as though God laughed with his cheeks or mocked with his nose. Rather, we must understand the power he gives to his saints, so that, seeing future things—that is, the name of Christ, his dominion spreading among posterity and winning over all nations—they may understand that those people meditated on vain things. This power by which these things were foreknown is God’s laughter and mocking.

By the heavens we understand the holy souls, through whom God, knowing beforehand what will happen, will laugh and mock.

**VERSE 5.**—“Then he will speak,” etc. The anger and fury of God must not be understood as a disturbance in him, but as the power by which he most justly avenges all creation subject to him for service. Nevertheless, God’s anger may rightly also be understood as the very darkening of mind that follows those who transgress God’s law.

**VERSE 6.**—“But I have been established,” etc. Some interpret Zion as “speculation,” which we must understand as the Church, where the mind is daily raised to contemplate God’s charity. It is also called a mountain because of its eminence and firmness.

**VERSE 7.**—“The Lord said to me,” etc. That day may appear in prophecy to be the day on which Jesus Christ was born according to his humanity. Yet because “today” signifies presence, and in eternity nothing past has ceased to be, as though it were no longer, nor is anything future absent, as though it did not yet exist, “today” may also be understood, with utterly sincere and Catholic faith, as the eternal generation of the power and wisdom of God, who is the only-begotten Son.

[Col. 0756D] **VERSE 8.**—“Ask of me,” etc. That is, so that the nations may be joined to the Christian name and thus be redeemed from death, so that they may be possessed by God.

**VERSE 9.**—“You shall rule them with a rod,” etc. With an iron rod, with inflexible justice, crushing in them earthly desires and the muddy affairs of the old person.

**VERSE 10.**—“And now, kings,” etc. “And now,” that is, already renewed. For spiritual people are signified, those who judge the earth. Whatever we judge is beneath us; whatever is beneath the spiritual person is rightly called earth.

**VERSE 11.**—“Serve the Lord,” etc. “Rejoice” is most appropriately added, lest what was said—“serve”—seem to lead to misery. But again, lest that same rejoicing turn into an outpouring of rashness, “with trembling” is added, so that it may serve as a warning to exercise careful prudence.

**VERSE 12.**—“Take hold of instruction,” etc. To understand and be educated is to take hold of instruction. In the phrase “take hold,” sufficient indication is given that it is a kind of protection and defense against everything that could do harm, provided it is grasped with such care. To perish from the righteous way is a great punishment, feared by those who have tasted something of the sweetness of righteousness.

**VERSE 13.**—“When he burns in a short time,” etc. That is, when the vengeance comes that is prepared for the ungodly and sinners, it will not only fail to touch those who trust in the Lord, but will also advance them toward blessedness, where the sum and fullness of all good things are found.

As for what is added—“in a short time”—I think it signifies that something sudden will occur, since sinners regard this as remote and far in the future.

# ON THE THIRD PSALM

**VERSE 1.**—“A psalm of David, when he fled from the face of his son Absalom.”

David, whose name is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable,” signifies our Lord Jesus Christ, whose voice is introduced in this psalm speaking about his passion and resurrection.

Absalom signifies either Judas the betrayer or the persecuting people. Judas was still among the apostles when the Lord said: “The children of the bridegroom cannot fast as long as the bridegroom is with them.” And concerning the people he says through Moses: “Israel is my firstborn son.”

Therefore Truth fled from the mind of Judas, or from the persecuting people, even though he did not cease to enlighten them. Or, as the Gospel relates: “Jesus said these things, and he departed and hid himself from them.”

Since Absalom is interpreted as “the Father’s peace,” it is rightly understood that Christ displayed peace toward his betrayer, although the latter was being ravaged by the inward warfare of so wicked a thought. Christ also showed himself so peaceful toward the persecuting people that he pleaded with the Father on their behalf, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

**VERSE 2.**—“Lord, how they have multiplied,” etc. They were so greatly multiplied that even from the number of the disciples there was one who joined the number of the persecutors.

**VERSE 3.**—“Many say,” etc. It is clear that, unless they despaired of his rising again, they would certainly not have killed him. Therefore Judas too would not have betrayed him unless he had belonged to the number of those who despised Christ, saying: “There is no salvation for him in his God.”

**VERSE 4.**—“But you, Lord, are my protector,” etc. He calls the Lord his glory, even that man whom the Word of God received in such a way that he became God together with him.

Here “head” should, I think, be understood as the human mind itself, which so adhered and, in a manner, coalesced with the transcendent excellence of the Word receiving humanity that, amid such humiliation of the passion, it was not cast down.

These words can also be understood as spoken from the perspective of the Church. For in that man the Church too was received by the Word, which became flesh and dwelt among us. Let the Church therefore speak together with its head, established amid the storms of persecution throughout the whole world: “Lord, how they have multiplied,” etc., with its head exalted, the one who, firstborn from the dead, ascended into heaven.

**VERSE 5.**—“With my voice I cried to the Lord,” etc. Not with the bodily voice, which is uttered with the noise of struck air, but with the voice of the heart, which is silent to human beings but sounds like a cry to God when the soul alone speaks to the Lord, drawing nothing bodily and nothing belonging to carnal intentions into prayer, where God alone hears.

This is also called a cry because of the force of the intention itself.

He says that the Father heard him from the mountain, that is, from his righteousness. For it was just that he should raise from the dead the innocent man who had been killed and to whom evils had been repaid for good, and that he should repay his persecutors with what they deserved. For we read: “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God.”

The Church too is heard from that mountain, which is also its head, concerning which the Prophet says: “The mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared at the top of the mountains.”

**VERSE 6.**—“I slept,” etc. It may appropriately be observed that “I” signifies that he endured death by his own will, according to the saying: “For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, and I will take it up again; no one takes it from me.”

It is rightly understood as: “I slept and was drowsy”—I permitted myself to the passion, and death followed.

The saying is also addressed to the people of the Church: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will touch you,” because he was taken from sinners.

“Nor will I fear thousands,” etc. The words “arise” are not spoken to God as though he were sleeping or lying down. Rather, it is the custom of the divine Scriptures to attribute to God’s person what he does in us—not everywhere, but wherever it can suitably be said—or so that he may be said to speak when the various messengers of truth speak through his gift.

**VERSE 7.**—“For you have struck all,” etc. They have been shattered—that is, reduced to nothing—the words of sinners tearing apart and cursing the Son of God.

The teeth of sinners may also be understood as the leaders of sinners, by whose authority a person is cut off from the fellowship of those who live rightly and, as it were, incorporated among those who live wickedly.

**VERSE 8.**—“Salvation belongs to the Lord,” etc. Therefore no one should presume upon himself, since it belongs to the Lord to save from the death of sin. But you, Lord, bless your people who hope for salvation from you.

# ON THE FOURTH PSALM

**VERSE 2.**—“When I called, he heard me,” etc. “God of my righteousness,” from whom my righteousness comes: from the narrowness of sorrow you led me into the breadth of joys. For “tribulation and distress are upon every soul of one who does evil.”

But the one who says, “We rejoice in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces testing, and testing produces hope; hope does not disappoint, because the charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us,” does not have a constricted heart, even though persecution is inflicted from without.

This voice is either that of the Lord Jesus Christ after his resurrection, or that of the Church believing and hoping in him: “Have mercy on me and hear me,” etc. The devout mother says that she is to be pitied if her prayer is heard on behalf of her children, because whatever is granted to the members is without doubt granted to the whole body.

**VERSE 3.**—“Children of men,” etc. At least let your error have lasted until the coming of the Son of God. Why, then, are you still heavy-hearted? When will your deceits come to an end, if you do not possess the presence of Truth?

Since truth alone makes people blessed, and from it all things are true, why are you held back by love of temporal things? Why do you pursue what is, as it were, first and last, when it is vanity and falsehood? For you desire things to remain with you, although all things pass away like a shadow.

**VERSE 4.**—“And know that,” etc. Whom else but the one whom he raised from the dead and placed at his right hand in heaven? The human race is therefore rebuked, so that at last it may turn from love of this world toward him. And just as people rejoice over illumination in this life, so they should know that they must pray for rest after this life.

**VERSE 5.**—“Be angry and do not,” etc. This can be understood in two ways.

Either: Even if you are angry, do not sin. That is, even if a movement of the soul arises which, because of the punishment of sin, is no longer within one’s control, at least let reason and the mind, regenerated inwardly according to God, not consent to it, so that we may serve the law of God with the mind, even if we still serve the law of sin with the flesh.

Or: Do penance—that is, be angry with yourselves over past sins and cease sinning thereafter.

What follows—“the things that you say in your hearts”—is a complete sentence: “The things that you say in your hearts, say,” that is, do not be the people of whom it was said: “They honor me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.”

The chambers themselves are the hearts, concerning which the Lord also admonishes us to pray inwardly with the doors closed.

## Psalm 4

**Verse 6.—“Sacrifice the sacrifice,” etc.** He says the same thing in another psalm: “A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit.” Therefore, it is not improperly understood here as the sacrifice of righteousness itself, which is accomplished through repentance. For what is more just than that each person should be angry at his own sins rather than at those of another, and, punishing himself, slay himself as an offering to God? Or certainly the sacrifice of righteousness consists in just works after repentance.

There are, however, many foolish people who doubt or despair concerning the future life promised to us. They often say: “Who knows whether these things are true? Or who came back from the dead to announce them?”

**Verse 7.—“You have marked us,” etc.** This light is the whole and true good of the human being, perceived not by the eyes but by the mind. He said “marked in us,” as a denarius is marked with the image of the king. For the human being was made according to the likeness and image of God, which he corrupted by sinning. His good, therefore, is true and eternal if he is marked anew by being reborn. Joy, then, is not to be sought outside, but within, where the light of God’s countenance has been marked.

**Verse 8.—“From the fruit of grain,” etc.** It is not without purpose that *his own* has been added; for there is also grain, wine, and oil belonging to God. But those devoted to temporal pleasures are always inflamed by desires and cannot be satisfied. Distracted by manifold and wretched reflection, they are not permitted to see the simple good. Therefore the faithful man rejoices and says:

**Verse 9.—“In peace, in the same place,” etc.** It is rightly hoped by such people that the mind will be wholly estranged from mortal things and forget the miseries of this age. This is fittingly and prophetically signified by the terms “falling asleep” and “sleep,” in which supreme peace can be interrupted by no disturbance. But this is to be hoped for after this life. Therefore he appropriately adds at the end and says:

**Verse 10.—“For you, Lord, uniquely,” etc.** He says well, “uniquely.” This can be understood in contrast with the many who, enriched by the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil, say: “Who will show us good things?” For this multiplicity perishes, and the saints are held together as one, concerning whom it is said: “The multitude of believers had one soul and one heart.”

## Psalm 5

**Verse 1.—“For the end, for her who attains the truth, a psalm of David.”** The Church is understood, receiving an inheritance unto eternal life through our Lord Jesus Christ, so that she may possess God himself, to whom she clings and is blessed, according to the saying: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance.” Therefore this is the voice of the Church, called to the inheritance and so that she herself may become God’s inheritance.

**Verse 2.—“Perceive my words with your ears,” etc.** He aptly shows what this cry is, since the voice of the body is heard, while the spiritual meaning is understood.

**Verse 3.—“Attend to my voice,” etc.** The Scriptures commonly call the Son a king. According to what was said, therefore, “Through me one goes to the Father,” he is first “my king” and then “my God.”

**Verses 4–5.—“For to you I shall pray, Lord,” etc. “In the morning I shall stand,” etc.** He says: You are not one who can be seen by those whose eyes have not yet been freed from the night of sins. When the night of my error has been completed, and the darkness that I made for myself through my sins has departed, you will hear my voice.

But what is “I shall stand” except “I shall not lie down”? To lie down is to rest upon the earth, which means seeking blessedness from earthly pleasures. We must not cling to earthly things if we wish to see God, who is perceived by the pure in heart.

**Verse 6.—“Nor shall he dwell,” etc.** That is, they will not see in such a way as to cling to him, because their mind is beaten back by the light of truth on account of the darkness of sins. Through their habitual attachment to these sins, they cannot endure the radiance of right understanding.

**Verse 7.—“You hate all who practice,” etc.** He hates those whom he does not permit to remain in him. They do not remain because they are unable to endure him. Falsehood, however, is contrary to truth. But lest anyone suppose that some substance or nature is contrary to truth, let him understand that falsehood belongs to what is not, not to what is. If what is said is what exists, it is truth; if what is said is what does not exist, it is falsehood. Therefore he begins: “You will destroy those who speak falsehood,” because, departing from what exists, they turn toward what does not exist.

“Men of blood and deceit,” etc. Understand “men of blood” as those who practice iniquity, and “deceitful” as those who cherish falsehood. Those who are rejected are commonly said to be disinherited. But this psalm is for her who attains the inheritance, and she follows with the exultation of her hope, saying:

**[Col. 0761B] Verse 8.—“I shall enter into your house,” etc.** “I shall enter into your house,” as though, I believe, this were said of a stone in a building. For what else is the house of God than the temple of God, concerning which it was said: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are”? The cornerstone of this building is the one whom the coeternal power and wisdom of God the Father assumed.

It must be considered that he did not say “into the temple,” but “toward the temple.” For the holy temple is the body of the Lord the Savior, which the Church rightly worships; concerning it he himself said: “Destroy this temple.” He adds, “in your fear,” which is a great protection for those proceeding toward salvation.

**Verse 9.—“Lord, lead me,” etc.** Nothing is clearer than that he commends the time in which a person makes progress. For this is a journey accomplished not through earthly places but through the affections of souls. “In your sight,” he says, “is my way,” in accordance with what is also said in the Lord’s Prayer: “Hallowed be your name.” This does not mean that what is holy in itself is made holy by our prayers, but that we ask that what is holy by its nature may also be made holy in us. Thus the Prophet now asks that God’s way, which is straight in itself, may also be made straight for him.

**Verse 10.—“For there is not in their mouth,” etc.** How can truth be in the mouth of those whose heart is deceived by sin and the punishment of sin?

**Verse 11.—“Their throat is an open grave,” etc.** Flatterers and heretics are called open graves because, although they themselves are dead through not possessing the life of truth, they receive into themselves the dead whom they kill with lying words. When he says, “Judge them, O God,” he is not wishing that this should happen, but perceiving what will happen.

“Let them fall,” etc. Let them fall through the thoughts accusing them, through their own conscience. And because they are greatly impious, drive them far away from that inheritance which is possessed by understanding and seeing God.

**Verse 12.—“And let them rejoice,” etc.** He himself, therefore, will be eternal exultation, as the righteous become the temple of God.
