“And they will glory,” etc. This is the blessing: to glory in God and to be inhabited by God.

**Verse 13.—“Lord, as with the shield of good will,” etc.** God’s good will precedes our will, so that he may call sinners to repentance. These are also the weapons by which the enemy is conquered, against whom it is said: “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect?” And again: “For if, while we were still enemies, Christ died for us, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved from wrath through him.” This is the unconquerable shield by which the enemy is driven away, the enemy who suggests despair of salvation through the multitude of tribulations and temptations.

## Psalm 6

**Verse 1.—“For the end, in songs, for the eighth, a psalm of David.”** The day of judgment can be understood as the eighth, because eternal life is received after the end of this age. Then the souls of the righteous will no longer be subject to times. And since all times revolve in the recurrence of seven days, that day may perhaps be called the eighth because it will not possess this variation: assigning to each person what is owed according to merit, it transfers the saints to eternal life but condemns the impious eternally. Fearing this condemnation, the Church prays, saying:

**Verse 2.—“Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger,” etc.** On the day of judgment all who lack the foundation, which is Christ, are reproved—that is, accused. Those who build wood, hay, and straw upon this foundation are corrected—that is, purified—and yet they will be saved, as through fire. But this person prays that in the Lord’s anger he may neither be condemned nor corrected, but may be so perfectly healed here that he will fear not only death but also not have to endure the hand of the burning or cutting physician. Therefore he continues and says:

**Verse 3.—“Have mercy on me, God,” etc.** That is, be the soul’s foundation or strength; for this is what bones signify. Therefore the explanation is supplied by what follows:

**Verse 4.—“And my soul,” etc.** Who would not understand a soul struggling with its illnesses, but kept waiting for a long time by the physician so that it might be persuaded into what evils it had plunged itself by sinning? What is healed easily is not guarded very carefully. From the difficulty of healing, however, more diligent protection of the health that has been recovered will arise.

**Verse 5.—“Turn, Lord,” etc.** Turning himself, he prays that God also may turn toward him, as it is said: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you, says the Lord.”

**Verse 6.—“For there is not,” etc.** He understands that this is now the time for conversion, because when this life has passed, nothing remains except the repayment of merits. This may also be understood in the sense that he calls sin death—the sin committed by despising God’s law. In this death, that is, in being forgetful of God and despising the law and commandments, he says that hell is the blindness of the soul which receives and envelops the sinner, that is, the dying person. The soul asks to be kept safe from this death and this hell while it strives to turn toward the Lord and experiences difficulties. Therefore it continues, saying:

**Verse 7.—“I have labored,” etc.** The bed is called in this passage the place where the sick and weak mind rests, that is, in bodily pleasure and every worldly delight. He washes it with tears who strives to withdraw himself from it, and is compelled to suffer, as though through alternating feeling, by day and night. When he says, “In my mind I serve the law of God,” he seems to experience day; again, when he says, “But in the flesh I serve the law of sin,” he is bent toward night, until the whole night passes and one day comes, concerning which it is said: “In the morning I shall stand before you.” We understand “bed” here as also “couch,” although “I will water” is more than “I will wash.” Something may be washed on the surface, but watering reaches the interior; this signifies weeping down to the depths of the heart.

**Verse 8.—“My eye is troubled,” etc.** Because of the Lord’s anger, he confesses that the eye of his heart is troubled. For what is more terrifying than that the one who, unless he has mercy, destroys, should be angry? When he adds, “I have grown old among all my enemies,” he finds himself surrounded by every vice. Since these belong to the former life and to the old person, whom we must strip off in order to put on the new, he rightly says, “I have grown old.” By “all my enemies,” he either means the vices themselves or people who refuse to turn to God. Even if they do not know it, and even if they show leniency, they are nevertheless enemies to those who turn toward God because their purpose is opposed.

But since what is asked with such intensity cannot be fruitless, and since he is the fountain of all mercies, it is most truly said: “The Lord is near to the brokenhearted.” After so many difficulties, the pious soul signifies that it has been heard—and it is also possible to understand the Church—when it adds:

**Verse 9.—“Depart from me,” etc.** This may have been said prophetically: for the impious will depart, that is, be separated from the righteous, when the day of judgment comes. Or it may refer to the present, since even if they are contained together in the same gatherings and associations, the grains are already separated from the chaff on the bare threshing floor, although they remain hidden among the chaff.

“The Lord has heard,” etc. The repeated recurrence of the same statement shows not the necessity of a narrator but the emotion of one who is rejoicing.

**Verse 10.—“Let them be ashamed,” etc.** This will be fulfilled on that day, when the rewards of the righteous and the punishments of sinners have been revealed. For the impious are so far from being ashamed that they do not cease insulting us.

This may also be understood here as follows: now that God has heard the one who groans and weeps so often and for so long, she is understood to have been freed from sins and to pray even for her enemies, that they may repent of their sins—which cannot happen without shame and distress—and turn to the Lord, being ashamed that they gloried previously in the darkness of their sins. What he adds, “very swiftly,” refers either to the emotion of the one who prays or to the power of Christ, who converted the nations that had persecuted the Church on account of their idols to faith in the Gospel with such astonishing rapidity.

## Psalm 7

*Chusi* is interpreted as “Ethiopian.” It signifies the devil, or Judas the betrayer, or the Jewish people, who, after receiving blessedness, turned toward the blackness of sins. He is also written as the son of Jemini, that is, “son of the right hand.” Although they fell through their own fault, they were created good by God in their nature. For they conspired against Christ and the Church in the persecution with equal agreement.

**Verses 1–2.—“Lord my God, in you I have hoped,” etc. “Lest he seize,” etc.** The Apostle says: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.” Therefore, although he had said in the plural, “Save me from all those who persecute me,” he later introduced the singular, saying, “Lest he seize my soul like a lion.” He does not say, “Lest they seize,” as though, once every battle and adversity of the vices had been overcome, no one could resist the perfected person except the envious devil. What he adds, “while there is no one to redeem,” is to be understood as meaning: let him not seize while you neither redeem nor save.

**[Col. 0764B] Verse 4.—“Lord my God,” etc.** What he means by “if I have done this” he explains below when he says: “If there is iniquity in my hands.”

**Verse 5.—“If I have repaid,” etc.** He does not say, “If I have repaid those who did something,” but “those who repaid me evil.” For the one who repays has already received something. It requires greater patience not to repay evil even to one who, after receiving benefits, returned evil in return for us than it does if he had wished to do harm without having received any benefit. He aptly adds: “May I rightly fall away empty before my enemies.” For a person boasts emptily when, although he is himself human, he desires to avenge himself upon another human being. While he openly seeks to overcome a human being, he is secretly overcome by the devil, made empty by the vain and proud joy that he, as though unconquerable, could not be defeated. Understanding where the greater victory lies, he therefore conquers anger rather than a human being.

**Verse 6.—“Let the enemy pursue,” etc.** He names as “the enemy” the one whom he earlier called a lion. He pursues the soul, and if he deceives it, he seizes it and, by trampling its life down into the earth, makes it his food. For he is called not only a lion but also a serpent, to whom it was said: “You will eat earth.” He also brings its glory down into dust, which the wind casts from the face of the earth. This is vain and foolish boasting, like a globe of dust lifted by the wind.

**Verse 7.—“Arise, Lord,” etc.** He does not pray these things against human beings but against the devil and his angels, whose possession is sinful and impious people. It is punishment for them when this possession is taken away from them, since they desire to rule over it. He calls this punishment God’s anger against the devil: that he cease possessing those whom he possesses. He called this possession “boundaries,” where he wishes God to be exalted—that is, honored and glorified—rather than the devil, as the impious are justified and migrate into the temple of God.

“Arise, Lord my God,” etc. Because you commanded humility, appear humble, and you first fulfill what you commanded, so that by your example those who conquer pride may not be possessed by the devil.

The “assembly of the peoples,” that is, the multitude of believers through his humility, surrounded him in such a way that it was most truly said: “Blindness in part has happened to Israel until the fullness of the nations should enter.”

**[Col. 0765A] Verse 8.—“And on account of this,” etc.** That is, on account of this assembly, return to the heights. This is understood to have occurred when he rose again and ascended into heaven. He continues appropriately:

**Verse 9.—“The Lord judges the peoples,” etc.** For from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. Therefore observe how this soul, which prays perfectly, does not fear the day of judgment, and how it truly says with desire in prayer:

“Judge me, Lord,” etc. That is true innocence which harms not even an enemy. Therefore he rightly asks to be judged according to his innocence, since he could truly say: “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil.” What he adds, “over me,” shows the same thing: that the soul is righteous. It is as though a burning and shining lamp were to say: “Judge me according to the flame that is over me”—that is, not according to what I am, but according to the flame with which I shine, having been kindled by you.

**Verse 10.—“Let the wickedness be completed,” etc.** “Let it be completed,” he says; let it be perfected, that is, let it reach the height of wickedness, so that this judgment may now come. But since it was said not only of filth, “Let him who is filthy be filthy still,” but also, “Let the righteous become more righteous,” he adds: “You will direct the righteous, God who searches hearts and kidneys.” How, then, is the righteous directed amid such great confusion of pretense, unless God, searching hearts and kidneys, sees everyone’s thoughts—which are signified by the word “heart”—and their pleasures, which are understood by “kidneys”? Searching our heart, therefore, and observing that we do not yield to flesh and blood but delight in the Lord, he directs the righteous in the very conscience before him, where no human being sees, but only the one who observes what each person thinks and what delights each person.

**Verse 11.—“Righteous is the help,” etc.** It is righteous help that is now granted to the righteous. If he provides the medicine by which we, the sick, are healed, how much more will he provide that by which we, once healthy, are preserved? For if, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, how much more, now justified, shall we be saved from wrath through him. Thus it happens that God, searching hearts and kidneys, observing right thoughts in the heart and no inferior pleasures in the kidneys, provides righteous help to the upright in heart, where heavenly pleasures are joined to pure thoughts.

**[Col. 0765D] Verse 12.—“God is a righteous judge,” etc.** He is righteous because he repays each person according to his works; strong because, although most powerful, he endured impious persecutors for our salvation; patient because he did not immediately after the resurrection snatch those who had persecuted him away to punishment, but endured them so that at some time they might turn from that impiety to salvation. He is not angry every day because he still endures them, reserving the final punishment for the final judgment.

**Verses 13–14.—“Unless they are converted,” etc. “And in it he prepared,” etc.** Coming at his second advent to judge the living and the dead, the righteous Judge will flash forth in the manifest splendor of his glory as light for his righteous and as terror for the impious. He calls the Holy Scriptures a bow, in which, through the strength of the New Testament, the hardness of the Old Testament has been bent and subdued as though by a bowstring. From this bow the apostles are sent forth like arrows, or divine proclamations are shot. He made these arrows burning, so that those struck by them might blaze with divine love.

The “vessels of death” may be understood as heretics, who leap forth from the same bow—that is, from the same Scriptures—not to inflame souls with love but to destroy them with poisons. This happens only according to merits, and therefore even this arrangement must be attributed to divine providence. Or the “vessels of death” may be the same apostles, because to some they are “the fragrance of life unto life,” and to others “the fragrance of death unto death.”

**Verse 15.—“Behold, he was in labor,” etc.** Every wicked person conceives sorrow when he desires something unlawful; he is in labor with injustice when he meditates upon it through desire; he gives birth to iniquity, because when sin has been completed it generates death.

**Verse 16.—“He opened a pit,” etc.** This is what is said in another psalm: “The sinner has been caught in the works of his own hands.”

**Verse 17.—“His sorrow will return,” etc.** His iniquity will rightly be upon him when he has voluntarily subjected himself to his iniquity, just as it is said in another psalm: “My iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden, they have been made heavy upon me.”

**Verse 18.—“I will confess to the Lord,” etc.** This is not a confession of sins but of God’s righteousness. We speak in this way: “You are truly righteous, Lord, when you protect the righteous in such a way that you illuminate them through yourself, and order sinners in such a way that they are punished not by your wickedness but by their own.”

This psalm may also be understood as spoken in the person of the Lord’s human nature, provided that what is said there humbly is referred to our weakness, which he bore.

## Psalm 8

We can understand the “winepresses” as the Churches, for the same reason that we understand the threshing floor as the Church. For whether in the threshing floor or in the winepress, nothing else is done except that fruits are cleansed from impurities—impurities necessary both for their coming into being and for their growth and arrival at the maturity of harvest or vintage. This is what now takes place: the good are temporarily separated from the evil not by place but by disposition, although in the Churches they associate in bodily presence. There will be another time when either the grains are separated into barns or the wines into storerooms.

The winepresses are also commonly understood as martyrdoms, as those who confessed the name of Christ were trampled under the affliction of persecutions, so that their mortal remains remained on the earth like grape-stems, while their souls flowed forth into the rest of their heavenly dwelling.

The divine Word can also be understood as a grape. When, because of the necessity of expression, it uses the sound of the voice so that it may reach the ears of those listening, understanding is enclosed in that same vocal sound like wine in grape-stems. Thus this grape comes into the ears as though into the pressing vat of the winepress. There it is separated: the sound reaches the ears, while the understanding is received in the memory of those who hear as though in a certain place, and from there passes into the discipline of conduct and the disposition of the mind, as from a vat into storerooms. If negligence has not made it sour, it will be strengthened by age. For among the Jews it did turn sour, and with this vinegar they gave the Lord drink.

**Verse 2.—“Lord, our Lord,” etc.** As though he were saying openly: “Lord, who are our Lord, how greatly you are admired by all who inhabit the earth, because your magnificence has been raised above the heavens from earthly humility!” From this it became evident that you had descended, since you were seen by some, while others believed that you had ascended.

**Verse 3.—“From the mouth of infants,” etc.** The infants and nursing children may be understood as those to whom the Apostle says: “As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not food.” They were signified by those who went before the Lord praising him, in which testimony the Lord himself made use.

As for the enemies of this dispensation accomplished through Christ Jesus—and him crucified—we must generally understand all who forbid people to yield to what is unknown and promise certain knowledge, as all heretics do, as well as those who are called philosophers within the superstition of the nations. The devil, however, the fiercest enemy, may also be understood as the avenger. For sinners are handed over to him for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord. But he eternally possesses all who have not been rescued from his jaws by divine grace.

**Verse 4.—“For I shall see the heavens,” etc.** “I shall see,” he says, “the heavens, the works of your fingers”—that is, I shall perceive and understand the Scriptures, which you wrote through your ministers by the operation of the Holy Spirit, who is called the finger of God.

Thus the enemy is destroyed when the Scriptures proclaimed even to the slowness of infants are understood. The moon and stars are established in the heavens because both the universal Church, which is often signified by the moon, and the individual Churches in their various places, which I believe are indicated by the name “stars,” have been placed in those same Scriptures, which we believe are designated by the term “heavens.”

**Verse 5.—“What is the human being,” etc.** It is possible to ask what distinction there is between “human being” and “son of a human being.” For if there were no distinction, it would not be phrased in this way: “or son of a human being,” with a disjunction. Every son of a human being is a human being, although not every human being can be understood as a Son of Man. Adam was a human being but not a son of a human being. Christ, however, is both human being and Son of Man.

A human being, then, is called one who bears the image of the earthly human being. God remembers this one as absent. But the Son of Man, who bears the image of the heavenly one, he visits as present; this is the Word of God in the assumption of humanity. Hence it follows:

**Verse 6.—“You have made him a little lower,” etc.** We have heard and believe that he was made a little lower than the angels through the humility of bodily generation and passion. This is read more magnificently in Hebrew: “You will make him a little lower than God.” There he is clearly shown to be equal to the Father according to divinity and declared to be destined to be lower than the Father according to humanity.

**Verse 7.—“You have subjected all things,” etc.** He excludes nothing when he says “all things.” And lest it be understood otherwise, the Apostle commands us to believe this when he says: “Except the one who subjected all things to him.” Yet it does not seem that he adds anything especially significant when he says: “Sheep and oxen,” etc., unless we understand sheep and oxen as holy souls, either producing the fruit of innocence or working so that the earth may bear fruit—that is, so that earthly people may be regenerated into spiritual abundance.

These holy souls must therefore be understood as belonging not only to human beings but also to angels, on the basis of the Lord’s saying that he left ninety-nine sheep in the mountains—that is, in higher places—and descended on account of one. The matter of the oxen is readily explained, since human beings are called oxen for no other reason than that, by proclaiming the word of God, they imitate the angels.

The “animals of the field” are most suitably understood as people rejoicing in the pleasures of the flesh, in which they climb toward nothing arduous or laborious. For the field is the broad way that leads to destruction.

**Verse 8.—“The birds of heaven,” etc.** Consider now also the proud birds of heaven, of whom it is said: “They have set their mouth in heaven.” See how high they are carried by the wind, those who say: “We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own; who is our lord?” Observe also the curious fish of the sea, which traverse the paths of the sea—that is, they search in the depths of this age for temporal things, which, like paths in the sea, become worthless and perish. He said “they traverse,” showing their most persistent devotion to seeking empty and passing things.

**Verse 10.—“Lord, our Lord,” etc.** After the body of the discourse, it is fitting to return to the beginning, to which the same familiar statement must be referred.

## Psalm 9

One may ask about “the hidden things of the Son.” But since he did not add whose hidden things they are, the only-begotten Son of God must be understood. The Lord himself also, when he says “the Son” without qualification, wishes himself to be understood as the Only-Begotten, as where he says: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free.”

What the hidden things of the Son are, the edition translated from Hebrew clearly shows when it says: “To the victor over the death of the Son.” Therefore, in this psalm the hidden things of the Son must be observed: his humble coming, through which he benefited the nations amid the blindness of the Jews; and the punishment now taking place secretly—not yet the condemnation of sinners, but either the testing of those who are converted, or an admonition that they should convert, or blindness preparing for condemnation those who refuse to convert.

For the inscription written in the title, “For the end, for the hidden things of the Son,” and the translation mentioned above from Hebrew, “To the victor for the death of the Son,” fit these matters most appropriately. Beyond doubt, Christ is their author, who said: “Take courage; I have conquered the world,” when he triumphed equally over death and hell. He himself is also the end, that is, the completion of the law, as he says: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it.” Since he will also win the victory over the world, he is the end of future goods.

**Verse 2.—“I will confess to you, Lord,” etc.** He does not confess to God with his whole heart if he doubts in any respect about his providence. He recounts all God’s wonders because he sees them taking place not only openly in bodies but also invisibly in souls, though in a far more sublime and excellent manner.

**Verse 3.—“I will rejoice and exult,” etc.** Not in this age, where joy is deadly; not in the ambitions of the world, where sins are bitterly sweet; but in you, where secure joy continually increases.

“I will recount all your wonders” can especially be understood as spoken in the person of Christ, who said to his disciples: “Everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.” Indeed, the person of the Lord who speaks begins already to appear in this psalm. For it continues:

**Verse 4.—“When my enemy is turned back,” etc.** His enemy was turned backward when he was told: “Get behind me, Satan.” For then the one who desired to place himself first through temptation was made backward, having no power against him. No human being precedes him or makes him backward except one who, laying aside the image of the earthly human being, bears the image of the heavenly one—forgetting what lies behind and stretching toward what lies ahead.

It is not unreasonable to understand “my enemy” generally, as the Hebrew edition teaches. After saying, “I will sing to your name, Most High,” it immediately adds: “When my enemies have fallen backward, they will stumble and perish from your presence.” Why?

**Verse 5.—“For you have carried out judgment,” etc.** That is, you executed that judgment in which I appeared to be judged, and the case in which human beings condemned me as just and innocent. These things served him for our liberation, just as sailors call the wind they use for good sailing “their own.”

**Verse 6.—“You rebuked the nations,” etc.** We understand this more appropriately as spoken to the Lord Jesus Christ than as spoken by him. For who else rebuked the nations and caused the impious person to perish except the one who, after ascending into heaven, sent the Holy Spirit? Filled with him, the apostles boldly proclaimed the word of God and freely reproved human sins. Through this rebuke the impious person perished, because he was justified. The name of the impious was blotted out, for those who believe in the true Lord are no longer called impious.

**Verse 7.—“The enemies have failed,” etc.** Whose enemies, unless the devil’s weapons? These are understood as the various opinions of error, with which he kills souls as with swords. “Unto the end,” however, means “in Christ,” who destroyed his cities when he expelled their ruler, concerning whom it was said: “The ruler of this age has been cast out.”

“Their memory has perished,” etc., either because a noise occurs when impiety is overthrown, or because the very noise in which impiety rages also perishes.

**Verse 8.—“He prepared his throne for judgment,” etc.** Since he will also come openly and manifestly to judge the living and the dead, he prepared his seat in the hidden judgment.

**Verse 9.—“And he himself openly judged the world in righteousness.”** That is, restoring things worthy of their merits.

**Verse 10.—“And the Lord became a refuge for the poor,” etc.** He explained what it means to be a helper in times of opportunity when he added: “in tribulation.” For the soul is not converted to the Lord unless it is turned away from this age. Nor is it turned away opportunely from this age unless its frivolous, harmful, and destructive pleasures are mingled with labors and sorrows.

**Verse 11.—“And let them hope in you,” etc.** When the soul is being torn away from this world, it seeks where to fix its hope. The knowledge of God’s name fittingly receives it. God’s name itself has been proclaimed everywhere, but there is knowledge of the name when the one whose name it is is known.

**Verse 12.—“Sing praises to the Lord,” etc.** This is said to those whom the Lord does not abandon when they seek him. He dwells in Zion, which is interpreted as “watchtower” or “contemplation,” and bears the image of the Church, which now exists and to which it was said: “The temple of the Lord is holy, which you are.”

**Verse 13.—“For, as one who seeks blood,” etc.** It is as though those who were sent to evangelize among the nations, zealous for God, were answering and saying: “Lord, who has believed our report?” And: “For your sake we are put to death all day long.” Or it is as though someone less instructed and of weaker faith were asking: “How will it be announced, when the unbelief of the nations is about to rage?” It appropriately continues by saying that Christians would die in persecution not without great fruit for eternity, because the one who seeks their blood has remembered it.

**Verse 14.—“Have mercy on me, Lord,” etc.** One person intercedes for the saints—the one who first became poor for us, although he was rich—when above he said in the plural: “He has not forgotten the cry of the poor.” And he himself says:

**Verse 15.—“You who exalt me,” etc.** Each one of us is exalted in him, in his members, above all depraved desires, which are the gates of death because through them one goes into death. The “daughters of Zion” are all the best endeavors through which one comes to the vision of peace. In the holy Church, the daughters of Zion are also the sacraments and beginnings of faith.

**Verse 16.—“I will exult in your salvation,” etc.** “I will exult,” that is, I will be held in blessedness by your salvation, which is our Lord Jesus Christ, the power and wisdom of God. Next, observe how punishment is preserved for the sinner from his own works.

“In this snare,” etc. The hidden snare is a deceitful thought. The foot of the soul is rightly understood as love: when it is perverse, it is called desire or lust; when it is right, affection or charity. Their foot, therefore, was caught in a fraudulent scheme when, through love, it reached vain joy by deceit.

## Psalm 9

**Verse 17.**—“The Lord shall be known,” etc. These are the judgments of God, when he repays each person according to his work.

**Verse 18.**—“Let sinners be turned back,” etc. That is, let them be delivered into their own hands when they are spared, and let them be ensnared by deadly pleasure.

**Verse 19.**—“For forgetfulness shall not be unto the end,” etc. Those who now appear to be, as it were, forgotten are called poor: while the wicked flourish, they are afflicted. But their patience, by which they now endure the wicked, will not perish; it will be rewarded at the end.

**Verse 20.**—“Arise, O Lord; let man not prevail,” etc. The future judgment is invoked. What he says—“in your sight”—signifies “in secret before God,” understood by a few holy and righteous people.

**Verse 21.**—“Set over them, O Lord,” etc. He seems to signify the Antichrist, concerning whom the Apostle says: “When the man of sin is revealed.” Those who do not wish to be liberated by the Son of God, to belong to the Son of Man, and to be sons of men—that is, new men—will serve a man, that is, the old sinful man, because they are men. And because he is believed to come to such a pinnacle of empty glory, and will be permitted to do so much against all people and against God’s saints, that at that time some weak people will truly think that God neglects human affairs, he adds, as though in the voice of those groaning and complaining, why judgment is delayed.

**Verse 22.**—“Why, O Lord, have you withdrawn,” etc. That is, you disregard what is timely, and you produce tribulations in order to inflame minds with desire for your coming. For that fountain of life is sweeter to those who thirst greatly. Thus he intimates the reason for the delay, saying:

**Verse 23.**—“While the wicked man is proud,” etc. It is marvelous and true how greatly the little ones of good hope are inflamed toward right living by comparison with sinners. By this mystery it comes about that even heresies are permitted to exist, so that those who are known to God may be openly shown among men. The wicked, however, are caught in their schemes, because their thoughts become bonds for them. But why?

**Verse 24.**—“For the sinner is praised,” etc. The tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins. It is pleasing to do things in which one not only does not fear a reprover, but even hears a praiser.

**Verse 25.**—“He has provoked the Lord,” etc. He is greatly angered when he does not inquire, when he seems to forget, when he does not attend to sins, and the wicked man reaches wealth and honors through frauds and crimes. This will happen especially in that Antichrist, who will appear so blessed to men [Col. 0771D] that he will even be thought to be God. But how great this anger of God is, the following words teach.

**Verse 26.**—“God is not in his sight,” etc. What punishment, then, does he suffer, when through the prosperity of his sins he is brought to the point that God is not in his sight—that is, he is abandoned by the light of truth—and his ways are defiled for all time, meaning that his thoughts and plans are unclean?

“Your judgments are removed,” etc. For a mind conscious of evil, when it seems to itself to be suffering no punishment, believes that God does not judge; and thus your judgments, O God, are removed from his face, although this itself is a great condemnation. “He will rule over all his enemies,” because he is said to surpass all kings and to obtain the kingdom alone, when, according to the Apostle, he will also sit in the temple of God, exalting himself above everything that is worshiped and called God [Col. 0772A].

**Verse 27.**—“For he has said in his heart,” etc. That is: “My fame and my name will not pass from this generation to the generations of posterity unless by evil arts I obtain such an exalted rule that later generations cannot remain silent about it.” Or certainly he will imagine that he will pass from human generation into divine generation by magical practices.

It should be known, however, that the Hebrew translation signifies that the condemned man is so persuaded by the devil that he thinks he will reign forever without any adversity. It reads as follows: “He speaks in his heart: I shall not be moved; from generation to generation I shall be without evil” [Col. 0772B].

**Verse 28.**—“His mouth is full of cursing,” etc. It is a great curse to seek heaven by such monstrous arts and to acquire such merits in order to seize an eternal dwelling. His mouth, however, is full of this curse. This desire will not achieve its effect, but beneath all things it will serve only to destroy him, because he dared to promise this to himself. “With bitterness and deceit”—that is, with anger and ambushes, by which he will turn the multitude to his own side.

What follows—“Under his tongue are labor and pain”—refers to what he said in his heart: “I shall not be moved.” Therefore it says “under his tongue,” not “in his tongue,” because he will think these things silently, while speaking to people in such a way that he may appear good, just, and the Son of God [Col. 0772C].

**Verse 29.**—“He sits in ambush,” etc. Which rich people does this mean, if not those whom he will heap up with the gifts of this age? Therefore he is said to sit in ambush with them, because he will display their false happiness in order to cast men down. “In secret,” I think, refers to the places where it is not easily understood what should be sought and what should be avoided. To kill the innocent, however, is to make the innocent guilty.

**Verse 30.**—“His eyes look upon the poor,” etc. For he will persecute the righteous above all, concerning whom it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit.” He calls him a lion in the den, in whom both force and deceit will operate. The first persecution of the Church was violent, when through confiscations, tortures, and killings Christians were compelled to sacrifice [Col. 0772D]. The second persecution is deceitful, and is now carried out through heretics of this kind and false brothers. The third remains, which will come through the Antichrist; nothing will be more dangerous than it, because it will be both violent and deceitful. He will have force in his rule and deceit in his miracles. “Lion” refers to force; “in his den” refers to deceit. And again the same things are repeated in reversed order: “He lies in wait to seize,” etc. For lying in wait belongs to deceit, while seizing belongs to violence. The things that follow are likewise the same:

**Verse 31.**—“In his snare he humbled,” etc. The snare aptly signifies ambushes; domination, however, most appropriately conveys terror. Hence it says: “He will bow down and fall,” etc. [Col. 0773A]

**Verse 32.**—“For he has said in his heart,” etc. This is the most wretched bowing and falling: when the human mind seems to prosper in its own iniquities and thinks that it is being spared, while it is being blinded so that it may be preserved for the final and appropriate vengeance. Concerning this he now speaks, saying:

**Verse 33.**—“Arise, O Lord God; let your hand be exalted,” etc. That is: let your power be made manifest. At that time the suffering Church, like a ship amid great waves and storms, awakens the Lord as though he were sleeping, so that he may command the winds and tranquility may return. Then, understanding and rejoicing in the manifest judgment, they say:

[Col. 0773B] **Verse 34.**—“Why has the wicked provoked God?” etc. That is: “What benefit was there in doing so many evil things?” Then it continues:

**Verse 35.**—“You see that you consider labor,” etc. This passage requires careful phrasing; if it is wrongly pronounced, it becomes obscure. Thus the wicked man said in his heart: “God will not inquire,” as though God were considering labor and pain in order to deliver them into his hands—as though he were afraid to labor and suffer, and therefore spared them lest their punishment be burdensome to him, or lest he be disturbed by a storm of anger. Human beings often act this way, concealing vengeance so that they may not labor or suffer.

“To you the poor man is abandoned,” etc. He is poor because he despised all the temporal goods of this world [Col. 0773C], so that you alone might be his hope. He called him an orphan because this world, through which he was carnally begotten, dies as his father. Yet he can now say: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.” To such orphans God becomes a father, saying to them: “Do not call anyone on earth your father.”

**Verse 36.**—“Break the arm of the sinner,” etc. This refers to the one of whom it was said above: “He will rule over all his enemies.” Therefore he called his arm his power. “His sin will be sought”—that is, he will be judged for his sin—and it will not be found, because he himself will perish on account of his sin.

**Verse 37.**—“The Lord will reign forever,” etc. He called the nations sinners and wicked people.

**Verse 38.**—“The desire of the poor,” etc. That desire with which they burned when, amid the straits and tribulations of this age, they longed for the day of the Lord.

The preparation of the heart is that of which another psalm sings: “My heart is prepared, O God; my heart is prepared.” Concerning it the Apostle also says: “But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience.” We must understand, in the proper way, that the ear of God is not a bodily member but the power by which he hears. For it is not right to think that the Lord God is corporeal: he heard not a sounding voice but the preparation of the heart.

**Verse 39.**—“To judge the orphan and the humble,” etc. To judge the orphan is one thing; to judge for the orphan is another. Even one who condemns judges the orphan; but one who pronounces a sentence on behalf of the orphan judges for the orphan [Col. 0774A]. Men are intended here—not only those of whom it was said, “Set over them, O Lord, a lawgiver, so that the nations may know that they are men,” but also the one who is understood to be set over them in that same passage. He will be a man, concerning whom it is now said: “So that man may no longer continue to exalt himself upon the earth,” namely, when the Son of Man comes to judge for the orphan, having stripped off the old man and, in this manner, as it were, lifted up the father.

## Psalm 10

This psalm is sung against the heretics who endeavor to turn us away from the breasts of Mother Church, asserting that Christ is with them and piously, as it were, advising us to pass over to them and migrate to Christ, whom they falsely claim to possess. Since Christ was allegorically indicated in prophecy by many names, he was also called a mountain. Therefore they must be answered in this way:

**Verse 2.**—“In the Lord I trust; how can you say,” etc. I hold to one mountain in which I trust. How can you say that I should pass over to you, as though there were many Christs?

**Verse 3.**—“For behold, sinners,” etc. “They have bent the bow,” namely, the Scriptures, from which they shoot poisoned opinions by interpreting them carnally. “They have prepared arrows in the quiver,” namely, the same words that they launch with the authority of Scripture, so that when they perceive that the light of the Church has been darkened because of the multitude of the ignorant and carnal, and that they cannot be refuted, they corrupt good morals through evil conversations [Col. 0774C].

**Verse 4.**—“For they have destroyed what you perfected,” etc. All heretics, insofar as it lies within them, have destroyed the praise that God perfected from the mouth of infants and nursing children. They harass the little ones with empty and scrupulous questions and do not allow them to be nourished by the milk of faith. But if heretics or Jews have destroyed the praise or law of God, what has Christ done, who said: “I give you my peace,” which they violated by their wicked dissension?

**Verse 5.**—“The Lord is in his holy temple,” etc. It is so, as the Apostle says: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are.” The Lord is in this holy temple of his, which consists of many members, each performing its own functions, built by love into one edifice. It is also understood as heaven, in which he reigns and from which God judges.

“His eyes look upon the poor,” etc. For the poor man has been abandoned to him, and he has become a refuge for the poor. Understand “the sons of men” as those regenerated from the old by faith. In certain obscure passages of Scripture, as though by God’s closed eyes, they are exercised so that they may seek; and again, in certain clear passages, as though by God’s open eyes, they are enlightened so that they may rejoice. This frequent opening and operation in the holy books is like God’s eyelids, which examine—that is, test—the sons of men [Col. 0775A]. They are neither wearied by the obscurity of things, but are exercised by it, nor inflated by knowledge, but strengthened.

**Verse 6.**—“The Lord examines the righteous and the wicked,” etc. Why, then, do we fear that the wicked may harm us if they perhaps share the sacraments with us without a sincere heart, when he examines the righteous and the wicked, and the lover of iniquity harms only his own soul?

**Verse 7.**—“He will rain upon sinners,” etc. “He will rain” refers to the words of preachers flowing down from heaven, which are showers to the devout but snares to those who understand badly or do not believe. The former bear fruit in faith by understanding rightly; the latter, by handling them perversely, strangle their souls in the very act of their distortion. Their punishment and end are those by which the name of God is blasphemed: first they are ravaged by the fire of their desires; then, through the shame of their evil works, they are cast out from the assembly of the blessed; finally, seized and overwhelmed, they pay unspeakable penalties. This is the portion of their cup. I think it is called a cup so that we may not suppose that anything occurs beyond measure or proportion, even in the punishments of sinners, under divine providence [Col. 0775B].

**Verse 8.**—“For the Lord is righteous,” etc. “Righteousnesses” is understood in place of “the righteous.” For among many righteous people, many righteousnesses seem to exist, although God’s righteousness is one and all participate in it. It is as if one face looked into several mirrors: what is singular in the face is reflected plurally in the many mirrors. The face of God is the power by which he makes himself known to those who are worthy. Or certainly, “his face has seen equity,” because he does not make himself known to the wicked but to the good. And this itself is equity.

## Psalm 11

The “eighth” may be understood as the day of judgment, or it may represent the preaching of the Gospel, in which the Jews or heretics, by transgressing the Decalogue of the law, fell as though into the number eleven. Therefore the body of the Church, which is of one voice and one heart, prays to the Lord to be rescued from their condemnation:

**Verse 2.**—“Save me, O Lord, for,” etc. “The holy man has failed,” that is, he is not found, as we speak when we say: “The grain has failed,” or “the money has failed.” Truth, however, is one, by which holy souls are enlightened. But since there are many souls, many truths can be spoken of in them, just as many images appear in mirrors from one face [Col. 0775D].

**Verse 3.**—“Everyone has spoken vain things,” etc. “Neighbor” must be understood as every human being, because there is no one with whom evil should be done, and love of neighbor does not do evil. When he says twice, “in heart and heart,” he signifies a double heart. For someone who knows in his heart that what is true is true nevertheless, in a certain other heart, with truth suppressed and deceit urging him, lies.

**Verse 4.**—“May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips,” etc. He says “all,” so that no one may think himself excepted. By “a tongue speaking great things,” understand pride [Col. 0776A].

**Verse 5.**—“Those who have said, ‘With our tongue,’” etc. Proud hypocrites are signified, placing their hope in their own speech in order to deceive men, and not being subject to God.

**Verse 6.**—“Because of the misery of the needy,” etc. This must be understood as spoken from the person of God the Father, who, because of the needy and the poor—that is, those lacking spiritual goods—sent his Son.

“I will place him in salvation,” etc. “In salvation” must be understood as “in Christ,” according to the saying: “For my eyes have seen your salvation.” In him he is understood to have placed what pertains to removing the misery of the needy and consoling the groaning of the poor. “He acted confidently in him,” according to the Gospel: “For he was teaching them as one having authority” [Col. 0776B].

**Verse 7.**—“The words of the Lord are pure words,” etc. “Pure,” that is, adulterated by no lie, but tested like silver that is assayed, by the sevenfold fire of the Holy Spirit. What he says, “tested on the earth,” the Hebrew edition expressed more clearly by saying: “separated from the earth.”

**Verse 8.**—“You, O Lord, will preserve us,” etc. Here as needy and poor; there as wealthy and rich.

**Verse 9.**—“The wicked walk around,” etc. “They walk around” means in the desire for temporal things, which revolves like a wheel through the repeated cycle of seven days. Therefore they do not reach the eighth, that is, eternity, for which this psalm is titled. “The sons of men are multiplied” means that the righteous are multiplied according to the height of God, when they go from strength to strength [Col. 0776C].

## Psalm 12

**Verse 1.**—“How long, O Lord, will you forget me to the end?” etc. That is: “How long will you delay me from understanding Christ spiritually, who is the wisdom of God and the true end of every intention of the soul?” God is said to turn his face away when he does not grant the soul knowledge of himself, because it does not yet possess a pure eye of the mind.

**Verse 2.**—“How long shall I place counsel in my soul?” etc. Counsel is needed only in adversity. Therefore, “How long shall I place counsel in my soul?” is said as if to mean: “How long shall I remain in adversity?” Or it may be understood as a response, with this sense: “You will forget me to the end, O Lord, and turn your face from me for as long as I place counsel in my soul, so that it may perfectly perform mercy.” God does not direct him to the end, nor grant him full knowledge of himself, which is “face to face.” In the phrase that follows, “sorrow in my heart by day,” we must supply: “How long shall I place it there?” “By day” signifies either continuation, or “day” is understood as the time from which a person, desiring to be freed, places sorrow in his heart, entreating to ascend to eternal things and not to endure the human day [Col. 0776D].

**Verse 3.**—“How long will the enemy be exalted?” etc. This enemy is the devil, or the ungodly people, or carnal habit.

[Col. 0777A] **Verse 4.**—“Look upon me” refers back to what was said: “How long will you forget me to the end?”

**Verse 5.**—“Enlighten my eyes, lest ever,” etc. He prays that the eyes of his heart may be enlightened, lest they be closed by the pleasing failure of sin. The devil’s mockery must indeed be feared: through detestable habit he becomes joyful when he knows that he possesses those whom he has deceived.

“Those who trouble me will rejoice,” etc. Those who trouble are the devils and their angels. They did not rejoice over the righteous man Job when they afflicted him, because he was not moved—that is, he did not depart from the stability of faith. But the fact that a person is not moved and remains fixed in the Lord must not be attributed to himself, lest, when he boasts that he has not been moved, he be moved by that very pride [Col. 0777B].

**Verse 6.**—“My heart will rejoice in your salvation,” etc. “My heart will rejoice in your salvation,” that is, in Christ Jesus, who grants me spiritual goods, not things belonging to the human day. Therefore I will sing to the name of the Most High—that is, I give thanks with joy and use my body in the most orderly manner, for it is the song of the spiritual soul. If some distinction is to be observed here, I will sing with my heart and sing psalms through my works to the Lord, who alone sees; but I will sing to the Lord’s name, which is made known among human beings, and which is useful not to him but to us.

## Psalm 13

Christ is the end of the law. We return to him when we begin to enter upon the good way; we shall see him when we arrive. Therefore he is the end whom the Jews, seeing him come in humility in assumed flesh, did not understand to be the one foretold by the prophets. Thus the psalm begins:

**Verse 1.**—“The fool has said in his heart,” etc. This is more serious because they did not say it merely with their lips, but in their heart, so that unbelief might be joined to an evil desire and become worse. This may also be understood of the nations, who, denying divine providence, think that the world is governed by chance.

“They are corrupt and abominable,” etc. That is, while they love this age and do not love God, these are the very pursuits that corrupt the soul and blind it, so that the fool can even say in his heart: “There is no God.” For because they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a debased mind, so that, stained by the most wicked unbelief, they might be made abominable to the Lord by their errors. What he says, “even to one,” may be understood either as including that one, so that no human being is meant, or as excluding that one, so that the Lord Christ is meant—just as we say: “This field extends to the sea,” without including the sea itself in the field. The latter is the better interpretation: no one is understood to have done good “up to Christ,” because no human being can do good unless he grants it. And the one thing is this: until each person knows the one God, he cannot do good [Col. 0777D].

**Verse 2.**—“The Lord looked down from heaven upon the sons of men,” etc. This may be understood as referring to the Jews, whom he called more honorably “sons of men” because of their worship of the one God, in comparison with the nations. The Lord looks down in order to see through his holy souls, which is signified by the phrase “from heaven.” For nothing is hidden from him in himself. Unless perhaps it is understood in the sense that “he may see” means “he may cause to see,” just as it was said to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear God,” meaning, “Now I have caused it to be known.”

**Verse 3.**—“All have turned aside,” etc. That is, the Jews became such as the nations also are.

“An open tomb,” etc. In an open tomb, either the voracity of a gaping appetite is signified, or, allegorically, those who kill and, as it were, devour those whom they persuade to adopt the perversity of their morals. The opposite is similar to what was said to Peter: “Kill and eat,” so that he might convert the nations to his faith and good morals. It is clear what follows: “They acted deceitfully with their tongues.” Flattery is indeed the companion of the voracious and of all evil people. He calls deceit “poison”; “of asps,” because they do not wish to hear the words of the charmer. The Jews are most appropriately compared to asps: against words of salvation, in their misery they introduced a deadly deafness [Col. 0778B].

“Their mouth is full of cursing,” etc. He calls the feet the advances of a plan, by which we move from an undertaking toward the outcome of affairs. By saying “swift,” he shows that their plans lacked moderation. They were swift to pour out blood—namely, the blood of the divine Savior—so that the enormity of the crime might increase through the deed [Col. 0778C].

“Destruction and misery are in their ways,” etc. All the ways of evil people are full of labors and misery. Therefore they did not know the way of peace, which says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you; and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light.”

**Verse 4.**—“Will they not all know?” etc. The Lord threatens all the ungodly with judgment, saying that at the universal retribution they will know the vengeance, though now they practice wickedness under the freedom they have. “They devour my people,” he says, “as though eating bread”—that is, daily. Bread is daily food; they also devour the people because they derive their own advantages from them, not directing their ministry toward the glory of God and the salvation of those over whom they preside [Col. 0778D].

**Verse 5.**—“They did not call upon the Lord,” etc. For someone who desires what displeases the Lord does not truly call upon him. The Jews also feared losing an earthly kingdom where there was no cause for fear. They said: “If we let him go on in this way, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our nation and our place.” Thus they lost the kingdom of heaven, which they ought to have feared losing. The same is to be understood of all temporal advantages: when people fear their loss, they do not come to eternal things.

**Verse 6.**—“For the Lord is in the generation,” etc. What is said, “For God is in the righteous generation,” refers to what precedes, so that the sense is: “Will they not all know who practice iniquity that God is in the righteous generation?” That is, he is not in those who love the age. For it is unjust to abandon the creator of the ages, love the age, and serve the creature rather than the Creator. “You have confounded the counsel of the poor,” etc., means: “You despised the humble coming of God because you did not see in him the pomp of the age, so that those whom he called might place their hope in God alone, not in passing things.”

**Verse 7.**—“Who will give salvation from Zion?” etc. “Who will give?” Supply: “unless it is he himself, whose humility you despised.” He will come in glory to judge the living and the dead, and to establish the kingdom of the righteous. Because through this humble coming blindness occurred in part in Israel, so that the fullness of the nations might enter, through that other coming what follows will take place: “and thus all Israel will be saved.” On behalf of the Jews, the Apostle also accepted that testimony from Isaiah which says: “Let him come from Zion who will deliver and turn away ungodliness from Jacob,” just as it is placed here: “Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion?”

But if, as often happens, “Jacob” means the people of the Jews, while “Israel” is understood as the nations, it must be considered for different reasons why the particular words have been assigned. For he says: “Jacob will rejoice”—that is, he will be filled with inexpressible joy when he sees what he desired with the most ardent hope; “Israel will be glad,” because it has received the medicine it did not hope for.

## Psalm 14

**Verse 1.**—“Lord, who will dwell in your,” etc. Although “tabernacle” is sometimes used for an everlasting dwelling, when it is taken in its proper sense a tabernacle is a military object. For a time we fight with the devil, and then a tabernacle is necessary in which we may be refreshed. This signifies above all the faith of the temporal dispensation, which was accomplished temporally for us through the incarnation of the Lord. The holy mountain signifies the everlasting dwelling itself.

Observe, however, how beautifully the suitable words are distinguished according to their various senses: “Who will dwell in the tabernacle?” is said of one who is still struggling in the contest of this age; “Who will rest on the mountain?” is said when each of the faithful, after the labors of this age, is refreshed by the security of eternal peace.

**Verses 2–3.**—“He who enters without blemish and practices righteousness. He who speaks,” etc. Some have truth on their lips but do not have it in their heart. It is as if someone deceitfully pointed out a road, knowing that there were robbers on it, and said: “If you go this way, you will be safe from robbers,” and it happened that robbers truly were not found there. The man spoke truth, but he had something else in his heart: he thought otherwise and unknowingly spoke the truth. Therefore it is not enough to speak truth unless the same truth is also in the heart. Deceit is practiced with the tongue when one thing is brought forth by the mouth and another is understood in the breast.

“He did not do evil to his neighbor,” etc. It is well known that every human being must be understood as a neighbor. One does not accept reproach against him who does not readily and rashly believe an accuser [Col. 0780A].

**Verse 4.**—“He has been brought to nothing,” etc. This is perfection: that the malignant one should have no power in a person. And so that nothing may exist in his sight, he must know with complete certainty that the malignant one is present only when the mind turns away from its eternal and unchangeable Creator toward the form of the creature, which was made from nothing. He glorifies those who fear the Lord; such a person can say with the Prophet: “But to me your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honored.”

“He who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive,” etc. These things are not great. But whoever cannot do even these things is much less able to speak truth in his heart, to avoid deceit with his tongue, to bring forth truth as it is in his heart, and to have in his mouth “Yes, yes; No, no”; nor can he refrain from doing evil to his neighbor—that is, to any human being—or from accepting reproach against his neighbor. These are the qualities of the perfect, before whose eyes the malignant one has been brought to nothing. Nevertheless, he concludes even these lesser matters as follows:

**Verse 5.**—“He who does these things will not be moved forever.”

## Psalm 15

Our King speaks in this psalm from the person of his assumed humanity. Concerning him, the royal title written at the time of his Passion shone forth: “Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews.” But in this passage those are truly understood as Jews who retain faith in Christ in their heart for righteousness and confess him with their mouth for salvation.

**Verses 1–2.**—“Preserve me, O Lord, for I have hoped in you. I said to the Lord: You are my God, because you do not need my goods.” That is: “You do not await the achievement of blessedness from my goods.” If these words are understood as spoken from the person of the Lord, it must be noted how perfectly they correspond to the title, which is read in Hebrew in this way: “the humble and simple one of God,” namely, the one who said: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart.”

It must also be observed that he alone is truly Lord who, as he is most excellently defined here, does not need the goodness of a servant. For when we act well, we provide not for God but for ourselves [Col. 0780C].

**Verse 3.**—“To the saints who are in his land,” etc. To the saints who have placed their hope in the land of the living, citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, whose spiritual way of life is anchored in that homeland by hope. It is rightly called God’s land, although they still live in the flesh in these earthly regions. The Father has made his purposes for me marvelous in their progress, through which they understood what benefited them: the humanity of my divinity, by which I died, and the divinity of my humanity, by which I rose again [Col. 0780D].

**Verse 4.**—“Their infirmities have been multiplied,” etc. These infirmities are errors. By seeing through the teaching of the Gospel that they possessed many such errors, they hastened to seek salvation from Christ.

“I will not gather their assemblies from blood,” etc. Their assemblies, therefore, will not be carnal, nor will I gather them after being propitiated by the blood of animals. Rather, through a spiritual transformation they will forget what they were. They will no longer be called by me sinners, friends, and men, but righteous people, my brothers, and sons of God [Col. 0781A].

**Verse 5.**—“The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and my cup,” etc. For they will possess the Lord himself as an inheritance with me. Let others choose for themselves earthly and temporal portions in which to take pleasure; the portion of the saints is the eternal Lord. Let others drink deadly pleasures; the Lord is the portion of my cup.

When I say “my,” I include the Church, because where the head is, there also is the body. For in the inheritance I will gather their assemblies, and through the drunkenness of the cup I will make them forget their former names, so that the glory that I had with you, O Father, before the world existed, may be known also to those whom I liberate. For you will not restore to me what I did not lose; rather, you will restore knowledge of that glory to those who lost it, in whom you will restore it because I am in them [Col. 0781B].

**Verse 6.**—“The measuring lines have fallen for me in splendid places,” etc. The boundaries of my Passion have fallen by lot within your glory, like the possession of the priests and Levites, whose possession is God. What his splendid inheritance is, the Hebrew text explains more clearly by turning toward the Lord: “And you are my beautiful inheritance.”

**Verse 7.**—“I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding,” etc. By this understanding the inheritance can be seen and possessed. But the lower part—my assumed flesh—disciplined me in addition to understanding, even unto death, so that I might experience the darkness of mortality, which that understanding does not possess [Col. 0781C].

**Verse 8.**—“I set the Lord always before my eyes,” etc. For, coming among things that pass away, I did not remove my eye from him who always remains. I arranged this so that, after accomplishing temporal things, I might return to him who is always at my right hand, so that I might remain steadfastly in him.

**Verse 9.**—“Therefore my heart rejoiced,” etc. As if he were saying openly: “Therefore there is gladness in my thoughts and exultation in my words.” Moreover, the flesh will not fail into destruction, but will sleep in the hope of resurrection.

**Verse 10.**—“For you will not abandon my soul in the underworld,” etc. For you will neither give my soul to the underworld to be possessed there, nor allow the sanctified body—through which others too are to be sanctified—to be corrupted [Col. 0781D].

“You have made known to me the ways of life,” etc. Through me you have made known the ways of humility, so that human beings might return to life, from which they fell through pride. In that life you will fill them with joy, so that they will seek nothing further when they see you face to face. In them, because I am in them, you will fill me. There is delight in your favor and propitiation, leading us through the journey of this life to the end of the glory of your sight.

## Psalm 16

This is to be attributed to the person of the Lord, with the Church joined to him, since she is his body.

**Verse 1.**—“Hear, O Lord, my righteousness,” etc. Before the Lord, righteousness certainly has its own voice, which recognizes silent things by the power of its understanding. His is the perfect prayer whose cause and tongue cry out together. “Not from deceitful lips,” that is, it does not proceed toward you from deceitful lips. He prays well whose lips contain no deceit [Col. 0782A].

**Verse 2.**—“Let my judgment come forth from your face,” etc. Let my true judgment come forth from the illumination of your knowledge. Or he says “from your face” in accordance with what you look upon and recognize in me. He rightly asked this because he knew that he possessed no pollution of sin.

**Verse 3.**—“You have tested my heart and visited it by night,” etc. My heart has been tested by the visitation of tribulation. But the tribulation itself should be called not only night, because it usually disturbs, but also fire, because it burns; through it I was examined and found righteous [Col. 0782B].

**Verse 4.**—“So that my mouth may not speak the works of men,” etc. So that nothing may proceed from my mouth except what pertains to your glory—not the works of men who act against your will. Because of the words of your peace and of your prophets, I guarded the difficult ways of human mortality and Passion.

**Verse 5.—“Make my steps firm in your paths,” etc.** May the love of the Church be perfected along the narrow ways by which one comes to your rest. Let the markers of my journey not be moved—those which, like footprints, have been impressed through the sacraments and the apostolic Scriptures, so that those who wish to follow me may look upon and observe them. Or certainly, let me now remain steadfastly in eternity, after I have traversed the hard roads and completed my steps along the narrow paths of your ways. [Col. 0782C]

**Verse 6.—“I cried out, because you heard me,” etc.** Whoever cries out because he is heard is evidently recognized as pure, innocent, and undefiled; for he prayed confidently, because from the purity of his conscience he presumed that he could be heard. Or certainly, it should be understood in this way: I directed toward you the free and vigorous intention of my prayer, because, in order that I might possess this, you heard me when I was praying more weakly. Therefore, let your hearing not abandon my humility.

**Verse 7.—“Make your mercies wondrous, you who save those who hope in you,” etc.** Let your mercies not become cheap, lest they be loved less.

[Col. 0782D]

**Verse 8.—“From those who resist your right hand,” etc.** From those who resist the favor with which you favor me, guard me as the apple of the eye. It appears small and tiny, yet through it the beam of light is directed, by which light and darkness are distinguished. So, through Christ’s humanity, divinity exercises judgment, discerning between the righteous and sinners.

**“Protect me under the shadow of your wings,” etc.** That is, protect me under the shelter of your love and mercy.

**Verse 9.—“My enemies have surrounded my soul,” etc.** His enemies were the Jews. They surrounded his soul—that is, his temporal life—and sought to take it from him.

[Col. 0783A]

**Verse 10.—“They have enclosed themselves in their fat.”** That is, they were covered with the fatness of their joy after their desire had been satisfied by their crime. Therefore their mouth spoke arrogance: “We have no king but Caesar”; and, “You who destroy the temple,” and other such statements.

**Verse 11.—“Now, casting me out, they have surrounded me,” etc.** After casting me outside the city, they now surrounded me on the cross, and fixed the intention of their heart upon earthly things, thinking that the one who was being killed was suffering a great evil.

**Verse 12.—“They have received me like a lion ready for prey,” etc.** They received me like that adversary who goes about seeking someone to devour, and like his cub—namely, the people to whom it was said, “You are from your father the devil”—thinking of the ambushes by which they might surround and destroy the righteous.

[Col. 0783B]

**Verse 13.—“Arise, O Lord; go before him and trip him up,” etc.** Arise, O God, whom the unbelieving people suppose to be sleeping and not to care about human iniquities, before their wickedness is carried out, so that your vengeance may forestall their deed; and thus trip him up. But rescue my soul by raising me from the death inflicted upon me by the wicked. My soul is your sword, which your hand—that is, your eternal power—took up, in order through it to wage war against kingdoms of iniquity and to divide the righteous from the wicked. Rescue it, therefore, from my enemies.

**Verse 14.—“Lord, divide them from the few upon the earth,” etc.** The good are few in comparison with the wicked. But the Jews have been scattered throughout the world, separated from the few among them who believed, and separated from the Church, the land of the living, in their own life—that is, in this life, which they think is their only life because they despair of the eternal one. Nor has only this visible punishment overtaken them: their memory has also been filled with sins which, like darkness, are hidden from the light of God’s truth, so that they have forgotten God.

[Col. 0783C]

“They have been filled with sons, and have left their remnants to their little ones”; that is, they have been filled with the fruits of evil works and have left the sins of their unbelief even to their descendants.

**Verse 15.—“But I shall appear in your righteousness,” etc.** But I, who did not appear to those whose filthy and darkened hearts cannot see the light of wisdom, shall see your face in your righteousness, and shall be satisfied when your glory appears, as will those who understand me.

[Col. 0783D]

It must be carefully noted and diligently impressed upon the memory how clearly the glory of the resurrection of the faithful is declared, according to the Hebrew edition, in these final verses, where it says: “In righteousness I shall see your face; I shall be filled when I awake with your likeness.” For since it is certain that no one can see the face of God, who is the fountain of righteousness, unless the body of Christ has been justified by his grace, he not only gives thanks for so great a gift but also confidently trusts that he will be filled with his likeness when he awakes—that is, when he rises again. For what else is meant by “I shall be filled when I awake with your likeness” than what the blessed Apostle John says: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is”?

[Col. 0784A]

## Psalm XVIII

What is this day on which the body of Christ knows that it must be rescued from the hand of all its enemies, except that day whose glory he clearly expressed at the end of the preceding psalm when he said: “I shall be filled when I awake with your likeness”? For when the Church of Christ has been filled with the likeness of God in awakening—that is, in the resurrection—then it will rejoice that it has been rescued not only from the hand of its other enemies but also from the hand of Saul, by whom death is signified. At the resurrection the saints will mock death, saying: “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” Saul, whose name means “asked for,” bears the likeness of death, concerning which Scripture says: “God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living.” And shortly afterward: “But the ungodly have summoned it by their hands and words.”

[Col. 0784B]

**Verse 2.—“I shall love you, O Lord, my strength; the Lord is my firmament,” etc.** Christ and the Church speak these words—that is, the whole Christ, head and body. “I shall love you, O Lord, through whom I am strong, who strengthened me, to whom I fled.” I fled to you because you set me free.

**Verse 3.—“My God, my helper, and I shall hope in him.”** You first granted me the help of your calling, so that I might be able to hope in you. “My protector, and the horn of my salvation, and my receiver.” You are my protector because I did not presume upon myself, as though I were raising against you the horn of arrogance. Rather, I found you yourself to be the horn—that is, the firm exaltation of salvation; and in order that I might find it, you received me.

[Col. 0784C]

**Verse 4.—“Praising, I shall call upon the Lord,” etc.** Seeking not my own glory but the Lord’s, I shall call upon the Lord, and there will be no source from which the errors of ungodliness can harm me.

**Verse 5.—“The pains of death surrounded me,” etc.** The pains of mortality—that is, of the flesh—surrounded me, and unrighteous crowds, stirred up for a time, acted like rain-swollen streams that soon dry up, in order to trouble me.

**Verse 6.—“The pains of hell surrounded me,” etc.** In those who surrounded me in order to destroy me were the pains of envy, which produce death and lead to the hell of sin. They went before me because they wished to inflict harm first, which would later be repaid to them. Such people ensnare for destruction those whom they have persuaded to evil by their boast of a righteousness in whose name, though not in its reality, they glory against the nations.

[Col. 0784D]

**Verse 7.—“In my tribulation I called upon the Lord,” etc.** From the temple—that is, from my heart, in which he dwells—he heard my voice. My cry, which I possess inwardly before him, not in the ears of human beings, entered his ears.

**Verse 8.—“The earth was shaken and trembled; the foundations of the mountains were disturbed.”** When the Son of Man was glorified, sinners were shaken and trembled, and the hopes of the proud—which had existed in this world—were disturbed, so that temporal hopes would no longer possess a foundation in human hearts.

[Col. 0785A]

**Verse 9.—“Smoke rose in his anger,” etc.** The tearful entreaty of penitents rose when they recognized what God threatened against the ungodly. The fervor of love, arising from knowledge of him, blazed up after repentance. Those who had already died—deserted by the fire of good desire and the light of righteousness, and who had remained cold and dark—were kindled and illumined again, and came back to life.

**Verse 10.—“He inclined the heavens and descended,” etc.** He formed the apostles in humility, while the ungodly, who set their minds on earthly things, did not recognize the darkness of their own wickedness.

[Col. 0785B]

**Verse 11.—“And he mounted upon the cherubim and flew,” etc.** He was exalted above the fullness of knowledge, so that no one might come to the Lord except through love. For love is the fullness of the law. He quickly showed himself to be incomprehensible to those who loved him, lest they suppose that they could grasp him through bodily imaginings. That swiftness by which he showed himself incomprehensible is above the virtues of souls, by which they raise themselves from earth into the air of freedom as though on wings.

**Verse 12.—“And he made darkness his hiding place.”** He made the obscurity of the mysteries and the hidden hope in the hearts of believers the place where he might remain concealed without abandoning them. We are still walking by faith, not by sight, in these same darknesses, as long as we hope for what we do not see and await it with patience. Yet those who believe in him, turning toward him, surround him, because he is in their midst, favoring all equally—in them he dwells at this time as in a tabernacle.

[Col. 0785C]

Therefore no one should suppose that he is already in that future light, when we shall pass from faith to sight, if he understands the Scriptures correctly. For in the prophets and in all preachers of the divine word, teaching is obscure in comparison with the splendor that will be present at his manifestation. Hence it continues:

**Verse 13.—“Because of the brightness before his presence, his clouds,” etc.** His clouds—that is, the preachers of his word—are no longer confined within the boundaries of Judea but have crossed over to the nations. The rebukes by which hard hearts are struck as though by hail, if a gentle and devout spirit receives them, are dissolved into satisfying instruction; when the fire of love has been kindled, hearts revive. All these things have crossed over to the nations in his clouds.

[Col. 0785D]

**Verse 14.—“And the Lord thundered from heaven,” etc.** So that heavenly things might be heard in the depths of human affairs.

**Verse 15.—“And he sent his arrows and scattered them; lightnings,” etc.** He sent evangelists, flying along straight paths on the wings of virtues—not by their own power but by that of the one who sent them—so that to some they might be the fragrance of life leading to life, and to others the fragrance of death leading to death. He also multiplied miracles and troubled them.

[Col. 0786A]

**Verse 16.—“And the springs of waters appeared,” etc.** The prophets, who had not been understood, were revealed, so that upon them the inhabited world, believing in the Lord, might be built. This came from your rebuke, O Lord, and from the inspiration of the spirit of your anger—namely, of the one crying out: “The kingdom of God has drawn near to you”; and: “Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.”

**Verse 17.—“He sent from on high and took me,” etc.** By calling the Church from the nations into a glorious inheritance—a Church without stain or wrinkle—he took me from the multitude of peoples.

**Verse 18.—“He rescued me from my strongest enemies,” etc.** He rescued me from my enemies, who prevailed in afflicting and corrupting this temporal life of mine.

[Col. 0786B]

**Verse 19.—“They went before me on the day of my affliction,” etc.** They harmed me first during the time in which I bear a mortal and laborious body. Since, through the bitterness of miseries, the foundation of earthly pleasure had been shaken and torn apart, the Lord became my protector.

**Verse 20.—“And he brought me out into a broad place; he saved me because he desired me.”** Because I was suffering carnal narrowness, he brought me out into the spiritual breadth of faith, because he desired me before I desired him.

**Verse 21.—“And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness,” etc.** The Lord will repay me according to the righteousness of good will. He first granted mercy before I possessed good will, and according to the purity of my deeds, since he enabled me to do good by bringing me into the breadth of faith.

[Col. 0786C]
