**Verse 22.—“For I have kept the ways of the Lord, and I have not acted wickedly against my God.”** So that perseverance in endurance may attain the breadth of good works which comes through faith.

**Verse 23.—“For all his judgments are before my eyes,” etc.** That is, I continually consider, in persevering contemplation, the rewards of the righteous, the punishments of the ungodly, the scourges of those being corrected, and the temptations of those being tested. I have not cast his righteousness away from me, as those do who fail beneath its burden and return to their vomit.

[Col. 0786D]

**Verses 24–25.—“And I shall be blameless with him, and I shall keep myself from my iniquity. And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness,” etc.** The Lord repays me not only on account of the breadth of faith, which works through love, but also on account of the length of perseverance—not according to what human beings see, but in the sight of his eyes. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal; this pertains to the height of hope.

**Verses 26–27.—“With the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent; with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will appear perverse.”** There is also a hidden depth in which you are understood to be holy with the holy, because you sanctify; and innocent with the innocent, because you harm no one, but each person is bound by the cords of his own sins. You are chosen by the one whom you choose, and with the perverse you appear perverse, because they say, “The way of the Lord is not right,” while their own way is not right.

[Col. 0787A]

**Verse 28.—“For you will save the humble people,” etc.** What seems perverse to the perverse is that you save those who confess their sins, while you humble those who, ignorant of God’s righteousness, wish to establish their own.

**Verse 29.—“For you illumine my lamp,” etc.** Our light does not come from ourselves; rather, you illumine my lamp, O Lord. We are darkness because of our sins, but my God will illumine my darkness.

**Verse 30.—“For in you I shall be rescued from temptation, and in my God I shall leap over a wall.”** Not in myself but in you shall I be rescued from temptation; and not in myself but in my God shall I leap over the wall which sins have raised between human beings and the heavenly Jerusalem.

[Col. 0787B]

**Verse 31.—“My God, his way is undefiled; the sayings of the Lord are tested by fire,” etc.** My God does not come into human beings unless they have eaten the way of faith by which he may come to them, because his way is undefiled. The sayings of the Lord are also tested by the fire of examination, and all who hope not in themselves but in him are not consumed by the same tribulation; for hope follows faith.

**Verse 32.—“For who is God besides the Lord, or who is God besides our God?”** Who is God besides the Lord, whom we serve? And who is God besides our God, whom we, as sons hoping for an inheritance after good service, shall possess as our inheritance?

[Col. 0787C]

**Verse 33.—“God, who girded me with strength and made my way undefiled.”** He girded me so that I might be strong, lest the flowing folds of desire impede my works and my steps. He made the undefiled way of love by which I shall come to him, just as the undefiled faith by which he comes to me.

**Verse 34.—“Who made my feet like those of deer and set me upon high places.”** He perfected my love so that I might pass beyond the thorny and shadowy entanglements of this world, and fixed my intention upon the heavenly dwelling, so that I might be filled with all the fullness of God.

**Verse 35.—“Who trains my hands for battle,” etc.** He teaches me to work for the overcoming of the enemies who try to shut us out from the heavenly kingdoms. He also established the tireless intention of my good works.

[Col. 0787D]

**Verse 36.—“And you gave me the protection of your salvation, and your right hand received me.”** You gave me the protection of your salvation, and the favor of your grace received me.

**“And your discipline corrected me to the end, and your discipline itself will teach me.”** Your discipline, not allowing me to go astray, corrected me so that whatever I do I may direct it toward the end at which one clings to you. That same discipline will teach me how to arrive at the place toward which it directed me.

**Verse 37.—“You widened my steps beneath me, and my footprints were not weakened.”** Carnal narrowness does not impede me, because you have made my love broad, enabling it to act joyfully even with regard to the mortal things and members beneath me. My ways—or the signs impressed upon them for imitation by those who follow—have not been weakened.

[Col. 0788A]

**Verse 38.—“I shall pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I shall not turn back until they fail.”** I shall pursue my carnal affections, lest I be overtaken by them; rather, I shall overtake them so that they may be consumed. I shall not turn away from this intention toward rest until those who hinder me have failed.

**Verse 39.—“I shall crush them, and they will not be able to stand; they will fall beneath my feet.”** I shall crush them, and they will not endure against me. I shall set before them the directed fears by which I walk forever.

**Verse 40.—“And you girded me with strength for battle; you tripped up those who rose against me beneath me.”** You restrained the flowing desires of my flesh by your strength, so that I would not be hindered in such a struggle. You caused those who pursued me to be deceived, so that those who wanted to be above me would be beneath me.

[Col. 0788B]

**Verse 41.—“And you gave me the backs of my enemies,” etc.** You turned my enemies around and made them be my back—that is, you made them follow me. But you destroyed the others who persisted in hatred.

**Verse 42.—“They cried out, but there was no one to save them to the Lord, nor did he hear them.”** For who could save those whom you did not save? They cried not to just anyone but to the Lord, yet he judged them unworthy of being heard because they did not withdraw from their wickedness. This is to be understood especially of the Jews, who cry out in their synagogues but are not heard because they desire the earthly Jerusalem, not the heavenly one.

[Col. 0788C]

**Verse 43.—“And I shall crush them like dust before the face of the wind,” etc.** They became dry because they did not receive the rain of God’s mercy, so that, lifted up by pride, they might be swept away from firm and unshaken hope as from the solidity and stability of earth. They became like the mud of the streets, because they luxuriate and slip along the broad ways of destruction on which many walk.

**Verse 44.—“You will rescue me from the disputes of the people,” etc.** You will rescue me from the disputes of those who said, “If we let him live, the whole world will go after him.”

**Verse 45.—“The people whom I did not know,” etc.** The people of the nations, whom I did not visit in bodily presence, served me. They did not see me with their eyes, but, receiving my preachers through the hearing of the ear, they obeyed me.

[Col. 0788D]

**Verse 46.—“The sons of strangers have lied to me,” etc.** Those who should not be called my sons but rather strangers—those to whom it was rightly said, “You are from your father the devil”—lied to me. These foreign sons, to renew whom I brought the New Testament, remained in the old human being. Like men disabled in one foot—because they held to the Old and rejected the New—they became lame, even in the old law itself, following their own traditions rather than God’s.

For they slandered concerning unwashed hands, because such were the paths they themselves had made and worn smooth through custom, straying from the way of God’s commandments.

[Col. 0789A]

**Verse 47.—“The Lord lives, and blessed is my God,” etc.** I do not understand the God of my salvation according to an earthly custom, nor do I hope for that salvation as earthly; rather, I hope for it from him on high.

**Verse 48.—“God, who gives me vengeance,” etc.** God, who vindicates me by placing peoples beneath me, is my deliverer from my enemies, the Jews, who cried out, “Crucify, crucify.”

**Verse 49.—“And from those who rise up against me you will exalt me,” etc.** From those same people who rose against me while I was suffering, you will exalt me when I rise again, and you will rescue me from their wicked kingdom.

[Col. 0789B]

**Verse 50.—“Therefore I shall confess to you among the nations, O Lord,” etc.** Therefore the nations will confess you on my behalf, O Lord, and you will become more widely known through my good works.

**Verse 51.—“Magnifying the salvation of his king,” etc.** God magnifies and makes beloved the salvations which his Son grants to believers. He shows mercy to his Christ—to that deliverer himself, who by a strong hand conquered this world—and to those whom he begot eternally as believers through the Gospel.

Whatever has been said in this psalm that cannot properly apply to the Lord himself, that is, to the head of the Church, must be referred to the Church. For the whole Christ speaks here, in whom all his members are present.

## Psalm XVIII

The title is known; it is not the Lord Jesus Christ who says these things, but they are said concerning him.

**Verse 2.—“The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands.”** The righteous evangelists, in whom God dwells as in heavens, expound the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, or the glory by which the Son glorified the Father upon earth. The firmament proclaims the Lord’s mighty works: for confidence in the Holy Spirit became a firmament and a heaven, though formerly it was earth through fear.

[Col. 0789C]

**Verse 3.—“Day pours forth speech to day, and night makes known knowledge to night.”** The Spirit brings forth to spiritual persons the fullness of God’s unchangeable wisdom: that the Word in the beginning is God with God. The mortality of the flesh, by insinuating faith to carnal persons as though far removed, announces the knowledge that is to come.

**Verse 4.—“There are no utterances nor speeches through which the voices of the evangelists have not been heard.”** This is so when the Gospel has been preached in every language.

[Col. 0789D]

**Verses 5–6.—“Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. He set his tabernacle in the sun,” etc.** The Lord, about to wage war against the kingdoms of temporal error and to send not peace but a sword into the earth, placed in time, or in manifestation, as it were a military dwelling-place—namely, the dispensation of his incarnation. He came forth from the virgin womb, where the Lord of human nature was joined like a bridegroom to a bride. “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course,” etc. He rejoiced as the strongest, surpassing all other human beings by incomparable strength, not to remain but to run his course.

**Verse 7.—“His going forth is from the highest heaven.”** That is, his equality with the Father, born from the Father, is not temporal but eternal. “And his meeting is unto its height,” etc. He reaches, in the fullness of divinity, unto equality with the Father. But when the Word also became flesh and dwelt among us, taking up our mortality, he allowed no mortal to excuse himself on account of the shadow of death; even this was penetrated by the heat of the Word.

[Col. 0790A]

**Verse 8.—“The law of the Lord is undefiled, converting souls,” etc.** The law of the Lord is he who came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it. The law is undefiled because he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth; it does not oppress souls with a yoke of servitude but converts them in freedom to imitate him. His testimony is faithful, because no one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom he wills to reveal what is hidden from the wise and revealed to little ones; for God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.

[Col. 0790B]

**Verse 9.—“The righteousnesses of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts,” etc.** All the Lord’s righteousnesses are right in him who did not teach what he himself did not do, so that those who imitated him might rejoice in them in heart, because they acted freely with love, not slavishly with fear. His commandment is bright, without the veil of carnal observances, illuminating the sight of the inner person.

**Verse 10.—“The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever,” etc.** This is not the penal fear under the law, dreading the loss of temporal goods, through love of which the soul is defiled; rather, it is the holy fear by which the Church, the more ardently she loves her bridegroom, the more diligently takes care not to offend him. Therefore perfect love does not cast this fear out, but it endures for ever and ever. His judgments also—he who judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son—are truly and unchangeably justified. For God, whether threatening or promising, deceives no one; nor can anyone rescue either the ungodly from his punishment or the pious from his reward.

[Col. 0790C]

**Verse 11.—“More desirable than much gold and precious stone,” etc.** Whether “much” qualifies the gold and stone themselves, or “precious,” or “desirable,” God’s judgments are nevertheless more desirable than the pageantry of this world. Desire for that pageantry causes God’s judgments not to be desired, but to be feared, despised, or disbelieved. If anyone himself is gold and a precious stone, so as not to be consumed by fire but taken into God’s treasury, let him desire God’s judgments more than himself, whose will he sets before his own. Whether anyone is already honey, because, released from the bonds of this life, he awaits the day when he comes to God’s feast; or is still a honeycomb, so as to be wrapped about as it were with wax by this life—not congealed to it, but filling it—he needs some pressure from God’s hand, not a crushing hand but one that presses out, by which he is transferred from temporal life into eternity. God’s judgments are sweeter to him than he is to himself, because they are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.

[Col. 0790D–0791A]

**Verse 12.—“For your servant also keeps them,” etc.** He says: This is why they are so sweet to me: because I keep them. For the day of the Lord is bitter to one who does not keep them. Thus there is great recompense not in any external advantage, but in keeping God’s judgments itself, because one rejoices in them.

**Verse 13.—“Who understands transgressions? Cleanse me from my hidden faults,” etc.** But what sweetness can there be in transgressions, where there is no understanding, since who understands transgressions? They shut up the very inner place to which truth is sweet, to which God’s judgments are more desirable and sweeter; and as darkness prevents the eyes from seeing, so transgressions prevent the mind from seeing either the light or itself. Therefore, “Cleanse me,” he says, “from my hidden faults, O Lord, and do not lead me astray through things alien.” For one who is clean from his own faults is not captured by alien ones. Spare, then, your servant from alien desires—not one who is proud and wishes to be in his own power.

[Col. 0791B]

**Verse 14.—“If they have not ruled over me,” etc.** A translation from the Hebrew makes the sense of this verse clearer, where it reads: “Deliver your servant also from the proud; if they have not ruled over me, then I shall be undefiled.” The proud and alien ones are understood to be malignant spirits, irrevocably alienated from God by the enormity of their pride; their dominion has oppressed the human race through sin. Therefore, after praying above, “Cleanse me from my hidden faults,” he appropriately adds at once: “If they have not ruled over me, then I shall be undefiled.” For if those spirits, proud and alien to God, obtain no power in us through the desert of sin, then, having received swift remission, we shall truly be undefiled. Since pride is the root and tinder of all sin, by which both the devil fell and the first human being brought death into the world, we too shall be cleansed from this greatest transgression when freed from the power of demons. Their prince is lord over the proud, as is written of him: “He is king over all the children of pride.”

[Col. 0791C]

But if we read, as some manuscripts have it, “if mine have not ruled, then I shall be undefiled,” the sense is this: if my own hidden and alien things have not ruled over me, then I shall be undefiled. For there is no third origin of sin besides one’s own hidden fault, by which the devil fell, and the alien fault by which the human being was deceived so as, by consenting, to make it his own. “And I shall be cleansed,” he says, “from the greatest transgression,” namely pride. For there is no greater transgression than apostasy from God, which is the beginning of human pride. Truly undefiled is the one who is free even from this transgression, because for those returning to the Lord it is the last thing, though for those departing it was the first.

[Col. 0791D]

**Verse 15.—“And the words of my mouth shall be such as please,” etc.** The meditation of my heart is not for the boastful purpose of pleasing human beings, since pride is now absent, but is always before you, who behold a pure conscience.

**“O Lord, my helper and my redeemer.”** O Lord, you are my helper as I stretch toward you, because you are my redeemer, so that I might stretch toward you. Thus no one who attributes to his own wisdom his conversion to you, or to his own strength his arrival at you, may be driven further from you, who resist the proud; for he has not been cleansed from the greatest transgression and has not pleased in your sight. You redeem us so that we may turn, and help us so that we may arrive at you.

[Col. 0792A]

## Psalm XIX

The title is known, and it is not Christ who speaks, but the Prophet speaks to Christ, singing in the form of a wish about things that are to come:

**Verse 2.—“May the Lord hear you on the day of tribulation; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you,” etc.** May the Lord hear you on the day when you said, “Father, save me from this hour.” For the people born afterward belong to you, because “the greater shall serve the lesser.”

[Col. 0792B]

**Verse 3.—“May he send you help from the sanctuary,” etc.** May he make the sanctified body—the Church—for you; it awaits you as though from a watchtower, watching for your coming from the wedding feast.

**Verse 4.—“May he remember all your sacrifice,” etc.** May he make us mindful of all the injuries and insults you endured for us, and may he turn the cross, on which you were offered wholly in soul and body to God, into the joy of the resurrection.

**Verse 5.—“May he grant you according to your heart,” etc.** May he grant you not according to the heart of those who thought that they could destroy you by persecuting you, but according to your heart, since you knew what benefit your suffering would bring. May he confirm all your counsel—not only the counsel by which you laid down your soul for your friends, so that the grain that had died might rise more abundantly, but also the counsel by which a partial blindness came upon Israel, so that the fullness of the nations might enter and thus all Israel might be saved.

[Col. 0792C]

**Verse 6.—“We shall rejoice in your salvation,” etc.** We shall rejoice because death will harm you nothing; for in this way you will show that it can harm us nothing either. The confession of your name will not only not destroy us but will also magnify us.

**Verse 7.—“May the Lord fulfill all your requests,” etc.** May the Lord fulfill not only the requests you made on earth but also those by which you intercede for us in heaven. For now it has been shown to me through prophecy that the Lord will raise up his Christ.

[Col. 0792D]

**“May he hear him from his holy heaven,” etc.** May he hear him not only from earth, where he asks to be glorified, but also from heaven, where, already interceding for us at the right hand of the Father, he poured out the Holy Spirit upon those who believe in him. Our powers, however, are the salvation of his favour, since he even gives help in tribulation, so that when we are weak, then we may be strong. For vain is the salvation of human beings, which is not his right hand but his left. Behold, all who have been made temporally safe while sinning are lifted up in great arrogance.

**Verse 8.—“Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we shall call upon the name of the Lord our God.”** Some are dragged along by the revolving succession of temporal goods, while others are lifted up in pride and exalt themselves through honors, rejoicing in them. But we, fixing our hope upon eternal things and seeking not our own glory, shall rejoice in the name of the Lord our God.

[Col. 0793A]

**Verse 9.—“They are bound and have fallen,” etc.** They were bound by desire for temporal things. Fearing to spare the Lord lest they lose their place from the Romans, and rushing against the stone of stumbling and rock of offense, they fell from heavenly hope. A partial blindness came upon Israel, because they were ignorant of God’s righteousness and wanted to establish their own. But we, so that the fullness of the nations might enter, were raised up from stones as sons of Abraham. Though we were not pursuing righteousness, we seized it and rose; we were raised upright not by our own strength but by faith, having been justified.

[Col. 0793B]

**Verse 10.—“Lord, save the king,” etc.** Lord, save the king, and may he himself, who showed us through his suffering an example of fighting, also offer our sacrifices—the priest raised from the dead. Now that he offers on our behalf, hear us on the day when we call upon you.

## Psalm XX

The title is known; it is sung about Christ.

**Verse 2.—“O Lord, the king will rejoice in your strength,” etc.** O Lord, the man Christ Jesus will rejoice in your strength, because the Word became flesh; and he rejoiced greatly in this, that you give life to all things.

**Verse 3.—“You granted him the desire of his heart,” etc.** He desired to eat the Passover, and, when he wished, to lay down his soul and take it up again; and you granted it to him. “I leave you my peace,” he said, and it came to pass.

[Col. 0793C]

**Verse 4.—“For you went before him with blessings of sweetness,” etc.** He had first drawn in the blessing of your sweetness; therefore the gall of our sins did not harm him. At the beginning of his preaching, precious stones—his disciples—came around him, and from them the proclamation of his message would begin.

**Verse 5.—“He asked life of you, and you gave him length of days,” etc.** He asked for the resurrection, saying, “Father, glorify your Son.” You gave him the long ages of this world, which the Church would possess, and thereafter eternity forever and ever.

[Col. 0793D]

**Verse 6.—“Great is his glory in your salvation,” etc.** Great indeed is his glory in the salvation by which you raised him; but you will add glory and great splendor to him when you place him in heaven at your right hand.

[Col. 0794A]

**Verse 7.—“For you will make him a blessing,” etc.** This is the blessing that you will give him forever and ever: you will make him rejoice with joy at the sight of your face, according to the human nature which he raised to you.

### Verse 8

For the king hopes in the Lord, etc. Because the king does not grow proud, but hopes in the Lord with a humble heart, and will not be disturbed by the mercy of the Most High, humbling himself and becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross.

### Verse 9

Your hand shall be found by all your enemies, etc. May your power, O King, be found when you come to judge all your enemies, who did not understand it in your humility; and may the glory with which you reign at the right hand of the Father find, on the day of judgment, those who hated you, to be punished—because now they themselves did not find it.

### Verse 10

You shall make them like a fiery furnace, etc. You will establish them burning inwardly with the consciousness of their impiety at the time of your manifestation. Then, troubled by the Lord’s vengeance after the accusation of conscience, they will be handed over to an everlasting fire to be devoured.

### Verse 11

You will destroy their fruit from the earth, etc. You will destroy their fruit from the earth because it is earthly; and you will not count their works, nor those whom they led astray, among the sons of men whom you have called to an everlasting inheritance.

### Verse 12

For they have turned evil against you, etc. This punishment will be repaid to them because the evils which, while you reigned, they thought were impending for themselves, they turned against you to be killed; and they devised plans, saying: “It is expedient that one man should die for all.” And: “Come, let us kill him, and we have his inheritance.” These plans they could not establish because they did not know what they were saying, nor did they obtain what they desired.

### Verse 13

For you will set them as a back, etc. You will arrange them among those things from which, after they have been rejected and despised, you turn away; and among those things which you leave behind—that is, the desires of an earthly kingdom—you will prepare for yourself their shamelessness for the Passion.

### Verse 14

Be exalted, O Lord, in your strength, etc. O Lord, whom they did not recognize in humility, be exalted in your strength, which they thought was weakness. But we shall celebrate your wonders with heart and deed, and make them known.

## Walafrid Strabo, monk of Fulda: Epitome of Rabanus’s Commentaries on Leviticus

(Colvenerius, *Works of Blessed Rabanus Maurus.)* (G)*

## Preface

I, Strabo, have endeavored to abridge the briefest possible annotation of the following book, that is, Leviticus, with the abbot Rabanus—an illustrious man, splendidly adorned in many forms of knowledge of divine utterances—handing it on to me, insofar as the weakness of my little intellect permitted. Since I do not recognize in myself a tenacious memory, I may at least, by returning to these scraps of little glosses, recover some portion of what was handed down to me.

But because I could by no means conceal this from the knowledge of others [lacuna; Note: Col. 0795C, something is missing], I earnestly beg you, whoever you may be who reads this, that if you find anything in it said otherwise than it ought to be said, you should begin to attribute it not to the man who, drawing from this full fountain of wisdom, transmitted it to me, but to my own incompetence, since through lack of understanding I could easily have gone astray.

For I have taken care, in accordance with the Catholic faith, insofar as the author of faith has deigned to grant faith to me, to store up for the nourishment of my soul what has been sown within me. In the exposition of this book, however, my guide was Hesychius, presbyter of Jerusalem, sound in faith and supported by truth, together with the other holy teachers.

Read happily.

## Chapter One

**VA-YIQRA**, that is, Leviticus, as though it were “the book of offering” or “the priestly book.” The clear order of things proves that this book is connected with the preceding one, because in it the tabernacle was being constructed, and concerning this tabernacle the commands contained in the book [of Exodus] were given for observance. That tabernacle signifies either the Church or Holy Scripture, from which the fullness of all sound doctrine is supplied to us.

Moreover, when it is said that the Lord called Moses from the tabernacle of testimony, this signifies that the Lord instructs the teachers of the Church in the disciplines of the Church through Holy Scripture, for the salvation of the faithful. They speak to the children of Israel—that is, they impose the counsel of salvation upon the faithful.

“Any man who offers a sacrifice.” He says “man” so that the one who desires worthily to offer vows to God may use well the reason implanted in him and not be made like foolish beasts.

It is called a *hostia*—a sacrificial victim—from the fact that it was led to the door of the tabernacle and there offered to the Lord.

“From the cattle,” that is, from the works of active life which are performed according to the flesh. In what follows he makes mention of the contemplative life, where he treats of birds.

“From oxen and sheep.” In oxen we understand good works performed for the brethren; in sheep, works of simplicity by which one abstains from every injury. Hence the Lord says: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10). As though he were saying: “Wise,” so that you may distribute works of mercy to the brethren; “simple,” so that you may not willingly harm anyone.

“Offering victims.” A victim is so called because it was bound and killed for victory, and was offered; it signifies every good work offered to the Lord.

“If his offering is a burnt offering.” A burnt offering is something wholly burned, and it signifies those works which are judged worthy of God in every respect.

“From the herd,” that is, from the multitude of good works.

“A male without blemish,” that is, the work in which there is nothing fragile or languid with feminine softness.

“One year old,” that is, such a sacrifice as is perfect and tested.

“To the door of the tabernacle” it is to be brought, that is, to the teaching and examples of the holy Fathers—namely, of the apostles and the others.

“He places his hand upon the head of the victim”: the one who, at the beginning of good will, does not delay to devote himself to the efforts of good works, and thus may advance toward the remission of sins.

“And he shall sacrifice the calf before the Lord.” Since a calf is a joyful creature, it teaches that the work of the Lord is to be performed with spiritual joy.

“The sons of Aaron,” who offer the sacrifice, are to be Christians and faithful people, whom the apostle Peter calls “a chosen generation, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2). For just as Christ is both priest and victim, so Christians ought to offer spiritual victims both through themselves and in themselves.

They offer blood—that is, their soul—because in Genesis blood is called the soul of the flesh. It is poured around the altar. Every good work is perfected in remembrance of Christ’s incarnation. Hence the Lord says: “Whenever you do this, do it in remembrance of me.”

Concerning this altar it is said above: “You shall make an altar of earth for me.” “Which is at the door of the tabernacle,” because at the entrance of faith we are immediately instructed in the faith of Christ’s incarnation.

The skin is removed when the excess of riches and possessions is diminished, so that the victim of good work may be sacrificed with greater freedom. That the skin signifies these riches is shown in Job when it says: “Skin for skin” (Job 2), and so forth.

The limbs are cut into pieces when the individual senses in the body are prepared for the service of the Lord.

A pile of wood is arranged when the examples of Peter and the Fathers are taken up for imitation. Fire is placed beneath when a good work is consecrated by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

The head is the primacy of the mind. In the liver every desire is understood. For philosophers say that the liver is the seat of heat for digesting food and the root of desire.

“With the intestines and feet washed.” The intestines are soiled with dung, in which filthy thoughts are shown. The feet, which often touch unclean things, signify those works which cannot in any way be separated from worldly affairs. Yet both these and the former must be cleansed with the water of compunction and thus fitted for sacrifice to the Lord.

When anyone offers such a victim, he is the Lord’s priest, because the Lord receives from his hand the fragrance of sweetness, being pleased by such sacrifices.

“But if the offering is from the cattle,” and so forth. In oxen we understand strong works; in sheep, simplicity of life; in goats, repentance for sins.

We have spoken above of the unblemished burnt offering and the year-old victim. It is commanded that it be sacrificed beside the side of the altar facing north, so that everything may be done in remembrance of Christ, just as we confidently implore all petitions through our Lord Jesus Christ, adding after the petition, “Through our Lord Jesus Christ,” and so forth.

The northern side, dark as though far from the sun, signifies that whatever a person labors at in this life, he does not know how highly it is valued by God, except that the firmness of hope teaches him to hope. For it is written here: “There are righteous people whose works are in the hand of God, but no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred” (Wis. 3; Eccles. 9).

Alternatively, the north signifies the nations that have grown sluggish in the coldness of unbelief. In every work of that propitiation, however, it is fitting that we be mindful, because Christ cared for the Gentiles, freeing them from the lord of the devil, who boasted that he sat in the sides of the north.

We have spoken of the blood and the altar. The limbs are divided when right discernment is preserved in all virtues. Of the head and the other things that are to be offered, and of the wood, fire, and priest, we have already spoken above.

“But if the offering of a burnt offering is from birds,” and so forth. Until now he has discussed the labors of the active life; now he adds a discussion of the purity of the contemplative life.

The turtledove, which does not join itself to another after the death of its mate, signifies chastity. The dove, however, which sits in a tree and watches the water, foreseeing the hawk’s arrival, signifies simplicity and vigilance. For holy souls, resting in a tree—that is, in the height of the virtues—and in water—that is, in meditation on the divine law—know how to anticipate the snares of the ancient enemy.

The head is bent back toward the neck, so that Christ, although he surpasses all in divinity, may not, in the estimation of any faithful person, be separated from the unity of the Church, which is his body.

Alternatively, when you draw near to heavenly things, do not entirely neglect care for the flesh, from which you may stand more firmly. For although the Apostle says, “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13), it is said elsewhere: “Who has ever hated his own flesh?” (Eph. 5).

“When the place of the wound is opened, the blood runs down upon the edge,” or “the *hasim* of the altar,” as another edition reads. This occurs when, once good intention has been disclosed, the whole of life is consecrated according to evangelical teaching.

The vesicle, which always appears swollen, and the feathers—the roots of gentleness—are thrown down beside the altar on the eastern side, where the ashes are customarily poured out. This signifies that, for Christ’s sake, every swelling of pride and the vanity of gentleness are restrained in remembrance of our origin, where we understand our corruption, so that the offering of contemplative purity may be completed without any admixture of malice; so that we may not think more highly than we ought (Rom. 12), and may not attempt to add anything unworthy to these things.

The armpit is the part where the wings are joined to the body. The armpits are commanded to be broken, not divided with iron, so that in the contemplation of God nothing may be attacked or investigated by the iron of deceit and schism. Rather, it is to be received, observed, and offered in the service of the Lord by the hand—that is, by the simplicity of understanding which the Lord grants.

The remaining matters added concerning these things have been discussed above.

## Chapter Two

“When a soul offers an offering of sacrifice to the Lord.” He uses “soul” for the whole person, just as he says that Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy souls, and so forth. He says “soul” because he is going to speak of spiritual matters. Spiritual understanding is perceived by the capacity of the mind, not of the body.

The sacrifice was offered to the Lord in bread and in the fruit of the earth. Fine flour, nobler than every kind of bread, while bread is stronger than every food, signifies divine wisdom. Elsewhere it is compared with gold, which is more precious than all metals. Isaiah named it first among the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the Lord placed it at the point of perfection in the list of beatitudes, after the lesser qualities had been enumerated, saying: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5). For there is no greater wisdom than to become a son of God through the merits of the virtues.

Oil denotes charity and mercy, without which wisdom perishes. The same meaning is signified by it everywhere in what follows.

Frankincense indicates continual prayer. “For if anyone,” says the apostle James, “lacks wisdom, let him ask it of God, and it will be given” (James 1), and so forth.

These things are commanded to be offered to the sons of Aaron, so that whoever has received from God the knowledge of understanding may confer with spiritual teachers, lest perhaps, while praying, he fall into the devil’s snares. For Paul, although he had learned the Gospel through God’s revelation, nevertheless, as he himself testifies, went down to the apostles and conferred with them, lest he should be running or should have run in vain (Gal. 3).

“One of whom,” and the rest. “One” is understood in relation to the unity of faith, and Paul says: “One Lord and one faith” (Eph. 4), and so forth. The same apostle says elsewhere: “I beseech you to think the same thing and all to speak as one” (Phil. 2).

A full handful is sacrificed so that each person may attempt to investigate as much as he is able to grasp, and not attempt more than he can contain.

A portion of the flour and oil is sacrificed, but all the frankincense, because the perfection of wisdom, charity, and mercy is not fulfilled in this life in any of the saints. For Paul says: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 13). Concerning charity he says: “But greater is charity than these,” because in this life it cannot be perfected together with hope and faith; rather, it remains to be perfected in the future.

Concerning mercy also he says that one ought to desire beyond one’s powers. It is therefore not perfected here, because we ought to desire to do what we cannot do.

The frankincense, however, is burned entirely, because one must pray without interruption, so that whatever we do, we may do in the name of the Lord.

A memorial portion is placed upon the altar in remembrance of the Lord’s incarnation, as was said above. The remainder is given to the priests. This agrees with the fact that the apostles gathered up the fragments left over from the crowds, so that what the lesser are unable to understand may be reserved for the greater to take up.

“But when you offer a sacrifice baked in an oven, from fine flour—namely, loaves kneaded without leaven and mixed with oil.” The oven is the womb of the Virgin, where the bread that descended from heaven was prepared for our salvation through the operation of the Holy Spirit.

When you treat of these matters, bring forward loaves from fine flour—that is, the firmness of evangelical teaching—without leaven, that is, without the bitterness of error. Hence the Lord says: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Matt. 16), meaning their malicious teaching.

Let the loaves themselves be mixed with oil: that is, let the very inquiry and investigation of wisdom be seasoned with mercy and charity.

Unleavened cakes spread with oil are bread, broad and thin. To the extent that they lack the firmness of bread, the Law and the narrative of the prophets are weaker than the brightness of the Gospel and the knowledge of the apostles. Yet they are spread with oil, because in the precepts of the Law the observance of charity and the effect of mercy are purified; and the prophets foretold the coming mercy and charity of the arriving Christ.

An offering from the griddle, made from fine flour mixed with oil, is commanded. The griddle, which lies between the fire and the food, protected against the fire by its very great strength, hardening some soft things and softening some hard things, signifies the cross of Christ. It was a mediator because it supported the food, and through it the heat of the Passion was kindled.

Unless the heavenly bread had been roasted upon it, the mystery of his body would in no way have been disclosed for the salvation of the human race. For the whole dispensation of his incarnation looked toward the consummation of the cross. Hence all our creation is subjected to him because of the power of the cross.

For the Apostle says: “He became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him a name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2), and so forth.

The power of this cross subdued some hard hearts into the gentleness of meekness, while it raised up other soft and weak hearts through the strength of steadfastness, so that both might be joined to the body of Christ.

Therefore, if anything is to be discussed, let it be investigated with the fine flour of wisdom and with true charity.

We have already spoken of the leaven. It is divided into small pieces when the individual aspects of his Passion are worthily enumerated: namely, what was accomplished by the betrayal, the scourging, the placing of the crown of thorns, the mockery of the blows, and other things of this kind.

A sacrifice from the grate is a worthy discussion of Christ’s death. Just as a strong fire is kindled beneath the griddle so that the food may be cooked, while beneath the grate the coals of consumption are placed, so also the force of the Passion roasted Christ’s flesh through the cross; and after these things had been accomplished, death received it for a moment, so that it might strip it of the condition of mortal life.

Therefore, whenever the matter is to be discussed, let the fine flour be mixed with oil, let it be handed over by the hands of the priest, let the memorial portion be burned, and let what remains be left to the priests. We have already spoken above concerning all these matters.

“Every offering that is offered to the Lord shall be made without leaven,” that is, every work of service to God must be free from the malice of alien teaching.

Nor shall any leaven or honey be burned in the sacrifice to the Lord. Honey signifies the sweet and sonorous eloquence of philosophy, by which unstable people are enticed toward depraved judgments.

Only their firstfruits and offerings are presented, because the elements of letters and the instruments of the liberal arts, which philosophers discovered, are to be used for the benefit of the holy Church. Their false theology is not to be repeated as offerings to the Lord, nor are divine matters to be investigated through their disputations.

“Whatever sacrifice you offer, you shall season with salt.” He exhorts us to apply the sweetness of divine wisdom to every good work.

An offering of firstfruits is made from green ears of grain when the beginning of some good work and discipline is commended to the grace of the Lord. Since it has not yet reached maturity—that is, perfection—it must also be cleansed and strengthened by the fire of the Holy Spirit. It must be crushed in the manner of meal: once the veil of the letter has been opened, the discipline itself must immediately be investigated to its marrow, in the likeness of perfect wisdom.

For there are certain things that receive wholly an inner sense, not an outward one.

We have already spoken of the oil, the frankincense, and what follows.

## Chapter Three

“But if his offering is a sacrifice of peace offerings, and if he wishes, he shall offer from the cattle a male or female without blemish.”

The burnt offering, which was wholly burned, signifies the works of the highest and greatest kind, such as virginity, concerning which it is said: “Let the one who is able to receive it receive it” (Matt. 19). Likewise, to leave everything is perfection, as is said to that rich man: “If you wish to be perfect” (ibid.), and so forth. These things belong to the few. Hence only a male is commanded to be offered.

Peace offerings, however, are to be offered by either sex—that is, by the strong and the weak—because one is offered from oxen, that is, from strong works, while another offers a gift from sheep, that is, from simplicity of life. Both are to be without blemish, namely, with error and vices laid aside.

The hand upon the head, the entrance of the tabernacle, the blood, and the altar have already been discussed.

The fat that covers the vital organs—that is, the heart and the parts attached to it—signifies anger or some appetite of desire that is nourished inwardly, because the rational soul is said to be rational, concupiscible, and irascible. Whenever it happens that one becomes angry, this ought to be offered to the Lord, so that it may be done for the Lord’s sake and one may not sin in the very agitation, and so forth.

“The kidneys, with the fat by which the flanks are covered,” signify the desire for intercourse. They are offered to the Lord when marriage is undertaken not for lust but for love of offspring.

“The network of the liver”—because the liver is said to digest food—signifies the desire of the appetite, which must be offered to the Lord through abstinence, so that, together with the other virtues, the virtue of moderation may also be sacrificed.

These three kinds of entrails, when they are found in the following she-goats, are understood in the same sense.

From sheep a lamb is offered as a peace offering, when any simple person presents to the Lord the innocence of his life. Its tail also—that is, perseverance in the good all the way to the end—is commanded to be offered, and so forth.

The intestines are understood as above.

“The sons of Aaron” are the teachers, through whose ministry the gifts of the faithful are offered to the Lord.

A goat is present in the offering when someone seeks to obtain the Lord’s favor for himself through repentance.

The things that follow concerning it are understood as the preceding things were.

But what is said in each case—“with the wood placed upon the fire”—is not to be understood as though the Holy Spirit were inferior to our works. Rather, it means that he is the foundation in each work and that, through his help, these works are raised before God’s eyes.

“All the fat shall belong to the Lord by a perpetual ordinance,” that is, all our desire is preserved in the service of the Lord.

He says “by a perpetual ordinance,” not because the rite of the victims was perpetual, but because what it signified in its meaning was perpetual.

“In all your generations,” that is, to the end of the age; “in all your dwelling places,” that is, in every calling or order—of apostles, clergy, monks, or laypeople.

“You shall eat neither fat nor blood at all,” lest anyone live for himself and serve his own desires. What blood does in animals, the soul does in human beings. The soul itself is life, and life principally consists in reason. Everything that reason accomplishes in a human being is to be offered to the glory of the Lord.

## Chapter Four

“When a soul sins,” and so forth. Here he first turns to two chapters, which he explains more fully immediately afterward. Therefore he says “soul,” meaning either a priest or the whole congregation.

“If the priest who has been anointed sins,” and so forth. If we wish to understand these words above the true priest, anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit—namely, Christ—we can say that he patiently endures sinners so that they may return. For Paul says: “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance?” (Rom. 2).

He is said to sin, although he is completely without sin, because he often does not immediately proceed to punish sins. For the sinner, seeing that punishment is delayed, sins more obstinately.

Or our priest is said to sin because of the weakness of his members. For these sins—that is, both the sins of those who, not recognizing God’s patience, sin, and the sins of his members—he offers a calf, namely himself, without blemish and free from every fault. It is sacrificed at the door of the tabernacle, that is, according to what the apostles and the other teachers teach: his Passion has been accomplished.

“He places his hand upon its head.” He himself, since he is both priest and victim, has the power to lay down his soul and to take it up again (John 10).

“He shall sacrifice it before the Lord,” because in all things he fulfilled the will of the cooperating Father.

“He brought the blood into the tabernacle,” because, as the Apostle says, he now appears before the face of God for us (Heb. 9).

“He dipped his finger in the blood”: that is, he completed his entire work in the Passion. For he said: “It is finished” (John 19).

He sprinkled seven times, granting the remission of sins and the grace of the Holy Spirit.

“Against the veil” he sprinkled the blood: that is, he made his flesh a mediator between us and the sanctuary of divinity.

He dipped his finger in the blood—wounded by nails, pierced in the side, and so forth.

He placed some of the blood upon the horns of the altar of incense. The altar of incense signifies the angelic virtues, overflowing with the fragrance of virtues. If certain human beings shine with heavenly virtues, how much more do those whose life never strays outside righteousness? Christ restored their number when he redeemed us.

Thus the Apostle also says: “He made peace by his blood not only between the things on earth but also between the things in heaven” (Col. 1).

He poured the remaining blood at the base of the altar. He himself is the altar in his body for sinners and for those at the lowest places, and he poured out blood for the peoples of the human race, so that it might benefit the angels inwardly and us outwardly.

He pours it at the entrance of the tabernacle because he himself is the door.

We spoke above of the inner organs, showing that they signify various desires. But because some of these are not found in Christ—such as the desire of lust—we should speak generally and say that all his desires worked for our salvation, whether he thirsted, hungered, went to sleep, or desired anything else according to the human nature which he assumed.

He burned these upon the altar of burnt offering when, by right, he completed all things and committed them to be celebrated in his memory.

The head, together with the intestines, and the skin, together with the flesh and feet, are burned together. The head of Christ is God, for Christ is God and man; “with the intestines,” that is, with the rational soul; “and with the skin, flesh, and feet,” that is, the substance of flesh through which he suffered for us. The one God is indivisible.

Dung is also burned there, because he would bear our sins, although he himself did not commit them.

He suffered outside the camp—that is, outside the gate.

He suffered in a clean place, for he cleansed us from sins, where the ashes are customarily poured out—that is, where the heat of our crimes was extinguished by his redemption.

They are burned upon a pile of wood, that is, in accordance with what the prophets foretold, he fulfilled everything completely. For to each individual event the evangelists add: “So that what had been spoken might be fulfilled” (John 19).

The sin of the whole congregation, moreover, signifies the lamentable hardness of the Jews. For, condemning Jesus, they cried: “We have no king but Caesar” (Matt. 27), and: “His blood be upon us,” and so forth (ibid.).

This is not like the sin of the priest, because it occurred through their ignorance and lack of understanding. Peter says to them: “I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your rulers,” and so forth (Acts 3).

Some of them, later understanding their sin, offered a calf—that is, they believed in the crucified one according to the whole truth of his Passion.

The elders of the people placed their hands upon his head, because the chief priests and scribes delivered Christ over to death.

The fact that in this calf the intestines, which signify desires, are likewise commanded to be offered, as in the preceding one, seems to show that the same desires which Christ had for our salvation he commended to us to have for ourselves and for our brethren.

All the other things said concerning the calf are to be understood according to the preceding meaning, so that what was prefigured as something to be done in that sacrifice may be understood as something to be believed in this one.

“If a ruler sins,” that is, one who knows the Lord’s will, to whom the Lord has granted authority and the power of knowledge, “through ignorance,” that is, through negligence, he shall offer a he-goat, that is, strong repentance.

The ruler offers a he-goat, while any soul from the people offers a female goat, because “the servant who knew his master’s will and did not do it shall be beaten severely, but the one who did not know shall be beaten lightly” (Luke 12). “The powerful shall suffer powerful torments” (Wis. 6).

For this is what it means to produce fruits worthy of repentance (Matt. 3): repentance is to be extended according to the character of the faults.

“He places his hand upon its head” when he adorns the beginning of repentance with the exercise of good works.

In the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered, the victim for sin is also slaughtered, because repentance is pleasing to the very Lord to whom the highest works are offered.

The priest dips his finger in the blood and touches the horns of the altar, because Christ receives the offering of repentance—the redemption which he accomplished on the horns of the cross. For he says to his disciples: “This cup shall be poured out for you and for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. 26).

The altar signifies the remembrance of his Passion; its horns signify the horns of the cross on which our redemption was accomplished.

The blood is poured at the base of the altar because, at the beginning of evangelical preaching, the Lord preached repentance, as is read in the Gospel.

Concerning the intestines, as above: every desire is to be offered to the Lord.

The priest prays for the ruler. Christ prays according to his humanity, because he shows the Father the form which he assumed for us, and he is daily our propitiation.

Or this is said by metonymy: he prays in the sense that he causes prayer to be made. For, by his gift, the saints pray for us sinners, which we also implore daily.

“If a soul from the people of the land sins,” that is, a person inferior in status and knowledge, he is released through an easier repentance.

He recognizes his sin, either through divine inspiration or through the admonition of teachers.

All the rest is as above.

He offers a sheep from the flock who sacrifices simplicity of life to the Lord.

All these victims are commanded to be without blemish, so that nothing false may be displayed either in repentance or in works; thus past sins may be mourned, and sins not yet committed may be avoided.

He burned incense upon the altar of the Lord. Let everything be done in remembrance of the incarnation and Passion of Christ, and thus the offering will be acceptable to the Lord.

The rest is as above.

## Chapter Five
“If a soul sins and hears the voice of one swearing an oath,” and so forth. Whoever is aware of another’s sins, if he consents either by approving them or even by failing to judge them, is guilty together with the one who committed them, since he knows himself to be liable [the text reads *reverse esse*, probably for *reum se esse*]. For not only those who commit such acts, but also those who consent to them, are worthy of death.

“The soul that touches anything unclean,” and so forth. The Jews had many categories by which they thought a person was contaminated, such as animals that do not chew the cud, or do not divide the hoof, or do one of these two things but not both. The Lord rebukes them for this superstition: “You are mistaken, not knowing the power of God” (Mark 12). “For it is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth,” and so forth (Matthew 15). He commands us not to consent to sins, whether they are introduced by the devil—such as envy and hatred, pride, and the like—which is to have been killed by a beast, or whether they originate in the person himself, with the devil as instigator—such as lust and gluttony, and the rest—which is to have died of itself. He also calls a sin that clings to earthly filth a creeping thing. A soul is said to be defiled either through negligence or contempt: “For whoever despises small things gradually falls away and slips into greater ones” (Ecclesiasticus 19).

“If he touches anything unclean from a human being,” and so forth. Whoever suffered a discharge of semen was judged polluted, together with everything he used; the same applies to a woman’s menstruation. By forbidding contact with these things, he forbids us to share in anyone’s sins.

“Afterward he has come to know it,” whether through divine prompting or another’s admonition, “he shall be liable to guilt”—that is, he must do penance for the offense.

“The soul that swears and utters it with its lips,” and so forth: that is, if he swears that he will do some evil, or if he vows some good under oath [Col. 0804C] and does not accomplish it, he is guilty of the offense. Herod was deceived in this respect: he wickedly promised something to his daughter under oath and, having fallen into the evil, carried it out fully [the manuscript reads *poenis*, probably for *plenius*].

Whoever does this shall offer a lamb or a she-goat—that is, the innocence of life, as the Apostle commanded: “Let the one who used to steal steal no longer” (Ephesians 4), meaning that the one who previously caused harm should now live innocently. Or let him offer a she-goat, that is, let him undertake strict penance, so that Christ, the true priest, may become his propitiation.

But if he cannot offer livestock—that is, severe penance through fasts, vigils, sackcloth, and the other practices belonging to this—“let him offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons.” That is, let him abandon the world, since the turtledove is solitary; let him pursue chastity and strive to live simply in a monastery or in the desert [Col. 0804D], having a groan instead of a song, like the dove, so that he may mourn his sins and sigh for the desire of eternal life. This also means offering “one for sin and the other as a burnt offering.”

“He shall give them to the priest,” namely, let him entrust his devotion to Christ.

“He shall twist its head back toward the wing-feathers,” and so forth. Because a wing lifts up a bird, he commands the mind likewise to be joined to contemplation without neglecting the necessary care of the flesh, as we said above.

He sprinkles the side of the altar with blood when he offers his life to Christ’s mercy. He pours the remaining blood at the base of the altar when he subjects whatever he does in his life to evangelical teaching.

The priest shall pray for him—that is, Christ himself as man, a member of the priesthood, who offers a sacrifice of praise to the Lord [Col. 0805A].

But if he cannot even abandon the world or fulfill what we have said, let him offer a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour. An ephah contains three measures, and signifies knowledge of the Holy Trinity. He offers a tenth part of it when he places perfect confidence in the humanity of Christ, which the Holy Trinity joined to itself. For the denarius is an indication of perfection.

He does not put oil or any frankincense into it. For one so weak that he does not know how to repent perfectly cannot confidently use spiritual joy or place confidence in his prayer, because he does not know how the Lord’s mercy toward him may be revealed, as the prophet says: “Who knows whether he will turn and forgive, God?” and so forth (Joel 2).

He hands the fine flour to the priest when he entrusts that confidence itself to Christ, admonishing him to fulfill by his generosity what he himself commanded his disciples, saying: “Whenever your brother sins against you and says, ‘I repent,’ forgive him”; and likewise to Peter: “I do not say to you seven times, but seventy-seven times” (Matthew 18) [Col. 0805B].

“He shall burn a full handful of it,” when, mindful of his promise, he bestows his mercy. For since letters are formed by the hand, the firmness of the promise is represented through it.

“He himself shall have the remainder of the flour,” because everything is entrusted to his clemency.

“If a soul, transgressing the ceremonies, should through error sin in matters sanctified to the Lord,” and so forth. This concerns the many things that were sanctified and were not to be appropriated by the rest of the people: for example, the prohibition against making the composition of the anointing oil and incense, and the command that, among certain sacrificial offerings, only males descended from Aaron might eat, while in the case of others both sexes might do so [the citation at Col. 0804C follows the preceding reference].

For such transgressions these commands are given according to the historical sense; but for us it is prescribed that whoever exceeds what is right in holy places and in all things consecrated to the Lord, especially in the handling of the Eucharist, “shall offer for his offense an unblemished ram from the flocks.” That is, by doing penance he should trust in the redemption accomplished through the humanity of Christ.

“One that can be bought for two shekels,” or “for shekels,” as the Septuagint translated it. The number two signifies the two commandments of charity, from which we reach fifty, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit. For penance is corrected in vain unless the commandment of charity is preserved for the one to whom the Holy Spirit is to be poured out [Col. 0805D].

“He shall restore what he caused to be lost”; that is, he shall discharge through penance what he committed as sin.

“He shall add a fifth part to it.” There are five bodily senses: whoever was a minister of one of these must afterward be guarded in the praise of the Lord and in the observance of good works, and so forth, as above.

“If a soul sins through ignorance,” and so forth. He mentioned the same matter above and commanded that a she-goat or a lamb be offered; now he teaches that a ram is to be sacrificed, because penance is nothing if it is undertaken outside the hope of Christ’s forgiveness and redemption.

“According to the valuation of the sin,” because he produces fruits worthy of penance when he tries, with the Lord’s mercy, to amend his life in proportion to the seriousness of his offense. The rest has often been discussed.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0806A]

“The soul that sins and, despising the Lord,” and so forth. He despises the Lord who neglects to amend his life and does not understand that his sin can be exposed and punished by him. Whoever, deceived by such hardness, has in some respect opposed the Lord and gone against his commands, or has knowingly injured his neighbor, shall add a fifth part of the price—that is, confessions made with the tongue. Taste, one of the five senses, belongs to the tongue.

“Let him repay,” and so forth. “And everything intact”—that is, a worthy compensation of penance. And let him offer a ram—that is, let him trust firmly in the Lord’s mercy and prepare himself as one worthy to be heard.

“He shall pray for him,” because he is the protector of all who hope in him.

“Falsely denying,” that is, denying [Col. 0806B]. The rest as above.

“This is the law of the burnt offering: It shall burn on the altar throughout the night until morning.” He seems here to be speaking of the burnt offering in which one lamb was to be offered every day in the morning and another in the evening. As for the rest, we have explained above what the burnt offering signifies spiritually.

Throughout the night until morning, the fire that is on the same altar burns, because the charity that Christ commended when he said, “Remain in my love, just as I have loved you” (John 15), must blaze in the hearts of the faithful until the morning of the future life, when the light of perfect knowledge will shine forth.

The priest is clothed in a tunic, as David says: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Psalm 101). He is also clothed in linen undergarments when he preserves continence and chastity, as the Lord says: “Let your loins be girded,” and so forth (Luke 12).

He places the ashes beside the altar when he entrusts the completion of good works to the Lord, as Paul says: “He is able to guard my deposit,” and so forth (2 Timothy 1) [Col. 0806C]. Alternatively, the altar is understood as the altar of the heart, because eternal charity must be preserved and the completion of labors stored up. Paul says: “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1).

Until it is carried outside the camp—that is, until, after the end of this life, in a completely pure place, when, as the Apostle testifies, “the Lord will bring to light the hidden things of darkness,” and so forth (1 Corinthians 4), he causes it to be consumed down to the ash, that is, stripped of all corruption, and establishes it in the eternal kingdom.

The priest puts on other garments when every believer advances from virtue to virtue. He removes his own garments when, “forgetting what lies behind,” he reaches forward to what lies ahead [Col. 0806D].

The fire on the altar is fed with wood placed beneath it in the morning when, by the examples of the Fathers and the sayings of Scripture in the light of knowledge, the hearts of the faithful are stirred to the ardor of charity.

The fat is the richness of charity. Fine flour mixed with oil is perfect knowledge joined to works of mercy. We have spoken above of the full handful and the incense.

The sons of Aaron eat the remainder because the few offer up the greatest mysteries of divine knowledge, while the lesser perceive the lower mysteries of Christ’s incarnation and the other mysteries. These are eaten in the holy place without leaven—that is, within the holy Church, without philosophical or Jewish superstitions. Only males use them: that is, the stronger, those less inclined to consent to softness and pleasure, are admitted to holy things [Col. 0807A].

“Everyone who touches them”—that is, whoever shows himself worthy of holy things through pure faith and true love—“shall be sanctified,” with holiness and the reception of salvation.

Aaron and his sons shall offer on the day of his anointing a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour, because in his incarnation Christ, when his humanity was anointed with the oil of gladness, established for the faithful the tenth part of an ephah, which contains three measures—that is, the fullness of good works in the knowledge of faith in the Holy Trinity.

“Half of it in the morning and half in the evening.” In the morning he stood before the governor, condemned to death; in the evening, after his passion had been completed, he was placed in the tomb.

This fine flour, mixed with oil, is to be fried in a pan and offered hot, because Christ’s passion was accomplished on the cross on account of the excessive love with which God loved the world [Col. 0807B]. That it is offered hot “as a most pleasing aroma to the Lord” shows that, having suffered out of love for us, he “now appears before the face of God on our behalf, to be our propitiation” (Hebrews 9).

“The priest who succeeds his father by right.” Christ succeeded the legal high priesthood, and the evangelical sacraments succeeded the service of legal sacrifices.

“For every sacrifice of the priests is consumed by fire, and no one shall eat of it.” Since Christ is God and man, born and having suffered for our salvation, he must not be divided by the distinction of human separation. Rather, the entire administration of his incarnation must be entrusted to the knowledge of the Holy Spirit and held by sincere faith.

“In the place where the burnt offering is offered, the sacrifice for sin shall be slaughtered” [Col. 0807C], because the fruit of good penance leads to the holy perfection of the saints. Peter, David, and the other saints are believed, after falling and doing penance, to have been restored to their former dignity; therefore it is called “the holy of holies.”

The priest eats the sacrifice in the court of the tabernacle. Christ receives penance in the Church; for unless he himself receives it and forgives through the remission he has granted, it will not be acceptable to God.

“Whatever touches its flesh shall be sanctified.” The works of penance are fasts, vigils, and many other things. Whoever performs them, even if he has undertaken them beyond the proper measure of penance, will be rewarded with a sure recompense, just as the saints often chastise themselves as though they were involved in the greatest sins.

“If any of its blood is sprinkled on a garment,” and so forth. That is, if the substance of the body of the penitent is stained in the course of his life, he must have hope of election through the baptism he received in the Church [Col. 0807D]. For unless he was first rightly baptized, he will not be corrected by penance. Through baptism past sins are forgiven, and, when preceded by penance, forgiveness for future sins is prepared.

“But the earthen vessel in which it was cooked shall be broken.” If, after remission has been granted through penance, he fastens himself to fragile works, he should already fear that he will be punished by the Lord’s judgment.

Therefore the bronze vessel is scrubbed and washed with water—that is, if he has persevered in the solidity of virtue and steadfastness, he will be cleansed by the fire of the Holy Spirit and by the compunction of tears.

Every male, as above.

“For the sacrifice that is slaughtered for sin,” and so forth. Here he seems to be speaking of the calf that he previously commanded to be offered for sin; it has been discussed in its proper place [Col. 0808A].

“It shall not be eaten, but shall be burned with fire.” Since Christ suffered for our sins, he must not be diminished by teeth, so that he might be said to have died for his own sins—for “he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2). Rather, that mystery must be entrusted to the knowledge of the Holy Spirit and commendably presented with complete faith.

## CHAPTER VII

“This also is the law of the sacrifice for an offense.” An offense may be called what is committed against divine things, while sin refers to what is committed against human beings. The remedy for an offense is acquired through true penance by those wholly devoted to perfection.

Let its blood be poured around the altar [Col. 0808B], so that his life may be entirely inclined to the imitation of Christ. The tail and intestines have been discussed above, and likewise the male animal.

“It shall belong to the priest who offered it.” It belongs to Christ, who offered himself for us; our action belongs to him, through whom we hope to implore forgiveness.

“The priest who offers the victim of the burnt offering shall have its skin.” The skin signifies the outward substance, which is to be given in almsgiving to Christ, that is, to his members, so that penance may thereby be brought to completion. For the Lord says: “As long as you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” (Matthew 25).

“And every grain offering that is baked in an oven,” and so forth. That is, every understanding concerning the incarnation, passion, or death of Christ must be entrusted to him, and no rash opinion should be held about these matters [Col. 0808C].

“Whether mixed with oil or dry”: that is, whether it belongs to one whose knowledge overflows with the gentleness of eloquence, or to one who has the means to give alms; or whether it belongs to one whose knowledge is weaker, who is sluggish because of the slowness of his speech or lacks material resources to distribute.

“Yet it shall be divided in equal measure among each one.” For all must be made equal in the equality and unity of faith, as Paul urges us “to have the same mind” and “to say the same thing” (Philippians 2).

“For thanksgiving”: a gift offered by one who is not compelled to repent by the enormity of his sins, but gives thanks for the divine mercy granted to him.

He offers loaves mixed with oil—that is, he follows the teaching of the Fathers of the New Testament. He also offers unleavened cakes smeared with oil—that is, the understanding of the Fathers of the Old Testament. To be mixed with oil is greater than to be anointed with oil [Col. 0808D], because the former preach the truth of what the latter dreamed would come.

He offers round cakes—that is, the teaching of the orthodox, through whose labor we understand the canonical books. All these are without leaven—that is, without the bitterness of another’s teaching.

He offers leavened loaves—that is, the firmness of faith. For leaven also signifies faith, as the Lord indicates when he speaks of the woman leavening flour.

One loaf is offered among the firstfruits when every good work is begun in the unity of faith.

“And it shall be the priest’s who pours out the blood of the sacrifice,” because faith must be shown to him through whom the offering of our service is presented to the Father.

“Whose flesh shall be eaten on the same day,” because in this life we must preserve the entire perfection of faith in Christ’s passion and present within ourselves a sacrifice pleasing to God. “For after the morning of the future life,” as Solomon says, “there is no wisdom, nor counsel, nor understanding where we are hastening” (Proverbs 21) [Col. 0809A].

“If anyone offers a sacrifice by vow or voluntarily,” and so forth. That is, whether someone offers it by vow, like monks, clerics, and those who renounce the world; or whether someone, suddenly considering a good work, begins it, he must complete that work on the same day—that is, in the present—and tomorrow, meaning during the remaining periods of his life.

“For whatever the third day finds, fire will consume.” Nothing imperfect should be left here to be completed there, that is, in the future life, because “each one’s work will be shown for what it is, for the fire will test it; if anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss,” and what follows (1 Corinthians 3).

“If anyone eats the flesh of the victim on the third day,” and so forth [Col. 0809B]. If anyone thinks that he can complete in the future life what he leaves imperfect here, his work does not please the Lord, and therefore he is liable to condemnation.

“The flesh that has touched anything unclean,” and so forth: that is, a work stained by vices must not be counted as progress or taken as an example; it is reserved for vengeance, as for fire.

“Whoever is clean shall eat of it,” and so forth. It should not be understood as referring to the preceding verse, as though the clean were commanded to eat what is unclean, but to the following verse: the clean person may eat the sacrifice whose flesh is forbidden to the unclean soul.

We are forbidden to receive the body and blood of Christ unworthily, as the Apostle teaches fully; what is commanded is to be handled by the clean.

Alternatively, an unclean soul eats the Lord’s sacrifice when someone outwardly pretends to perform God’s work without good intention—for example, when someone sows or gives away his possessions out of arrogance, and in many similar cases [Col. 0809C].

“And whatever touches the uncleanness of a person,” and so forth. The uncleanness of a person includes the discharge of semen and the other things that, according to the Law, are counted as uncleanness for him.

But he forbids sharing in vices, whether those of a human being—that is, one clever in evil—or those of an animal—that is, one dull-witted and publicly delinquent.

“The fat of a sheep, an ox, and a goat,” and so forth: that is, do not turn toward anything else the desire directed to God by one who acts simply, works courageously, and does penance, but keep it as he rightly intended.

“The fat of a carcass that died,” and so forth: that is, do not turn to your imitation the will of one who is dead through his own sins, as the Apostle says: “The widow who lives in pleasure is dead” (1 Timothy 5); or of one who has been deceived by the devil.

“You shall not eat the blood of any animal,” and so forth: that is, do not envy anyone’s life. For the Apostle says: “See that, if you bite and devour one another, you are not consumed by one another” (Galatians 5), whether the person is spiritual or simple and carnal.

“Whoever offers a sacrifice of peace offerings,” and so forth. Whoever renders thanksgiving to the Lord should add an offering of charity, without which nothing pleases God.

The breast signifies faith and steadfastness; the shoulder signifies good works, which we ought especially to preserve for God.

This is what he says: “It falls to the share of Aaron,” “the one who offers the blood and the fat,” and so forth. It speaks of one person, and therefore faith and good work belong to the one Christ [Col. 0810A].

“The breast of the elevation offering” is so called because faith raises us. It is as though he said: this is the rite of Aaron’s priesthood, to which he was anointed, so that what has already been said may pertain to him.

“On Mount Sinai.” Sinai is interpreted as “bush” or “temptation.” It signifies this present time, in which we are worn down by temptations and the goads of sins and need God’s commandments, which we also receive.

We spoke of Aaron’s consecration in Exodus. Moses signifies either the Law, which foretold Christ’s incarnation, or Christ’s divinity, which raised his humanity to such glory, as it is said: “God, your God, has anointed you with oil,” and so forth (Psalm 44).

The sons of Aaron are Christ’s apostles and their followers.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0810B]

“You shall assemble the whole congregation,” and so forth. Through Christ’s passion the Church is gathered for evangelical teaching.

The garments of the priests, whether you refer them to Christ or to any saint, have already been discussed above.

The tabernacle is smeared with oil, and the altar with its base and the basin are sprinkled, because every instrument of the Church is confirmed both by baptism and by the grace of the Holy Spirit. Its sevenfold sprinkling displays the sevenfold grace.

The calf that is offered signifies Christ. We place our hands upon its head when we preach about his divinity. The foundation of the altar is evangelical teaching, according to which Christ’s passion was accomplished; the rest is as above.
