The rams also represent Christ, and two are mentioned because they commend the two sacraments of his body [Col. 0810C]. The tip of the ear is touched because of obedience, since Christ himself “became obedient to the Father unto death” (Philippians 2).

All the matters included below are to be understood according to the meaning that we have distributed above concerning the sacrifices, whether of Christ or of his members, while each matter is associated with whatever interpretation suits it.

“Taking from the basket of unleavened bread,” and so forth. The various loaves in the basket signify the variety of wisdom in Holy Scripture. For just as that material is joined together from branches, so Scripture, composed of holy sayings, ministers the word of life to the faithful.

For it is also said of Christ according to his humanity: “The child Jesus advanced in wisdom, and age, and grace” (Luke 2). We have explained the meaning of the loaves above.

These things are rendered acceptable to God upon the altar—that is, in memory of Christ’s passion.

The breast of the ram belongs to Aaron as his portion, because Christ seeks that right faith concerning himself be offered to him.

“Taking the anointing oil and the blood,” and so forth. Aaron with his garments and sons—that is, Christ in his holy members—is adorned with grace, with the infusion of the Holy Spirit, and with his redemption; for the Holy Spirit is also read to have descended upon him.

Regarding his garment, it is said that all these are clothed as with an adornment, namely, the congregation of the Church formed from the sons; thus “he gave them power to become children of God” (John 1).

“Cook the flesh before the entrance of the tabernacle,” and so forth [Col. 0810D]. By the fire of the Holy Spirit, according to apostolic teaching, the sacraments of Christ’s incarnation and passion are ministered to the faithful for the support of life [Col. 0811A].

The basket and the loaves have often been discussed.

“Aaron and his sons shall eat them.” Aaron, that is, Christ, is said to eat them because he makes his sacraments effective for us.

“Whatever remains,” and so forth. Whatever remains for us from these things, let us leave to the Holy Spirit, who knows the secrets.

“You shall not go out from the entrance of the tabernacle,” and so forth. Either he commands that the Lord be served in the Church throughout the whole time of life, or it signifies what he commanded his disciples after the passion: “But you,” he said, “remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Acts 1), and so forth.

For from the Lord’s resurrection there are seven weeks, that is, seven times seven days, making forty-nine days. To this number you add the fiftieth day, which comes when the sevenfold cycle of days has been completed on the day of the resurrection. In what follows he calls it the eighth, because, when the preceding days have been counted off in sevens, it comes after seven sevens and so becomes at once the first and the eighth.

“You shall remain day and night,” and so forth: that is, in prosperity and adversity within the Church, observing the watches and the rest; attending to his commands so that you may be made worthy of eternal life.

## CHAPTER IX

“When the eighth day had come,” and so forth. The apostles are to be believed to have celebrated the ministry of Christ’s body on the day of Pentecost, that is, to have sacrificed the calf.

The ram for the burnt offering pertains to him, because he is the leader of the flock, and his entire passion was accomplished by God’s dispensation.

The sons of Israel upon whom hands are imposed are the faithful who were with the apostles. For they are said to have been one hundred and twenty.

They offered a male goat, either by preaching the glory of Christ’s passion, since he was offered for our sins, or because Peter preached penance on that same day.

They offered a living innocent lamb [the text adds, correctly: “living”]; the ox signifies strong works, as they courageously struggle for Christ; the ram is as above.

“In the sacrifice of each one,” and so forth. In each one they displayed divine wisdom, as it is said: “They began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2).

“For today the Lord will appear to you,” as it is written: “Suddenly there came a sound from heaven,” and so forth (ibid.). And shortly afterward: “There appeared to them divided tongues,” and so forth (ibid.) [Col. 0811D]. The rest follows: for the Holy Spirit is God and Lord.

“And Moses said to Aaron: Approach the altar,” and so forth, and afterward, “and pray for yourself.” Christ is said to pray and offer for himself, which he does for his body; or he prayed for himself according to his humanity: “Father,” he said, “into your hands I commend my spirit” (Matthew 27), and many similar passages.

He prays for the faithful people because he offers their vows to the Father, and he is the propitiation for their sins.

He offered the calf. If you apply this to Christ, he offered himself for us; if to a member of the high priesthood, then the calf signifies the strong works that we offer through Christ.

What follows concerning the calf has been discussed above, and likewise the burnt offering.

“Adding libations to the sacrifice”: that is, the instruments of spiritual wisdom in all things [Col. 0812A].

“Without the ceremonies of the morning burnt offering”: that is, of the lamb that he commanded to be offered every morning.

The sons of Aaron offer the blood, which, as the Apostle commanded, the faithful offer whenever they do so in his remembrance.

“They placed the fat of the ox and the tail upon the breasts,” because we must offer every desire and perseverance through faith and in faith.

“Extending his hands,” and so forth. The extension of the hands signifies earnest prayer, as David says: “The lifting up of my hands” (Psalm 140), and so forth.

“And when the sacrifices had been completed, he descended.” The descent signifies that a teacher must sometimes pray and sometimes condescend to teach others, as Paul says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober-minded, it is for you” (2 Corinthians 5) [Col. 0812B].

Alternatively, he extends his hands when he exercises himself in prayer privately; he descends when he returns again to examine his own actions.

“But Moses and Aaron entered … and came out, and blessed the people.” Before the eyes of the Lord, as though at the time of going out, prayer should be poured forth in secret, so that from there, as though at the time of going out, the blessing may be received.

For Paul says: “Blessed be God, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ” (Ephesians 1). First he says “blessed,” that is, he praises God, and afterward recounts the blessing that was given.

“And the glory of the Lord appeared”: that is, on the day of Pentecost, at the coming of the Holy Spirit.

“And fire came out from the Lord,” and so forth. The Holy Spirit, coming from God, consecrated the vows and desires of the saints to the Lord [Col. 0812C].

“When the crowds saw this, they praised the Lord, falling on their faces.” When the Jews saw the grace in the apostles and heard Peter’s words, as Luke reports (Acts 2), they were cut to the heart and were baptized, and about four thousand souls were added.

The statement “falling on their faces” signifies their humility and readiness to do penance.

## CHAPTER X

Nadab and Abihu are condemned by divine fire when they offer foreign fire. Thus those who kindle the fire of error or greed in the Church are condemned by divine vengeance, as are heretics; they are anathematized here and reserved for fires in the future.

“I shall be sanctified in them,” and so forth. This means: I appear holy when I cast down by just condemnation those who approach improperly [Col. 0812D].

“But Moses summoned Mishael,” and so forth. Mishael is interpreted as “touching of God”; Elsaphan as “mirror of God.” Aaron here bears the type of the Law; Uzziel, Aaron’s uncle, bears the type of the Gospel, because by a certain affinity the Law tends toward the Gospel, and the Gospel toward the Law.

His sons—that is, the followers of the New Testament—who touch God, meaning that they seek him by good works, and contemplate his majesty with a pure mind, drive heretics, who remain silent in their sins, away from the unity of the Church.

They wear linen tunics because deceivers assume the appearance of piety in order more easily to lay snares.

“Do not uncover your heads,” and so forth [Col. 0813A]. That is, do not divide Christ, who is the head of the Church.

The cap that he forbids removing from the head is Christ’s humanity, in which his divinity lay hidden. For we confess one Christ in two natures.

“And do not tear your garments”: that is, do not tear the unity of the Church.

“And over the whole congregation,” and so forth. Often anger is provoked against subjects because of the sins of their leaders.

“Let your brothers mourn the burning,” and so forth. Compassion must be shown on account of the equality of nature, but not in such a way that what is greater is violated because of it.

“Wine and everything that can intoxicate,” and so forth. At the time of their ministry they are forbidden cups; for us, drunkenness must never steal upon us, because we must persevere continually in holy conduct.

“So that you may have knowledge,” and so forth: that is, do not burden yourselves with gluttony, so that you may have the knowledge, with sound judgment, to distinguish between just and unjust, false and true [Col. 0813B].

For the Apostle warns: “Do not be drunk with wine,” and so forth (Ephesians 5). This does not mean that bodily necessity is to be rejected, since he says to Timothy: “Use a little wine,” and so forth (1 Timothy 5); rather, it rejects drunkenness, which makes a person like one dead or insane, because “wine causes even the wise to fall away” (Ecclesiasticus 19).

“What he spoke to them through the hand of Moses.” The Lord dictated and commanded, while Moses transmitted it by writing. Likewise, to this day the saints write outwardly for the benefit of many what they have learned inwardly through the revelation of the Spirit.

He commanded the sons of Aaron—that is, teachers—to take up the mysteries that remained from the sacrifice in the place of the holy Church beside the altar, in memory of Christ’s passion, and so forth, as above.

Sons and daughters—that is, the strong and the weak—are saved by the same sanctification.

The goat that was offered for sin is found burned up when the sinner, truly penitent, perishes in the plague of his sins. When the Lord rebukes the teachers concerning the destruction of these people, they say: “They plainly fell before us in their sins; therefore we could not receive their penance,” because the blood was not brought into the holy place—that is, their life was not inclined toward the Lord.

Thus the Lord receives satisfaction, not because he rejoices in the destruction of the wicked, but because they receive what is worthy of their deeds.

## CHAPTER XI

“Whatever has a divided hoof and chews the cud among the livestock, you shall eat.” It must be asked why they declare some creatures unclean, when Genesis says: “Everything was very good” (Genesis 1), and after the flood the Lord says to Noah: “Everything shall be food for you, like green plants” (Genesis 9).

He did not prohibit certain creatures because of the uncleanness of creation, but because of the teaching that he reserved for us in these figures.

Everyone who divides the hoof—that is, who understands Holy Scripture with discernment, knowing how to separate the mystical sense from the literal, as it is said in Jeremiah: “If you separate the precious from the worthless, you shall be as my mouth” (Jeremiah 15)—and whoever chews the cud, that is, continually meditates on the law of the Lord, should be followed as an example.

But whoever chews the cud and does not divide the hoof—that is, whoever does the Lord’s will but does not discern it properly—is to be rejected [Col. 0814A]; likewise, whoever divides the hoof but does not chew the cud.

The camel signifies those who, although they know the Lord’s law, subject themselves to the burdens of the world and do not follow discernment, contrary to the Apostle, who says: “No one serving God entangles himself in worldly business” (2 Timothy 2).

The *chaerogrillus*, a spiny animal larger than a hedgehog, slow but rapacious and beastlike, signifies those who, although they possess only limited capacity, turn everything they understand toward evil.

The hare is a swift and timid animal. It signifies those who are ready for evil but reluctant toward good, like the Jews: prepared to kill Christ, but fearful of repenting, when they said, “If we let him go, the Romans will come” (John 11), and so forth. “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Psalm 52).

The pig, which does not chew the cud but does divide the hoof, represents those who lead unclean lives without searching the law of the Lord.

“You shall not eat their flesh,” and so forth. It is as though he proclaimed: Do not imitate the feigned virtues of such people, and do not share in works liable to death.

“Everything that has fins and scales you shall eat.” Those who, having been reborn in baptism, pursue a heavenly way of life and are involved only in lighter sins because of the weakness of the flesh—follow their examples. But those who do not have these qualities, who are subject to more serious sins and do not know how to desire heavenly things, are to be rejected.

“These are the birds that you must not eat.” He did not set forth a particular distinction concerning birds to be avoided, as he had concerning those mentioned above, but specified them by name, because many measure out a heavenly manner of life and are therefore recognized in various species. [Col. 0814C]

The griffin is a winged, four-footed animal. This kind of wild beast is born in the northern mountains; in part of its body it is like a lion, and in its wings and face like an eagle. It is exceedingly hostile to horses and tears apart human beings when it sees them. The sea-eagle, resembling an eagle, is a large bird, though smaller than a vulture. The eagle, the griffin, and the sea-eagle—that is, although they fly, they nevertheless serve rapacity—signify certain people who pretend to live in contemplation but seek unjust gain.

The vulture delights in the slaughter of the slain and signifies those who sow discord and devote themselves to quarrels. The kite hunts prey around houses and represents “those who go around houses and take captive little women burdened with sins” (II Tim. III). [Col. 0814D] The raven, in its own kind, signifies the blackness of unbelievers in their sins.

The ostrich has feathers but does not fly; it signifies those who outwardly pretend to perform a good action, yet cling to earthly desires. The owl can see clearly in darkness, but not when the sun has risen, like those who sin openly and are unable to receive the light of the Gospel. The gull lives both in water and outside water, signifying those who accept baptism and circumcision equally.

The hawk, according to its kind—Pliny says that there are sixteen kinds—is accustomed to being tamed but delights in plunder. It resembles those who, as the Lord says (Matt. VII), “come in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves.” [Col. 0815A] The owl, as Pliny says, when seen in cities or at all in daylight, is considered an ominous portent. When it seeks food, it indicates one who lives and feeds in the darkness of sins.

The diver, a black bird, plunges beneath the waters to seek fish. *Dubfusal* or *alacfra* or *tu afri* [Note: These may have slipped into the text from a gloss.] [Col. 0815D] signifies those who have been reborn in baptism but desire the lowest things of the world.

The ibis is an African bird with a long beak. Josephus writes: “The ibis is an animal hostile to serpents; for when they approach, the serpents flee and try to hide, but, as though carried away by the breath of stags, they are devoured. Ibes, however, are generally very tame, though they are fierce against serpents.”

Pliny writes: “The Egyptians also invoke their ibises against the approach of serpents; and the Eleans invoke Musagoras [Another reading: *Myiagron*] as a god when a multitude of flies brings pestilence; the flies immediately perish as soon as sacrifice has been offered to that god.” [Col. 0815B]

The swan and the *onocrotalus*, which make a sound in the water, are those who do not know how to live in quiet, although they have been cleansed in baptism. Pliny, however, writes as follows:

> The *onocrotali* resemble swans and would not be thought to differ from them at all, unless there were in their throats a kind of second stomach. Into this they gather all their food, so great is its capacity. Then, when the food has been fully swallowed, they gradually return it to the mouth and bring it back into the true stomach, like a ruminant. Gaul, near the northern Ocean, produces them.

According to Pliny, the *porphyrio* alone drinks by biting: that is, according to its particular nature, it repeatedly dips all its food in water and then brings it from its foot to its beak, as though with a hand. The *herodius*, a falcon, is spoken of in the same way as the hawk. Some call the *caradrion* a *lerax*. [Col. 0815C] The hoopoe, or *opopa*, which builds in dung and imitates a groan in its song, represents those who cling to earthly things and perish through worldly sorrow.

The bat has wings, but although it flies in darkness, it usually walks upon the ground, like those whose knowledge is darkened by the darkness of sins and whose hope lies in lowly things.

“Whatever among the flying creatures walks on four feet,” and so forth. He speaks of those who do not use the doctrine of the four Gospels correctly, or of those who rely upon bodily pleasures, since the body consists of the four elements.

The *bruchus* resembles the locust. Alternatively, the *bruchus*, the locust, and the caterpillar are one and the same. The *attacus* and the *ophiomachus* are hostile to serpents. For *ophis* means “serpent,” while *machus* means “fighting,” as though *ophiomachus* meant “fighting with a serpent,” like those who struggle against the devil’s snares. [Col. 0815D]

The fact that the locust, the *bruchus*, and the *attacus* are said to leap signifies those who, strengthened by works of righteousness, pass over the thorny growth of vices and feed upon the grass of divine Scripture. We ought to share in the examples of such creatures; but whoever is contaminated by the vices of those mentioned above “is unclean until evening,” that is, harmful until perfect repentance.

“And if it should be necessary for him to carry any of them,” and so forth. That is, if someone should happen to be subject to such uncleannesses, he shall “wash” the habit of his conduct with the tears of repentance, and he is held guilty until the fervor of evil desire subsides. [Col. 0816A]

“Whatever walks upon its hands,” and so forth: one who pollutes his conduct through the filth of vices. The weasel, as though *mus longa* (“a long mouse”), is a malicious animal and signifies the fraudulent and deceitful. The mouse is always laboring because of its gluttony and denotes those who follow the greed of the belly, “whose god is their belly” (Phil. III).

Concerning the crocodile, Pliny writes:

> The Nile has the crocodile, an evil quadruped, hostile alike on land and in the river. This is the only land animal that lacks the use of its tongue. It inflicts a bite with its one movable upper jaw, while elsewhere a terrible [Another reading: *terribilem*] row of teeth encloses it like a comb. It usually exceeds eighteen cubits in length. It lays eggs as large as those of geese. It is armed with claws against every attack, and its hide is invulnerable. It spends the day on land and the night in water.

[Col. 0816B] It represents those who are clothed in savagery on every side, whose hardness is not penetrated by the dart of the divine Word, and so forth; such is the form that this beast displays.

The chameleon does not have one color but is sprinkled with varied hues like a leopard. It is called this because the little body of the chameleon changes with the greatest ease into different colors, whereas the bodies of other animals are not so readily capable of change. It signifies the unstable, who are driven into the byways of every vice.

Some call the *mygale* a *haramo*. The *stellio* is a poisonous beast—that is, a kind of lizard, or a *moll*, as others wish. Both of these, namely the *mygale* and the *stellio*, although weak, are nevertheless malicious. They signify those who turn whatever they can toward evil and serve the belly. For *mygale* [Col. 0816C] means, as it were, “gluttonous mouse.”

The lizard is likewise agile and malicious. The mole, which is said to be born from rain and mud, is blind as it digs the earth. It denotes one who, blinded in mind by the desire of the flesh, clings to earthly things.

“Whatever of their carcasses falls upon something shall make it unclean,” and so forth. There is a distinction between the one who touches and the one upon whom something falls. It touches the person who pollutes himself; it falls upon the person who is deceived by some accident, as David, while walking on the roof, was suddenly captivated by the beauty of a woman (II Reg. XI).

The wooden vessel signifies gentleness; the garment, the habit of one’s conduct; the skin, mortification of the flesh; the sackcloth, repentance. If any of these should pollute another person through someone else’s vice, he is cleansed by the water of compunction [Col. 0816D] until perfect repentance.

“But an earthen vessel,” and so forth. An earthen vessel draws liquids into itself. He says: If someone, sharing in another’s vices, persists in increasing them, let him be severely corrected through excommunication, as the Apostle says: “Deliver such a one to the destruction of the flesh,” and so forth (I Cor. V).

“Every food that you eat, if water has been poured over it,” that is, water in which those vessels previously described as polluted are washed; “and every liquid that is drunk from any vessel,” and so forth—namely, the things that he has already declared unclean before they are cleansed. Food and drink are understood as spiritual doctrine or good works. If they admit the uncleanness of the things mentioned above, they are no longer worthy to be received. [Col. 0817A]

“Whether ovens or cooking-pots,” and so forth. Cooking-pots are earthen vessels having feet. Ovens and cooking-pots, in which bread and food are prepared, are teachers, who ought to prepare the nourishment of life for others. If they are defiled by examples of evil, let them be deprived of their teaching office.

“But springs and cisterns,” and so forth. That is, although many have strayed from divine knowledge, the catholic faith and its doctrine nevertheless remain unconquerable.

“If anything falls upon seed,” and so forth. That is, if evil examples of the same kind touch a catechumen who is to be buried with Christ in baptism so that he may be given life, he will be cleansed in baptism. “But if someone should pour water over the seed,” and so forth—that is, after he has been baptized, if he should then entangle himself in the matters already mentioned, he will be guilty. [Col. 0817B]

“If an animal should die which you are permitted to eat,” and so forth. If any righteous person, whose example appears right to follow, should fall through his own fault and incur the death of the soul, whoever shares in his life or follows his example must cleanse himself in the fountain of tears until perfect repentance.

“Everything that creeps upon the earth,” and so forth—that is, whoever relies upon fleeting desires. “Whatever four-footed creature walks upon its breast,” and so forth: one who places all his confidence in earthly things and tries to confirm his obstinacy by the sayings of the four Gospels and the testimonies of many other books, claiming for the pleasure of his desires what the Lord did out of mercy; if, when invited to the banquets of sinners, he consents, and so forth.

“Be holy, because I am holy,” and so forth, so that the righteous may serve the righteous, the holy the holy, the good the good, and servants may serve.

## CHAPTER XII

“If a woman, having received seed, gives birth to a male,” and so forth. In this chapter he recalls the first transgression, so that, since the human being is conceived in iniquities and brought forth in sins, he may know how he is to be cleansed from the ancient curse.

Moreover, a human being born under such a condition has an unclean mother. For seven days—that is, throughout the whole period of this life—he is to recognize himself as bound under innate weakness. “According to the days of her separation because of her menstruation,” that is, when she flows with blood either after childbirth or during childbirth, she is unclean for seven days.

“On the eighth day the infant shall be circumcised,” [Col. 0817D] because the righteous, on the day of resurrection, after laying aside every stain of mortality, will be released from the bonds of the primordial condemnation.

“But she shall remain in her blood for thirty-three days,” and so forth. When the thirty-three days have passed—that is, when perfection in good works has been completed in faith in the Trinity—we hasten to the temple, that is, to the dwelling of the heavenly Jerusalem, with thanksgiving. For until we are freed from the foulness of original sin, we cannot approach the sanctuary.

The reason that seven and thirty-three make forty is that the purification takes as many days as the human being is formed in the womb. Human conception is said to proceed and reach completion in this way: during the first seven days it is like milk; during the following nine days it is changed into blood; then during twelve days it becomes solid; during the remaining eighteen days it is formed until the limbs have their complete outlines; and from then on, throughout the remaining time until birth, it increases in size.

Seven, nine, twelve, and eighteen together make forty-six. Therefore, include the lesser number within the greater, and you will see that the commandment requires a person to be cleansed in nearly as many days as he is formed in the womb, although this number forty points toward a higher interpretation.

For God formed the human being in his own image. He who is said to be formed in the womb under this condition destined his own Son, by this law of birth, to enter the womb of the Virgin through the work of the Holy Spirit, “in whom all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily [Col. 0818B] (Coloss. II),” who is the image of the invisible God. After completing the dispensation of the incarnation, following the victory of the passion, he ascended into heaven on the fortieth day and sat victoriously at God’s right hand. Thus, after the periods of this life, to which the number forty corresponds, may we, for whose liberation he came as a human being through birth and did not fear to share our nature, be raised with God’s help to immortality and into the heavenly kingdom after achieving victory over the devil, and may we deserve to be numbered among the sheep who will reign with Christ at his right hand.

“But if she gives birth to a female, she shall be unclean for two weeks,” and so forth. Since the woman first deceived herself and then deceived the man, she is therefore subjected to a greater curse. For it was said to the man: “Cursed is the ground in your work,” and so forth; and again: “When you have worked it,” and so forth; and: “By the sweat of your face you shall eat,” and so forth. But to the woman it was said: “In pain you shall bear children, and you shall be under the power of the man” (Gen. III). [Col. 0818C] Labor is foretold for the man outwardly, for the woman inwardly.

They also say that the flow of blood lasts seven days for a male child but fourteen days for a female, and that the weaker the sex, the more polluted it is at birth. Moreover, fourteen and sixty-six make eighty. In this the higher number is doubled, because the woman consented to the serpent’s persuasion and compelled the man to consent to her persuasion, whereas the man consented only to the woman.

The number eighty itself can also be bent toward a signification of the resurrection. It must also be said that the weaker the human being is, the greater the correction he needs.

“He shall offer a lamb and a young pigeon or a turtledove,” [Col. 0818D] that is, he shall offer to God the innocence, simplicity, and chastity of life—he who, cleansed from sins, wishes to be brought into the sanctuary. The priest is Christ, as has often been said.

“But if her hand does not find what is required,” and so forth. Just as in all things God’s providence takes merciful care of the human race, so here also he has relieved the poverty of the poor. For whoever cannot lead a lamb—that is, preserve complete innocence—shall take two turtledoves or young pigeons, that is, compunction and chastity.

Because these birds have a moan instead of a song, two are prescribed because there are two kinds of compunction. At times the mind is pierced by fear of Gehenna; this is the offering of one bird for sin. At times it is pierced by desire for the heavenly kingdom, that is, for the vision of God; this is the offering of the other as a holocaust.

## CHAPTER XIII

“The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron,” and so forth. Why does he speak to both, when in Exodus he promised that he would speak to Aaron through Moses? Because God speaks to human beings in two ways: through inward inspiration and through the ministry of the Gospel or of other human beings. The Lord spoke secretly to Moses and through Moses to Aaron.

“A man in whose flesh and skin,” and so forth: namely, a Jew who has transgressed the Lord’s commandment, or any Christian in whose flesh and skin iniquity and a conspicuous sin have appeared through his life and works. [Col. 0819B]

“Or a pustule”: a greater or lesser offense.

“Or something apparently shining,” that is, manifest sins, concerning which the Apostle says: “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment” (I Tim. V).

“He shall be brought to Aaron the priest,” that is, he shall be made known for examination to spiritual teachers. “When he sees leprosy on the skin and the hairs changed to a white color,” and so forth—that is, sin in conduct, thoughts changed from the uprightness of their proper state, and the action of his former life made more shameful and lower than before—“he shall be separated at his discretion,” that is, if he is judged worthy, he shall be excommunicated.

“But if there is a shining whiteness on the skin,” and so forth. If the sin is indeed revealed, but the person has not fallen away from the condition of his former life, and if his thoughts have not turned toward persisting in sin or toward despair, he shall shut him away for seven days—that is, through repentance and the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is represented by the number seven—and promise him forgiveness of sins.

The hairs are ordered to be examined to determine their color because careful investigation is needed to discover whether the sin arose from a long premeditation of malice or happened accidentally, according to the weakness of human nature.

“But if the leprosy has not spread further,” that is, if the person has not persisted in the habit of sin, “nor crossed its boundaries,” that is, if he has not violated his other ways of life, “he shall shut him away again for another seven days.” He commanded that the person be shut away twice because of the carefulness of the examination; nevertheless, forgiveness is always promised through the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0819D]

“If the leprosy is darker,” and so forth: if the sin has been erased through repentance, “he shall cleanse him,” that is, judge him clean. “And the man shall wash his garments,” that is, his conscience shall be cleansed by tears of compunction.

“But if, after he has been examined by the priest,” and so forth: if, after completing repentance and receiving forgiveness, he should presume to repeat the sin, he shall be judged contaminated; and if he persists, he must be separated.

“If the plague of leprosy is in a man,” and so forth—that is, the contagion of error and sin. He shall be brought to the priest, that is, to Christ or to the teacher who holds Christ’s place.

“When the color is white,” and so forth—that is, a cooling of charity, for whiteness often becomes gray because of cold—“and it changes the appearance of the hair,” that is, the condition of the thoughts. Hairs are so called as though they were “hairs of the head.” “And the living flesh appears,” that is, a carnal observance of the law: “it shall be judged a very old leprosy,” that is, the work and pollution of the old human being, “inolitacuti” [uncertain reading; “in the skin”], that is, clinging to one’s manner of life. [Col. 0820A]

“The priest shall contaminate him,” and so forth: he shall judge him unworthy of communion, because, as the Apostle says, “If you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you” (Gal. V); and again: “Avoid a heretical person after one and a second correction, knowing that such a person is perverted” (Tit. III).

“But if the leprosy breaks out and spreads,” and so forth. According to the historical sense, it does not seem consistent that one whose whole flesh is covered with leprosy should be clean, while one in whom leprosy appears in a single place should be unclean. [Col. 0820B]

Allegorically, however, leprosy occupies the whole flesh when either a sinner, confessing his entire life to have been sinful, does not conceal his evil, or when, openly doing penance throughout the whole period of his life, he seeks to be whitened by Christ’s grace. “He shall be clean,” that is, near to salvation.

“But when living flesh appears in him,” and so forth, the carnal superstition of the law must be investigated by the judgment of the priests to determine whether it is so obstinate that it should rightly be condemned. “For if living flesh is sprinkled with leprosy, it is unclean,” that is, observance of the law, if it is in error, provides no benefit. Whoever believes that there is no salvation under grace without observance of the law is ensnared by error.

“But if it should again turn white,” and so forth: if, after forgiveness, he should again deviate from the right way, he is judged unclean.

“The flesh and skin in which an ulcer has arisen and been healed,” and so forth. An ulcer is a wound that bursts forth from within, whereas a wound is a lesion inflicted from without. If sin has proceeded from a person’s will, not from accident, and has been healed through repentance, “and a white scar appears,” that is, carnal Judaism, “or reddish,” that is, a transgression committed after the grace of the Gospel, making the flesh lower—that is, worse—than the former life, and so forth, as above. [Col. 0820C]

“But if the hair is of its former color,” that is, if the intention of the thoughts has not abandoned its former state, and if he has refrained from sin, forgiveness is to be promised him through the Holy Spirit. But if he persists in evil, let him be condemned.

“The flesh and skin that fire has burned,” and so forth: the life and conduct wounded by envy and hatred. If, while correcting himself, he follows either the superstition of the law or accepts a transgression of the Gospel and of sound doctrine, he shall be condemned. But if his good intention is not changed, let it be as above.

If, after careful examination—represented by a full waiting period of seven days—the person is found subject to error, let him be condemned. The plague of a burn is the suspicion of envy, not envy itself. For one who previously envied someone unjustly, if he later rebukes that person justly, is thought to be acting from a repetition of envy. The teacher must carefully investigate whether this is so. [Col. 0820D]

“A man or woman on whose head or beard leprosy shall grow,” and so forth. Strong or weak, wise or less wise, whoever is stained by error concerning the divinity or humanity of Christ—“if the hair is yellow and thinner than usual,” that is, if the intention of the thoughts has abandoned its proper state and become more skillful at investigating evil, let him be condemned.

“But if he sees that the place of the spot is level with the neighboring flesh,” that is, an error that does not deviate greatly from the truth, and “the hair is black,” according to the thoughts of his proper state, “he shall shut him away for seven days,” that is, examine him through the doctrine prescribed by the Holy Spirit; “and the man shall be shaved except at the place of the spot,” that is, his remaining vices shall be examined. What he has confessed is manifest and does not require investigation; the rest is as above. [Col. 0821A]

“Somewhat dark,” that is, not entirely clear.

“A man from whose head the hair shall fall,” and so forth. This means one whose intellectual discernment and agile understanding for probing deep matters have failed, who applies himself to simplicity; he is judged clean.

There are two kinds of such simplicity. One is found in those who are prudent so that they are not deceived, and simple so that they deceive no one. The other is found in those whose mind, seized by dullness, is unable to distinguish good from evil, because they are called by the Greeks *moriones* [Note: “Fools,” from *μωρία*, “foolishness.”]. [Col. 0821D] The rest concerning baldness is as above. But if a transgression occurs in simplicity, the one who committed that sin must himself be examined according to a just judgment.

“Therefore, whoever is stained with leprosy,” and so forth: that is, whoever is rightly excluded from communion on account of his guilt, “shall have torn garments,” that is, he shall declare himself abandoned to his own strength; “his head shall be bare,” that is, he shall declare himself unworthy of the helmet of salvation; “his mouth shall be covered with a garment,” that is, restraining it from the loquacity of depravity, and at all times publicly declaring himself a sinner while doing penance, so that he may be justified by the Lord. [Col. 0821C]

“Alone he shall dwell outside the camp,” persisting unanimously in the penance assigned to him until he receives pardon from the Lord.

“A woolen or linen garment,” that is, the highest and the lower virtue. A woolen garment is more valuable and provides greater color, while linen is cheaper and provides less. The chastity of widowhood or marriage is not equal to virginity, martyrdom, renunciation of possessions and of the world; nor is preaching without persecution equal to the giving of alms, although each of these things is good and useful.

The warp, which supports the other threads, can express God’s command; the weft, our intention. From these, with God’s help and the grace that precedes the virtues, the garment is woven. [Col. 0821D]

The skin signifies the hardship and tribulation that we impose upon ourselves through fasts, vigils, and other exercises.

In these virtues, “if the spot is white or reddish,” that is, if a stealthy form of pride or boasting appears, “the priest shall shut it away for seven days,” as above. But if, after careful examination, the vice is found to have adhered to the virtue, “let it be burned with flames,” that is, let the condemnation of excommunication be imposed or the terror of punishment in Gehenna be displayed.

If he makes no progress through punishments, let him be washed with the tears of repentance and examined with greater caution to determine whether he persists in pride; let him be shut away for another seven days. [Col. 0822A]

If he sees that the person in whom it exists is raised up by greater boasting and rejoices in his previously acquired favor as though it were lawful, he shall judge him damnable.

“But if it is darker.” That is, if there is some sign of sin, let him cut it away from the person’s conduct where he determines that pride has begun to sprout in him.

“But if it appears further in these places,” and so forth: that is, if the former offense, once recovered, appears again, he is subject to greater danger.

## CHAPTER XIV

“He who has gone out from the camp,” and so forth. Christ, the true priest, came into the world, going forth from the Father without abandoning the Father. Through his redemption the sinner is cleansed, provided that, in right faith, he offers what is commanded: “two living sparrows,” namely, the two natures in Christ, without the contagion of sin.

The cedar wood signifies his cross. The scarlet signifies the blood of the passion. Hyssop, having a good smell and cleansing the lungs, signifies the power of the Holy Spirit, who purifies sins. [Col. 0822B]

“He shall sacrifice one of the sparrows in an earthen vessel over living waters.” Let him firmly believe that Christ’s humanity suffered in mortal flesh after the consecration of baptism.

“But he shall dip the other living sparrow, together with the cedar wood, the scarlet, and the hyssop, in the blood of the sacrificed sparrow; with this he shall sprinkle the one who has been cleansed seven times, so that he may rightly be purified; and he shall release the living sparrow so that it may fly away into the field.”

The living sparrow signifies his divinity. The living sparrow is dipped with the wood and hyssop in the blood of the sacrificed sparrow because true divinity was in him who suffered on the cross—namely, Christ, God and man—although divinity itself did not suffer the passion. It is dipped with hyssop because the Holy Spirit did not abandon him in his passion. [Col. 0822C]

The one who is to be cleansed is sprinkled seven times because, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, forgiveness of sins is granted. The living sparrow is released into the field because the divinity is recognized as free from suffering.

“When the man has washed his garments,” that is, cleansed his conduct, “he shall shave all the hair of his body,” that is, he shall cut away his illicit thoughts. “He shall wash in water,” that is, in tears of compunction; and, having been purified, he shall enter the camp. Once cleansed from transgressions, he shall be restored to communion with ecclesiastical unity.

“He shall remain outside his tent for seven days,” that is, until perfect repentance; he shall judge himself unworthy of the company of the others. [Col. 0822D]

“He shall shave the hair of his head, his beard, and his eyebrows,” that is, he shall cleanse his inner and outer thoughts through which the mind sins either in the secrecy of the heart or through external affairs; then, having again washed his garments and his body—that is, his conduct and his life—

“On the eighth day,” and so forth. The eighth day is also the first day. It is called the eighth because it follows the seventh; for after the passion the Lord rose on the eighth day, which is also the first day. Therefore the sinner is commanded to be cleansed on the eighth day: that is, he must firmly believe in the Lord’s resurrection.

“He shall take two lambs,” and so forth. The two lambs signify Christ, who redeemed both sexes; or the innocent life that must be preserved both inwardly and outwardly. [Col. 0823A]

“A year-old ewe,” that is, perfect gentleness.

“Three-tenths of fine flour,” the faith of the Holy Trinity, infused with the oil of mercy.

“A sextary of oil,” the catholic faith, in which all virtues are contained, as smaller measures are contained in a sextary.

The door of the tabernacle is the doctrine of the apostles. The offering for a trespass or for sin is the presentation of repentance. The rest is as above.

“And the priest, taking some of the blood of the sacrifice, shall place it upon the tip of the right ear of the same person,” that is, through Christ’s redemption he shall teach him to have a favorable and willing hearing for listening to righteousness.

“And upon the thumbs of his right hand and right foot,” namely, to direct his outstanding works and his progress in the commandments of God. [Col. 0823B]

“And from the sextary of oil he shall put it into his own left hand,” that is, he shall commend the holding of complete faith in this life. For eternal life is understood to be in the right hand.

“He shall dip his finger in it,” and so forth—that is, with the discernment of judgment, he shall obtain for him from the Lord complete forgiveness, sprinkling him, as it were, seven times.

“The rest of the oil he shall pour upon the tip of his right ear,” that is, although because of his weakness a person cannot fulfill all God’s commandments in action, he should nevertheless strive to hear and learn, so that, knowing the Lord’s will, he may compensate through good will for what he cannot accomplish in deed.

“And upon the blood that was poured out for the trespass.” Oil is poured over the blood because after redemption one must devote oneself to works of mercy, and everything must be done in the name of the Redeemer. [Col. 0823C]

“Then he shall sacrifice the holocaust,” and so forth. First we must fully perform repentance for what we have committed, in remembrance of the passion and resurrection in which we recognized the work of our Redeemer; then, having been purified in our senses, we must wholly sacrifice ourselves upon the altar of the Lord’s praise, so that we may live no longer for ourselves but for him. Finding us dead, he redeemed and helped us so that we might live through him.

“But if he is poor and his hand cannot find the things that have been mentioned,” and so forth. If someone, overtaken by the weakness of frailty, has been unable to preserve perfect innocence, let him offer a lamb: that is, let him carefully preserve faith in Christ’s passion.

“A tenth part of fine flour mixed with oil,” either the faith of the Trinity or theology, which we are commanded to confess and believe, together with the oil of charity and mercy; “and a sextary of oil,” the integrity of faith. [Col. 0823D]

We have spoken above in many places about the turtledoves and young pigeons; likewise, what is said here concerning the eighth day and the other matters that follow in this chapter has already been discussed above.

The seven nations of the Canaanites express the chief vices, which God destroyed when, by his coming, he purified us who are from the nations. In that land, after the unbelievers have been uprooted, anyone possesses a house when a teacher governs the congregation entrusted to him.

If anything erroneous appears in it, the one who presides should report it to an ecclesiastical assembly, just as Paul sought counsel from the apostles at Jerusalem concerning the deception of the Antiochenes.

“Therefore it is commanded that everything be removed from the house,” [Col. 0824A] that is, that those who have been deceived separate themselves from association with the unclean, so that afterward the doctrine itself may be discerned by true judgment.

The little cavities (*valliculae*) signify perverse opinions; the pallor and redness signify boasting and pride.

“He shall immediately shut it up,” that is, he shall condemn that error and strive to seal it off so that it may not spread further.

“And when he returns on the seventh day,” that is, after careful examination, “if he finds that the leprosy has increased,” and so forth—that is, if he sees that the error persists, “he shall command the stones themselves to be torn out,” or he shall place the seducers themselves and their doctrines outside the Church among the heretics.

“As for the house itself within,” that is, he shall cleanse the congregation itself; “and the dust,” that is, he shall assign the contagions of error to the uncleanness of the heretics, appoint other teachers in their place, and join the members of that same body together in concord through true doctrines. [Col. 0824B]

But if, after new teachers have been appointed, the restored error should defile them together with the rest of the house, the malice is persistent. Therefore the stones, wood, and dust are thrown outside the city into an unclean place. That is, whether teachers or those who ought to have produced the fruit of good works, together with their doctrines, are to be anathematized outside the Church, after their certain recognition, among those in error.

“Whoever enters the house,” and so forth: whoever joins himself to condemned error “is unclean” until he has completed repentance.

“Whoever sleeps in it and eats,” and so forth: whoever trusts that he will find rest in that error, or shares in it—if he has not been rightly baptized, let him be washed in the sacred font; otherwise, let him be released through the tears of repentance. [Col. 0824C]

If, then, the error is found to have been restrained through the Lord’s help and earnest repentance, the house must be purified. Everything that follows in this chapter has been fully discussed above. For it is believed that all things can be obtained through right faith. The variety of leprosy demonstrates the variety of errors.

## CHAPTER XV
“Then the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron,” and the rest: that is, through the law and the priesthood the Lord instructed the children of Israel. “A man who suffers an emission of semen”: that is, a teacher who ought by the strength of his spirit to press forward—if he suffers error in his teaching, or practices the indulgence of worldly things—is unclean, especially if he nourishes the vice by habit. “Every bed on which he sleeps” [Col. 0824D]: that is, the habit in which he seems to find rest is condemned. If anyone touches his bed—that is, shares in his torpor—let him cleanse his deeds until perfect repentance. If he sits where that man sat—that is, imitates his torpor, as above. “Whoever touches his flesh”: that is, whoever follows his examples. “If such a man spits upon one who is clean,” and the rest: namely, if by his cunning and feigned wisdom he defiles one who rightly believes; the remainder is as above.

A *sagina* [term uncertain], a *filtrum*, a covering, or whatever else is prepared for sitting—together with the other things subsequently included—signifies the various perversities which the defiled employ. “Whoever carries any of these things”: that is [Col. 0825A], whoever subjects himself to these pollutions. “Everyone whom such a person touches, without having first washed his hands,” and the rest: that is, whoever that unclean man has contaminated by his examples without first cleansing his deeds, and the remainder as above. “The earthen vessel that he touches shall be broken.” If he has led astray someone fragile, who cannot easily be corrected, let him who permitted himself to be deceived be restrained by strict discipline. “The wooden vessel” signifies the gentleness of some people, which, when it falls away, is restored through the tears of repentance.

“If the one who suffers such an affliction has been healed”—that is, if the person described above has been corrected—“he shall count seven days”: let him believe that forgiveness will come to him through the grace of the Holy Spirit, cleansing his deeds together with his garment, that is, his outward manner of life, through the tears of repentance. “On the eighth day” [Col. 0825B]—in faith in the Lord’s resurrection—“he shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons”: chastity, gentleness, and meditation on the divine law, as it is said, “I will meditate like a dove” (Isa. 38); we have often spoken of these birds.

“A man from whom the emission of intercourse proceeds,” and so forth: that is, one who pours himself out in worldly desires shall be cleansed, as above, and shall cleanse “the garment and the skin,” that is, his manner of life. The skin may be understood as his wife, since she too needs to be cleansed, because conception is completed in iniquities; or the skin may be understood as labor in vigils and other works.

“A woman with whom he has intercourse,” and so forth. There are two parts of the inner person: the spirit, which deals with what is above and within, and the soul, which orders outward desires. This lower part, if it has been polluted because the spirit has inclined itself toward lower things [Col. 0825C], must necessarily be cleansed.

“A woman who suffers an emission of blood when her period returns,” and so forth: that is, the soul which, when the visitation of the Lord’s grace arrives, is defiled by idolatry is entirely unclean. “She shall be separated for seven days”: that is, by divine judgment she shall be excluded from communion outside until perfect repentance. Her touching and the other matters that follow are to be understood as above concerning the man who suffers an emission of semen.

According to the historical sense, vessels may be understood as all kinds of utensils, just as we speak of vessels of war. “If a man has intercourse with her during the time of her blood”—that is, if someone sacrifices with idolaters, or reclines in an idol-shrine while eating sacrificial food—“he shall be unclean for seven days”: that is, he shall complete the perfect repentance appointed for him. For one who was compelled by persecution to sacrifice, but afterward returned of his own will, repentance was certainly prescribed.

“A woman who suffers an emission of blood for many days, not at the time of her menstruation,” and so forth: that is, the soul which, after knowing grace, is occupied in idolatry. It is not the time of menstruation—that is, when the blindness of the nations has already been almost illuminated by the light of truth, whereas previously almost the whole world wandered in the service of the devil. The rest is as above.

“If the blood has ceased”: that is, if the error of folly has ceased, “she shall count seven days,” as above; the other matters likewise are as above.

“You shall therefore teach the children of Israel to beware of uncleanness, lest they die in their filth when they have defiled my tabernacle,” and the rest. That is, let the faithful beware of every uncleanness of idolatry [Col. 0826A], vices, and sins, lest they corrupt the Church, which is the house of the Lord; or lest they corrupt those who ought to become the temple of the Lord, as the Apostle says: “You are the temple of God,” and the rest (2 Cor. 6).

## CHAPTER XVI

“Speak to Aaron, so that he may not enter the sanctuary at all times, which is within the veil before the mercy seat.” He commands teachers not to usurp, according to their own desire, matters that exceed human understanding by disputing about the mystery of divine things. For it is dangerous to permit oneself or others to investigate how the eternal Word appeared in the flesh as a true human being, and many other matters of this kind, in which the greatest caution is necessary.

“Because I shall appear in a cloud over the oracle.” [Col. 0826B] The Lord appears either in the sayings of the prophets, concerning which it is said, “I will command the clouds not to rain upon it” (Isa. 5), or in human flesh; hence it is said, “The Lord will enter Egypt upon a swift cloud” (Isa. 19), that is, into the unclean one in flesh, while himself free from sins; or he appears in the hidden things of the mysteries, in which it is not easy to investigate him completely.

“Unless you do these things beforehand”—that is, he shall not enter upon the oracle in Holy Scripture—“he shall offer a calf for sin.” The calf, born from bulls and cows, signifies Christ, begotten according to the flesh from the patriarchs and from the Synagogue, which had borne the yoke of the law; the ram likewise signifies him, as was said above.

“He shall put on a linen tunic,” and the rest. The linen tunic signifies chastity; the undergarments, continence; the belt, vigilance of mind; the turban, vigilance of the bodily senses. It is fitting that the one who is going to discuss the Lord’s mysteries be clothed with these. These four kinds of garments may also signify the four principal virtues: the linen tunic, justice; the undergarments, temperance, which is the mother of chastity; the belt, fortitude; the turban, which covers the head, prudence, by which the mind is adorned.

“With these, when he has been washed, he shall clothe himself”: that is, after baptism.

“Two male goats for sin.” These goats signify Christ, who bore our sins, for which he was offered. They are said to be two because of Christ’s twofold nature. “And when he has offered,” and the rest. Christ is the priest who laid down his soul for us; and he prayed for himself and for his household—that is, for the humanity of our weakness, and for the condition of the Church, which is his body. He “shall make the two goats stand [Col. 0826D] before the Lord,” and the rest.

It pleased the Holy Trinity that Christ should suffer for the human race: he is one Son of God in two natures, God and human. A lot is cast over the goats, because it had been ordained that, insofar as he was human, he should die for the dead. One goat is slaughtered for sin, because his flesh was sacrificed for us sinners on the altar of the cross. The scapegoat is set alive before the Lord, because his divinity underwent no change in itself when he suffered in human flesh; but by eternal and living power he sought the deserts of heaven—not by changing place, since God is everywhere, but by restraining his power so as to give room for suffering. This is the desert where the good shepherd, having left the ninety-nine sheep, went to seek the one that had been lost (Luke 15).

The priest pours prayers over the goat, because Christ, through his divinity, reconciles us to the Father: “No one can forgive sins except God alone” (Luke 5).

Some say that the two goats signify the two portions of the people: the one sacrificed signifies those who, believing in Christ’s passion, slaughter themselves daily on the altar of faith; the one sent into the wilderness signifies those who, persisting in sins and refusing to convert, go toward darkness burdened with sins. That both are offered for sin shows that all are found in original sin, but that some are received by the Lord because of faith, while others are condemned because of the stubbornness of unbelief. Both are set before their Lord, because “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22). The Gospel reaches everyone.

Let them say that prayers are poured over the scapegoat when eternal condemnation is imposed upon unbelievers. They are sent into solitude—that is, into perpetual condemnation—while Christ’s divinity always has been and is in the bosom of the Father. It is called solitude because, apart from the Trinity itself, it is not entirely clear to anyone how their eternal essence contains them—I mean, theirs in persons, his in substance. This interpretation concerning Christ’s two natures appears more suitable: he alone bore the sins of the world, not in order to keep them for himself, but in order utterly to destroy them. Let the prudent reader choose what seems more appropriate to follow, provided that in all things he does not waver from the authorities of the faith.

“After taking the censer,” and the rest. We understand this fire-pan as the Lord’s tongue, with which he supplied us with coals from the altar—that is, from the heavenly secret—with the burning heat of spiritual teaching. “And taking the composed incense in his hand,” and the rest: that is, he strengthened all his teaching by works of virtue. This teaching was prepared as incense for the Lord, because everything he did was acceptable to the Father as the sweetest fragrance, of which he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3).

“He shall enter within the veil into the holy place.” For he ascended into heaven, “having found eternal redemption” (Heb. 9), “with the spices placed upon the fire.” Everything he did he presented because of love, saying: “No one has greater love than that he should lay down his life,” and so forth.

“The cloud and vapor of them shall cover the oracle”: that is, the reconciliation which he made for us with the Father reached above all the angelic powers.

“He shall take from the blood of the calf and sprinkle with his finger seven times,” and the rest. Christ’s passion was not only the restoration of human beings but also of the order of the angels. Therefore it is said of the blood of the calf that was brought in, “he sprinkles with his finger”—he who now “appears before the face of God for us” (Heb. 9).

“Toward the east.” The East itself is Christ, who showed himself to us as the sun of righteousness; concerning him it is said: “Behold the man; East is his name” (Zech. 6). The same applies to the following goat.

“Let him cleanse the sanctuary.” The present Church has been cleansed by Christ’s blood from the filth of unbelief. “Which is fixed in the midst of the filth of their inheritance”: because the Church is in the midst of the nations, from whose original filth Christ’s coming rescued it.

“Let no human being be in the tabernacle when the high priest enters the sanctuary,” and the rest. When the Lord Christ joined himself to his Church through the Virgin’s womb, her unity had not yet been gathered together, although we believe that the ancient saints belonged to the building of that structure. Christ the priest prays “for himself,” according to his humanity, and “for his household,” that is, for the Church.

“When he has gone out to the altar that is before the Lord.” That altar is the heavenly powers, over which God presides. Upon them the blood of the goat and the calf is placed, because Christ’s passion benefited them greatly. For the Apostle does not say without reason: “to renew all things that are in heaven and that are on earth” (Eph. 1).

This altar has four horns because those angelic powers employ the adornments of the four principal virtues. We have written in Exodus how these are observed by them. He shall sanctify it “from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel”: that is, by his passion he reconciles the angelic choirs, so that because of original sin they would no longer display hostility toward them.

“After he has cleansed the sanctuary, the tabernacle, and the altar.” The King is making ready the heavenly and earthly things through Christ’s passion. The living goat is offered—namely Christ himself, without sin—and he is presented as about to forgive our sins by the power of his divinity.

“Having placed both hands upon its head.” We ought, with hands extended, remembering that he extended his hands for us on the cross, and with the deepest supplication confessing our sins, to entreat his majesty, because he is faithful and will forgive. Truly, he himself bore our infirmities, and so forth.

“He shall send it away by a prepared man,” and the rest. We send him by means of himself, because he came to us by his own will and, as it pleased him, returned himself to make atonement, as he himself says: “I have power to lay down my life,” and so forth (John 10).

“Aaron shall return to the tabernacle of testimony”: this is what he himself says: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28).

“After he has removed the garments”: that is, after laying aside mortal flesh, he put on the glory of immortality. “He shall wash his flesh in the holy place”: Christ immersed the flesh he had assumed in the blood of his passion. He offers the burnt offering after coming out, because, ascending to the Father, he completed the whole dispensation for our salvation. He offers the fat—that is, his desire by which he thirsted for our salvation.

“But the one who has sent away the scapegoat,” and the rest. Christ, who forgives sins, cleansed the Church, which is his body and garment, from confessed sins by the water of baptism, and thus established his dwelling among the saints; or, alternatively, he entered the camp—that is, after completing redemption, he ascended into heaven.

“But the calf and the goat that were for sin,” and the rest. Each victim signifies Christ. Their being burned with flesh, skin, and dung outside the camp indicates that the Lord Jesus Christ, inseparable in his person and true God, suffered for us outside the gate. The dung displays the filth of our sins.

“But the one who burned them,” and the rest. For if anyone among those who killed him believed, he was cleansed through repentance and received into the number [Col. 0829A] of the faithful.

“In the seventh month, on the tenth day,” and the rest. The seventh month indicates the fullness of time in which God sent his Son, and so forth (Gal. 4). The tenth day signifies the perfection of the law; likewise, Andrew is read to have come with his brother to Jesus in the Gospel at the tenth hour of the day.

“Whether native-born or resident alien”: that is, whether Jew or Gentile. “You shall afflict your souls,” according to the literal sense: fasting for three days until evening. This, however, is the beginning of Christ’s preaching: “Repent,” and so forth.

“You shall do no work,” namely work belonging to carnal desires, as it is said: “Work not for the food that perishes,” and so forth (John 6).

“On this day atonement shall be made,” and the rest. For in this time a period of correction has been granted.

“For it is a sabbath of rest,” as the Psalmist says: “Be still and see that I am God,” and so forth (Ps. 45).

“So that he may exercise the priesthood in place of his father.” Just as a son follows his father, so Christ follows Aaron, “whose hands were initiated,” because eternal power was given to him, in whom we have our atonement.

“He shall put on a linen vestment”: that is, he receives the Church into the unity of his body, and it shines with the whiteness of chastity.

“The priests also and all the people.” Both the greater and the lesser need the Lord’s help.

“Once a year.” What was commanded to the priests in shadow, the Lord Jesus fulfilled by entering once a year into the holy place of reconciliation, which proclaims that, by offering himself, he found eternal redemption (Heb. 9).

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 0829C] “If a man kills an ox.” According to the historical sense, this prohibits idolatry; mystically, however, if he offers to the devil and not to the Lord an ox—that is, a strong work—, a sheep of innocence, a goat of repentance, or any other work, “he shall be guilty of blood”: that is, of homicide, by which he loses his own life.

“Whoever offers a burnt offering or a sacrifice,” and the rest, belongs entirely to the preceding interpretation. Whoever eats blood—that is, whoever pursues bloody deeds, whether hatred or every kind of wickedness, concerning which corrupt blood many things are read—“because the life of the flesh is in the blood.” For the confidence of carnal people is in the corruption of pleasures; we must mortify this weakness in the love of the Lord and take it as an example for ourselves.

“If he has caught a bird or a wild animal by hunting or fowling” [Col. 0829D]: that is, if someone has brought any carnal person, or someone endowed with greater intelligence, to the confession of Christ’s name through the teaching of salvation, “let him pour out its blood and cover it with earth”: that is, let repentance cover his carnal life, not taking the blood as food—that is, not contracting a stain from his wicked life.

We may also say that he prohibits eating blood, which signifies the life of the flesh, because no one ought to live for himself, but should do everything in the name of the Lord.

“You shall not eat the blood of any flesh.” This was first commanded when the eating of flesh was permitted in Noah’s time, and likewise by the Apostles under grace; but it signifies homicide. The Apostle John says what homicide is: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (John 3). Hence we are prohibited here:

“The soul that eats an animal that has died of itself or one torn by a beast”: that is, the soul that mingles itself with the examples of a person dead in sins or corrupted by the devil must cleanse itself and its deeds by the washing of repentance. It remains guilty until perfect repentance, and only then will it be cleansed. But if it does not devote itself to amendment, it will incur the punishment of transgression.

## CHAPTER XVIII

“According to the practices of the land of Egypt you shall not act,” and the rest. In this chapter he especially prohibits idolatry by repeatedly impressing upon them the remembrance of his name; spiritually, he also warns them to beware greatly of past and present vices.

“You shall carry out my judgments, keep my precepts, and walk in them”: that is, fulfill them. “The person who does them shall live in them,” for truly the one who keeps the Lord’s commandments lives.

“No man shall approach his nearest relative by blood,” and the rest: that is, he teaches that they must not marry outside legitimate union. Nor shall he uncover her shame—that is, do not publish the sins of one who confesses them to you; do not spread the deeds of pagans and criminals among those who might thereby be harmed. In what follows he wholly prohibits adultery. There is no need to seek an allegory in these matters; it seems sufficient that they be kept according to the letter.

“Into concubinage,” that is, into her rejection or concubinage; for concubines are called *pellices*. Concerning a woman’s menstruation, it was said above.

“You shall not have intercourse with your neighbor’s wife”: that is, do not be deceived by the philosophy of the pagans, who are your neighbors in weakness.

“You shall not give any of your offspring to be consecrated to the idol Molech,” who was the god of the Ammonites; universally, however, he includes all idols in this one. “Nor shall you profane the name of your God.” The one who lives disgracefully while professing the religion of God profanes the Lord’s name, as Paul says: “Because of you the name of the Lord is blasphemed among the nations” (Rom. 2).

“So that it may vomit out its inhabitants”: that is, reject them contemptuously.

## CHAPTER XIX

“Speak to the entire assembly of the children of Israel: Be holy, because I am holy,” and the rest. This [Col. 0830D] is commanded not only to the sons of Aaron, nor only to the Levites—that is, to the greater members of the Church—but also to the entire assembly of Israel, that is, to all the faithful, so that they may pursue holiness in everything, because it is fitting that he have holy servants who partake of his holiness. [Note: The passage is corrupt, as are very many others.]

“Each person shall fear his father and his mother.” This is entirely right, and it is especially fitting to fear the Lord the Father and to venerate the Church as mother.

“Keep my sabbaths”: all the solemnities appointed for you. We, however, are always commanded to refrain from servile things—that is, from works of sin.

We have already spoken above about eating the sacrificial victim on the same day and on the following day.

“If you reap the grain of your land,” [Col. 0831A] and the rest. The Jews are commanded, while they abounded in the Scriptures, not to deprive foreigners—that is, Gentiles—of communion with them, but to leave them the ears of grain, that is, the abundant interpretations available to themselves. Likewise, “in your vineyard you shall not gather the clusters and berries”: that is, Israel should allow the prophets and their sayings to be shared with the Gentiles.

“You shall not steal”: that is, do not entertain any desire to acquire something unjustly; and do not, like the Jewish people, invent that Christ, having risen, was secretly carried away.

“You shall not lie.” He teaches that, after abandoning truth, no lie should be uttered in anything, whether in speech or in teaching.

“Nor shall each person deceive his neighbor”: namely, in the two matters mentioned above.

“You shall not swear falsely by my name.” Just as in the Gospel he prohibited anger because of homicide (Matt. 5), so he forbade swearing lest we swear falsely. Whatever is beyond this and more abundant is from evil, because if we swear when we are not willing to do so, what we swear comes from the malice of the one who does not wish to believe the truth.

“Nor shall you profane the name of the Lord”: by living wickedly and unjustly appropriating his name.

“You shall not oppress your neighbor,” and the rest: that is, you, Jew, must not trouble the Gentile people—that is, the ecclesiastical people.

“The work of your hired servant shall not remain with you,” and the rest: that is, pay him for his labor, by which perhaps he must live; spiritually, do not deny your preacher the necessities of bodily life.

“You shall not curse the deaf, nor place a stumbling block before the blind”: that is, do not set traps of seduction before the simple person who does not know how to be on guard.

“You shall not show partiality to the poor,” and the rest: that is, although mercy must be shown to the wretched, the sinner must nevertheless be rebuked justly, and the rich must not be treated more leniently because of their power.

“You shall not be an accuser or a whisperer,” and the rest: a slanderer and a grumbler.

“You shall not seek vengeance.” Here he teaches patience.

“You shall not make your animals mate,” and the rest: that is, do not make the simple mingle with the wickedness of evil people.

“You shall not sow your field with different kinds of seed”: that is, do not fill the Church with true and false teaching at the same time.

“A garment woven from two kinds of material,” and the rest: that is, do not accept in yourself a diversity of faith or a dissimilarity of teaching, nor mingle imitations with true virtues.

“If a man sleeps with a woman in an emission of semen,” and the rest. That is, if an ecclesiastical man turns toward the error of the Synagogue, which the Apostle calls a slave woman, though she is also noble because she was descended from the patriarchs, “yet not redeemed for a price”—that is, Christ’s passion does not benefit her because she persists in hardness—“nor granted freedom”—that is, by her unbelief she herself bars herself from liberation—“both shall be scourged”: that is, the seductress and the seduced shall acknowledge themselves worthy of punishment, “and they shall not die”: that is, let them repent, lest they perish.

He enacted a lighter penalty concerning this because involvement with the Jewish sects is not as destructive as union with pagan madness: the former worship one God, the latter none. Nevertheless, we must not understand the wickedness described above as applying to the entire Synagogue, but only to those in whom blindness has occurred.

“For his offense he shall offer to God at the entrance of the tabernacle a ram”: that is, returning to apostolic teaching, let him preserve faith in Christ’s passion, which is his redemption.

“You shall remove their firstfruits [foreskins]”: that is, by devoting yourselves to divine Scripture, cast away the carnal observance of the law, at least in those matters that presented nothing but a shadow.

“ The fruits are unclean,” because such interpretations are observed superfluously.

“In the fourth year all their fruit shall be sanctified”: that is, when evangelical grace appeared through the Lord, the same figure would be taught to be kept spiritually.

“But in the fifth year you shall eat their fruit”: that is, in the time of the Apostles, because after the Lord’s resurrection, on the fiftieth day—that is, with five multiplied by ten—the Holy Spirit came in grace, and the vigor of spiritual understanding appeared. Before his passion the Lord said to them: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will announce all things to you,” and the rest (John 16).

“You shall not eat blood”: that is, you Jews must not put your confidence in the pouring out of the blood of figurative sacrifices.

“You shall not practice augury.” *Augurium* is so called as if from *avigarrium*, that is, the inspection and observation of birdsong; *auspicium*, however, is as if “inspection of birds,” that is, consideration of their flight.

“Nor shall you observe dreams”: that is, false dreams. Some claimed prophecy for themselves from dreams; therefore he prohibited the observation of dreams. For these things should be observed all the less because we cannot discern from where they come.

“You shall not cut the hair of your head into a circle”: that is, do not fix your thoughts upon earthly pleasures, for a circle is round.

“Nor shall you shave your beard” [Col. 0832C]: that is, do not strip your soul of virtues.

“You shall not make cuts in your flesh for the dead”: that is, do not lacerate your soul through carnal pleasures. “Nor shall you make any figures or marks”—that is, paintings, and so forth—“lest you be defiled by a variety of error or by hypocrisy.”

“You shall not prostitute your daughter”: that is, do not hand her over to a brothel. Spiritually, however, do not hand your soul over to the will of demons and heretics.

“And you shall fear my sanctuary”: that is, honor my Church; or the sanctuary may also be understood as the body of Christ, which must be honored.

“Do not turn to magicians, nor inquire of anything from diviners.” He prohibits every rite of sorcery. Diviners are called inspectors of altars, or of hours, who practice their magical divinations in the entrails of animals. Mystically [Col. 0832D], however, they signify heretics, who, promising knowledge that they do not possess, are caught by the devil’s deception.

“Rise before a gray head”: that is, honor the wise, for the gray hairs are the thoughts of a human being. Concerning these elders—that is, the wise—Paul says: “Let the presbyters be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and teaching” (1 Tim. 5). And the Lord said to Moses: “Choose seventy men whom you know to be elders of the people” (Exod. 24).

“If a resident alien dwells in your land,” and the rest: that is, let a Jew treat a Gentile who converts to the Lord as a brother, remembering that he himself by nature had been a son of wrath, just as the others.

“You shall not do anything unjust,” and the rest.

“In the rule”: that is, in the measuring rod, and in every correctness of division, and in the other matters that follow. In these we are commanded to avoid fraud, lest we wish to give a smaller measure and demand and receive a larger one.

“Keep all my commandments,” and the rest. Without doubt, blessed is the one who possesses the will to fulfill all the Lord’s commandments.

## CHAPTER XX

“If anyone gives any of his offspring to the idol Molech.” He mentions this one alone because *Molech* is interpreted as “prince” or “principal,” signifying the devil, who is the prince of this world. If anyone consents to him through his works, he is guilty of punishment.

“The people of the land shall stone him”: that is, he shall be convicted by harsh judgments. “And I will set my face against that man”: that is, the anger of vengeance, “because he has defiled my sanctuary”: whether his own soul, which is the image of God, or the congregation, namely the house of God.
