“But if the people of the land, being negligent and treating it as though it were of little importance,” and the rest: that is, if the teachers dissemble and do not rebuke the sinner as is fitting, the Lord’s face is set against him, “and against his family”: anger against him and those who consent to him.

“The soul that turns to magicians and diviners”—heretics and pretenders—“shall perish from the assembly of the saints.”

“Whoever curses his father and mother”: that is, whoever blasphemes the Church of the Lord.

“If anyone commits adultery with another man’s wife,” and the rest: that is, if anyone sends a Church entrusted to the care of another shepherd into communion with his own error, both the persuader and the one who consents shall be condemned.

“Whoever lies with an animal,” and the rest: that is, whoever mingles himself with the error of fools.

“Whoever lies with a male,” and the rest: that is, whoever corrupts one who is capable of performing strong works.

“A woman who lies beneath any animal,” and the rest: that is, the soul that consents to the folly of any error.

“Whoever lies with a woman during her menstrual flow,” and the rest: that is, whoever falls into error through the philosophy of the Gentiles. Menstruation is so called from *mensis* (“month”), and *mensis* from *mensura* (“measure”), according to the etymology of the Latin language. Finally, the wisdom of the Gentiles may be compared to menstruation for this reason: from measurements of natural philosophy they undertook their intellectual skill.

“Whoever lies with his uncle’s wife,” and the rest: that is, whoever, instructed by his predecessors, touches the stains of error shall perish without the reward of good works.

“Whoever takes his brother’s wife,” and the rest, as Herod did. Whoever corrupts by his persuasion a necessary friend, whom the Lord commended under the image of the right hand and foot, shall likewise perish.

“Lest the land vomit you out when you are about to enter it,” and the rest: that is, lest you be shamefully expelled from the Church if you live wickedly within it. The Church is the land that produces suitable vegetation with blessing. The land is said to vomit out its inhabitants when it does not permit the disinherited to remain in it.

“But to you I say: Possess their land,” and the rest: that is, make yourselves worthy of the inheritance by good morals, for they themselves readily possessed it. Mystically, however, the faithful people are commanded to inhabit and preserve by holy conduct the land of the Church, which through Christ has been freed from the devil and from errors [Col. 0834A].

“A land flowing”—that is, overflowing—with every sweetness. Of all foods that are prepared, milk and honey are prepared most easily. By these he indicates to them that, if they kept his commandments, they would possess the promised land without any labor and with complete joy. The same sweetness of spiritual teaching and gifts is promised in the present to us who fear God, and in the future, rest without labor.

“I have separated you from the other peoples,” because he gave them the law. He has also separated us, since he caused us to know his power.

“Separate the unclean animal”: that is, the common person lying in the folly of error from the one who is poor in spirit through his simplicity.

“Do not defile your souls with animals and birds”: that is, do not be deceived by the folly of those who wander or by the cleverness of philosophers.

“You shall be holy to me”: living holy lives; the rest is as above.

“A man or a woman in whom there is a pythonic spirit,” and the rest. Whether greater or lesser, those who follow error and false prophets are guilty of death; if they do not repent, let them be convicted by the harsh darts of judgments and perish in their sins.

## CHAPTER XXI
“Let the priest not defile himself among the deaths of his fellow citizens.” For the Lord speaks to Ezekiel concerning all priests, saying: “I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel: if you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, he will die in his sins; but I will require his blood at your hand” (Ezek. [Col. 0834C] 33), and so forth. Thus teachers are commanded not to be polluted by the sins of their fellow citizens. “Except only among his blood relatives,” and so forth. It often happens that someone is promoted to the priesthood after managing his household affairs. But because that marital relationship cannot be maintained without an admixture of sin, the priest is permitted to be defiled by human frailty—that is, to care for persons necessarily joined to him—where, as we have said, it would scarcely be possible to be free from sin; not because we detest marriage, but because we know that we are entangled in the filth of the original stain. For, according to the Apostle, the man who is to be ordained is commanded to preside well over his household, to have chaste children, and to have a good reputation among those outside (1 Tim. 3).

“But he shall not be defiled among the ruler of his people,” that is, he must not consent to their sins by flattering them. [Col. 0834D] “They shall not shave their heads or their beards,” that is, the thoughts of their minds must not incline toward consenting to sins. By the beard we understand the vigor or understanding of the soul. The same interpretation should be applied here as in the case of the thoughts mentioned above. “Nor shall they make incisions in their flesh,” that is, they must not permit scandal in their life. For they offer to God “the incense of the Lord,” that is, prayers, and “the loaves,” that is, sacrifices of praise.

“He shall not take a prostitute or a disreputable harlot as his wife,” that is, he shall not mingle with heretics and pagans, nor imitate one who has been repudiated—that is, the Synagogue, cast away from Christ through superstition. “If the priest’s daughter is caught in fornication,” and the rest: the soul of one subject to another, if it falls into error, is purified by the flames of repentance or burned in Gehenna. [Col. 0835A]

“The high priest, that is, the chief priest among his brothers,” and the rest. Christ is the eternal high priest, anointed with the Holy Spirit above all the saints. “Whose hands have been consecrated,” that is, stretched out upon the cross for our justification. “And he has been clothed in holy garments,” in the assembly of the saints. “He shall not uncover his head,” that is, he shall not dishonor his divinity; for, being subject to the Father in his humanity, he honors the Father while being equal to him in divinity. “He shall not tear his garment,” that is, he does not allow the Church to be torn apart. “He shall not enter upon any dead person,” for he was a participant in no sin. “Not even for his father or mother,” that is, for the Jewish people and the Synagogue. “Nor shall he go out from the holy place,” that is, from the Father’s will, “lest he defile the sanctuary,” that is, the Church [Col. 0835B] or his own body—which he certainly does not do.

“He shall take a virgin as his wife,” to whom the Apostle says: “For I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” —“A widow, a repudiated woman, or a prostitute,” and the rest, that is, the Synagogue and pagan superstition; “but he shall take a maiden from his own people,” that is, the Church, regenerated by the water of baptism from the universality of the nations. He calls it his own people because, since he is human, he regards the whole human race as related to him. “Nor shall he mingle with any branch of his kindred,” and the rest. For he does not permit his members to be mingled with the wicked.

Let us understand these things as prophesied chiefly of Christ rather than as commands, so that we may have him as our patron, truly fulfilling all these things: “Whoever has a blemish shall not offer loaves to God,” that is, whoever has a defiled conscience must not presumptuously handle the mysteries of the Lord. [Col. 0835C] “If he is blind,” that is, if he does not possess the light of knowledge; “if lame,” that is, if he does not walk properly in the Lord’s commandments; “if he has a small, large, or crooked nose,” that is, little discernment, or excessive and perverse discernment; “if he has a broken foot,” that is, if he does not walk rightly on God’s way; “if he has a defective hand,” that is, corrupt action; “if he is hunchbacked,” that is, weighed down by the burden of sins; “if he is bleary-eyed,” that is, if he sees the Lord’s commandments but does not carry them out in worthy deeds; “if he has a white spot in his eye,” that is, an obscured light of knowledge; “if he has a continual scab,” that is, wantonness of the flesh; “if he has an eruption,” that is, avarice; “or if he is herniated,” that is, weighed down by the superfluities of the mind.

These vices are to be understood as comprising the number twelve, to show that all of them are contrary to apostolic teaching. Therefore, whoever remembers himself to be burdened with such blemishes should not condemn himself by taking the body and blood of the Lord unworthily. “Yet he shall eat of the loaves,” and the rest: that is, although he is such a person, he should nevertheless be provided with the nourishment of spiritual teaching, so that at some time he may come to his senses. [Col. 0835D]

“He shall not enter within the veil,” that is, he should not easily be admitted to reconciliation, nor to the opening of the mysteries, nor presume that he will enter the heavenly kingdom, since nothing unclean will enter there. “He must not defile my sanctuary”: he wrongfully claims holy things for himself. “Moses therefore spoke to Aaron,” and the rest. The Law indicates all the Lord’s commandments to priests, together with the whole Christian people.

## CHAPTER XXII

[Col. 0836A]

“That they may beware of the things that have been sanctified,” that is, that they handle them carefully. Shortly afterward he explains what he had warned them to avoid: “Any man, he says, who approaches from your offspring,” up to “in whom there is uncleanness.” Here he recalls the matters mentioned above. We too must pay the greatest attention lest we touch the mysteries of Christ unworthily.

“And they shall not profane the name of the sanctified things,” and the rest. He profanes the name of the sacrifice who offers it unworthily, not according to its dignity. “Whoever is a leper or suffers from an issue of semen,” and the rest. A heretic, disfigured by vices, and one who serves fornication and carnal pleasure must not communicate until he has been healed through repentance. “Whoever [Col. 0836B] touches something unclean upon a dead person,” and the rest—that is, whoever is polluted by some corpse; concerning these matters it has been fully said above.

Mystically, however, this varied touching of unclean things signifies communion with sin. Whoever is polluted by such things “is unclean” until repentance has been completed; but “when he has washed his flesh,” that is, cleansed his conscience, and after “the sun has set,” that is, when the fervor of completed repentance has passed beyond him, then, if he has been thoroughly cleansed, he may lawfully use the sanctified things.

“An animal that has died of itself or has been torn by a beast”: concerning these things we have spoken above. “Let them keep my commandments,” and the rest. Let us observe this carefully, lest we be overthrown by the second death. [Col. 0836C] “No foreigner shall eat of the sanctified things,” that is, a pagan must not be admitted to the mysteries of Christ. Hence the Lord forbade casting pearls before swine.

“A resident alien of the priest and a hired servant,” and the rest. A resident alien is so called as one who is within the household and serves in domestic duties; a hired servant, however, is one who works in agriculture or in the keeping of sheep. Neither serves so as to remain in the household, but is always ready to leave and does not cease to seek his wage in the present. They signify those who behave hypocritically in the Church, not for the sake of an eternal reward, and thereby show themselves unworthy of the Lord’s body.

“But one whom the priest has bought,” and the rest—that is, one who, bought through evangelical teaching, ought to render faithful service to Christ in the Church is not to be alienated. “If the priest’s daughter is married to anyone from the people,” and the rest: that is, if a soul joins itself to the baseness of the vicious, let it be suspended from receiving the sacred things. [Col. 0836D]

“But if she is a widow or repudiated,” and the rest—that is, if she has separated herself from vices and been freed from evil, let her be restored, apart from those hardened in evil ways. “Whoever eats of the sanctified things through ignorance,” and the rest: whoever presumptuously handles something in divine matters, as though ignorant of its power, shall pay for it through repentance and restore a fifth part—that is, instruct each of his five senses toward correction.

“But whoever offers his offering,” up to “it shall be an unblemished male,” and the rest. Whatever we offer must be presented in the strength of firm action, without the stain of malice. “From cattle,” that is, strong action; “from sheep,” that is, the virtue of innocence; “from goats,” that is, the fruit of repentance. “If it has a blemish,” and the rest: for if a good work is done for any reason other than the one it ought to serve, “it will not be acceptable.” [Col. 0837A]

“The man who offers a victim,” and the rest. Understand as a bull one who appoints someone to a teaching office; as a sheep, a humble hearer; as a goat, repentance. Let him offer such persons as are commanded here. “If it is blind,” that is, lacking the light of knowledge; “if broken,” that is, not walking properly; “if it has a scar,” that is, a mark of past sin. For there are certain sins which, if they are openly discovered in one who is to be ordained, cause him to be rejected from what he has begun; “if it has pustules,” that is, the vice of detraction; “a scab,” restlessness and avarice; “or an eruption,” which fatigues the body without pain and corresponds to fornication, sweet to the flesh but destruction to the soul. Those polluted by such vices must by no means be promoted to the ranks, because they are not acceptable to the Lord.

[Col. 0837B] “A bull or a sheep with its ear or tail cut off,” and the rest. He has a cut-off ear who is disobedient, or flees from hearing the word of God, or willingly listens to vain things. He has lost his tail who does not take care to foresee his last things. Such persons may be offered voluntarily, but a vow cannot be fulfilled with them: they are to be instructed toward repentance and conversion, yet they must not be admitted to teaching.

“Every animal that has crushed, bruised, or cut parts, or has had its testicles removed,” and the rest. The testicles signify the capacity to produce offspring; therefore, whoever is fruitless—that is, empty of hope for good works—cannot be acceptable to the Lord.

[Col. 0837C] “You shall not offer the loaves of your God from the hand of a foreigner,” and the rest. If pagans give anything to be offered, it must not be accepted. Nevertheless, we pray for catechumens and for the conversion of unbelievers; but if they wish to persist in error, their vows are detestable.

“When a bull, a sheep, or a goat is born, it shall be under its mother’s udder for seven days.” Whether strong, innocent, or repentant, let a person at this time remember that he is held under the weakness of nature. But on the eighth day, and so forth—that is, on the day of resurrection, once immortality has been received, the elect will serve God alone without failing.

“Whether it is a bull or a sheep, it shall not be slaughtered on the same day as its young,” that is, the newness of the Gospel must not be observed together with the superstition and antiquity of the Law. Concerning eating the same sacrifice, it has been said above. [Col. 0837D]

“I brought you out from the land of Egypt”: Christ also delivered us from the power of the devil. “I am the Lord”: therefore he appends the remembrance of his name to each command, so that he might instill fear in them and prevent them from sinning, while also planting love in them, so that he might teach them to regard his commandments more diligently.

## CHAPTER XXIII

“These are the feasts of the Lord, which you shall call holy,” that is, abstentions from evil works, which are called “the Lord’s” because they fulfill the Lord’s will. “For six days you shall do work,” and so forth. He shows that in this life we must devote ourselves to pious labors, because once we have reached rest, there will no longer be time for working. He rightly says, “in all your dwelling places,” because in the future life there is a dwelling, whereas in the present there is a pilgrimage. [Col. 0838A]

“In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month,” and so forth. This refers to the time of Christ’s passion, for redemption is the beginning of all our conduct. When he says that the Passover is to be celebrated on the fourteenth day and the solemnity on the fifteenth, he shows that the Lord’s humanity, with the shadow following under the Gospel, begins the true solemnity of understanding.

The seven days of unleavened bread are counted from that day because we who have been redeemed by Christ must throughout our whole life be free from the bitterness of Jewish perversity and from other errors. “The first day shall be most solemn for you,” up to “the seventh day shall be more solemn and holier.” The first day is the entrance into the new life; the seventh day is the completion of labors. In both, we must take the greatest care that we are not found doing “servile work,” that is, work subject to sin. If anyone has grown sluggish through negligence at the beginning, let him strive to be found among the good at the end. [Col. 0838B]

“When you have entered the land,” and the rest—that is, when the faithful dwell in the Church; “and you have reaped the grain,” that is, when you have led peoples to faithfulness. Concerning them the Lord said: “Look at the regions, for they are white for harvest.” You shall bring sheaves of grain, namely, the assembly of the saints in the primitive Church; and this happened when three thousand souls were added on one day and five thousand on the next.

[Col. 0838C] “He shall lift the sheaf before the Lord,” and the rest. Since the offering of the faithful is made acceptable to God through the help of Christ, the great priest. “On the day after the Sabbath, and he shall sanctify it,” and the rest. In his resurrection he joined together the unity of the saints.

But if you wish to understand the sheaf as Christ’s flesh, from which the bread of life is supplied to us, the second day may be understood as the day of the passion. For on one day he celebrated the mystical supper, and on the next he completed his body’s offering for us in the punishment of the cross.

“On the same day on which the sheaf is consecrated, an unblemished lamb shall be slaughtered,” that is, when Christ was sacrificed on the altar of the cross, the unity of the faithful was sanctified in Christ’s blood. “Libations shall be offered with it,” that is, when he suffered, the sacraments of our redemption flowed from his side.

“Two tenths mingled with oil,” and the rest. The tenths signify the completion of the Law. The two signify either the two Testaments or the Law and the Prophets, in which the Lord’s passion is most clearly announced. [Col. 0838D]

“For a pleasing fragrance to the Lord”: the work which the Son was accomplishing was most pleasing to the Father. “Also a libation of wine, a fourth part of a hin.” Wine is spiritual teaching; it is called a fourth part of a hin because the fullness of wisdom is found in each of the four books of the Gospels.

“Bread and meal and porridge,” and the rest: that is, strive to prepare yourself for that rest of the soul before you know that you have been initiated into the faith of that redemption.

“You shall therefore count from the day after the Sabbath,” and the rest. The sheaf was taken and sanctified, as Josephus testifies, on the sixteenth day of the moon; but now he seems to command that the counting begin from the fifteenth day of the moon, when the firstfruits themselves were brought, though they had not yet been sanctified by sacrifice.

We, however, count “from the day after the Sabbath,” [Col. 0839A] that is, from the resurrection, the series leading to the fiftieth-day solemnity. For just as on Mount Sinai, in the presence of the Lord, the indications of the Law—[f. judgments]—not yet written down were shown to the Hebrew people on the fiftieth day after they had gone out from Egypt, so, after redemption, the grace of the Holy Spirit was sent down from heaven to the faithful on the fiftieth day.

“Until the day after the seventh week is completed,” that is, after seven weeks had been completed, with one day added, the observance was fulfilled. “A new sacrifice from all your dwelling places”: with a new kind of proclamation, they hastened to offer new gifts of virtues throughout all their assemblies.

“Two loaves of firstfruits”: either the two commandments of love or the gathering of the two peoples. [Col. 0839B] They are called two tenths of fine flour because both Testaments were formed by the deepest wisdom. The flour is called fermented, that is, filled with the firmness of teaching. It is baked as firstfruits of the Lord, that is, established by the Holy Spirit for the sanctification of beginners.

The seven unblemished lambs signify Christ, who willed to be offered through the Holy Spirit; or the innocence of life, which the grace of the Holy Spirit has bestowed upon us. The calf signifies Christ; the two rams signify either Christ in his two natures or teachers imbued with the two Testaments. The libations signify either the mysteries of our redemption or the admixture of spiritual wisdom. The goat signifies repentance, which the Lord first preached. The two lambs signify peace and holiness, or humility and gentleness. Concerning these the Lord says: “Learn from me, for I am gentle” [Col. 0839C] (Matt. 11), and so forth.

“They shall serve for its use.” Everything that we do pertains to Christ the priest, because it is received by him. “And you shall call this day most solemn,” and the rest. Truly it is most holy, on which the whole Church has been sanctified. Concerning the rest, as above.

“After you have reaped the grain of your land,” and the rest. O Jews, do not twist the understanding of the Law into the letter away from its spiritual meaning; rather, leave what you cannot grasp to be investigated by the people of the Church, poor in spirit, through allegorical subtlety. The rest that was said above has been fulfilled spiritually under grace, and it must be believed by us daily, so that we may please the Lord.

“In the seventh month, on the first day of the month,” and the rest. This is in the fullness of the times, when the Lord Jesus proclaimed the acceptable year of the Lord, in which we are commanded, as though by the number seven, to rest from evil works. [Col. 0839D]

“On the first day of the month,” that is, at the beginning of preaching; “when the trumpets sound,” that is, when the cries of teaching resound. “It shall be a Sabbath of remembrance,” that is, a continuing practice of abstaining from vices.

“On the tenth day of this seventh month,” that is, in the fullness of that same period, “there shall be a day of atonement”: we are to afflict our souls, because this is an acceptable time; through repentance we should chastise ourselves, so that we may find the atonement granted to us in Christ’s passion.

“Every soul that is not afflicted on this day,” and the rest—that is, whoever, while able to repent of evil works, neglects to do so, will be cut off from the assembly of the saints throughout all generations. [Col. 0840A] For in the Church, when others exhort them, the same worship of righteousness must be maintained.

“You shall afflict your souls on the ninth day of the month; from evening to evening you shall celebrate your Sabbaths.” To keep Sabbath from evening to evening is to remain in the affliction of repentance until the end, until the future morning dawns.

“From the fifteenth day of this seventh month there shall be a feast of booths to the Lord,” and the rest. The number fifteen contains within itself the most excellent numbers, namely seven and eight. The former is suitably compared with the Law because of the Sabbath observance, the latter with the Gospel because of the resurrection. During the whole period of this life we must remember these things in our observance, because “we have no lasting city here, but we seek the one that is to come” (Rom. 13), so that we may live as guests hastening toward their homeland. He has given us the Spirit, having snatched us from the slavery of the devil, just as they continually observed this solemnity in remembrance of their liberation and exodus from Egypt.

[Col. 0840B] By calling the first and eighth days solemn, he shows that the intervening days must be observed with similar devotion and commands that our whole life be guarded from beginning to end. For it is called a gathering and a collected assembly—that is, “day of gathering” in the genitive, as though it meant “of congregation.” The day of the gathering is called collected because seven days have been gathered into it, that is, completed, since it was the end of the festival. The eighth day may also be understood as the resurrection, which is the day of gathering and collection, because then all will be gathered into the kingdom of God and the end of the ages will be brought together.

[Col. 0840C] “You shall offer offerings to the Lord on them, burnt offerings and libations according to the rite of each day,” and the rest. We ought to offer varied progress in virtue, according to what the time dictates, because “there is a time for speaking, a time for keeping silence, a time for weeping, and a time for laughing” (Eccl. 3), and what follows. “Except for the Lord’s Sabbaths,” and the rest: let us do what has been commanded, and otherwise add whatever we are able.

“From the fifteenth day of the seventh month,” and the rest. He recapitulates what was said above, whose meaning is plain.

“You shall take for yourselves on the first day the fruits of a very beautiful tree,” that is, at the beginning of grace, the fruits of virtues produced by Christ and the keeping of his teaching. He himself is the very beautiful tree, of whom he says: “If they do this in the green wood,” and the rest.

“And branches of palms,” that is, by the virtue of righteousness. For the palm crowns victors, the laurel soldiers, and the ivy poets. He says “branches,” using a diminutive form, as though in the likeness of a longer sword. [Col. 0840D]

“And branches of a tree with dense foliage,” that is, forms of manifold virtues, such as charity, mercy, and humility; or he calls the sayings of the holy Scriptures branches. “And willows from the torrent,” that is, chastity in the shortness of this life. For the willow produces no fruit, and the torrent passes quickly. “And you shall rejoice before the Lord your God.” Spiritually, the one who knows that he is adorned with these virtues can rejoice. The rest is as above.

[Col. 0841A] “Everyone who is of the stock of Israel,” that is, who belongs to the fellowship of Christians, “so that your descendants may learn that I made the children of Israel dwell in booths,” and so forth. We therefore celebrate commemorations of our redemption, so that we may know how great a kindness God has shown us and may make the same kindness known to those newly arriving, so that praise and thanksgiving may be rendered to Christ throughout eternal ages.

“Moses spoke concerning the solemnities,” and the rest. The Law speaks to the faithful concerning all observances of God’s commandments.

## CHAPTER XXIV

“That they may bring you pure olive oil for preparing the lamps outside the veil of testimony,” and the rest. The children of Israel, who are the faithful, should offer true mercy for the adornment of their works within the Church; to them the Lord says: “Let your light so shine before men” (Matt. 5), and so forth. In another sense, the lamps are the lights of God there, where mercy is especially commended.

[Col. 0841B] “And Aaron shall set them from evening until morning,” and the rest. This means Christ, who establishes in his Church his own brightness and the beauty of his works throughout the night of this life until the morning of the resurrection. “Upon the purest lampstand,” that is, upon Christ, who contains the entire state of his Church.

“You shall also take fine flour and bake twelve loaves from it,” and the rest. Let teachers be instructed in divine wisdom according to apostolic teaching. “They shall have two tenths,” that is, let them preserve the perfection of both Testaments; “six on each side upon the table.” They agree in Holy Scripture. In another sense, those loaves signify the Eucharist and the table the altar; and the fact that they were twelve signifies its perfect meaning.

[Col. 0841C] “And you shall place upon them the purest frankincense,” that is, prayer or the illumination of God’s word, because frankincense benefits the eyes. “They shall be changed every Sabbath,” that is, good teachers are said to be transferred from here to rest, while others are appointed in their place on the Sabbath because of that same rest. “Received from the children of Israel”: for holy teachers are taken from the faithful. “They shall belong to Aaron and his sons,” because Christ receives them into himself.

“Now the son of an Israelite woman went out, whom she had borne to an Egyptian man among the children of Israel, and he quarreled in the camp,” and the rest. This man signifies one who, born within the Christian religion, has an Egyptian father—that is, one who has fallen into error through the philosophy of the gentiles. This is what it means to quarrel; and because he blasphemed the name of the Lord, he is sent, as one who has gone astray, into prison, because he must be severely disciplined. [Col. 0841D]

Afterward he is commanded to be stoned outside the camp, because one who persists in error must be driven outside the Church by the harsh judgments of excommunication.

“A man who curses his God,” and the rest—that is, one who through error attempts to violate the worship of God shall be punished either by the penalty of repentance or by eternal condemnation. “Whether citizen or foreigner,” that is, whether Jew or gentile. “Whoever kills a man,” that is, whoever leads astray someone useful to many, shall be punished as above.

“Whoever strikes an animal shall pay its equivalent,” that is, whoever leads astray a simple and foolish person must expiate the guilt of that seduction through worthy repentance. “Whoever inflicts a blemish,” and so forth: whoever harms the life of a neighbor in any way must cleanse it through worthy correction. [Col. 0842A]

“Let there be equal judgment among you, whether a foreigner or a citizen has sinned”: whether a Jew or a gentile comes into the Church, let each cleanse himself from transgression by the same correction.

## CHAPTER XXV

“When you enter the land, let the land keep a Sabbath to the Lord,” that is, when you enter the Church, seek the rest that is to come. “For six years you shall sow your field,” that is, in this life labor in the commandments of the Law and in the grace of the Gospel, which is to prune the vineyard for six years; “and you shall gather its fruit,” that is, labor so as to attain the fruit of life.

“In the seventh year the land shall keep a Sabbath,” and the rest: that is, in the future rest there will be no time for laboring, nor will fruit be sought through toil; therefore he commands that it not be harvested. [Col. 0842B] “But they shall be food for you”: what is granted by the Lord will be received without labor. For there the reward will not be increased by anyone’s labor, but by the mercy of God, according to what he grants as food—that is, refreshment of life—for master and servant, that is, for teacher and subjects, and for the hired servant who serves in the Church for an eternal reward; and for the resident alien and the beasts, that is, for the gentile who has been converted and for the simple.

“For there are many dwelling places in the Father’s house” (John 14), because each person will be rewarded according to his own measure.

“You shall also count seven weeks of years, that is, seven times seven,” which signifies the perfection of rest, “and you shall sound the trumpet.” For the trumpet will sound, and the dead who are in Christ will rise first (1 Cor. 15). “On the tenth day of the seventh month,” that is, in the perfection of the promised rest, “you shall sanctify the fiftieth year.” We have shown in many places that fifty signifies remission. For in the future rest remission will be perfect, when all the elect are called to the kingdom.

“A man shall return to his possession,” that is, to paradise, from which he had long ago fallen; “he shall return to his family,” that is, to the company of the angels, according as each person’s merits require. Concerning not sowing and not reaping, it has already been said. “But you shall eat what is offered immediately,” that is, let us immediately use what the just Judge, the Lord, will repay, without seeking a later exercise of labor.

“You shall not gather the firstfruits of the vintage,” that is, according to the letter he commands that they not gather wine to be pressed. “In the year of jubilee everyone shall return to his possessions,” that is, at the separation of body and soul, or at the universal resurrection, the elect shall return to paradise, where the thief went from the cross.

“When you sell anything to your fellow citizen or buy it from him,” and the rest: that is, when you commend teaching to your brother or buy obedience from him, “do not distress him,” that is, do not demand from him greater knowledge or action than he has received from you. This is to buy according to the number of the jubilee. “The more years that remain after the jubilee, the greater the price will increase,” and so forth. The longer someone has adhered to a teacher, the more excellent fruits he must repay.

“So that you may be able to dwell in the land,” and the rest. Let us keep the Lord’s commandments, so that, living in the Church without fear of the devil’s cunning, we may acquire the fruit of life in it. “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4).

[Col. 0843A] “I shall give you a blessing in the sixth year.” That is, in the sixth age, when the Lord was made incarnate, as the Psalmist says: “The Lord’s blessing is upon you; we bless you in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 128). The Lord’s blessing is upon us, who, redeemed in Christ’s blood, are able to produce the fruit of virtues. We are blessed in the name of the Lord because through Christ’s coming we know the Father; hence he himself says: “Whoever sees me sees my Father also” (John 14).

“And it shall produce the fruit of three years.” For such a blessing was given that in the faith of the Holy Trinity we may abound in all things. “And you shall sow in the eighth year.” This means that, rising again, you will stand before Christ’s tribunal, giving an account of your good works, for which you will be crowned. [Col. 0843B]

“And you shall eat the old produce until the ninth year.” That is, in the good works acquired in the body you will rejoice unto eternity and beyond. “Until the new things grow, you shall eat the old.” That is, may the merits of your good works, with God’s grace, lead you to the place where eternal things are supplied to you.

“The land shall not be sold forever, because it is mine.” Although many depart from the Church, it will not be overturned forever, because Christ is in it. “And you are resident aliens and settlers with me.” Although a person is born in the Church, he must be born again in order to enter it.

“Therefore, throughout the whole region of your possession,” and the rest. If anyone has converted his body or soul into slavery to sin, he can be released through repentance. “If your brother has become poor,” and the rest: if a brother has become weak in faith or action and has subjected himself to iniquity; “and his relative wishes,” and so forth—that is, any teacher, if he wishes, can recall him through word and reason. To him James says: “Whoever brings a sinner back from the error of his way,” and so forth.

[Col. 0843C] “And if he himself can find the price with which to redeem himself,” and the rest: that is, if he lacks another’s help and has himself been corrected by some zeal of remorse, “the fruits shall be reckoned,” and the rest—that is, let him consider how long he served the devil and henceforth redeem his life through the worthy fruit of repentance.

“But if his hand does not find enough to repay the price, the buyer shall have what he bought until the year of jubilee.” That is, if he has not yet raised himself through the zeal of amendment, he remains in the teacher’s power until he reaches the jubilee, that is, true remission through repentance. [Col. 0843D]

“For in it every sale returns,” and the rest. In the perfection of repentance, the sinner is restored to his former liberty.

[Col. 0844A] A house sold in a city may be redeemed within one year. Not afterward, when the year has passed, because worship under the Law, made worse by the traditions of the Pharisees, could be redeemed from transgression in the year—that is, in the time of Christ’s incarnation—if they had wished to believe. For Satan possessed those who remained obstinate in error. “Nor could they be redeemed in the jubilee,” that is, in Christ’s passion, when the Lord said: “Father, forgive them,” and so forth (Luke 23). But those who believed in his incarnation redeemed their conduct in one year, and this prayer benefited them.

A house in an unwalled village is sold under the condition of the fields, because the conduct of the gentiles, not bound by the guardianship of the Law, if it deviates from the truth after acknowledging it, is redeemed through repentance. Concerning the jubilee, as above.

“The houses of the Levites that are in the cities may always be redeemed,” that is, the assemblies of the apostles, which they gathered, were cleansed through repentance from what they had previously done wrong. “Because they are their possessions among the children of Israel,” because those whom they converted through their prayers were saved by the Lord’s mercy, not by their own merits.

[Col. 0844B] “Their surrounding lands shall not be sold,” and the rest, that is, virtues must never be abandoned, because we cannot live without them. There are, however, certain virtues that cannot be possessed continually, such as fasts, vigils, and similar practices; but there are others of which a person must never be deprived, such as charity, humility, and so forth. The former, too, are possessed continually if, when they are not present in action, they are made present in intention.

“If your brother has become poor,” and the rest. If one joined to you in Christianity becomes weak in action and you “take him in” to instruct him, demand from him as much as you have given him—that is, according to your teaching, seek his obedience.

[Col. 0844C] “You shall not give him your money at interest,” and the rest: when you entrust the treasure of teaching to one who is weak, do not demand from him an operation beyond his capacity. There is another interpretation: giving money to money-changers so that it may be returned with interest. The abundance of crops signifies immoderate obedience.

“If your brother, compelled by poverty, sells himself to you,” and so forth—that is, if, having become weak, he chooses you as his teacher, do not despise him as a servant, that is, as a pagan. Rather, let him labor with you for the sake of the future reward until the jubilee, that is, the remission of sins. For Paul says: “If a man is overtaken in any trespass, you who are spiritual,” and so forth (Gal. 6). “He shall work with you,” that is, let him gather virtues; “and afterward he shall go out with his children,” that is, with his works, “to return to his kindred,” that is, to evangelical conduct, “and to the possession of his fathers,” that is, paradise.

“You shall not oppress him by force.” This is what the Apostle commands: “Not lording it over the clergy, but becoming examples to the flock” (1 Pet. 5).

“Let male and female slaves be your property,” and the rest, that is, regard pagans as inferior to you; “and from the resident aliens who sojourn among you, or from those born from them,” that is, catechumens, or those who follow their way of life; “these you shall have as servants,” and the rest: excel them forever in virtues.

[Col. 0844D] “If the hand of a resident alien or sojourner among you grows strong,” and the rest. If a weak brother consents to some sin; “but if one of his brothers wishes,” that is, one of the Christians, he can free him through prayer or teaching. Or, if he himself has the zeal to repent, let him reckon the time of his sale, during which he served sin, and strive to practice worthy repentance in the life that follows. “You shall not oppress him violently in your sight,” as if he were saying: You are his debtor, so that you must not allow him to be oppressed but must set him free.

[Col. 0845A] “But if after these things he cannot be redeemed,” and the rest—that is, if he is not redeemed sooner by himself or through another, nevertheless, at some time, if he repents and receives remission, he will be restored to liberty together with good works. “I brought you out of the land of Egypt,” that is, I redeemed you from the power of the devil.

## CHAPTER XXVI
“‘You shall not make idols for yourselves,’ and so forth—that is, do not possess greed, ‘which is the service of idols’ (Eph. 5). ‘Nor shall you erect pillars’: according to the literal sense, he speaks of many altars; mystically, of principal vices and capital crimes. ‘Nor shall you set up a conspicuous stone,’ and so forth. This is clear according to the historical sense; allegorically, however, he forbids, through the worship of greed, amassing a heap of precious things—whether stones, other metals, or things of any kind. ‘I will give you rains in their seasons’: that is, the teaching of the Scriptures or of good teachers. [Col. 0845B] ‘And the earth shall yield its growth’: that is, your life shall produce the virtues of good works. ‘And the trees shall be filled with fruits’: that is, with holy virtues. ‘The threshing of the harvest shall overtake the vintage,’ and so forth. The completion of one virtue is followed by another as its reward, as Paul says: ‘God, who works in you both the willing and the advancing, according to his good will’ (Phil. 2). By “good will” he means that perfection is supplied through good works. ‘And you shall eat your bread to satisfaction’: that is, spiritual teaching; ‘and you shall dwell without fear.’ For whoever keeps the Lord’s commandments is not caught by the devil’s ambushes.

“‘I will give peace within your borders’: that is, in the Church or in each individual person. True peace exists when a person no longer feels the conflicts of vices within himself. [Col. 0845C] ‘You shall sleep, and there shall be no one to terrify you’: that is, you shall rest, with no one disturbing you. ‘I will remove evil beasts’: that is, spiritual enemies. ‘The sword shall not pass through your borders’: that is, the sword of discord or vengeance. ‘You shall pursue your enemies,’ and so forth: that is, by doing good you shall overcome the devil. ‘Five of you shall pursue a hundred strangers’: that is, a few of the faithful who then govern their senses well and follow the divine law shall drive away the full force of the opposing power. Just as perfect numbers are understood in a good sense, so they have corresponding numerical forms in evil things. ‘Your enemies shall fall by the sword’: that is, the evil spirits shall fall by God’s vengeance. ‘I will look upon you’: through mercy.

“‘You shall eat what is oldest of the old, and you shall cast out the old when the new arrives.’ He says this because of the fertility of the land. Mystically, we do this when, according to the Apostle, we ‘forget what lies behind’ (Phil. 3), that is, when we stretch ourselves toward what is within. For the saints are always, as it were, at the beginning of virtue, since they do not think that past good deeds are sufficient for them. [Col. 0845D] ‘I will set my tabernacle in your midst’: that is, I will make my dwelling in each righteous person. ‘I will walk among you’: that is, so that I may cause you to walk in my commandments. ‘I broke the chains of your necks so that you might walk upright’: that is, I removed the burdens of sins so that you might know God and keep him in remembrance, and not devote yourselves to earthly desires.

“‘I will visit you swiftly with poverty and burning heat,’ so that you may always thirst and never be [Col. 0846A] satisfied; ‘which will waste away your eyes’: that is, the burning heat will make your eyes fail, and they will see what they do not wish to see; ‘and consume your souls,’ because of your anguish. By burning heat and poverty he signifies that those who despise God’s commandments are afflicted with a thirst for spiritual understanding. ‘You shall sow your seed in vain,’ and the rest: that is, you who wish to be without Christ imitate certain virtues in vain, because the devil corrupts them through his perversity. What follows belongs to the same meaning.

“‘You shall flee when no one pursues you’: that is, possessing no confidence, you shall waste away in your sins while your conscience accuses you. ‘I will add your chastisements sevenfold’: that is, complete vengeance. The same applies in what follows. ‘I will make your heaven above like iron and your earth like bronze.’ He speaks simply of barrenness, because when rain does not come from above the earth produces nothing. Mystically, those who despise Christ have neither divine help nor any fruit in the Scriptures or in their hearts. [Col. 0846B] ‘Nor shall the trees yield fruit’: that is, those who ought to appear to produce fruit shall be distinguished by no virtues. ‘I will send the beasts of the field’: that is, evil spirits, ‘which shall consume both you and your cattle’: that is, both the wise and the dull. ‘And your roads shall become desolate’: that is, your actions, because no one will practice them.

“‘I too will walk against you in hostility.’ Those who are contrary to the Lord’s will should know that the Lord is not sufficiently present to them as a helper. ‘And I will bring a sword upon you,’ and so forth: that is, the word of God, which will convict you Jews that, without the grace of the Gospel, the Law cannot save you. All these things that surround the passage concern the Jews, who did not receive Christ when he came.

“‘When you flee into the cities,’ and so forth: that is, through your prophets their meaning will convict you of thinking in a merely mortal way. ‘After I have broken the staff of your bread,’ and so forth: that is, the strength of Scripture, which you observe carnally. For the Law is worthless without Christ. [Col. 0846C] ‘So that ten women shall bake your bread in one oven,’ and so forth: that is, the ten commandments shall prepare understanding within the narrowness of the Law, ‘but they shall by no means give it for satisfaction,’ because they do not possess the breadth of spiritual understanding.

“‘So that you shall eat the flesh of your sons and your daughters.’ Both things happened in the Babylonian and Roman captivities. Moreover, they ate the flesh of their sons and daughters when they deceived their disciples by perverse teaching. [Col. 0846D] ‘I will destroy your high places and break your images’: that is, the priests and teachers. ‘You shall fall among the ruins of your idols’: the scribes and Pharisees—idols because they preferred their superstitions to the Lord’s commandments. ‘I will reduce your cities to desolation’: do not follow a carnal sense in the prophets. ‘And I will make your sanctuaries desolate’: that is, I will cause you to abandon your worship and religion. ‘I will no longer accept the most pleasing fragrance’: that is, of the sacrifices which pleased me in the shadow. ‘And I will destroy your land’: that is, I will not allow Scripture understood carnally to remain in that condition.

“‘And all your enemies shall be astonished at it when they have become its inhabitants.’ That is, those converted from the nations, who received the inheritance of faith in your place, will marvel at your hardness. He calls them enemies as though they were opponents. ‘But I will scatter you among the nations,’ as we see happened afterward, following Christ’s Passion. ‘And I will unsheathe the sword after you.’ For the word of God attacks them everywhere. [Col. 0847A] ‘Then the land shall enjoy its Sabbaths’: that is, the Scriptures shall rest from carnal observance, for you did not grant them the rest of rightful observance.

“‘And to those who remain I will give fear in their hearts.’ That is, if those who previously believed return, I will give them anxiety while they live among a Christian people, driven from their former dwellings. ‘The sound of a flying leaf shall terrify them’: that is, the sentence of the prophets. For whatever the nations see them presume to do concerning what the Law forbids terrifies them, and they shrink from seeing it. [Col. 0847B] ‘And so they shall flee as though from a sword,’ and so forth. When someone shows them something from the Scriptures, ‘they shall fall when no one pursues them’: that is, they think this is being done to their detriment, although such charity is shown to them for no other reason than goodwill. ‘They shall fall, each upon his brother’: that is, they shall lead one another to ruin.

“‘A hostile land shall consume you.’ The evangelical Scripture, namely, will convict you of error. ‘But if some of them remain, they shall waste away in their iniquities,’ and so forth. Those who wish to persist in the error they began, after their homeland has been lost, will themselves also be worn down by punishments, ‘until they confess their iniquities,’ either here through repentance or in the future, when they must give an account. [Col. 0847C] ‘And I will bring them into a hostile land’: that is, into evangelical teaching, ‘until their uncircumcised mind grows ashamed,’ overcome by the truth. ‘And I will remember my covenant,’ and so forth: the spiritual promise. ‘I will also remember the land’: that is, their synagogue. What was said above concerning the Sabbath-rest of the land applies here.

“‘Nevertheless, while they are in a hostile land, I will not utterly reject them,’ and so forth. This is what the Apostle says: ‘A hardening has come upon Israel in part, until the fullness of the nations should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved’ (Rom. 11). ‘And I will remember my former covenant,’ and so forth, because the promises were given to them.

## CHAPTER XXVII

“‘Whoever has vowed his life shall give its price according to the valuation.’ Whoever has vowed his life to the Lord [Col. 0847D] should serve him according to the measure of his abilities. ‘If he is male, from twenty years to sixty’: that is, strong for doing good, from the completion of the Law, which consists in the Decalogue, which must be observed both literally and allegorically up to the age of sixty—that is, the perfection of works. The number six, which is perfect, is multiplied by ten, which is equally perfect, as is proposed here. ‘He shall give fifty shekels’: that is, he shall live his entire life spiritually.

“‘If female, thirty’: that is, weaker in action, she should offer the faith of the Trinity together with observance of the commandments. ‘From five years up to twenty, the male shall give twenty shekels’: that is, after he has learned to use the five bodily senses, he should, up to the completion mentioned above, diligently exhibit observance, if he is the stronger. [Col. 0848A] ‘But if female, ten’: that is, though weaker, she should observe the Decalogue historically.

“‘From one month up to the fifth year’: that is, from the beginning of one’s way of life up to the observance of the senses, the stronger shall give five shekels—that is, mastery of the five senses; the weaker shall offer three, that is, faith in the Trinity, to God. To such beginners Peter says: ‘Like newborn infants’ (1 Pet. 2), and so forth.

“‘A male of sixty years and older shall give fifteen shekels.’ A man of sixty is no longer sufficiently suited to war and marriage, and he signifies one who is less capable of ascending to the summit of the highest virtues, such as virginity, martyrdom, and the upright way of life of monks. Whoever can now fulfill these things less fully should pay [Col. 0848B] fifteen shekels: that is, he should preserve the five senses courageously together with observance of the Law. ‘The female, ten’: that is, the weaker person should observe the Decalogue or its historical sense.

“‘If he is poor,’ and so forth: that is, if he lacks virtues and cannot repay what he has promised, he should complete whatever is imposed upon him by his superiors, with his ability duly taken into account.

“‘An animal that may be sacrificed to the Lord,’ and so forth. A disciple whom you have appointed for the Lord’s service should not be rejected so that you may seek another: ‘neither the better for the worse, nor the worse for the better.’ Do not exchange what is good for what is bad. But if he is bad, do not cease correcting him or reject him entirely; rather, strive to present him according to the promise.

“‘Whoever changes it,’ and so forth: that is, if you acquire another, better person in his place, remember to save both. [Col. 0848C] ‘An unclean animal that cannot be sacrificed to the Lord,’ and so forth. That is, if someone has promised to the Lord a person whose vices prevent him from being offered, let his price be assigned—that is, let effort be expended so that he may be freed from that uncleanness.

“That the priest judges whether it is good or bad signifies that the teacher must consider whether the person is corrigible or not; and if he is, he should apply the effort of correction to him. If he wishes to do this, he shall add a fifth part: that is, he shall accomplish it through his understanding. We call the fifth part understanding because it presides over each of the five senses.

“‘If a man vows his house,’ and so forth: that is, his household Church. Let him test what sort it is and how much it is worth, and let it be devoted to the Lord’s service to that extent. ‘But if the one who vowed it wishes to redeem it’: that is, if he wishes to manage it again according to his understanding, let him repay its fruit.

“‘But if he vows a field of his possession,’ and so forth: that is, the meditation he ought to have in divine Scripture. It shall be valued according to the measure of the seed: that is, let it be promised according to the capacity of his understanding.

“‘If it is sown with thirty measures of barley,’ and so forth. If, through faith in the Trinity, he grasps the sense of the Law hidden beneath the letter, let him meditate in order to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0848D] ‘If he vows it immediately from the year when the jubilee begins,’ and so forth. If, at the beginning of his way of life, he commits his meditation to searching out the divine Law, he shall be rewarded according to how much he has been able to labor.

“‘But if after some time,’ and so forth: that is, if he turns to this task at a more advanced age, he shall receive a lesser reward, just as he will be able to grasp less. [Col. 0849A]

“‘If he wishes to redeem the field that he vowed,’ and so forth. That is, if he wishes to recall his meditation so that he may instruct himself in the Scriptures—not always listening to another and never providing nourishment for himself—let him receive it according to his understanding of the truth, so that he may repay its fruit to the Lord to whom he promised it and reap from it the fruit of sweetness for himself.

“‘But if he does not wish to redeem it, and it has been sold to another citizen,’ and so forth. If he delays reclaiming his meditation so that he may read and understand for himself, and wishes always to rely upon another, it may happen that he clings to someone from whom he acquires error, from which he is not easily redeemed.

“‘For when the day of the jubilee comes, it shall be sanctified to the Lord,’ and so forth. When the day of recompense comes, ‘it belongs by right to the priest,’ because the reward of the labor remains with the one through whom it was offered to the Lord, even if the person himself later perished. For the one who vowed it is the priest of God.

“‘If the field was purchased and was not from the ancestral possession,’ and so forth. That is, if a disciple coming from elsewhere brings meditation to you, though he is not from your school, calculate how much labor you can undertake in him, and apply yourself to winning him. [Col. 0849B] ‘But in the jubilee it shall return to its former lord’: that is, the reward of labor shall be given to the one who first worked in him, while you receive the recompense for your own effort.

“‘Every valuation shall be weighed by the shekel of the sanctuary’: every diversity of judgment and business shall be weighed according to ecclesiastical teaching. ‘The shekel has twenty obols.’ [Col. 0849C] The very measure of divine teaching is contained in the Decalogue, which is doubled in the number twenty—either because it contains the two commandments of love, or because it must be observed both historically and allegorically.

“‘The firstborn that belong to God,’ and so forth. Those who dedicate themselves to God at the beginning of their way of life cannot have others appropriate for themselves the fruit of that way of life in them. ‘Whether ox or sheep,’ as above.

“‘But if the animal is unclean,’ and so forth. He speaks of the uncleanness of weakness. If someone has bound himself by a vow, such as a promise of virginity, and afterward has become vicious in some respect, what he has preserved from his promise cannot be offered to God by another; but in what is less perfect he requires redemption according to consideration of the need. [Col. 0850A] ‘If he does not wish to redeem it, it shall be sold to another.’ If one person does not redeem him, another may restore him through his own effort.

“‘Everything consecrated to the Lord, whether man,’ and so forth—that is, whether a rational and wise person, a subordinate, or meditation is consecrated to be offered to the Lord—must not be exchanged for another, as was said above; ‘nor can it be redeemed’: that is, by an exchange for another. ‘He shall die the death.’ Whatever is promised to the Lord must in no way be neglected, but must be preserved [Col. 0850B] to the point of death. The Apostle also says of the Lord’s faithful: ‘They have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires’ (Gal. 5).

“‘All the tithes of the land,’ and so forth: that is, the perfection of all works must be consecrated to the Lord. ‘If anyone wishes to redeem his tithes,’ and so forth: that is, if he wishes to establish good works for himself by a sound understanding, let him repay their fruit to the Lord. ‘Of all the tithes,’ and so forth: of all the orders that are under Christ’s discipline. ‘Whatever comes as the tenth,’ and so forth: that is, whoever possesses a just understanding of the Law is offered to the Lord as a sacrificial victim, without any exchange; the rest as above.

“But I earnestly beseech your goodness, almighty God, to make me always an acceptable sacrifice of praise to you, so that I may truly recognize what must be done [Col. 0850C] and accomplish what I have recognized through the faithful execution of works. May the fire of the Holy Spirit and of venerable charity—which you commanded to be preserved forever and which you confirmed in my heart and breast through the shedding of true blood—not fail, but burn forever for the praise and honor of your name in the service of your love. Amen.

[Col. 0849]

# WALAFRID STRABO, MONK OF FULDA: HOMILY ON THE BEGINNING OF THE HOLY GOSPEL OF MATTHEW

(Pez., *Thesaurus noviss. Anecd.*, vol. II, p. 41.) (G)*

[Col. 0849D] ## BEGINNING OF THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW

The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham. Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob, Jacob begot Judah and his brothers, and so forth.

Moses, a holy man supported by divine authority, composed the book of the creation of heaven and earth, in which he had woven the origin of perishable humanity. Matthew, apostle of Christ and evangelist, appropriately wrote the book of the generation of Jesus Christ, in which lies the beginning of our salvation and which [Col. 0850D] is the perfection of our eternal blessedness, because Jesus is interpreted as “Savior”; Christ, “anointed,” which is the name of the highest dignity, because ancient kings, prophets, and priests were anointed with the oil of sanctification. Jesus Christ our Lord, however, is read to have been anointed by the Lord with the oil of gladness above his companions.

He came into this world through chosen and circumcised fathers, whose names Matthew therefore placed in order at the beginning of his [Col. 0851A] book, because he understood, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, that in them was the figure of our redemption and eternal salvation, and that these same figures were fulfilled in truth through Christ. For just as Christ came into this world through the genealogy of these patriarchs for our salvation, and bore in himself the role of them all, so also, through the interpretation of all their names, he wished our salvation to be signified spiritually. We too, insofar as we can with his inspiration and help, ought to imitate their interpretation, as the evangelist John says: Whoever desires to imitate Christ ought himself to walk as Christ walked. Now let us return to the order of the book itself.

### VERSE 1.—The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of [Col. 0851B] David, son of Abraham

Here a question arises: Why is David placed before Abraham? Because there is a greater election in David than a promise. For there is election in David, of whom it is said: “I have found David, son of Jesse, a man after my heart, who will do all my will.” And again: “From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne.” The promise, however, was made to Abraham, to whom it is said: “In your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed.”

David is interpreted as “strong of hand,” because he alone conquered and killed the exceedingly proud Goliath. Abraham is interpreted as “father of many nations.” Both meanings are understood of Christ. For he is our most powerful warrior, who alone fought against the devil, the strongest enemy, overcame him, and condemned him. After this victory he became the father of many peoples, [Col. 0851C] that is, the father of all believers, granting all who believe in him permission to invoke the Father, saying: “You shall pray thus: Our Father who are in heaven.”

We too, renouncing all the devil’s works in baptism and rejecting all the devil’s pomps, have entered into a most difficult spiritual struggle against him. And just as he never ceases to lie in wait for us, so we must remain in that same struggle with the greatest vigilance and care until the day of our departure, continually imploring the most merciful kindness of almighty God, so that in his great mercy he may grant us victory and allow us to be fathers of many virtues. These are the weapons of spiritual warfare. [Col. 0851D]

### VERSE 2.—Abraham begot Isaac

Isaac is interpreted as “joy.” Christ, rightly the father of all believers, has also become the joy of all his peoples, because at his birth the angel spoke to the shepherds, saying: “Behold, I bring you good news of great joy, which will be for all the people.” So we too ought, through increase in perseverance in good works, to prepare for ourselves the joy of eternal life with the holy angels. Let us always hope to remain in that same joy, as the Apostle urges when he says: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice.” This means that we ought to rejoice in Christ’s birth, Passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven in such a way that we may deserve to reach eternal joys. [Col. 0852A]

Isaac begot Jacob. Jacob is interpreted as “supplanter.” After Christ granted the world the joys of his birth, he also supplanted the devil, the destroyer of the human race, through his Passion and despoiled his vessels. So we too, through the joy of the second birth—that is, after receiving the remission of all sins in baptism—must be supplanters of all vices and carnal pleasures, and supplant the devil’s temptations within us, avoiding his deceptions and snares entirely, as far as we can through God’s gracious gift.

Jacob begot Judah. Judah is interpreted as “confession.” Confession does not always concern repentance; [Col. 0852B] sometimes it concerns the praise of God and thanksgiving. Thus Christ, having supplanted the devil’s temptations, rightly offered confession—that is, praise—to God the Father, as when he says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth,” which pertains to praise.

We too, when, with the help of the mercy of the Lord our Savior, we have been able to overcome and perceive that we have overcome even a little of our vices and carnal pleasures within ourselves, should attribute all of this to God’s mercy and assign nothing to our own merits. Rather, we should always go before his face in confession of our sins. By day and by night, let us remain always in his praise, so that he may graciously deign to defend and protect us from the snares of the ancient enemy. Let us confess his holy name [Col. 0852C] and glory in his praise forever and ever.

### VERSE 3.—Judah begot Phares and Zara

Phares is interpreted as “division,” and Zara as “rising.” Christ may rightly also be understood as division, because he separated the holy Church from the fellowship of unbelievers. Likewise, at the judgment he separates the righteous from sinners and will repay each according to his works. We too must separate ourselves from the impious and unbelieving, and distinguish our actions from association with them, so that at the final division we may not be condemned with the impious but deserve to be crowned with the righteous.

In Zara, who is interpreted as “rising,” Christ is rightly understood, of whom the Prophet says: “For you who fear the name of the Lord, the sun of righteousness shall rise.” At the beginning of his preaching, using the testimony of Isaiah, he himself also said: “The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. For those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, light has risen.” And elsewhere: “I am the light of the world.”

So too, after we separate ourselves from the actions of unbelievers and flee carnal desires, the splendor of eternal light arises in our hearts—the sun of righteousness, Christ—and may he himself deign to dwell in us. Thus, through the practice of virtues, what he himself commanded may be fulfilled in us: “Let your light shine in such a way that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” [Col. 0852D]

Phares begot Esron. Esron is interpreted as “the arrow of the Lord’s salvation.” Christ may be understood as the arrow of our [Col. 0853A] salvation, because when a poisoned arrow is driven into any living thing, it kills it. So Christ, the arrow of his preaching, kills our vices and sins within us, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.”

The holy apostles, preachers of the Church, are also called the Lord’s sharp arrows. Through their preaching unbelievers are rebuked and believers corrected, when they are pierced with remorse for their sins and moved to repentance. We too should place before our eyes the arrow of the strict examination of God’s just judgment, mourn with worthy repentance the evils we have committed, and, so that we may deserve pardon for our sins, provide others with an example of salvation.

Esron begot Aram. Aram is interpreted as “chosen.” [Col. 0853B] Christ is God’s chosen one, of whom the Father speaks: “Behold my servant, my chosen one, whom I have chosen.” We too should choose with the greatest care what God’s will is and do it as far as we can, as the Apostle Peter says: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood.”

### VERSE 4.—Aram begot Aminadab

Aminadab is interpreted as “my spontaneous people.” Christ is rightly interpreted as “spontaneous,” because he freely offered himself as an unblemished sacrifice for our salvation. We too ought freely to obey the Lord our God and strive to perform his will, as far as we can, not under compulsion but willingly. In the Gospel he also declares that those who do his will are his brothers, sisters, and mother, saying: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.” [Col. 0853C]

Aminadab begot Naasson. Naasson is interpreted as “a strong augur,” which is understood of Christ, who is the powerful prophet. Speaking to his disciples about the day of judgment, he said: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, then he will sit on the seat of his majesty to judge the world in righteousness, and he will repay each according to his works.”

We, however, through Christ’s strength, should abandon the worldly auguries of the pagans, place faith in the divine promises, and locate the prosperity of all things in God’s will alone, not in false divinations, but trust fully in the divine oracles.

Naasson begot Salmon. Salmon is interpreted as “perceptive.” [Col. 0853D] Christ is perceptive, the one who said to the woman touching the hem of his garment: “Someone touched me, for I too know that power has gone out from me.” He knows all things before they happen, and knows all things past, present, and future.

We too ought to be perceptive in the Lord, hold fast only to what is good, and, perfect in our understanding, be infants in evil, so that with one mind and one voice we may honor the Lord and the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ. Instructed by the meanings of sacred Scripture, let us become teachable by God, according to Isaiah’s prophecy: “And they shall all be taught by God.”

### VERSE 5.—Salmon begot Booz

Booz is interpreted as “strength of virtue,” which is Christ. Speaking to his disciples about his Passion, he said: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I will draw everything to myself.” And elsewhere: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again.”

We too should be strengthened in the Lord and act manfully, with Christ confirming our hands for battle and our fingers for war, so that, strengthened by the power of patience, we may endure every kind of temptation and triumph over our enemies. Let us have our senses trained for the discernment of good and evil, holding fast to the apostolic saying: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me.” [Col. 0854A]

Booz begot Obeth. Obeth is interpreted as “serving.” Christ is rightly understood as serving, for he said: “I did not come to be served but to serve,” taking the form of a servant [Col. 0854B] and being found in human form; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death.

Let us too serve the Lord with joy—that is, with the kind of service in which the Lord is served not through the spirit of fear but through the spirit of adoption. Through perfect service, let us present ourselves to the Lord as perfect servants, so that when the time of service has ended, we may be called by the Lord to the joys of the eternal kingdom.

Obeth begot Jesse. Jesse is interpreted as “incense.” Christ is rightly called incense, for he said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and I desire that it burn.” He says that he sows the fire of divine love in the hearts of the faithful.

Let us too continually burn the incense of our prayers upon the altar of our hearts and blaze with the highest desire in love of our Lord, saying with the Psalmist to the Lord: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight.” [Col. 0854C]

Jesse begot David. David is interpreted as “desirable” or “powerful warrior.” Both meanings are understood of Christ, of whom the Prophet says: “Beautiful in form above the sons of men.” And the Evangelist says: “His face shone like the sun, and his garments became white as snow.”

He is also a powerful warrior when he conquered the devil and humbled our accuser. In the likeness of Christ and of David the prophet, let us forgive personal injuries and become desirable to the Lord. Let us have an eager desire for the Lord, so that, loving the Lord, we may be loved by the Lord.

Let us also be powerful warriors: that is, through perfect action let us kill the spiritual giant, the devil, with his own sword, and rescue from his power both our own souls and those of our neighbors. Then, when the final judgment comes, may we shine as desirable ones like the sun in the kingdom of our Father, and, having fought the good fight, may we receive from the just Judge of righteousness the crown of justice laid up for us in heaven. [Col. 0854D]

### VERSE 6.—David begot Solomon

Solomon is interpreted as “peaceful.” Christ is our peace, as the Apostle says: he makes both one, that is, from Jews and Gentiles he made one Church for himself, which he redeemed with his precious blood and reconciled to God his Father.

We too, with the Apostle, insofar as it depends on us, should be at peace with all people. Victorious through spiritual virtues in the inward war against vices, and with both our persons—that is, the inner [Col. 0855A] and outer person—reconciled into one heavenly desire, let us have peace with God and our neighbor. Let us not merely be at peace with all, but let us also be peacemakers for all, bringing brothers who are at odds back to harmony. “Blessed,” says the Lord, “are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.”

### VERSE 7.—Solomon begot Roboam

Roboam is interpreted as “the breadth of the people.” Christ is rightly understood as the breadth of the faithful people, because many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. That is, the faithful are called from every part of the world to the kingdoms of heaven.

Let us too fulfill the broad commandment of love, showing fraternal charity to all without any respect of persons, and let us enjoy spiritual joy in heaven. [Col. 0855B]

Roboam begot Abia. Abia is interpreted as “the Lord Father.” Christ is our Father, who said: “Do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven.”

Let us too exercise ourselves in worthy works, so that we may have the Lord as Father and be brothers in the Lord, so that we may truly say: “Our Father, who are in heaven.” Thus may we deserve to be heirs of God and co-heirs of Christ.

Abia begot Aser. Aser is interpreted as “taking away.” Christ is the one who takes away, of whom John says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” Let us too lift our minds from present things to future things, from earthly things to heavenly things.

### VERSE 8.—Asa begot Josaphat

Josaphat is interpreted as “judging in Josaphat.” Christ is called the judge, who says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.”

We too, in order to judge rightly, should examine both our own sins and those of our subordinates, remembering what the Lord himself said: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.” And: “With the judgment with which you judge, you shall be judged.” [Col. 0855C]

Josaphat begot Joram. Joram is interpreted as “exalted.” In Joram Christ is rightly understood as exalted, for he says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the Son of Man, who is in heaven.” And the Psalmist says: “The Lord is exalted above all nations.”

We too, so that we may rise from the death of sins through works of righteousness with Christ, should seek the things that are above—that is, heavenly things, not earthly things—so that, made exalted in the Lord, we may have our way of life [Col. 0855D] in heaven.

Joram begot Ozias. Ozias is interpreted as “strong in the Lord.” This fits Christ, because by the voice of his power he raised Lazarus, who had been four days in the tomb. We too, according to the Apostle, should be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might, so that, while our Lord Jesus Christ strengthens us and fights for us, Satan may swiftly be crushed beneath our feet.

### VERSE 9.—Ozias begot Joatham

Joatham is interpreted as “perfect.” This rightly fits Christ, who said to his baptizer John when John objected: “Let it be so for now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” And elsewhere he says: “I did not come to destroy the Law but to fulfill it.”

Through his disciples he also commanded us to be perfect in our work, saying: “Be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect.” Therefore, doing perfect works, let us be perfect and whole, giving no consent at all to wicked temptations. [Col. 0856A]

Joatham begot Achaz. Achaz is called “the one who apprehends.” This is understood of Christ, who weighed heaven in his palm and enclosed the earth in his fist, as he himself says: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father.”

We too, so that we may apprehend and enclose Christ in our hearts, should forget what lies behind and always stretch ourselves toward what is ahead, so that we may apprehend true life.

Achaz begot Ezechias. Ezechias is interpreted as “strong in the Lord” or “the Lord strengthening.” This is Christ, [Col. 0856B] of whom the Apostle Paul says: “But we preach Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God.” And, strengthening his disciples, he said: “Take courage; I have conquered the world.”

Let us too continually praise the strength of the one who fights for us, so that he may strengthen us in his will. Let us humbly beseech him to free us from every evil through his mercy and grant us eternal life.

### Verse 10

Ezechias begot Manasseh, whose name is interpreted as “forgetful.” For Christ is forgetful of our sins, who says through the prophet Ezekiel: “On whatever day the sinner turns back, I will remember none of his iniquities any longer.” He also teaches us to forget our injuries, saying: “When you stand to pray, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, from your hearts, so that your heavenly Father may also forgive you your offenses.” Let us too, in the night of the present age, forgetting past evils, remember the name of the Lord; let us not seek vengeance, but forgive the debts of our brothers, so that ours may be forgiven us by the Lord.

Manasseh begot Ammon.
