Ammon is interpreted as “faithful.” Christ is faithful for all, who said: “Ask and you will receive; seek and you will find; knock and it will be opened to you.” Concerning him John says in the Apocalypse: “He is the faithful witness.” He is faithful because his promises are both to be hoped for and to be feared. Let us also stand courageously in the faith of Christ and cling faithfully to the faithful Lord, because “the righteous person lives by faith.” He himself also says: “Whoever believes in me has eternal life.” He grants the faithful servant entrance into the joys of his Lord and will set him over all his goods.

Ammon begot Josiah, whose name is interpreted as “the salvation of the Lord.” For Christ is our salvation, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.” Let us also work out our salvation through works of righteousness and piety, so that by invoking his holy name we may deserve to attain eternal salvation.

### Verse 11

Josiah begot Jeconiah, whose name is interpreted as “the preparation of the Lord.” This is Christ, who said: “If I go away and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself.” Let us also continually prepare ourselves for the Lord’s coming, always vigilant and watchful, lest that sudden day overtake us, which falls like a snare upon all who dwell upon the face of the earth. Let us beware lest, following the example of the foolish virgins, we be shut out from the wedding when the Lord comes; rather, let us be admitted with the prudent to the wedding and to eternal joys.

Jeconiah begot Joachim, whose name is interpreted as “the resurrection of the Lord.” For Christ is our resurrection, who said: “I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me will not die forever, but I will raise him up on the last day.” Let us also rise from the death of sin to the way of righteousness, so that through this resurrection of the soul we may deserve to possess eternal joys with the saints and the righteous in the final resurrection.

### Verse 12

Joachim begot Salathiel, which means “the Lord is my petition.” Christ petitioned the Father for us when he said: “Holy Father, keep them in your name, those whom you have given me from the world.” Let us also ask one petition from the Lord: that we may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of our life. For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to whoever knocks it will be opened.

Salathiel begot Zerubbabel, whose name means “teacher.” Christ is the teacher of all believers, who said to his disciples: “Do not be called teachers, because your one teacher is Christ.” Let us also strive with every effort to become both disciples of the heavenly and true teacher and teachers of the unlearned, so that, fulfilling in our works whatever we have learned, we may teach others, as it is written: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’”—that is, let the person invited to the spiritual banquet invite the others also, so that the house of eternal life may be full of those reclining at table.

### Verse 13

Zerubbabel begot Abiud, whose name is said to mean “this is my father.” This is Christ, who said: “I and the Father are one.” He is the Father and head of all believers. Let us train ourselves in worthy works, so that the Lord Christ himself may be a Father to us and we may be sons and daughters to him, and so that such offspring may reign with the Father in heaven.

Abiud begot Eliakim, whose name is interpreted as “the Lord raising up.” This is Christ, who says: “Whoever believes in me will not die forever, but I will raise him up on the last day.” Let us also rise daily in soul through confession and lamentation over our sins, passing from vices to virtues, so that we may deserve to live for the Lord in the Holy Spirit.

Eliakim begot Azor, whose name is said to mean “helped.” This is Christ, who says: “I am not alone, but the Father who sent me is with me.” Let us also, with the Lord’s help, conquer the aerial powers and, trusting in the Lord alone, say: “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

### Verse 14

Azor begot Zadok, whose name is interpreted as “just.” This signifies Christ, concerning whom John says: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.” Let us also implore his clemency, so that we may deserve to be justified by him who justifies the ungodly, who says through the prophet: “For on whatever day the ungodly person turns from his ungodliness, he will be justified, and he will live and not die.”

Zadok begot Achim, whose name is interpreted as “my brother.” For Christ is our brother, who granted that we too should invoke the Lord his Father as our Father, saying: “You shall pray in this way: Our Father who are in heaven.” And in the Gospel he says: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother.” And to the women after the resurrection: “Go, announce it to my brothers.” Let us also continually do his will with every effort, so that we may deserve to receive the dignity of this name in the heavenly kingdom.

[Col. 0858B] Achim begot Eliud. Eliud is interpreted as “this God,” as Thomas said to Christ: “My Lord and my God.” Let us have no other Lord but God the Father, and his only Son as our Lord, and the Holy Spirit.

### Verse 15

Eliud begot Eleazar, whose name is interpreted as “my God is helper.” For Christ is the helper of all who believe in him, who says: “The one who sent me is with me and has not left me alone.” And again: “Amen, amen, I say to you, whatever you ask for in my name while praying, you will receive.” Let us also confess that our salvation consists solely in the Lord Jesus, remembering that saying: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.”

Eleazar begot Mathan, whose name is interpreted as “giving.” Through Christ, God the Father forgave us all our debts; and when he ascended on high, he gave gifts to human beings—that is, the blessedness which we lost through Adam’s transgression, he restored to us through his passion, resurrection, and ascension; or when he gave the Holy Spirit to the apostles. Let us also forgive the offenses of our neighbors and, receiving the gifts of the Holy Spirit, deserve to be enriched by God’s grace.

Mathan begot Jacob, whose name means “supplanter.” For Christ is the supplanter of our ancient enemy, who gave his faithful the power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and upon all the power of the enemy. Let us also spiritually trample down the rulers of these darknesses, together with the vices and desires of the flesh, by the power and strength of God, as the Apostle Peter says in his Epistle: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” For without combat, eternal victory in war cannot be acquired.

### Verse 16

Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ. Joseph is interpreted as “increased,” signifying Christ, who said: “I came so that they may have life and have it more abundantly.” And again: “I will ask my Father, and I will send you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive.” Although our outward person is corrupted through the mortification of vices, the inward person is nevertheless renewed from day to day and increased by the progress of spiritual growth, until it may spiritually be said of each one of us: “Joseph is a son who increases.” Let us therefore grow in charity until we all attain the perfect person, to the measure of the fullness of Christ’s maturity, so that, passing from virtue to virtue and ascending by stages of perfection from the fear of God—which is the beginning of wisdom—to charity, which is the end of the whole commandment, we may afterward be able to see the God of gods in Zion.

Mary, as most people judge, is interpreted as “illuminating woman” and “star of the sea.” In Syriac speech she is called “Lady.” She is rightly called “illuminating woman,” because through her Christ, the light of the whole world, was born. For just as through Eve’s transgression the whole earth was condemned to darkness and the shadow of eternal death, so through the merits of blessed and ever-virgin Mary and through her childbirth the whole earth was liberated, sanctified, and illuminated. Sailors have the custom, when they plan to row toward some land, of choosing a particular star, by whose sign and radiant light they may be guided without error toward the place they desire. The same has been observed in the name of holy Mary. For to us, sailing upon the sea of this world, she has been called the star of the sea. Whoever, as an ecclesiastical sailor, is endangered by the disturbances of this world, if he looks with the full attention of his mind toward the light of this star—that is, toward Christ born of the Virgin Mary—and fixes his hope upon him, and follows the guidance of his words and examples, will reach the harbor of eternal life without any shipwreck or loss of salvation, Christ himself saying: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of eternal life.” The reason she is called “Lady” requires no explanation, since she bore the Lord and Savior. Indeed, the mother of Christ, King of kings, ought to be called queen; the mother of the Lord of lords ought to be called Lady. Through her, may we receive the light of faith and divine grace and be led to the ineffable vision of almighty God, in which, rejoicing and freed from every sorrow of this age, we may deserve to reign with Christ in eternal blessedness.

After passing through the generations, Matthew again summarizes, saying: “From Abraham to David there were fourteen generations.” Why, then, are they arranged three times in three divisions, unless these three divisions of generations correspond to the order of the three kinds of seed—namely, the thirtieth, the sixtieth, and the hundredfold? The thirtieth order, which is assigned to married believers, appropriately corresponds to Abraham, who is recorded as having begotten Isaac through a faithful marriage—Isaac whom he offered to the Lord as a sacrifice in the likeness of Christ. The second order, assigned to widows, is also appropriately extended to the transmigration of Babylon, at which time the royal stock was deprived of royal dignity. The third order is counted from there to the Virgin Mary and to the very head of virgins, because the crown of virgins is signified by the perfection of the number one hundred.

Or else this is because the faithful are saved and attain eternal life through confession of the Holy Trinity and through observance of the New and Old Testaments: the perfection of our salvation is shown through the ten commandments of the Law and the four Gospels. Or else it is because the number of the faithful is completed from the three parts of the world—namely, Asia, Africa, and Europe.

Thus all the generations from Abraham to Christ number forty-two, because the children of Israel, having departed from Egypt—which signifies this world or darkness—entered the promised land after forty-two encampments. In this way our liberation and redemption came to us through forty-two fathers. Or else this number forty signifies the whole perfection of our life, in which we live through body and soul amid the labor and danger of temptations, hoping for what we do not see and awaiting with patience until we may deserve to reach the promised homeland of eternal happiness.

You have heard and understood, beloved, how blessed Moses, describing from the beginning the book of the creation of heaven and earth and of all the elements, visible and invisible, and the formation of the whole world, also described the loss of the human being who was destined to perish from paradise. We have also heard how the evangelist Matthew, in the same likeness, fully described the restoration of the whole world in Christ, just as it had been proclaimed or prefigured by the holy Fathers. Therefore blessed Matthew, both apostle and evangelist, not without reason had woven the succession of so many fathers into the birth of Christ, because he understood that in all of them, through the Holy Spirit, the mystery of our salvation was prefigured; because each one of them bore within himself a type of our Lord and Savior; and because the Lord and Savior himself completed in his own person the work of restoring all of them. For in the patriarchs he is patriarch, in the prophets prophet, in the priests priest, and in the judges judge, as is sufficiently and clearly demonstrated above by corresponding testimonies.

As we examine these matters with the utmost care, we too must understand that Christ, in his own person, truly fulfilled all the same interpretations and figures for the redemption and salvation of us all, and left them to his disciples and their successors to imitate. Therefore, beloved, we must weigh this most seriously and consider it with great fear: we who have been appointed vicars and successors of the blessed apostles and holy Fathers must, if we desire to attain eternal life, imitate as far as we can, with the Lord’s help, those things which the Lord himself granted to his disciples as an example. These things are great, brothers; but the greater and more numerous the things we must imitate, the greater and happier are the rewards we may hope for, if we faithfully strive to observe and fulfill what has been entrusted to us—not merely out of concern for our own salvation, but also for that of those placed under our care. Let us remember the Apostle’s saying: “The one who labors more will receive more reward.” The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “Whoever perseveres in my commandments to the end will be saved.”

May Jesus Christ himself deign to grant this to us, he who lives and reigns as God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages. Amen.

[Note: In another manuscript this conclusion is found: “Through him who lives and reigns as God throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.”]

[Col. 0861]

## Walafrid Strabo, Monk of Fulda: Exposition on the Four Gospels (G)*

### Martianay’s Notice

*(Works of St. Jerome, vol. V.)*

I found an exposition on the four Gospels, divided into short sections, in manuscript codices falsely attributed to Jerome and so full of barbarisms and solecisms that it seemed altogether unworthy to be brought to light. But since works of this kind are not displeasing to everyone, I wished to publish this Exposition here together with others of the same sort, especially because Strabo of Fulda may have been the author of this Commentary, which some utterly unlearned person later copied with a mass of barbarisms and solecisms. Whatever its quality, I have handed over this little work, transcribed from an ancient codex of Jumièges, to our printers for publication, together with nearly all its faults. I did not consider it worthy of being corrected according to our usual practice, nor did I wish to waste time, effort, and labor in amending it.

## The Exposition of the Four Gospels Begins

[Col. 0861A] First, the time, place, person, and purpose of all the books must be sought: and why are not twelve Gospels received, but only four? Because the whole world consists of four elements—namely, heaven, earth, fire, and water.

Through heaven John is indicated, because just as heaven surpasses everything, so does John, who said: “In the beginning was the Word.” Through Matthew, earth is indicated, for he said: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ.” Through Luke, fire is indicated, for he said: “Was not our heart already burning within us?” Through Mark, water is indicated, for he said: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness.”

That is, the four rivers from one source signify the four evangelists, namely Christ. Pishon, “breathing” or “inspiration,” signifies John; Gihon, “swiftness,” signifies Matthew; Tigris, “happiness,” signifies Mark; Euphrates, “fertility,” signifies Luke. They water the world—that is, the Church—and signify the four virtues: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. Just as four rivers water paradise, so these four virtues water our heart. The human being also consists of four elements: air, fire, water, and earth. From air comes breath; from fire, blood; from water, flame; from earth, the body. The head signifies heaven, where there are two lights; the breast, air; the belly, water; and the feet, earth.

Again, Adam received his name from four letters and from four stars, which are *artis*, *dosis*, *anatholis*, and *mesimbrio* [the terms are obscure and perhaps corrupt]. Alternatively, the four signify the evangelists. Just as every human being is born from Adam, so through the four evangelists all come to the faith.

Again, Noah’s ark is read to have been made square from wood: its length was three hundred cubits, its width one, and its height completed at thirty-one cubits. It signifies the Church. Through the four evangelists, its length signifies the hope of eternal life, its width charity, and its height faith in the Trinity; the one cubit signifies worship of the one Lord. The bitumen inside and outside signifies love of God and neighbor.

Again, the ark of the covenant, in which were the two stone tablets and Aaron’s rod, was carried by four golden rings, and the poles covered with gold signify the four evangelists. The ark signifies the Church and the poles the teachers. Just as those poles were surrounded by rings, so priests instructed from the Old and New Testaments—the four evangelists—carry the Church by defending it from heresy. Through the rod the cross is shown. Just as a square piece of wood stands firm whichever way it is turned, so a human being instructed by the four evangelists may become firm against heresy and tribulation.

Again, Matthew means “given”; Mark, “lofty gift”; Luke, “rising”; John, “the grace of the Lord.”

Again, “a wheel within a wheel” signifies the Spirit within the wheel; the preaching of the Gospel revolves throughout the world. The Spirit within the wheel signifies the Holy Spirit in the Gospel.

Again, the linen vessel, and four lines above it, signify the four evangelists. These are the clean and unclean, Jews and Gentiles.

Again, the four living creatures have eyes before and behind and cry out, “Holy.” They are the four evangelists.

Again, Jacob supplanted his brother three times: first through the blessing, second through the lentils, and third through the blessing [the wording appears corrupt]. Esau signifies the devil; Jacob, Christ, who conquered and supplanted him three times. So we too must supplant our brother, the devil, three times—in thought, in word, and in deed. He is called our brother because God created him, as he created us; we have one Father, God, and he created him good, but through his own vice, by becoming proud, he deprived himself of that goodness.

The four evangelists are signified as follows: Matthew by the face of a human being, Luke by that of a calf, Mark by that of a lion, and John by that of an eagle. The Lord Jesus Christ fulfilled all of these: he was human in being born, a calf in being sacrificed, a lion in rising, and an eagle in ascending.

“Wheel within wheel” means law within law, the Old within the New.

Why are there four evangelists, and why are they not written by four apostles, except that they were written by two disciples and two apostles? This is because the sons of Jacob were born from two free women and two slave women.

Matthew is honey; Mark, milk; Luke, oil; John, wine.

## On the Gospel of Matthew

[Col. 0863B] “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.” He names two fathers for this reason: of David it is said, “From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne”; of Abraham it is said, “In your seed all nations will be blessed.” David is written before Abraham because he is closer to Christ, who was to be born from that stock.

“Jacob begot Joseph”: he said this according to creation. Luke spoke according to the law, so that he might be the son of Heli. Women are therefore included in Christ’s genealogy because they themselves come to eternal life as men do. Sinners are also named in Christ’s genealogy because he said: “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”

When Luke speaks of Christ from Adam, he shows that through Christ Adam is released from sin, or that those who return to the Father proceed from Christ.

The figure of the forty-two men in Christ’s genealogy signifies the forty-two encampments of the children of Israel from Egypt to the promised land—that is, from the world to heaven. This signifies that through threefold divisions we come to Christ through faith, hope, and charity.

What do the fourteen signify, except the ten words of the Law and the four virtues? The first is prudence: serving God rather than idols. The second is temperance: not coveting. The third is justice: not committing adultery. The fourth is fortitude: forgiving rather than killing.

The world was ruined through four things: through a man, through a woman, through a tree, and through a serpent. It is restored through four things: through Christ, through Mary, through the cross, and through the man Joseph.

The serpent that was in Israel signified Christ. It was made of bronze, with four round wheels; those who looked upon it were healed. He lifted it up to the top of the staff so that all might see it, and the animals of the desert fled from fear of the wheels. Thus each person is healed if he looks upon Christ at the top of the staff—that is, upon the cross. The four wheels signify the four evangelists. Thus the devil flees from the Gospel when it sounds in heaven.

“Now the generation of Christ was as follows.” That is, according to the flesh. They said: Christ is called “Christ” so that Christians might be called from that derivative name. Again, through etymology, Christ means “anointed,” because through him, after the washing, we received the anointing of chrism.

“Thus it was according to eternity.” Mary signifies “star of the sea,” because a star is sweet, whereas the sea is bitter [one word has been deleted; perhaps “truly”]. Thus Mary was in the sea of the world among sinners like the star of the sea, because it is customary for a star to lead sailors to port if they follow it. So Mary, in the world where Christ was born, leads everyone to life if they follow him.

His mother was betrothed for four reasons: so that she would not be stoned as an adulteress; so that she might have comfort in flight; so that Christ’s genealogy might be traced through Joseph; and so that the birth might be hidden from the devil. Before they came together—that is, before they had lived together—she was found by Joseph to be pregnant, not in the womb in the ordinary manner of a woman, but as a virgin conceiving from the Holy Spirit; that is, he was made from the Spirit by the Spirit [the text reads *Spirius*, apparently an error], just as he makes an apple upon a tree and made Eve from Adam’s bone.

“Joseph her husband.” He is therefore called her husband, and therefore just, lest anyone suspect a human union. “He did not wish to expose her”—that is, in judgment—lest he transgress the Law, because he knew that she was a virgin, so that the devil might remain unaware of her childbirth.

“While he was considering these things”—that is, he was considering whether to dismiss her or keep her—this prophecy is fulfilled: “A helper in times of trouble.” The angel of the Lord said in a dream: “Do not say ‘in sleep,’ because the angel often came to him in dreams. Do not say ‘once,’ because the mystery of God cannot be understood all at once.”

“Joseph, son of David”: that is, prophecy was fulfilled in Joseph through David—“from the fruit of your womb,” and so forth.

“Do not be afraid”: that is, love and rejoice in your non-marital spouse—not through marriage or generation, but through cohabitation. He said “your,” so that he might believe that the child had been conceived not by another man but from the Holy Spirit.

“She will bear a son”: that his joy in the son might be greater, as is customary among human beings. “And you shall call his name”—for his joy he named him Jesus, and he also called him Savior, because he saves his people. He did not say “all,” except those who believe in him, from their sins. That is, what no other physician could do, this one did entirely.

“Now all this took place”—that is, what the angel said—“so that what had been spoken by the Lord might be fulfilled,” namely through the prophet Isaiah concerning Christ. Here it is according to the letter alone: “Behold, a virgin will have a child in the womb, and she called his name Emmanuel.” Therefore this name is interpreted because, in both languages, it is said to mean “God with us”—that is, God and human being are one in the faith.

“He did as the angel of the Lord commanded him,” showing that he deserved to see the Lord’s vision, because he did what the angel commanded him.

“And he did not know her until she had borne her son.” “Until” is understood earlier [the text says *pronum quam*, perhaps for *priusquam*]. He is called “firstborn” according to the Law because he first opened the womb. It does not mean one followed by other children, but the one born first. Christ is called firstborn for three reasons: in the resurrection from the dead, from Mary, and from created beings.

“When Jesus had been born,” three things are confirmed: place, time, and person.

“In Bethlehem,” which is appropriately interpreted as “house of bread,” so that the living heavenly bread might be born where bread is named. “Juda, look toward Bethlehem of the nations” [the wording is uncertain].

“In the days of King Herod”: this refers to the kings and rulers of Judea, as it was said: “The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes to whom it was promised; he himself will be the expectation of the nations.” He therefore says “Herod the king” against the Jews because they themselves said at the cross: “We have no king but Caesar.”

“Behold, magi come from the East.” The East is the one who is sought; therefore they are indicated as coming from the East. He leads us to himself. They came to Jerusalem because “from Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.”

Saying, “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?”—that is, king of confessions—they add a reason for those who inquire: “Who told you?” “For we saw his star in the East.” The star is mute but luminous; the light leads to the Word.

He is given a star, not one of heaven and earth; it did not belong to them but to the Son of God. There was neither before nor afterward anything like Christ in the flesh. Therefore the star led them, heavenly beings, to the heavenly one; and therefore it was not another creature but a mute one, so that the mute might lead them to the mute. They were mute because they worshiped idols [the printed *munerant* is perhaps an error for *muti erant*].

“King Herod was troubled”—that is, through envy, lest he and his sons be surpassed; or all were afraid, lest things go badly for them. A just king being present under an unjust king means that the king’s companions are not as dear to another king; or they were troubled so that they might please the king. According to the literal sense, the good is displayed to the wicked through their disturbance, and the evil eye is troubled at the rising of the sun.

“And gathering all the chief priests and scribes of the people”—that is, hoping that they would come to him, or that he might receive their counsel, as God says: “Ask your father, and he will announce it to you; your elders, and they will tell you.” He asked the chief fathers, elders, and scribes where Christ would be born.

He did not say, “Where has he been born?” but, “Where is he?” They said, “In Bethlehem of Judea.” In words they say what they deny by their deeds. The blind grope as Isaac did for Jacob. They neglect to go to the one whom they point out by their worship.

The three magi signify the three sons of Noah; with their three gifts, they signify worship of the Trinity.

“Then Herod secretly summoned them.” Here the historical account fails, since he disclosed privately the time of the star. For this reason opinions differ about when the magi came. Some say that they came after one or two years; others say that they found him not in Bethlehem but in Egypt. And if they came in twelve days, how could Persians from a distant land—or from Havilah, Arabia, or Kedar—have come in twelve days? But God can do this, at whose word rocks fly and mountains move, whose nature it is that what he commands comes to pass.

Nevertheless, he carefully learned from them the time of the star, so that he might know at what time it had appeared. Perhaps he thought that a son had been born from himself or from his own lineage.

“When they had heard the king, they departed.” When he sends them to seek Christ, he must be obeyed; when he orders them to return to him, he must be disregarded. When he was leading the Savior upward, he refused, and the Savior did not refuse; but when he ordered him to be sent downward and to worship him, he refused according to the Law: “You shall worship the Lord your God,” and so forth.

Thus, when they went out, they knew how to leave but did not know how to return. “And behold, the star which they had seen,” and so forth. It is uncertain where it hid itself when they had departed. Some human reasoning is involved here, because the Lord concealed it from our hearts so that it might also be sought: is the star faith or the Law? It is the compunction that leads us to Christ.

The star went before them. When they came to Christ, the star led them there; but it did not lead them to Herod. Herod signified the devil, because whoever goes from the devil’s suggestion toward Christ goes with the star of faith.

“When they saw the star, they rejoiced,” and so forth, because it is customary for everyone to rejoice when what was lost has been found. Therefore he showed them the child in a higher place than his mother.

“And entering the house,” and so forth. Was it a house or an inn? “And falling down, they worshiped him.” They worshiped before the star; the creature ceased when the Creator was worshiped.

“And opening their treasures,” and so forth: gold for the king, frankincense for God, myrrh for the tomb. Did one offer gold, another frankincense, and a third myrrh? It is not known whether each offered three gifts. The text does not state this appropriately, but both interpretations are possible in the figure.

They do not disagree, because the three faithful are one, and in one there would be three fruits: the thirtieth, the fortieth, and the hundredfold. The thirtieth signifies faith in the Trinity; the fortieth, perfection of active life; the hundredth, contemplation of eternal life.

Each offered three things: through gold, a pure conscience; through frankincense, upright prayer; through myrrh, mortification of the will. Again, the three gifts signify holy thought, good speech, and perfect work.

The star appeared in this way only at his birth, just as the dove appeared at his baptism. When the star went before them, it was not far from the earth.

“And receiving an answer in a dream,” and so forth. It was in a dream, with the eye closed, so that they might worship the invisible and incomprehensible God, and so that their vigilant eyes would not be opened toward the creature but toward the Creator.

“They should not return to Herod”—that is, after repentance, they should not return to the devil. “They returned to their own region by another way.” The region is paradise. A person returns by another way when he reforms his entire life and comes from depravity to holiness.

“When they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord,” and so forth. Gabriel is called “the strength of God.” It was fitting that the strength of God should strengthen the weakness of human nature. Alternatively, the angel approaches us when we have withdrawn from Herod the devil.

“Flee into Egypt.” This shows the victory of flight, as with Jesus son of Nave when he said: “Divide yourselves and flee until the inhabitants go out; afterward turn back, and you will conquer them.” Christ first fled until he conquered the devil from behind. Thus Joseph fled from his mistress in Egypt when she made an illicit advance, and afterward he himself became king over Egypt.

“Until I tell you.” This shows that the devil is not always to be fled from, as the Apostle Paul says: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”

“By night”: this shows that he withdrew from the darkness of the letter of the Law. Among the Jews, after Christ, he waits until Herod’s death—that is, three years. The Gentiles signify the Trinity to be believed. He did not continue until death; Herod indicates the Jews who come to Christ after the death of the letter of the Law.

“Out of Egypt I have called my son.” At first, Moses and Aaron are called forth; they prefigure Christ.

“Then Herod, seeing that he had been deceived by the magi”—here the prophecy is fulfilled: “This dragon whom you formed to mock them.” He sent and killed all the boys so that he might find the newborn king. Here he is mocked even more, because those whom he thought dead he sent alive into paradise.

“From two years old and under”: that is, from the preceding and following year, because the name of infancy [or “childhood”; the text is corrupt] encompasses two years.

“A voice was heard in Rama,” and so forth. Rachel is interpreted as “a sheep seeing God.” Rama means “high.” Rachel signifies the Church, which weeps in the valley of tears for those whom she has lost, those who sinned previously; she does not wish to be consoled because they are not Christians. Rachel was the mother of Benjamin, or because she died and was buried there, where the children were killed. They died, and so forth. This is therefore a synecdoche, a part standing for the whole.

“He came and dwelt in the city called Nazareth,” which means “flower of purity.” It was appropriate that he should dwell there who said: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.”

Archelaus means “the lion investigating”; Nazarene means “holy.”

“Rise, take the child and his mother.” First he commands the person who abandons earthly things to rise from the earth; afterward he commands him to take the child and then the mother—that is, to love God first and afterward his neighbor.

Archelaus signifies heresy, whose adherents think they are what they are not and are blind.

“In those days”: this should not be understood as referring to King Archelaus, but to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, because in that year the word of the Lord came upon John. Before Christ there was the voice before the Word, the lamp before the sun, and the flower before the fruit.

“Repent, and do not work.” Since “works” is said of external bodily actions, work inwardly; let repentance be enacted in the inner person and proceed from the heart. True repentance is to mourn what has been lost and, by repenting, not to commit it again.

[Col. 0867D] “For the kingdom of heaven will draw near”: that is, baptism or the Gospel, the martyrdom of Christ, or the Church. “The voice of one crying in the wilderness”: John’s cry has a threefold sense. First, if someone is far away: salvation is far from sinners. Second, from the deaf, if he is deaf like an asp, and so forth. Third, he is indignant: that is, “your fury has been indignant.” “In the wilderness”: that is, without law, without a king, without a priest, or without prophecy—the Jews were there. And just as a friend joins a bride to the bridegroom whom he loves, so John joined the Church to Christ. Therefore he is called “the friend of the bridegroom.”

John had a garment made of camel hair. He himself was born into fasting and had fasting as his clothing and food. This was fitting while he taught repentance, so that he might first fulfill it in himself, so that everyone who preaches the word might confirm it by example. John’s garment of camel hair signifies the Church of the Gentiles, or their riches, which Christ gathered and made into the Church. The belt signifies the mortification of vices, around the loins—that is, because fornication between men and women is there, at the navel. His food was locusts, most wretched birds; they signify the Jews who used the letter of the Law like a locust uses a flower. Wild honey signifies the sweet sayings of God, or the Jews who received the sweet preaching and came to Christ.

“Then Jerusalem and the rest went out to him.” That is, Judea is named for its inhabitants. Jerusalem means “vision of peace”; it indicates the peaceful who come to Christ through confession. Jordan means “descent”; it signifies those descending in humility to Christ.

[Col. 0868B] “And they were baptized in the Jordan”: this shows that the humble came to baptism through descent. “Confessing their sins”: this shows that one must confess sins before coming to communion. “Pharisees”: that is, “divided”; they are also called *sarabatae*. “Sadducees”: justified in their own eyes.

“And he said to them, ‘Brood of vipers’”: the same venom is only in the tongue, for a viper kills both father and mother. The Pharisees and Sadducees imitate this: they killed their mother, the synagogue, and the Fathers and Prophets. “Who showed you,” and so forth: that is, who did not say “according to possibility,” but according to the difficulty implied when it is said, “Produce good fruit”—that is, put away every vice—or “produce fruit worthy of repentance.” Thus, whoever has two tunics should give one to him who has none; whoever acts unlawfully should abstain from unlawful things.

“God is able from these stones,” and so forth. They were stones because they worshiped stones, but many of them came from there to faith in Christ. He calls them stones figuratively because they are heavy, hard, and cold in faith. “The axe has been laid”: that is, the Gospel has been laid at the root of the trees, namely, the Jews. The axe consists of iron and wood; so Christ consists of divinity and humanity. “Roots” means the thoughts of sinful trees, or the roots of sons, the trees being their parents.

“Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down”: that is, it will be separated from the Church. “It is thrown into the fire”: that is, on the day of judgment. “He who is stronger than I”: this refers not only to John but to all; Christ is stronger. He is stronger because he baptizes in the Holy Spirit and in fire. “To carry his sandals”: therefore I cannot fully explain his incarnation.

[Col. 0868D] “He himself baptizes you with fire”: that is, in judgment, or in the Holy Spirit and fire. “Whose winnowing fork,” and so forth: that is, just judgment is in his hand, meaning in his power. “The threshing floor”: that is, the world or the Church. “The wheat”: the holy, into the barn, meaning the kingdoms of heaven. “The chaff”: sinners, because chaff is light, is carried by the wind, and is burned by fire. So it is with sinners. They themselves preserve the fire, because the fire does not fail unless the wood fails.

“Then Jesus came to Galilee to be baptized,” and so forth. Christ came to John: that is, the bride kisses the bridegroom, because John is the bridegroom’s representative through the Church. Here he says, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” Or Christ was baptized by John so that the servant would not excuse himself from being baptized by his Lord, or so that the Lord would not disdain to be baptized by his servant.

“I ought to be baptized by you.” For this reason John recognized Christ among the many: when the Jordan fled from him and the mountains exulted, because creation recognized its Creator. He therefore came to John to cleanse the waters and to be manifested through the Holy Spirit.

“Four causes without limit”—that is, until both had been baptized, Christ from the waters or through martyrdom. “To fulfill all righteousness,” and so forth: that is, the law of nature or the law of the letter, because it was their custom to honor elders. John’s baptism profited nothing [Col. 0869B] except that it foreshadowed Christ’s baptism, so that John’s baptism would not be distinguished from Christ’s baptism: water washes and extinguishes; therefore baptism was through water. Thus John washes and extinguishes sin, gives life and satisfies.

Baptism is therefore like the sea; and because they are baptized through two substances—water and the priest’s voice, the visible and invisible, body and soul—those ascending from the water signify that they will afterward ascend through good works and descend by the degree of humility, because Jordan means “descent.”

“Behold, the heavens were opened”: that is, he revealed baptism. Heaven is opened to each person after Adam’s sin. “And he saw the Spirit descending like a dove”: this shows that it was only in the form of a dove, because the Spirit received a body from the air. The likeness of a dove was made for this purpose; previously it had not existed. Therefore the Spirit came upon Christ in the form of a dove because a bird is gentle; so Christ is gentle and without blemish.

Alternatively, the dove has seven forms, signifying the Spirit in seven forms. Therefore the Spirit came upon Christ through a dove, just as a star appeared that had not existed before and would not exist afterward. Or it was because the Son was in a body: just as human beings could not endure the presence of the Son of God without a body, so they could not endure the Spirit without the appearance of a dove.

Why did the Spirit appear as fire over the apostles and as a dove over Christ? This must be stated literally: the signs indicate it. “And a voice came from heaven”: here the Trinity is compared. The Father’s voice speaks of the Son; the Spirit is represented through the dove: “This is my Son,” and so forth, because the first son, Adam, was displeasing, whereas in Christ he was pleasing.

[Col. 0869D] “Then Jesus was led”—that is, led by the Holy Spirit—into the wilderness after baptism. This shows that the devil is conquered through fasting and prayer. We too must be led into the wilderness away from vices so that we may conquer them. “To be tempted by the devil”: that is, so that he might conquer the devil.

“For forty days and forty nights”: lest heretics say that he ate during the night. Forty is a sign because Moses fasted forty days on the mountain, and Elijah also fasted forty. He was with his disciples for forty days after the resurrection, and the flood lasted forty days, because through these things he was to erase Adam’s sin. Afterwards he was hungry: this indicates the true human being, so that the devil might be deceived concerning his birth.

“Approaching, the tempter”: just as a fish tests the hook and is caught, so the one who conquered the first human being through the throat is conquered by the second through abstinence. “If you are the Son of God, say that these stones,” and so forth. By etymology, *panis* (“bread”) comes from *pascere*, “to feed,” so that he might see whether he could do this from stone. Or, mystically, the devil’s food is stony and hard human beings in sin. But the one who produced wine from water and water from rock could have done this if he had wished.

[Col. 0870A] “Man does not live by bread alone,” and so forth: that is, man would not have lived if God had not willed it; and he would have eaten bread. If he had willed it, he would have lived even without eating bread, as Moses and Elijah did for forty days. “By the word of God”: that is, the soul’s eternal life.

“In the holy city,” that is, Jerusalem. “Upon the pinnacle of the temple”: that is, upon the wall of the ancient structure; these signify arrogance. “It is not,” so that he might tempt him from the head, he who allowed himself to be crucified through a limb by Pilate.

These are the three temptations. The devil first demanded them from Adam: through the throat he said, “Taste”; through vainglory, “You will be like gods”; through avarice, “knowing good and evil.” But through these three he again tempted Christ: through gluttony, that bread should be made from stone; through vainglory, “Throw yourself down”; through avarice, “I will give you all these things,” and so forth.

But the one who casts him into the abyss says this through the word of preaching. Through these three he shows that the devil is conquered. Here he shows the true God and true human being: the human being whom the devil tempts is God, to whom angels ministered.

The forty days signify tenths of years, so that just as we ought to give tithes from all things, so we should strive to give God the tithe of the days of our life.

[Col. 0870C] “For he will command his angels,” and so forth: the devil tried to conquer Christ by example, but Christ conquered him by his own example through Scripture. Yet the devil does not correctly understand that psalm as referring to Christ. Jesus said to him, “You shall not tempt the Lord your God.” Here he says: “Since I am the Lord your God, why are you tempting me?”

“And he showed him all the kingdoms of the world”: that is, “I will give you gold, silver, all these things,” and so forth. Truly he falls who worships the devil. Whoever, even a monk, serves a ruler for the sake of payment, gives himself over to the devil. “Go away behind me”: that is, your kingdom now, or in judgment, in hell.

“You shall worship the Lord your God,” and so forth. Through three examples from Deuteronomy, which signify the Gospel—that is, the repetition of the Law—the Lord conquered the devil. It also signifies the temptation involving David and Goliath. The five stones are the five books of Moses; with one of them he killed the devil—that is, with one book as with a stone—through the three temptations: suggestion, delight, and consent. But Christ he tempted only through suggestion, because suggestion comes from the devil.

[Col. 0870D] “When Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee”: that is, he went from the Jews to the Gentiles. Or, leaving the synagogue with its Law, he established the Church and the Gospel. Galilee is called “volubility.” He came to those who turn from evil to good. And because he came for the healing of the girl, and healed the woman on the way, this signifies the synagogue and the Church.

Leaving the city of Galilee, he came to Capernaum, the most beautiful village, [Col. 0871A] which represents the Church. Nazareth is called “flower,” because fruit comes from a flower. Capernaum means “village of fatness.” Light illuminates, and fatness lacks blood; this shows that Christ passed from the flower of the letter of the Law to the fruit of the fatness of the Gospel, which is light, that is, knowledge.

“In the region of Zebulun and Naphtali.” Zebulun is called “dwelling of beauty”; Naphtali means “forgetfulness.” Here he shows that the one who forgets his sins dwells in beauty. “Beyond the Jordan,” and so forth: because, through fear of the nations and peoples, this man remained in the field at night.

“He saw a great light,” as it says: “Light has risen for them.” They were sitting in darkness, that is, in ignorance of sins. Light has risen for them, that is, Christ.

[Col. 0871B] “Repent”: that is, he puts wine into the wound. “For the kingdom of heaven will draw near”: that is, he puts oil into the wound and gives consolation. For in the Old Testament they sacrificed animals; in the New, each person will offer himself to the Lord.

“He was walking”: this shows us that we are in the present world, passing through it rather than loving it. “Beside the sea”: beside worldly flesh. The Sea of Galilee is itself the Lake of Gennesareth, the lake of salt-pools, the Sea of Tiberias, and Lake Cinnereth.

“Come after me,” and so forth: that is, to draw souls from the sea of sin to the shore of eternal rest. For it is customary for fishermen to have a boat and a net in the sea; so the apostles have the Church, the Gospels, and the world. The fish are human beings; casting nets into the sea means preaching in the world.

[Col. 0871C] “They left their nets and their father and followed him.” The father is likewise the devil; the nets are the dwellings and business of the world. Peter and Andrew cast their nets into the sea. This shows that the Lord chose some who desired and clung to the affairs of the world. James and John were repairing their nets in order to cast them into the sea. This means that he chose others who desired to cling to the affairs of the world.

Who left more of these four? Peter and Andrew left more, because their possessions were their own; the other two had possessions that were not their own.

“I will make you,” and so forth: he changed their affection, not their office. These four constitute the first chariot. Now they are sent into the Church two by two, just as in Noah’s ark the animals entered two by two. They signify the four virtues: justice, prudence, fortitude, and temperance.

The peoples were called through three vocations. The first, through John, was to friendship: “Behold the Lamb of God.” The second was to belief, when John said, “Jesus performed this first sign in Cana of Galilee,” so that his disciples might believe in him. The third calling was to the apostolate: “Come after me,” and so forth.

[Col. 0871D] “Jesus went around all Galilee,” and so forth. Just as Gideon conquered the Philistines, so Christ conquered demons. “Teaching”: he preaches the things that belonged to the Law. “Preaching”: the Gospel. “Every sickness”: he was a physician. “The people”: Israel. Bodily sickness signifies weakness of the soul.

“And his report went out through all Syria”: that is, through all the nations. “All who were afflicted”: they were insane through many sins or through bad faith. “Those who had demons” [Col. 0872A]: that is, in the soul, they believed in idols. “Lunatics”: they thought that their illness came from the rising of the moon.

“They brought him paralytics”: that is, those slow to do good. “And great crowds followed him”: first, disciples for faith; second, the sick for healing; third, experts in the Law, to accuse; fourth, the poor, for almsgiving; fifth, women, so that they would not despair; sixth, little children.

As he said, “Let the little children come.” “The Decapolis”: that is, those who observe the words of the Law. “From Jerusalem”: those who, seeing peace, would have followed Christ. “From Judea”: those who followed Christ through confession.

[Col. 0872B] “When Jesus saw the crowds,” another four crowds followed Christ, and four kinds follow the Church. The first follow Christ through fear and love; likewise they come to the Church. The second come for desire of food or drink. The third come through envy, so that they may have something to accuse. The fourth are teachers.

Christ had three places of refuge in which to escape the crowds: the mountain, the wilderness, and the boat upon the sea. He leaves these three to us: ascent into the height of the commandments; descent into the wilderness, abandoning vices; and entry into the unity of the Church. The boat signifies the Church, which has a helmsman and sailors and those who cast things into the water. These are the bishops, the laborers, and those who carry out the ministries within.

Three things assail the boat: danger in the waves, in the wind, and in the hair-shirt. So the Church has danger in the waves, meaning the devil’s temptations; in the wind, meaning the sins; and in the hair-shirt, meaning false brothers.

[Col. 0872C] When he ascended the mountain, it signified *theorica*, that is, contemplation. When he descended, he taught *practica*, that is, action. And when he sat down, it indicated that his incarnation had not appeared, because one who sat protected his body with his clothing.

“His disciples approached him”: that is, body and soul. “And opening his mouth”: that is, he who opened the mouths of the Prophets.

“Blessed are the poor in spirit”: those who are poor for the sake of the Holy Spirit, even though they could be rich. “Blessed are the meek”: those who return evil to no one for evil. “For they shall possess the earth,” of which it is said, “I believe that I shall see,” and so forth.

“Blessed are those who mourn now.” He does not speak of every kind of weeping, but of three kinds of weeping which the world ought to have. The first is weeping for one’s own sin; the second, for the sin of one’s neighbor; the third, for heavenly love.

Tears have three qualities: bitter tears, for mourning over sin; hot tears, through the heat of charity, for mourning over the offenses of one’s neighbor; and tears shed from heaven, for weeping out of love for him. Tears are poured out for three reasons: some through remembrance, others through fear of the future, and others through exile.

[Col. 0872D] “Blessed are those who hunger,” and so forth: that is, those for whom whatever good they do is not enough, unless they wish to do more. They will be filled, that is, in the kingdom of God.

“Blessed are the merciful”: those who show mercy are freed from misery and will go to heaven with their gift. “Blessed are the pure in heart”: those who, with a pure heart, are touched by no consciousness of sin, because God, who is pure, looks upon the pure in heart.

[Col. 0873A] “Blessed are the peacemakers”: that is, in four relationships: between God and human beings; between body and soul; between a person and his neighbor; and between a person and his friend. One ought to hate the vice and love the person.

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake”: that is, in Christ. These eight beatitudes pertain to the eight people who were in the ark and who now ought to be in the Church. They can also be seven, like the seven women who had one husband, Christ—that is, in the resurrection.

These eight beatitudes are fulfilled in Christ:

“Blessed are the poor in spirit”: the Son of Man had nowhere to recline his head.

“Blessed are the meek”: “Learn from me, because I am meek.”

“Blessed are those who mourn”: when he saw the city, he wept over it.

“Blessed are those who hunger”: “My food is to do the will of my Father.”

“Blessed are the merciful”: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice.”

“Blessed are the pure in heart”: “Be holy, because I am holy.”

“Blessed are the peacemakers”: “I give you my peace,” and so forth.

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution”: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you.”

[Col. 0873B] “You are the salt of the earth”: this is said of the apostles and teachers. The earth means this world. “If the salt has lost its savor,” and so forth: if a teacher has erred, by what is he corrected? Salt gives flavor, kills worms, and is thrown out and trampled by people. This means that they go out from the Church and are counted among the Gentiles.

“You are the light of the world”: light reveals what is hidden and illuminates darkness; so you too must illuminate the darkness of sins. Alternatively, just as the sun always remains in heaven, so you should remain there.

[Col. 0873C] “A city cannot be hidden”: the Church upon the mountain, that is, upon Christ. “Nor do they light a lamp”—the apostles and teachers—and put it under a bushel, that is, under fear or love.

The apostles have four likenesses: salt, sun, lamp, and city. “Upon a lampstand,” that is, the Church, so that they may shine for all who are in the house, meaning in the Church or in the world. “Let your light shine”: that is, your teaching or good works, “and let them glorify your Father,” that is, through your good deeds.

[Col. 0873D] “Do not think that I came to abolish the Law.” That is, whatever work was done, he himself fulfilled it. When the children of Israel sinned, Moses and Levi took three swords for vengeance against them. Christ did the same when he said, “I have not come to bring peace but a sword.”

“To fulfill” means to complete what was lacking. For the old Law commanded that anyone who committed adultery be punished; now the Law is not abolished but fulfilled when it says, “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her,” and so forth. Again, it says that one must give an account of every idle word on the day of judgment. Behold: he did not come to abolish the Law but to increase what the old Law had not said. “Amen, I say to you.”

“Amen” means truly or faithfully. “One iota”: the name of a letter. By adding one stroke it becomes the letter *deca*, that is, the ten words of the Law. Among the Greeks it is the letter κ, which we have called “one.” “One dot”: literally, one point; in meaning, the least commandments of the Law. “Until all things come to pass”: because what was least in the Law becomes full of mysteries. The iota is the old Law; the dot is the New.

[Col. 0874A] “Whoever abolishes one of these least commandments”: that is, whoever teaches much but fulfills very little, like the Pharisees who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel. This means one who preaches lesser things to others but commits greater offenses himself. “He will be called least in the kingdom of heaven,” that is, in the Church.

“Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees”: for they taught great things but did little, or they rejected some commandments of the Law that they did not love and spoke only of those they loved.

[Col. 0874B] “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not kill.’” This does not abolish the Law. “Whoever is angry with his brother”: that is, anger in the heart without words; he will be liable to judgment, that is, on the day of judgment.

“Raca”: that is, empty or worthless. “Fool”: that is, without a brain. He will be liable to the fire of Gehenna. Gehenna is a double punishment because it punishes both soul and body.

“If you offer your gift at the altar,” and so forth: “Go and be reconciled to your brother.” The gift means prayer, an offering, or yourself, which you offer for communion. One must never come to the Church until one has been reconciled to one’s brother.

“Leave your gift there.” How will this be fulfilled? He rebukes both equally: if the brother is near, it is good; if he is far away, one must nevertheless reconcile oneself in one’s mind. Thus what has been said is fulfilled: “Be at peace with all people.”

[Col. 0874C] “Be consenting with your adversary.” That is, with the Gospel while you are on the way with him, meaning in this life. Or with your adversary, the devil: do not do what he suggests to you, lest he increase the punishment for your sin.

If an infant asks for a sword, do not hand him something with which he can stab himself; thus you consent to him. “Lest your adversary hand you over to the judge”: that is, lest the law of the Gospel hand you over to Christ the judge, because you did not consent to the Gospel; and then to the minister, that is, the angel who sends souls into punishment; and to prison, that is, hell.

[Col. 0874D] “You will not leave there”: that is, no one will leave hell until he has paid the last quadrans. “Until” is understood as forever. A quadrans is the fourth part of a coin, which is given as payment for washing, or it is used for a very small sin. “To pay the quadrans” means to be sent into hell, or it refers to the fact that the human being was made from four elements.

“You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not commit adultery’”: that is, you shall not commit adultery. “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her”: there are two kinds of desire. The first is desire which, even if opportunity follows, does not lead to the act. The second is completed when opportunity is present; adultery is committed in body and in heart.

[Col. 0875A] “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you.” The eye means your ruler or teacher. “Tear it out”: separate him from yourself if he prevents you from serving God. “One of your members”: it is better for your ruler to perish than for you to go into hell with him.

The eye also means your desire, because the body is sent into Gehenna on its account. “The right hand”: your minister or your anger. “Causes you to stumble”: correct it within yourself. “The hand”: cut off the evil work.

[Col. 0875B] “Do not swear”: that is, do not swear falsely. “Do not swear at all”: that is, never swear. “Nor by heaven, because it is God’s throne.” Otherwise, “is” means “is”; “no” means “no”: the word must be spoken both in the mouth and in the heart. “Anything more than this is from evil”: that is, from the unworthiness of the one who is not believed.

“An eye for an eye”: do not return evil for evil. “If someone strikes you on the right cheek”: if a heretic strikes you with a dogma of evil Scripture, offer him another dogma of divine Scripture for living.

“Whoever wishes to take your tunic”: strip away the crime that people know about you. “Give him your cloak also”: the crime of which you alone are conscious; give him a confession of it.

“If someone forces you to go a thousand paces, go with him another thousand”: once you have left the body, go also in your mind. “Whoever asks something of you, give it to him”: whoever questions you, answer him. Or give alms to the poor.

[Col. 0875C] “It was said to the ancients, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’” How did he say this without abolishing the Law? He rightly fulfills it, because in the Old Testament the enemy to be hated is the devil. Here, however, we love enemies in three ways: with the heart, the one who hates us in his heart; through good works, the one who persecutes us in his actions; and through prayer, the one who slanders us in words.

“While people slander you”: that is, falsely accuse you, “so that you may be sons of your Father,” and so forth. It is as though someone had carried gold and silver to us; even if he had cursed and struck us, we would love him. When those things failed, we too would fail; therefore life is promised without failing.

“He makes his sun rise,” and so forth, “and sends rain upon the just”: because the whole world is contained in both—in the sun, dry and hot; in the rain, moist and cold. The world was made from these four qualities. So we ought to give our enemies food and drink, clothing, and a word of love.

[Col. 0875D] “For if you love those who love you,” and so forth. A publican is called so because he sins publicly, or because he administers public affairs. “Gentiles”: that is, pagans.

“Be perfect”: that is, fulfill these things perfectly—in almsgiving, fasting, and prayers. “So that you may not be seen by people”: good works must not be done for human praise.

“When you give alms”: to a priest, a poor person, or an enemy. “Hypocrite” means a pretender. “They have received their reward”: not from God.

[Col. 0876A] “Let your left hand not know”: the left hand means vainglory. “Your right hand”: do everything for God. “Enter your room”: the secret places of the heart. “With the door shut”: against vainglory.

“Do not speak at length”: do not learn many petitions or many words, nor ask God through excessive loudness of voice. “For your Father knows what you need.” Therefore pray thus: “Our Father.” Let us live on earth in such a way that we may have a Father in heaven.

We show charity and brotherhood when we say “our.” The emperor says this, and the beggar; the Lord says it, and the servant; together they say, “Our Father.” Therefore those who have one Father are brothers. Let the Lord not disdain to have his servant as a brother, since the Lord Christ wished to be his brother. Let us therefore act so that we may be heirs to the Father, for human law also makes sons heirs.

[Col. 0876B] “Hallowed be your name.” Here we ask that his name be made holy in us, that is, in our works; for his name is always holy.

“Your kingdom come”: just as sons desire the kingdom for their father, so we pray that he may reign in us and not the devil; he, and not sin—whether in the Church or in the Gospel.

“Your will be done,” and so forth. Just as angels serve without blame in heaven, so should we; or just as in souls, so in the body; or just as Christians, so heretics; just as the Church, so the synagogue; just as righteousness, so sin. Let them be converted, so that your will may be done in them.

[Col. 0876C] “Our daily bread”: that is, every day until the beginning of the year. “Today”: that is, always. “Bread”: Christ. We must act so that we may receive him daily as a remedy.

“And forgive us,” and so forth: here we make a pledge with God: if you forgive, it is forgiven to you.

“And do not lead us into temptation”: as you led people astray in the flood, or those in Sodom, or Pharaoh in the sea; or into the devil’s temptation, or the snares of human beings.

“But deliver us from evil”: that is, from the devil, from sin, and from an evil person. These seven prayers have four common to all, so that he may have prayed for the seven graces of the Holy Spirit. Three petitions concern heavenly things: “Hallowed be your name,” “Your kingdom come,” and “Your will be done.” Four concern this present life.

[Col. 0876D] “When you fast,” and so forth: “They disfigure their faces.” That is, they transform themselves so that they may be seen by people to be fasting.

“Anoint your head and wash your face”: what you wish to give to the Lord, who is your head, give to your neighbor.

“Do not store up treasures on earth”: store them in heaven, lest rust—that is, vainglory or anger—and moth—that is, envy or pride—and thieves, that is, demons, destroy them. Gold means understanding; the world means clothing; food means divine preaching.

[Col. 0877A] “The lamp of your body”: that is, your teacher or ruler. “Body”: the inner human being. “If it is single”: if it is directed toward one thing.

“No one can serve two masters.” “Where your treasure is,” and so forth. “He will hate one”: the one who is not good to him. “He will love the other”: the one who is good to him. This means despising the devil and loving God. Whoever serves riches serves demons. Mammon means riches, or it is the name of the devil.

“Is not the soul more than food?” That is, those who give lesser things to God and greater things to the devil.

“Look at the birds of heaven,” and so forth. It is customary for birds to fly upward and sing a song, and when they desire something on earth, they receive it from the Lord. So human beings ought to think about heavenly things and praise God. When they are in need on earth, they receive restoration from the Lord together with the citizens of heaven. How much more will your Father, who is good by nature, give good things to those who ask him—that is, faith through charity?

[Col. 0877B] “Enter through the narrow gate,” where sinners cannot enter unless they lay aside [uncertain: *portam fides palasticas* II]. That is, the love of God and neighbor. The two lights are the upper one, the Gospel, and the lower one, the Old Law. Whoever gives offense does not enter.

“How broad is the gate,” and so forth: that is, those who serve riches and their own will.

“Beware of false teachers”: that is, guard yourselves against them. “In sheep’s clothing”: good teachers. “Ravenous wolves”: they seize souls for destruction. “By their fruits”: that is, by their works you will recognize them.

“Do they gather grapes from thorns,” that is, from heretics? Grapes mean virginity. “Or figs from thistles”: that is, a spouse from heretics. A good tree is a good person; a bad tree is a bad person, one who does evil works.

[Col. 0877C] “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’” and so forth. He speaks of those who love to stand praying in the corners. But “the one who does the will of my Father” is the one who keeps the commandments.

“Many will say to me, ‘Lord’”: many are those who enter through it. “I never knew you”: that is, whether good or heretical. “Depart from me”: those who hope that there will be no forgiveness of sins.

“Everyone who hears my words,” and so forth: the one who does not act against the preaching will be like a wise man who built his house upon rock, that is, upon good work.

“Lest rain enter it”: that is, heretical teaching. “Rivers”: persecutions of heretics. “Winds”: demons. The clouds receive rain from the sea; heretics receive doctrine from the world. “The house did not fall”: that is, he does not fall who stands upon faith in Christ.

[Col. 0877D] “And everyone who hears my words and does not do them.” It was the custom in the Law that anyone in the people who was not clean, if he received healing, should show himself to the priest, and an offering should be made for him: two turtledoves or two young pigeons.

A piece of wood, hyssop, and scarlet were with them. The scarlet was fastened around the top of the wood, and the blood of one bird was sprinkled upon that wood and upon the other bird; the latter was then released into the air.

The wood signifies the cross of Christ; the scarlet, his passion. One must go to martyrdom through Christ’s passion, and our blood must be sprinkled upon his cross. Thus one ascends to the Church after the passion of our body in martyrdom.

[Col. 0878A] “As a testimony to them”: that is, so that he would not abolish the Law, or so that they might see that he had been cleansed of leprosy.

The centurion represents the teachers. The paralytic servant, contracted and unable to move, signifies the human race enclosed in sins.

Jesus found three mysteries in the centurion. First, humility, when he said, “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.” Second, faith, when he said, “Only say the word, and he will be healed.” Third, prudence, when he said, “I am a man under authority.”

Jesus marvels at the centurion: that is, he found wisdom in him, by which he had been taught through divine preaching.

“From the east”: those converted from infancy. “From the west”: those converted from old age. “From the south”: those converted from youth. “From the north”: those who come from the power of the devil to faith. “They will recline”: that is, they will dwell.

“Why with only three?” That is, because of forgiveness. Those who desire will weep there. There will be gnashing of teeth for those whose god is their belly.

“Peter’s mother-in-law lying with a fever”: that is, the synagogue’s uncertainty.

[Col. 0878B] “He touched her hand”: he provided assistance. “The fever left her”: unbelief ceased. “She ministered to him”: she blessed him.

“Toward evening”: this reveals the end of the world.

“Demons”: sins. “Foxes”: unbelieving people. “Birds”: rich people. “He has nowhere to recline his head”: where there is no faith. “Let the dead bury their dead”: the body burying the soul. Alternatively, if a sinner praises a sinner, the dead buries the dead.

“The boat”: the Church. “Movement and waves”: temptation. “He slept”: he was incarnate or crucified. “Wind”: sudden temptation.

“The demoniac”: the Gentile, a nation with unbelief. “Among the tombs”: these are bodies. “No one passed by that road”: that is, through paganism to the kingdom. “The herd of pigs”: they show human beings before conversion. “They were drowned in the sea”: that is, in the deep. “The herdsman”: he represents the philosophers.

[Col. 0878C] “He arose”: that is, he was healed. “He returned to his own house”: that is, to the first creation.

“The bridegroom”: Christ. “The bride”: the Church. “The sons of the bridegroom”: the apostles.

“Unfermented bread”: the teaching of the Gospel. “Torn garments”: these are old people. “New wine and old wineskins”: new preaching given to old people.

“The ruler”: he represents the Prophets or Patriarchs. “The girl”: this is the synagogue. Jesus took the girl’s hand: that is, he gave her assistance.

“A great harvest”: prepared hearts. “Harvesters”: teachers.

“Not two tunics”: that is, not of double mind and not with double confidence, either in the New or in the Old Testament. “No sandals”: that is, no testimony of evil. “Nor a staff”: that is, not strength, but patience.

“Peace returned”: that is, the reward was received. “Dust”: defilement. These things are so because dust acts in three ways: it binds the feet, darkens the eyes, and soils garments.

“The crucified serpent hides its head”: that is, the apostles, crucified and not denying Christ. “Persecution”: these are heresies.

“From one city to another”: that is, through the individual questions of the books.

Nothing is covered that will not be revealed: that is, the passion of Christ [Col. 0878D] and of all teachers. “What I say in the darkness”—that is, to the Jews—“say in the light”—that is, in the Church. The two sparrows signify the body and soul, or Christ and Barabbas. The penny signifies faith; the sword signifies the word of preaching. Alternatively, the two sparrows signify the two Testaments; this is Christ. “To separate father from son” means to separate the faithful from the unfaithful. “He took up the cross” means, “Crucify yourself.” “To be scandalized by Christ” means to deny Christ. The reed shaken by the wind signifies flattering, empty, fruitless people. “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence”: this means that one reaches the kingdom of God through the crucifixions of the flesh and through repentance. He himself is Elijah who is of John, because the same spirit was in Elijah; at the second coming, it was in John at the first coming. The children sitting in the marketplace signify the prophets. “We piped to you and you did not dance”: we announced the coming, and you did not believe. “We lamented and you did not mourn”: we announced repentance, and you were terrified of confession. Praises are made in four ways.

“I will confess to you, Lord”: the Father of heaven is faith—“I believe in God the Father”; of the martyrs—“who confesses me before men”; of sinners—“Confess to the Lord, for he is good.” “You have hidden these things from the wise,” that is, from those who use the wisdom of this world; “you have revealed them to little ones,” that is, to the disciples. The calling was made in the New Testament in four ways.

“Come to me, all you who labor”: in the Old Testament, “Come, children, hear me”; in the future, “Come, blessed ones.” The yoke, that is, doctrine, is light for those who desire it and heavy for those who do not. Perfection is understood in three ways: of the disciples, through baptism; of sinners, through remission; of the Jews, through renewal of the New Testament. The fields signify the harvest, which signifies the ancient Law. The Sabbath signifies the rest of the New Testament. The disciples plucking ears signify drawing testimonies from the Old Testament to confirm the New; rubbing them with their hands signifies expressing them in a spiritual sense.

The man with the withered hand signifies avarice: he is eager to receive and greedy in giving. The one who used to steal should learn to give. He stretched out his hand, that is, he cleansed his heart; it was restored, signifying conversion to the faith. The smoking wick signifies the hearts of the gentiles prepared for the faith. The demoniac, mute and blind [Col. 0879C], signifies the human race. “He bound the strong man in the house”: Christ bound the devil; his vessels are the hearts of the gentiles. “Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil?” Through the viper he signifies the synagogue; through the brood, the Jews. Just as a son kills the viper, his mother, so the Jews killed Christ, who is the wisdom and mother of all. “An evil and adulterous generation” means those who abandon the Lord and cling to idols.

“The queen of the south came from the ends of the earth”: she signifies the gentiles, hearing the wisdom of Solomon, that is, the doctrine of Christ. The unclean spirit went out from the man, that is, from the Jews; it went through dry places, that is, through the gentiles; it returned to the house, that is, to the Jews. It found it swept clean, that is, by ancestral traditions [Col. 0879D]. It took with it seven spirits more evil than itself: these signify all their days turned toward evil works. Entering the house, that is, the hearts of the persecutors—for they persecuted Christ and the prophets.

“Mother and brothers,” that is, the synagogue and the Jews, standing outside, that is, outside the Church, seeking to speak with you: this signifies the future conversion of the Jews to the faith. Jesus went out from the house and sat beside the sea. This is understood in two ways: from heaven into the world, and from the Jews to the gentiles. He went up into a boat, that is, into heaven; the crowds remained on the shore, signifying the present life. “In a parable”: this means in parables. The one who sows is the one who preaches; the seed is the word of God. “Beside the way” signifies one who hears the word of God and does not understand it. “On rocky ground” signifies one who hears the word of God and receives it, but when temptation comes, denies it. “Among thorns” signifies one who hears the word but, because of riches, chokes it. “In good soil” signifies one who hears and understands.

“And it bears fruit”: thirtyfold signifies the order of married people who follow the commandment of God. Sixtyfold signifies the order of widows and perseverance in the Lord. A hundredfold signifies the orders of martyrs, monks, or virgins. “To the one who has, it will be given”: this signifies the apostles; those who have Christ will be given understanding. “From the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away”: this signifies the Jews; the very Law that they possessed will be taken away from them.

“Seeing, they do not see”: these are the Jews, who saw with their eyes but did not believe with their hearts. “Hearing, they do not hear”: this signifies the concerns of the body; they heard but, because of the hardness of their hearts, did not understand [Col. 0880B]. “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field.” The sower is the Son of Man; the seed is the word of God in the hearts of believers; the field is the world. The weeds are the sons of the wicked, that is, workers of iniquity. The enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the consummation of the age. The reapers are angels. Why is it said “bundles”? Because not all are judged equally, but adulterers with adulterers, and all alike with their equals.

The mustard seed signifies Christ. The man who sows is God the Father; the field is the world.

“Smallest of all the seeds”: this signifies Christ, rejected by the Jews. “When it has grown,” that is, when he has risen; “a tree,” that is, he ascended into heaven. Its branches are the apostles; the birds in its branches are the saints who despise earthly things and desire heavenly things.

Alternatively, the mustard seed signifies the word of the holy Gospel. The man who sows is Christ; the field is the world. “Smallest of all” means preserved in the hearts of the faithful despite the wisdom of philosophers. “A tree” means that it ascended above all worldly wisdom. Its branches signify the explanations of the individual teachers; the birds signify lovers of knowledge, receiving it from the seed, that is, from the doctrine of the Gospel.
