The woman signifies wisdom. She hid it in the flour, that is, in the hearts of the faithful. The three measures signify the three sons of Noah, until the whole was leavened, that is, until the Gospel was preached throughout the whole world.

“The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden”: the treasure is Christ or wisdom. “In the field” means in the Church or in the divine Scriptures. “He sold everything” means that he abandoned worthless things, or earthly possessions, and bought the field, that is, the kingdom of heaven. The merchant is one who seeks divine teaching; he found one pearl, that is, the wisdom of Christ, and sold everything, that is, vices.

“The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea.” Through the net the word of preaching is signified; the sea is the world. It gathers fish of every kind, that is, the whole human race. It hears the word of God beside the shore, that is, near the end of the world. The householder is Christ. The scribes and teachers are the apostles. “He came into his own country” means that he came to the Jews. A tetrarch is the appointed part of a kingdom.

[Col. 0881A] “He bound John and sent him into prison”: this signifies the end of the old Law. Herodias signifies the synagogue. The girl danced at the banquet, signifying the gentiles dancing before an idol. John’s head on a platter signifies the body of Christ on the altar; his head in the hearts of the faithful was given to the girl, that is, to the Church from the gentiles. She brought it to her mother, signifying the future conversion of the Jews.

“Those who followed” signifies those proceeding on foot; it shows that a person ought to follow God not with money or possessions, but through his own labor. He healed the sick, that is, he washed away sins and idols. “The hour has already passed,” that is, the letter of the Law. The five loaves signify the five books of Moses. The two fish signify the two Testaments, or two orders, namely of priests and prophets, or the two books of Joshua.

The crowd reclined on the grass [Col. 0881B], that is, on dry hearts, or reclined upon vices. Having taken the loaves and looked toward heaven, he drew up the meaning; he broke them, that is, he expressed the history of the Law in a spiritual sense, and understanding appeared. He blessed them, that is, multiplied them. The twelve full baskets signify the twelve apostles from holy doctrine.

Why are women and children not counted like men? Because children are unable to struggle against their vices, and likewise women, since the sex is imperfect. He ordered them to go up into the boat, that is, into the Church, and to go ahead across the water, that is, from the Jews to the gentiles.

He is called in four ways: first, by nature; second, by kinship; third, by nation; fourth, by affection. In four ways a person is described: what is said may be good, well; “Repent,” and so forth. Evil, badly: “His blood be upon us.” Good, badly: where it is said concerning the blind man, “Are you also his disciple?” Evil, well: where the Apostle says, “I handed such a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved.” When evening came, he was alone: this signifies the end of the world; alone he came to redeem the human race.

The boat was in the middle of the sea, that is, the Church in the middle of the world. It was tossed by the waves, that is, it suffered persecutions. The contrary wind signifies the devils. Jesus came in the fourth watch of the night, signifying the fourth Law, that is, the Gospel. Jesus walking on the sea signifies trampling upon the bitterness of the age. Peter walked on the waters, that is, upon bitterness, or trampling the vices of sinners.

When Peter sank into the sea, this signified doubt of faith. Thus everyone who doubts in faith sinks [Col. 0881D] into sin. Jesus stretched out his hand and seized him, that is, gave him the help of faith. These are the four Laws: the first in nature; the second, the Law of the letter; the third, that of the prophets; the fourth, that of the Evangelists.

When he had crossed over, that is, when he had passed across, they came to the land of Gennesaret, that is, from the Jews to the gentiles. They brought to him those who were suffering, that is, those serving idols.

The Canaanite woman signifies the primitive Church. Her daughter, afflicted by a demon, that is, the Church of the gentiles corrupted by idols, was healed. The girl was healed from that hour, signifying the conversion of the gentiles from the hour when they believed in Christ.

“I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel”: this refers bodily to the Jews [Col. 0882A]. Alternatively, all who believe in the God of Israel are called “Israel.” To take the children’s bread means doctrine; the children are the Jews; to give it to dogs means to give it to the gentiles. The little dogs eat: the gentiles receive crumbs, that is, the lesser commandments.

“I have compassion on the crowd”: this shows that God is wholly merciful. “They have remained with me three days”: this signifies faith in the Trinity. “They have nothing to eat”: they have no word of preaching. “I do not want to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way”: lest they perish on the way of error in the present life, because faith without works is dead.

The seven loaves signify the Heptateuch. The few fish signify the order of the prophets or priests. Sitting upon the ground signifies those already more perfect, having trampled their vices. The seven baskets signify the seven teachers of the Holy Spirit.

The Pharisees are divided; the Sadducees are justified. A clear sky signifies the resurrection of Christ; a red sky, the shedding of blood; a dark sky signifies the passion of Christ; a glowing storm signifies persecution.

“Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees,” that is, their doctrine. Simon means “obedient”; “son of Jonah” means “son of a dove,” which is interpreted as the Holy Spirit. “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you”: that is, father and mother have not shown it to you. The gates of hell are the sins of human beings. The keys of the kingdom of heaven are the power of binding and loosing; through repentance they will be opened.

“To suffer many things from the elders and scribes”: by saying this, Jesus showed his passion and resurrection. He says to Peter, “Go behind me”: this shows that he himself would be crucified. “After me, let him deny himself” [Col. 0882C], that is, let him despise the pleasure of the flesh. Whoever loves his own pleasure loses his soul. Here “soul” is used for “pleasure.” “Whoever loses his soul will find it”: a person loses his soul in two ways, through martyrdom and through denial of the body. “He will find it,” that is, in the kingdom of God. He gives an exchange for his soul, the one who crucifies his flesh and nourishes his soul.

“After six days”—already on the seventh—he shows the ages of the world; the seventh signifies rest. Peter, James, and John signify here the whole Church. He leads them up the mountain, that is, into the kingdom of God. His face shone like the sun, that is, the saints in the glory of the Father. Alternatively, the Old Testament shone into the New.

His garments were white like snow, that is, the gathering of all the faithful [Col. 0882D]. Through Moses he shows the letter of the Law; through Elijah, the order of the prophets; Christ with the disciples shows the New Testament. The dark cloud is the letter of the Law; the bright cloud is the preaching of the Gospel; the rain cloud is the preaching of the apostles, who produced the fruit of repentance after Christ’s ascension. “When he came to the crowds” means when he descended into the world.

The man prostrated on his knees signifies the order of the prophets, who prayed for themselves as though for the Church. His lunatic son signifies the people of the gentiles worshiping idols. He falls into fire, that is, into desire; repeatedly into water, that is, into lust. From here he passes from the Jews to the gentiles: “Go to the sea,” that is, to the gentiles.

[Col. 0883A] “Cast a hook,” that is, the word of preaching. The fish that first comes up on the hook signifies the [uncertain: cornemium]. In its mouth you will find a stater, that is, confession of faith in the humanity and divinity. “Give it to them for me and for you”: for me, faith; for you, an excuse.

The little one enters the kingdom of heaven, not one who is little in age but one pure in mind; hence the Apostle says, “Be little ones in malice.”

“Whoever causes one of these to stumble”: whether through bodily injury or through opposition to the faith. “Let a millstone be hung”: that is, the care or circuit of this age. “Around his neck”: in the labor of the age. “Let him be drowned in the sea”: that is, in the age.

“Your hand” means your equal. “Feet” means your minister. “Eye” means your bishop, priest, teacher, or elder. “Do not despise one of these” [Col. 0883B], lest you act against their innocence.

The sheep that went astray signifies the human race. The shepherd is Christ. The sheep left on the mountains signify the orders of angels who dwell in the heavens.

“If your brother sins, rebuke him between yourself and him”: so that the exposure of the sin does not become public and reproach does not arise against the brother. “Tell the Church,” that is, the congregation of the faithful. “A gentile,” that is, a gentile and a tax collector, is one who sins publicly. Let not their likeness be hateful to you, but their works.

“If two agree,” that is, flesh and soul. If the flesh agrees with the soul, the one who asks receives through faith.

“The kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants.” The one who owes ten thousand talents is the one who sins against God. The one who owes one hundred denarii is the one who sins against his brother. The fellow servants who judged are angels.

When Jesus had finished these sayings, he moved to Galilee, that is, at the end of the world, from the gentiles to Judea.

“A man leaves father and mother”: this shows that Christ leaves the Father in heaven, yet leaves him in such a way that he does not abandon the mother, that is, the synagogue. “He will cling to his wife”: Christ will cling to the Church. “The two will be one flesh”: this shows that Christ is the head and the Church the body.

“To abandon a wife from the true [order]”: when someone departs from Christ, then he joins himself to heresy in one crime. Four souls perish: the one who dismisses his wife without reason, and the one who marries a dismissed woman.

“It is difficult for a rich man to enter,” and what follows: he speaks of those who possess under the power of avarice. The eye of a needle is called a little gate of Jerusalem. Alternatively, the eye of a needle signifies confession of faith or repentance. The rich are called the Jews; the camel is the people of the gentiles. In a third interpretation, the eye of a needle signifies the passion of Christ; the camel is the one who bears the sins of the human race.

“In the regeneration” means through the resurrection.

“The last will be first, and the first last.” The last were the people of the gentiles; the Jews were first and became last. So it is with Peter and the thief; so with the infant and the elder.

The householder hired workers for his vineyard. The Father is Christ. Early morning signifies the beginning of the world. The workers are cultivators of the commandments of God. The vineyard is the Church; in the Old Testament the vineyard is the Law or the synagogue. The daily denarius is eternal life.

At the first hour Abel came; at the third hour Noah and his sons; in the marketplace, that is, in the world, Abraham came at the sixth hour. Moses and David came at the ninth hour. At the eleventh hour the people of the gentiles came.

Alternatively, the first hour signifies infancy; the third, adolescence; the sixth, youth; the ninth, old age; the eleventh, extreme old age. At whatever hour a person is converted and groans with all his heart, he receives the daily denarius. Evening means the end of the world. The steward of the vineyard is Christ. Those who murmured are the Jews, saying, “We have borne the burden of the day,” that is, bearing the Law and the prophets.

Jericho is interpreted as “moon” and signifies the decline of the people. The two blind men signify the Jews and the gentiles, sitting beside the way [Col. 0884B], that is, in the present life near its end.

“Jesus passed by” signifies that through the incarnation and humanity he passed through the world. “Jesus stood” shows his divinity. “When he drew near Jerusalem” means when he came into the world.

Bethphage means “house of the mouth” or “of the jaw.” The Mount of Olives signifies the name of the three lights: refreshment of labor, consolation of work, and knowledge of the true light. The village opposite you signifies Jerusalem, which resisted the law of the Gospel. “Untie them and bring them to me” shows the conversion of the Jews or the gentiles through the preaching of the apostles.

“The Lord has need of it”: he needs nothing other than faith. “To Zion” means “watchtower of life.” The daughter of Zion is the congregation of the faithful. Through the garments he shows doctrine. They made him sit upon them, that is, Christ in the hearts of the faithful. They spread garments on the way, showing the conversion of humility.

The branches from the trees signify the doctrine of the gentiles. The crowd going before signifies the Jews; the crowd following signifies the gentiles. “Hosanna” means “Save me,” or “Save”; just as you save the Jews, save the gentiles; just as you save the angels, save the human race.

Alternatively, the branches from the trees signify simple teachers who, through the simplicity of their doctrine, cut off the teaching of the fathers like shoots.

Jesus entered the temple, that is, the Church. He cast out the sellers and buyers, that is, those who sell and buy the gifts of the Holy Spirit, baptism, or any consecration. The chair signifies doctrine; the table signifies the commandments of the Law. The children crying out in the temple, that is, in the Church, signify the children. Having left them, he went outside, showing that the Jews had been abandoned; he went to the gentiles.

Bethany means “house of obedience.” He remained there, showing that Christ remains in the heart of the obedient. He returned to the city, showing that at the first coming he came to the Jews. “Who was hungry except for the faith of the Jews?” The fig tree signifies the synagogue, beside the way, that is, according to the letter. He found nothing on it except leaves, that is, the outward show of the Jews and ancestral doctrine.

The withered fig tree shows the synagogue without repentance. “The mountain,” that is, Christ: “Take it from here,” that is, cast the Jews into the sea, into the hearts of believers.

The man who had two sons is Christ. The two sons are the Jews and the gentiles. “Which of them did the father’s will?” The one who said “I will go” and did not go signifies the Jews [Col. 0885A]; the one who said “I will not go” and went signifies the people of the gentiles, who acted through confession of faith.

The householder planted a vineyard. The man is God the Father. The vineyard is the synagogue. He surrounded it with a hedge, that is, with the protection of angels. The winepress signifies the temple of martyrdom. The tower in the middle signifies the doctrine of the Law. The cultivators are the teachers.

When the time of the fruit drew near, that is, the coming of Christ, the servants sent were the prophets. The first whom they killed was Jeremiah; Isaiah was the one whom they stoned; [uncertain: “Barth”], or Stephen. “They cast him outside the vineyard,” that is, outside Jerusalem, onto Mount Calvary. “He will give the vineyard to other tenants” signifies the Church of the gentiles, who return fruit, that is, confession of repentance and faith.

The stone is Christ. The stone cut from the mountain without hands signifies without human act or intercourse, from a mother without seed, from the Father without time. It became the head of the corner and contains two walls, signifying the New and Old Testaments, the Jews and the gentiles.

Whoever falls upon the stone will be broken: this signifies the gentiles, who, falling upon Christ, are broken away from unbelief into faith, broken upon him, that is, into humility. Upon whomever the stone falls, it will crush him: this signifies the superstitious Jews.

The man who is a king and made a wedding feast for his son: the man is God the Father. The wedding signifies the union of Christ and the Church. Just as Eve came from Adam’s rib, so the Church was redeemed from Christ’s side; and just as Adam came forth from virgin earth, so Christ was born from the virgin Mary.

He sent his servants, that is, the patriarchs. Again he sent others, that is, the prophets. The prepared meal signifies Holy Scripture. The slaughtered bulls signify those who shed their blood for Christ. The fattened animals signify the well-fed.

Some went away to the farm, that is, into desire; others to business, that is, into the world, as the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself.” The rest seized his servants, showing the violence of persecution.

He says to his servants, that is, to the apostles: “The wedding has been prepared,” that is, the hearts of believers have been joined to Christ through the love of charity. “Go out to the exits of the roads,” that is, to the gentiles. They gathered the good and the bad, showing the present life.

The king entered among those reclining, showing the second coming. The man without a wedding garment signifies charity, as it is said: “Faith without charity is dead.”

[Col. 0885D] The woman, that is, the synagogue, through seven husbands signifies the Heptateuch. The woman who died signifies the dead letter, passing from the Old Testament into the New. “In the resurrection, whose wife will she be?” means, “Of the Church of Christ.”

“The Lord said”—that is, God the Father—“to my Lord”—that is, to Christ—“until I place your enemies as a footstool under your feet.” This shows that he humbled the Jews and the gentiles beneath his feet through patience, or that the persecutors will be punished through vengeance in the future.

“Upon the chair of Moses,” that is, upon his doctrine. The phylacteries are the ten words of the Law written on a small scroll, which the Pharisees wore on their foreheads.

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem”: the repetition shows the affection of grief. “As a hen gathers her chicks under her wings” [Col. 0886A], that is, under raised wings, so Christ spread his palms on the cross to gather his children, as the Song of Deuteronomy declares: “He spread his wings and took them up upon his shoulders.”

“Behold, your house will be left desolate”: this shows that they have been abandoned by their Law, prophecy, and priesthood. “You will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’”: this shows that at the second coming every flesh will see him, and all the tribes of the earth that pierced him will mourn over him.

“Not one stone will be left here upon another”: this shows the dispersion of the Jews. “Then many will be scandalized”: this shows that, because of the magnitude of the persecution, they will deny Christ.

The abomination signifies the statue of the Antichrist placed in the temple. Desolation means consummation. “Those who are in Judea” means those who are in the confession of faith. They flee to the mountains, that is, to the doctrine of the apostles. Whoever is on the roof, that is, in the contemplative life, should not descend into the house, that is, into the active life; or into the field, that is, into the preaching of the Gospel. “Let him not take his cloak”: let him not return to his former way of life.

Woe to pregnant women, that is, to those desiring the possessions of others. Woe to nursing women, that is, to those committing sin in their works. Through the desert he shows persecution; through the Sabbath, the end of the world.

“Wherever the body is, there the eagles will gather”: the body is Christ; the eagles are the souls of the saints. Alternatively, in the resurrection each soul will take up its own body.

Through the sun he shows the preaching of the Gospel; through the moon, the Church; through the stars, the saints or preachers. The powers of heaven will be shaken: this is the appearance of the hosts of angels for judgment. The sign in heaven is the cross of Christ. Through the trumpet he shows the sound of the angels.

“There will be two in the field,” that is, in the preaching of the Gospel. One will be taken, that is, the one who completes the preaching in works; the other will be left, that is, in the work of righteousness. “At the mill,” in the world: the two grinding signify those in the Catholic Church and those among the heretics.

“The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins who took their lamps.” This means their bodies in the resurrection. They are virgins because they did not deny Christ. The five wise ones signify those who labored for the kingdom of God; the five foolish ones signify those who acted for the sake of human reward.

To become drowsy means to grow weak before death; to sleep means to rest in death. Midnight signifies error, or negligent security. “I do not know you” means, “I do not know your good works.” The man going away is Christ. “He went abroad” means that he went from the world to the Father.

He called his servants, that is, the teachers, and gave them his possessions, that is, the doctrine of the Gospel. The five talents signify the five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Through habit he used to move them, or he turns transient causes toward the eternal.

Thus it is said concerning sight: “Turn my eyes away,” and so forth. Concerning hearing: “Fence your ears so that they may not hear the tongues of blasphemy.” Concerning smell: “We are a good fragrance to God among those who are being saved.” Concerning taste: “Do not curse, but bless” [Col. 0887A]. Concerning touch: “Let the one who used to steal steal no longer, but labor with his hands so that he may give to the one in need.”

For this reason the talents become ten. The two talents signify understanding and action. Whoever has these, fulfills them by example and teaches by words; he saves himself and instructs others. For this reason the talent is doubled.

The one talent signifies understanding. He hid it in the earth, that is, the one who teaches the preaching of the Gospel for earthly things. “After a long time,” that is, at the end of the world: “You reap where you did not sow,” that is, where there had been no preaching.

“Take the talent,” that is, understanding, “and give it to the one who doubled it in good works.” The five senses, as the Apostle says, are a law for themselves; they show the work of the Law in their hearts. To the one who has faith and charity will be given understanding and the working of virtues [Col. 0887B]. From the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away: that is, whoever has faith but does not have charity, that faith itself will die in him.

Majesty means power and dignity. The Jews are the goats; the people of the gentiles are the sheep. The right signifies what is prosperous or straight; the left signifies what is adverse or punitive, since with God there is nothing left-handed.

When he was in Bethany, that is, in the house of obedience, “house” is here used for the world.

The woman signifies the future Church. The alabaster signifies the human body. Through the ointment he shows the faith of confession. The head of Christ is God the Father; reclining, Christ is upon the Church.

“You will always have the poor”: spiritually, those who need doctrine; or bodily, those who need food. “You will not always have me” shows the time according to the flesh.

Joseph was sold into Egypt for twenty pieces of silver to satisfy the hunger of the body. Christ was sold for thirty pieces of silver for the sins of human beings and the hunger of faith.

Opportunity means a suitable time. Through the unleavened bread he shows sincerity of mind. “I will drink it with you in the kingdom of my Father”: that is, in his members, in the kingdom, that is, in the Church.

“I will strike the shepherd”: that is, Christ. “The sheep will be scattered”: these are the apostles. “I will go before you into Galilee”: this means that, leaving the Jews behind, he went to the gentiles.

“If it is possible, let this cup pass from me”: the cup is the passion. He said this on account of the part belonging to the flesh. Through the sword he shows the divine word.

“Cut off the ear”: this signifies the Jews’ severed hearing. In the cleansing of the Jews he accepted it so that he might purify our uncleanness. He was scourged and endured it [Col. 0888A] so that he might free us from the scourges of sins.

Just as Adam stretched out his palm toward the tree of life, so the Jews stretched out their palms against Christ. Therefore Christ stretched out his palms upon the wood of the cross so that he might free us from every goad. Through the crowing of the cock he shows the restoration of the Holy Spirit. He was bound and led away so that he might loosen the bonds of our sins.

“Corban” in Hebrew, “gazophylacium” in Greek, is called in Latin “the treasury of riches.” Through the shedding of Christ’s blood the human race was redeemed. Through the price of blood the field was bought for the burial of strangers.

Hyrus Pompeius [uncertain reading] is; Barabbas was led into the desert, that is, into hell. The other was sacrificed, that is, Christ for the sin of human beings.

They stripped Christ, that is, stripped him from the faith of the Jews; they dressed him in a scarlet cloak, that is, Christ clothed in the faith of the gentiles. The scarlet cloak signifies Christ clothed in the faith of the gentiles. Alternatively, through the scarlet cloak he shows the shedding of his blood or martyrdom.

They stripped him of the cloak and dressed him in his own garments, showing the conversion of the Jews at the end of the world.

The soldiers who divided his garments hold the figure of the Gospel: they divided the doctrine of Christ among themselves. Through the tearing of the veil he shows the tearing apart of the kingdom of the Jews.

Alternatively, the veil was torn: this shows the tearing of the letter of the Law through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, or the ascension of Christ; the heavens were torn open for the human race.

The earth was shaken, showing the grace of God, moved from the Jews to the gentiles. The rocks were split [Col. 0888C]: these are the hearts of the gentiles, split open for the faith. The tombs were opened, that is, hearts opened to the faith.

The tomb signifies the Church from the gentiles. “New” shows that the word of God had not previously been preached to the gentiles. The tomb cut out in the rock shows the Church cut out from the hardness of gentility. The stone rolled to the entrance of the tomb shows hardness in the hearts of the Jews.

“On the evening of the Sabbath,” that is, at the end of the world. “The first of the Sabbath” shows the day of the resurrection. The stone being rolled away signifies the future rolling away of the hardness of the Jews. Through the brightness he shows terror; through the whiteness of the garment he shows the consolation of restoration. “In Galilee, on the mountain” shows the movement from the Jewish people to the gentiles.

## THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK

[Col. 0887]

[Col. 0887D] The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, Son of God. By saying “Son of God,” he shows birth according to divinity; according to the flesh he shows it when he says “Jesus.” “Behold, I send”—that is, the Father’s voice—“my angel,” that is, John, “before your face,” that is, the forerunner of Christ, making his coming known.

The voice of John is “crying out.” Christ is in the desert, signifying the Jews, abandoned by the Law, the kingdom, and the priesthood. “Prepare the way” means the hearts or works. “Make his paths straight” [Col. 0888D] means the thoughts of your hearts.

Through the baptism of water he shows the washing of body and soul. The baptism of repentance is the remission of sins. He came into the house of Simon and Andrew, that is, to the Jews. Rising very early, he shows the coming of Christ and the beginning of the New Testament. He went into a deserted place, that is, to the Jews, and there he prayed, that is, there he preached.

He could not enter the city. This was because of the multitude of the people [Col. 0889A]. Through the paralytic he shows the human race; through the bed, the body. He was carried by four: these are the four elements from which a human being is constituted, or the four orders of the Gospel, or the four virtues of the soul, namely fortitude, justice, prudence, and temperance.

Fortitude is fighting against vices. Justice is loving God with all one’s heart and one’s neighbor as oneself. Prudence is anticipating the future. Temperance is restraining every movement of anger.

They uncovered the roof, that is, making the history of the Law open. They lowered the pallet, showing the letter of the Law stripped bare and the manifest meaning of the Gospel. He commanded them to serve him in the boat, that is, to preach in the Church.

He ascended the mountain, signifying his ascension with the flesh into heaven [Col. 0889B]. “Thunder” is Christ; the sons of thunder are the apostles. The clouds are the prophets; the rain is preaching.

The lamp under the bushel signifies the one who teaches for the sake of worldly desire. Under the bed, that is, in the darkness of sinners, nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest. The hidden things of the Law among the Jews were made manifest to the gentiles.

The man who sowed shows the teacher. What he sowed is the divine word, in the earth, in the human heart. Sleeping signifies ignorance. Night shows adversity or ignorance; day shows prosperity or knowledge. The shoot signifies compunction of heart; the grass, faith in works; the ear, perfection of action; the full grain in the ear, the completion of works. Through the sickle he shows the cutting off of the present life and the consummation of the age.

When the crowd of Jews had been dismissed, he went into the boat, that is, into the Church from the gentiles. Other boats were with him, that is, the various Churches of the heretics. Through the storm of the wind he shows persecutions against the faithful. The waves were striking it so that the boat might be filled: this shows the persecution of the Antichrist, or the most savage persecution, so that they would come close to denial.

Many beloved of God persevere in the faith. Christ sleeping in the stern indicates the testing of the faithful in persecution; their awakening him means that they invoke him for help in persecution. “There arose a great calm” means after the persecution of the Antichrist and after the resurrection. A man having an unclean spirit signifies the human race. Breaking chains indicates the Gentiles transgressing the law of their [Col. 0889D] nature—or the teaching of the philosophers—and likewise the Jews breaking the letter of the Law or the prophecy. “He cut himself with stones” indicates the Gentile people worshiping stones. “The man sitting, clothed and in his right mind,” indicates one clothed in faith in Jesus, faith, and charity, with a pure and sincere mind. “He had spent his substance on physicians” means that he had placed all his faith, conduct, and hope in the philosophers.

He sent them out two by two: this indicates the two Testaments, so that they might preach the same things everywhere; likewise, because charity does not consist in fewer than two. By the staff, consolation or discipline is indicated, as Paul says: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in a spirit of gentleness and consolation?” They were to wear sandals for three reasons: [Col. 0890A] because of thorns, that is, the entanglement of riches or the anxiety of the world; because of cold, that is, the desire of the mind or unbelief; and because of serpents, that is, the teaching of heretics.

“Not two tunics” means not a divided mind, nor doubt between faith and unbelief, nor a divided confidence in the New or in the Old [Testament]. Not like hypocrites who seek praise from human beings, through a supper that is not followed by a meal: the consummation of the world, when Christ came and saw its consummation, has already passed—the hour, that is, the letter of the Law. Hence he says: “The old things have passed away, and behold, new things have come to be.”

Ships in the middle of the sea mean the Church amid the turbulence of the world. Jesus alone on the sea signifies that he alone was born on earth without sexual contact. The contrary wind indicates the persecution [Col. 0890B] of the devil against the Apostles after Christ’s ascension. “He wanted to pass them by” indicates that he wished to test them. Gennesaret is interpreted as “a suitable harbor.” He went into the region of Tyre and Sidon, that is, to the Gentiles; entering a house means entering the world.

He did not want anyone to know: this indicates humility. “He could not remain hidden” means that his works are always manifest. The woman signifies the primitive Church. She comes before the feet of Jesus; the Apostles are indicated. “First let the children be satisfied” means the Jews, so that they may receive the commandments of the Law and of the Gospel. If they should judge the kingdom of God unworthily, then let the Gentiles receive it. He found the girl lying on a bed, that is, he found her in her former [state—lacuna] of her body. “Deaf and mute” indicates the human race: he was deaf because he did not hear the [Col. 0890C] commandments of God; nor could he speak, because he could not render a confession of praise and did not possess a confession of faith. “Take him outside the crowd” indicates a life removed from the world, because in withdrawal a person continually recognizes the blindness of his sins. Alternatively, “take him out of the crowd of sinners” means returning to his former conduct of good nature.

He put his fingers into the ears of his heart and opened his mouth in the confession of faith. Looking up toward heaven indicates that all should render praises to God. He groaned, that is, over the sins of the human race that prevailed in the world. Alternatively, this was done to give us an example, so that we might ask God with supplications. By the blind man he indicates the human race; those who brought him to Jesus indicate the teachers.

[Col. 0890D] He took him by the hand, that is, he gave him the power of action. He led him outside the village, indicating withdrawal into the contemplative life, or outside his former conduct. By spitting upon his eyes, the incarnation of Christ is indicated through which the human race was enlightened. By laying on his hands, he gave the assistance of action.

“I see people like trees”: here he gives an example of humility, so that no one may become exalted because of his virtues, but may consider himself lesser and lower than everyone. Again he laid his hands upon his eyes, and they were opened. This indicates that he opened the hearts of human beings so that they might clearly see the knowledge of God and believe without doubt. “He was restored,” that is, to good works.

[Col. 0891A] He sent him to his own house, that is, he recalled him to the former condition of worldly nature. Christ’s descent from the mountain indicates his descent from heaven. Here the disciples hold the order of the Prophets or Patriarchs. The crowds inquiring of them indicate the coming of Christ. What the crowds were seeking was the Law from the Prophets and Patriarchs. They greeted him; here salvation is understood on account of humility. The one who brought his son maintains the order of the Patriarchs; the son indicates the human race. By foam he indicates pride; by the gnashing of teeth, avarice; by withering, he indicates avarice. The disciples could not heal him. Here the disciples bear the figure of the Patriarchs, because neither the Prophets nor the Patriarchs could heal the human race, until Christ came and redeemed it by his [Col. 0891B] blood, as the Prophet says: “A brother does not redeem”—that is, Moses did not redeem through the Law.

The man means Christ. “From childhood” means from the first age of the human race. The father said to the child, “I believe; help my unbelief.” This indicates that he said: If faith is lacking, increase it. “He tore him violently” indicates that, when he saw the devil about to be expelled from the earth at the end of the world, power was then given to him to do whatever he wished because of God’s elect. When he saw himself being expelled from each person through confession and repentance, he then stirred up greater vices and the most savage assaults against them. He became like a dead man. Here he gives an example of a purified person, that is, one who through confession and repentance mortifies himself. Here Jesus appears to have performed two miracles: [Col. 0891C] he healed him from the demon and raised him as though from death. Thus he raised the human race from the death of sins and freed it from the slavery of the demon. The millstone indicates the circuit of the world; the ass indicates the uncleanness of sins.

To be thrown into the sea means to humble oneself in sackcloth through repentance, or to perish in one's own sin, because it is lighter to endure punishment for oneself alone than to cause others also to be driven from the kingdom of God. By worms he indicates those who repent late: the worm continually consumes that person in punishment, because, while he had time, he did not amend himself. “Everyone will be salted with fire”: by fire the kindling of the Holy Spirit is understood, because just as all flesh perishes without salt, so every person without knowledge of the word of God becomes foolish. “Have salt in yourselves” means: have the wisdom of God in yourselves. He came [Col. 0891D] into the borders of Judea, indicating that the Jews would in the future return to faith in Christ.

Beyond the Jordan means toward the grace of baptism. “Let the little children come to me”: here the little children bear the figure of the Gentiles. The disciples who were preventing them bear the figure of the Jews. Camels could not pass through the eye of a needle unless they laid down their burdens; likewise, the Jews cannot enter the kingdom of God unless they lay down the burdens of their sins, or their riches. What did Peter leave when he said, “We have left everything”? This indicates that a person leaves much when he puts himself second. “Let him go before them” means that he should precede his sheep by his example. By the cup he indicates the Passion; by baptism, the mortification or sleep of the Church. [Col. 0892A] Just as Adam sinned in three ways—he desired, transgressed, and acted proudly—so Christ was three days in the tomb. Likewise, and for this reason, a person is immersed three times beneath the water of baptism. Hence the Apostle says: “For we have been buried with Christ through baptism; indeed, we were baptized into his death.” “Whoever wishes to be first among you shall be the servant of all”: here he indicates the teachers of the Church. The blind man bears the figure of the Gentiles; he was sitting beside the road, that is, beside the faith.

He cried out to Jesus, “Have mercy on me.” In the moral sense, when we devote ourselves to prayer, the crowd of phantoms—that is, the minds of the faithful—rebukes us to be silent, wishing to exclude us from persevering prayer. Then Jesus, standing beside us—for standing belongs to divinity, while passing by belongs to humanity—[Col. 0892B] commanded them to call him, that is, through the preaching of the Apostles. He calls the Gentiles to faith. He threw off his garments, that is, his former conduct. “Leaping up” means moving from ignorance to knowledge and from unbelief to faith.

“You will find a colt tied up”: this indicates the Gentiles bound by the guilt of sins, upon which no one had sat, that is, where no teacher had preached. “Untie it and bring it to me” means: bring it to faith through preaching. He saw a fig tree, indicating that the faith of the Jews was far from Christ.

“It was not the season for figs” means that it was not yet the time for the Jews to believe, because they had judged themselves unworthy. The kingdom did not know how to transfer the vessel through the temple, which signifies the hearts of the faithful. Christ does not wish any work to be done or carried out except what is holy. [Col. 0892C] “To hand it over to the tenants” means to guard the Law. The winepress means the temple of Solomon. Alternatively, it indicates martyrdom. He came to the synagogue; the synagogue is often the guardianship of the angels. The tower means the Law. “They cast him out of the vineyard” means from the Jews to the Gentiles. Alternatively, it means from the city of Jerusalem to Mount Calvary.

The widow put in two coins, which make a quadrans; through them he understands a person who is a quadrans, one who has offered himself to God. “Whatever you ask for, believing in prayer, will be done for you.” How, then, does Saint Paul say: “Three times I asked the Lord concerning the thorn, and it did not depart from me”? The devil asked to tempt Job, and God permitted him; Paul was not heard, so that through that thorn he might be crowned. The devil was heard so that through his temptations Job might be crowned. Therefore the [Col. 0892D] Apostle says: “We do not know what we should ask for,” except for Christ, who intercedes for us.

“Nation will rise against nation” means pagans against Christians. Morally, it means flesh against soul; the kingdom of the devil against the kingdom of Christ; the vices of the flesh against the spirit of good action. An earthquake means a movement from unbelief to faith, that is, the body or soul hearing the word of God. “Those who stand on account of me as a testimony to them” means: if they believe your testimony, it will be for them unto life; if they do not believe, it will be for them unto punishment.

Concerning the day and the hour, no one knows, except the Father. This is said with respect to the part that is the body, because the body of Christ is the Church. When he says, “You do not know the time,” he means the departure of each person or the consummation of the world.

[Col. 0893A] A man went abroad, that is, Christ went from the world with his flesh into heaven. He left his house, that is, the Church, to teachers of every work, that is, of every grace and virtue. By the begetter he indicates a bishop or teacher. In the evening fire and sulfur rained down upon Sodom from heaven. At midnight Egypt was struck in its firstborn. In the morning Sodom was overthrown, and its smoke rose up to heaven. “Lest he come suddenly and find you sleeping” means in ignorance or in the security of negligence.

The alabaster flask signifies the body of Christ wounded on the cross. By the ointment the confession of faith is indicated. The head of Christ is God the Father. He sought an opportune time to hand him over; this indicates that the appropriate [Col. 0893B] time had come for the destruction of the Jews, or of Judea, and for the redemption of the Church.

On the first day of Unleavened Bread—that is, on Thursday—the unleavened bread of sincerity was made into the Church. “Passover” is spoken of in four ways: from the world to the Father; from the Jews to the Gentiles; from unbelief to faith; and from death to life.

A man carrying a pitcher of water bears the figure of the Apostles, or of their successors and of those baptized, through whom baptism is effected. The pitcher signifies the baptism of the Trinity. “To eat the Passover with his disciples” indicates that he was with his disciples among the Jews. Alternatively, he eats in his members, who are the Church. By the upper room the higher life is indicated. By the large furnished room the breadth of the Church is indicated.

The lamb sacrificed in Egypt indicates the mystery of the body and blood sacrificed in the New Testament [Col. 0893C], since the ancient Jewish sacrifice—the blood of goats and bulls—has passed away. For our sacrifice, which is called wine, was offered by Melchizedek when Abraham returned from the slaughter. Why did they question him individually? This indicates that no one should rely upon his own conscience.

Leaving the linen cloth, he fled naked from them. This indicates that the malice of the Jews had been abandoned. He fled naked, showing that the Apostles, naked of the superstitions of the Jews, went to the Gentiles. Peter was warming himself by the fire; this signifies the lukewarmness of the Apostles, his own denial, and the unbelief of the Jews.

“They will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power”: this indicates that Stephen saw him; Saul also saw him when he was thrown down on the road; and [Col. 0893D] many others saw him.

Pilate is interpreted as “mouth of the hammerer.” He who fashions but is not fashioned: likewise, persecutors fashion the souls of the righteous for the kingdom of heaven, while they themselves remained unformed by the grace of God. The Lord took the crown of thorns upon himself in order to wash away the thorns of our sins. Hence it was said to Adam: “Let thorns and thistles spring up for you.”

When Jesus says that he was [Col. 0894A] crucified at the third hour, he indicates that he was judged so that he might be crucified. At the sixth hour he was raised upon the cross. “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani”—that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” This is said with respect to the flesh: he was not forsaken according to his divinity, because there is unity of power. He forsook the flesh of the Son for a time in the Passion, so that through his own Son he might have adopted sons.

Just as a sponge was full of cavities and vinegar, so the Jews were full of superstitions and a mass of teaching. Joseph bears the figure of the primitive Church. From the Gentiles he bought a linen cloth for a price; the linen cloth indicates confession of faith. By the linen cloth he indicates the mortification of the Church, or the grace of those baptized. The body of Jesus wrapped in a new linen cloth means Christ surrounded by the Church and the restoration of regeneration.

By the tomb [Col. 0894B] and the linen cloth he indicates the altar on which the body of Christ is placed. Alternatively, it indicates the Church: those who received Christ through faith in their hearts, or who receive his body to eat and his blood to drink. The stone is Christ.

The tomb cut out in the rock indicates the Church built from the side of Christ. He rolled the stone to the entrance of the tomb: this indicates Christ hidden in the Law and the prophecy. The stone rolled away indicates the history of the Law opened in the New Testament, revealing Christ.

“He is not here” means that he is not among the Jews, but among the Gentiles. “Go, tell his disciples and Peter”: he names Peter because of his denial, so that he might not despair, and because of his primacy in the Apostolate.

Mary, from whom he had cast out seven demons. Through the seven [Col. 0894C] demons he indicates that her whole life had been defiled, because it revolves through seven days.

“Preach the Gospel to every creature” means to every human being, because a human being shares something with each other creature: with angels, understanding or discernment; with animals, sight and sensation; with trees, life. A tree lives through its greenness, and so a human being lives through youth. With stones he shares being, because there are also human beings who believe like stones.

“They will cast out demons,” either spiritually or bodily. “They will speak in new tongues,” either in diverse languages. The new tongue is the preaching of the Gospel. “They will take up serpents,” that is, the poison of serpents or the teaching of heretics. If they drink something deadly, it will not harm them; nor will the teaching of heretics harm them. They will lay hands upon the sick, whether of body or of soul.

We read of three who were taken bodily [Col. 0894D] from the world into heaven. The Lord was lifted up by his own power, because he was neither begotten through sexual intercourse nor did he beget through sexual intercourse, but was born from a virgin. Enoch was taken away because he begot through sexual intercourse. Elijah was carried off in a chariot because he was begotten through sexual intercourse, but did not beget through sexual intercourse, since he remained a virgin.

# ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE

[Col. 0893]

[Col. 0893D] Luke himself, rising up, was Syrian by nationality, from Antioch, a physician by profession, and a disciple of the Apostles. He followed Paul, serving God without blame, and never having a wife. He died at the age of eighty-three in Bithynia, full of the Holy Spirit, and was buried in Constantinople. In Achaia he wrote the Gospel in the Greek language. Matthew [Col. 0895A] wrote for faithful Jews; Mark for penitents; John for the perfect; Luke for faithful Greeks.

“There was in the days of Herod,” and so forth. Here he completed the order: he indicates the king and the region in which he was, the priest and his people, and his wife. “Of the course of Abijah,” that is, in the days of the Lord. Zacharias is interpreted as “mindful of the Lord.” The angel of the Lord appeared to him at the right side of the altar; this indicates that, because he is mindful of the Lord, the mystery of God is shown to him.

Abijah is interpreted as “father of the Lord.” It was fitting that, at the time of the service of the Father of the Lord, this man should begin who would preach the Lord as Father. Elizabeth is interpreted as “the fullness of my God.” She bears the figure of Mary, who was full of God. “And both were righteous before the Lord, not before human beings,” because formerly a barren woman was accursed [Col. 0895B] under the Law. “Walking in all the commandments” means that they observed the whole Law.

They had no child because Elizabeth was barren, and both continued in their days. Therefore these two causes are mentioned as a testimony, so that the power might be greater. Zacharias entered the temple, that is, Christ entered Mary. The people were praying. At first the people asked Zacharias for freedom from captivity. An angel appeared to him; he did not say “he has come,” because he was already there.

Zacharias was troubled, that is, because the Jews were troubled when Christ came. “Your prayer has been heard” means more than you asked. You asked for the liberation of the people, and a forerunner was given to you; and many will rejoice at his birth, because after destruction they will rejoice in eternal life. For he himself said, “Behold, the Lamb of God,” [Col. 0895C] and so forth. He precedes Christ: he is baptized first, preaches first, appears before him, and is born and dies first. There were six reasons, because six months separated them.

“I am Gabriel,” that is, “the strength of God.” Elizabeth conceived; he did not say “from Zacharias.” He knew his wife because the desire of their will had failed in them. She hid herself out of modesty, to test whether what she had conceived was true. “For five months” means five thousand years of the world, or the five books of Moses.

“Take away my reproach” means the reproach of barrenness and of conceiving in old age among human beings, because it was not a reproach before God. Just as in the sixth month Gabriel was sent by the Lord into the city, so in the sixth millennium of the world Christ was sent. Joseph is interpreted as “savior,” because he saved Egypt from [Col. 0895D] famine; or [Joseph signifies] Mary. “Blessed” means from the flesh of Christ.

She was troubled because she did not know whether what the angel said referred to the past or the future. “The Holy Spirit will come upon you”: Spirit is the name of every grace when it is breathed into someone. How did Mary know what the angel said? Either because, being full of the Spirit, she knew what the angel had said to her, or because she was already filled with the Spirit. “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” means that he hid her in Egypt when she fled.

She is called your kinswoman because Elizabeth was of the tribe of Levi, that is, of the tribe of God. “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord,” as he says, “the son of your handmaid.”

She went into the mountain in haste. Everyone who wishes to fulfill the will of God ought to hasten. The infant leaped in his mother’s womb; this means that the son honored the Son, just as the woman honored the woman. She cried out [Col. 0896A] with a loud voice. This was fitting, because it was said concerning John: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness.”

“John is his name.” Why did he not say, “He will be John”? Because he was named by the angel before he was conceived. “And they marveled”: there was agreement between the father and the mother. “Blessed is the Lord our God”: while Zacharias asked for the liberation of the people, a forerunner was given to him by the goodness of God.

“He raised up a horn of salvation,” that is, Christ, because a horn is neither flesh nor bone. Likewise, Christ is neither flesh nor flesh [uncertain]; only divinity. “The child grew,” that is, in body, and “was strengthened,” that is, in Spirit.

This first census was made, that is, for the Romans, because Julius was the first to rule the Romans, though he did not hold the whole world. After him Augustus ruled, and after Augustus, Tiberius. In the time of Augustus and Tiberius the time of Christ was completed for his [Col. 0896B] baptism. In the fifteenth year of the reign of Augustus, Augustus and his son Tiberius came together in one chariot to their own city. After they had seen the Lamb of the world, this indicated that he would be born during his reign, the one who would rule over the whole world, and that the Father and the Son were united in will.

At that same time a bronze circle appeared around the sun. This indicated that he would be born during the reign of the one whose power, beauty, light, and wisdom would encompass every power, the first beauty, light, and wisdom. At that same time a spring of oil flowed from the inn of a prostitute [uncertain] all day until evening. This indicated that he would be born in the time of the one from whom a spring of oil would flow, that is, spiritual anointing, throughout the whole Gospel until the end of the world.

Augustus represents the Father; [Col. 0896C] Tiberius, the Son. The census was taken so that the king might know the number and greatness of the people. From Persia to Syria, it indicates the place from which Christ came, so that each might prophesy in his own place. The city is indicated so that no one outside the Church might render the census to God.

He was placed in a manger, that is, the body of Christ upon the altar. The ox and the ass in Christ’s manger indicate the Gentiles and the Jews sharing upon the altar. The place in the lodging-house—that is, a house between two walls with two doors—bears the figure of the Church between paradise and the world. The army of soldiers indicates that they follow Christ the commander.

The shepherds were speaking. It was fitting that the shepherds should speak; it was fitting that the shepherds should give testimony concerning the true Lamb. “Let us go over to Bethlehem” indicates that we should look neither backward nor to the right nor to the left, but only to [Col. 0896D] Christ. They found Mary, Joseph, and the infant; through these three the world was healed.

Mary kept all these words, that is, what the angel had said to her. After the eight days had been completed, he was circumcised. In the eighth beatitude he indicates the Passion of Christ, when it is said: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution.” The circumcision of Christ on the eighth day indicates the blood of the martyrs until the day of judgment, or because he fulfilled the Law and did not abolish it.

After the days of her purification had been completed—that is, twelve days for a boy and thirty for a girl, according to the Law, so that a woman might not enter the Church—the offering was a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons. Through the wildness of the turtledove he indicates prudence, as with serpents; through the [Col. 0897A] dove, simplicity. The pair indicates that a person should offer his whole self to God. “A revelation to the Gentiles” means the glory of faith.

“Behold, he is appointed for the fall” means for those who do not believe in the resurrection. For those who believe in him he is a sign, that is, the Gospel. “I have come to separate a man against his mother,” and so forth. As he himself says: “Who is my mother?” and “Blessed is the womb that bore you,” and so forth—that is, so that many may conceive good thoughts, since Mary alone is not the mother of Christ.

“And your own soul a sword will pierce”: this means the word of God, or the Passion of Christ. She had lived with her husband for seven years, that is, the synagogue with the Heptateuch. She did not depart from the temple, that is, the Church ought not to depart from heaven.

The child grew, that is, in body, and was strengthened, that is, in Spirit. When he was [Col. 0897B] twelve years old, this means the twelve tribes that came to Christ. After three days they found him. The father, that is, the Church, and the mother, that is, the synagogue, sought him through the three Laws and did not find him except through the Gospel. “And he was subject to them” indicates that the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve.

From the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, the first king, the first governor at the birth of Christ, are mentioned, that is, while they had not yet begun to teach. But now a fourth king, the tetrarch, is mentioned, when he came to preaching and baptism. The king signifies Christ, and the four tetrarchs indicate the four Gospels. There were two priests, indicating the two Laws. Through the number six the world was made.

The first king [Col. 0897C] of the Romans indicates the unity of the Roman kingdom; the fourth tetrarch over the Jews indicates the division of the Jewish kingdom. The word of the Lord came to John: “Go and preach baptism.” The valley will be filled, that is, the Jews and the Gentiles. “Mountains and hills will be humbled,” that is, whoever humbles himself will be exalted. “The crooked places will become straight,” that is, let the lustful become chaste. “The rough places into level roads,” that is, let the proud become humble. “All flesh will see the salvation of God,” that is, Jews and Gentiles, men and women.

He came from Nazareth, where he had been raised. This indicates the Church in which he was raised, so that a person may not forget. He rose to read. Here he indicates that if something is revealed to a younger person, the elder should keep silent, that is, the Evangelist and the Pentateuch. Peter also rose and [Col. 0897D] stood in the midst of the disciples. This indicates that what is to be preached should not be withheld.

“Because he has anointed me”: this means not with common oil but with spiritual oil. “To preach the Gospel to the poor” means “Blessed are the poor in spirit.” “And release to captives” means to the Jews from Pharaoh and to the Gentiles from the devil. “Sight to the blind” means to the Jews and the Gentiles. “Release the broken” means the Jews. “Clay to be fashioned” means the Gentiles supplicating idols.

“The year of the Lord” means that, because a year has four seasons, it indicates the four Evangelists; and because it has twelve months, it indicates the twelve Apostles; “and the day of recompense” means the day of judgment. Literally: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your ears.”

There were many widows in Israel, that is, in the Church. Elijah signifies Christ. Naaman the Syrian signifies the Gentiles. [Col. 0898A] The daughter means the synagogue. Gehazi means the Church. “Having a demon” means believing in idols. “What have we to do with you?” means torments for us and glory for you.

Beside the lake means beside the Law. Two ships mean two Churches. “Put out into the deep” means Christ ascending into heaven. “We have labored all day and caught nothing” means that through the Old Law we brought no one to life. They filled both ships, because through the Church and the synagogue he converted them. They were so full that they began to sink, that is, a person who can neither bear riches nor poverty.

“Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man”: this indicates that the Lord did not depart, because he does not abandon true humility.

“Do not be afraid” means that the sinner should not fear the physician. The report about him spread increasingly, that is, concerning healing and [Col. 0898B] teaching. When he prayed, he indicated the contemplative life; when he sounded forth, he indicated the active life. Through the tiles, divinity is indicated. “Rise and walk” indicates the resurrection of all.

He went up onto the mountain to pray and then departed to the crowds. This indicates the contemplative and active life joined into one.

Four beatitudes are read because the four cardinal virtues are contained in them. “Caudes” is said in Latin for “of the heart” [text uncertain]. These four gentle things indicate the four parts of the world. Likewise, the eight refer to the eight souls who were in Noah’s ark, through whom he indicates the whole human race.

“Your reward is great in glory” means on account of preaching, persecution, and patience. “According to these things their fathers did to the Prophets” means that they hated them, reproached them, expelled them, and reviled their [Col. 0898C] names. “Woe to you who have your consolation” means that you have it and do not give thanks to God, but to your riches. “Woe to you when people bless you” means your enemies. Not despairing of what you have, give it, so that you may receive your reward from the Lord in glory.

“Can a blind man lead a blind man?” means a foolish person teaching a foolish person. Both will fall into a pit, that is, into destruction.

He was going into a city called Nain. This indicates that, after healing the sick man, he raised the dead, because sickness precedes death. The only son of his mother means Adam, carried from the earth by the four elements from which the human being is made. The place is touched by God, that is, the wood of the cross, because Adam perished through wood.

A person is carried by earth when he thinks only about earthly things, or when he is sick and cannot [Col. 0898D] walk. He is carried by water when he thinks about indulging in lust, or when his body cannot be touched because of excessive cold. He is carried by air when he does everything for human praise, or when, because of illness, he cannot breathe. He is carried by fire when he thinks about avarice, or when, because of excessive fever, he cannot be touched.

The Lord raised three dead people: the son of one mother, the daughter of the ruler, and Lazarus. The first was in a house, that is, in thought; the second at the gate, that is, in speech; the third in a tomb, that is, in action.

“Whoever is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he,” that is, Christ, because the angels were not born. Hence it says: “You made him a little lower than the angels.” Nevertheless, Christ is greater than John. When he reigns with the Father, [Col. 0899A] Wisdom was justified by her children, that is, by the people and the publicans who justified God.

The alabaster of ointment means the body together with faith. Standing behind means after the Lord’s ascension. Beside his feet means beside the Apostles. She watered them with tears, that is, with inward charity in God. The hair means superfluous food and giving clothing. She kisses his feet, that is, having peace with everyone.

One owed five hundred denarii, that is, the sins of the Gentiles committed through the five senses. Another owed fifty, that is, the sins of the Jews. This woman was Mary Magdalene, from whom seven demons had been cast out. “Who is he who forgives sins?” means divine power and strength. This Mary figures the Church, from which he cast out seven vices, because a person sinned through the seven days.

[Col. 0899B] A certain man means the people of the Gentiles. “For a long time” means from the beginning of the world. “He wore no clothing” means that he was without faith. “Nor did he remain in a house” means in the Church, but among tombs, that is, in the habit of sinning. Chains on his feet mean the law of nature and the written Law.

“Sitting” means being in faith after baptism. “Clothed” means clothed in immortality. “At his feet” means at the feet of the Apostles. He dismissed him and said, “Return to your house.” This indicates the contemplative life, not coming to the active life.

The woman means the Church. The flow of blood means the law of nature. “For twelve years” means two ages.

She touched the fringe of his garment, that is, she believed in the least commandment of Christ. “Who touched me?” means: who believed in me? “Power has gone [Col. 0899C] out from me” means that it went forth to make manifest the one who had faith.

Peter, John, and James mean faith, hope, and charity. The father means the bishop; the mother, the Church. The villages and cities mean servants and lords. They told him what they had done. The day began to decline, that is, to become night. He dismissed the crowd, the Jews.

“You give them something to eat” means: preach to the Gentiles. He blessed, that is, the Gospel. He broke, that is, literally. “The Son of Man must suffer many things” means that he must die.

Those sailing from the city [or polity; uncertain] through the danger of the voyage, who saw calm after danger, suffered many reversals [text uncertain] on the following day, that is, under the second Law.

A man from the crowd cried out, that is, Abraham. “An only son” means the whole human race. Suddenly crying out means becoming angry, and he cast him down in the flattery of a neighbor. “He tears him apart” means [Col. 0899D] in despair, with foam, that is, with foolishness.

“Putting his hand to the plow” means placing the work upon the Gospel. “Backward” means in the world. Plowshares mean charity. The four oxen mean the four Evangelists.

The Lord appointed another seventy disciples, just as Moses chose seventy elders from the twelve tribes. This indicates that the seventy languages, which had been divided through pride, should be united into one language through humility. The two animals in the ark and the two disciples sent to preach indicate charity. He shows the New and Old Testaments, body and soul, man and woman, and the two disciples.

“I am sending you like lambs among wolves.” I am the shepherd; you are the sheep. The wolves are the scribes and Pharisees. “The demons [Col. 0900A] are subject to you,” that is, something that was not in the mouth under the Law.

“Over serpents” means over pagans, because the serpent does not kill but pours out the poison of its teaching. A scorpion with tail and head equal kills; this is the devil, who wishes to deceive at the beginning and at the end.

A man was going down, that is, the world, which is called anathema, among robbers, that is, demons. They stripped him, that is, of good faith. They scourged him, that is, they made him sin. They left him half-dead, that is, with a living body but a dead conscience and soul.

The priest means Aaron. The Levite means the tribe of Levi with its Law. The Samaritan means Christ, who is from the outskirts of Samaria. “Samaritan” itself is interpreted as “guardian,” because it refers to Christ God, who guards the little ones.

He bound up his wounds, that is, through repentance he restrained [Col. 0900B] his sins. He poured in oil and wine, severity and gentleness, the reward and punishment of Scripture. He placed him on his beast, that is, in his body, because through his Passion he brought the human race to the inn, that is, to the Church.

The two denarii mean the two Laws. He gave them to the innkeeper, that is, to the order of teachers. “Whatever more you spend” means whatever you accomplish through your diligence in teaching others; “when I return,” that is, at the judgment, “I will repay you.”

Martha means the active Church.

Maria, that is, the contemplative Church, which always hears Christ’s words: Martha said that her sister should help her, because the active life ought to assist the contemplative life: “Friend,” that is, a teacher. “At midnight,” that is, at the opportune time: “three loaves,” he shows the faith of the Trinity: “My friend,” that is, another person doing penance [Col. 0900C] “from the road,” that is, from the world. “I have nothing to set before him,” that is, I do not know how to teach him: “the door being shut,” that is, the door of heaven, which is opened only by charity. “My children are with me,” that is, the heavenly virtues: “what is outside and inside,” that is, the one who made the body also made the soul: “Give alms, and everything is clean”; and if you do not give, everything you have is unclean. “Do not fear, little flock”: these are the Jews, he says, because they believed; for it was said in the Law that the one who became poor was accursed.

“Let your loins be girded”: he shows chastity. “Burning lamps,” that is, good works. “So that when he comes,” that is, in sorrow, “and knocks,” that is, when the soul is passing through death, “they may immediately open,” that is, that one should always be ready: “he will pass through and minister to them,” that is, after the judgment, eternal life [Col. 0900D]. “I have come to cast fire upon the earth,” that is, charity: “the Galileans and the eighteen” signify those upon whom the tower fell, that is, the Holy Spirit, because it is said to have been sent into the forest: “Let it alone this year,” that is, the Gospel: “I will dig around it,” that is, I will preach: “a basket of manure,” that is, confessing sins, “in the future,” that is, on the day of judgment. “The woman,” that is, the human race: “with a spirit of infirmity,” that is, in faith and works: “eighteen years,” that is, the two Laws—or those who did not fulfill the ten words of the Law and did not believe in the resurrection, since it takes place on the eighth day. Through three sixes he shows that she was infirm before the Law, under the Law, and under grace: “bent toward the earth,” that is, toward earthly desires: “to look upward,” that is, she did not seek heavenly things through repentance [Col. 0901A]. “He called her to himself,” that is, through confession, “and laid his hand upon her,” that is, good examples: “she was healed,” that is, the hope of healing. “The first day of the week,” that is, the future rest. “Tell that fox,” that is, Herod, because the devil is an animal that dwells within and destroys the vineyard; thus Herod, the devil, destroys the vineyard, as it is said: “You brought a vine out of Egypt.”

“The man with dropsy,” that is, the human race: the fornicator, when seized, was healed; he shows that the assault of fornication is thereby healed. “A certain man,” that is, God the Father: “a great dinner,” that is, the Gospel. “He invited many,” that is, the Jews: “he sent his servant,” that is, Christ in the flesh: “everything is ready,” that is, what was prophesied about Christ. “I have bought a farm,” that is, because of avarice I have not come to Christ. “Five yokes of oxen,” that is, pride [Col. 0901B]; alternatively, the five yokes of oxen are the five senses, or the five books of Moses. “I have married a wife,” that is, lust. “The poor and the weak,” that is, those who acknowledge their sins. “Go out into the roads,” that is, to the Gentiles: “compel them to enter,” that is, through confession. “To build a tower,” that is, to follow Christ. “The cost,” that is, renouncing the world. “What king,” that is, the Apostles, “when he goes to war,” that is, the recompense of works, “against another king,” that is, against Christ, “with ten thousand,” that is, with the works that a person perceives, “with twenty thousand,” that is, with the works that are hidden and in the open, “and, while he is still far away, sends an embassy,” that is, by showing mercy and giving alms, he asks for what makes for peace, as in: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord.” “On the earth,” that is, in riches: “into the dung heap,” that is, into poverty. “A certain woman” [Col. 0901C], that is, riches. “A lamp lit,” that is, the Gospel: “a drachma found in the house,” that is, a sinner converted in the Church. “A certain man,” that is, God the Father.

“Two sons,” Jews and Gentiles, because the Law was first given to the Jews. “Give me my portion,” that is, the present life. “He divided the substance,” that is, he gave freedom of choice to both peoples. “He went away into a far country,” that is, away from God. “Living luxuriously,” that is, worshiping idols. “A severe famine,” that is, a famine of the word of God. “To one of the citizens,” that is, to a philosopher. “In his own farm,” that is, in the world. “To feed pigs,” that is, he lived like pigs. “And on the pods,” that is, to fill the belly without becoming fat. “The pigs,” that is, fools. “The hired servants of my father,” that is, those who are lesser servants of God. “They will be filled with bread,” that is, with doctrine [Col. 0901D]. “I have sinned against heaven”: those who say this have the devil as father, the one who sinned in heaven. “Moved by mercy,” that is, he came in the flesh. “To his servants,” that is, to the Apostles. “The first robe,” faith, which Adam lost. “The ring,” that is, the cross on the forehead. “The sandals,” that is, the Gospel. “The fattened calf,” that is, Christ, who died according to the two Laws; that is, Adam. “He came to life again,” that is, through baptism. “He had perished,” that is, in despair. “He was found,” that is, in hope. “The elder son,” that is, the Jews. “In the field,” that is, in unclean desire. “Music and dancing,” that is, prophecy and the Gospel. “The two servants,” that is, Isaiah.

“Lazarus, a beggar”: he gives the name of the poor man, but not of the rich man; he shows that good people are written in heaven, but evil people are not [Col. 0902A]. “Full of wounds,” that is, sins: he signifies the rich Jews; the poor man signifies the Gentiles. “The dogs,” teachers who heal wounds with their tongue. “In Abraham’s bosom,” that is, in rest. “Buried in hell,” that is, in the letter. “Lifting up his eyes,” because the Jews had eyes—that is, they lived well up to the time of Christ. “He saw”: thus Abraham will be after the judgment; from hell they see the kingdom of God, so that they may have greater punishment and greater joy. “The tip of his finger in water,” that is, those who give small alms. “I am tormented in this flame,” that is, in his own punishment. “A great chasm” [perhaps *chaos magnum*], that is, the confusion of all things, or the Old Law. “You received good things in your life,” that is, you did good and received it. “Lazarus received evil things,” that is, because he received the punishment for his evils during his life. “Five brothers,” that is, they observed the five books of Moses [Col. 0902B]. “If someone should rise from the dead as a sign”: this happened when Christ rose; others among the Jews believed. “If a millstone,” that is, if the Gentiles . . . like a horse that turns a mill and does not see whom it serves; or he teaches philosophers a philosophy that profits them nothing but the holy Church. “Increase our faith,” that is, while you increase the commandment.

“To this mulberry tree,” that is, the Gospel, which proclaims the red cross of Christ; just as the mulberry is red: “to uproot it,” that is, from the Jewish people, “and transplant it into the Gentile people.” The mulberry tree’s fruit is first white, then red, and afterward black. So too the devil, while he was a white angel, became black in Adam’s killing, and red in the murder of Cain and Abel. “Two women grinding,” he shows two Churches, or two Testaments. The judge and the widow are from the half-filled vessels, and he will have patience with them, but they will not always remain silent [Col. 0902C]. “Two went up”: one magnified his holiness and lost it; the other magnified his sins, and they perished. “I fast twice on the Sabbath,” that is, without food and without a woman. “What must I do to have eternal life?” That is, as was said above, the kingdom of God belongs to such people. Nicodemus was thinking similarly: “How can a person be born again?” “You shall not kill,” and the rest. Why did he say these things? Because he fell in this very matter. “When he drew near Jericho,” that is, when he came to the incarnation.

“A man named Zacchaeus,” that is, he was a Jew and signifies the Jews. His name is interpreted as “justified,” just as the Jews justify themselves. “Because of the crowd,” that is, of riches and vices. “In a tree,” that is, the cross. “Of half my goods,” that is, of my substance, “I give to the poor,” that is, “break your bread for the hungry” [Col. 0902D]. “And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold”: this is said in the Law concerning souls, and in the Gospel concerning every creature. “A nobleman,” that is, Christ, “went away to a distant country,” that is, to heaven, “to receive a kingdom for himself,” that is, the heavenly kingdom, “and to return for judgment.” “Ten servants,” that is, the whole human race. “Ten minas,” the ten words of the Law. “His citizens,” that is, the Jews.
