“They sent an embassy,” that is, the killing of the Apostles. “The first servant and the second,” the order of the Apostles. “The mina of each servant,” that is, Scripture. “He found each like himself,” that is, he found both alike. “The stone cried out”: these are the Gentiles; the Jews were silent. “He wept over it”: he shows that we ought to weep for our sins. “They will surround you,” that is, the Romans surrounded it on every side [Col. 0903A], inside and out. “The other,” that is, into hell. “Children,” that is, virtues; what he did by day, he fell into at night. “Entering the temple,” that is, because he entered the temple on the Lord’s Day. “They sought to destroy him”: he shows the nine servants who were not rejected from their ministries. “A certain man,” that is, God the Father, “planted a vineyard,” that is, the Jews. “Tenant farmers,” that is, legislators. “He himself went away,” that is, he left them all in the freedom of their own choice. “The first servant,” that is, Isaiah. “The second,” that is, Jeremiah. “The third,” that is, Daniel. “Outside the vineyard,” that is, outside Jerusalem. “What will the lord of the vineyard do?” “He came and destroyed them,” that is, the evil man will be crushed by evil; he will crush his desires by the cross. “He crushed him,” that is, in the vengeance of the cross. “Nation against nation,” that is, nation against the Romans. “Kingdom against kingdom,” that is, some against the Romans [Col. 0903B]. “Terrors,” that is, chariots were heard in the air. “There will be signs,” as happened previously over Jerusalem. “The star with a fiery sword,” these things occur in testimony, that is, from the Jews to the Gentiles. “Therefore I give you a mouth and wisdom”: in Moses it is said, “God has shown you wisdom.”

“Not a hair from your head will perish,” that is, through mortality. “Jerusalem will be trampled,” that is, idols will be worshiped in it, “until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled,” that is, until the Jews are converted at the end of the world. “Signs in the sun,” literally. “The sound of the sea,” that is, the Sodomite sea came into being. “It casts its fish upon the earth.” “Coming in the clouds of heaven,” that is, in the prophets and Apostles. “The fig tree and the other trees,” that is, the synagogue and human beings. “By day teaching in the temple,” that is, he labored with the Jews. “By night, on the Mount of Olives,” that is, he rested with the Gentiles [Col. 0903C].

“A man carrying a water jar,” that is, Moses and John the Baptist. “The house with an upper room,” that is, the Church. “A bed,” that is, the faith of the Trinity. “Until the kingdom of God is fulfilled,” that is, the great ministry. “Two cups, one with water and the other with wine,” that is, with a mixture of water and wine in the cup; one wine with water shows the passion through baptism. “Did anything fail you,” when he was with them in the flesh? That is, he commanded them not to care for the world; but when he separated himself from them, they were to have one faith. “Let him buy a sword,” that is, the Law. “Two swords,” that is, the two Laws.

“The Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power,” as the Lord said, “The Lord said to my Lord,” and the rest [Col. 0903D]. “In a white garment he sent him back to Pilate” [Col. 0904A], that is, in the faith of the Trinity. He came to the Gentiles, to the people of Israel. “They became friends,” that is, both peoples came to the faith of Christ. Herod signifies the people of the Gentiles; Pilate, the Jews. Leviathan—*densi seduna* [uncertain]—Barrabas is called the son of the devil. “Weep over yourselves,” that is, over your nation. “Then they will begin to say,” that is, the people of Israel. “Say to the mountains,” that is, to the Patriarchs; “to the hills,” that is, to the Prophets. “Forgive them,” that is, let them drink the blood they poured out, so that they may become vessels of mercy, though they are vessels of wrath. “They do not know what they are doing”; and if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty, because they did it through ignorance. “Today you will be with me in paradise,” that is, whoever follows Christ has no darkness but the light of life.

“Joseph,” that is, the people of Israel. “Aromatics and ointments,” that is, faith, hope, and charity. “The first day of the week,” that is, the Gospel, which shines through the night of the Old Testament [Col. 0904B]. The women first saw the resurrection. It was fitting that salvation should first run through those through whom death had first run. “And behold, two men stood”: in Matthew, first an angel; in Mark, a young man; in John, two angels; in Luke, two men are mentioned. This means either that the women made many journeys and the visions were different, or that there was one event and one vision, while the Evangelists’ accounts differ.

“The linen cloths lying alone” show that bodies do not need clothing after the resurrection, just as he marvels at what leaves the garments behind. “Two of them were going,” he shows the Gentiles, because he appeared both to those who were outside and to those who were inside. “The village,” that is, the world.

[Col. 0904C] “Jerusalem,” that is, heavenly. “A stadium,” that is, an eighth of a mile. “Sixty stadia” shows the number of days in which the world was made. The name of the village was Emmaus, and he pretended that he was going farther away: that is, to the Gentiles. “They recognized him in the breaking of the bread,” but they did not recognize him when they heard him preaching. “He vanished from their eyes”: he shows that we cannot delay in contemplation, and that he was farther away from them when they did not recognize him, because we can remain longer in the active life. “When he opened the Scriptures to us.” “Peace be with you”: now he gathers them into one peace. Why did he not rise and ascend in one place? Because honor descended from Jerusalem to the Gentiles. Here the Lord fulfilled what he himself said: “Pray for those who persecute you.” He dismissed them [Col. 0904D].

# IN THE GOSPEL OF JOHN

[Col. 0903]

[Col. 0903D] “In the beginning was the Word,” that is, because all things begin and end in him. “The Word of the Father, the Son, was with God,” because the Son is always with the Father. “The Word was God,” that is, the Son was God. “He was in the beginning with God.” “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made”: these are the idols. “What was made”: in him was life; that is, all things live in him before they come into being. “The life was the light of men”: Christ is both light and life. “The light shines in the darkness,” that is, among the Jewish people through the Law and the Prophets. The Jews did not recognize him [Col. 0904D]. “There was the true light which enlightens every person,” and the rest. The true light enlightens by being born, being nourished, and living, and through the grace of baptism by the Holy Spirit. It enlightens knowledge. “He came into the world”; the world did not recognize him, that is, the Jewish people. “A part belonging elsewhere”: some part recognized him. “He came to his own,” that is, to his own people according to the flesh. “His own did not receive him.” “But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God,” through faith. They were born from him through the renewal of baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0905A] “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” that is, through the assumption of flesh. “We saw his glory,” that is, through his transfiguration and resurrection. “He came after me”: he shows birth according to the flesh. “He was made before me,” that is, all things were made through him. And because he existed before me, “from his fullness we have all received”: by being born, being nourished, and living, “grace upon grace.” The grace of the Old Testament and of the New Testament. Again, through faith and charity; through the letter of the Law or prophecy. Three modes: through the grace of baptism, the eternal grace of the Son who is in the bosom of the Father, that is, in his heart or in secret. He confessed that John was not the Christ.

“He did not deny” that he was Christ’s forerunner. Alternatively, he shows the New Testament. “And I did not know him” [Col. 0905B]: John shows that he did not know through baptism that the world had been redeemed by Christ, although he knew that he was the Son of God and had been born in the flesh.

“Rabbi, where do you dwell?” That is, in what teaching? “Where do you stay?” or, “teach.” “Come, learn my teaching,” since he wishes everyone to come to him. “They stayed with him that day”: they show the New Testament, or the present life. “The tenth hour” signifies the evening of the world. “On the following day he wished to go out into Galilee,” that is, after his resurrection, to the Gentiles. “Under the fig tree,” that is, under the letter of the Law or the synagogue. “The heavens opened,” that is, to the human race. “Angels ascending and descending,” that is, in the ministry of Christ. “On the third day there was a wedding,” that is, the third Law; the wedding is understood as the joining of the Church with Christ. “Mary, the mother of Jesus, at the wedding” [Col. 0905C] shows the synagogue. “Jesus and his disciples,” a figure of the Church. “When the wine failed,” that is, the failure of the letter of the Law.

“My hour has not yet come,” that is, the time of Christ’s passion has not yet come. “Six water jars,” the six ages. “Into wine,” Christ. The master of the feast—John shows that John drank the passion before Christ. “The water made wine” shows renewal and the Old Testament changed into the New. Alternatively, through the water, John’s baptism; through the wine, Christ’s passion. Again, through the wine, Christ’s blood, as he himself says: his blood is true drink. “To preserve the good wine” shows the mystery. The mysteries of the Old Testament are shown by the oxen: the teachers who sell sacred gifts. By the sheep he shows simple people [Col. 0905D]. “A whip of cords,” that is, vengeance for various sins, by which they are driven out of the Church. Jesus did not entrust himself to them, that is, for the sake of the flesh. Nicodemus came to him by night; through the night he shows the letter of the Law, or the ignorance of the heart, so that it might be enlightened by the light of the knowledge of God. “We know that you have come from God”: he shows those who received Christ through faith. Flesh is born from flesh and blood, so that it may live bodily in the world; the soul is born again ineffably through the Holy Spirit, so that it may live forever.

“The Spirit blows where he wills,” that is, he enlightens whom he wills, as the Apostle says: “Whoever clings to Christ is one spirit.” “You hear my voice”: they show the enlightenment of the ear of the heart [Col. 0906A], whence the Prophet says: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me.” “What we know we speak; what we have seen we testify.” “What we say, we know”: he shows this through the modes of speech—either the whole Trinity, or Christ together with the Apostles and Prophets. “We testify,” that is, we give testimony. “You do not accept our testimony,” that is, you do not believe our preaching. Christ descended from heaven by assuming flesh.

“No one has ascended into heaven except Christ,” together with the tree, that is, the Church. “As the serpent was lifted up in the desert,” so Christ was lifted up on the Lebanon of the cross. Just as those who were struck by serpents were delivered by looking at the bronze serpent, so a person struck by the devil will be delivered by believing in Christ’s passion. He came into the land [Col. 0906B] of Judea, the land of confession. “In Aenon,” that is, the name of the place where they sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons, from which it received the name Gehenna, “near Salim,” which is interpreted as “of peace.” They called it Jebus, from which they received the name Jebusites. “For John was not yet in prison”: he shows that the consummation of the letter of the Law had not yet occurred. “He must increase, but I must decrease.” The one who was thought to be a prophet was found to be Christ, and the one who was thought to be Christ was found to be a prophet. “What I have seen and heard,” according to divinity: “this he testifies.” According to divinity, no one accepted his testimony. Here the whole is placed for the part. Likewise, “Believe, because God is truthful.”

“He had to pass through Samaria”: he shows that just as he preached to the Jews, so he would preach to the Gentiles. “A farm” [Col. 0906C], that is, a field. “A spring for flowing, a well for drinking.” “Jesus, wearied from the journey”: he shows that through the incarnation he came upon the history of the letter of the Law. Through the sixth hour is understood the faith of the Samaritans, who were fervent. “The woman,” that is, the synagogue. “To draw water,” that is, to learn the history of the letter of the Law. “Jesus asked to drink,” that is, he asked for the woman’s faith. “The well was deep,” that is, the depth of the Law’s mystery. “A spring of water welling up to eternal life,” that is, the preaching of the Gospel bubbling forth from the mouths of the Apostles or of believers. “Five husbands”: he shows the five books of Moses. “And this one whom you have is your husband”: he shows the book of Joshua. “She left her water jar,” that is, her former way of life. “She went into the city”: he shows the primitive Church, as though going to the Gentiles or to the people. “Lift up your eyes,” that is, the eyes of faith. “The fields are white,” that is, the hearts of the faithful [Col. 0906D]. “Those who sowed,” that is, the Prophets; “those who reap,” that is, the Apostles. “He stayed with them two days,” that is, after the two Testaments had been handed down to the Jews. “He went into Galilee,” that is, to the Gentiles. Alternatively, those who died bodily will hear his voice in the future and be raised. “As the Father has life in himself, so also the Son”: what is said to have been given to the Son is said with respect to the flesh. “Those who have done good will rise to the resurrection of life”: that is, whoever judges himself will rise. Alternatively, those who died in sins live through conversion of faith to life; they rise to judgment, those who did evil here. When he says, “I do nothing of myself,” he shows that this is with respect to the body. “As I hear, I judge.” “My judgment is just.” “I do not seek my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me”: here he placed his will in the members [Col. 0907A].

“If I bear witness about myself, my witness is not true”; as Solomon says, “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth.” “Nor do they ever hear his voice”: he shows the unbelievers who did not receive his preaching. “He went up the mountain with his disciples,” that is, attempting to ascend to a higher life. He tested Philip, that is, to prove, not to destroy him. “Five loaves,” the five books of Moses. “By the roughness,” the harshness of the letter of the Law is understood. “Much grass,” he shows the perfection of the people. “So that nothing may perish of what remains,” that is, do not send doctrine where it does not build up. “He went up alone into the mountain,” that is, to the Father. “The disciples went down to the sea,” that is, to the Gentiles [Col. 0907B]. “They went up into the boat,” that is, into the Church. “Darkness came,” that is, as the world grew toward evening, or the onset of persecution after Christ’s ascension. “Rowing,” that is, taking refuge in Christ.

“Jesus walking on the sea,” that is, trampling the vices of the world. “The crowds going up into the boat and seeking Jesus”: he shows that all seek Christ through their own labor. “The hand” is called *manu* among the Hebrews, from which it received the name *manna* among the Latins; that is, living bread, or the body of Christ transfigured in mystery. A person is raised in three ways: from unbelief to faith, from sin to repentance, and bodily on the last day, to the resurrection. “I live because of the Father”: they show this according to divinity. “The Feast of Tabernacles,” that is, the construction of tents. “You go up to the feast; I am not going up” [Col. 0907C]. “You, for whom the world rejoices; I will not go up, because I am not of the world.” “In the middle of the feast.”

“Jesus went up to Jerusalem,” with the zeal of the Jews burning most fiercely. “My teaching is not mine”; and, “If it is mine, how is it not mine?” It is mine insofar as it proceeds from my mouth to them; it is not mine insofar as what I heard from the Father, these things I speak to you. Alternatively, according to the flesh it is mine, but according to divinity it is not mine. “I performed one work, and you all marvel”: I made the whole human being sound on the Sabbath; that is, the whole human race in the New Testament. “Do not judge according to appearances,” that is, do not accept the person of a human being. “You do not know where I am from,” that is, according to the flesh.

“Yet a little while I am with you”: he shows that this lasts until the passion [Col. 0907D]. “You will seek me and will not find me,” that is, bodily; “and where I am, you cannot come,” that is, because of unbelief, unless through faith. “On the last day of the feast,” that is, when the feast of the Jews had been completed. “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink,” that is, let whoever thirsts for the word of God come and drink the teaching of the Gospel. “Rivers from the belly,” that is, doctrine from the heart. “Living waters will flow,” that is, the preaching of the Gospel, which gives perpetual life. “For Jesus had not yet been glorified”: he shows the glorification of the passion and resurrection. “They returned, each to his own house,” that is, to his own wickedness.

“A woman caught in adultery”: he shows the synagogue, which committed adultery against the Law of Moses by following ancestral traditions [Col. 0908A]; or the Church from the Gentiles, which, leaving God, fornicated with demons. “They brought her into the midst”: he shows the Jews, because they are accusers of Christ’s Church. “Moses commanded us to stone her; what do you say?” They tested him for two reasons: if he had said, “Stone her,” they would have said to him, “He does not do what he teaches; refer the case to us.” If he had said that she should not be stoned, they would have said, “He is an opponent of the Law.” “Jesus bent down,” that is, from the seats of the Father into the world, to redeem the sins of the human race. “He wrote with his finger on the earth”: he showed their sins. He raised himself up in order to raise those who were walking in sins. “Again he bent down and wrote on the earth”: he showed that the woman’s sins had been forgiven. “Jesus alone remained with the woman in the house,” that is, with the Church in the world. “Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness”: he shows that this concerns not only the steps of the feet but also the affection of the heart. “Not in darkness,” that is, of ignorance, nor in the darkness of sins, “but he will have the light of life,” that is, the light of knowledge and everlasting light. “I have many things to say and judge concerning you”: he shows that if they believe, he will teach them many things; and if they do not believe, he will say many things for your excuse.

“He was a murderer from the beginning,” because he killed himself through pride. Alternatively, he killed the first human being, whom God had created immortal, making him mortal; and through his suggestion Abel was killed. “Who among you will convict me of sin?” “Whoever is from God hears God’s words,” that is, whoever understands and does them. “You are a Samaritan and have a demon”: here he silently agreed to what was neither true nor possessed, and to what was true [Col. 0908C]. “I do not seek my own glory”; there is one who seeks and judges: God the Father. I do not seek it as hypocrites do, who judge unjustly. “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and rejoiced,” that is, he saw faith in the spirit and saw him in the person of angels. He saw three as one and greeted him as one when he said, “Turn aside, my lords, to the house of your servant, if I have found favor in your sight.” “Amen, amen, I say to you”: *amen* is doubled in meaning, “truly” or “faithfully,” announcing the New and Old Testaments. “Before Abraham was, I am”: this passage concerns divinity. “They took up stones to throw at him,” that is, because they had hearts of stone. “Jesus hid himself”: he showed himself hidden from their hearts. “He went out of the temple,” that is, from the Jewish people. “Jesus passed through the midst of them,” that is, he went to the Gentiles [Col. 0908D].

“He saw a man blind from birth”: the blind man signifies the human race. “Neither did this man sin nor his parents”: understand what he said, “neither did he sin.” Adam, the first man created to see, had his eyes closed to evil when he transgressed God’s commandment; he kept his eyes open to evil and closed to good. What, then, are the parents, except the human race? Or do they signify the instigators of vices, or vices themselves? “I must work,” that is, preach, “while it is day,” that is, while I am in the world. “Night is coming,” that is, the persecution of the Apostles or the persecution of Antichrist. “Night, when no one can work,” that is, after each person’s departure [Col. 0909A]. “He spat on the earth,” that is, the incarnation of Christ.

“He made clay and anointed my eyes”: he shows that just as he first formed the human being from the clay of the earth, so through that same kind of clay he reformed the human race. “Go and wash in the pool of Siloam,” demonstrating baptism. “The parents” are understood as the devil or vices. They said, “He is of age; let him speak for himself”: the man did not wish to confess Christ. “We do not know where he is from”: he shows that they did not know his divinity. “For judgment I came into this world”: he shows that whoever hears the word and receives it receives judgment for condemnation. “So that those who do not see may see”: he shows the Gentiles, who did not receive the Law. “And those who see may become blind,” that is, the Jews, who saw through the Law but became blind because they did not believe in Christ [Col. 0909B].

“Those who do not enter through the door”: he shows bishops who enter through rewards, not through the calling of God or of the people. “They are shepherds of the sheep,” those who labor for the profit of souls, not from worldly ambition. “To him the doorkeeper opens”: the first doorkeeper was John, the forerunner of Christ. The divine Scriptures call and name them; that is, the Lord knows who are his. “He leads them out” into doctrine or into the kingdom. “He goes before them,” that is, he first did the example that he taught. He precedes them into the kingdoms of heaven; likewise, all good teachers precede by their examples.

“They hear my voice,” that is, the doctrine. “They follow a stranger,” that is, the faith and doctrine of heretics. “All who came were thieves and robbers,” that is, false prophets [Col. 0909C], who existed and will exist in the time of Antichrist. “Through me, if anyone enters, he will be saved”: that is, whoever is saved through Christ’s doctrine will enter the Church through repentance and will go out from the present age into the kingdom of God. Alternatively, “go out” means going forth to fight against heretics. “The thief comes only to kill and destroy”: these are the orders of priests who enter for the sake of disgraceful profit, not for the profit of souls. “I came so that you may have life,” that is, my doctrine, “and have it more abundantly,” that is, eternal life. “The hired servant” is one who teaches for earthly profit. “He saw the wolf and fled,” that is, the devil or a heretic. “I have other sheep that are not of this fold”: he shows the Gentiles. “There will be one flock and one shepherd,” that is, the Church and Christ. Here is the cornerstone between the intervening wall, which makes both into one [Col. 0909D].

“I have power to lay down my life and to take it up again”: he shows this with respect to the flesh. “The Father who gave me is greater than all”: he shows that Christ, or the Spirit of God, is greater than all the works of the world. “I said, You are gods”: this is said in three ways: essentially, of the one who always exists, that is, God; by designation, “you are gods”; falsely, gods are said to be demons or idols.

“He went away across the Jordan,” that is, to the Gentiles, where John first remained baptizing. He shows the Church. Lazarus figures the Jews, because the Jews were weak in the faith of Christ. Martha and Mary show the teaching of good Jews. “This sickness is not unto death”: he shows that those who are dead to human beings live to God [Col. 0910A]. “He remained there two days,” that is, the two Testaments. “Let us go again into Judea”: faith will return to the Jews through Elijah and Enoch at the end of the world. “There are twelve hours in the day”: the day is Christ. The twelve hours are the twelve Apostles. “If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble”: in the day, that is, in the teaching of Christ or of the Apostles, he does not stumble into sin, because he sees the light of this world, that is, he sees Christ through knowledge.

“If anyone walks in the night, he stumbles”: by night is understood the darkness of sins or the ignorance of the heart. “He was not there”: he shows that he knew the presence of the flesh to be dead, because he knows all things. The first was raised in the house of the ruler of the synagogue, the second, the son of the widow, at the city gate, and the third, Lazarus, from the tomb: in the house, that is, in the heart; at the gate, that is, in the mouth; in the tomb [Col. 0910B], that is, in the work. Through these same things a person dies and through these same things is raised again.

“When Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went to meet him.” Here Martha signifies the Church, which met Christ through faith. “Mary sat at home,” showing the contemplative life. “Whoever believes in me, even though he has died, will live,” whether bodily or in sins through repentance. “Everyone who lives and believes in me will never die forever”: whoever here lives in good works lives in Christ.

“Jesus wept”: he shows that, as true God and true man, he is an example of compassion. “With his hands and feet bound”: he shows the bonds of sins. “His face bound with a cloth,” that is, the veil over the hearts of the Jews. “Release him,” that is, through the preaching [Col. 0910C] of faith. The greater the signs the Jews saw, the more they were blinded. “They took away the place and the nation”: the place, Jerusalem, is possessed by the Romans; and the Gentiles are those who are scattered throughout the regions. The ruler said the reason: “It is better for one man to die than for the whole nation to perish,” because he had the ministry of God before him and spoke this through the Spirit of God, so that the Son of God might gather into one those who were divided throughout the whole world. “Martha served”: he shows the active life.

“Lazarus reclining with Jesus” signifies the Church. “Mary took a pound of ointment”: so did the whole world, which means the hearts of the faithful. Through the ointment, the fragrance of confession. Mary signifies the Church. “She anointed Jesus’ feet,” that is, through the confession of repentance. “The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” [Col. 0910D]: so too the whole world was filled with the passion and resurrection of Christ.

“When the crowd heard that Jesus had come, they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet Jesus.” He shows that three, according to the second coming, are snatched into the air with the Lord. “He found a donkey”: through the donkey he shows the people of the Gentiles. “He sat upon it,” that is, through the confession of faith. “Do not fear your destruction, because your Savior has come.” “Daughter of Zion” shows the gathering of the faithful from Jews and Gentiles. “The whole world went after him,” because through his passion and resurrection he redeemed the whole world from sin, and it followed him. “They approached Philip and asked him to see Jesus”: he shows [Col. 0911A] the Gentiles converted to faith through the preaching of the Apostles. “A grain of wheat” bears the figure of Christ: if it dies, it produces many grains. So Christ also . . . multiplied his Church.

I will glorify and will glorify again—that is, glorify him in the resurrection of Lazarus, and glorify him again in his own resurrection. “The ruler of this world is cast out,” that is, with the devil expelled from his power over the world through the passion of the cross. “Walk while you have the light,” that is, while you have Christ with you bodily and spiritually, lest the darkness overtake you—that is, the darkness of ignorance and the persecutions of sins. “He hid himself from them,” that is, bodily or spiritually. “Lord, who has believed our report?” “Who” is used either because of the rarity or the difficulty of hearing; faith is what we heard through the Holy Spirit. The arm of the Lord is the Son of God, who has been revealed—that is, one portion has been revealed from the Jews, another from the Gentiles. “He who believes in me” does so not only according to his humanity but according to his divinity; otherwise, not only in me but also in the Father, because I am in the Father and the Father is in me. “He who sees me sees him who sent me”—as if he had said plainly: he who has seen me to be truly human and believes me to be truly God sees the Father also according to divinity.

“I did not come to judge, but to save the world”: he shows that through the pouring out of blood he would redeem the world. “I loved you,” because he was in the world and loved them to the end. He gave an example so that all might remain in the truth of God to the end. “When supper had been served”: he shows the passion of Christ. Just as a meal is not served after supper, so, after Christ had suffered once, he does not show himself as going to suffer again. “Rising from supper”: he signifies our passion, resurrection, or ascension. “He lays aside his garments”: he shows that his garments were to be removed at the cross.

## THE SUMMARY BEGINS.

“He took a linen cloth and girded himself with the linen cloth,” that is, his mortification. “He poured water into a basin”: he shows the grace of baptism. “He began to wash the feet of his disciples and to wipe them with the linen cloth”: by the washing of the feet, the baptism of the apostles is understood; by the wiping with the linen cloth, he shows the wiping away of sins through Christ’s passion. “You shall never wash my feet”: terrified with fear, he said this. “If I do not wash you, you will have no part with me”: he shows that whoever has not been washed through baptism and through the confession of repentance will have no part with the Lord. “He took his garments”: it is shown again that at the end of the world he will return to the Jews. “A servant is not greater than his master, nor is an apostle greater than the one who sent him”—that is, if I suffer, you also suffer. Alternatively: if I humble myself even to your feet, so you also humble yourselves before everyone. “He will lift up his heel against me”: the heel is the extremity of the limb.

“And through the morsel Satan entered into him”—that is, as the Apostle says, whoever receives the body and blood of the Lord unworthily eats and drinks judgment. “I give you a new commandment, that you should love one another.” In the Old Law it is said, “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy”; the Lord says, “Love your enemies.” This is the new commandment. “Let not your heart be troubled”: here he preaches to the apostles about his passion. “Believe in God, and believe in me,” because I am the Son of God.

“Believe in the house of my Father”—that is, in the Church. “There are many dwelling places”—that is, just as in one person the understanding is divided, so in the Church, which is the body of Christ, there are many graces. “I go to prepare a place for you”—that is, I will prepare life for you. As the Apostle says, we have an advocate with the Father who intercedes for us. “I am the way, and the truth, and the life”: Christ is the way without error, the truth without falsehood, and himself the life without death.

[Col. 0912B] “From now on you know him and have seen him”—that is, they knew him with the eyes of the body, and they knew him with the eyes of the heart according to his divinity, through the illumination of the Holy Spirit. “He will do greater works than these,” because Christ healed the woman through his fringe, while the apostles will heal the sick through their shadow.

## The Passion Ends.

“I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete”: the Spirit received twice signifies love of God and of neighbor. “The Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive”—that is, whoever loves the world does not receive him. “I will not leave you orphans”—that is, I will not leave you according to my divinity. “On that day you will know”—that is, in the future, or in the resurrection of Christ. “I am in the Father”—that is, according to divinity; “you are in me,” because you are my members; “and I am in you”—that is, in the love of your hearts. “I will manifest myself to him”—that is, to those who believe in his divinity we will make our dwelling with him, as he himself says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I also,” and so forth. “I give you my peace”—that is, just as I patiently endure all things, so you have patience. “I leave you my peace”—that is, just as I have suffered, so you also will suffer. “Not as the world gives do I give to you”: the world gives interrupted peace; God gives eternal peace. “The ruler of the world is coming to me, and he finds nothing in me”—that is, the devil came to the cross and found no sin in the Lord; he sought to seize him and was himself seized by him. “As my Father commanded me, so I do”: the Father sent him to pour out his blood for the human race, and so he did. “I am the true vine,” from which blood and water flow; “and my Father is the farmer”—that is, the cultivator of the Church. “You are the branches”—that is, the apostles or the faithful of the Church. Just as a branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains on the vine, so no one bears fruit unless he remains in Christ.

“In this my Father has been glorified, that you should bear fruit first”—that is, just as I have borne fruit through preaching and through suffering, so do you. “As the Father loved me, so I loved you”—that is, just as the Father sent me to preach and to suffer, so I send you. “No one has greater love,” and so forth: love is stronger than death. I suffer for you out of love, and you also suffer for the Church. “All that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you”—that is, the commandments of the Gospel. “I chose you out of the world”—that is, out of worldly actions. “You are not of the world”—that is, because you do not love the world. As Solomon says, “Such is the adulterous woman: when she has eaten, she wipes her mouth and says, ‘I have done no wrong.’” This represents the Church from the Gentiles, which through confession cleansed itself of the uncleanness of sins. “From the beginning these have been with me”—that is, from the beginning of preaching.

“If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you. When the Paraclete comes, he will convict the world concerning sin”—that is, because it does not believe in me, so that it may believe through the preaching of the Gospel; “concerning judgment,” because the ruler of the world has been judged. He convicts concerning sin so that through your preaching they may be converted to repentance; concerning righteousness, so that just as one loves his neighbor, he may also love God with his whole heart; concerning judgment, so that whatever people wish others to do to them, they also may do to them—for this is the Law and the Prophets.

“A little while and you will not see me”—that is, while I lay in the tomb; “and again a little while and you will see me”—that is, through the resurrection. “The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will openly declare the Father to you”—that is, through the resurrection. “On that day you will ask in my name”—that is, because I ascend to the Father by rising again, with authority. “The Father loves you because you love me.” “I leave the world and go to the Father”—that is, in the bodily presence; for according to divinity he does not leave the world. “You have tribulation”—that is, tribulation from worldly people. “I have overcome the world”—that is, I have bound the strong one in the world, who is the devil.

“Father, the hour has come: glorify your Son”—that is, through the resurrection; “that the Son may glorify you”—that is, through the Son may they be converted and believe. “I glorified you upon the earth”—that is, I made you known to everyone. “I manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world”: he shows that according to divinity he was with the Father, while bodily he was on earth. “Those whom you gave me were yours”: in foreknowledge they were yours from the beginning. “You gave them to me”—that is, for teaching. “And they kept your word”—that is, they remained in faith. “I pray for them, not for the world,” because God knows who are his. “All that is yours is mine, and mine is yours. And I have been glorified in them”—that is, I have been manifested in these same Gentiles, because they believed in me. “I am in the world bodily, and I am not in the world bodily.” “And for their sake I sanctify myself”—that is, through martyrdom and resurrection. “The glory which you gave me I have given them”—that is, the divine commandments. “He went out with his disciples across the torrent Cedron”: he shows the violence of persecution.

“Again Jesus passed over with his disciples”—that is, from the world to the Father, and from the Jews to the Gentiles. “They came with lanterns and torches”—that is, they themselves kindled for themselves a punitive light. “They led him to Annas”: Annas is interpreted as “the grace of God”; he had received the dignity of the priesthood by the grace of God. But she appeared as the doorkeeper who introduced Peter into the courtyard; she signifies the primitive Church. He reproached him because he had said that he was the Son of God: “He did not regard it as robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself and took the form of a servant.”

“Jesus bearing his own cross”: he gave the example, as he himself said: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself,” and so forth. Two thieves were crucified with Jesus: the one who remained in his unbelief signifies the Jews; the one who confessed signifies the Gentiles. “It was written in the title, ‘King of the Jews’”—that is, king of those who confess. They made four portions of Jesus’ garments: the four soldiers signify the four Evangelists. The divided garments signify preaching, incarnation, passion, and resurrection, which they preached in the four parts of the world. But the seamless tunic, woven from above, shows that divinity in the Father and the Son is inseparable. “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for whose it shall be”: he shows that Catholic men do not tear apart the unity of divinity.

“Woman, behold your son”; “Disciple, behold your mother”: here he entrusted the Virgin so that he might preserve her undefiled. They did not break Jesus’ legs—that is, what had previously been represented by the lamb in Egypt: “You shall not eat it raw or boiled in water, but roasted with fire.” It shows Christ’s passion. The staff in the hand shows Christ’s cross, from the world to the Father. “You shall not break any of it”: he shows that Christ’s cross was not to be broken. They pierced his side with a lance, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled: “They will look upon him whom they pierced.”

“Blood and water came out”: just as Eve was taken from Adam’s side, so redemption for the Church came out of Christ’s side—remission through the blood, baptism through the water. Two disciples were running, Peter and John: he shows two peoples running, the Jews through the letter of the Law, and the Gentiles through the law of nature.

John ran ahead more quickly; he saw the linen cloths lying there but did not enter. The Jews, through the Law and the Prophets, saw that Christ was to come, but they did not receive his coming. Peter came, following him; he saw the linen cloths and entered. He signifies the Gentiles, who believed in Christ’s coming or in his teaching. Through the linen cloths the incarnation of Christ is understood; through the napkin the mystery of divinity is understood. The napkin was not with the linen cloths but wrapped separately in one place. He shows that divinity is far removed from human senses, in one place—that is, in the universal Church. Then the other disciple, who had first come to the tomb, also entered: he signifies the Jews returning to the faith at the end of the world. The angels sitting at the head and at the feet signify the beginning and the end.

Mary said, “I do not know where they have laid him”: she shows that according to the flesh she loved the world, and through faith believed. What Mary said shows the thought expressed in the words, because through love of neighbor a person knows God. Jesus said, “Do not touch me”—that is, in your heart; “I have not ascended to you” according to divinity. The disciples went fishing through the whole night and caught nothing. The fishermen are the ancient teachers. The night shows that before Christ’s coming no one had reached perfection through the preaching of the Old Law.

“When morning came”: he shows that the coming of Christ had taken place. “Cast the net on the right side”—that is, cast the preaching among the Gentiles. Peter was naked—that is, they were naked of the faith of Christ. He girded himself with a tunic—that is, the faith of the Church. He threw himself into the sea—that is, into the waves and bitterness of the world through love of Christ. The other disciples came in a boat—that is, in the Church, treading upon the turbulence of the world. They saw coals, and a fish, and bread placed there: through the fish he signifies faith; through the coals, the warmth of charity; through the bread, the divine Word. “They dragged the net onto the land”: by the shore he signifies the end of the world. It was full of large fish—that is, the fullness and greatness of the Church through the remission of sins. Through the number three he signifies the Trinity. The net was undivided and unbroken—that is, the Church incorrupt in the future. Jesus ate after the resurrection: he shows the true incarnation of the body, so that believers might believe.

Jesus said, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” He shows that, just as Peter denied him three times, so he should confess the faith of the Trinity three times. “Feed my sheep”—that is, in the Church. Jesus entered through closed doors: he shows that he entered through closed doors from the womb; so also all the saints, after the resurrection, will put on a spiritual body and be able to enter everywhere without fear. Hence, whole and incorrupt in marriage, three witnesses confirm this interpretation.

“The disciple whom Jesus loved.” The second miracle is what Jesus did in Cana of Galilee: he drew wine from water, a prepared work. John’s virginity is signified, because a bride was joined to him. The testimony that Jesus entrusted his mother to John: Mary is represented as the Church. John signifies primacy. Just as John was a virgin in marriage, so he was undefiled in death. John narrates the genealogy according to divinity, whereas the others narrate it according to humanity. John speaks of divinity: “In the beginning was the Word.” He lay upon Jesus’ breast, and the knowledge of divinity that had been in Jesus’ breast rose into John through the joining of the two breasts. An implanted tree produces the fruit of one tree in another, the one in which it is planted.

If, according to the order of the canon, this book were to be placed before Matthew, and if it has been placed last, this is because the earth was sanctified first, then water, and finally fire, because fire is brighter and more subtle. Likewise, this corresponds to the two Laws, the Old and the New: the Old was given first, yet the New is brighter and greater, because it distinguishes what is heavenly and is more abundant. This pertains to the Gospel of John, according to what was stated above.

[Col. 0915]

## WALAFRID STRABO, MONK OF FULDA: ONE BOOK ON THE ORIGINS AND DEVELOPMENTS OF ECCLESIASTICAL MATTERS, ADDRESSED TO BISHOP REGINBERT

(From *The Library of the Ancient Fathers*, ninth century, part II, volume XV.) (G)*

## AUTHOR’S PREFACE

[Col. 0919A]

In the name of God the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Many people have said many things about the ministers of the Church and their ministries, and also about the manifold meanings of the sacraments, offices, and observances, so that few or almost none remain that have not already been demonstrated through the illumination of the Holy Spirit—not only how they ought to be performed, but also how each ought or can be understood mystically, after careful examination. You possess the abundance of all these things, venerable Father in Christ Reginbert, burning with a wholesome curiosity, since you have grasped them both in books and in memory according to your most diligent study of ecclesiastical matters. Yet you desire me to add certain things not entirely omitted by those earlier writers, but touched on more briefly than you wished, as though something had escaped them [Col. 0919B] that we might be able to examine. Rather, we ought truly to confess that we cannot attain, even through our eagerness to learn, all the things they discovered and left to us in their writings. Yet some matters of this kind seemed clear through the liveliness of their own understanding.

I shall therefore write, insofar as the Lord grants me the ability, what I have been able to learn from the statements of authoritative writers whom I have so far encountered. I shall indicate the beginnings of certain churches and the causes of matters, the origins of this or that custom, and how it has developed in the course of time, so that, even if I do not win praise for knowledge, I may nevertheless receive a sure reward for obedience. And first, it seems necessary to speak of the sacred buildings in which the sacred rites themselves are celebrated.

## TO THE READER

This little work Walafrid, poor and dull,

has gathered, following the broad teachings of the Fathers.

But he did not venture upon such great undertakings of his own will;

the harsh command of Reginbert compelled him.

If anything in this pleases you, reader, remember

to attribute it to the Lord; whatever displeases you, attribute to me.

## THE BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0919]

### CHAPTER ONE. On the Origins of Temples and Altars

[Col. 0919C]

Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, as we read, built altars to the Lord (Gen. VIII, XII, XXVI, XXXIII). Moses, however, was the first to erect the tabernacle in the wilderness of Sinai, according to the pattern divinely shown to him, after the children of Israel had been freed from Egyptian slavery. Solomon too, when that same people had already lived for a long time in the promised land, and when he surpassed the surrounding nations in the height of royal dignity, built that marvelous temple in Jerusalem—of which David his father had established the capital of the kingdom—at great expense, and endowed it with various ornaments.

In both of these, namely the tabernacle and the temple, the ark of the Covenant, the altars with their utensils, and other forms appropriate to the religion of that time are said to have existed. They were so numerous and provided with such deliberate planning that whatever is now celebrated in the Church’s spiritual practices seems to have been entirely and, so to speak, distinctly outlined and constructed in the figures of those buildings.

We also recognize that the pagans made temples for their gods, or rather for the demons who deceived them, not only from their own books but also from the testimonies of divine Scripture. For we read of the temple of Dagon in Samuel and of King Sennacherib being slaughtered in the temple of Neserach (I Sam. V; II Kings XIX); and we read that Daniel exposed the tricks of the priests in the temple of Bel (Dan. XIV). We also know that Antiochus, the most grievous persecutor of the remnants of God’s people and violator of the temple rebuilt after the return from captivity, fell in the temple of Nanea (II Macc. I). There are many other examples by which what we say is confirmed. We do not wish to summon witnesses to the same matter from the books of the pagans, lest amid the words of ecclesiastical edification we occupy the reader’s mind with useless fables.

### CHAPTER TWO. How Different Religions Imitated One Another, and What They Had in Common and What They Had Differently

In the earliest times, we should believe that both true worshipers of God and worshipers of demons celebrated the rites of their religion in suitable places beneath the open sky. But because the demons persuaded human beings, as an insult to the Creator, to exchange the image of the incorruptible God for the likeness of corruptible man, birds, four-footed animals, and serpents, and to serve the creature rather than the Creator (Rom. I), they consequently also demanded, to exact a more severe penalty for the error they had instilled, that temples be built for them and that not only animal but also human blood be sacrificed.

Therefore the almighty and patient Creator, wishing to care for his creation in every way, knew that, because of the weakness of the fleshly, all customs could not be abolished at once. He permitted and commanded certain things to be offered obediently to him by the devout, things that the impious offered damnably to demons: such as the construction of buildings and various kinds of sacrifices. Thus it came about that the things granted to the earlier people because of their weakness, once the error had been excluded, were disclosed to us who came later through Christ’s passion and served the cause of perfection. In those material structures we perceive the spiritual building of the Church, and in the fleshly victims and solemnities we perceive Christ’s passion and examples of the virtues.

Just as God willed certain moral precepts to be common to us and to the ancients—such as those that concern moral integrity and the preservation of justice among human beings—so he ordained that certain shameful practices, instituted according to the pleasure of demons, should be avoided in every way by them and by us: namely sorceries and lies, fornications, superstitious errors, and similar things.

Since this has been said, it should be understood that some things are common to every religion, such as: “What you do not want done to you, do not do to another” (Matt. VII; Tob. IV), and whatever is found, according to the natural law, to agree with the divine commandments. There is, however, this difference among them: some observe these things for the sake of moral integrity, like the philosophers; some out of fear, like the Jews; others out of love, like the Christians.

To return to our subject: just as God, in order to destroy the works of the devil, willed certain things to be offered to him by his worshipers—things that demons had first persuaded the erring to offer—so, afterward, the demons demanded for themselves the worship instituted by God, especially in the multiplicity of sacrifices and ceremonies. Thus it is written that the nations searched the books of God’s Law for a likeness of their idols, so that, just as the Law commanded service to the Lord through its rites, deceived nations might worship their deceivers, the demons.

For in the times of the Caesars Tiberius and Gaius, we read that idols were placed in the temple of the Lord. Julian the Apostate also attempted to twist the entire order of ecclesiastical rites to the honor of devils. And the devil himself wished to be worshiped by Christ as God (Matt. IV).

### CHAPTER THREE. On the Progress of the Christian Religion

After the time came when true worshipers began to worship the Father in spirit and truth (John IV), not only in Jerusalem or on Mount Samaria—that is, not locally but spiritually—and when saving teaching had been sent among all nations according to the Lord’s command, the faithful began to seek clean places, set apart from the disturbances and affairs of those living according to the flesh, where they could celebrate pure prayers, the holy mysteries, and the consolations of mutual edification.

Although, according to the Evangelist, the disciples were always with the believers in the temple or the upper room, praising God and devoting themselves to prayer and fasting, nevertheless, after the coming of the Holy Spirit (Acts I, II), we read that they celebrated prayers and the breaking of bread around houses. They met not only among the buildings of cities but also outside, in secluded places. For Paul is said to have gone out at Philippi, beyond the gate, beside the river, where prayer seemed to be offered; and he himself prayed with the Ephesians on the shore (Acts XVI, XX).

When the number of believers increased, they began to make their houses churches, as is very frequently read in the acts of the saints, and they dedicated private dwellings to the public needs of the faithful. Often, too, while avoiding the fury of persecutors, they held assemblies in crypts, cemeteries, caves, and deserted mountains and valleys.

Then, as the marvel of the Christian religion advanced more and more, and as Christ’s gains replaced the devil’s losses, not only were new houses built for prayer, but even temples of the gods, once the idols and their most foul rites had been cast out and destroyed, were changed into churches of God.

### CHAPTER FOUR. Toward Which Regions of the Sky Those Who Pray Should Turn

[Col. 0922D]

Because the diversity of idolatry had built temples in different ways, the righteous of that time did not greatly concern themselves with which direction they should turn places of prayer, provided only that wherever the filth of demons had been expelled, there the God who created all things, who is everywhere, might be worshiped and adored.

Although the wise man says that we worship God toward the east of light, and although it is truly fitting and has been established as a wholesome custom that in prayer we turn our faces toward the east, because just as with the body we look for the coming of bodily light from the east, so in our prayers we ask that the face of him should shine upon us, of whom it is written, “Behold, the Man whose name is Orient” (Zech. VI), and, “The Orient from on high has visited us” (Luke I), nevertheless, since the entrance of the tabernacle-temple was also from the east, where the altar and laver were, and where all the rites of victims and sacrifices were performed, it is certain that in both cases many prayed from the east toward the west.

Indeed, when Solomon dedicated the temple, he stood before the altar, stretched out his hands toward heaven, and poured forth a prayer remarkable both for its devotion and its length (III Kings VIII). The eastern and front parts of the temple or altar therefore faced east. Hence among the ancients the eastern parts of temples were called the front; the western, the rear; the northern, the left; and the southern, the right.

This is also written concerning the southern side of the Lord’s temple: “The door of the middle side was in the right-hand part of the house” (III Kings VI). Since the gates of the three courts were placed opposite one another and opened in a straight line toward the east, the equinoctial sun, rising, would raise its rays evenly through them toward the middle of the temple, and in the same way would extend through the entrances of the portico and of the temple itself to the entrances of the Holy of Holies, placed opposite on the other side.

As the elders relate, those who stood in the outer courts and were prevented from entering the inner court by certain seemingly reasonable causes directed their eyes, through the open view of the gates set opposite one another, as far as the entrance of the temple. They were not permitted to approach it with their feet, but approached with prayers, vows, and salutations.

Solomon himself, in that celebrated prayer concerning the people who would come into exile because of their sins, said to God: “If they pray toward the city which you have chosen and toward the temple which I have built for your name” (I Chron. VI), and so forth. The prophet Daniel, too, a man in whom no suspicion could be found, is read to have done this. With the windows of his upper room open toward Jerusalem, he prayed three times each day (Dan. VI).

Taught by these and other examples, we know that those who established altars in temples, whether newly constructed for God or cleansed from the squalor of idols, in various directions because of some convenience of location, did not and do not err, because there is no place where God is not.

For we have learned through a most truthful account that in the church which the emperor Constantine, together with his mother Helena, established at Aelia over the Lord’s tomb, of marvelous size and circular form, and likewise in Rome, in the temple formerly called the Pantheon, which Pope Boniface, with the permission of the emperor Phocas, consecrated in honor of all the saints, and also in the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the altars are distributed not only toward the east but also toward other directions.

Since these arrangements were made according to will or necessity, we do not dare to condemn them. Nevertheless, the more frequent practice—as we mentioned above—and the one closer to reason is for those praying to turn toward the east, and for churches to be arranged in that direction. Let each person abound in his own understanding. “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth, and salvation is far from sinners” [Col. 0924A] (Ps. CXLIV). “Draw near to the Lord, and he will draw near to you” (James IV). Otherwise, even if a sinner flees, he cannot escape him who is everywhere. For neither from the east nor from the west nor from the deserted mountains—understand, no place of flight is open—because God is judge: he humbles one and exalts another. To him the Prophet also says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit? And where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. LXXIV, CXXXVIII).

### CHAPTER FIVE. On the Vessels Simply Called Signals
Concerning cast or wrought vessels, which are simply called signs, because by their sound, aroused through certain strokes, the hours are indicated at which the appointed offices are celebrated in the house of God: concerning these, I say, it seems necessary to say that their use is not reported as having been customary among the ancients to the same extent, because they did not have such a frequent succession of assemblies as exists now. Among some peoples, devotion alone compelled people to gather at the appointed hours. Others were summoned by public announcements and learned which hours were soon to follow at a given solemnity. Among certain peoples the hours were announced by tablets, and among others by horns.

The use of the vessels of which we have begun to speak is said to have been first invented among the Italians. Hence, from Campania, which is a province of Italy, these larger vessels are called *campanae* (“bells”); the smaller ones, which are also called *tintinnabula* (“little ringing objects”) from their sound, are called *nolae*, from Nola, a city of the same Campania, where these vessels were first devised. Since, moreover, we have bronze and silver trumpets in the Law (Num. X), and the prophet commands the voice of preaching to exult like a trumpet (Isa. VIII), we appropriately use these vessels in the calling together of the faithful, so that our preaching in the Church may be signified as pure in silver, durable and sonorous in bronze—that is, so that it is neither defiled by the rust of heresy, nor wearied by the sluggishness of negligence, nor suppressed by human fear.

## CHAPTER VI. An exposition of certain names associated with sacred things

We have said these things as best we could. Now let us say a little about the names that have been assigned to the sacred places or buildings themselves—not accidentally, but rationally—so that the reader, once he has learned the reasons for the buildings and their beginnings, may also understand why they have been called this or that.

*Ecclesia* is indeed a Greek name, and it means “calling together” or “assembly.” It may refer either to the universal unity of the saints, joined together in one faith and love, whence it is called the one and catholic Church; or to the holy association of individuals in particular places, whence many churches are also called churches. Yet the very house in which the multitude of the faithful gathers either to learn or to celebrate divine things is also called an *ecclesia*: we borrow that name from what is done there.

The Apostle indicates examples of these meanings when he says: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. V); and: “As I teach in all the churches of the saints” (I Cor. IV); and: “Let women keep silence in the Church” (I Tim. II), with many similar passages.

Each of the elect is also called a house and temple of God, as the Apostle confirms both by his own example and by that of the prophet: “The temple of God is holy,” he says, “which you are” (I Cor. III); as the Lord says: “I will dwell in you” (II Cor. VI), and so forth. And Peter says: “You, as living stones, are built up into a spiritual house” (I Pet. II), and so forth.

Therefore, just as in the Church, so many houses and temples are gathered together in the house and temple of God. A house (*domus*) is so called from *domate*, which in Greek means “roof.” *Domus* also denotes the association of an entire family dwelling under one roof, just as a city is the dwelling-place of an entire people and the world the dwelling-place of the whole human race.

A *templum* is said to mean, as it were, a spacious roof. Hence the name is appropriate to more distinguished buildings: thus the most wise king Solomon had a temple in the royal city, whereas Moses is said to have erected a tabernacle while traveling. The tabernacle (*tabernaculum*) was so called from boards and curtains, because curtains were stretched above the intervening boards. Hence the tents of soldiers, in which they avoid the heat of the sun and the violence of storms, rain, and cold while traveling, are also called tabernacles.

Some think that *aedes* and *aedificia* (“buildings”) are derived from *edere* (“to eat”), as though they were originally made for eating. Hence Plautus says:

> “If I had invited you to the house for dinner.”

For it is possible that houses were first made for eating in them, just as dining rooms (*coenacula*) were made for dining, and that later, through long usage, the word was transferred to another meaning. Likewise, *tabernae* were originally called the little houses of commoners because they were made from six wooden boards; hence some wish *tabernaculum* to be derived from that word. Now, however, the shops of tavern-keepers are so called.

*Basilica* is Greek; in Latin it means “royal” or “regal,” from *basileus*, that is, “king.” The palaces of earthly kings are also called by this name, as it is written concerning Esther: “She stood in the inner court of the royal house, opposite the king’s basilica” (Esth. V).

Our house of prayer is called royal because the King of kings is served in it, or because kings and priests—that is, members of the supreme King and Priest, who rule the movements of the body and offer spiritual sacrifices to God—are there regenerated from water and the Spirit and nourished with saving doctrine.

An *apsis* is called *lucida* in Latin, “bright,” because through an arch it admits the light it has received. An *exedra* is a kind of apse, somewhat separated from a temple or palace, and is so called because it projects outward. In Greek it is called *cyclon*.

Some have said that an *ara* (“altar”) is so called because slaughtered victims burn there; others derive it from prayers, which the Greeks call *arai*. Hence curses or imprecations are also called *antara* [the printed term is uncertain]. An *altare* is named as though from *alta ara*, “high altar.”

A *porticus* is named from *porta*, either because it is said to be open or because it is chiefly made so that people may enter and pass through it.

A *coemeterium* is the resting-place or sleeping-place of the dead. They are therefore called “sleeping” by the Church, because they are believed to be destined to rise again.

*Crypts* are underground caves, named from their abrupt depth, just as we call the abrupt upper edges of any bodies *crepidines*.

*Martyria* were called churches built in honor of certain martyrs. The canons decree that fitting honor should be shown to their tombs and churches. They also decree that places constructed under uncertain names and relics, or merely under the designation of the dead, are not to be honored. The blessed Martin and Germanus of Paris are read to have confirmed this by their examples.

A *sacrarium* is so called because sacred things are placed and preserved there. An *analogium* is so called because the word of God is read and proclaimed from it. For *logos* in Greek means “word” or “reason.”

A *pulpitum* is so called because it is set up in a public place, so that those who stand there may be seen by everyone. An *ambo* is named from *ambire* (“to surround”), because it surrounds and encloses the person entering it.

*Cancelli* seem to be so called because they are made with smaller columns. For *cancri* are called the larger columns, especially square ones. Or *cancelli* may be derived from *cubitus*, which in Greek is called *ankos*. They are commonly not built higher than the point at which those standing above them can lean on them with their elbows.

*Januas* (“doors”) are named from a certain Janus, to whom the pagans consecrated every entrance and exit. *Ostia* (“entrances”) are called so either from *obstare* (“to stand before”), because they are placed outside, or from *ostendere* (“to show”), because they show the way in. *Valvae* (“folding doors”) are named from *volvere* (“to roll” or “turn”). *Fores* are so called because they are placed on the outside. *Portae* (“gates”) are so called because through them things are carried and conveyed.

Properly speaking, *januas* are the first entrances into a house; *ostia* are the entrances within a door leading to any places; *valvae* are those that roll inward, that is, turn and fold together, like doors that turn outward. *Portae*, properly speaking, belong to walls and courtyards.

A *camera* (“vault”) is so called from its curvature, which is customary in buildings closed above with masonry. Because of its upper concavity, it is also called a *testudo* (“tortoise”), after the likeness of that animal. In Greek, *camyron* means “curved.”

*Coffered ceilings* or *lacunar* are hanging ornaments of temples, so called because they shine in the air. Since it would be lengthy to explain and go through one by one all the parts of sacred buildings, and since there is as much variety of names and forms in them as in other structures, let what has been said about their more prominent parts suffice. For the remaining parts, these signs of the entrances will make access easier for those who are diligent.

## CHAPTER VII. How the house of God is called in the Theotisc language

I shall nevertheless also say, according to our barbarous language, which is Theotisc, by what name this same house of God is called. I would become a laughing-stock to Latins if anyone who happened to read these things wished to count misshapen, monkey-like offspring among the children of the poor. Yet we know that monkeys were also brought to Solomon—who in many things represented the type of the Lord and Savior—among the peacocks (III Kings X). And the Lord, who feeds the doves, gives food to the young of the ravens that call upon him (Ps. CXLVI).

Let our people therefore read, and understand that, in rational speech as well as in religion, we imitate in many respects the true philosophy of the Greeks and Romans. Among individual nations there are many things whose names, before the things themselves are known, are unknown to other peoples. Thus it very often happens that, as people learn the understanding of things from one another, they also draw their names and designations into their own language—either whole or corrupted—together with the new understanding. Thus the Greeks, Latins, and barbarians borrowed from the Hebrews *Amen*, *Alleluia*, and *Hosanna*.

From the Greeks, the Latins and all who use Latin books and language received *ecclesia*, *baptisma*, *chrisma*, and almost all the roots of spoken expressions. From the Latins, the Theotisci received many words in common speech, such as *schamel* (“stool”), *fenster* (“window”), and *lectar* (“lectern”); in matters associated with divine service, they received almost everything.

Likewise, following the Latins, we received from the Greeks such words as *kylch* for “chalice,” *vatter* for “father,” *mutter* for “mother,” and *genez* from *gynaeceum*. In Greek these are written κύλιξ, πάτηρ, μήτηρ, and γυναικεῖον. In some of these matters, not only do the Latins have their own words, such as *genitor* and *genitrix*, but the Theotisci also have their own, such as *atto*, *amatodo*, and *toda*.

From the Greeks themselves we received *kyrch* from *kyrios*, and *papst* from *papa*, which is a name of a certain fatherhood and suits the dignity of clerics; and *herr* from *heros*; and *monn* and *monath* from μήνη (*mēnē*, “month”); along with many other words.

Therefore, just as the house of God is called a basilica—that is, a royal building—from *rex* (“king”), so it is also called *Kyriaca*, that is, “the Lord’s,” from the Lord, because the Lord of lords and King of kings is served there.

If it is asked by what occasion these traces of Greekness came to us, it must be said that barbarians served in the Roman state, and that many preachers skilled in Greek and Latin speech came among these beasts to fight against errors. For these reasons our people learned from them many useful things they had not previously known, especially from the Goths—who are also called Getae—since, at the time when they were led to the faith of Christ, although not by a straight path, they lived in the Greek provinces and possessed our language, that is, the Theotisc tongue.

And, as histories testify, afterward learned men of that nation translated the divine books into the particular form of their own language; some remnants of these translations are still possessed by certain people. We have also learned through the report of faithful brothers that among certain Scythian peoples, especially the Tomitans, divine offices are still celebrated in that same language.

These mixtures and translations of words are so numerous in all languages that scarcely more words now belong exclusively to individual languages than are shared with others or translated from others.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning images and paintings

**[Note: What Walafrid Strabo discusses here concerning the veneration of images must be read cautiously, since he was one of those theologians of Gaul who, through an inverted error, judged that images should be retained for the adornment of churches and for historical instruction, but should in no way be worshiped.]**

Now something must be said about images and paintings, by which the beauty of churches is increased. Their variety is neither to be honored with an immoderate cult, as certain fools think, nor is their beauty to be trampled underfoot with a kind of contempt, as certain advocates of vanity suppose.

For what sound-minded person would think that Moses and Solomon, in constructing the tabernacle or temple, acted against what is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. VI); and again: “You shall not make for yourself any likeness of them that are in heaven, or on earth, or in the waters under the earth” (Exod. XX)? Yet Moses, according to the divine command, adorned the variety of the curtains and the priestly vestment with different figures (Exod. XXVI); and Solomon, according to the wisdom divinely bestowed upon him, distinguished almost the entire work of the temple with paintings and sculptures, not only of animals but also of trees and plants (III Kings VI). Moreover, both of them placed the likeness of cherubim above the ark and the mercy-seat.

It is certain that they understood this in the following way, and that we ought to understand it likewise: things made by them or by us, or the entire structure of the tabernacle and temple, are not to be honored with the cults and honors due to God, whether they are made to signify some mystery, as the structure of the tabernacle and temple, or to commemorate past events, as paintings of histories, or because of love for those whose likenesses are to be impressed more firmly upon the minds of those who see them, as images of the Lord and his saints.

For it was not without reason that the earlier command added: “You shall not worship them or serve them.” From this we are to understand that the devotion and usefulness we seek to arouse or provide through making these things are not to be condemned; rather, the superstition and dullness by which misguided people attempt to transfer spiritual worship to bodily things are to be condemned in worshiping them.

Certainly, if anyone thinks that the art of painters or craftsmen should be condemned because the things they make, through the beauty and appropriateness of their art, entice foolish people to worship them, then he could consequently reproach God for his works: why did he create the heavenly lights with such splendor, or herbs and vegetables with such beauty and fragrance? For these things, like other creatures, have been worshiped and honored with divine honors by certain people in error. That error is not to be attributed to the author of good things, but to the persuasion of demons and to the wicked consent of human beings, who have learned to abuse good things for evil.

It must also be noted that, just as some people venerate these same images beyond what is sufficient, so others, while wishing to appear more cautious than others in religion, reject them as forms of idolatry and, through the arrogance of their presumption, scandalize the hearts of the simple.

This question often aroused such great controversies among the Greeks that, under the younger Pope Gregory, the emperor Constantine removed all the images at Constantinople; and under Gregory III a synod was held at Rome against the aforesaid heresy, as they called it, in which it was established that images of the saints should be restored according to the ancient custom of the catholic Church.

Finally, the complaint of the Greeks was brought into Francia during the time of the emperor Louis of blessed memory, and through the foresight of that ruler it was refuted in synodal writings. A certain Claudius, bishop of Turin, who was wavering on the path of truth because of the resemblance of his name [to another?], wished to renew this complaint among his other foolish vanities. Before he could be pierced by the darts of the writings of various opponents, he perished, condemned by his own judgment. Perhaps the man who recorded the emperor’s image among the number of the faithful also paid before his tribunal the penalty for his insolence and disturbance.

For the powerful of this world did not think an insult done to them a light matter if they discovered that their image or name on any coin had been despised and trampled underfoot by their subjects.

But because the people of Israel in the desert, or King Jeroboam, offended God by making calves (Exod. XXXII; III Kings XII), the bronze serpent that Moses made at the Lord’s command was not therefore to be despised (Num. XXI). Indeed, those struck by real serpents were healed by looking upon the imagined serpent. Yet because the people, always prone to idolatry, later venerated it with a superstitious devotion, King Hezekiah of Judah, a most religious man, is read to have broken it (IV Kings XVIII).

Thus, since the Christian people have been led with such teachability in divine matters into the inner chambers of spiritual wisdom that they do not believe that even paintings and images—or even holy people themselves, whether living or dead—are to be honored with divine honors or worshiped, we ask the saints not to grant by themselves the things necessary for our salvation, but to obtain them from the author of good things, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes (James I). Being closer to him through their merits, they are therefore more certainly heard, and they request what they know to be suitable for the salvation of those who ask.

We pray to God that, through his gratuitous goodness and through the merits and intercessions of the saints, he may bestow what he judges beneficial for us. To him, as God, Lord, judge, creator, almighty one, and Savior, we offer supplication; but we call upon the saints for assistance as friends of God, servants of the Lord, patrons, truly honored and completely saved.

Those who know how to consider the public prayers of the Church cannot doubt that this is the character of the prayers of the faithful. Since this is the perfected understanding of a Christian, honors paid to images that are entirely respectable and moderate should not be rejected.

For if, because we know that icons are not to be worshiped or served, paintings are to be trampled underfoot and destroyed as unnecessary or harmful, then, because we believe that the Creator of all things, who is everywhere and fills heaven and earth, does not dwell in things made by human hands, temples too should be destroyed, lest we seem to believe that the Creator is enclosed by walls and roofs. In this way it could happen that, while guarding against the existence of anything anywhere by which the minds of foolish people might go astray, we would possess almost nothing by which either to exercise our devotion or to draw the simple and unlearned toward love of invisible things.

How much usefulness comes from painting is evident in many ways. First, painting is a kind of literature for the unlettered, so much so that one of the ancients is reported to have learned the histories of former times from paintings.
