Then—to pass over much for the sake of brevity—it is read in the deeds of Pope Sylvester that the emperor Constantine recognized the apostles by their *thoracidas* (“portraits” or “busts”), because he had seen them in a vision [the printed term is uncertain].

Sometimes we see simple and uneducated people who can scarcely be brought by words to believe the events of the faith, yet who are so moved by a painting of the Lord’s Passion or of other miracles that, through their tears, they testify that the outward figures have been impressed upon their hearts as though by letters.

Therefore, just as all things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean because their mind and conscience are defiled (Tit. I), so all ways are full of occasions of offense to the wicked. And just as the good use even evil things well, so the wicked use even good things badly.

Images and paintings, then, should be possessed and loved in such a way that usefulness is not canceled through contempt, and that this irreverence does not redound to the injury of those whose likenesses they are; nor should the soundness of faith be wounded by immoderate devotion, nor excessive honor paid to bodily things accuse us of contemplating spiritual things less attentively.

## CHAPTER IX. On the dedication of temples and altars

That the temples of God should be consecrated by solemn dedication is taught by the examples of the ancients and by fitting reason. For Jacob the patriarch is read to have erected a stone, anointed it by pouring oil over it, and called it the house of God; and he invoked the mighty God of Israel over the altar he had erected.

Moses is read to have consecrated the tabernacle, and Solomon the temple, by the most celebrated dedications (Exod. XL; III Kings VIII). Hence, as a testimony of divine manifestation and visitation, fire descended from heaven and consumed the offerings, and over both houses appeared smoke and the cloud of divine protection.

It must be noted that dedication was celebrated not only at the first construction of a temple, but also a second or third time, after the same temple had been overturned and profaned because of the sins of the people and by foreign nations, when it had been rebuilt under Zerubbabel (Hag. II), or purified under the Maccabees and followed by a renewed dedication (I Macc. V).

Hence the dedication that was most recently performed in winter is known to have been observed until the time of Christ’s Passion, as it is written in the Gospel of John (chapter X): “The Feast of the Dedication took place at Jerusalem, and it was winter,” and so forth. The other two are reported to have taken place at other times of the year, namely in the seventh and first months.

It is also found to have been established by the Council of Agde that the altar should be anointed and blessed. We have these and other examples of the dedication of temples and altars, and we are led to this observance by no less persuasive reasoning.

For if pagans are known to devote and dedicate temples and statues—the testimonies of their error—to deceptive demons through certain curses rather than sacraments, so that they might more closely display their devotion to the gods whom they desire to please and win the favor of demons for visiting them by this familiarity, as it is read that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, dedicated the statue he had erected in the plain of Dura (Dan. III), why should we not rather take care to dedicate temples and altars, signs of our religious devotion, to God our Savior through undefiled sacraments (John XIV)? Thus we may please the divine majesty through the duties of our devotion, and he may deign always to visit us and make his dwelling in us, who says through the prophet: “Revere my sanctuary” (Lev. XXVI), and so forth.

## CHAPTER X. What should be done in places consecrated to God

What should be done in places consecrated to God, the Lord makes known through the prophet and through himself, saying: “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations” (Matt. XXI; Isa. LVI). The Psalmist likewise says: “I will enter into your house; I will worship toward your holy temple” (Ps. V), with many similar passages.

Jacob also recognized that angels are present in such places when he saw the angels ascending and descending on the ladder set upright at Bethel (Gen. XXVIII). David testifies to the same, saying: “In the sight of the angels I will sing praise to you, and I will worship toward your holy temple” (Ps. CXXXVII).

The Law of Moses also teaches fully that vows and sacrifices should be offered to God in these places (Deut. XII), and the Psalmist recalls this: “I will pay my vows to the Lord in the sight of all his people” (Ps. CXV), and so forth.

Moses also showed that the word of doctrine should be dispensed to the people in the Church when he explained the Lord’s commandments to the people at the entrance of the tabernacle. The Lord himself was found in the temple, sitting in the midst of the teachers, at the age of twelve (Luke II); and it is very frequently found in the Gospel that he spoke in the temple, just as in his Passion he confesses that he taught openly in the synagogues and in the temple, where all the Jews gather (John XIX).

Peter also prayed in the temple with John, and Paul fulfilled his vows (Acts III); all the apostles taught there (Acts XXI). Hence, since the same house of God is called an *oratorium* (“place of prayer”), it may be thought to receive this name both from the supplications made there and from the utterance of doctrine. For *oratio* means, as it were, “the reasoning of the mouth,” and by this name is understood not only humble petition but also rational speech.

This is why the first orders in the Church make use of oratories, because the duty of teaching belongs to them. Public declaimers and wise composers of speeches are also called *oratores* (“speakers” or “orators”).

Baptism is also most appropriately celebrated there, because we read that before the tabernacle there was a basin, and before the temple a sea and ten stands, in which the priests who were about to offer sacrifices and the flesh of the victims were washed (Exod. XXX; III Kings VII). It is entirely fitting that Christians should be regenerated in the temple of Christ.

## CHAPTER XI. What likewise should not be done

The Lord himself shows that other works of worldly business should not be carried out in buildings consecrated to God—not to mention things permitted nowhere, but also certain things that are sometimes lawfully performed elsewhere and must therefore be removed from there—when, moved by zeal for the house of God, he cast the sellers and buyers out of the temple (John II).

Through the prophet he also asks in one place: “My beloved has committed many crimes in my house” (Jer. XI). The Apostle likewise rebukes the Corinthians for having dissensions in the church and for feasting there, saying: “First of all, when you come together, I hear that there are divisions among you” (I Cor. XI), and so forth; and later: “When you come together into one place, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper. For each one takes his own supper beforehand to eat. One is hungry, and another is drunk. Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the church of God and shame those who have nothing?”

After much more, he adds: “Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you do not come together for judgment.” Earlier he had spoken of the disorderly gestures of those who pray: “This I command, not praising you, because you come together not for the better but for the worse.”

Hence the blessed Father Benedict, in the Rule of Monks, commands that an oratory should be what its name signifies, and that nothing else should be done or stored there. This shows that those who, without being compelled by necessity, commit unworthy acts there are blameworthy, as are those who turn holy places into granaries and storerooms. For the canons have also frequently forbidden banquets or meals to be held in churches, unless someone is compelled by the necessity of travel.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the manner of praying and the variation of voices

The same Father concludes how one should pray in brief words, especially these, saying: “Prayer should be brief and pure. Let us know that we are heard not through many words, but through purity of heart and compunction expressed in tears; not through a loud voice, but through tears and the intention of the heart.”

And again: “Let us consider how we ought to stand in the sight of the Divinity and of the holy angels, and let us stand to sing psalms in such a way that our mind agrees with our voice.”

Let us therefore understand from these examples what the Lord wishes to be done in his temples and what he forbids. He punished the sons of Eli for their crimes committed around the tabernacle; but he heard Hannah, the mother of the blessed Samuel, praying in the secrecy of her heart, with only the movement of her lips and without the noise of her voice, when she asked for a son. He also chose Samuel himself as prophet, priest, and leader, rejecting the old man, because Samuel faithfully ministered in the house of the Lord.

From his most modest mother one may learn humility and perseverance in prayer. It is indeed read of her that “her face was no longer changed in various ways.” For whoever asks in prayer for something other than what he ought, or entreats in a manner other than the Teacher of humility indicates, either does not know how to pray or gains less than he could have gained. Whoever, after completing a prayer, immediately leaps without reflection either into his customary wrongdoing or into new crimes loses the fruit of prayer.

Some people beat their breasts with their fists in prayer, strike their heads, lower their voices with feminine softness, and do not fear, shortly afterward, to disturb others by word or deed and to make themselves culpable. Such people fight by their conduct against the judge whom they honor in prayer.

Concerning the difference of voices, the voice suitable for divine praises is that which, however it may sound, proceeds from the good treasure of the heart and agrees with the inward intention. A loud voice is also spoken of in a good sense when, at the dedication of Solomon’s temple, the voice of the priests and Levites crying out amid crowds and hymns is said to have sounded far away (III Kings VIII); and the holy martyrs are read to have cried out with a loud voice beneath the altar of God (Rev. VI).

Here it may be understood, as in many other passages, that the great voice is one which, although low in sound, proceeds from good devotion. Thus God says to Moses: “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exod. XIV), although Moses is not said there to have cried out at all. Nevertheless, it is good, and preferable to every quiet manner, to labor decently and simply in the praise of God.

Although every kind of divine praise, when offered according to reason, should be praised, that form is more commendable which contains the least vanity and ostentation. Read the books of the Confessions of Saint Augustine, and you will find how great a danger he judged there to be in songs with the sweetness of melody.

## CHAPTER XIII. For whom divine worship is beneficial, and for whom it is not

It must certainly be understood that the worship of temples and sacred offices is acceptable to God, the creator of all things, only when the hearts of the people—for whose sake he permits or commands these things to be offered to him—are worthy of his indwelling.

They polish wood and stones in vain if they do not reform their conduct. They bring gifts and money in vain if inwardly they do not please the eye of divine discernment. Because the Jews did not listen to the Lord inwardly, he despised and rejected their outward things, saying through the prophet: “I have forsaken my house; I have abandoned my inheritance” (Jer. XII). And through himself: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII).

Therefore, that sacred places are neglected by God because of human sins is witnessed by the ark captured by the Philistines (I Kings IV), by the temple so often overturned or profaned, and by many Christian churches now devastated or overthrown by barbarians, now laid waste by fire or lightning, now destroyed by earthquakes or whirlwinds.

Hence the Lord also takes away from the sinful people their greatest confidence through Jeremiah, saying: “Do not trust in lying words, saying: ‘The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord,’” and so forth (Jer. VII).

It is certain from this also that not only God’s protection but likewise the guardianship of angels and the care of the saints depart from places once holy when the inhabitants or worshipers of those places have first departed from God. For the whole host of the saints stands before the throne of God, and where God is not, they cannot be.

I say this with respect to the manifestation of grace, not with respect to the immensity of divine power, since he who fills heaven and earth is not absent even from the realms of hell. Josephus writes (*The Jewish War*, book VII, chapter 17) that, when the destruction of the city was imminent because of its sins, the voice of invisible guardians was heard from the interior of the temple: “Let us depart from these dwellings.”

Nor do sacred places benefit those who cast holiness away, just as dreadful places do not harm those protected by the Lord’s grace. For in the aforementioned destruction of Jerusalem, those crushed by every evil, turning their tear-filled eyes toward the temple, did not deserve to be delivered, as it is written: “They cried out, and there was no one to save them; to the Lord, and he did not hear them” (Ps. XVII). The same psalm adds the reason: “The sons of strangers lied to me,” and so forth.

Presumptuous and negligent people are punished in holy places, as were Nadab and Abihu, who offered strange fire (Lev. X). Korah and the rebellious men with him were devoured by the fire of God before the tabernacle (Num. XVI). Eli the priest breathed his last in a holy place with his neck broken (I Kings IV). The men of Beth-shemesh were condemned in the presence of the ark (I Kings VI). Joab was killed beside the altar (II Kings II). Uzziah, unlawfully usurping the priesthood, was covered with leprosy (II Chron. XXVI).

Conversely, the humble and God-fearing are saved in weak and deadly places when justice protects them. Joseph did not perish in the cistern and was not abandoned in prison (Gen. XXXVII and XLI). Moses was not drowned in the river (Exod. II). Job was raised up from the dungheap (Job XLII). Jeremiah was lifted out of the muddy pit (Jer. XXXVIII). Daniel was preserved unharmed among the lions, and the three young men amid the fire (Dan. VI and III). Peter was delivered from prison (Acts XII), and Paul escaped from the sea (Acts XXVII).

And what more shall I say? Iniquity cast angels down from heaven; justice freed human beings from hell.

## CHAPTER XIV. That God desires just offerings, and virtues more than bodily gifts
Finally, the builders or decorators of sacred buildings must be admonished to show the devotion of their hearts through goods acquired justly, because the Lord testifies through the prophet that he hates robbery in a burnt offering (Isa. 61). Elsewhere it is written: “Whoever offers a sacrifice from the goods stolen from the poor is like one who slaughters a son before his father” (Ezek. 34). And in Proverbs: “The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable, because they are offered from crime” (Prov. 21). Likewise: “Honor the Lord from your just labors,” and so forth (Prov. 3).

Let him also remember King David, who refused to accept the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite for building an altar to the Lord, although Araunah wished to give it freely, unless he first repaid the full just price (2 Sam. 24). Indeed, there is no remedy for sin if, having disregarded the commandment of salvation, one presents to the commander the very signs of one’s contempt. Furthermore, whoever offers justly but sets aside the greater and more useful commandments of the Law hears Cain’s words: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? Be still” (Gen. 4, according to the Septuagint). The Savior says to such people: “Woe to you who tithe mint and rue and every herb, but pass over the weightier matters of the Law—mercy, judgment, and truth” (Matt. 23).

We say this, however, not to blame the devotion of those who build and decorate holy places, but to teach that almsgiving to the poor is to be preferred to this. For, as blessed Jerome says: “It is superstitious for walls to shine with gold while Christ suffers hunger and nakedness before the doors.” He himself commands us to store up treasure where neither rust nor moth destroys it, where thieves neither break in nor steal (Matt. 6). And when he comes in judgment, he will inquire not whether we have built churches, but whether we have benefited his least members (Matt. 25).

The Apostle calls these ornaments a “worldly sanctuary” (Heb. 9), because there are other ornaments that are, as it were, holy and heavenly, namely, the ornaments of souls. The less splendor these possess in human eyes, the more merit and reward they possess before the Lord.

For it is read of blessed Pope Gregory that he did not labor like others in the construction of churches, but in teaching and distributing alms; and he took care to exercise this generosity not only among his own people but also among those living far away and in foreign provinces. If, therefore, the highest holiness consisted in founding or decorating sacred buildings, those most devoted to such works ought to surpass in merit, by a corresponding degree, those who had applied themselves less to carrying them out. But since we read that Moses, the builder of the tabernacle, offended the Lord at the waters of contradiction (Num. 20), and for that reason did not enter the promised land; and that Solomon, after the unique and marvelous construction of the Temple, incurred the Lord’s displeasure when he was seduced by love of women (1 Kings 11)—whence the power of the kingdom, until then united, was torn from his offspring and partly transferred to another tribe through a ruinous division—we understand, and without any doubt confess, that the construction of sacred buildings is to be praised as arising from religious devotion, yet that the virtues, which are spiritual structures, and the enduring ornaments of souls in whom God dwells, are to be preferred to them by far.

For however great a beauty earthly ornaments may be fashioned with, they become worthless to God without virtues. The virtues, however, which he also loves in his angels, he shows to be pleasing to him always even without material adornment, saying through the prophet Micah: “I will show you, O man, what is good and what the Lord requires of you: surely, to do justice, to love mercy, and to walk carefully with your God” (Mic. 6). Hence we know that many saints pleased God even before the use of sacred temples; and others, after sanctuaries had been established for God in various places, while dwelling in deserts and desolate regions, served the almighty Lord by virtues alone.

## CHAPTER XV. On the offerings of the ancients

What we have recalled concerning the construction and uses of sacred buildings is sufficient for us, considering the limits imposed by our slowness and negligence. Now let us add what he himself has given us to say about the sacrifices and offerings presented to God in them.

Abel and Cain are read to have been the first to offer gifts to the Lord: Abel, from the natural offspring of the sheep he tended; Cain, from the fruits of the earth that he had acquired by skill and labor (Gen. 4). That the gifts of the two were not received with equal favor, because they had been offered in unequal manner, is shown by the judgment of the divine regard, as well as by Cain’s madness, which, envying his brother’s happiness, fell even into the guilt of murder.

Noah likewise, after the Flood, offered the Lord clean animals as a pleasing odor (Gen. 8). Abraham and Jacob, too, as well as Job, the model of patience, are read to have offered sacrifices and burnt offerings to the Lord.

But how numerous the commands concerning offerings were under the Law must be learned from the books themselves. There the flesh and blood of quadrupeds and birds, the produce of the earth, and the fruits of trees are commanded to be offered in various ways. Although all these things, in accordance with the observance of the legal ordinances, prefigured the truth of the Gospel through their presentation, they were imposed for observance upon a people weak and, as it were, understanding only flesh and blood, until the Lord of the Law and the prophets should come and complete everything that had been foretold concerning him in explicit or mystical sayings, or prefigured through the figurative rites of victims, sacrifices, and solemnities.

This was so arranged that, when the truth of the Gospel dawned, neither believers from the Jews would be forbidden to observe those practices as though they were sacrilegious and profane things, nor would those coming to faith from the Gentiles be compelled to undertake them as though they were necessary for Christian salvation.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the sacrifices of the New Testament, and why the sacrifices were changed through Christ

Accordingly, Christ, who is the end of the Law for believers, assumed the dispensation of the flesh and did not reject the statutes of the Law, since they were from God; rather, he fulfilled them in himself in order to bring them to an end. He handed down the new mysteries of the New Testament for the instruction of the new man; by his death he brought the old things to completion, and by his resurrection he confirmed the new.

At the supper that he held with his disciples before his final betrayal, after the solemnities of the old Passover, he handed over to those same disciples the sacraments of his body and blood under the substance of bread and wine, and taught them to celebrate them in remembrance of his most holy passion.

Nothing more suitable for signifying the unity of the head and the members could therefore have been found. For just as bread is formed from many grains into one body through the coagulation of water, and wine is pressed from many grapes, so the body of Christ is completed from the multitude of the saints gathered into one.

Hence the ancients wisely decreed that wine should not be offered in the sacrifice without the admixture of water, so that this might signify that the peoples who, according to John, are waters (Rev. 17), ought not to be divided from Christ, whose blood is in the chalice. Thus neither wine without water nor water without wine is offered, because Christ suffered in no other way than for his people, nor can the people be saved in any other way than through Christ’s passion.

Since Christ is said to be a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, as the Apostle Paul establishes at great length (Heb. 7), while preserving the meaning of the many figures in which Jesus Christ, the Son of God and priest of the Most High God, who offered himself to the Father for us, is recognized as having been proclaimed, our Lord, the true priest, graciously provided an appropriate kind of sacrifice as the mystery of his body and blood.

Just as Melchizedek, before circumcision and the ceremonies of the Law, is read to have lived by faith and offered bread and wine, so the Lord himself, made high priest according to the order not of Aaron but of Melchizedek—righteous, and justifying the one who is of faith—after the completion of the Law, handed these same sacrificial elements over to his faithful.

Let us not doubt, therefore, that we are justified by faith without the works of the Law, while in the freedom of faith and devotion we imitate those whom we know to have pleased God through faith without the servitude imposed by the Law.

Thus, while God was known in Judea and sacrifices had to be offered in one place, that is, in the one tabernacle or temple, carnal people were commanded—or rather permitted—to present various costly offerings, so that a servile religion might labor through burdensome acts of service. But after the Lord’s praiseworthy name had shone over the whole earth, and a priesthood that was not particular but universal was exercised in every place and among all nations, with the whole unity of the faithful converging not bodily upon one place but spiritually upon one faith, it was decreed that the faithful should consecrate simple offerings to the Lord. These would contain the truth of the mystery and would not burden the adopted sons with any difficulty of expense.

Human reasoning must not investigate why the one who is always the same and cannot change established or commanded this or that at this or that time as though the things were different and contradictory. The creator and arranger of times disposes everything that occurs in time justly, suitably, and beneficially—not according to a temporal reasoning of his wisdom but according to an eternal one, although he often does so secretly.

It should nevertheless be noted that he did not call the human race from greater, stronger, holier, and more useful things to lesser, weaker, more worthless, and useless things. Rather, just as the person of the Son, placed before servants—namely, angels or human beings—surpasses them in the majesty of his nature, so he himself, coming in the flesh, established greater things for them and taught the passage from carnal things to spiritual, from earthly to heavenly, from temporal to eternal, from imperfect to perfect, from shadow to body, and from images to truth.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the power of the sacraments, and why criminals are suspended from them

Since the Son of God himself says, “My flesh is truly food and my blood is truly drink” (John 6), the same mysteries of our redemption are to be understood as truly the body and blood of the Lord, so that we ought to believe them to be pledges of that perfect unity which we already possess in hope with our head and shall possess in reality hereafter.

For this reason they are also called sacraments, from sanctification or a hidden power. Hence those who, through the foulness of capital crimes, have departed from the members of Christ are suspended from the sacraments themselves by ecclesiastical judgment.

Whoever worthily eats and drinks the body and blood of the Lord shows that he is in God and God in him. Whoever either does not possess the medicine or uses it unworthily testifies, through his languishing, that he is far from the physician.

The one who says, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves,” and so forth, does not lie. For it must be understood that the holy Fathers established this especially so that those who sin mortally might be kept away from the Lord’s sacraments, lest, receiving them unworthily, they become involved in greater guilt—like Judas, whom, after he had rashly received bread from the Master, the devil is said to have seized more completely, so that the crime he had first conceived through wicked premeditation he might complete through an even more wicked deed.

They also acted lest those who presume, as the Apostle says concerning the Corinthians, incur bodily weakness and feebleness, and even death itself. And, once suspended from communion, they might be driven by fear of that exclusion and by a kind of condemning anathema to seek more earnestly the medicine of penance and to long more eagerly for the recovery of salvation.

## CHAPTER XVIII. What should be offered on the altar

Although the use of these sacraments, handed down by the Lord himself and transmitted by the apostles and apostolic men throughout the whole extent of the Catholic Church, has been established, we nevertheless understand from the canons—especially those of the apostles—that in the earliest times some people were accustomed to offer other kinds of offerings.

The third canon says:

> “If any bishop or presbyter, contrary to the Lord’s ordinance, offers anything else upon the altar in the sacrifice—that is, either honey or milk, or for wine, fermented drink, or prepared foods, or birds, or any animals, or vegetables—acting against the Lord’s constitution, let him be deposed at the proper time.”

And the fourth says:

> “Nothing may be offered on the altar except new ears of grain and grapes, and oil for the lamps, and spices, that is, incense, at the time when the holy offering is celebrated.”

Since certain things are forbidden to be offered, it is shown that some people had applied them to offerings, although contrary to the established order.

Hence Eutychianus, the twenty-eighth bishop of the Roman see, decreed that only beans and grapes should be blessed upon the altar. This perhaps was because the mystery of the Lord’s blood is celebrated in wine, while the bean is the food of those who abstain.

It was otherwise decreed that different kinds of things should be blessed by priests everywhere; or, if any such things were brought to the altar for blessing, they were in every respect to be distinguished from the consecration of the Lord’s sacraments by a special blessing. Thus, just as the Lord made the word of the Gospel brief upon the earth in place of the innumerable commandments of the Law (Isa. 10), so in place of the various rites of sacrifice the simple offering of bread and wine should suffice for the faithful. They do not seek the truth as something destined to appear amid a multitude of shadows, but possess it clearly in the manifestation of deeds.

Hence the error of certain simple people, born from the seedbed of Jewish superstitions and extending certain traces of antiquity even to our own times, has already been suppressed to a great extent through the efforts of the wise. If anywhere the pernicious germ of this plague is still shown to be sprouting again, it must be cut off at the root with the spiritual sword.

I mean the error by which certain people placed the flesh of lambs beside or beneath the altar at Easter, consecrated it with a special blessing, and on the very day of the Resurrection partook of that flesh before other bodily foods. The sequence of this blessing is still possessed by many.

How unnecessary this practice is, and how contrary to the sacraments of Christian perfection, is readily understood by anyone who truly understands that “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5), and who wishes to feast not on the old leaven but on “the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XIX. That communion should be received only by those who are fasting

It should also be recalled that some people are read to have received these very sacraments while fasting, and others after eating. Thus it is read in the canons of the Council of Africa, chapter 8, in these words:

> “Let the sacraments of the altar be celebrated only by people who are fasting, except on the one anniversary day on which the Lord’s Supper is celebrated,”

and so forth.

Those people judged that communion should be received after the meal on that day because the Lord is read to have handed the sacraments of the New Testament to his disciples after the supper of the legal Passover.

Others, following a particular practice, judged that they ought to be refreshed with bodily food before receiving the sacraments not once a year, like the former group, but more frequently. After meals and a full stomach, as though strengthened, they approached the sacred things under bodily necessity. Socrates testifies to this in his Ecclesiastical History (Tripartite History, book 9, chapter 3), where, mentioning the different customs of the Churches and, after many variations of fasts and solemnities, he reports among other things:

> “There is also some diversity concerning the celebration of assemblies. For while sacrifices are celebrated throughout the Churches established across the entire world on each Sabbath of every week, this is not done in Alexandria and Rome according to the ancient tradition. The Egyptians living near Alexandria and the inhabitants of the Thebaid do hold assemblies on the Sabbath, but they do not receive the sacraments as is customary. For after they have feasted and been filled with every kind of food, they receive communion toward evening after the offering has been made.”

A little farther on he says:

> “In Syrian Antioch, however, they have the altar not toward the east of the church but rather toward the west.”

On this matter we too have discussed above (above, chapter 4).

> “These people,” he says, “received communion every Sabbath; those others, after lunch or dinner. By what authority they wished to do this is not altogether clear. But the fact that the former were permitted to receive communion after eating on the anniversary of the Lord’s Supper seems to have arisen from the circumstance explained above.”

It is known, however, that subsequent generations established through an honorable and reasonable deliberation that the most holy mysteries should always be celebrated by those who are fasting.

We ought not to eat first and then receive communion merely because the Lord, the fulfiller of the Law and author of grace, first completed the legal Passover and afterward instituted the evangelical sacraments. Nor are we first compelled to be circumcised bodily and afterward baptized, since we know that our Lord was born of a woman and made under the Law, first circumcised according to the ordinances of the Law, and afterward, for the fulfillment of all righteousness, underwent the saving washing and consecrated its beginnings for us.

Therefore, that these same sacraments ought always to be celebrated by those who are fasting is proved both by the general practice of the whole Church and by the statements of the Synod of Braga. There, the previously mentioned practice of receiving communion after breaking the fast on the day of the Lord’s Supper is abolished by the imposition of an anathema.

If, then, it is not permitted to receive communion after eating on that day, although both the Lord’s example and the assent of certain people seemed to support it, much less is it permitted at other times, when neither of these is known to have been granted.

This practice was demanded not only by the propriety of sobriety, through which it is fitting that the chambers of the heart be prepared to receive such holiness, lest the medicine, if received unworthily, become a judgment; but also by the great logic of necessity. For when people eat before communion, it is believable that, as a bad habit usually advances toward worse things, they sometimes fall from small refreshments into the excess of drunkenness.

And what is more absurd than to receive spiritual and life-giving nourishment at the very moment when, because of the excess of what has been consumed, a person overcome by gluttony cannot even handle bodily food honorably? The Apostle commands, saying: “Let all things be done honorably and according to order” (1 Cor. 14).

Although these forms of moderation are necessary in each of the works of the saints, they must be observed especially and repeatedly in the veneration of the most holy blood and body of the Lord. Thus, as honorably—that is, humbly—holding peace and charity in our hearts, fasting and sober, with purity of body and heart, we should touch the sacraments themselves insofar as possible.

We should do so according to order as well: knowing that their sanctification is to be kept far apart from other foods, since they signify the life of the soul, and that we should first be refreshed by their consolation and afterward take the supports of the body.

The canons also speak discreetly and clearly, and we mentioned this above (chapter 11): there should be no banquet in the churches either before or after communion.

## CHAPTER XX. That some say communion should be received more rarely, others more frequently, and others daily

Since we have touched briefly upon the ordering of the sacraments, it seems appropriate to append an account of how the practice of celebrating these mysteries daily came about.

Because teachers give many different accounts of this matter, let us collect briefly what we can, without setting down the names of each author because of the length involved. We shall not attempt to assert anything that we have not either read in this form, inferred from our reading, received from the words of truthful people, or learned through the indication of practice.

As we learn from the discussions of the Fathers, some judged that communion should be received once a year, so that, purifying body and soul through prolonged preparation, people might finally approach the table of heaven worthily.

Some of these held their annual celebration itself on the day of the Lord’s Supper, so that the grace of the sacraments might be repeated there alone, where it had first been revealed. Hence on that day they also broke their fast, as we are accustomed to do on feast days, and completed their assemblies before midday. This is partly shown and entirely prohibited in the canons.

But others, more cautious, thought that these people were all the less worthy to arrive at the annual celebration of their observance because they believed that, after a long delay, they had become sufficiently cleansed and could approach the reception of the sacred things as worthy. They believed it better, even if the soul was unworthy, to repeat sacred things more frequently, because spiritual medicine is such that it both helps the healthy persevere in health and assists the wounded in restoring strength.

The sacrament is received more worthily when those receiving it, kept low through the guardianship of humility, never consider themselves sufficiently worthy to receive it.

Those who, according to the judgment of spiritual physicians, are admitted to this remedy only more slowly ought therefore to abstain for a time, lest, by prematurely taking medicines appropriate to the illnesses of others, they become more seriously ill, and what is restoration for others become condemnation for them.

Others, celebrating Mass every Sunday or every Sabbath in the East and in Spain, thought it sufficient to commemorate the Lord’s passion every week. Hence some believed that the Lord’s Prayer, which, as we believe, was said by the apostles themselves or in the apostolic age before communion and the breaking of the bread, should be recited only at the time when the sacrifices were celebrated. They wished the bread requested in that prayer to be understood as supersubstantial, not daily bread.

Thus those who received communion once a week also recited the Lord’s Prayer once a week.

Cyprian, however, shows that it should be said daily, saying:

> “Therefore, in the Lord’s Prayer we ask that our bread, that is, Christ, be given to us daily, so that we who remain and live in Christ may not depart from his sanctification and body.”

Hilary likewise says:

> “And because it is a daily prayer, daily also the prayer is made that the bread of life may be given.”

Saint Augustine says:

> “Concerning the daily and lesser sins without which this life is not lived, the daily prayer of the faithful provides satisfaction for error.”

The earlier group was pleased with the practice just described. Others judged that the mysteries of divine gifts should be celebrated not only on Sundays and the general feast days—such as the Nativity, Epiphany, Easter, the Lord’s Ascension, and Pentecost—but also on the birthdays of the saints.

For it is read that Felix, the twenty-seventh pope, established that Masses should be celebrated over the memorials of the martyrs. But blessed Pope Gregory, the sixty-sixth in order, commanded that Masses be celebrated over the body of the blessed apostle Peter.

Once these practices had been observed, the younger generations began in the following period to increase the fasting days, correctly understanding that daily bread was to be requested daily and that it was to be offered and received daily by those to whom this was appropriate.

But because Melchiades, the thirty-third to hold the episcopate at Rome, established that no Christian should fast on Sunday or Thursday—for pagans frequently practiced fasts on those days—blessed Gregory mentioned above, in arranging the offices of the year within Lent, left Thursday vacant, so that, because it was festive like Sunday, it might also be celebrated with the office of Sunday.

Because this Thursday later began to be assigned to fasting like the other days, Gregory the Younger established that it should be solemn with Masses and prayers, and, gathering material from every source, increased the offices of that day.

Since the Hebrews are read to have celebrated their carnal offerings daily at the Lord’s command, why should Christians not offer their spiritual sacrifices daily and repeat them in memory of their salvation?

For we read, as blessed Gregory—whom we mentioned above—testifies, that Cassius, bishop of Narnia, after his ordination sacrificed the sacrificial offering to the Lord every day. By divine favor he was admonished to persist in his customary works and strengthened to persevere by the grace of a great promise.

Gennadius, a presbyter of Marseille, standing in ecclesiastical doctrine midway between the older and younger generations—that is, when some were still receiving communion only on Sundays while certain others were already receiving it on daily occasions—moderates his judgment with this balance: he says that he neither praises nor condemns daily reception of the Eucharist. He does, however, urge people to receive communion every Sunday, provided that capital sins do not prevent them and that their minds are not set upon the pleasure of sinning.

Among the Greeks, those who have passed two or three Sundays without communion are likewise said to be excommunicated.

Since the venerable Pope Silvester, thirty-fourth after blessed Peter, taught that the clergy should observe feast days, so that, just as among the pagans only certain days marked by particular feasts were called holidays—for thus it is said through Moses, “These are the holidays of the Lord” (Lev. 23)—so among Christians, and especially among clerics, every day might be counted as a holiday, it seems entirely reasonable that we should be occupied with sacred offices every day.

And whenever more serious stains of mind or body do not obstruct us, let us continually seek and desire the bread and blood of the Lord, without which we cannot live. Let us receive them out of desire for his protection rather than presumption concerning our purity, imitating the salutary devotion of the primitive Church, concerning which it is written in the Acts of the Apostles:

> “They were persevering in the teaching of the apostles, in communion, in the breaking of bread, and in the works” (Acts 2).

And farther on:

> “Every day they continued unanimously in the temple, and breaking bread in their homes, they took food with gladness and simplicity of heart, praising God” (Acts 2).

And again:

> “Every day in the temple and in the homes they did not cease teaching and evangelizing Jesus Christ” (Acts 5).

Note that it says that they first broke the bread and afterward took food.

## CHAPTER XXI. Whether it is appropriate to offer and receive communion once or several times in a day

A certain disagreement commonly arises among priests. One priest wishes to celebrate Mass only once a day, believing, of course, that the same mystery of Christ’s passion is the general support for all necessities, because the one who is ruler and judge of the living and the dead died once for our sins, to take away the sins of many.

Another thinks it appropriate to repeat the same mysteries twice, three times, or as often as desired in one day, believing that God is moved all the more to mercy the more frequently Christ’s passion is commemorated.

Perhaps he thinks his custom can be confirmed by the fact that Roman practice sometimes has two or three Masses of a single solemnity, as at the Nativity of the Lord and on certain feasts of the saints.

Indeed, Telesphorus, ninth in order among the bishops of the Roman see, established that three Masses should be celebrated at night on the Nativity of the Lord.

[Note: It appears from the examples cited by Walafridus that it was once customary for one priest to celebrate several Masses in a day; and that this custom has now rightly been abolished for serious reasons. On the Nativity of the Lord it is permitted to say only three Masses.]

I should truly not consider it absurd if, when several Masses must be celebrated on one day, one priest, persuaded by necessity or inclination, celebrates two or three rather than omitting some of them.

Furthermore, the practice of the whole Church is to celebrate Masses frequently for the living, for the dead, for alms, and for various other causes, as the offices assigned to these purposes also testify.

On days distinguished by public solemnity, therefore, either those various necessities must be interrupted, or, when public observance and private necessity coincide, the fulfillment of both must be distinguished through their respective offices; or, as we mentioned above, different causes must be fulfilled through one offering.

The testimony of reliable men has brought it to our knowledge that Pope Leo, as he himself admitted, often celebrated the solemnities of Mass seven or nine times in one day, whereas Boniface, archbishop and martyr, celebrated Mass only once a day. Both lived not long before our own times, and both were outstanding in knowledge and rank.

Therefore, let each person abound in his own judgment (Rom. 14), provided that faith teaches those who offer more frequently not to think that God cannot otherwise distinguish petitions, and those who sacrifice offerings once a day not to suppose that the subtlety of their own faith is more acceptable to God than the devotion of their predecessors.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the order of Mass and the manner of offering

Since we have shown, in whatever way we could, how the solemnities of daily Mass came about, let us now explain what was established, when, and by whom concerning the office of the Mass, insofar as we have been able to discover.

What we now perform through the manifold office of prayers, readings, songs, and consecrations was all performed by the apostles and, as is believed, by those closest to them, simply through prayers and remembrance of the Lord’s passion, as he himself commanded. Hence, according to the testimonies mentioned above, they broke bread in their homes.

Luke also declares this in another passage, saying:

> “On the first day of the week, when we had assembled to break bread,”

and so forth (Acts 20).

The report of our predecessors is that in the earliest times Masses were customarily celebrated as we now receive communion on Good Friday of Easter—for on that day Masses are not celebrated among the Romans—that is, after the Lord’s Prayer had been said and, as our Lord himself commanded, after his passion had been commemorated. Those whom reason permitted were admitted to the Lord’s body and blood.

As religion subsequently advanced and grew, the offices of Masses were expanded by the worshipers of Christ. Either the peace that had been granted extended the Church’s boundaries more widely, or the abundance of saints, as their number increased through the strengthening of the practice, made this possible more frequently.

We have already said that the same thing occurred in the construction and decoration of sacred buildings—not because any of those who came later were greater than the apostles in knowledge or devotion, but because the apostles were chiefly concerned with calling people from unbelief to faith and from darkness to light, and with making them firm in the truth. Through the very simplicity of religion, they were better able to persuade the inexperienced of what they wished.

Hence, as is read, the first believers from the Gentiles wished to be weighed down by the burden of the legal commandments.

Many among the Greeks and Latins therefore established the order of Mass as seemed appropriate to them. The Romans, receiving their practice of observances from blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, added in each period whatever was judged suitable.

Many nations admire their practice in sacred matters for this reason: its beginnings shine with the eminence of such a great teaching received from the apostolic summit, and no Church throughout the world has remained equally pure from every dross of heresies throughout all past ages as the Roman Church.

Ambrose, bishop of Milan, also arranged the order of Mass and of the other offices for his own Church and for the other people of Liguria; these observances are still maintained today in the Milanese Church.

Let us therefore follow, as best we can, the order of the Roman Mass.

Pope Celestine, the forty-fifth, instituted the singing of antiphons at the entrance, as is read in the Acts of the Roman Pontiffs. Until his time, only one reading from the Apostle and the Gospel had been read before the sacrifice.

The litanies that follow—that is, “Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison” (“Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy”)—are believed to have been taken from Greek practice, because the words are Greek and the Greeks themselves repeat them frequently in their Masses.

As for the angelic hymn, in which certain words spoken by the angels in praise of God around the Lord’s Nativity are expressed briefly, the holy Fathers who followed added very sweet and suitable phrases for the common praise of the holy and undivided Trinity. Thus, just as its beginning was ordained by the heavenly ministers, so its entire sequence might also be filled with divine mysteries.

I mean that Telesphorus, the ninth Roman pontiff, established that hymn should be sung before the sacrifice, so that the minds of those assembled for the celebration of such great holiness might be soothed by the sweetness of angelic melody. But here one may ask: If this same hymn began to be sung before the sacrifice in the time of this pope, why is it recorded that long afterward, under Coelestine, only the reading of the Apostle and the Gospel preceded the sacrifice, so that Coelestine necessarily appears to have placed before them antiphons from the Psalms of David to be sung before those very readings [Col. 0945B]?

The answer must be either that Telesphorus indeed ordained that this hymn be sung at the beginning of the Mass, but that among his successors this ordinance itself was discontinued until the entire order of the Mass was more fully arranged by those who followed; or that he decreed that the hymn itself should be used on the greatest festivals and by bishops alone. This too seems to be indicated at the beginning of the book of sacramentaries. Therefore it was written that, up to the time of Coelestine, only the readings had been given before the sacrifice: this is to be understood as meaning that, although that hymn was sometimes sung before Masses, as we have said, it was nevertheless not something regularly placed before the readings in every Mass by all priests [Col. 0945C], before Coelestine established that antiphons should be sung at the entrance.

Or it may have happened that Coelestine taught that *Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus, Dominus Deus*, and the rest, should be said before the sacrifice. This too can be called an angelic hymn, since the prophet Isaiah (chapter VI) records that the seraphim proclaimed its beginning. But by certain uninstructed persons, at the same place where Telesphorus is said to have placed an angelic hymn before the sacrifice, the words *Gloria in excelsis Deo* may have been added, because they thought that no other hymn could be understood as the angelic hymn except the one that the angels sang when the Lord was born.

If the words *Gloria in excelsis Deo* had not been included in the chapter on Telesphorus, the foregoing question would not have arisen, and the angelic hymn [Col. 0945D] would have been understood as the one sung before the *actio*—that is, the Canon. This assertion appears to be supported by the statement that Symmachus, the [perhaps read: fifty-third] Roman pontiff, established that *Gloria in excelsis Deo* should be said every Sunday and on the birthdays of the saints. Either, then, Telesphorus did not add that hymn, as we said above, or, if he did, his ordinance remained incomplete for a long time.

The prayers that we call Collects—because we gather together, that is, conclude, their necessary petitions in concise brevity—were composed by different authors, according as it seemed appropriate. For it was customary not only during the offices of the Mass, but also in other suitable prayers and conversations, wherever persons more eminent than the rest were present, to conclude the matter with a brief prayer [Col. 0946A]. We recognize this also in the examples of the holy Fathers, when some, as a mark of honor, asked others to conclude the prayers.

The venerable teacher Augustine also ended his address to the people in certain sermons in such a way that he said at the conclusion, “Let us turn to the Lord.” This is understood to mean that, in an extemporaneous prayer, he directed the common petition to the Lord. So even now priests customarily append brief prayers—namely, Collects—at the conclusions of the nocturnal or daytime assembly. Some prayers of this kind are such that they ought to be said only in connection with the celebration of the sacrifice. Others, however, may be used both in the office of the Mass and, equally, in other places.

As the worship of the divine religion increased, as we said above, the composition of the prayers and offices of the Church also gradually increased [Col. 0946B]. Many people—some possessing the highest learning, others moderate learning, and others the least—added what seemed suitable for expressing the matters at hand. Therefore we believe that the Councils of Carthage and Milevis decreed that prayers and petitions composed by anyone should not be said unless they had been approved by a council. For Pope Gelasius, fifty-first in order, is likewise said to have arranged both the prayers composed by himself and those composed by others.

The Churches of Gaul also used their own prayers, many of which are still retained. And because many things, having authors of such uncertainty, seemed uncertain [variant: inserted] and lacked integrity of meaning, blessed Gregory took care to assemble whatever was reasonable. After excluding what seemed excessive or ill-composed, he composed the book called the *Sacramentary*, as its title most clearly indicates [Col. 0946C]. If anything in it is found to limp with respect to this meaning, it should be believed to have been added afterward not by him, but by others who were less careful.

It is not altogether certain who first established the apostolic or Gospel readings before the celebration of the sacrifice. It is nevertheless believed that this arrangement was made by the first successors of the apostles, chiefly for the following reason: in the Gospels these same sacrifices are commanded to be celebrated, while in the Apostle it is taught how they ought to be celebrated. Moreover, before the mystery of the most holy *actio*—that is, the Canon—they were to recognize from the Gospel the foundation of their salvation and faith, and from the Apostle to receive the instrument of that same faith and of conduct pleasing to God. [Col. 0946D]

What is lower in dignity is placed first, so that the minds of the hearers may progress from lesser things toward the apprehension of greater things and ascend step by step from the lowest to the highest.

Pope Anastasius, forty-first in order, established that whenever the holy Gospel was recited, priests should stand not upright but bent over, so that they might also demonstrate bodily the humility taught by the Lord.

It appears that at that time no other readings were placed before the Gospel except those of the Apostle Paul. The author who wrote the *Gesta of the Pontiffs* mentioned only these when he added his reference to the antiphons: “Previously this was not done, except that the Epistle of the blessed apostle Paul and the holy Gospel were read.” Saint [Col. 0947A] Pope Damasus also shows this, writing to Jerome, in almost the same words. Perhaps at first only readings from Paul were read in that place. Later, however, when everything had been more broadly expanded, other readings—not only from the New Testament but also from the Old, as the order of the feasts required—were interspersed.

Nor should it seem surprising that the offices are said to have increased gradually, while many things necessary to them were still lacking. For even to this day, when almost everything is already abundant, we see readings, Collects, and various kinds of praises still being added, so that in this too that prophetic saying may appear to be fulfilled: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. XII).

But one must observe, as blessed Augustine says, that those things should be sung which have been written to be sung [Col. 0947B]. The Responsories and the Alleluia sung before the Gospel appear to have been added later, after the practice of saying antiphons at the entrance had come to an end. These seem also to have been prohibited by the canons of the Spanish bishops, which were established long afterward. For those canons command that no hymn be placed between the apostolic reading and the Gospel in the order of the Mass. From this it is understood that some people attempted this at that time, but that, because of the novelty of the practice, their effort had not yet been accepted by certain others. Later, however, having been approved by Roman usage, it spread to all the Churches of the Latins.

The Creed of the Catholic faith is also rightly recited in the solemn celebrations of Mass after the Gospel [Col. 0947C], so that through the holy Gospel faith may be believed in the heart for righteousness, while through the Creed confession may be made with the mouth for salvation.

It should also be noted that the Greeks transferred that Creed—which we adopt within the Masses in imitation of them—rather than another, into the sweetness of song, because it belongs properly to the Council of Constantinople and perhaps seemed more suitable in musical melodies than the Nicene Creed, which is earlier in time. It was also so that, against the poisons of heretics, the devotion of the faithful might repeat, even during the celebration of the sacraments, the remedies prepared at the see of their royal city. Thus that practice is believed to have passed from them to the Romans.

Among the Gauls and Germans, however, after Felix the heretic had been deposed and condemned under the glorious Charles, ruler of the Franks, the same Creed began to be repeated more broadly and more frequently in the offices of the Mass [Col. 0947D].

The Council of Toledo also decreed that the same Creed should be recited every Sunday according to the custom of the Eastern Churches, so that, before the Lord’s Prayer was said, true faith might have a more manifest testimony, and the breasts of the people, purified, might approach to taste beforehand the body and blood of Christ.

At the council held in the same place it was also decreed that the hymn of the three youths should be sung every Sunday at Mass from the pulpit. The Romans, because of the multiplicity of their offices, do this only on four days of the year, on which the number of twelve readings is completed.

The Offertory, which is sung during the offering, is said to have entered Christian usage from the custom of the former people [Col. 0948A]. Nevertheless, we do not clearly read who specifically added it to our offices. We may make the same admission concerning the antiphon that is said at Communion. For we truly believe that in ancient times the holy Fathers offered or communicated in silence; we still observe this practice on Holy Saturday of Easter.

But, as was said above, the dignity of the Church has advanced over time in various ways and stages, and will not cease to increase until the end. Finally, it is handed down that blessed Gregory, just as he brought the arrangement of the Masses and consecrations to its present form, also brought the discipline of the chant, for the most part, to the arrangement that has continued to be regarded as especially fitting, as is also recalled at the beginning of the *Antiphonary*.

[Col. 0948B] It should be known, however, that some people make offerings in a disorderly manner. They pay attention to the number of offerings rather than to the power of the sacraments, and often make an offering in passing at Masses at which they do not wish to remain. It is more reasonable to offer where one intends to remain, so that, having offered a gift to the Lord, one may likewise present a devout petition for receiving that same gift.

For it is not without reason that the *actio* says, “Those who offer to you”; it does not say, “Those who have offered,” so that we may understand that they ought to persist in offering until the things offered reach the purpose for which they were offered.

There also appears to be a considerable error in the belief of some that they cannot make a full commemoration of those for whom they offer unless they offer individual offerings for each person, or in their failure to think that the living and the dead may be offered for together [Col. 0948C]. For we truly know that one person died for all, and that there is one bread and one blood which the universal Church offers.

If someone wishes to offer separately for each person, let him do so because of the breadth of his devotion and his desire to increase his prayers, not because of the foolish opinion that one sacrament of God is not a general remedy. In a certain sense, a person is imperfect in faith if he thinks that the Lord does not discern, when many are asked for in a single petition, what each one needs; or if he supposes that the Lord is wearied when the same offering is presented now for one person and now for another.

We do not know who first arranged the Preface of the *actio*, by which the disposition of the people is stirred up to give thanks and then the petition of the human voice seeks admission to the praises of the heavenly powers, or who first arranged the *actio* itself, by which the most holy mystery of the Lord’s body and blood is accomplished. The Romans also call this the Canon, as is frequently found in the *Pontificals* [Col. 0948D].

We understand from the added sections that it was enlarged not once but repeatedly. The Preface, for example, is said differently on certain feasts than on ordinary days; and sometimes it is not itself changed, but special commemorations of particular matters are inserted in the middle.

The *actio*, or Canon, is recognized as having been composed in sections especially from the fact that the names of the saints whose communion and fellowship are requested there are found in two places. It is not true that some people say two orders of names were made there because those placed later had not yet been crowned when the earlier ones were put into the Canon [Col. 0949A]. We know that John the Baptist was not only equal in time to the apostles but earlier than they; that Stephen was their contemporary and that both had been crowned before the apostles; and that the others who are listed in the later order lived in the same periods as those placed earlier.

It is therefore clear that the later teachers of the Church added to the ancient ordinances of the Fathers whatever seemed appropriate, so that, just as the multitude of the religious had increased, the institutions of religion might also increase.

We recognize that the first part of the aforementioned Canon is especially ancient from the fact that the order of the apostles is not arranged in it as it is found in the more accurate Gospels. This perhaps happened because that section was composed before the Gospels were corrected to the form in which they are now found among the Latins [Col. 0949B]. For in the earlier editions, as Jerome testifies, not only was the order of the Evangelists changed, but there was also a confused mixture of words and sentences.

Alexander, seventh in the papal sequence, introduced the Passion of the Lord into the priestly prayer when Masses are celebrated. Since this is written about him in the *Pontificals*, it is doubtful whether he arranged only that part of the *actio* in which the Passion of the Lord is commemorated, or the whole section from the beginning up to that point.

The second opinion seems to be contradicted by the fact that in that section saints are named who lived both before him and long after his time—unless we say that he commemorated only those who lived before him, while the names of the others were added later by different persons at their respective times [Col. 0949C]. Hence Alexander’s own name is also found in the later order.

Gregory, whom we have mentioned so often above, added to the prayer of the Canon the words: “And order our days in your peace.” Some wish the entire continuation of the Canon from that point to the end to be understood as having been composed by him. This view seems to be contradicted by the fact that the Passion of the Lord, which Alexander inserted into the same prayer, occurs after these verses.

Therefore some believe that Gregory added no more than those three petitions to the earlier ordinances: namely, petitions for peace in our times, deliverance from eternal punishments, and the attainment of fellowship with the saints [Col. 0949D].

Leo, who held the forty-sixth place in the Roman pontificate, also established that the words “A holy sacrifice,” and the rest, should be said within the *actio* of the sacrifice. Here too one may ask whether he added what follows from that point onward, or merely inserted in that place the words themselves, namely, “a holy sacrifice, an immaculate victim.” Since we do not read this explicitly, we do not wish to decide the matter.

It nevertheless follows that Gregory, who lived long after Leo, did not compose the entire Canon from the place where he inserted his additions to the end.

Gregory III, the third pope of that name, built an oratory in the Basilica of Saint Peter in honor of all the saints and established that daily offices and Masses should be celebrated there in their veneration. At the same time, he instituted that the priest should say in the Canon: “Whose solemnity is celebrated today in the presence of your majesty, Lord our God, throughout the whole world” [Col. 0950A]. Since this specifically pertains to that celebration, it was not noted in the Canon, which is said in general.

The *actio* is called the Canon itself because the Lord’s sacraments are accomplished in it; the Canon, in turn, is called the same *actio* because in it the sacraments are accomplished lawfully and according to rule.

The Lord’s Prayer follows, with appropriate additions. The first addition that precedes it proclaims the confidence by which we dare to call the Lord, our Creator, “Father”; the second, which follows it, explains from what evils and by whom we ask that the Lord deliver us.

Because the Lord’s Prayer was taken up in the consecration of the sacrifices before the other prayers, it is fittingly placed at the completion of that most sacred *actio*, so that those who are going to communicate, purified by it, may worthily receive for true salvation what has been sanctified.

Pope Innocent established by his decrees that the peace be given before Communion, so that by the act itself we might demonstrate ourselves to be at peace in accordance with what we promise in the holy prayer under the pledge of forgiveness.

Sergius, eighty-sixth among the Roman pontiffs, established that the *Agnus Dei* should be sung by clergy and people during the breaking of the Lord’s body, so that, while the Lord’s body is being prepared for distribution, those who are to receive it might pray that the innocent one who was offered for them would cause them to receive safely the pledges of eternal salvation [Col. 0950C].

Moreover, concerning the command of the canons that one who does not communicate should not come forward for the peace, some understand it to mean that no one should receive the peace at other Masses except those at which he communicates. Others, however, wish only the person who has been suspended from Communion by priestly judgment to be prohibited from the peace.

But they hold that a person who for some reason postpones Communion at that time [variant: “of times,” with *illo* (“that”) deleted], while nevertheless not being outside communion, should not be separated from the grace of peace, lest his humility be marked with suspicion of graver crimes.

Since we have already said something about the differing practices concerning Communion (above, chapter 9), it seems appropriate to add that some believe it sufficient to communicate once a day, even if they have attended several Masses; while others wish to communicate at every Mass they attend on that day [Col. 0950D].

I do not consider either group blameworthy, because, as Augustine says concerning those who communicate daily and those who do so less often: “Reverence for holy things holds the former back, while love of things that bring salvation invites the latter.” The priest himself also does not fail to communicate as often as he celebrates Masses during the day.

If he does not do so, he is to be struck by canonical judgment (*De consecratione*, distinction 2, chapter “Relatum”). Nor is it surprising that this is understood of the priest, since the Councils of Zaragoza and Toledo jointly decreed concerning everyone that whoever receives the Eucharist but does not consume it is to be rejected as a sacrilegious person.

The proper time for communicating is before the final prayer, which is called the prayer “for completion,” because its petition is directed especially toward those who communicate [Col. 0951A]. This is also why the desire of those who wish to communicate at every Mass appears to be kindled: throughout the whole Mass, prayer is offered especially, and almost by name, for those who offer and communicate there.

We may and ought to say that, so that the same holy celebration of the Mass may be believed to benefit not merely a few but many, the others who persist in the faith and devotion of those who offer and communicate are also said to be and are participants in the same offering and Communion.

Although, when priests alone celebrate Masses, it may be understood that those for whom the offices are then celebrated are fellow-workers in the same *actio*, and that the priest represents them in certain responses, nevertheless we must acknowledge that the legitimate Mass is one in which the priest, the respondent, the offerer, and the communicant are present, as the very composition of the prayers clearly demonstrates [Col. 0951B].

The Council of Orléans also decreed that the people should not leave the Mass before the priest’s blessing. This blessing is understood to be the priest’s final prayer.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Time of Mass

The time for celebrating Mass varies according to the character of the solemnities. Sometimes it is celebrated before midday, sometimes around the ninth hour, sometimes in the evening, and sometimes at night.

For Pope Telesphorus established that no one should presume to celebrate Mass at any time before the course of the third hour had passed [Col. 0951C], since according to the Gospel of Mark our Lord is said to have been crucified at that hour.

In this connection it should be noted that one should not fast on Sundays and major feast days, unless necessity compels it, as the canons also show; nor should the angelic hymn, that is, *Gloria in excelsis Deo*, or [for *et*, “and”] the *Alleluia*, be said on fasting days or ever after midday, except on the two Saturdays of Easter and Pentecost, which are adorned with special mysteries.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Sacred Vessels and Vestments

The vessels in which our sacraments are chiefly placed and consecrated are chalices and patens. *Calix* (“chalice”) derives from the Greek name κύλιξ (*kylix*); *patena* derives from *patere* (“to be open”), because it is broad and open; *ampulla* means something “of little breadth.”

Zephyrinus, the twenty-sixth Roman pontiff, established that Masses should be celebrated with glass patens. Then Urban, the eighteenth pope, made all things consecrated for the ministers of silver, and twenty-five patens [perhaps: four, etc.] [Col. 0951D].

Here, as in the other forms of worship, the dignity of the Church increased more and more with the passage of time.

Boniface, martyr and bishop, when asked whether it was permissible to accomplish the sacraments in wooden vessels, replied: “Once there were golden priests who used wooden chalices; now, on the contrary, wooden priests use golden chalices.”

Pope Sylvester established that the sacrifice of the altar should be celebrated neither on silk nor on dyed cloth, but only on linen produced from the earth, just as the body of the Lord Jesus Christ was buried in a clean shroud [Col. 0952A].

The priestly vestments also gradually increased toward the ornamentation they possess today. In the earliest times priests celebrated Mass dressed in ordinary clothing, as certain Easterners are reportedly still accustomed to do.

Stephen, however, the twenty-fourth [pope], established that priests and deacons should not use the sacred vestments in daily life, except in church. Sylvester ordained that deacons should wear dalmatics in church and that their left side should be covered with a linen pallium.

At first, priests wore dalmatics before the use of chasubles; later, when they had begun to use chasubles, they granted the dalmatics to deacons. That bishops themselves were nevertheless to use them is clear from the fact that Gregory and other Roman pontiffs permitted their use to some bishops and prohibited it to others [Col. 0952B]. This shows that the privilege was not then granted to everyone, whereas now nearly all bishops and some presbyters consider themselves permitted to wear a dalmatic beneath the chasuble.

The Council of Braga decreed: “Let a priest not celebrate Mass without an orarium.”

Various people added various things to the sacred vestments, either in imitation of those used by the ancient priests or to express mystical meaning. What each of the vestments we now use signifies has already been sufficiently explained by our predecessors.

In their number, however, the present vestments correspond to the ancient ones: just as there were the tunic, the linen *superhumerale*, the *superhumerale*, the breastplate, the belt, the undergarments, the tiara, and the plate, so here there are the dalmatic, the alb, the *mappula*, [Col. 0952C] the orarium, the girdle, the sandals, the chasuble, and the pallium.

Therefore, just as among those ancient vestments only the pontiffs used the last, so among these present vestments only the chief shepherds use the last.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Canonical Hours and the Bending of the Knees; on Hymns, and Likewise on Chants and Their Development
Having set forth what seemed necessary to say concerning the order of the Mass, let us add, if the Lord permits, what is to be said concerning the appointed canonical hours. It should be understood that many ages passed after the revelation of the Gospel before the solemn observances of certain hours by day and night were arranged as they are now. In the Old Testament we read (Exod. 29) of certain fixed hours of prayer, such as the times of the morning and evening sacrifice. And when Daniel is said to have knelt in prayer three times a day (Dan. 6), we must believe that he did so for good reason.

In the New Testament, too, many examples are found not only of prayer but also of kneeling. For the Lord Jesus Christ, before his Passion, fell on his face and adored the Father (Luke 22). And Stephen, having knelt, prayed for those who were stoning him (Acts 7). It is also written of the apostle Bartholomew that he knelt a hundred times by day and a hundred times by night.

Although the whole Church observes the practice of kneeling, the nation of the Scots is especially devoted to this practice. Many of them appear to undertake it at numerous intervals, others at fewer intervals, but always at fixed and counted times by day or night, not only to lament their sins but also to fulfill their daily devotion.

The canons state at which hours or times one should pray during the public offices without kneeling: namely, on Sundays, on the greater feast days, and during Quinquagesima. According to these canons, public penitents must always kneel.

The canonical hours, therefore, although all are celebrated with rational authority and although nothing is observed in them that is not confirmed by the examples or sayings of the holy Fathers, have nevertheless been assigned in certain cases to more explicit precedents. Thus we read that our Lord himself spent the night in prayer (Luke 6); and Paul and Silas, praying at midnight in prison, were shown by the earthquake to have done so (Acts 16). Around the third hour the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles while they were praying (Acts 2). At the sixth hour Peter went up to the upper room to pray (Acts 10); and likewise, with John, he went into the Temple at the ninth hour, the hour of prayer (Acts 3), at which hour an angel also appeared to Cornelius while he was praying.

Philo, too, is a witness [Note: [Col. 0953D] See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*.] that the primitive Church among the Alexandrians, among its other good practices, celebrated “Lucan” (*lucanos*; reading uncertain) hymns before cockcrow.

From these and similar examples we understand that many observed hours which are also now highly celebrated, though not with the distribution of psalms or prayers that we now use. We observe that this distribution was begun around the time of Theodosius the Elder and subsequently completed for many reasons.

For Ambrose of Milan, as blessed Augustine testifies in his books of *Confessions*, composed hymns of divine praise for the people and thereby eased the persecution of the empress Justina through this novel course of action. At that time, as is also written in the *Life of Ambrose*, antiphons, hymns, and vigils began to be celebrated in the Church of Milan. Hilary of Poitiers likewise composed hymns. And it is written of Pope Gelasius that he composed treatises and hymns after the manner of blessed Ambrose.

Damasus, however, established that psalms should be sung day and night in all churches and monasteries, and he commanded this of bishops and priests.
