Then John of Constantinople [Chrysostom] was the first to increase the prayers in the nocturnal hymns, chiefly for this reason: the Arians held gatherings outside the city, while on Saturdays and Sundays they assembled inside the gates and porticoes, singing hymns and antiphons composed according to Arian doctrine. They did this for much of the night, and at dawn, with the same antiphons, they entered through the middle of the city by the gate and hurried to their church.

Since they did not cease doing this frequently, as though to reproach the orthodox—for they often sang this also: “Where are those who say that the three are one in power?”—John then, so that simple people would not be drawn away by such songs, instructed his own people to occupy themselves with nocturnal hymns as well, so that the work of the Arians might be obscured and the profession of the faithful strengthened.

John’s zeal, therefore, so useful though it was, ended amid crowds and dangers. These matters are inserted in the tenth book of the ecclesiastical history called the *Tripartite History*. A little farther on it adds the following:

“Yet it must be said from where the practice of singing antiphons in the Church first arose. Ignatius of Antioch in Syria, the third bishop after the apostle Peter, who also lived with the apostles themselves, saw a vision of angels singing antiphons and hymns to the Holy Trinity. He is believed to have transmitted the manner of that vision to the Church of Antioch, and from there it passed to all the Churches.”

It should be noted that “hymns” means not only those that proceed in meters or rhythms, such as those composed by Ambrose, Hilary, Bede, the Father of the English, and Prudentius, the scholar of Spain, together with many others, but also the other praises that are expressed in appropriate words and sweet sounds. Hence among the Hebrews the Book of Psalms is called the Book of Hymns.

Although metrical hymns are not sung in certain churches, general hymns—that is, praises—are sung in all of them. That those which are legitimately composed should also be sung is shown by the authority of the Council of Toledo, which says among other things:

“And since some are known to have been composed with great devotion in praise of God, the apostles, and the triumphs of the martyrs, such as those published by the most blessed teachers Hilary and Ambrose—and since certain people specifically reject them because they do not derive from the books of the holy canons or from apostolic tradition—let them also reject that hymn composed and approved by everyone, which we say daily in both public and private offices at the end of all the psalms:

‘Glory and honor to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.’

“Let them also reject the hymn that the angels sang to Christ born in the flesh:

‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.’

“The remaining words that follow there were composed by ecclesiastical teachers. Therefore, are these not to be sung in the churches either, because they are not found in the books of the Holy Scriptures? Masses, prayers, orations, commendations, and impositions of hands are composed; if none of these are sung in the Church, all ecclesiastical offices are empty.”

These words show that many things are newly composed in the Church which, provided they do not depart from the faith of truth, are not to be rejected.

Moreover, metrical and rhythmic hymns are sung in the Ambrosian offices. Some have also been accustomed to use them occasionally in the solemn celebrations of Mass, for the sake of the compunction that is increased by harmonious sweetness. It is indeed reported that Paulinus, patriarch of Forum Julii, often, and especially at private Masses, celebrated hymns composed either by others or by himself around the offering of the sacramental gifts.

I would certainly believe that a man of such learning and such stature did this neither without authority nor without careful reasoning.

Hymns are also sung at the canonical hours in the offices that blessed Benedict, an abbot distinguished by every holiness, ordered. Calling them Ambrosian, he either intended those composed by Ambrose himself or others composed in imitation of the Ambrosian hymns.

It should nevertheless be understood that many hymns are thought to have been made by Ambrose which were not published by him at all. For it seems incredible that he composed such pieces as many of those that exist—namely, pieces that have no continuity of meaning and display, in their very diction, a rusticity foreign to Ambrose.

Concerning the hymn inserted into all the offices in honor of the holy and unique Trinity, it should be said that the holy Fathers arranged it in different ways. The Spaniards, as we mentioned above, wished it invariably to be said in the form stated above.

The Greeks say:

“Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, now and always, and for ever and ever. Amen.”

The Latins sing this hymn in the same order and with the same words, adding only in the middle:

“As it was in the beginning.”

Because of these additions, certain less discerning Greeks in recent times attempted to attack the Latins with accusations.

Nevertheless, we understand that we do not err in this, since we believe in the coeternity of the glory of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. We also know that the Romans, most steadfast guardians of the faith, would not have accepted this form of the hymn, after removing other compositions, unless they had recognized it as pure from every error.

Many indeed affirm that this hymn was issued by the most sacred decree of the Council of Nicaea, so that, interwoven with all offices and prayers, it might impress upon the mind the faith of the coeternal Trinity and, in each petition, cause that same confession to obtain more effectively the favor of divine hearing.

Some therefore attach this hymn to nearly all psalms, and sometimes to the divisions of psalms, but to fewer responsories, as do those who follow the statutes of Father Benedict in the canonical hours. The Romans repeat it less often in the psalms and more often in the responsories.

Certainly, the verse customarily said at the beginning of all offices—except the Mass—that are performed at the canonical hours, namely, “O God, come to my assistance,” and what follows, is found to have been prescribed by the ancient Fathers in their *Collations* to precede everything, not only the offices but also their works. Thus the invocation of divine assistance, assumed at the beginning of every action, makes both the constancy of asking and the power of obtaining easier.

In the offices for the dead and around the solemnity of the Lord’s Passion, the beginnings and completions of the offices are not performed as in the other offices, in order to signify sadness, unless some more weighty decree intervenes.

Since there is such great diversity among the offices—not only according to the variety of peoples and languages, but also within one people or language because of changes in time or the deliberate instruction of teachers—if I wished to repeat everything that I have already read concerning this multiplicity, I would seem more burdensome than useful to my listeners. I shall therefore omit what is endless, affirming only this: the complete order of the offices now observed throughout the Roman world was established after many ages of antiquity had passed, and was expanded through regulations to the highest dignity of holy religion.

As the number of the faithful increased, and the plague of heresy increasingly stained Catholic peace, it was necessary for the worship of true observance to be increased, so that a more splendid religion might invite the minds of those approaching the faith, and an enriched worship might display the steadfastness of Catholics against their enemies.

Indeed, the practice of memorizing and exercising songs or psalmody was so rare among earlier generations that, concerning nearly the last of the Roman bishops, men who lived scarcely two hundred years before our own time, it is written as something memorable and extraordinary if any of them appeared more distinguished than the others in these matters.

Hormisdas, the fifty-fourth in succession, organized the clergy and trained them in the psalms. Leo, the eighty-second, and Benedict, who followed him immediately, as well as Sergius, the eighty-sixth, are said to have flourished in knowledge of psalmody and song.

Of Gregory III something apparently unheard-of and new is reported: that he knew all the psalms by heart. This indicates that few of his predecessors had learned the Psalter in this way. For they used to insert the psalms into their offices, partly by reading them, just as they did the other Scriptures. If you consider this carefully, it is evident from many scriptural testimonies.

Blessed Gregory is believed to have distributed the order of the chant to be said at the hours of the day and night in a complete arrangement, just as we said above in the book on the Sacraments, although many composed prayers, antiphons, or responsories either before or after him. We also spoke above of the beginning of the antiphons (chap. 22).

Responsories, moreover, are said to have first been invented by Italians—whether by Ambrose or by someone else who rejoiced in a new increase of divine praises. And because the Gallican Church, equipped with men no less learned, possessed a considerable repertory of sacred offices, some elements from it are said to have been mingled with the Roman offices. Many acknowledge that these can be distinguished from the other chants both by their words and by their melody.

Nevertheless, by observing the privilege of the Roman See, and because the rational appropriateness of the arrangements made by that See recommends it, it came about that the custom and teaching of that same See prevailed in nearly all the churches of the Latins. For no other tradition is equally to be followed, whether in the rule of faith or in the teaching of observances.

That order of offices is also worthy of praise which blessed Father Benedict established for monks to observe: namely, that those who are distinguished from others by their profession should strive to discharge something more than others in the burden of continual service.

We believe that church leaders do not prohibit this arrangement because it is close to the authority of the Roman Church and because blessed Gregory, in describing the outstanding life of Father Benedict, praises the Rule composed by him, in which this same order of offices is found, and by his own authority appears to support its statutes.

There are, however, some who, I do not know through what presumption, do not wish to use this constitution. They want to excuse their laziness or insolence by the permission that the most holy man, through the greatness of his humility, appears to grant: that if anyone dislikes the distribution of the psalms which he made, he may arrange it otherwise if he judges another arrangement better.

It is as though they could devise something better and more suitable to their own order than the man who is said to have been filled with the spirit of all the saints.

As for the psalms, while the Romans still possess them according to the Septuagint translators, the Gauls and some of the Germans sing the Psalter according to the revision that Father Jerome produced from the Septuagint edition. Gregory, bishop of Tours, is said to have borrowed this from the Roman Fathers and transferred it to the churches of Gaul.

As for a more perfected knowledge of chant, which nearly all France now cherishes, Pope Stephen introduced it through his clerics, at Pippin’s request, when he came to Pippin, the father of Charlemagne—first into Francia—to demand justice for Saint Peter from the Lombards. From there its use grew strong far and wide.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the development and immersion of baptism, and the reasons for baptizing

[Col. 0957B]

Something must also be said about baptism. It is known to have been clearly prefigured in the crossing of the Red Sea (Exod. 14) and of the Jordan (Josh. 3), and more secretly prefigured by many other figures.

John first displayed this at the beginning of the new grace to those converted to faith in Christ—not through his own invention but because it had been provided by divine ordinance, as he himself testifies when he says: “He who sent me to baptize in water,” and what follows (John 1).

He baptized not for the remission of sins, which is customarily accomplished by Christ’s baptism, but unto repentance, telling them to believe in the one who was to come—that is, in Jesus. Concerning him he also bore witness, saying:

“I indeed baptize you in water for repentance. But he who is to come after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry; he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3).

And plainly it was fitting that, in the new salvation of the human race through the coming of the Son of God in the flesh, a new mystery of purification should be opened. Just as the priests of the Levitical order were accustomed to wash before offering bodily sacrifices, so all heirs of the Christian name, who are called a royal priesthood (1 Pet. 2), should, cleansed from the stain of sins by a spiritual washing, offer spiritual sacrifices to God as a sweet fragrance.

It should be understood that at first believers were baptized simply in rivers or springs. Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, so that he might consecrate the same washing in us, was baptized by John in the Jordan. And as we read elsewhere: “John was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there” (John 3). The evangelist Philip also baptized the eunuch in a spring that he found beside the road (Acts 8).

As we showed above that, with the progress of time, the honor of religion and the institutions of the churches grew toward their full splendor, so the celebration of this mystical washing gradually increased through the passage of time.

Some added anointing with chrism. No one should doubt that this was taken from ancient custom, since in the earliest times baptism was customarily confirmed by the laying on of hands, which Peter and John are read to have performed in Samaria (Acts 8).

This confirmation belonged then to the first pastors of the Church, and there is no doubt that it still belongs to them. Hence the canons often forbid priests to prepare chrism or to mark the baptized on the forehead, since this is reserved to bishops.

The decrees of Pope Innocent and the statutes of Silvester testify to this. Silvester himself established that a priest should anoint the baptized person with chrism in case death was approaching. If someone baptized by a deacon or by any other person should happen to die before confirmation, it should not be believed that he perishes for this reason, because he may be saved under the faith in which he believed, provided that subsequent sins do not destroy him. Read the decrees of the Council of Elvira.

Some added exorcisms to the sacrament of baptism, others the consecration of the font, others the infusion of salt or saliva, and others the formal instruction of catechumens. Others established the scrutinies with the greatest care as preparation for so great a mystery.

Many other practices were also introduced, discovered through examples of divine actions or sayings and recognized as full of highly appropriate meanings concerning spiritual progress, as the abundant testimonies of earlier writers concerning these matters demonstrate.

True baptism is celebrated only in the name of the highest Trinity, as the Lord himself showed and the canons of the apostles teach. Therefore, whoever has been baptized either by heretics who baptize in the Trinity or by any other person under the legitimate invocation of that same Holy Trinity must not be rebaptized, lest the invocation of the highest dignity appear to be annulled. Rather, what was incomplete must be completed by chrism and the laying on of hands. This is frequently found in the canons and decrees of the Fathers.

It is also read in the last book of the *Ecclesiastical History* that Athanasius, while still a boy, played at imitating baptism among his companions. When Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, learned the question put by the baptizer, the responses of those being baptized, and the other actions that, although performed as play, had nevertheless been carried out according to our religion, he judged that they should not be rebaptized but confirmed with the customary mysteries of the Church.

The Council of Elvira also permits the faithful who possess full baptism to baptize in an emergency.

Victor, the fifteenth Roman pontiff, likewise established that, when necessity required it, anyone coming from paganism could be baptized wherever water was found—whether in a river, the sea, or springs—provided that the confession of Christian belief had been made.

These and similar provisions do not grant indiscriminate permission to everyone to baptize, since the Council of Carthage forbids women to baptize. Rather, they show that when unavoidable necessity demands it, it is better for someone to be baptized anywhere and by anyone in the name of the Trinity than for a person in danger to perish without a remedy.

Accordingly, the legitimate times for baptism are not to be observed in such emergencies. According to the decrees of Leo, those endangered by illness, persecution, siege, or shipwreck must always be assisted. The Council of Gerunda likewise orders that an infant one day old, if in danger, should be baptized.

Concerning those whose status is uncertain—that is, those who cannot establish by any testimony that they have been baptized—we learn from the Council of Carthage and the decrees of Leo that they ought to be baptized.

Those who know that they have been baptized but do not know under what profession of faith were established by the decrees of Pope Leo to be received with the laying on of hands.

The legitimate times for baptism are designated as Easter and Pentecost, according to the decrees of the bishops Siricius, Leo, and Gelasius, although the Council of Gerunda names the Nativity of the Lord and Easter. Others also wished baptism to be administered on the Epiphany of the Lord, because tradition says that our Lord was baptized at that time; others prohibit this.

Since, according to the Apostle, we are baptized into the death of the Savior (Rom. 6), and since the Lord himself shows that those who will enter the kingdom of heaven must be reborn of water and the Spirit (John 3), the Roman bishops appropriately designated only these two times for the celebration of baptism: Easter and Pentecost. At the one, the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection are celebrated; at the other, the coming of the Holy Spirit.

Some require a threefold immersion, in imitation of the Lord’s three-day burial, as is established in the canons of the apostles and observed by Roman custom. Others insist upon a single immersion because of the unity of the Godhead, as is set forth most fully in the Council of Toledo.

There it is also recalled that, when Leander asked blessed Gregory about this matter, Gregory replied among other things that, since the faith is one, differing customs do not harm the Church.

We, however, by immersing three times, signify the mystery of the three-day burial, so that when the infant is brought up from the water for the third time, the resurrection after the three-day period may be represented.

If someone should think that this is also done in honor of the highest Trinity, that does not prevent a person from being immersed once in the water. Since one substance exists in three subsistences, it can in no way be blameworthy to immerse the infant in baptism three times or once: in the three immersions the Trinity of persons can be signified, and in the single immersion the unity of the Godhead.

Although this single immersion pleased the Spaniards at that time—they said that threefold immersion should be avoided because certain heretics had dared to teach that the substances in the Trinity were unlike one another, thereby denying the consubstantiality of the Holy Trinity—the more ancient practice and the reason stated above prevailed.

For if we abandon everything that heretics have twisted to their own perversity, nothing will remain for us, since they have erred even concerning God himself and have claimed as their own, through their errors, everything that appeared to belong to his worship.

It should also be noted that many people have been baptized not only by immersion but also by water poured over them, and that they may still be baptized in this way if necessity requires it. Thus, in the Passion of blessed Lawrence, we read of someone being baptized after a pitcher had been brought.

This can also occur when the greater size of an adult body does not permit a person to be immersed in smaller vessels.

[Note: [Col. 0959D] There is no doubt that in the earliest periods of the Church many adults and elderly people were sometimes baptized; indeed, some postponed baptism through a wicked custom until the end of life. But it is the common assertion of the orthodox that, from the very beginnings of the Church, there was an apostolic tradition, always practiced, of baptizing infants before the age of reason. See Bellarmine after the other authorities, Book VII, *On Baptism*, chapter 8.]

It should be noted that in those earliest times the grace of baptism was customarily given only to those who had already reached such bodily and mental maturity that they could know and understand what benefit was to be obtained in baptism, what was to be confessed and believed, and what, once reborn in Christ, was finally to be observed.

The venerable Father Augustine reports of himself in his books of *Confessions* that he remained a catechumen almost until the age of twenty-five. His intention was that, through this delay, he might be instructed concerning each matter and freely led to choose whatever he wished; then, when the passions of slippery youth had cooled, he would be better able to preserve what ought to be followed.

But as devotion to the divine religion increased, Christians who understood the teaching of the faith came to recognize that Adam’s original sin holds liable not only those who increased their transgression through their own deeds, but also those who committed no personal sin. For, according to the Psalmist, they were conceived and born in iniquities (Ps. 50) and cannot be free from sin while they proceed from a polluted root.

Thus the Apostle rightly says of all: “All have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace” (Rom. 3). And concerning Adam: “In whom all sinned” (Rom. 5).

Those who followed sound faith, therefore, understanding this, judged that infants should be baptized for the remission of sins, lest they perish if they died without the remedy of the grace of regeneration.

Certain heretics who resisted the grace of God argued that infants should not be baptized under any necessity because they had not yet sinned. If that were true, they should either not be baptized at all, or, if baptized without necessity, the sacrament of baptism in them would be incomplete and not true—the very sacrament that we confess in the Creed to be given for the remission of sins.

Therefore, since all whom the grace of God does not liberate perish in original sin, infants too are necessarily baptized, even though they have not added the increase of their own crimes.

Saint Augustine demonstrates this in his book *On the Baptism of Infants*. The African councils and the many testimonies of other Fathers also bear witness to it.

For this reason the practice of having godfathers and godmothers was introduced: they receive the infants from the font and answer on their behalf all that the infants themselves cannot confess because of the weakness of their age.

Likewise, the spiritual father or mother ought, when the person whom he or she received from the font of regeneration has reached the age of understanding, to explain to that person the confession made on his or her behalf. Having been freed from the sickness of sins through another’s confession, just as the paralytic was freed through the faith of those who carried him (Luke 5), the person should strive to live worthily of the salvation granted and, by personal action, fulfill what the sponsors confessed with their mouths—if he does not wish to lose the salvation he obtained through their faith.

A father or mother should not receive his or her own child from the font, so that a distinction may exist between spiritual and bodily generation. If this should happen by accident, the couple who have received the spiritual bond of co-parenthood through their common child may no longer have the relations of bodily marriage with one another.

Therefore not only those who, because of their age, can speak and understand what is being done are to be baptized, but also those who cannot yet speak either for themselves or on their own behalf.

Thus the Council of Carthage also established that sick people who can no longer speak are to be baptized when they have expressed their will through witnesses, or when they themselves have been able to confirm it by some signs.

The council at the place mentioned above prohibits baptism or the Eucharist from being given to the dead, although in the earliest times of evangelical preaching some are reported to have possessed such fervor in their belief in God that, for certain beloved persons who had died before the proclamation of the truth or the reception of baptism, they sought to be baptized.

The Apostle Paul recalls this in support of belief in the resurrection (1 Cor. 15), because unless they believed that the dead would rise, it would have been foolish to seek baptism for those who no longer existed.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the giving of tithes

Abraham indicates by his deeds that tithes are to be given to God and to the priests of God (Gen. 14); Jacob indicates this by his promises (Gen. 28); then the Law establishes it (Lev. 27; Num. 18), and all the holy teachers recall it.

It was certainly fitting that the Israelites should give the Lord tithes of their livestock, crops, and all their money. To free them, he struck the Egyptians with ten plagues; in the final plague he destroyed the firstborn of all, and he granted his own people the favor of plundering Egypt by obtaining its wealth.

Concerning these tithes the remarkable teacher Augustine says:

“ Tithes are demanded as a debt. What if God were to say: ‘You are mine, O human being; the earth that you cultivate is mine; the seeds that you scatter are mine; the animals that you weary are mine; the warmth of the sun is mine. Since everything is mine, you who contribute so little—did you deserve only a tenth? Keep nine parts for yourself; give me the tenth. If you do not give me the tenth, I shall take away the nine. If you give me the tenth, I shall multiply the nine.’ ”

Since the Jewish people observed the commandment of tithes with such diligence that, as the Lord himself testifies (Matt. 23), they paid tithes even from the smallest garden plants—rue, mint, and cumin—why should the evangelical people not fulfill the same command with greater zeal, since they have both a greater number of priests and a purer worship of the sacraments?

Tithes must therefore be given so that, through this devotion, God may be appeased and may more generously provide what is necessary, as we showed above.

They are also given so that priests and ministers of the Church, relieved of the care and anxiety of bodily necessities without which this life cannot be lived, may be freer for meditation on divine law, the administration of teaching, and the willing fulfillment of spiritual service.

They are also given so that the offering of the people may be sacrificed to the Lord as a daily oblation and, according to canonical statutes, may contribute to the support of the poor and the restoration of churches.

For, according to the canons, the offerings of the faithful are to be divided into four parts: one for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth reserved for the restoration of churches.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the performance of litanies

The Romans customarily perform litanies—that is, public rogations, which we call the Greater Litanies—annually on a designated day, namely the seventh day before the Kalends of May [25 April].

Pope Gregory instituted them at the beginning of his pontificate, when, after an extraordinary flood of waters, an unusual and pestilential disease of the groin was ravaging the Roman people following the death of Pope Pelagius.

At that time he arranged the litany in seven groups, as Paul recalls in the *Deeds of the Lombards* (during the reign of Maurice), so that those praying to the Lord might be distributed into seven companies and might implore the Lord’s mercy with greater intensity.

The first choir consisted of the clergy; the second, all the abbots with their monks; the third, all the abbesses with their communities; the fourth, all the children; the fifth, all the laymen; the sixth, all the widows; and the seventh, all married women.

The three-day litanies, which are celebrated annually throughout the churches of Gaul and Germany on the days immediately preceding the Ascension of the Lord, were established in Gaul.

In the time of Clovis, king of the Franks, who with his people was the first to become Christian, the city of Vienne was repeatedly shaken by earthquakes and laid waste by attacks of beasts. Saint Mamertus, bishop of that city, is reported to have instituted these litanies on account of the evils just mentioned.

The Council of Orléans both orders that they be performed at that time and commands everyone to abstain from servile labor so that they may be celebrated more fully.

The Spaniards, however, because it is written, “The children of the bridegroom cannot mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them” (Matt. 9), refused to fast during the fifty days of Easter. They therefore placed their litanies after Pentecost, performing them on the Thursday, Friday, and Saturday of that same week.

Some of them established a three-day fast on the Ides of December; others on the Kalends of December.

It should be noted that “litanies” means not only the recitation of names by which the saints are invoked for assistance in human weakness, but also that everything done through supplications is called a rogation.

The litany of the names of the saints is believed to have been adopted into use after Jerome, following Eusebius of Caesarea, composed the *Martyrology* over the course of the year. He was asked by the bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus to compose this work for the following reason: the devout emperor Theodosius, in a council of bishops, praised Gregory, bishop of Córdoba, because every day, when completing the Masses, he mentioned many of the martyrs whose anniversaries were being celebrated.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the sprinkling of water

[Col. 0963A]

Pope Alexander established that water for sprinkling should be blessed with salt and sprinkled in the dwellings of the faithful.

Just as the former people, serving under the ordinances of the Law, were purified with blood (Exod. 24), so the new Christian people, reborn through the sacrament of baptism, are rightly sprinkled with blessed water. Thus, just as the blood of the lamb was placed on the doorposts to repel the destroyer (Exod. 12), so the mystery of water may protect the bodies and dwellings of those who have been reborn.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the blessing of the candle

[Col. 0963B]

Pope Zosimus established that the candle should be blessed not only in the principal churches but also in parish churches.

The Council of Toledo shows that this practice itself was observed by some of the Spaniards and neglected by others.

## CHAPTER XXXI. A comparison of the ecclesiastical and secular orders
Around the conclusion of these matters, it pleases me to insert a comparison of certain secular and ecclesiastical dignities, although I am not unaware that the arrangements of powers and offices are so perplexed by the diversity of peoples, places, and times that scarcely anything certain can be set forth about them. For who, after all, would admit that he knows how the empire—not to speak of the Assyrians, Medes, and Macedonians, but even of the Romans, whose case is better known and nearer to us—was distributed and organized among administrations and offices? Over the long course of time, some powers have been exchanged for others, some subordinated, and others concealed, so that the very instability of affairs proves that what is human is temporary: by a certain inconstancy it is both extended into greater magnitude and contracted into less.

Setting aside, therefore, what is uncertain, let us compare matters that are better known to one another, so that we may show how the arrangements of worldly wisdom have been transformed by sacred distinctions into the spiritual commonwealth of the universal Church—just as, according to the ancient history, either the money of the Egyptians was put to the use of the tabernacle (Exod. XI), or cedars cut from Lebanon were employed in the construction of the temple (III Kings V); and how Rahab, Ruth, and Achior are said to have been transferred into the number of God’s people (Joshua II; Ruth IV; Judith VI).

Just as the Roman people are said to have held the monarchy of the whole world, so the supreme pontiff, occupying the place of blessed Peter in the Roman see, is exalted to the summit of the whole Church. Concerning him, the Council of Sardica decrees that the decisions of all should be referred to him and that what he himself has decreed must be observed. Just as the supreme principate of the secular world was at times held not only among the Romans but also among the peoples of other regions, so other Churches are associated with the dignity of the Roman see: namely, the Church of Antioch in Asia and that of Alexandria in Africa. For at the Council of Nicaea it is shown that the privilege of these three Churches should be placed before that of all the others.

Yet the eminence of these three places may be referred to a single dignity, because Peter himself sat in two of them; while he nevertheless made the third, Alexandria, his see through Mark, his son, and through the Gospel which Mark himself had written from Peter’s mouth. The same should be understood of the principalities of the secular world: although they shone forth in different parts of the world at their appointed times, nevertheless, in the end, almost all were referred to Roman law as to a single summit.

Let the Roman pope, therefore, be compared with the Augusti and Caesars; the patriarchs with the patricians, who appear to have been first after the Caesars in the empires; for these men, who are quite few in number, are regarded as first after the prelates of the three sees. Next, let us compare with kings the archbishops, who preside over the metropolitans themselves. Let us compare the metropolitans [Col. 0964B] with dukes, because just as dukes are placed over individual provinces, so one metropolitan is appointed in each province. Hence the Council of Chalcedon orders that one province is not to be divided between two metropolitans. What counts or prefects accomplish in the secular sphere, the other bishops accomplish in the Church. For it is reported that in the regions of the East there are, in each city and prefecture, separate episcopal governments.

Just as tribunes were placed over soldiers, so abbots are known to preside over monks, the spiritual athletes. Just as palaces have preceptors or counts of the palace, who deal with secular cases, so there are those whom the Franks call chief chaplains, placed over the cases of clerics. Minor chaplains are like those whom, in the Gallic custom, we call royal vassals [vassi dominici].

The chaplains were first called by this name from the cloak [cappa] of blessed Martin, which the kings of the Franks used to carry with them as an aid to victory in battle. Because clerics carried and guarded it together with the other relics of the saints, they began to be called chaplains.

Furthermore, just as certain counts place their own representatives over the common people to settle lesser cases while reserving greater ones to themselves, so certain bishops have co-bishops who carry out the matters entrusted to them that are appropriate to their office. The centenarii, also called centenariones, or vicars, who are appointed throughout the districts, may be compared with the parish priests who hold the baptismal churches and preside over the lesser priests. The decurions or deans, who carry out certain lesser duties under those vicars, may be compared with the lesser priests of the titular churches [Col. 0964D].

Under the ministers of the centenarii there are still lesser officials, who may be called collectors, quaterniers, or duumvirs, because they gather the people and, by their very number, show themselves to be inferior to the deans. These names themselves have been borrowed from ancient custom, in which the offices of superiors were named according to the number of their subjects: thus the Greek chiliarchs, in Latin millenarii; centenarii or centurions; pentacontarchs or quinquagenarii; deans or decurions; quaterniers and duumvirs.

Corresponding to these are deacons and subdeacons, assistants to the priests in preaching, baptism, and daily office. There are also archpriests, who exercise care over the canons under the bishops. Secular powers have counselors in domestic affairs and tutors for their children; they themselves have stewards of their household property. Likewise, in certain Churches there are archdeacons, to whom the governance of the household pertains.

Among secular officials there are investigators, that is, those who examine the accused; in the Church there are exorcists, expellers of demons. The palaces of the powerful have doorkeepers, and the house of God has doorkeepers. The world has couriers, record-keepers, producers of games, and ceremonial reciters of songs; the Church has acolytes, readers, singers, and psalmists.

In any case, through the union and love of both orders one house of God is built and one body of Christ is formed, with all the members contributing the fruit of their offices to their mutual benefit: the eye being in the wise, who perceive and convey the true light; the mouth in teachers; the ear in willing hearers; the nose in lovers of discernment; the hands in those who perform works; the feet in those who make progress; the belly in those who show compassion; the shoulders in those who endure labors [Col. 0966A]; and everything else in the remaining members. Thus there is to be no schism in the body; but if one member rejoices, all the members are to rejoice with it, and if one suffers, all are to suffer with it. This harmony must be maintained until we all come to a perfect man, so that God may be all in all (I Cor. XI).

## CONCLUSION OF THE LITTLE BOOK

At last released from a heavy burden—and would that it had been as fruitful as it was great—in concluding this work I entreat my readers not to attribute to rash presumption what I undertook in obedience. For I confess that I neither discovered everything I wished to clarify nor included everything I discovered: the magnitude of the subject inflamed the desire to know, while the confusion of its variations produced an excess of weariness [Col. 0966B]. Nevertheless, my reader’s careful inquiry will find in these matters, even if not an abundance sufficient for satisfaction and delight, at least some kind of reason for investigation by which he may be better exercised.

[Col. 0965]

## SERMON, OR TREATISE, OF WALAFRID STRABO, MONK OF FULDA, ON THE DESTRUCTION OF JERUSALEM

(From Canisius, *Lectiones antiquae*, vol. II, p. 277.) (G)*

[Col. 0965C] From many passages of Holy Scripture, but especially from the present reading, we can learn how greatly the almighty Lord rejoices in the progress of human beings and how deeply he grieves over their ruin. Indeed, when the Jews wished to kill the Son of God and were plotting his death, he himself, like a merciful father, mourned their destruction. For when the Lord grieves over the Jews who were seeking to kill him, he openly shows how greatly he rejoices in the progress of the human race: he was then grieving over the Jews’ future death, which would occur long afterward.

The preceding text of the Gospel relates how the Son of God sent disciples for the colt of a donkey, and, riding upon it, came to Jerusalem. Then all the crowds descending with joy began to praise the Lord with a loud voice for all the mighty works they had seen, saying: “Blessed is he who comes, the King in the name of the Lord; peace in heaven and glory in the highest” (Luke XIX). Some of the Pharisees said to him: “Teacher, rebuke your disciples” (ibid.). He replied: “I tell you, if these were silent, the stones would cry out” (ibid.).

In accordance with these words, the evangelist Luke adds: “And when Jesus drew near to Jerusalem, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: ‘If you also had known,’ etc.” (ibid.). The Lord grieved over the destruction of the faithless city, which did not know that this destruction was to come upon it. We must not suppose that the Lord wept over the city’s beautiful walls, or the buildings of its walls, or the heights of its towers; rather, by metaphor he wept over the inhabitants of the city.

Metaphor is a figure of speech, as the learning of the Greeks and Latins teaches, through which Scripture very often appears to speak—namely, by means of the inhabited place for its inhabitants, the irrational for the rational, and the inanimate for the animate. Let us omit the other cases and speak of those before us: by means of the inhabited place for its inhabitants, as here; and as elsewhere the Lord says: “Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to you” (Matt. XXIII). There, as here, he did not weep over Jerusalem but over the inhabitants of that city, to whom the weeping Lord says: “If you also had known”—that is, you would have wept—“and indeed in this your day, the things that are for your peace, but now they are hidden from your eyes” (Luke XIX).

In its own day the perverse city possessed the things that belonged to its peace, because it was lifted up by honors, gloried in possessions, rejoiced in riches, in abundance of goods, in the fruitfulness of offspring, and in bodily health. And because it possessed what belonged to present peace, it did not foresee the future conflict. Hence it is rightly added: “But now they are hidden from your eyes” (ibid.). The present joy was bringing tribulation. Concerning that tribulation it is rightly continued: “For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart, and they will surround you and your children who are within you; and they will not leave in you a stone upon a stone, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation” (ibid.).

How these words were fulfilled according to their literal sense, in the destruction of that city and of the Jewish people, the historian Josephus recounts in full. Among other things, he also relates how two Roman commanders, Vespasian and Titus, father and son, came with a military force to destroy that city in the forty-second year after the Lord’s resurrection and his most glorious ascension. And rightly and deservedly: those who had denied God the Father and the Son were killed by a father and son.

For after his Passion the Lord waited forty-two years for the Jewish people to repent. But for the most part they refused to convert, and therefore they encountered enemies so harsh. When the Roman people were burning the entire surrounding region with fire, and the whole population, with women and children, entered the city as one man on the solemn day of Passover to celebrate the feast, suddenly the city was surrounded by a siege, so that no one could enter or leave. This happened by God’s will, so that those who on the solemn day of Passover had cruelly fastened the Son of God to the cross might, on that same day, be oppressed and afflicted by their enemies.

The famine within tormented their entrails so dreadfully—while the sword afflicted them from without—that some did not even refrain from eating their own shoes, as Josephus himself says. Others chewed the remains of old hay, the refuse of grain, and straw; some, tearing off the coverings of the gates, put them between their teeth to be consumed. In this necessity and tribulation all modesty and shame had departed from them, because powerful hunger had claimed everything for itself.

Women snatched inedible food from the hands of men, children from their parents, and—more pitiable still—mothers themselves from the teeth of their children. Women were dragged about with their hair disheveled so that hidden food might be exposed. No respect was shown to the gray hair of the aged, and no pity to the little ones.

In addition to all this, robbers had risen among them, afflicting them more grievously within than they were afflicted by the enemies outside. For if they saw anyone’s doors closed, this was a sign that people inside were eating; immediately they broke down the doors and tore the food from their hands. No one, therefore, dared set a table in the customary manner, but they ate their own food as though it had been stolen. Grain was lacking in the city, and if anyone wished to go outside to gather herbs, he was immediately detained by those within, as though he intended to make peace with the Roman army.

The bodies of young men therefore lay through the streets of the city, weakened more by hunger than by age. No one was buried according to custom, because neither the multitude of the dying nor the weakness of their strength allowed it. Some who took care to bury the bodies of their loved ones breathed out their own lives over their graves. When the city had become full of decay and an intolerable stench, they began throwing the bodies of the dead outside the walls, until the corpses seemed to be level with the walls themselves.

One day Titus was going around the outside of the city—for his father Vespasian had already gone to Rome on account of the empire—and, seeing all the ramparts of the city filled with the corpses of the dead and the bodies of the dying nearly level with the walls, he called God to witness that this deed was not his own. Raising his eyes to heaven with a great groan, he is said to have exclaimed:

“O Roman citizens, I shall not hesitate to report what I think. I believe that, if the Roman army were to withdraw for a little while from this most pestilential city, its inhabitants would either be swallowed up by an opening in the earth, or consumed by fire like that of Sodom, or destroyed by the waters of a flood.”

After saying this, although perhaps he intended to give the army rest on the following day, he immediately armed the soldiers, stationed guards, and began once more to hold the city. They were deservedly tormented by a cruel famine, for they had killed the bread of life.

Josephus also relates an unheard-of crime committed there: there was a certain woman named Mary, the daughter of Eleazar, extremely wealthy and born of a very noble family. She had come to the city with the rest of the multitude. When the property she possessed in the surrounding region had been devastated and burned by the enemy, and what she had brought with her into the city had also been consumed, she is said, in this necessity and tribulation, to have armed herself against nature itself.

Indeed, she had a small son at her breast. Placing him before her eyes, she is said to have spoken as follows—I will convey the meaning, although I shall omit the exact words:

“O unhappy mother, and still more unhappy son, for whom shall I preserve you amid famine, war, and the devastation of robbers? Even if life could be hoped for, we are pressed under the yoke of slavery. O dear child, be food for your mother; be the fury of the robbers, a tale for the ages, and a most grievous remembrance of famine.”

Having said this, she immediately killed her son, roasting one part of him in the fire and reserving the other part for herself later. When the robbers, as usual, came because of the smell of the burned flesh, they began to threaten the wretched woman with death unless she revealed the food she had hidden.

Then she, with a savage expression—and more savage even than the robbers themselves—said: “I have reserved the finest portion for you.” At that she uncovered the remaining limbs of the infant and said: “It is my offspring, it is my son, and it is my crime. Eat, for I was the first to eat the one whom I bore. Do not be more religious than a mother, nor softer than women. But if compassion conquers you and you abominate my food, I, who have been nourished on such things, will feed on them again.”

The robbers were then struck dumb with amazement and horror at so great a crime. They reported it throughout the city, and each person, placing this deed before his eyes as though it were his own abomination, mourned it. Amid great wailing, weeping, and shouting, the city gate was immediately opened. Titus entered with the entire Roman army, killed some by the sword, burned others with fire, and sent into captivity the young men whom he found to be more robust.

The historian, gathering the number of those killed by hunger and the sword, found eleven hundred thousand. Those who were scattered into captivity numbered ninety thousand. The number of the robbers who died in various ways after the city was captured is uncertain. The city itself was so utterly destroyed from its foundations that no stone was left upon another.

[Col. 0969A] We have recalled these events from Josephus to establish that the Lord’s pronouncement was true, for he said: “For days will come, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart; and they will surround you and hem you in on every side; and they will cast you down to the ground, and your children who are within you; and they will not leave in you a stone upon a stone, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation” (Luke X).

Elsewhere also the Lord says to his disciples: “Truly I say to you, not one stone will be left upon another in it that will not be destroyed” (Matt. XXIV). And elsewhere: “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by enemies, know that its desolation is near” (Luke XXI).

The place is shown even to this day, because in the same place where it then stood, not one stone was left upon another. Later it was rebuilt outside the city gate, where the Lord was crucified, by Aelius Hadrian, and it is now called Aelia. Such was the cheapness in the purchase of Jewish slaves that those who paid one silver coin bought thirty Jews for themselves. It was fitting that those who had bought the Lord for a paltry price should be sold in a paltry bargain.

At that time the prophecy of the prophet Ezekiel was also fulfilled, the prophecy that the Lord had spoken to him: “And you, son of man, take for yourself a sharp sword that scrapes away hair, and draw it over your head and your beard, and divide it into four parts. Scatter one part to the wind, throw another into the fire, cut a third with the sword, and bind the remainder at the top of your cloak” (Ezek. V).

All this was fulfilled then, when one part of the people was killed by the sword, another burned by fire, and another sent into captivity—a captivity that continues to this day among the wretched Jews throughout the whole world. By the part that the prophet threw into the fire, we should understand those from the Jewish people who perished by fire, or even the city itself, burned from its foundations. By the part that he cut with the sword, he indicated those who were killed by the sword. By the part that he scattered to the wind, he represented those who were scattered into captivity through the various regions of the world. By the sword that he was ordered to draw after these things, the general striking of the Lord against that same people is understood. By the remnants that he was ordered to bind at the top of his cloak, he signified those of that race who will believe at the end of the world.

Why such harsh things happened to them is added: “Because you did not recognize the time of your visitation” (Luke XIX). He visited them then, when he wished to become incarnate among them. The Psalmist desired this visitation when he said: “Visit us, Lord, with your salvation” (Ps. CV). Of this visitation Zechariah also says: “He has visited and accomplished redemption for his people” (Luke I). And: “The Dawn from on high has visited us” (ibid.).

But the faithless city did not recognize this time of visitation, because when Christ appeared in the flesh, the Jewish people disdained believing in him. Hence, to testify against their hardness of heart, the birds of heaven are brought forward, when it is said: “The kite in heaven has known its time; the turtledove, the swallow, and the stork have observed the time of their coming; but Israel has not known me, and my people have not understood” (Jer. VIII).

Nor did the Lord deign to visit them only through himself. After his ascension, for forty-two years he visited and terrified them not only by various signs, miracles, and portents but also by warnings. For, as Josephus himself relates, one day a heifer brought forward for sacrifice gave birth to a lamb. The temple gate, moreover, so heavy that it could scarcely be moved by twenty men, opened of its own accord. At midnight a light shone so brightly in the temple that some thought it was midday.

When the ignorant saw this, they believed that prosperity was about to come to them; but the wise were not at all unaware that the destruction of the city was being signified. Noise and voices were also heard in the temple saying: “Let us depart from these dwellings.” Chariots and fiery horsemen were seen being carried through the air, threatening the destruction of the wretched city.

Two years before their siege, a star entirely resembling a sword appeared in the sky above the city for a whole year. And one year before their destruction, a certain man named Jesus, a commoner and rustic, began on the solemn day of Passover to cry out among the crowds:

“A voice from the east, a voice from the west, a voice from the four quarters of heaven, a voice against bridegrooms and brides, a voice against Jerusalem and the temple.”

Although the crowds beat him severely, he did not cease at all. As he breathed out his spirit amid the blows, he said: “Woe, woe to Jerusalem!” Although they had been visited and terrified by so many and such great miracles and signs, their hearts were not softened toward repentance; rather, they persisted in their wickedness and sins.

Nor was it fitting that they should remain unpunished, since they had been responsible for such great crimes. Their punishment had been prefigured in the deeds of the prophet Elisha, when, as he was coming down from Gilgal, boys mocked him, saying: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead” (IV Kings II). But he cursed them in the name of the Lord, and two bears came out of the forest and devoured forty-two of the boys.

By Elisha we understand the Lord Christ, who was led by the Jews to the place called Calvary in order to be crucified. Just as Elisha was mocked by the boys, so the Son of God was derided by the Jews when, bending their knees, they said: “Hail, King of the Jews” (Matt. XXVII). And again: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross, and we will believe in him” (ibid.). And striking him, they said: “Prophesy to us, Christ; who is the one who struck you?” (Matt. XXVI).

By the forty-two boys are signified the forty-two years during which the Lord waited for them to repent. But when they refused to repent, two bears came out of the forest—that is, two great Roman commanders, coming from the forests of the Gentiles, namely Vespasian and Titus—and killed them.

“And he entered the temple and began to cast out those who sold and bought in it, saying to them: ‘It is written, My house is a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves’” (Luke X). King Solomon built the house of the Lord (III Kings VIII) so that it might be a house of prayer, but it had been made a den of thieves by the priests, who ought to have been guardians and makers of the law, because merchandise was being prepared there.

The children of Israel had been told to assemble three times a year to celebrate the feasts in Jerusalem (Exod. XXIII). The Law also commanded: “No one shall appear empty-handed before me” (ibid.). Therefore, when they came from distant regions and were unable to carry with them the gifts they were to offer, the temple ministers compelled them to buy from them. When the people gave gifts, the priests defrauded them: they did not sacrifice the gifts to the Lord as commanded, but reserved them for themselves so that they could sell them again to others and multiply the price of the offering for themselves.

Hence, as the other evangelists state, sheep and oxen, turtledoves and pigeons were sold in the temple; and so that they might have no excuse for buying, money-changers sat in the temple (Matt. XXI; Mark XI). They had made the house of prayer a den of thieves because they sold again what had been wrongly bought. They sat in the temple for this purpose: if anyone offered gifts, the priests would praise them with great acclamations; but if there were people who offered no gifts, they would strike them with whips.

Therefore, in order to [perhaps: teach] those who understood these things less fully, we have touched on them briefly in their historical sense; now we must return to them in a short discourse. What we said pertained to the destruction of the material temple [Col. 0971C] may also be referred to every sinful soul.

At that time the most merciful Lord himself wept over the city that was being destroyed; every day, through holy teachers in the Church, he weeps over the souls of those who are perishing. Those in the Church are to be mourned by teachers who do not know how to mourn for themselves, who do not understand why they are being mourned, who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things. Thus the apostle Paul, in Christ’s place, mourned the fallen disciples, saying: “I shall mourn many of those who sinned previously” (II Cor. XII). And again: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV).

What was therefore said by the Lord as he wept over the city that was to perish also applies to the soul that is perishing. The Lord says to the city that is to perish: “If you also had known” (Luke XIX)—that is, if the sinful soul knew, it would weep—the tribulation and anguish that are growing for it in the future, where there are worms that do not die and fire that will not be extinguished (Isa. LXVI), it would choose to mourn for a time with the elect in this world rather than rejoice with the reprobate.

“And indeed in this your day, the things that are for your peace” (Luke XIX). The sinful soul has its own day when it rejoices in what is transitory and quickly ending in this world, when it is inflated by honors, lifted up by riches, and glories in its possessions; but what it has in its own day, and what scandal it will suffer in another’s day, it does not foresee, nor does it look ahead to the future tribulation.

Hence it is rightly added: “But now they are hidden from your eyes” (ibid.). Self-love blinds the eyes of the heart; and just as dust blinds bodily eyes so that they cannot see clearly, so love of this world and present riches blind the eye of the mind, so that it cannot foresee the future judgment.

Concerning that tribulation it is rightly continued: “For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart” (ibid.). “Days will come upon you”—that is, times of death, days of tribulation, days of anguish, days of calamity and misery—when the unhappy soul will begin to quarrel with itself and, as it were, say:

“Why did I give myself over so fully to evil works? Why did I not repent of my past sins? Why did I not exercise myself in good works?”

Then it will begin to repent, when no fruit of repentance will remain, but only the strictness of punishment.

“And they will surround you and hem you in on every side” (ibid.). The unhappy soul has no worse enemies than unclean spirits. From these the Psalmist desired to be rescued when he said: “Deliver me from my enemies, my God” (Ps. LVIII). And again: “Deliver me from those who work iniquity” (ibid.).

Thus the enemies of the wretched soul surround it with a rampart when, around the day of death, unclean spirits recite to it all its sins; and they hem it in most tightly when those who were first to persuade it toward crimes become exactors of its torments.

“And they will cast you down to the ground.” The unhappy soul is cast down to the ground when it loses the virtues it thought it possessed; or the flesh, which was taken from the earth, returns to the earth. As it is written: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. III).

“And your children who are within you” (Luke X). In Holy Scripture, sons—and sometimes daughters—signify works, sometimes good and sometimes evil. Good works, as the Psalmist says: “And may you see the children of your children; peace upon Israel” (Ps. CXXVII). Evil works, as in this passage, where it says: “And your children who are within you” (Luke XIX).

The children of the sinful soul are cast down to the ground because we shall give an account not only of an evil deed but also of the thought itself—not only of lying, perjury, and murmuring, but even of an idle word. The Lord says: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matt. XII).

“And they will not leave in you a stone upon a stone, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation” (Luke XIX). Just as, in the building of a city, one stone is placed upon another so that the construction may grow, so an evil thought is placed upon an evil thought, and an evil habit is joined to evil works, so that a kind of diabolical building may be constructed.

In the destruction of the city, no stone is left upon another because on the day of judgment not only evil works but also wicked thought will cease and perish. As the Psalmist says: “On that day all their thoughts will perish” (Ps. CXLV).

Therefore, while we are in this world and have the opportunity, it is necessary not only to abstain from evil but also to strive to do good in everything. Above all, let us place the day of death before our eyes, because the one who always thinks that he will die easily despises everything. Hence Solomon exhorts us, saying: “In all your works remember your last things” (Ecclus. VII). And again: “On the day of good things do not be forgetful of evils; and on the day of evils do not be forgetful of good things” (Ecclus. XI).

The merciful Lord, who patiently waits for us, will judge us severely on the day of judgment if we have not been converted. Hence he also admonishes us in the Gospel: “Run while you have the light, lest the darkness of death overtake you” (John XII). And again: “Be quickly reconciled with your adversary, while you are on the way with him, lest perhaps your adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be thrown into prison. Truly I say to you, you will not leave until you have paid the last quadrans” (Matt. V).

The apostle Paul says: “While we have time, let us do good to all” (Gal. VI). And again: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI). And Solomon says: “Whatever your hand can do, perform it diligently” (Ecclus. IX).

“Because you did not recognize the time of your visitation” (Luke XIX). In the present life God visits the sinful soul in many ways. He first visited it through the coming of his Son and through his miracles; every day he visits it through the preaching of teachers; he visits it through prosperity and adversity; he visits it through scourges; he visits it through persecution. But the perverse soul does not recognize where it is going with closed eyes toward the fire. It does not humble itself in prosperity, nor recognize itself in adversity.

I omitted earlier that earthly Jerusalem is to be understood in four ways. First, historically: the city situated on Mount Moriah, built by Shem, son of Noah, and called Salem. Second, it was possessed by the Jebusite, from whom it received the name Jebus. Third, it was possessed by Solomon, and from this it was called Hierosolyma, from Jebus and Solomon, as it were, Jebusolyma. Later, after being destroyed by the Romans, it was rebuilt by Aelius Hadrian, from whom it is now called Aelia. This is the literal sense.

Allegorically, Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace,” signifying the holy Church. For the Jerusalem above can contain only those who are peaceful in the faith of Christ [Col. 0973D].

In the anagogical sense, however, it signifies the holy soul, which by contemplation of the mind continually merits to see the Lord.

“Then he entered the temple and began to drive out those who were selling and buying in it, saying: ‘It is written: My house is a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers’ (ibid.).” What the Lord then did bodily by himself, he does every day spiritually in the Church. Spiritually, the temple of God is the Church, because it can rightly be called a house of prayer, where the Church does not cease daily to offer pure prayers to God, saying with the Psalmist: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Psalm 140).

In this temple, that is, the Church, the sellers and buyers are those who seek ecclesiastical office not for the profit of souls but for earthly gain, or for human favor. Hence, according to the other evangelists, sheep and oxen, turtledoves and doves were sold in the temple (Matthew 21; Mark 11). In Holy Scripture the name “ox” sometimes designates preachers, as the Lord says to Moses: “You shall not plow with an ox and an ass together” (Deuteronomy 22)—that is, do not join together in preaching or teaching the wise with the foolish.

The sheep signifies innocence or simplicity, for the sheep is the simplest of animals. Therefore whoever displays holiness or innocence before others in order to seek praise from human beings carries a sheep for sale in the temple. Of such people the Lord says in the Gospel: “They do all their works so that they may be seen by men” (Matthew 23). And again: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6).

The dove signifies the Holy Spirit. Thus the same Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove above the baptized Lord (Matthew 3). Therefore those who bestow the grace of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands—which they ought to have given freely, since the Lord says, “Freely you have received, freely give” (Matthew 10)—not for God’s sake but for gifts or earthly profit, sell doves, as it were, in the temple. Of such people it is written: “Fire will devour the tents of those who willingly accept gifts” (Job 15). And again: “You shall not show partiality to the poor in judgment, for gifts blind the eyes of the wise and overturn the words of rulers” (Exodus 23).

The Lord drives such people from the temple. Although in the present age they may appear bodily joined to the Church, on the day of judgment they will be separated from the Church, when he says to them: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25).

“And he was teaching daily in the temple” (Luke 19). The Lord teaches daily in the temple through holy preachers whenever the holy Gospel is read, the Apostle is recited, and teachers preach. The Lord always teaches in the Church, as he himself says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). He says this so that no one may be able to offer any excuse for sin on the day of judgment. For when a teacher announces the word of God in the Church, Christ teaches in the temple; and whoever despises the preacher’s word refuses to hear Christ, who himself says: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10).

Let us fear this destruction of the city as the destruction of our soul. Let us therefore beseech the Lord that he who permitted earthly Jerusalem to be destroyed, and afterward ordained that heavenly Jerusalem should endure, may destroy the sins of our body and soul, so that he may bring us into the chambers of his bride, where we may see with him without end the good things that are in Jerusalem.

# THE SECOND PART OF ALL THE WORKS OF WALAFRID STRABO, MONK OF FULDA—HISTORICAL WORKS

## THE LIFE OF SAINT GALL, ABBOT IN ALAMANNIA

*(G)*

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS OF MABILLON

*(Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict)*

### 1.

It is certain that Walafrid Strabo, or Strabo, undertook to compose the deeds of Saint Gall, abbot, as is shown by Hepidannus, a monk of St. Gall, in these words from his Annals:

> In the year 849, Walahfred, abbot of Augia, died. This learned man elegantly compiled the Lives of Saints Gall and Othmar at the request of Abbot Gozbert. He undertook this work while still young, after another anonymous author, whose footsteps he confesses in his Preface (no. 1) that he followed. To the Life of Saint Gall he added a book of Miracles, which the monk Gozbert had already partly published in writing (at the end of the Life).

### 2.

Moreover, Walafrid promised and supplied a metrical Life of Saint Gall for Abbot Gozbert at the end of the Preface reproduced below. Since this Life has not yet been published, the following is circulated as its opening:

> Mindful of my promise, behold me, Gozbert, which once…

This is Gozbert, or Gotzpert, abbot of Saint Gall, who, according to Ratpert in book 1, chapter 6, *On the Misfortunes of Saint Gall*, succeeded Werdoni “in the year 816 from the incarnation of the Lord.” Then, “in the year 830, he began to build a new basilica for Saint Gall, which he completed fully by building it over a period of seven years.” Finally, “as time passed,” the same author says in chapter 7, “when he realized that the gravity of age and the weakness of his body were no longer sufficient for the urgent needs of his affairs, he obtained from the most merciful Emperor Louis that the monk Bernwicus should become his successor; and as soon as he made the request, it was carried out … in the year 837 of the Lord’s incarnation.”

### 3.

Walafrid Strabo first attended the schools of Saint Gall monastery as a young man. From there he was sent to Fulda to hear Rabanus, and remained there until Rabanus’s elevation to the see of Mainz. Then, leaving Fulda and going to Augia, he held the dignity of abbot, and finally died in the year 849.

For this reason Gerardus Vossius, in book 2, chapter 33 of *On Latin History*, and Goldast, in the *Life of Saint Gall*, rightly refute Trithemius and others who wish to distinguish Walafrid the abbot of Saint Gall from Walafrid of Fulda. Certainly no Walafrid is numbered among the abbots of Saint Gall by Hepidannus, Ratpert, or others, although Mezler and Vossius believe that Walafrid Strabo, first educated in the schools of Saint Gall, was dean there.

Augia—called in antiquity Auva, Ouva, and Sinthleoheswa, and commonly Richenow or Richenaw—was once a distinguished abbey for holiness, nobility, and wealth, and was therefore called “the Rich,” by which name it is distinguished from Greater Augia, or Brigantina. It lies on an island in the Rhine a little below Constance and is said to have been founded in 724 by Saint Pirminius with the assistance of Charles Martel.

Not far from the island of Augia lies the monastery of Saint Gall, still exceedingly famous for its religion and dignity, and lending distinction to the town of Saint Gall. It stands beside Lake Acronium, in the territories of the Helvetians and Vindelicians. Its abbot holds a place among the princes of the Empire and presides among the Fathers of the congregation of Saint Gall. We shall speak of this monastery in the following century, in the *Life of Saint Othmar, On Illustrious Men*. (See below.)

### 4.

After Walafrid, Notker, a monk of Saint Gall surnamed Balbulus, sang the life of his patron in three books. This author, distinguished by the name of holiness, is recorded by Hepidannus as having died in the year 912. Since it has not been possible to obtain Notker’s metrical work, Walafrid alone will suffice; we shall reproduce his composition, divided by its author into chapters, from volume 1, part 2, of Goldast’s *History of Alamannia*.

# PREFACE OF THE AUTHOR TO GOZBERT, ABBOT, AND THE MONKS OF SAINT GALL

### I.

Unless the authority of the holy Scriptures, and especially that saying of the truthful prophet in which obedience is preferred to sacrifice (1 Samuel 15), compelled me to the necessity of obeying, I would oppose this kind of apology to your commands, most holy Fathers.

If the prophet who was chosen by the Lord before he was formed in the womb, and sanctified before he came out of the womb, complained of weakness of age and ignorance when the Lord, enlightening him with his Spirit, devoted him to the office of the word (Jeremiah 1), what am I, a sinner, to do? I was conceived in iniquity and brought forth in sin; because of the filth of life I am uncircumcised in heart and ears, since I neither properly grasp what must be known nor faithfully preserve what I have heard.

How shall I declare the righteousnesses of the Lord and take his covenant upon my lips, when neither age nor knowledge has yet completed or commended me; when neither doctrine strengthens my words nor life confirms them? Especially since you command me to write and arrange matters whose dignity I scarcely comprehend with my sluggish mind.

Nevertheless, I find a way to dare such things for three reasons. First, because I believe that I shall be raised up by the Lord, for whose commands and promises alike I have undertaken, in my desire to obey, what I feared when I considered my strength. Second, because I trust that I am aided by the intercession of blessed Gall and by your prayers; for the sake of your reverence and love I have fitted a great burden upon weak shoulders. Finally, because I follow in the footsteps of others and am compelled to measure the path of truth that must be preserved only with new steps.

You therefore wish me to adorn with the light of upright speech the life of the holy confessor of Christ, Gall, our patron, whose bodily treasure you preserve with faithful watchfulness, though noble in substance and mean in writing; and you wish the confused sequence of chapters to be distinguished by boundaries.

### II.

Since I cannot excuse myself from this task, I choose rather to be torn apart for laziness than condemned for disobedience. Now, when I recently read through the work itself, I found that its author repeatedly called the land inhabited by us Alamanni, or Suevi, “Altimannia.” But when I sought the origin of that name, I found no mention of it in any writer whose knowledge has reached us.

Unless I am mistaken, the moderns invented this name from the elevated situation of the province.

**[Note:]** Walafrid does not approve this conception of Alamannia, about which the authors dispute.

For according to trustworthy writers, that part of Alamannia—or Suevia—

**[Note:]** Here the preposition *vel* (“or”) is not disjunctive. Among ancient authors, the Alamanni and Suevi, because they were neighbors, are sometimes found confused together.

—which lies between the Pennine Alps and the southern bank of the Danube is called Raetia. What lies toward the northern region is assigned to Histria of Germany.

And lest we seem to be making this assertion ourselves, we shall call forward certain witnesses to the matter. Paulus Orosius, whose statements command universal agreement, writes the following, among other things, in describing the situation of the lands:

> Pannonia, Noricum, and Raetia have Moesia to the east, Histria to the south, the Pennine Alps to the southwest,

**[Note:]** The words contained in this clause are missing in Surius.

> Gaul Belgica to the west, the source of the Danube to the northwest, and the Danube and Germany to the north.

Since Noricum is the region of the Bavarians, and its northern boundary is the Danube and Germany, Raetia, which is mentioned together with it, must necessarily have the same northern boundaries.

Solinus likewise, in his *Polyhistor* (chapter 24 of Solinus), when mentioning Gaul, describes these provinces, situated in one continuous stretch of land, in the following words:

> From this gulf—that is, from Gaul—whichever direction in the world you wish to travel, if you are making for Thrace, the Raetian territory receives you, rich in crops and famous for Lake Brigantinus. From there comes cold Noricum, less fruitful; but where it withdraws from the Alpine ridges, it is exceedingly fertile. Then come the strong men of Pannonia, whose land is level and rich, encircled by the famous rivers Dravus and Savus.

If Raetia lies only below the Alps, as many maintain, what follows? Traveling from Gaul to Noricum, must we cross the ruggedness of the Alps, rather than proceed directly through Greater Raetia all the way to Noricum?

In that same Raetia, according to the statement just cited, the town of Brigantium, now fallen into ruin through age, gave its name to the lake formed by the Rhine flowing through it. This lake is also called Potamicus, according to its Greek etymology.

Thus, because the Alamanni and Suevi, intermixed, occupied one part of Germany beyond the Danube, one part of Raetia between the Alps and the Hister, and one part of Gaul around the Arar,

**[Note:]** That is, the Arola, commonly called the Aar, a river of the Helvetians flowing into the Rhine. Hadrianus Valesius observed in *History of the Franks*, book 24, page 478, volume 3, that among the ancients the name *Arar* was sometimes used for the Arola.

let us preserve the truth of the ancient names and derive the name of the homeland from its inhabitants, calling it Alamannia or Suevia. Since there are two names signifying one people, the surrounding nations that speak Latin call us by the first name, while custom among the barbarians calls us by the second.

Similarly, we know that the Franks subjected parts of Germany and Gaul not only to their power but also to their own name.

### III.

Since we have touched upon descriptions of provinces, let us briefly recall, according to the same authors, the situation of the island of Ireland, from which so great a glory has shone upon us.

The island of Ireland, as Orosius writes, lies between Britain and Spain and extends farther from southwest to north. It is nearer to Britain and narrower in extent, but more favorable in climate and sunlight.
