As the aforementioned Solinus testifies, it is so rich in pasture that the cattle there, unless they are sometimes kept away from grazing in summer, are brought into danger by surfeit.

There are no snakes there, and birds are rare. But whatever horrors he himself or others may testify concerning the character of its inhabitants, now that the faith of Christ is shining, we should pass over them; for where sin abounded, grace abounded still more. From the rising of the sun, from the Indians and Ethiopians, to the setting of the sun, among the Britons and Scots, the name of the Lord is now praiseworthy. For the Lord is exalted above all nations, and his glory is above the heavens.

### IV.

I therefore beseech you, dearest Gotzpert, abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall, and all the brothers who serve under you in spiritual warfare, to assist me with your prayers, so that I may be worthy to expound this work, and others thereafter, in a manner pleasing to God.

For if you gratefully accept what we have correctly set down, kindly correct what is uncertain, and if the Lord permits it, I shall later season this rustic dish of a work with certain poetic embellishments. It is indeed worthy that he whom the Lord sent from the farthest ends of the earth for our salvation should be celebrated throughout the world by our praises.

May the Holy Trinity deign to preserve your Fatherhood in good health and mindful of us forever. Amen.

> O Father, O Offspring of the Father, O gracious Spirit,  
> One and triune God, have mercy on us and guide us.  
> Your commands bind me; may your promises govern me;  
> May your light shine, I ask, upon my words.  
>
> In you, Gall, I shall confess God; in the Lord, Gall, I shall confess you.  
> Pour forth holy prayers for me to the Lord,  
> That he may grant pardon for my offenses and restraint to my words;  
> May he uproot what harms and increase what helps.

# BOOK ONE

## CHAPTER ONE  
### The progress by which blessed Gall advanced from childhood under the instruction of Saint Columbanus to the dignity of the priesthood

Since the renowned way of life of the most holy man Columbanus, who was also called Columba, was celebrated throughout all Ireland, and since, like the splendid radiance of the fiery sun, he drew everyone’s love to himself by his singular excellence—as the book of his deeds fully indicates, showing that this had been ordained concerning him before his birth—the parents of blessed Gall, religious before God and noble according to the world, were among those whom the fame of his virtues had attracted.

They offered their son, radiant in the flower of early youth, to the Lord, and entrusted him to Columbanus’s instruction so that he might advance in the discipline of the regular life and imitate, among the many followers of spiritual warfare, the examples of obedience and stricter purpose.

As the young man of good character was nurtured in loving—or, according to another reading, chaste—affection, he grew greatly in virtue. With heavenly grace going before him, he drank so deeply from the divine Scriptures that he could bring forth new things and old from his treasure. With an able intellect he also mastered the rules of grammar and the subtleties of poetic meters.

He disclosed the obscure things of Scripture so wisely to those who wished to understand them that all who heard his wisdom and words judged him worthy of the highest admiration and praise. Through this maturity of wisdom it came about that, by the common counsel of all and by the command of Abbot Columbanus, he ascended through each rank of sacred promotion and, though unwilling, accepted the dignity of the priesthood.

Thus, while he devoted himself to sacred offices, he pleased the Lord day and night with prayers and tears. Desiring to please the eyes of the heavenly overseer, he was loved by all for the merits of his virtues and life, and he was pleasing to everyone.

**[Note:]** The reports transmitted by Goldast concerning blessed Gall’s royal ancestry do not seem sufficiently established. It is said that Kethernach, the father of blessed Gall, was born of Unuchun, king of Ireland; that Kethernach, called *Gallach* in his native language, rejected the kingdom.

## CHAPTER TWO  
### How the holy men, undertaking pilgrimage for the Lord’s name, came to King Sigibert and began to inhabit Luxeuil

While these things were taking place, blessed Columbanus, desiring daily to attain evangelical perfection—that is, to leave everything he possessed, take up his cross, and follow the Lord naked—acted in council with the brothers whose hearts the same fervor had inflamed, so that, spurning the sweetness of relatives and estates, they might prove the ardor of their minds by their deeds.

They therefore boarded a ship, came to Britain, and from there crossed over to Gaul. When the man of God reached King Sigibert with his companions, the king asked him to settle somewhere within Gaul and not, after leaving those lands, migrate to other peoples. He promised that he would provide everything the holy Father requested.

To this the man of God replied:

> We who have abandoned our own possessions in order to follow the Lord according to the evangelical command must not embrace the wealth of others, lest we become transgressors of the divine command.

The king answered this objection as follows:

> If you desire to take up your cross and follow Christ, seek the quiet of a vast wilderness; only do not leave the soil under our rule and pass over to neighboring nations. By this plan you can both increase your own rewards and look to our salvation.

Thus he consented to the king’s persuasion and, having accepted the choice offered him, entered with his companions the wilderness called Vosagus (the Vosges). They found there a place enclosed by ancient walls, watered by hot springs, but already collapsed through age, which was commonly called Luxovium (Luxeuil).

There they built an oratory in honor of blessed Peter the Apostle and made small dwellings in which they could live together. As they lived there and cultivated the place itself, many came to them—not only from the people of Burgundy but also from the Franks—out of love for their praiseworthy life.

Instructed by their spiritual admonitions, these people received such grace of compunction from their words that some handed over all their possessions to that place, cut off the hair of their heads, and voluntarily embraced the monastic habit in poverty.

**[Note:]** What Jonas relates about Gall’s fishing in the *Life of Saint Columbanus*, no. 16, ought to be supplied here.

## CHAPTER THREE  
### By what authority blessed Columbanus rebuked King Theodoric; by what hatred Brunichildis drove him from that kingdom; and how he came with his companions to King Lothar and from there to Theudebert

As this discipline of those living together continued to advance ever more happily, the singular holiness of blessed Columbanus, confirmed by frequent miracles, began to be proclaimed throughout the provinces of Gaul and Germany.

He was praised by all and honored by everyone, so much so that King Theodoric, son of Childebert and grandson of Sigibert, who at that time ruled the Burgundians, often came to him and sought the support of his prayers with the greatest devotion.

When the holy Father rebuked him because he was polluted by the embraces of concubines and did not instead enjoy the marriage of a lawful wife, he obeyed his admonitions and promised that he would avoid all such unlawful conduct.

But Brunichildis, the king’s grandmother, seeing him obey the counsels of the man of God, was stirred by the goad of malice and armed her mind with the serpent’s venom of fury. She feared that, if the concubines were cast off and a queen were taken into partnership in the kingdom, her own dignity would be diminished by the loss of honor.

Troubled by this fear, she began to harbor hatred against the man of God. After contriving many injuries against him, as the account of his holy conduct bears witness, she consulted with the king about driving him from the kingdom. She sent her envoys with a letter to the holy man, ordering him not to remain any longer in that kingdom.

Avoiding the snares of Jezebel, he set out with his companions and reached King Lothar. After staying with him for some time, he asked that, with the king’s assistance, he might reach Theudebert, king of the Austrasians.

When he had been honorably sent to Theudebert according to his request, Theudebert received him with every honor and great joy. He therefore remained with him for several days, opening the sacred Scriptures and explaining the truth to him.

When he also asked the king to have him escorted by royal command through Alamannia to Agilulf, king of the Lombards, the king, distressed at the departure of such men, promised that within the boundaries of his kingdom he would find pleasant places suitable for the servants of God to inhabit and well situated for instructing the surrounding peoples by the word of truth.

The man of God, desiring to plant the seed of the word in the hearts of the nations, promised to remain for a while if royal authority confirmed its words by deeds.

## CHAPTER FOUR  
### How, after being given the choice of seeking a dwelling-place, they came to Tuggen, and what they accomplished there

Having received permission from the king to choose a place wherever they wished, they traveled through many regions and came within the territories of Alamannia to the river called Lindimacus.

**[Note:]** Surius calls it the Limagus; it is commonly called the Limmat, a not insignificant river of present-day Switzerland. It enters Lake Zurich, here called Lake Tigurinum, washes the city of Zurich, the chief city of the Zurich region, and afterward flows into the Arola, together with which it descends to the left bank of the Rhine. Walafrid places Tuggen here at the head of Lake Zurich. Compare the *Life of Saint Columbanus* by Jonas, beginning at no. 49. Goldast notes that Tuggen is now called Tuggium, or, in the vernacular, Zug, because the ancient Alamanni liked to change Greek *tau* (τὸ T) into *Z*: hence Tigurinum became Zurich, Tabernae became Zabern, Durae Aquae became Zurzach, and similar names.

Following this river upstream, they came to Lake Zurich. As they walked along its shore, they reached the head of the lake, at a place called Tuggen, and the character of the site pleased them as a place of habitation.

The people living there, however, were cruel and impious. They worshiped images, honored idols with sacrifices, observed omens and divinations, and followed many superstitious practices contrary to divine worship.

When the holy men began to live among them, they taught them to adore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and to preserve the truth of the faith. Blessed Gall, disciple of the holy man, armed with zeal for piety, set fire to the shrines in which sacrifices were offered to demons, and cast into the lake whatever offerings he found.

Moved by this, the people pursued the saints with anger and hatred. By common counsel they wished to kill Gall, but to scourge Columbanus and drive him from their territory after subjecting him to insults.

The blessed Father, having learned of their plan, invoked justice against them, saying:

> God, by whose providence the world subsists and all things are governed, cause the insults that they have prepared for your servants to return upon the head of this generation.  
> May their offspring perish quickly, and before they grow old may they be forced to rave through sudden derangement. May they themselves, together with the land they inhabit, be oppressed by the harsh domination of the powerful, so that their disgrace may be revealed to all forever; and, as it is written, “May their sorrow return upon their own head, and may the iniquity they have committed descend upon the crown of their heads” (Psalm 7).

## CHAPTER FIVE  
### Their arrival at the presbyter Willimar at Arbon, his kindness, and their stay at Brigantium

After this, not terrified by fear of persecution but persuaded by love of spiritual gain, he left behind the barren crowd of obstinate people, lest he water dry hearts fruitlessly for too long, when meanwhile he could have benefited benevolent minds greatly.

Proceeding from there with his companions, he reached the fortress called Arbona (Arbon). There he found a presbyter distinguished for goodness, named Willimar. When Willimar saw him, he said:

> Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, and so forth.

The man of God replied:

> The Lord has gathered us from different regions.

The presbyter then took him by the right hand, led him into the oratory, and, after they had prayed together, brought them into the guesthouse. They invoked peace upon the house and set down their little bundles.

After they had reclined, at the abbot’s command Gall recited the divine words, unlocking the depths of truth. During the sacred feasts of saving doctrine, the priest was so amazed at the man’s wisdom that he could not restrain himself from weeping.

For a full cycle of seven days he ministered to them with the greatest honor and care. He who had refreshed them with bodily delicacies was himself daily nourished by them with the food of the Scriptures.

During their conversations concerning sacred edification, Abbot Columbanus asked the presbyter whether he knew of any place in the wilderness where a small cell could be built, somewhat suitable for regular observances.

The host of the holy men answered this inquiry:

> There is in this wilderness a certain place with remains of ancient construction amid the ruins. Its soil is rich and suited to the growth of fruit trees; lofty mountains surround it; a vast wilderness rises above the town; and its broad plain does not deny the fruit of labor to those seeking sustenance.

After praising the situation of the place at length, he indicated its name: Brigantium.

## CHAPTER SIX  
### How they visited that place, what blessed Gall did in the gathering of the people, how they restored the oratory, and how long they remained there

Since they desired to go there, the presbyter prepared a small boat and placed rowers in it. The venerable abbot, boarding the vessel with his companions Gall and a certain deacon, invoked the name of the Lord and reached the desired place by a direct route.

Leaving the boat, they approached an oratory built in honor of Saint Aurelia, which blessed Columbanus later restored to its former dignity. After praying and surveying everything around them with their eyes, they were pleased with the character and situation of the place.

Then, after prayer had been offered, they made small dwellings for themselves around the oratory. In the temple they found three gilded bronze images fixed to the wall. The people, having abandoned the worship of the sacred altar, adored them and customarily said, while offering sacrifices:

> These are the ancient gods and the old guardians of this place; through their protection both we and our possessions have endured down to the present.

Columbanus therefore assigned blessed Gall the task of recalling the people from the error of idolatry to the worship of God through salutary exhortation, since he had merited from the Lord the grace of possessing considerable knowledge not only of Latin but also of barbarian speech.

When the solemnity of that temple was being celebrated, a considerable crowd of both sexes and all ages arrived, not only out of respect for the festival but also to see the strangers whom they had learned had come.

As they gathered for the hour of prayer, Gall, at the command of the venerable abbot, began to show the people the way of truth and to admonish them to turn to God. He urged them, casting away their empty practices, to adore God the Father, creator of all things, and his only-begotten Son, in whom there is salvation, life, and the resurrection of the dead.

In the sight of everyone he seized the images, smashed them to pieces with stones, and threw them into the lake. At this sight some were converted to the Lord, confessed their sins, and gave praise to the Lord for enlightening them. Others, stirred to anger and fury by the destruction of the images, withdrew in a turbulent rage of indignation.

Blessed Columbanus ordered water to be brought. After blessing it, he sprinkled the temple with it; then, as they went around singing psalms, he dedicated the church. Next, invoking the name of the Lord, he anointed the altar and placed the relics of Saint Aurelia in it. After clothing the altar, they completed the Mass according to due rite.

When everything had thus been properly accomplished, the people returned to their homes with great joy.

Blessed Columbanus then remained there with his fellow soldiers for three years.

**[Note:]** Not, of course, three complete years. For in the year 612, when Columbanus saw that Theudebert had been defeated by Theodoric, he left Gaul and Germany and entered Italy, says Jonas in his *Life*, no. 56.

A cell was built there. Some worked the garden; others cultivated fruit-bearing trees. Blessed Gall, meanwhile, wove nets, and, with the mercy of God assisting him, caught such an abundance of fish that the brothers were never without them. He also aided travelers who arrived with such provision and, from the same labor, continually bestowed blessings upon the people.

## CHAPTER SEVEN  
### What voices of demons Gall heard, and how that error departed

Once, while he was casting his nets into the deep in the silence of night, he heard a demon calling another demon by name with a great uproar of voice from the summit of a nearby mountain, as though the latter were dwelling in the deep.

When the one who was being called answered from the lake that he was present, the first said:

> Rise and come to my aid, so that we may drive these strangers from these settlements. They have come from far away and expelled me from my temple, shattered my images, and turned away the people who followed me. Let the injury I suffer move you, and with united strength let us keep our common enemies from our territories.

The other replied:

> Alas that you tell of your misfortunes! From my own contempt I understand them. For one of them presses me in the deep and devastates what is mine. I cannot ever damage his nets or deceive him, because the invocation of the divine name never departs from his mouth. Protected by continual vigilance, he despises our ambushes. Therefore cunning stratagems will not overcome such cautious warriors of the faith.

Having heard this, the man of God fortified himself on every side with the sign of the holy cross and said to them:

> In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, I adjure you to depart from this place and presume to harm no one here.

Then, returning quickly to the shore, he reported to his abbot what he had heard. When the abbot received this report, he went to the church and, striking the signal, summoned the brothers.

Before they had begun the psalmody, dreadful voices of demons were heard across the mountain peaks, together with the confused howling of those who seemed to be departing in terror. Hearing this, the servants of God prostrated themselves in prayer, asking for the Lord’s protection and offering him praise and thanks because he had deigned to free them from the terrors of the wicked.

## CHAPTER EIGHT  
### The plotting and malice of the inhabitants against the holy men, and their decision to depart after the command of the duke

Meanwhile, certain citizens, angered by the abolition of their idols and despising the admonitions of the holy men’s preaching, began to stir up hatred against them and contrive ambushes.

With this intention they also approached the duke of the region, named Gunzo, and accused the saints before him, saying that the public hunt in those same lands had been disturbed because of the infestation caused by the strangers.

When the duke heard this, he was inflamed with fury and sent messengers ordering the servants of God to leave that place.

But this was not enough for the demons’ henchmen. They even stole the brothers’ cow and drove it into an inaccessible part of the woods. When two of the brothers pursued them immediately, the brigands rose up, killed them, stripped them of their possessions, and departed.

When the brothers wondered why they delayed returning for so long, they sent others to search for them. Following their tracks, these men found them dead, placed their bodies upon their shoulders, and carried them back to the cell.

Amid these waves of distress and sorrow, the duke’s messenger arrived and ordered them to depart from that place—and not without reason, for light has no fellowship with darkness.

The devil accomplished this by his own device, so that the people whom he had begun to lose in the presence of the light might be seized by ancient darkness once the radiance of holiness had departed.

The holy men, therefore, distressed that they were being driven from a beloved dwelling-place, decided by common counsel to seek Italy. While they were overwhelmed by excessive grief, the holy Father Columbanus began to console them with these words:

> Indeed, brothers, we have found in these regions a golden shell, but one filled with poisonous serpents. Nevertheless, let the deadly weakness of sorrow give way, because our confidence in the protector’s aid is certain. For the God whom we serve will send his angel with us, who will lead us to Agilulf, king of the Lombards. There, as his mercy prepares human goodwill, we shall find a dwelling-place full of peace.

## CHAPTER NINE  
### How Gall remained behind because of illness when the others departed, and with what care he was received by the presbyter Willimar
After this, when the time for departure was approaching, a sudden fever seized blessed Gallus. He therefore threw himself at the feet of his abbot and informed him that he was suffering from a severe illness [Col. 0985C] and consequently could not complete the journey he had undertaken. But the abbot, supposing that Gallus was being held there by his love for the place, in order to complete his labors there and avoid the hardship of a longer journey, said to him:

“I know, brother, that it has now become burdensome for you to be worn out by such great labors on my behalf. Nevertheless, as I am about to depart, I warn you not to presume to celebrate Mass while I am alive in the body.”

And after giving him permission to live as a solitary on his own, he set out on the road to depart.

After his master and companions had left, Gallus placed his nets and seine in a boat and went to the priest Willimar. When he had offered him the nets, amid tears and sighs he recounted everything that had happened concerning his brothers. Then, explaining the causes of his illness, he asked Willimar to be willing to care for him. Willimar received him with every service of charity, granted him a house near his church for his needs, and entrusted this responsibility to two of his clerics, Magnoaldus and Theodorus, so that they might devote themselves with every diligence to his recovery.

After several days had passed, the Lord—the true physician—granted him healing. He began to take food, and, strengthened as time passed, he attained complete health. O illness stronger than all human strength! O fever worthy of every praise! O sickness to be counted among health and joys! For, following the example of the Lord, Gallus suffered on our behalf so that through sacred preaching he might drive away the diseases of souls; he could not go with his master so that he might show us the way of truth. Truly the Lord is patient and merciful: having long been despised in his preachers, while he endures the conversion of sinners, he keeps the teacher from abandoning those who are in error.

## CHAPTER X. Hiltibold the deacon’s indication of the place of solitary habitation desired by the man of God

The deacon of the aforementioned priest, named Hiltiboldus, knew all the paths and retreats of the wilderness. For he was accustomed to roam the solitude frequently in order to catch fish and hawks, and through daily practice to learn the hidden places of the region.

When the holy man had shown him the favor of his intimacy, he asked whether he had ever found in the wilderness a place abundant in pure and wholesome waters, spread out on level ground [Col. 0986B], and suitable for human cultivation.

“I am consumed,” he said, “by the desire of a fervent spirit, longing to spend in solitude the days granted to this life, in accordance with what the Psalmist declares:

‘Behold, fleeing, I have gone far away and remained in solitude. I was awaiting him who would save me,’ and the rest (Psalm LIV [55]).”

The deacon replied:

“Father, this solitude is watered by many streams, terrifying in its ruggedness, full of lofty mountains, winding through narrow valleys, and inhabited by the fiercest beasts. For, besides deer and herds of harmless animals, it produces many bears, countless boars, and wolves beyond number, remarkable for their savagery. I am therefore afraid that, if I lead you there, you will be devoured by such enemies.”

To this the holy man replied:

“It is the Apostle’s judgment: ‘If God is for us, who is against us?’ [Col. 0986C] (Romans VIII). And: ‘We know that for those who love God all things work together for good’ (ibid.). He who delivered Daniel from the lions’ den can also rescue me from the hand of beasts.”

The deacon answered him:

“Put provisions and a very small net in your bag, for tomorrow I will lead you into the wilderness. If you find a place acceptable to you, give thanks to God and fulfill the strictness of the Lord’s command. The God who led you out of a distant region will himself, just as he gave a heavenly companion to his servant Tobias, send his angel with us and show us a place suited to your holy desires.”

Accordingly, the blessed man remained fasting that same day and spent the night until dawn of the following day in prayer. It was fitting indeed that what he was beginning through divine love should be commended to the Lord by the most earnest prayer.

## CHAPTER XI. How, penetrating the wilderness with the deacon, he found the desired place and chose it for himself, and concerning the obedience of the bear

When the morning star, advancing, had revealed the hiding places of night, and the sun, leaving the lower regions, had visited the higher zones of the world along its accustomed course and displayed its fiery radiance to mortals from the eastern sky, the champion of God, taking with him what his guide had said, set out on the road with the blessing of prayer, the deacon leading the way.

When they had traveled throughout the day, around the ninth hour the deacon said:

“Father, the hour of refreshment is now approaching. Let us take a little bread and water, for, strengthened in this way, we will be able to complete the remainder of the journey more easily.”

The man of God replied:

“Son, take refreshment according to the need of the body. I will taste nothing before the Lord shows me the place of the dwelling I desire.”

And the deacon said:

“As we are companions in suffering, so shall we also be companions in consolation.”

After these words they began to travel more quickly, because the day was already declining and the sun’s heat was nearing its setting.

They came to a certain little river called the Stemaha [alternative forms: Stemiha, Staina]. Following its course, they reached a rock from which it descended forcefully and formed a broad pool. There they saw many fish, and, placing their nets, they caught them. Then, after lighting a fire, the deacon roasted the fish and placed the bread on the bag.

Blessed Gallus, having withdrawn a little from him for the sake of prayer, was walking amid the dense thickets of brambles when his foot caught and he fell to the ground. When the deacon saw this, he hurried to lift up the fallen man. But the man of God, foreseeing what was to come, said:

“Leave me. ‘This is my rest forever and ever; here I shall dwell, for I have chosen it.’”

When he had risen after prayer, he took a hazelwood staff [Note: [Col. 0987D] That is, a staff made of horn, or of the shrub called *cornus* or *coryllus*, commonly called *cornouiller* (dogwood).] and made a cross, fixing it in the ground.

He wore around his neck a small reliquary containing relics of the blessed Mother of God Mary and of the holy martyrs Mauritius and Desiderius. After hanging it upon the cross, he called the deacon, and they prostrated themselves together in prayer.

Then the venerable man offered this prayer:

“Lord Jesus Christ, who for the salvation of the human race deigned to be born of a Virgin and to undergo death, do not despise my desire because of my sins. Rather, in honor of your holy Mother and of your martyrs and confessors, prepare in this place a dwelling suited to your service.”

When the prayer was finished, the day also came to an end as the sun set. At last they took food with thanksgiving and, again giving thanks to God, lay down on the ground to rest for a little while.

But when the holy man thought that his companion was held in deep sleep, he rose and prostrated himself in the form of a cross before the reliquary, pouring forth devoted prayers to the Lord.

Meanwhile, a bear descended from the mountain and cautiously gathered the crumbs and fragments that had fallen from the meal of the diners. When the man of God saw this, he said to the beast:

“I command you, beast, in the name of the Lord: take a piece of wood and put it in the fire.”

At his command the animal turned, brought a very large piece of wood, and threw it into the fire.

Then the most benevolent man approached the bag, took a whole loaf from the small store of food, and offered it to the servant. As the bear received it, he commanded:

“In the name of my Lord Jesus Christ, leave this valley. You shall have the surrounding mountains and hills in common in such a way that you harm no human being here and injure none of the livestock.”

While this was happening, the deacon pretended to be asleep, but observed what the man beloved of God was doing with the beast. He then rose [Col. 0988A], prostrated himself at Gallus’s feet, and said:

“Now I know truly that the Lord is with you, since even the beasts of the wilderness obey you.”

But Gallus said to him:

“Be careful not to tell anyone at all about this until you have seen the glory of God.”

## CHAPTER XII. How the holy Father drove away the apparitions of demons shown in the form of women in that same place

When the night had passed and the golden light illuminated the dark woods, the deacon said:

“My father, what shall we do today?”

He replied:

“I beg you, son, not to be displeased by what I say. Since the Lord has enabled us to find what we sought, let us spend this day also in this place. Take the net and go to the pool; I too will follow you as quickly as possible. Perhaps the Lord will show us his customary generosity, so that, when we return to the fortress, we may offer our father the priest a blessing from this place, which the Lord has granted us to find.”

The deacon replied:

“I am glad of what you command, Father.”

He rose quickly, invoking the name of the Lord, took the little net, and went to the river. When he wished to cast it into the pool, demons in the form of women stood for a long time on the bank, stripped as though they wished to enter a bath. When they displayed the indecency of their bodies to him, they picked up stones, threw them at him, and said:

“You brought this man into the wilderness, an unrighteous man full of envy, who has always been accustomed to overcome us by his sorceries.”

The deacon returned to the man of God and told him what he had seen and heard. The chosen warrior of God prostrated himself with the deacon and prayed to the Lord in these words [Col. 0988C]:

“Almighty God, ineffable goodness, immeasurable majesty, according to your mercy and not according to my merits, receive these prayers with a gracious hearing, and command these demons to leave this place, so that it may be sanctified in honor of your name.”

When they had risen from prayer, they came to the pool. Immediately the demons turned to flight and went along the course of the little river toward the nearest mountain.

Saint Gallus said to them:

“I command you, apparitions, by the power of the immeasurable Trinity: leave this place, go into the deserted mountains, and have no further confidence of returning here.”

Then they cast the net into the pool and caught as many fish as they wished. While they were freeing the fish from the meshes of the linen net, they heard at the summit of the mountain [Col. 0988D] voices like those of two women lamenting the dead. They said to one another:

“Alas! What shall we do, or where shall we go? This stranger does not allow us to live among human beings, nor does he permit us to remain in the wilderness.”

These voices were heard not only then, but afterward on three occasions. Whenever the deacon himself had entered the forest to catch hawks, he heard the demons crying out from a certain mountain called Himilimberg [Note: Himilimberg was sometimes called by monks Mons-Coeli, formerly Monkelen, and is now called Menkelen, as Goldastus noted.] and asking whether Gallus was still in the wilderness or had already departed.

## CHAPTER XIII. The choice of the place itself and the departure of the serpents

[Col. 0989A]

After the departure of the demons, those faithful lovers of the wilderness surveyed the valley. Seeing many desirable features between two little rivers—a beautiful forest, mountains all around, and a plain in the middle—they judged the place to be excellent for building a cell.

The holy man then recalled the statement that Jacob had uttered after his vision of the ladder and of the angels ascending and descending upon it:

“Truly, the Lord is in this place” (Genesis XXVIII).

Until that time, the same valley had contained a very great multitude of serpents. From that day, however, they departed so completely that afterward they did not appear there.

This miracle agrees with what came before. For once the devil had been expelled from the place, it was fitting that the animal through which he had deceived humanity should yield to the dwelling of holiness.

## CHAPTER XIV. How he consecrated that place by fasting and, returning to the fortress, learned of the bishop’s death

When they had returned to the place of their first station, where the man of God had earlier fixed the little cross, the deacon said to him:

“Let us take the bag and the net and return to the fortress.”

But Gallus replied:

“Son, return to your own place, as you wish. I, however, will remain in these regions for a little while and, after three days, with the Lord as my guide, will follow you.”

The deacon said:

“I will certainly not return to our father while you are absent, lest you perhaps say that I killed you for the sake of your possessions. Or, if I wished to deny the murder, he might object to me: ‘Why did you leave him in the wilderness? Return quickly and bring him to me.’ In that case I should have both doubled labor and manifest disgrace.”

To this the holy man replied:

“Go, son. I will hasten after your footsteps as quickly as possible.”

After the deacon had departed, the champion of God remained fasting from all bodily nourishment for the entire three days, in order that he might consecrate through the beginnings of abstinence the place he was preparing for spiritual warfare.

On the fourth day, therefore, he left the wilderness and revisited the priest’s house. Amid the duties of friendly greeting, he rendered due thanks to God with fitting praise for all the good things God had shown him.

The priest received him joyfully and ordered the table to be set. When they had sat down, blessing God, they took food with thanksgiving. During the meal the deacon said to the priest:

“If the bear had been present, perhaps Gallus would have offered him a blessing.”

When asked why he had spoken in this way, he recounted everything that had happened in the wilderness.

From that day and thereafter, they regarded him as a prophet and holy man, measuring daily the greatness of his merits by the severity of his life and his devotion to virtue.

Meanwhile, while they were living together, a messenger came to the priest and announced that the bishop of Constance, named Gaudentius, had departed this life. When they heard this, they all joined together fervently in prayers and tears for the repose of the deceased shepherd.

## CHAPTER XV. How he was summoned to the duke with the priest, refused to go there, traveled through Raetia, and was received by the deacon John

Seven days afterward, a letter from Duke Gunzo arrived for the priest, ordering him to come on the twelfth day to the estate of Iburningas [Note: Iburningae was a royal estate, or fortress, on the right side of Lake Potamicus. At that time it was the seat of the dukes of Alamannia and Swabia; it is now called Oberlingen, a free city of the Roman Empire, as Goldastus observed.] and to bring the man of God with him.

For a malignant spirit had invaded his only daughter, named Fridiburg, who shone with exceptional beauty. While she was tormented by various afflictions, she endured almost continuous fasting; often thrown to the ground, she writhed in pitiable madness amid dreadful foam, to such an extent that she could scarcely be restrained by the efforts of four men.

After the passage of thirty days from the beginning of this affliction, the evil inhabitant began through her to utter dreadful voices. For this reason her father sent messengers to King Sigibert, son of Theodoric, who had betrothed her [Note: If this account is true—for some modern authors reject it as a fable—it cannot refer to Sigibert, son of Theodoric, who, according to Fredegar, Chronicle, chapter 42, was killed together with his brother Corbo by order of King Chlothar after the battle of Tolbiac, when he was scarcely twelve years old. It must therefore refer either to Sigibert, son of Dagobert—as the ancient documents of the abbey of Saint Martin of Metz show, preserved by Meurisse, bishop of Madaura, in his History of the Bishops of Metz, under Pappolus—or certainly to Sigibert, or Sigbercht, king of the East Angles, a good and religious man who, while he was formerly living in exile in Gaul to escape the hostility of Rædwald, received baptism during the reign of Dagobert, as Bede testifies in Book III, chapter 18 of his History.], so that they might inform him of everything that was happening concerning the girl.

The king immediately sent two bishops, on whose merits he particularly relied, with royal gifts to the girl, so that they might cure her through the remedy of their prayers from the sickness of her frenzied madness.

Accordingly, the priest Willimar, wishing to come to the duke at the time fixed by letter, said to blessed Gallus:

“You know the duke’s command. Let us go to him.”

But Gallus replied:

“This journey is yours, not mine. You go, therefore. What have I to do with the princes of this world? I will return to the wilderness from which I came.”

“Do not act in this way,” said Willimar. “Come with me, lest perhaps the duke, who is deeply distressed by his daughter’s affliction, should be provoked to anger and send soldiers to have you brought there in chains.”

The man full of God replied:

“I will go first to my cell, so that I may provide for the welfare and necessities of the brothers who are there and who will serve the Lord.”

He said this in order not to go to the prince. Then, rising, that distinguished soldier of the Lord made his way toward the place of the habitation previously chosen.

On the following day he forbade the brothers who were with him to tell anyone where he was going. If they were questioned too insistently by anyone, he ordered them to say that he had been invited to Italy by a letter from his master.

After saying this, he took two of his disciples [Col. 0991A] and traveled through the wilderness of Raetia Curiensis [Note: They call this First Raetia, bordering Italy, whose chief town is the settlement of Curia, Chur. They call the region extending from Curia to the Danube Second Raetia.] When they had crossed the nearest mountain, they came into a wilderness called Sennia. From there they went down to the nearest village, called Quaradaves, and found there the deacon John, a just man who feared God. He received them as guests and fostered them with every act of kindness.

They pretended that they had come from far away, and they remained with him for seven days.

## CHAPTER XVI. How the bishops sent by the king, after the priest had been sent for the man of God, were unable to free the duke’s daughter and returned to the king in confusion, the demon confessing the power of blessed Gallus

The aforementioned priest, the guest of the holy men, heard that the man of God had left his cell. He boarded a ship, crossed over to the duke, and reported what had happened concerning the man of God.

The duke ordered him to return quickly and, after sending messengers in pursuit of the man of God, to ask him devotedly to come. He added:

“For if, through his prayer, the Lord frees my daughter from the demon, I will give him the bishopric of the Church of Constance and will also honor him with abundant gifts of reward.”

The priest promised that he would do as commanded if he could find the man they sought. He then sought a boat and returned to his own place.

Meanwhile, the bishops sent by the king arrived. They found the girl herself suffering from an excessive frenzy, while her parents, the entire household, and her relatives wept over her, weighed down by pitiable grief. The whole house was wasting away beneath a single calamity: the girl was tormented by madness, and the others by sorrow.

After the bishops entered and presented the gifts sent by the king, they poured out prayers to the Lord in the girl’s presence. But she tore herself free from the hands of those restraining her, seized one of their swords by force, and wished to kill the bishops.

When she could not accomplish this, the unclean spirit said to one of them:

“If you wanted to drive me from this vessel, as you promised the king, why did you not make your daughter, whom that old woman conceived and bore by you, come with you?”

Then he said to the other:

“And you have committed fornication with three women. By your command—which is strengthened by no merit of holiness—I shall never depart.

“There is, however, a certain man of great power with almighty God, named Gallus. He forcibly expelled me from Tucconia, where I had long enjoyed the rest I desired, and boldly destroyed my dwellings. Later, when he found me living at Brigantium, he dispossessed me by that same power.

“Because this duke expelled him from that place, I seized this girl in revenge for the injury done to him. Unless he himself comes, I shall in no way be removed from this possession.”

One of the bishops then struck the frenzied girl in the face, saying:

“Be silent, Satan, deserter from truth, lover and author of falsehood!”

He thought that the demon was speaking of a rooster, *gallus*, rather than of Gallus the man.

After the evil spirit had subjected them to many further verbal insults, they remained there for only three days. Then they returned to their own place and reported to the king everything that had happened.

## CHAPTER XVII. How the man of God came to the duke through the priest

The priest, following the man of God step by step in accordance with the duke’s command, found him in a cave, nourishing his spirit with the consolation of reading. Approaching him, he greeted him humbly and said:

“Do not be afraid, servant of God, to come to the duke. Under oath he has promised that he will inflict no injury upon you. Moreover, when you lay your hand upon the girl’s head and the unclean spirit departs from her through your prayers, he will raise you to the honor of the episcopate in the see of Constance.”

While they were discussing these matters, the deacon John arrived and, according to custom, offered him unleavened loaves, a small flask of wine, oil and butter, and honey in small vessels, together with roasted fish.

When the man of God recognized that he was coming, he gave thanks to God, full of joy. The three most faithful companions sat down to eat and received the Lord’s gifts with thanksgiving.

During this meal the holy man said to the priest:

“Stay with us for the coming night, and tomorrow, with the Lord’s will, I will depart with you.”

When the priest had agreed to this proposal, the deacon John said to the man of God:

“I will come here at first light and bring my mule, equipped with a pack saddle, so that you may travel together. I myself will be the guardian of the cave and will watch over it carefully.”

Saint Gallus replied:

“You have spoken well, son. I shall return by the road through the wilderness by which they came to my cell and visit the brothers. Afterward, as soon as I can, I shall hurry to the fortress.”

The priest, however, bound him by a solemn adjuration never to do anything contrary to his words. They then departed together. John also, after receiving a blessing, returned to his own house.

When the blessed man had reached his cell by the direct road, he spent that night there resting with the brothers. On the following morning, taking two brothers with him, he went to the fortress. There he found the duke’s messenger with the priest, urging them to travel with all haste. The messenger also reported that the girl had now remained for three continuous days without nourishment.

They therefore boarded a small boat and, hastening forward with all their strength, cutting across the deep waters with their floating timber, reached the duke on the following night.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How by prayer and a word he freed the duke’s daughter from the demon

When the sun, after conquering the darkness of deep night, restored bright day to the earth with joy, the duke ordered them to come into the chamber where the possessed girl was being kept.

At that time she lay in her mother’s lap with her eyes closed and her mouth gaping open. Her limbs were also so sprawled that she appeared almost dead. A foul odor burst from the depths of her mouth, so strong that the room itself seemed to have been sprinkled with sulfur.

The father entered with his household to see what the man of God would do. Certain of the Lord’s generosity, Gallus humbly prostrated himself and poured out these prayers to the Lord with tears:

“Lord Jesus Christ, who for the salvation of the human race deigned to take flesh and to be born through a Virgin; who commanded the winds and the sea, and also ordered the devil, intent upon the deceits of his cunning, to retreat; who through your Passion deigned to redeem the world and restore it to freedom: command this most unclean spirit to depart from this girl for the glory of your name, so that the proud invader may leave your creation, and your creature, rejoicing, may serve you, its Creator.”

When he had risen from prayer, he took her right hand and lifted her up—for the evil spirit had thrown her into confusion. Placing his hand upon her head, he said:

“I command you in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, unclean spirit, to go out and depart from this creation of God.”

When he had said this, she opened her eyes and looked at him. The evil spirit addressed him in these words:

“Are you Gallus, who earlier expelled me from my dwellings? I certainly invaded the daughter of this duke in revenge for the injury that he inflicted upon you and your companions—and you are driving me out in this way? If I leave here, where shall I go?”

“To the place,” he replied, “where the Lord has prepared for you the eternal punishment of the abyss.”

Immediately, in the sight of those present, it came out of the girl’s mouth like a pitch-black bird, terrifying with infernal horror. At that very hour she rose healed, and the man of God joyfully restored her, rejoicing, to her mother.

## CHAPTER XIX. How he rejected the honor of the episcopate offered to him, distributed the duke’s gifts among the poor, and urged his disciple to almsgiving

After these things had been accomplished, the duke ordered the gifts that the king had sent for the girl to be offered to Gallus. He also asked him to accept the highest dignity of the episcopal rank.

The blessed man replied:

“While my lord and father Columbanus lives, I shall not usurp the ministry of the altar unless he permits me. Therefore I cannot undertake the burden of this governance that you offer. If you certainly wish this to happen, wait for the time being until I send a letter to my abbot to inform him of your desire. If I learn that he has granted permission, then and only then will I accept the burden of pastoral care that has been offered.”

The duke said to him:

“You have spoken well. Let it be according to your word.”

And he dismissed him in peace.

Gallus took the things that had been given to him and crossed the open water by rowing. The duke, deeply moved by such a clear sign of his holiness, ordered the prefect of Arbon to go with the entire service of the people to the place of the Cell, and to construct, according to the disposition of the man of God, whatever buildings necessity required.

After the venerable Father had entered the fortress of Arbon once the rowing chant had been sung, he summoned all the poor and needy and distributed among them the gifts he had brought.

When one of his disciples, named Magnoaldus, saw this, he said to him:

“Father, I have a precious silver vessel, distinguished by engraved work. If you wish, I will reserve it so that we may make sacred vessels for the ministry from it.”

He replied:

“Son, remember the statement of blessed Peter the apostle, which he spoke to the lame man who hoped for money: ‘Silver and gold I do not have’ (Acts III). Do not therefore be found acting contrary to that salutary example. Take care to give the vessel you possess to the poor.

“For my most blessed teacher Columbanus customarily offers the sacrifice of salvation to the Lord in bronze vessels, since it is also said that our Savior was fastened to the cross with bronze nails.”

When all these things had been completed, Gallus returned to the sanctuary of his beloved solitude.

## CHAPTER XX. With what fervor of charity he summoned the deacon John by letter and instructed him

[Col. 0994B]

Then he sent a letter to the deacon John, asking him to come to him. When John received the letters of his beloved master, he took whatever he could offer as a blessing and came to him. After presenting the customary gifts, he greeted the father and was honored with a fatherly greeting.

When John asked the holy man about the success of his journey, Gallus replied:

“By the divine mercy that went before us and followed us, everything turned out well. The prince received us with the greatest joy, God freed his daughter from the demon, and he himself gave us considerable gifts. In addition, he offered me the honor of the episcopate. I did not agree to accept it before receiving my abbot’s command.

“Therefore, son, heed my counsels. Remain with me, read the books of divine knowledge, and, with the grace of God cooperating, I will teach you the meaning of the Scriptures.”

The deacon fell at his feet, giving thanks. He sent back to their own place the young men who had come with him, but he himself remained with the venerable man. Gallus began to introduce him into the storehouses of Scripture, showing him the hidden things of the New and Old Testament.

Thus illuminated by heavenly mercy, John progressed through the diligence of such instruction, to such an extent that, nobly learned in the whole breadth of divine Scripture, he displayed the fruit of his teacher’s labor.

## CHAPTER XXI. In what words the duke’s daughter, recounting the life and virtues of blessed Gallus, obtained for him the favor and support of King Sigibert

[Col. 0994D]

When King Sigibert heard that the girl had recovered her health, he ordered her father to present her before him. Taking immense gifts and a multitude of boys and girls, the father led her with a great retinue of his people as far as the Rhine; from there he sent her on to the king by way of the counts.

When she had been received graciously and was asked how she had obtained a remedy for her illness, since the bishops sent for that purpose had been unable to restore her to health, she gave this account:

“My lord, there is a certain man in the province that I left when I was brought here, an inhabitant of a solitude and a member of the Scottish people, named Gallus. He possesses such power and merit with God that he exercises a singular strength against demons.

“When I, your servant, was almost at the dangerous end of a wavering life under the severe assault of my tormentor, that same man of God came at my father’s request. Fortifying me with the sign of the saving standard, he ordered the tyrant in an authoritative voice to depart.

“In the sight of all who were present, it came out of my mouth like a raven, black as pitch and terrifying as Tartarus. When he had strengthened me with the nourishment of the heavenly sacrifice, I was restored to my former health.”

After recounting these things, the girl fell at the king’s feet and said:

“I beg you, lord, to cherish that man with the kindness of your favor and not to hesitate to offer him fitting thanks on my behalf.”

The king asked her in what wilderness the extraordinary man lived.

She replied:

“In the forest adjoining the territory of Arbon, which is held under public law. It lies between the Alps of Raetia and the shore of Lake Brigantium.”

When the king heard that Gallus was living on public property, he ordered a charter of confirmation to be drawn up, so that by royal authority the holy man might possess the place where he lived.

He also sent the man of God, through his messengers, two pounds of gold and an equal weight of silver together with the letter of grant, commending himself most earnestly to Gallus’s holy prayers. He ordered Duke Gunzo to provide the inhabitant of the solitude with whatever assistance was necessary for building a cell, if he wished to remain there as a solitary.

## CHAPTER XXII. By what plan the same girl escaped the king’s marriage chamber and submitted herself to divine service
[Column 0995C] After not many days had passed, the same king, wishing to take the girl as his wife, ordered by a public edict that the senate of his priests and nobles should attend the solemnities of the wedding. When he had entered, surrounded by a procession of nobles, where she was staying, he said to her: “Let us go up to the palace, for the wedding is ready; the priests and chiefs of the peoples have arrived with suitable blessings [that is, gifts].”

When she heard this, she fell at his feet, saying: “My lord, since my former illness has wasted me by its weight, adverse health has drained my strength, and sickness has weakened the functions of my limbs, grant me at least seven days’ respite, so that I may recover some of my lost strength and thus be able to present myself before you.”

When the king graciously received this request, he returned to the palace, while she remained in a private chamber. In both places immense preparations for celebration were made, and many wondered why, after being separated for so long, they had postponed the wedding feast. Meanwhile, when the seven days had passed, around the time of the morning office the girl entered the church of blessed Stephen, the first martyr, with two men and an equal number of women. Withdrawing behind the doors of the church, she removed her royal garments and assumed the habit of a holier purpose, without the men who had come with her knowing this.

Having laid aside the clothing of earthly dignity, and following the splendor of holiness with a certain contempt for herself, she approached the altar and, throwing herself face down, worshiped the Lord with great devotion. Then, when she rose, she grasped the horn of the altar and uttered these words:

“Blessed Stephen, who by your blood bore witness to Christ, commend my prayer to the Lord through your merits, so that through your intercession today he may turn the heart of my lord the king according to my will, lest he remove from my head the veil that I have taken up for the love of God.”

The men who were with her, seeing these things, went to the king and reported what had happened. He summoned the priests and some of his nobles and began to ask them what they thought should be done in this matter.

[Column 0996A] Cyprianus [Note: [Column 0995D] Saxius proves in *Pontif. Arelat.*, no. 39, that no bishop of this name presided over the see of Arles.] of Arles replied to the king: “Since it is plainly evident that, when this girl was delivered from the demon, she bound herself by this vow, which she appears to have fulfilled, you must take care lest, if you invalidate her vow, she should perhaps be seized by a renewed assault of demons, and her last state become worse than the first; and you incur the guilt of so great a crime.”

The king, steadfast in justice and full of fear of the Lord, gave the counsel the assent of a devoted heart. He entered the church, ordered the garment prepared for the wedding to be brought, and ordered the crown intended to adorn the bride to be brought. When these things had been brought, he ordered the girl to come to him. But the bride of God, already clinging to the companions of the Lamb, could not be pulled away from the altar, because she feared that she would be dragged out of the church.

When she clung even more tightly to the horns of the altar, the king urged her not to be afraid, saying: “Today you shall see the fulfillment of your will in every respect.”

She, placed between hope and fear, rested her head upon the altar and said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to his will.”

The king then ordered the priests to lift her up and bring her to him. This done, at his command she was dressed in royal clothing and crowned with the sacred veil. The devout king looked upon her and said: “Behold, prepared for my wedding, I hand you over to the embraces of the heavenly Bridegroom, our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Taking her right hand, he placed it upon the altar. Then, as he crossed the threshold of the church, he revealed in tears the love he had kept hidden. Afterward he summoned her and had her sit beside him in the palace. He honored her with immense gifts and placed her in charge of the monastery of the handmaids [Column 0996D] of God, built in the city of Metz in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, where all the events we have just related took place.

[Note: [Column 0995D] The women’s monastery of Saint Peter was founded within the walls of the city of Metz by Eleutherius, duke of the Franks. Blessed Waldrada presided over this community during the reigns of Theoderic and Theodebert, kings of Gaul and sons of King Childebert.]

In accomplishing all these things, the girl followed the counsel of the most blessed Gallus, who, with the Lord’s help, had freed her from the demon.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How the aforementioned John advanced for three years through the teaching and example of the man of God

During this same period, the deacon John, remaining with the venerable Father, drank eagerly from the prudence that abounded in him from heaven—especially in resolving difficult questions of divine Scripture and in matters of undefiled faith. He not only loved the knowledge of the daily work which that outstanding imitator of apostolic discipline pursued with diligent zeal, but also acquired it.

For, enlightened by divine grace, whatever he learned by sight or hearing he quickly stored in his deep memory and, so to speak, in the treasury of his heart. Under the discipline of this instruction he spent three years, preserving every form of gentleness and humility.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How blessed Gallus excused himself from promotion to the episcopate at the principal council

[Column 0997B]

After this, the duke already often mentioned asked the man of God by letter to come to the town of Constance to choose a bishop to preside over that see. He summoned the bishops of Autun and Verdun, together with a multitude of clerics. He also had the bishop of Nemidona—which modern people call Speyer—come; and through messengers and letters he ordered the priests of all Alamannia and all the companies of clergy generally to assemble at Constance on the appointed day, namely the Sunday immediately following Easter. He himself also attended this gathering with his nobles and counts.

When this synod was being celebrated with the arrival of such a multitude, and its future duration was announced as three days, the most blessed Gallus, full of divine counsel, set out for the town, taking with him John and Magnoald, who had been raised to the office of deacon. When he entered the council chamber, the duke spoke these words:

“May almighty God, by whose providence the entire body of the Church is increased and governed, through the intervention and merit of blessed Mary ever-virgin, in whose honor this place has been consecrated, pour out the Holy Spirit upon us today, so that we may choose a pontiff suited to govern the people of the faithful and filled with pastoral diligence for directing the Church of God.”

He then exhorted the bishops and the whole clergy to provide a ruler for the Church according to the most salutary decrees of the canons.

All the clerics began saying to one another: “This Gallus has a good testimony from everyone who knows his life. In the divine Scriptures he has attained the summit of knowledge, and in every honorable aspect of life he shines with the light of wisdom. He joins bodily chastity to a life of justice; he possesses gentleness together with humility; and to salutary continence he adds patience. He is a giver of alms, a father to orphans, and eager to comfort widows. It is fitting that this follower of every virtue should be pastor of the peoples.”

When the duke heard this, he said to him: “Do you hear what these men are saying and affirming?”

The holy Father replied: “They speak well; would that what they confess were true. But while they discuss such matters among themselves, they do not know that the canons prohibit someone who moves from his own place from easily being ordained in another place.

[Column 0998A] There is with me, however, a certain deacon named John, a native of the neighboring region, to whom the testimony they have given me can rightly be applied. Believing him chosen by divine judgment, I offer him to you for promotion.”

## CHAPTER XXV. The promotion and consecration of the aforementioned John, and the care they afterward showed him

By this testimony the most holy man stirred everyone’s affection for John—for they could not believe anything about him other than what the man beloved of God had asserted. The duke therefore had the deacon brought forward.

“You are John the deacon?” he asked.

“I certainly am,” he replied.

“From where,” said the duke, “do you derive your family line?”

He answered: “I was born in Chur-Raetia of a family of moderate rank.”

The duke then said to him: “Can you bear the burden of the episcopal mitre?”

At that point the venerable Gallus promised that he would answer for his son.

While they were discussing these matters in mutual conversation, the deacon withdrew and, fleeing, sought refuge in the church of Saint Stephen the martyr, which stood outside the town. The priests and the people followed him. They seized him, drenched in the joyful tears of those who were glad, and although he resisted, dragged him into the presence of the bishops and the duke.

All together they raised their voices, saying: “Today the Lord has chosen John as his pontiff.”

All the people replied: “Amen.”

The bishops then led him to the altar and ordained him bishop through the solemn ministry of blessing. When the sacred promotion had been completed, they asked him to celebrate the mysteries of the saving sacrifice.

After the customary introductory rites of the divine offering, following the reading of the Gospel they asked the venerable Gallus to provide the assembled multitude with the nourishment of sacred instruction through preaching. He took the bishop John with him and ascended the steps, on the understanding that Gallus would gather the instruments of edification, while the bishop would convey them for the benefit of the Barbarians by interpreting what had been well expressed.

He therefore began to speak about the beginning of creation and recalled Adam’s sin, on account of which he was driven from paradise. Moving from there to the Flood, he passed in succession over the times and deeds of the patriarchs. He also recounted the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, their passage through the Red Sea, the giving of the Law through Moses, and the miracles of the heavenly food.

Then, briefly touching upon the succession of the kings and the times of the prophets, he unfolded the time of the Lord’s coming. Recalling also the Savior’s baptism and the glory of his miracles, he truthfully added the shame of the cross together with the various forms of persecution by the impious.

Hearing these things, the pastors of the Church and the multitude of the people shed abundant tears and said to one another: “Truly the Holy Spirit has spoken today through the mouth of this man.”

He continued his preaching up to the resurrection of Christ and ended it with a commemoration of the universal judgment. All who were present were filled with joyful exultation of spirit; they blessed the Lord and returned home with gladness.

The venerable teacher remained with Bishop John for seven days and, among many words of saving consolation, repeatedly impressed these upon him: “Whomever God has chosen, no human being shall despise; rather, the one commended by divine judgment will be exalted in everyone’s veneration.”

Then, having received John’s blessing, Gallus returned to his cell.

The bishop ordered those in charge of the episcopal property to come to the man of God with those subject to them and to obey his command. After this, mutual love was preserved between them with such devotion that, joined always by the bond of spiritual service, they seemed separated only in body.

The master nurtured his disciple with fatherly concern, prayers, and salutary counsel; the disciple, in turn, supported his teacher with filial honor and every form of assistance in his needs. Thus the holy fellowship of the devout grew in honor and became increasingly renowned for its multiplied love.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How Saint Gallus, having previously learned through a vision of the passing of blessed Columbanus, discovered it afterward through the mission of his disciple

At a later time, the outstanding cultivator of virtue began to build an oratory, with small dwellings arranged around it for the brothers to live in. By instruction and example he had already stirred twelve men, strengthened by the holiness of their monastic purpose, to desire eternal things.

One day, as they were returning to their beds at first light after the labor of the morning office in order to rest, the man of God called his deacon Magnoald and said to him: “Prepare the ministry of the sacred offering, so that I may celebrate the divine mysteries without delay.”

The deacon replied: “Are you going to celebrate Mass, Father?”

He said to him: “After the vigils of this night I learned through a vision that my lord and father Columbanus has today departed from the distress of this life to the joys of paradise. Therefore I must offer the sacrifice of salvation for his repose.”

When the signal was sounded, they entered the oratory, prostrated themselves in prayer, and began to celebrate Masses and devote themselves to prayers in commemoration of blessed Columbanus.

When the sacred service of devotion was finished, the venerable Gallus said to the deacon Magnoald: “My son, do not regard the burden of my request as troublesome; take up the road and go to Italy. When you have crossed through to the monastery called Bobbio, inquire carefully [Column 0999D] what has happened concerning my abbot. Mark the day and hour, so that, if you discover that he has died, you may learn whether my vision is supported by the outcome of truth. After learning all these things through careful investigation, you shall return and report to me.”

The deacon fell at his master’s feet and complained that the journey was unknown to him. But the blessed man, in a gentle voice, urged him not to be afraid.

“Go,” he said, “and the Lord will direct your steps.”

Strengthened by this consolation, the pupil of the devout teacher obeyed the command. After receiving the provision of his blessing, he hastened onto the road.

When he reached the monastery as instructed, he found that everything had happened just as it had been revealed to his Father through the vision. He remained there for one night [Column 1000A] and received from the brothers a letter for blessed Gallus reporting the venerable passing of Columbanus.

They also sent by the deacon his staff, which is commonly called a *cambotta* [variant *cambutta*, that is, a pastoral staff], saying that the holy abbot, before his passing, had ordered Gallus to be released through this well-known pledge.

After being dismissed by them, Magnoald hastened his journey. Proceeding successfully in all things, he reached his lord and Father on the eighth day, carrying the letter of report and the token of release.

When the holy Gallus read the letter, retaining the love of his dearest father in a full heart, he shed abundant tears and, having gathered the brothers, disclosed the reasons for his grief. Thereafter they frequently commemorated so great a father in holy prayers and saving sacrifices.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The miracle revealed through the enlargement of a board

[Column 1000B]

One day, while he was working with the brothers on the construction of the oratory, a certain board intended to be placed in the wall appeared to be four palms shorter in length than the others. When the craftsmen working on the same project wanted to add something to it, blessed Gallus, conscious of the power he possessed in the Lord, ordered them to leave their work and enter the house to take the meal that the Lord had prepared with him.

When they had done as he commanded, he handed them blessed bread with his own hand. After the meal, when they all resumed the unfinished work together, they found that the board which, because of its shortness, they had previously wanted to discard was longer than all the others by half a foot.

Amazed at what had happened, they fitted the wood, which had miraculously grown, into its place in the wall. From then on, when sought by the faithful, it effectively healed toothache for a long time; besides preserving the memory of the ancient miracle, it was continually honored by new effects.

In this event we can weigh the greatness of his merits and the power of his prayer: dry wood was enlarged contrary to nature, and, so that the old miracle would not be erased, it was continually repeated through renewed testimony of signs.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How he satisfied the brothers who came from Luxeuil, and how wonderfully he refreshed them with the abundance of a heavenly gift

After this, Eustasius, abbot of the monastery called Luxeuil, whom Columbanus of blessed memory had appointed over that place, departed from the exile of this life to the heavenly homeland.

The brothers living in that monastery therefore took counsel to recall the venerable Gallus and submit themselves to his rule. They sent six brothers from among those who had come from Ireland, to carry a letter explaining the reasons for their mission.

When they had reached the man of God’s cell by the direct route, they announced their arrival and were led to prayer. When the prayer was finished, they entered the house and handed him the letter.

[Column 1001A] When the holy man had read it through, he said to them:

“I, brothers, desiring to imitate the words of the Prophet who says, ‘I have become a stranger to my brothers and a sojourner to the sons of my mother’ (Psalm 68:9), have abandoned my acquaintances and relatives. In order that I might serve the Lord more freely, I chose the solitude of secluded places. And, to pass over the renunciation of parents and estates, I did not consent to accept episcopal honor or the riches of the world.

“How, then, after this renunciation and voluntary poverty, shall I become entangled in worldly affairs, be exalted by honors, and weighed down by burdens? Far be it from me, having put my hand to the plow, to look back at what I have left behind and, like a dog, return to my vomit.

“You yourselves know that, when I was placed among you, I always devoted myself to humility and submission. How, then, do you believe that I can be summoned to so lofty a height? Revise your plans and turn elsewhere. What the Lord has once fixed in my heart, he will not allow to be changed.”

By these and similar words he removed their hope of obtaining this request.

Then he called one of the brothers and asked him what they would have for the meal. When the answer was given that only a sextarius of flour was available for everyone’s use, he ordered bread to be made, saying: “God is able to prepare a table in the desert.”

When he had ordered vegetables to be gathered, he himself took a net and, with one of his disciples and the visiting brothers, went to a pool. He said: “Let us see whether the merciful Lord wishes to grant some little fish to meet our needs.”

When they reached the pool, they saw [Column 1001C] a large fish swimming in the collected water, with two otters pursuing it, as though they wanted to seize the fleeing creature. They cast the net and dragged the fish, once caught, to the bank. It was twelve palms long and four palms wide.

When this was done, the otters plunged into the depths. The holy fishermen cast the net again and disturbed the fish hiding places by striking the water. The otters appeared a second time, driving such a multitude of fish into the net that, because of their number, they tore it apart in several places.

After the catch had been brought to the bank, the man full of discernment, with the help of those present, threw some of the fish back into the water and said to the brothers: “Today, because of your arrival, the Lord has deigned to reveal an extraordinary manifestation of his generosity.”

They, on the contrary, attributing what had happened to his merits, returned joyfully to the house with him leading the way.

And behold, near the entrance to the cell a man appeared, carrying two wineskins [Column 1002A] full of wine and three modii of flour as an indication of his devotion. They received these gifts with thanksgiving, took food, and after refreshing their bodies, endeavored to nourish their souls with the banquets of spiritual conversation.

Blessed Gallus kept them with him for several days and, out of regard for charity, treated them with every form of human kindness. He also told them what he had learned through a reliable report concerning their common Father, blessed Columbanus.

Then, after offering them the kiss of peace, he dismissed them. Armed with the blessing of so great a Father, they returned home.

## CHAPTER XXIX. How the most holy Father departed to the Lord at Arbon amid his labors of construction

[Column 1002B]

[Column 1002B] Not long afterward, when the Author and Source of every good wished to remove his champion from the contest of the world and adorn him with the everlasting crowns of reward, the priest Willimar came to the holy man’s cell and asked him to go out with him to the fortress. To obtain what he desired, he humbly set forth this complaint in a sorrowful voice:

“Why, Father, have you abandoned me—though I am drawn by the counsels of your words—as though I were despised, and deprived me, a willing hearer, of the salutary precepts of your teaching? To what else could I ascribe this reproach than to the stench of my sins? If my life did not displease your judgment, you would not deprive me of the beloved consolation of your edification.

“Therefore do not now reject us because of our sins. Moved by the Lord’s commands, open the way of truth [Column 1002C] to those who desire it and grant us the gift of your customary kindness.”

Moved by this supplicant’s appeal, he who loved compassion went down with him, and they came to the fortress.

On a solemn day, when the multitude had been summoned, the holy man refreshed the hearts of eager hearers with the sweetness of preaching and clothed everything he said in such a light of wisdom that he was heard with universal rejoicing and honored with complete veneration.

After spending two days there, on the third day he was seized by a fever. Its violence so rapidly weakened him that he could neither return to his cell nor take nourishment. After suffering from this illness for fourteen days, on the sixteenth day of October—that is, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November—having completed ninety-five years of life, he was released from the prison of this life in a good old age and, with his soul full of merits, rendered it up to the good things that were to endure forever.

[Note: [Column 1001D] From the statements at the beginning of this chapter, blessed Gallus died not long after blessed Eustasius, who is known to have departed to heaven in the year 625. In the *Life of Saint Magnus*, or Magnoald, Gallus is said to have survived blessed Columbanus, who died in 615, by only ten years, so that he seems to have left the world in 625.

Yet many considerations overturn this calculation. If Gallus died at the age of ninety-five, who would believe that, ten years earlier, the clergy of Constance thought of promoting to the vacant see—as is read above in chapter 22—a man already decrepit and more than eighty-five years old? Indeed, who would believe that the monks of Luxeuil, after the death of Eustasius, thought of Gallus as almost a centenarian and summoned him as their abbot from a distant region?

Moreover, if Gallus died more than ninety years old in 625, it is necessary to say that Gallus was already advanced in age and older than his blessed master Columbanus when he came to Gaul. Finally, we have already noted in chapter 14 that Gallus survived blessed Dagobert, the son of Chlothar. Evidence for this is the statement that the illustrious Talto, chamberlain of King Dagobert, honored Saint Gallus while he was still alive (*Ratpertus, On the Affairs of Saint Gallus*, chapter 1).

We shall discuss in its proper place the authority of the writer of the *Life of Saint Magnus*. It should further be noted that Saint Gallus is commemorated in the authentic martyrologies of Usuard and Ado not on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, the day on which Walafrid and Wandalbert celebrate him here, but on the tenth day before the Kalends of March.
