Thus Usuard writes: “In Alamannia, Saint Gallus, priest and confessor.” And Ado: “In Alamannia, Saint Gallus, confessor.”

Walafrid and Wandalbert accordingly assign the day of his death to the twenty-second day before the Kalends of November; Usuard and Ado place it on the tenth day before the Kalends of March. Perhaps they record the memory of his elevation, when the body of Saint Gallus was transferred by Boso, bishop of Constance, to a more suitable place, as is reported in the following book, chapter 2.

Saint Gallus therefore died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, around the year 645. See Notker’s *Martyrology*, seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, in Henricus Canisius, volume VI.]

## CHAPTER XXX. How Bishop John attended his funeral, and how he learned that he ought not to be buried there

[Column 1003A]

When John, prelate of the Church of Constance, heard that blessed Gallus was ill at Arbon, he boarded a small boat and took with him kinds of drink and food that he knew were suitable for one suffering from illness, so that by his visit he might refresh his most faithful friend.

As he drew near the harbor, he heard in the priest’s house a great lamentation being made over the funeral of the man of God. He asked what was the cause of so much weeping.

When he learned that the venerable Gallus, the most steadfast guardian of their friendship, had departed from the dangers of this world, he threw himself into the water—for he could not endure, on account of his excessive grief, to wait until the boat reached the shore. He went down with those who had come with him and entered the priest’s house, expressing the grief of his heart in a mournful voice and through the gestures of his body.

He found the holy man’s body wrapped and placed in a coffin. He opened the sarcophagus, looked upon the lifeless corpse of his friend, and shed even bitterer tears, saying:

“Alas, alas, beloved Father; alas, outstanding teacher! Why, after bringing me out of my father’s house, have you left me like an orphan amid these dangers, and by an untimely death broken the confidence I placed in your counsels, upon which I relied so greatly?

“For you, indeed, this death is fruitful, since it brings you to receive the reward you desired so ardently; but for us, struggling amid so many storms of worldly disturbances, it is grievous in many ways.

“Yet we who grieve over the interruption of bodily life must rejoice over the freedom of the immortal soul, confident that you will not cease to assist by your prayers those whom you were accustomed to strengthen by counsel and example.”

During these words, the priest urged him to rise, so that he might pray more fervently to the Lord for the repose of the deceased. They therefore entered the church, and the bishop offered the saving sacrifices for his dearest friend.

When the service of fraternal commemoration was completed, he looked behind him and saw the grave in which they intended to bury the holy body. Taking up the cross and the things used for funeral rites, they entered the house, wishing to carry the treasure of the precious body to the place of burial.

When they tried to carry the coffin containing the corpse, set upon a bier, to the burial pit, it could not be moved in any direction by any strength. While they discussed this new kind of miracle in mutual amazement, Bishop John said: “I truly understand that this site of burial does not please my Father Gallus.”

He ordered the priest to find two unbroken horses and have them brought in. When this had been done, they harnessed them with great difficulty and led them to the place where the body lay. The bishop then offered this prayer with the clergy:

“God, who through the power of your majesty are wholly present everywhere, for whose love this man left his homeland in order to keep your commandments: cause his body to be carried by these unbroken horses to the place that your will has foreseen for him because of his merits.”

When the prayer was ended, everyone present responded: “Amen.”

## CHAPTER XXXI. A cripple healed after receiving a gift of the holy man’s garments

It seems fitting to recount here the miracle that the Lord deigned to display during the funeral of his confessor, clearly showing to everyone that his servant was then truly living with him, when he was freed from the prison of the flesh.

There was there a beggar so contracted by weakness in all the joints of his limbs that, amid the other troubles of his illness, he was entirely deprived of the ability to walk. When the priest was distributing the holy man’s garments to the poor, he gave this man Gallus’s leggings together with his shoes.

At once the cripple, filled with the greatest joy at receiving the gift, fitted the sacred garments to his legs and feet. Suddenly all the joints of his limbs were released; he sprang up, cried out in a loud voice, and gave thanks to the Lord and to Gallus, through whose merits he saw that health had been restored to him.

When the bishop and everyone present saw this miracle of healing, they glorified God with one accord and said: “Today the Lord has deigned, by a manifest act of power, to show us the glory of his servant.”

They gave the healed man a candle, and he followed the funeral with the rest of the people. This was the first sign that the Lord revealed in his memory after his passing.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Signs of his mortification discovered after his death

During the same funeral of the blessed shepherd, another significant indication of his holiness appeared.

The man of God had a small leather case, carefully fastened, whose key he kept under such vigilant custody that, as long as he lived in the body, none of his disciples could discover what was kept inside. He used to carry it hanging from his shoulders wherever he went.

But when he had departed from this life, they took the key and opened the case. They found in it a small hair shirt and an iron chain splattered with blood.

Then, examining the master’s body, they found the place where the chain had often been fastened around him. The flesh itself had been deeply furrowed by the chain in four places, so deeply that blood flowing from those wounds had soaked the hair shirt in several places.

They placed the case with the hair shirt beside his head in the bier and carried them with the body to [Column 1005A] the place of the tomb. They hung these three tokens of his mortification near his head beside the tomb. Through them, thereafter, the Lord graciously displayed many miracles to those who sought them, for the manifestation of his merits.

From this we can understand that, although this man was not sacrificed by a persecutor through the shedding of his blood, he nevertheless offered himself to the Lord as a living sacrifice, in the fragrance of sweetness. Taking up his cross and following the Savior daily, he obtained as a confessor both the labor and the palm of martyrdom.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How he was carried by unbroken horses to the place of his burial

After the holiness of the venerable Father had been openly demonstrated to all who attended the affairs of his funeral, both by the greatness of the miracle and by the manifestation of these signs, the bishop approached the bier. Lifting it from one side while the priest raised it from the other, he placed it upon the horses and said to those standing nearby:

“Remove the bridles from their heads, so that, once liberty has been granted, they may go wherever the Lord wills.”

They took up the cross and candles and began the journey while singing psalms and melodies. The horses, turning toward neither side, proceeded by the direct route to the man of God’s cell.

When they reached it, the bier was set down before the oratory. His disciples lifted the relics of the devout teacher, carried them inside, and placed them before the altar.

Then, praying for him together with the bishop, they dug a grave for the burial between the wall [Column 1005C] and the altar. After offering prayers suitable to the occasion, they buried him there.

When everything had been duly completed, the multitude that had gathered for the funeral of so great a man, strengthened by the bishop’s blessing, returned to their homes.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. The miracle displayed through the candles

When the fortunate place had received within itself the treasure of the blessed body, the Lord wished to offer consolation and healing to those grieving over the death of his servant. By the novelty of a miracle, he revealed with what brightness the spirit of his friend shone before him.

Two candles had been lit in the fortress when his body was raised, and they were carried burning all the way to the place of burial. Once placed there—one at his head and the other at his feet—they continued burning for thirty days thereafter, without being consumed; and, marvelously, they burned without failing and did not fail as they burned.

To show that the power to endure had been divinely bestowed upon the melting wax, many miracles afterward flowed from the substance of this miracle. Whoever suffered from toothache, or from dimness of the eyes, or from obstruction of the ears, took a little wax from these same candles and applied it to the places afflicted by such ailments; they quickly received the desired gift of healing.

After this, such power to heal those afflicted by various illnesses appeared at the tomb of the blessed man for all who came there and faithfully sought the assistance of his prayers that the fame of so great a merit became known throughout all the surrounding regions, and the place itself was frequented by crowds to no small degree.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Conclusion of the little work

Since, therefore, most blessed Fathers, the life and virtues of Saint Gallus, if joined together in a single book, might because of their length impose some weariness upon the reader, I have decided to divide this work into two small books.

The first of them shall carry his life and deeds, by a truthful account, up to his burial. The second shall recount the miracles that the Lord afterward displayed through his merits: first, those that have been transmitted to us in writing by earlier generations; then, those reported by most trustworthy witnesses and committed to writing in our own age by our dearest brother Gotzbert.

Thus what has been written piecemeal will not be separated by a ragged division; rather, what is joined by the similarity of its events will also be joined in the comprehension of its words.

Let this, then, the end of the first little book, conclude what has been set forth above, and reserve without prejudice for the following book what remains to be included.

# BOOK TWO. ON THE MIRACLES PERFORMED AFTER THE DEATH OF BLESSED GALLUS

[Column 1005]

## CHAPTER I. How the enemies violated the tomb of Blessed Gallus

[Column 1005D]

The merits of the most blessed Gallus shone forth daily through signs of miracles and soothed the peoples dwelling far and wide around him with the golden sweetness of his fame. When forty years had already passed since his death [Note: [Col. 1005D] In the published Acts of Saint Magnus, this is said to have happened three years after the death of Saint Gallus. Although those Acts are extremely corrupt, they nevertheless provide grounds for doubting whether a copyist’s error has entered Walahfrid’s text. Certainly, since in the next chapter Walahfrid mentions Magnoaldus and Theodore as survivors of this assault, and since it seems certain—if anything in the history of Saint Magnus is true—that they died much later, so long an interval cannot have elapsed between the death of Saint Gallus and the disaster described here. Compare the following note.], Othwinus came, invested with authority over those regions [Col. 1006D] and accompanied by a large army. Inflamed by intolerable anger, he devastated no small part of the district called Turgowe from the river flowing through it; he also began to lay waste and set fire to the territory of Constance and the borders of the district of Arbon. He put to the sword all the men who could be found and led their wives and little children into captivity. After their livestock and all their household goods had been carried away, he ordered all their crops to be utterly destroyed [Col. 1007A].

The people of Arbon, compelled by the enormity of this terror, fled into the wilderness with everything they possessed and took refuge at the cell of the man of God. Then they dug a pit in the field, hid there whatever they had, covered the excavation with earth so that their secret would not be discovered, and scattered flaxseed over it. When the enemy had laid waste the district of Arbon, they followed the fugitives’ tracks, came to the cell of the holy Father, seized and bound the fugitives whom they found, and sent their young men into captivity.

Erchonaldus (also called Erwinus), the prefect’s deputy, lived in places near the wilderness and was very familiar with the possessions of that cell. Entering the oratory, he found a certain beggar sitting inside, whom he knew well, and said to him [Col. 1007B]:

“Tell me where these people—whom we have found so naked and wretched—have their clothing, utensils, gold, and silver stored, of which they had hitherto enjoyed an abundance.”

He replied: “Is it not better for me to reveal their secrets than to incur the anger of your severity?”

“If you do so,” he said, “you will be one of us and will rejoice in sharing our fellowship.”

Persuaded by this promise, the beggar rose and led him to an underground storeroom. When the deputy had it opened, he distributed the objects he found there among those who were with him, after dividing them. Having done this, they supposed that similar things were hidden everywhere and went about examining each place carefully by means of various indications.

For the same purpose Erchonaldus entered the oratory with seven boys. When they struck the level pavement with the doors closed [Col. 1007C], evidently hoping to find money, one of them came behind the altar and struck the pavement. Hearing a sound coming back from the hollow of the tomb, he said: “Here is what you greatly desire.”

The hostile grave-robbers hurried up and began to dig. When they reached the little coffin, they lifted it out, saying: “Since these Raetians possess such natural cunning, let us see whether anything remains hidden beneath this chest.”

As they set about this sacrilege, an immense horror seized them. Turning to flee, and each trying to reach the oratory door first, they were driven mad, drew their swords, and cut one another down. Erchonaldus, the author of this crime, compelled by fear, tried to leap through the doorway, struck his head against the lintel, fell to the ground, and lay there out of his mind [Col. 1007D].

When his servants carried him home, he began to be tormented by extreme illness and new pains. Throughout the course of that entire year he was afflicted with the most severe sufferings, lost the dignity of his hair and the surface of his skin, and even lost the nails of his fingers. And [Col. 1008A] so that the signs of the divine vengeance inflicted upon him might be evident to everyone for a long time, he remained marked by this disfigurement throughout all the days of his life.

## CHAPTER II. How Bishop Boso Reburied His Body

When the bishop of the Church of Constance, named Boso [Note: [Col. 1007D] Here Goldast sets against Walahfrid’s calculation Hermannus Contractus, who says that Ernfrid succeeded Boso as bishop of Constance in the year 736. In that year Boso could not have been alive if he had already witnessed the disaster inflicted by Othwinus. A much stronger argument could be drawn from the age of Magnoaldus and Theodore, disciples of Saint Gall, who cannot have survived into the eighth century. Yet in Hermannus it is not Boso but Audonius who is said to have been Ernfrid’s predecessor; and even if the text read otherwise, the authority of Hermannus, much later though he is, would not be preferable to Walahfrid’s. In the catalogue of the bishops of Constance compiled by Gabriel Bucelinus, a Benedictine and prolific author, Boso—also called Obihardus or Obbaldus—is listed after John, the disciple of Saint Gall; six bishops are inserted between Boso and Ernfrid, the last being Audonius or Ausonius.], heard that the tomb of the most blessed Gallus had been violated by the enemy and that no one remained in the cell except the two brothers Magnoaldus and Theodore, who could restore the relics of the sacred body to the tomb, he came there with his clergy.

He found the cell deserted, the body of the holy Father cast out of the tomb, the altars stripped, and the two brothers who had remained lying plundered in the oratory, declaring the magnitude of their calamity with groans [Col. 1008B] and tears. Moved by compassion, he began to console them with many words, repeating the Psalmist’s saying:

“In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he answered me in a spacious place. The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me” (Psalm 117).

After saying this, he took the little coffin in which the holy body was kept and placed it on the ground between the wall and the altar. Above it he built a higher chest, as is customary, and filled the pit with earth. He also supplied the brothers with clothing from his own resources and arranged for their sustenance, then returned to the episcopal residence.

## CHAPTER III. With What Punishment the Violators of That Place Were Stricken

[Col. 1008C]

After a long time, Pippin the mayor of the palace [Note: Namely, Pippin, father of Charlemagne, who is reported to have attacked Alamannia in the year 745. See Hadrian Valesius, *Rer. Franc.*, book XXV.] sent a large army to devastate the province of the Alamanni and subject it once again to Frankish rule. When the whole land was being crushed by hostile invasion, greedy plunderers roaming through the district of Arbon came to the cell of the man of God. They led away as captives all whom they found there, for many had fled there hoping in the mercy of God and the protection of his saint.

Five soldiers of the aforementioned prince entered the oratory and found there certain female servants of that place with their children. They asked who they were. When the women proclaimed that they belonged to the household of the saint, the plunderers said to them: “Out! Go out! We do not know the saint you speak of.” And they led them away as captives to Francia [Col. 1008D].

In that same year, however, seized by evil spirits and driven mad, the five men ran naked in every direction. Wherever they entered cities or villages, they disclosed the cause of their torments, saying: “Abbot Gallus has bound us.” And while miserably passing their lives amid this wretched recollection of their crimes, they ended them in lamentation [Col. 1009A].

## CHAPTER IV. By What Miracle the Cloth over the Saint’s Bed, after Being Burned, Was Restored

At another time, a deacon named Stephen was serving as custodian in the church of the same holy Father. One evening, bringing a lighted candle into the oratory, he placed it on a candlestick beside the tomb of the blessed man. Leaning away from its upright position, the candle fell burning onto the altar of the tomb. The force of the fire caught one of the pallia and burned it as far as its middle; then the fire went out, causing no damage to the bed, to the staff hanging upon it, or to the other linen cloths spread over the tomb [Col. 1009B].

From this it is clear that the fire occurred for the manifestation of the holy man’s virtues rather than to damage his belongings. For, as appears below, the power made whole the pallium that a slight flame had diminished.

At daybreak the brothers entered the oratory, saw what had happened, and were struck with no little astonishment. On the third day, when they gathered for the office of Matins, they found candles burning in the oratory and two young men standing there, one at the head and the other at the foot, stretching between them the pallium that had previously been touched by the fire’s heat.

When they saw this, they were overcome with great fear, quickly went out, and returned to their beds. As they settled down, the church bell sounded, and two choirs were heard resounding with the extraordinary sweetness of alternating voices [Col. 1009C]. That day they did not dare enter the oratory at all.

On the following day they gathered unanimously before its door and prostrated themselves in prayer. When they had risen, they entered with great fear and found the pallium that the fire had partly consumed spread over the bed as it had formerly been spread, showing no sign of diminution. Rather, its breadth or length appeared to have been increased by three cubits.

Made joyful by the clarity of this miracle, they blessed the Lord, who had deigned to reveal the merits of his servant through such manifest powers of grace.

## CHAPTER V. The Miracle of the Bird That Was Sent

[Col. 1009D]

At one time the same Stephen, when he and those who were with him had no meat to eat as a certain fast approached, sat in the cell to speak with the others about their poverty. While they offered one another consolation in their poverty through varied conversation, a bird of unknown appearance settled on the threshold.

One of those sitting there seized a burning log from the fire and struck the bird. After they had prepared its flesh for their use, they discovered an incredible sweetness of flavor in it. We believe that the merits of the blessed man brought this about: just as, in imitation of the ancient miracle by which the people of God were fed with quail in the wilderness, an unknown bird was sent to his servants, so the flavor of the food provided from heaven possessed the delight of a new sweetness [Col. 1010A].

## CHAPTER VI. On the Multitude of the Holy Man’s Signs

Such is the abundance of the miracles that the Lord has displayed at his tomb at various times that it cannot easily be encompassed by the effort of writing. Because of this abundance, many are omitted; a few and more outstanding examples are inserted in this little work for the memory of posterity.

Apart from the raising of dead bodies, remedies for other illnesses have been and continue to be granted there by the Lord with great frequency. Demoniacs have been restored there, the sick revived, the barriers of the ears opened, the darkness of the eyes wiped away, the silences of the mute removed, and the weakness of the paralytics driven out [Col. 1010B].

Moreover, whoever, compelled by a need of soul or body, carries out an earnest prayer at the tomb of Saint Gallus with undivided faith is never deprived of the fruit of his prayers, since the Lord confirms the merits of his confessor. Rather, such a person rejoices without delay upon experiencing the gifts of divine generosity.

## CHAPTER VII. How a Gift Intended for the Saint Was Preserved from Fire

[Col. 1010C]

In the time of Carloman the mayor of the palace, we judge it useful to insert into this work a miracle brought about through the merits of the holy Father and worthy of remembrance.

A certain poor man in the district called Perahtoltespara, moved by the deepest devotion, decided to go with his wife to the cell of Saint Gallus for prayer. In keeping with this devout intention, his wife prepared a small cloth that she was to offer at the shrine. She wrapped it around a formella [Note: That is, a wax ring. Thus, in 1 Kings 17:18, “ten formellae of cheese.” The Septuagint has τρυφαλύδες, a word which Gaza, in Aristotle, rendered as *formaginem*—a word by which the Franks and Italians still call cheese. This is Goldast’s note.] of wax, which she also intended to offer, and placed it in their chest among other garments.

While they were preparing to leave, it happened that their house, together with everything inside it, was consumed by fire. When everything had been destroyed and the fire had died down, they began searching among the heaps of ashes for the remains of their iron tools [Col. 1010D]. And behold—they found, marvelous to relate, the wax wrapped in the small cloth among the ashes and coals. No damage whatever was visible in it, although the fire had utterly consumed the chest itself and everything else stored in it.

Having witnessed the miracle of such great power, they blessed God and completed the journey they had planned. They told the brothers what had happened and offered the gift, which, consecrated to this vow, could not perish even amid the greatest dangers. These same objects were preserved there as a testimony for future generations until the time of Abbot Othmar.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Correction of the Man Who Fraudulently Kept the Horse He Had Vowed

[Col. 1011A]

Nor does it seem that the event reported to have occurred in the aforementioned district in the time of King Pippin should be passed over in silence.

A certain man named Willimarus, weighed down by a serious illness, promised under a vow that, if he were restored to his former health, he would donate to the church of Saint Gallus a living horse and two oxen. When he was strengthened that very day and had recovered full health, it happened that he came to the cell of the holy man riding that same horse with his lord Bicthilo, for the sake of prayer.

After the prayer, all those who had come together had gone some distance from the church. Then the horse—which its faithless sponsor had fraudulently kept after making the vow—suddenly stopped. Although its rider urged it with spurs and wearied it with blows, he could not move it at all.

Those present, seeing this, began to inquire into the cause of the miracle. The man, seized with shame appropriate to the matter, disclosed his guilt and confessed the fraud he had committed in making the vow. They all turned back together, offered the horse at the threshold of the church, received a blessing, and returned home without hindrance.

In this event both divine mercy and the power of the holy man were revealed: the man who had refused to repent of his own accord was brought to correction through chastisement.

## CHAPTER IX. Wax Offered from a Theft Turned into Stone

I also wish to commit to memory the miracle that occurred in the fourth year of King Carloman [Col. 1011C] in the district mentioned above.

A certain poor man living near the royal estate called Rotenwila wished to go to the cell of the holy man Gallus but had nothing that he could bring there as a token of devotion. Yielding to the devil’s persuasion, he broke into the courtyard of a wealthy man, secretly carried away a hive with its honey and bees, and brought it into his own house.

After killing the bees, he made wax from them. Not long afterward, he went with this stolen gift among his neighbors and friends to the church of the venerable Gallus. When each person brought what he had offered, the man who had unlawfully wished to offer a gift from robbery found the wax changed into the hardness of the most solid stone [Col. 1011D].

Struck with immense fear, he confessed his guilt to one of those who had come with him. When that man then reported what had happened to the guardians of the church, the fame of this miracle became known to everyone with astonishing speed.

## CHAPTER X. The Writer’s Statement Concerning the Nature of the Work Undertaken

Having described what the diligence of the ancients transmitted to us in writing concerning the life, death, and virtues of Saint Gallus, we shall now attempt to set down in writing what was reported by the most faithful witnesses and committed to writing by our dearest brother Gotzpert.

First, these materials clearly explain how and when the institutions of regular life began to be observed in the monastery of Saint Gallus; then they credibly set forth through what miracles the power of the same Father shone upon all, while also naming the individual authorities for the assertions introduced.

We have therefore wished to arrange these materials with new expressions, so that they may possess some similarity of language to the earlier accounts while remaining concise through brevity and not becoming burdensome to readers inclined to boredom.

Indeed, we omit the names of those who are or were witnesses to what must be written because of their barbarous character, lest they stain the dignity of the Latin language. We know that faithful people must not doubt the truth of their statements, since they understand that none of the things we report is impossible for God, in whom everything wondrous and praiseworthy accomplished through the saints takes place [Col. 1012B].

If anyone wishes to know the witnesses to these events, he will be able to find them in the written account that we follow. We shall also insert into this work certain matters that we learned not from written testimony but from the reports of truthful men.

In all these matters, so far as concerns us, we shall strive to preserve the line of truth, inserting nothing of our own through love of falsehood and concealing nothing true through envy. Since we follow the writings or statements of others, the truth of the events belongs to them, while the abridgment of the wording and the joining together of the arguments belong to us.

## CHAPTER XI. How Pippin Commended the Same Place to Othmar with a Privilege and Gifts

[Col. 1012C]

After the glorious burial of the venerable Father, namely Gallus, confessor of Christ, certain devout clerics—either inspired by the memory of his discipleship or inflamed by divine love—kept daily vigils beside the relics of his sacred body for many years, from approximately the time of King Dagobert down to Charles, the father of Carloman and Pippin, administering them for the praise of Christ.

When the fame of the virtues that the Lord graciously deigned to display to those who sought them through the merits of his confessor had delighted the ears of peoples dwelling far and wide, people began to hurry from every direction with eager devotion to seek the intercession of so great a Father. They also enlarged the same place with many gifts of property and possessions, in honor of the lasting memory of the saint [Col. 1012D].

When the things bestowed through the generosity of the faithful seemed sufficient to support a modest congregation of monks, a certain Waldramnus, whose paternal property appeared to include the boundaries of the vast wilderness in which the man of God had built his cell, saw that the donated goods were being handled disorderly by certain usurpers. He obtained from Victor, then count of the Curienses, a devout priest named Othmar to whom he could entrust all these possessions, and he commended the cell to him together with everything belonging to it [Note: Hepidannus, a monk of Saint Gall, reports that this happened in the year 710 in his *Annals*. Ratpertus says the following in Book I, chapter 2, *On the Affairs of Saint Gall*: “Thieltolt was the son of Taltonis; Talto had been chamberlain of King Dagobert. Thieton was the son of Thieltolt; Pollo was the son of Thieton; Waldpertus was the son of Pollo, and he begot Waltramnum. Waltramnus, desiring to enlarge this place in every way for love of Saint Gall and wishing to establish regular life there, obtained the holy man Othmar from Victor, count of Raetia Curiensis, entrusted to him the aforesaid cell with everything belonging to it, and appointed him abbot. Later, as time passed and the condition of the monastery improved, the aforementioned Waltramnus presented the same Abbot Othmar to King Pippin,” and so forth. The same Othmar governed that monastery successfully for forty years, while the aforementioned Waltramnus assisted him for twenty years.]

Afterward, persuaded by the counsel of a certain duke named Nebi [Col. 1013A], he went with that duke to the aforementioned prince Charles, transferred the same cell to him by right of ownership, and begged him to place the priest Othmar in charge of it.

The prince granted his request. He summoned Othmar into his presence, entrusted the place to him, and ordered him to strive to establish regular life there. Othmar returned and immediately undertook the beginnings of a good shepherd’s work. Building suitable dwellings for the monks in an orderly manner in every direction, he adapted the condition of the same holy place to various useful purposes.

When the aforementioned prince had reached the end of his earthly reign and life, he left the administration of the kingdom to his two sons, Carloman and Pippin. After a few years had passed, Carloman, for love of the heavenly kingdom, laid aside the pomp of worldly [Col. 1013B] glory [Note: That is, in the year 745, as the same Hepidannus writes.]. As he was traveling toward Rome for the sake of a quieter life, he came into the vicinity of the aforementioned place and visited the same monastery for prayer.

Hearing that the place was being illuminated by the Lord through the merits of the holy man’s continual miraculous signs, he is said to have remarked:

“This place is indeed poor in resources, but because of the merits of Saint Gallus it is celebrated and widely renowned.”

He wished to provide some support from his generosity to those living there, but he hesitated because, being separated from the affairs of the kingdom, he could not accomplish what he wished. He therefore wrote to his brother, asking him, for love of him, to deign to bestow some support from the royal generosity upon the monastery.

When Prince Pippin received the letter presented by Abbot Othmar, he agreed to his brother’s request, gave the abbot the book that Benedict the Father had composed concerning the way of life of monks, and bestowed other gifts of royal dignity. He charged him with the utmost diligence to establish in the place entrusted to him an order of regular life, in order to provide for the vigils kept in honor of Saint Gallus.

To enable him to accomplish what he had been ordered to do more effectively, he granted him certain tributaries from the same district, so that, with their assistance, he could build workshops necessary for the monks’ use and could devote to the support of the brothers the taxes they were accustomed to contribute annually to the royal revenues, in remembrance of his generosity.

Among his other gifts of munificence, at the abbot’s request he gave one bell as an ornament for the holy place. It remained in the same monastery down to the times of our own age as a memorial of his benefactions.

And so that no one’s greed might obstruct the growth of so great a good, he had a document of lasting validity written and, as is customary, confirmed it with carefully considered safeguards. Thus, thereafter, both the prince who was then present and his successors would hold the same monastery by royal authority, and it would be subject to no coercion except that of the rulers of the realm.

Bestowed with these supports of royal piety and elevated by these honors, Abbot Othmar returned joyfully to the monastery. From that time the beginning of monastic life in the monastery of Saint Gall was established, and its growth and progress have continued to expand laudably down to the present day.

## CHAPTER XII. How a Sign Was Given by Divine Power When the People Prevented Victor’s Incursion

Having completed the foregoing account, by which we believe it has been shown with sufficient truth how the sacred place merited the privilege of immunity and at what time it was adorned with monastic dignity, we may now turn more freely in our writing to the miracles of Saint Gallus.

Victor, count of Raetia Curiensis, whom we mentioned above [Col. 1014B], had frequently learned that innumerable virtues were displayed at the tomb of Saint Gallus through the saint’s merits. Driven by envy, he grieved that our people were distinguished by such a wealth of new virtues. As rumor then reported, he secretly wished to approach through the hidden paths of the wilderness and, if he could somehow manage it, carry away the treasure of the precious body.

When those living around the cell of the man of God learned of this malicious intention, they appointed guards in turn by companies and strove with every vigilance to defend the place against hostile attack, so that they would not be deprived of the radiance of so dear a jewel.

One night, when armed guards were stationed at the summit of the mountain overlooking the monastery to prevent suspected attacks, they happened by chance to see a light coming from heaven and flooding the walls of the entire church [Col. 1014C]. Astonished at the immensity of the light, they hurried to the church. While they stood there trembling and amazed, gazing at the same brilliance, the light gradually gathered itself together, sank away, and joined the stars.

Seeing the miracle, they gave thanks to the Lord and returned home in safety, believing that the body of the man of God could not be carried away by force from the place that the Lord had foreseen for him before the ages and adorned in those times with the honor of his illumination.

From this it may be understood how great this man’s merit was with God: the place of his burial was illuminated from heaven, so that the light his soul perfectly enjoyed in heaven would not be absent from his dead body on earth.

## CHAPTER XIII. By What Punishment He Was Restrained from the Same Presumption

When the aforementioned count heard that the guards had departed from the cell of the holy man, he wished to carry out his attempt. He gathered a crowd of men so that he might accomplish what he had wickedly planned by a sudden and secret approach.

But because he was not seeking the good of his own devotion and was instead envious of another’s prosperity, he is known to have been quickly restrained by God’s will. At the very moment he undertook that journey, he fell from the horse on which he was riding, and his thigh was broken in the fall. The Lord thereby also rewarded the merits of the holy man, preventing him from being carried away from the place he had chosen—the man whom he had sent from the farthest regions of Ireland to Raetia for the salvation of many.

The neighboring people had shown the service of their devotion by keeping watch; but God, the guardian of all good things, kept watch there as well to restrain the thief, where the vigilance of the people taking turns was absent.

He did this, we believe, so that the faithful people would not be deprived of the treasure they sought with fervent zeal, and so that the man who had wished to seize this glory through wickedness would not attain the result of his perversity. Above all, he took care that, if the relics of the holy man were removed, the companies of monks who were to serve God there with praises would not fail to be present.

Thus the count, punished and carried home by his servants, was tormented for a long time by excessive pains, so that at least through his punishment he might understand how arrogantly he had contemplated what he believed could be accomplished by his own strength.

## CHAPTER XIV. A Paralytic, Blind, and Deaf Man Healed through the Merits of Saint Gallus

Since, then, while the Lord kept watch, the body of the pious shepherd could not be carried away from the enclosure of his devoted sheep, it was fitting that the power of his merits should shine openly there before all through miracles that confirmed faith [Col. 1015C].

A certain man from the neighboring territory (also read: Tucinum), afflicted by a long illness and lying on a bed, lost the sight of his eyes and the sense of his ears when a harmful fluid gradually invaded him. Then, with the soles of his feet twisted back toward his buttocks, he was so overwhelmed by illness that only the faintest signs of his fleeting life issued from his breast.

His family carried him by wagon to the monastery. When the custodian allowed him, at the request of his friends, to spend one night in the church of Saint Gallus, he remained there alone overnight. Around the time of the cockcrow, in a sudden ecstasy of mind, he saw four men dressed in brilliantly white garments enter the oratory.

As they approached the altar and sang for a very long time with the sweet alternation of melodies [Col. 1015D], one of them, when the praises were finished, came to the bed on which the sick man lay and said:

“What is the reason, man, that you spend the horror of this darkness here alone through the night? Only believe, and from now on you will be safe from this illness. Therefore rise up healthy and go out free.”

He immediately rose, and when all his weakness had been removed, went out and returned home in good health.

## CHAPTER XV. How Abbot Othmar Was Afflicted by Wicked Magnates

Abbot Othmar had governed the same monastery vigorously for many years. As religious people living all around it bestowed abundant gifts from their generosity upon the possessions of the place for the sake of an eternal reward, he enlarged them to such an extent that within a few years, as external resources increased and the purity of his life became renowned, he became the father of many monks.

Certain counts, Warinus and Ruodhardus [Note: Hepidannus, under the year 758, says: “Warinus and Ruodhardus afflicted the blessed and holy man Othmar with many injuries. He, full of days and also full of the holiness of his merits, was delivered from the straits of this life and buried on an island in the Rhine River called Stein.” Saint Othmar will be treated in its proper place.], who administered responsibility for almost the whole of Alamannia, attempted within the boundaries of their authority to subject a considerable portion of ecclesiastical property to their own ownership by force [Col. 1016B]. They seized for themselves a large share of the possessions of the same monastery.

They took away the taxes that Pippin of blessed memory had granted to the brothers, and with the insolence of their rapacity they carried off many other things that had been transferred to the monastery through the donations of various devout people.

Moreover, when the abbot accused them of this before the prince, they threw him into chains and confined him in custody on an island in the Rhine River near the place called Stein. After he had remained there for some time under the strictest confinement, he passed from the prison of this life into heavenly joy, having completed no fewer than forty years of governance, during which he had nobly enlarged and increased the condition and glory of that holy place [Col. 1016C].

## CHAPTER XVI. How, at Their Instigation, Bishop Sidonius Invaded the Same Place

After he had thus been removed from human affairs, the aforementioned counts retained the possessions they had taken from the holy place and installed a certain monk named John from a nearby monastery in his position. Then, to increase the crime of their tyranny, they incited Sidonius [Note: Hepidannus, already cited above, says of him: “In the year 746 Sidonius, bishop of the Church of Constance and abbot of Reichenau, condemned the blessed Othmar, accused of adultery, in a synod and immediately sent him into exile.” After Abbot Othmar’s death, this Sidonius is said to have “taken over the administration of the monastery” of Saint Gallus by force in the year 757.] the bishop of the Church of Constance to strive to subject the same monastery to the authority of the episcopal see [Col. 1016D].

They did this so that, with the bishop favoring their schemes, they might more freely retain what they had unjustly seized. The bishop willingly yielded to their persuasion, entered the monastery, and attempted to oppress the brothers and subject the place to the property and authority of the episcopal see.

The brothers, however, since they did not dare resist his power, preferred to obey his authority rather than become entangled in so many adversities. But what follows proves how perversely he acted when, through the disease of greed, he dared to violate the privilege of the sacred place.

## CHAPTER XVII. What Loss He Suffered in His Property for This Same Rashness

[Col. 1017A]

It is reported that on one occasion the same bishop ordered provisions for a hostile expedition to be prepared from the resources of that monastery. The brothers did not dare disregard his orders. They loaded what had been commanded onto a boat and sent it to the bishop by the hands of certain brothers.

When those who had been sent began to sail, a certain bird appeared before them—as they themselves often testified—and flew ahead easily, as though it were about to perform the service of a guide. They followed its guidance across the entire expanse of the lake, though they did not know where it was taking them.

At last, arriving successfully at the harbor, they wondered what the service of this strange guide signified [Col. 1017B]. As they carefully watched the direction in which it went, it entered a house adjoining the shore, where the supplies prepared for the aforementioned journey were stored.

Marvelous to relate, at once a flame seized that same building and burst upward, utterly consuming everything that had been gathered there, so that nothing whatever remained of those things after the fire.

Thus, by God’s just judgment, the man who had seized another’s property through power was deprived of his own through heavenly justice.

## CHAPTER XVIII. With What Severity He Pressed the Brothers, and How Shamefully He Died
At another time, the same bishop came to the monastery and, attempting by a certain act of violence to subject that place to the bishopric and to afflict with various insults the monks who did not consent to his tyranny, as though they were justly rebellious, [Col. 1017C] Tello, a bishop of the Church of Chur, sent to him, humbly begging that, for the sake of his affection—since some of those brothers were related to him by blood—he cease his injuries against them and inflict no harm upon the servants of God. In his arrogance, dictated by fury, he contemptuously rejected this request and sent back word that he would yield in no way to Tello’s pleas, but would swiftly exact vengeance for their resistance.

Immediately afterward he entered the oratory of Saint Gall the Confessor, as though to pray, and stood before the altar consecrated to that saint’s name. He who did not deserve to be heard for his salvation received, by a fitting retaliation, the afflictions he had sworn to inflict upon others. [Col. 1017D] For his intestines began to seethe like a frying pan set over a fire, and such dreadful twisting of his entrails suddenly seized him that he could not possibly leave without assistance from others. But—shameful to relate—an evacuation of nature burst forth with disgraceful violence, burdening those standing nearby with an excessive stench. Without delay he was driven from the church and placed in a vehicle, as he had requested, so that he might leave the monastery.

Thus, with an immoderate discharge lacking nature’s customary control, he departed while sitting over a vessel into which the excrement might flow, and [Col. 1018A] was taken to the neighboring monastery called Auva [Note: [Col. 1017D] The monastery of Auva, or Augia, commonly called Reichenau, mentioned above in the preliminary Observations. Ratpert, *Book I of the Deeds of Saint Gall*, chapter 2: “After this,” he says, “Sidonius, the bishop of Constance, who also held in his power the monastery called Auva, at the urging of the counts began to investigate our monastery and reduce it to the authority of the bishopric,” and so forth.], over which he was then presiding. There, as his illness grew worse, he became so intolerable to those serving him because of the excessive stench that scarcely anyone could continue to attend him as usual. Punished in this way, after a few days he breathed out his spirit from the bodily sewer, receiving this as the reward of his schemes.

## CHAPTER XIX. The miracle displayed in the fattening of pigs

Having completed in the preceding accounts the narrative by which we believe we have sufficiently and truthfully shown how the holy place was renowned and enlarged in its possessions through the merits of Saint Gall, by what machinations of certain ill-wishers it was attacked, and what vengeance humbled some of them, we now think it necessary to relate how great a protection the blessed man provides for those who serve him, in guarding or defending his property, and with what authority he comes to the aid—through manifold kinds of miracles—of those who ask his help and place their hope in him. In this way the Lord declares the greatness of his merits to mortals through the constant occurrence of signs.

At a certain time, when the sterility of the land denied the fruits of trees not only to pigs but also to wild beasts and other animals, so that no fodder could be found anywhere in the neighboring regions of the wilderness with which the swine raised for the monastery’s use might be fed, a herd of pigs, driven by some hidden impulse, began to withdraw at a rapid pace through the pathless forest. After fording the bed of the Rhine, it penetrated [Col. 1018C] the secluded parts of a more distant wilderness.

The swineherd, astonished at the sudden flight of his animals, followed immediately and found the herd lingering amid abundant pastures. Since he did not know how to lead them back, he remained there, living on the fruits of trees and on meat, until the whole herd had become fully laden with rich flesh. Wishing to return home, he began anxiously to consider by what means he might undertake the unknown route.

That night he saw in a dream an old man of venerable appearance and bearing, honored by his white hair, who said to him: “Since, as I see, the pigs you are following have been abundantly fattened, prepare now to return.” When he replied that he did not know the way, the old man said to him: “Kill the sow whom the whole herd customarily follows as its leader, and direct your steps wherever she goes ahead.”

When he did this and carefully followed the sow as she led the way, he reached the monastery without error, unexpectedly, while everyone suspected something else. What else was revealed in this event than the merits of Saint Gall, when he showed animals unknown pasture for the use of those serving him and then, in a wondrous order, brought them back again to their own place?

## CHAPTER XX. How those who burned the barns were discovered

A certain brother of the same monastery, having several of its estates under his care, built barns in a more remote place for feeding the livestock and stored a great quantity of hay there. Two men, instigated by diabolical persuasion, set fire by night to these storehouses and to everything that had been gathered there.

Although the perpetrators concealed themselves for almost a whole year, one of them, seized by a demon, began to run through the surrounding places, publicly proclaiming: “I burned the barns of Saint Gall’s livestock, and therefore, in turn, I am being invisibly burned by him.” Since divine judgment was continually manifest in him, and many people, stirred by his persistent cries, gathered from every direction to witness this pitiable spectacle, he begged them all to extinguish his fires.

But although they threw water upon him in competition with one another, the punishment inflicted by God could not be extinguished by human strength. After several days had passed amid this pitiable kind of torment, the madman ended his life.

When the other man saw that his accomplice in crime had been condemned to such torture, he went to the aforesaid provost. Voluntarily fearing divine judgment, he confessed his offense, offered two oxen as compensation, and bound himself by a vow never again to inflict harm upon the property of Saint Gall. The brother, recognizing his repentance, did not accept the oxen but allowed him to depart with what was his.

## CHAPTER XXI. How the man who had publicly burned the forest was punished

[Col. 1019C] On one of the monastery’s estates, a small woodland was guarded for the grazing of pigs, so that it would not be consumed by many people cutting it indiscriminately. A certain poor man used to visit it secretly and, furtively cutting down many trees there, inflict great damage.

One day, then, when he entered secretly according to his custom and cut down a few shrubs, the sword he was holding adhered so firmly to his hand that he could not put it down in any way. Recognizing why he had been punished, he hurried to the basilica built in honor of Saint Gall and, devoting himself for a long time to prayer, released his hand and left the sword before the altar.

Afterward, as he departed, he began to think that it would do no harm if he carried home the wood he had cut, whereas it would be of no benefit if it were left to rot. So he yoked oxen to a cart [Col. 1019D], returned to the forest, and gathered the cut wood into one pile.

When he wished to load it onto the vehicle, he was suddenly struck in the buttocks by a powerful pain, as though he were being driven by goads. When he immediately reached out his hand to the place, he happened by chance to recover the sword he had left before the altar. Grasping the hilt with his fingers, he held that detestable object so tightly that the joints of his fingers seemed to be coming apart.

Then the wretched man, compelled by pain, ran back to the church. There, prostrate, he begged forgiveness for his offense and release for his hand. After he had remained in prayer for a long time, unable to let go of the sword, he finally promised by oath and vow that he would never again inflict harm upon the property of Saint Gall. [Col. 1020A] Immediately his hand opened and released the sword. As a testimony to the miracle, it was hung in that same place, where it remained for a long time, striking those who invaded ecclesiastical property with a great burden of fear.

## CHAPTER XXII. What vengeance the perjurer suffered

A certain man named Frumold violently took two female servants from one of the monastery’s estates and subjected them to his own service. After he had repeatedly been summoned by the advocate on behalf of these women, he was finally compelled by the judgment of the judges either to return them to the monastery or to confirm his right to them by an oath sworn at the altar of Saint Gall.

Driven by greed and treating the oath as worthless, he went with his people to the monastery and boldly carried out what had been adjudicated. But for his contempt of the saint, God’s vengeance overtook him swiftly. After completing the oath, he left the basilica to return to his own property. When he brought up a pack animal and tried to mount it by jumping onto it, he lost his mind and, sitting on the horse, turned his face toward its rear.

Thinking that this had happened through the negligence of his servants, he leapt down in great anger and ordered them to turn the horse around quickly. When, on the second and third attempts, he was mocked by the same error as he tried to mount, he was finally placed on the horse with the help of his attendants and left the monastery in shame. Not far from there, a terrible pain suddenly seized his eyes. Then, as his sight diminished moment by moment, he was condemned to the horror of blindness and deprived completely of material light.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How the holy man, when invoked, saved someone from death

The following example will show how promptly the venerable Gallus provides help when invoked. A certain man was traveling through a forest and, cautiously trying to avoid by hurrying the attacks of robbers who usually lived there and harmed many people, when such a heavy sleep suddenly overcame him that he could scarcely walk.

Fearing the dangers that might befall him on the road and wishing to turn aside for a while in order to sleep, he encountered a peasant. He began to ask him to act as his guard for the time being, until he could drive away the oppressive sleep by resting briefly. The other, pretending to be peaceful, pledged his good faith.

Turning aside a little, the traveler placed his cloak beneath his head and, lying down, implored the aid of the blessed man in these words: “Saint Gall, guard me with your protection.” After strengthening himself with the sign of the cross, he fell asleep. The faithless guard, forgetting his pledge, took up weapons and approached the sleeping man as though he intended to kill him. He pulled the garment away from his neck, so that he might more easily kill the sleeper with a single blow.

But when he wished to bring down his sword for the stroke, his limbs were numbed by rigidity, and his arms could not bend. Meanwhile someone stood beside the sleeper and said to him in his dream: “Why are you weighed down by sleep, when I have just protected you from imminent death?”

He awoke and saw his faithful companion standing over him with a bared sword. He leapt up, seized him, and asked for what reason he wished to commit such a crime. When the man confessed that he had intended to do this in order to take his possessions, his arms, which had been stiffened by divine command, immediately dropped.

Recognizing that by the merits of Saint Gall he had been saved from death through divine mercy, the other made peace with him and allowed him to depart unharmed.

## CHAPTER XXIV. A girl freed from a demon

Moreover, so many people have been freed from demonic madness through the merits of this holy Father that, if we wished to recount the healing of all of them, we would give fastidious readers an occasion for complaint. We shall therefore repeat one case among many, lest anyone think that this kind of power was lacking in the holy man.

A certain girl, held by the fiercest torment of the ancient enemy and brought to the monastery through the efforts of parents who were not of low station, entered the oratory of Saint Gall the Confessor. Immediately, seized by a horrifying demonic assault, she fell to the ground, tearing herself miserably and beginning to pour forth the foulest words in a dreadful shriek.

For this reason one of the brothers, named Stephen, moved by compassion for her misery, recited an exorcism over her for so long that the affliction ended. When the girl returned to her senses, he imposed upon her forms of penance and began to discipline himself on her behalf through prayers and fasts.

But as soon as the wretched woman consumed anything from the forbidden foods, the demon immediately attacked her so fiercely that she could scarcely be restrained by many people. When she had been brought back to the same place repeatedly and the aforementioned Stephen had recited the exorcism over her again, a small animal, black and resembling a caterpillar, slipped from her mouth.

When the same brother, seeing this, applied himself more attentively to the adjuration, three times an animal resembling a caterpillar fell from the woman’s mouth. As those standing nearby tried to catch the creatures with their hands, they suddenly vanished. At that very hour the girl rose unharmed and spent the remainder of her life without any further demonic assault.

## CHAPTER XXV. The custodian’s anxiety rebuked by the miracle of the flowing oil

It is also pleasing to show by an evident miracle how the holy man rebuked certain people in his service who were anxious over scarcity of goods and strengthened their faintheartedness arising from weak faith.

The custodian of his church, at a time when he did not have enough oil to supply the lamps, extinguished one night the light that customarily burned every night in the crypt. The light burning above, before the upper altar and the tomb, was directing its rays through a certain window toward the altar situated below in the crypt, and it was thought sufficient for both places.

In the same glass lamp that, as we have said, the custodian extinguished, there was water below and the oily substance above it. I shall relate a wondrous event: all the oil flowed drop by drop through a crack found at the bottom, down to the ground, while the water seemed not to have diminished at all.

The same liquid ran across the floor [Col. 1022A] as far as the altar, and, rising up, covered its linen altar cloth. It stained it up to the middle in such a way that afterward it could never be washed clean.

I cannot determine which part of this is most worthy of wonder: whether that the oil sank beneath the water, or that the water did not flow out through the same fracture, or certainly that the oil rose upward from the pavement onto the altar cloth. Yet in all these things I have no doubt that the power of the holy man was displayed and the servant’s foolish parsimony rebuked.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How a fugitive monk was unwillingly recalled

It must not be left unspoken by what power the blessed Father restrains those who abandon his service and flee deceitfully, either recalling those who have fallen or striking the obstinate in their wrongdoing.

A certain brother of the same monastery, plotting flight, stole a horse and departed during the night. When the fugitive came to the banks of the Rhine, he attempted to cross the river on horseback. From the middle of the river, however, without knowing how, he was carried back by the horse to the place where he had entered. He returned to the monastery with great haste, thinking that he was departing toward some distant region.

When morning came and he realized that he had labored in vain, he hid during the day. At night he attempted flight again, but in the river, as before, he suffered the salutary consequence of his error and, having made a circuit, unknowingly returned by the same route.

Joining obstinacy to his shame, he hid himself during that day as well. When night followed, he took the familiar road for the third time and was likewise recalled in the manner already described. [Col. 1022C] Finally, overcome by weariness, he gave himself over to sleep in a field on the third day. He was captured by certain people who recognized the horse and was restored to his proper place.

And because he did not achieve what he desired, he was overcome, even against his will, by the power of the holy man and came to the proper path. Many people customarily testify that all who have fled from the household of this saint must either undergo correction very soon or succumb to manifest vengeance; no one who has scorned to keep full faith with him escapes unpunished.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Disfigured by lightning, healed partly at Rome and partly in this holy place

That the Lord restrains certain people from sins by his scourge and afflicts them for their offenses is shown by the paralytic to whom the Savior forgives sins before healing him. Sometimes he strikes in such a way that, with the merits of his saints assisting, he restores them to health. Thus the divine action is indicated when the inner person is restrained from sin through the scourge, and the power of the saints is clearly proven when outward health is granted through their merits.

It also sometimes happens that a person who, by God’s hidden judgment, is subject not to one but to several infirmities does not lose all of them at the same time, but loses his afflictions at different times and through different intercessors. Thus, while a remedy for some illness is granted through the merits of one saint, the restoration of health is reserved for the prayers and honor of another. The account that follows will provide clear evidence of all these matters.

A certain man, struck by the force of lightning, after a prolonged illness lost the entire form of his body and the functions of his limbs to such an extent that he seemed to represent something monstrous rather than a human being. His stature had been reduced by miserable contraction, and the ability to walk had been taken away. His face had been so disfigured by the ugliness of burning, and the sockets of his eyes had been so flattened by flesh and skin growing over them, that he presented a horrible spectacle to those who looked at him.

With the aid of his parents he was taken to Rome. There the bonds of the rest of his body were loosened, and he recovered his former strength and posture; but he remained in the squalor of blindness.

When his family brought him to the monastery of Saint Gall and he attended the nocturnal praises on a certain Sunday, he was overcome by sleep. He saw, as it were, two burning arrows sent forth from the altar and fixed in the places of his eyes. Terrified immediately by this vision, he cried out and fell trembling to the ground.

After he had rolled about on the floor for a long time, the skin that had grown over his eyes was cut away as though by a sword. Immediately he rejoiced in the restoration of the light he had lost. As time passed, the sharpness of his eyes appeared so clear to those who observed him that his sight seemed to surpass that of perceptive boys.

Certainly, as we firmly believe, that eminent apostle to whom the Lord granted the power of binding and loosing could have freed him from every kind of infirmity by his merits and prayers. But divine providence arranged that, through the novelty of this miracle, the venerable Gallus should be made equal to apostolic deeds, so that the greatness of his merits might also shine forth to all in this way.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. A deaf and mute man restored to health there

On the following Sunday, a certain deaf and mute man, very well known to many of the brothers there because he had been accustomed to frequent the same monastery, was attending the nocturnal vigils when he was suddenly thrown violently onto the pavement. Immediately, when a great quantity of blood burst from his mouth and ears, he recovered the functions of both organs without delay and departed healed.

## CHAPTER XXIX. A theft revealed through a vision

It seems appropriate to insert into this work an account of how greatly the servant of God watches over the property of those who devoutly strive to seek his aid.

A certain boy, who was later incorporated into the same community and used to testify to these events, was then still enjoying the flower of early youth and was attending the solemnities of a Sunday night among the students of a certain monastery. A man from the neighboring territory broke into his lodging, stole his book and whatever else he could find there, and departed.

The boy, returning from the basilica, grieved bitterly over the loss, shedding abundant tears. But that same night an old man appeared in a dream to the boy’s brother, who was outside the monastery, standing before him with a peaceful expression. He disclosed everything that had happened to the boy. He also identified the thief’s name and the place where he lived, and stated the time at which the theft had taken place.

Trusting the vision, the brother returned to the monastery and found that what he had heard in the dream had happened. Then, following the indications he had received, he caught the thief without difficulty and recovered everything that had been stolen.

## CHAPTER XXX. How a religious woman received the use of her arms there

At another time a certain religious woman from the bishopric of Constance arrived. Her arms were twisted rigidly as far as her breasts and could not be bent for any kind of work. After she had prayed for a while before the tomb of Saint Gall, she obtained health and departed rejoicing.

## CHAPTER XXXI. How a theft of tools was exposed

A certain man, who later proved that he had not come with an innocent intention, noticed that some monastery laborers, having ceased their divinely appointed work of farming, had left their tools in the plows overnight. Thinking that the dark hours were opportune for his fraud, he took as many tools as he thought he could carry.

Hurrying away, he spent the entire night laboring in vain. At the very rising of the light he unexpectedly reached the monastery gate. Recognizing that his deed could not remain concealed, he openly confessed that, prompted by the devil, he had committed this wicked presumption against the property of Saint Gall. Thus, returning what he had attempted to steal, he went back empty-handed after asking forgiveness.

## CHAPTER XXXII. A disabled man restored

A certain disabled man was so contracted in all his limbs that he could not possibly move anywhere by himself. His relatives carried him to the memorial of Saint Gall and placed him every day beside the tomb in the crypt. He remained there devoted to prayer until evening, when they carried him back to the guesthouse.

After this had been done for several days, a certain priest of the same community was one day, not far away, performing the sacred offerings in that very church. Suddenly, when no one else was present, the sick man was visited from heaven, as we believe, through the merits of Saint Gall, whose aid he earnestly implored. He began to cry out in a confused and terrifying voice, so that the priest, during the solemn celebration of Mass—as he often used to testify—was shaken by no small terror and fear.

After looking around and examining everything with his eyes, he wished to overcome the intensity of his fear by the presence of someone else. Then, as the wretched man’s limbs returned to their proper state, he heard a cracking like dry branches being broken. Turning himself this way and that in distress, shortly afterward he saw the man who had been disabled emerge from the crypt healed.

Immediately such complete health came to him that thereafter, without the obstacle of infirmity, he enjoyed the walking he had desired.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. A certain man freed from the danger of loathing food

[Col. 1025A]

In the same province of the Alamanni, a certain rich man was so wasted by an adverse illness that, suffering from loathing for almost an entire year, he was wasting away and could neither take nor retain nourishment sufficient for the recovery of health, as it appeared to require.

He was brought to the monastery of Saint Gall for this very reason. After prolonged prayers and sighs, when the service of the sacred offering had been completed, he received the bread of blessing from the priest’s hand. After eating it, he was freed from his loathing. Having properly regained his appetite for food, he blessed the Lord, marveled at the merits of Saint Gall, and returned home healthy and joyful.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Another freed from iron bonds

[Col. 1025B]

A certain poor man [Note: [Col. 1025D] Goldastus adds: “a priest.”], because of guilt for homicide, was bound with iron rings around his neck and around both arms. How severe were the torments he suffered daily he demonstrated to those who saw him by the furrows that the iron had cut into his flesh.

After visiting many holy places in search of relief from this torment and remission of the crime he had committed, he was finally regarded with divine mercy and deserved to lose the bonds that constricted his neck and one of his arms. When he happened to come into the vicinity of the monastery of Saint Gall, he was commanded in a vision—as he used to relate—to seek the holy man’s patronage and visit the monastery. It was also revealed to him that there he would lose the ring that he still carried on one arm and would obtain the grace of the health he desired.

Burning with desire for the promised health, and held by such torment that his whole arm, immersed in the iron, had already become a swelling, he hastened his journey to the monastery. While attending the nocturnal vigils there and overcome by deep sleep, he saw an old man standing beside him, venerable in his white hair, dressed in a chasuble, who said to him: “Why, man, while the others are celebrating the praise of the Lord, are you weighed down by the torpor of sleep?”

Terrified by his presence and afraid to answer, he felt the old man touch the place of his wound with the staff he carried in his hand. The iron sprang farther apart, and from the pain he felt at the touch he frightened those standing nearby with horrible cries. When they asked why he was disturbing those who were singing psalms, he recounted in order everything he had seen.

Although he still had a fresh wound, he nevertheless rejoiced greatly at the loss of the iron whose bonds had bloodied him, because healing was now at hand.

## CHAPTER XXXV. A lamp-holder miraculously preserved with its lamps

At another time a certain brother, who served as custodian in the same church, needed to lower the lamp-holder [Note: [Col. 1026D] That is, a hanging apparatus by which lamps are suspended in churches.] hanging before the altar of Saint Gall in order to light the lamps. Carelessly, he pulled back the rope from which the lamp-holder was suspended. The rope immediately slipped from his hand and pulled the peg to which it was attached out of the wall.

When the lamp-holder was approaching the ground with excessive speed, it suddenly stopped and remained suspended in the air without any human support or artifice. The custodian, struck with amazement at the miracle, brought fire and lit all the lamps. While many people witnessed the event, he drew the lamp-holder higher than it had usually hung, without spilling any oil or diminishing the lamps’ contents.

Accordingly, all gave praise to God and everyone returned thanks, for, in order to proclaim the merits of the eminent Father through the astounding novelty of the miracle, God did not allow the light prepared for holy uses to be absent even for an hour from that venerable place.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Lamps not damaged by a fall

[Col. 1026B]

The same brother was washing glass lamps in the same church at another time. Another man, walking carelessly, suddenly turned in a different direction and knocked some lamps lying nearby to the floor with his clothing. They were thrown with such force that they rolled all the way to the church screen.

Yet, through the wondrous manner of divine action, they were found without damage and immediately restored to their places, not without the amazement of those present.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. By what remedy the physician in danger was helped

A certain brother of the same community, well trained in medical knowledge, had a vein opened by a phlebotomist at a certain time. Shortly afterward, while carelessly undertaking some task in excessive haste, not only the arm whose vein had been wounded by the incision but his entire body became distended with swelling.

For this reason he began to fear death, especially since he saw that the skill of his own profession, applied with the greatest care, was of no benefit. The following night he saw in a dream an old man of calm gravity standing beside him and gently asking about the causes of his illness.

When he related the entire course of events in order to the man questioning him, the old man said: “Remember, my son, when daylight has been restored to the earth, to anoint the place of the wound with the oil that customarily burns before the altar in the crypt; for you will immediately recover your health.” 

When morning came, he reported to the church custodian what he had heard in the dream. He entered the basilica with him and, as he had been instructed, carried out the command, confident in the promise. Without delay, after being anointed with the sacred liquid, the swelling subsided throughout his body, and he attained complete health.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. A girl blind from birth given sight

A certain woman carried her only daughter to the monastery on her own shoulders. The girl, as the woman related, had been blind from birth. She laid her down before the altar of Saint Gall, prostrated herself on the ground, and devoted herself for a long time to prayers on her behalf.

[Note: [Col. 1025D] See the preface.]

While she was praying with greater devotion, the girl suddenly rolled about on the pavement from side to side and cried out piteously. Amid her distress and groans she was granted the sight she desired and, through the evident manifestation of the sign, offered a most welcome spectacle to everyone present.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. A sick boy restored by sarcophagus dust and oil

At that time there was among the students in the same monastery a certain little boy, born to poor parents but very devoted to the pursuit of learning. When he was deprived of the support of both parents by their premature deaths, he continually sought his daily food through his own labor. Nevertheless, even when compelled by necessity, he did not abandon his diligence in the pursuit of good studies.

Struck by a pain in his side, he wasted away through a long period under such a severe illness that, on one side—from the shoulder, that is, to the extremity of his body—numerous ulcers lay open, emitting pus. He was so weighed down by this illness that he could scarcely move a step without assistance from others.

Since bodily medicine, although applied very frequently, did him no good, and everyone was already despairing of him, the church custodian, on the feast of Saint Gall, gathered ashes from his sarcophagus, mixed them with the oil that burned before the same altar, and anointed the boy’s body on the part occupied by the pain.

The next day he was found healed, the ulcers already covered over. In memory of the health restored to him, he spent the remainder of his life in the vigils of that same holy place with faithful devotion.

## CHAPTER XL. A girl’s withered hand restored

After some time, a certain girl arrived at the monastery with her mother. For many years she had borne the useless burden of a withered and crooked hand. With pious devotion, she placed a small ball of flax upon the numb hand and approached the altar of the holy confessor in order to lay down what she had brought. Immediately the hand itself was restored to health.

## CHAPTER XLI. The wax that a peasant stole from the church was turned into stone

[Col. 1027D]

At another time a certain peasant secretly stole from the altar in the basilica of the blessed Father a piece of wax intended for his own use. Returning from there to his lodging, he pulled the wax from his bosom in order to make something from it. He found that it had been turned into the hardness of stone.

Immediately he ran back to the church, restored what he had taken to its place, and, making a salutary confession of his insolence before those present, reported what had happened. Astonished by the novelty of the event, they lifted the same piece from the altar in order to investigate the matter more certainly. Amazingly, they found that it had been changed back to the former softness of its own nature.

## CHAPTER XLII. A mute endowed with the gift of speech

[Col. 1028A]

A certain poor young man, visiting the monastery for the sake of prayer, brought with him his brother, who had long been grieving over the loss of his voice. When he had approached the altar of Saint Gall, he saw a certain priest there performing the sacred mysteries. Waiting for the completion of the sacred action, he threw himself at the knees of the priest as he returned from his ministry and urgently begged him to deign to offer some prayers to the Lord for the mute man.

The priest granted this request: first he prayed for the unfortunate man, then strengthened him with the sign of the cross and fortified him as though with the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood.
