Once this had been done, the bonds of his tongue were loosened, and the man who had arrived mute recovered the functions of his former speech.

## CHAPTER XLIII. A boy crippled by weakness set free

Certain people who were accustomed to carry a boy whose limbs were so contracted that he could not move anywhere by himself abandoned him alone not far along the road leading to the monastery.

A certain herdsman traveling along the same road from the forest toward the monastery saw the wretched boy lying there and said to him: “How and from where, O pitiable one, have you come? By what confidence did you not fear to remain in this desolation? Where, then, did you wish to go?”

The boy replied: “Because of these calamities, whose multitude you see surrounding me, I had long desired to reach the protection of Saint Gall. But look: those whose labor I had hoped would carry me there, now wearied by the length of the road, have left me, miserable as I am, in this wilderness, to be tormented by hunger and torn apart by beasts.”

Moved by compassion to mercy through these complaints, the herdsman placed the boy on his shoulders and carried him one mile to the monastery. A brother entrusted with the care of receiving the poor then took him in and provided him with suitable lodging.

One night, around the time of the nocturnal vigils, while the other people who had likewise been received were hurrying to the church, the boy began earnestly begging everyone to carry him to the basilica. When they all denied him what he requested, he began repeatedly invoking the name of Saint Gall with loud cries. Then he made an even more dreadful uproar, causing no small terror to those who heard him.

Some people entered to learn the cause of his distress and found him healed. With thanksgiving, he hastened to the church.

## CHAPTER XLIV. A paralytic woman restored to health
A girl who had long been suffering from paralysis was brought by her people to the monastery. Carried into the church, during the reading of the Gospel that is recited at the night watches according to the custom of the regular office, she began asking those standing around to lift her from the ground and support her among their hands. When she had been raised, she asked to be released. Since they were afraid to do so, lest she perhaps be injured by a sudden fall, she confidently asserted that she was able to stand. Accordingly, when released, she stood on her own; thereafter, having recovered the strength of her whole body, she departed healed.

## CHAPTER XLV. A blind woman given sight

A maidservant of a certain householder living not far from the monastery, when she happened by chance to open the doors of the house, was struck in the face and eyes by a whirlwind that drove dust and chaff against her. Immediately, as the affliction increased, her use of sight gradually failed, until she was completely surrounded by dreadful darkness. Brought to the church of Saint Gall, when she most devoutly sought his intercession upon her first entrance, she received back the light she had lost and departed rejoicing.

## CHAPTER XLVI. A candle kindled from heaven

Not long afterward, while the festival of the octave of Epiphany was being celebrated with its annual rite, everyone came together in the church at the time of the sacrifice, and lamps and candles were being lit according to custom. One candle, however, left without a light among the others that were burning, at the solemn celebration of the Mass, first began gradually to emit a thin smoke. Then, in the sight of many, it caught flame and shone more brightly than the others, commending the effect of the sign by the singularity of its radiance.

## CHAPTER XLVII. A Scot cured of many infirmities

Recently, too, certain men from the nation of the Scots—for whom the custom of pilgrimage has almost become a natural characteristic—came and left one of their traveling companions, afflicted by a manifold disease, at the same monastery. After he had remained there for several days and daily sought a remedy for his illness with complete faith, one night he saw in a dream an old man standing beside him, venerable in gesture and appearance. When he asked who he was, he learned that he was the most blessed Gall.

Immediately he said to him: “You see, lord, that my whole body is disordered, and that every day I await some manifestation of your merits. Therefore do not delay any longer what I believe you will at some point do. For I understand that I have been preserved until now for this purpose: that, just as your power shines most widely among these barbarians, so also the splendor and glory of your merits may become known among the people of your own nation. You yourself know—you know, I say—how far I am separated from my native land, and how greatly, amid the hardships of pilgrimage, I am oppressed by bodily weakness. Come to my aid more quickly; help me without delay.”

Moved by this complaint, he replied briefly with a calm expression: “When day has been restored to mortals, go to the church, and you will see that you are raised up by divine providence better than by the comfort of your homeland or your parents.”

When morning came, he hurried to the basilica, rejoicing with the utmost ardor of spirit, and, remembering the promise, devoted himself to prayer beside the tomb of Saint Gall. After prayer and tears, leaning against the corner of the sarcophagus, he began gradually to raise himself. He did not leave the corner of the bed on which he was leaning until, standing upright and having regained his strength, he was able to walk back and forth on his own. As time went on, he was granted complete health and continued to live in that monastery, serving through prayer and holy living.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. The author’s conclusion

From the exceedingly abundant harvest of Saint Gall’s virtues, I have been pleased to consign these grains to the granaries of memory, where they may benefit both our nourishment and that of others. For these accounts can greatly contribute to the edification of those who love righteousness: they convey moral uprightness and inflame the mind of the devout reader or hearer to praise the Lord, who so glorifies his saints.

Moreover, so many and so great are the miracles of this holy Father that, because of their abundance, they could neither be encompassed by diligent writers nor read through without weariness and a wrinkled brow by fastidious readers. Those miracles alone have been inserted into this work that preserve the truth through the testimony of truthful witnesses and, by their moderate brevity, do not offend anyone’s mind, even one that grows weary of useful things.

### Prayer of Walafrid

Therefore we beseech you, blessed Gall, confessor of Christ, that, just as we have related that you bestowed bodily health through your many merits, so you may deign to implore for our minds the healing of divine mercy. Amen.

---

# LIFE OF SAINT OTHMAR, ABBOT OF SAINT GALL

*(G)*

## Mabillon’s Preliminary Observations

*(Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, vol. IV.)*

1. Among the ancients, the name of Saint Othmar was written in more than one way. In the charters published by Melchior Goldast in volumes II and III of *Alemannic Affairs*, one finds Audemarus, Audomarus, Autmarus, and Otmarus, the abbot of Durgau or of the monastery of Saint Gall, whom others, and the common usage, call Gallus or Gall.

Walafrid Strabo, abbot of Reichenau, committed the lives of both saints—namely Gall and Othmar—to writing, at the request of Gozbert, abbot of Saint Gall, as Hepidannus testifies in his *Annals*, together with Walafrid himself in his prologue. Walafrid died in 849, specifically on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, according to the Necrology of Saint Gall preserved by Goldast.

2. Iso, a monk of the monastery of Saint Gall, who was almost his contemporary, wrote two books on the translation and miracles of Saint Othmar. Ekkehard the Younger praises him highly in book 2 of *The Misfortunes of Saint Gall*, where he is said to have had Notker the Stammerer, Tutilo, and Ratpert as pupils. According to Hepidannus, Iso the teacher died in 871, on the day before the Ides of May; Hermannus Contractus also assigns him that year. Two hymns are likewise preserved in Canisius, volume V of the *Ancient Readings*, pages 757 and 767: one composed by Notker the physician, the other by an anonymous author in honor of Saint Othmar.

3. Immediately after his death, Othmar was regarded as a saint. Accordingly, ten years after his burial, his body was brought back from the island of Stein to the monastery of Saint Gall. Yet he was not honored by public worship before the year 864, when Solomon, bishop of Constance, decreed this after the solemn raising of his body from the tomb. Ekkehard, chapter 1 of *The Misfortunes of Saint Gall*, writes that blessed Othmar was raised as a saint by Roman authority. I fear, however, that he said this with regard to his own period—namely, the eleventh century—when it was customary to await the approval of the Roman pontiff for raising the bodies of saints from the earth. For the monk Iso, witness and historian of the translation carried out by Solomon, does not mention that the authority of the Roman pontiff intervened in book 1, chapter 2 and the following chapters. Saint Wolfgang, bishop of Regensburg, honored Saint Othmar with particular devotion.

4. Notker, physician and monk of the monastery of Saint Gall, calls Othmar a martyr in a hymn he composed, in these verses:

> He grieved over the savage plunderings of princes.  
> Thereafter, burdened by the schemes of the plunderers,  
> He earned the martyr’s palm and deserved  
> To ascend to the heavenly kingdoms.

At that time, certainly, it was customary for innocent people who had suffered any violent death at the hands of others to be called martyrs. Yet even if Saint Othmar ended his life in exile for the sake of justice, he should not therefore immediately be called a martyr; we read that this title was attributed to him only by Notker. Cuonradus Camerarius established a light to burn every night before the altar of Saint Othmar, as is recorded in the Gallican Necrology on the eighth day before the Ides of October.

5. The monastery of Saint Gall, situated in the diocese of Constance beside Lake Constance, was formerly called Durgau, because it was situated in the district of Durgau, which is also called the district of Arbon. This monastery, I say, celebrated to the present day for its renown and greatness, owes its beginnings and growth to Othmar the abbot. He enlarged the small cell founded by Saint Gall and almost abandoned, equipped it with the necessary buildings, and assigned it to Benedictine monks; he himself also became a monk, although previously he had been a secular priest.

Indeed, when King Pippin entrusted the cell of Saint Gall to Othmar, he gave him the book that Father Benedict had composed concerning the manner of life of cenobites, as Walafrid testifies in *The Miracles of Saint Gall*, chapter 2, where he describes the former state of Saint Gall’s cell. There is no doubt that Pippin did this with the intention that the new monastery should be formed according to Benedictine institutions.

Kero, a monk of Saint Gall, during the reign of Pippin, the father of Charlemagne, rendered the Rule of Saint Benedict into Alemannic for the benefit of unlearned monks, as is recorded by Goldast in volume II of *Alemannic Affairs*. Hence the frequent mention of the Rule of Saint Benedict in the history of Ekkehard the Younger. Before him came Hartmann, a monk of the same monastery in the ninth century, in the metrical Litany in volume V of Canisius, page 732, reported in these verses:

> O beloved of God, radiant with flashing virtue,  
> Holy Father Othmar, join your prayers with ours.  
> Supreme worshiper of God, ruler and abbot of monks,  
> O holy and kind Father Benedict,  
> Sanctify this monastery and the company serving you,  
> And together watch over all that is ours.

6. Various donations made to Saint Othmar are recorded by Goldast in volumes II and III of *Alemannic Affairs*, where Othmar’s name is expressed in various forms, as we noted above.

7. Several devout and illustrious men flourished in that monastery. Among them, besides Othmar, were Saint Eusebius the Scot in the ninth century; Notker, surnamed the Stammerer, who died in 912; Wiborada, a recluse; and Foillanus the Scot, of blessed memory, in the tenth century. More will be said about them in their proper places.

There were also men endowed with learning to the extent permitted by their times: Master Iso, Tutilo, Ratpert, Ekkehard the Elder and the Younger, Hepidannus, Burchard, Berthold, and other monks of Saint Gall—not to mention the many distinguished by episcopal and abbatial dignity who emerged from the same school. Notker, bishop of Liège, must be counted among them, as we shall establish elsewhere.

There also flourished there an inner school for monks and an outer school for laypeople. It is worth noting here that the venerable Father Agino, bishop and head of the monastery of Saint Gall, is named in a charter of Ruakerus dated in the twenty-fourth year of Charlemagne’s reign, preserved by Goldast in his notes on chapter 14 of Burchard’s history, *The Misfortunes of the Same Monastery*. At that time, however, Werdo is said to have presided as abbot.

# HERE BEGINS THE LIFE

## PROLOGUE

### To the brothers of the monastery of Saint Gall

Having completed the two little books on the life and virtues of the blessed confessor Gall, which we composed more truthfully than elegantly according to the account that had reached us in writing or by word of mouth, I am pleased, at your command, dearest brothers—who, established in the monastery of that holy Father, display by the holy vigor of your purpose an example of the fervor he showed in the things of God—to append the account concerning the endeavors of Saint Father Othmar and the virtues manifested through his merits, which has been committed to writing by your truthful testimony and care.

Since it is full of truth and clear in its reasoning, we have repeated it for no other reason than that our dearest brother Gozbert, who published this little work and to whose affection we neither wish nor ought to refuse anything, requested—indeed, commanded—that this be done. In this task we gladly endured, without weariness, his most persistent urging as an *ergodioctes*.

[Note: Greek ἐργοδιώκτην, that is, “an exactor of work, an overseer who urges the work on”; Jerome used this word in the *Epitaph for Nepotianus*.]

Therefore let this abridgment of ours suffice for the trusting reader. But whoever is unbelieving, returning to the written account that we follow, will be confronted by the manifold corroboration of witnesses and, if he is fair-minded, will not be slow to accept its truth.

## CHAPTER I. How, on account of the holiness of his life, the man of God Othmar was placed over Saint Gall’s cell and established regular life there by royal authority

Othmar, born of the Alemannic people, was brought by his brother in childhood to Raetia Curiensis [Note: Raetia Curiensis, or First Raetia, whose chief city was Curia (Chur) on the Rhine, comprises the county of Tyrol; another, called Second Raetia, extends from the city of Curia to the Danube and is separated from Bavaria by the river Lech.] and was placed for a long time in the service of Victor, count of those regions. Advanced in knowledge of letters, a follower of virtue and possessor of praiseworthy morals, he rose to the priesthood. Kindly retained by the aforesaid count, he was placed in charge of a church dedicated to Saint Florinus the Confessor.

When the integrity of his morals and the purity of his holy life had spread far and wide, sprinkling the ears of many with a sweet report, a certain Waltramnus—who claimed the wilderness in which Saint Gall had built his cell as though it had passed to him by hereditary right from his parents—asked the aforementioned Victor to place Othmar in charge of that cell. Having obtained his wish, he solemnly entrusted to him the cell and everything belonging to it.

[Note: More precisely, to Charles, the father of King Pippin, as is clear both from Walafrid himself in *The Miracles of Saint Gall*, chapter 11, and from the monk Hepidannus in *The Misfortunes of Saint Gall*, as well as from Hermannus Contractus in his *Chronicle*, where Othmar is said to have been “appointed first abbot of Saint Gall’s cell in the year 720, established cenobitic life there, and nobly governed it for forty years.” Moreover, Walafrid says that Victor, “persuaded by the advice of a certain duke named Nebi, hastened with that duke to the aforesaid prince Charles, surrendered that same cell to him by right of ownership, and begged him to place the priest Othmar in charge of the place.” Yet from Iso’s first book *On the Miracles of Saint Othmar*, chapter 5, we learn that Othmar was first brought by Victor to Charles and then, after Charles’s death, to his son Pippin, so that he might be confirmed in possession of the place that had been granted.]

Accordingly, he went to King Pippin, presented Othmar to him as abbot, and surrendered to the prince by right of ownership the place over which he had previously appointed him, earnestly requesting that Othmar be established there as abbot in full accordance with royal authority. The aforementioned prince granted his request, entrusted the place given to him to the venerable man, and ordered him to establish regular life there.

On his return, Othmar immediately put into effect the zeal of a good shepherd. At the very beginning he constructed suitable dwellings for the monks on every side and most diligently reformed the condition of the sacred place for the advancement of divine service. He also invited various religious men to devote themselves to this calling by his generosity, so that through the donations of some of them he greatly enlarged the possessions of the monastery, and within a few years attracted many to the service of the sacred life, whom he guided and governed most fittingly by his instruction and care.

## CHAPTER II. With what perfection of holy conduct he shone

With these matters preliminarily set forth, let us briefly touch upon the holiness of his life, so that it may clearly appear to all by what degrees of progress he rose to this glory.

He was an outstanding devotee of frugality, frequently mortifying his body by fasting, so that on the principal days of fasting he often continued the abstinence customary for two days. Fortified by these shields against the darts of temptation, he loved vigils and, through constant prayer, drove back spiritual wickedness.

He was especially endowed with the grace of profound humility and loved voluntary poverty so greatly that he fled earthly glory by every means. He also had this custom: if necessity required him to travel anywhere for the benefit of the monastery, he would ride upon the humble back of a gentle little ass.

Among his other qualities, he possessed such great concern for the poor that he preferred to care for them personally rather than through others. In the work of mercy called almsgiving, scarcely anyone was his equal. For receiving lepers, who customarily lived apart and separated from other people, he established a small hospice not far from the monastery, outside the dwellings in which the other poor were received. He personally cared for them in every way, so attentively that even at night he often left the monastery and ministered to their illness with remarkable devotion.

He washed their heads and feet, cleaned their pus-filled wounds with his own hands, and supplied what was necessary for their sustenance, always turning over in his mind the sentence that the just Judge will pronounce to the merciful, saying: “What you did for one of the least of my brothers, you did for me” (Matthew 25).

Thus it came about that, exalted in the reverence of all who knew him, he was called by many the Father of the Poor. Such was the fullness of his devotion to mercy that, if he saw a poor person numbed by the injury of nakedness, he would often remove his own clothes and cover the miserable person’s limbs, sometimes returning to the monastery without a tunic, clothed only in a cloak.

[Note: That is, a *cuculla*, as we learn from the letter of Theodemar, abbot of Monte Cassino, to Charlemagne.]

For he preferred, through contempt for present splendor, to attain the garment of eternal incorruption rather than, through the loss of a good work, to endure the disgrace of future nakedness.

## CHAPTER III. How great was his mercy toward the poor

At one time, coming to King Pippin, he was received honorably. Among the other benefits of the king’s generosity, he received seventy pounds of silver to relieve the needs of his brothers.

[Note: Walafrid states in *The Miracles of Saint Gall*, chapter 11, that at the request of his brother Carloman, Pippin granted Saint Othmar many gifts, among them a copy of the Rule of Saint Benedict and a bell, and confirmed the estates of the monastery of Saint Gall by a charter.]

But as soon as he departed to return to his own monastery, he distributed the greater part of that money to the poor before the gates of the palace. He was scarcely compelled by the brothers who were with him to retain a few solidi, with which he later purchased a certain tract of land near the monastery.

Not forgetting the Lord’s commandments, he did not think about the morrow for his own sake, knowing that a monk ought to be content with food and clothing. Therefore he chose poverty for himself and his people rather than the superfluous possession of passing things, which weighs upon minds that should be free.

## CHAPTER IV. How, because of the zeal for justice with which he burned, he was subjected to many insults by certain wicked men

When the Lord had already determined to repay him with rewards worthy of his merits, the cunning enemy of all goodness, jealous of his good works and grieved that the lives of others were improving through his example, attempted to disturb the peace that Othmar had possessed in the service of Christ, though not without considerable labor.

Yet although the cedar of paradise was struck by the blasts of temporal adversity, because it had fixed its root in the rock of truth it remained unshaken. For Warinus and Ruadhardus, who at that time administered the affairs of all Alemannia, prompted by the devil and afflicted by the monstrous disease of greed, forcibly drew a large part of the property of the churches under their authority into their own ownership.

[Note: A letter of a certain Scalcomannus, preserved by Goldast in volume II of *Alemannic Affairs*, item 45, is dated “in the first year of King Carloman, under Count Roadhardus”; another of Winibert, item 43, is dated “on Sunday, the sixth day before the Ides of October, in the tenth year, while Lord Pippin, king of the Franks, reigned under Count Warinus.” There is likewise another, item 67. Count Warinus was still in office in the fourth year of Charlemagne, according to charter 29. Compare Walafrid’s chapter 15, *On the Miracles of Saint Gall* (above). Stumpf makes Warinus count of Hegau and Ruadhardus count of Thurgau; Goldast, in his notes on Ratpert’s chapter 2, calls them messengers of the court, drawing on Ekkehard’s *The Misfortunes of Saint Gall*, chapter 1, near the beginning.]

After they had claimed many possessions of blessed Gall by the same violent act, the man of God Othmar did not covet earthly possessions. Rather, he foresaw the impending lack of resources for the cenobitic life in that place, and therefore went to King Pippin. He laid before him their tyrannical presumption and likewise declared that the king would incur serious guilt if, by consenting to their actions, he supported them.

For this reason the benevolent prince summoned both men and threatened that they would lose his favor entirely if they did not immediately restore to the Church of God what they had unjustly taken. But they returned to their homeland, infected with the vice of rapacity and inflamed by bestial savagery, and disregarded the royal command. Moreover, when the man of God Othmar wished to approach the prince again over this affair, they secretly dispatched soldiers after him and had him forcibly brought back in chains. They also persuaded a certain Lambert, who was counted among Othmar’s brothers by profession, though not by holiness of life, to bring a charge of sexual misconduct against him by means of a contrived plot. They worked to find an opportunity to depose him after his holiness had been defamed by such suspicions.

For this reason many people, unaware of the treacherous conspiracy, were summoned to a council.

[Note: Namely, in the year 745, as Hepidannus testifies in these words: “Sidonius, bishop of Constance and abbot of Reichenau, accused blessed Othmar of adultery; then he was sent into exile.”]

## CHAPTER V. What moderation he maintained when accused of a fabricated crime, and what punishment his accuser suffered

Accordingly, the venerable man, sound in *castae vitae* (“a chaste life”) [variant: *castitate*, “chastity”] and advanced in years through the maturity of his morals, was placed in the midst of the council. Lambert, the instrument of falsehood, was brought before everyone to accuse him. Having received permission to speak, and having forgotten the truth, the advocate of falsehood said that he knew a certain woman who had suffered sexual violation at the hands of the holy man.

He is said to have given no answer to this. When many people compelled him to respond to the accusations, he moderated his speech with words of this kind: “I confess,” he said, “that I have sinned exceedingly in many things. Concerning this accusation, however, I call God, the examiner of my secret life, as witness.”

When they pressed him more intently to clear himself by an apology for this deed, secure in mind and free in conscience, he continued silently. Since he recognized that the judges permitted the freedom to accuse, he preferred, for the sincerity of his heart, to please the divine judgment rather than the human judgment in defending himself against the charge.

Then, so that it might become clear to everyone that his chastity had been falsely defamed, divine vengeance seized Lambert. Seized by a fever, he gradually lost the strength of his limbs and began to contract. As all his limbs lost their upright posture or natural form, with his head bent toward the ground like that of a four-footed animal, he was terrifying not only in the deformity of his appearance but also because, with a living voice, he confessed that he had sinned against the saint throughout his life.

## CHAPTER VI. How he ended his life amid the narrow confines of custody

After the plot had been wickedly begun and brought to a still more wicked conclusion, the man of God Othmar was confined in the palace at Potamum.

[Note: Potamum was formerly a town, renowned as a royal palace, according to Ekkehard, cited below. Lake Potamicus took its name from it; the lake was otherwise called Lake Constance and Lake Brigantinus. The town was destroyed after the year 917, on whose site the fortress of Bodman or Podman was later rebuilt. It is now inhabited by the noble family of Bodman, as Goldast noted in Ekkehard’s chapter 1. Not far from there lies Stein, situated beside the place where the Rhine emerges from Lake Constance, where Othmar died.]

Since no one was permitted to enter or converse with him there, he spent several days without bodily nourishment. When he was suffering from prolonged hunger, a certain Peragosus [Surius: Patgozus], one of his brothers, used to come by night and provide him with food.

Later, a certain Gozbertus, a powerful man, having obtained permission from the wicked rulers for the man of God to be entrusted to him, assigned him to custody on an island in the Rhine called Stein, near his own estate.

[Note: In Goldast, volume III of *Alemannic Affairs*, pages 54–55, there is a record of a donation made by Gautzpertus to Audomarus, abbot of Durgau, concerning the monastery of Saint Gall, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, in the third year of Pippin’s reign.]

There the holy Father, devoting himself solely to spiritual exercise—that is, to prayers and fasts—served the Lord all the more freely because he had been released from human company and worldly cares.

Persisting in these and similar works of renowned devotion, after not much time had passed he departed from the narrow confines of worldly disturbance into the broad expanse of heavenly joy, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December.

[Note: Chesnius incorrectly reads “the seventeenth.” Walafrid says that he died after completing no fewer than forty years of rule, in chapter 15 *On the Miracles of Saint Gall*. He died in the seventh year of Pippin’s reign, according to Ivo below, book 1, chapter 5; therefore not in the year of Christ 758, as in Hepidannus, nor in 760, as in Albert, abbot of Stade, but in 759, as Hermannus Contractus correctly reads. Certainly, John, Othmar’s successor, formerly a monk of Reichenau, presided over the monastery of Saint Gall in 761, or rather in 760. This is clear both from charter 44 in Goldast, dated on Sunday, the fifth day before the Nones of May, during Pippin’s reign—that is, in the year 761—and from charter 59, dated in the eighth year of King Pippin, on January 15, in favor of John the abbot, which corresponds to the year 760.]

His body was buried on the same island and thereafter remained there for many days without corruption.

[Note: At this point Walafrid omits the death of Sidonius, bishop of Constance, on account of his seizure of the property of the monastery of Saint Gall; this should be supplied from chapter 18 of *The Miracles of Saint Gall*.]

## CHAPTER VII. How, after a long time, his body was found incorrupt

Ten years after his departure, his brothers were warned by the Lord in a vision to bring the body of their dear Father back to the monastery. Once the divine will had been revealed, eleven of those same brothers came by night to the place where the remains of the holy man were kept. Opening the tomb, they found his body unharmed by every form of corruption, except that the end of one foot, which the water had washed, appeared somewhat decayed, its color alone having changed.

By a sufficiently fitting miracle, the first signs of his healing became clear: his body was found as free from corruption as he himself had been free from the crime by which, for a time, he had seemed to be overcome.

Thus the devout brothers, instructed more perfectly by the novelty of the event, reverently took up the body and placed it on a raft. They lit candles, placing one at the head and another at the feet.

[Note: Hermannus Contractus correctly assigns this event to the year 769.]

## CHAPTER VIII. How the storm was miraculously calmed during the translation of his body

When they had left the shore and entrusted themselves to the uncertain paths of the deep, rowing with the utmost effort and eager to return as quickly as possible, such a force of rain and wind suddenly broke out that they scarcely believed they would escape.

But through the wondrous providence of almighty God—and, as we believe, through the merits of the holy man—it came about that even the elements, which seem insensible to us, recognized how great a man’s relics were being carried there, serving the command of their Creator.

For although the sea all around was stirred by a rain-bearing storm, lifting its waves high into the air, it caused no trouble at all to the rowers. In whichever direction the boat moved, the swelling waves that rose against it were driven back and subdued. Thus, after the masses of water, the torrents of rain, and the blasts of wind had been driven away from every side over a considerable distance, the boat seemed to be surrounded by a kind of hedge, so that not even one drop of the rain that was pouring violently here and there descended upon it.

The wax candles that had been placed burning at the head and feet in service to the blessed Father did not lose the light of their first kindling until his body had been brought to the monastery.

## CHAPTER IX. The abundance of drink supplied from heaven, and where his body was buried after the translation

One further miracle remains, which the Lord revealed to the devout brothers during the same translation of the sacred body.

When they had been exhausted by their excessive exertion in rowing and, as the hour of refreshment approached, had sat down after first offering praises to the Lord in order to recover their strength through bodily nourishment, they finally remembered that the solace of drink should be added to their fortunate meal. One of the servants then reported that no drink remained there except what was kept in a small flask, from which scarcely anything could be offered to each person for tasting rather than for drinking.

They, however, recalling the Lord’s miracles—how he had fed a great multitude of people with a few loaves—ordered that the small amount they had be distributed lovingly to everyone present. In a wondrous manner, the amount of liquid in that same little vessel began to increase with each draught, so that, despite continuous pouring, it appeared not to diminish at all, until the drinkers were overcome by the abundance of cups.

Astounded at the novelty of the event, they offered fitting thanks and praises to the Lord, giver of all good things, who had provided them with such miraculous sufficiency. As soon as they resumed the journey they had begun, the drink in the vessel ceased.

When they reached the harbor of the desired shore, they recounted in order to the brothers who came to meet them with praises of God what had happened. After celebrating together, they carried the body of the holy man with great honor to the monastery and placed it in a sarcophagus between the altar of Saint John the Baptist and the wall. There also, afterward, the Lord deigned to reveal miracles worthy of remembrance through the merits of the saint.

## CHAPTER X. A mute and deaf man was healed at his tomb

Finally, at one time a deaf and mute man came with certain people from the neighboring regions who were going to the monastery for prayer. Since from earliest childhood he had been deprived of both speech and hearing, he carried two tablets hanging from his neck. By striking them together and making a sound, he asked for the work of mercy that he could not request with his voice.

When he entered the church with his traveling companions and saw them placing small pieces of wax on each of the altars, as is the custom of the poor, he approached the tomb of the man of God, placed the tablets he was carrying upon it, and prostrated himself before it as though he were about to pray.

Immediately overcome by deep sleep, he later reported that he saw an old man, radiant in face and glorious in monastic dress, emerging as if from the tomb and saying to him: “Man, why are you overcome by sleep here?”

When he was entirely unable to answer the questions put to him, the old man said to him: “Rise, and know that a remedy for the troubles from which you have suffered until now has been obtained for you from me.”

Thus he left the tablets there, immediately departed from the monastery, and was told not to disclose to anyone in that place the gift granted to him by God. When he awoke and rose, he left the monastery in great haste. As the day was already declining toward evening, he turned aside to the lodging of a powerful man named Ratgozus.

When Ratgozus asked him where he was coming from, he explained in order where, when, and how he had obtained the gift of healing. But not believing his account, Ratgozus ordered him to be held and guarded. He himself, wishing to investigate the truth of the matter more reliably, came to the monastery that same night and found the tablets placed upon the tomb.

He also found the travelling companions of the healed man, who were still unaware of what had happened. He carefully asked them whether, as they were going to the monastery, they had had such a man in their company. Immediately, from their account, he discovered that what he had heard at home was true.

The event soon became known to those present and has reached us through a truthful report.

## CHAPTER XI. How a light given from heaven appeared in that same place

A certain priest from the same community, named Tanco, while serving as custodian of that church, was accustomed to enter the basilica during the time of night’s rest in order to replenish the lights. On three occasions he found nearly everything extinguished.

When he reached the tomb of the holy man, however, he found a candle burning beside it. Knowing that the radiance of that light had been supplied from heaven, he did not dare to extinguish it. When he departed, the light that had come of itself was likewise withdrawn of itself.

As a further indication of the greater miracle, the fire shone in the candle as usual, but the wax seemed not to diminish at all from its heat. This venerable priest repeatedly confirmed the event in his own account, dispelling every basis for doubt by the force of its truth.

## CHAPTER XII. How easily a certain man, despairing of life there after an accident, recovered
At another time, while the roofs of the same church, having fallen into disrepair through age, were necessarily being restored, one of the monastery’s household servants, overburdened by a load of tiles which he was supposed to carry to the basilica’s roof, fell from the very height of the roof onto the tomb of the man of God [Col. 1040A]. Immediately, another immense mass of timber, driven down by the impact of the collapsing structure, covered him from above at the very moment of his fall. When those standing nearby came running to perform the funeral rites for the man whom they already believed lifeless, they lifted away part of the weight of timber. He lay there showing no movement of his limbs; then, drawing breath again through long sighs, he rose unharmed without any injury and returned joyfully to the work he had begun. In this miracle, therefore, the merits of the holy Father unquestionably shone forth: the height of the roof from which the man had fallen was no less than forty feet above the ground, while the weight that followed the falling man—enough to crush several people—could cover him in his descent but could not crush him.

## CHAPTER XIII. A Contracted Man Restored to Health

[Col. 1040B]

At another time a certain blind man arrived and was received in the lodging prepared for the needs of the poor. That same night, when he wished to go to the church, the little boy who was supposed to guide him refused his assistance because of the excessive severity of the cold. The blind man was deeply distressed that he was not worthy to attend so great a solemnity—for it was the vigil of the Lord’s Day. A certain young man, whose limbs were so completely contracted that he could move nowhere except by crawling on his hands, was resting in the same place. Taking pity on the blind man’s distress, he dragged himself from his bed and guided the blind man’s steps with whatever assistance he could provide.

When they entered the church [Col. 1040C], they came by a fortunate mistake to the tomb of Othmar. The blind man’s kindly predecessor—for so he was acting—thought that a doorway opened in that very corner, through which they could enter the crypt adjacent to the place. Thus, unexpectedly striking against the sarcophagus of the man of God, which rose somewhat higher above the ground, he suddenly recoiled and fell immediately to the ground, filling the whole church with terrifying cries. Hearing this, the blind man thought that his guide had been seized by madness and tried to flee as best he could.

But the merciful Lord, author and lover of every good, because he had seen that the weak boy had wished to perform an act of charity beyond his strength, and because the merits of blessed Othmar also secured this outcome, deigned to reward his kindness with the gift of health. For immediately, when his limbs were restored to their proper condition, he led the blind man—whom shortly before he had dragged to the church while crawling on his hands—through the remaining places of prayer in the same enclosure, now with firm steps. Since he remained in the monastery for some time afterward, he made the matter so clear even to those who had had less involvement in the event that no one thereafter could doubt it.

## CHAPTER XIV. Earth Turned into Stone

A certain member of the schoolmen secretly stole a small piece of wax from the tomb of blessed Othmar. On returning to the lodging, he treated his deed as insignificant; but immediately, through an evident correction from God, he shamefacedly recognized the error of his folly. For [Col. 1041A], when he drew the same piece from his bosom, he found that it had been changed into the hardness of stone. Yet when he joined obstinacy to his rashness, he concealed this event for a long time from everyone’s knowledge—except, of course, from the man who at that time was aware of these matters and who now remains the most faithful narrator of the miracle we have related.

## CHAPTER XV. A Cleric’s Hands Restored

At another time a certain cleric arrived, for whom the use of both hands had been denied in a completely pitiable manner. His fingers were twisted into the palm, and his nails were driven down to the very bones of his hands; he was tortured without interruption by excruciating pain [Col. 1041B], so that some parts of his hands had even rotted and emitted a foul stench over a considerable distance.

While he was standing not far from the tomb of the blessed man, his fingers suddenly began to rise one by one, in their proper order, and to return to the coordinated movements of nature. Yet the man who ought to have rejoiced in the gift of health granted to him testified to the magnitude of his pain with a terrible cry; and in that same hour, with his hands restored completely, he afterward departed in good health.

## CHAPTER XVI. How the Same Tomb Remained Unharmed during the Destruction of the Basilica, and How the Relics of the Holy Man Were Transferred to a Higher Place

We think that what recently happened concerning the tomb of this same holy man, when the church of Saint Gall was being demolished in order to rebuild it [Col. 1041C], should not be suppressed in silence. In the same basilica, beside the altar of blessed John the Baptist, a certain chest stood adjoining the wall. It was constructed on four sides of masonry with cement and fairly large stones; above it, transverse boards, three or four fingers thick, appeared to have been laid and covered with cement spread over them. Within it the little body of the holy man lay raised somewhat above the pavement, with only a wooden board placed beneath it [Col. 1042A].

> **Note:** Observe the ancient practice of preserving the relics of the saints. Thus, Bede says in Book IV, chapter 30 of his *History*, that the monks of Lindisfarne raised the body of Saint Cuthbert from the earth, “placed it in a new chest, and set it above the pavement of the sanctuary.” The same author should be read in Book IV, chapter 3, where he describes the tomb of Saint Ceadda, bishop: “covered with a wooden tomb made in the form of a little house, having an opening in the wall through which those who come for devotion customarily put in a hand,” and so forth. Gregory, bishop of Tours, writes much the same about the tomb of Saint Venerandus, bishop, in his *Book on the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 37, and likewise in chapter 44. Bishop Tranquillus is said to have had a tomb above the ground. In approximately this form the monuments of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy at Clairvaux are still visible. The monk Iso records in Book I, chapter 5 of his *Miracles* that the body of Saint Othmar was placed on the right side of the altar; Bede likewise states this concerning the relics of Saints Aidan and Ceadda in *History*, Book III, chapters 17 and 23.

Many therefore believed that the body of the holy Father had been placed beneath the ground and that the construction of the chest had been cemented merely to indicate the location of the burial. Believing for that reason that the tomb itself could remain undisturbed, they attacked the church walls with machines and forced them to collapse under repeated blows from battering rams. Since the walls were of great height on every side, they almost all fell together under the powerful thrusts of the machines and came crashing down over the tomb of the man of God. Yet, in a remarkable manner, they did not damage any part of the chest. When the ashes had been carried away, it was found untouched on every side, as though it had not been struck by the impact of any falling wall.

Afterward, however, when someone carelessly threw a not very large stone upon it, it was immediately broken on one side. At last, when it became known that the relics of the holy Father were kept within it [Col. 1042B], they transferred them from there with great honor and placed them in the church of Saint Peter behind the altar.

> **Note:** This occurred not in the year 729, as Hepidanus seems to think, but in the following year, as may be inferred from the subsequent account of the translation. Certainly Ratpertus, chapter 6, shows that the restoration of the basilica of Saint Gall was begun in the year 830; and the monk Iso, in Book I, chapter 5 of *The Miracles of Saint Othmar*, writes that this translation took place “on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, on Good Friday,” that is, in the year 830, when Easter fell on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

## CHAPTER XVII. What Vision Was Revealed to a Certain Brother in the Same Oratory

After a few days had passed, a certain brother entered the same oratory one night to pray before the nocturnal vigils. With all his devotion he applied himself to prayer and directed his attention toward the altar. There, on the right side of the altar, he saw—he could not say whom—standing in the radiance of an angelic brightness. The figure was resplendent in priestly dress, its face turned toward the east, and its bodily posture displaying the appearance of the most intense prayer [Col. 1042C]. He declared that the garments themselves shone with such brilliance that they dazzled human eyes.

After he had gazed at this for a long time and anxiously weighed in his mind whether he ought to approach more closely, the figure that had appeared withdrew, leaving him overwhelmed by the miracle and his astonishment. It is therefore not incredible that the same venerable man wished to declare, by a vision of his presence, that the brotherly devotion repeatedly shown toward his translation had been pleasingly diligent.

[Col. 1043]

# LIFE OF SAINT BLAITHMAIC, ABBOT OF IONA AND MARTYR

*(In Mabillon, Acta Sanctorum of the Order of Saint Benedict, third century, from Canisius and Bollandus.)* (G)

## I. PROLOGUE

[Col. 1043A]

If those who have sung in their own poems  
the ways and deeds of wicked men  
and raised them to heaven with praises,  
drenched in the art of the demon,  
weaving frivolous memorials of human evils,  
have deserved so great a reputation,  

why should we not sing more freely  
the deeds of the saints,  
whom the miracles they perform  
show to have pleased God?  
They perform these things through the power of faith,  
by the gifts of Christ.  

For Scripture sings, with the Lord promising the lowly:

> “Open your mouth, and I will supply the words.” (Psalm 80)

Therefore, venerable Father, dearest Felix,  
ready from the heart to obey your commands,  
I, Strabus, whom the Alamannian land sent forth by birth,  
have resolved to write of the life and death  
of blessed Blaitmaic [Col. 1043B],  
whom wealthy Ireland brought forth into the world  
and whom perfect martyrdom, following after, sent to heaven,  
so that through his merits I may obtain forgiveness throughout the ages.

## II. BLAITHMAIC’S HOMELAND AND ROYAL DESCENT

Born from a royal stock and possessing  
the supreme beauty of nobility,  
this holy man, the royal heir, flourished  
while living a chaste life.  

And what is rarely done and seldom seen:  
the greater he was, the more he humbled himself.  

The hope of his homeland, his father’s fortune,  
a future king;  
just in judgment, prudent, and chaste in body;  
temperate, well adorned, cheerful, cautious, honorable;  
noble in illustrious lineage, nobler still in conduct;  
rich in service, made richer by virtues [Col. 1043C];  
he practiced as a layman what a cleric accomplished.

His honorable name, in Latin speech,  
is *Pulcher natus* (“beautifully born”) [Note: Among the Irish, *brah* or *braa* now sounds like “beautiful,” and *mac* means “son”; from Bollandus.].  
And he was rightly worthy of that name,  
for he chose the almighty Father  
and sought God with beautiful love.

## III. HE FLEES TO THE MONASTERY

Earthly things seemed worthless to his mind,  
which was seeking divine things.  
The hidden secret remained in his heart alone  
until the holy will came to fulfillment.

Secretly, without a witness,  
he sought a certain monastery.  
He who had once been prince of his homeland  
through royal power  
was then made, for Christ’s name,  
a lesser servant.

He who had once terrified everyone  
in the midst of the emblems of power  
now served everyone admitted there,  
without a soldier at his side.

## IV. HIS FATHER’S AND THE NOBLES’ TEMPTATIONS DISPELLED

[Col. 1043D]

When chance, flying rumor,  
brought the news to his father’s ears,  
astonishment and grief enclosed the parent’s mind.  
He mourned the heir who had been taken away  
and sent the senate [Col. 1044A],  
armies, magistrates, the people, orders, and companies.

Leader and companion went;  
the bishop hurried to his side,  
along with a company of abbots, neighbors,  
and relatives by blood.  
Their only aim was this:  
if by any means they could make him return,  
to cause him to enter another heart  
while avoiding danger.

O how blind such a purpose was!  
He had scarcely withdrawn himself  
from the whirlpool of storms;  
after seeking a harbor for a long time,  
he stood there wavering like an anchor.  
He had not yet been able to loosen  
the ropes of his cares  
or set his foot firmly on land,  
when a wind stirred up by the sea  
drove the ship, with its arrow-bearing blasts,  
and the wave by its own force  
would have broken the trembling keel  
had not the one who governs all ages  
guided the prow.

## V. BLAITHMAIC’S VIRTUES AND GOVERNANCE

[Col. 1044B]

Soon, embraced by everyone with extraordinary love,  
he strove to become—and to be called—  
the servant of all:  
humble in mind, a guardian of his speech,  
and a model of goodness.

He gladly received God’s words  
with a thirsty heart.  
He possessed an eager desire to learn  
and, through books, learned by an astute mind  
the divine teachings.

Thus, flourishing in the brightness  
of learning and character,  
he governed a venerable company  
of many men.  
He proved his words by his example  
and regarded empty favors as nothing.  
For him Christ alone was praise and glory:  
Christ was his speech, Christ his teaching.

Peace was his shield, prayer his cuirass,  
patience his warfare,  
the word of God his sword,  
hope and love his whole armor.

He disparaged no one  
and heaped abuse upon no one.  
Why is it necessary to speak of each thing  
in separate words,  
when he properly possessed  
whatever virtue one reads of,  
and avoided whatever vice Scripture displays?  
Happily becoming all things to all people,  
he caused everyone to bring their gains to Christ.

A useful and prudent servant  
among Christ’s sheepfolds,  
at the appointed time distributing  
the measure of rich grain to his fellow servants,  
he shone everywhere as a faithful man.

## VI. HE DESIRES THE PALM OF MARTYRDOM

So that nothing of merit  
or of moral excellence might be lacking,  
he sought the palm of martyrdom  
with a gracious mind.  
For this reason he often tried  
to visit foreign lands,  
but rested from his undertaking  
when the people held him back.

Then, in his mind,  
he settled for a while  
to attempt the desired journey  
by a hidden path, with a small company of disciples,  
carrying with him precious jewels  
of virtues beneath their weight.  
Breaking through the darkness  
and fleeing by night,  
he prepared to depart in haste.

[Col. 1045A] Behold, a crowd of pursuers  
overtook the fugitives  
and dragged the captured shepherd back  
to the sheepfolds.

I will not keep silent about this also:  
the Holy Spirit revealed to him  
the secrets of events,  
in the manner of the prophets.  
For while rumor proclaimed  
that his father had flown far and wide  
to the heavenly powers  
because of the blessed man’s flight from this life,  
he, taught by holy inspiration,  
declared that this was not yet the case,  
but would be so after a short time.

## VII. HE WITHDRAWS TO THE ISLAND OF IONA

An island of the Picts is pointed out  
on the coasts, suspended  
in the wave-wandering sea.  
It is called Eo [Note: Also called Jova and Iona, the island on which the monastery of Iona stands.],  
where Saint Columba rests in the flesh.

He sought it in his desire  
to suffer the scars of Christ.

For there a numerous pagan host of Danes  
was accustomed to arrive,  
armed with evil madness.  
But the holy man of the Lord,  
resolving in his mind to test such lions,  
stripped fear from his heart.  
Armed with the shield of faith  
and the helmet of salvation,  
he did not dread the weapons  
of wicked men.

He could have sung with the eloquent prophet:

> “God is my helper; let wicked fear be absent from me.” (Psalm 117)

He had already learned through public wars  
to despise demonic agents—  
the very tyrant whom he had rightly overthrown  
and whom, alone among all,  
he had conquered with every weapon.

## VIII. HE FORETELLS THE ARRIVAL OF THE DANES

It was the time when God’s great mercy  
planned to join his servant  
to shining heavenly companies  
and to confer a certain crown  
upon the good victor [Col. 1045C].  
Then the holy man’s mind, foreknowing events,  
perceived with deep understanding  
that wolves would soon come  
to divide the limbs of the faithful sheep.

“Companions,” he said,  
“ask with discerning minds  
whether you have the courage  
to endure sufferings for Christ’s name.  
I beg all of you who can  
to await them with me,  
arming your minds with manly resolve.

“But those whose inner hearts tremble in weakness,  
let them hurry to flee  
so that they may avoid the dangers prepared,  
arming their limbs with better hopes.

“An assured temptation of death  
stands close before us.  
Let firm faith keep watch,  
suspended over future events.  
Let the cautious protection of flight  
preserve those who are less strong.”

At these words the company was moved,  
and each resolved in his heart  
to do what he saw himself able to do.  
Some rejoiced with tranquil minds  
to look upon sacrilegious hands  
and to place their heads beneath  
the furious sword.

[Col. 1046A] But others, whom confidence of mind  
had not yet persuaded to do this,  
took flight by familiar paths  
through known places.

## IX. HE IS CROWNED WITH MARTYRDOM

The golden dawn, dispersing  
the dripping darkness, shone forth,  
and the bright sun gleamed  
in its beautiful sphere.

At that moment this holy teacher,  
celebrating the sacred rites of the Mass,  
stood before the holy altar—  
an unblemished calf,  
a sacrifice pleasing to God,  
to be offered beneath the threatening sword.

The rest of the company lay prostrate,  
commending to the Thunderer  
through tears and prayers  
the souls that were about to depart  
from the burden of the flesh.

Behold, the furious accursed band  
rushed through the open buildings,  
threatening the blessed men  
with savage dangers.

After the other companions had been slaughtered  
by rabid ferocity,  
they came to the holy Father,  
forcing him to return the precious metals  
in which the sacred bones of Saint Columba lay.  
For they had lifted the chest from its place  
and, knowing already of the wicked plague,  
had placed it in a hollow dug in the earth,  
beneath a dense covering of turf.

The Danes desired this booty.  
But the saint, unarmed, stood firm—  
[the text is lacunose here]—  
with the steadfast determination of his mind,  
skilled in standing against the line  
and challenging the battle,  
unaccustomed to yield.  
He addressed the barbarian in these words:

“I know absolutely nothing  
of the gold you seek,  
where it has been placed in the ground,  
or beneath what coverings and hiding places.

“And if, with Christ’s permission,  
I were allowed to know it,  
my mouth would never report this  
to your ears.

“Barbarian, draw your swords;  
take hold of the hilt,  
and now slaughter me.  
Holy God, I commend  
this humble man to your help.”

Thus the pious victim was torn apart  
with severed limbs [Note: The Danes harassed the island of Britain and its neighboring regions more than once. I think this incursion occurred in the year 793, when they destroyed the church of Lindisfarne. Later martyrologies and the Benedictine calendar assign his day of death to 19 January.].

What the savage soldier could not obtain by treasure,  
he began to search for  
amid the cold fibers of the wounds.

Nor is this surprising.  
For there will always be,  
and will always rise again,  
those whom evil fury arouses  
against all the servants of God.

Thus, what Christ’s judgment accomplished  
for the sake of all,  
may all perform for Christ,  
even if the deed is unequal.

## X. CONCLUSION

He, therefore, made a martyr of Christ  
for Christ’s name,  
and, as rumor relates,  
rests in that same place.

There, many miracles  
are granted to the saints according to their merits;  
there the Lord is worshiped  
with worthy and reverent honor,  
together with the saints,  
through whose merits I believe  
my sins are forgiven,  
to whom, as a suppliant,  
I have offered gifts of praise.

Christ denies nothing to these men,  
who have brought him the greatest gains.  
With the loving Father  
and the holy Spirit  
he reigns forever  
and possesses eternal splendor without end.

[Col. 1047]

# LIFE OF SAINT MAMMES THE MONK

*(In Canisius, Ancient Readings, vol. II.)* (G)

## PREFACE OF STRABUS

[Col. 1047A]

You have read, and your keen judgment remembers,  
how ancient men often entrusted their fame  
to their own poems,  
whose literary gifts either explain  
or celebrate their deeds:

so that you may learn the rest from a few words,  
Mars is invoked while singing of wars,  
and Hercules;  
countrymen prefer the Nymphs  
and Pan.

Apart from these there are various subjects,  
but all are empty.

For us, however, the Lord must be invoked  
with the mouth  
and praised with a devout heart  
and by our deeds—  
the Lord whose work is displayed  
by whoever fittingly celebrates  
the names of the saints.

Anselm, keep watch;  
dear Wulfing, do not be silent  
in asking the Judge in prayer;  
Lantwine, cry out to him persistently,  
for whoever asks him for more  
has deserved more good.

These little verses, which I wish to append,  
proclaim for me through unbroken days  
until I complete what you now request—  
a difficult task even for perfected minds.

Though I myself am covered  
with many foul stains,  
I faithfully hope to receive forgiveness  
through the prayers of the saints,  
whom I honor in song,  
for the great and excessive burdens  
that I carry.

## PRAYER OF THE SAME AUTHOR

O dreadful creator of all things,  
who wondrously created  
the human race  
and powerfully restored it  
while, innocent, you endured  
the punishments of the cross,

hear me, wretched and weighed down by evils,  
in whom you find nothing but ruin.  
You alone can heal my vices;  
I seek you alone as physician—heal me.

Unworthy as I am even to ask you for anything,  
I can deserve nothing through my own merits.  
In the things where my resources for prayer fail,  
may the prayer of your Mammes come to my aid.

I wish to recount his deeds in verse  
to your praise and glory, Creator,  
from whom the saint receives blessedness  
and the sinner receives restoration.

Now I shall begin, blessed Mammes;  
I beg you, and the gift of the Holy Spirit,  
to aid my labor,  
so that I may speak words worthy  
of the triune God—and worthy of you.

## CHAPTER I. The Homeland and Childhood of the Holy Man

The Cappadocians inhabit a city  
which, as he reports, Mosoch fathered,  
coming from the seed of Japheth.  
Toward the west, the countryside of Lesser Asia  
and the side of Armenia touch its borders;  
the plain of the Amazons lies toward the east,  
while the cloud-bearing Taurus,  
on the side of the north,  
opposes its warm ridges to the south.

Perseus once built it, mighty in virtue;  
later, after Roman power had rejoiced  
in its own affairs,  
it gave it the name Caesarea.

Mammes, a stranger and guest  
in body and in the world,  
dwelt there happily as an inhabitant,  
though in mind he was seeking heaven.

So that the faith of their offspring  
might be much more precious,  
his devout parents maintained perfect faith  
and taught their son, through reverent fear,  
to keep the bright commands of God.

He was found not slow to obey.  
With a maturity of character  
he surpassed his tender years in understanding:  
a child in flesh, but an old man in heart.

After his parents’ death,  
as a most careful guardian  
of the blessed life,  
he observed God’s commandments  
and quickly gave an example  
and model of the narrow way.

A city seated on a mountain  
cannot remain hidden;  
nor does a lamp covered by a bushel  
lose its flame.  
Rather, carrying its light upon the roof,  
it turns everyone’s pure love  
toward itself.

## CHAPTER II. How, during the Persecution, at Twelve Years of Age He Sought Solitude with the Flocks, and What He Did There

He had now reached twice six years,  
the flower of childhood,  
when the savage law of the wicked Aurelian  
was slaughtering the sheep of the Church  
and laying waste the sheepfold,  
while, at the tyrant’s command,  
the lictors pursued the devout everywhere  
and afflicted the bodies of those unwilling  
to offer sacrifices and prayers  
to various gods  
with various punishments.

As soon, therefore, as the boy saw  
these things happening in Caesarea,  
and saw choirs seduced  
into serving profane shrines,  
he could not endure such wickedness  
with an inactive mind.  
He despised whatever wealth  
his parents’ care had prepared  
and sought the mountain,  
following with his flesh the mind  
that had always remained above,  
contemplating God.

He considered the rich delights of kings  
equal to the milk of the flock.  
He brought these possessions alone  
to the mountain,  
pastured the sheep himself,  
and sought his food from them.

Persisting often in prayer  
and drawing out long hours of leisure  
in reading books,  
he lived his life without crime.

That he sought the mountain  
was in accordance with the warnings of Jesus.  
The one who sings the signs of destruction  
adds that this should be done:

> “Then let those who inhabit the plains  
> hasten toward the highest peaks  
> and speed their flight.”

Imitating the customs of his ancestors,  
the simple boy pastured sheep,  
a follower of the great Jacob:  
another Abel,  
holy offspring of the patriarchs.

## CHAPTER III. How, Called by the Lord into the Field, He Found a Staff and the Gospel

In the midst of these things he was instructed by a voice  
to seek the Lord’s field.  
As he went, he said:

“Where are you calling me, Christ?  
Where shall I follow you?”

Immediately a shining staff fell  
through the clear sky,  
and a voice fell with it:

“This is sent to you; take it, Mammes.  
Whatever your holy mind advises you to seek,  
it shall be given through this.”

Then, joyfully raising his face to heaven,  
he gave thanks to the Lord.  
As soon as the staff touched the western edge  
of the field,  
a holy Gospel was given  
in wondrous order.

After he had humbly taken it  
and read it open, he said:

“I believe, knowing that by the staff  
a shepherd is appointed,  
and by the book a great teacher.”  
He reverently adored the Lord and said:

“And who will show me  
what these words mean?  
You have already granted me the will to speak;  
grant that alien hearts  
may believe my words.”

He spoke, and heard the voice  
of the speaker:

“Hurry, Mammes.  
When you return to the mountain,  
quickly build a small house.  
Then, at my command,  
I will give you these sacred words,  
through which you shall distribute  
what must be learned by a teacher.”

## CHAPTER IV. How, According to the Command, He Built a House on the Mountain and Was Honored by the Forest Herds

Following the venerable commands  
of his pious Father,  
he climbed the mountain.  
Skillfully cutting down trees on every side,  
he built not so much caves  
as intricately fashioned roofs  
with lofty domes,  
and at the same time constructed  
an altar to the Thunderer.

After the burden of his labor,  
he settled his limbs, flowing  
with holy sweat, into a seated position  
and opened his book.

While he brought forth sacred verses  
from his blessed mouth,  
the forest herds came—  
animals driven there by God’s command—  
and patiently adored him  
with fixed knees.

While he recited, they were silent  
and stood listening with attentive ears.  
After the word, when all the males  
had gone off to seek the forest lairs,  
they left behind the female herds  
whose udders were swollen  
with fresh milk.

Having been tamed without conflict,  
they remained together;  
the honor of the holy man  
had joined them.  
If it is fitting to say so,  
thus instructed,  
Macedonia serves her Paul.

She gives bodily nourishment  
through the one from whom she received  
heavenly things.

Let us marvel at the work of virtue  
and grieve over the wickedness  
and brutish hearts of human beings.  
When the teacher spoke the word,  
the attentive wild beasts were astonished;  
but human beings, endowed with reason,  
deaden their hearing and understanding  
with noisy speech.

The wild beast gives a reward  
to the teacher;  
we offer impious insults.  
Thus the wild beast has no guilt,  
but the hard mind bears the blame.

## CHAPTER V. How He Milked the Wild Creatures Together with the Tame and Distributed Cheese to the Poor, and Was Reported to the Governor

The man of God, recognizing that he had remained there  
so that he might willingly milk the wild creatures  
together with his own flock,  
approached and filled his bosom  
from the snow-white spring.

Gradually, cheese was produced  
from the milk as it curdled.  
The basket grew rich  
with the forms placed within it.

He saw the abundant fruits  
of the gift of milk  
and asked that the Lord show him  
what he wished to come of it.

Then a holy command immediately ordered the man  
to hurry to the gates of Caesarea  
and, once he had found the poor,  
widows, and orphans deprived  
of the light of their parents,  
to place in their open hands  
what the Lord had granted.

He completed this promptly and lovingly,  
just as he had been commanded.

Often, when the citizens saw these wonders  
taking place here and there,  
they were present as envy’s evil goad  
struck them.

“Mighty Alexander, sent as governor  
by the man who stirred up the ninth storm  
throughout the world against the worshipers of Christ,”  
whose dreadful law drove holy Mammes  
onto the mountain: listen, O merciful governor.

“We have seen a certain man  
from the race of magicians  
changing the laws of wild beasts  
by celebrated [perhaps: illicit] incantations.  
Skillfully suppress the complaints  
that have arisen.”

## CHAPTER VI. With What Kindness He Received the Governor’s Agents

Moved by these words,  
the anger of the furious governor  
ordered two horsemen to go  
and bring back the holy man.

As they climbed the mountain heights,  
Mammes met them and said:

“Where are you hurrying?”

“We are looking for Mammes,” they replied.

“If you know him, show us the way  
to where he himself lives  
or where he pastures his sheep.”

“I know no man of that name here,” he said,  
“nor is any dwelling of that name known.”

He did not say this out of fear;  
rather, he fulfilled the words  
of the Lord who commanded the saints  
to avoid open threats,  
and by speech alone  
he accomplished his escape.

For in all other trials  
he endured courageously,  
preferring to lay down his life for Christ  
rather than preserve it.  
His following words show  
that he was not afraid:

“Why is Mammes being sought?  
Explain it to me,  
and I will show him to you.”

“They say,” they replied,  
“that the governor’s ears have been assaulted  
by an accusation:  
he hears that this boy trusts in magical arts,  
tames wild beasts,  
and commands the creatures of the countryside.”

Warned by God’s gift,  
he answered:

“Let us go first and taste some food;  
then it will be time to carry out your orders.”

He led them home  
and prepared a generous meal,  
setting before them bread, water,  
and gifts of snow-white milk.

He had not loved his enemies  
only through his own prayers;  
rather, remembering the holy diligence  
of Paul,  
he would not allow them  
to suffer hunger or thirst.

Here you may see that their minds  
were touched by burning coals,  
while they revered Mammes  
as though he were a kinsman and friend.

Then they returned  
as noble witnesses of holy virtue.

## CHAPTER VII. How He Comforted Them When They Were Frightened by the Gathering of the Country People, and Concerning the Variety of His Name

While they were dining together,  
a country crowd entered in a mass,  
as the holy man was reading  
the teachings of the Gospel word.

The men’s hearts, unfamiliar  
with what they saw, were troubled.  
One, in supplication, embraced the altar;  
another, terrified, clung  
to the sacred knees of Mammes.

Struck by a new terror,  
they already held the hope of salvation  
in their uncertain hearts.  
Seeing them afraid, he said:

“Do not be afraid.  
You see Mammetes—behold,  
the very man you are seeking.  
Know that you have found him.  
Take courage;  
you see nothing here except gentleness.

“Yet I still have some doubt  
about this name.  
For the name is found as *Mammas, Mammae*,  
and *Mammes, Mammetis*,  
while earlier writers left it written  
as *Mammes, Mammis*.

“Whatever the form,  
heavenly writing preserves the matter:  
whatever we express,  
we designate the same holy man.

“If you wish, come of your own accord;  
if not, permit me to return.”

“Go,” he said.  
“Let fear trouble your hearts no longer,  
for wherever the Spirit of God drives me,  
I shall go.”

Immediately they returned,  
both rejoicing and afraid.

How easily the Almighty  
can suddenly change human hearts  
and grant praise to his saints—not merely  
so that these men fear them,  
but so that all created things do.

## CHAPTER VIII. How, Warned by the Spirit of God, He Called the Lion That Was to Follow Him

[Col. 1051B]

The eminent Spirit taught Mammes  
lofty things. He said:

“Rise, and now call from the mountain  
the lion who possesses great strength  
and excels in body.  
Let him call Jews and nations,  
together with their wicked race.”

Joyfully Mammes looked up  
toward heavenly Olympus:

“O gracious God of our fathers,  
holy creator of the world,” he said,  
“now have mercy,  
and do not abandon your servant, Father.  
Look upon what the faith  
of Mammetes’ heart is pondering,  
and guard him as he is about  
to suffer many things for your name.”

He spoke, and from the region  
of the wilderness there came a roar.  
A lion, terrifying in neck and mane,  
gave forth dreadful sounds.

To it Mammes said:

“Wherever Christ calls,  
I shall go without delay.

“You too shall come, by divine command,  
to the contests.  
While the spectacles take place  
in the hollow amphitheater,  
let the impious crowd, as it dies,  
feel you to be its enemy.

“And like a soldier following the standards,  
learn to strike down the enemies  
of your commander with drawn swords.”

## CHAPTER IX. How, Coming to Caesarea, He Became Known to the Governor

After these events  
the venerable boy went to Caesarea.  
Near the gates he found  
the men whom the governor had earlier sent  
to capture him, sitting there with the gates open.

When the saint arrived,  
they were astonished and greeted him  
with humble speech:

“We rejoice to find you safe and present.”

They embraced his feet  
and honored him with friendly words.

Then the men rose  
and hurried to the governor’s lofty court,  
saying:

“O governor, the man you seek as an enemy  
is here. He is not a magician,  
as the foolish opinion of the crowd imagined,  
nor is he guilty of the things  
that idle rumor was spreading.  
He is a blameless servant and soldier  
of the supreme God.”

The judge replied:

“This man is known to have corrupted  
my agents with payment,  
so that they might spread falsehoods  
willingly.”

“We did not tell you falsehoods,” they said,  
“but what we saw.  
We do not wish to exchange truth  
for payment.

“We saw, when he customarily invoked Christ by name,  
the forest animals stand before him  
as though they were tame,  
and surround him as he prayed  
with a sufficiently humble posture.

“We do not know that this man is a magician.  
If you consider us unworthy of belief,  
he is at hand, for he came voluntarily.  
Examine us by your judgments  
and learn that we have spoken the truth.”

When these things were heard,  
many of the devout came to Mammes  
seeking fellowship in the sacred word,  
their hearts refreshed  
by holy joys [Col. 1052A].

## CHAPTER X. How He Answered the Governor, Who Sought a Confession of Magical Arts

Meanwhile the governor ordered Mammes  
to be brought before the tribunal  
and attacked him with bitter words.

“You are called Mammes,” he said,  
“the man whom rumor proclaims a magician?”

“I am called Mammes,” the servant replied,  
“a servant of Christ and an inhabitant  
of the mountain.”

“Tell me,” said the governor,  
“how you restrain wild beasts  
by magical art and tame them.  
You must reveal this;  
you are able to do so.”

“I serve Christ,” the saint replied,  
“who governs all things,  
at whose command the substance  
of the world bends.  
The earth fears him, heaven fears him,  
the sea and every spirit fear him.  
This I know and this I confess;  
the rest I have never known.”

Alexander said:

“If you evade revealing  
your magical frauds by concealing them,  
you will be forced by powerful torments  
to expose what you keep hidden.  
Therefore tell me what I desire.”

“I have not learned  
the foul mysteries of magicians,” he replied.  
“But I invoke Christ,  
whose venerable name makes all things holy.  
I surrender my flesh to you to be mangled;  
you can torture it,  
but this free spirit remains  
in the power of the Lord,  
whom all things tremble before.”

The governor said:

“I see that you despise punishments  
for magical rites.  
Yet do not think that I can be moved  
by the inventions of your wickedness  
or by the tricks of your incantations.”

He spoke, and in reply  
the holy Mammes said:

“God hates both the life  
and the race of magicians.  
A man who burns with love for the Lord  
cannot be a magician.

“Know this, wretched man:  
I do not fear your torments  
or your threats.  
I possess the shield of the Savior,  
who guards the stars,  
who holds both you and me  
under his judgment and authority.  
I worship him;  
taught by his law,  
I adore him alone.”

The governor said:

“You strive to oppose different things  
to the truth.  
Until now the artificer  
has been allowed to play with words.  
Let the secrets of the mountain  
be disclosed to me more quickly.”

“And what,” he said,  
“shall I confess to you, wicked judge?”

## CHAPTER XI. How He Refuted the Governor’s Flattery with Matching Replies

Then the judge’s madness  
began to try another path.

“By the laws of the unconquered Caesar,”  
he said,  
“by Fortune and by the divine power of the gods,  
swear that there is no forbidden art  
in the case of Mammes,  
and you will quickly depart safely.”

“By the name of God the Father,”  
Mammes joyfully replied,  
“I affirm everything,  
and by the power of the Son  
together with the Spirit.

“But I cannot follow the inventions of men  
or by any means condemn my soul, redeemed,  
to savage demons.”

Seeing that the governor’s anger  
was sending back his own strong weapons,  
the judge grew enraged and burned inwardly  
with words such as these:

“Despise the name of God,  
and now deny the laws of your own God.  
Bring offerings to our gods;  
let Aurelian’s decree  
be fulfilled by everyone.”

The man of God, relying  
on his accustomed trust in the Thunderer,  
said:

“I shall follow what I have learned.  
I wish to offer sacrifice  
to the one who governs all things,  
whom alone I have always adored.

“Let him worship demons who does not know  
the Lord of heaven.”

“Foolish boy,” said the governor,  
“you are being led astray too much.  
I grieve for you,  
for now you possess a beautiful youth,  
and your early years display  
their first tender blossoms.  
You will not be able  
to endure completely  
the punishments prepared for you.

“Great strength burns  
in your raw young heart,  
but fiery courage grows weak  
in wars once begun.

“Yield; break your faith.  
An easy escape—perhaps the punishment  
of our anger—lies before you.  
Denying the Lord and God,  
offer sacrifices burned  
to the mighty gods.  
That is what Augustus commands.  
If you do so,  
you will depart free.”

Supported by friendship. Mammes replies to him:

“Now cease, wretched man, to hope that my prayers will be turned back, and remember rather to have grieved at last for your sake, and to lament your years; cease grieving for me, for the Lord is my protector.”

“I wish at once,” said the governor, “that you yourself deny the one whom you say must rightly be worshiped.”

“I do not deny the Lord,” said the saint. “Order every torture to be prepared: I shall gladly endure it for the name of Christ.”

## CHAPTER XII. How, suspended on the rack, he confessed that he had felt no blows.

Vehement anger inflames the wretched breast of Alexander with great fury; therefore he orders the saint to be hung higher and, crazed with rage, beats both his sides with savage torments. While he is torn by hooked claws, Mammes utters none of the sounds customarily made by those in pain.

“Have you not yet felt the blows, you block of stone?” says the governor. “Hard man, error does not allow you to possess human feeling in a youthful body.”

Mammes, joyfully turning his gaze toward the stars, says:

“We give thanks to the God of earth and heaven, because I myself have not yet felt inwardly, secure in the citadel of my mind, more than the cruel punishments that have touched you as you sit there.”
