O holy patience of the saints, surpassing every hardship by wondrous means! Seeking heavenly things in mind, they despise the flesh, whether they see it with the eyes of memory or behold it directly. Thus they lose their life, having found life without end.

Everything they endure is light, fleeting in a moment, and vanishes swiftly; the hope of reward sharpens it, and the ardor of love. Heavenly glory grants them the immense weight of its reward. Why do you marvel that the recruit is always eager for battle? The victor has his rewards: he fights for a kingdom, and after the battles he rests as a king.

## CHAPTER XIII. How, tortured more harshly, he was strengthened by a heavenly address.

[Col. 1053D] When the governor perceived that Mammes remained unshaken through his wounds, steadfast in spirit and unwilling to turn back toward the aid of the laughing world, he said:

“Let the man’s innermost parts now be beaten with hooked hands, so that at last he may cease trusting in empty magic and, at least unwillingly, follow our footsteps.”

Mammes fixed his eyes upon the starry heaven and, with better hope, drove away his fear of punishment.

“I believe what Christ said: those who kill bodies, which are subject to common death, are not to be feared, because they cannot destroy souls that will live without end by any punishments. Therefore, while Mammes suffers such things—”

[Col. 1054A] —a voice sent through heaven ran forth:

“Now there is need of courage, O Mammes; now there is need of a strong heart. Take courage: victory is near, the crown is complete. Use your manly endurance, unconquered soldier.”

Some of the holy brothers received this voice with blessed hearing and rejoiced with full hearts. But the others, who perceived none of the sacred words’ consolation, were equally oppressed by fear and grief.

## CHAPTER XIV. How the governor ordered a furnace to be prepared and committed the saint to prison.

After the judge saw Mammes endure the raging hands of the executioners and scorn them, he changed his purpose and ordered him to be taken down from above and the furnace to be built with every effort, so that the man whom the savage claws had not bent might be consumed by fire.

[Col. 1054B] Madman! Ignorant that a great flame reigns in the breast of the saints, he did not fear to apply perishing fires, although fire is not usually extinguished by fire but rather increased; nor can blessed fires of the saints be overcome by mighty waters. Scripture bears witness, proclaiming with its sacred mouth that the devout ardor of love cannot be extinguished by many waters.

While the soldier prepares such tortures, the governor, pressed by an inward judge, carries out commands that oppose his commands and orders blessed Mammes to be bound in the furthest recess of the prison and in darkness. He himself is more deeply pressed by blind darkness and gloom: lacking the Lord as guide, he seeks the outer darkness where weeping and gnashing remain, without light.

But for the saints the world is a prison, from which the Psalmist prays to be released so that he may joyfully enter the house of paradise.

## CHAPTER XV. How, after entering the prison, he fed those confined there.

The saint, led into the narrow cavern of the prison, found forty men enclosed there under a harsh lot for various crimes. At once, fixing his knees on the threshold before the Lord, Mammes poured forth these words:

“Almighty, boundless God, whom at last our fathers loved because you, in compassion, loved them, hear the prayers I pour forth. Do not abandon me, your creature, who live by your aid; deem me worthy of your help.”

[Note: [Col. 1053] Hankius reads *Mammem* in the manuscript note; but the old reading should be retained. BASN.]

Immediately, when the prisoners heard the name of Mammes, they threw themselves everywhere at his sacred feet.

When Mammes asked them aloud what they wanted, he heard that hunger had already driven its fury through all the bones of the weakened men, that their steps wavered beneath their exhausted strength, and that the use of their tongues had been dulled.

Meanwhile a dove was seen entering through the open window, carrying gifts of honey and also snow-white milk. At the same time a voice cried out:

“This is sent to you; receive it, Mammes. Take this gift, sweeter than all precious things.”

Mammes received the sacred gifts with upturned hands, ate them, and the blessing joined to them satisfied the gathered crowd.

Just as the Lord once gave five loaves, which one boy happened to carry, to five thousand people, so what the bird carried was able to satisfy this crowd in honor of blessed Mammes. These gifts befit the saint threefold: he was free from gall, pleasant with the sweetness of life, and possessed of a threefold power—life, faith, strength, love, hope, the way, and the palm.

## CHAPTER XVI. How the prisoners escaped and how the governor conversed with Mammes about sacrifice.

When the stars gliding across the sky marked the middle of the night, suddenly the bolts’ fastenings were lifted and opened a way for all whom the prison held.

The wretched men now hasten their flight and leave their companion alone beneath the night. Fear therefore reveals that they had endured punishment as guilty men, while he, guilty of no crime, wished only, through strength of spirit and amid battles, to follow his own King and attain the palm of rest.

[Col. 1055B] When the governor heard that the prison’s shadows had been scattered, that the prisoners had escaped, and that Mammes alone remained, he ordered the saint to be brought before him by a summoned guard. When he had been brought, he addressed him thus:

“This one choice alone is granted to you, Mammes: I offer forgiveness for all your evils, if only, in a straightforward declaration, you deny the Lord whom you worship, confess, and invoke as God in word and life.”

The saint said: “The sentence once pronounced shall stand.”

The governor said: “It is necessary for you, fool, to offer sacrifice to the gods.”

Mammes replied: “Let that cease; I worship Christ. Your order is empty.”

The judge said: “Your words will be overcome by the blazing furnace.”

“Come, then,” said joyful Mammes, “prepare whatever tortures you finally wish.”

The judge replied:

“Since by your usual magical arts you despise even fires, sacrifice, bring gifts to the gods, and offer presents to the temples.”

“Tell me,” said Mammes, “which gods do you think should receive sacrifice?”

Although anger forbade the governor to speak, he nevertheless answered:

“Let Alcides and mighty Apollo be worshiped, the holy offspring of Jupiter.”

Then Mammes immediately said:

“Your words agree with your errors. ‘Apollo’ means destruction: he is accustomed to ravage his worshipers with savage fire, not to save souls destined to be held there.”

As soon as he heard these words, the judge, with an angry heart, gave the sorrowful order to Dionysius, Satan, and Zosimus, his attendants, and commanded them to torture the saint with the fires of the furnace, so that the flame might reduce his whole body to ashes.

## CHAPTER XVII. How he gave thanks to God in the furnace because he could not be harmed by the fire.

When the soldier of God, led to the mouth of the furnace, saw the ministers of punishment sweating as they prepared the tortures, he looked with all his eyes toward the heavenly Olympus and poured forth these sacred words from his devout heart:

“O fear of our fathers and of us, while obeying your commands I suffer the anger of the frenzied judge for your sake. Hear the prayers I pour forth. May blessed endurance direct our path; may the fire’s strength likewise grow faint; and may Mammes, unharmed, overcome the tyrant’s tortures, so that those ignorant of the light may plainly receive the evident proofs of your power and know that you alone can conquer all things.”

Then fortified by the holy name of Christ, and having made the sign of the cross over every part of himself, he did not hesitate to enter the midst of the flames’ heat.

As soon as he entered, all the fire’s heat withdrew, and the coals, extinguished, began to grow sparse.

[Col. 1056A] Seeing the wonder, Mammes said these words with devout lips:

“Father of all things, best of fathers, we give you thanks, because you have deigned to visit us with salvation in no other way than once, when you gave the faithful youths of sacred Babylon, who despised the honor of the furnace with loyal hearts, the grace to celebrate you in the midst of the furnace; you saved them by means of dew.

For your Mammes does not feel fire amid the fires.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. How the governor renewed the conflagration and, hearing that he was unharmed, summoned him.

While the third dawn still held the sky and the chariot of the tireless sun climbed the heights, the governor ordered much wood to be added to the flames, renewed with great fury, so that no ash or bone might remain from the burial.

[Col. 1056B] Dry fires crackle beneath their terrifying roof with a great roar; black smoke flies into the air.

Nor was there delay: a beautiful dove, released, came swiftly swimming down from heaven, separated the flames, and bent the entire burden of fire in the chamber as though it were a vault. Before long, the furnace’s violence was extinguished.

But after five days the judge, wishing to know whether any ashes of the body remained after such a great fire, ordered the furnace to be opened. Then a great crowd, mixed with soldiers, rushed there—wonderful to relate! Applying their ears, they heard him speaking within, singing psalms to God and offering praises and thanks.

Perhaps Mammes mingled these words with his sacred songs:

“Great God, you made us pass through fires and rivers, and after all hardships you restore us to rest.”

Astonished, they hurriedly withdrew their steps and carried these words to the judge’s furious anger:

“This man is not a magician, excellent governor, believe us; rather, by God’s power, not by an incantation, he conquers your savage tortures; he prevails as he diligently prays under Christ the Savior.”

But when the governor heard that the fire had not touched the man, he said:

“Now I think we can overcome the magicians’ tricks. Yet you, soldier, shall go and bring the man here. While I live, he shall not depart safe and unharmed; he will be conquered by bitter punishments.”

## CHAPTER XIX. How the governor promised wild beasts after he had brought him out and he denied that he was a magician.

When the soldier had opened the great mouth of the furnace, he saw angelic choirs standing there and surrounding Mammes, who was sitting peacefully in the middle of the furnace and properly invoking the Trinity’s power with humble prayer, intent upon the praises of the Lord and enclosed by a holy throng.

The Christ-worshipers likewise, destined to be witnesses of his power, watched this deed.

“Come out,” the soldier said. “Mammes, the governor calls you; he wishes to see you.”

When he had taken the appointed path, shining thousands of saints immediately sought their heavenly dwelling places. For who would doubt that blessed citizens had come for their fellow citizen, bringing holy consolation? They do not abandon him as he hastens toward the certain rewards of his palm, but secretly urge him to stand firm, so that the saints may lead the victor, as one of their citizens, to the heights.

[Col. 1057A] When the governor saw Mammes standing before the savage tribunal, he struck his holy mind with these words:

“What work of magical art is this, which is seen to accomplish so much in every respect, so that the strength of the flame has been destroyed by trickery? Are the fires, and likewise our tortures, to be despised by you in this way? Tell us by what arts you recently called the wild beasts, alien to their own laws, to their death. The same error is at work here, and the frauds seem the same. Tell us these arts of your own accord, and then you will depart free, so that no fire may harm you, however great.”

“The name of Christ,” said Mammes, “has given me such proofs of great power. No empty superstition instructed me. At God’s command I fed the wild creatures that came, and, following the Thunderer, they used to praise him with me in their own voices.

Know that Mammes accomplished these things.”

[Col. 1057B] “Let there now be an end,” said the governor, “of this great waste of words. I want you finally to bring forth the truth. If you have unquestioning trust in empty things, I too have means of overcoming your efforts with punishments. Deceived man, madman, now reveal by what method you have overcome the wild beasts and by what means you have so greatly conquered the fire.”

“I have learned no magic,” he said, “nor do I bring forth frauds. Rather, I have worshiped the Son of God, from whose name I have a name; for such a king I shall exchange my life.”

The governor, in anger, said:

“I promise you wild beasts, which always delight in human blood. I want to deliver you swiftly to them as sweet food.”

“We are not afraid,” said Mammes. “Send them; we shall endure.”

## CHAPTER XX. How a bear and a leopard brought him not punishment but honor.

When these words had been spoken, the judge, as usual, summoned the attendants whose duty was hunting:

“Go quickly,” he said, “prepare the wild beasts that you know possess bloody and savage spirits, so that they may seem to desire not merely to kill bodies but to make food of their prey.”

While he then sat in the hollow amphitheater, they brought Mammes in. A bear was released, young but pretending threats of savagery. After it came out of the cage and reached the brightness of heaven, it joyfully approached Mammes, driven by its former memory of savagery and its love of prey. Yet, ignorant of what had happened, having already passed beyond the limits of its former path, it was astonished at the blessed man’s face and his appearance.

For the beast excused its rash approach by falling prostrate on the ground and reverently worshiping the man whom human madness condemned to such great things.

Then he ordered a leopard to be released. The beast, rushing toward Mammes to offer obedience, embraced the blessed martyr’s neck and surrounded him with its tender arms. It wiped the sweat from his sacred body and, devoted to his service, cherished the one whom it had been ordered to strike down.

From this we can also weigh the saint’s merit. When the first man, created by the Lord as maker, stood as the image of God, free from sin and guilt, he first received, by God’s gift, the insignia of that power by which all created things in the world were subjected to him alone in obedience.

[Col. 1058A] After he hardened his neck in proud spirit and abandoned God, wishing not to be regarded as the Lord’s servant but rather, unworthy as he was, to seize dominion himself, the power previously granted to him began to flee from him. He, who had recently been exalted in honor, now suffers punishment from all things, having become an apostate.

The saints escaped this plague of the first parent and, having received Christ’s remedy through humble strength of spirit, merited the insignia of the first right.

## CHAPTER XXI. How, when a lion had been captured to kill him, the one whom he had previously summoned came and imitated a human voice.

When the judge saw that Mammes had not been injured by any wound, he said:

“Go, men, with all your efforts. Search the mountains; let the forests be covered with nets; set ambushes throughout all the valleys; scour every hiding place until you station in the city an excellent lion that can sharpen its strength in spirit and its anger in power, and that can first mingle its jaws with Mammes in fury. And lest lack of time hinder my orders, behold, I grant you twice ten days.”

Soon they obeyed his commands, departed, and, having found the creature of remarkable strength, quickly led the lion to the high buildings.

When the governor heard from repeated reports that the beast had been enclosed in cages, he ordered the amphitheater to be decorated.

Then, as the third day rose at the appointed hour, he came forth and ordered the monster to be released against the saint.

While the frightened hand hesitated to undo the bonds—for the lion was savage—the lion descended from the high mountains. This was the lion which, when it had earlier been summoned, the martyr had commanded; approaching the city, it harmed no one beneath the city’s walls.

It came through the open, festive gates toward the spectacle, bringing mourning rather than laughter. Soon, when it looked upon the face of blessed Mammes—wonderful to relate!—it assumed a human voice and first used these words:

“Hail, venerable worshiper of the supreme Thunderer—O man whose nature is filled with the holy Spirit and likewise with the merits of life. At an angelic command we are at last compelled, contrary to nature’s gifts, to utter human sounds; we serve your honor, beloved shepherd. For what nature itself gives in lesser measure, your great faith equally merits.

You are our shepherd; it is right for us to serve you willingly.”

Let us marvel at the work of virtue and grieve over the wicked deeds of human beings. The brute lion praises the master’s good deeds in the speech granted to it and confesses his merits. Out of love for the teacher it fears neither crowds nor weapons; ready to serve, it wishes to endure destruction. We wretched people, by contrast, conceal all the good deeds of our teachers.

We delight in inventing falsehoods, or willingly spread deeds. We certainly wish to know, but regard our own labor as more helpful than a teacher’s aid. Few now fear to wound teachers with insults; many rejoice not in breaking down doors but in constructing ambushes with polluted hearts. Christ’s holy judgment calls such men equal to dogs and swine and commands that they be deprived of *nitela* [reading uncertain; the verse is mutilated].

[Note: [Col. 1057D] The verse is mutilated.]

## CHAPTER XXII. With what severity, after the doors had been closed, he struck down Jews and gentiles.

[Col. 1059A] After the lion had completed its flying words, all the doors of the place were closed fast from heaven with a bolt, so that no easy escape could rescue the wretched people before they all suffered the fiercer enemy.

At once it entered with dreadful fury to strike everything down, staining its ravening jaws with human blood. It tore some with its teeth and cut others with savage claws; running forward, it drove down some and killed them by a bitter fall. Fear of sudden death struck others helpless through various accidents. It attacked gentiles and likewise pressed upon Jews.

When all had been overthrown, only the governor and a few attendants remained exempt from destruction, their deaths being postponed at Mammes’ command, so that the man might not lack the suffering he desired. He himself prepares life for those preparing tortures; he himself seeks the palm through death. The judge remains alive, so that his crimes may not yet reach their end.

Who could know the number of those falling—thousands perhaps—when fragments were scattered everywhere across all the steps? A head, torn far from its neck, floated in red dew mingled with the slaughter. One could see severed hands joined to foreign bodies, trunks carried without either knee, and all the limbs either cut off from their proper place or left wounded where they lay.

So great was the sudden blood that ran from the shores filled with slaughter, as evidence of the terror of the deed, that you would have thought a river was flowing from its banks. It was like when enormous hail falls from the highest mountains and the sky thunders at once with mingled rains:

[Col. 1059C] then the collected streams descend into the lowest valleys, dragging rocks and carrying away forests, wandering across the whole plain of the fields, while the farmer gives a groan from the depths of his heart. No differently were the bodies of the slain carried away, swept along by their own blood.

Such was the end of the evil crowd’s spectacle. Mammes then called the lion and ordered it swiftly to hide in its own den.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How the holy Mammes overcame the lion’s extraordinary cruelty.

Yet the governor’s anger, even after such a wound to the people, did not find rest. Rather, so that Mammes might not escape, he hardened himself still more and, summoning him in his former fury, addressed him:

“Mammes, either you shall offer libations to the gods, or you shall die a bloody death.”

The martyr replied:

“I am amazed that, as a participant in demons, you dare to test God’s servant after such events. For I know my Lord, who, I believe, will never wish to abandon me. But he will condemn you to avenging flames: your impiety makes you criminally deny the Lord, and you worship gods of wood, stone, or metal, which the hands of craftsmen assembled in empty honor. The judgment of death will bind you as guilty.”

When the governor heard these words with an angry heart, he said:

“Know that the lion is held under our authority. If in proud spirit you regard my commands as contemptible, the beast will tear your flesh more savagely. Do not doubt it, for you will be overcome.”

Then Mammes said:

“Whatever you think must be done, you may finally do, provided that you swiftly complete what you have mentioned.”

Immediately the governor went to the stadium and ordered the lion—an animal of remarkable power—to be released. He believed that the beast, which he had earlier ordered them to seek for twenty days and had now considered captured, would inaugurate his victory.

Mammes rebuked the governor as he spewed forth beastly commands and pressed the wretched man with biting words:

“Impious, empty, wretched, accursed, insane, profane man! You follow the commands of your father Satan, which, in your wicked mind, you think must be done. We shall conquer both you and him.”

After these words they sent the lion forth with a great shout.

As soon as the beast arrived and saw the saint looking upward and uttering praises to God with steadfast meditation, it prostrated itself suppliantly at his feet and licked his blessed soles, seeking pardon for its offense.

As Scripture reports, against the commands of the Thunderer no counsel, reason, wisdom, or will can prevail. The governor prepared tortures in vain, since the devout right hand of the Lord protected Mammes.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How, stoned by the people, he remained unharmed.

When the people saw this, they raised long murmurs with growling and threatening faces. Then, with a loud voice, each man urged the others to take punishment from the enemy’s blood and remove the magician from their midst by savage torment.

Immediately, with their spirits inflamed to gather stones, they broke through the obstacles in their way. Hail without rain arose; stones flew and fell upon the saint in a heap.

[Col. 1060C] They departed rejoicing, thinking that they had conquered, but the outcome of events showed that they themselves had rather been defeated. They did Mammes no harm beneath that great storm, but condemned themselves to eternal punishments by their crime.

After a short time, when Mammes perceived that silence had fallen around him, he rose unharmed from the piled-up heap and departed, repeatedly praising and thanking the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXV. How, called by a heavenly voice, he prayed for his enemies and rested in peace.

As he proceeded, a voice came through the clear air and said:

“Ascend, O most holy Mammes. The gate of heaven and the open entrance of paradise receive you into their embrace. Christ rejoices that you are approaching and that you have finally merited the crown he brings you.

[Col. 1060D] Hasten now; the holy Breath guides you everywhere. You will see the angelic citizens, their contest ended.”

Here Mammes praised the Lord and soon prayed these words:

“I beg you, forgive them, and do not, as judge, demand with strict examination that they receive what they did to me. You who command such things, mercifully hear such prayers, and permit my soul to return in peace to its rest after the battles of the world.”

He spoke, and his spirit ascended to the heavenly palace, free to remain forever in eternal honor.

Then sleep closed the eyes of his holy flesh.

The seeds which Mammes bore, sown with tears, he here reaped joyfully in their fruit: he who went weeping now comes bearing full sheaves in gladness for his reward.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How he equaled the other saints not only in life but also in virtues.

[Col. 1061A] Now that we have brought the blessed life and death of Mammes to a close, though in an unworthy style and in a certain order, we may add something to the accumulation of his praise: gifts by which the deeds of the Lord’s faithful servant may also be recounted, and by which the humble poet’s reward may be filled with offerings added from his own sacred praise.

Which of the saints would Mammes not equal in devotion and faith, in conduct and signs, and also in steadfast struggle? His holy life represents for you the saints who came before him, displaying the deeds of them all:

the simplicity of the first shepherd was always in him; the devout life of long-lived Enoch; Noah’s perfection; Lot’s sacred diligence; Abraham’s trusting virtue;

[Col. 1061B] Isaac’s fatherly caution; Jacob’s blessing; Joseph’s counsel; the wisdom of holy Moses; Samuel’s grace; fruitful Job’s patience; the peace of great Jedidiah; David’s mutual love; apostolic ardor and prophetic fervor equally held their proper place in him.

He also gave such manifest miracles as are the world’s two lights. From these it is pleasing to compose a few examples for the praise and fame of so great a patron, drawn from the deeds of the ancients, so that you may clearly recognize how this man shone with the gift of all the godly.

In the beginning the people were called into the desert and, receiving the law from God, prepared a sacred tabernacle with skins and boards. So Mammes, seeking the desert, while he built a dwelling, merited the venerable gift of an evangelical book.

Like Solomon, whatever he might ask for was granted to him from heaven. When Mammes read the sacred words, the astonished wild beasts marveled, offering wonderful obedience to the teacher, just as sweetness was given to Samson from the lion’s mouth.

In his own walls the follower of Elisha nourished his enemies. That wild creatures obey is so familiar among the saints that it is unnecessary to rehearse it. Nor is it surprising that a foolish judgment called the Lord Beelzebub, since the Jewish people did so.

Together with the three youths, who likewise despised the idols of the world, he was enclosed in furnaces blazing with fire.

He endured blows with Paul. He follows both alike in punishments, and likewise, in overcoming them, follows both: here he was pierced by claws; Isaiah was tortured by saws.

[Col. 1061D] Ravens fed Elijah; doves fed Mammes.

As Jonah was found alive after being swallowed by the sea-monster, so wild beasts were able to preserve Mammes without harming him.

Elisha’s disgrace was wiped away by two bears, and the fiercest lion struck down Mammes’ enemies.

Just as the Lord opened the tongue of the dumb ass so that the unjust prophet might not bring destruction upon the people, so the lion, with a human voice, proclaimed the honor of Mammes, so that at least through such a teacher the bloody judge might come to his senses.

Pressed also by a hailstorm of stones, he prays to God for such men together with Paul and Stephen, having in his body the example of Jesus dying.

Administering these and other most illustrious gifts of God, at last he was called by eternal goodness to the kingdom of heaven prepared for all the saints. Blessed without end, he enjoys the highest peace of God.

There, holy Mammes, remember your poet, whom fortunate Augia nourishes under the name of Strabo.

# STRABO’S HYMN FOR THE BIRTHDAY OF SAINT MAMMES

Let us, suppliants, sing the praise  
of the blessed martyr  
to the glory of the Trinity,  
which gives a crown to its witnesses.

He endured the world’s adversities  
and trampled its prosperity.

Mammes returned to the Thunderer  
what he had suffered here for the guilty.

In virtue, life, and conduct,  
most delightful in speech,  
he always remained exceedingly rich  
in the grace of charity.

Despising wealth together  
with the world’s misfortunes,  
he pressed on toward heavenly things.

He departed free from perishable things,  
desiring nothing from below.

Gentle, he subdued the savage  
and disclosed mysteries to them.  
He lived among wild beasts,  
where the angels rejoice as fellow citizens.

Aided by the weapons of the spirit,  
he conquered the rulers’ fury,  
crushing the head of the savage dragon  
with sacred efforts.

Great praise is owed  
to this martyr,  
for whom Christ was life,  
and to be released was the greatest gain.

Faith remained in his breast,  
and blessed, whole hope in his mind.  
Greater than these, charity  
possessed him within and without.

Let every assembly of suppliants  
rejoice with serene joy,  
asking with bowed hearts  
the intercession of this father.

[Col. 1062D] Therefore, martyr Mammes, we ask you:  
favor those who beseech you.  
Protect with sacred prayer  
those whom you instruct through struggle.

Be lavish in your care;  
in your mercy take away evil;  
grant the consolations of goodness,  
preparing the rewards of life.

To the Trinity be glory,  
power, and honor through the ages,  
which may always aid us  
through the intercession of the blessed martyrs.

Amen.

# THE THIRD PART OF ALL THE WORKS OF WALAFRID STRABO, ABBOT OF FULDA—POEMS

(From Canisius, *Antiquae Lectiones*, vol. II.)

[Col. 1063]

## ON THE VISIONS OF WETTIN [Note: [Col. 1063C] See the prose account of the same man’s visions among the works of Hetto, Bishop of Basel, in *Patrologia*, vol. CV, col. 767. EDIT.]

(G)*

## PREFACE TO GRIMALD THE CHAPLAIN

[Col. 1063A] To the lord Father, truly blessed and venerable in the purest sincerity, GRIMALD the chaplain, WALAFRID STRABO sends greetings of eternal blessedness in the Savior of the world.

Ever since, most blessed Father, you deigned, in a certain familiar kindness, to acknowledge my insignificance, I have held in diligent and tenacious memory the one whose presence I thirsted for with the greatest ardor, as I still do. For although long stretches of intervening earth separate us, and the winding passes of vast mountains and forests divide us, nevertheless, burning with spiritual fire in my mind, though absent I constantly gaze upon your countenance as though upon a kind of mirror.

Finally, at the command of the venerable Father Adalgis in the Lord, I was compelled secretly to render in hexameter verses the vision of your kinsman Wettin [Note: [Col. 1063C] Namely, Grimald’s brother. BASN.], which the blessed Father Hetto [Note: [Col. 1064C] Abbot of Reichenau in 801, Bishop of Basel, and Charlemagne’s envoy to the East. BASN.], adorning it with the honeyed flowers of polished eloquence, composed most learnedly in prose.

[Col. 1063B] I therefore present this to no one for approval; I have merely satisfied his will, and obedience was greater than ability. For I knew that whoever obeys spiritual men never goes astray.

And if I have erred in the measures of the feet and in the placement of elisions, I shall undertake no contest against anyone, since I did not work to scatter little branches [Note: [Col. 1064C] Perhaps “little branches,” as somewhat farther below. CAN.], but rather for the preservation of my purpose. Indeed, neither my age is suited to such work, nor do I possess the requisite learning. There is a certain spark within me, and it needs fuel.

In this first poem, however, neither leisurely time was granted for caution, nor did I have control over my own language. I think that, if opportunities for wandering through the fields had been given me, I might perhaps have plucked some little branches by which my rusticity could have been covered for a while.

[Col. 1063C] Thus, for one reason, willingness overcame impossibility. For we have learned that there are some who, judging this to be no more than empty dreams, do not deign either to possess, believe, or hear it. But once they hear of this presumption, they take it up in their swollen hands, and, eagerly examining the faults with which it overflows, they will find, whether they wish it or not, the very thing they hate, while seeking what they desire.

Let them nevertheless know that I burst forth into this work under compulsion and wrote it, as often happens, driven on as though by goads. Yet the love of him who saw these things and desired them to be made known encouraged me in this confidence.

Therefore, most blessed Father, I ask your holiness to deign to correct whatever, in this little document, your judgment decides is suitable for correction or discordant with the truth. It is necessary that the lord Erlebald and Tatto, my teacher, should not be unaware of this matter, since it is not right for a monk to conceal anything from his abbot.

[Col. 1064B] If, therefore, on examining it, they find that it is defiled by excessive falsehoods, they will immediately prick me; they will not stroke me. And, as I fear, since I have now nearly completed my eighteenth year, I shall be beaten with deserved blows. For they are very well trained in this art, as also in others, though they love it less.

Therefore deign to defend my usefulness and protect the weakness of this little sheet. Certain names hidden in the text, if someone investigates carefully, will also be found impressed in these verses.

May almighty God deign to preserve you, in eternal happiness, in good health and mindful of Strabo, most holy Father. Amen.

# THE BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 1065]

## Prayer to Christ

[Col. 1065A]

Christ, who grant me a new Passover to celebrate,  
receive the offerings of my prayers  
and the saving vows of my praise,  
seeking my willingness rather than my gifts.

As much as you grant me the power,  
so much am I prepared to will,  
when your majesty supplies  
both the will and the ability.

I pray you, gracious God, disperse childish games  
and implant the gentle leaven of your teaching in me,  
so that the Father’s judgment may be mild and sweet to me.  
I follow his commands, lest he begin  
to tear my back with a harsh whip  
and swiftly condemn my song in his mind.

Indeed, I first resolved to compose this poem  
from no other source than the holy commands of those who came before,  
bringing first fruits to God,  
for whom the fat of the heart is offered upon the altar,  
consecrated with the fragrance of holy praise.

[Col. 1065B] Jesus Christ, I beg, by the merits of the blessed cross  
and of the risen Lion through the greatest festivals,  
whose venerable feast is present today for all,  
deign to cleanse me from wicked sins,  
so that what I approve with my voice  
may not be condemned in my conduct.

What more shall I say? Have mercy on the world, Redeemer,  
and through the divine power of the threefold majesty come to our aid.

## On the Abbots of Reichenau—Hetto’s Childhood, Governorship, and Death

Where the Rhine, led down from the Ausonian Alps,  
mingles with the waters, spreading vast  
through the western regions, an island hangs  
in the midst of its current.  
It bears the name Reichenau, and Germany lies around it.

This place is accustomed to produce  
remarkable companies of monks.

The first holy bishop, Pirminius,  
built walls here  
and protected the flock for three years.

If anyone wishes to learn the life  
of this saint,  
let him seek the tomb itself;  
he will find sufficient proof at Hornbach.

After him, Eto presided for seven years.  
Then came the praiseworthy priest Geba, who held office for two years;  
Ermenfredus then completed two lustrums as abbot.  
Sydonius ruled there for thirteen years.

John then held office for twenty-two years.  
After him venerable Peter received five years,  
and Waldon’s authority then endured four lustrums.

During their time, like a golden star,  
a young man arose, destined soon  
to be proclaimed throughout the dark world:  
for, five years old, he entered the monastery of the Island.

The city built upon a raised summit  
is not hidden from men,  
nor does a potsherd go beneath a bushel;  
the foreign fame of so great a man, flying abroad,  
strikes royal ears.

Later he was taken away, unwilling,  
from his beloved prison;  
and he who had been free became,  
with his freedom surrendered, a shepherd  
watching over a sheepfold,  
a great part of which, persisting in profane acts,  
had wandered away from Christ’s valley.

For God’s provident wisdom appointed such a Father,  
who, restraining everything under sacred laws,  
renewed what had been destroyed down to the countryside,  
raised up a twofold ruin,  
and transformed it into varied honor for God,  
healing what was within  
and reforming what was without.

[Col. 1066A] No abundance of speech is sufficient for me  
to describe his character,  
since he shone uniquely in the world:

learned, casting sacred seed into uncultivated furrows;  
generous in assistance; upright in life; suited to love;  
just in judgment; clever in skill;  
more perfect in deed.

Why do I delay singing these things,  
when I may rightly confess  
that I know no one who could be compared with him?

Meanwhile he was compelled to be regarded  
as the shepherd of the monks:  
once a disciple, he himself was appointed master.

He was the guardian of the prison  
in which he had often wished  
to await the approaching day,  
then, after conquering death,  
to enjoy the everlasting crown  
through Christ’s gift.

Even if his mouth brought forth words  
in seven languages,  
there would still be no capacity  
to recount everything in which  
he completed immense labor.

He did everything that by right had to be governed in Christ’s sheepfolds, and with constant peace he firmly established salvation for Christ’s worshipers.

Supported by a royal gift,  
he was sent across the vast sea  
to the leaders of the Greeks.  
But when the ship struck the rocks,  
it discharged its entire load and all the men,  
while the bishop from the waves—
He recovered himself and his companions, with the Lord extending his hand [Note: [Col. 1065] That embassy to the Greeks, sent by Emperor Charles, fell in the year 811. MAB.].

After this he suffered no further dangers of the raging sea, but rather, on a straight course and with favorable fates, he brought the Argive replies to the Franks in due order.

Finally, after he had endured long distresses, he began, in his obscure mind, as a fugitive, to consider withdrawal from so great an office, lest, captivated by the love of holding it,

[Col. 1066C] he should abandon the eternal One, to whom his service had always clung.

Therefore, in the tenth year of Emperor Louis, when twice nine years of his tenure of that office had passed, and he had already completed sixty years of life, illness dragged his patron to a deadly end.

That beloved pain was a cherished fever; death was despised, and this was the first opportunity for escape. The time came for him to return to the adopted cavern of the prison, so that, contemplating the face of another commander, he might now carry out what that superior had earlier imposed upon him.

He was released from his burden and rejected the authority subject to him; thereafter he enjoyed a silent and happy rest.

Tell me, I beg, whoever you are who seek honor: what will be your reward, when evil reputation troubles your mind and the harshest punishment follows that reputation?

[Col. 1066D] Behold, you see me, carried along by sweet rumor, having reckoned as nothing the empty and soft splendor of favor, so greatly pitiable to righteous men.

O great day, lest it condemn and dishonor you: despise honors, and come to your senses according to the rule of the holy Father!

In a few verses I have sketched briefly the deeds of Hetto; yet you may learn greater things beneath the envy, if your mind is not burdened.

## Concerning Erbald and his election as abbot

[Col. 1067A]

Sister Muse, tell greater things and, on swift wings, set forth the melody, and reveal the torch of praise and the hidden lineage whose heir is said to have been handed down to Hetto from his origin.

There was a famous tribe, learned in the arts of law, which earned the right to sit in the foremost senate of the people and, by just judgment, to distinguish good laws.

From her stock arose a descendant, called Erbaldus—an audacious man, as his name, rendered in reverse, is said to indicate.

After seventeen years he reached the soil of Insula, joined those brothers, and was entrusted to the kindly instruction of Hetto.

Under his guidance he was instructed to no small degree in the sacred books and in the various seven arts, which the ancients impart to the ears of nobles.

[Col. 1067B] For that Scripture of John reports that the holy creatures had eyes before and behind. The meaning is this: a learned man, by a twofold rational understanding, looks before him toward heavenly things, while behind him he guards against earthly things, lest on this side he become blind with closed eyes.

From there he was sent, accompanied by a companion, to a certain Scot, whose wisdom flourished in many doctrines [Note: [Col. 1067D] Perhaps Clement the Scot, whom the monk of Saint Gall, in his *Life of Charlemagne*, says taught letters [Col. 1068D] in Gaul? MAB.].

The one whom I called his companion seeks an abundant poem, for his life reaches its goal and his strength triumphs in death.

Now I shall follow what I have begun; after a little I shall prepare to address that subject.

Finally, after his return, his conduct shone forth more perfectly: ardor dwelt in his character, and faithful love stood in his speech.

Truth shone in his understanding; he was upright, suitable, honorable—the standard of goodness, equitable in faith, holy in affection—

and he glittered with countless virtues, all of which I cannot pursue under this brevity, lest you refuse to listen.

[Col. 1067C] After these things concerning Hetto had been spread abroad to the ears, he himself approved, through his governance everywhere, that they were true enough, and carried them across the backs of the flowing fields, cutting through the waves and entering Argos, as we said above; then they returned beneath the cavern of Augia.

Therefore, when the authority of Hetto’s arguments fell silent after much had been said, and while it was permitted to transfer the rights of another, it became clear, by the art of prayer, and the request passed in turn from mouth to mouth, that Erbald should be given the fortress in these walls.

God himself assented, granting that all had desired this with one mind, and entrusted to the shepherd the care of those whom the fertile earth, rejoicing in grain, feeds.

Then an ever more perfect willingness to serve the Lord took hold of him, and the best vows revealed the distinguished man.

[Col. 1067D] How much greater his inward desire had previously been to be kind, you will be able to prove from the goodness added to it.

I shall indeed say what I recognize here from the ancient figures, recalling the old prophets: that venerable man succeeded Elijah—Elisha—and, being carried lightly into the air, addressed him:

“Please, let your spirit be doubled in me.”

But he replied: “You ask for great things, son; nevertheless, let that very will be done.”

The greatest deeds of Hetto shone throughout the world; yet, if anything can be added to them, he is surpassed by this man, who, powerful in his customary virtue and equally benevolent, guardian of virtues and fiercest enemy of vices,

[Col. 1068A] remained such from boyhood all the way to old age.

How beautifully, worthily, and with great distinction the heir flourishes—both Fathers blessed in life and rank!

The one was previously the father; now he stands as the son and obeys him, and through his own son he desires to be governed with a father’s heart.

This son, previously subject, is ordered to be his father’s leader; yet he attends to how he should conduct himself according to the judgment of the learned elder, and follows in every respect the abundance of peace.

Swift concord joins the flock of shepherds; no deceit, no anger, provokes anyone.

A peace born within masters is truly a praiseworthy thing. May the Almighty, discoverer of life, peace, and light, grant both of them life through many ages.

## Concerning Wettinus and his age. Vision of armed demons. An angel drives away a demon. Wettinus asks for prayers. The angel’s consolation and instructions

[Col. 1068B]

Come, nourishing Spirit, and join yourself to our Muse, so that I may bring to completion the life of a distinguished man.

Proceed, Camoena, and raise up the man whom I mentioned above; for Wettinus was a master of celebrated reputation,

instructed, according to the custom of earlier men, in the seven arts. Fortune granted him attachment to those schools in which bright and wanton youth commonly delights.

Nevertheless, as far as our judgment can discern outwardly, he led a moderately disciplined life in chaste conduct, and was widely proclaimed in the praises of men.

After the Lord had descended from on high into the lodging of the flesh, in the year eight hundred and twenty-three [Note: [Col. 1068D] The year 823.], in the eleventh year of the pious Emperor Louis, and while October was declining on its twenty-fifth day,

[Col. 1068C] that day arrived which stands seventh in order. As was his custom, he took some drink for the health of his body, which he did not then take alone.

Companions were added, together with the other wholesome practices. He himself suffered immense new pains: vomiting undigested matter, he grew disgusted with nourishing himself by food intended for the body.

The first day had now come from its beginning, and the great anguish had scarcely withdrawn. Then he recovered, though he did not abandon the nausea that had begun, nor did he consider that he was in any danger of bearing death, since that food had restored him to life.

The third light arose, and Hesperus brought the wheel of night. The company gathered, and they sat down to eat.

Then he said to a brother: “The table does not please me; food does me no good. Give me room, for the violence of pain compels me to see my bed. Carry these things beneath another roof.”

The bedding was lifted and carried into another room, adjoining the cell which he had previously entered for supper.

When, therefore, he placed his weary limbs upon his bed, he could not sleep at all with his eyes closed.

Behold, a spirit of deceit came forth through the open doors, in the form of a cleric. The windows of his forehead were hidden, so that not even the signs of small eyes could be seen.

Already carrying torments in his hands and approaching his head, he embraced great joys in his burning heart and said: “Tomorrow you will be tortured, and every merit will be repaid.”

[Col. 1069A] O human mind, bereft of understanding, where do you seek to lead yourself blindly, when the One whose seven stars are held in his palm is set against you by bitter hostility?

While you lack the light, you are surrounded by black darkness. That one—fierce, rapacious, threatening, deceitful, and cunning—lying in wait at the boundaries, stains you to the depths of hell; but if the Lord is your guide, he carries you across to Olympus.

While he made such threats to the defenseless man, a crowd accompanied the pitch-black master in ranks. It poured in and filled the entire place with its dreadful host.

Armed, as if rushing to war, they ran through the hall, preparing the narrow cavern of a punitive prison, leaving no gift of escape from fear.

This place suggests what Jesus said concerning Jerusalem:

“Behold, the days will come when you will be surrounded by a rampart and brought down to the ground; the infant will be killed by the sword, and in this slaughter stone will not be left upon stone.”

The city signifies the soul; the stones, certainly, signify its dealings. The rampart is recognized as the anxiety imposed upon it.

The destroyer will be the demon, and destruction will be the end. This happens to the one who despises the Jesus who has been made known.

After these things, fear choked his utterance [F. *ora*, “mouth”], and terror seized his limbs. There was now no hope of avoiding the black host.

But divine mercy soon arrived. He had seen monks sitting in the cell, radiant in appearance and wearing unfamiliar armor.

One of them, whom fortune had placed in the middle, said:

“The injustice is evident. Flee, enemies, from these seats. This man will still receive the benefits of this life.”

[Col. 1069C] When he had said this, just as a threatening torrent is carried into a valley, the host withdrew from sight in sudden departures. The anxiety ended, and a beautiful angel entered the hall, shining in a red garment.

Standing in his footsteps, he called out in friendly speech:

“I have come to see you, beloved soul, at this moment.”

As he spoke these words, Wettinus, reclining, replied in Latin:

“If the Almighty deigns to forgive our sins, he increases the work of mercy to perfection. Otherwise, we are all confined by his hand; whatever he ordains, we willingly follow.”

“For from the first face of the holy patriarchs appointed in the beginning, then from the holy gathering of the ancient prophets, and finally from the sacred company of the apostolic order, all these have borne the human race with great labor.

“Now the present moment also seeks greater consolations.”

In the middle of their conversation the vision of the two was broken off—not yet the words, but the end of the vision was reached.

He awoke and asked whether anyone was present for him. He saw two men there, who, when everyone had returned to their beds, happened to be entering the house.

One of them was then prior in the monastery, my own master, flourishing in exceptional goodness and surpassing everyone in conduct, wishing to remain hidden but known everywhere.

He found this man and another brother standing in the house, and, calling them near, poured into their hollow ears everything he had learned about the events of that brief time.

He grew pale and afraid. When the pain of the flesh had passed, he rose from his watch, lay prostrate upon the ground, and stretched his limbs in the shape of an extended cross.

[Col. 1070A] “Now, men,” he said, “with all your strength I ask you, worshiping with frequent prayer: ask pardon for us; form earnest prayers. Great is the mercy.”

They saw him groaning in such terror. They persisted in their songs, stretched their hands toward the stars, sang the seven songs of tears, and firmly added many melodies of psalms, as such great anxiety required them to continue.

Then he rose from the ground and sat upon his bed, breathless. He requested that the final words of Saint Gregory be read to him, in the writing known to be his—the *Dialogues*, in which he constructed many instructions for good ministers and discussed the circumstances of death at length.

[Col. 1070B] A substantial reading from this book was read to the brother.

Then he said: “I beg you, Fathers, lay your bodies upon the earth and relieve the heavy labor with peaceful rest. Grant me also whatever portion of the night remains, so that my weakened body may be nourished by empty sleep.”

After they laid their weary limbs upon their own bedding, while he himself wished to restore such dreadful labors of soul and body, an angel sent from the summit of heaven came clothed in whitened garments.

Standing at his head, he displayed the figure he had previously shown in a purple garment, standing beside his feet, and offered the gentle words of his speech beforehand.

He praised the devotion by which he had fled for refuge to the gracious Lord in prayer, and praised the fact that holy reading had pleased him at a time when oppressive anguish had weighed heavily upon him.

[Col. 1070C] “You shall preserve this,” he said, “and henceforth you shall not neglect it. There is also a more perfect psalm, one among many, in which moral virtue resides, constant after the songs, [Note: [Col. 1069D] That is, ‘existing.’] seven and ten and a hundred [i.e. Psalm 117]; you shall often turn to it.

“When it is read, and the psalms are sung openly, it is held as a joyful gift with truthful faith. Such devotion also rises beneficially toward the Lord and appeases Christ, who has been calmed in this contest, because of the punishment of wicked priests.”

After these words, that same angel took the sick man and led him along a pleasant path.

As they went, they saw mountains touching the stars, beautifully mingled with the appearance and color of marble. Around them a fiery river encircled the circuit, granting inexhaustible fires to those who entered.

In it a very great crowd of the guilty was displayed. In other places, following different deeds, he recognized the punishments of many whom he had once known lying there.

There was a large group of priests in the waters, bound to a fixed stake, their backs given over to bonds. Behind each of them stood a woman, for the sin of fornication, the companion and fuel of adulterous punishment in hell. When the third dawn had sent forth its rays, both were said to be struck upon their genitals.

Of these, he said that he recognized some.

“A large part of the priests,” said the angel, “seek earthly profits and cling to the things they covet.

“They seek perishing rewards through courtly services and adorn themselves more with polished clothing than with the rays of life. They prepare to glorify dishes upon splendid tables, while abandoning the gain of souls.

“Led by luxuries, they roll headlong through prostitutes. For this reason they can defend neither others nor themselves.

“If they were to return their profits to God with all their strength, they could console the world impoverished by plague and famine.

“This is the sum of the reward received by those who devote themselves to such things: at the end they shall receive eternal wrath.”

## An address to priests. The torment of monks. Concerning a bishop who refused assistance to a dead man. Charlemagne is tortured for impure lust, yet is nevertheless numbered among the elect. Description of the life of courtiers

O Fathers! If I add a few things, do not despise them, I beg you.

[Col. 1071B] What does the bishop do? The wolf rushes into the fold while no one closes the doors, and he lies buried in drunkenness.

Shepherd, how will you dare to commit adultery against the bride of the Lord? You ought to lead her even into the king’s bedchamber—and do you not fear that you yourself were the first to invade the marriage bed?

I am astonished that avarice possesses a consecrated heart.

For whom are you saving it? Come to your senses, I beg you; no heir is born.

What are you accumulating? You did not acquire it under your own authority, but these are God’s gifts, which you are commanded to distribute.

No one resists goodness if you maintain the will to do what is right.

Why do you seize and sell doves, after the fashion of the people of Jerusalem?

Take great care lest the Lord, having expelled you, torture you with dark scourges and condemn your pomp to grim hell.

Why should you think yourself great, if you remember that you must render account to mighty God for the number of sheep entrusted to you?

[Col. 1071C] You often close sighs within your hidden breast. If you do not grieve over your losses, let shame lead you away from the fire.

And when you see your sheep on your right, while yours are on the left, former leader, and you do not follow them, you will endure burning punishments, suffering penalties for all.

I do not want the prophet to sing this for you, consecrated bishop: “The priest will be like the foolish people in sinning.”

Strive to be the praise of your flock, and you will deserve the heavenly kingdom.

There he also saw a dreadful work of wood and stone, constructed out of material and set there like a fortress, confused in arrangement and filled at the top with vapor.

Terrified by these things, the brother asked who inhabited it. He heard that a crowd of monks was confined there for purification, remaining in various groups according to their fathers and places.

Among them one brother was held under a special distinction, a man who had fallen into the unlawful crime of possessing wealth.

He had heaped up secret treasures by an unjust burden. He had a chest of oak, which a leaden box possessed, to be vomited out at the uncertain end until the day of judgment.

By this fraud the married couple Sapphira and Ananias first armed themselves, common vessels of danger.

Concerning this brother, previously, while someone was suffering from disease, a similar sentence had been seen ten years earlier, when he was being snatched away in an ecstatic vision.

That old matter had already dissolved, until it was recalled by this event.

[Col. 1072A] Even he to whom it was now revealed had not heard of it before.

This place indicates a vice that is often noted and that monks must beware of more and more. It is useful to cut down what adds such a weight.

O monk, you desire to be what you have now denied that you wished to be: rich in possessions, although none of the Fathers gave you this instruction, but rather taught poverty, of which Christ is considered a part.

If you sell Christ, let the hell you see remain for you.

You abandoned the common good and chose theft and private property; you will not receive the crown allotted to the common lot.

Yet you, Almighty, rule as leader your own disciples.

After these things they saw a lofty mountain close to heaven, while the guide said:

“In this fortress is held the abbot [Note: [Col. 1071D] This abbot was Waldo, as is clear from the acrostic letters of the following verses. Waldo was first abbot of Reichenau, then of Saint-Denis near Paris. He died in 814. BASN.], who had left his body ten years ago.” [Note: [Col. 1072B] In Migne, the initial letters of the following lines have been printed sideways to emphasize the words “WVALDO ADALHELMUS.”]

The assaults of winds and the violence of storms,

[Col. 1072B] The force [Note: [Col. 1072D] The verse is corrupt.] of rain and great danger there

washed away whatever he had neglected through careless conduct.

May he be led joyfully into the hall of the eternal King, obtain sacred delights in the seat of the saints forever, and, free of punishment, follow life where it continues.

The angel added:

“A certain bishop ought to have helped that same man with kind prayers and deeds. Many days earlier he had appeared, as he had instructed him, to a messenger, whom in a dream he urged to carry his words to the Father.

“But that bishop [Note: [Col. 1072D] This bishop was Adalhelmus, as is clear from the acrostic beginning with the verse ‘The angel added.’ His see is unknown. MAB.], thinking the usual lies of dreams empty, received the message mockingly, despising the brother’s love.

“Sluggish in mind, not discerning in heart, slow to bring help, he now bitterly succumbs to the force of torments and receives punishments for his own crime.”

To him the brother said: “Where is the one whom you say is confined?”

He replied: “He is held on the other side of the mountain.”

“But the dream which we have now related in a few words, we set forth in the words of the man who himself saw these things.”

He began:

“I saw myself sleeping in a squalid hut. I saw the one whom we mentioned above, the abbot, sitting in the place assigned to him, with his shins and legs flowing with blood.

“He said: ‘Son, carry these words to the Father. Do you see this dwelling? We are commanded to inhabit this shapeless place in pairs, for two companions customarily wash themselves in these baths, swimming in the pool, and they sprinkle this house with the odor of deadly pestilence, so that the wretched inhabitants may be driven from it.

“‘Go to the places of the saints and ask that he send men who, requesting the consolations they freely provide, may restrain the immense burden of stench where there is no wall and relieve the suffering.

“‘My son, I beg you, do not forget these things.’”

After this, when the bishop heard everything from the mouth of the messenger, he said:

“I believe these were phantoms, and therefore I do not lend faith to these fabricated words.”

What he refused to believe, this angel now discloses: because, warned yet remaining incredulous about the dead, he delayed in bringing help through prayer to the one in need, and therefore enjoys punishments without his own gift of merit.

[Col. 1073A] Finally, we have passed through in a few songs what was seen, which the man who now brought these renewed things had not heard before, and, as it were, carried up from the deepest abyss to the heavens.

This place teaches that pious vows are very deserving.

But do not trust that, after the time of life has passed, you will be released through the words of another from the fires which he himself gathers by wicked deeds. Although intercession may cleanse the sins of many, no one can be considered secure in this matter, because he does not know by what weight his own deeds are measured.

Therefore I say that it is useful for me to cleanse first what I have done; each person’s deeds will follow him. [Note: [Col. 1073A] In Migne, the initial letters of the following lines have been printed sideways to emphasize the words “CAROLUS IMPERATOR.”]

He also contemplated a certain man [Note: [Col. 1073] This concerns Charlemagne, who was suffering on account of impure lust. The acrostic of the verses proves this, beginning with the verse “He also contemplated.” BASN.], as his gaze surveyed him—

the one who once held the kingdoms of Ausonia and of the lofty Roman people—standing with fixed step, while an opposing animal tore at his genitals as he stood.

[Col. 1073B] The rest of his body was free from the foul affliction.

He had seen these things and, astonished with great terror, spoke:

“While this man lived his life in the body, he was, according to the lot of men, a nourisher of justice and in keeping with the present age.

“He made the greatest examples of devotion to the Lord flourish and protected the sacred people with pious guardianship.

“And as though he had taken a special summit in the world, he desired what was right and flew through the kingdoms with gracious favor.

“Yet here he is held under such a cruel condition and bears such a dreadful mark of severe disease. Tell me, I beg you, why.”

Then the guide said:

“He remains in these torments because he defiled his good deeds with shameful lust, thinking that temptations could be taken up beneath the weight of his good works, and he wished to end his life in his accustomed filth.

“Nevertheless, he will seize an abundant life and joyfully enter the honor appointed by the Lord.

“This warns the man who wishes to preserve these hours with worthy conduct not to lose everything through some single crime and to pour out all goodness in a ruin that destroys everything.

“Such a man draws water by catching it in a vessel full of holes, and loses what he has long poured in through the devouring opening.

“This is a heavy, evil, and most wretched labor: he always suffers loss and never receives the honor of reward.

“Let him who wishes to retain an everlasting kingdom in heaven govern his life in every matter while still in the fields of this world.”

There he saw splendid gifts prepared with magnificent ceremony in the hands of a demon, cloaks already being brought forward, and vessels of gold and silver metal.

A horse was furnished with gleaming linen trappings, and a great abundance of shining reins adorned it.

[Col. 1073D] Then he asked from what group of men these things had come and what they represented.

The angel answered:

“These are the possessions of courtiers who remain throughout the various kingdoms of the earth, of rulers who govern legal rights unjustly.

“They have been led here so that they may see what they gathered through plunder and what they greedily devoured with a lesser mouth.

“He clearly named some of them and said that these gifts would never end until each person, overtaken by death, received into his own bosom whatever he had sent ahead to the lodging of the eternal hall.

“No one can adequately relate in what dreadful language he defiled the life of the courtiers.”

[Col. 1074A] They are regarded not as avengers of crimes belonging to Satan, but certain among them, binding people with many dangers, habitually condemn the just and justify the guilty, despising the law.

They are joined to thieves and companions in every vice. Captured by gifts, they do nothing for the sake of the future reward; but when they enforce certain obligations under the law, they rage without piety.

The ardor of avarice knows how to grant nothing. It extorts everything and sends everything to Tartarus, accumulating wrath for the hour when fury comes.

They never devote themselves to justice in the pursuit of a blessed life; and the soul that they appear to offer freely, they carry for sale, giving it as a pledge.

He said that certain of them were already succumbing to judgment, just as the Lord once said concerning those who do not believe:

“Judgment has overtaken whoever remains unbelieving.”

Enough has now been said. Blessed is the one who guards this in his heart, so that love of money does not become greater than the dwelling of heaven.

Suddenly poverty will seize those who abound in greatness.

O courtiers, consider whose courtiers you are!

Christ says: “Whoever seeks to climb to heaven must set his step upon the narrow path.”

Likewise, the servant who follows the broad tracks of death descends into eternal fire amid miserable lamentation.

Let everything be cast aside; now the sad will possess what was joyful, and those who wished to rejoice will be beaten into sad shadows.

Enter into what pleases you; it is better then to retain what is joyful.

## Prayers of the saints for the faithful. Visions of deceased saints. Concerning the seat of martyrs and virgins. The angel’s prayer to Wettinus. Wettinus’s response. Concerning the guardian angel. He withdraws from the vicious

[Col. 1074C]

He also saw innumerable phalanxes, divided according to different lots: monks, people of other ranks, and the senate of the people, from various places far away and from distant homelands.

Some rejoiced happily, while others gnashed their teeth in groaning. Paradise holds these; Tartarus tears apart those.

After seeing these and many other things, which it would be lengthy to write and which a running pen leaves aside in compressed brevity, he was led to the walls of a certain exceedingly beautiful seat, which seemed to stand as a natural mass.

This work shone with immense splendor, glittering with arches, gleaming with various golden ornaments, and bearing much silver metal in its structure.

[Col. 1074D] Through its craftsmanship it offered the eyes sculpted images to nourish the mind.

The walls possessed so broad and long a measure, and so beautiful and wondrous a form, and they opened their lofty summits to the flying winds to such an extent that no effort of the mind can contain their appearance—or their use—in thought, nor can anyone express in speech or assign a truthful form to so great a work, or arrange its surpassing beauty in adequate words.

The holy angel then said to the brother who was looking at these things:

“Tomorrow you will depart, leaving the boundaries of earthly life. Meanwhile, we two shall strive in piety to lay prayers before the saints of Christ, so that at least a small concession may be made to your deeds.”

From there they came with equal flight to the seats of the blessed priests. What glorious order receives the burden of merit and possesses enduring honor?

The angel said:

“The Lord of all has enriched these men with excellent merits; therefore no one can describe the crown with which each person shines, whom Christ overshadows.

“And those whom you honor with offices at the altars, let us ask them to intercede for you before the Lord.”

Then, supported at the feet of the venerable men, each of them prayed that the allurements of one man might be relieved by prayers.

Immediately the companies of the saints rose together. Approaching the throne, they prostrated themselves and begged Christ to loosen rather than to return what was deserved.

Then a voice resounded from the sacred shell, saying:

[Col. 1075B] “He ought to have inflamed many brothers by his examples, but, drenched in sluggishness, he ceased to bear the labor.”

At this the responses fell silent, and they ceased to emit a voice.

The angel and the brother stood apart while the saints peacefully revisited their seats.

He said that he recognized Dionysius, Hilary, and the saints Martin and Anianus by their appearances.

How did he recognize those whom he had never seen bodily? It may be hoped that he heard these things either through the speech of the blessed guide, or that the grace which had shown him everything made him recognize some of them silently.

Then, urged on again by his guide, they turned back their steps and resumed the road toward the shining seats, where the rich glory of the blessed martyrs reigns.

You would not be able to believe their appearance or how many there were.

[Col. 1075C] “These,” he said, “were brought into these realms by an unconquered triumph.

“You honor these men on earth with heavenly praise. Let us ask these holy men, entrusted with your prayers, to release your sins.”

Immediately they threw themselves before the sacred feet, and the holy assembly quickly rose from there and prostrated itself before God’s golden hall.

As they asked that sins be dismissed, a voice came back from the seat:

“If anyone, teaching evil, has deceived them with the gall of sin and, enticing them, has made them leave the path and fall headlong, let him call them back again; their debts will be released freely.”

They asked by what means he could release the crimes and how he could remove from others the pitiable poison of evil teaching.

Then a voice came forth to them:

“Let him summon all those whose minds he has perverted through empty doctrines, or whom he has ever harmed in their deeds,

[Col. 1075D] or to whom he has offered an example, whether in speech or action, by which they could corrupt their lives and conduct.

“Let him prostrate himself upon the ground and say that in every respect he is guilty, that he has acted badly and has shamefully taught others.

“Thus let him ask forgiveness, and immediately add to those standing there:

“‘I beg you, children of the Lord, by the powers of the Most High and by the holy men,’ adding also, ‘and by the blessed souls and all the inhabitants of heaven: let none of you hand these crimes on to another by doing or teaching them.’

“It is clear how greatly the person who corrupts another’s actions sins, whether through a bad example or through wicked doctrine.

“The evil man is accustomed to invite many to join him; yet he will bear the whole commerce of crimes, wretched as he is, unable to endure his own burdens and seeking greater ones.”

Meanwhile, two men stood at a distance on the other side. Behold, he recognized Sebastian, flashing with great splendor, and Valentine in unmistakable appearance.

[Note: [Col. 1075D] The verse is mutilated.]

From there, with the guide turned away, they approached the virgin crowds, where supreme splendor, flashing with light, adorned them in shining seats.

“These,” he said, “are the holy women whose names you honor in divine service under the worship of the Thunderer. Grant that they may be sent ahead to the Lord on behalf of a long life for you.”

He spoke, and they strove to prostrate themselves at their feet. Immediately the women rose and quickly went to the lofty threshold of the throne to ask a long life for the brother.

But before they could prostrate themselves in prayer, the majesty before them and Christ’s immense power

[Col. 1076B] raised them, bowed down, shining with wondrous splendor—such as no human form can ever be granted to see or recognize.

Christ, gentle toward the maidens standing there, gave them words while teaching what is right: “If he acts rightly and offers all a worthy example, recalling to the precincts of life those whom he has betrayed to eternal fire by teaching what is contrary, then your honor will obtain my forgiveness of all things.”

O sublime merit of yours, most holy mother Virginity, who, chaste, hold supreme power over heaven and earth; you who, nearest to the Lord Christ, have established an inviolate eternal dwelling above the stars!

She alone, unmarried, will possess so great a title.

Yet even if a corrupted soul, after its crimes, turns back and returns submissively to the Lord,

[Col. 1076C] certain rewards remain for it, even if it will lack that name forever.

After these things had been accomplished, they began to depart with an easy step, and the holy angel followed them along their way with these words:

“Who could relate how many vices the human race rolls about in?

“For although the human race, suffering from numerous plagues, withdraws from the Lord, abandoning its Creator, and is accustomed to burden its neck with Satan’s yoke, the Creator, when offended, punishes no sins with such fury as those that are contrary to nature—sins that everyone should strive to avoid.

“Therefore all must strive exceedingly lest Sodomite lust, the mother of crimes, enter in and the temple of the Lord be changed into the dreadful shrine of the black serpent, in which it rejoices to dwell.

[Col. 1076D] “This filthy disease does not merely spread contagion by shamefully attacking males in turn and staining souls with the burning desire of fornication.

“Rather, it is also accustomed to violate the marriage bed in many ways with filth, when each person, following the madness of lust and driven by the violent impulse of the demon, abandons the pleasures granted by nature to spouses, turning permitted passion toward fornication and proceeding into Satan’s hostile brothel.

“Therefore, in the name of our Creator, I command you to proclaim these things openly, to repeat them in a clear voice, and not to conceal how great a danger attaches to women who have been introduced and are suited to many men.

[Col. 1077A] “For as long as they persist in such foul filth, they do not attain the entrances of heaven or blessed life.

“O all who desire to subject ourselves to such great evils, let the punishment of future torment come to mind.

“Sweet indeed to mind and flesh is insane pleasure; but, alas, a harsher fire will then come with heavy lamentation, when the end arrives that will follow each person.

“I ask you: would you be willing to test whether you could easily carry a finger through this fire? Certainly you refuse to endure it.

“How, then, will you walk with the whole mass of your body through eternal heat, in which worm and fire remain forever and give black exchange to all vices?” [Note: [Col. 1077D] *Incendis* according to Hanck., manuscript note.]

Then Wettinus said:

“Lord, I am afraid to proclaim these things. I am an insignificant person, and I am not suited to this judgment, which we transmit to human ears.”

[Col. 1077B] But the angel, driven to great anger, rebuked him:

“What the supreme judgment of God has commanded, you do not dare to proclaim because you are held back by sluggish torpor.”

Then he sufficiently instructed him to order his own conduct and illuminate his life with blessed rays.

He added:

“I am the one who was ordered to preserve you. I remain the angel and guardian of your affairs.

“Holy Scripture proclaims me throughout the world as Samson’s guardian. I used always to remain in his assistance.

“By God’s favor, the two of us accomplished marvelous things. By God’s command I accompanied him from the beginning, until, through Delilah, he ran into the Lord’s anger and sold the sacred gifts of Christ, his Creator, to a prostitute.

“Polluted by that crime, he abandoned the Lord and God. Then I departed from him, offended by his vices.

[Col. 1077C] “Therefore, while you were a good and chaste boy, you pleased me; but after you began to live according to your own desires, your life displeased me, for you went astray into wickedness.

“Now, grieving with tears and returned with your whole heart, I once again embrace you with peaceful love.

“Sacred writings report that heavenly beings are guardians of human beings, and the Lord Jesus, teaching, shows that they stand before the Father’s face to guard the faithful. The book of the Shepherd also shows the same assistance.”

## Admonitions for monks; commandments concerning the observance of poverty

The angel added that monks in monasteries must be strongly admonished to cut away every root of vice, so that the beautiful shoots of virtues may flourish.

[Col. 1077D] For the greater number cling to worldly things, rather than those who, with God urging them and heavenly admonitions guiding them, bring these things to the camp and adorn their lives faithfully.

The carnal person does not know what belongs to the gracious Spirit.

Therefore it is necessary to strive with all one’s strength lest the carnal multitude oppress the sacred teachings of life, or lest the pledge of eternal love, which holds many hearts in hope, grow cold under the weight of sins.

Let the sacred remedies drive back the wound of avarice. When it rules, no one becomes humble in the name of Christ, and from there can enter heaven.

To whomever this concern enters—
To avoid gluttony in food and drink, we admonish you:

Let the allowance of nourishment be sufficient, though small;

[Col. 1078A] Let the best use be made of water, which nature gave to be drunk.

Let the clothing’s adornment be changed so that it merely drives away the cold

And covers the naked limbs.

Let humble-mindedness flourish through serious pursuits, not be lost in fictitious ones,

And let perverse pride abandon the whole mind:

For some appear gentle with necks bent,

Yet swell with an erect heart and prove false.

The beautiful order of apostolic life is corrupted

When the rights of virtues are oppressed by various vices,

And while, under the appearance of piety, guilt secretly enters,

Constantly increasing, it is retained as one’s own practice,

And now, as though sanctioned by law, is reckoned among righteous acts.

Therefore we instruct the people in the western regions of this order,

Whom we know to inhabit the Gallic countryside,

And all whom this Germany produces,

[Col. 1078B] To follow true poverty with devoted mind,

So that heaven’s gate may not be closed against them,

Nor they, driven away from it, perish in the jaws of fire;

How the omnipotent Creator and Redeemer of humankind

Through me gives this terrible warning to all.

Seeing that these things are sufficient, I can add nothing for those

Who ought to surpass all others in the merits of their life,

Who are said to have crucified the world for themselves, and themselves for the world—

Something which, indeed, we have all promised to God:

For we know the teachings and paths of the Fathers,
