And every day the words of books resound through our ears.

The world attacks: happy is the one who flees it,

And who avoids casting his eyes backward upon the age left behind.

## Against widowed abbesses. Further commands of the angel. The cause of the plague. The blessed death of Count Gerold.

[Col. 1078C]

Explaining how great are the harms that arise among the female throngs

Who accustom themselves to serve God in the manner of monks, the angel said:

“Very many gains of the devil flourish, and great slackness overtakes God’s gain,

While, in a confused order, a dead woman is preferred to the living,

Because, deprived of a husband’s pleasures, she has died sufficiently;

Yet the wealth placed under her control prevents her from living, and they take on the confines of a living death,

While following examples perverted by their own deeds.”

Thus the riches that faithful people amassed

For the preservation of honorable virginity are squandered:

The woman who thirsts for the world’s fleeting pleasures receives them

And carries sober gifts into wicked delight:

The virgin lives, but the sinful woman will undergo death.”

[Col. 1078D] Finally, when widows assume the rights of governance,

They overturn a corrupt life by a supposedly righteous exertion of power;

Few can withdraw themselves from their customary filth,

And some are not proved to abstain even from intercourse.

Thus the deceived band follows its leader through everything.

“O Prince, who seem to have joined together such an evil,

Give the chaste to the chaste; let the widowed woman receive something else;

It is certainly not beneficial to destroy the morals of many.

For indeed a woman is believed to be better than a man.

She receives that rank, although rarely is this the law among men,

That the governance of holy places should sooner be entrusted to a married man.”

Nature demands that the confused arrangement be discerned.”

The brother likewise asks where, in the modern age,

[Col. 1079A] The perfect standard of apostolic teaching might stand.

“In regions beyond the salt sea,” he says, “that rigor is found, and the steadfastness of the ancient Fathers flourishes.”

[Note: [Col. 1079D] “In overseas regions,” Hetto writes. In the island of Britain or in Greece? Yet in Gaul too the observance of regular discipline was flourishing again through Benedict, abbot of Aniane. MAB.]

Those who have attained poverty without various possessions

Seek nothing earthly that might delay their vows,

And thus, penetrating the realms of heaven, take possession of them.

Happy are the lands whose soil produces

The finest ornaments of gleaming gems for heaven,

The aid of their homeland, the glory of merit, the honor of the world.”

After these words the holy angel again introduces a statement

About the ancient crime of Sodom, which destroyed the countryside,

For he had once warned against the other detestable vices.

This disease, harmful to morals and souls,

Prompted by the devil, quick to destroy nature,

He warned them five times, or more, that they must beware of it.

[Col. 1079B] Then the brother asks why so great a number

Of the faithful common people and populace should perish in the destruction of the plague.

[Note: [Col. 1079D] In the year 823 a great pestilence throughout all France consumed an innumerable multitude of people of both sexes, as Einhard testifies. MAB.]

He replied: “From their wicked dealings people receive these things,

And an advancing judgment condemns the guilty,

Signifying that the day destined for the world is drawing near,

So that at last an end may be set to the order of the age.

Behold, the day will come; let each person be prepared.

Behold, the Lord is coming, to gather up our deeds.

Now it is fitting to keep watch, so that when he comes he may crown each person.

Above all he admonished everyone to serve the divine praises

With good effort and diligent zeal;

Commanding that no one, overcome by heavy sluggishness,

Neglect to pay continual praises to the Lord,

And that the glory of the Church be celebrated in holy order.

Whoever anxiously seeks his own salvation,

[Col. 1079C] Let him do these things, and he will be able to withdraw himself from the flames.

The Lord does not need these things, but we need to perform them.”

Moreover, that holy angel declared that once Count Gerold

Had sought blessed rest,

Equal to that of the martyrs, by which the highest glory

Grants the blessed citizens of eternity a draught of sweetness.

“And when he had conceived zeal for the Lord,” he said,

“To defend Christ’s people against faithless nations,

He entered into the hazards of this life in combat;

Therefore he deserved to shine with eternal trophies,

Receiving the great gifts of everlasting life.

This man shone with supreme goodness in this land,

Distinguished in character, truthful, gentle, honorable.

His sister was Queen Hildegard,

The beloved mother of Louis,

Beautiful with equal goodness,

[Col. 1079D] And he was powerful in strength, yet more powerful in holy action.

He had lacked offspring, and likewise lacked an heir.”

Therefore he began to restrain himself with these words:

“God denies an heir; he himself remains as survivor.

What he gave, he will take away. I commend him to blessed Mary.””

Thus his vow follows his deeds; more than all others,

He benefited that place, whose gifts make Augia shine.

Then Charles, the emperor, waged war against the fierce Huns.

[Col. 1080A] Gerold fell in that war, while the people were fighting.

Then his servants, filled with tears,

Took up the body and brought it back here by so long a route through wilderness,

And the soil of the island covered it in the church of Mary.

## Wettinus reports what he had seen and orders it to be written.—Various writers on Wettinus’s visions.

[Note: [Col. 1080D] The verse is mutilated.]

Seeing these and many more things, whose number almost resists enumeration,

Which a hurrying hand, running on, left untouched,

He awoke. Then the messenger of light shook off the now-blind silence of night

By resounding through the buildings.

He summoned the brothers whom he saw had spent the night

Keeping watch with him. Trembling and deeply frightened,

He sang, recounting the vision in order,

And poured the hidden secret into eager ears.

[Col. 1080B] He asked that the abbot, when he came,

Immediately receive these words and order them to be committed to writing.

Those standing there restrain the speaker’s words:

“Now the brothers are occupied with the customary order of the night;

Now they devote themselves to prayer; now the cloister must be silent.

For we dare not disturb either ourselves or him with these things.”

“But meanwhile,” he said, “paint these things upon soft wax,

So that when the shining day comes they may be revealed more quickly.

Lest, with my tongue grown numb, I be unable to bring forth publicly

The vision imposed upon me beneath so great a burden of threats—

A vision that must be sung aloud

And told to all as quickly as possible in a clear voice.

For I fear that, if I leave anything unspoken in silence,

I shall not obtain forgiveness, pressed down by grave guilt.”

The final intercession of the virginal throng

[Col. 1080C] Left me placed in uncertainty; for I do not know what sort of life

We should think they implored from God, the giver of life—

Whether an everlasting one, or the bitter life of this present age.

If the comforts of present life should fail me,

Then, without doubt, tomorrow my body will possess death.

“My leader said these things, and his promise to me is certain.”

With these words he encouraged those brothers,

And, explaining himself, began again to unfold what he had said.

They immediately impressed it upon a tablet of melting wax.

Meanwhile, when the praises of the Lord had been properly completed,

The abbot entered, accompanied by others;

For customary affection urged him to revive the one who lay there.

They drew nearer; the sick man received them into his secret.

The rest withdrew, and five remained seated there:

Hetto was first; Erbald was second;

[Col. 1080D] Of these two we have composed brief verses at the beginning.

The third was the silent master, wise in heart,

[Note: [Col. 1080D] It is unclear whether this is a proper name or a metaphorical designation, perhaps given to him by Walafrid through an allusion. MAB.]

The fourth was an elder, advanced through many years:

Theganmar, servant of the Lord, to whom long old age

Had bestowed venerable gray hairs as an eternal gift—

A great honor of the head, and greater wisdom of mind—

The confessor of the brothers,

[Note: [Col. 1080D] In each monastery one brother was appointed to receive the confessions of the brothers. ID.]

Skilled in applying remedies,

Following the ancient fathers in character, without fault.

[Col. 1081A] The fifth present was Tatto, to whom great grace,

In his kindness, granted the task of leading an excellent life.

Indeed, as a boy he had been transferred to the palace halls,

But, burning with zeal for Christ, he dismissed his fellow servants,

Who rejoiced in the reward of their service,

And, entering this monastery, bound himself by the rule as a monk,

Remembering that he had first received instruction there.

Even today he is upright, fortunate, distinguished, and capable.

“I rejoice that I deserve to obey such a master,

Through whose help my present life sustains me.”

To these five, then, he clearly related what he had seen and heard,

Which he had recorded in words and writing during the night,

With a swift-running hand.

Rising and prostrating himself upon the ground,

He asked that his sins be forgiven,

And sought to appease the thundering Lord with prayers.

[Col. 1081B] Entrusting the secrets of God to them,

So that, if he were snatched away by death,

They might bring them into the light in word and writing;

But if otherwise, he asked them to leave them to be revealed at the proper time.

For he desired to proclaim the whole matter to the open world

With wide-open mouth, and to make it known through the ears of all people.

Finally, if he remained alive and continued in this body,

He wished to carry his strict way of life further,

So that he might drink water and never drink intoxicating cups,

Along with many other things that it would now take too long to explain.

They inspect his face, and it does not appear pale;

No wasting disfigures him, nor do his limbs stiffen with pain.

They touch his veins, which rejoice in living blood,

And see no fatal sign or danger of death.

Confident in spirit, they promise him an extension

Of his present life, and say that death is withdrawing far away.

[Col. 1081C] To them he gave the answers that he had given before:

“For tomorrow’s day will drive the soul from the body.”

Thus the brother spent that day,

And, while explaining the approaching cycle of night

And the following day, withdrew from flesh heavy with fear;

Sighing and sending groans from the depths of his heart,

He strove to entrust himself to the brothers and to all,

And sent brief requests to many close friends,

Asking them to strive to implore forgiveness through holy prayers.

I wrote these things with the hands by which I recorded them.

Finally, when the dawn had first brought forth its rays,

He ordered me to be summoned, and, sitting down,

Commanded me to impress them in wax.

He dictated twice five brief messages,

Attaching them to the same meaning,

Which we undertake to mark here,

So that complete trust may shine forth for all.

[Col. 1081D] There had been ten of them, and their written form was as follows:

“To the most venerable Father in Christ, ill. [abbreviation uncertain], Wettinus, now your devoted servant, eternal salvation in the Lord. I have written to you in danger of death; and because youth still flourished, deign to console my weakness concerning the other world, so that, after laying aside the burden of this corruption, I may not there be bound by the weight of punishments as well. If the prayer should reach one hundred Masses and one hundred Psalters, the reward will be certain. Farewell, you whom I shall no longer deserve to see.”

He ordered this ending to be appended to every brief letter.

But when I wished to alter it and write it differently,

He said that I might express it in these unambiguous words:

[Col. 1082A] “Unknowingly I wrote this, and was utterly shaken by astonishment,

For we spent that whole day alone.

Now we read; now it is pleasant to arrange our limbs upon the bed.

Sleep overcame me; I did not touch that waking state.

He prays during the vigil, rises, and walks vigorously.

Evening comes, and at last he spoke to me thus:

‘Go, boy, and remember to refresh your body with food,

And be willing to give thanks for your labor.’

I departed, while the sun, threatening night, sank toward the sea.

Already the stars were painting the shining center of the heavens.

The brothers arrived, and many stood in the house.

‘Behold,’ he said, ‘the final limit is pressing upon us:

To finish the exile of the flesh, to return earth to earth and bury it.

We ask you in every way: extend your sacred hands,

And, persevering in prayer, defend our end.’”

[Col. 1082B] What an unwelcome matter! Before all the others he began

The psalms and antiphons, like a cantor,

Uttering from his mouth the beginning of each one.

When the chants had been completed,

He breathed for a little while in fear,

And the brothers returned to their beds.

He rose and tried to turn his path here and there;

He was agitated, recognizing that his passage was swiftly approaching.

He fell upon the bed, receiving the mysteries of Christ,

And closed the final hour of his changeable life.

“Behold, venerable Father, I have been compelled to come to the end

Of that whose beginning it was dreadful to approach.

I do not deny that my song is sullied by faults:

Protect the lines I have wrested out, if you are able.

For every bird that is compelled to fly ahead of its wings

Falls from above, seeking the depths.”

[Col. 1082C] I know that this is of no use, yet obedience is necessary.

This is what the Lord was able to do—he who desires sacred incense.

Following your commands, I, your humble servant, have completed this,

Unequal to the work in age and understanding.

Do not consider what I cannot do; see instead that I am willing,

And may you flourish in a good condition through long ages.

Amen.

## On the death of Wettinus. To Grimald, the chaplain.

Writing gives me no pleasure, since our writer has died,

He who displayed new teachings to our hearts.

He wished to build structures made stable for a long age,

But, overtaken by untamed death, he could not

[Col. 1082D] Raise the summit of the temple along its lofty courses.

Perhaps we were unworthy of so wise a teacher;

Yet although we do not doubt that he has reached the heavenly places,

We must nevertheless mourn that he has departed from us.

He was the first to entrust seeds to uncultivated furrows,

[Note: [Col. 1081] In these verses Walafrid indicates that Wettinus taught the letters at Augia. MAB.]

So that the gathered harvest might be carried into Christ’s granaries,

And the splendid sower might possess his own reward.

This was his study, this his vow, this also his very will.

Struck within by sorrow, we beat our hearts in mourning:

We weep that the field has suddenly been deprived of so great a cultivator.

And I, in particular, repeatedly clasp my arms

In the manner of the bereaved, lamenting my gentle patron.

[Col. 1083A] Often what I add to the lamentations of another is this alone:

That no heir of great teaching is brought forth.

Such estates lie vacant, with no one cultivating their vineyards;

The wisdom hidden in the mind perishes through lack of use.

It is said—alas for the wretched man—of one who falls,

Who has no one to raise him, that he lies pitiable before the whole world.

You, now that your brother’s seed has been abandoned,

Bring it forth.

It is not a matter for idleness, since holy law commands it;

Rather, it is fruitful if someone holds it under the law.

He has fallen from me, and no one stands in his place.

He gave beautiful dishes; who will offer me restricted nourishment?

He adorned me with clothing; who will provide coarse coverings?

He had surpassed every measure in innumerable good things;

Who now, wretched that I am, demonstrates the word to me with encouragement?

[Col. 1083B] Who compels me to recall the days in the annals

And mark his death, unless he carefully reflects in his mind

That he was commanded, in the name of Christ, to be nearest to him,

So that offspring might not be taken away from his brother’s order?

Read these words now, best Father, receiving them into your heart.

From now on deign to be gracious to me,

And in hidden matters console our sorrow.

For we carry a spark which, if someone increases it,

Will multiply the aid of pardons at the final end.

When God comes in peace, may he seek his gifts,

Which may bring us the holy protections of many.

Sitting among banqueters and sweet throngs,

I, eager, heard of the banquets of the ancient assembly,

Which, when God was feeding it, deserved to be satisfied with God himself

By five loaves, and then by two fish in due order.

Since these things, accomplished in reality, reveal certain mysteries,

There are also present for us, through the gracious gifts of the Creator,

Loaves, little fish, and an abundance of gentle new wine,

Because he always and everywhere gives consolations to his servants,

Mercifully renewing all things that perish, as their creator.

Meanwhile a pleasant small portion of warm ascon-fish [term uncertain] is brought to me,

and then a vessel of wine,

Desired and warm, sent generously by the prince,

[Col. 1084B] Which the abbot, deserving of praise, transmitted . . .

[Note: [Col. 1083B] Perhaps Grimald. ID.]

Would that I might praise anyone, if only I had so much time!

No sooner had I begun than the instruments of the signal sounded,

Which reminded me to fulfill the customary vow of Christ.

While there is time, my Muse will gladly sound of him,

And multiply the melodies that lack of space leaves aside.

Meanwhile, may he prosper and rise blessed in all things,

Joyful on earth and rejoicing in the heavenly shores.

## On the individual festivals of the year. (G)*

### On the Nativity of Christ

[Col. 1083B]

For today the Creator and Redeemer has been born,

Christ, made human from the Virgin Mary,

So that he might have us as sharers in holy Divinity,

Cleansed of vices and pleasing through our merits.

### On the Lord’s Octave

Jesus, already circumcised, also received the name,

So that the cleansed human being might be the offspring of the Lord.

### On the Epiphany

Receiving worthy gifts, he himself appeared;

Thus, in his gracious coming, he sees our gifts.

### On the Hypapante

He who was without sin was offered upon the altar in the temple;

He calls us sinners to his dwelling.

His mother is present—yet a perpetual virgin—

And remains glorified by her Son.

### On Septuagesima

[Col. 1083D]

Behold, we are preparing to celebrate the coming festivals;

It is beneficial to prepare our hearts in holy conduct.

### On Lent

Following the Lord’s example, we begin bodily fasts outwardly;

Let our minds abstain from vices.

### On Palm Sunday

The welcoming crowd spread its garments before gracious Christ;

So that he may sit upon these, we offer our own bodies.

### On the Passion

He endured the cross, wounds, blows, and harsh spittle,

Showing how much it is fitting for you to endure.

### On the Resurrection

[Col. 1084C] Despoiling Tartarus and rising after conquering death,

He saw you lying fallen, so that he might give you life.

He died so that we might die, our sins having been taken away;

He rises so that he may establish us at the threshold of life.

### On the Ascension

He ascended into heaven, carrying triumph through the ages,

So that he might summon us, as conquerors, to the high stars.

### On Pentecost

The Spirit of the Lord descended to earth in fire,

Giving fiery hearts to apostolic men.

Present, he refreshes them with his protection,

Whose minds he sees burning with chaste love.

### On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist

Today holy John the Baptist was born,

By whose prayers may the Lord’s right hand help us.

### On the Nativity of Saint Boniface, Archbishop

[Col. 1084D]

May the joys of this present day, holy Boniface,

Save us through your merits, with the Lord granting it.

### On the Assumption of Saint Mary

The Virgin, Mother of God, drawn from a chaste body,

Behold, passed into the rest of her own Lord.

May the nourishing offspring of the eternal Virgin

Wish us to pass to her through her prayers, which aid us.

### On the Apostles

These are the ones whom divine election

First chose throughout the world and preferred in rank.

May those who do not always follow the commands of their faith

Receive the kingdom of heaven through their prayers.

[Note: [Col. 1083D] “Now,” Hanck, manuscript note.]

### On Confessors

[Col. 1085A]

Perfect confession, preserving these men for their King,

Made them companions in heavenly rest.

Remaining at peace through their examples and words,

We are instructed to love the way of supreme peace.

### On Martyrs

Those who gained heavenly rewards through their own blood,

Which God, in his recompense, bestowed upon them,

Warn us that, by enduring, we may easily undertake

The precious insults suffered for Christ, which prepare the sacred kingdoms.

### On Virgins

[Col. 1086A]

A strong steadfastness flourished in the weaker sex,

Which joins a virginal office to itself.

By this we are admonished that, even if the world’s assault is absent,

At least our devout mind should wage war against vices.

### On the Nativity of Saint Martin, Bishop

This holy man, a teacher venerable to the world,

Gave examples of life and helps us by his prayers.

Whoever reads these things, remember to ask forgiveness for Strabo,

And call all these saints to your aid.

## Hymn on the Nativity of the Lord. (G)*

[Col. 1085B]

The angels sang glory to Christ who was born;

They proclaimed the report, and the shepherds

Resounded with clear voice

New joys for the world.

“Praise in the highest, holy peace in the fields,”

Is said to be celebrated with great prayers;

At the Lord’s coming the whole fabric of things

Is stirred.

The Virgin is made pregnant by a holy conception.

The mute and barren wombs of married women

Now flourish through the gifts of the womb;

The prophet prophesies from prison.

They gave forth the shining torch of heaven;

The sacred light of the Magi stirred their ardor;

The new reports terrify the savage people of the Jews.

[Col. 1085C]

Late, aged Simeon, seeing the fulfillment of his vows,

Proclaims to all that the salvation of the Father,

Desired so long before,

Is at hand.

Anna, now advanced in age,

Suddenly penetrated by the touch of holy light,

Joyfully fulfilled the long life

That she had patiently endured.

The savage murderer tortures Christ’s flowers—the martyrs—

in their many thousands,

Greedily seeking blood

With the coldness of an evil mind.

Therefore, since we know him to be the light and head

Of our hope,

Let us celebrate him with full joys,

Striving for the love of holy peace.

Brought forth eternally from the sacred mouth of the Father,

The Maker wished to endure, within the chaste womb of the Virgin,

The narrow constraints of nature—

The duties of our humanity.

The venerable Virgin carries him who carries her;

She nurses the Nourisher, and bears the Parent,

Pregnant through the Spirit working within her:

Mother and Work.

[Col. 1086B]

Truth has sprung from the earth, and righteousness has been born;

He removes the losses of the first curse,

And, in place of thorns and thistles,

The earth supplies fruit.

This fruit of the earth, previously indicated

By a prophet of great exaltation,

Was able to satisfy holy flocks

With living bread.

Shining here beneath human appearance,

He wished to bear a humble crib as his dwelling,

By which he announced himself as pasture

for the flock.

Let the choir of heaven rejoice, since the Creator,

In order to renew its number,

Himself descended and at the same time

Struck down the proud enemy.

Let the earth rejoice, irradiated by the course

Of so great a light;

And let the redeemed race, rejoicing in its vows,

Make and offer its due promises with grateful mind.

Christ, ruler of kingdoms, increase

Glory and triumphs for our prince,

And preserve his offspring safely

Together with his chaste wife.

May his happy bride, under such great protectors,

Flourish in merit and position,

Surpassing the world,

And remain faithful in lasting peace.

[Col. 1086D]

Christ, grant us to follow your commands

With a truly sincere heart,

And through blessed deeds to deserve

The shining emblem of eternal life.

May the blessed Divinity of the Father and Son,

And likewise of the Holy Spirit,

Reigning in supreme devotion,

Grant these things to us throughout all ages.

## Hymn on the Martyrs of Agaunum. (G)*

[Col. 1085]

Happy Gaul, rich in mighty trophies,

In the fertility of its soil and the splendor of its men,

Purpled by the great name of its kingdom,

Sister and partner of the city of Rome:

This land, I say, more nobly dedicated to Christ’s signs,

Stained with the blood of martyrs,

[Col. 1087A] More gloriously frequents these robes,

Which no impious enemy disturbs.

It cherishes treasures enclosed by the current of the Rhône,

Beneath the very Alps;

Yet it alone does not possess the sacred glory

That is seen to excel throughout the whole world.

I speak of Mauritius, great in steadfastness,

With whom Candidus and Exsuperius,

Following the loyalty of their comrades in arms,

Helped inflame the courage of the excellent commander.

The blessed Theban legion of that people,

Entrusted with these military obligations,

Following the warfare of the true King,

Blocked the enemy beneath the banner of the cross.

They inflicted no slaughter upon the guilty;

Rather, themselves sacrificed to God by swords,

They reveal in the western camps the faith

Which they received in the lands of the East.

The savage emperor increases his crimes,

He whom it is not worthy even to name in song,

When he orders the saints to sacrifice to idols

And commands the unwilling to undergo death.

The first commander exhorts his companions,

Gathered together, to maintain steadfastness of mind:

“Let no one fail through fear. Let no one,” he says,

“Be disturbed. At last, let us follow God.

With our perishable weapons we have already slain

Enough enemies, with our right hands eager for the contest;

Now the greater enemy must be subdued by courage of spirit,

For a greater crown remains.”

[Col. 1087C]

Therefore the reward of the emblem is not delayed long;

Behold, if you conquer today,

The trophies of your laurel will remain with God.

They stand firm without fear and speak with one voice:

“Command, Caesar, that the soldiers, ready for battle,

Fight for the protection and public interests;

We shall obey.

But if, having abandoned God, you wish us

To serve your gods, profane man,

We despise you, as well as the trials

Of your severity and your worthless threats.

Now break the delays; go, officer;

Report these efforts to the tyrant.

Let him burn us, destroy us, and kill us,

Whether by the water of the river or by cutting stones.”

[Col. 1087D]

They stand unbending and remain fixed;

They do not offer libations to the gods or bend the knee.

For Christ is King and Creator, and for them

To live and die is gain.

When the savage and impious executioner

Reported these things to his cruel master,

The stirred crime immediately burned

In his bloodstained heart, and increasingly throughout it.

“This,” he said, “is a mark that I can scarcely endure

Amid grave complaints: that the order of our office

Should dare to send back such a reply.

I shall now provide an example for those to come through these men.

[Col. 1088A] Soldier, go; kill the insolent men,

And first cut down every tenth one;

At least in this way they will fear my commands.”

When this had been done, the same fury was found.

The guilty man renews and completes the slaughter,

And moves his sword against the whole flock.

The devout crowd competes to anticipate one another;

Each thinks that what is coming has been too long delayed.

They are cut down by swords; the valleys themselves

Are filled with bodies, and streams of sacred blood flow.

The Rhône itself, made sacred by the blood

Of the saints, flows out through the gore.

From this point, now nobler and greater in its course,

It seeks the great sea with greater splendor,

Crowning the whole kingdom of Gaul

With the death of the martyrs.

[Col. 1088B]

O how noble is the stream which, performing

The blessed funeral rites, deserved to wash their wounds,

And to carry them away as sacred,

And to possess their bodies around it.

The places that formerly indicated only a light name

Now delight in the blessed name of Agaunum;

Between narrow approaches it shines,

Which the loving four-square world admires.

After the executioners had completed their crime

And closed it, they gave themselves over to feasting.

Amid the funerals, instead of mourning for grief,

They dared to pursue playful merriment.

An old man, Victor by name, sounder in mind

Than those senseless hearts,

Came to the banquets and said:

“Why do you carry, malignant soldier,

Joys amid the blood of slaughter?”

“They say that the provident emperor has ordered

The whole army to appease him by worshiping the gods,

Because this rebellious crowd, unwilling,

Has paid the penalty in its fury.”

The old man sighed and said:

“Why, wretched man, have I passed through this span of life?

How I wish, if a choice were granted,

To end my burdensome old age among these holy men!”

As he spoke, they seize him and slaughter the old man.

He becomes a martyr and companion of the white-robed assembly,

And is immediately added to the ranks

With those to whom he had previously desired to be joined.

O legion of saints, worthy to be honored

[Col. 1088D] With the highest praises, washed in blood,

How much more perfect than every figure

Is the beauty that this number six arranges.

They are said to have been six thousand,

Six hundred, sixty-six—

A complete number.

Nothing can better adorn the saints.

Let us all rejoice in so great a gift,

Who trust that above the stars of heaven

We have so many illustrious patrons,

Whose prayer obtains what it asks.

If you take care to offer them faithful service,

O Father Conrade, worthy of my honor,

[Col. 1089A] With all your strength,

Peace will follow you through great and continual deeds.

For although I am wretched and sinful,

I nevertheless believe that through this small labor

I may, by the merits of the saints,

Deserve from God the long-sought forgiveness

Of Strabo.

[Col. 1090A]

To the holy glory of the Trinity

Be glory, praise, power,

One might, and everlasting salvation,

Throughout all ages;

May it always crown us through the prayers of the martyrs.

Amen.

## On the Virgin Mary. (G)*

[Col. 1089A]

May the Lord be with you; may your grace always be with me,

As a sign of peace. Extend and give your hand.

To us who cry out to you, praying with tears and voice,

[Col. 1090A] Make your people safe through your help on every side.

Cheer the sorrowful, most merciful one; comfort those who weep,

And wipe away our troubled state through your peace.

## Verses composed at the Palace of Aachen in the sixteenth year of Emperor Louis. (G)*

### On the image of Tetricus

[Col. 1089B]

**Strabo.**

Why should there not be sweet beauty, when the season has arrived

And spring, joyful with flower-bearing South winds, raises itself,

And great Phoebus climbs the burning heavens by his steps?

Now the days have grown longer, and the shade becomes sweet;

Fresh grass, trees, and every kind of living creature

Are given to flowers, new offspring, and the joys of fruit—

Whatever crosses the sea, the woods, the countryside, or the air.

Do you permit me to ask you, while you request that I answer?

For learning is my desire, and speaking is ready for you.

**Scintilla.**

Nor, I believe, are you unaware of the custom by which ancient poets

Sang songs worthy of great gods and earth,

Whether following the solitary ridges

Of a broken mountain,

[Col. 1089C] Or summoning the great, quiver-bearing Echo

From caves, hollows, or remote valleys and glens.

[Note: [Col. 1089D] The verse is corrupt.]

With their temples well crowned by their own rough ivy,

With the grove as witness, and the wild beasts as witnesses,

And the timid birds,

Their minds at peace, far from the drunkenness of raging cares.

But for woods, ivy, Echo, and the tragic buskin,

We endure monstrous tumult on every side,

And scarcely does the pupil of the eye itself withdraw from the mud.

And, shamefully, every extremity bristles with dung.

Here comes the clamor of detractors, there the shouting of beggars;

Naked legs grow filthy with little black rags.

If the Muses ever loved these little black things—

Dung, shouting, muddy streams, and tumult—

I do not delay answering you. But if I speak a little,

Because there is not room, I ask you to criticize gently.

**Strabo.**

[Col. 1089D]

First I would like to know, beside which we so often walk,

Why the image has been represented in this way,

With its particular features.

**Scintilla.**

Tetricus, once ruler on the Italian shores,

Keeps only great wealth for himself, avariciously;

But, unhappy in himself, he walks through pitch-black Avernus.

Nothing remains for him in the world except scarcely a withered reputation.

Although the crowd prepares the waters of the baths for him,

Not without reason: for he is cursed by every mouth,

[Col. 1090B] And the judgment of the world condemns the blasphemer of God himself

To eternal fires and to the great abyss.

If craftsmen perhaps gave him this statue while he was alive,

Believe that in this art they were flattering a mad lion;

Or, what I believe more likely, the wretched man himself ordered

These images to be given, because pride often dictates such things.

For no one is unhappy unless he himself abandons

Knowing what he is, daring to believe himself to be what he is not.

If you see proud men standing in chariots and upon horses,

You will never admire a man merely because he has sat upon a horse.

**Strabo.**

We see aerial doves arriving together,

Coming three times a day—at dawn, midday, and evening.

I shall add such spectacles to realities that are not vain.

**Scintilla.**

Do you not see humble people seeming to love savage tyrants?

Not from the heart, however, but for the sake of the peace of the present time

They seek food; they do not rest by building nests.

**Strabo.**

Why does he seem to carry a bell in his right hand,

Naked for this sole reason, I suppose, so that he may enjoy a dark skin?

**Scintilla.**

Even if he did not sing, he would certainly not lack a skin,

The one he had once put on.

But there will be something that you can say:

Certainly they celebrate the praises of the wicked

With the highest commendations, though they lack every virtue.

More truly, let me say it: the naked man gives reproaches

To the naked man.

**Strabo.**

If there is anything else in these matters, tell us; you know.

**Scintilla.**

[Col. 1090D]

Avarice shines, golden in its ornamented limbs;

It carries darts which, though it is often joyful to strike them,

May grow sluggish, and which kindle hearts with solid plunder.

That the golden ruler is surrounded by a black attendant

Portends nothing other than this:

As luxury stretches some people’s minds wide with avarice,

So poverty devastates and burns others,

Under which the waters flow below.

For, as the poet testifies,

The avaricious person is always in need.

You will notice that the reins are missing,

And that, over stones, lead, and empty metal,

[Col. 1091A] He rides on a horse.

The beast, with its hard breast,

Marks that proud power rules with sluggish heart

And hollow understanding.

O endlessly harmful plague! It has not been enough

To fly throughout the whole world with wars and the slaughter of the powerful;

You may also see it placing its wicked face

Opposite splendid palaces and Christian flocks.

Before its feet, supported everywhere by threefold bonds,

That horse of yours will rise, swimming above empty air,

And will be displayed white among the swans.

How fiercely you wish to stain devout hearts with your weapons!

Yet you have not even lifted one foot

Against the best counsels by your empty efforts.

For whenever you have tried to join some nobleman to yourself,

So often either black barriers of death

Have unexpectedly come against you,

Or the caution of the Fathers—whom the most holy citadel

Has always appointed—has restrained the dark plague

By their admonitions.

May their scepter never fail from their seed,

Until the King, flashing in a fire-breathing cloud, shall come.

**Strabo.**

It is fitting, as I see, then,

After the preceding sad matters,

To offer the princes the vows of due praise.

**Scintilla.**

I know it indeed; yet it has never harmed the fortunate man

To strengthen his spirit through adversity,

Nor does any evil occur without good preceding it.

Thus the ancient prophets said that the golden ages

Were woven by the gods.

In your great age, Caesar, we see this come to pass.

You fill with devotion whatever may be lacking;

Let others be more adorned with treasures; may you be more adorned with merits.

You please through goodness, while others delight in tyranny.

You alone, great King, advance to triumphs of every kind.

For what should I call you except the great Moses among the people,

You who lead peoples, after taking away their darkness, through light;

You who build new temples of character;

You who offer to all the gifts of Christ

That have been granted to you for the common good?

He had the shadow; you have the substance.

He, in a remote wilderness, skillfully built a tabernacle

And bound the bronze serpents;

He drew water from the rock and received manna from the frost.

But you rule temples, great King, among peoples summoned to the pleasant places of paradise,

Temples founded with sacred stones.

Their weight your great father once increased for you,

He whose golden images play upon the highest columns.

[Col. 1091D]

I do not compare Plato’s teaching with his genius.

You flow with milk and honey together,

And you lavish the waters of the following rock,

When Pharaoh has been slain by the waves.

You celebrate the Father enthroned on high with praises through the ages,

For whom spectacles worthy of the place of delight

Will always exist.

From here comes Solomon’s great work; from here temples shine,  
comparable to the highest structures. Beneath, glazed galleries  
display a splendid grove, and flying creatures cross the green meadow.  
The murmuring streams play, and wild beasts and cattle graze—  
aurochs with stags, timid does with roe-deer.  
If you should wish it, lions too will properly leap,  
as will bear, boar, panther, wolf, lynxes, and elephants;  
rhinoceroses and tigers will come, and tamed dragons,  
having been allotted a common pasture with cattle and sheep.  

[Col. 1092A] All the animals are present, their quarrels settled.  
Birds in the air, from the summit of the oak,  
modulate their songs with joyful beaks and murmur sweetly.  
But on the other side, shining with glittering splendor,  
a golden horseman rides about, accompanied by a marching foot-corps.  
Some strike bells, others play organs;  
so sweet a melody began to beguile empty minds  
that a woman, departing from her senses,  
lost her very life in the sweetness of the sounds.

Let the great creations of your Colossus yield;  
Rome will desire it; great Caesar will move to the citadels.  
Whatever the wretched world of the Franks has forged—  
behold, those things in which Greece especially used to boast—  
the great King does not count organs among the greatest things.

[Col. 1092B] Yet if they preserve the songs they have begun untouched,  
the idle man will often be one who strikes the bronze with his plectrum.  
Before that, however, having rejected the skin, he will boast a cloak,  
and, raving after seizing iron, will recklessly  
smash the noisy logs and the unjust hemlocks with his voice.  
Nor is this without reason, since he has earned no gifts  
for his song—at least so that some outer part of his golden  
limbs might be painted black through the rewards bestowed on gold.

Meanwhile the platforms resound with great crowds,  
and a most beautiful throng follows the illustrious Moses.  
I confess that I was astonished by the adornment of gems and gold;  
I saw it, and, turning it over in my mind, considered each detail:  
whether I was seeing pious Solomon or great David.  
I knew that it was not Herod, nor a participant in such honor—  
may the best King of heaven make him one.

[Col. 1092C] At last I understood, after the stiffness had left my bones:  
these were the bones of the holy Father, corrupted,  
but flashing with radiant splendor. The fellowship of the divine Word  
had bestowed this brilliance upon him,  
who among earthly beings is the gentlest.

## From the First Book of Maccabees

When the Maccabean threatened his enemies  
and joined weapons with his terrible hand,  
the swift sun shone upon the golden shields,  
with flashing chaos [Note: [Col. 1091D] “Fleeing,” Hanck., manuscript note.].

The legion secured a number,  
Israel surpassing the battle-line  
which the hostile cohort had earlier formed  
in powerful ranks  
[Col. 1092D] to crush the people of the Lord.

This is an example that the devout must imitate—  
those whom the furious rage of the envious demon  
drives on or holds back,  
and whom savage dangers stir  
to pierce the threats of Mars.

While you wish to overthrow the ranks opposed to your laws,  
which your mind sustains by its nurturing care,  
fly forth, with the Lord’s assistance,  
against the camp of swift destruction,  
carefully recognizing the enemy’s weapons.

Receive rightly the guide of light  
and seek the level places in peace.  
May the broad open field delight you;  
[Col. 1093A] do not remain sluggish in unfamiliar things,  
where you are worn down by vices at night.

The Sun of justice rises for you  
and glows upon your shields.  
These are the reliable teachings of the Fathers,  
by which your life must be protected,  
lest you be overcome by your enemy.

You accomplish this under the leadership of Maccabee,  
who himself is also called Judas,  
while you do not hesitate to disclose your deeds  
to the pious Lord and always perform  
work beneficial to yourself.

Look upon me, great Father of mankind,  
and protect me, though I am frail.  
I pray, Almighty One, favor me,  
lest my arms perhaps be unable  
[Col. 1093B] to break the daily battles by deceit.

## On Saint Gall

Offended by the thorn-bushes, the holy man said, “Here is my resting-place,”  
while the Levite, eager to raise up the fallen man, was at work.  
Soon, with the cross fixed in the ground, they sang a holy hymn  
and sought from Christ, their helper, consolations for themselves.

Behold, bears serve Gallus, having received bread,  
while the Levite pretends to sleep as he lies across the field.  
Female-shaped demonic furies terrified the holy leader  
when he wished to catch fish.

May Christ’s grace be present to King Henry,  
driving away every evil and joining every good.

## On the Emperor Lothar

[Col. 1093C] At the saint’s right side proceeds the best hope of the kingdom,  
the heir of Joshua, whose name is prophetic.  
Nothing will be lacking in his character, virtue, or honor.  
If he remains safe, after the kingdoms of heaven  
have lifted you up and you rejoice at the sight of God’s face,  
then, under Christ the Prince, praise will be sung on earth and in heaven,  
and a good end will complete such beginnings.

## On King Louis

Thereafter we contemplate your joyful, most sweet countenance,  
Jonathan; a corresponding grace of peace is present in you,  
a corresponding integrity of character, and victory always equal to it.  
You will rightly bear back your father’s name through your virtue.  
Although your burden is lighter, you share his glory;  
[Col. 1093D] do not grieve that treasure is lacking: concord supplies it.

## On King Pippin

May the third jewel never lose its honors.  
From his merits—what he did not impress upon my sight—  
I draw, with the joyful sweetness of a flower-bearing reputation.

## On the Empress Judith and Charles, Son of the Emperors

The foulness of the sea meets the vast prow  
of the storm-tossed vessel, which the newly begun voyage  
now urges to cut a path; but the mass of water  
and the rolling obstacle inspire fear.

[Col. 1094A] Indeed, I saw beautiful Rachel, the solace of her ancestors,  
bringing forth Benjamin in due order at her right hand.  
His abundant welfare refreshes holy old age through the ages.  
I believe that he remains as the fifth part above the other,  
which he gladly receives; for he himself will shine in his honor.  
He himself will create tribe and lineage through pious virtue,  
and in him the rejoicing mother, although she had suffered grief,  
brought forth the blessed joys of the whole world.

Grace, which wondrously clothes tender youth,  
now shapes mature thoughts in an honorable heart.  
Happy the offspring who will remain in such a descendant!  
Christ, grant that he whom he follows in name may also follow him  
in deeds, character, intelligence, life, virtue, triumphs,  
peace, faith, devotion, courage, speech, daring,  
doctrine, counsels, success, and faithful offspring.

[Col. 1094B] And if you perceive that the name “Judith” is not without reason,  
she also reflects Judith in virtue and religion:  
the fierce Assyrian robber submitted his harsh head to her,  
and she cut the throat of death with the sword of faith,  
increasing the aid of freedom for her rescued fellow citizens.

Mary struck tambourines with their hoarse-sounding skin;  
Judith ran her fingers over organs with a sweet-sounding plectrum.  
If only eloquent Sappho, or Holda, would visit us,  
you would be able to dance with your feet or foretell the future.  
For whatever the poverty of your sex has taken from you,  
cultivated and disciplined life has restored through your talents.  
In you we see many admirable qualities together:  
rich in seed, you appear rich in doctrine;  
you are powerful in reason, chaste in devotion,  
sweet in love, strong in courage, and witty in speech.

[Col. 1094C] May you be joyful as you lie down, joyful as you sit,  
joyful as you rise again;  
and may the blessed woman rejoice, established in the seat of heaven.

## On Hilduin [Note: [Col. 1093D] He later became abbot of Saint-Denis. He wrote the life of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite both in verse and in prose. He was Hincmar’s tutor and chief of the clergy of the sacred palace, as Hincmar himself says (Letter to Charles, *Annales*, [Col. 1094D] I, letter 60); for it was the duty of the chief chaplains to preside over the palace clergy. BASN.] the Archchaplain

At once great Aaron advances in a great procession,  
girded with the honor of his vestment in wondrous order.  
Pomegranates answer the bells with ringing sound;  
the pomegranates signify faith, the bells resound with teachings of salvation.  
Through both, the pious father shines in varied order  
and swiftly celebrates divine rites in sacred worship.

Sooner would it happen that watery Thetis lacked her waters  
than that so great a Priest should burn the accursed idols.  
The idols that felled the holy people with axes—  
the greedy man possesses idols; you proclaim yourself an apostle of Christ.

Go, honor; go, make use of the world’s better fortunes.  
[Col. 1094D] Live happily for God and attain a happy end.

## On Einhart, the Great Eginhard

Nor should less reverence be paid to the great father:  
Bezalel, the craftsman, first to comprehend every work  
of the artisans, watchful and thus eminent.  
God himself, choosing the weak, thus despises the strong.

For who has ever received greater things from the great  
than those which we marvel shine forth from a very small man?

## On Grimald [Note: [Col. 1094D] He was the emperor’s chaplain and the brother of Wettin, to whom Walafridus dedicated the visions of that abbot. BASN.] the Master

Although you lead your life beneath the archives of kings,  
[Col. 1095A] I do not overlook you. Will you hide in Homer’s caves?  
For I know that the Sicilian grottoes please you,  
where alone you enjoy the feasts and love of the Muses.  
Yet you often forge the best songs for great victors;  
[Note: [Col. 1095D] “You forge,” Hanck., manuscript note.]  
there will be a time when you must be without the radiant Sun.

But if the individual limbs of my body  
were turned by varied use into tongues speaking of things,  
or if sharp hemlocks could grow from bristles,  
I would still be unequal to proclaiming the praises of the great.  
As is fitting, we keep silent about the more wondrous deeds of the nobles,  
rather than diminish so great a weight with humble speech.

I had made it my concern to learn about such offices  
and, with keen inquiry, examined the duties of such great affairs.  
While we had almost quenched our thirst with a sacred draught—  
and so great and ardent was the desire to see [Note: [Col. 1095D] Variant: *rura*, “fields.”]—  
[Col. 1095B] it was asked where I came from and on whose commission I had arrived.  
I was astonished and, trembling, set out the whole matter to the king in order.

It is enough to have seen once; enduring love presses me  
to praise you forever. May divine mercy cause your hand  
to retain trophies among all peoples,  
and your happy, toga-clad reputation among the fathers,  
and cause those admitted into the great senate through the ages  
to fear your bows in joyful glades—  
the bear, boar, timid hare, and fleeing stags,  
the doe, wolf, and enormous herd of wild cattle.

Thus may the Bulgar, the evil guest of the Sarrae and Cynes,  
the Iberian, Brutus the Briton, the crafty Dane, and the grim African  
submit their terrified necks to your honored right hands.

Now at last the commonwealth has flourished,  
since kings have become wise and the wise themselves rule.

Farewell, foolish Tetrice, since at your urging I was singing.  
It is no wonder that our song is sullied by vices.  
You do not know how to show me either material or words;  
if reason brings anything to you, then you will strive with the Muse.  
Here I have decided to set down my pen: evening is now rising.

Strabus, the smallest portion of the brothers, published this.  
The island of Augia nourishes them through your prayers.  
Although grammatical rule insists that I should be called Strabo,  
I myself wish to call myself Strabus; I shall be Strabus.

What the maker corrupted in the work—if it is permissible to say so—  
I shall publish under this corrupted name as well. Spare me, God.

## To the Empress Judith

I confess that everything has been done by the will and command  
of Him alone who guards the secrets of all things  
and offers rewards to devoted minds of faith:  
I, who long ago resolved in humble heart to be wholly faithful to you,  
was at last, by I know not what chance, drawn into your service  
and that of your blessed offspring,  
whom the gracious piety of God has allowed to rise  
for your welfare and that of this kingdom alike.

May God’s power, ever compassionate toward you and yours,  
protect, exalt, strengthen, govern, arm, and adorn you.

The humble Strabus sends these little gifts to the Empress—  
pledges of many entrusted to the Lord, their mediator.  
Lover of peace and friend of light, you who guard all good things  
in your mind, receive these writings of mine with mercy.

## To the Same, Concerning a Dream

[Col. 1096A]

While, under the unhappy power of time and grief,  
the devices of deceit were oppressing the pious people and their father  
and were preparing to erase holy faith  
through decrees, exile, hatred, force, imprisonment, and the sword,  
then the good lay prostrate beneath a cloud of dark sorrow.  
Treacherous audacity alone displayed its foolish boldness  
amid the terror of a tottering kingdom.

While I was anxious and grieving for the cause of justice,  
great cares flowed repeatedly into my heart,  
and prophetic rest did not come to me in dreams, until God,  
by unmistakable power, dispelling the black clouds  
of ancient fear, taught me to hope for a shining calm,  
while night enclosed the pale thing that we call earth  
and the long emptiness that we call the void.

[Col. 1096B] While sleep released creatures weary in their inner marrow  
and moderated the long anxieties and cares of the day  
with divine gift and equal governance,  
there appeared before my eyes a most beautiful sequence of a long book,  
which, in metrical verses, properly set forth its entire subject-matter  
full and arranged in order.

As I, an eager yet cautious reader, went through each matter,  
I noticed that the series itself, concerning the fortunes  
of both kingdom and king, resounded in prose.  
Here the name of Caesar appeared in a certain image,  
and there, in place of the sacred name, “Equitatius”  
was always written for Louis. The novelty of this surname  
did not disturb me, since the very subject expressed the person,  
whose deeds were known through familiar signs.

For it was read there: the separation of a double deceit,  
[Col. 1096C] impiety, and a double seizure; victorious patience;  
the ruler’s glory, and the ever-restorable honor of affairs.

While my eyes, senses, ears, and the innermost chambers  
of my heart burned to reread or read it,  
a brother snatched the book from my sight, after it had displayed its marvels,  
and added these words from memory:

[Note: [Col. 1096D] The sense appears incomplete. CASS.]

“A sadder [reading uncertain: *humeros*; Hanck reads *humor*, ‘moisture’] issue from the eyes than befitted all hearts,  
not far from suffering the losses of ruin.”

Awakening, and wishing at the same time to retain what I had absorbed,  
I could scarcely remember two verses at the end  
and the added name, while forgetting the rest.  
From the omen of the name I immediately increased my hope a little:  
that Equitatius foretold swift resources of virtue,  
and the following assertion confirms the same—  
that one who bears harsh burdens ought not to grieve excessively  
and will quickly make his return to joyful things.

Since I see these things fulfilled in deeds,  
what more should I conceal? I decided to set before you  
the things that nourished the joys of our long hope.

Empress, the poor Strabo gives ten times five gifts,  
asking pardon; the same tally marks the reckoning.

## To the Emperor Louis

These little gifts are paltry in comparison with your merits,  
but they are given from a full heart of love and faith.  
I shall strive to preserve this faith toward you for a long time,  
indeed through all the ages, until death.

What could ever stand more clearly before me  
[Col. 1097A] than the continuing glory of the pious Lord?

The holy coming of Christ, by powerful virtue,  
increased this into affection and new joy.  
That little one, called forth from the flesh,  
bears six great and splendid names.  
He himself is mighty God, wondrous, and Father of the age;  
he is powerful in peace and counsel.

May he grant the pious king strength and divine gifts  
and a bright support for eternal time.  
May he cause him to retain peace through wholesome counsel—  
him whom he prepares for eternal peace and its gifts.

May God bring you and yours, unharmed,  
again and again through the years to these feasts.

## To Judith Augusta

Many things indeed come to us that our merits do not deserve  
but that can cheer us through their own goodness.  
A few adverse things, however, stir up a harsher wind; some of them are apparent to you  
even though I remain silent.

Nor is this the least of them: no command of yours  
binds me to any cause in which I am permitted to be present.  
I do not see your face, nor drink in your words;  
I hesitate between hope and fear: shall I displease or please?

Yet hearts conscious of faith, and faithful to their vows,  
teach me not to despair of better things.  
Let the faith already established suffice. I shall pray  
for what I have prayed for until now, and for what I think should be sought:  
that you and yours may enjoy, for all time,  
life, protection, peace, and Christ’s consolation.

We believe and wish that we shall carry this out more fully  
at the approaching feasts of the saints.

## On the Bone of a Doe from Which a Little Tree Grew, to the Emperor Louis

[Col. 1097C]

A sheath that once nourished a tree has a shinbone holding a shoot in its marrow: surely this is a good omen.  
We marvel that it lacks the bark’s moisture, that it is harder than wood,  
and that such strength exists in a bone.

Great Caesar, no leisure is left to you: hunt does  
from whose bones a forest will arise. Hail!

## To the Young Charles

Born nobly and reared with princely cultivation,  
learn what you should render to the Lord who created you.  
May the virtue of justice grow from your earliest years,  
and may this work grow old with you in a sound mind.

Fear, in any respect, to fall short of your father’s devotion rather than of your royal lineage.  
If we recall grandfathers, great-grandfathers, and the great names  
of former generations, this lineage will benefit you only  
if sacred nobility shines through the beautiful spectacle of character,  
with the clouds of ignorance driven away.

Let the obedient crowd of your servants therefore rejoice,  
refreshed by the promise of so great a disposition.  
For nothing yet draws you away from fortunate years;  
everything you do gives hope to men’s hearts.

Your form shines with beauty, your mind is more capacious than your age,  
and—most important of all—your zeal and love for God.

[Col. 1098A] Begin what a more mature age will one day complete;  
the vessels imbibe things at first and retain them long.

May the majesty of God always grant you every prosperity  
and bring you the sweet gifts of eternal life.

## To the Elder Hilduin

If I could season my verses with the sweetness of honey,  
holy father, or adorn them with roses,  
even then such display would not be worthy of the refinements  
that you bear in character and understanding together with integrity.

Your clemency has received me with such honor  
as I could wish I had deserved.  
I have rendered no service and deserved nothing, yet behold:  
suddenly, though unworthy, I have been admitted as a poor man  
and enjoy honor.

May I continue to do so, and rejoice forever in your peace,  
in life, merit, and holy salvation.

[Col. 1098B] I am unable in any respect to repay what has been done for me,  
but the Lord will be its recompense.  
For his sake you have not despised either us or what is ours,  
but have endured it with pious affection.

Therefore I am, and shall remain, wholly faithful in heart  
to you and yours for all time.  
I beseech, ask, and pray that the Lord’s protection  
may cover you, govern you, strengthen you, exalt you, and love you.

## To Bishop Heribald [Note: [Col. 1097] He was bishop of Auxerre; Rabanus wrote to him, and he is listed with him among the Stercoranists. BASN.] in the Person of Charles

Do not think, Heribald, that we wish to repay  
your great merits with insignificant thanks  
or small rewards. You send these little letters,  
trembling yet not sluggish, written with full affection  
for the honor we hold.

The Prophet’s words, which testify, have indeed been fulfilled;  
we know them repeated with a new effect.  
And praise full of fear has come to the Lord:  
the North brings gold, often stiff with cold.

For the little flame carried in your writings  
shows that earlier flames burn in your breast.  
And because you know how, in our just moderation,  
we spare subjects and endure the wicked,  
for these gifts rewards will be returned to you,  
greater than the profits that treachery’s love would have brought you.

If the sweetness with which you begin  
extends to the outermost part of you just as sweetly,  
my sweetness toward you remains ever sweeter.

Learn to make your steps firm, lest the hanging path  
again depart onto a rocky road.  
Learn already to grow old happily in the ancient nest,  
until white plumage covers your wretched head.

[Col. 1098D] Then, enduring fevers, a severe cough, and shameful gout,  
you will die beside your own hearths.  
To wish these things for you is the sign of a friend who loves in return,  
whether of a gentle lord or a patient master.

Be happy, and know that you have pleasingly mingled  
serious matters with jokes in our hearts.  
By carrying this often, weigh faithful hearts  
and learn the nature of my mutual goodwill.

Whenever you are in need, at every time, farewell through the ages;  
but never wish to be forgetful of us.

## To Luitger the Cleric

[Col. 1099A]

To Luitger, whom he honors with sweet services  
and a friendly mind, Strabus gives a few words.

Although the affection on our side may have been small,  
I nevertheless believe that you remember me well enough.  
Whatever you have on your right side, I gladly desire;  
if anything is present on the left, I grieve for it in the little enclosure of my heart.

As an only child to a mother, as sunlight to the earth,  
as dew to the grasses, as water of the sea to fish,  
as air to birds, and the murmuring of streams to meadows,  
so, little boy, your dear face is to me.

If it could happen—what we think can happen—  
I beg you to bring yourself swiftly before my eyes.  
For since I have learned that you are standing closer to us,  
I do not rest until I see you quickly.

May your glory, life, welfare, and health exceed  
the number of stars, drops of dew, and grains of sand.

## Also to Him

Dear one, you come suddenly, and suddenly, dear one, you depart.  
I hear but do not see you; yet inwardly I see you, and inwardly  
I embrace you as you flee, in body though not in affection.

For I was certain, and shall always be, that I am cherished  
in your heart and you in mine. Let no time  
persuade you otherwise, nor persuade me otherwise.

If you can come to see me, it will be enough—  
if I see you, it will be welcome. If not, write something back.  
I know your sorrows and recall them with grief.  
Grief is the possession of the world;  
and the things you think serene flee more sadly  
into clouds and darkness, in the swift world that hangs in space.

Now it rises, now it descends; thus the wheel of the world draws it along.  
[Note: [Col. 1099D] I would prefer *orbem*. Hanck., manuscript note.]

## To Louis the Cleric

To you, Louis, who gave me the gift of your affection,  
Strabo gives these words of greeting: hail.

Your promise, though it made me insignificant,  
has emboldened me to admonish you in my verses.  
For although you hold the great honors of the world,  
I do not believe that you despise us, the very least.

I say nothing of human riches. When hope and faith have withered,  
love alone will then remain.  
I bring you no garment, nor any gift of metal;  
I seek only to serve you in love.

For with all my understanding, speech, and deeds  
I shall strive to repay you with the work of love you promised.  
Remember one who remembers you; and, with the Lord’s favor, farewell,  
receiving as many good things as it is enough to have deserved.

## To Bodo the Subdeacon

Strabo gives you these few little words to read,  
dearest little Bodo, whom he loves.

The shoot that we long ago fixed in the fields  
with equal ardor—may it rise toward the heavenly south winds.  
May pure affection rise through continual movements,  
until it can reach the firm heavens and stars.

Remember me in your prayers as you offer vows to the Thunderer;  
Strabo too always remembers you.

Love what pleases the Lord and what he has commanded;  
hope for what he promises, flee what he forbids.  
Love the virtues and remain far from every vice.  
A sure reward is given to the good, punishment to the wretched.

May God lead all your thoughts toward better things  
and bring you great gifts forever.

Farewell, bright one, dear one, ever and everywhere most dear;  
bright little boy, bright little dear one.

## To Gotabert the Italian

Verona did not rejoice more greatly in her son Catullus,  
nor Mantua itself so greatly in her Maro;  
nor did Greece pour forth Homer with greater joy,  
nor Cordoba herself send forth two Senecas,  
than Ticinum will grow happier in you, if you prosper,  
fortunate boy: you will be another Cicero.

Whatever you are, farewell; whatever you are destined to be,  
you will be ours. May you prosper, we ask, in the Lord.

## To Thomas, Tutor of the Palace [Note: [Col. 1099D] Walafridus explains elsewhere who the tutor of the palace is: “Just as there are tutors in palaces, or palace counts, who investigate secular cases.” [Col. 1100D] The tutors were therefore the same as the palace counts, entrusted by the prince with the investigation of civil cases. BASN.]

You have begun to deserve the summit of the apostolic name,  
as heir, through deeds and words.  
You whose breast has taught twice six people through its gift—  
Strabo knows that you retain him in your heart.

I rejoice not so much because worldly prosperity smiles upon you  
as because you please everyone through your goodness.  
We often see that this is common to the wicked;  
that distinction belongs only to those who please God.

Honor does not bestow merit; merit itself is rewarded with honor,  
nor do perishable things bind hearts that are full of God.

[Col. 1100C] As salt, dew, the face of leaders, flesh, grass, and war  
are not without stain, so I, holy father,  
bid you farewell without end in the Lord, and remember us;  
for we are members of one head.

## To Count Conrad

Ever since I received the praise of your reputation,  
frequent and true, I drank it in with judgment.  
Although obscure in talent and birth,  
I strove to rejoice in my heart at these praises.

I have done this, I do it now, and shall always do it,  
while living warmth nourishes my breast.  
Whatever I can do in deed, prayer, heart, and faith,  
I dedicate entirely to your service.

And even if my presence is not empty of purpose,  
which might gladden you, I nevertheless behold you in my mind.

I shall test, with humble words, whether one who desires  
may entrust more sacred words to you.  
For if confidence in speaking is finally granted me,  
I shall not be silent before you at an unsuitable time.

May the summit of nobility, the one Father of mankind,  
who binds nobles and poor men alike by their condition,  
increase, strengthen, multiply, and cherish  
your virtue, life, and peace through the ages.

## To Ruadbern the Layman

Ever since the fame of your celebrated name  
brought me the breath of your reputation,  
and I learned the strength of your faith and the sequence of your deeds,  
I embraced you, bending toward you with great love,  
and continually honored you in my heart.

And because at last I was worthy to know what I had sought,  
my love increased as the nearer knowledge of your piety increased.

For who could count how many labors you often endured,  
or in how many dangers, Rodbern, you entrusted your life,  
groaning over your lords’ sufferings?  
While savage deceit, harmful to itself, oppressed the pious king  
and the humble queen, and had shut them in the city of Liguria,  
you placed your life in your hands.

You did not consider the destruction and dangers of your own fortunes  
a great matter, if you could contrive some force  
on behalf of justice.  
Whenever I recall these things carefully in my mind,  
I marvel and, my breast stirred, dissolve into tears.

[Col. 1101B] And because I understand that the Lord’s consolations  
gave you these strengths as a certain gift, I believe it.

Alas, with what snares did alert watchfulness surround  
the narrowest paths amid the Alps!  
How greatly the constriction of enormous rivers terrified you,  
and how often hiding-places held you in fear;  
poverty pressed you, immediate danger and every hardship.  
No time was filled with secure ease.  
Dark night feared the day, and daylight itself feared the night.  
There was rest in neither house nor field,  
with fear striking from every side.

Only faith and a mind conscious of what was right  
urged you to this task and taught you to hope for some salvation.  
But all other dangers, in the fury of excessive terror,  
gave way to the savagery of men.  
Often compelled by it, you changed your clothing,  
and, with cleverness suited to the role of a servant,  
you humbly performed servile tasks  
and carried out a thousand things  
that you could not have accomplished through exceptional virtue.

[Col. 1101C] Yet your mind, full of faith and wearied by no labor,  
did not rest from what it had undertaken  
until fear alone had abandoned its power  
and you had brought the first hearts of the powerful  
throughout the West to give birth, by writing and speech,  
to sacrilegious wickedness.

Then, through these counsels, it was accomplished  
that the queen, long exhausted and oppressed  
by the weight of evils, was led out of savage darkness  
without loss of honor. At last, concealed  
and using a disguised stratagem, you came,  
and swiftly and willingly received sweet commands  
in the presence of the pious Caesar,  
being the first to carry them to the friends who had joined him.

Nor was that journey less troublesome to you,  
full again of fear, snares, and deceptions on every side,  
when a close guard tried to block the Cumaean lake against you.  
But the right hand of the Lord, sending favorable winds,  
carried you from the hostile shore.

Again, in the lofty Alps, the force of the snows  
made you linger in the heights,  
a season hateful to rest.  
Yet, shaking off these delays through the benevolent duties imposed upon you,  
you reported the messages in due order to the anxious king.

For these deeds, and for such fortunate daring, I say that  
the returning king, the freed queen,  
and all the faithful together, full of devotion,  
will assign you higher praise and an honorable name.

Moreover, the Almighty, who established laws and faith,  
who created lords and servants from one root  
but does not make them agree through equal authority,  
rather through love and honor, will give you true rewards  
for your unquestionable faith—rewards that will not perish  
with the praise of fleeting time but will overflow through all ages.

[Col. 1102A] In this age, while these feeble years  
had not yet blossomed with the down of youth  
beneath tender adolescence,  
while rival poverty forbade great deeds  
in your integrity, we marvel that you were able and willing  
to do what God, in a definite order, enabled you to do.

Who, then, will be permitted henceforth to doubt  
how greatly you will labor for your lords,  
for justice, and for faith, if a better place  
and greater opportunity should arise?  
You endured the first hardships with a courageous spirit,  
not conquered by bitter circumstances,  
and, balanced between hope and fear in uncertain danger,  
you turned death before your eyes as a hard burden.

[Col. 1102B] Therefore, go: give thanks to the Lord,  
offer gifts of praise, and attend at the same time  
to the justice owed by your lords.  
Leave sorrows behind and return again to joyful things.

For what was so hopelessly sad for the kingdom  
as that its rulers, once deposed, should be able to return  
again to their scepters and recover their former state?

But God, hidden Judge and impartial Arbiter,  
helped these and those faithful people by his power.  
Rejoice; exult with me. For I rejoice with you  
because we see this being fulfilled and fulfilled in part—  
what I wished for, and at least wished to hear,  
and what you properly sought through immense labor.

Happy is the person who recognizes himself  
as a participant and companion in an honorable work,  
as deeply as that man conscious of treachery  
wastes away, confounded by the turmoil in his heart.

[Col. 1102C] Let all the sources of joy be with him—  
or rather, much more abundantly—with those  
who preserve faithful hearts for their lords  
and remain unconquered through every misfortune.

I now seem perhaps to have used too many talkative hexameters,  
while the greatness of the subject extends my affection;  
and I am ashamed to have said briefly what is worthy  
of profound talent and a long poem.

At last Strabo gives you ten times ten humble verses,  
asking, as usual, that you meditate with me in love  
upon the commands of God, and prosper through all the ages.

## To Adalheid

If I should strive to remain silent about something  
that resounds through a thousand reports  
and is established as true by the abundance of its witnesses,  
perhaps I shall incur the mark of envy.

[Col. 1102D] Let it therefore not happen that this pleases my mind.  
Rather, I wish to hear it kindly  
and publish it without deceit.

For whatever good is reported about good people,  
I confess that such a great rumor about your integrity  
nourishes and carries away our minds  
that, if I should refuse to favor praise,  
it would be contrary to the conscience I carry.

We admire the beauty of conscience  
with which it is known that you especially shine.  
We admire your merit and honorable character,  
by which it is beyond doubt that you please everyone.

Whoever praises you crowns himself with honor;  
whoever praises you loves and honors the truth;  
whoever praises you will be considered kind;  
whoever praises you does what ought to be done.

[Col. 1103A] I do not bring these things forth from the mouth of a flatterer,  
nor do I desire to please with falsehoods.  
Rather, I have undertaken to prepare a straight way of speaking  
with words suited to the truth.

For if I discover that this is permitted to us,  
and if the All-Powerful, granting his assent,  
mercifully gives it, then you will read  
the figures that reveal our heart,  
now, always, and hereafter.

Hail in the Lord, farewell, and greetings to you—  
you, holy Father, and the Father’s blessed offspring.  
May the Spirit also help you through the ages.

## An Admonitory Fable to Someone

[Col. 1103B] I am considering what I should do. Recently it happened to me  
that I fell in one place; there I was torn apart by dogs.  
Here, submerged by the kicks of the people in the deepest mire,  
if you give me advice, I shall avoid forever  
this road, whose treading brings me such disgrace.

For I fear that perhaps the tide of the sea may overwhelm me—though from its assault  
I had scarcely found refuge on land  
and escaped the open anger of the raging whirlpool.

## A Comparison of Impossible Things

Let him capture white ravens and black swans,  
also talkative silent cicadas;  
let him acquire horned horses and mutilated young bulls;  
let him forbid fish to swim and birds constantly to fly;  
let him make swift springs stand still and mountains run;  
let him compel waters to flow upward and flames downward;  
let mud become moisture and wax harden in fire;  
let bones swell with blood and sinews with marrow;  
let earthworms leap and stags crawl in the dust;  
let hens give birth to kids and goats lay eggs.

## Epitaph of Werdo

After the sentence of savage death,  
justly avenging, came from the mouth of God  
against the first man,  
and although fame may have celebrated certain people  
throughout the wide world and carried the breath of their name  
as far as the heavens,  
nevertheless, when justice decrees, it is established  
that dying limbs can be contained in small tombs.

This small enclosure holds the body of so great a man,  
whose spirit remains in the heavenly citadel.  
[Col. 1103D] The patron and abbot of this place was  
Werdo, a man filled with love for his God.  
Distinguished in understanding, rich in polished speech,  
he commended teachings through exceptional character;  
pleasing through diligence, approachable to everyone,  
and worshiping the Lord with devoted religion.

He is known to have ruled this flock piously  
for seven five-year periods and to have heaped upon it  
every kind of good.

While March, with its thirtieth sun, was approaching the Kalends of April,  
[Col. 1104A] Werdo died and ascended to the stars.

Whoever reads this inscription for his repose,  
pour forth prayers to the Lord from a peaceful heart.

## In the Church of the Monastery Called Rura

This temple is celebrated as dedicated in honor of Stephen,  
together with James, our brother in the Lord.  
Under their prayers, received through Christ’s mercy,  
may we attain the abundant gifts of the supreme Good.

Hildigrim built it; Bishop Hadabald  
consecrated it. Certain honor remains to both.

Over one altar of the same church.

Dantbert Martin holds this altar;  
through their pious prayers, Christ, protect us.

Above another altar:

[Col. 1104B]

Here, holy Gregory, you are joined to the Mother of the Lord;  
ask God’s scepters for us.

Another epigram:

Abbot Grimald renewed and enlarged this house  
under the honor of Saint Peter, through love of the light.  
Here, whoever asks from his heart will receive by divine gift  
what he desires and gifts corresponding to his prayers.

Another:

This chapel too, venerable Virgin and Mother of God,  
Grimald, the humble, adorned in your honor.  
Ask God to grant him and all who pray here  
the reward for what they piously undertake.

Another:

[Col. 1104C]

It is fitting to give a poet verses and meters,  
just as what a merchant loves is dear to him.  
If you bring military arms to a farmer covered in dirt,  
he despises them, and a great gift to him is a mattock.  
Likewise, if a brave soldier receives gifts of a plowshare,  
he prefers trumpets and a spear.

Thus each person seeks more eagerly what he cherishes.  
For this reason I wished to entrust a few little verses to you, holy father.  
How much your affection delights me, I scarcely know  
well enough even to express it.

Your discipline is natural to you, and your sterner practice…

He erased “Scottus” [Note: [Col. 1103D] William of Malmesbury, in the second book of *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*, under Alfred II, says: “At this time John Scotus is believed to have lived, a man of penetrating intellect and great eloquence, who, when the clash of wars was long resounding everywhere, had crossed over in France to Charles the Bald.” See this passage. [Col. 1104D] SCRIVERIUS, manuscript note in Canisius. — But since the time when Scriverius wrote this, that John Scotus has become much better known; concerning him you will find more in Cave, Pinius, and also in our *Ecclesiastical History*. I am reluctant to repeat it here. BASN.] and replaced it with *probum*.

[Col. 1104D] If you consider what I said a joke, nevertheless Chronmal, departing from you, gave me these words to speak.
