Here I send you Fortunatus’ little books,

and the *Surveyor of the World*; read them through, write, and return them.

I am yours; be mine; let whatever either of us possesses belong to the other.

Thus may I be you, and you my other self.

By your nose I adjure you, my dear friend: farewell,

and, I beg you, pray willingly to the Lord for me.

## On the Hymn of the Three Boys

[Col. 1105A]

Let them bless the Almighty,

and let the stars of the heavens,

the sun and its sister,

likewise bless him;

the waters also,

the dew and the rains,

fire and summer,

cold and heat,

snow and ice,

light and darkness,

[Col. 1105B]

the dry lands and mountains,

rivers and springs,

all living things,

whatever the air carries,

the entire human race—

let them always worship

through every age

the Almighty.

All things, and the lights

of heaven’s choir,

the Almighty;

and whatever belongs to the heights,

every spirit,

the Almighty;

the heat and the frost,

and the hoarfrosts,

the Almighty;

night and day,

the lightning and clouds,

the Almighty;

buds and hills,

the sea and its waves,

the Almighty;

whatever the sea carries

and the earth nourishes,

the Almighty;

Israel itself—

the Almighty.

## Verses on a Certain Mantle

Eager to depict things in gleaming images, the skillful artist painted this mantle by art and hand [the damaged word after *hanc* is uncertain].

If so many artists fashioned one figure with such workmanship,

how beautifully does a single love unite two people.

The wantonness of shining flesh, rolled about in its own sphere,

perishes when the wind blows; yet fitting love remains.

## To Werdrich the Monk

There is no faith with you; lies possess you altogether,

for you seem to be like the foxes.

## Verses on a Staff

If my foot should slip, be a staff in place of my foot and raise me up.

## Verses on a Whip

After no shoots had grown upon my branches

to carry threats against Ceres, I began to yield fruit again.

## On the Handle of a Little Knife

Through the iron I accomplish what no one else does;

so may the iron be useful to you—keep me.

## Likewise on Another

[Col. 1105D] What does nature imitate in me, and what does the image produce?

Tell me, wise man, in a single name, if you are wise.

## On Sleeves

Behold, we are twin sisters, joined in equal partnership,

yet each in turn avoids the other’s place.

Tell me, teacher, what can do what it has never accomplished?

Or let the mute little lips give forth a sound clearly.

## On a Tablet

I reveal what I do not know, and I do not contradict the petitioner.

## On a Candle

Christ, direct the hands that made this candle.

## At a Feast

Salt, bread, leek, fish, wine, and food are present;

I do not wish to see the delicacies of kings just now.

## To Bishop Ferend

[Col. 1106A]

Behold, a new gift appears, bearing a royal emblem:

city, person, place, region, tribe, island, and world,

with profits gathered from every side without number or measure,

striving through rival vows to win your favor.

India sends ivory; Tmolus gives saffron-scented perfumes;

the Hermus pours forth more turbid gold than usual;

for your sake wealthy Canopus is defrauded of its twin harvests;

the Pontus and the oyster-bearing straits of Abydos are emptied;

Engaddi pours forth for you a tear made joyful by its bark;

learned Tyre complains that its purple dyes seem duller,

admitting that, in your judgment, their colors are unworthy;

Epirus and the Moselle together compete to produce

new palms and winged horses for you;

Swabia brings forth shining mountains of silver.

[Col. 1106B] Promising that, while you live, you will enjoy golden ages,

a faithful servant sends you, among these things,

with a willing heart, a gem discovered in an unsafe valley,

a bright little gem, rare, dear, and precious.

Oholiab carved it, and Bezalel likewise marked it,

the gem being proved genuine by its Greek name:

for *agathes*, from *agathos*—“good”—is the stone, as you yourself acknowledge.

No Bactrian black stone shines with such a form,

nor do amethyst gems adorn a noble neck in such a way,

nor does jasper enclosed in yellow gold flash so brightly.

If this gem were seated upon King David’s crown,

it would surpass every kind of flame with its own light.

Finally, if it were placed beneath the breast of the prophet Moses’ brother [Aaron], and compelled

to claim for itself the right to be one of the twelve gems,

[Col. 1106C] if this servant should please you, though black-faced,

then, should Swabia perhaps produce any little stone from its river—

milky, snowy, Parian, or simply white—

your servant’s generous right hand would offer it to you.

Nor will you call Alemannia sparing when it brings rocks,

nor will Saxony offer you more satisfactory stony gifts.

But in our stead, O stone, press eagerly on in service,

until, when I come, I may be able to complete what I desire.

## To Another Bishop

Alas, dictation refuses my grieving mind,

fleeing sadly from the confused chambers of my heart.

Father of all, help me, poor wretch that I am,

and you, merciful Son, who govern all the ages;

come, gracious Spirit, and grant words to one who prays.

[Col. 1106D] Holy Mother of God, we beg you, have mercy on us.

Now songs worthy of a serene man must be spoken,

in the clear name of the lord . . . .

You are powerful through the offspring of the virtues,

and you shine with doctrine;

by your art you surpass eloquent sages.

All whom pleasant France produces praise you;

the Norican realms likewise strive to honor you.

Faithful Swabia, now springing forth in adorned songs,

sings great joys and resounds above the stars.

Young men rejoice, and glad old men likewise,

over the outstanding bishop whom Swabia has produced,

who supplies the peoples with the king’s honor and abundant consolations;

you are gentle, generous, and compassionate toward all.

If nature prepared a hundred tongues for me,

and a thousand voices for my mouths,

I could not speak songs worthy of your praise,

nor can any sound of the voice grasp everything.

The nobility of your family is recognized at every hour.

A glorious lineage has joyfully produced you:

in body sufficiently handsome, in the virtues of your mind exalted,

in every respect adorned and good.

You stand illustrious, you bright and excellent ruler [*archos*, prince],

noble in words, nobler in deeds.

You surpass Phoebus and the seven wandering stars;

Hesperus, however beautiful, cannot surpass you.

Adorned with the character of faith, a most steadfast champion,

you are altogether beautiful, down to your feet.

You refresh the needy, and, being good, give them every excellent thing.

May you likewise receive everlasting joys.

[Col. 1107A] Now I pray that you may prosper happily throughout the regions of the world,

and do not hesitate to remember me, your servant.

## Another Epigram

If the beauty of silver were my wealth, or if it were gold,

or if by chance I possessed beautiful little gems,

I would gladly have bestowed such great gifts upon you, Father.

Since I do not have these things, I freely give what I can.

## Another

As a weary sailor is accustomed to rejoice,

when he sees the familiar shores he has long desired,

so a writer, at the wished-for end of his little book,

exults when he sees it, though he himself is weary.

## To a Female Friend

When the splendor of the moon shines pure from the heavens,

stand beneath the open sky, gazing with wonderful sight,

and observe how the moon shines with its pure lamp.

With its single radiance it embraces those dear to one another,

separated in body but joined by the love of the mind.

If one face could not look upon the face of its beloved,

[Col. 1108B] at least let this light be a pledge of love between us.

Your faithful friend has sent you these little verses,

if on your side the chain of faith stands firm.

Now I pray that you may prosper happily through all the ages.

[Col. 1107]

# Verses of Walafrid Strabo, Published after He Had Completed Fifteen Years of Age, on Various Subjects (G)*

## To Hēbo, Archbishop of Rheims, in the Person of Tatto

[Col. 1107B]

Although this voice is unworthy, may I be permitted to admonish you,

most holy bishop, sublime head of the pontiffs,

[Col. 1107C] that with all your strength you build up the laws of heaven.

A great part of the good that you accomplish can appear

to the whole world, because the opportunity itself

has voluntarily presented itself, so that the court might willingly obey you,

and the Lord has given you, for the present time, a special light

of intellect, by which supreme wisdom has established its dwelling;

nor does your venerable will retain less of this power.

Since the great Judge of all justice has appointed you over all these things,

and causes you to grow rich through your own gifts,

it will not be unworthy if, with your whole mind,

you nurture the members of the blessed and holy Church,

strengthened in the marrow of their unity, with sacred doctrine.

Let the eyes first flourish, for the daylight

by which the whole body is instructed toward right footsteps.

The only-begotten Son of the Lord calls you salt and light,

[Col. 1107D] forbidding sacred commands to be dissolved by wrongful deeds;

he has given you the power of binding and loosing,

a power that remains in heaven and on earth,

and he commands nourishment to be supplied to fellow servants at the proper time.

Therefore, if a worthy life has suitably adorned you,

those subject to you will be drawn by your example to the crossroads of life;

and those not subject to you will be enticed by the most beautiful sequence of morals

to avoid the errors of their former life

and, with humble neck, to bear the yokes of the Thunderer.

For this first is fitting, and it must be pursued with all one’s heart:

that the pious rule be strengthened by Catholic deeds,

[Col. 1108B] before other hearts are tested by sacred words.

What good is it to drive healthy sheep into diseased folds,

when you desire the flock to be sound?

First let every vice be driven from the sacred stalls;

then let the young multitude be summoned.

Was this not likewise the concern of the gracious teachers—

[Col. 1108C] that they should walk through every aspect of life without stain,

lest holy authority should perhaps give a place to blasphemers?

Paul, the herald of God, desires to be all things to everyone,

so that from many he may gain blessed profit.

“Let us give no offense,” he says, “to the Jew, to the Gentiles,

or to the Church of God,” which has fled from every wrinkle

and carefully joins itself from its members to its head.

For as much as the head, for the whole body,

possesses smell, hearing, taste, sight, and touch,

so much more strictly does the law restrain you;

and so much more must you survey the citadel of the supreme image

with an intrepid step.

Yet we do not pursue these matters because we think

that you lack any virtue;

great love supplies the things that must be said.

For we desire your efforts to be led toward a holy end,

[Col. 1108D] and we plainly know that this is a place worthy of the highest attention,

provided only that the will is not lacking.

We do not doubt that you already recognize our desire;

the perfection of Christ will be its gift.

May the triune power of God grant you, through all the ages,

eternal life and a crown without end,

so that you, with the Lord, and the joyful multitude following with you,

may reap firm sheaves in great peace.

## To Degan, Chorepiscopus of Trier, in the Person of Tatto

[Note: [Col. 1107] This was the celebrated man also called Thegan, who wrote the deeds of Louis the Pious while the emperor was still alive. He died in the year 837. BASN.]

In these little verses, most holy teacher Degan,

[Col. 1109A] humble Tatto sends you words of joyful greeting.

I am constrained by conflicting judgment in uncertain matters:

whether I should say little, or rather remain silent.

Mutual affection compels me to write,

but I fear that I may not offer you anything worthy, Father.

Even if Tullius should return from the deepest underworld,

or great Plato should again open his eloquent mouth;

even if Titus Livius should bring Cato himself with him,

or loquacious Sappho should polish her smooth tongue,

they could never adequately express

the wondrous praises that belong to you,

for they are sufficiently numerous.

We rightly admire the gifts of your wise mind:

your learning, character, poems, words, and spirit.

No less do we admire outwardly the holy growth

of your stature, your limbs, hands, and face.

[Col. 1109B] We are small and humble; our form has made us subject to a mouse,

while the glory of our bulk makes our mouth a giant.

But setting these things aside, we pray with all our strength:

do not tear apart the verses given to you, beloved bishop.

Rather, send back writings answering writings,

by which, we beg, you may admonish us when corrected.

Indeed, we shall give you a few things for boys to read,

some jokes of ours, so that you may cut away what is faulty.

But, for the rest, if you wish to entrust us with anything,

we are wholly prepared to follow your commands.

We earnestly ask that you not deprive us, whom you love,

of the honey-sweet melodies of your teaching.

Thus, for our part, we shall dare humbly

to send you words bearing the gift of greeting.

And may he cause you to rejoice in attaining the realms of heaven.

[Col. 1109C] Now prosper and flourish, strong in merits through the ages,

and remember us, as we remember you in our prayers.

## The Same to the Same

Receive, most holy bishop Degan,

the small gifts of your Strabo, which he sends you joyfully.

Remember Strabo in your prayers while you offer vows to the Thunderer;

he too always remembers you.

I shall send the songs of the pygmy, together with those of the giant,

as soon as there is leisure. Farewell everywhere and always.

Amen.

## Riddle

There is a certain monitor who himself admonishes many,

yet sings no utterance without a word that admonishes in turn.

While the heat is cooking, he is completely silent and refuses

songs, but in the midst of the cold he cries out more loudly.

## To Drogo, Bishop of Metz

While Paul was examining the decrees of God with keen understanding,

he could not, stunned and amazed by such extraordinary emotions,

not merely speak of the greatness of so great an honor,

but could not even touch it.

“O how far distant,” he says, “are the divine inner chambers from man,

hidden away in secret paths, which those enclosed in the body

see through a mirror and only partly in obscure figures.

For who can discern what the wisdom of the world is?

What is its way? What is the hidden knowledge of things spread abroad?

What is the judgment by which God rules and orders all things, so that they may exist?

By what path are the vessels of destruction permitted,

through scourges and peace, to proceed upon their course,

while the vessels of mercy are led through adverse and favorable outcomes

[Col. 1110A] to love the way of light?”

By this it came to pass—and I shall piously confess it was providentially ordered, Father—that from his earliest years he should often be shaken by harsher misfortunes,

yet never broken;

for God’s praiseworthy judgment wished to preserve him

through joyful days and the goods of perpetual salvation.

If, in their secure circumstances, they laughed at leisure,

freedom would slowly generate a more grievous danger.

Long rest produces the fuel of labors;

constant exercise brings peace and adds honor.

He who preserved the seeds of the world amid the wandering flood,

and restored the human race from a small stock;

he who gave Joseph reign after the shadows of prison;

he who himself brought the house of Israel out of harsh chains

and, after hiding places, hatred’s deceits, and battles,

called them together to the promised fields;

[Col. 1110B] David, to whom he gave sovereignty,

and whose son’s monstrous deeds he turned to their author [the transmitted wording is difficult], then received him again into his kingdom;

he for whom peace itself existed;

he who rescued the prophet from the lions’ jaws

and the boys from the midst of the flames,

and in the furnace’s deep womb scattered dew instead of heat;

he who, after scourges, the cross, curses, and the tomb,

made Christ rise and sit at the Father’s right hand;

he who changes the darkness and blind silences of night

into new light through the bright rays of the sun;

he who purifies the cloudy and rainy day when fair weather returns,

and after the cold of winter restores spring to the lands

with fruits, leaves, and flowers,

the fields previously disturbed by white frosts;

[Col. 1110C] he also equips and calms the seething murmurs of the sea—

he himself, through the immense gift of his mercy,

has granted you to change things that were sad into joyful things,

so that, because you have learned to trust in the Lord’s gifts,

you may not thereafter wish to cling to goods destined to fall.

Indeed, blessed is the man who hopes in the Lord;

but cursed is the one who believes that the arms of the flesh suffice

and foolishly despises the Lord’s consolations.

For one who trusts in the Lord, like illustrious Zion,

will not fear being shaken through the ages by blows of misfortune.

For whoever drinks in the words of God with attentive ears

and strives to fulfill what he has learned through devoted deeds,

eternal Wisdom calls such a man like one

who supports the foundations of a lasting house

on the mass of the sacred rock—Christ is present there—

where the temples of good works must be established.

If suddenly a wave of deceit and error should come,

or the strong floods of oppression,

and a violent wind, bringing a roar from the Scythian North,

whistles its temptations hidden by ancient deceit,

or if it should perhaps weary the structure with an immense storm,

[Col. 1110D] the builder stands, and the house he built stands,

because the foundations of blessed rock are firm,

and he is shown to have built upon them.

Upon this mass of rock Peter stands, truly bearing that name,

in whom the order of the power of binding and loosing was received.

Rightly he is called by your name,

since it is clear that you possess him through right deeds and doctrine.

The more someone deserves to possess him,

the more he is rightly believed to possess him.

Therefore, to the one who holds it,

[Col. 1111A] honor does not give merit; rather, merit itself is given to him.

These above all are the qualities by which your person shines distinguished:

virtue, wisdom as its root,

order, affability, goodness, patience, strength,

life, rank, doctrine, position, moderation, way of life,

zeal and love of God, unconquerable strength of faith,

religion, duty, judgment, modesty, and conduct.

May the power of God grant you to grow in these things

through many years,

and in return grant the eternal rewards

which the Lord of life, the way, life, and redeemer,

declares must be given to faithful servants.

If no profound forgetfulness of my name oppresses me,

I shall never be forbidden to remember you.

And what I have recited above, Strabo, a sinful and sluggish man,

wishes with kindly prayers for the outstanding shepherd:

[Col. 1111B] twenty-five verses offered as a gift.

## To Bishop Muatuuinus [Modoinus]

If any confidence could make a path for my prayers,

I would have wished long ago to write to you often.

Now at last receive, most beloved bishop,

what my simple mind offers in humble fashion.

I trust that you will not disdain so small a thing of mine,

you whom the love of the world honors.

Yesterday the wealth of a rich man received golden vessels as household goods,

counting up various forms of silver.

That same wealth does not reject vessels made of unfired clay or wood,

but assigns them to their proper uses.

He who gives great gems from the Erythraean shore

seeks amber at the borders of Europe;

he who is accustomed to tear whales from the ocean’s depths

calls common tench to his nets.

The goldsmith’s craft, fashioning precious necklaces,

sometimes hammers out a slender needle in bodily form.

Seeking balsams and narcissus throughout the regions of the world,

he gathers field violets and coriander.

You too, nourished by the virtue of the highest foods,

deign to accept the banquet of a small gift.

And just as, after honey, one takes heavy cups of myrrh—

although it is harsh, it is of assistance to many—

the great glory that has grown in your songs,

I ask, stooping, not to tear our little wheels:

I desire poems precious with mature old age,

sayings of youth, which I read many times.

Although you sing many things worthy of being celebrated

by the crowds of the age,

you are silent among us, whose fame is lesser.

[Col. 1111D] Do not permit, gracious Father, that I remain long

without a share in the gift which you freely offer to all.

I would now hope for the consolations of your Muse,

if such great evils had not rolled through the kingdom.

Now the teacher is regarded as a soldier, and the bishop as a warrior;

those who bear what belongs to others ruin what belongs to themselves.

Alas, how openly honor is rendered to Satan,

and peace is absent from peace, driven far away from the world.

O helmsman, direct your efforts toward pious labor,

lest the raging wave engulf one who is in a small vessel.

[Col. 1112A] May the Lord be with you always, and may your grace be with me always.

In the Lord, poet Modoinus, farewell.

## The Same to Someone

If you have an abundance of grain,

and are able either to give us some freely or to sell us something,

there is a need, since I have certain people to feed,

to whom, willingly or unwillingly, I must ultimately be of service.

Dear friend, farewell; please salute your lord yourself

with a submissive voice.

If you advise me to write thereafter,

it will be written promptly as a worthless letter.

Believe me, I have recorded these trifles on this parchment without wax.

## To Agobard, Bishop of Lyon

When I had scarcely completed three times six years of life,

my name reached you, gracious Father.

I know that it arrived, since I received your reply,

which was for us the equivalent of great love.

For if you remember—and surely you can remember—

I rejoice, and I ask that you remember everywhere.

Love itself still burns in our hearts,

and the desire itself remains strong:

to see you and enjoy your face.

If the queen who ruled the Ethiopians,

if she left the fields of Sheba in order to seek Solomon,

why should we not, for whom another kingdom is being prepared,

remain always in the love of the Creator alone?

For I confess that, if a definite choice were now given me,

whether I should receive the gifts of the world or of intellect,

I would pursue the freer, secure leisure of knowing the truth,

rather than golden ages, though they are destined to perish.

But concerning the new flower that has sprung up among you,

this region nourishes the report and spreads its fragrance everywhere.

Once Flora came, while the various gods

each addressed her, bearing thyme from the hills and meadows.

The judgment of Christ’s worshipers attributes to this flower

whatever flourishes in doctrine and speech.

For this flower follows the flower from the stock of Jesse,

and conveys what that loving one brought to humanity.

What bee will be so sluggish as to be ungrateful for heavenly gifts,

and not willingly feed itself on this nectar?

May this flower not wither;

may it always bear fragrant, flower-filled breaths to God,

until, extending its summits toward the star-bearing abodes,

it raises them up and already possesses fruit without end.

Let ambrosia yield, and the rose, lilies, grain, and saffron;

let all sweet things yield together, and may love of this flower prevail.

[Col. 1112D] May I enjoy this, use this, be warmed by this,

delight in this, abound in this;

may I be nourished and instructed by hearing and seeing it.

May God one day grant that we may bestow mutual gifts upon one another,

and that each side may reap something.

By divine favor I pray: farewell without end,

while you send, in turn, your sweet writings.

## To Hrabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda, His Teacher

Receive, best Father, the words of your servants,

and may the Almighty approve your prayers.

Make sluggish Strabo make up for his delays,

lest he read too many reproaches against his own masters.

Receive with merciful heart the little book of a dung-dweller [F., *patricolam*, “a father-worshipper”],

[Col. 1113A] so that it may bear contents corrected by your mouth.

Deign to grant your servants the doctrines scarcely restored by you,

so that they may know how warmly you burn with love.

Grow strong, flourish in increase, and strengthen us in blessedness

always in the Lord, illustrious Father, I beg you.

## To the Same, Concerning Shoes

In a letter addressed to Father Hrabanus, Strabo,

some months ago promised us

that what our poverty had requested would be sent here

at the autumn season for our use.

But vain hope deceived me in my misery,

as my unexpected want presses me while I remain suspended in uncertainty.

Although countless complaints strike my heart,

what troubles me more is that I am compelled

to endure going barefoot,

unless your consolations first regard our circumstances

and, at the words of one who says little,

your hand—which is the most generous mother to all—

comes to meet me.

We pray that you may prosper through all the ages.

## To the Same, Concerning Giving a Servant

We beg you, best Father, to remember mercifully

your small servant who is ours.

Our house is narrow for two people;

if there were three of us, it would be wide enough.

Therefore we await the promises of your favor.

May you mercifully help us, and may the Lord help you. Amen.

## On the Five Parts of Rhetoric

The first part of rhetoric is skilled invention;

the second consists in a well-ordered arrangement of speech.

The third part follows—“condignis ... narrow for two” [text corrupt; Note: [Col. 1113D] The passage is corrupt.]

The fourth asks the teacher, once he has gathered [things], to retain them in memory.

The fifth completes the speaker’s formula with ornament.

## To Wenibert, Abbot

Receive, holy Father, the poor gifts that Strabo

sends you, and willingly turn over in your mind what is sent from the heart.

For what among those who understand is more precious than every treasure,

that our inmost being wishes to present to you.

Not gold, nor any gifts subject to harmful cares,

which often overthrow the unwary,

but only gifts that nourish pure minds—

when I bring these to you, I bring them multiplied a hundredfold.

Therefore, if you let these words enter your pious ears,

I shall give more, if God grants me life.

[Col. 1113D] Live, farewell, reply, and teach, kind Wenibert;

remember one who remembers, and remember your own [servant].

## To Sigimar, Now Abbot

Holy Father, deign to read through this brief page,

which Strabo has produced with slender talent.

For I have fathers who hold the most celebrated rights,

yet who take care not to recite verses of this kind.

That is why I entrust my attempts to unknown little mouths,

so that at least I may find someone to carry pious words.

Look upon the one whom you will see gazing with a sidelong eye.

This boy sends these words to you, Father,

desiring that eternal salvation remain with you.

Remember your servant as you give mutual gifts.

## To the Teacher Tatto

[Col. 1114A]

Little letters are accompanied by our bitter tears,

as we long to see your face.

May you see the Giver in the seat of heavenly life

and receive the many good rewards of a worthy recompense.

## On the Wantonness of the Flesh

Whoever on a sloping path

sets a sphere [Note: [Col. 1114D] *Sphaeram*, with the first syllable shortened, according to the custom of this age.]

in a level place,

unless he holds it fast with his hand,

immediately sees it glide toward the lowest point

in a rolling course.

Whoever entrusts a feather or a leaf

to a light hand

while the pole is shaken by the winds,

unless he catches its flight with his hands,

the wandering thing quickly attempts escape

and is carried into the air.

When harsh necessity compels someone

to give a light boat to the river

and its savage waves,

unless he quickly subdues the sluggish craft with a pole and oars,

the channel carries you away with it.

Fire flying through straw,

or over the tops of shrubs

which the force of the sun had scorched,

unless a stronger spring checks it,

immediately consumes the wandering material

and perishes together with it.

It is useful to keep a wild creature of the countryside,

once captured, in cages,

or a bird under a keeper,

unless you tame it with constant care;

otherwise it proceeds through pathless lairs

seeking its former way of life.

If, in recent years, you should entrust a foal

of noble father to the fields,

unless you hold it firmly with reins,

trusting in its wantonness

it throws you down and flies away.

I know rivers more readily

to run in their first channels;

but if you should compel them

to leave their familiar courses,

unless you enclose them on every side,

they immediately break their bonds.

Let these things concern our flesh,

most foolish human being,

which is accustomed to live badly:

the boat, the feather, the hearth, the sphere,

the foal, the river, the bird, the wild creature.

Pay close attention to these.

Unless, watchful against evils,

you disarm it of its inborn impulses

and, by your innermost efforts,

draw it back to the true path,

it stretches toward the black regions of hell,

and you groan forever.

O you who, through your begotten Son,

healed the lands ruined by vice through your gift,

do not allow the horrible power of the demon

to claim for itself the minds

which you washed in baptism.

## To Lipharus the Monk

Strabo sends you greetings from inward love,

that you may prosper in your Lord, beloved teacher.

Remember Strabo and, in reply, send back

the mutual gifts of peace;

if I live, I shall give more words.

The bearer is hurrying; thoughts in my heart are slow.

If a better thought comes, love presses on.

## To Altger, Monk of Elawang

Strabo wishes the aid of the Lord to be present for the old arrow;

he himself prays that Strabo may prosper greatly.

I mourn, I confess, your departure, beloved supporter,

and now water my face with abundant tears.

I remember the help that you used to offer me,

and I recall the gift, the work of peaceful love.

We beg you to taste kisses from your sweet-sounding mouth—the little letters which I have given with hand and mouth.

Now you are seen to let your arrow rest securely in its quiver,

and behold, to feed on peaceful blessings.

And let it not fall from your mind who you were,

whoever you now are;

the instructions are complete in upright conduct.

I, Strabo, pray that Marcuvardus and the worthy Bertus

may possess all gifts of salvation for a long time.

Now may all the brothers prosper, and may the good abbot prosper;

I am your little servant—indeed, I ask this as a small one.

Remember me in holy speeches, Altger;

Strabo everywhere remembers you in the Lord.

## In the Person of a Certain Monk to His Abbot

Receive mercifully, best Father, these few verses;

receive the vows of my prayers and behold my sorrowful mind.

Behold, you bear Christ’s role, with mercy as your guide;

I believe that you are pious through the piety of God.

Never has a storm like this struck or touched me,

by whose attack I should fail so quickly.

Your suspicion, based on imagined matters, shakes me so greatly

that, miserable as I am, I fear there will be no escape for one who swims.

Yet if it had been permitted to turn the oar toward the wind,

I would have drawn myself from the sea with a secure heart.

This I beg, earnestly begging through the powers of the Most High:

either now allow me to be cleansed,

or permit me to remain guilty.

I would endure being driven more gently from the lot of my own people

than having deserved your anger in this way.

Forgive these words, more forceful than usual;

behold, gracious Father, necessity compelled me to speak thus.

## To the Monk Gottschalk, Also Called Fulgentius

Swift Calliope, frequent the road

where Fulgentius [Note: [Col. 1115D] He follows the custom of that age, in which the names of kings and learned men were changed. Gottschalk was called Fulgentius because he shared his views with him concerning grace and predestination. BASN.]

is found.

You sought him, traveling farther after his cradle,

following uncertain rumor.

Sometimes rumor wandered, loudly carrying word of him

as he lived in the city of Rome,

thinking of foreign lands with devoted heart,

and willingly visiting distant fields.

At last seek him, restored to his proper place,

and always say “hail” and “farewell” to him,

to whom you once gave a name derived from honor.

He directs to you the greetings of the one who bears that name.

When the sweet joys of the holy birthday

were now drawing nearer and filling our loves with desired prayers,

the shining gifts of a second festival were added,

which your letter poured upon us while we waited—

[Col. 1116B] a rest for the weary, a sweet spring of water for the thirsty;

mother’s milk for lambs, rain for parched fields;

for those bound in prison, a vein of daylight.

Thus the palace verses you wrote with your own hand,

so eagerly desired by me, drove away the clouds with their brightness.

But because clouds often follow a light-bearing calm,

the North Winds likewise disturb my joys,

while your writings declare that I can do without you in person,

although deep in my heart there is a witness:

an ardent hope that I wish to gain much from you

and to share in your light.

Let it also be certain to you, with many as witnesses,

that you are able to instruct me and others

with the lamp of your examples and words,

and to pour wisdom into us with well-seasoned speech.

There is something else that must be lamented with greater sorrow:

although your life is more precious than the law of Lycurgus,

do not lie alone, ungenerous, upon received gold,

nor let bound napkins weigh down the entrusted talent.

Yet the following words are materially corrupt: “but he who in poverty endured than our youth . . .”; I have not found you, dear friend, less kind, nor less concerned for those who asked.

Why does biting rumor now declare, I wonder,

that your generous hand conceals its private resources [the construction after *in amplis* is incomplete]?

The merciful Father left them to be increased through interest.

The sun does not begrudge its rays to the blind world,

nor does the moon withhold its own.

Rain falls upon the fields below,

and rivers flow willingly in their accustomed manner.

The air draws forth its offspring;

the earth bears grasses,

and the tree clothes itself spontaneously with leaves and fruits;

milk flows from the breasts of mothers.

God himself gives light to all without distinction

[Col. 1116D] and commands the rains, followers of his work, to proceed.

Who persuaded me to block sacred gifts with a grasping heart,

unless it was one who thinks contrary to the Creator?

Rather, the page of holy Paul admonished us:

“Let us preserve what is good and practice it toward all,

but especially toward the saints,”

whom household life nourishes.

Therefore, Father and brother, the sole portion of my mind,

I would not have you think that I wish to tear apart my words,

but I cannot remain silent about your dangers,

if my mind knows anything and is able to preserve faith faithfully.

I shall not be such a man to you as they remember Philip to have been,

through the ancient records of deceit in friendship.

[Col. 1117A] I beg you to be for me a far greater friend than I have deserved.

As great as I am to you, so great shall I be;

reply through this man, a lover of our peace

and a faithful mediator.

And pray for the one who asks,

so that, not carried away by an evil storm,

he may be able not to forget you.

Farewell from here through the ages.

## On a Certain Dream, to Erluinus

It was night, and the distant stars increased their radiance

with alternating fires across the regions of the great sky.

Pollachar, steeped in sleep by the gift of Lethe,

loved the night’s resources, his cares removed.

Suddenly, rumor says, the arm-bearer of Jupiter appeared

to the man, shaking the deep darkness before his eyes.

“Proceed,” he said, “and cross beyond the clouds weighing upon the earth;

for I shall lead you where great rewards await you.”

At this he rejoiced, seeing all things, because the guide wished to satisfy his weary soul after its long search.

The winged creature flew to the heights and carried the timid man through the air,

until purer ether dispelled his terror.

That new Daedalus, partly urged on by fear

and partly by excessive haste, dreads the path he is treading.

“Will he carry me,” he said,

“with these filthy things weighing down my limbs,

into the shining hall of the star-bearing heaven?

Rather let the evacuation of my distended belly run out;

let the earth keep its own burden, and I shall depart light.”

Knowing what was to come, Unguirapus held his tail in his mouth

and said, “Quickly purge every foul thing.”

Then, that the world might endure for a long age,

he emptied his bowels with all his efforts.

“It is absurd,” said the eagle, “to introduce into divine dwelling places one who will sprinkle the lofty places with filth.”

Therefore return, and attend to the filth left behind on the bed;

do not hope again to follow the stars with your excrement.”

Awakening, he found that whatever he had seemed

to pour down from the upper heavens

had run across his own bed.

Shame and abomination! Deceived by wicked visions,

[lacuna] [Note: [Col. 1117D] Some pages seem to have been cut out here from the manuscript codex, I do not know by whose fraud. CAN.]

(Here, in Canisius, thirteen poems follow, in honor of blessed Mary and the twelve apostles. But these ought to be attributed to Saint Aldhelm, and have been reprinted by us in volume LXXXIX of the *Patrologia*, column 291.)

## The Psalm Begins

Behold how good it is for all brothers to dwell together in concord,

like the clear folds of a soothing mantle once poured from the crown of the head,

and like the moist peaks of the dew-bearing hill:

Hermon and Zion moisten the dewy fields.

There the Father’s gifts will flourish forever,

and life will remain safe through the ages to its very end.

## The Lord’s Prayer

Almighty Creator, ruler of heaven in your royal hall,

may your praiseworthy name be sanctified in honor.

May the enemy who harasses us with hatred be driven far away,

and may your glorious will be done in our lands,

just as your revered will stands established at the summit of heaven.

Most High Father, grant us our daily bread

[Col. 1118A] until our faith grows into holy merit.

Forgive the many things we do that are dear to us,

so that, by granting forgiveness, we may release our brothers’ debts.

Let no evil temptation break our nature,

nor prevail, lest it bring upon us the snares of the wicked enemy.

Therefore, defend us from great dangers of evil,

so that we may deserve to enter the lofty rewards of your kingdom.

Reader, learn from this speech who I am.

## ANOTHER

To Hartpert, enclosed beneath the diadem of the heavenly kingdom,

you who climb by steps of virtues a life made holy,

never grow slack in all the service of the Lord;

a devoted person announces this in a faithful heart, N.

All things that can be done in any service,

all things altogether of salvation together with faithful prayers,

[Col. 1118B] I have long wished for an answer from you to come,

such as might bring us consolations from you.

I truly doubt whether you wish to fulfill these things for us,

so that, as our ears have heard your remarks,

you may either speak more clearly or ask outright to be refused,

so that the bonds of an uncertain heart may quickly be loosed.

As a bird rejoices and chattering birds rejoice in the branches,

so shall I rejoice when I see your body safe;

this I ask: may true love join us, and error not divide us.

## DISTICHS TO THE RULER OF GOOD THINGS

To the beloved father, serene in the flower of virtues,

Mathytes [Note: [Col. 1118D] Greek μαθητής, “disciple.”] the faithful everywhere wishes honor.

If melodies were to flow for me in thousands of buzzing voices,

they could not sound worthy of so great a man.

[Col. 1118C] Yet I praise you as I can with devoted heart,

with a resounding voice calling you worthy of praise.

Let waters resound for you with triple symphonies,

and let every splendor of harmony echo for you.

Let four-stringed instruments be joined with triple melodies;

let one sound the octave for you, another the fifth.

Let the player of the great-sounding hydraulic organ praise you;

let a Colchian instrument be fashioned for you from diamond.

Let the harmonious Sisters praise you in their accustomed manner;

their number is twice four and once more.

They who, as myth bears witness, flew with many wings,

as companions of golden-haired [Apollo] and thundered through the heavens.

Only one remained in the fields for my purposes,

whom the tardy swan brought to this work.

She, by wandering with me through muddy pools,

teaches me to keep watch in your praise.

Finally, the truthful and happy little wretch

had revealed the various rivers of the star-wandering number.

Now that the rest of them have been withdrawn to some distance,

the outermost wave of the harsh ford afflicts us.

In that stream, surrounded only by twin swans,

our Thalia sits and grows stiff with cold.

Finally, she grieves that her bright feathers

are soiled beneath the black torrent, when no other pain is present.

She would make use of these when a river of milk were available;

therefore she asks other companions for herself here.

If someone were to send her an Alpine crow

or a Strymonian crane, she would give pleasing gifts.

With castanets, ringing sounds, and lyres,

she herself, in her leisure, would make a clamor surpassing Thracian music.

O sweet one, radiant in every art,

I beg you, dear friend, let her have leisure for this work on your behalf.

For she recalls your name, one above all others,

which Perdia mentions and counts also by night. [The supplied reading *Perdia* is uncertain.]

Yet, that you may believe these things without doubt,

look at what the mistress herself has written to you.

## THALIA’S VERSES TO THE SAME MAN

Hail, beloved equal; illustrious glory of our company, be well,

you whom experience of affairs makes suitable for us,

and whom no one is considered able to equal in our arts.

For your name, always a beloved light to me,

will dwell with me through all nights and days,

which, binding it together in numbers after the manner of heavenly honor,

I compose in fixed rhythms, making known what I have learned.

Its face, marked five times and then ten times five,

gives three, ten, and finally three signs to its side.

Finally, taking twice two little letters from the name itself,

I mark a square through the quarters of the world;

then, drawing as many further characters from the remaining elements,

four eminent men are marked, spreading Christ’s teachings through the broad world.

But if, watchful, you observe these two quadrangles,

you will note two hundred numbers with five added,

which, if skillfully divided by seven circles,

leave two remaining, signifying a double peace.

“Seven,” for the same number marks heavenly gifts.

But if you first see a pentagon through the letters,

which with a certain sound resounds like a messenger from on high,

three little letters remain from the summit of the name;

the Trinity itself offers them to holy faith.

Now behold, brother, the clear and serene name;

rejoice with the Lord, and remember me.

## IN THE BASILICA OF SAINT PETER AND SAINT PAUL

Here Peter and Paul, the square lights of the world,

guard the splendid apse with their twofold power;

and also Andrew, who once gladly suffered death

and hung upon the gallows with his holy flesh.

[Col. 1120A] This temple, built with beautiful workmanship,

the noble Bugga, daughter of King Cenuvium, raised.

Her father had previously ruled the Saxons’ realm by right,

until, scorning the heights of the present kingdom,

he abandoned the world’s riches and the reins of worldly affairs,

and bestowed many estates upon new basilicas,

where Christ-worshipers now observe monastic law.

Then he went to seek the consecrated life,

when he abandoned his own kingdom for Christ’s name.

Yet before this he had fought three battles

and likewise brought wars to an end with three triumphs.

After him succeeded, famous in war and arms,

King Caejivunalla [Note: [Col. 1119C] Cendualla. He died at Rome after receiving baptism in the year 689, on 20 April. See Alford, *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Anglo-Saxons*, under the years 688 and 689.] powerful, possessor and heir of the kingdom.

But soon abandoning the world’s rule and scepter,

seeking the lofty kingdoms of the heavenly realms,

he cleft the bright summit of star-bearing Olympus.

But when these princes had penetrated the high heavens—

the two names of whom I described earlier—

a third ruler received the rich scepter,

whom they call Ini, by the customary name of his people,

and who now governs the Saxons’ kingdom by right.

While he reigned, Bugga, the humble handmaid of Christ,

built a new chapel of lofty structure.

Therefore let us all celebrate the present day with rejoicing,

and let us sing responsive songs to God and Christ.

Thus he ruled the kingdom happily for many years,

until, converted, he withdrew into a blessed cell.

From there he sought the heights above through shining merits,

led to the summit of heaven by angelic bands,

and joined to the heavenly citizens, rejoices in the lot above.

He plowed the blue sea with curved ships

and traversed the ocean plains with the oarsman.

The cold sails crackled beneath the windy blasts,

until the boat struck the shores with its rough prow.

Then he crossed the cloud-covered Alps,

enclosed by snowy ramparts and mountain summits;

at his arrival Rome rejoiced in mercy,

when he was deemed blessed to plunge into the baptismal waters.

Therefore, after the white garments [Note: [Col. 1120C] That is, after baptism.], seized by illness, he departed,

until he closed the breathing passages of mortal life.

[Col. 1119]

# WALAFRID STRABO’S *HORTULUS* TO GRIMALD, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT GALL (G)*

## CANISIUS TO THE READER

Although this *Hortulus* of Strabo was published long ago, I have nevertheless wished to publish it again here, so that Strabo’s poems, as far as possible, might finally be gathered into one body. Would that it had been possible to add the *Life of Saint Gall*, written by the same author in verse! But we were deterred by a manuscript written with extreme corruption, from which you would extricate yourself no more easily than from the leaves of the Sibyl scattered by the wind.

But so that you may know who this Grimald was, to whom Strabo dedicates this little garden, I am pleased to set down what the Reverend Father Jodocus Metzler, professed member of the monastery of Saint Gall, recorded about him. He says:

“Louis, king of Austrasia, substituted Grimald, his archchaplain and a secular cleric, for Engelbert, the deceased abbot, in the year of the Lord 841, according to the manuscript *Chronicle*, or, according to others, 842. This abbot governed the monastery very well—not so much in the care of temporal matters as in that of regular and divine affairs, and so forth.

“Grimald raised the oratory of Saint Othmar, and transferred his body there from the church of Saint Gall through Solomon, bishop of Constance, in the year of the Lord 867, on 24 September, in the first indiction. Under this abbot Saint Notker the Little was received into the monastery; under him also many excellent books were purchased and written at great expense.

“There were likewise within the monastery famous schools, one for the monks and another outside it for secular persons, in which the sons of princes and nobles were carefully educated. He died in the year 872, after having governed for thirty-one years. And, as I gather from the following epitaph, he was buried in the church of Saint Othmar; no other church is recorded as having been built by him. The epitaph is this:

Here within rests a lover of the divine law,

the humble Grimuuald, who ordered this temple to be built.”

## AUTHOR’S PREFACE

[Col. 1121A]

Although tranquil life possesses many distinctions,

it is no small thing, if one is devoted to the Paestanian art,

to know how to attend to the cares of obscene Priapus.

For whatever property of land is available—whether

where rotten gravel lies inert along a sandy stretch,

or where rich soil, softened by heavy moisture, produces abundant growth,

whether it lies high upon raised hills,

or upon an easy slope of level plain,

or bristles with rough valleys—

it does not refuse to produce the noble fruits of vegetables,

provided that your care, compressed by heavy sluggishness,

does not train itself through foolish daring

to despise the gardener’s manifold resources,

and does not shrink from darkening calloused hands with the day’s work,

or avoid laying full baskets of manure

upon the thirsty dust.

[Col. 1121B] This knowledge was revealed to me not only by the report

of common fame, nor by reading sought in ancient books,

but labor and study, to which I postponed the long leisure of my days,

taught me through tested experience.

## I. THE BEGINNING OF CULTIVATION

Winter, the old age of the entire year,

the belly and savage consumer of abundant labor,

when, at spring’s arrival, driven beneath the earth,

it had hidden far away in its dark retreats,

and returning spring prepared to erase the dreadful traces

of greedy winter from the ancient crown [Note: [Col. 1121C] That is, the crown.],

and to restore the languishing fields to their former splendor—

spring, the first head and glory of the world and of the year—

when purer air had begun to open the clear day,

and, following the west wind, grasses and flowers

began to extend the slender tips of roots,

long hidden in the blind bosom, and hating hoary frosts;

when the forests were fresh with leaves, the mountains with rich grass,

and the meadows with conspicuous, joyful greenery—

nettles filled the little forecourt which, before my doors,

a small open area turns toward the rising sun,

and, smeared across the level of the little field,

their shafts grew with burning poison.

What was I to do? Beneath, the order of the roots was so dense and interlocked

that it was like the latticework which a master of the stable

skillfully weaves with pliant green withes;

as the hoof of horn-footed horses, when harmed by gathered moisture,

imitates the rotting forms of withered fungi.

Therefore, breaking through the hidden delays with Saturn’s tooth,

I attack the clods and the torpid fields;

I raise up the naturally regrowing nettles,

tearing apart their intertwined masses,

and destroy the burrows inhabited by shade-loving moles,

bringing the worms back to the edges of the light.

Then the small plot is baked by the winds of the south and the sun’s heat,

and, lest it fall apart, is enclosed with squared timbers;

raised slightly higher than the level ground, it slopes gently upward.

The whole is crushed bit by bit with hooked rakes,

and rich fermenting manure is spread over it.

With seeds we attempt to bring some vegetables to life;

others we try to recall to their ancient youth from old roots.

Finally, the little crop is sometimes sprinkled with spring rain,

and the tender moon in turn nurtures its delicate shoots.

Again, whenever dry seasons denied the help of dew,

driven by my love of cultivation

—for I feared that thirst would make the slender fibers languish—

I took care, with keen diligence, to bring pure streams

in capacious jars and pour them out with my own palms,

drop by drop, lest by chance a faster rush [Note: [Col. 1121C] Hanckius, manuscript note, reads *ne fors*, “lest by chance.”]

pour in excessive waters and disturb the seeds that had been cast.

Nor is there delay: the whole plot is clothed with tender shoots.

Although one part lies beneath a high roof,

dry and rough, deprived of the gift of rain;

another part escapes the sun beneath perpetual shade;

another, because it is higher, blocks the approach

of the fiery star with a hard barrier—

nevertheless, none of the things once entrusted to it

closed beneath the turf without hope of slow growth.

Rather, whatever was almost dry, transplanted and received

in cultivated furrows, it restored, full of renewed green,

repairing the seeds with abundant fruit.

[Col. 1122C] Now the work calls for ingenuity;

now for an obedient heart and tongue,

so that I may touch upon the names and powers

of so great a harvest, that small things may be adorned with great honor.

## II. SAGE

*Elelifagus* [Note: [Col. 1121C] Greek ἐλελίσφακος. The verse seems to limp; but if the first syllable is shortened, as was customary in this period, before *praefulget*, it will stand; or, if preferred, one may understand the first syllable of *elelifagus* as absorbed by the final word of the preceding verse, while nevertheless reading *primo* for *prima*. EDIT.] shines first in honor among the plants,

sweet in smell, weighty in virtue, and useful when drunk.

Found beneficial for many human diseases,

it has deserved to rejoice in perpetual green youth.

But it tolerates a domestic evil: for its savage offspring of flowers,

unless removed, burns its parent

and, enviously, causes the old branches to die.

## III. RUE

This shady grove is painted by the very green rue,

a little blue-green forest endowed with small leaves,

which, shooting out short umbrellas,

lets the breaths of wind and the rays of Phoebus

pass through its stems to their lowest parts,

and gently scatters powerful scents by its touch.

Since it flourishes with manifold healing power,

it is said especially to resist hidden poisons

and to drive away the harmful toxins that invade the fibers.

## IV. SOUTHERNWOOD

Nor is it less wonderful to admire deeply

the budding shoots of southernwood,

and the ears which the abundance of its branches raises,

imitating slender hairs.

Its fragrant crown, with its pliant stem,

when plucked, is useful to mix with paeonian remedies.

For it resists fevers, drives away the dart,

and helps limbs oppressed by the uncertain injury

of a furtive drop.

Moreover, it possesses as many powers as there are strands of hair.

## V. GOURD

[Col. 1123B]

[Note: [Col. 1123D] That chapter on the gourd is ingenious and seems not to have been composed better by better authors. BARTHIUS.]

Likewise the high-climbing gourd, rising from cheap seed,

raises immense shade on the shields of its leaves

and throws out holding tendrils through its numerous branches.

Just as ivy has entwined a tall elm with its foliage,

it has given its loose arms an embrace around

the whole tree, from the bosom of the countryside,

and, following the highest summit,

has concealed the wrinkles of its bark beneath green protection.

Or like a vine, a shrub-like species,

when it has spread itself upon any tree,

clothed the high branches with clusters,

and raised itself upward of its own accord:

thus one sees a red bunch hanging in a foreign dwelling;

Bacchus weighs down the green rafters,

and the broad vine-leaf separates the lofty foliage.

[Col. 1123C] So my gourd, rising from a fragile stem,

loves the supports placed beside it, its forks,

and, embracing its own alders, holds them with hooked claws.

Lest it be torn away by a mad whirlwind,

it thrusts out as many tendrils as it produces knots.

And since each one produces a double cord,

they seize support on every side, right and left.

Just as girls spinning thread pass soft skeins

through the spindle, and with enormous spirals

measure out the whole series of threads into beautiful circles,

so these wandering tendrils bind the poles

with twisted chains, quickly wrap the smooth rods,

and by borrowed strength learn to climb

the lofty roofs of hollow porches with winged movement [Note: Hanckius reads *meatu*, “by passage.”].

Who could worthily marvel at the fruits

hanging everywhere from the branches?

They are formed by no less regular paths

than if you were to inspect turned wood,

shaved in the middle, which consists of *mymphure* [uncertain term].

At first, lowered by a slender stalk,

they carry huge bodies upon a long and thin neck;

then the weight widens into the flanks.

The whole is belly, the whole abdomen,

and within it many seeds are nourished,

separated in a hollow chamber,

which can promise you a similar harvest.

Indeed, while the tender fruits are still young,

before the moisture hidden within their organs

thins with the arrival of late autumn,

and the skin has remained dry around them,

we often see them pass among stores of food

and absorb rich fat in the burning frying pan,

and, drunk with it, provide the palate

with a gentle flavor many times at subsequent meals.

But if the fruit is allowed to endure

the sun’s summer breath with its mother,

and to be cut down by the ripe sickle,

the same offspring can be shaped for constant uses as vessels,

when we have removed the interior from its great belly

and scraped the flanks with an easy lathe.

Sometimes a great sextarius is hidden in this belly;

or a full amphora, a still larger measure, is enclosed.

When smeared with pitch, it preserves unspoiled for a long time

the generous gifts of Lyaeus.

## VI. MELONS

[Col. 1124B]

In the same space, in the field where this joyful crop

is fixed in the lowest ground, which I have portrayed in humble song,

another vigorous kind of vine is seen

to creep across the dusty surface

and nourish round fruits.

This species, commonly lying covered upon the dry earth,

takes on the most beautiful growth,

until, dyed yellow by the summer suns,

it fills the reaper’s baskets with ripe produce.

Then you may see some with their belly lowered

in an elongated form, like a revolving nut or egg;

or like a bubble of washing paste (*lomentum*), once suspended from upturned hands,

which shines, drawing a film of moisture around itself,

before fresh foam is softened in water poured back upon it [the construction of this supplied line is uncertain];

while it is still made pliant by struggling fingers,

and, alternately, by the same rubbing motion

between both hands, a small opening

produces a small exit.

Here the gentle force of the south wind passes through the tightened mouth,

stretches the hollow weight beneath a glass-like appearance,

and forms a shifting center in the middle of the bottom,

where the curve of the roof may meet from every side.

Therefore, while the steel blade penetrates the inner parts of this fruit,

it draws out abundant streams of moisture

with many seeds.

Then, scattering hollow fragments by hand

through its many sides, the joyful guest

takes rich delicacies from the gardens;

whiteness and flavor delight the throat.

The food does not make the hard molars hesitate,

but, easily chewed, nourishes the body’s cold

through the inner parts by its natural power.

## VII. WORMWOOD

Next to it the plot raises sharp shoots of wormwood,

imitating the mother of herbs with its pliant stem.

Its leaves have one color, its branches another scent,

and its taste is far more bitter when drunk.

This remedy, proven by clear virtue,

usually subdues burning thirst and drives away fevers.

If, moreover, your head should suddenly be struck

by sharp pain, or if dizziness should weary you,

seek the aid of this plant.

Boil the bitter leafy growth of wormwood,

then pour the decoction into a capacious vessel

and wash the crown of your head with it.

After you have bathed your slender hair with the liquid,

remember to lay the bound leaves upon it.

Then let a soft bandage bind the moistened locks,

and after not many hours have passed,

you will marvel at this among its other powers.

## VIII. HOREHOUND

What shall I say of the nearby and exceedingly powerful

kind of horehound, not worthless,

although it bites the mouth more sharply

and separates taste from scent by a great distance?

For it smells sweet but does not taste sweet;

yet, when taken in a sad draught,

it suppresses the painful distress of the chest,

especially if such a drink is heated by fire

and is made to close the meal with frequent cups.

Whenever the poisons sought by a hostile stepmother

are mixed into drinks, or aconite is mingled

with treacherous foods and confounds them with sorrow,

a healing drink of horehound, taken immediately,

presses down the suspected dangers.

## IX. FENNEL

Nor should the honor of fennel be left unmentioned.

It rises on a strong stalk

and extends its branches widely;

it is sufficiently sweet in taste

and adds a sufficiently sweet scent.

They say it benefits eyes oppressed by shadow.

Its seed, taken with the milk of a lactating she-goat,

is said to soften the swelling of the belly

and immediately dissolve the delays of a sluggish bowel.

Moreover, the root of fennel, mixed with wine,

when taken, drives away a breathless cough.

## X. GLADIOLUS

Nor will I pass you by, whose free Latian tongue

has fashioned eloquence into the name of the sword-leaf.

You produce for me the glory of a purple flower,

bearing in early summer the pleasing gifts

of the dark violet,

or like Hyacinthus, newly arisen upon Apollo’s lofty table

after the boy’s death, and having marked the king’s name upon his crown.

We crush and dissolve the dried shavings of your root

in flowing wine,

and by such an art suppress the savage pain of the bladder.

By your pledge, fuller, you make the white woven linen

stiff [Note: Barthius reads *vigeant*, “may thrive”],

and cause it to imitate sweet scents.

## XI. LOVAGE

Love of the little garden, spreading more widely,

urges me to mention the fragrant grove of lovage.

Although this plant, alike in juice and scent,

is thought to cause double vision

and bring on darkness,

its seeds nevertheless often add a little

to carefully sought remedies

and win a reputation through another’s praise.

## XII. CHERVIL

You who complete, with your sacred voice,

so many monuments of wars and famous great deeds,

do not disdain, Erato, to touch with me in verse

upon the riches of my vegetables.

Although the Macedonian plant spreads in feeble branches

and produces an unremarkable seed on frequent ears,

it nevertheless, recoverable throughout the whole year,

relieves the poverty of the unworthy [Note: Barthius reads *indiguae*, “needy.”] common people

with a generous gift,

and by its easy taste is accustomed to check

the streams of blood diffused through the body.

When the belly is perhaps disturbed

by an attack of hostile pain,

it too applies no ineffectual fomentations,

adding pennyroyal and poppy leaves to itself.

## XIII. LILY

With what verse, or in what song,

could the arid weakness of a fasting Muse

sufficiently extol the gleaming whiteness of lilies?

Their whiteness displays the likeness of snowy splendor.

Their scent is sweet; in their flower they imitate the forests of Arabia.

Neither Parian stone in whiteness nor spikenard in scent

surpasses our lilies.

And if a treacherous serpent, having gathered poison

through its innate cunning,

sows it from its pestilential mouth,

sending death through a blind wound

into the innermost heart,

have lilies thoroughly crushed with a heavy pestle,

and drink their juices in Falernian wine.

If the crushed preparation is placed in small spots

on the surface of the livid opening [apparently the wound’s mouth],

then the magnificent powers of this remedy

will readily be recognized.

This bruising is also beneficial to loosened limbs.

## XIV. POPPY

And in this section of agricultural trifles

I am pleased to mention the cereal poppy,

which Latona is said to have devoured

so that, as the mother of the stolen girl,

she might cast immense forgetfulness over her mind

and strip away her cares.

With this aid, the carbuncle too—

the black swelling at the bottom of the chest,

which rolls up excessively bitter belches

as far as the gates of the mouth—

often seems to be restrained.

Its head, fertile with a seed of grains,

usually raises itself upon a long and fragile neck,

and, in the manner of the fruit

to which the Punic region gave its name,

it encloses many seeds of celebrated virtue

beneath a single open covering of skin.

From the sound made by one who chews it

it derives its suggestive name.

## XV. CLARY SAGE

Here, amid the shady new greenery,

clary sage rises on a powerful stalk [Note: Our clary sage does not rise on a stalk. SCRIVERIUS, manuscript note.]

and lifts its branches and foliage higher.

Although, sought less often by anyone for aid,

it is thought to have almost escaped the hands of physicians,

nevertheless, added to warm drink,

it supplies both strength and the ferment

of its fragrant flavor.

Nearby, a grove of garden costus, not at the garden’s far edge,

lies hidden;

with the beneficial aid of its cooked root,

it stimulates the stomach and the sluggishness of the belly.

## XVI. MINT

Nor will I lack the abundant supply of common mint,

with its many kinds and diverse species, colors, and powers.

They think that one variety of it can restore

a hoarse voice to clear song,

if someone drinks its juices while fasting,

when frequent hoarseness torments the throat.

There is another exceedingly rich kind of this shrub,

which spreads the shade of a no longer small shoot,

and, rising like elder from a strong stalk,

extends larger wings of leaves in every direction.

It has another scent,

and its taste is somewhat harsher.

But if anyone can fully recount

the powers, species, and names of mint,

let that person know that he must also know

either how many fish fly in the Erythraean sea,

or how many sparks Lemnian Mulciber sees

rise into the high air from the vast furnaces of Aetna.

## XVII. PENNYROYAL

The narrowness of this poem does not allow me

to encompass all the powers of pennyroyal in a swift verse.

It is said to be worth as much among the experts of India

as the mass of black Indian pepper is worth among the Gauls.

Who, then, could doubt that many ailments

can be soothed by this herb?

That richest people eagerly purchase it at such prices,

a nation flowing with ebony and gold,

bringing to the world whatever is wondrous to desire—

O virtue and providence of the great Thunderer,

which opens the generous gifts of its power

to no land without exception!

What you commonly see as rare beneath this sky,

in other regions lies in such abundance

as the most worthless things produce among you.

Again, certain things which seem contemptible to you

are purchased by rich kingdoms at great price,

so that one land may possess another’s wealth,

and throughout the whole world one household may exist in separate parts.

Pennyroyal, boiled, will kindly cure

a sluggish stomach, both by drink and by fomentation—

believe me.

While we sing matters which we hold firmly

through serious reasoning, license and usage permit us

to mingle some things we have heard with truth in the tragic style [the supplied word is incomplete: *cothurn-*, referring to the tragic buskin]:

join a sprig of pennyroyal

to your ear, lest the heat of the sun

disturb your head if it blows upon you

in the open air.

If Thalia, hastening to lower her sails,

did not compel me and urge me at last

to enter harbor,

I could pluck many more flowers for you from here.

## XVIII. CELERY

Although celery had become cheap in our gardens,

and many people observed that it was useful

through its customary taste,

it nevertheless displays many remedies

through its own powers and sharp assistance.

If you take its bitter seeds,

it is said to break the knots of tormenting urine;

and, when chewed with its tender shoot,

it digests the wandering foods

in the recesses of the stomach.

If nausea disturbs this ruler of the body,

let celery soon be drunk in water and bitter vinegar;

then the affliction will yield,

overcome by swift healing.

## XIX. BETONY

Although the precious abundance of betony,

collected in mountains and forests,

meadows and deep valleys,

surpasses almost every place everywhere,

our garden nevertheless has it too,

and teaches it to grow gentle in cultivated soil.

It has earned so much praise under its general name

that, if my Muse should wish to add anything,

at last, overcome by the mass of her task,

she would feel that whatever she brought forth

was inferior to its usefulness.

If you should happen to gather it green

for your own use,

or lay it aside dried for sluggish winter,

whether cloudy cups delight your throat,

or whether you prefer gifts clarified

by long labor,

the wondrous power of this herb will suffice for everything.

We know that some value it so highly

that, if misfortune attacks the whole body within,

they think they can fortify themselves

with its powers,

and habitually drink this sharp, health-giving medicine

on successive days.

Moreover, if the head, shattered by a hostile wound,

should have wasted away,

then repeatedly pound and apply

the leaves of sacred betony.

You will immediately marvel at its powers

when the scar has closed completely.

## XX. AGRIMONY

Here too it is easy to distinguish

sarcocolla, which covers many fields everywhere

and grows beneath the exhausted shade of forests,

by its beautiful rows.

Besides the varied honor of its broad powers,

when crushed and drunk it subdues

the very severe pain of the belly.

If hostile steel should happen

to inflict wounds upon our limbs,

we are ordered to try its aid

and place its cut shoots upon the open part,

to obtain renewed vigor by this method,

provided that biting vinegar is added to the poultice.

## XXI. AMBROSIA

Not far away ambrosia rises,

as it is commonly called.

It is praised, but many doubt

whether this is the plant so frequently mentioned

in ancient books.

Physicians nevertheless cultivate it according to their art,

and, when drunk, it absorbs as much blood

as the drink has introduced into the belly.

## XXII. CATNIP

Among the herbs which that little garden

always produces in fresh offspring,

no less vigorous a shoot of catnip emerges,

imitating nettle in its leaves

and spreading a very pleasing scent widely

from its lofty crown.

Once suitable for various treatments of diseases,

it is not counted among the least of herbs.

For its juice, mixed with rose oil,

makes an ointment which, they say,

can remove wounds in injured flesh

and the ugly marks of new scars,

restore them to their former beauty,

and restore the hairs which the gaping sore of a recent wound,

corroded by pus and decay, may have carried away.

## XXIII. RADISH

From here the radish, strong in root,

raised beneath a covering of leaves

and lifted from seed,

makes the outermost row visible.

Its sufficiently bitter root, when chewed,

suppresses the cough that shakes the entrails;

and a drink of its crushed seed

often cures the same diseased condition.

## XXIV. ROSE

If a longer journey did not impede me,

weary as I am,

and if the rough sequence of a new poem

were not being worn away,

I ought to surround the precious viburnum-like rose

with Pactolian metal

and the snowy gems of Arabia.

Because Germany is not spread with Tyrian purple,

nor does broad Gaul boast of blazing murex,

it renews its yellow growths every year

with purple flowers—

an abundance of blossom which is said immediately

to surpass all the beauty of herbs

in virtue and scent,

so that it is rightly called the flower of flowers.

[Col. 1129A] It infuses an oil named after itself.

No human being can remember or say

how often this has proved useful

to the cares of mortals.

The famous lilies set their flowers against it,

and their scent, breathing farther,

already fills the air.

But if someone grinds the gleaming white shoots

of the snowy fruit,

he will immediately marvel

that all the supposed promise of nectar

has perished in swift passage.

Because this flower shines with the reputation

of blessed virginity,

if no labor has disturbed it with impurity

and no illicit passion has broken it,

it blazes with its own scent.

But if the glory of integrity should fall,

I confess, it will change its fragrance.

For these two celebrated kinds of worthy flowers

mark the highest triumphs of the Church through the ages:

the roses gather the gifts of martyrdom in blood,

and the lilies bear them in the shining whiteness of faith.

O virgin mother, mother in fruitful offspring,

untouched branch of faith, bride in the name of the bridegroom,

bride, dove, house, queen, faithful friend,

pluck roses in battle; seize lilies joyfully in peace.

A flower has come to you from the scepter-bearing stock of Jesse,

the only restorer and founder of the ancient line.

He who consecrated lilies through words and life,

dying and staining roses,

left peace and battles to his members in the world,

embracing both virtues,

and preserving eternal rewards for both triumphs.

## DEDICATION OF THE LITTLE WORK

These humble little gifts of service

your Strabo, servant with devoted heart,

offers to you, most learned father Grimald,

though they are of no weight.

So that, when you sit within the enclosure of a green garden,

beneath apple trees shaded by leafy growth,

where the peach tree divides its foliage into uneven shadows,

while playful boys, the joyful school of your people,

pluck pale-fuzzed tender fruits for you

and place huge fruits in your capacious palms,

attempting to enclose the large bodies in their hands—

may this remind you, gracious father, of my labor,

when you reread what I willingly offer.

And while reading, I ask you to cut away

whatever is defective and strengthen what pleases.

May God make you flourish with eternal virtue

and allow you to touch the palm of unfading life.

May the Father, the Son, and the gracious Spirit grant this.

# APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF WALAFRID STRABO

[Col. 1129]

## SERMON ON THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS

(See among the works of Saint Augustine, *Patrologia*, volume XXXIX, part II, column 2135, sermon no. 209.)

[Col. 1129]

## POEM ON SAINT MICHAEL, TO BE REJECTED FROM THE WORKS OF WALAFRID (G)*

[Col. 1129C] To you I flee, Michael; I ask your divine power,

outstanding light of the world, who receive the prayers of those praying

and lead them to the stars in peaceful flight,

bringing heavenly protection to suffering mortals.

First grant pardon, remitting sins

harmful in deeds, words, or in thought alone.

Then heal mind and body with your medicine,

binding wounds completely and various pains,

and cherish my household in peace;

make my mind joyful throughout the ages,

so that sorrows may yield to better consolation.

You are the trust of my lineage,

you are the trust of our marriage.

[lacuna]

Let no disaster, rushing upon me from there,

torment my heart;

turn away diseases, or consume the danger

that threatens me.

May you wish to ward off what hangs over me

and scatter the powers of the mighty,

who weary me with rabid hatred.

May I not pass through life in lowliness,

nor indeed without glory,

but may it become clear how much your right hand can do for me—

the hand which once gave me victory

and fame in the toga.

You yourself, ruler of affairs,

be watchful over me,

and cover me fearless;

may I be cherished by fortunate counsels,

and, attaining a higher rank,

be made illustrious, blessed by just work and understanding.

Make it so that harsh hunger

or shameful poverty does not engulf me in disgrace.

Grant perpetual food and firm health

to the children whom you yourself have given.

May I always be grateful, dear, and approved

by my Martianus.

As you preserve him unharmed,

struggling toward the highest summit,

defend him, weighed down by dangers,

and protect him.

Now, saddened, I am compelled

to see him depart [Note: Perhaps *re linquere*, to be divided as two words.]

[Col. 1129]

## EPITAPH OF COUNT GEROLD [Note: [Col. 1129D] He was killed in battle against the Huns in the year 799. See the book on the visions of Wettinus above, [Col. 1130D] column 1063.] (G)*

[Col. 1129D] Beneath this mass the limbs of the great Gerold are preserved,

the man who increased the rights of this place with all his strength.

Slain by the Pannonians for the true peace of the Church,

he fell beneath the savage sword on the Kalends of September,

and gave his soul to the stars.

His faithful Saxon carried away his limbs,

brought them back here,

and enclosed them here with fitting honor.

[Col. 1131]

# THE METRICAL LIFE OF SAINT LEODEGAR [Note: [Col. 1131B] See the prose Life of the same Leodegar in Patrologia, volume XCVI, column 336. The text presented here has been borrowed from the work of R. P. D. Pitra, entitled *Histoire de saint Léger, évêque d’Autun*, enlarged with notes and revised anew by him. D. Pitra suspects that this Life is the same one that Vossius attributes to our Walafrid. The very learned scholar will bring forward the arguments supporting this conjecture in one of the volumes of the *Spicilegium Solesmense* soon to be published. Editors of the *Patrologia*.] OF THE BISHOP AND MARTYR, attributed by some to Walafrid Strabo [Note: [Col. 1131B] That author revealed almost nothing—whether his period, homeland, or status—by any indication. Only two things, and those uncertain, can be conjectured: first, that he lived in the first part of the ninth century, since he sings that the martyr’s bones still rested intact in the cell of Saint Maxentius; for nowhere does he mention the depredations of the Normans, who invaded the territory of Poitiers around the year 886, scattering Saint Leodegar’s relics throughout Gaul; and secondly, that he wrote not far from the Jura or Vosges region. Indeed, I think he visited the monastery of Luxeuil, since he devotes himself entirely to describing it carefully and almost pictorially. Finally, the one manuscript so far discovered, a Saint Gall manuscript dating from approximately the ninth century, suggests that he flourished among the people of Saint Gall. Compare Mabillon, *Veterum Analecta* IV, 639.]. (G)*

## I. Prologue

[Col. 1131A]

Many poems shine, completed through flourishing diligence,  
which distinguished men, renowned for genius, have composed.  
With their sweet-flowing melody they feed teachable minds  
and pour sweet honey into them through their plectra.

Each master took up whatever subject pleased him,  
so that from it he might bring forth a pure and excellent work.  
One, with the Muses’ sweet song resounding, wove  
the history of the Gospel and gave true poems.  
Another mingled the Old and New Testaments with wondrous art,  
and composed a book adorned with flowers.  
Another drew the apostolic labors from his mouth  
and expressed their noble deeds in verse.  
Nor did Christ’s worshipers compose with less devotion
