the life-giving deeds accomplished by the fathers [Note: [Col. 1132B] Here, as also in the preceding lines, the author alludes to Juvencus’s Gospel history, Sedulius’s Paschal poem, Arator’s metrical Acts of the Apostles, and finally the various poems of Prudentius, Paulinus, and Fortunatus on the deeds of the saints.].

As far as the western region is distant from the east [Note: [Col. 1132B] Wherever the text fails or remains incomplete, we have supplied the passage according to our modest ability, though not always with unimpaired Latin, meter, or judgment.],  
so Phoebus (perhaps “surpasses”) the stars and fiery-haired lights,  
and lowly broom-shrubs swell upward above the beech,  
while the ash surpasses the dense hazel trees.

[Col. 1131B] Verse 18

[Col. 1132A]

So, overcome by the teaching of the wise, while I search out their words,  
I lie low, with a kindly heart within me.  
Yet if, though slow, I cannot pluck  
the fruit of the great cedars from their leafy tops,  
nor bring forth the tender fruits that the palm produces from its bark,  
it is enough for me merely to lie in shady places,  
from which I may gather into my lap the fruits that fall,  
and thus satisfy my already unsavory [Note: [Col. 1132B] *Insuavidam*, perhaps *his avidam*, “greedy for these things.”] hunger.

Our patron urges me to say a few words,  
now that the annual day [Note: [Col. 1132B] *Annali* for *annuali*, “annual.”] is swiftly returning [Note: [Col. 1132B] “As the day returns,” namely the fifth day before the Ides of October],  
while the turning orbit has recalled from every direction  
the returning crowd that celebrates the martyr’s sacred blood.

Whoever loves to recite my verses in order,  
if a letter is sullied or a syllable falters,  
if the scansion of the meter does not proceed in its customary course,  
if the time-measure does not hold its proper places,  
correct it, and guide the paths in a straight order;  
with your smoothing pumice and scraping knife, remove the defects.

Verse 36.

# BOOK ONE. THE LIFE OF LEODEGAR THE MARTYR

[Col. 1131]

## II. On the Recurrences of the Ecclesiastical Year [Note: [Col. 1131D] “Recurrences,” because Saint Leodegar’s annual feast is celebrated around the Ides of October.]

[Col. 1131C]

Times yield to times [Note: [Col. 1131D] The manuscript reads *caedunt*, “cut”;], the wheel of the age moves on  
with rapid whirlwinds [Note: [Col. 1131D] *Turbinibus* is absent from our copy.], and knows no return,  
like flowing water, which as it runs onward  
rushes headlong with vast resounding collapse.

The annual order proceeds, and its ruler bends it with the reins,  
guiding the swift chariot beneath a varied, radiant pattern.  
A fitting crown is inserted into it in equal parts;  
the twelve months of the year never delay their course.

The year has four seasons: winter and spring are mingled twice,  
and autumn and summer run in balanced chariots.  
Spring brings forth lilies blooming upon the renewed earth;

Verse 47.

[Col. 1132C]

summer thrusts golden ears of grain from its bosom;  
in autumn the vine-dresser leans upon the heavy grapes;  
melancholy winter scatters the warm fire of Vulcan into the air.

Each season rejoices in what its own gift has bestowed.  
In winter the Father, resting in fortunate destiny, cherishes  
the heavenly offspring whom the Most High sent from the stars;  
he brings back the return of the Morning Star,  
at which spring rejoices to be present, victorious,  
from the depths of the unhappy abyss [Note: [Col. 1131D] The manuscript reads *imus*, “the lowest place.”].

Summer, reclining beneath the burning sun upon the breezes,  
bears the apostolic summit in its radiant embrace [Note: [Col. 1132D] “The apostolic summit” means the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, or perhaps Saint Peter’s Chair throughout the West, celebrated in summertime—that is, on those days when the world is illumined by the sun’s brighter and longer-lasting light.].

Autumn is honored by those whose merits ascend  
to the heights of heaven, rejoicing as they despise the threshing-floor.

Verse 59.

## III. Praise of Saint Leodegar and the Poet’s Devout Prayer

[Col. 1133A]

Autumn brings back the annual vows, on the second day  
after the beginning of the holy martyr’s day,  
the day that divides the middle of October,  
on which the outstanding victor rendered his noble weeping to the stars.

We gladly honor him, for his merits shine everywhere;  
wherever the sea extends, or whatever the waters surround,  
all peoples together bear witness that this renowned fosterling  
shed his own blood for the Lord.

Now, therefore, may the Lord of heaven prosper my undertaking;  
the fitting time has come for me to unfold again  
the deeds of the outstanding martyr.  
Unfasten the little bolts of my tongue,  
you who are present as the Father’s Word; grant gifts to my tongue,  
you who gave me a tongue and gave the beginnings of life.

Although my barbarous tongue may resound, compressed between my lips,  
you can do this—you who once formed the throat of a donkey  
to speak by shaping it in the likeness of human lips [Note: [Col. 1133D] “The throat of a donkey.” This very humble comparison, taken from Balaam’s donkey, is nearly proverbial and frequent among the ancient hagiographers. Compare the second-century Benedictine Prologue, passim.].

My mind now longs to set forth the praises  
of so great a prophet, but my slender powers grow warm with sluggishness.

[Col. 1133B]

I am not so despairing that I think you cannot do everything;  
for I remember that it is written, as the prophet declares:  
“Open your mouth willingly; I shall fill it with gifts.”

## IV. Saint Leodegar’s Noble Birth and His Youth Flourishing in Study

Distinguished parents begot distinguished offspring,  
born from the great race of the Frankish nobles.  
Their parental care gave him the name LEODEGAR,  
at the time when King Chlothar held the scepter  
of the Frankish kingdom, rich in possessions and faithful in arms.

While he was still very young and growing toward maturity,  
he was attached to the service of obeying the harsh ruler,  
so that he might often be able to stand before his face.  
But the king entrusted the teachable boy to a prophet  
who surpassed all others in distinguished learning.  
At last the young man, delaying none of the commands,  
went without deceit to be instructed in divine disciplines.

This prophet is said to have been his uncle.

[Col. 1133C]

At once Christ’s wisdom was present with the tender boy  
and filled the dwelling of his heart with bright light.  
After he had been taught and reached mature years,  
he began to shine in intellect and devout eloquence.

As is related, he was strong in an excellent body,  
learned in speech, prudent, and a lover of chaste virtue.  
Pleasant beauty radiated from his appearance,  
and foul desire never darkened his limbs;  
rather, he remained an innocent virgin throughout his life.

Now joined to the virgins, he follows the Lamb in purity;  
and the Lamb guided him, leading him to pleasant green pastures [Note: [Col. 1133D] The manuscript reads “the straight way,” *via recta*.],  
which Paradise nourishes in flowering and blessed fortune.

## V. Saint Leodegar as Archdeacon and Abbot

Grant, God, that I may be able to proclaim such great virtues;  
water my hearts, dry of fertile gifts,  
lest a scanty draught drawn from poor water  
restrain such abundant streams from the prophet.

The days passed; his age rolled forward through the years,  
and the rapid cycle was now returning twice ten times.

[Col. 1133D]

Meanwhile the deacon was brought to the holy altars;  
the rights and duties of sacred ministry were entrusted to him;  
immediately he began to grow through holy inspiration.

His fame already spread him among all people  
with praises that gave life. Suddenly, like a burning lamp [Note: [Col. 1133D] *Lichinus*; read *lychnus*, “lamp,” despite the meter.],  
he shone forth, driving darkness from many minds.

Having become a devout deacon, he then carried out the commands  
of the bishop of Poitiers, who ruled the heights  
of the holy Church. Thus he scattered seeds throughout the people,

Verse 120.

[Col. 1134A]

cleansing the rough fields by removing their thorns,  
so that they might become the Lord’s harvest,  
and so that savage weeds would not burn the young plants  
planted by the devout plow.

The lands entrusted to him by right the prophet held busily,  
and with swift step he hurried across them all.  
He consoles the sorrowful and also cares for the needy;  
here he raises the humble from the lowest depths  
and overwhelms the proud [Note: [Col. 1134D] *Mersat* is a barbarous word, used for *mergit*, “submerges” or “overthrows.”].  
He prepares to offer gentle things to the devout,  
but harsh things to the wicked.

Like a father to all, desiring soothing medicine,  
he restores what had been ruined for the better  
and renews what was old.  
Things previously neglected, cleansed of filth, shine.

The man’s rich and fragrant fame was already spreading everywhere.  
Lest this lamp be submerged in gloomy darkness,  
he hurled fire-bearing flames. But toward the heights of heaven,  
as his merits increased, he himself became chief minister;  
he now shone among the people as a bright lamp.

But when, by chance, a certain father had suffered death  
and had closed his appointed day by the lot of death—  
he who had formerly held and ruled the company of brothers—  
so that the group might not long remain deserted  
and deprived of a ruler’s help,

[Col. 1134B]

but might instead grow stronger through increased instruction,  
the devout deacon, at the command of the illustrious master,  
undertook its governance. He ruled it chastely  
for six years and enriched it with abundant resources.

## VI. Leodegar Is Raised from the Palace to the See of Augustodunum

More and more widely the fame of the devout man  
spread its fragrance; the people multiplied their sacred praises.  
Meanwhile sweet-flowing rumor, overflowing from a pure spring,  
was carried no less to the ears of the king,  
who at that time ruled the peoples from his lofty position [Note: [Col. 1134D] Here, unless I am mistaken, the order of the verses has been transposed, and they should be read:

“Meanwhile sweet-flowing rumor was carried no less to the ears  
of the king, who at that time ruled the peoples from his lofty position,”  
and so forth.].

Then the nobles alike, and the already nameless common people,  
loudly praised him as worthy to stand beside the king  
in meritorious service. The petitions of those who asked were fulfilled.  
At once, brought forward at the command of the lofty ruler,  
he was presented; commanded to serve in obedience before his countenance,  
he appeared. The long-returned pledge of affection was present:

[Col. 1134C]

thus at last Leodegar was joined to the lofty courts.

There he was honored by all with extraordinary affection;  
everyone rejoiced to have him as a devout father  
and everyone desired him as a teacher, both young and old alike.

There was a city called by the ancient custom of the people  
Aedua, rich in possessions and also distinguished in arms [Note: [Col. 1134D] Virgil, *Aeneid*, book I.].  
A younger age called it Augustodunum, changing the name;  
there the shepherd fell from his highest shores.

Suddenly, while the nobles came together from every side  
by a swift road, they uttered these words from their hearts to the king:  
“Let the lofty king order Leodegar, his distinguished fosterling,  
to become bishop.” After this, the petitions delayed nothing;  
soon, beloved by all with wondrous affection,  
he was joyfully appointed bishop of Christ’s Church,  
which Aedua, his nurse, embraces in a beautiful bosom.

As a cultivator cleans a rough little field,  
so that it may be fit for grain, and cuts away harmful woods,  
entrusting sweet grain to the furrows  
so that the gathered harvest may rise upon its stalks,  
so the prophet, cultivator of the divine field,  
calm in judgment, generous, and serene in countenance,  
a rejoicing and upright shepherd, second to none in compassion,  
cuts away with the sickle of his speech  
the sins of Christ’s worshiping people, arising from useless roots;  
he nourishes virtues and restrains harmful growth.

The heavenly walls receive a hundredfold harvest,  
while the prophet thunders from his devout mouth  
the teachings of the Scriptures.

Verse 182.

## VII. King Childeric Is Raised to the Throne Through Leodegar’s Care, and Ebroin Is Exiled to Luxeuil, Whose Site Is Described Accordingly

[Col. 1135A]

When the bishop possessed these virtues, the tenth year had now passed.  
Meanwhile a trumpet sounded with mournful music  
and announced that King Chlothar had suddenly departed this life;  
it proclaimed that he was dead and that he was being honored  
in a sorrowful urn [Note: [Col. 1135D] *Celebrarier* for *celebrari*, according to a very common practice among ancient poets. Compare below, verses 249, 305, and 336.].

After these events, the structure hung uncertain amid doubtful affairs,  
and the condition of the kingdom wavered. Then companions chosen from every side  
came together, traveling by a swift road.  
The prophet too quickly returned to the familiar court;  
he gathered companions like himself, to whom the armed soldier  
who held the scepters of the kingdom said these words:

“Behold, your [kingdom] lies dead; come to its aid more quickly [Note: [Col. 1135D] *Vester*; perhaps *Neuster* or *Auster* should be read, designating the Frankish kingdom.],  
O companions; now, now come to the aid of our exhausted affairs.  
Hasten and put off no delay: let him who will govern  
the scepters of the kingdom now take his place.”

Perhaps two brothers remained behind,  
Theodric the elder and Hiltrich the younger,  
sons of the kings. While the wavering crowd remained divided,  
one party strove to join the elder to the scepters,  
another the younger; the party prevailed  
which the holy bishop favored.

The defeated party remained, and at last the author of the schism  
led it into opposition—he who had held the heights of the kingdom,  
who had been chief of the nobles and second to the king:  
for Ebroin was at last held in contempt.

But what should he do? In fear he turned to every faction.  
For before the king he fell upon his knees,  
beat his face upon the ground while weeping,  
and, sobbing, fixed kisses upon the king’s feet;  
as a suppliant he begged for his life and limbs  
and asked that he might be permitted to assume a monk’s habit.

The bishop appeared as intercessor. Then immediately Ebroin  
sought the community of Luxeuil with rapid steps;  
he joined himself humbly to the company  
and hastened to cut off the hair of his head.

This monastery, long called by a word of light,  
is said to be Luxeuil, which nourishes a shining flock.  
It is enclosed on every side by tall, leafy forests,  
and all around, the beauty of flowering meadows  
delights the eyes of those who look.

Through its midst a river murmurs in a swift torrent,  
the Lignifer, carrying fish covered with scales in its whirlpool.  
Although the land is sterile, clothed in turf where mistletoe grows,  
it nevertheless belches forth from its deepest springs  
hot waters, which bathe the limbs and provide healing.

Here Christ’s worshipers continually serve the Lord in rejoicing;  
the brothers, joined to angelic choirs,  
sing a hymn of renown with joyful mouths  
and sweet-flowing melody.

## VIII. Leodegar Takes Up the Government of the Kingdom

Then Hiltrich obtained the summit of the kingdom,  
with affairs secured on every side, and shone in royal lineage.  
His brother Theodric was held under a careful guardian [Note: [Col. 1135D] The manuscript reads *tuetur*, “protects.”].

The fortune of the two returned in alternating turns:  
one flourished through happy successes, while the other declined.  
The lofty prophet was placed at the head of affairs;  
he was called prince of the Frankish nobles, according to custom.

For he was appointed chief of the household and ruler;  
the bishop, by his merits, undertook the rights of governing  
the court after the king. Then the people everywhere, rejoicing,  
filled the king and the prophet with glorious praises.  
They rejoiced that they had gained such patrons for themselves,  
so that the wise one might bend the reins of the kingdom’s scepters  
and king and bishop alike govern the lofty palaces.

Having assumed the administration [Note: [Col. 1135D] *Suscepto*; rather, for the sake of the meter, read *accepto*.],  
the prophet, at the senate’s request,  
strives to restore the kingdom to its former condition.

Peace in the fatherland, devotion among the people,  
and reverent worship among Christ’s faithful increased;  
at the same time the boundaries of the empire were enlarged in honor,  
and monuments of ancient times were brought to light.

The hero was always eager to imitate the wise nobles,  
whose minds were conscious of what was right,  
whom vain desire had never deceived,  
and who were accustomed to safeguard their homeland’s borders and kingdoms [Note: [Col. 1136D] *Imitarier*; compare verse 186.].

Verse 243.

## IX. The Bishop Returns to His Own City with the King and Faces Danger to His Life

After the affairs of the kingdom had been completely and happily settled,  
the third cycle of years now returned to the earth.  
But the demon, who had long been turning fearful hearts within him,  
could no longer bear to behold with his eyes or perceive with his face this situation [Note: [Col. 1136D] It seemed necessary to reconstruct this verse almost entirely. Who would not be wearied by the manuscript’s senseless reading: “The demons, long turning fearful hearts…”].

For, renewing his ancient deceits with an evil mind,  
he scattered between the two—the prophet and the ruler—  
seeds of the accursed darnel, staining their peace;  
and such frauds, sprung from a savage mind, he summoned to arms.

By chance the beautiful day of Easter had arrived,  
which was celebrated by all the people,  
the day on which the world was rescued through Christ’s blood.  
The prophet spoke these words from the king’s mouth:

“Let your authority command, O king—for I humbly seek your rule—  
that the Easter day be celebrated at Augustodunum,  
for your power is glorious there.”

The king promptly carried out the petitioner’s words. After this,  
the petitions delayed nothing; rejoicing together,  
with a great company accompanying them,  
they reached the city ruled by the holy bishop.  
There they decided to celebrate the peaceful feast.

While they were in the midst of these festivities,  
the savage enemy sent an evil man, who approached  
and began to speak from a doubtful mouth:

“Bishop, you must protect yourself with cautious care.  
While, in the middle of the night, you are taking sleep  
with a peaceful heart, the king intends  
to hand you over to savage throats,  
piercing your limbs so that you may pour out your soul in blood.  
Do not think that my words are flying empty through the air.  
Tonight, as my words assure you, the appointed end is near.”

At these words the prophet, overcome with grief,  
held his heart in silence and sorrow, turning great cares  
within his breast; quietly he beat his inward organs with sobs.  
Here he scattered his swift thoughts, there he divided them.  
He did not greatly fear for himself,  
but he shuddered at the king’s shameful deed  
and sought rather to spare the king, cautiously,  
lest he disgrace the honor of the feast by so great a crime.

Thus he thought to himself, while showing the people  
a cheerful face, until he had duly completed  
all the solemn rites before God.

When these things were done, he called upon the Lord in humble prayer:

“Grant, God, that I may fulfill my vows to you alone  
and not be held captive by the image of the deceptive world;  
but permit me to break the harmful bonds of the age.”

After speaking, he chose faithful servants from the entire assembly  
and unfolded these words to them in order:

“Hasten our flight, dear friends, lest that traitor,” he said,  
“cut down the bishop and pour out his blood,  
lest he stain the great annual feast with the bishop’s death.”

## X. Yielding to Envy, Leodegar Withdraws to Luxeuil and Soon Is Recalled to His City

At last he abandoned all the chains of the world.  
Throughout the night he hurried away upon a swiftly moving course,  
until daylight drove away the dark shadows  
and Phoebus breathed across the fields  
with his pale, rose-colored chariots.

The king himself remained exceedingly sad  
and filled the house with complaints at the bishop’s departure:

“What are we doing? Hurry, men; why are you abandoning him?” he said.  
“Let the men take up arms; let the strength of the young seize weapons.  
Let horsemen pursue this man; arm swift companies.  
Run after the prophet! What madness has seized us?”

From every side the crowd rushed forth, hastening to recall its master.

Verse 304.

[Col. 1137A]

Yet the prophet himself humbly prayed to be released [Note: [Col. 1137D] *Absolvier*; compare verses 186 and 249. As he imitated Virgil earlier, so now the author imitates Lucretius.].  
He sought the community of Luxeuil with rapid steps.

There Ebroin had indeed already remained in the sacred order as a cleric.  
Then both of them, seeking peace and pardon,  
poured abundant tears over their faces,  
and in turn they thus broke the bonds of their sins.

The outstanding father instructed them with friendly counsels—  
he who had ruled the sacred company of monks with zeal—  
and taught them what commands of the Lord must be observed.  
For a time he had separated them by a definite order,  
until devout peace should thoroughly join their discordant minds;  
then at last he instructed them to join their bodies together as well.

They carefully carried out the commands of the outstanding father  
and at last assumed the kindly form of monks.

At no other time had the final hour  
of the life of the ruler Hiltrich reached its limit.  
The people celebrated his savage funeral;  
his limbs were buried in dark tombs.

At last Theodric took up the authority over the peoples,  
sent out from the strict cloisters  
where he had previously remained.

But behold, the people approached from different directions  
and came before the king:

“We humbly ask that you not despise our petitions,  
but order our patrons to return.”

Everyone longed to see the face of both men,  
so that each might joyfully be restored to his former seat:  
Ebroin, and also the holy bishop Leodegar.

The king calmly replied to their opening words:

“Go quickly and report my words to the illustrious men:  
let it be permitted for the patrons to return to their own seats.”

Immediately the nobles, traveling by a swift road,  
returned to the monastery with these words:

“Father, return the familiar fathers; return them now, we beg you,  
for without them it is now wearisome to feed upon the upper air [Note: [Col. 1137D] *Quis* in the manuscript.];  
see how exhausted we are—we have come across  
long stretches of road to this place.”

At these words the father remained astonished.

“Do not, do not constrain me to such circumstances,” he had said,  
“so that I should compel Christ’s worshiping servants  
to return backward.”

At last, unwillingly, he granted the petitioners  
time to depart; but they, even more unwillingly,  
yielded to the place. Nevertheless, the outstanding father blessed them as they went:

“May the highest peace now follow you;  
you must continually preserve harmonious hearts;  
may devout peace always rejoice in your hearts.”

## XI. While the Citizens Joyfully Welcome Leodegar, Ebroin Plots New Frauds and Returns to the Palace

Together they went forward and drew near the city,  
which the distinguished man had once consecrated  
through his holy counsels.

No delay: rumor summoned the people; the crowd rushed together;  
the populous city resounded, and the shout was hurled to Olympus.  
The people went to meet him in a great triumphal procession;  
young and old alike hurried joyfully,  
fathers and young men, boys and unmarried girls,  
mothers joined together, and infants at their mothers’ breasts.

Every age hastened forth; hymns resounded joyfully.  
They welcomed the distinguished father, whom they had once mourned  
when he departed from his own seat.  
The crowd ceased from that activity [Note: [Col. 1137D] *Actu*. Perhaps *luctu*, “grief,” should be read—as though the poet had said, or intended to say, that the city was relieved of its mourning once Leodegar had been restored to his seat, after those who had acted in his place while he was in exile had been removed. Why not read *aestu*, “distress,” as in verse 398?]. Then the companions settled down  
to peaceful banquets and jointly filled the joyful feasts;  
they strove to surround the tables with prepared dishes.

Thus they spent the joyful day, until evening closed Olympus  
and the falling stars counseled sleep.

But when the savage Ebroin saw these things with an evil mind,  
he pressed down his livid heart, infected with dreadful poisons.  
He could not remain calm amid these events  
or give his limbs their customary nightly rest.  
Rather, he concealed his fraud beneath a serene face,  
until, covered by wicked darkness, he fled away,  
departing without companions and deprived of great honor.

Verse 369.

[Col. 1138A]

The prophet had wished to enrich him with generous wealth  
and return him joyfully to his own dwelling with an escort:

“Why do you silently raise yourself and depart in the middle of darkness?  
Come, tell me, I beg you: had you not also given your limbs to rest?  
It would have been better to travel for a while  
through the pleasant light of day;  
but the hours of night are sought by robbers.  
The son of light, however, avoids the darkness of night.

Or are you plotting frauds, fleeing with an evil mind?”

When Ebroin had been restored to his own place,  
he first sent peace agreements to those whom he had previously held as enemies;  
thus, after their offenses, he joined himself to them as a friend.

But he carried out all these things as a pretender with a treacherous heart.  
The outcome proves this: afterward he gathered wicked allies  
around the king, offered himself voluntarily,  
and, at the command of the great ruler,  
was received again in his former rank.  
From then on he was made chief of the household,  
prince of the nobles, and second to the king in authority.

## XII. Ebroin Proceeds Tyrannically Through Every Wicked Deed and Resolves to Crush Leodegar

[Col. 1138B]

Soon, raging, he drove on the goads beneath his black breast.  
Like a savage wolf, when its dry throat is parched,  
he ravages the gentle flock, greedily biting and dragging it.  
Like a lion, he terrifies the defenseless beasts with dark roars;  
full of anger, he strains their trembling necks  
and raises them up, or else, driven by furies and rage,  
presses on with dreadful slaughter and pours out innocent blood—  
men are struck down in the manner of battle [Note: [Col. 1138D] *More*; perhaps *morte*, “by death,” should be read.].

For he deprived many nobles of life and arms,  
strove to drive many from their native lands,  
and proscribed other nobles, stripping them of their beloved riches.  
After committing such crimes, he raged in wicked action [Note: [Col. 1138D] *Actu*; perhaps *aestu*, “in fury,” should be read.].

Meanwhile the prophet remained in residence, governing the city  
entrusted to him and consecrated by his holy counsels.

At once the wretched Ebroin, with a grim heart,  
planned to drive the prophet from his own seat.

“He will not escape unharmed from my hands,” he said,  
“he who so often opposed me in my undertakings,  
without suffering the punishment for what he formerly did.  
Rather, he will receive it; he will feel vengeance!

Because of him I was compelled to lose my hair,  
driven from the kingdom and forced to assume a monk’s habit.  
I abandoned my wife’s sweet embraces and kisses;  
I no longer held the kisses of my offspring hanging upon my neck.

Oh, if only some faithful person would avenge this anger for me!  
Come here, whoever you are, seeing what sort of wrong has been done.”

While he was considering such things, two men of wicked mind stood by him.  
They are said to have soothed his grief with flattering words:

“Now cease, prince, to cast miserable words into the air.  
Willingly disclose what your heart has decided.  
Speak: we shall gladly obey your words of our own accord.  
Look, we are already here, ready to fulfill what you desire.”

One was called Diddo, and the other Wegemarus [Note: [Col. 1138D] Wegemarus is elsewhere called Waimerus, Vaimirus, or Vagemar. Compare verse 609.].  
Ebroin said:

“Behold my sufferings, beloved hands, you who have taken pity on them.  
I have always held you firm. Now go and prepare an ambush;  
drive the prophet from his seat.”

## XIII. Augustodunum Is Besieged by Arms

They quickly strove to fulfill the command  
and the savage order of the ruler.  
A swift crowd rushed from every side, threatening with hard iron  
and with dark clubs.

Some sounded the empty trumpet; others shouted loudly.  
Some rushed behind them, burdened with round shields.  
Others carried broad spear-shafts in their hands.  
Some trusted in nimble feet; others bent the necks  
of wing-footed horses and thrust forward javelins  
from hollow quivers.

With such weapons, the raging crowd challenging battle  
went across the fields and held the city.

Verse 432.

[Col. 1139A]

The companions encouraged one another:

“Surround the walls with a rampart,  
or now climb the roofs by tall ladders.  
Let one party repeatedly shake the foundations  
of the wall below with a battering ram;  
let another hurl arrows from bowstrings [Note: [Col. 1139D] *Jactata*; perhaps *jactate*, “hurl,” should be read.].  
Let the better archer be present; provide strong weapons.  
Now, young men, we must complete what we have begun:  
come together, all of you.”

The servant of God had perceived these things.  
Then he gathered the entire clergy  
with crosses and wax lamps [Note: [Col. 1139D] The manuscript reads *laudibus*, “with praises.”]:

“Carry the crosses and adorn the bright lamps.  
Bring the holy relics and the ashes of the devout.  
Let us joyfully imitate the shining example of the Lord.  
He himself had gone forth first to meet the crowds;  
let us too, undaunted, hasten to meet these crowds.”

He spoke. He wished to preserve the innocent sheep  
and joyfully offered himself to the palm of martyrdom.

## XIV. Leodegar Is Horribly Blinded and Again Confined in a Monastery for Two Years

But at that time the executioner’s sword  
did not yet deliver the blow,  
when he wished to seize the heavenly wreath.  
The crown of martyrdom was delayed, not taken away.

Yet, alas, the impious faction, scorning reverence for Christ,  
laid hands upon him.  
It tore out his exceedingly bright eyes  
from beneath his serene brow  
and pierced them through with a sharply drawn weapon.

He therefore repaid the Lord with praises and thanks.  
For he is said to have praised the highest Thunderer in prayer:

“May salvation, power, and grace be yours, great Christ,  
who have wished me today to glorify you in so great a manner.”

Although the open windows beneath his brow were empty,  
the inner light nevertheless shone with the greatest brightness.

The savage hand entirely closed his bodily eyes;  
the exalted hand opened the radiant eyes of his heart.

A humble, patient man, a man of prayer, worship, and love,  
he remained continually, so that he might win the blessed palm.

When these excessively wicked deeds had thus been carried out,  
the prophet was held under the guard of a certain cautious monastery  
while the sun completed two circuits of the heavens.  
There he lay hidden patiently, providing examples for many.

## XV. Saint Garinus, Leodegar’s Brother, Is Buried under Stones and Adorned with the Jewels of Martyrdom

[Col. 1139C]

He had a brother, called Garinus,  
who, driven away by fear from his native shores,  
wandered as an exile here and there with uncertain steps.

Meanwhile the exiles were ordered to return  
and attend to the king’s customary services [Note: [Col. 1139D] *Insistere*. The copyist wrote *insiste* in error.].  
Garinus was ordered to be present among them.

Nor was the prophet afterward excluded from the court.

When Prince Ebroin looked upon them with an evil mind,  
he mocked both brothers with various blasphemies:

“Behold, stand here in accordance with your merits, you wretches,” he said.

Moved by these words, the blessed prophet is said to have spoken,  
silently drawing out long sighs from his heart:

“We suffer these things because of our merits,  
for we have committed many sins before God,  
whose losses we now endure.  
Yet Christ’s mercy is always greater than these things;  
he deigns to grant us eternal life.

Wretched Ebroin, cease now from your deeds.  
Behold, you have prepared many for death with a drawn sword.  
You, rather, pitiable man, are undergoing severe torments.  
Look: the gate beneath of burning hell stands open for you,  
with weeping companions of the flames  
and Gehenna prepared for you,  
unless you quickly earn pardon for these deeds.”

On hearing these words, inflamed still more by furies and anger,  
Ebroin immediately said:

“What madness deceives you?  
Go quickly away from here; drive such men away at once.  
Let them cease to carry such speeches through the air;  
they enjoy empty conversations and words alike.

Let Garinus quickly be punished by a hail of stones.

Verse 496.

[Col. 1140A]

Hurry, men; at last condemn the proud man.  
Bind him tightly with hard stakes and thongs.”

Seeing this, the prophet spoke from his heart:

“O honor, O brother, always most beloved to me,  
bend your ear here to a few counsels; I shall instruct you.  
Dear brother, now keep your heart firm.

This brief and passing end carries everything away [Note: [Col. 1139D] *Finis*. It is scarcely possible to restore this awkward text without often falling into solecisms. At this point the copyist had written, without any sense: *Est opus ista brevis currens vehit omam finis*. We have attempted, as best we could, to repair the text, though without preserving the Latin fully.].

Since the bitter decree of death holds us,  
it is established that we must submit our bodies  
to punishments for Christ’s name.

Yet a bright life awaits us at the summit of heaven,  
a life that remains, that has no end,  
and that endures in blessedness.

Do not fear. Let us hasten joyfully  
to the place where we shall reign.”

There was no delay: they strove to pour out their garments to the winds.  
The impious crowd rushed forward, barely touching the ground  
with its feet; stones flew through the thin air,  
hurled by arms drawn back.

Suddenly a harsh cloud thickened;  
a stony hail fell. Impious fury supplied the weapons,  
and the hard rocks were scattered with rosy blood.

Amid the stones that clattered around him,  
he prayed to the Lord with outstretched palms:

“O God, you who deem me worthy to be taken away  
from this life through torment like a martyr’s,  
give me the crown of eternal life.”

The prophet himself also wished to receive the crown  
together with his brother and to close the limit  
of their fragile life,  
so that together they might enjoy the blessed citizens in heaven.

## XVI. Leodegar Is Subjected to Various Torments and Handed over to Waningus for Custody

The wretched Ebroin delayed hastening  
the day of the holy martyr.  
He wished to postpone the crown he had earned,  
so that he might assail the Lord with harsh blasphemies  
and prevent the martyr from being regarded as equal  
in merit to the saints.

What the Lord preserves for his devoted servant to receive,  
human impiety desires to take away from the brothers  
as they rise to the lofty seats;  
yet divine devotion joins them with heaven forever.

Thus the madman thinks that he can bend the divine mind  
in a human fashion.  
But God is not bent by any fraud;  
he never turns his devout ear away from his servants.

[Col. 1140C]

When he saw that the prophet’s inner resolve was firm,  
his mind, infected with evil, groaned,  
turning goads beneath his black breast;  
burning fury added anger.

Then he ordered the gentle, humble, patient man,  
walking barefoot, to tread in a certain pool  
which contained beneath its vast waters sharp stones  
in the manner of nails.

When ordered to do so [Note: [Col. 1140D] *Quo jussus*; perhaps *jussu*, “by command,” or *qui jussus*, “he who was ordered,” should be read.], he stepped into the stream barefoot.  
Horrible blood flowed from his torn skin  
and poured over the thirsty sand in rosy streams.

Already exhausted in his feet and wearied in body,  
he stopped and beat his trembling limbs  
with repeated blows.

At last, compelled, he was thrown down upon the broad ground,  
while they ordered his lips to be cut away with iron,  
or his tongue [to be cut out].

With his eyes removed, his tongue and both lips gone,  
and his steps exhausted—or rather, his whole body—  
he could no longer praise the highest Thunderer  
with his customary offices;  
but he carried praises to the Lord in his mind  
and directed devout prayers to Christ’s ears.

When he saw that human assistance  
was increasingly absent from him,  
he desired Christ’s constant aid to be present.

Then the merciless Ebroin, carrying a heart full of poison,  
empty of understanding, savage, harsh, and bitter,  
summoned someone quickly and finally said to him:

“You have seen him before; now, with an inflated spirit,  
seize the proud man. Bind him in the tight chains  
of imprisonment, Waningus.”

Spare neither care nor ears; my command will come, and it will condemn him, according to his merits, to the ultimate punishment. Go quickly.” He goes swiftly, striving to conduct the man cautiously all the way to the monastery, which is known to have once been called Fiscamnus; there the virgin company remained under a single mother.

*Verse 564.*

[Col. 1141A] Endowed with holy deeds throughout all ages, there she continually resounded with hymns to the Lord in measured voices; dwelling there for so long a time as the martyr did, she reverently worshipped the high-throned Lord in supplication. [Col. 1141D] *Fruteta* [“thickets”], written incorrectly as *frutecta*.

For she spared food, taking little drink as well; rarely did she allow straw to her wearied limbs, and often, leaning against a wall, she rested her body. With face, hands, and entire body intent upon the task, she sought with utmost effort the King of the stars, asking him to loosen crimes, grant pardon, and remit guilt.

The tireless bishop performed these things night and day. Then, when the lips had suddenly been cut away and the tongue was silent, by divine gift the voice of speech was restored. At once the organs and throat returned to life; the jaws resumed their accustomed functions and strove to speak. Without delay, teachings flowed from his sweetly speaking mouth, and sacred words were opened to the virgin flock.

Whenever he expounded teachings to the holy virgins, he poured them into their hearts like sweet honey.

[Col. 1141B] In a flower-bearing field, at the first season of spring, shoots emerge while rain is scattered from heaven; at the appointed times, slowly, they swell, and the thickets grow, [Col. 1141D] *Spernebant* [“they despised”]. The codex is corrupted by many errors in this passage; I have not yet corrected all of them:

“They despised him greatly for his sinister deeds,

and rejoice in giving themselves to the work of a better life.”

and the pregnant ears of grain grow heavy with full stalks.

In the same way the bishop, watering the hearts of Christ’s worshippers, pours forth doctrine flowing from a pure spring. There many despised their wicked deeds; [Col. 1141D] *Militibus* [“by the soldiers”]. The copyist wrote *milibus* so that the meter might be satisfied to some extent. they rejoiced to devote themselves to the pursuit of a better life, believing that through his admonitions they had escaped everlasting danger.

From every side eager peoples gather to hear the words of salvation that the holy man, joyful, drew forth from his mouth, providing nourishment for all.

### XVII. Leodegarius, at Ebroinus’s instigation, is stripped of his office and condemned to be beheaded

At that time the king ordered a council to be held. Bishops came, and at the same time crowds came from every direction: Theodricus, the illustrious prince, and Ebroinus himself. The two expellers also hurried there: [Col. 1141C] the treacherous Wagemarus, and likewise the wicked Diddo, Wagemarus’s associate; equal guilt bound them together.

Others also assembled, men whom swift and deserved vengeance had not allowed to go unpunished. First, cast out by that council and made a defendant, Diddo was already falling, mocked by the soldiers [Col. 1141D] *Perditor* [“destroyer”], the codex, he who had once driven the seer from his own seat; and, as a mad traitor, he was condemned. [Col. 1142D] *Concilium* [“council”]. To bring some light to these tangled words, one should consult what Ursinus, another author of the *Life of Saint Leodegarius*, wrote at nearly the same point: “Then they summoned him also to the same synod; yet it is not confirmed that he was within the council, but rather that the king and Ebroinus conferred with him separately. It is clearly established that in this conversation he foretold many future events to them, and that these came to pass.” No. 19.

Therefore, because of his deserts, he was driven away in exile from the beloved shores, and the sentence of death punished the wretched man.

Unhappy Wagemarus, thrown down from a similar honor, then followed—the accomplice or wicked supporter in the case of the righteous man. At last, it is said, he was worn down by savage beatings; his faction saw him shamefully afflicted by punishments, he who had assumed an honor he did not deserve. It is believed that this happened by the will of the supreme ruler of Olympus: for afterward the unhappy man tied his throat in a noose, hastened toward the shades of death, and sought the seat of Tartarus, bitterly punished.

With this reward Ebroinus presents his friends who had driven the righteous seer from his own seat. [Col. 1141D]

Now the final contests remain for the just man, contests by which, already victorious, he ascends Olympus. He is led out from the strict enclosure where he had previously remained, where the saint had sanctified virginal ears with his teaching. At the command, he arrived before the face of the prince and Ebroinus. They held a council outside, in one particular place, seeking to investigate hidden matters and things to come.

*Verse 626.*

[Col. 1142A] They tested the holy man, to whom all the sentence that awaited them—or others—was known in advance; the outcome soon proved everything. Against him the grim and wicked man spoke as follows:

“Why do you so often vaunt yourself with empty words, wicked man? Do you hope that you can earn the palm of martyrdom? Once you have been found worthy, you may take up the garland and palm. No crown of life is granted for deeds such as these, nor do I deem you worthy to close your course with such a gift; for you are closing your life by a hastened death, proud man.”

Unhappy Ebroinus had spoken thus, turning over in his mind that, as he had formerly stripped him of worldly honour, so he would utterly drive him from the realms of heaven, from which he strove to expel him by this pious recompense. Yet the saint adhered all the more closely to the eternal realms.

Then he repeatedly summoned a certain man:

“Take him, Rotbert, and strive to bind him in the enclosure of chains,” he said. “The time will now come when I shall send him, as he deserves, beneath Tartarus to worthy punishments.”

The man, impetuously, took up the commands that had to be obeyed, [Col. 1142B] and strove cautiously to lead him to his own house.

### XVIII. How the blessed man, even before his martyrdom, was endowed with heavenly light

While they strove to cover the road with alternating steps, they suddenly saw him, exhausted in his feet and weakened in his limbs, come to a halt in the middle of the fields. Taking pity on him, the man offered assistance, or poured out a drink, while the cupbearer prepared to pour the soothing liquid.

For a shining figure came with a great light; a flame sent from heaven, radiant, rushed forth, and, caressing the martyr’s head, settled above it. It touched the saint’s uninjured hair and preserved it.

When the men saw this, they were afraid; their voices stuck in their throats, their hair stood erect, trembling seized their limbs, and repeated sobs beat upon their breath and entrails.

When they had recovered themselves, they broke into these words from their breasts:

“At last, worshipper of the Lord, tell us, best of men: behold, suddenly we are traveling along a road with unequal steps, while this light is flying and gliding from the hinge of heaven; and now it is above your head, flashing with brilliant radiance. This terrifies everyone; we all stagger on our feet. We have never seen a sign like this from heaven: it encircles your temples in a burning circle.”

The martyr heard this, fell prostrate upon the ground, and addressed these words and thanks to the Lord in supplication:

“You who dwell in the heavenly citadels, guarding the realms; you who are present as maker of heaven and creator of the universe; you who rule the fourfold world with supreme authority: I worship you, to you I willingly offer vows and thanks, whose command sent this light from heaven, since you deign to place such a sign above me.”

The people, stirred by these holy words, softened their hearts. Turning to the Lord with their whole hearts, despising tribulation and pursuing better things completely, they avoided the road of death and sought the heavenly kingdoms.

The servant of the Lord taught them what holy commands were:

“You see, my children, how the unstable machinery of the universe turns, flying through the clear air like smoke. So the pompous glory of the world collapses in its flourishing. The court of God calls us all, and the blessed dwellings; the angelic beings desire to cherish us in their own bosoms and embraces as fellow citizens, if only our mind does not now grow sluggish and cold. Wretched people who despise the Lord hasten beneath Tartarus.”

Then the male and female servants together—Rotpertus and his wife, the whole household—venerated the seer with chaste love. *Verse 689.*

[Col. 1143A] They all utterly rejected their former error. They persisted in holy deeds and continually attended upon Christ.

### XIX. The final passion and victory of the holy martyr

While the martyr was doing these things, not much time afterward, the savage mind, ever thirsting for the righteous man’s death, did not rest; neither the insane fury of slaughter nor anger ceased until it struck the limbs of the holy seer with a blade, delivered his body to death, and poured out his blood.

For the final day and the sacred passion came, when the Lord ordained that his servant should be enriched with blessed kingdoms, and should carry the saintly spirit to the stars, where he would receive the sacred rewards due to his merits.

Then Ebroinus sent horsemen at headlong speed, threatening the saint from behind with shields and iron. The earth gave a sound; the hoof struck the rotten field. [Col. 1143C] *Altum*, read *agrum* [“the field”]. The horse ground its teeth against the bit and shook its bloodied mouth; watery moisture poured forth, and fire boiled in its bones.

Four able men hurried to Robert’s house, [Col. 1143B] to seize the holy seer. Having seized him, they carried him through the deep woods by stealthy steps, turned back over unknown hills, and led the blessed man away.

While they were doing this, the martyr suddenly restrained them. He said:

“O children, do not lose your way in these expanses. Behold, exhausted, stop at last after so many efforts. I am here, not unaware; fulfill the command. Here I shall end my life and the labors of my course. The time is coming quickly; children, do not delay the orders.”

Then suddenly they rushed forward, while the fourth remained arrogantly standing; three of them fell at his humble feet and begged pardon:

“We ask you now to forgive our crimes,” they said; “bless us also, venerable priest.”

At once he extended his hand and blessed them.

The fourth rebuked them:

“Stand away from here, defeated,” he said. “But what shall I do? Speak now with a fearful mind. Extend your head to the throat,” he said, “or bow your neck.”

He himself stood upright, flashing with his drawn blade.

At once the martyr knelt and stretched out his palms, asking these things in supplication and striking the stars with his prayer:

“Benevolent Father, you sent your Son [Col. 1143C] *Direxit*, the codex, is defective in both sense and metre; perhaps read *direxti*, since *direxisti* is metrically inadmissible even by synaeresis. You sent him to take away the sins of the world and to heal its wounds by holy blood;

*Verse 729.*

[Col. 1144A] through him the world deserved to know you as the true Creator, all ancient error having been removed. Empty error departs; the images of the gods fall. [Col. 1144C] *Caedunt fincmenta*, the codex. Grace returns ready, faithful worship comes; the whole world worships you everywhere—the earth, the sea, and the stars. The sheep, birds, and fish that cross the rivers all testify that you, the true Maker, created everything.

Have mercy on all and forgive them, and spare all my enemies and these men, because their hearts do not know the truth, though they inflict savage torments and death.

For this reason, benevolent Redeemer, before your clear presence I believe that I shall be presented and shall take up this everlasting life. Now receive my spirit in your gentle hands.”

After these words, the armed man cut off his head with a drawn sword and, with accursed hands, drenched the earth with the sacred blood. Thus the victor ascended to the bright heavens.

Immediately the Lord performed great miracles, as the Psalmist sings: “All of you now behold with your eyes. Behold, the Lord adorns his saint with great honor.”

[Col. 1144B] After his head had been cut off, the body remained standing erect, it is said, for as long as the sun takes to complete one hour’s course across the sky.

A living heat remained in his limbs; warmth held his bones. The murderer, impatient, struck him with his heels so that the body would fall more quickly to the earth.

—Unhappy sword-bearer, stained with the martyr’s rosy blood, you who struck the sacred body with your heel: you were not permitted to endure these punishments with impunity. Soon, seized by a manifold plague of the demon, you were held fast and, cast into the midst of flames, gasped for breath.—

Ash fled from his mouth until he hastened toward the shades.

Afterward the married couple were pleased secretly to entrust the limbs to graves, together with the garments sprinkled with the aforesaid blood. The sacred limbs were buried in a small basilica; they remained there, hidden beneath the ground, for approximately two years and six months.

On this day, when these things had been accomplished with clear signs, on the second day of the month of [Col. 1144C] October—*Octoribus*, for the second day of October, dedicated to the holy martyr—believe the solemn rites truly.

With scant ability, a certain portion of the flower-bearing life has now been completed. [Col. 1144C] Let the end of this book now be at hand, and let the beginning of another at last be taken up again. [Col. 1144C] *Reputatur*, read *repetatur* [“let it be taken up again”].

*Verse 768.*

## BOOK TWO. ON THE MIRACLES OF SAINT LEODEGARIUS

[Col. 1143]

### I. On the miracles of the holy martyr before the elevation of his body

[Col. 1143D]

The earlier little book contains the deeds of the consecrated martyr, which he performed peacefully while clothed in the covering of flesh. Now, stripped of his bodily vesture, behold, this second book gathers together the deeds he performed through wondrous powers.

Thus far I have set forth the holy gifts of the righteous seer, in a dry style indeed, but with deeds rich in substance. Yet greater are the things he accomplished after trampling down his faults, when, victorious, he already sat upon Olympus, by the Lord’s grant; these are preserved as manifest through various holy signs.

O discourse that gives shape to my tongue, glide into it, though it lies sluggish. Before the tongue could speak, let everything first be spoken by human lips in song, so that from a little I might recount it widely to many.

Meanwhile, a priest, ever watchful in devoted spirit, kept vigil at the small basilica. Gazing from afar at night, he saw a lantern shining; supported by no human attendant, behold, suddenly it revealed itself voluntarily in its own flames.

*Verse 783.*

[Col. 1144D] It appeared, and the news immediately spread here and there in pleasant report; they celebrated the martyr’s tomb in shining speech. Then greater signs radiated forth in succession.

The beloved gift returned to blinded eyes; firm strength was restored to the feet of the lame; the pleasing stroke of the air returned to their ears; the dreadful apparition, falling from the limbs of the possessed body, departed, and by its departure lifted both body and mind.

Through these powers the benevolent man first became renowned everywhere.

Meanwhile, the church’s custodian remained at the seer’s tomb, steadfast in vigilant devotion. At last, in the dark of night, a thief maliciously stole property that the guardian himself had previously gathered by his own labor.

The thief left the guardian’s empty dwelling behind him, taking with him one shoe, which he had held reverently. [Col. 1143D] *Queiscum, quem tenuit reverenter, calceus unus …*—words plainly disordered and almost nonsensical, unless perhaps they are understood as follows: “One shoe of the martyr, which the cleric had held reverently, is said to have been carried away from these buildings.”

*Verse 800.*

[Col. 1145A] The same cleric, returning so that he might promptly visit his own dwelling, discovered that this *acerram* had been stripped of its fittings. [Col. 1145D] *Haspe acerram*, that is, a house deprived of its door or of the hinge of its doorway. Compare Cangius.

He hurried back to the venerable tombs, tearing his hair and beating his breast with his fists. His cheeks were not without tears, nor his throat without cries; shouting and weeping, he rushed about with excessive lamentation. Persisting in supplication and adding the night to his daily prayers, he begged that the stolen property be restored to him.

The exhausted thief returned in madness; when the burden of the shoe weighed upon him, he unwillingly restored the great spoil to its master.

But the master perpetrated false perjury against his servant. Soon worthy and pitiless vengeance followed them both: the master surrendered his life in a swift death, and the servant-thief was condemned to bitter punishment.

### II. The miracles are reported to Ebroinus, and his envy and sudden death are recounted

The growing signs did not long remain hidden from the deceitful Ebroinus. A report everywhere makes clear by certain indications what he had previously concealed through the evil art of envy. [Col. 1145B]

—Look upon this, envious, rapacious, murderous, pitiless adulterer, now that the martyr reigns with the Lord in the citadel: the signs of the holy seer shine, radiate, blaze, are displayed, and are loved; his virtue, adorned, gleams.

Now what will you be able to say against these things with false speech? What else, Ebroinus, except that you groan in your heart and tremble silently?

Each person strives to obtain from the tomb the desired healing for his limbs. One rejoices that healthy steps have returned to him; another rejoices that clear rays have returned to his eyes, darkness having been expelled and the harmful discoloration removed.

Another rejoices that he has vomited forth the demon’s grim poison, and the power granted cures everyone. This proves that he whom you promised to the savage realms of Tartarus reigns in heaven: your power has been driven away.—

Struck by such signs, Ebroinus grieved. Breaking this utterance from the depths of his breast, he spoke these complaints into his wife’s ears:

[Col. 1145C] “Alas for me! Why do I hear so many people celebrating the tomb? Why is such a great gathering of the people carried there? Tell me, wife: do these things appear true or false? I judge that they are more likely false stories traveling through the common people’s ears—that a martyr [the text is uncertain here: *Martyra (quam?)*] deserved to receive such crowns. I believe that the crowd has been deceived by such omens.

“Yet, to make us certain, let there be a messenger who goes and returns swiftly; let him bring us reliable information and resolve our doubts.

“Come, dear companion, let some servant be sent. Let him go to the tomb and inquire into everything.”

The carrier, proceeding to the tomb, ordered the guardians to tell him what firm judgment they held concerning these matters, which the people were proclaiming and which they confessed to be true.

The wretched messenger delayed celebrating the holy tomb and uttered empty words:

“This dead man lying here, covered by a worthless turf,” he said, “will not be able to provide powerful healing.”

Having spoken thus foolishly, he immediately struck the urn with his foot, looked down, and departed. At once an evil disease seized him; tearing him apart and torturing his entrails, it finally ended his life with a mournful death.

They did not laugh at your arrival, nor do you bring joy, traveler, to those masters who sent you. Learn from your punishments not to despise any saint: certainly it would have been better to pray to the blessed man on bended knees than to strike the sacred tomb with your feet.

Ebroinus waited anxiously, wondering what the messenger would bring him; uncertain, he wavered in a mind divided by conflicting thoughts. Sadly, he murmured to himself in a silent voice:

“Why does the servant who was sent keep delaying? Why is he also late in returning? Is it not for some reason? Or has the ultimate fate carried him away, just as earlier it carried away the man who killed the seer with his sword?

“We discovered that his limbs were immediately reduced to ashes. This man too is now held by a similar fate. Perhaps a pursuing punishment struck him on his return and brought him, with equal destruction, all the way to ashes.

“What shall we do? The glory of the man whose fame is now growing everywhere makes our former deeds appear excessively shameful. His fame flies about, fragrant with radiant report; and we, as guilty men, are driven along by the voices of everyone.

“But lest the fame of this man flow forth still more in gentle speech, let us try, by an evil stratagem, to heap false and wicked words upon him, so that the glory of our praise among the people may not be diminished.”

While he was considering such things, death seized him in a swift course. The savage throat of the abyss enclosed him—the man who had forced many to death with a drawn sword. A burning sword stripped him of life and weapons.

God’s sentence, expressed in true words, was fulfilled: whoever in madness should stain the limbs of the martyr would himself pour out his blood when struck by a sword.

[Col. 1146B] Let it suffice to say that the tyrant was finally punished by such an end; from here I shall now tell the remaining events.

### III. A dispute arises among three bishops concerning the elevation of the holy martyr

When these things had happened, the blessed power of the martyr became manifest and burned throughout the entire kingdom.

Just as incense grows warm in fires, or crushed mustard seeds emit a fragrant and shining odor, or scented herbs are pounded with their heavy flowers, and precious ointments gleam in hollow vessels, so the fame that spread through every place flew about in holy report; the peoples thronged to the great miracles that hostile treachery had previously hidden from many.

Meanwhile, the blessed fame of all the seers and nobles was carried to the ears of the great king. Bishops, clergy, monks, and high and low alike hurried eagerly along the road, competing with one another. [Col. 1146C] Both sexes with one accord celebrated the virtues.

Everyone joined the clear, life-giving miracles of the martyr to praises beneath a starry circle beyond the clouds.

Three bishops rose from the great assembly: Vincianus, Ansoaldus, and Ermanacharius. Each had decided that the body belonged to his jurisdiction, and each desired to carry the blessed man away from the tomb.

“Behold, the consecrated bones lie in land belonging to my jurisdiction,” said the first. “Here, while the saint journeyed to the stars, he received rest; here he was first revealed through blessed signs.”

“Stop contending in such words, brother,” said the second. “It is clear that he was related to me by beloved flesh; this is the parish that I govern as bishop, and he was born from here and took the beginnings of his life here. [Col. 1146D] This opinion favors those who maintain that Saint Leodegarius was born at Poitiers, or originated from the people of Poitiers. Therefore the blessed martyr is granted to me by right.”

At these words the third restrained both seers:

“Cease at last to burden the assembled crowd with such words, and instead attend to what I say.

“Let the blessed remains consecrate the seat that the bishop held, the seat that the fortunate man instructed with sacred teaching; it is fitting that he rest in the allotment of the other see.”

All fell silent and pressed their fingers to their mouths. After these words, they desired to obtain the help of a better counsel; they decided to join fasting to their prayers.

Together they strove to appeal to the supreme Thunderer, asking to whom he would rather grant the man on account of his merits.

The entire day was prolonged with holy hymns, and the night itself was held in vigilant watchfulness. Then, as dawn reddened—the day on which he would wish the sacred palm to be handed over after the darkness had been driven away—Phoebus also rose from his ruddy rising.

The bishops adorned the altars and celebrated Masses; they fed the attentive people with sacred offerings.

*Verse 943.*

[Col. 1147A] On three tablets the names had been written; each carried the name of its particular seer, and the tablets were kept beneath the covering in the middle of the altar. When the sacred Masses had been duly completed, they ordered a single servant, who knew nothing of the matter, to open the tablet and take whichever one God wished him to choose. He promptly carried out the command.

The first page, brought to the light, declared Ansoaldus and showed that he had remained endowed with such a gift. Everyone’s voices testified that he was worthy of this honor, since he had received so precious a gift. Joyfully they all gave him the palm and the right hand; at last, without doubt, they abandoned the restraints of the dispute.

### IV. How many miracles were performed during the translation of the sacred body as far as Poitiers

Then the servant of the Lord entrusted the task to a faithful disciple whom the martyr had once nurtured with careful instruction, who governed the monks whom the martyr had previously governed. He was called Audulfus, according to the care of his parents. Let him gladly perform the duty and carry out the command; let him reverently lead the holy limbs all the way to Poitiers.

“Go quickly,” he said. “Take companies of the brothers with you. Do not delay. Carry both patrons to their proper seat with sonorous hymns. Perhaps I myself shall dedicate the house and place of rest.”

They went quickly and fulfilled the commands of the shepherd who had given the order. They loaded the sacred bones into baskets, and all returned joyfully along the desired roads.

As soon as the limbs were moved, their great power was not lacking. The sick departed healed of various diseases; limbs long weakened received the desired remedy.

Giving thanks to the High-Throned One as they witnessed such miracles, those present reported them and prepared to continue along the road.

Then the pedestrian crowd also followed and rushed onward. Devoted in mind to the holy ministers, both sexes joined them and ran eagerly. They burned with the blessed man’s holy power and desired to be blessed through the worthy merits of his martyrdom.

Some strove to carry a part of the bier, others to touch the sacred veil, so that they too might bear the blessed man upon their shoulders. With lights, crosses, and bright lamps, the worshippers of Christ hurried in alternating companies. They rivaled the angelic citizens and struck at the stars; they sang shining praises with incense-bearing fragrance.

Whoever had been pressed by a powerful disease or an evil weakness, or whoever had long been tormented by an oppressive illness, if he touched the sacred veil or the holy bier, returned with healed limbs and a sound step.

Let true faith prevail, once false error has been removed, while the body itself is carried swiftly along the roads.

They were already approaching the houses of a certain village. Behold, distressed parents hurried toward them, carrying in their arms a daughter whose sight had been blinded. For seven periods she had endured dumbness and lay exhausted in her limbs; a threefold weakness continually condemned her body.

While they desired the girl to touch the saint or the threads of the bier, night, advancing on blue wings, had arrived. Meanwhile a deep sleep held her exhausted.

In a shining vision she reported that two men had come to her and strengthened the sick girl with these words:

“Behold, the salvation you desire is yours; do not delay in believing. It will come.”

The healing immediately followed her. When she awoke, she possessed her eyes, her step, and her tongue.

Soon healed, she offered praises and thanks to God, because through the martyr’s merits she received a long span of the present life, her old illness having fled.

Nor is your healing small, woman, when the blessed martyr acts as physician. A demon had long occupied the caves of your breast; it tightened its grip, but its madness fled as you were dragged by both hands and both arms bound, so that you could touch the cloth of the bier.

*Verse 1013.*

[Col. 1148A] Do not be afraid, madwoman, though you are shaken by such a great illness. Thousands of gifts were nevertheless being bestowed. Behold, suddenly, through the holy servant of Christ, as you touched the bier, the hostile spirit quickly left your limbs.

From there the men, joyful and enriched by various successes, entered the shining buildings of the city of Tours. At that point the ready bishop, accompanied by a great crowd, came out to meet them with honor befitting the miracles; striving to lead the body through the middle of the city, he was hailed with exalted praises, and Olympus rang aloud.

Behold, a woman was dragged along, bound with harsh chains, accused of the wicked death of her own husband and soon destined to lose the dear life from her body, unless the Lord should perhaps bring aid to the poor woman.

When she saw them carrying the bier of the holy martyr, she cried out with a mighty voice, breaking from her breast these words:

“Behold, merciful Leudegar, look upon my punishments now; [Col. 1147D] The editor reads *nunc* from the three letters *snc* written by the copyist, of which the first appears to have entered by error. Deign to release me, wretched woman, from unjust chains, and remove the threats and drive away the wicked death that now unjustly threatens me, condemned as I am.

“Help me, I beg you; grant pardon and hear the one who asks. I stretch my suppliant hands to the stars, martyr.”

With such tears she thundered forth. Suddenly the cords burst apart, and the chains yielded to the hands around her neck. The executioners stood stupefied and withdrew; at last they left the innocent woman far behind.

The people often repeated this deed in their speech.

### V. So many miracles, especially in the territory of Poitiers, that speech can scarcely describe them

My mind, drawing out long periods of idleness, wastes away in sluggishness. In the midst of my throat, compressed by lazy lips, the tongue lies still; the fingers will not be able to guide the pen gracefully; the eyes are sunk in dark gloom; the mind itself remains swollen with excessive earthly vapors.

Shake off your sluggishness; drive away your lazy torpor. Give, God, to my fingers their accustomed service and to my tongue speech, so that they may grasp these things; let familiar breaths return, and let sacred songs rise through the veins. [Col. 1147D] *Per venias*, or perhaps *per venas* [“through the veins”].

[Col. 1148C] We do not sing of fierce battles or the grim duel of luckless Hector and equally savage Achilles, when the Argive force destroyed its ancestral Pergamene kingdom; nor do we sing of the torches stained with dreadful blood, which Turnus and Aeneas are said to have sought with twofold sword, the false household gods having been led away while Latinus held the kingdom.

Rather, we sing of the sacred trophies of the saints, who through their own blood deserved lasting honor.

Let me recount the long-interrupted miracles of the martyr, who healed two needy sufferers in swift succession.

One was lame in his feet, wearied by many years; sluggish and long wasting away, with the road denied to him, he could not take the beloved step upon his feet.

He was carried to the saint and invoked him in supplication. Joyfully he obtained the desired healing for his feet.

A woman hastening forward, afflicted by a malignant disease, stretched hands with fingers deformed and bent toward the stars:

“Look now, martyr, at the claw so often cruelly driven into my limbs, and how it does not cease to increase the pain throughout my body. Quickly grant that this harmful plague depart; grant, physician of Christ, grant now the remedies of health.”

Immediately, with a cry, the disfiguring disease withdrew. Its lurid color departed and left the dry bones; by Christ’s gift the former strength returned to her hands.

When the bishop heard that the company of his companions had hastened to a certain estate belonging to his own authority, Ansoaldus, moved by devoted love, sent disciples to meet them, so that they might provide food for the weary people:

“Go,” he said, “and aid the weary people with provisions. Let there be abundant banquets for everyone and an ample supply of bread. Provide delicacies as well, and clear drink, so that the holy body may properly be carried forward without delay.”

*Verse 1083.*

[Col. 1149A] The crowd, made joyful by such blessings, now rested. But the high Judge had performed a marvelous deed for all: the liquid had returned in doubled streams; sweet must flowed, and it increased even through its own vessels.

No longer contained by its enclosures, it flowed abundantly across the fields, and the level ground was drenched by streams. One sign was added to another, miracles to miracles.

From there they made their way swiftly toward a village beside which a river flowed beneath a vast whirlpool. The pedestrian crowd gladly approached this river, called the Vienne and the Sannonavius.

Behold, a threatening storm swelled with roaring force and rushed across the surface of the strait, driven by furies. The turbulent sea boiled with black waves; the south wind rolled the sands toward the upper air.

There was no open space for crossing, nor any suitable passage for boats amid the waves:

“Do you see,” it said—[Col. 1149D] *Scopulis*. The text is rough and mutilated and seems to require *speculis*: “Do you see? It resounds from the rocks”—“how the waters mingle with a great roar, and how the winds likewise prepare to clash with their weapons? East Wind and South Wind contend with one another in combat.

[Col. 1149B] From the summits of the mountains the echo of the waves resounds.

“It is better to restrain our swift steps on these banks than to be submerged beneath the swollen waves after the ship is wrecked. At last, cease trusting the faithless winds.”

But the fearless father, entrusted with the care of affairs, said:

“Surely God can restrain these shallows—the God who once, commanding the sea, broke its anger:

‘You, sea, give way to your place; and you, swollen winds, be silent.’

The former calm has returned; the sea’s blue expanse has ceased its agitation.—He too will be able to lay low the disturbed waves.

“Go forward confidently; bring the body aboard the ship.”

When these things had been done, the threats fell silent, and the savage storm, turned aside, came to rest as gentle water.

Here a foreign woman, with her blind child, approached, wishing to obtain healing for her child. Spending the night in vigils and prayers, she remained where the healing limbs of the life-giving martyr rested. His customary gifts returned to her with healing.

Thus the windows long closed in her forehead were opened. The mother rejoiced, enriched by such remedies.

### VI. On the miracles performed in the city of Poitiers

[Col. 1149C]

At last the bishop, who had long held back, obtained what he desired; he learned that the swift company was near. He himself came out from his seat to meet them, accompanied by many noblemen, the clerical order, and a procession of monks; the people, the crowd, the poor, and both sexes were mixed together, with shining crosses and bright lamps filled with incense.

All the clouds thundered above, and the fields trembled together. Each person strove to outstrip the others along the swift road: one to touch the horns of the bier, another the fringe of the veil, another to bear the burden upon his shoulders, another to carry its great weight.

At last, having received so great a pledge, the joyful bishop proceeded with it to the city of Poitiers.

Here too came a woman who, with the sinews of her entire body bent, looked down toward the earth; compelled by an illness of many years, she could not raise her bent neck or lift her face.

“Grant healing to me also, martyr, as you grant it to many through God’s power,” she said resolutely.

She remembers the bright orb [Col. 1149D] *Clarum*, namely the sun; “she remembers the bright orb.” Compare verse 1242. through bodily sufferings.

Immediately she offered praises and thanks to the Lord alone.

From there, with joyful steps, they sought Saint Radegund, who shines through sacred merits and is known above the heavens. Here a young man had lain, tormented by dreadful pain, sluggish, cold, and weakened in all his limbs.

*Verse 1149.*

[Col. 1150A] Here too he rose healthy through the martyr’s merits. At once he was added as a sound companion to the companies. Along the more prosperous road they entered the dwelling of the eloquent seer, who had once been driven from his own shores by a savage schism: Hilarius, when he condemned with pious speech the false doctrines that the unhappy Arius had scattered through the regions of the world.

Such a dispute had arisen between the two men. [Col. 1150D] Add, as I think, *viris* [“between the two men”] for sense and meter, namely between Hilarius and Arius; otherwise shape the verse as follows: *Lis fuerat cum tanta viris* [“Such a dispute had arisen between the men”]. These verses are especially crude; some may perhaps accept them in such a way that our poet turns out to be Poitevin, and from this they may wish to discern the author’s homeland.

Hilarius proclaimed such teaching from his mouth:

“There are three persons; God’s substance is simple.”

Arius joined a threefold *ousia* [Greek: οὐσία, “substance”] to the three persons.

Here a man who had lain sluggishly on his bed with a cold body was healed of his twofold weakness; a girl who had long been deprived of her sight in the night was also healed.

The girl herself remained beside the sacred altar because of these events, intent upon holy duties for as long as life remained; she celebrated the martyr’s tomb with great honor.

### VII. By what miracles the cell of Saint Maxentius, which Leodegarius once governed, is illuminated

[Col. 1150B] The martyr loves to obtain peaceful rest for his limbs and to enjoy the station where he once governed the flock.

Now at last, bishop, do not allow your vows to be delayed. Go quickly, accompanied by the great triumph of the people; yourself, in supplication, place your shoulders beneath the horns of the bier!

The monks await the return of their former father, and the benevolent Maxentius watches from his peaceful dwelling. He already desires to warm again the blessed limbs.

The martyr, carried upon the bishop’s shoulders, went forward, while across the broad spaces a numerous flock came to meet him—the flock to which he had formerly provided nourishment through sacred teaching.

And the happy ranks of the monks received their father.

Among so great a throng there moved a woman; sorrowful, she carried beneath her breast a half-dead child—only a faint breath remained in his throat—and, her eyes covered with tears, she held him. The mother cried out in supplication with a very loud voice:

“Give me back my child, since I carry only a corpse. Behold the unhappy mother—and now no longer a mother. ‘Death and I,’ she says, ‘are fighting one another with blows.

[Col. 1150C] She—Death—raging in darkness, seeks to strike down my child. You, merciful martyr, grant him to recover consciousness once more—or else let the earth, gaping open, receive us both together [Note: “Receive us.” The copyist had written without sense: “Or bear him before our face receive.”].

I shall not be able to leave kisses upon my beloved child.”

Behold, suddenly the boy answered in a feeble voice:

“Tell me where you are, mother; receive me, your child.”

“I am here, dearest son,” said his mother.

He brought great joy to his mother in return for so great a gift. The rejoicing mother returned with her child restored to health.

A one-eyed man approaches the bier with his blind wife. The man bore beneath his brow a single clear eye; his wife had been deprived of both eyes, and her ungrateful husband had so often guided her along the slow road with a rope.

Then the woman, trusting in her heart that the martyr could restore her lost sight, came forward; but the man doubted. Thereafter the doubtful man lost even the one eye he possessed, while the woman, endowed with both eyes through the martyr’s merits, departed. Thus the faithless blind man went away, while the faithful one saw.

Nor should I be silent about the miracles that were performed at the enclosure of blessed Maxentius.

[Col. 1150D] The ready ranks of the monks prepare to go to meet their father. Meanwhile a girl, long disabled in the use of her limbs and thereby unable to perform her duty, lay there for many years.
