As soon as her open ears received the saint’s name, repeatedly proclaimed by common report, one hand at once recovered its native strength; after three days, when the blessed man arrived, her whole body was granted once more to rejoice in its accustomed health.

Verse 1213.

[Col. 1151A] Great joys, martyr, you bring back, witnessed by your people:

When you arrive, the desired health, entering among all,

runs everywhere; no sickness could remain.

As soon as the holy man, arriving, touched the sacred court,

a woman deprived of sight was restored to the shining light;

a boy was rescued whom the burning rage of a demon tormented;

here too a woman, tossed by a similar madness,

vomited foul poison together with a stream of blood.

Her youth, destined to live, will endure for many years.

## VIII. Summary of the preceding miracles, and description of the tomb

Who could set them all forth with a pen? Yet now I am pleased to touch upon the signs one by one, briefly, as they were recorded in order—signs that he performed by the power of God, now restored to the stars.

The body remained raised aloft for the space of one hour [Note: “Of an hour,” according to the manuscript; do not attend too closely to the imperfect verse].

The executioner, cast into the midst of flames, gasped;

a lantern was seen shining in the middle of the night;

a thief seized the guardian’s object by wicked cunning;

the master suffered death [Note: “Suffered death”: if one wishes to conjecture and disregard the meter, one should read “fled.” Cf. verse 810], but the object was restored;

he died a cruel death who struck the urn with his feet;

the sword deprived the perpetrator of life and weapons;

a letter secretly obtained suppressed the dispute;

a sick seven-year-old recovered sight and speech;

an evil spirit left a woman’s limbs;

a wife escaped death, in place of the false death of her husband;

a lame man departed on his feet, exhausted by many years;

a woman with crooked fingers was healed and revived;

behold, liquid had returned once more in double streams;

at the martyr’s arrival the disturbed storm grew calm;

a poor mother gained light for her child;

a woman once bent down now remembers the circle of the sun;

a young man is freed from the dreadful pain that tormented him;

two men are healed beneath a cold body; a poor girl,

long deprived of her eyes beneath the night;

a mother was granted to see her half-dead boy living once more;

thus the faithless blind man went away, while the faithful one saw;

thus the girl rejoices, made sound in her whole body;

a woman deprived of sight was restored to shining light;

[Col. 1151C] Verse 1249.

[Col. 1152A] there is the boy rescued from the burning rage of a demon;

and here too the woman tossed by a similar madness.

From the sea’s depths we have gathered these things drop by drop; many more remain, passed over by my slender talent.

Who could search out all the miracles that have been related, however richly endowed with teachable skill and understanding he might be—miracles that the servant of the Lord accomplished by his radiant power?

Let us gladly turn our pleasant pen to the tomb.

At last the bones were brought back to their own dwelling and buried in a beautiful tomb within the bosom of the church. Here and there the frequent hymn-singing choir resounded: clergy and monks alike, young and old, each greater and lesser, devotedly present at the rites, until everything had been properly completed for the servant of God.

The appearance of the church is distinguished by varying form. At the front it is marked by four walls; farther along, it is extended lengthwise by two walls. Beyond this, an elegant structure remains, built for the people [Note: “Beyond this …” Since our author is here reviewing the individual parts of the basilica [Col. 1152C], these words seem to refer to the apse. Hence I think one should read at this point: “Beyond this, the stronghold remains,” or, more willingly: “Beyond this, an arch remains … built with elegance.”].

Beneath it, a crypt contains the sacred altar in its embrace; from the upper doorways one proceeds by steps toward it.

[Col. 1152B] From there one climbs again by stairs to the upper buildings. There the altar gleams, constructed of yellow metal; in its sacred bosom it contains venerable treasures.

A solid pavement extends between these altars.

Here blessed Maxentius received rest beside the peaceful buildings and guards the sacred palace.

A single accessible portico joins these halls, where the monks sing a hymn again in sacred harmonies.

This gift, great Father, I, your devoted servant, bring to you:

for your servant presents these bronze offerings to his lord.

Others may be able to carry great treasures and pour gold and gems into your riches; others may possess the weight of silver through abundant wealth.

Although colder blood covers my heart, nevertheless my mind, with burning devotion, always desires you. Willingly I venerate you, and in supplication I seek your divine power; I confess that I am your servant, O Lord, subject to your authority.

By your accustomed aid, martyr, protect me always.

[Col. 1152C] Verse 1287.

## BOOK ONE—LIFE OF SAINT LEODEGARIUS THE MARTYR

II.—On the seasons of the ecclesiastical year. 1131  
III.—Praise of Saint Leodegarius and the poet’s pious prayer. 1133  
IV.—Saint Leodegarius’s noble birth and childhood flourishing in study. 1133  
V.—Leodegarius as archdeacon and abbot. 1133  
VI.—Leodegarius is raised from the palace to the see of Autun. 1134  
VII.—King Childeric, through Leodegarius’s efforts, is elevated to the throne, while Ebroin is exiled to Luxeuil; that place is described accordingly. 1135  
VIII.—Leodegarius assumes the reins of the kingdom. 1135  
IX.—The bishop returns with the king to his own city and undergoes danger to his life. 1136  
X.—Yielding to envy, Leodegarius withdrew to Luxeuil, and shortly afterward was recalled to his own city. 1136  
XI.—While the citizens joyfully welcome Leodegarius, Ebroin, plotting new frauds, is restored to the palace. 1137  
XII.—Ebroin proceeds tyrannically through every wicked act and resolves to crush Leodegarius. 1138  
[Col. 1160] XIII.—Autun is besieged with arms. 1138  
XIV.—Leodegarius, cruelly blinded, is again confined in the monastery for two years. 1139  
XV.—Saint Garinus, Leodegarius’s brother, buried beneath stones, is adorned with the jewels of martyrdom. 1139  
XVI.—Leodegarius is subjected to various tortures and handed over to Waningus for custody. 1140  
XVII.—At Ebroin’s instigation, Leodegarius is stripped of his dignity and condemned. 1141  
XVIII.—How the blessed man, even before his martyrdom, is endowed with heavenly light. 1142
